en: Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Dhammapada in the Khuddaka Nikāya.
(First Part) Introduction to the Composition:
To the world enveloped in the darkness of great delusion, [the Buddha], who perceives the end of the world...
Having paid homage at the feet of that glorious Sambuddha, by whom the lamp of the True Dhamma was kindled with blazing splendor,
and having honored his True Dhamma and extended a reverential salutation to the Saṅgha.
Having encountered various causes, the Teacher— skilled in what is Dhamma and what is not, having attained the state of the True Dhamma—
taught the beautiful *Dhammapada* with a mind impelled by the surge of compassion.
This subtle commentary on its meaning, which increases the joy and gladness of gods and humans, has been handed down in succession;
it is established in the language of the island within the Island of Tambapaṇṇi.
"He does not accomplish the attainment of welfare for other beings;
perhaps he might even accomplish that welfare for the entire world.
Thinking thus, one who is self-controlled and lives in equanimity should aspire [to this].
I was earnestly requested by the Elder Kumārakassapa,
whose mind is steadfast and who desires the endurance of the True Dhamma,
to explain that teaching which had become overly prolix and its sequence of words disordered.
Having set aside and replaced the beautiful web of threads— that is,
the phrasing and wording of the verses which was not fully elucidated there—
I have explained only that, while the remainder remains exactly as it was in meaning.
I shall speak in another language, bringing forth the discerning one, with joy and gladness of mind, supported by the meaning and the Dhamma. 1.
The Chapter on Pairs.
1. The Story of the Elder Cakkhupāla “Mind precedes all phenomena; mind is their chief, they are all mind-wrought.
If one speaks or acts with a corrupted mind, [suffering follows].”
"Suffering follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws.
Where was this teaching on the Dhamma spoken? At Sāvatthī. With reference to whom? With reference to the Elder Cakkhupāla.
It is said that at Sāvatthī there was a householder named Mahāsuvaṇṇa, who was wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments, yet he was childless.
Thus, one day, having bathed at a bathing place and returning after his ablutions, he saw along the way a forest tree with fully developed leaves and branches.
Thinking, "This must be possessed by a deity of great power," he had the area beneath it cleared,
had a surrounding wall constructed, had sand strewn over it, and [hoisted] banners and streamers.

Having raised up the forest tree and adorned it, he joined his palms in reverence and made this aspiration: "If I should obtain a son or a daughter, I shall pay you great honor. Having spoken thus, he departed.
Then, before long, a fetus was established in the womb of his wife. She [perceived] that the fetus had taken root.
Having learned of this, she informed him. He provided for the sustenance of her pregnancy. After ten months had passed, she gave birth to a son.
On the day of the naming ceremony, because the boy was obtained by relying on the forest tree that the merchant himself had protected, he gave him the name Pāla.
Later, she obtained another son, to whom he gave the name Cūḷapāla.
Having done so, he gave the other the name Mahāpāla. When they reached maturity, they were bound by the ties of marriage.
Later, their mother and father passed away. All of their wealth was managed solely by the others.
At that time, the Teacher, having set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dharma, arrived there in due course, accompanied by the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika.
Having spent fifty-four crores of wealth to have the Great Monastery of Jetavana constructed,
he dwelt there while establishing the great multitude on the path to heaven and the path to liberation. For the Tathāgata had spent only a single rainy season in the Great Monastery of Nigrodha,
which was built by eighty-two thousand kinsmen— eighty thousand from his mother’s side and eighty thousand from his father’s side.
He dwelt for nineteen years in the Great Monastery of Jetavana, built by Anāthapiṇḍika, and for six years in the Eastern Park, built by Visākhā through her gift of twenty-seven crores of wealth;
thus, out of regard for the greatness of the virtues of these two families, he spent the rains retreat based on Sāvatthī for twenty-five years.
Both Anāthapiṇḍika and the great female lay disciple Visākhā were constant [in their support].
Twice a day they go to attend upon the Tathāgata;
and as they go, never having gone before with empty hands, they think, "The young novices will look at our hands.
Those going before the meal take along various kinds of hard and soft foods, while those going after the meal take the five tonics and the eight kinds of drinks. In their residences...
Furthermore, for those two groups of two thousand bhikkhus, seats were always prepared in advance.
Regarding food, drink, and medicine, whatever anyone desired was provided to him exactly as wished. Among them, Anāthapiṇḍika had never before asked the Teacher a question even on a single day.
It is said that he thought: "The Tathāgata is delicate by nature, refined like a noble kshatriya."
Thinking, "The householder has been very helpful to me; he might weary himself teaching me the Dhamma," he did not ask a question out of excessive affection for the Teacher.
But as soon as the merchant was seated, the Teacher thought: "This wealthy man protects me from what ought not to be protected against.
For four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons, I have remained adorned and prepared..."
"Having cut off my own head, plucked out my eyes, and torn out the flesh of my heart, and having renounced my wife and children who were as dear to me as life itself,
I fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) solely for the sake of teaching the Dhamma to others. It is this very [perfection] that protects me in situations where I ought not to be protected," he said,
and delivered this very discourse on the Dhamma.

At that time, seven million people lived in Sāvatthī. Among them, after hearing the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, about five million people became noble disciples (ariyasāvaka), while about two million remained worldlings (puthujjana). For those who were noble disciples, there were only two duties:
they gave alms before the meal, and after the meal, with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in hand, they provided robes, medicine, drinks, and so forth.

Having had them recited, they would go for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma. Then one day, Mahāpāla saw noble disciples going to the monastery with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in their hands;
having asked, "Where is this great multitude going? and heard that it was "for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma," he said, "I too will go.
Having gone there, he paid homage to the Teacher and sat down at the edge of the assembly.

When the Buddhas teach the Dhamma, they do so by observing the underlying potential (*upanissaya*) for taking refuge, undertaking precepts, going forth, and so on, and they teach the Dhamma according to the inclinations of those present.
Therefore, on that day, the Teacher, having observed his potential while teaching the Dhamma, delivered a gradual discourse (*anupubbikathā*).
That is to say: a talk on giving, a talk on virtue, a talk on heaven, and [a talk on] the dangers of sensual pleasures...
He proclaimed the danger, the misery, and the defilement [of household life], as well as the benefit in renunciation. Having heard this, the householder Mahāpāla thought:
"When one goes to the next world, neither sons nor daughters, nor brothers, nor wealth follow;
even one's own body does not go with oneself. What is the use of my living at home? I shall go forth. At the conclusion of that teaching, he...
Having approached the Teacher, he requested the going-forth. Then the Teacher asked him, "Do you have anyone among your relatives who ought to be consulted?
"I have a younger brother, Bhante," he replied. "In that case, consult him," said the Teacher.
Accepting this with the words, "Very well," he paid homage to the Teacher, went home, summoned his younger brother, and said, "Dear one, whatever..."
"In this house of mine, whatever wealth there is—both animate and inanimate—all that is your burden;
manage it. He asked, "But what will you do? "I shall go forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher.
"What are you saying, brother? You are like a mother to me when my mother has died, and like a father to me when my father has died."
“You have obtained a father like this, and your home is of great wealth; it is possible to perform meritorious deeds while still living as a householder, so do not act in this way.
“Father, having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, I am unable to live the life of a householder.
For the Teacher, having applied the three characteristics with extreme subtlety and delicacy, [taught] that which is beautiful in the beginning, middle, and end...”
“The Dhamma has been taught; it is not possible for one living in the midst of a household to fulfill it.
I shall go forth, dear brother. “Brother, you are still young; wait until you are old before you go forth.
“Father, when one is old, even one’s own hands and feet become unresponsive and no longer obey one’s will; how much more so, then, one’s relatives?”
“Indeed, how could I not do as you say? I shall fulfill the very practice of a recluse.
“When one is worn out by old age, and hands and feet are no longer obedient;
when one’s strength is destroyed, how can such a person practice the Dhamma?”

“I shall indeed go forth, dear father,” he said; and while his father was still crying out, he went into the presence of the Teacher, requested the going-forth, and having received the ordination, lived for five years in the presence of his preceptor and teacher.
When the rains retreat was over and he had performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony, he approached the Teacher, paid homage, and asked: “Venerable sir, how many duties are there in this Dispensation?”
“There are only two duties for bhikkhus: the duty of study (*ganthadhura*) and the duty of insight (*vipassanādhura*). “But what, venerable sir, is the duty of study, and what is the duty of insight?

“Having mastered one or two Nikāyas, or the entire word of the Buddha consisting of the Three Piṭakas, according to the measure of one’s own wisdom, its retention, exposition, and recitation [constitute the duty of study].”

“This is called the burden of the scriptures (*ganthadhura*). However, for one who lives simply, delights in remote lodgings, and—having established the perception of decay and fall within his own person—increases insight through the practice of constant perseverance and thereby attains Arhatship, this is called the burden of insight (*vipassanādhura*).
“Venerable Sir, I went forth in my old age; I will not be able to fulfill the burden of the scriptures.”
"But I shall fulfill the duty of insight; please tell me a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). Then the Teacher explained to him a meditation subject leading all the way to Arahantship.
Having paid homage to the Teacher, he sought out monks who would accompany him and, having found sixty monks, [set out].
Having set out with them and traveled a road of two hundred yojanas, they reached a large frontier village;

there, together with his retinue, he entered for alms. Seeing the monks who were perfected in their conduct, the people, with hearts full of faith, prepared seats, invited them to sit, and served them with excellent food. Then they asked, "Venerable sir, where are the masters going?"
When they had asked this and were told, "Lay followers, go to whatever place is convenient," the wise men,
realizing that "the venerable ones are seeking lodgings for the rainy-season residence," said, "Venerable sirs, if the masters would stay here for these three months,
we would establish ourselves in the refuges and undertake the precepts. They [the monks] also [thought], "We [shall rely] upon these families..."
“We shall effect our deliverance from existence,” they consented.
Having obtained their promise, the people maintained the monastery, provided night-quarters and day-quarters, and gave them to them.
They entered that very village regularly for alms. Then a certain physician approached them and said:
“Venerable sir, even in the dwelling place of many people there are times when it is uncomfortable; if such a thing should arise, please tell me, and I will prepare medicine,” he invited him.

On the day of entering the rains retreat, the Elder addressed those monks and asked, “Friends, during these three months, through how many postures will you pass your time? “Through four, venerable sir. “What—”
"Friends, is this not fitting? Should we not indeed be heedful?
"For we have come having received our meditation subject from the presence of the Buddha who is currently living; and Buddhas cannot be satisfied by negligence;
they must be pleased by a noble disposition. To one who is negligent, the four states of misery are like his own home."
“Be diligent, friends,” he said. “But what about you, venerable sir? “I shall pass my time in three postures;
I will not stretch out my back, friend. “Very well, venerable sir; may you be diligent.
Then, as the Elder did not fall asleep, when the first month had passed and the middle month arrived, an ailment of the eyes arose.
[It] arose. Streams of tears flowed from his eyes like a stream of water from a leaking jar.
Having practiced the duties of a recluse throughout the entire night, he entered the womb-chamber and sat down at the break of dawn.
When it was time for the alms-round, the monks went to the Elder and said, "Venerable sir, it is time for the alms-round. "In that case, friends, take [the bowl]," he replied.
“Bowl and robes,” he said. Having had his own bowl and robes brought, he departed.
When the monks saw tears streaming from his eyes, they asked, “What is this, venerable sir? “Friends, my eyes are being pierced by wind,” he replied.
“Venerable sir, did the physician not dismiss us? What shall we say to him? “Very well, friends,” they said, and they informed the physician.
Having thus prepared the oil, he sent it. The Elder sat down and poured the oil into his nose while remaining seated;
having finished pouring, he entered the village. When the physician saw him, he said, "Venerable sir, it is said that wind is piercing the eyes of the noble one?
"Yes, lay follower. "Venerable sir, I prepared the oil and sent it; you have poured the oil into your nose? "Yes."
“Lay followers,” he said. “What is it like now? “It is indeed worsening, lay followers. The physician thought, “I sent oil that was capable of bringing about relief in a single application;
why has the disease not been cured? He asked, “Venerable sir, was the oil poured over you while you were sitting or while you were lying down?
The Elder remained silent. Though he was asked again and again, he did not speak.
Thinking, "I will go to the monastery and look for the Elder's dwelling place," he dismissed the Elder, saying, "In that case, venerable sir, you may go.
Having gone to the monastery and looking for the Elder's dwelling place, he saw only the places where the Elder had walked and sat, but not the place where he slept.
Not seeing a bed, he asked, "Venerable sir, did you sit when you were here, or did you lie down? The Elder replied:
He remained silent. “Venerable sir, do not do this; that which is called the duty of a recluse can be performed by one who maintains his body.
Lie down and have [the oil] poured on you,” he entreated him again and again. “Go for now, friend;
having consulted, we shall know,” he sent the physician away. Now, the elder had neither kinsmen nor blood-relations there—whom could he consult with?
But speaking with his body made of kamma, he said: "Tell me first, friend Pālita, will you look at your eyes, or will you look at the Buddha’s teaching?
For in this beginningless cycle of existence, there is no counting the number of times your eyes have been destroyed;
indeed, hundreds and thousands of Buddhas have passed away. Among them, not even a single Buddha—"
"I have served [the Teacher]; now, for these three months of the rainy season, I shall not lie down. I will exert constant effort for these three months.
Therefore, let your eyes perish or be destroyed; uphold the Buddha’s teaching alone, and not your eyes.
Thus, exhorting the body of elements, he spoke these verses:
“May my eyes that are cherished perish;
may my ears and likewise my body perish;
may all this that depends on the body perish.”
"For what reason, O Pālita, do you neglect [the teachings] that you have protected? 'May my eyes decay;
likewise may my ears and my body decay.'"
"May all this that depends on the body decay!
For what reason, O Protector, do you neglect me?
Let my eyes, which I have cherished, perish!"
“Let the ears break apart, and likewise the body;
let all this that depends on the body break as well.
For what reason do you protect it and neglect me?”
Having thus given his own exhortation with these three verses, he performed nasal medication while still seated and entered the village for alms.
When the physician saw him, he asked, "Venerable sir, why have you performed nasal medication? "Yes, lay follower," he replied.
"Of what kind was it, venerable sir? "It was indeed painful, lay follower. "Venerable sir, did you perform the nasal medication while sitting?"
“...having lain down. The Elder remained silent; though questioned again and again, he said nothing.
Then the physician said to him, “Venerable sir, you are not doing what is suitable for yourself.
From this day forward, do not say, ‘Oil was prepared for me by so-and-so,’ nor shall I say, ‘Oil was prepared for you by me. Thus spoke the physician. He [the Elder]—by the physician...
“Having been rejected, you went to the monastery; you have been rejected even by the physician. Do not abandon your posture, O ascetic!
“Rejected from medical treatment and shunned even by the physician, you are destined for the King of Death. Why, Pālita, do you neglect [your duty]?”
Having exhorted himself with this verse, he practiced the duty of a recluse.

Then, when the middle watch of the night had passed, his eyes and his defilements were shattered simultaneously—neither before nor after the other. Having become an Arahant through dry-insight (sukkha-vipassaka), he entered the womb and sat down.
When the time for alms-round arrived, the bhikkhus came and said, "It is time for alms-round, venerable sir.
"Is it time, friends? "Yes, venerable sir. "In that case, go then. "But what about you, venerable sir?
"My eyes have failed me, friends. They looked at his eyes and, with tears filling their own eyes, said, "Venerable sir, do not..."
They thought, "We shall look after you," and having thus comforted the Elder and performed the appropriate duties and services, they entered the village for alms.
Not seeing the Elder, the people asked, "Venerable sir, where is our noble master?
Having heard what had happened, they sent rice-gruel and went themselves with alms-food; upon arriving, they paid homage to the Elder.
Turning around at the base of his feet and weeping, they comforted him, saying, “Venerable sir, we shall look after you;
do not worry,” and then departed.
From that time on, they regularly sent rice porridge and food to the monastery itself. The Elder, as well as the other sixty monks—

He exhorted them continuously. Abiding by his exhortation, when the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) was near at hand, they all together attained *arahantship* along with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
Having completed the rains retreat and desiring to see the Teacher, they said to the Elder, "Venerable sir, we wish to see the Teacher. Hearing their words, the Elder thought: "I am weak..."
“On the way there is a forest inhabited by non-human beings;
if I go with them, they will all become exhausted and will not even be able to obtain alms-food. I shall send these ahead.
Then he said to them, “Friends, you go on ahead. “But what about you, venerable sir? “I am weak,” he replied.
“On the way there is a wilderness inhabited by non-human beings; if I were to go with you, we would all become exhausted.
You should go on ahead. “Do not do this, venerable sir; we will go together with you.
“Do not insist on this, friends; if that were the case, it would cause me discomfort.”
"He will be there; however, when my younger brother sees you, he will ask about me, so you should inform him that my eyes have failed.
He will then send someone to me, and I shall come with him.
In my name, please pay homage to the One of Ten Powers and the eighty great elders," he said, and dismissed them.

Having asked forgiveness of the Elder, they entered the village. When people saw them, they had them sit down, gave them almsfood, and asked, "Venerable sirs, does it appear that the masters intend to depart? "Yes, lay followers; we wish to see the Teacher.
Having entreated them again and again, and perceiving their firm desire to go, the people followed them for a while, lamented, and then turned back.
Gradually reaching Jetavana, they paid homage to the Teacher and the eighty great elders according to the elder’s instructions.
On the following day, they entered the street where the elder’s younger brother lived for alms.
Recognizing them, the householder had them sit down, exchanged greetings, and asked, "Venerable sirs, where is my brother, the elder?"

He asked. Then they reported that matter to him. Upon hearing it, he wept while rolling at their feet and asked, "Venerable sirs, what should be done now? "The Elder is waiting for someone to come from there;
when he arrives, he will come along with him. "Venerable sir, this is my nephew named Pālita."
“Send him along. “It is not possible to send him in this way; there are obstacles on the road. It would be better to ordain him and then send him.

“Do so and send him, venerable sirs. Then, having ordained him and instructed him for about half a month in matters such as carrying the bowl and robes, they sent him off after pointing out the route.
Thus, having reached that village by stages, he saw an elderly man at the entrance of the village and asked, "Is there any forest hermitage (āraññaka-vihāra) dependent on this village?
"There is, venerable sir," he replied. "Who lives there?
"The elder named Pālitatthera, venerable sir. "Show me the way. "Who are you, venerable sir? "I am [the disciple] of the elder..."
“I am your nephew. Then, taking him with him, he led him to the monastery.

He paid homage to the Elder and, for about half a month, performed his duties and services, properly attending upon the Elder. Then he said, “Venerable sir, my maternal uncle’s family is waiting for your arrival;
come, let us go. [The Elder replied,] “In that case, take this walking-staff of mine.”
So, taking hold of the end of the staff, he entered the village together with the Elder.
The people, having seated the Elder, asked, "Venerable sir, does it appear that you are intending to go? "Yes, lay followers; having gone, I shall pay homage to the Teacher.
When they failed to obtain [their wish] despite entreating him in various ways, they dismissed the Elder halfway along the road.

Having gone and wept, they turned back. As the novice was walking along, carrying the Elder by the tip of his staff, he reached a village named Kaṭṭhanagara, which had been established by the Elder in the middle of the wilderness.
Having left the village and gone into the forest, he heard the sound of singing from a woman who was gathering firewood while singing.
He took up every sign. For there is no other sound besides the sound of a woman capable of pervading a man’s entire body.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Bhikkhus, I do not see even a single other sound that persists by so completely seizing a man’s mind as does the sound of a woman, bhikkhus.”
The novice, having observed a sign there, released the tip of his staff and went toward her, saying, "Wait a moment, venerable lady, I have business. Seeing him, she remained silent.
He fell into moral transgression with her. The Elder thought: "Just now, the sound of singing was heard; and yet..."
“The sound of the woman has ceased, and the novice is also delaying; he must have fallen into a breach of virtue with her.
Having finished his own business, the novice also returned and said, “Let us go, venerable sir.
Then the Elder asked him, “Have you become a wicked person, novice? He remained silent, and though questioned repeatedly by the Elder, he said nothing at all.
Then the Elder said to him, “I have no need for a staff-tip to be grasped by such a sinner as you.
Stricken with spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), he removed his saffron robes, put on the dress of a layman, and said, “Venerable sir, previously I was a novice, but now I have become a householder.
Furthermore, when I went forth, I did not do so out of faith, but out of fear that my path was being obstructed.”
“Having gone forth, come, let us go,” he said. [The other] replied, “Friend, the misdeed of a householder and the misdeed of a recluse are both indeed evil.
Even while standing in the state of a recluse, you were unable to fulfill even the mere measure of virtue; being a householder, what good could you possibly do?
There is no need for me to hold onto the tip of the staff of such an evil person. “Venerable sir, the path is infested by non-human beings.”
“You are blind and without a guide; how will you live here? Then the Elder said to him, “Friend, do not think thus.
Even if I were to lie down right here and die, or even as I turn over from side to side, there is no going with you.
Having said this, he spoke these verses:
“Alas, I am sightless, having come halfway across the wilderness;
lying down, I shall not go on—there is no companionship for a fool.
“Alas, I am sightless, having come halfway across the wilderness...”
“I shall die, I will not go; there is no companionship with fools.
Having heard this, the other was seized with a sense of spiritual urgency and thought, “Alas, what a grievous, reckless, and unseemly deed I have committed!
Wringing his arms and weeping, he rushed into the thicket of the forest and remained there, having thus departed. As for the Elder as well—

Through the power of his virtue, the stone seat of Sakka, the king of the gods— the Pāṇḍukambala stone throne, sixty yojanas in length, fifty yojanas in width, and fifteen yojanas in thickness, colored like a *jayasumana* flower, and naturally inclined to sink or rise at the times of sitting down or standing up—
manifested a sign of heat. Sakka, looking about with his divine eye, wondered, "Who indeed wishes to displace me from my position?"
He saw the Elder. Regarding this, the ancients said:
“The thousand-eyed Lord of Devas purified his divine eye;
this protector Pāla, censuring evil, purified his livelihood.”
“The Lord of Devas, Sahassanetta, purified his divine eye;
this noble one (pāla) reveres the Dhamma and sits delighting in the Teaching.
Then it occurred to him: “If I do not go into the presence of such a noble one who reviles evil and reveres the Dhamma, may my head split into seven pieces! I shall go into his presence. Thereupon—
“The Lord of Devas, Sahassanetta, the upholder of the glory of divine kingship, having arrived at that very moment, approached Cakkhupāla.
And having approached, he made the sound of his footsteps not far from the Elder. Then the Elder asked him, “Who is this?”
“I am a traveler, venerable sir. “Where are you going, lay follower? “To Sāvatthī, venerable sir. “Go then, friend.
“But where will the noble sir go, venerable sir? “I too shall go to that very place.
“In that case, let us go together, venerable sir. “Friend, I am weak; for one traveling with me—”
“You will have much trouble. “I have no urgent business; as I go along with the noble one, I shall obtain one of the ten bases of meritorious action. Let us go together, venerable sir.
The Elder, thinking, “This man will become a true person (sappurisa),” said, “In that case, I will go with you. Take hold of the tip of my staff.”
“Lay followers,” he said. Sakka did so, and contracting the earth, he brought him to Jeta’s Grove at the time of evening.
Hearing the sound of conchs, drums, and other instruments, the Elder asked, “Where is this sound? “In Sāvatthī, venerable sir.
“Previously, when we were traveling, we took a long time to get there. “I know the direct route, venerable sir. At that—
In an instant, the Elder perceived: "This is not a human; it must be a deity.
"The Lord of Devas with a thousand eyes, the bearer of the glory of divine sovereignty, having shortened that path, quickly arrived at Sāvatthī."
Thus, having led the Elder there and brought him to the leaf-hut built for the Elder’s sake by the younger householder, he had him sit upon a wooden plank.
Then, approaching the householder in the guise of a dear friend, he called out to him, “Friend Cūḷapāla! “What is it, friend?
“Do you know that the Elder has arrived? “I do not know; but has the Elder come?”
“Yes, friend,” he replied, “I have just now come from the monastery after seeing the Elder sitting in the leaf-hut you had built.

Having said this, he departed. The householder also went to the monastery; upon seeing the Elder, he rolled at his feet, weeping, and said, “Venerable sir, having seen this, I did not allow you to go forth,” and so on, as he spoke to the two slave children.

Having made them his servants and having had them ordained in the presence of the Elder, he assigned them the task, saying, "Bring alms-gruel, rice, and other provisions from within the village and attend upon the Elder.
The novices performed their duties and services and attended upon the Elder.
Then one day, monks living in various directions, thinking, "We shall see the Teacher," arrived at Jetavana and [approached] the Tathāgata.
Having paid homage to the eighty great elders, and having paid homage to those wandering on their alms-round through the monastery, they reached the dwelling place of the elder Cakkhupāla.
Thinking, "We shall see this place as well," they turned toward it in the evening. At that moment, a great rain cloud arose.
They thought, "It is now too late in the day, and a cloud has arisen; we will go and see it early in the morning," and so they turned back. The rain—

Having rained during the first watch, it had ceased during the middle watch. The Elder, being one who had initiated energy and was accustomed to walking meditation, entered upon the walking path during the last watch.
At that time, however, many earthworms (*indagopaka*) emerged from the ground because of the recent rain.
As the Elder walked, they mostly perished under his feet. The pupils [of the Elder] [watched] the Elder’s place for walking meditation...
They did not sweep at the proper time. The other monks, thinking, "We shall see where the Elder lives," arrived and, seeing dead insects on the walking path, asked, "Who has been walking here?
"Our preceptor, venerable sirs. They complained, "See, friends, the deed of this ascetic! Having lain down while his eyesight was still present..."
"While sleeping and doing nothing at all, he has now killed so many tiny creatures while walking, thinking 'I am walking,' even though his vision is impaired;
thus, thinking 'I shall do good,' he does harm.
Then they went and reported this to the Tathāgata: "Venerable Sir, the elder Cakkhupāla, while thinking 'I am walking'..."
“You have killed many living beings. “But was he seen by you while killing? “He was not seen, venerable sir.
“Just as you do not see him, so too he does not see those living beings. There is no such thing as a ‘volition to kill’ for those whose taints are destroyed, monks.
“Venerable sir, since the necessary conditions for Arahantship were present, why was he born blind?”
“By virtue of his own past deeds, monks. “But what, Bhante, did he do?
“In that case, monks, listen—In the past, while the King of Kāsi was ruling in Bārāṇasī, a certain physician, having traveled through villages and market towns, practiced his medical craft.”
While traveling, he saw a woman with impaired vision and asked, "What is troubling you? "I cannot see with my eyes," she replied.
"Shall I prepare medicine for you? "Do so, Master. "What will you give me in return?
"If you are able to restore my eyes to their natural state, I shall give myself as a slave along with my sons and daughters."
"I shall become [his wife]," she thought. He replied, "Very well," and prepared the medicine; with that single medicine alone, his eyes were restored to their natural state.
She thought, "I promised that I would become his slave along with my sons and daughters, yet he will not treat me with gentleness or proper conduct; I shall deceive him. Then the physician arrived.
When asked, "What is it like, my lady? she replied, "Previously my eyes were only slightly painful, but now they are even more so.
The physician thought, "This woman wishes to deceive me and refuses to give me anything;
I have no need for the fee she has given me, so I shall make her blind this very moment. Having thought thus, he went home and [related] this matter to his wife.
He explained it to her, but she remained silent. Having prepared a medicinal ointment, he went to her and, saying, "Lady, apply this ointment," he had her apply it.
Then both her eyes were extinguished like the flame of a lamp.
That physician became a protector of sight.
"Monks, the deed committed by my son then followed close behind him.
For indeed, this evil karma follows one like a wheel follows the hoofprint of a draft ox bearing its burden.
Having related this story, and having established the connection between the past and the present, the Dhamma King—like one sealing moist clay with a royal seal—uttered this verse:
“Mind precedes all phenomena; mind is their chief, they are all mind-wrought.
If one speaks or acts with a corrupted mind, suffering follows him even as the wheel follows the hoof of the draught-ox.”
Therein, "mind" (*mano*) refers to all consciousness belonging to the four planes, including the wholesome and other types of sense-sphere consciousness (*kāmāvacara*).

However, in this particular context, being specified, determined, and delimited according to the state of mind that had arisen in that physician at that time, only the consciousness associated with aversion (*paṭigha*) and accompanied by mental distress (*domanassasahagata*) is obtained. "Foremost" (*pubbaṅgamā*): by means of that which goes first.

Having offered [the sacrifice], they were endowed [with these qualities]. "Dhammas" refers to four types of phenomena by way of virtue, teaching, the scriptures, and the absence of a self or a life-principle. Among them:
"For neither Dhamma nor non-Dhamma both yield the same result;
non-Dhamma leads to hell, while Dhamma brings one to a happy destination."
This is called the Dhamma as quality (*guṇadhamma*). “Monks, I will teach you the Dhamma that is good in the beginning,” this is called the Dhamma as teaching (*desanādhamma*).
“But here, monks, some clansmen master the Dhamma: the discourses, the songs,” this is called the Dhamma as the doctrine (*pariyattidhamma*).
“At that time, indeed, there are phenomena (*dhammā*), there are aggregates (*khandhā*)”—this refers to the Dhamma as phenomena (*dhammadhamma*).

This is called the "dharma devoid of a sentient being" (*nissatta-dhamma*), and it is also the same as the "dharma devoid of a life-principle" (*nijjīva-dhamma*). Among these, in this context, the "dharma devoid of a sentient being and a life-principle" is intended.

In terms of its actual meaning, it consists of the three formless aggregates (*arūpa-khandha*): the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-khandha*), the aggregate of perception (*saññā-khandha*), and the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhāra-khandha*).
For these have the mind as their precursor; thus, they are called "mind-precursors" (*manopubbaṅgamā*).

But how is it that the mind—which arises simultaneously with these [mental factors], sharing the same basis and the same object, neither before nor after them—is called the "forerunner"? It is in the sense of being the condition for their arising.

For just as when many people are performing deeds such as plundering a village together, if one asks, "Who is the forerunner among them?", it is whoever is their leader—that is, the one who is their condition—relying upon whom they act.
They perform that action, and he—whether it be Datta or Mitta—is called their "forerunner"; this should be understood as being exactly like that.
Thus, because mind is the forerunner of these [mental states] in the sense of being the condition for their arising, they are called "mind-forerunners" (*manopubbaṅgamā*).
For they are not able to arise unless mind arises; however, even when some mental factors do not arise, mind [does].
It indeed arises. Furthermore, because the mind is the dominant factor (*adhipati*) among these, it is called "mind-preeminent" (*manoseṭṭha*).

For just as among thieves and the like, the chief thief and so forth are the dominant and preeminent ones, so too for these [mental phenomena], the mind is the dominant factor, and thus the mind alone is preeminent.
And just as various articles produced from wood and other materials are called "wooden" and so forth, so too these...
They are called "mind-made" (*manomaya*) because they are produced from the mind.
"By the corrupted" means by adventitious defilements such as covetousness. For the natural mind is the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*), which is uncorrupted.
Just as clear water, when fouled by adventitious impurities such as blue dye, becomes distinguished as "blue water" and so forth; [so too is the mind].

It is not new water, nor is it merely the previously clear water; likewise, that [mind] too becomes defiled by adventitious faults such as covetousness, yet it is not a new mind, nor is it merely the previous *bhavaṅga* (subconscious) mind.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, this mind is luminous, but it is defiled by adventitious secondary defilements."
"...is defiled. Thus, if one speaks or acts with a mind corrupted by covetousness and the like, while speaking he utters only the fourfold verbal misconduct;

while acting he performs only the threefold bodily misconduct; and while not speaking or acting, through that state of a mind corrupted by covetousness and the rest, he fulfills the threefold mental misconduct. In this way, his ten...
The unwholesome courses of action reach completion.
"Then suffering follows him" means that from those three kinds of misconduct, suffering follows that person;
by the power of that misconduct, whether he goes to the four states of deprivation or among human beings, suffering follows him both in his physical basis and in other respects.
In this manner, he follows after bodily and mental resultant suffering. How is this?
It is like the wheel of a beast of burden following the foot of the ox yoked to the pole as it carries the load.
For just as that ox, carrying the load for even one day, or two, or five, or ten, or half a month, or a full month, cannot turn back the wheel—
He is unable to abandon it. Then, as he walks forward, the yoke strikes against his neck;
as he walks backward, the wheel strikes against the flesh of his thighs. Thus, being oppressed by these two ways, the wheel follows upon his footsteps;
in the very same way, one who stands having fulfilled the three types of misconduct with a mind corrupted by thought.
"Wheresoever a person goes among the realms of hell and so forth, there bodily and mental suffering rooted in misconduct follows them.

At the conclusion of this verse, thirty thousand bhikkhus attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Thus, even for those who had merely come to hear it, the teaching was meaningful and fruitful.
The First Story: The Elder Cakkhupāla.
2. The Story of Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī.
The second verse, "Mind precedes all phenomena," was also spoken at Sāvatthī concerning Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī.
It is said that in Sāvatthī there was a brahmin named Adinnapubbaka (Never-Giver). Because he had never given anything to anyone before, they knew him by the name "Adinnapubbaka.
He had an only son who was dear and beloved to him.
Then, wishing to have jewelry made for him, [the father thought], "If I have it made by goldsmiths, I will have to pay them food and wages."
Having ground the gold himself and fashioned polished earrings, he gave them to her.
Because of this, his son became known as Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī (the Polished-Earring). When he reached the age of sixteen, a disease of jaundice arose in him.
His mother, looking at her son, said, "Brāhmaṇa, a disease has arisen in your son; have him treated. "Madam, if a physician..."
“I will bring it back; you must pay the fee for the meal. Will you not consider that you are depriving me of my wealth?
“Then what will you do about it, brahmin? “I will act in such a way that I do not suffer the loss of my wealth.
He went to the physicians and asked, “What medicine do you prescribe for such-and-such a disease?”
Then they pointed out to him various things such as tree bark and so forth. Having brought those, he prepared medicine for his son.
While he was still preparing it, the disease became severe and reached a state beyond cure. When the brahmin realized its weakness had departed, he summoned a physician.
Upon merely looking at him, the physician said, "We have a certain task..."
“There is another physician; summon him and have him treat you. Having said this, he left, abandoning him.
The brahmin, knowing the time of his son’s death, thought, “Those who come to see him will see the family wealth within the house;
I shall take him outside. He had his son carried out and laid him down on the outer porch.
On that day, at the time of the powerful dawn, the Blessed One arose from the attainment of great compassion and,
for the purpose of seeing those kinsmen among those to be trained— who had performed services for previous Buddhas and possessed abundant roots of merit—
he surveyed the world with his Buddha-eye and spread the net of his knowledge over ten thousand world-systems. Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī was outside on the veranda.

His body was visible inside [the house] in the very posture in which he had lain down. When the Teacher saw him, he realized that the youth had been brought out from inside the house and laid down there;
then, reflecting, "Is there perhaps some need for me to go there? he perceived this:
"This young man, having placed his mind in faith toward me, has passed away and been reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven in a palace thirty yojanas in size."
He will be reborn in a golden celestial mansion, attended by a retinue of a thousand nymphs; and the brahmin, having cremated him, will wander about the funeral pyre weeping.

The son of a deva, beholding his own form—measuring three gavutas in height, adorned with ornaments weighing sixty cart-loads, and surrounded by a retinue of a thousand nymphs—will wonder: "By what kamma have I attained this glorious success?"
Having observed this and realized that [the benefit] had been obtained through the clarity of his mind toward me, he thought:
"This brahmin, out of fear of losing his wealth, has not prepared my medicine and is now weeping at the cremation ground; I shall cause him to reach a state of extreme distress.
While his father was weeping, he approached with the appearance of Maṭṭhakuṇḍali and, lying down not far from the cremation ground, began to weep.
Then the brahmin will ask him, "Who are you? He will reply, "I am your son, Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī.

When asked, "Where have you been reborn? he will say, "In the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. When asked, "By what deed were you reborn there? he will explain that he was reborn there through his confidence of heart toward me.
The brahmin will then think, "Having placed confidence in you, he has indeed been reborn in heaven."

If he asks me, "Are they? I shall reply to him, "It is not possible to define their number by saying there are so many hundreds, thousands, or hundreds of thousands," and then I will recite a verse from the *Dhammapada*.
At the conclusion of that verse, eighty-four thousand living beings will attain the realization of the Dhamma, and Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī will become a stream-enterer.

It will come to pass. Likewise for the Brahmin who has never before given. Seeing that through this son of good family there will be a great realization of the Dhamma, the Teacher, having attended to his physical needs on the following day and surrounded by a great community of monks, entered Sāvatthī for alms and proceeded step by step to the door of the Brahmin’s house.
At that moment, Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī was lying with his face turned toward the interior of the house.
Then the Teacher, knowing that the youth did not see him, released a single ray of light. The young man, thinking, "What is this radiance?", turned over while still lying down;
seeing the Teacher, he thought, "Having approached such a Buddha on account of my blind and foolish father, I shall perform services for his body."
“I was unable to perform a service, give a gift, or hear the Dhamma; now even my hands are no longer under my control, and there is nothing else left for me to do,” he said, gladdening his own mind.
The Teacher, thinking, “Enough with this much gladness of heart on her part,” departed.
As soon as the Tathāgata had passed from the range of her vision, she died with a mind full of serene confidence.
Like one awakened from sleep, he was reborn in the heavenly world in a golden celestial mansion thirty *yojanas* in extent.
The brahmin, having cremated his body, remained intent on weeping at the funeral pyre; going to the pyre every day, he wailed, "Where is my only son?
Where is my only son? The son of the gods, too, looked upon his own splendor and—
Reflecting, "By what deed was this obtained by me? he realized, "It was through my mental confidence in the Teacher.
Thinking, "This brahmin did not have medicine prepared for me when I was unwell, yet now he has gone to the cremation ground and weeps;
it is right to treat him with contempt," he approached in the guise of Maṭṭhakuṇḍali and, standing not far from the cremation ground, raised his arms and cried out:
He stood there weeping. When the brahmin saw him, he thought, "I am weeping because of grief for my son; for what reason is this man weeping?
I shall ask him. And asking him, he spoke this verse:
"Adorned, with polished earrings..."
"O garland-bearer, adorned with yellow sandalwood paste,
why do you weep with outstretched arms,
distressed in the middle of the forest?"
Then the young man said:
"A radiant chariot-fender made of gold has appeared for me."
“I do not find even a pair of wheels for it;
because of that suffering, I am giving up my life.
Then the brahmin said to him:
“Tell me, O auspicious young man, [whether it was] made of gold, made of gems, made of red coral, or made of silver.”
“I shall provide you with a pair of wheels.

Hearing this, the young man thought: “This brahmin, instead of providing medicine for his son, sees me as a mere substitute for his son and, weeping, says, ‘I will make a chariot wheel made of gold and other precious materials. Very well; I shall rebuke him. Having thought thus, he said:
Having said, "How large will you make my wheel-yoke?
and being told in reply, "I shall make it as large as you desire," he requested, "I have need of the moon and the sun; give them to me," and spoke thus:
"That young man explained it to him..."
“Both the moon and the sun are seen here;
my chariot is made of gold,
and it shines with that pair of wheels.”
Then the brahmin said to him:
"You are indeed a fool, young man,
you who aspire to that which is not to be aspired to."
"I think you will die,
for you shall not see the moon and the sun.
Then the young brahmin said to him:
“Is it for the sake of something that is manifest that one weeping is a fool, or rather for the sake of something that is not manifest? Having said this, he continued:
“The coming and going is seen, And the element of beauty is present on both sides of the path.”
“The dead who has passed away is no longer seen;
who here is more foolish than those who weep?
Having heard this, the brahmin perceived, “He speaks what is fitting,” and—
“You speak the truth indeed, young man;
I alone am the more childish among those who weep,
crying like a child at the moon.”
"‘He has longed for one who is dead and gone,’ he said;
and having become free from sorrow through those words, he spoke these verses in praise of the young man:
‘Alas! While I am burning like a fire fed with clarified butter, [you have brought this news].’"
Like sprinkling with water, he extinguished all my distress:
“Truly, you have extracted the arrow, the grief residing in my heart,
you who have dispelled the sorrow for my son from me as I was overcome by grief.”
“I have extracted the arrow, I have become cool, I am extinguished;
I do not grieve, nor do I weep, having heard you, O young man.
Then, asking him, “Who are you by name?”—
“Are you a deity, a gandhabba, or perhaps Sakka Purindada?
Who are you, whose son are you, and how may we know you? Thus he spoke. Then the young brahmin—
“Though you weep and though you wail,
having yourself cremated your son on the funeral pyre— I, for my part,
having performed wholesome karma, [shall go to heaven].”
“He has gone to the company of the Thirty-three gods,” he replied.
Then the brahmin said to him:
“Whether it be little or much, we have not seen it.”
"While giving gifts in your own home,
or performing such an act as the Uposatha ceremony—
by what deed have you gone to the world of the gods?"
The young brahmin said:
"I am afflicted, suffering, and ill;
I am in a state of distress within my own home."
I beheld the Buddha, free from dust, who has crossed over doubt,
the Well-Gone One of peerless wisdom.
"Thus, with joyful wealth and a clear mind,"
I paid homage with joined palms to the Tathāgata;
having performed that wholesome deed,
I went to the company of the Tidasas.
Even as he was speaking, the entire body of the brahmin was filled with rapture. Proclaiming that rapture, he said:
"How wonderful! How marvelous!
Such is the fruit of this act of joining the palms!"
“I too, with a joyful mind and a serene heart,
go this very day for refuge to the Buddha,” he said.
Then the young brahmin—
“Go this very day for refuge to the Buddha,
with a mind full of confidence, and to the Dhamma and the Saṅgha;
likewise, undertake the five training precepts.”
Take up these unblemished flowers.
Quickly abstain from taking life,
and avoid what is not given in the world.
"Do not drink intoxicants, do not speak falsehood,
and be content with your own wife," he said.
Having accepted this with the words "Very well," he spoke these verses:
“You are one who desires my welfare, O yakkha; you are one who desires my benefit, O deity.
I shall do as you say, for you are my teacher.
I go for refuge to the Buddha and also to the unsurpassed Dhamma.”
And the Saṅgha of the God among Men, I go for refuge.
“I shall quickly abstain from taking life;
I shall avoid what is not given in the world.”
“I drink no liquor, nor do I speak falsehood;
I am content with my own wife.

Then the deva said to him, “Brāhmaṇa, there is much wealth in your house; go to the Teacher, give alms, listen to the Dhamma, and ask a question,” and having said this, he vanished right then and there.
The brahmin, having gone home and addressed his wife, said, "My dear, today I shall invite the ascetic Gotama and ask him a question;
please prepare the hospitality. Having spoken thus, he went to the monastery, but neither saluted the Teacher nor exchanged greetings with him;
instead, standing to one side, he said, "Master Gotama, please accept tomorrow’s meal."
“Together with the community of monks,” he said. The Teacher consented.
Having understood the Teacher’s consent, he returned quickly and had various kinds of excellent hard and soft food prepared in his own residence.
The Teacher, surrounded by the community of monks, went to his house and sat down on the seat that had been prepared. The brahmin served him with great care, and a great crowd of people gathered.
It is said that when one who holds wrong view invites the Tathāgata, two groups of people assemble:
those with wrong view assemble thinking, "Today we shall see the ascetic Gotama being harassed as he is questioned";
and those with right view assemble thinking, "Today we shall see the domain of the Buddha and the play of the Buddha. Then...
When the brahmin had finished his meal, he approached the Tathāgata and, sitting on a low seat, asked a question:

"Master Gotama, is it possible for people to be reborn in heaven merely through mental confidence alone, without having given gifts, without having performed acts of worship, without having heard the Dhamma, and without having observed the Uposatha? "O Brahmin, why do you ask me this?"
“Did not your son Maṭṭhakuṇḍalin, having inspired confidence in me, declare that he had been reborn in his own heaven?

“When was that, Master Gotama? “Was it not today, when you went to the charnel ground and were weeping, that you saw a young man nearby who, raising his arms, was also weeping, and [said], ‘Maṭṭhakuṇḍalin is adorned, wearing garlands and anointed with yellow sandalwood’?”
Explaining the story told by two people, he related the entire account of Maṭṭhakuṇḍala.
For that reason, this came to be known as "spoken by the Buddha.
Having related that, he said: "Indeed, Brahmin, it was not one hundred, nor two hundred; rather, my mind..."
"Having inspired confidence, there is no counting those reborn in heaven," he said.
Then the great multitude remained without full conviction; perceiving their lack of conviction, the Teacher resolved:
"Let the deva-son Maṭṭhakuṇḍali come together with his celestial mansion. He arrived with a celestial mansion measuring three gavutas, adorned with divine ornaments.
Having come in her own form, she descended from her celestial mansion, paid homage to the Teacher, and stood to one side.
Then the Teacher, asking her, “By what deed did you obtain this prosperity? said:
“O goddess, you who stand here with such exquisite beauty—”
“Illuminating all directions like a star among the herbs, I ask you, O god of great power: what merit did you perform while being a human?”—thus he spoke this verse.
“Venerable sir, this prosperity of mine as a son of the gods was obtained by inspiring confidence in your mind.”
“Did you obtain this by inspiring confidence in my heart? “Yes, venerable sir,” he replied.
The great multitude, looking at the son of the gods, expressed their joy, saying: “How wonderful indeed are the qualities of the Buddha!
Even the son of a brahmin who had never before given anything, having inspired confidence in the Teacher without performing any other merit, has obtained such a state of prosperity.”
Now, for these beings, the mind is the forerunner in the performance of wholesome and unwholesome kamma; the mind is supreme.
For kamma performed with a clear mind does not abandon a person as they go to the world of the gods or the world of humans, just as a shadow does not leave its bearer.
Having related this account, having established the connection, and having joined the sequence, he sealed the teaching—which had just been established—with the royal seal.
As if bestowing a reward, the Dhamma King spoke this verse:
“Mind precedes all phenomena; mind is their chief, they are all mind-wrought.
If one speaks or acts with a pure mind, [happiness follows one] like a shadow that never departs.”
"Then happiness follows it, like a shadow that never departs. In this context,
although the term "mind" (*mano*) generally refers to all consciousness belonging to the four planes of existence,
when it is being defined, determined, and delimited in this specific passage, it refers specifically to the eightfold wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
It is obtainable. However, when considered according to its basis (*vatthu*), only a consciousness associated with knowledge and accompanied by joy is obtainable even there.

"Preceded by" means being endowed with that which goes first. "Phenomena" refers to the three aggregates beginning with feeling (*vedanā*). For these have the mind associated with joy as their precursor in the sense of being the condition for their arising.

"Mind is the forerunner" means this: just as when many people have gathered together and are performing meritorious deeds—such as giving robes and so forth to the great Saṅgha of bhikkhus, or performing sublime acts of worship, listening to the Dhamma, or making offerings of garlands, perfumes, and honors—if someone were to ask, "Who is the leader among these?
it is that person who serves as their condition, depending upon whom they perform those meritorious deeds.
Just as when Tissa or Phussa performs a deed, he is said to be their leader, so too should this be understood.
Thus, because mind is the precursor to these [mental states] in the sense of being their condition for arising, they are called "mind-preceded" (*manopubbaṅgamā*).
For they are not able to arise unless mind arises; however, mind itself certainly arises even when some of the other mental factors do not arise.
Thus, because mind is the foremost among these by way of sovereignty, they are called "mind-foremost" (*manoseṭṭhā*).
Just as a person who is the leader of a group or an army is called the "best of the group" (*gaṇaseṭṭho*) or the "best of the army" (*seṇiseṭṭho*), so too is mind the foremost among them.

Furthermore, just as articles produced from gold and other materials are called "made of gold" (*suvaṇṇamaya*) and so forth, so too these are called "mind-made" (*manomaya*) because they are produced from the mind.
"With a serene mind" means with a mind serene through qualities such as non-covetousness.
"He speaks or acts"—when speaking with such a mind, he speaks only the fourfold good verbal conduct; when acting, he performs only the threefold good bodily conduct;
and when neither speaking nor acting, through that state of a mind serene by way of non-covetousness and so forth, [he cultivates] the threefold good mental conduct.
He fulfills them. In this way, his ten courses of wholesome action reach completion.
"Then happiness follows him" means that from those three kinds of good conduct, happiness follows that person. Here, the wholesome [kamma] pertaining to the three planes is intended;
therefore, by the power of the good conduct belonging to the three planes, the person reborn in a happy destination—

Whether one is situated in a state of misfortune or in a place of experiencing happiness, bodily pleasure—whether based on the body, based on something else, or baseless—follows and does not abandon the mental pleasure that is a result (*vipāka*).
This is how the meaning should be understood. How so? "Like a shadow that never departs.
For just as a shadow is bound to the body and moves when the body moves, [so too does this pleasure follow].

When [the body] stands, it stands; when it sits, it sits. One is unable to make it turn back—either by speaking gently or harshly, or by striking it—saying, "Turn back! Why? Because it is bound to the physical body.

In the same way, the bodily and mental happiness belonging to the sense-sphere and other realms, which is rooted in the wholesome roots that have been repeatedly practiced through these ten courses of wholesome action (kusala-kammapatha), [persists].
"Like a shadow that never leaves one who has gone to a place, it does not abandon him.
At the conclusion of the verse, eighty-four thousand living beings attained realization of the Dhamma;
the deva-son Maṭṭhakuṇḍali was established in the fruit of stream-entry, as was the brahmin Adinnapubbaka. He [the Buddha], with such great majesty—
"It was scattered throughout the Buddha's teaching.
This is the second story, that of Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī.
3. The Story of the Elder Tissa.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, related this teaching on the Dhamma concerning the Elder Tissa.
It is said that the Venerable Elder Tissa was the son of the Blessed One’s paternal aunt;
having gone forth in old age, he enjoyed the gains and honors bestowed upon the Buddhas, and his body became stout from wearing robes that were repeatedly beaten and pressed.
Having dressed himself, he usually sat in the assembly hall in the middle of the monastery.

When visiting monks who had come to see the Tathāgata saw him, they thought, "This must be some great elder," and approaching him, they asked for instructions regarding their duties and requested such services as having their feet massaged. He remained silent. Then [the visitors] said to him:
A certain young bhikkhu asked, “How many years of seniority do you have? When they replied, “We have no years;
we went forth at an advanced age,” he said, “Friends, you are ill-behaved and old; you do not know your own measure.
Seeing so many great elders, you do not perform even the slightest act of courtesy; when asked about your duties, you remain silent, and you feel not even the slightest pang of remorse.”
“They do not exist,” he said, and snapped his fingers. Having conceived a sense of pride as a kshatriya, he asked, “Whom have you come to?
When they replied, “To the Teacher,” he said, “But you should consider who I am; I shall cut off your very roots!
Weeping, pained, and dejected, he went into the presence of the Teacher. Then the Teacher [addressed him].
“Tissa, why have you come here so distressed, dejected, with tears on your face, and weeping? he asked.
Those monks, thinking, “He might cause some commotion once he has gone,” went along with him; having paid homage to the Teacher, they sat down to one side.
When questioned by the Teacher, he said, “Venerable Sir, these monks are reviling me. “Where [have you been]? he asked.
“But where were you sitting? “In the assembly hall in the middle of the monastery, venerable sir.
“Did you see these monks as they were coming? “Yes, I saw them, venerable sir. “Did you rise and go out to meet them?
“I did not, venerable sir. “Did you ask for their requisites? “I did not, venerable sir.”
“Did you ask for the *vatta* (duty) or the water? “I did not ask, venerable sir. “Did you remove the seat, pay homage, and perform the foot-massage?
“I did not do so, venerable sir. “Tissa, all this *vatta* must be performed for senior monks;
it is not permitted for one who does not perform this *vatta* to sit in the middle of the monastery. It is yours alone [to attend to].”
“Is it not your fault? Ask these monks for forgiveness. “These monks abused me, Bhante; I will not ask them for forgiveness.
“Tissa, do not act thus. It is your own fault; ask them for forgiveness. “I will not ask them for forgiveness, Bhante.
Then, when the monks said, “He is difficult to speak to, Bhante,” the Teacher replied, “Monks, he was not difficult to speak to only now.”
“Even in the past, he was difficult to speak to,” he said. When they asked, “Venerable sir, we have now known his difficult-to-speak-to nature;
what did he do in the past? he replied, “In that case, monks, listen,” and he related a story of the past.
In the past, while the King of Bārāṇasī was reigning in Bārāṇasī, an ascetic named Devila dwelt for eight months in the Himālaya mountains.
Having stayed for four months for the purpose of practicing the salt-and-vinegar regimen, the ascetic, desiring to dwell near the city, came from the Himālayas.
Seeing some boys at the city gate, he asked: "Where do the renunciants who have arrived in this city reside?
"In the potter’s hall, venerable sir," they replied. The ascetic went to the potter’s hall and stood at the door.
“If it is not troublesome for you, Bhaggava, we would like to stay in the hall for one night,” he said. The potter replied, “I have no need for the hall at night;
it is a large hall, so please stay as you wish, venerable sir,” and he offered the hall to them.
When he had entered and sat down, another ascetic named Nārada arrived from the Himālayas and approached the potter.

He requested a stay for one night. The potter thought, “Whether he wishes to stay together with this man who arrived first or not, I shall free myself from him,” and said, “Venerable sir, if the one who arrived first approves, you may stay by his consent.
He approached him and said, “If it is not troublesome for you, teacher, and if we—”
“May we stay for one night,” he requested. When [Devila] replied, “There is a large hall;
enter and stay in a corner,” he entered and sat down behind Devila, who had already entered earlier. After both had conversed on friendly topics, they lay down to sleep.
At the time of going to bed, Nārada took note of Devila’s place of rest and the location of the door, and then lay down. He...
But when Devila lay down, instead of lying in his own place, he lay across the middle of the doorway.
As Nārada was going out at night, he stepped on his matted hair. When [Devila] asked, "Who has stepped on me?
he replied, "Teacher, it was I. "You rogue of a matted-hair ascetic! Having come from the forest, you have stepped on my matted hair! "Teacher, yours..."
“I do not know that you were lying here; please forgive me,” he said, and even as the other was crying out, he went outside.
The other thought, “If he enters while I am inside, he might step on me,” so he turned over and lay down with his head where his feet had been.
As Nārada entered, he thought, “First I offended my teacher; now I shall enter by his side.”
Having thought this, as he was coming, he stepped on [the teacher’s] neck. When asked, “Who is this? he replied, “I am, Teacher.
Upon being told, “You rogue ascetic! Having first stepped on my matted locks, you now step on my neck;
I shall curse you! he said, “Teacher, there is no fault in me. I did not know that you were lying down in such a manner. Even at first—”
“I have offended you; now I shall enter by the side of the tree,” he said, and so I entered.
“Forgive me! he pleaded. “O Kūṭajaṭila, I shall curse you! “Do not do this, Teacher! he replied. But he, disregarding his words, said:
“The thousand-rayed one, of constant brilliance, the sun that dispels darkness;”
“When the sun rises, may your head split into seven pieces! Thus he uttered a curse against him.
Nārada said, “Teacher, you are cursing me even as I say, ‘I have no fault. May the head of whoever has a fault split apart, but not that of one who is innocent. Then he added:
“The thousand-rayed sun, of constant brilliance, the dispeller of darkness;”
“When the sun rises, may your head split into seven pieces!”—thus he cursed him.
Furthermore, that man of great power could recollect eighty eons—forty in the past and forty in the future.
Therefore, reflecting on whom his curse would fall upon, he realized it was his own teacher.
Out of compassion for him, he used his power of psychic potency (*iddhi*) to prevent the rising of the dawn.
When the dawn did not rise, the citizens went to the king’s gate and cried out, “Your Majesty, while you are ruling the kingdom, the dawn does not arise;
please cause the dawn to rise for us! The king, examining his own bodily actions and the rest, saw nothing amiss.
Seeing that this was improper, he thought, "What could be the reason?
Suspecting that there must have been a dispute among those who had gone forth, he asked, "Are there any who have gone forth in this city?
When it was told to him, "Your Majesty, they arrived yesterday evening at the potter's workshop," the king went there at that very moment with torches being carried before him, and [found] Nārada.
Having paid homage, he sat down to one side and said:
“O Nārada, the work of Jambudīpa does not proceed;
by what has the world become shrouded in darkness? Tell me this when asked.”
Nārada, having related all that had occurred, said: "For this reason I was cursed by him.
Then I said, 'I have no fault; let the curse fall upon whoever has the fault,' and so I cursed him.
Having cursed him, I reflected, 'Upon whom indeed will this curse fall? and while searching, [I saw] at the time of sunrise—"
“...the head of the teacher will split into seven pieces. Having seen this, out of compassion for him, [the deity] thought, “I shall not allow the sun to rise.
“But how, venerable sir, might there be no obstacle for him? “If he were to ask my forgiveness, there would be none.
“In that case, ask his forgiveness,” was said. [The deity replied: “Great King, he seized me by the matted locks...”
He stepped on his head, his hands, his belly, and his neck, saying, "I will not ask this fraudulent ascetic for forgiveness. "Forgive him, venerable sir;
do not act thus," [the king said]. "I will not forgive him," he replied. Even when it was said, "Your head shall split into seven pieces," he still would not ask for forgiveness.
Then the king, thinking, "You will not ask for forgiveness of your own accord," [seized him] by the hands, feet, belly, and neck.
Having made him seize [the teacher], he caused him to bow down at the feet of Nārada. Nārada said, “Arise, Teacher; I forgive you.
Then he said, “Great King, this man does not forgive me of his own accord. Not far from the city there is a lake;
place him there with a lump of clay upon his head, standing in water reaching up to his neck. The king did so.
Nārada addressed Devila, saying, "Teacher, when the heat of the sun arises from my released supernatural power, you should dive into the water and emerge at another spot before departing.
"As soon as it was touched by the rays of the sun, even a lump of clay would split into seven pieces; he dived and fled by another way."
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said, "Bhikkhus, at that time King Ānanda was Devila, Tissa was Nārada, and I myself was Nārada;
even then he was difficult to speak to. Having said this, he addressed the Elder Tissa:
"Tissa, for a bhikkhu it is not fitting to say, 'I have been reviled by so-and-so, struck by so-and-so, defeated by so-and-so; such-and-such a person has stolen my goods.'"

"For one who thinks, 'He has struck me,' 'He has beaten me,' 'He has defeated me,' or 'He has taken away what is mine,' hatred is not appeased; but for one who does not harbor resentment, it is indeed appeased.
Having said this, he spoke these verses:
"He has reviled me, he has beaten me, He has defeated me, he has taken away my wealth;”
"And for those who harbor resentment toward him, their enmity is not appeased.
'He reviled me, he struck me, he defeated me, he robbed me'—
for those who do not harbor such thoughts, their enmity is appeased."

In this context: *akkocchi* means he reviled; *avadhi* means he struck; *ajini* means he conquered, either by deceiving with false witnesses, by counter-arguing in debate, or by making a superior legal plea;
*ahāsi me* means he took away something belonging to me, such as a bowl or other articles;
and *ye ca taṃ* refers to whoever—whether deities or humans, whether householders or those gone forth—who [perceived] that basis [of the offense], namely, "He reviled me," and so forth.
They harbor resentment by repeatedly wrapping it around like a cart-yoke with leather thongs, or like rotten fish and the like wrapped in kusa grass;
for them, the enmity that has once arisen does not subside—that is, it is not pacified.

And those who do not harbor it do so either through lack of mindfulness or lack of attention, or by means of reflecting on their past actions (*kamma-paccavekkhaṇa*), and so forth—those who [do not harbor] that [resentment] based on grounds such as verbal abuse.
"Someone must have reviled you in a previous existence when they were innocent; someone must have struck you; someone must have defeated you by bringing false witnesses;
or something must have been forcibly seized from you by someone. Therefore, even though you are innocent, you have encountered such abuse and so forth.
In this way, they do not harbor resentment. Even if enmity should arise among them through negligence, [they do not let it persist].
“By this lack of provocation, he will be extinguished like a fire without fuel.

At the conclusion of the teaching, one hundred thousand bhikkhus attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages. The preaching of the Dhamma was fruitful for the great multitude. Even the ill-spoken became well-spoken.
This is the third story, concerning the Elder Tissa.
4. The Story of Kāḷayakkhinī:
"Not by hatred," this teaching on the Dhamma was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain barren woman.
It is said that when a certain son of a householder’s family had passed away, he himself performed all the work in both the fields and the house.
While doing so, he looked after his mother. Then his mother said, "Dear son, I shall bring you a young woman.
He replied, "Mother, do not say such a thing; I will look after you for as long as I live. She said, "Son, you alone perform all the work in the fields and at home;
because of that, I have no peace of mind. I shall bring one. Thus he spoke again and again.
Having refused, she remained silent. Desiring to go to a certain family, she departed from her home.

Then her son asked her, "To which family are you going? When she replied, "To such-and-such a family," he forbade her from going there and pointed out a family of his own choosing. She went there, requested the maiden, and fixed the day.
Having brought her, he made her his wife in his house. She became barren. Then her mother said to him, "Son, you chose this girl according to your own preference;
now she has turned out barren. A family without offspring perishes; the lineage will not continue.
Therefore, I shall bring another girl for you. Although he was told by her, "Enough, mother," [he did not listen].
She spoke again and again. Having heard those words, Vañjhītthī thought, "Sons are unable to transgress the command of their parents;
now he will bring another fertile woman and enjoy me as a slave-girl. What if I were to bring a maiden myself?
Having thought this, she went to a certain family and [asked for] a maiden for his sake.
Having been refused by them with the words, "What is this you say, mother?", she pleaded, "I am barren;
a family without children perishes. But your daughter, having obtained a son or a daughter, will become the mistress of the household;
give her to my husband. Having thus entreated and obtained their consent, she brought her back.
She performed [the service] in her husband’s house.
Then this thought occurred to her: “If she should obtain a son or a daughter, she alone will become the mistress of the household.
It is right that I act in such a way that she does not obtain a child. Then she...
She said, "Mother, when a fetus has taken root in your womb, then you must inform me.
She consented, saying, "Very well," and when the fetus had taken root, she informed her. But the other woman herself constantly gave her rice-gruel and food;
then, along with that very food, she gave her a medicine for inducing abortion, and the fetus fell out. A second time...
When she had become pregnant, she informed [the other woman], who likewise caused her to miscarry a second time.
Then the women living in the neighborhood asked her, "Is your co-wife causing you obstacles? Having reported the matter to them, she said, "O blind fools, why did you do this?
This woman, out of fear of your authority, has prepared and given you an abortifacient."
When she was told, "Because of that, your fetus falls; do not speak thus again," she did not say anything on the third occasion.
Then, seeing the other woman's belly, she said, "Why did you not tell me that my pregnancy had been established?
When the other replied, "You brought me here and deceived me by causing my fetus to fall twice; for what purpose should I tell you?"
Thinking, "I am now ruined," she watched for her negligence; then, once the pregnancy had matured, she found an opportunity, prepared a medicine, and gave it to her.
Because the fetus was mature, it was unable to fall out and instead lay crosswise;
sharp pains arose, and she reached a state where her life was in danger. She said, "I have been destroyed by you! You yourself brought me [here], and you yourself..."
She had already caused two children to perish; now she thought, "I too shall perish.
Having passed away from here, may I be reborn as a female spirit (*yakkhinī*) capable of devouring your children. Having made this aspiration, she died and was reborn in that very house as a cat.
Her husband also took the other child and said, "By you, my family line has been destroyed."

Thinking, "What have I done?", she pounded [her body] until it was well-massaged with *kappara*, *jaṇṇuka*, and other substances. She died from that very affliction and was reborn right there as a hen.
Not long after, the hen laid eggs, and a cat came and ate those eggs. A second time...
A third time as well, she ate them. The hen thought, "Having eaten my eggs three times, he now wishes to eat me too.

Making a wish, "May I, upon passing away from here, be able to eat him along with his children," she passed away from that state and was reborn in the forest as a leopardess. The other was reborn as a doe. When it was her time to give birth...
The leopardess came and ate the two cubs on three occasions. At the time of her death, the doe made a wish, thinking:
"She has eaten my two cubs three times; now she will eat me as well. Having passed away from here, may she be permitted to eat this one along with her cubs.
Having passed away from there, she was reborn as a *yakkhinī*. The leopardess likewise passed away from there and was reborn in Sāvatthī.
Having been born as a daughter of a noble family, she grew up and went to her husband’s home in a neighboring village.
Later, she gave birth to a son. Then a yakkhinī, having come in the guise of her dear friend, asked, "Where is my friend?
When told, "She has given birth in the inner chamber," she thought, "Has she given birth to a son, or perhaps a daughter? Shall I see her?"
Having entered the womb, she appeared as if looking at the boy, then took him, ate him, and departed.
On the second occasion, she did exactly the same. On the third occasion, the other woman became heavily burdened with her pregnancy;
she addressed her husband, saying, "Husband, a certain yakkhinī has come to this place, eaten my two sons, and departed. Now, having gone to my own family home, I shall give birth."
Having gone to her family home, she gave birth.
At that time, the yakkhinī had gone for her turn at the water. For the yakkhinīs of Vessavaṇa bring water from Lake Anotatta in a succession of sal-tree branches according to their turn;
they are released only after the lapse of four or five months.
Other yakkhinīs, their bodies exhausted, even reached the point of death.
But she, as soon as she was released from the water-vessel, went quickly to that house and asked, "Where is my companion? "How could you see her?
A yakkhinī comes here and eats every child born in this place; therefore, she has gone to her own family home. She—
