“Wherever he may go, he shall not escape from me! Thus, her mind incited by the impulse of her enmity, she set out toward the city.

The other woman, having bathed the boy on the day his name was given and having bestowed a name upon him, said, “Husband, let us now go to our own home,” and taking her son, she proceeded along the path through the middle of the monastery together with her husband.
Having given her son to her husband and bathed in the monastery lotus pond, she stood on the bank giving the child breast-milk after her husband had finished bathing.
Seeing the *yakkhinī* approaching and recognizing her, she cried out at the top of her voice, "Husband, come quickly!
Here is that *yakkhinī*! Come quickly! Here is that *yakkhinī*! and remained there until he arrived.
Unable to remain still, she turned back and rushed toward the interior of the monastery.
At that moment, the Teacher was teaching the Dhamma in the midst of the assembly.
She laid her son down at the feet of the Tathāgata and said, "I have given him to you; grant my son his life. At the gateway, she...
The yakkhinī named Sumanadevī, being possessed by [the spirit], did not allow her to enter.
The Teacher addressed the Elder Ānanda, saying, “Go, Ānanda, and summon that yakkhinī. The Elder summoned her.
The other said, “Venerable sir, she is coming. The Teacher said, “Let her come; do not make a sound,” and as she stood there having arrived, he spoke.

"Why do you act thus? If you had not come into the presence of a Buddha such as I, your enmity would have lasted for an eon, like that between snakes and mongooses, cats and shrews, or crows and owls.
Why do you return enmity with enmity? For enmity is appeased by non-enmity, not by enmity," he said, and then spoke this verse:
“Indeed, enmities are never stilled here by enmity;
they are stilled by non-enmity. This is the eternal law.
In this context, “indeed, not by enmity”: for just as a place smeared with impurities such as saliva and snot cannot be cleansed by those very same things, [so too enmity is not stilled by enmity].
Just as those who wash with impurities are unable to make something clean and odorless, but rather that place becomes even more unclean and foul-smelling;
even so, one who reviles in return while being reviled, or strikes back while being struck,
is unable to appease hatred with hatred, but rather increases hatred all the more.
It acts [thus]. Thus, those things called "enmities" are never appeased by enmity at any time; rather, they only increase.

But as for the phrase "they are appeased by non-enmity": just as those impurities such as phlegm, when washed away with clear water, perish and that place becomes clean and fragrant, even so, through non-enmity—that is, the water of patience and loving-kindness—applied with wise attention...
Through attention and through reflection, enmities are stilled, they subside, and they come to non-existence.
"This is the ancient Dhamma" means that this—namely, the stilling of enmity by one who is without enmity—is the ancient Dhamma;
it is the path traversed by all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and those whose taints are destroyed.

At the conclusion of the verses, the female spirit (yakkhinī) was established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). The teaching of the Dhamma was also beneficial for the assembled multitude.
The Teacher said to that woman, “Give this child back to her. “I am afraid, Bhante,” she replied. “Do not fear;
there will be no obstacle for you because of this,” he said. She gave him the child. Having kissed and embraced him, she—
Having given it back to her mother, she began to weep. Then the Teacher asked her, "What is this?
She replied, "Venerable Sir, although I previously made my living in whatever way possible, I could not even obtain enough to fill my belly; how shall I live now?
Then the Teacher comforted her, saying, "Do not worry," and said to that woman: "Take her and..."
“Having had him reside in her own house, she attended to him with the finest rice gruel and meals.
She took him there, established him upon a wooden beam, and tended to him with the finest rice gruel and meals;
when it was time for her to harvest the rice, he appeared as if he were striking her head with the end of a pestle. She addressed her companion, saying, “I am unable to live in this place.”

"Establish me elsewhere," she said; yet even though she was established in these places—the water-tub in the pestle-hall, the oven, the corner of the hearth, the heap of refuse, and the village gate—here it appeared to her as if someone were splitting her head with a pestle;
here children poured out leftover water; here dogs lay down; and here children...
“They make it unclean; they throw rubbish here; village children use this place for playing with clay.

Thus she rejected all those locations. Then, having established her in a secluded spot outside the village, they brought her the finest rice gruel, alms-food, and so forth, and looked after her there. That female spirit thought to herself: “This is my companion.”
“Now she has been very helpful; come now, I shall do something in return. She then informed her friend: “In this year there will be good rain;
sow your crops on high ground. In this year there will be poor rain; sow your crops only in low-lying places.
The crops planted by the other people were [destroyed] by excessive water.
Whether it was with too much water or without water, the crop would fail; yet for her, it always turned out exceedingly well.
Then the other people asked her, "Mother, the rice you have planted neither fails when there is too much water nor when there is not enough.

You perform your work having known whether there will be good rain or bad rain; what indeed is this? She replied, "A female spirit (*yakkhinī*), our companion, [knows] the state of good and bad rain..."
"She explains it thus: 'By her word we cultivate crops on both high and low ground, and because of that we prosper.
Do you not see how the rice-gruel, food, and other provisions are constantly being carried away from our house?
It is she who takes them. You too should carry the best rice-gruel, food, and so forth for her; she will look after your work as well.'"
Then all the inhabitants of the city paid her honor. From that time forward, she supervised the work of everyone and attained the highest degree of prosperity, possessing a large retinue.
Later on, she established eight *salākā*-meals (tickets for meals), which continue to be given even until the present day.
The Story of Kāḷayakkhinī, the fourth.
5. The Story of the Kosambī Bhikkhus:
"And others do not understand"—the Teacher spoke this teaching on the Dhamma while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the bhikkhus of Kosambī.
At the Ghosita Monastery in Kosambī, two monks lived with five hundred followers each:

one was an expert in the Vinaya, and the other was a preacher of the Dhamma. One day, after the preacher of the Dhamma had washed his body, he placed the remainder of the rinsing water in a vessel at the water cistern and went out. Subsequently, the expert in the Vinaya entered that place.
Seeing that water, he went out and asked the other, "Friend, did you set this water down? "Yes, friend.
"But do you not know that there is an offense here? "Yes, I do not know. "There is an offense here, friend.
"In that case, I shall make amends for it. "But if, friend, it was unintentional on your part or due to forgetfulness..."
He said, "There is no offense," and thus he held the view that there was no offense for that transgression.
The holder of the Vinaya also informed his own dependents, "This preacher of the Dhamma does not even know when he incurs an offense.
When they saw his dependents, they said, "Your preceptor, even after incurring an offense, does not recognize its existence as an offense."
They said this. Having gone, they reported it to their own preceptor. He spoke thus:
"This master of the Vinaya previously said there was no offense, but now he says there is an offense; he is a liar. They went and said, "Your preceptor is a liar.
In this way, they increased their mutual quarreling. The master of the Vinaya was brought to his senses.
Having obtained [the opportunity], they carried out a formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) against the Dhamma-preacher for his refusal to acknowledge an offense.
From that time on, those who provided them with requisites and their attendants split into two factions;

likewise, the nuns who received their exhortations, the protective deities, their friends and kinsmen, and even the deities dwelling in the sky—all of them, as far as the Brahma-world—split into two parties.
The worldlings were divided into two factions. However, from the realm of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṭṭha heaven, there arose a single cry and a great clamor.
Then, a certain bhikkhu approached the Tathāgata and [reported] regarding those who had suspended the *vinaya*-holders and their pupils.
The Blessed One reported that they held the view, "He has been suspended by a legal act of the Vinaya," while the disciples of those Dhamma-preachers who followed the suspended monk held the view,

"He has been suspended by an illegal act," and he reported their continued wandering about in attendance upon them even though they were being restrained by those who had suspended them, saying, "Let them indeed become united."

Having sent [messengers] twice and hearing that they did not wish to be in concord, O Bhante, he went to them on the third occasion, saying, "The Saṅgha of bhikkhus is split! The Saṅgha of bhikkhus is split!

There, he spoke of the danger in the suspension of those who had suspended others, and in the non-confession of offenses by the others; then, right there within the same boundary, he performed the Uposatha and other ceremonies with them.
Having authorized [the rule], he established the procedure for the dining hall (*bhattagga*) and other such places, stating: "Those who have fallen into quarreling must sit with a seat between them.
Later, hearing that they were still living in quarrel even then, he went there and said, "Enough, monks!
Do not quarrel," and so forth, adding: "Monks, these quarrels, strifes, disputes, and contentions..."
“They cause harm. For it was on account of a quarrel that even the little bird Laṭukikā brought about the destruction of life for a great elephant,” he said, and related the Laṭukikājātaka.

Then he said, “Monks, be united; do not dispute. For it was on account of a dispute that even many hundreds of thousands of quails met their destruction,” and he related the Vaṭṭakājātaka. Thus it was.
When they were not heeding the word of the Blessed One, a certain proponent of the Dhamma—one who did not wish for the Tathāgata’s affliction—said:
“Let the Blessed One come, O Lord, Master of the Dhamma; let the Blessed One remain at ease, devoted to dwelling in the happiness of the present life;
we ourselves shall be known by that quarrel, strife, contention, and dispute. Having said this, he brought up a past event:
Once upon a time, monks, there was a king of Kāsi in Bārāṇasī named Brahmadatta.
After Brahmadatta had seized the kingdom from Dīghīti, the king of Kosala, he killed his father while the latter was living in disguise.
When Prince Dīghāvu gave him his own life, from that time forth they lived in harmony; having related this account of their mutual reconciliation, [he said:]...
“Monks, even those kings who have taken up the rod and taken up the sword will possess such patience and gentleness!
Yet, monks, it would truly befit you that, having gone forth in this well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya, you yourselves should be patient and gentle.
Even after he had exhorted them thus, he was still unable to bring them into harmony.
He was unable [to remain]. Distressed by that state of being crowded, he thought: "I am now living in suffering because I am surrounded;
moreover, these monks do not follow my word. What if I were to dwell alone, withdrawn from the group?
Having reflected thus, after walking for alms in Kosambī, he took his own bowl and robes and departed alone, without taking leave of the Saṅgha of monks.
Having gone to Bālakaloṇakagāma, he spoke there to the elder Bhagu about the practice of wandering alone;
then, having spoken to three young men of good family in the Pācīnavaṃsamigadāya forest about the benefits of concord, he arrived at Pālileyyaka.
There, indeed, the Blessed One stayed near Pālileyyaka, in the protected grove of Rakkhitavana, at the foot of a bhadrasāla tree, together with Pālileyyaka the elephant.
Being attended by an elephant, he spent a comfortable rainy-season residence there.
The lay followers living in Kosambī also went to the monastery; not seeing the Teacher, they asked, "Venerable sir, where is the Teacher?
"He has gone to the Pālileyyaka forest grove. "For what reason? "I was striving to bring about harmony among you."
“But we were not in harmony. “Venerable sir, having gone forth in the presence of the Teacher, why did you not remain in harmony while he was practicing in concord?

“It is so, friend. “These men, having gone forth in the presence of the Teacher, failed to become harmonious even while he was practicing in concord; we [will go forth] depending on these very people for the sake of the Teacher.”
"We shall not even give them a seat, nor shall we perform prostrations and other marks of respect toward them.
From that time on, they did not offer them even the slightest gesture of courtesy. Due to their lack of food, they became emaciated;
after only a few days, they straightened up, confessed their transgressions to one another, and asked for forgiveness, saying, "Lay followers, we have become reconciled; you too..."
“Do not be like you were before,” they said. “But has the Teacher been asked for forgiveness by you, venerable sirs? “He has not been asked for forgiveness, friend.
“In that case, ask the Teacher for forgiveness; when the Teacher has been asked for forgiveness, we too shall become like you were before.
Because it was the middle of the rainy season, they were unable to go into the presence of the Teacher, and thus, with great difficulty...
They spent the rainy season there. The Teacher, however, dwelt in comfort, being attended by that elephant.
For that noble elephant too had abandoned his herd and entered that forest grove solely for the sake of living in peace.
As it is said: "I was dwelling crowded with male elephants, female elephants, elephant calves, and elephant cubs."
"I eat grass with its tips cut off; they eat my broken-off branches;
I drink turbid water; and when I have emerged from the bathing pool, female elephants come trailing along, rubbing their bodies against mine.
What if I were to dwell alone, withdrawn from the herd? Then that bull elephant departed from the herd.
He went to Pālileyyaka, the protected forest grove at the foot of the Bhaddasāla tree, where the Blessed One was staying;

having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he looked around but saw nothing else, so he struck the foot of the Bhaddasāla tree with his trunk, stripped off a branch, and swept [the ground] while holding the branch in his trunk. From that time on, with his trunk...
Taking a water jar, he provides drinking water and water for washing. When there is a need for hot water, he prepares hot water.
How so? Rubbing wood with his hand, he produces fire; throwing pieces of wood into it, he kindles the fire;
placing stones therein, he cooks them; and turning them with a wooden stick, he prepares them until they are thoroughly heated.
He threw it into a small vat; then, having lowered his hand and ascertained that the water was hot, he went and paid homage to the Teacher.
The Teacher said, "The water has been heated for you, Pālileyyaka," and having gone there, he bathed.
Then [the elephant] brought various kinds of fruits and gave them to him. But whenever the Teacher entered a village for alms,
Then, taking the Teacher’s bowl and robe and setting them down in the water-jar, he went along with the Teacher.
When the Teacher reached the vicinity of the village, he said, "Pālileyyaka, from now on you will no longer be able to go;
bring me food and my bowl and robe. Having had these brought, he entered the village for alms. He [the elephant] remained right there until the Teacher departed.
Upon his arrival, having stood there and gone out to meet him, he took his bowl and robe in the same manner as before, set them down at the dwelling place, and performed the proper duties;

then he fanned him with a branch. At night, holding a large staff in his trunk to ward off wild beasts and obstacles, he remained within the forest grove until the rising of the dawn, thinking, "I shall protect the Teacher."
From that time forth, it is said, that forest grove became known as the Pālileyyaka Protected Forest.
Beginning with the offering of water for his face at sunrise, he performed all the duties in that very same manner.
Then, one monkey, rising up day after day, [performed] the Tathāgata’s duties of personal service.
Seeing him doing so, the monkey thought, "I too shall do something," and as he wandered about, one day he saw a honeycomb free of bees.

He broke off a branch, brought the honeycomb along with the branch to the presence of the Teacher, cut a leaf from a plantain tree, placed it there, and gave it to him. The Teacher accepted it. The monkey thought, "Will he [eat it]?"...
Thinking, "He will not consume it," and looking [to see], he saw that [the Teacher] had taken it and was sitting there. Pondering, "What could this be?
he took hold of it by the tip of its stalk, turned it over, and examined it; seeing the seed-pods, he slowly removed them and gave it back.
The Teacher consumed it. With a joyful heart, he took various branches and danced as it were.
He stood there. Then, both the branches he had grasped and those he had stepped upon broke.
He fell onto the top of a tree stump, and with his body resting there, he passed away with a mind full of faith toward the Teacher.
He was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven in a golden celestial mansion thirty yojanas in size, surrounded by a retinue of a thousand nymphs, as the deva-son named Makkaṭa.
The fact that the Tathāgata was residing there, being attended by the noble elephant Hatthināga, became well known throughout the whole of Jambudīpa.

From the city of Sāvatthī, great families such as those of Anāthapiṇḍika and the great female lay disciple Visākhā sent a message to the Elder Ānanda, saying, "Venerable sir, please let us see the Teacher. Those living in other regions did likewise.

Five hundred bhikkhus who had completed the rains retreat approached the Elder Ānanda and requested, "Friend Ānanda, it has been a long time since we have heard a discourse on the Dhamma from the presence of the Blessed One.
It would be well, friend Ānanda, if we might receive a discourse on the Dhamma from the presence of the Blessed One.
Taking those bhikkhus with him, the Elder went there.

Thinking, "It is not appropriate for me to approach the Tathāgata in his presence with so many bhikkhus after having lived alone for three months," he left those bhikkhus outside and approached the Teacher all by himself.
When Pālileyyaka saw him, he took up his staff and rushed forward. The Teacher looked at him and said, "Go away, go away, Pālileyyaka; do not hinder me."
“This man is an attendant of the Buddha,” he said. Right there, he cast away his staff and asked for permission to receive his bowl and robes.
The Elder did not give them to him. The Nāga thought, “If he has mastered the proper conduct (vatta), he will not place his own requisites on the stone seat where the Teacher sits.
The Elder placed the bowl and robes on the ground. Those perfected in conduct—
Indeed, they do not place their own requisites upon the seats or couches of their teachers.
The Elder approached the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down to one side. The Teacher asked, "Ānanda, have you come alone?
When he heard that [the Elder] had arrived together with five hundred bhikkhus, he asked, "But where are these?"
When it was said, “I have come here without knowing your minds and have left you behind,” he replied, “Call them here. The Elder did so.
Those monks came, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down to one side.
The Teacher exchanged greetings with them, and those monks said, “Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is indeed delicate and accustomed to luxury...”
When it was said, "And you, O delicate son of a Khattiya, have performed what is difficult by standing and sitting alone for three months;

I suppose there was neither one to perform the duties of attendance nor anyone to provide water for rinsing the mouth and other necessities," [the Buddha replied], "Monks, all my needs were attended to by the elephant of Pālileyyaka.
For one who obtains such a companion as this, [it is easy] to dwell alone."
"It is fitting to dwell [with others], but for one who does not find such a companion, the state of wandering alone is better. Having said this, he spoke these three verses from the Nāga Chapter:
"If one should find a prudent companion, a wise co-traveler who dwells in virtue;..."
Having overcome all dangers,
one should wander with a mind at ease and mindful.
"If one does not find a wise companion..."
Having abandoned a wise companion who walks with him and dwells virtuously—
just as a king leaves behind a conquered kingdom—
one should wander alone like a tusker elephant in the forest.
“It is better to wander alone;
there is no companionship with a fool.
One should wander alone and not commit evil deeds.”
“Free from anxiety, like an elephant in the Mātaṅga forest.
At the conclusion of this verse, those five hundred bhikkhus were established in Arahatship.
The Elder Ānanda, having announced the message sent by Anāthapiṇḍika and others, said: “Venerable Sir, led by Anāthapiṇḍika, there are five crores of noble disciples...”
“I am waiting for your arrival,” he said. The Teacher replied, “In that case, take your bowl and robes,” and having had him take his bowl and robes, he departed.
The nāga went and stood across the path they had traveled. “Venerable sir, what is the nāga doing?
“Monks, he is waiting to give you alms; moreover, for a long time he has been [waiting] for me.”
"It is not right to provoke the mind of one who is a benefactor; turn back, monks! Having said this, the Teacher took the monks and returned.

The elephant, too, having entered a forest grove and gathered various fruits such as jackfruit and plantains, made a heap of them and gave them to the monks on the following day. The five hundred monks were able to consume them all.
They were unable to do so. At the conclusion of the meal, the Teacher took his bowl and robe and departed.
The nāga went between the monks and stood across the path before the Teacher. "Venerable sir, what is the nāga doing?
"Monks, this one has sent you and wishes to turn me back. Then the Teacher said to him, "Pālileyyaka,..."
"But this is my journey without turning back; you have no jhāna, nor insight, nor the path or fruit in this present body;
stay where you are," he said. Upon hearing this, the elephant thrust his trunk into his mouth and followed behind him weeping.
For had he been permitted to turn back the Teacher, he would have tended to him in that very manner for the rest of his life.
But when the Teacher reached the vicinity of that village, he said, "Pālileyyaka, from now on this is no longer your domain; it is a human habitation fraught with dangers.
Stay here. Weeping, he remained right there, and as soon as the Teacher passed out of his sight, his heart burst and he died.
Through his faith in the Teacher, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven at thirty yojanas [in height].
He was reborn in a golden celestial mansion in the midst of a thousand nymphs, and his name was Pālileyyaka-devaputta.
The Teacher, too, gradually arrived at Jetavana. Hearing that the Teacher had come to Sāvatthī, the monks of Kosambī went there to ask for his forgiveness.
The King of Kosala heard that those monks from Kosambī were quarrelsome...
Hearing that the monks were coming, he approached the Teacher and said, "Venerable Sir, I will not allow them to enter my kingdom.
"Great King, these monks are virtuous; they simply did not heed my words because of their mutual dispute.
Now they are coming to ask my forgiveness; let them come, Great King."
Anāthapiṇḍika also said, "Venerable sir, I will not allow them to enter the monastery," and having been thus refused by the Blessed One, he remained silent.
When they arrived at Sāvatthī, however, the Blessed One had a secluded lodging prepared for them in a private place and assigned it to them.
Other bhikkhus neither sat together with them nor ate together.
They did not remain; as each person arrived, they asked the Teacher, "Venerable Sir, who are these quarrelsome monks of Kosambī?
The Teacher pointed them out, saying, "These. As those who had come one after another pointed their fingers at them, saying, "It is surely they! It is surely they!
they were unable to lift their heads for shame and fell down at the feet of the Blessed One. The Blessed One—
They asked for forgiveness. The Teacher said, "Bhikkhus, you have done a grievous thing.
For having gone forth in the presence of a Buddha such as I, while I was acting with harmony, you did not follow my word.
Even the ancient wise men, upon hearing the advice of their parents who had reached the point of execution, did not transgress it even when those parents were being deprived of life."
"Later, they exercised sovereignty over two kingdoms," he said; and having further related the Kosambika Jātaka, he continued:
"Thus, monks, although Prince Dīghāvu was being deprived of his parents' lives, he did not transgress their advice.
Later, having obtained the daughter of Brahmadatta, he ruled over the two kingdoms of Kāsi and Kosala. You [should do likewise]."
"But by those who did not act upon my words, a grave wrong was committed," he said, and spoke this verse:
"Others do not understand that we here are striving for peace;
but those who do understand therein, from them the strife is stilled."
In that context, "others" refers to those other than the wise—namely, others who engage in quarreling.
While creating a clamor there in the midst of the Saṅgha, they do not realize: "We are dying, we are ceasing, we are perishing; we go constantly and continuously into the presence of Death.
And as for those who do realize it there: those wise ones there [realize], "We are in the presence of Death..."

“They understand: ‘Let us go. Then they settle their disputes. For by understanding thus, they arouse wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) and proceed toward the pacification of disputes (*medhaga*). Then, through that practice, those disputes of theirs are settled.
Alternatively, “and others” refers to what was previously stated by me: “Monks, do not engage in quarreling,” and so forth.
"Even though they are being exhorted, because they do not accept my exhortation and transgress it, others are indeed 'not of my kin. They do not realize:
'Having grasped a wrong view through the influence of desire and so forth, we are here in the midst of the Saṅgha striving for an increase in quarreling and the like.
But now, as you reflect wisely upon that, [you will see] your own..."
Furthermore, those wise men who, in the interim, realize, "Previously, striving under the influence of desire and so forth,
we practiced wrongly," and who, by relying on those [other] wise men, now settle these disputes known as quarrels—
this is the meaning here.
At the conclusion of the verses, the monks who had assembled were established in the fruit of stream-entry and the other stages.
This is the fifth story, concerning Kosambī. 6.
The Story of the Elder Mahākāḷa.
While residing near the city of Setavyā in the Siṃsapā Grove, the Teacher delivered this teaching on the contemplation of beauty with reference to Cūḷakāḷa and Mahākāḷa.
For there were three brothers who were householders living in the city of Setavyā: Cūḷakāḷa, Majjhimakāḷa, and Mahākāḷa.
Among them, the eldest and the youngest would travel abroad and bring back goods in five hundred carts, while Majjhimakāḷa...
He sold what had been brought [to him]. Then, on one occasion, both brothers took various goods in five hundred carts and went to Sāvatthī; they unyoked the carts between Sāvatthī and the Jeta Grove.
Among them, in the evening, Mahākāḷa, with garlands, perfumes, and other items in his hands, [encountered] the noble disciples living in Sāvatthī who were going for the hearing of the Dhamma.
Seeing them going along, he asked, "Where are these people going?
Having heard the matter, he thought, "I too shall go," and addressing his younger brother, said, "Dear brother, be diligent regarding those wagons; I am going to hear the Dhamma.
Having gone there and paid homage to the Tathāgata, he sat down at the edge of the assembly. The Teacher, seeing him, [said:]

Speaking a gradual discourse according to his disposition, he explained in many ways—by means of the *Dukkha-khandha Sutta* and other discourses—the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures. Having heard this, Mahākāḷa thought: "It seems one must depart having abandoned everything;
when going to the world beyond, neither wealth nor kinsmen follow. What use have I for the household life?"
Thinking, "I shall go forth," he paid homage to the Teacher while the great multitude was departing;
then, having requested the Teacher for the going-forth, when the Teacher said, "There is no one you must consult," he replied, "Venerable Sir, I have a younger brother.
When [the Teacher] said, "In that case, consult him," he said, "Very well, Venerable Sir," and having gone and summoned his younger brother, he—
“Father, take charge of all this property,” he said. “But what will you do, brother?
“I shall go forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher. Although he entreated him in many ways, he was unable to turn him back, so he said, “Very well, master;
do as you intend. Mahākāḷa went and went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher.
“I shall go forth only after taking my brother with me,” said Cūḷakāla, and he too went forth.
Later on, after Mahākāla had received full ordination (*upasampadā*), he approached the Teacher and asked about the duties in the Dispensation.
When the Teacher explained two such duties, Mahākāla said, “Venerable Sir, because I went forth at an advanced age, I am unable to fulfill the duty of textual study (*ganthadhura*).”

"I shall not be able [to fulfill it], but I will fulfill the duty of insight (vipassanādhura)," he said; and having had the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) explained until he reached Arahantship, he undertook the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) of the charnel-ground dweller.
When the first watch of the night had passed and everyone had fallen asleep, he would go to the charnel ground and return to the monastery at dawn, before anyone else had even risen.

Now, a certain female cemetery-keeper named Kālī, who was a cremator, having seen the Elder’s place for standing, his place for sitting, and his place for walking, thought, "Who is it that comes here?

I shall observe him. Being unable to observe him, one day she lit a lamp right inside her cemetery hut, took her sons and daughters with her, and went to hide herself in a secluded spot during the middle watch of the night.
Seeing the elder approaching, she went to him, paid homage, and said, "Venerable sir, does our noble master dwell in this place?
"Yes, lay follower," he replied. "Venerable sir, it is right for those dwelling in a charnel ground to learn the proper conduct (vatta)," she said.
Without saying, "But shall we practice the conduct you have described?", the elder asked, "What, lay follower, is it right to do?"

He said, “Venerable sir, it is proper for those who dwell in the charnel ground to inform the guardians of the charnel ground, the resident elder of the monastery, and the village headman that they are living there.

“For what reason, elder? “Because thieves who have committed a crime, pursued step by step by their owners, abandon their goods in the charnel ground and flee; then people [suspect] those who dwell in the charnel ground.”

“They create obstacles; however, if one speaks to them, they will ward off such calamities, saying, ‘We know that this venerable sir has been staying here for such a long time; he is no thief. Therefore, it is appropriate to speak to them.
“What else should the Elder do? “Venerable sir, for a noble one living in a charnel ground, fish, meat, sesame flour, oil, sugar, and so forth—”
These things are to be avoided: one must not sleep by day; one must not be indolent, but must be energetic;
having become free from deceit and guile, one must have a noble disposition; when everyone has gone to sleep at evening, one should return from the monastery;
and at dawn, while everyone else has not yet risen, one should go to the monastery. If, venerable sir, ...
"Noble sir, if you dwell in this place, you will be able to bring the duties of one who has gone forth to their ultimate fulfillment.
If they bring the dead body here and discard it, I shall place it upon the Kambala gabled house, honor it with perfumes, garlands, and the like, and perform the funeral rites.
If you are not able [to do so], I shall place it on the pyre and set fire to it."
"Having set it on fire, pulled it out with a stake, thrown it outside, hacked it with an axe until it is in pieces, and cut it into fragments, I shall throw it into the fire and burn it," she said.
Then the Elder said to her, "Very well, Bhaddā; however, when you see a visual object, please tell me about it.
She replied, "Very well. Then the Elder went to the charnel ground according to his inclination.
He practiced the duties of a recluse. But the Elder Cūḷakāḷa, rising again and again, brooded over his household life and remembered his wife and children.
He thought, "My brother is performing very heavy work.
Then, a daughter of a noble family died in the evening from a disease that had arisen at that very moment, her body neither withered nor exhausted.
Then his kinsmen and others, having taken him to the cemetery in the evening along with wood,
oil, and other necessities, gave wages to the cemetery-keeper, handing him over with the instruction, "Burn this man," and departed.
She removed the cloth he was wrapped in and, seeing at that moment his body— so very plump, golden-hued, and radiant— thought, "This is a fitting object to show to my master."
Having reflected on this, he went and paid homage to the Elder, saying, "Venerable sir, there is an object of such a nature; please look, noble sir.
The Elder said, "Very well," and having had his upper robe removed, he looked from the soles of his feet up to the tips of his hair.
Then he said, "This form is exceedingly plump and golden-hued; were it cast into a fire, at the very moment it is seized by great flames—"
“Inform me,” he said, and having spoken, he returned to his own place and sat down. She did as instructed and informed the Elder.
The Elder went and looked; the color of her body was like that of a speckled cow at every spot struck by the flames.
Her feet were bent and hung down, her hands were curled back, and the skin on her thighs and forehead had been stripped away. The Elder—
“This body, which until just now was appearing limitless to those who were looking at it, has just now reached its destruction and reached its decay.
Having gone to his night-quarters and sat down, contemplating its destruction and decay, he [recited]:
“Impermanent indeed are conditioned things, subject to arising and passing away;”
"Having arisen, they cease; their subsiding is blissful.
Having spoken this verse, he developed insight and attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
When he had attained arahantship, the Teacher, wandering on tour surrounded by the community of monks, arrived at Setavyā.

He entered the Siṃsapā forest. When the wives of Cūḷakāḷa heard that "the Teacher has reportedly arrived at the Siṃsapā forest," they sent word, saying, "We shall take our husband [with us]," and invited the Teacher.
However, because there was no place where the Buddhas had previously been served, one monk, while indicating where the seat should be prepared, went ahead of them.
It is appropriate. For after arranging a seat in the central place for the Buddhas, one must arrange seats for the Elder Sāriputta to the right of that and for the Elder Mahāmoggallāna to the left;
starting from there, seats for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus must be arranged on both sides.
Therefore, the Elder Mahākāḷa stood in the place where the robes were being put on and said, "Cūḷakāḷa..."
“Go ahead and announce the preparation of the seats,” he sent Cūḷakāḷa.
From the moment the householders saw him, they began to joke with him, spreading low seats at the edge for the senior monk of the Saṅgha and high seats at the edge for the junior monk of the Saṅgha.
The other said, “Do not do this; [spread] low seats...”
"Do not arrange them above; arrange the high seats above and the low seats below," he said.
The women, as if not hearing his words, asked: "What are you doing wandering about? Is it not proper for you to arrange seats?
Whom did you ask for permission to go forth? By whom were you ordained? Why have you come here?"
Having spoken thus, they tore off his lower and upper robes, dressed him in white garments, placed a wreath upon his head, and sent him forth, saying, "Go and bring the Teacher;

we shall prepare the seats. Having remained in the state of a monk for no long time, he did not know how to feel shame because he had renounced the robes while still young; therefore, in that attire, he went forth without any hesitation.
Having gone and paid homage to the Teacher, he returned taking with him the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
At the conclusion of the Saṅgha’s meal, Mahākāḷa’s wives thought, "Our husband has been won over by these women; we too shall win our own husband.
Having so reflected, they invited the Teacher on the following day. At that time, however—
Another monk arrived for the purpose of arranging the seats. At that moment, unable to find space, they seated the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha and gave them almsfood.
Cūḷakāḷa had two wives, Majjhimakāḷa had four, and Mahākāḷa had eight. The monks, wishing to perform their meal duties, sat down and completed their meal.
Desiring to go outside, they rose and departed. But the Teacher remained seated and performed his meal duties.
At the conclusion of his meal, those women said, "Venerable sir, Mahākāḷa will come to deliver the blessing;
you should go on ahead. The Teacher said, "Very well," and went on ahead. Upon reaching the village gate, the monks—
They complained, "What is this that has been done by the Teacher? Was it done knowingly, or perhaps unknowingly?
Yesterday, because he went before Cūḷakāḷa, an obstacle to the going-forth arose; today, because he went before another, no obstacle arose.
Now he has come having set aside Mahākāḷa; moreover, this bhikkhu is virtuous and endowed with proper conduct—he will surely [cause an obstacle]."
“Could this indeed be an obstacle to his going forth? Having heard their words, the Teacher turned back, stood still, and asked, “What are you discussing, monks? They reported the matter to him.
“But do you, monks, perceive Mahākāḷa as being like Cūḷakāḷa? “Yes, venerable sir. For he had two wives.
“It has eight [supports],” he said. “Venerable sir, what will it do, being held after being encircled by eight?
The Teacher said, “Monks, do not speak thus. Cūḷakāḷa dwells rising up again and again, full of beautiful objects;
he stands on a precipice like a weak tree. But my son Mahākāḷa dwells contemplating foulness.”
"Unshakable like a solid mountain of rock," having said this, he spoke these verses:
"One who dwells contemplating beauty, who is unrestrained in the sense-faculties,
who knows no moderation in food, who is lazy and lacking in energy..."
Māra indeed overpowers him, as the wind does a weak tree.
But one who dwells contemplating the foul, well-restrained in the sense faculties,
moderate in eating, endowed with faith, and aroused in energy— [him Māra cannot overcome].
“Māra indeed cannot overcome him, just as the wind cannot move a rocky mountain.
In this context, “dwelling contemplating the beautiful” means contemplating what has been heard; the meaning is that he dwells having released his mind from desirable objects.
For that person who, while grasping at signs (*nimitta*) and secondary characteristics (*anubyañjana*), [perceives] “the nails... [and so forth].
One perceives: "The hands are beautiful," one perceives: "The fingers are beautiful," one perceives:
"The hands, feet, calves, thighs, hips, belly, breasts, neck, lips, teeth, mouth, nose, eyes, ears, eyebrows, forehead, hair of the head, and [other parts] are beautiful.
One perceives: "The hair of the head, body hair, nails, teeth, and skin are beautiful. [And so on with] the complexion...
"Beautiful" means the shape is beautiful; this is what is called "contemplating the beautiful.

While he is dwelling thus contemplating the beautiful, regarding the "faculties," that is, the six faculties beginning with the eye, "unrestrained" means not guarding the doors of the eye and so forth.
Regarding food, it is because he does not know the measure of this—namely, the measure of seeking, the measure of receiving, and the measure of consumption.

"Immoderate": furthermore, because he does not know even this measure—that is, mere reflection or mere verbal response—he is "immoderate," meaning he does not know that "this food is lawful" or "this food is unlawful. "Lassitude" refers to being overcome by thoughts of sensual desire, ill will, and cruelty.
"Weak in energy" means lacking vigor, devoid of the exertion of energy in the four postures. "Overcomes" means...
It overcomes and overwhelms. "Like a strong wind to a weak tree" means like a powerful wind [acting] upon a weak tree growing on a precipice.
For just as that wind causes even the flowers, fruits, and shoots of that weak tree to fall, breaks its small branches, breaks its large branches, and uproots that tree together with its very roots—
Just as [a tree] goes with its roots upward and its branches downward, even so, the Māra of defilements that has arisen within such a person overcomes him;
just as a strong wind causes the falling of the flowers, fruits, and shoots of a weak tree, it causes him to incur minor and very minor offenses;
and just as there is the breaking of small branches, it causes him to incur offenses such as those involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). It is like the breaking of the great branches.
Just as one might cause a tree to fall by uprooting it, placing the roots above and the branches below, so too does he cause one to incur an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*);

likewise, just as one might cause a tree to incur thirteen offenses of formal meeting (*saṅghādisesa*), he causes one to fall from the well-proclaimed dispensation and, within a few days, reduce them to the state of a householder.
Thus, the meaning is that the Mara of defilements brings such a person under his own power.
"Contemplating foulness" means contemplating any one of the ten kinds of foulness while observing repulsiveness;
it refers to one who contemplates hair as foul, and likewise contemplates body hair, nails, teeth, skin, complexion, and shape as foul.

"In the sense faculties" means in the six sense faculties. "Well-restrained" means having the doors [of the senses] closed, being free from grasping at signs and so forth. By way of the negation of "lack of moderation" (amattaññutā) ...

"And moderate in food": "Faithful" means endowed with both mundane faith, characterized by conviction in karma and its fruit, and supramundane faith, consisting of verified confidence in the three objects.
"Aroused in energy" means one whose energy is exerted and perfected. "Such a one" refers to a person of this kind.
Just as a weak wind, blowing gently, is unable to move a solid mass of rock,
so too the weak Māra of the defilements, even when arising within, does not prevail; the meaning is that it is unable to disturb or shake that person.
Then his former wives surrounded the Elder and said, "Whom did you ask for permission when you went forth?
Now, will you become a householder again, or not? and so on; they desired to take away his saffron robes.
The Elder, observing their behavior, rose from his seat, ascended into the air by means of psychic power, and stood upon the pinnacle of the gabled roof.
Having split himself in two and come through the air, he descended from the sky while the Teacher was still finishing the verse,
and bowing at the feet of the Tathāgata, he praised the Teacher’s golden-hued body.
At the conclusion of the verse, the assembled monks were established in the fruits of stream-entry and the other stages.
The sixth story: The Elder Mahākāḷa.
The seventh story: Devadatta.

While residing at Jetavana, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning Devadatta’s acquisition of a yellow robe in Rājagaha. It began with the words: "One who is not free from impurity... (Anikkasāvo).
On one occasion, the two chief disciples, each taking his own retinue of five hundred followers, took leave of the Teacher, paid homage to him, and departed from Jetavana for Rājagaha.

The residents of Rājagaha, whether in groups of two, three, or many, gathered together and gave alms to these newcomers. Then, on a certain day, the Venerable Sāriputta delivered a discourse of thanksgiving.
He explains: "Lay followers, one person gives a gift himself but does not encourage others;
he obtains abundance of wealth in each place where he is reborn, but not abundance of retinue. One person does not give himself but encourages others;
he obtains abundance of retinue in each place where he is reborn, but not abundance of wealth. One person..."
If one neither gives nor encourages others to give, in every place where they are reborn, they do not obtain even a bowlful of sour gruel to fill their belly;

they remain destitute and without resources. If one gives themselves and also encourages others to give, in every place where they are reborn—even in a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand successive existences—they possess an abundance of wealth and an abundance of attendants.
“...obtains,” thus he taught the Dhamma.
A certain wise man, having heard this teaching, thought: “How wonderful, indeed! How marvelous, indeed! This teaching of the Dhamma is truly excellent;
a sound reason has been stated. It is fitting for me to perform the action that brings about these two attainments.”
Having reflected, he invited the Elder, saying, "Venerable sir, please accept my almsfood tomorrow.
"How many monks do you require, lay follower? "But how large is your retinue, venerable sir? "About a thousand lay followers.
"Then please accept the almsfood tomorrow together with all of them, venerable sir. The Elder consented.
As the lay follower was walking through the city streets, he encouraged the people, saying:
"Mistresses and masters, I have invited a thousand bhikkhus; how many bhikkhus can you provide with alms, and how many can you?
The people, according to their own respective means, replied: "We will give for ten; we will give for twenty..."
“We are indeed [worthy],” they said. The lay follower replied, “In that case, let us gather in one place and serve you all together;
collect sesame, rice, ghee, honey, molasses, and so forth. He had them gathered in one place.
Then a certain householder, having given him a fragrant yellow robe worth a hundred thousand pieces, said, “If your practice of giving...”
"If it is not sufficient, set this aside and fill whatever is lacking.
If it is sufficient, you may give it to whichever monk you wish," he said. At that time, his entire duty of giving was fulfilled; there was nothing at all lacking.
He asked the people, "Venerable sirs, this saffron robe was spoken of by a certain householder in such a manner..."
“The gift has become an excess; to whom shall we give it? Some said, “To the Elder Sāriputta.
Others said, “The Elder is in the habit of coming and going during the harvest season of the green gram;
Devadatta, however, is our constant companion in all matters of good and ill fortune, standing by us like a water-jar. Let us give it to him. Thus they spoke in a large assembly.
“‘It should be given to Devadatta,’ said the majority; then they gave it to Devadatta.
Having cut it, sewn it, dyed it, and put it on as an undergarment and upper robe, he went about. Seeing him, people said: ‘This is not suitable for Devadatta;
it is suitable for the Elder Sāriputta. Devadatta [is like] himself...”
“They are wandering about having put on and dressed in what is unsuitable,” they said. Then a certain resident monk from the surrounding districts went from Rājagaha to Sāvatthī;
having paid homage to the Teacher and received his greetings, he was asked by the Teacher about the well-being of the two Chief Disciples.
He reported the entire occurrence from the beginning. The Teacher said, “Indeed, it is not fitting...”
"This monk is wearing clothing that is unsuitable for him even now; he must have worn it in the past as well. Having said this, he related a story of the past:

"In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, a certain elephant-killer living in Benares made his living by killing elephants one after another, and then selling their tusks, claws, entrails, and thick flesh."
He made this arrangement. Then, one day, many thousands of elephants, while going out to forage in a forest, saw the Paccekabuddhas;
from that time on, whenever they went out or returned, they would kneel down, pay homage, and then depart.
One day, the elephant-killer, having seen this practice, thought: "I kill these with great difficulty, yet they—whenever they go out or return—"
While reflecting, "They pay homage to the Paccekabuddhas; what have they seen that they pay them homage? he observed, "It is the saffron robes.

Thinking, "It is fitting for me, too, to obtain saffron robes now," he went down to the bathing pool of one Paccekabuddha who was bathing, and having stolen a robe from among those placed on the bank, he [placed it] on the path by which those elephants came and went.
Taking his spear and covering himself from head to foot, he sat down. When the elephants saw him, they took him for a paccekabuddha, paid homage to him, and departed.
He followed right behind them, struck one with his spear, killed it, and taking its tusks and other parts, he buried the rest in the ground and went on his way. Later, the Bodhisatta—
Having taken rebirth in the womb of an elephant, he became the leader of the herd, the chief of the elephants. Even then, he acted in the same manner.
The Great Being, perceiving the decline of his own retinue, asked, "Where have these elephants gone? They have become sluggish.
When they replied, "We do not know, Master," he said, "While going somewhere, they did not ask me for permission."
“They will not go; one must lie in wait as an ambush,” he said.

Suspecting that an ambush might come from someone sitting in a certain place wearing a saffron robe, he thought, “It is right to surround him,” and sent all the elephants forward while he himself followed behind at a slow pace. As for the other elephants...
When they had departed after paying homage to the Great Man, [Devadatta], seeing him approaching, gathered his robe and hurled a spear.
The Great Man, having established mindfulness as he came forward, stepped back and avoided the spear.
Then Devadatta lunged at him, thinking, "I shall seize him by saying, 'It was he who drove these elephants away. The other [the Great Man] moved to a tree in front of him.

Having done so, he hid himself. Then, thinking, "I will encircle him with my trunk along with the tree, seize him, and dash him against the ground," the elephant saw the saffron robe displayed by the man as he was led out.

He reflected, "If I were to betray him, my sense of shame toward the many thousands of Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and those whose taints are destroyed would be shattered. Having thus resolved, [he said: "By you..."
“How many relatives of mine have been ruined by you? he asked. “Yes, master,” they replied.
“Why did you commit such a grave deed? By wearing a robe suitable for those free from passion—which is not at all fitting for yourself—and performing such an act, you have done something heavy.
Having said this, and further seeking to restrain him, he continued: “One who is not free from the taints (anikkasāvo)…”
Having recited the verse, “The saffron robe... he indeed is worthy of the saffron robe,” and having said to him, “You have done what is improper,” he released him.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka by saying, “At that time, Devadatta was the elephant-killer, and I myself was the elephant who subdued him. Then he said, “Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, Devadatta...”
“Only one who wears a robe that is not suitable for himself [should wear it],” he said, and then spoke these verses:
“He who, being impure, shall put on the saffron robe,
Devoid of self-control and truthfulness, does not deserve the saffron robe.”
“But he who has vomited out impurities, who is well-composed in the precepts,
and who is endowed with self-control and truth— he indeed is worthy of the saffron robe.
This meaning should also be illustrated by the *Chaddanta Jātaka*.
In this context, "one who is not free from impurity" means one who possesses impurities such as lust and the like.

"He will wear" means he will make use of [the robe] by way of wearing it as an undergarment (*nivāsana*), an upper garment (*pārupana*), or a covering (*attharaṇa*). There is also a reading, "he will don. "Devoid of self-control and truth" means devoid of both the restraint of the sense faculties and the verbal truth that belongs to the side of ultimate truth (*paramattha-sacca*);
the meaning is that he is separated from, deprived of, or abandoned by them. "Not he" means that such a person [is not worthy of] the saffron robe (*kāsāva*).
It does not deserve to burn him. "One whose taints have been vomited out" means one who has vomited out the taints, discarded the taints, and abandoned the taints by means of the four paths.
"In the precepts" means in the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*). "Well-composed" means thoroughly composed and well-established.
"Endowed" means arrived at through the taming of the faculties and through the truth of the aforementioned kind. "He indeed" refers to one of such a nature.
"Such a person is worthy of that fragrant saffron robe.

At the conclusion of the verse, that resident monk became a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), and many others attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages. The teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.
This is the seventh story concerning Devadatta.
8. The Story of the Elder Sāriputta The Teacher, while residing at Veḷuvana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning the failure of Sañjaya to come, as reported by the two Chief Disciples.
Herein is the sequential narrative: For our Teacher, from four incalculable eons and one hundred thousand aeons ago, until now—

In the city named Amarāvatī at the head [of the Ganges], having been a young brahmin named Sumedha and having attained perfection in all arts, after the passing of his parents, he renounced wealth numbering many millions.

Having gone forth into the ascetic life of an *isi* and dwelling in the Himālaya, he developed the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*). While traveling through the air, he [encountered] the Fortunate One Dīpaṅkara.
Seeing people clearing the road from the Sudassana monastery toward the city of Rammavatī for the purpose of entering it, he himself took a spot and cleared the path.
While that section was still uncleared, he made himself a bridge for the Teacher who had arrived;
spreading his deerskin upon the mud, he thought, "May the Teacher, together with the community of disciples, [cross] the mud..."
Lying down, he said, "Let him pass over me without stepping on me. When the Teacher saw him, he prophesied: "This is a sprout of a Buddha;
at the end of four incalculable eons and one hundred thousand aeons in the future, he will become a Buddha named Gotama.
Later, after that Teacher had passed away, [the Buddhas] Koṇḍañña, Maṅgala, Sumana, ...
Having illuminated the world with the names— Revata, Sobhita, Anomadassi, Paduma, Nārada, Padumuttara, Sumedha, Sujāta,
Piyadassī, Atthadassī, Dhammadassī, Siddhattha, Tissa, Phussa, Vipassī, Sikhī, Vessabhū, Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa—
he received his prophecy in the presence of these twenty-three Buddhas who had arisen.

Having fulfilled the thirty perfections—namely, the ten perfections (*pāramī*), the ten near-perfections (*upapāramī*), and the ten ultimate perfections (*paramatthapāramī*)—while abiding in his final existence as Vessantara, he gave great gifts that caused the earth to tremble;

having renounced his wife and children, at the end of his life-span, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven. Having remained there for the duration of his lifespan, the deities of ten thousand world-systems assembled and said:
“O Great Hero, it is time for you to arise in the mother’s womb;
saving the world including the gods, awaken to the deathless state.
When this was said—
“Having surveyed the time, the place, the island, the clan, and the mother—having looked upon these five great surveys—he of great renown was reborn.
Having thus performed the five great surveys, he passed away from there and took conception in the royal family of the Sakyans; after the lapse of ten months, [he was born].
He was born from his mother’s womb. At the age of sixteen, being attended to with great prosperity there, he gradually attained auspicious youth.

Experiencing royal splendor like the glory of the deva-world in three palaces suited to the three seasons, at the time of going for a pleasure excursion in the park, he [encountered] those known as the old, the sick, and the dead in succession.

Having seen the three divine messengers, he was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency; turning back, and on the fourth occasion seeing one who had gone forth, he conceived a longing for the going-forth, thinking, "Excellent is the going-forth!

Having returned to the park and spent the day there, while sitting on the bank of the Maṅgala lotus pond, he was prepared with ornaments by the divine son Vissakamma, who had arrived in the guise of a barber, for Prince Rāhula.

Having heard the proclamation and recognizing the intensity of his son’s affection, he thought, “I shall cut this bond while it has not yet grown tighter,” and as he was entering the city in the evening, he said:
“Surely that mother is at peace; surely that father is at peace.”
"Truly extinguished must be that woman, whose husband is such as this.
Upon hearing this verse spoken by her paternal aunt's daughter, named Kisāgotamī, [the King thought], "I have been addressed with the word 'extinguished' by her.
He then removed a pearl necklace, sent it to her, and having entered his own palace, he lay upon his royal couch.
Sitting there, he witnessed the disarray of the dancing girls who had fallen asleep;

with a heart weary of the world, he roused Channa, had Kaṇḍaka brought, and mounting him, accompanied by Channa and surrounded by deities from ten thousand world-systems, he made the Great Renunciation.
Having gone forth on the banks of the Anomā River, he proceeded by stages to Rājagaha.
There, having wandered for alms and sat on the slopes of Paṇḍava Mountain, he declined the invitation of the King of Magadha to rule his kingdom;
and having attained omniscience, having given his promise to come to his own realm,
and having approached Āḷāra and Udaka, he did not adorn himself with the special attainments reached in their presence, but [spent] six years.
Having exerted the Great Struggle, on the full moon day of the month of Visākha, he partook of the milk-rice offered by Sujātā early in the morning;
then, having cast his golden bowl into the river Nerañjarā, he spent the day on the bank of the Nerañjarā in a great forest grove by means of various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
At evening time, taking the grass offered by Sotthiya, [he sat down] with Kāḷa, the Nāga king.
Having had his virtues extolled, he ascended the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and spread out blades of grass.
Making the vow, "I shall not break this cross-legged posture until my mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging," he sat down facing the east.
Even before the sun had set, he shattered the host of Māra; in the first watch of the night, he attained the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsañāṇa).
Having attained the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings during the middle watch, and having applied his knowledge to the nature of conditions at the conclusion of the final watch,
he penetrated the knowledge of omniscience— adorned with all qualities such as the ten powers and the four grounds of self-confidence—
at the rising of the dawn. Having spent seven weeks at the seat of enlightenment, on the eighth week, he sat at the foot of the Goatherd’s Banyan tree.

While falling into a state of non-exertion through reflection on the profundity of the Dhamma, he was entreated to teach the Dhamma by Sahampati Brahmā, who was accompanied by a retinue of ten thousand Great Brahmas of the Cakkavāḷa.
Having surveyed the world with his Buddha-eye and having accepted Brahmā’s request, he looked about, thinking, “To whom indeed should I first teach the Dhamma? and [beheld] Āḷāra and Udaka.
Having understood that the time had come and recollecting the great service rendered by the group of five monks, he rose from his seat and set out for Kāsi-pura.

On the way, after consulting with Upaka, on the full-moon day of Āsāḷha, he arrived at the Deer Park in Isipatana, the dwelling place of the group of five monks; there, they were treating him with an unworthy reception.
Having instructed them, while bestowing the drink of the Deathless upon eighteen koṭis of Brahmās headed by Aññāta-Koṇḍañña, he set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion.
Having thus set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, on the fifth day of the fortnight, he established all those bhikkhus in Arahatship.
On that very same day, perceiving the excellence of the spiritual potential (*upanissaya*) of the young man Yasa, during that very night—
Seeing that he had become disenchanted with the household life and had gone forth, she called out to him, "Come, Yasa!
On that very same night, she enabled him to attain the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*), and on the following day, she enabled him to attain *arahantship*.
Furthermore, she ordained his forty-four companions through the "Come, monk" (*ehibhikkhu*) formula and enabled them to attain *arahantship*.

Thus, when sixty-one arahants had been born in the world, having spent the rains retreat and performed the *pavāraṇā* ceremony, he sent sixty bhikkhus out on tour in various directions, saying, "Go forth, bhikkhus, on your journey. He himself went toward Uruvelā;
on the way, in a cotton-tree grove, he disciplined thirty young men of the Bhaddavaggiya group. Among them, the last to be ordained became a stream-enterer, while the foremost became an arahant.
He became a non-returner (*anāgāmī*). Having ordained them all by means of the "Come, monk" formula (*ehibhikkhubhāva*), he dispatched them to the various directions.

He himself went to Uruvelā and, after displaying three thousand five hundred miracles, he converted the three brothers, the Jaṭilas, who were accompanied by a retinue of one thousand Jaṭilas, including Uruvelakassapa.
Having ordained them by the "Come, monk" formula and seated them at Gayāsīsa, [he taught] the *Ādittapariyāya* discourse.

Having established them in Arahatship and being surrounded by those one thousand Arahats, [the Buddha] thought, "I shall fulfill the promise given to King Bimbisāra," and went to the Laṭṭhivana Grove on the outskirts of the city of Rājagaha.
Hearing that "the Teacher has indeed arrived," the king came together with twelve hundred thousand brahmins and householders; to him, [the Buddha] delivered a sweet discourse on the Dhamma.
While preaching, he established eleven hundred thousand people along with the king in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), and established one hundred thousand in the refuges (*saraṇa*).
On the following day, his virtues having been extolled by Sakka, the king of the gods, who had assumed the form of a young brahmin, he entered the city of Rājagaha;
having performed his meal duties at the royal residence and accepted the Veḷuvana monastery, he departed.
He made his dwelling right there. There, Sāriputta and Moggallāna approached him.
Regarding this, the following is the sequential account: Even before the Buddha had appeared, there were two brahmin villages not far from Rājagaha, named Upatissagāma and Kolitagāma.
In those two, in Upatissagāma, a son was conceived in the womb of a brahmin woman named Sārī.
On the very day [the Bodhisatta] was conceived, a Brahmin woman named Moggalī also conceived a child in the village of Kolita.
It is said that these two families were bound together as close friends for seven generations;
they provided nourishment for the pregnancies of both women on the same day. Both of them gave birth to sons after exactly ten months.
They were born. On the day of the naming ceremony, because the son of the brahmin woman Sārī was the son of the eldest family in Upatissa village, they gave him the name Upatissa;
because the other was the son of the eldest family in Kolita village, they gave him the name Kolita.
Both of them, as they grew up, reached the further shore of all branches of learning. As for the young man Upatissa—

When they went for the sake of recreation to the river or to the park, they were accompanied by five hundred golden palanquins with attendants, and the young man Kolita had five hundred chariots yoked with thoroughbred horses. Both men were each surrounded by five hundred young male attendants.
Furthermore, in Rājagaha, there was an annual festival called the Giraggasamajja; both of them attended it at one and the same place.

They construct a platform. Even when both sit together and watch the festival, they laugh at what is laughable, feel spiritual urgency at what inspires urgency, and give gifts where it is appropriate to give gifts.
As they continue watching the festival in this very manner for one day, because their knowledge has reached maturity, at what was previously laughable on earlier days—
There was no laughter where there should have been a sense of urgency, nor was there any giving where it was appropriate to give.
Yet both men thought thus: "What is there here to look upon? All these people will pass away without reaching even a hundred years;
it is fitting for us to seek the Dhamma of liberation. Having taken this as their objective, they—
They sat down. Then Kolita said to Upatissa: "Friend Upatissa, you are not as joyful as on other days;
you are now dejected in spirit. What has been observed by you? "Friend Kolita, there is no essence in observing these things;
this is useless. It is fitting to search for the Dhamma of one's own liberation."
"I am sitting here reflecting on this. But why are you dissatisfied? He replied in the same manner.
Then Upatisso, knowing that they shared the same aspiration, said: "The thought is the same for both of us;
however, as we seek the Dhamma of liberation, it is fitting that we both take up the homeless life. In whose presence shall we go forth?"
Now at that time, a wanderer named Sañcaya was residing in Rājagaha together with a large assembly of wanderers.
Five hundred young men, saying, "We shall go forth under him," were sent off with the instruction, "Take palanquins and chariots and go!
They departed by means of one palanquin and one chariot and approached Sañcaya.
They went forth into homelessness in his presence. From the time they were ordained, Sañcaya attained an abundance of extra gains and the highest excellence.

Within just a few days, they had mastered the entirety of Sañcaya’s system and asked him, "Teacher, is this the extent of your knowledge, or is there more beyond? He replied, "This is indeed the whole of it; you have [mastered it all]."
When he said, "It is known," they thought: "If this is so, living the holy life (brahmacariya) in his presence is useless;
that Dhamma of liberation for which we have gone forth to seek cannot be realized in his presence.
Moreover, Jambudīpa is vast; by wandering through villages, market towns, and royal capitals, we shall certainly find one who teaches the Dhamma of liberation."
“We shall find some teacher. From then on, wherever they heard it said that there were wise recluses or brahmins, they would go to those places and engage them in discussion.
When others were unable to answer the questions posed by them, the two of them would provide the answers. In this way, having searched throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, they...
Having returned to their own respective places, they made an agreement, saying, "Friend Kolita, whichever of us first attains the Deathless shall inform the other.
While they were living there after having made this agreement, the Teacher, following the aforementioned sequence, arrived at Rājagaha and reached the Veḷuvana.

Having accepted [the invitation], he dwelt in Veḷuvana. At that time, among the sixty-one arahants who had been dispatched for the sake of proclaiming the virtues of the Triple Gem with the words, “Go forth, bhikkhus, on a journey for the welfare of many people,” the Elder Assaji—who was one of the group of five—returned and came to Rājagaha;
early the next morning, having taken his bowl and robe, he set out.
He entered Rājagaha for alms. At that time, the wanderer Upatissa, having finished his morning meal and was on his way to the wanderers’ park, saw the Elder and thought:
“I have never before seen such a renunciant. He must be one of those monks in the world who are Arahants or who have attained the path to Arahantship.”
A certain person thought: "What if I were to approach this bhikkhu and ask him:
'Friend, for whose sake have you gone forth? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you approve of? Then it occurred to him:
"It is not the right time to ask this bhikkhu this question; he has entered among the houses and is walking for alms."
"What if I were now to follow behind this bhikkhu, for he is traveling on a path prepared by those in need?

Seeing the elder going toward a certain place after receiving almsfood, and perceiving his desire to sit down, he spread out his own recluse's seat and gave it to him; then, when the elder had finished his meal—
He gave water from his own water-pot.
Having thus performed the duties toward his teacher and having finished his meal, he exchanged pleasant greetings with the Elder and said:
"Friend, your faculties are serene; your complexion is pure and radiant."
"Friend, for whose sake have you gone forth? Who is your teacher? Or whose Dhamma do you approve?
he asked. The Elder thought: "These wanderers are indeed opponents of the Teaching; I shall demonstrate the profundity of this Teaching.
Showing his own status as a junior, he said: "I am, friend, a newcomer..."
“I have not long gone forth; I have only recently come to this Dhamma and Vinaya.
I am not yet able to teach the Dhamma in detail. The wanderer thought, “I am named Upatissa.
Whether you speak little or much according to your ability, it is within my power to penetrate this through a hundred or a thousand methods,” and he said:
“Whether you speak little or much, tell me only the meaning;
it is the meaning alone that I seek. What will you do with many words?
When this was said, the Elder recited the verse beginning, “Of those phenomena that arise from a cause. The wanderer [understood] only the first two lines.
Having heard this, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), which is adorned with the thousandfold method;

he brought the other two stages to completion at the time of his becoming a stream-enterer. Having become a stream-enterer, and observing that no further distinction arose, he reflected, "There must be a reason for this," and said to the Elder:
"Venerable sir, do not increase the teaching of the Dhamma beyond this much."
“Very well, where does our Teacher dwell? “In the Bamboo Grove, friend. “In that case, venerable sir, you go on ahead;
I have a companion with me, and we made a pact with one another:
‘Whichever of us first attains the Deathless shall inform the other. I must now fulfill that promise.”
“Taking my companion, I shall return to the presence of the Teacher by the very path you have taken,” he said.
Then, prostrating himself at the Elder’s feet with the fivefold salutation, circumambulating him three times, and bidding the Elder farewell, he set out toward the Wanderers’ Park.
Then Kolita the Wanderer, seeing him approaching from afar, thought: “Today, for my companion...”
His facial complexion was not like it had been on other days; "surely he must have attained the Deathless," [Kolita] thought, and so he asked about his attainment of the Deathless.
He (Upatissa) acknowledged to him, saying, "Yes, friend, the Deathless has been attained," and recited that very same verse.
At the conclusion of the verse, Kolita was established in the fruit of stream-entry and said, "Friend, where indeed does our Teacher dwell?"
“In the Bamboo Grove, friend, this is what was said by our teacher, the Elder Assaji. “In that case, friend, let us go;
we shall see the Teacher. Now, the Elder Sāriputta was always a worshipper of his teachers;
therefore he spoke thus to his companion: “Friend, the Deathless has been attained by us, and it is for our teacher, the wanderer Sañjaya, as well...”
“We shall speak; if he awakens, he will penetrate [the truth]; if he does not penetrate it, he will have faith in us and go into the presence of the Teacher;
having heard the teaching of the Buddhas, he will achieve penetration of the path and its fruits.
Thereupon, both men went into the presence of Sañjaya.
Upon seeing them, Sañcaya asked, "What is it, dear ones? Have you found someone who can show you the path to the Deathless?
"Yes, teacher, we have found one. A Buddha has appeared in the world; the Dhamma has appeared in the world; the Saṅgha has appeared in the world.
You wander about in vain and without essence; therefore, come, let us go into the presence of the Teacher. "Go then, you yourselves," [Sañcaya replied].
“I shall not be able to do it. “For what reason? “I have lived as a teacher among the great multitude;
for one who has lived thus, living as a pupil is like a water-jar turning into a water-drawing wheel. I shall not be able to live the life of a pupil.
“Do not do this, Teacher! “Enough, dear ones; you may go, I shall not be able to do it.”

“Teacher, from the moment the Buddha appeared in the world, the great multitude will go with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in their hands and worship him alone; we too shall go right there. “What will you do?
“Dear ones, are there many dullards in this world, or are there many wise ones? “There are many dullards, Teacher; the wise are few.”
"And so, there will be only a few of us. "In that case, dear ones, the wise shall go into the presence of the wise ascetic Gotama;
the slow-witted shall come into my presence, the slow-witted. You go; I will not go.
They departed, saying, "You shall be known, Teacher! As they were going away...
The assembly of Sañjaya split; at that moment, the monastery became empty. Seeing the monastery empty, he vomited hot blood.
Of the five hundred wanderers who were traveling with him, two hundred and fifty turned back. Then, together with their own two hundred and fifty disciples, those wanderers departed.
Together they went to the Bamboo Grove.
As the Teacher sat in the midst of the fourfold assembly teaching the Dhamma, he saw them from afar and addressed the bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, those two friends, Kolita and Upatissa, are coming; they are my pair of disciples."
“...there will be a supreme, auspicious pair. Having paid homage to the Teacher, they sat down to one side;
and having sat down, they said this to the Blessed One: “May we receive the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One, Lord;
may we receive the full ordination. “Come, monks,” the Blessed One said, “the Dhamma is well-expounded.”
“Practice the holy life for the complete ending of suffering.
Then all of them, wearing robes and bowls produced by supernormal power, appeared like elders of sixty years’ standing.
Thereupon, according to the conduct of their assembly, the Teacher expanded his discourse on the Dhamma. With the exception of the two chief disciples—
The rest attained Arahatship, but for the two Chief Disciples, the task of the three higher paths was not yet completed.
Why was this? Because of the greatness of the knowledge pertaining to the perfections of a disciple (sāvakapāramiñāṇa).
Then, on the seventh day after his ordination, while the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was dwelling near the village of Kallavāla in the Magadha country, he fell into sloth and torpor.

Stirred by the Teacher, he dispelled sloth and torpor; while listening to the meditation subject on the elements bestowed by the Tathāgata, he completed the work of the three higher paths and reached the pinnacle of the disciple’s supreme knowledge (*sāvakapāramiñāṇa*).
The Elder Sāriputta, too, having passed half a month from the day of his going forth, [lived] together with the Teacher near that very city of Rājagaha.
While dwelling at the Sūkarakhatā Cave, as the *Vedanāpariggaha-sutta* was being taught to his own nephew, the wanderer Dīghanakha, he sent forth his knowledge in accordance with the discourse;
thus, like one partaking of food increased by another, he reached the pinnacle of the knowledge of the perfections of a disciple.
Is it not true that this venerable one possessed great wisdom? Then why [was he surpassed] by Mahāmoggallāna?
Why does he attain the knowledge of the disciple’s perfection only after a longer time? Because of the greatness of the preliminary work (*parikamma*).

For just as destitute people who wish to go anywhere depart quickly, whereas kings must perform great preliminary work such as preparing elephant-vehicles and the like, so too should this be understood.

On that very day, however, as the shadow was lengthening, the Teacher assembled his disciples in the Veḷuvana grove, assigned the positions of chief disciples to the two elders, and recited the Pātimokkha.
The monks murmured, "The Teacher distributes alms by looking at their faces; in assigning the position of chief disciples, he should have first given them to those who were ordained earliest."
It is permissible to give it to the group of five; disregarding them, it is permissible to give it to the fifty-five monks headed by Venerable Yasa;
