disregarding them, to the thirty members of the Bhaddavaggiya group; disregarding them, to the three brothers beginning with Uruvelakassapa.
But setting aside all these great elders, the position of Chief Disciple belongs to those who went forth last of all.
“Having looked at his face, it was given by him,” they said. The Teacher asked, “What are you discussing, monks?
When they replied, “This very thing,” he said, “Monks, I do not give almsfood after looking at a person’s face;
rather, I give exactly what each of them has individually desired. For Aññāta Koṇḍañña, during a single harvest, nine times—”
“While giving the gift of the finest food, he did not give it aspiring for the position of chief disciple;
rather, he gave it aspiring to be the very first to penetrate the supreme Dhamma, which is Arahatship. “But when, Blessed One?
“You shall hear, monks,” said the Blessed One. “Yes, venerable sir,” they replied. Then the Blessed One related the past:
"Monks, ninety-one aeons ago, a Blessed One named Vipassī appeared in the world.
At that time, two brothers who were householders, Mahākāḷa and Cūḷakāḷa, had a large field of rice sown.
Then one day, Cūḷakāḷa went to the rice field, split open a spike of rice, and ate it; it was exceedingly sweet. He [offered it] to the community headed by the Buddha..."

Desiring to give a gift of a rice granary to the Saṅgha, he approached his elder brother and said, “Brother, let us split open a rice granary, prepare it in a manner befitting the Buddhas, have it cooked, and give it as a gift.
“What are you saying, dear one? As for giving a gift by splitting open a rice granary, such a thing has never occurred in the past, nor will it ever occur in the future.”
"It will grow; do not ruin the crop. Although he was told this, he begged again and again.
Then his brother said to him, "In that case, divide the rice field into two portions;
without touching my portion, do whatever you wish in your own portion of the field. He replied, "Very well," and having divided the field, [he employed] many men...
Having requested manual labor, she split open a rice pod, had it cooked in waterless milk, and combined it with ghee, honey, sugar, and other ingredients;
then, after giving this gift to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, at the conclusion of the meal, she said:
"Venerable Sir, may this supreme gift of mine lead to the first penetration of the Supreme Dhamma."
The Teacher gave his blessing, saying, "May it be so.
Having gone to the field and looking about, he saw the entire field covered with rice heads as if bound together by stalks;
attaining the fivefold joy and thinking, "What a gain for me!", he [partook of] the finest of the harvest at the time of the harvest.
He gave the first-fruits; together with the village dwellers, he gave the first-fruits of the chief crops. At the time of harvesting, he gave the best of the harvest;

at the time of binding into sheaves, the best of the sheaves; from the bundles and so forth, the best of the bundles; the best of the threshing floor, the best of the threshing-floor grain, and the best of the granary.
In this way, he gave the first-fruits nine times for a single crop. In all these instances, the place from which each portion was taken became completely full; the crop—
It became abundant and endowed with excellence. For this Dhamma indeed protects one who protects themselves. Therefore the Blessed One said:
“The Dhamma truly protects the one who lives according to the Dhamma;
the Dhamma well-practiced brings happiness.”
“This is the advantage when the Dhamma is well-practiced:
one who lives according to the Dhamma does not go to a state of misery.
Thus, at the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Vipassī, he aspired to be the first to penetrate the supreme Dhamma. Nine...

On that day she gave the foremost gifts. Furthermore, one hundred thousand kappas ago, during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara in the city of Haṃsavatī, she also gave a great almsgiving for seven days;
then, prostrating at the feet of that Blessed One, she made a resolution solely for the sake of being the first to penetrate the supreme Dhamma.
Thus, what I have given was given precisely because of that resolution; it was not I [who acted independently].
“...monks, I give [this] after looking at the face.
“Venerable sir, what deed did the fifty-five people, headed by the noble youth Yasa, perform?
“These too, having made many meritorious deeds while aspiring for arhatship in the presence of a certain Buddha, at a later time when [that Buddha] had passed away...”

Having become companions in the Buddha’s dispensation, they wandered about performing meritorious deeds by binding themselves in groups and tending to the bodies of the deceased who were without protectors.
One day, seeing a pregnant woman who had died, they carried her to the charnel ground, thinking, “We shall cremate her.
Having left five men at the charnel ground with the instruction, “You cremate her,” the rest entered the village.
The youth Yasa, piercing that dead body with stakes and turning it over again and again while burning it, acquired the perception of foulness (*aśubhasaññā*).
He also showed it to the other four men, saying: "Look, sirs, at this body!
Its skin is pierced here and there; like a speckled ox-hide, it is impure, foul-smelling, and repulsive. They too—
There, they acquired the perception of foulness (*asubhasaññā*). Those five men went to the village and told their remaining companions.
But the youth Yasa went home and told his parents and his wife; they all likewise cultivated the perception of foulness.
This was their past karma. For that very reason, the perception of a cemetery arose for Yasa even within the women’s quarters.
“Through that excellence of supporting conditions, the attainment of distinction arose for all of them as well. Thus, these too obtained exactly what they had themselves aspired to.
I do not give by looking at their faces.
“But, Bhante, what karma did the companions of the Bhaddavaggiyas perform? “These too, under previous Buddhas...”
"Having made a vow for Arahantship in my presence and performed meritorious deeds, at a later time when no Buddha had yet appeared, these thirty men became libertines;
having heard the Tuṇḍila-advice, they observed the five precepts for sixty thousand years.
Thus, even these obtained exactly what they themselves had vowed for. I do not give gifts by looking at people's faces."
“But what deed did Uruvelakassapa and the others perform, venerable sir? “They too performed meritorious deeds while aspiring for arahantship itself.
For ninety-two aeons ago, two Buddhas named Tissa and Phussa appeared.
King Mahinda was the father of Buddha Phussa. When that Buddha had attained enlightenment, the king’s younger son became his first chief disciple.”
The son of the family priest became the second chief disciple. The king went into the presence of the Teacher and, having looked upon them, saying, “The Buddha is my eldest son;
the first chief disciple is my younger son; the second chief disciple is the son of my family priest,” he declared, “The Buddha belongs to me alone;
the Dhamma belongs to me alone; the Saṅgha belongs to me alone! Homage to that Blessed One, the Arahant!”
Having uttered this inspired exclamation three times—"To the Perfectly Enlightened One!"—he prostrated at the feet of the Teacher and said:
"Venerable Sir, now that I have reached the end of my lifespan of ninety thousand years, it is as if it were time for me to lie down and sleep;
therefore, until I pass away, please accept from me the four requisites without my having to go to the doors of others' homes."
Having obtained his promise, he made a regular practice of attending upon the Buddha. Now, the king had other sons besides him;
among them, the eldest had five hundred warriors as his retinue, the middle one three hundred, and the youngest two hundred.
Thinking, "We too shall entertain our brother," they requested permission from their father, but not obtaining it, they [continued] again and again...
Although they had gone begging and received nothing, they were sent to pacify the unrest in the border regions;
having pacified the border regions, they returned to their father’s presence. Then their father embraced them, kissed them on the head, and said, “Sons, I grant you a boon.
They replied, “Very well, Your Majesty,” and accepted the boon. After a few days had passed, the father said to them again, “Take it, sons!”
They said, "A boon," and spoke thus: "Your Majesty, we have no need for anything else; from now on, we shall feed our brother ourselves.
Grant us this boon. He replied, "I will not grant it, dear ones. They said, "If you will not grant it forever, then grant it for seven years, Your Majesty.
He replied, "I will not grant it, dear ones. They said, "In that case, for six, five, four, or three [years]..."
“‘O gods, give us one year,’ they said. ‘I will not give it, dear ones,’ he replied. ‘In that case, O god, give us seven months,’ they said.
‘Give six months, five months, four months, three months, O gods,’ he said.
‘I will not give it, dear ones,’ he replied. ‘Very well, O god; having given each of us one month, give us three months,’ they said. ‘Excellent, dear ones! Therefore—’”
"Indeed, you should feed them for three months," he said. Delighted, they paid homage to the king and returned to their respective places.
Now, those three had but one storekeeper and one overseer, who was accompanied by a retinue of twelve hundred thousand men.
He summoned them and said: "For these three months, we shall observe the ten precepts and wear two saffron robes."

"We shall dwell in the company of the Teacher; you, having undertaken this much duty as almsgivers, should provide daily all kinds of hard and soft food for ninety thousand bhikkhus and a thousand warriors.
From now on, we shall say nothing further," they said.
“Those two men, taking along a retinue of a thousand people, undertook the ten precepts, donned saffron robes, and lived right there in the monastery.
The storekeeper and the overseer joined together; taking turns from the storehouses of the three brothers, they established a custom of giving alms and provided gifts.
Furthermore, the sons of the laborers [provided] rice gruel, food, and so forth.”
They wept for the sake of [the monks]. Even before the Saṅgha of bhikkhus had arrived, they gave them rice gruel, alms-food, and so forth.

It had never happened before that there was any surplus remaining after the Saṅgha of bhikkhus had finished their meal. Thinking, “We shall give this to our children later,” they took some for themselves and ate it.
Upon seeing such delicious food, they were unable to restrain themselves. But they—

There were eighty-four thousand of them. Having consumed the merit of the offerings given to the Saṅgha, at the breaking up of the body after death, they were reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts (pettivisaya).
However, those three brothers, having passed away together with a thousand men, were reborn in the world of the devas;
and as they transmigrated from the world of the devas to the human world, and from the human world back to the world of the devas, for ninety-two eons—
They threw [the lot]. “Thus those three brothers, aspiring for Arahatship, performed wholesome deeds at that time.
They obtained exactly what they had aspired for. I do not give by looking at faces.
At that time, however, their overseer was King Bimbisāra, and the storekeeper was the lay follower Visākha. The three...
The three princes became ascetics with matted hair. Their laborers, having been reborn as ghosts (*peta*), wandered through the cycle of existence via good and bad destinations;
within this eon, they were reborn in the ghost realm itself during four intervals between Buddhas.
At the very beginning of this eon, they approached the Blessed One Kakusandha, whose lifespan was forty thousand years.
They asked, "Tell us the time when we shall obtain food. He replied, "You will not obtain it during my time;
after I have passed away, when the great earth has risen by a league, a Buddha named Koṇāgamana will appear.
You should ask him. They waited for that length of time, and when he had appeared, they questioned him.

He also said, "You will not obtain it during my time; after me, when the great earth has risen by a yojana, a Buddha named Kassapa will appear. You should ask him. They spent that much time, and when he had appeared, they asked him.
He too said, "You will not obtain it during my time; however, after me..."
"When you have ascended the great earth by the measure of a *yojana*, a Buddha named Gotama will arise.
At that time, a kinsman of yours named King Bimbisāra will exist; he, having given a gift to the Teacher, will cause you to obtain the merit (*patti*), and then you shall receive it," he said.
For them, the interval between Buddhas was like a single day. When the Tathāgata...
When King Bimbisāra had given his first-day alms-offering, they failed to receive a portion;
consequently, during the night, they raised a terrifying sound and revealed themselves to the king. On the following day, the king went to Veḷuvana and reported that matter to the Tathāgata.
The Teacher said, "Great King, ninety-two aeons ago, at the time of Buddha Phussa, these were your kinsmen who [acted thus] toward the Saṅgha of bhikkhus."

"Having consumed the merit of the gift you gave, we were reborn in the world of the *petas* and wandered through saṃsāra. We questioned the Buddhas Kakusandha and the others, who told us this and that:
'For so long a time we have been waiting for the fruit of your gift;
since we did not receive the merit when you gave your gift yesterday, we have remained thus. He asked, "But, venerable sir, will they receive it now as well?"
“Yes, Great King,” he replied. The king invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, and on the following day, after giving a great almsgiving, he dedicated the merit, saying:
“Venerable sirs, may divine food and drink accrue to those hungry ghosts from this. It happened for them exactly as he had said.
On the next day, they appeared naked. The king asked: “Venerable sirs, why are they naked today?”
“Having offered [the robes], show yourself! he announced. “The robes were not given to you, Great King,” [they replied].
On the following day, the king also gave a gift of robes to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, dedicating it with the words, “From this, may divine robes appear for those peta beings.
At that very moment, divine robes appeared for them. They abandoned their peta-existence and—

They established themselves in celestial bodies. As the Teacher offered his expression of appreciation, he delivered the "Tirokuṭṭa" (Beyond the Walls) benediction beginning with the words, "Standing beyond the walls.
At the conclusion of that benediction, eighty-four thousand living beings attained realization of the Dhamma.
Thus, having related the story of the three brothers who were matted-hair ascetics, the Teacher delivered this teaching on the Dhamma.
"But what did the Chief Disciples do, venerable sir? "They made a resolution for the state of being Chief Disciples.
For at the head of an incalculable aeon, exceeding one hundred thousand aeons from now, Sāriputta was reborn in a family of great brahmin landowners;
by name he was known as the young brahmin Sarada. Moggallāna was reborn in a family of great householders."
There was a householder named Sirivaḍḍhana. Both of them had been companions since childhood, playing together in the dust.
Among them, when the father of Sarada Māṇava passed away, he took charge of the great wealth that remained; one day, having gone into seclusion, he thought:
"I know only the existence of this world, not the existence of the world beyond. And of beings who are born..."
“Death is certain; it is fitting that I go forth into homelessness and seek the Dhamma of liberation.
He approached his friend and said, “Friend Sirivaḍḍhana, I shall go forth and seek the Dhamma of liberation;
will you be able to go forth with me, or will you not? “I will not be able,” he replied.

“Friend, you yourself should go forth. He thought: “When one goes to the next world, there is no such thing as going having taken one’s companions or kinsmen along; what one has done belongs to oneself alone.
Then, having opened his storehouses of jewels and given a great alms-giving to the poor, the destitute, the needy, and the beggars, he entered the foothills of the mountain.

He went forth into the ascetic life of a seer (*isi*). Following him, one, two, three, and so on, went forth in succession until there were seventy-four thousand matted-hair ascetics (*jaṭila*) who had likewise gone forth.

Having realized the five supernormal powers (*abhiññā*) and the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), he instructed those matted-hair ascetics in the preliminary practice of the meditation objects (*kasiṇa-parikamma*).
They all, too, realized the five supernormal powers and the eight meditative attainments.
At that time, the Perfectly Enlightened One named Anomadassi appeared in the world. The city was named Candavatī;
his father was the kshatriya Yasava, and his mother was Queen Yasodharā.
His Bodhi tree was the Ajjuna tree, and his two chief disciples were Nisabha and Anoma. His attendant was named Varuṇa, and his two chief female disciples were Sundarā and Sumanā.

They existed. Their lifespan was one hundred thousand years, their bodies were fifty-eight cubits in height, the radiance of their bodies pervaded twelve yojanas, and they were surrounded by a retinue of one hundred thousand bhikkhus.
One day, at the time of dawn, having emerged from the attainment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-samāpatti*) and surveying the world, he saw the ascetic Sarada and thought: "Today, for me..."
Because of my having gone into the presence of the ascetic Sarada, there will be a great teaching of the Dhamma;
he will aspire to the position of chief disciple, and his companion, the householder Sirivaḍḍhana, to the position of second disciple.
At the conclusion of that teaching, seventy-four thousand matted-hair ascetics from his retinue will attain arahantship.
"It is fitting for me to go there. Taking his own bowl and robe, and without informing anyone else, he went alone like a lion.

When the disciples of the ascetic Sarada had gone out for fruit, he resolved, "Let him know my state as a Buddha," and while the ascetic Sarada was looking on, he descended from the sky onto the earth.
He established himself. Seeing both the Buddha’s majesty and the perfection of his physical form, the ascetic Sarada contemplated the marks and mantras and thought:
"One endowed with these marks, if he lives as a householder, becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin) king;
if he goes forth, he becomes a perfectly enlightened Buddha (sabbaññubuddha) who has removed the veil from the world. This person is undoubtedly a Buddha."
Having recognized him, he went out to meet him, paid homage with the fivefold prostration, prepared and offered him the seat of honor.
The Blessed One sat upon the prepared seat of honor. The ascetic Sarada also took a seat suitable for himself and sat down to one side.
At that time, seventy-four thousand matted-hair ascetics arrived, carrying various excellent and succulent fruits.
Having arrived in the presence of the teacher and observed the seats occupied by both the Buddhas and the teacher, they said:
"Teacher, we wander about thinking, 'In this world there is none greater than you,' yet this man appears to us to be even greater than you.
"Dear ones, what are you saying? [How can he compare] with mustard seeds when his height is six million eight hundred thousand yojanas?"
“O children, you wish to make Mount Sineru level; do not compare me with the Omniscient Buddha.
Then those ascetics thought, “If this were a being of limited power, our teacher would not have brought such a comparison.
How great indeed this man must be! Thereupon, they all prostrated themselves at his feet and paid him homage with their heads. Then...
Then the teacher said: "Sons, we have no gift worthy of our Buddhas;
however, since the Teacher has arrived here at the time for the alms-round, we shall give a gift according to our ability and strength.
Bring whatever choice fruits you have. Having had them brought, he washed his hands.
He himself placed [the food] into the Tathāgata’s bowl. As soon as the Teacher had accepted the various fruits, the deities added divine nourishment.
That ascetic also strained the water himself and gave it to him.
Then, after the Teacher had finished his meal and was seated, he summoned all his resident pupils and, in the presence of the Teacher, delivered a discourse of consolation.
He sat down and spoke. The Teacher thought, "Let the two chief disciples come together with the community of monks.
Knowing the Teacher's mind, they arrived accompanied by a retinue of one hundred thousand who had destroyed the taints; having paid homage to the Teacher, they stood to one side.
Then the ascetic Sarada addressed his pupils: "Sirs, even the seats upon which Buddhas sit are low; [so it is for] even a hundred thousand recluses."
“There is no seat; today it is fitting for you to perform a sublime honor for the Buddha. Fetch flowers endowed with color and fragrance from the foot of the mountain.
To one who speaks, time seems like an obstacle, yet the domain of the power of a possessor of supernormal abilities is inconceivable;
thus, in just a moment, those ascetics brought back flowers endowed with color and fragrance, [covering] an area of a league around the Buddhas.
They prepared flower-seats. For the two Chief Disciples, the seats were three *gāvutas* in length; for the rest of the monks, they varied from half a *yojana* downwards;
and for the youngest member of the Saṅgha, it was the measure of a bull (*usabha*). One should not wonder, "How is it that such vast seats were prepared in a single hermitage?
For this is the domain of psychic power (*iddhi*). When the seats had been thus prepared, the ascetic Sarada...
Standing before the Tathāgata with palms joined in reverence, he said, “Venerable Sir, for my long-term welfare and happiness, please ascend this flower-seat. Thus it was said:
“Having prepared various flowers and perfumes together;”
Having prepared a flower-seat, he spoke these words:
"O Hero, this seat of mine is prepared as befits you;
sitting upon this flower-seat, please gladden my heart."
“For seven days and nights the Buddha sat upon the flower-seat,
gladdening my heart and causing the world with its devas to rejoice.
When the Teacher had thus sat down, the two chief disciples and the remaining bhikkhus each sat down on their own respective seats.
The ascetic Sarada stood holding a large flower-parasol over the head of the Tathāgata.
Thinking, "May this honor paid to these matted-hair ascetics bear great fruit," the Teacher entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Knowing that the Teacher had entered the attainment, the two chief disciples and the rest of the monks also entered the attainment.
While the Tathāgata sat having entered the attainment of cessation for seven days, his resident disciples, when the time for alms-round arrived, partook of forest roots and fruits;
at other times, they stood with palms joined in reverence toward the Buddhas.
But the ascetic Sarada, without even going on alms-round, spent those seven days in joy and bliss while holding a flower parasol.
He spent the time. The Teacher emerged from the attainment of cessation and addressed the Elder Nisabha, his first chief disciple, who was seated on his right side:
"Nisabha, offer words of appreciation for the flower seats provided by these ascetics who have shown such honor.
The Elder, his heart filled with joy like a great warrior who has received a magnificent reward from a wheel-turning monarch, [applied himself] to the knowledge of the perfections of a disciple.
Having stood there, he began the *anumodanā* (expression of appreciation) for the flower-seat. At the conclusion of his teaching, he addressed the second disciple:
"Bhikkhu, you too should teach the Dhamma. The Elder Anoma, having reflected upon the entire word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas, delivered a discourse on the Dhamma.
Yet, despite the teachings of the two chief disciples, not even one among them attained realization (*abhisamaya*). Then the Teacher, [addressing] the immeasurable...
Standing upon the domain of the Buddhas, he began the teaching of the Dhamma.
At the conclusion of the discourse, with the exception of the ascetic Sarada, all seventy-four thousand matted-hair ascetics attained Arahatship;
the Teacher extended his hand, saying, "Come, monks," and at that very moment their hair and beards vanished, and the eight requisites became fastened upon their bodies.
Why did the ascetic Sarada not attain Arahatship? Because his mind was distracted.

It is said that from the moment he began to listen to the Dhamma teaching of the Chief Disciple—while the latter sat on the second seat of the Buddhas and taught the Dhamma while established in the knowledge of the perfections of a disciple—he thought:
"O, may I too, in the future, under the dispensation of the Buddha who shall arise, [be like him]..."
He gave rise to the thought: "May I attain the burden already attained by this disciple. However, because of that reflection, he was unable to achieve penetration of the Path and its Fruit.
Then, having paid homage to the Tathāgata and standing before him, he asked:
"Venerable Sir, who is the name of the bhikkhu sitting on the seat immediately behind you in your teaching? [The Buddha replied: "It is the Wheel of Dhamma set in motion by me..."
“Not falling away from it, having penetrated the sixteen types of wisdom that reach the pinnacle of the disciple’s perfection-knowledge,
this one named Nisabha stands as the foremost disciple in my teaching. “Venerable Sir, as for the honor I performed by holding a flower-parasol for seven days,
through the fruit of this, I do not desire any other sovereignty, whether as a Sakka or as a Brahmā.”
"I make this aspiration: in the future, may I become the chief disciple of a Buddha, just like this Elder Nisabha.
The Teacher, wondering, "Will this man's aspiration be fulfilled?
sent forth his knowledge of the future and, looking into it, saw that it would be fulfilled after the passing of one incalculable eon plus one hundred thousand aeons.
He saw him. Having seen him, he said to the ascetic Sarada: "This aspiration of yours shall not be in vain.
However, after one incalculable aeon (*asaṅkhyeya*) plus one hundred thousand aeons have passed, a Buddha named Gotama will arise.
His mother will be the queen Mahāmāyā, his father the great king Suddhodana, and his son Rāhula."
“His attendant will be named Ānanda; his second chief disciple will be named Moggallāna;

and you, however, will be his first chief disciple, the General of the Dhamma, named Sāriputta. Having thus prophesied for the ascetic and delivered a discourse on the Dhamma, he leapt into the air, surrounded by the community of monks.
Sarada the ascetic also went to the presence of his resident elder disciples and sent a message to his friend, the householder Sirivaḍḍhana:

"Venerable sirs, tell my friend: 'Your friend, the ascetic Sarada, has made a resolution at the feet of the Buddha Anomadassi to attain the position of the first chief disciple in the dispensation of the future Buddha Gotama.'"
“You should aspire for the position of the second foremost disciple.
Having said this, he went aside before the elders and stood at the gate of Sirivaḍḍhana’s residence.
Sirivaḍḍhana, thinking, “It has been a long time since my noble master arrived,” had him seated on a seat and sat down himself on a low seat. However, [he saw that] the assembly of his students—
“Venerable sir, this is not known to you,” he asked. “Yes, friend, the Buddha Anomadassī came to our hermitage;

we paid him honor according to our own means. The Teacher taught the Dhamma to all of us, and at the conclusion of the teaching, with the exception of myself, the rest attained arahantship and went forth. I [sought] the Teacher’s first chief disciple...”
“Having seen the Elder Nisabha, I aspired to the position of the first chief disciple in the dispensation of the future Buddha Gotama;
you too, aspire to the position of the second chief disciple in his dispensation.
“Venerable sir, I have no acquaintance with the Buddhas,” [he replied]. “Let the conversation with the Buddhas be my responsibility.”
“You must prepare a great reception.
Having heard his words, Sirivaḍḍhana had an area eight *karīsa* in extent made level at the gate of his own residence according to royal measurement;
he had it strewn with sand, scattered flowers with parched grain as the fifth [ingredient], and provided a canopy of blue lotuses.
Having caused a pavilion to be built, having prepared a seat for the Buddha, and having arranged seats for the remaining monks as well, he made extensive preparations for a great offering and honor.
He then gave notice to the ascetic Sarada to invite the Buddhas.
The ascetic took the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha and went to his residence. Sirivaḍḍhana too—
Having gone out to meet the Tathāgata and taken the bowl from his hand, he led him into the pavilion;
then, after the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha had sat down on the prepared seats, he offered them water for the hands and served them with exquisite food.
At the conclusion of the meal, he [honored] the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha with costly garments.
Having covered [the ground], he said, "Venerable sir, this is not for the sake of a mere trifle;
out of compassion, please remain according to this very arrangement for seven days. The Teacher consented.

Having offered a great almsgiving for seven days according to that same arrangement, he paid homage to the Blessed One and, standing with palms joined in reverence, said: "Venerable sir, my friend..."
“I wish to become the first chief disciple of that Teacher who will have Sarada the ascetic as his first chief disciple,” he aspired; I too aspired, “May I become his second chief disciple.
The Teacher, looking into the future and seeing that his aspiration would be fulfilled, prophesied: “You—”
“After passing beyond an incalculable eon plus one hundred thousand aeons, you shall become the second chief disciple of the Buddha Gotama.
Having heard this prediction from the Buddhas, Sirivaḍḍhana became overjoyed.
The Teacher, having delivered his expression of thanks after the meal, returned to the monastery together with his retinue. “Monks, this [Sirivaḍḍhana] was among my sons...”
"Then their prayers were fulfilled; they obtained exactly what they had prayed for. 'I do not give by looking at a person's face,'" he said.

When this was said, the two chief disciples paid homage to the Blessed One and said, "Venerable Sir, while we were still householders, we went to see a festival on a mountain top," and so on, up until the realization of the fruit of stream-entry from the presence of the Elder Assaji.
Having related the entire present matter, they said: "Venerable sir, we went into the presence of our teacher Sañjaya with the desire to bring him to your feet;
we explained to him the essencelessness of his own tenets and spoke of the benefits in coming here.
Now, for him, staying as my pupil is like a water-pot turning into a water-drawing wheel."

Having said, "I will not be able to live as a resident pupil," when he was asked, "Teacher, now that the great multitude, with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in their hands, will go and worship the Teacher alone, what will become of you?
he replied, "In this world, are the wise many, or are the dull-witted many? When it was said, "The dull-witted are many," he said, "In that case, let the wise [be the ones who]..."
“They will go into the presence of the ascetic Gotama; being slow-witted, they will come back to me slowly.

You go! Having said this, he did not wish to come, Venerable Sir. Hearing that, the Teacher said, “Monks, Sañjaya, because of his own wrong view, has taken the worthless for the essential and the essential for the worthless. But you—”
“Having understood through your own wisdom what is essential as essential and what is non-essential as non-essential, abandon the non-essential and grasp only that which is essential.
Having said this, he spoke these verses:
“Those who perceive the essential in the non-essential, and see the non-essential in the essential;”
Those whose range of activity is wrong intention do not attain the essence.
But those who know the essential as essential and the unessential as unessential,
and whose range of activity is right intention, they attain the essence.

In this context, "those who perceive the substantial in the insubstantial" refers to the four conditions, the ten-based wrong view, and the teaching of the Dhamma that serves as its decisive support (upanissaya);
this is called "the insubstantial," and the meaning is those who have the perception of substance in that which is insubstantial.

"And those who perceive the insubstantial in the substantial" refers to the ten-based right view and the teaching of the Dhamma that serves as its decisive support; this is called "the substantial," and in that...
“‘This is not the essence’—thus they see what is not the essence. Yet, having grasped that wrong view, they stand upon it;

being within the range of wrong intention through sensual thoughts and so forth, they do not attain the essence of virtue, the essence of concentration, the essence of wisdom, the essence of liberation, the essence of the knowledge and vision of liberation, nor the ultimate essence, Nibbāna.”

"Knowing the essence" means knowing that very essence, such as the essence of virtue (*sīla-sāra*), as "this is indeed the essence," and knowing the aforementioned lack of essence as "this is indeed the lack of essence.
"Those [who attain] the essence" means that those wise ones, established in such right vision,
become the domain of right intention through the intention of renunciation (*nekkhamma-saṅkappa*) and so forth, and thereby attain that aforementioned essence.
At the conclusion of the verses, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages. The teaching of the Dhamma to those who had assembled was truly beneficial.
This is the eighth story, the Story of the Elder Sāriputta.
9. The Story of the Elder Nanda.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, delivered this teaching on the "House" concerning the Venerable Nanda.
For after the Teacher had set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma and gone to Rājagaha, he was staying in the Veḷuvana grove.

There, ten thousand messengers—each accompanied by a retinue of a thousand—one hundred thousand in all, had been dispatched by King Suddhodana with the command: "Bring my son back and show him to us."
Having gone last of all the messengers, the Elder Kāḷudāyi, who had attained Arahatship, recognized the time for departure;
after praising the beauty of the road, he was escorted to Kapilavatthu surrounded by twenty thousand monks whose taints were destroyed.
At the gathering of his kinsmen, he established the occasion for the discourse by raining down lotuses and related the Vessantara Jātaka. On the following day, he entered the city for alms.
Having established his father in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*) with the verse, “Arise,
do not be negligent,” he established Mahāpajāpatī in the fruit of stream-entry and the King in the fruit of once-returning (*sakadāgāmi-phala*) with the verse,

“One should practice the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the meal, however, having related the *Candakinnarī-jātaka* based on a discourse concerning the virtues of Rāhula’s mother, [he continued] from then on the third day...
While the auspicious ceremonies for Prince Nanda’s consecration, entry into his new home, and marriage were taking place, [the Blessed One] entered for alms;
having placed his bowl in Prince Nanda’s hand and pronounced a blessing, he rose from his seat and departed without taking the bowl back from Prince Nanda’s hand.
Out of reverence for the Tathāgata, Prince Nanda said, "Venerable Sir, please take your bowl."
He was unable to speak. However, he thought to himself: "The Teacher will take the bowl at the top of the stairs.
But the Teacher did not take it there either. The other thought: "He will take it at the foot of the stairs.
The Teacher did not take it there either. The other thought: "He will take it in the royal courtyard. The Teacher did not take it there either. The prince then desired to turn back.
Going along with a lack of desire, he was unable to say, "Take the bowl," out of reverence for the Teacher.
He went on thinking, "He will take it here; he will take it there.
At that moment, other women saw him and pointed him out to the Janapadakalyāṇī, saying, "Noble lady, the Blessed One..."
“Having taken Prince Nanda, he has gone; he will do it without you.
With her hair still half-combed and dripping with drops of water, she went in haste and said, “May you return quickly, noble son!
Those words of hers remained as if engraved across his heart. The Teacher [took him] from his hand...
Taking the bowl and leading him to that monastery, he said, "Nanda, will you go forth?
Out of reverence for the Buddha, he did not say, "I will not go forth," but replied, "Yes, I will go forth. The Teacher said, "In that case, let Nanda go forth.
The Teacher went to Kapilavatthu and on the third day caused Nanda to go forth.
On the seventh day, Rāhula’s mother, having adorned the prince, sent him into the presence of the Blessed One, saying:
“Look, dear child, at this ascetic surrounded by twenty thousand monks, golden-hued like the form of Brahmā;
this is your father. Great jars of treasure belonged to him, yet we have not seen them since his departure.”
“Go and ask him for his inheritance, saying: ‘Father, I am the prince; having received the consecration, I shall become a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti).
I have need of wealth; give me wealth. For a son is the master of what belongs to his father.
The prince, having gone into the presence of the Blessed One and immediately feeling paternal affection, with a joyful heart said: “May you have a pleasant shadow, ascetic.”

Having spoken thus, he stood there speaking much more that was appropriate to himself. The Blessed One, having finished his meal and performed the expression of thanks, rose from his seat and departed.
The prince also followed after the Blessed One, saying, "Give me my inheritance, ascetic! Give me my inheritance, ascetic!
The Blessed One, however, did not make the prince turn back. His attendants also [followed] the Blessed One...
He was unable to turn back the one who was going along with him. Thus, he went to the monastery together with the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One thought: "The wealth from his father's estate that this man desires is part of the cycle of existence and fraught with suffering;
well then, I shall give him the sevenfold noble wealth obtained at the foot of the Bodhi tree, as an inheritance of the supramundane."
“I shall make him my master. Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Sāriputta:
“In that case, Sāriputta, let Prince Rāhula go forth. The Elder ordained the prince.
But once the prince had gone forth, an excessive sorrow arose within the king. Unable to endure it, he [approached] the Blessed One...
Having made his offering, he requested this boon: “It would be well, venerable sir, if the masters would not ordain a son who has not been permitted by his parents.
The Blessed One granted him that boon. Then, on another day, having partaken of breakfast at the royal palace, the King sat to one side and said to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, when you were practicing austerities, a certain deity approached me and said:”

When he said, “‘Your son has died,’ they told me. Not believing their words, I rejected them, saying, ‘My son does not die until he has attained enlightenment,’” [the Buddha replied]: “Now what will you believe?
Even previously, when his bones were shown and it was said, ‘Your son is dead,’ you did not believe it. This is the origin of this account.
He related the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka. At the conclusion of the verses, the king was established in the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).
Thus, having established his father in the three fruits, the Blessed One, surrounded by the community of monks, returned once more to Rājagaha.
Thereafter, having given his promise to Anāthapiṇḍika to come to Sāvatthī, he went to the Jetavana when it was completed.
Having gone there, he took up residence in that monastery.
While the Teacher was dwelling thus at Jetavana, the Venerable Nanda became disenchanted and reported this matter to the monks:
"Friends, I am not finding delight in living the holy life; I am unable to maintain the holy life."
“Having renounced the training, I shall return to the lower life. When the Blessed One heard of this occurrence, he summoned the Venerable Nanda and said to him:
“Is it true, Nanda, that you announced this to many bhikkhus:
‘Friends, I am practicing the holy life without interest; I am unable to endure the holy life’?”
“Having renounced the training, I shall return to the lower life. “So be it, Bhante.
“But why, Nanda, do you live the holy life dissatisfied? Why are you unable to maintain the holy life and intend to renounce the training and return to the lower life?
“Bhante, the Sakyan lady, the most beautiful woman in the land, [left me] as I was departing from my home.”
With his hair still half-shorn, he looked at me and said: “Noble son, you should come back quickly.
Venerable sir, recollecting that, I am living the holy life without delight;
I am unable to maintain the holy life, and having renounced the training, I shall return to the lower life.
Then the Blessed One, taking the Venerable Nanda by the arm, brought him to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven by means of his psychic power; on the way,
he showed him a disfigured female monkey sitting on a charred stump in a burnt field— her ears, nose, and toes severed—
and [he showed him] those who had come to the service of Sakka, the king of the gods, in the Tāvatiṃsa realm.
He showed him five hundred celestial nymphs with feet like those of a wild cock;
"feet like those of a wild cock" means their feet were like those of a *pārevata* bird because of their reddish color. Having shown them, he said: "What do you think, Nanda?
Which is more beautiful, more lovely, or more charming—the Sakyan lady Janapadakalyāṇī, or these five hundred celestial nymphs with feet like those of a wild cock?"

Having heard that, he said: "Venerable sir, just as a female monkey with its ears, nose, and toes cut off would be utterly ruined, even so, venerable sir, that Sakyan lady, though she was the most beautiful woman in the land, does not even bear comparison with these five hundred nymphs;
she does not come within a fraction, nor a part, nor a portion of them. Indeed, these five..."
“...these hundreds of nymphs are more beautiful, more lovely to behold, and more charming.
“Rejoice, Nanda! Rejoice, Nanda! I am your guarantor for the acquisition of five hundred nymphs with feet like those of a rooster.
“If, Blessed Lord, you are my guarantor for the acquisition of five hundred nymphs with feet like those of a rooster...”
“I shall delight, Bhante, in the holy life under the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, taking the Venerable Nanda with him, vanished from that place and reappeared right there at Jetavana.
The monks heard it said: “The Venerable Nanda, they say, is the Blessed One’s brother, the son of his maternal aunt; he has [gone to] the nymphs...”
"He practices the holy life for the sake of a cause; the Blessed One is indeed his guarantor for the acquisition of five hundred kakuṭapāda nymphs.

Then the venerable Nanda’s companions addressed the venerable Nanda with the words "hireling" and "debt-slave," saying, "The venerable Nanda is indeed a hireling; the venerable Nanda is indeed a debt-slave."
"Nanda practices the holy life for the sake of celestial nymphs; the Blessed One has indeed given his guarantee for his acquisition of five hundred kakuṭapāda nymphs.
Then the Venerable Nanda, being distressed, ashamed, and disgusted by his companions' monks addressing him with the terms "hireling" and "servant," withdrew alone.

Dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute, before long he realized for himself through direct knowledge and attained in this very life that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness;
he dwelt having entered upon it, [knowing]: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived."
"What was to be done has been done; there is nothing further for this state of being"—thus he directly knew. And the Venerable Nanda became one of the Arahants.
Then, during the night, a certain deity, illuminating the entire Jeta’s Grove, approached the Teacher, paid homage, and announced:
"Venerable sir, the Venerable Nanda, the Blessed One’s brother and son of his maternal aunt, through the destruction of the taints, has realized the taintless..."
“Having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, he dwells having attained them.

Then the knowledge arose in the Blessed One: “Nanda, through the destruction of the taints, dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and has attained them.”
When that night had passed, the Venerable Nanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and said this:
“Venerable sir, regarding the Blessed One’s guarantee for me to obtain five hundred kakuṭapāda nymphs—I release the Blessed One from that promise. “Nanda, I too [know] you with my own mind...”

"Having encompassed his mind with my own, I have known: 'Nanda, through the destruction of the taints, dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, abides therein. Deities also have declared this matter to me:

'Venerable sir, the Venerable Nanda, through the destruction of the taints, has realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom...'"
‘Having realized it for oneself through direct knowledge in this very life, he enters and dwells in that state.
Nanda, the moment your mind was liberated from the taints through non-clinging, at that very moment I was released from my promise.
Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired exclamation:
“He whose mire has been crossed over, who has crushed the thorn of sensual desire, and who has reached the destruction of delusion—he, that bhikkhu, does not tremble in the face of pleasure and pain.
Then one day, the bhikkhus asked the Venerable Nanda: “Friend Nanda, formerly you—”
“You said, ‘I am weary,’ but now what is your intention? “Friend, I have no attachment to the state of a householder.
Hearing this, the monks thought, “The Venerable Nanda speaks what is untrue; he gives a contrary explanation.
Having previously said, ‘I am weary,’ he now says, ‘I have no attachment to the state of a householder. Having gone [to the Buddha], they reported it to the Blessed One.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, “Monks, in days past Nanda’s physical form was like a poorly thatched house, but now it has become like a well-thatched house.
For from the time he saw the celestial nymphs, he has striven to reach the pinnacle of the purpose for which he went forth, and he has now attained that goal. Having said this, he spoke these verses:
“Just as rain penetrates a poorly-thatched house,
so passion penetrates an undeveloped mind. Just as rain does not penetrate a well-thatched house, [so passion does not penetrate a developed mind].”
“In this way, lust does not penetrate a well-developed mind.
In this context, “house” refers to any kind of dwelling. “Ill-thatched” means poorly covered, full of holes and gaps.
“Penetrates” means that the falling rain breaks through it. “Undeveloped” [mind] is so called because, like that house, it is devoid of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
An uncultivated mind is pierced by lust. Not only lust, but all defilements—such as hatred, delusion, pride, and so forth—pierce such a mind exceedingly.
"Well-cultivated" means well-developed through the cultivation of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
A mind of this kind, like a well-roofed house, cannot be pierced by defilements such as lust, just as rain cannot penetrate it.
At the conclusion of the verses, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages. The teaching was fruitful for the great multitude.
Then, in the Hall of Dharma, the monks initiated this discussion: "Friends, the Buddhas are indeed wonderful!
By means of Janapadakalyāṇī, the Venerable Nanda—who was so deeply distressed—was made to regard a celestial nymph as a bait by the Teacher..."
“He has been disciplined. When the Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
and they replied, “About this very one,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, he was disciplined by me after being enticed by a woman.
Having said this, he related the past:
In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, there was a merchant named Kappaṭa living in Benares.
He had a donkey that carried loads of jars and could travel seven *yojanas* in a single day.
On one occasion, having gone to Taxila with his donkey-loads, he remained there until the goods were disposed of.
He released a donkey to graze. While that donkey was grazing on the edge of a ditch, he saw a female donkey and approached her.
She, exchanging greetings with him, asked: "Where have you come from? "From Bārāṇasī," he replied.
"For what purpose? "For the business of trade. "How much of a load do you carry? "A load of jars."
“Carrying such a burden, how many yojanas do you go? “Seven yojanas.
“In the places you have already traveled, are there anyone who performs foot-massage or back-massage for you? “No. “If that is so, you must experience great suffering.
“Even though there are indeed no one to perform foot-massage and the like for those who have gone to the animal realm,”
“But why did he speak such words for the sake of agitating the fetter of sensual desire? He became weary of that talk.
Kappaṭa, having disposed of his wares, came to him and said, “Come, dear one, let us go.
“You go; I will not go,” he replied. Then, after repeatedly entreating him and, when he was unwilling, rebuking him—
Thinking, "I will lead him away," he spoke this verse:
"I shall make for you a goad with thorns as sharp as śāla-needles;
I shall cut your body to pieces—know this well, O donkey!"
Having heard that, the donkey said, "If that is the case, I too shall know what must be done for you," and spoke this verse:
"You shall make for me a goad with thorns sixteen finger-breadths long;
standing in front, having pulled it up from behind."
“I shall cause your teeth to fall out; know this, you rag-picker!
Hearing this, the merchant thought, “For what reason does he speak thus?
Looking here and there, he saw that female donkey and realized, “He must have been instructed by her in this way: ‘[If anyone says] such a thing as this...’”
“Thinking, ‘I will bring a she-camel,’ I shall entice him with a woman and lead him away,” he spoke this verse:
“A four-footed woman with a conch-like face, beautiful in every limb—I will bring such a wife for you; know this, O camel.”
Hearing this, the donkey, with a joyful heart, spoke this verse:
“A woman with four feet, a conch-like face, beautiful in every limb— you shall bring such a wife for me;
know this well, rag-picker!”
“I shall go further, for fourteen *yojanas*, O rag-picker.
Then the rag-picker, saying, “In that case, come,” took him by the hand and went to his own place.
After a few days had passed, he said to him, “Did you not say to me, ‘We will bring your wife back’? “Yes, it was said.”
"I shall not break my word to myself; I will bring you a wife, but I shall give the wages to you alone.
Whether those wages are sufficient for both of you or not, you yourself shall know.
However, through the cohabitation of you two, sons will be born; whether it is sufficient for you even with many of them..."
"Or else, you yourself shall know. Even as he was speaking, the donkey became indifferent.
Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said: "At that time, monks, the she-donkey was Janapadakalyāṇī, Nanda was the donkey, and I myself was the merchant.
Thus, in the past, he too was disciplined by me after being tempted by a woman."
He completed the Jātaka.
The ninth story, the account of the Elder Nanda, is finished. 10.
The account of Cunda the pork-butcher.
"Here he grieves": this teaching on the Dhamma was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Veḷuvana concerning a man named Cunda the pork-butcher.
It is said that for fifty-five years he made his living by slaughtering pigs, both eating them himself and selling them.
During times of famine, he would take rice in a cart and go to the countryside, where he would sell village piglets for the price of a single stalk or two stalks of grain.
Having purchased [the animals], filled his cart, and returned, he enclosed a single spot in his backyard like a sacrificial altar (*vajra*),
planted fodder right there for them, and once they had grown fat by eating various shrubs and the impurities of their own bodies,
whenever he wished to kill any one of them, he would tie it motionless to a post until the flesh of its body had swollen.
Having struck him with a square mallet to ensure the flesh has become thick, and knowing that "the flesh has grown," he opens his mouth,
inserts a stick inside, and pours boiling water from a copper vessel into the mouth.
That water enters the belly, takes up the boiled excrement, and exits through the lower part, even down to the last bit of excrement.
First, it comes out turbid; when the womb is clean, it comes out clear and free from turbidity.
Then the remaining water is poured over its back. That black skin peels away and falls off.
Then, having burned the hair with a grass torch, he cuts off the head with a sharp sword. The flowing blood is caught in a vessel.
Having accepted it, he kneaded the meat with blood, cooked it, and while sitting in the midst of his wife and children, ate it;
then he sold the remainder. As he maintained his livelihood in this very manner, fifty-five years passed by.
While the Tathāgata was residing at Dhuravihāra, he did not perform even a single day’s worth of worship, such as a handful of flowers or a ladleful [of food].

There was no gift of alms or any other meritorious deed whatsoever. Then a disease arose in his body, and even while he was still alive, the torment of the Great Niraya of Avīci manifested before him.
The heat of Avīci is such that even for one standing a hundred yojanas away and looking on, it is a fever capable of shattering the eyes. And this has been said:
“His ground is made of iron, blazing and filled with heat;
it stands pervading a hundred yojanas on all sides at all times.
This simile was spoken by the Elder Nāgasena because of its superior intensity compared to the heat of an ordinary fire: “Just as...”
“Great King, even a stone the size of a gabled chamber, when thrown into the fire of hell, dissolves in an instant;
yet the beings reborn there do not dissolve, for by the power of their karma they remain as if they were still in their mother’s womb.
As that torment presented itself to him, a form resembling his past action appeared. Even while in the middle of his house, he let out a cry like that of a pig.
Moving about on his knees, he goes from the eastern part of the house to the western part.
Then the household servants seize him firmly and cover his mouth. Indeed, the ripening of kamma cannot be warded off by anyone.
Even as he cries out, he wanders here and there. Consequently, the people in the seven houses surrounding him find no sleep.
But when the entire household, unable to prevent him from going out because he was terrified by the fear of death,
closed the house doors, surrounded the exterior of the house, and remained guarding him so that, like one standing inside who cannot move outside, he could not leave; the other,
wailing with the heat of hell even within the house, wandered here and there.
Having wandered about in this manner for seven days, he passed away on the eighth day and was reborn in the Great Niraya of Avīci.
The Great Niraya of Avīci should be described according to the Devadūta Sutta.
When the monks were passing by his house door, they heard that sound and, perceiving it to be the cry of a pig, [said]:
Having gone to the monastery and sat down in the presence of the Teacher, they said:
"Venerable Sir, today is the seventh day since the gate of Cunda the pork-butcher’s house was closed; we imagine some auspicious ceremony must be taking place in his house.
Venerable Sir, in one who slaughters so many pigs, there is not even a single thought of loving-kindness or compassion."
“Indeed, we have never before seen such a cruel and harsh being.
The Teacher said, “Monks, it was not he who killed these pigs during these seven days; rather, a result corresponding to his past action arose.
Even while he was still alive, the torment of the Great Niraya Avīci hell manifested before him. Because of that torment, for seven days he cried out with the cry of a pig.”
“Having wandered about in his own house, he died today and was reborn in the Avīci hell. When it was said, “Venerable Sir, having grieved thus in this very world,
he has now gone and been reborn in that very place where one must grieve,” the Buddha replied,
“Yes, monks, whether they be householders or those who have gone forth, those who are heedless surely grieve in both places,” and he spoke this verse:
“Here he sorrows, and after passing away he sorrows;
the doer of evil sorrows in both places.
He sorrows and he is tormented.”
"Having seen the defilement of his own karma.
In this context, "one who has done evil" refers to a person who has committed various kinds of unwholesome deeds;

at the time of death, they grieve here with absolute certainty, thinking, "Alas, I have not done what is good, but I have done evil. This is their "grieving over karma. [The result is] the ripening...
"But experiencing [the results], he grieves after passing away. This is his grieving for the ripening of the fruit in the next world. Thus, he grieves in both places.
For that very reason, even while still alive, Cunda the pork-butcher grieves.
"Having seen the defilement of his own karma"—having seen his own defiled karma, he dwells in distress, lamenting in various ways.
At the conclusion of the verses, many became stream-enterers and others. The teaching of the Dhamma had become fruitful for the great multitude.
This is the tenth story, the Story of Cunda the Pig-butcher.
11. The Story of the Lay-follower Dhammika.
"Here one rejoices"—the Teacher spoke this teaching while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the lay follower Dhammika.
It is said that in Sāvatthī there were five hundred lay followers named Dhammika, each of whom had a retinue of five hundred lay followers.
Of them, the eldest had seven sons and seven daughters. Among them—

For each of them, there was a single portion of rice-gruel, as well as meals on the fortnight, meals by invitation, meals on the Uposatha day, meals for newcomers, meals for the Saṅgha, and meals during the rainy season retreat. All of these were known as "sons born after" (anujātaputta).
Thus, for the wife of the lay follower and for the fourteen sons, sixteen portions of rice-gruel and other offerings were distributed.
Thus, together with his wife and children, he was virtuous, possessed of noble qualities, and delighted in giving and sharing.
Later, a sickness arose in him and his life-force began to decline. Desiring to hear the Dhamma, he sent messengers to the presence of the Teacher, saying, "Send me eight or sixteen bhikkhus.
The Teacher sent them. Having arrived, they surrounded his bed.
They sat down on the seats that had been prepared. When he said, "Venerable sir, it will be difficult for me to see the noble ladies; I am weak.
Please recite one discourse for me," [the Venerable Ānanda] asked, "Which discourse do you wish to hear, lay follower?
He replied, "The *Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta*, which has not been abandoned by any of the Buddhas. [The Venerable Ānanda then began: "Monks, this is the one-way path for beings..."

They established the Sutta, saying, "For the sake of purification. At that moment, from the six celestial realms, six chariots arrived, adorned with every ornament, yoked to a thousand thoroughbreds, and measuring one hundred and fifty *yojanas* in length.
Standing upon them, the deities cried out, "We shall take him to our own celestial realm!
We shall take him to our own celestial realm! O, break this earthen vessel and [take him] to a golden vessel!"
“Come here as if taking us with you; be reborn here so that we may delight in our own heavenly world!
they said. The lay follower, not wishing for an interruption in his hearing of the Dhamma, said, “Wait! Wait!
The bhikkhus, perceiving that he was forbidding them, remained silent.

Then his sons and daughters cried out, "Our father was formerly insatiable for hearing the Dhamma, yet now he has the monks summoned, makes them recite, and then dismisses them himself; there is no being who does not fear death.
The monks, thinking, "Now there is no opportunity," rose from their seats and departed. The lay follower...
After waiting a short while, having regained his mindfulness, he asked his sons, "Why are you weeping?

They replied, "Father, when you had the monks summoned and were yourself listening to the Dhamma, you prevented us from doing so; therefore, we wept, thinking, 'There is no being who does not fear death.
He asked, "But where are the masters? They replied, "'There is no room,' they said, and rising from their seats, they departed."
“Father! When he said, “I do not speak with the noble ladies,” she asked, “Then with whom do you speak?
He replied, “The deities from the six heavenly realms, having adorned six chariots and taken them along, stand in the sky and cry out, ‘Delight in our heavenly realms!
Delight in our heavenly realms! It is with them that I speak. “Where—”
“Father, chariots! We do not see them. “But do I have any flowers woven together? “I do, father.
“Which heavenly realm is most delightful? “The Tusita heaven, father, where all Bodhisattvas and the parents of Buddhas dwell, is the most delightful.
“In that case, let it be attached to the chariot that has come from the Tusita heaven.”
“Throw a flower garland! They threw it. It caught on the front of the chariot and hung suspended in the air.
The great multitude saw only that; they did not see the chariot. The lay follower said, “Look at this flower garland!
When they replied, “Yes, we see it,” he said, “This hangs from the chariot that has come from the Tusita heaven; I am going to the Tusita heaven.”

"I am going; do not worry about me. Desiring to be reborn in my presence, perform meritorious deeds according to the method established by me," he said, and having passed away, he was established upon a chariot.
At that very moment, his personal existence (attabhāva) manifested, measuring three gavutas in size and adorned with ornaments weighing sixty cart-loads.
A thousand celestial nymphs attended upon him, and a golden celestial mansion twenty-five yojanas in size appeared.
When those monks arrived at the monastery, the Teacher asked: "Monks, did you hear the lay follower’s teaching of the Dhamma?
"Yes, venerable sir," they replied. "But he stopped us right there, saying, 'Please wait,' for his sons and daughters were weeping. We..."
“‘Now there is no opportunity,’ he thought, and rising from his seat, he departed. “Monks, he was not speaking with you.
Deities from the six celestial realms, having adorned six chariots and brought them forth, summoned that lay follower.
Unwilling for there to be an interruption to the teaching of the Dhamma, he spoke with them. “So it is, Bhante. “So it is.”
“Monks,” [the Buddha said]. “Where has he been reborn now? “In the Tusita heaven, monks.
“Venerable Sir, having wandered about here among his kinsmen enjoying himself just now, and having departed this very moment, he has been reborn once again in that very place of enjoyment.
“Yes, monks; for whether they be householders or those gone forth, those who are heedful rejoice everywhere,” and having said this, he spoke this verse:
“Here he rejoices, and having passed away, he rejoices;
having performed merit, he rejoices in both places.
He rejoices, he exults.”
"Having seen the purity of one's own karma.
In this context, the "one who has performed merit" is a person who performs various kinds of wholesome deeds;

they rejoice here through the rejoicing in their karma, thinking, "Alas, evil was not done by me; what is auspicious has been done by me," and they rejoice after death through the rejoicing in its fruition. Thus, in both places...

"He rejoices," it is said. Regarding "purity of action": even a righteous lay follower, seeing his own purity of action—the success of his meritorious deeds—rejoices in this very world before passing away; and having passed away, he now rejoices exceedingly in the world beyond.
At the conclusion of the verses, many became stream-enterers and others; thus the teaching of the Dhamma became fruitful for the great multitude.
The Story of the Lay Follower Dhammika, the eleventh.
12. The Story of Devadatta:
"Here one suffers"—the Teacher spoke this teaching on the Dhamma while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning Devadatta.

The story of Devadatta has been related in detail by expanding upon all the Jātakas spoken concerning Devadatta, from the time of his going forth until his entry into the earth. This, however, is the summary:
while the Teacher was dwelling in the Anupiya Mango Grove near the Malla town named Anupiya, the Tathāgata—

On the very day the marks were received, eighty thousand kinsmen pledged themselves, saying, "Whether he becomes a king or a Buddha, he shall always move about surrounded by Khattiyas," and thus eighty thousand sons were promised. Of these, when the majority had gone forth into homelessness, there remained six:
King Bhaddiya, Anuruddha, Ānanda, Bhagu, Kimila, and Devadatta.
Seeing that other Śākyans were not going forth, they raised this question: "We have allowed our own sons to go forth, yet these six Śākyans do not seem to be relatives;
why do they not go forth? Then the Śākya Mahānāma approached Anuruddha and said, "Dear brother, there has been no one from our family who has gone forth. Either you go forth, or I shall go forth."
He said: "Furthermore, he was delicate and possessed of abundant wealth; even the word 'there is not' had never been heard by him before.
For one day, while those six kṣatriyas were playing with balls, Anuruddha lost with a cake and sent for one.
His mother prepared cakes and sent them. They ate them and played again. Again and again..."
He was defeated for that very reason. His mother, however, having sent cakes three times each time he sent a message, sent a message on the fourth occasion saying, "There are no cakes.
Because the word "there are none" had not been used before, he thought, "This must be some kind of cake," and sent back the message:
"Bring me the 'no-cake'! His mother, however, [sent back] the "no-cake"...
When she said, "Please give it, noble lady," [the other] thought, "My son has never before heard the word 'there is not.
But by this means, I shall make him understand this matter. So she sent an empty golden bowl, covered with another golden bowl.
The deities who guard the city thought: "At the time of Annabhāra, when Anuruddha the Sakyan was..."
Having given a portion of rice to the Paccekabuddha Upaṭṭhaka, he made this aspiration: "May I never hear the words 'there is nothing,' and may I never know the place where food arises.
He thought, "If he sees this empty bowl, we shall not be permitted to enter the assembly of the gods, and our heads too shall split into seven pieces. Then he...
They filled a tray with divine cakes (*dibbapūva*). When they placed them on a sugar-mound and merely uncovered them, the fragrance of the cakes pervaded the entire city.
As soon as a piece of cake was placed in the mouth, it circulated through the seventeen thousand vessels of the body.
He thought: "I am not dear to my mother; for all this time she has not baked these so-called 'cakes of nothingness' (*natthipūva*) for me. From now on—"
“From now on, I shall not eat any other kind of cake. Having returned home, he asked his mother, “Mother, am I dear to you or not?
“My son, you have been as exceedingly dear to me as one eye to another, or as my own heart,” she replied.
“Then why did you not bake any cakes for me all this time, Mother?”
She asked the junior attendant, "Is there anything in the bowl, dear? He replied, "The bowl is full of cakes, noble lady;
indeed, I have never seen such cakes before. She thought, "My son must be meritorious and one who has made a firm resolve;
the deities must have filled the bowl and sent the cakes. Then...
“My son, mother,” he said, “from now on I will not eat any other kind of cake; you should bake only *natthipūva* (‘no-more-cake’) for me.
From then on, whenever he said, “I wish to eat cake,” she would give him back an empty bowl after exchanging it for another one that was already empty.
As long as he lived in the household, the deities sent him cakes.
“Since he does not even know this much, what will he understand about going forth? Therefore, having asked his brother, ‘What is this so-called going forth?

and being told, ‘One must live with hair and beard shaven, clothed in saffron robes, lying down on a bed of wood or a mat of split bamboo, wandering for alms—this is what is called going forth,’ [he said], ‘Brother,…”
“I am delicate; I will not be able to go forth,” he said. “In that case, dear son, learn a craft and live the life of a householder.
For it is not possible for us to have even one who does not go forth.
Then he asked him, “What is this so-called ‘craft’? [The father replied,] “How can a gentleman who does not even know the proper places for eating and standing know what a craft is?”
One day, a conversation arose among three kṣatriyas: "From where does food arise?
Kimila said, "It arises from the granary. Then Bhaddiya said to him, "You do not know the place where food arises;
food arises in the cooking pot. Anuruddha said, "Neither of you two knows."
“Food, indeed, arises in a golden bowl with a jeweled rim,” he said.
It is said that one day Kimila, seeing rice being poured out from a granary, perceived, “These were born right there in the granary.
One day Bhaddiya, seeing food being increased in a cooking pot, [perceived], “In the cooking pot itself...”
He perceived it as "arisen. As for Anuruddha, he had never before seen rice being threshed, nor food being cooked, nor [the meal] being prepared;
however, he saw it placed right there in front of him once it had been prepared.
When he desired to eat, he perceived that "the food rises up into the bowl. Thus, none of those three [saw] the place where the food was originally situated.
They know this. Therefore, having asked, "What is this so-called 'work'?
and having heard the duties to be performed year after year—such as "first, the field must be ploughed," and so forth—they said, "When will the end of these works appear?
When shall we enjoy our wealth free from anxiety? Thus, the endlessness of their labors was made known to them.
“Then you yourself stay at home; I have no need for this,” he said. Approaching his mother, he said, “Mother, give me your permission;
I shall go forth. After she had refused him three times in various ways, she said, “If your friend King Bhaddiya goes forth, then go forth together with him. Having been told this, he—
Having approached him, he said, "My going forth, friend, depends upon you," and after persuading him in various ways,
on the seventh day he obtained his promise to go forth together with him.
Then these six kṣatriyas— Bhaddiya the Śākya king, Anuruddha, Ānanda, Bhagu, Kimbila, and Devadatta— [went forth].
Like the Upāli-kappa-devas who, having enjoyed celestial prosperity for seven days, set out for a pleasure garden, they departed with a fourfold army.
Upon reaching the territory of another king, they withdrew the army by royal command and entered that foreign realm.
There, the six kṣatriyas [removed] their own ornaments...
Having untied it and made it into a bundle, they said, "Come now, friend Upāli, let us return; this much is enough for your livelihood," and gave it to him.
He rolled at their feet and lamented, but being unable to disobey their command, he rose, took it, and turned back.
At the moment they were divided, the forest seemed to reach a state of weeping, as if the earth itself were trembling.
It was as if he were dead. Upāli the barber also went a short distance, then turned back and thought: "The Sakyans are fierce;
they might even kill me, thinking, 'By this man the princes have been sent away.
For these very Sakyan princes, having abandoned such prosperity and cast aside these priceless ornaments like a globule of spittle, will go forth into homelessness—how much more so, then, shall I?"
Having unfastened his bundle and hung those ornaments on a tree, saying, "Let whoever needs them take them," he went into their presence.
When they asked him, "Why have you turned back? he related the matter to them.
Then, taking him with them, they went into the presence of the Teacher and said, "Venerable Sir, we Sākiyas are indeed dependent upon our pride; this man has been [our servant] for a long time..."

"Let this attendant be ordained first; we shall perform the salutations and other duties for him, and in this way our pride will be humbled," they said. Having thus had him ordained first, they themselves were ordained afterwards.

Among them, the Venerable Bhaddiya became a possessor of the three knowledges (*tevijja*) within that very same rainy season, while the Venerable Anuruddha became possessed of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).
Having made the offering, he later heard the Mahāvitakka Sutta and attained Arahatship. The Venerable Ānanda was established in the fruit of Stream-entry.
Later, both the Elder Bhagu and the Elder Kimila increased their insight and attained Arahatship.
Devadatta attained mundane psychic power (iddhi).
Later on, while the Teacher was dwelling at Kosambī together with the community of disciples, great gain and honor accrued to the Tathāgata.
People, carrying robes, medicines, and other requisites in their hands, entered the monastery and asked, "Where is the Teacher? Where is the Elder Sāriputta?
Where is the Elder Mahāmoggallāna? Where is the Elder Mahākassapa? Where is the Elder Bhaddiya?"
They wandered about, looking for the seats where the eighty great disciples were sitting, asking, "Where is the Elder Anuruddha? Where is the Elder Ānanda? Where is the Elder Bhagu?
Where is the Elder Kimila? There was no one who even asked, "Where is the Elder Devadatta sitting or standing?
He thought to himself: "I too went forth together with these very men; they too are those who have gone forth from the kṣatriya caste."
“I too have gone forth as a kshatriya. People seek me out solely for the sake of gain and honor;
there is no one who even takes my name. With whom could I associate, and by pleasing whom, might I acquire gain and honor?
Then this thought occurred to him: “This King Bimbisāra, from our very first meeting...”
“Together with eleven hundred [monks], he has been established in the fruit of stream-entry;

it is not possible to be on the same footing as him, nor is it possible to be on the same footing even with the King of Kosala. However, this Prince Ajātasattu, the king’s son, knows nothing of virtues or faults; we shall be on the same footing with him. Thus, from Kosambi...
Having gone to Rājagaha and manifested the form of a young boy, he fastened four venomous snakes upon his four hands and feet,
placed one as a head-ornament, and draped another over one shoulder; then,
descending from the sky with this girdle of snakes, he sat upon the lap of Ajātasattu, who, being terrified, asked, "Who are you?"
Having said, "I am Devadatta," and in order to dispel his fear, he withdrew that manifestation of his own form;
standing before him clad in the outer robe, bowl, and robes, he gained his confidence and brought about gain and honor for himself.

Overwhelmed by that gain and honor, he conceived an evil thought, thinking, "I shall lead the Saṅgha of bhikkhus," and simultaneously with the arising of that thought, he fell from his supernormal power.
Having left the Teacher while he was teaching the Dhamma in the Veḷuvana Monastery to an assembly including the king, he rose from his seat, joined his palms in reverential salutation, and said:
“Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is now old, aged, and advanced in years;
may he devote himself to dwelling in happiness in this very life with little concern. I shall look after the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.”
Having said, "Give me the Saṅgha of bhikkhus," he was rebuked by the Teacher with the words "spittle-swallower" and rejected;
being displeased, he departed, having harbored this first grudge against the Tathāgata.
Then the Blessed One had a formal act of reconciliation performed for him in Rājagaha. He thought, "I have now been cast off by the ascetic."
“Now, since he has been raised by Gotama, we shall do him harm. Having approached Ajātasattu, he said, “In the past, prince, humans were long-lived;
nowadays they are short-lived. It is possible, indeed, that you might pass away while still a mere youth.
Therefore, prince, kill your father and become king. As for me, I shall [kill] the Blessed One...”
Having said, "I shall become a Buddha after killing him," and having appointed men for the sake of slaying the Tathāgata once he was established in that kingdom,
those men returned after attaining the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). Then, having ascended Mount Gijjhakūṭa himself, thinking,
"I alone shall deprive the ascetic Gotama of life," he hurled down a rock and committed the deed of shedding blood.
Having attempted this means as well, being unable to kill him, he again released Nāḷāgiri.
As the elephant approached, the Elder Ānanda stood in front, sacrificing his own life for the sake of the Teacher.
The Teacher tamed the elephant, departed from the city, went to the monastery, and after partaking of a great alms-offering brought by many thousands of lay followers, he remained there.

On that day, after he had delivered a graduated discourse to the eighteen koṭis of residents of Rājagaha who had assembled there, and when the realization of the Dhamma had arisen for eighty-four thousand living beings, they exclaimed: "Oh, how great are the virtues of the Venerable Ānanda!
