Even when such a noble elephant was approaching, he sacrificed his own life and remained right before the Teacher."
Having heard this account of the Elder’s virtues, [the Buddha] said, "Monks, it is not only now that he has sacrificed his life for my sake;
he did so even in the past," and at the request of the monks, he related the Cūḷahaṃsa, Mahāhaṃsa, and Kakkaṭaka Jātakas.
Furthermore, Devadatta’s deed was not made public, because the King had caused him to be killed, nor by the executioners.
It became evident not because the stone had been thrown, but because [the elephant] had been dispatched, just as in the case of the elephant Nāḷāgiri.
At that time, the great multitude raised a clamor, saying: "The king was caused to be killed by Devadatta himself; the assassin was employed, and the stone was cast down.
But now he has even caused Nāḷāgiri to be released! Having taken up such evil [counsel], the king goes about!"
Having heard the words of the great multitude, the king had five hundred pots of cooked rice removed and did not go to his service again;
nor did the city-dwellers give him even a mere morsel of alms when he approached their homes.
With his gains and honor diminished, desiring to live by deceit, he approached the Teacher and requested five boons, to which the Blessed One replied, "Enough."
“Devadatta, let whoever wishes be a forest-dweller. [To this] he replied:
“Whose words are more beautiful, friend—those of the Tathāgata or mine? For I speak thus on the basis of the highest standard:
‘It would be good, Bhante, if the bhikkhus were forest-dwellers for as long as life lasts, almsfood eaters, wearers of rag-robes, dwellers at the foot of trees, and abstainers from fish and meat.’”
"Let us eat. Having said, "Whoever wishes to be freed from suffering, let him come with me," he departed.
Hearing his words, some newly ordained monks of dull intellect thought, "Devadatta has spoken well;
we shall wander together with him," and they became one with him. Thus, he [was accompanied] by five hundred bhikkhus.
Together with those five points, seeking to persuade people who were inclined toward austerity, he strove for a schism in the Saṅgha by repeatedly making requests among the families.

When questioned by the Blessed One, “Is it true, Devadatta, that you are striving for a schism in the Saṅgha, a breaking of the Wheel? he replied, “It is true, Blessed One. [The Blessed One said: “Devadatta, this is indeed a grave matter.”
Although he was admonished with the words, "This is a schism in the Saṅgha," and so forth, he departed without heeding the Teacher's word.

Seeing the Venerable Ānanda wandering for alms in Rājagaha, he said: "From this day forward, friend Ānanda, I shall perform the Uposatha and carry out the formal acts of the Saṅgha apart from the Blessed One and apart from the Bhikkhu Saṅgha. The Elder—
He reported that matter to the Blessed One. Having understood it, the Teacher, moved by a sense of spiritual urgency regarding the Dhamma, reflected:
"Devadatta is performing an action that brings harm to the world with its devas—an action that will cause him himself to burn in Avīci. Then he said:
"Evil deeds are easy to do, as are those things that are harmful to oneself;"
"What is indeed beneficial and good is indeed most difficult to do.
Having spoken this verse, he further uttered this inspired utterance:
"What is good is easy for the good to do; what is good is difficult for the evil to do."
“Evil is easily done by the evil, but evil is difficult for the noble ones to do.
Then, on the day of the Uposatha, Devadatta sat to one side together with his own assembly and said,
“Let whoever approves of these five points take a voting ticket,” and thus he had five hundred newly ordained Vajjiputtakas [take the tickets].
When the voting sticks had been taken by those who did not know moderation, he split the Saṅgha and, taking those bhikkhus with him, went to Gayāsīsa.
Hearing that he had gone there, the Teacher sent two chief disciples to bring back those bhikkhus.
Having gone there, they instructed them through the miracle of mind-reading (*ādesanā-pāṭihāriya*) and the miracle of supernormal power (*iddhi-pāṭihāriya*).
And as they were instructing them, having caused them to drink the Deathless, they took them and returned through the air.
Kokālika also said, "Arise, friend Devadatta! Your monks have been led away by Sāriputta and Moggallāna.
Did I not tell you, 'Friend, do not place your trust in Sāriputta and Moggallāna'? Sāriputta and Moggallāna have evil desires; they are possessed of wicked intentions."
Having said, "He has fallen under [his power]," he struck the middle of the heart with his knee; there and then warm blood gushed from his mouth.
But seeing the Venerable Sāriputta approaching through the air surrounded by the community of monks, the monks said:
"Venerable sir, when the Venerable Sāriputta departed, he went accompanied only by himself; now he has a great retinue."
“...he shines as he approaches. The Teacher said, “Monks, it is not only now that Sāriputta shines;
even in the past, when he was reborn in the animal realm, my son shone just as much as he approached me. Having said this, he spoke:
“There is benefit for those of virtuous conduct who live with hospitality;”
“Behold the auspicious marks as he approaches, honored by his circle of kinsmen;
yet now we see this dark one utterly forsaken by his relatives. Thus he related this Jātaka.
Again, when the bhikkhus said, “Venerable sir, it is said that Devadatta has [driven away] the two chief disciples...”

When it was said, "Having seated them on the mountain passes, he is performing a service for you by teaching the Dhamma with the grace of a Buddha," [the Blessed One] said, "Monks, it is not only now that he has striven to perform a service for me, but he was unable to do so even in the past. And he said:
"Did you not see, Vīraka, the bird Mañjubhāṇaka?"
My husband, resembling a peacock’s neck, was adorned with earrings.
[He was] a bird that moved both on water and on land,
and who constantly fed on raw fish.
Having related the Jātaka beginning with, “Following him was Savitthaka,
who died, covered by water-weeds,” and so forth,
on subsequent days as well, he spoke in a similar manner concerning appropriate stories.
“Indeed, this one has wandered through the forests,
piercing trees that were mere wood and pithless;
yet he has now found the acacia tree, which possesses true heartwood.”
“Where the Garuḍa has split your head,” [he said].
“Your ichor is dried up, your skull is shattered, all your ribs are broken; today indeed you shine forth.”
He related such Jātaka stories as these. Then, concerning the discourse on how Devadatta was ungrateful, he said:
“We have done what was to be done for you, since we possessed such strength;
O King of Beasts, homage be to you! May we receive at least something [in return].”
“O blood-eater, who constantly commits cruel deeds,
though you have entered between my teeth, you live for so long!”— with these and other verses,
he recounted the Jātaka stories. Then, concerning his repeated efforts to kill him:
“‘This is known to the Kuruṅga deer: that you would lie down for a *sepaṇṇi* flower;
I shall go for another *sepaṇṇi*, for I do not like that fruit of yours’”—with these and other verses he recited the Jātakas.
On the following day [he said], “Devadatta has fallen away from both sides: from gain and honor, and from the state of a recluse.”
And while such talk was being circulated, [the Blessed One] said: "Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta has fallen away;
he had already fallen away in the past. Having said this, he spoke:
"The eyes were pierced, the cloth was lost, and there was a quarrel in my kinsman's house;"
"Both on water and on land, undertakings fail when corrupted by both sides.

He spoke such Jātaka stories. While staying thus at Rājagaha, having related many Jātakas concerning Devadatta, he departed from Rājagaha for Sāvatthī and took up residence in the Jetavana monastery. And Devadatta too—
For nine months he was ill, and in his final moments, desiring to see the Teacher, he said to his own disciples:
“I wish to see the Teacher; show him to me. When they replied, “During your time of strength you lived as an enemy toward the Teacher;
we will not take you there,” he said, “Do not destroy me! I harbored resentment toward the Teacher.”
"But toward me, the Teacher has not even a hair’s breadth of resentment. For that Blessed One was "even-minded in all circumstances—
toward the murderer Devadatta, the robber Aṅgulimāla,
Dhanapāla, and Rāhula."
“Show me the Blessed One,” he begged again and again. Then they took him out on a litter.
Hearing of his arrival, the monks informed the Teacher: “Venerable sir, it is said that Devadatta is coming to see you.
“Monks, he shall not be permitted to see me in that state of existence. Devadatta...
It is said that from the moment he requested the five points, he was no longer permitted to see the Buddha again;
this is the natural law (*dhammatā*). [The monk said: “Venerable Sir, he has come from such-and-such a place and such-and-such a place. [The Buddha replied: “Let him do whatever he wishes;
he shall not be permitted to see me. [The monk continued: “Venerable Sir, he has come from a distance of one *yojana* from here, or half a *yojana*...”
“...a *gāvuta* away, having come near the Jetavana lotus pond, venerable sir. “Even if he enters within the Jetavana, he will not be able to see me.
Having brought Devadatta along, they lowered his bed onto the bank of the Jetavana lotus pond and descended into the pond to bathe. Devadatta, too, rose from the bed and both—
Having placed his foot on the ground, he sat down. His feet sank into the earth.
Gradually, they sank as far as the ankles, as far as the knees, as far as the hips, as far as the breasts, and as far as the neck; and when the jawbone had entered the earth—he [thought]:
"By these bones, that Supreme Person..."
“I go for refuge with my life to the Buddha, the God beyond gods, the Charioteer who tames men, the All-seeing One, marked with a hundred merits.”
He spoke this verse. It is said that upon seeing this situation, the Tathāgata ordained Devadatta.
For had he not been ordained, having remained a householder, he would have committed heavy deeds and would not have been able to create the conditions for escape from existence in the future;
but having been ordained, although he will indeed commit heavy deeds, in the future—
Thinking, "He will be able to create the condition for escape from existence," the Teacher ordained him.
For he was to become a Paccekabuddha named Aṭṭhissara one hundred thousand kappas hence; having entered the earth, he was reborn in Avīci.
However, because he had offended against a Buddha while he was still stationary, [the Teacher thought], "Let him suffer while remaining stationary," and within a range of one hundred yojanas—
In Avīci, his body was produced with a height of exactly one hundred yojanas. From the top of his head down to his ears, it entered an iron slab;
from his feet down to his ankles, it entered the iron ground.
An iron stake, as thick as the trunk of a great *tāla* tree, emerged from the western wall, pierced through the middle of his back, and exited through his chest, entering the eastern wall.
It entered; then, emerging from the southern wall, it pierced the southern side, emerged through the northern side, and entered the northern wall.
Next, emerging from the upper roof-plate, it pierced the top of the head, emerged through the lower part, and entered the iron earth.
Thus he was tormented there, remaining motionless.
The bhikkhus raised the discussion: "Devadatta entered the earth because he did not get to see the Teacher while coming this far.
The Teacher said, "Bhikkhus, it was not only now that Devadatta entered the earth after offending me;
he entered it even in the past," and having said this, [He related the story] of the man who had lost his way during the time of the elephant king.
Having comforted him, he placed him upon his back and carried him to a place of safety;
then, returning three times more, he broke off the tusks at the tip, in the middle, and at the base respectively, so that on the third occasion,
as the Great Being passed beyond the range of his vision, it might be made known that the elephant had entered the earth.
“For the person who is ungrateful, who always looks for flaws;
even if one were to give him the whole earth, one would never satisfy him.
Having related this Jātaka, when the same discussion arose once more, he [the Buddha] spoke of himself as having been Khantivādin.
In order to illustrate how that king, having become a *kalābu* tree, entered the earth after he had offended him, he related the *Khantivādijātaka*;
and in order to illustrate how that king, having become King Mahāpatāpa, entered the earth after he had offended him when he himself had become Cūḷa-Dhammapāla,
he related the *Cūḷadhammapālajātaka*.
When Devadatta had entered the earth, the great multitude was delighted and joyful;
they raised up banners, flags, and plantain trees, set out full water-jars, and celebrated a great festival, exclaiming, "What a gain for us! They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "Monks, it is not only now that the great multitude rejoices at the death of Devadatta; formerly as well..."

Having said, "He is indeed satisfied," in order to demonstrate the state of joy among the great multitude when Piṅgala— the king of Bārāṇasī, who was dear to no one, fierce, and cruel— had died, he said:
"All the people were oppressed by Piṅgala..."
While he was alive, conditions were experienced [by others];
was he indeed dear to you, O dark-eyed one?
Why do you weep, gatekeeper?
“The one with dark eyes was not dear to me;
I fear returning to him.
For if he goes from here, he might harm the King of Death.”
“Indeed, having been harmed, he would return here again.
Thus he related the Piṅgala Jātaka. The bhikkhus asked the Teacher, “Venerable sir, where has Devadatta now been reborn?
“In the great Avīci hell, bhikkhus,” he replied. “Venerable sir, having wandered about here suffering...”

"Having gone again, he was reborn in that very place of torment. "Yes, monks, whether they be renunciants or householders, those who dwell in negligence suffer in both places," and having said this, he spoke this verse:
"He suffers here, he suffers after death; the doer of evil suffers in both places."
“I have done evil,” he suffers; having gone to a state of misery, he suffers all the more.
Herein, “he suffers here” means he suffers with mere mental distress through the torment of his actions in this world.

But “after passing away” means that in the next world he suffers with the extremely harsh suffering of the states of deprivation (apāya) through the torment of the ripening [of karma]. “An evildoer” refers to one who has committed various kinds of evil.
The doer of evil. "In both respects" means that by means of this aforementioned kind of burning, one is said to burn in both ways.
"Evil has been done by me"—for he, brooding over it, burns with the thought, "An evil deed was committed by me. That is a minor form of burning;
however, burning with the burning of the result (vipāka), having gone to a state of misery, he burns even more intensely with exceedingly harsh torment.
"By burning, he burns all the more.
At the conclusion of the verse, many became stream-enterers and others. The teaching proved beneficial to the great multitude.
This is the twelfth story, concerning Devadatta.
13. The Story of Queen Sumanā.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning Queen Sumanā, beginning with the words, "One rejoices here.
For in Sāvatthī, two thousand bhikkhus daily ate at the house of Anāthapiṇḍika; likewise...
[This was] for the great female lay follower Visākhā. In Sāvatthī, whoever wished to give a gift had to do so only after obtaining the permission of both of them.
For what reason? Because, having been asked, "Has Anāthapiṇḍika or Visākhā arrived at the head of your almsgiving?
and being told, "They have not arrived," even a gift performed by spending a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] would be [regarded as incomplete]. What [then of other gifts]?
“They criticize it, saying, ‘This is called giving. For both of them know very well the inclinations and the appropriate duties of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus;
while they deliberate, the bhikkhus eat as they please. Therefore, all those who wish to give gifts take them along and depart.
Thus, they do not wait for the bhikkhus to be served in their own respective homes.”
They received [the offerings]. Then Visākhā, reflecting, "Who indeed will stand in my place and serve the Saṅgha of bhikkhus?
and searching for someone, saw her son’s daughter and established her in her own position. She served the Saṅgha of bhikkhus in her mother-in-law's residence.
Anāthapiṇḍika also established his eldest daughter, named Mahāsubhaddā; she [served] the bhikkhus...
While performing services and listening to the Dhamma, she became a stream-enterer (sotāpanna) and returned to her husband’s family. Thereafter, she appointed Cūḷasubhaddā;
she too, acting in the same manner, became a stream-enterer and went to her husband’s family. Then, she appointed her youngest daughter, named Sumanadevī.
Having heard the Dhamma, however, she attained the fruit of a once-returner (sakadāgāmiphala) while still a young maiden.
Having made such an offering, she became afflicted by an illness that caused her great discomfort. Desiring to see her father, she cut off her food and summoned him.
Upon hearing her message at the conclusion of a gift-offering, he came and asked, "What is it, dear Sumana?
She replied to him, "What is it, father, about my younger brother? "Are you lamenting, mother? "I am not lamenting."
“...your younger brother. “I am not afraid, mother; he is my younger brother. Having said only this much, she passed away.

Although he was a stream-enterer, being unable to endure the grief that had arisen for the merchant’s daughter, he performed the funeral rites for his daughter and went into the presence of the Teacher while weeping. “What is it, householder? [the Teacher asked.]
When he was told, "You have come here suffering, dejected, with a tearful face, weeping," he replied, "Venerable sir, my daughter Sumanadevī has passed away.
"Then why do you grieve? Is it not certain that death comes to everyone?
"I know this, venerable sir; yet such was my daughter, endowed with moral shame and fear of wrongdoing, that at the time of her death she was unable to establish mindfulness."
“Unable [to speak], she died while lamenting; because of that, a great deal of sorrow arises within me.
“But what did she say, Great Merchant? “I addressed her, venerable sir, saying, ‘Mother Sumana.
Then she said to me: ‘What is it, dear one? ‘Are you lamenting, mother? ‘I am not lamenting, dear younger brother.’”
“‘Are you afraid, mother? ‘I am not afraid, younger brother,’ she said. Having said this much, she passed away.
Then the Blessed One said to him, “Your daughter, great merchant, is not lamenting. “But why, Bhante, did you say that? “Precisely because she was your younger [sister].
For your daughter, householder, has surpassed you by means of the paths and fruits. You, indeed, are a stream-enterer.”
“However, your daughter is a once-returner (*sakadāgāminī*). Because she is senior to you in terms of the fruits of the path, she spoke to you thus.
“Yes, venerable sir. “Yes, householder. “But where has she been reborn now, venerable sir? “In the Tusita heaven, householder.
“Venerable sir, my daughter, having lived here among her kinsmen in joy, even after departing from this world...”

“They were reborn right in the Nandana Grove. Then the Teacher said to him, “Yes, householder, whether they be householders or those who have gone forth, those who are heedful truly rejoice both in this world and in the world beyond,” and he spoke this verse:
“He rejoices here, he rejoices after passing away; having performed merit, he rejoices in both places.”
“He rejoices, thinking, ‘Merit has been done by me’; having gone to a happy destination, he rejoices even more.

In this context, “here” means he rejoices in this world through the rejoicing over his deeds. “After passing away” means he rejoices in the next world through the rejoicing over the result [of those deeds].
“One who has done merit” is one who is a doer of various kinds of merit. “In both places” means here, [thinking] “I have done what is wholesome,”...
One rejoices thinking, "I have not done evil," and rejoices while experiencing the result in the future.
But one who rejoices here thinking, "Merit has been done by me," rejoices by means of the very joy of the thought "merit has been done by me," based on the delight in the action itself.
Furthermore, having gone to a happy destination through the delight in the result, for fifty-seven hundred thousand million years and six million years...
"Experiencing divine splendor, he rejoices exceedingly in the Tusita city.
At the conclusion of the verses, many became stream-enterers and others. The teaching of the Dhamma became fruitful for the great multitude.
This is the thirteenth story, the Story of Queen Sumanā.
14. The Story of the Two Companion Monks.
While residing at Jetavana, the Teacher related this Dhamma instruction concerning two companions.
For there were two young men of good family living in Sāvatthī who, having become companions, went to the monastery and heard the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse.

Having abandoned sensual pleasures, having gone forth into the Dispensation with sincere resolve, and having lived for five years in the presence of his preceptor and teacher, he approached the Teacher and asked about the responsibilities within the Dispensation.

Having heard in detail about the responsibility of insight (*vipassanā-dhura*) and the responsibility of study (*gantha-dhura*), he first said: "Venerable Sir, I went forth at an advanced age; I shall not be able to undertake the responsibility of study."
“I shall fulfill the duty of insight (vipassanādhura),” he resolved;
thus, having been assigned the duty of insight until he reached Arahantship, he strove and exerted himself, attaining Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).

The other, however, thinking, “I shall fulfill the duty of the scriptures (ganthadhura),” gradually mastered the word of the Buddha consisting of the Three Baskets (Tipiṭaka) and preached the Dhamma wherever he went.
He expounded the Dhamma, recited the Sarabhañña, and wandered about teaching the Dhamma to five hundred bhikkhus.
He was the teacher of eighteen great assemblies. Bhikkhus who had received a meditation subject from the Teacher went to the dwelling place of that other elder;
by abiding in his instruction, they attained arahantship and [honored] the elder.
Having paid homage, they said, "We wish to see the Teacher. The Elder sent them off, saying, "Go, friends;
having paid homage to the Teacher in my name, pay homage to the eighty great elders, and say to my friend the Elder, 'Our teacher pays homage to you.
Those monks went to the monastery and [paid homage] to the Teacher and the eighty...
Having paid homage to the Great Elder, they went into the presence of the Elder Gaṇṭhika and said, "Venerable sir, our teacher pays homage to you.
When the other asked, "Who is he by name? they replied, "He is your friend, the monk, venerable sir.
As the elders sent word back and forth in this manner again and again, that monk waited for a short while.
Having associated with him, when he was unable to associate with him later on, and it was said, "Our teacher pays homage to you," he asked, "Who is this?
When it was said, "He is a bhikkhu who was your companion," he asked, "But what did you learn from him?
Is it one of the Nikāyas such as the Dīghanikāya, or is it one of the Piṭakas among the three?"
Having said this, he thought: "He does not know even a four-line stanza; having taken up rag-robe rags at the very time of his going forth, he entered the forest.
Indeed, he has gained many pupils; it is fitting that I ask him a question when he arrives.
Later on, the elder came to see the Teacher. [The Teacher] [placed] the bowl and robes in the presence of his friend, the elder.
Setting them aside and departing, he paid homage to the Teacher and the eighty great elders, then returned to the dwelling place of his friend.
After that friend had him perform the duties of hospitality and provided him with a seat of equal measure, he sat down, thinking, "I shall ask a question.
At that moment, the Teacher thought, "If this man were to harass my son in such a manner, he would be reborn in hell."
Out of compassion for them, as if on a routine visit to the monastery, he went to the place where they were sitting and sat upon the excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared.
For wherever monks sit, they do so only after having prepared a Buddha-seat.
Therefore, the Teacher sat on the seat already prepared by custom. Having sat down, he [addressed] the monk Gaṇṭhika regarding the first jhāna.

Having asked a question about that [first jhāna] and not receiving an answer, he asked questions regarding all eight attainments—beginning with the second jhāna—as well as concerning the realms of form and the formless.
Thera Gaṇthika was unable to explain even a single one. The other, however, explained them all.
Then he asked a question regarding the path of stream-entry. Thera Gaṇthika was again unable to explain it. Thereupon, he questioned the Elder Khīṇāsava.
He asked. The Elder explained. The Teacher, having expressed his approval, saying, "Excellent, excellent, monks," asked questions in successive order regarding the remaining paths as well.
Gaṇṭhika was unable to explain even a single one; however, the one whose taints were destroyed (khīṇāsava) explained each question as it was asked.
The Teacher gave him his applause for all four points. Having heard this, the earth-deities...
Beginning from the very outset up to the Brahma-world, all the deities as well as the nāgas and supaṇṇas gave their applause.
Hearing that applause, his pupils and co-residents complained against the Teacher, saying:
"What is this that has been done by the Teacher? Why did he give his applause in four places to an elderly elder who knows nothing at all?"
"He gave [to others], yet he did not offer even a word of praise for our teacher, who was a master of the entire scriptural tradition and the leader of five hundred bhikkhus.
Then the Teacher asked them, "Bhikkhus, what is this you are talking about?
When the matter had been reported, he said, "Bhikkhus, your teacher is like one who guards cattle for hire in my dispensation."
"But my son is like a man who enjoys the five products of the cow according to his own whim," he said, and then spoke these verses:
"Even if one speaks much that is well-composed,
if that heedless man does not act accordingly..."
One who counts the cattle of others like a cowherd does not partake in the fruit of the ascetic life.
Even if one speaks but a little that is well-composed...
He practices in accordance with the Dhamma;
having abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion,
he is possessed of right clear comprehension and is well-liberated in mind.
“Not grasping at anything here or in the world beyond, he becomes a partaker of the fruit of recluseship.
In this context, *saṃhita* is a name for the word of the Buddha consisting of the Three Piṭakas. Having approached a teacher...
Having learned much and speaking or teaching it to others, even upon hearing that Dhamma, he does not act in accordance with what must be done by a person who practices it.
He does not apply proper attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) even for as long as a cock flaps its wings, contemplating [the object] through such aspects as impermanence (*anicca*).
He is like a cowherd who, having guarded his cattle for hire all day long, [leaves them] at dawn without exception...
Having accepted it and taken it in the evening, she delivers it to her owners and receives only her daily wage;
yet she is not permitted to consume the five products of the cow as she pleases.
In the same way, one merely partakes in the performance of duties and services for the sake of the pupils, but does not partake in the fruit of asceticism itself. Just as...

Just as the owners themselves enjoy the dairy products of the cows delivered by the cowherd, so too, having heard the Dhamma spoken by him, those individuals who practice according to the instructions reach the first jhāna and so forth;

some, having developed insight, reach the paths and fruits. Thus, they become partakers of the "dairy" of the common goal (sāmañña), just like the owners of the cows are partakers of the dairy products.

Thus the Teacher spoke the first verse concerning a monk who is endowed with virtue and is very learned, yet dwells in negligence and is heedless regarding wise attention (yonisomanasikāra) through such aspects as impermanence; it was not spoken concerning one who is immoral.
The second verse, however, was spoken concerning a person who, though of little learning, performs the work of wise attention.
In this context, "even a little" (*appam pi*) means even a small amount, such as a single chapter or two chapters.

"One who lives in accordance with the Dhamma" (*dhammassa hoti anudhammacārī*) means that, having understood the meaning and understood the Dhamma, one who practices the Dhamma corresponding to the nine supramundane states—the preliminary path consisting of the fourfold purification, the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), the meditation subjects on foulness (*asubha-kammaṭṭhāna*), and so forth—is one who lives in accordance with the Dhamma (*anudhammacārī*). He...
“Today, indeed today!”—thus he wanders about desiring realization.

By means of this right practice, having abandoned lust and hatred, and having fully understood delusion through the correct cause and method regarding those phenomena that are to be fully understood, his mind is well-liberated by way of liberation through its constituent parts (*tadaṅga*), suppression (*vikkhambhana*), eradication (*samuccheda*), subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi*), and renunciation (*nissaraṇa*).
Not grasping at anything, whether in this world or the world beyond—that is, included within this world or the next world—[he remains].
Not grasping at internal or external aggregates, bases, and elements by means of the four kinds of clinging, he— having become one whose great taints are destroyed—

becomes a partaker of the "fruition-asceticism" (phalasāmañña) that comes by way of the asceticism known as the Path, and of the five aggregates of dhammas pertaining to those beyond training (asekha).
Thus, as if with a pinnacle of jewels, he took the summit of the teaching through his attainment of Arahatship.
At the conclusion of the verses, many became stream-enterers and others. The teaching thus proved beneficial to the great multitude.
This is the fourteenth story, concerning the two companion monks.
The commentary on the Yamaka Vagga is finished.
The First Chapter. 2.
The Chapter on Heedfulness. 1.
The Story of Sāmāvatī.
The Teacher, while residing at Ghosita’s Monastery near Kosambī, delivered this Dhamma teaching— "Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless"—
with reference to the calamity of death that befell five hundred women headed by Sāmāvatī, and five hundred kinswomen headed by Māgaṇḍiyā.

In this regard, the sequential narrative is as follows: In the past, in the kingdom of Allakappa there was a king named Allakappa-rāja, and in the kingdom of Veṭhadīpaka there was a king named Veṭhadīpaka-rāja.
These two, having been friends since childhood, learned their crafts in the same teacher’s household;
and upon the passing away of their respective fathers, they raised the royal parasol over territories each ten times ten yojanas in extent.
There were kings over the realm. From time to time, meeting together, they would stand, sit, and lie down as one;
seeing the great multitude being born, growing old, and dying, they thought: "There is no such thing as following one who goes to the next world;
even one's own body does not follow. One must go leaving everything behind. Why [grieve]?"

Having deliberated, "We shall not live the household life; we shall go forth," they entrusted their kingdoms to their wives and children, went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, and while dwelling in the Himalayan region, they reflected:
"We have gone forth having abandoned our kingdoms, not because we were unable to live [at home]. If we dwell in one place, we are just like those who have not gone forth. Therefore—"
“We shall dwell separately. You may dwell on this mountain, and I shall dwell on this mountain;
however, on every half-monthly Uposatha day, we shall come together. Then it occurred to them: “Even so, there will still be the socializing of a group.
But you should kindle a fire on your mountain, and I shall kindle a fire on my mountain.”
“By means of that sign, we shall know his existence. They did accordingly.
Later on, the ascetic of Veṭhadīpa passed away and was reborn as a powerful king of the gods.
When half a month had elapsed, the other, not seeing any fire, realized, “My companion has died. The other [the deity] also—
At the very moment of his rebirth, having observed his own divine splendor and reflecting upon his past karma, he saw his practice of asceticism from the time of his departure.

Thinking, "I shall go and see my companion," he discarded that celestial form and, like a traveler on the road, went into his presence, paid homage, and stood to one side. Then he [the companion] said to him:
He asked, "Where have you come from? "I am a man from Maggika, venerable sir; I have come from afar.
But, venerable sir, why does the master live alone in this place? Is there no one else here? "I have one companion. "Where is he?
"He lives on this mountain; however, on the Uposatha day, he does not kindle a fire, for he is dead."
“Surely it will be so. “Is that so, venerable sir? “It is so, friend. “I am he, venerable sir.
“Where have you been reborn? “Venerable sir, I have been reborn as a king of great power in the world of the devas;
I have come back again because I thought, ‘I shall see the noble ones. Is there perhaps some danger for the noble ones dwelling in this place?”
“Yes, friend, I am weary because of the elephants. “What do the elephants do to you, venerable sir?
“They drop dung in the place where we sweep; they kick up dust with their feet on the ground.
Thus, while I am clearing away the dung and smoothing out the dust, I become weary. “But do you wish for them not to come back? “Yes, friend.”
“Very well then, I shall ensure they do not come back,” he thought, and he gave the ascetic both the elephant-enticing lute and the elephant-enticing spell.
While giving them, however, he showed him three strings on the lute and had him learn three spells, saying:
“When you strike this string and recite this spell, the elephants will flee so swiftly that they will not even turn back to look.”
"Having struck this cord and when this mantra is recited, they turn back and flee, looking back again and again;
and having struck this cord and when this mantra is recited, even the leader of the elephant herd comes forward, presenting his back.
Having explained this, he said, "Do as you please," and after paying homage to the ascetic, he departed. The ascetic—
Having spoken the "fleeing-spell" and struck the "fleeing-chord," he caused the elephant to flee and took possession of it.
At that time, there was a king in Kosambī named Pūrantappa.
One day, he sat on an open terrace with his queen, who was pregnant, basking in the heat of the morning sun. The queen’s cloak was worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold].
Seated there, wearing a red woolen blanket and conversing with the king, she took from the king’s finger the royal seal-ring worth a hundred thousand pieces and placed it on her own finger.
At that moment, a bird called a *hatthiliṅga*,
traveling through the air, saw the queen from afar wearing the red woolen blanket and perceived her as a "piece of meat."
Having spread its wings, it descended. Terrified by the sound of its descent, the king rose up and entered his inner apartments.
Because of her advanced pregnancy and her timid nature, the queen was unable to move quickly.
Then that bird swooped down upon her, made her sit within the cage of its talons, and soared into the sky. It is said that those birds [belonged to] the five...
They carry the strength of elephants. Therefore, having carried her through the air and seated her in a place according to their pleasure, they eat the flesh.
As she was being carried by them, terrified by the fear of death, she thought: "If I cry out, the sound of a human is indeed terrifying to animals;
hearing it, they will abandon me. If that happens, I shall perish along with my fetus."
"I shall reach the end of my life; however, at whatever place he begins to eat me while I am sitting, I will make a noise there and cause him to flee. Through her own wisdom, she consented.
At that time, in a region of the Himalayas, there was a great banyan tree that had grown somewhat large and stood like a pavilion.
Thus, that bird would take deer and other animals there and devour them;

therefore, having taken him as well to that very place and placed him within the branches, he looked back along the path by which he had come. For it is said to be their nature to look back along the path they have traveled.
At that moment, the queen thought, "Now it is time to make him flee," and raising both her hands, she made a clapping sound with her palms.
Having made a sound with her mouth, she caused her to flee. Then, at the time of sunset, the winds born of karma stirred within her womb.
A great rain-cloud arose, thundering in all directions.
To the queen-consort, who was suffering intensely and could not obtain even a single word of comfort such as "Do not fear, noble lady," there was no sleep throughout the entire night.
As the night was turning into dawn, the dispersal of the clouds, the rising of the sun,
and her delivery from the womb occurred all at the same moment. Because she gave birth to her son while experiencing the conditions of the rainy season, the mountain climate, and the time of sunrise,
she gave the child the name Utena.
The dwelling place of the ascetic Allakappa was also not far from there.
By his very nature, on the day of the rains, he would not enter the forest for the sake of fruits and roots out of fear of the cold;

instead, having gone to that foot of a tree, he would bring back bones of meat eaten by birds, pound them, extract the essence, and drink it. Therefore, on that day, [he thought], "I shall fetch some bones."
Having gone there and searching for bones at the foot of a tree, he heard the sound of a child above; looking up, he saw the goddess and asked, "Who are you?
She replied, "I am a human woman. He asked, "How did you come here? When she said, "I was brought by the bird Hatthiliṅga," he said, "Come down.
She replied, "I fear the loss of my caste, noble sir. He asked, "What caste are you? She said, "I am a kṣatriya."
“I am a kshatriya as well,” he replied. “In that case, speak with the pride of a kshatriya,” he said. He spoke with the pride of a kshatriya.
“Then, having climbed up, take my son down,” he said. Having made a path for climbing by one side, he climbed up and took the boy.
When it was said, “Do not touch me with your hand,” he took the boy down without touching him at all.
The goddess also descended. Then, having led her to the hermitage, he tended to her out of compassion without breaking his virtue;
he brought honey free from flies, fetched wild-growing rice, cooked it into gruel, and gave it to her.
While he was thus tending to her, she later thought: "I know neither the path by which I came nor the path by which I must go."
“I know that there is not even a mere measure of trust between us. However, if he should abandon us and go elsewhere, we both will meet our death right here.
Therefore, by whatever means necessary, it is right to break his virtue so that he does not leave me. Then, by showing him poorly dressed and poorly clad...

Having enticed him, she brought about the destruction of his virtue. From that time on, the two of them lived together in harmony. “Do you have resentment toward him? “No, Bhaddā; it was because I saw his face looking withered by the stars that I spoke thus,” she said, and she wept.
Then, having asked her, “Why do you weep? and once she had declared to him that he was her husband, he said, “Do not weep, Bhaddā;
for one who is born, death is indeed certain. When she replied, “I know this, noble sir,” he said:
“Then why do you weep, O Rodasī? “My son is worthy of the kingdom inherited by my family;
had he been there, I would have raised the white parasol. Now he has been born as one who will surely bring great loss—out of grief for this, noble lady, I weep.
“Be at ease, blessed lady; do not worry. If he desires the kingdom, I shall provide the means for him to obtain it.”
“I shall do so. Then he gave him both a lute that mimicked the cry of an elephant and the spells for making elephants cry out.
At that time, many thousands of elephants came and sat at the foot of the banyan tree. Then he said to him: “Before the elephants have even arrived, climb the tree;
when they have come, recite this spell and strike this string, and they will all turn back.”
“Even those who are unable to look back will flee; then you should descend and come up.
He did so, and having returned, he reported what had happened. Then, on the second day, he said to him: “Today, after reciting this mantra, you should strike this rope;
all of them, looking back, will flee. On that occasion also, he did exactly so.
Having done so, he returned and reported it. Then, on the third day, he said to him: "Today, having recited this mantra, you should strike this string;
the leader of the herd will come along, presenting his back. He did exactly that once more and reported it. Then, addressing his mother, he said:
"Noble lady, please deliver this message to your son: 'The King has come from just this far.'"
“So it shall be,” he said. She addressed her son, saying, “Dear child, you are the son of King Pūrantappa of Kosambī;

a female elephant-heron brought me here while I was pregnant. Having spoken thus, she announced the names of the commander-in-chief and the others, and said, “If they do not believe you, you should show them this blanket with which your father wrapped himself, as well as his signet ring,” and then she sent him forth.

The prince asked the ascetic, "What shall I do now? He replied, "Sit beneath the lowest branch of this tree, recite this mantra, and strike this lute-string. An elder elephant will approach, placing its back near you;
sitting upon its back, go to the kingdom and seize the sovereignty. Having paid homage to his parents, he departed.
Having done so, he sat upon the back of the elephant that had arrived and whispered in its ear:
"I am the son of King Pūrantappa of Kosambī; having seized my paternal kingdom, give it to me, O Master!
Hearing this, the elephant let out a trumpeting cry, saying, "Let many thousands of elephants assemble! and many thousands of elephants assembled.
Again, he let out a trumpeting cry, saying, "Let the old elephants retreat! and the old elephants retreated.
Again, he let out a trumpeting cry, saying, "Let the very young elephants turn back! and they too turned back.
Surrounded by many thousands of herd-elephants, he reached a frontier village and said, "I am the king’s son; those who desire prosperity [should come] with me."
"Let them come," he said. From then on, gathering a multitude of men, he went and surrounded the city, sending a message:
"Give me either battle or the kingdom. The citizens replied, "We will give neither.
For our queen was carried off by the elephant-sign bird while she was heavily pregnant; we do not even know whether she still exists or—"
"Or rather, we do not know her non-existence; until we hear news of her whereabouts, we will neither give battle nor hand over the kingdom.
At that time, it was indeed an ancestral sovereignty.
Then the prince, saying "I am her son," and having stated the names of the commander-in-chief and the others, gave a blanket and a seal-ring to those who still did not believe him.
He showed them. Having recognized both the blanket and the ring, they became free from doubt, opened the gate, and consecrated him in the kingdom.
This, then, was the origin of Udena.
However, during a famine in the kingdom of Allakappa, a certain man named Kotuhalika, being unable to survive, [took] a kāpi...
Taking his young son and his wife named Kāḷī, he set out with provisions for the journey, thinking, "I will go to Kosambī and live there.
Some even say that he departed after seeing the great multitude of people dying from the plague of snake-bite (*ahivātaro ga*).
As they traveled, when their provisions were exhausted, they were overcome by hunger and were unable to carry the child. Then—
The husband said to his wife, “My dear, as long as we live we shall obtain another son; let us abandon him and go.
A mother’s heart is indeed tender. Therefore she said, “I cannot bring myself to abandon my son while he is still alive.
“Then what shall we do? “Let us take turns carrying him. The mother [then took her turn].
Lifting her up like a garland of flowers on a festival day, he laid her upon his chest, carried her in his arms, and gave her to his father.
As he was taking her away after receiving her, even stronger than the pain of hunger, a sensation arose within him.
Again and again he said, "My dear, as long as we live, we shall have our son; let us not abandon him. She too, again and again—
Having refused, she gave no reply. As it was his turn to carry him, the boy grew weary and fell asleep in his father’s hands.
Knowing that he was sleeping, the father placed his mother in front and, laying the child down upon a bed of leaves beneath a certain tree, set out on his way.
The mother turned back and, looking about, not seeing her son, cried out, “Husband!”
“Where is my son? she asked. “He was laid down beneath a certain tree,” they replied.
“Master, do not destroy me! I cannot live without my son; bring my son back to me! she lamented, beating her breast. Then, having turned back, he brought him [home].
Yet the son had already died on the way. Thus, in all these places, he [searched] for his son.
Having abandoned it, as a result of that, he was abandoned seven times in other existences. One should not underestimate this, thinking, "This evil deed is but a small matter.
As they were traveling, they reached a certain cowherd's family. On that day, the cowherd had a ceremony for his milch-cow.
A certain paccekabuddha used to eat regularly at the cowherd's house; having fed him, the cowherd performed the auspicious rite.
A great deal of milk-rice had been prepared. When the cowherd saw them arrive, he asked, "From where have you come?
and having heard the whole account, this gentle clansman felt compassion for them and had the milk-rice served with a large amount of ghee.
His wife said, "Husband, as long as you live, I too shall live; for a long time you have been hungry."
"Eat as much as you desire," he said; and having placed the ghee and curd directly before him, he himself ate only a small amount with a little ghee.
The other, however, ate a great deal, and for seven or eight days he was unable to quell his craving for food due to hunger.
When the cowherd had caused them to be given the milk-rice, he began to eat it himself. The curious man watched him closely.
Having sat down, he saw a ball of milk-rice being offered by a cowherd to a bitch lying beneath his seat.
Seeing this, he thought, "This bitch must indeed be meritorious; she receives such food regularly.
Being unable to digest that milk-rice during the night, he died and was reborn in the womb of that same bitch.
Then his wife, having performed the funeral rites for him, worked for wages in that very same house;
having obtained a measure of rice, she cooked it, placed it in the bowl of the Paccekabuddha, and said, "May this reach you, my slave," and thought:
"It is fitting for me to live right here; the noble one comes here regularly; whether there is a gift to be given or not..."
"Or rather, by worshipping daily, performing services, and gladdening my heart, I shall produce much merit.
She remained right there, working for wages. That female dog, too, gave birth to only a single puppy every sixth or seventh month.
The cowherd had the milk from one cow given to it. Before long, it grew large.
As he was eating, the Paccekabuddha would regularly give him a single morsel of alms-food.
Relying on that morsel of food, the cowherd developed affection for the Paccekabuddha. The cowherd also went regularly twice a day to attend upon the Paccekabuddha.
Even while walking along the path, when he encountered wild beasts, he would strike the bushes and the ground with his staff.
By making the sound "susū" three times, he drove away the wild beasts; the dog also went along with him.
One day, he said to a Paccekabuddha: "Venerable sir, when there is no opportunity for me, I shall send this dog;
you may come by that sign. From then on, on days when there was no opportunity, [he sent the dog].
“Go, dear one, and bring the noble sir,” he said, sending the dog.
At a single word, the dog sprang forward and barked three times at the spot where his master used to trample the ground with his feet.
Knowing from that sound that the wild beasts had fled, he attended to his body early in the morning, entered the leaf-hut, and [approached] the Paccekabuddha who was seated there.
Having gone to his dwelling place, he coughed three times at the door of the leaf-hut to let it be known that he had arrived, and then lay down to one side.
When the Paccekabuddha, having observed the time, set out, he followed behind, coughing as he went.
From time to time, the Paccekabuddha, testing him, would take another path; then [the man] went before him.

Standing across the path and barking, he would cause him to enter the other road. Then one day, having set out upon another path, even though the dog stood across his way in front and tried to restrain him, he did not turn back;
instead, he struck the dog with his foot and proceeded.
The dog, realizing that he would not turn back, bit the hem of his lower garment and pulled at it, [forcing him] onto the other road.
He placed it [on the Paccekabuddha]. In this way, he developed a strong affection for him.
Later on, the Paccekabuddha’s robe became worn out. Then the cowherd gave him pieces of cloth for a robe.
The Paccekabuddha said to him: "Friend, it is difficult to make a robe by oneself; one needs a comfortable place..."
“I will go and have it built. “Venerable sir, please build it right here. “It is not possible, friend.

“In that case, venerable sir, do not stay outside for long. The dog stood there listening to their conversation, while the Paccekabuddha, saying “Wait, lay follower,” turned back the cowherd, rose into the air, and headed toward Mount Gandhamādana.
Pāyāsi. Seeing the dog traveling through the air, he let out a cry and stood still;
when the dog passed from his sight, his heart burst and he died. Indeed, these animals are said to be of an upright nature and not crooked.
But humans think one thing with their hearts and speak another with their mouths. For this very reason it was said: "This is a thicket."
“Venerable sir, as for these humans, they are shallow; as for these cattle, venerable sir, they are even more shallow.
Because of that straightforwardness and lack of crookedness, when he passed away, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven surrounded by a thousand celestial nymphs, where he enjoyed great prosperity.
As he whispered into his ear, the sound spread across an area of sixteen yojanas.

The sound of his ordinary conversation, however, covered the entire city of the gods, ten thousand *yojanas* in extent. For that very reason, he received the name "Ghosaka-devaputta" (the Son of the Gods Ghosaka).
[Question: "What was the cause of this? [Answer: It was the result of shouting out of affection for a *paccekabuddha*.
He did not remain there for long and passed away; for from the world of the gods, sons of the gods fall due to the exhaustion of their lifespan or the exhaustion of their merit.
They pass away due to four causes: exhaustion of nutriment and anger.
Among these, one who has performed much meritorious karma, having arisen in the world of the devas and remained there for the full span of his lifespan, is reborn in progressively higher realms.
This is what is called passing away through the exhaustion of the lifespan. One who has performed limited merit...
Just as three or four *nāḷi* measures of grain placed in a king’s granary are exhausted in the interim, he likewise exhausts that merit and passes away in the interim.
This is what is called "passing away through the exhaustion of merit. Furthermore, another person, while enjoying the strands of sensual pleasure, forgets his food due to a lapse of mindfulness;
with his body weakened by hunger, he passes away. This is what is called "passing away through the exhaustion of food."
One indeed passes away [through anger]. Another, unable to endure another’s prosperity, dies while filled with rage; thus one indeed passes away through anger.
But this man, while enjoying the strands of sensual pleasure, became muddled in mindfulness and passed away due to the exhaustion of his food.
Having passed away, he took rebirth in the womb of a courtesan in the city of Kosambī. On the day she was born, [she asked]: "What..."

Having asked the slave-girl, "Is this so?", and being told, "It is a son, mistress," she said, "Well then, girl, place this child on a bamboo litter and throw him away on a heap of refuse. For the beauties of the city cared for their daughters, not their sons;
by means of a daughter, their lineage was maintained. Then crows and dogs surrounded the child.
They sat down. Because of the sound of their crying, which arose from their affection for the Paccekabuddha, not even a single person dared to approach.
At that moment, a certain man who had gone outside saw the gathering of crows and dogs;
wondering, "What is this?", he went over, saw the boy, and feeling the affection of a father, thought, "I have found a son."
He led him home. At that time, as the Kosambaka merchant was going to the royal palace, he saw the court chaplain returning from the king’s residence and asked, “What is it, teacher?
Have you observed the lunar day, the calendar, and the conjunction of the stars today? “Yes, great merchant; what other business do we have?
What will happen to the country? “There is nothing else; in this—”
"However, the infant born today in the city will become the chief merchant. At that time, the merchant’s wife was heavily pregnant.
Therefore, he quickly sent a man to his house, saying, "Go, my good man, and find out whether she has given birth or not.
Having heard that she had not yet given birth, and having seen the king, he returned home in haste and [instructed] the maidservant named Kāḷī.
Having summoned her and given her a thousand [pieces of money], he said, "Go, my girl;
having investigated this city and paid a thousand, bring back a newborn boy born today. She, while investigating, went to that house and, seeing the boy, asked the housewife, "When was this boy born?
When she replied, "He was born today," she said, "This one for me..."
Saying, "Give it to me," she began with a single kahāpaṇa and, increasing the principal, gave a thousand and brought him back to show him to the merchant.
The merchant thought, "If my daughter gives birth, I will marry her to him and make him the master of the merchant's estate;
but if my son gives birth, I will kill him. Having thought thus, he had him made a resident in his house.
Then, after a few days had passed, his wife gave birth to a son. The merchant thought, "If this boy does not exist, my own son will obtain the position of treasurer;
it is fitting that I kill him right now. Having thought thus, he addressed Kālī:
"Go, girl; at the time when the cattle are leaving the pen, lay this child across the middle of the gate."
"The cows will trample and kill him; however, once you have discerned whether he has been trampled or not, you may come back," she said.
She went there and, as soon as the gate was opened by the cowherd, laid the elephant down in that manner.
Although the bull, the leader of the herd, usually went out last of all at other times, on that day he went out first of all.
He stood placing the boy between his four legs. Several hundred cows emerged, rubbing their two flanks against the bull.
The cowherd also thought, "This bull used to come out last of all;
but today, having come out first of all, he stands motionless in the middle of the gate. What could this be?"
Having reflected and gone there, she saw a boy lying beneath him; overcome with maternal affection, she thought, "I have found a son," and took him home.
When Kāḷī returned and was questioned by the merchant, she reported the matter to him, saying, "Go, give another thousand [pieces of gold] and [bring him back]."
When she was told, "Bring her," Kāḷī gave a thousand [pieces of money] and brought her back again, handing her over. Then he said to her:
"Mother Kāḷī, five hundred carts in this city set out for trade at dawn;
having led her there, make her lie down on the track of the wheels. Either the oxen will trample her, or the wheels will crush her. [Report] the news..."
“Having known this, you should come. She led him there and had him lie down on the path of the wheels.
At that time, the chief of the carters was at the front. When his oxen reached that spot, they dropped their yoke;
though they were repeatedly harnessed and driven, they would not move forward. Thus, even as he was struggling with them, dawn broke.
Thinking, "What indeed have the oxen done? he looked along the road and saw the boy.
Reflecting, "Alas, what a heavy task I have undertaken," his heart was filled with joy at the thought, "I have gained a son. He took him home.
When Kāḷī returned and was questioned by the merchant, she related the events to him, saying, "Go; give him another thousand [pieces of gold]."
Having been told, "Give it and bring it back," she did accordingly. Then he said to her, "Now, having led him to the raw charnel ground, lay him down between two trees;
there he will die, either eaten by dogs and such creatures or struck down by non-human beings.
You must return only after you have ascertained that he is truly dead. She led him there, laid him down, and stood aside.
He stood there. Neither dog, nor crow, nor non-human being was able to approach him.
[The questioner asks: "But surely he has no mother, no father, and no brother or anyone else who might be called his protector; who protects him?
It is protected by nothing more than the mere sound of barking that arose from his affection for the Paccekabuddha during the time he was a dog. Then, a certain goat-herder...
Leading several thousand goats to their pasture, he was walking along the side of a cemetery. One goat, while grazing on leaves, entered the thicket;
seeing the boy, she stood on her hind legs and gave him her teat.
Even when the goat-herd called out "He! He!", she did not come out. [The herder] thought, "I will strike her with my staff and drive her out," and went into the thicket.
Having entered and stood on his knees, he saw a goat nursing her kid;
having conceived a motherly affection for the child, thinking, "I have found a son," he took him and departed.
Kāḷī went and, when questioned by the merchant, explained what had happened, saying, "Go, [pay] that thousand again."
Having been told, "Give it to him and bring him back," she did exactly so. Then he said to her, "Mother Kāḷī, take this man, climb the Corapapāta mountain, and throw him over the precipice.
Striking against the interior of the mountain, he will fall to the ground in pieces;
once you have ascertained whether he is dead or alive, you may return. She led him there and, standing on the summit of the mountain, said:
Standing there, he threw it. Now, that great bamboo thicket had grown along the side of the mountain, leaning against its interior;
at its summit, a dense cluster of *jiñjuka* trees had spread over it. As the boy fell, he landed upon it as if on a woolen rug.
On that very day, the head of the reed-makers had received his share of the bamboo tribute. He [was accompanied] by his son...
Having gone together with him, he began to cut down that bamboo thicket. As it shook, the boy made a sound.
Thinking, "That is the sound of a child," he climbed up by one side; seeing him, and thinking with a joyful heart, "I have found my son," he took him and departed.
Kāḷī went to the merchant’s presence, and when questioned by him, she explained what had happened.
Told, “Go, give him another thousand and bring him back,” she did so.
While the merchant was doing this and that for him, the boy grew up, and his name became Ghosaka. He [stayed] like a thorn in the merchant’s eye.
He was so crooked that he could not even look straight ahead. While contemplating a means to kill him, he went to his friend the potter, asked, "When will you fire the kiln?
and when told, "Tomorrow," he said, "In that case, take this thousand pieces of money and do a job for me. [The potter asked,] "What is it, master?"
“I have an only son of low birth; I will send him to you.
Then, having seized him and placed him in a cauldron, cut him into pieces with a sharp axe and cook him in the boiling oil.
This thousand coins shall be like a guarantee for your truthfulness. As for whatever else is appropriate for you to do thereafter, we shall arrange that later.”
The potter accepted, saying, “Very well. On the following day, the merchant summoned Ghosaka and sent him off, saying, “Yesterday I commanded the potter to perform a certain task;
go to him and say, ‘Please complete the work that was commanded by my father yesterday. He replied, “Very well,” and went there. While he was there—
As he was going along, the other son of the merchant saw him playing with the children at dice;

having called out to him and asked, "Where are you going, brother? and being told, "I am going to the potter's place on my father's message," [the merchant's son said], "I will go there myself. These children have won much from me at dice; having won that back from them..."
“Give it to me,” he said. “I am afraid of my father,” [the other] replied. “Do not fear, brother; I shall carry that message.
He has been defeated by many; until I return, please stake your winnings on my behalf.
It is said that Ghosaka was skilled at dice games, and for that reason he bound him with these words. He too then told him, “In that case, go and [inform] the potter...”
"Tell him: 'My father, it seems, was commanded by you yesterday to perform a certain task; please complete it,'" and having said this, he sent him away.
He went to the potter and spoke thus. Then the potter killed him according to the very instructions given by the merchant and threw him into the cesspool.
Ghosaka, too, having played for part of the day, went home at evening time and asked, "What?"
When he was told, "Father, you have not gone," he related both the reason for his own failure to go and the reason why his younger brother had gone.
Upon hearing this, the merchant cried out with a great roar, "Alas, I am ruined!
and as if his entire body were ablaze with boiling blood, he threw up his arms and wailed, "O potter, do not ruin me! Do not ruin me!"
He went into his presence. Seeing him approaching in that manner, the potter said, "Master, do not make a sound;

your work is finished. He was overwhelmed by a grief as vast as a mountain and experienced no small amount of dejection, like one who has committed an offense against someone who is innocent. Regarding this, the Blessed One said:
“He who, with a stick, strikes those who do not strike back,
who are innocent and free from malice— he quickly encounters one of ten states:
he experiences harsh pain, loss of wealth, or the breaking up of his body.”
One may encounter a severe illness, or even a lapse of mind;
or a calamity from the king, or a terrible false accusation;
or the ruin of kinsmen, and the fragility of wealth.
“Or else, fire shall consume his houses;
at the breaking up of the body, that one of poor wisdom will be reborn in hell.
Even though this was so, the merchant was still unable to look him straight in the face. Thinking, “How can I kill him? he—
Having devised a stratagem, thinking, "I will send him to the presence of the official in charge of my hundred villages and have him killed," and further thinking, "This is my base-born son;
having had him killed, let them throw him into a cesspit; once this is done, I shall later see what must be done for my maternal uncle," he wrote a letter to him, saying:
"Dear Ghosaka, we have an official in charge of our hundred villages."
"Take this letter and give it to him," he said, and tied the letter to the hem of his garment. However, that man did not know how to read or write.
For since his childhood, the merchant had been trying to have him killed and could not succeed in doing so;
why then would he teach him literacy? Thus, having merely tied the very letter intended for his own execution to the hem of his garment, he departed.
As he was departing, he said, "Father, I have no provisions for the journey. [His father replied: "You have no need for provisions for the journey.
On the way, in a certain village, there is a merchant who is my friend; having taken your breakfast at his house, proceed onward.
Saying, "Very well," he paid homage to his father and set out. Upon reaching that village, he asked for the merchant's house.
Having gone there, he saw the merchant’s wife. When she asked, "Where have you come from? he replied, "From within the city. "Whose son are you?
"The son of your friend the merchant, mother. "Are you named Ghosaka? "Yes, mother.
At the mere sight of him, maternal affection for her son arose within her. Now, the merchant had a daughter about fifteen or sixteen years of age.
She was beautiful and charming; having given her only a single maidservant as a messenger to guard her, they had her dwell in the bedchamber on the uppermost floor of a seven-storied palace.
At that moment, the merchant’s daughter sent the maidservant to the market.
When the merchant’s wife saw her, she asked, “Where are you going? and she replied, “On an errand for my noble lady.”
When she had spoken thus, he said, "Come here first; let the errand wait. Spread a mat for my son, wash his feet, anoint them with oil, and prepare a bed for him;
afterwards you may carry out your errand. She did exactly as she was told.
Then, because she had returned after such a long time, the merchant's daughter rebuked her. Thereupon, she said to her, "Do not be angry with me; the merchant's son..."
"Ghosaka has arrived; having done this and that for him, we have come here after going there.
As soon as the merchant’s daughter heard the name "Ghosaka, the merchant’s son," her love pierced through her skin and all else, reaching right to the marrow of her bones.
For during a time of festival, she had been his wife and had given a measure of boiled rice to a Paccekabuddha; by the power of that deed, she had come [to him].
She was reborn in this merchant family. Thus, he seized her, overcome by that former affection. Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Whether through former association, Or through benefit in the present, In such a way does love arise, Like a lotus in the water.”
Then she asked him, "Where is he, mother? "He is lying on his bed, asleep.
"But does he have anything in his hand? "There is a letter on the hem of his garment. Thinking, "What kind of letter could this be?
while he was still sleeping and her parents were unaware because they were otherwise occupied, she descended, approached him, and [took] that letter.

Having released him and taken him, she entered her own chamber, closed the door, opened a window, and read the letter—due to her skill in the art of reading scripts—thinking, "Alas, what a fool! He wanders about with his own death-warrant tied to his garment;
had I not seen it, he would have no life left. Having torn that letter apart, [she gave it] to the merchant.
With these words, he wrote another letter: "This is my son, named Ghosaka.

Having had a gift sent from a hundred villages, and having performed the auspicious marriage ceremony with the daughter of this chief merchant of the district, he has built a two-storied house in the middle of his own village, well-secured by a surrounding wall and guarded by men."
"Let him do so, and let him send me a message saying, 'This and that have been done by me.
When this has been done, I shall later know what is appropriate for my uncle to do. Having written this, he folded it up, descended, and tied it to his waist-cloth.
He slept for part of the day, and having risen and eaten, he departed. On the following day, early in the morning, [he went] to that village.
Having gone there, he saw the village official performing his duties. Seeing him, he asked, "What is it, dear sir?
"My father has sent you a letter. "What letter is it, dear sir? Bring it here.
Having taken the letter and read it, with a joyful heart he said, "See, sirs! My master, having developed affection for me, [has sent this] to his eldest son..."
“May he grant me good fortune,” she sent this message to my presence.
Having told the householders, “Bring wood and other materials quickly,” he had a house built in the manner described above in the center of the village.

He had gifts brought from a hundred villages, took a daughter from the leading merchant of the district, and after performing the auspicious ceremonies, he sent a message to the merchant saying, “This and that have been done by me.”
Upon hearing this, great dejection arose in the merchant, thinking, "Whatever I do does not work; whatever I do not do, that very thing happens.
This grief, joined with his sorrow for his son, produced a burning sensation in his stomach and brought on dysentery.
The merchant’s daughter also thought, "If anyone comes from the presence of the merchant, he must not speak to me [without my knowledge]."
"Do not speak of this to the merchant’s son first," he commanded the people.
The merchant, thinking, "Now I will no longer let that wicked son become the master of my wealth," said to an official:
"Uncle, I wish to see my son; send a footman and have my son summoned."
Saying, "Very well," he gave him a letter and dispatched a man.
When the merchant’s daughter heard that he had arrived and was standing at the gate, she had him summoned and asked, "What is it, father? He replied, "The merchant is ill;
he has had me summon you, my lady, to see his son. She asked, "What, father? Is he strong or weak? "He is strong."

“...he eats his meal just as before, noble lady. Without informing the merchant’s son, she had the house and the travel expenses provided for him and said, “You shall go when I send you; stay for now. The merchant spoke again to the official:
“What, uncle? Has nothing been sent by you to my son? “It has been sent.”
“Master, the man who went has not yet returned. “In that case, send another one,” he said. He sent him.
The merchant’s daughter behaved toward him in exactly the same way. Then the merchant’s illness grew severe; it would enter through one vessel and exit through another.
Again the merchant asked his official: “What is it, uncle? Is there no news from my son?”
“Has he been sent into my presence? “He has been sent, sir, but the man who went has not yet returned.
“In that case, send another one. He sent him. When the merchant’s daughter asked about his condition for the third time upon his arrival, he replied:
“Noble lady, the merchant is gravely ill; having cut off all food, he is heading toward death. One vessel [of excrement] comes out, and one…”
“...is entering,” he said. The merchant’s daughter, thinking, “It is now time to go,” informed the merchant’s son, “Your father, it is said, is ill.
When he asked, “What do you say, lady? she replied, “He is unwell, sir. “What should be done now?
“Sir, let us take provisions for a journey from a hundred villages and go to see him. He said, “Very well.”
Having had gifts prepared, he took them with carts and departed.
Then she said to him, "Your father is weak; if you go taking such a large amount of gifts, it will cause him great trouble.
Have this all returned. Having sent everything back to her own family home, she spoke to him again: "My lord,..."
“You should stand on your father’s foot-side, and I will stand on the head-side.
As soon as they entered the house, she commanded her own men, saying, “Take up a guard both in front of and behind the house.
Once inside, however, the merchant’s son stood on his father’s foot-side, while the other stood on the head-side.
At that moment, the merchant was lying on his back. His steward, however, while massaging his feet, said, "Master, your son has arrived. "Where is he? "He is standing at your feet.
Then, seeing him, he summoned the treasurer and asked, "How much wealth is there in my house? "Master, as for the wealth—"
When it was said, "There are forty million [pieces] of articles for enjoyment and use, as well as forests, villages, fields, bipeds, quadrupeds, vehicles, and mounts;
this and that is the limit," he, wishing to say, "I do not give this much wealth to my son Ghosaka," said instead, "I give it.
Hearing that, the merchant's daughter thought, "This man, speaking again, is saying something else..."
Thinking, "What shall I say? she, as if afflicted by grief, disheveled her hair and weeping said, "What is this, dear father?
Tell me! We hear even these words of yours; alas, we are truly unfortunate!
Having said this, she struck him in the middle of his chest with the crown of her head, falling down so that he was unable to speak again, thus pressing the crown of her head against his chest.
Striking her breast, she showed herself weeping. At that very moment, the merchant passed away. "The merchant is dead," they went and reported to King Udena.
After the king had ordered the funeral rites for him to be performed, he asked, "Does he have a son or a daughter?
"He has, Your Majesty; he has a son named Ghosaka, and all the property—"
“Having delivered it to him, he died, O King.
Later on, the king summoned the merchant’s son. On that day, it rained;
water pooled here and there in the royal courtyard. The merchant’s son set out, thinking, “I shall see the king. The king [was at] the window.
Opening the door and looking out as he approached, he saw him coming across the water in the royal courtyard;
having come forward, prostrated, and stood before him, he asked, "Are you Ghosaka, my dear?
When he replied, "Yes, sire," he comforted him, saying, "Do not grieve that my father has died; I shall give your father’s position as treasurer to you alone."
"Go, dear son," he dismissed him. But the king stood watching him as he departed.
On his way back, the prince leaped over the water; on his way out, however, he descended and proceeded slowly.
Then the king summoned him from that very spot and asked, "Dear son, why was it that when you came to me you leaped over the water, but when you were going away..."
“Having descended, you walk slowly,” he asked. “Yes, Your Majesty, at that time I was a young boy; it was, as it were, a time for play.

But now, since my position has been granted to me by Your Majesty, it is fitting that I should walk not as I did before, but having first sat down. Hearing this, the king thought, “This man is resolute; even now—”
"I shall grant him a position," he said; and having given his father's wealth, he bestowed the status of treasurer upon him with all his heart.
Standing in his chariot, he circumambulated the city. Wherever he looked, the ground trembled.
The treasurer’s daughter, sitting and conversing with Kāḷī the slave-girl, said: "Mother Kāḷī, such great prosperity as this for your son—me..."
“...arose depending upon him,” he said. “For what reason, mother? “Because this man came to our house having tied his own death-warrant to the hem of his garment;

then I tore that warrant apart, wrote another warrant for the purpose of performing an auspicious ceremony together with him, and for all this time I have maintained a watch over it. “Mother, you see only this much.”
"However, from the time he was a child, this merchant desired to kill him but was unable to do so;
instead, because of him, much wealth has been squandered. "Mother, what a grievous thing the merchant has done!
But seeing him enter his house after circumambulating the city, she thought, "This great prosperity [that I have] is because of him."
“...has arisen,” she said, and she smiled. When the merchant’s son saw her, he asked, “For what reason did you smile?
“On account of one thing,” she replied. “Tell me! he urged. She would not tell him.
He threatened her, saying, “If you will not tell, I shall cut you in two,” and drew his sword. She thought, “This great prosperity of yours...”
"Thinking, 'I have obtained this by relying on him,' he laughed," she said.
"If my father bestowed what was his own upon me, what business do you have in this? It seems that for so long he had known nothing at all;
therefore, he did not believe her words. Then she said to him, "Your father sent me after giving me a death-warrant; you..."
“Having done this and that, I protected him,” he said, recounting everything. Not believing him, thinking, “You are speaking what is untrue;
I shall ask my mother Kāḷī,” he said, “Is it really so, mother? “Yes, dear son.
From the time you were small, he desired to kill you, but being unable to do so, he squandered much wealth through you. Seven times—”
"In these circumstances you were spared from death; now, having come from the village of Bhoga, you have attained the status of a merchant chief together with all your followers.
Upon hearing this, he thought, "Alas, what a grave matter! It is improper for one such as I, who has been spared from death, to live a life of negligence;
I shall be diligent. Having reflected thus, he [spent] a thousand [pieces of gold] every day.
Having dismissed [his own retinue], he established almsgiving for travelers, the poor, and others. A householder named Mitta was occupied with the arrangements for these gifts.
This is the origin of the merchant Ghosaka.
At that time, in the city of Bhaddavatī, there lived a merchant named Bhaddavatiya, who had never before seen Ghosaka.

It came to pass that Ghosaka the merchant, having heard from merchants who had come from the city of Bhaddavati about the prosperity and the age of the merchant of Bhaddavati, and desiring to establish a friendship with him,
sent a gift. The merchant of Bhaddavati likewise [heard] of Ghosaka the merchant from merchants who had come from Kosambī.
Having heard of his wealth and youth, and desiring friendship with him, he sent a gift.
