Thus they lived as friends who had never seen one another before. Later on, a snake-epidemic broke out in the house of the merchant Bhaddavatiya.
When it broke out, first the flies died, and then, in due succession, [the others].
Insects, mice, chickens, pigs, cattle, female slaves, male slaves, and even all the other human inhabitants of the house die last of all.
Among them, those who escape by breaking through the walls obtain life;
at that time, however, the merchant, his wife, and his daughter likewise escaped and set out on the road to Kosambī, longing to see the merchant Ghosaka.
On that very journey, their provisions being exhausted and their bodies worn out by the wind, the sun, hunger, and thirst, they reached Kosambī with great difficulty.
Stopping at a place where the water was pleasant, they bathed and entered a hall at the city gate.
Then the merchant said to his wife, "My dear, traveling in this manner, one becomes even unpleasant to one's own wife."
“It seems my companion has been disbursing a thousand coins daily for the sake of travelers, the poor, and others, and causing them to give alms.
Having sent our daughter there to fetch food, we shall stay right here for one or two days to nourish our bodies and then see our companion.
She replied, “Very well, my lord. They remained in the hall itself. On the following day, at the proper time—
When it was announced that the poor, the destitute, and others were going out for food, the parents sent their daughter, saying, "Daughter, go and bring us some food.
The daughter of a wealthy family, who had lost her sense of shame due to her misfortune, took a bowl and went with the poor folk for food. [The father asked: "How many portions will you take?"
When asked, "How many? she replied, "Three. He then gave her three portions of food.
When she had brought the meal, the three of them sat down to eat together.
Then the mother and daughter said to the merchant: "Master, misfortune indeed befalls even great families; do not..."
“Look at us and eat; do not worry. Thus, having entreated him in various ways, they fed him.
Having eaten, he was unable to digest his food and passed away as the sun was rising.
The mother and daughter lamented and wept in many ways. On the following day, the young woman went out weeping for the sake of food, asking, “How many portions [of rice]...?”
When she was asked, "Will you take it? she replied, "Two," and having brought food, she requested her mother to eat.
But she, though entreated by her daughter, ate and was unable to digest the food; that very day she passed away.
The young girl, weeping and lamenting all alone, was overcome with an extreme hunger-pain caused by that occurrence of suffering. On the following day—
Weeping along with the beggars, she went for the sake of food; when asked, "How many portions will you take, mother?
she replied, "One. The householder Mitta noticed her taking food for three days in succession, and because of that, he said to her, "Begone, get out, you outcaste!
Today you have discovered the capacity of your belly! She was endowed with a sense of shame and moral dread.
The daughter of a noble family, having received a blow from a spear as if on her breast, and the pouring of salt water upon her wound as it were, said, "What is it, master?
"Yesterday you took two portions, and today you take one; previously you took three portions.
Today you have come to know the measure of your own belly. "Do not think, master, that I took [the food] for my own sake," she replied.
“Then why did you take it thus? [She replied: “Master, formerly we were three people; yesterday there were two; today I am born all alone.
When he asked, “For what reason? and had heard the entire account she related from the beginning, he was unable to restrain his tears.
Overcome by a powerful surge of grief, he said, “My dear, this being so...”
"Do not worry; from this day forward, you are my own daughter, the daughter of the merchant Bhaddavatiya," he said.
Having spoken thus, he kissed her on the head, led her home, and established her in the position of his eldest daughter.
Hearing the loud noise and great clamor at the place of almsgiving, she asked, "Father, why do you make these people silent before giving the gift?"
"Do not give it," he said. "It cannot be done, mother. "It can be done, dear son. "How can it be done, mother?
"Dear son, having surrounded the place of giving, construct two doors with a width sufficient for only one person to enter at a time, and say, 'Having entered by one door, exit by the other.
In this way, they will take [the gifts] without making any noise."
Having heard that, she said, "Mother, it is indeed a good plan," and acted accordingly. She too had previously been named Sāmā;
however, because the wall was built, she became known as Sāmāvatī. From then on, she put an end to the clamor at the almsgiving.
Previously, when the merchant Ghosaka heard that sound, he would rejoice, thinking, "The sound of my almsgiving. But for two or three days, no sound...
Not hearing [the sound], he asked his friend and householder who had come to attend upon him:
“Is alms being given to the poor, the needy, and others? “Yes, master. “Then why is no sound heard for two or three days?
“I have made an arrangement so that they take it silently. “Then why did you not do so before? “Because of ignorance.”
“Yes, Master. “How did you come to know this now? “It was told to me by my daughter, Master.

“I did not know that you had a daughter. He then related everything that had happened since the onset of the snake-poisoning illness, and informed him that she had been established in the place of his own eldest daughter. Then he—
The merchant said, "If that is so, why did you not tell me? My friend’s daughter is my own daughter.
He summoned her and asked, "My child, were you the merchant’s daughter? "Yes, father," she replied.
"In that case, do not worry; you are my daughter. Having kissed her on the head, he gave her five hundred women to serve as her retinue.
Having given her away, he established her in the position of his eldest daughter.
Then one day, a festival was proclaimed in that city.
On such a festival, even daughters of noble families who do not go outside would go to the river on foot with their own retinues to bathe.
Therefore, on that day, Sāmāvatī also went to bathe in the royal courtyard, surrounded by five hundred women.
King Udena, standing at the lion-window, saw her and asked, "Whose dancing girls are these? "They are not anyone's dancing girls, Your Majesty," they replied.
"Then whose daughters are they? "They are the daughters of the merchant Ghosaka, Your Majesty, O Sāmāvatī."
“Is this not she? Having seen her, affection arose within him, and he sent a message to the treasurer:
“I hear you will send my daughter. “I will not send her, Your Majesty. “Do not do this; you must indeed send her.
“We are householders, Your Majesty, and we do not give our daughters away for fear of being beaten, harassed, or dragged off. The king became angry.
Having had the house sealed, he seized both the merchant and his wife by the hand and had them led outside.
Sāmāvatī, having bathed and returned, finding no opportunity to enter the house, asked, "What is this, dear ones?
[They replied,] "Mother, the king sent for you. Then, when we said, 'We will not give you up,' he had the house sealed and us driven outside."
“...had it built. [The father replied: “Dear son, you have done a grave deed. When a king sends a message, one should not say, ‘We will not give her’;
rather, dear son, one should say, ‘If you take our daughter along with her retinue, we will give her.
[The son said: “Very well, mother. If it is your wish, we shall do so. And he sent such a message to the king. The king said, “Very well.”
Having accepted her, he brought her along with her retinue, consecrated her, and established her in the position of chief queen.
The others became merely her attendants. This was the origin of Sāmāvatī.
Furthermore, Udena had another queen named Vāsuladattā, who was the daughter of Caṇḍapajjota. For in Ujjenī—

There was a king named Caṇḍapajjota. One day, while returning from the pleasure garden, he surveyed his own prosperity and asked, "Is there anyone else who possesses such prosperity? When he heard the people reply, "What is this so-called 'prosperity'?
The prosperity of King Udena in Kosambī is far greater," the king said:
—“In that case, shall we seize him? —“He cannot be seized. —“By doing something, shall we certainly seize him?
—“It is not possible, O King. —“For what reason? —“He knows the craft called ‘elephant-enticing’;
by reciting a mantra and playing the elephant-enticing lute, he can both frighten away the elephants and capture them. He is as accomplished in riding elephants as anyone else like him.”
“There is no such name. “I am not able to capture him,” [the king replied].
“If, O King, this is your firm resolve, then have a wooden elephant made and send it to a place near him.
Hearing that there is an elephant-vehicle or a horse-vehicle, he will go even a great distance. When he has arrived there, you will be able to capture him.”

The king, thinking, "There is this means," had a mechanical elephant made of wood; he wrapped it outside with rags, applied painted decorations, and released it onto the bank of a lake near his kingdom.
Inside the belly of the elephant, sixty men walked back and forth, and having brought elephant dung, they placed it here and there.
They abandoned it. A certain forest-dweller, seeing the elephant, thought, "He is worthy of our king," and going to the king, he reported:
"Your Majesty, I have seen a magnificent elephant, entirely white and resembling the peak of Mount Kelāsa, who is truly worthy of you alone.
Having made that very man his guide, Udena mounted the elephant and set out with his retinue.
He departed. Knowing of his approach, scouts went and informed Caṇḍapajjota.
He arrived and, leaving the center empty, deployed his army on both flanks. Udena, unaware of his arrival, pursued the elephant.
The men stationed inside caused it to flee with great speed. The wooden elephant [escaped] from the king’s spell.
Turning the lute around and playing it, he fled as if not even hearing the sound of the strings.
Unable to catch up with the noble elephant, the king mounted a horse and pursued him; as he followed with such speed, the army was left behind, and the king was all alone.
Then, the men of Caṇḍapajjota stationed on both sides seized him.
They gave him to his own king. Then, his army, having learned that he had fallen into the power of his enemies, remained encamped outside the city, having established their headquarters there.
Caṇḍapajjota, moreover, had Utena seized alive and cast into a house for thieves;
having had the door closed, he drank the wine of victory for three days. On the third day, Utena asked the guards, "Where is..."
“Is this your king, dear father? [The son replied: “He drinks the victory-drink because he has captured his enemy.
“What kind of conduct is this on the part of your king, who acts like a common woman? Should he not rather capture rival kings and either release them or put them to death?
Yet he makes us sit in discomfort and, they say, drinks the victory-drink! They went and reported this matter to the king.
So he came and asked, "Is it true that you speak thus? "Yes, Great King," he replied. "Very well, I shall release you;
since you possess such a spell, will you give it to me? "I shall give it to you with pleasure;
but when the time comes for its reception, you must pay homage to me and then take it. But how will you pay homage to me? "How could I pay homage to you?"
“I will not pay homage. “Then I will not give it to you either.
“If that is the case, I will have the king issue an order for you. “Do so; the body is master over me, but not the mind.
When the king heard his heroic roar, he thought, “How indeed shall I cause him to learn this mantra? He considered, “This mantra cannot be learned from anyone else...”
"It is possible; having had my daughter learn it from him, I shall learn it from her.
Then he said to her, "Will you give it to one who learns it after first paying homage to another? "Yes, Great King," she replied.
"In that case, there is a certain hunchback in our house; you must pay homage to her while she is sitting inside the inner enclosure, and then sit yourself outside the enclosure."
“Teach the mantra while standing still. “Very well, Great King; whether she be a hunchback or a cripple, I shall give it to her as she pays homage.
Then the king went and said to his daughter Vāsuladattā: “My dear, there is a certain leper named Saṅkhakuṭṭhi who knows a priceless mantra;
it is impossible for anyone else to know it. You must sit inside the curtain and [teach] him...”
“Having paid homage, take up the mantra; standing outside the enclosure, he will teach it to you. I shall receive it from you.
Thus, out of fear of creating intimacy between them, he made his daughter hunchbacked and the other a conch-shell leper, and spoke.
She paid homage to him while sitting inside the enclosure, and standing outside, he taught her the mantra.
Then one day, when she was unable to recite the mantra words despite being told again and again, he said, "Hey, hunchback!
Your face has excessively thick lips; speak like this! She became angry and said, "Hey, you wicked leper with a conch-shell deformity! What are you saying?
How can someone like me be called a 'hunchback'? When he raised his ear and asked, "Who are you? she replied:
“I am the king’s daughter, named Vāsuladattā,” she said. “When your father spoke of you to me, he called you a ‘hunchback,’” [the prince] replied.

“And when he spoke of me to him, he described me as a ‘shell-cutter,’” she said. Both of them thought, “In that case, he must have said this out of fear of forming an intimacy with us,” and so they made love right there within the enclosure.
From that time on, there was no more learning of spells or crafts. The king also asked his daughter constantly, "Are you learning a craft, my dear?

"I am learning it, father," she would reply. Then one day, Uttena said to her, "My lady, neither mother nor father, nor brothers nor sisters, are able to do what must be done by a husband. If [you wish] for me..."
“I will grant you your life, and having given you five hundred women as your retinue, I will give you the position of chief queen.
“If you can abide by these words, I will grant you your life. “I can, my lady,” she replied.
Saying, “Very well, husband,” she went to her father, paid homage, and stood to one side. Then—
He asked her, "Mother, has your craft been completed? "It is not yet completed, dear father," she replied.
Then he asked her, "What is it, mother? "Dear father, we must obtain a door and a vehicle. "What is this, mother?
"Dear father, it is said that at night, for the purpose of the mantra's preliminary practice, by means of the perception of stars..."

“There is one medicine that must be taken. Therefore, at the time of our departure—whether it be the right time or not—it is necessary to obtain both a single gate and a single vehicle. The king accepted this, saying, “Very well.
They took possession of one gate of their own choosing. As for the king, however, he had five vehicles.
The female elephant named Bhaddavatī travels fifty yojanas in a single day; the servant named Kāka travels sixty yojanas;
the two horses, Celakaṭṭhi and Muñcakesī, travel one hundred yojanas;
and the elephant Nāḷāgiri travels two hundred yojanas.
It is said that before the Buddha had appeared, the king was an attendant to a certain lord.
One day, while the lord had gone outside the city to bathe and was returning, a Paccekabuddha entered the city for alms;
however, because all the city-dwellers were influenced by Māra, he did not receive even a single portion of alms and left with his bowl as clean as when it had been washed.

He departed. Then, when he had reached the city gate, Māra approached him in the guise of a stranger and asked, "Venerable sir, have you obtained anything? "But what have you done to prevent my obtaining it?
"In that case, turn back and enter again; I will not do it now. "I shall not turn back."
For had he turned back, he would have again directed his intent toward the bodies of all the city-dwellers and, clapping his hands, engaged in laughter and play.
When the Paccekabuddha had gone without turning back, Māra vanished right there.
Then that lord, seeing the Paccekabuddha approaching with his bowl as clean as it was when washed, paid homage and said, "Even..."
“Venerable sir, have you received anything? he asked. “We have come out after wandering for alms, friend,” he replied.
He thought, “The venerable one does not say what I asked; he says something else. He must not have received anything.
Then, looking into his bowl and seeing it empty, he acted boldly, being unaware of whether the meal in the house had been finished or not.
Being unable to catch the bowl, he said, "Venerable sir, please wait a moment," and ran home in haste.
Upon asking, "Is our meal ready? and being told, "It is ready," he said to his attendant, "Dear boy, there is no one else who possesses such great speed as you;
having reached the Venerable with swift velocity, [hand him] the bowl."
“Give it to me, venerable sir,” he said, and taking the bowl, he ran forward with speed.
At that single word, the man leaped up, took the bowl, and brought it back. The master, having filled his own bowl with food, said:
“Go quickly and deliver this to the noble one; I shall give you a share of my portion from here.”
He too, taking it, went with great speed and gave the bowl to the Paccekabuddha. After prostrating himself with the five-pointed salutation, he said:

"Venerable Sir, because I have come and gone with such extreme haste, saying 'the time is drawing near,' may I, by the fruit of this speed, obtain five vehicles capable of traveling fifty, sixty, seventy, and eighty *yojanas* respectively."
"Whether I am coming or going, my body has been scorched by the heat of the sun;
by the fruit of this, may my authority in every place where I am reborn be like the heat of the sun. This alms-food has been given to me by my master;
through its outflow, may I become a partaker of the present life [of happiness] with you," he said. Thus spoke the Paccekabuddha.
Having said, “So be it,” he added:
“May all that you desire and pray for be fulfilled;
may all your intentions be realized, like the moon on the fifteenth day.”
“May what you desire and have prayed for be fulfilled quickly;
may all your intentions be realized, just like the radiance of a wish-fulfilling gem.
Thus he offered words of appreciation. It is said that for Paccekabuddhas, there are only two verses here known as verses of appreciation.
In this context, "Jotirasa" refers to the wish-fulfilling jewel (*maṇiratana*). This was his conduct in a previous life.
He is now Caṇḍapajjota. Through the result of that karma, these five vehicles came into existence.
Then one day, the king went out for a pleasure excursion to the park. Uttena [thought], "Today we must flee," and [prepared] very large...
Having filled a leather pouch with gold and silver and placed it on the back of a female elephant, he took Vāsuladattā and fled.
When the guards of the inner palace saw him fleeing, they went and informed the king. The king sent out an army, saying, "Go quickly!
But Udena, perceiving the army's intent to charge, unfastened the pouch of coins and let them fall.
The people, having picked up the coins, rushed back inside again.
The other [man], having untied and dropped his gold bag, reached his own camp which had already emerged outside while they were distracted by their greed for the gold.
Seeing him approaching, his own army surrounded him and escorted him into the city. As soon as he arrived, he...
Having consecrated Vāsuladattā, he established her in the position of chief queen. This is the origin of Vāsuladattā.
Furthermore, another woman named Māgaṇḍiyā obtained the position of chief queen from the king.
She was, it is said, the daughter of the brahmin Māgaṇḍiya in the kingdom of Kuru; her mother’s name was also Māgaṇḍiyā, and her paternal uncle was also Māgaṇḍiya.

She was beautiful, resembling a celestial nymph. However, her father, unable to find a suitable husband for her, rebuked and sent away even those who came from very great families, saying, "You are not suitable for my daughter.
Then one day, at the time of dawn, the Teacher surveyed the world and [beheld] the brahmin Māgaṇḍiya.

Seeing that her husband possessed the necessary support for attaining the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), she took her own bowl and robes and went to the place where he was performing fire-worship outside the city.
There, beholding the Tathāgata’s physical form, which had reached the pinnacle of beauty, she thought:
"In this world, there is no other man equal to this person; he is a worthy match for my daughter."
Thinking, "I shall give my daughter for his support," he said, "Ascetic, I have a daughter;
for all this time I have not seen a man suitable for her, but you are suitable for her, and she is indeed suitable for you.
For she is to be your attendant, and you must obtain a husband for her."
"It is fitting; I shall give it to you. Stay right here until my return," he said.
The Teacher remained silent without saying anything further. The Brahmin hurried home and said, "Lady, lady!
I have seen a man worthy of my daughter. Quickly, quickly adorn her! Having thus had her adorned, he [set out] together with the Brahmin woman.
Taking her, he set out toward the presence of the Teacher. The entire city was thrown into agitation.

Thinking, "For so long a time there has been no one suitable for my daughter," and hearing it said, "Today I have seen one who is suitable for my daughter," the great multitude went forth along with him, wondering, "What kind of man is this? Shall we see him?"

As he was returning with his daughter, the Teacher did not stand at the place where he had spoken, but having manifested a footprint-relic (*padacetiya*) there, he proceeded and stood in another location.

For the footprint-relics of the Buddhas become manifest only at the very spot where they have stepped after having resolved upon it, and not elsewhere; and only those for whose sake it was resolved can see it. For them...
Furthermore, whether elephants and the like should trample him, or a great rain cloud should pour down, or the Verambha winds should strike him, no one is able to defile him.
Then the brahmin woman said to the brahmin: "Where is that man? [The brahmin replied:
"I told him, 'Stand in this place'; where indeed has he gone? From here...
Looking closely, he saw the footprint-shrine and said, "This is his track.
The brahmin lady, being proficient in the three Vedas and their manuals of marks, recited the manuals of marks and examined the characteristics of the footprint.
She said, "Brahmin, this is not the footprint of one who indulges in the five strands of sensual pleasure," and spoke this verse:
For the footstep of one who is angry is stamping;
that of one who is ill-tempered is suddenly pressing down;
the footstep of one who is deluded is dragging.
“This is the kind of state for one who has uncovered the veil.

Then the brahmin said to him: “Lady, you are like one who sees a crocodile in a water-pot and a thief in the middle of the house while reciting mantras; be silent! “Brahmin, say whatever you wish; this is not [the case].”
“They say he is one who indulges in the five cords of sensual pleasure. Then, looking here and there, the brahmin saw the Teacher;
saying, “This is that man,” he approached and said, “Recluse, I give my daughter to you to support.
Without saying, “I have need of your daughter or not,” the Teacher said, “Brahmin, one...”
Having said, "I shall tell you the reason," and being told, "Tell it, O ascetic," he related how,
from the time of the Great Renunciation until his arrival at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree, he had been pursued by Māra; and how, at the foot of that very Ajapāla banyan tree,
when Māra’s daughters arrived to soothe the grief of him who was afflicted with sorrow because he thought, "This realm is now past for me," [he remained unmoved].
Having described the seduction employed by means of the form of a young maiden and so forth, he said: “Even then, no desire arose in me.
And he added: “Having seen lust, aversion, and passion, there was no desire even for sexual union.”
"What is this thing filled with urine and excrement,
that one would not even wish to touch it with one's feet?"—
he spoke this verse. At the conclusion of the verse, both the brahmin and the brahmin woman were established in the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).
Māgaṇḍiyā thought: "If he has no need of me, then his lack of interest should simply be stated;
yet he makes me carry a vessel full of urine and excrement, and does not even wish to touch my feet. Very well;
having obtained such a husband on account of the excellence of my birth, family, country, wealth, and youth, I shall learn what is appropriate for a śramaṇa Gotama to do."
She harbored resentment toward the Teacher. [The questioner asks: "But does the Teacher know that resentment has arisen within her, or not?
[The answer is: "He certainly knows. Knowing it, why did he speak this verse? [It was] on account of the other two.
For Buddhas, disregarding resentment, teach the Dhamma only with regard to those who are worthy of attaining the paths and fruits. Her mother and father took her away...
Having entrusted their youngest sister, Cūḷamāgaṇḍiyā, to him, they went forth and attained arahantship.
Cūḷamāgaṇḍiya also thought, "My daughter is not suitable for a man of low status; she is fit only for a king.
Taking her with him, he went to Kosambī, adorned her with all kinds of ornaments, and [said], "This jewel of a woman for the King..."
"Suitable," he said, and gave her to King Udena. Upon seeing her, a powerful passion arose within him;
he performed the consecration ceremony, provided her with a retinue of five hundred women, and established her in the position of chief queen. This was the origin of Māgaṇḍiyā.
Thus, he had three chief queens, each accompanied by a retinue of fifteen hundred female dancers. In that regard...
Now at that time, there were three guild-leaders in Kosambī: Ghosaka-seṭṭhi, Kukkuṭa-seṭṭhi, and Pāvārika-seṭṭhi.
When the commencement of the rainy season was near, they saw five hundred ascetics who had come from the Himālaya and were wandering for alms in the city;
having gained confidence in them, they seated them, fed them, obtained their promise, and [attended to them] for four months.
Having had her live with them and having made her promise to return again during the rainy season, they sent her away.
From then on, the ascetics lived in the Himālayas for eight months and stayed in their presence for the four months [of the dry season].
Later, while returning from the Himālayas, they saw a great banyan tree in a forest tract and, at its base—
They sat down. Among them, the eldest ascetic thought: "The deity dwelling in this tree cannot be of minor power;
it must be a king of the gods of great majesty. It would be well indeed if he were to give drinking water to this company of seers.
He too gave them drinking water. The ascetic then thought of bathing water, and that too he gave. Then—
He thought of food, and that too he gave him. Then it occurred to him: "This king of the gods gives us everything we think of;
oh, that we might see him! He split open the trunk of a tree and revealed himself.
Then the ascetics said to him: "King of the gods, great is your prosperity; what indeed did you do to obtain this?"
They asked, “Did you receive it? “Do not ask, noble ladies,” he replied. “Tell us, O King of Devas!
Being thus urged by them again and again, he said, “In that case, listen,” and spoke. However, because the deed he had committed was so trifling, he was ashamed and did not dare to speak.
But being pressed repeatedly by them, he said, “Very well, listen,” and told his story.
It is said that there was once a man of poor fortune who, seeking employment, obtained a job as a hired laborer in the service of Anāthapiṇḍika and made his living by depending on him.
Then, when a certain Uposatha day arrived, Anāthapiṇḍika returned from the monastery and asked: "Has anyone told that hired laborer that today is the Uposatha day?"
“It was not mentioned, Master. “In that case, cook him an evening meal. Then they cooked him a measure of boiled rice.
Having worked in the forest during the day, he returned in the evening;
when the food was increased and given to him, instead of eating immediately, saying, “I am hungry,” he said, “On other days in this house you would say, ‘Give rice! Give soup! Give curry!’”
"Let us eat! he thought, "there was a great clamor; today they all lay down in silence, and they have increased the food for me alone.
What can this mean? Having reflected thus, he asked: "Did the rest eat, or did they not?
"They did not eat, dear one. "For what reason? "On the Uposatha days, in this house, there is no evening meal."

They eat, and everyone observes the Uposatha. Even as for infants who drink from the breast, the Great Merchant has them wash their faces and have honey-mixtures poured into their mouths, thus making them observe the Uposatha.
While scented oil lamps are burning, the children—both small and large—lying on their beds recite the Thirty-two Aspects. But as for you...
“We did not apply mindfulness to explain that it was an Uposatha day; therefore, this food has been cooked for you alone—please eat it.
[The other replied: “If it is now proper to observe the Uposatha, then I too shall do so.
[The first said: “The merchant knows this. [The others said: “In that case, ask him. They went and asked the merchant, and he spoke thus:
"But now, if you do not eat, rinse your mouth, and resolve upon the factors of the Uposatha, you will obtain half of the Uposatha merit.
Having heard this, the other did exactly so.
After he had performed his work all day long, his body became famished and his humors were disturbed. He bound his chest with a cord.
He was spinning, holding onto the end of a rope. When the merchant heard this news, he had torches carried and four kinds of sweet honeyed food brought;
he went into his presence and asked, "What is it, dear sir? "Master, my wind-humors are disturbed.
"In that case, get up and eat this medicine. "You should eat it too, master."
“There is nothing unwell with us; please eat,” they said. “Master, I was performing the Uposatha ceremony and could not complete it entirely;
let not even half the rite be deficient for me,” he replied, and would not consent.
Though told, “Do not do this, dear one,” he refused. As the dawn rose, like a withered garland, he passed away right there.
He was reborn as a deity in the Nigrodha tree. Therefore, after explaining this matter, he said:

"That merchant was devoted to the Buddha, devoted to the Dhamma, and devoted to the Saṅgha; it is through the result of the half-Uposatha observance performed in reliance upon them that I have obtained this success."
Upon hearing the word “Buddha,” the five hundred ascetics rose up, and extending their joined palms toward the deity, they asked, “Do you say ‘Buddha’?
Do you say ‘Buddha’? Having made him acknowledge three times, “I say ‘Buddha,’ I say ‘Buddha,’” they uttered this inspired utterance:
“Even such a sound as this is rare in the world! Then, O deity, [they said] regarding the many...
“We have heard a sound never heard before in hundreds of thousands of eons; you have caused us to hear it,” they said.
Then the pupils said this to their teacher: “In that case, let us go into the presence of the Teacher. “Dear ones, three merchants have been very helpful to us;
tomorrow, after receiving alms at their residences and informing them [of our success], we shall depart.”

“Please consent, dear ones. They consented. On the following day, the merchant prepared rice gruel and food, arranged seats, and, knowing that it was the day for the arrival of the noble ones, went out to meet them.
Taking them with him, he went to his residence, had them sit down, and gave them almsfood. When they had finished their meal, they [spoke] to the great merchant.
“We shall go,” they said. “But, venerable sirs, did you not already give us your promise four months ago during the rains retreat?
Where are you going now? “It is said that a Buddha has appeared in the world, the Dhamma has appeared, and the Saṅgha has appeared;
therefore, we shall go into the presence of the Teacher. “But what [is he like] in the presence of that Teacher?”
“Is it fitting for you alone to go? “Friends, it is not forbidden to others either. “In that case, venerable sir, please wait;
we too will go after making preparations for the journey. “If you make preparations, it will cause us delay. We shall go on ahead;
you may follow later,” he said. Having spoken thus—
Having gone there earlier, they saw the Perfectly Enlightened One, and after praising him and paying homage, they sat down to one side.
Then the Teacher, having delivered a gradual discourse, taught them the Dhamma.

At the conclusion of the teaching, they all attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Having requested ordination, at the very moment the words "Come, monks" were spoken, [they were ordained].
They became "Come, monk" (ehibhikkhu) disciples, wearing robes and bowls produced by supernormal power.
Those three merchants, having taken five hundred carts each filled with provisions for alms—such as food, clothing, ghee, honey, and molasses—arrived at Sāvatthī;
they paid homage to the Teacher, listened to his discourse on the Dhamma, and at the conclusion of the talk, [they were ordained].
Having established herself in the fruit of stream-entry, she gave alms for even half a month while staying in the presence of the Teacher.
Then, requesting the Teacher to permit her departure for Kosambī, the Teacher granted his consent;
when he said, "Householders, Tathāgatas indeed delight in empty dwellings," she replied, "Understood, Bhante, by the message sent by us."

"It is fitting for him to come," they said; and having gone to Kosambī, they had Ghosaka the merchant build the Ghosita Monastery, Kukkuṭa the merchant the Kukkuṭa Monastery, and Pāvārika the merchant the Pāvārika Monastery—these three great monasteries—and sent a message for the Teacher to come.
Having heard their message, the Teacher went there. They went out to meet the Teacher.
Having entered the monastery, they took turns looking after it. The Teacher stayed in one monastery each day.
In whichever monastery he stayed, he would go for alms at the door of that very house.
Now, these three merchants had a gardener named Sumana who served them. He said to those merchants: "I have [served] you for a long time..."
“I am a benefactor; I wish to feed the Teacher. Please grant me one day’s meal for the Teacher as well.
“In that case, my man, feed him tomorrow,” he replied. “Very well, master,” he said, and having invited the Teacher, he prepared the hospitality.
At that time, King [Bimbisāra] gave eight kahāpaṇas daily to Queen Sāmāvatī for her flower expenses. Her attendant was Khujjuttarā.
A slave girl named Nāma used to go regularly to a flower-garland maker and take flowers from him.
When she arrived on that day, the garland maker said to her: "I have invited the Teacher; today I shall honor the Teacher with flowers.
Stay here for now; you may act as my assistant at the meal distribution, and after you have heard the Dhamma, you may take what remains."

“Having taken the flowers, you shall go. She consented, saying, “Very well. Sumana served the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, and after the meal, he took up his bowl for the sake of giving the expression of thanksgiving.
The Teacher began the discourse on the Dhamma of thanksgiving. Even as she listened to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, Khujjuttarā was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
On other days, she would take four kahāpaṇas for herself and go with four flowers;
on that day, however, she went having taken eight flowers. Then Sāmāvatī said to her, “Mother, has the King given us double the price for the flowers today? “No, Noble Lady,” she replied. “Then why—”
“Why so many flowers? [He replied: “On other days, I take four kahāpaṇas for myself and bring four flowers.
“Why did you not take any today? “Because, having heard the Dhamma discourse of the Sammasambuddha, I have attained the Dhamma.
Then he said to her: “Hey, wicked slave! For all this time, the kahāpaṇas you took—”
Without coaxing her with the words, "Give it to me," he said, "Mother, you have drunk the Deathless; let us drink it too.
When she replied, "In that case, bathe me first," he had her bathed with sixteen jars of scented water and had two smooth, fine cotton cloths given to her.
She put on one as an undergarment and draped the other over one shoulder, prepared a seat, and had a fan brought.
Having sat down on her seat and taken up her variegated fan, she addressed the five hundred women and taught them the Dhamma according to the very same method taught by the Teacher.
Upon hearing her discourse on the Dhamma, they all became established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).
They all paid homage to Khujjuttarā, saying, "Mother, from this day forward, do not perform defiled deeds."
“Standing in the place of both mother and teacher, go to the presence of the Teacher, listen to the Dhamma taught by the Teacher, and then explain it to us,” they said.
Acting accordingly, she later became a bearer of the Tipiṭaka.
Then the Teacher declared of her: “Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my female lay disciples who are learned.”
He placed her at the head of those who are preachers of the Dhamma, saying: "Of all preachers of the Dhamma, this one is Khujjuttarā.
Then those five hundred women said to her: "Mother, we wish to see the Teacher; show him to us, so that we may honor him with perfumes, garlands, and the like.
She replied: "Noble ladies, the royal palace is a place of great importance; it is not possible for you to go outside taking yourselves with you."
“Mother, do not destroy it; let us see our Teacher.

“In that case, have holes made in the walls of your living quarters just large enough to look through, and having had perfumes, garlands, and other offerings brought, stand in those various places as the Teacher goes to the doors of the three merchants’ houses.”
“Look at him, stretch out your hands and pay homage, and offer worship. They did so;
watching the Teacher as he went and came, they both paid homage and offered worship.
Then one day, Māgaṇḍiyā, having stepped down from the upper terrace of her palace and was walking about, reached the place where they lived.
Having gone and seen a gap in the walls, she asked, "What is this? When those women—who were unaware that she harbored resentment toward the Teacher—replied, "The Teacher has arrived at this city;
we shall stand here and pay homage to and honor the Teacher," she thought, "The ascetic Gotama has indeed come to this city; now I shall know what must be done to him."
Thinking, "These women are her attendants; I shall know what must be done regarding them as well," he went and informed the king:
"Great King, Sāmāvatī and her companions have external designs; in just a few days they will take your life.
The king did not believe him, thinking, "They would not do such a thing. Even when this was said again and again, [he still did not believe].

He did not believe it at all. Then, even though he had been told this three times, the king still did not believe him, so [the monk] said, "If you do not believe me, Great King, go to their dwelling place and investigate.

The king went there, saw a hole in the walls of the rooms, and asked, "What is this? When the matter was explained to him, he did not become angry with them; instead, without saying anything, he departed.
Having had the openings closed, he had upper-ventilated windows installed in all the inner chambers.

It is said that such upper-ventilated windows were introduced at that time. Being unable to do anything to them, Māgandiyā thought, "I shall do what must be done against the ascetic Gotama," and after bribing the citizens, she said, "Once the ascetic Gotama has entered the city..."
“Drive him away by scolding and reviling him with slaves, laborers, and servants as he wanders about,” he commanded.
Those of wrong view, having no faith in the Three Jewels, followed the Teacher who had entered the city, saying: “You are a thief! You are a fool! You are deluded!
You are a camel! You are an ox! You are a donkey! You are a denizen of hell! You are an animal! There is nothing for you!”
“Only an unhappy rebirth, Sugata, is to be expected for you,” they said, reviling and abusing him with ten grounds for abuse.
Hearing this, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Teacher: “Venerable sir, these citizens of the city are reviling and abusing us;
let us go elsewhere. “Where, Ānanda? “To another city, venerable sir.”
“If people there abuse us, Ānanda, where shall we go? “To another city, Bhante. “If people there also abuse us, where shall we go? “To yet another city, Bhante.
“Ānanda, it is not proper to act in this way. Wherever a legal dispute has arisen, right there—”
“When that has subsided, it is appropriate to go elsewhere. But who, Ānanda, are those who revile us?
“Venerable sir, everyone from the slaves and laborers upwards is reviling us. “Ānanda, I am like an elephant that has entered the fray;
for it is a heavy burden for an elephant that has entered the fray to endure arrows coming from the four directions, even so [with] many...”
"Enduring the words spoken by the immoral is indeed my burden," he said, and while teaching the Dhamma concerning himself,
he spoke these three verses from the Nāga Vagga: "Just as I,
like an elephant in battle, endure the arrow fallen from the bow;..."
I shall endure harsh speech, for the majority of people are ill-behaved.
"The tamed one they lead to the assembly; the tamed one the king mounts upon his elephant.
Among humans, the tamed one is best—he who endures harsh speech."
“Better than those other tamed ones—the thoroughbred Sindh horses, the great elephants, and the noble tuskers—is one who has tamed himself.
This discourse on the Dhamma was beneficial to the assembled multitude. Having thus taught the Dhamma, [he said]: “Do not grieve.”
“Ānanda, these will revile him for only seven days; on the eighth day they will become silent.
For a legal dispute that has arisen against the Buddhas does not last beyond seven days.
Having failed to make the Teacher revile himself and drive him away, Māgandiyā thought, ‘What indeed shall I do? Then she considered: ‘These women are his supporters.’”
Thinking, "I shall bring ruin upon these as well," one day, while attending upon the king at his place for drinking liquor, she sent a message to her younger father:
"It seems I have need of chickens; let him come bringing eight dead chickens and eight live chickens.
Having arrived, let him stand at the top of the stairs, announce his arrival, and say, 'Please enter.'"
Even though this was said, he did not enter; instead, he first sent eight live cocks, saying, "Send the others later.
He also gave a bribe to the junior attendant, telling him, "You must do as I say.
When Māgandiya arrived and informed the king, and the king said, "Let him enter," he replied, "I will not enter the king's drinking hall. The other [woman] [instructed] the junior attendant...
He sent [a messenger], saying, "Go, dear one, to my younger father. Having gone there, he brought back eight live cocks given by him and said, "Your Majesty, the chaplain has sent this gift.
The king said, "A most excellent supplementary meal has appeared for us;
who indeed shall cook it? Māgaṇḍiyā replied, "Great King, the five hundred women headed by Sāmāvatī..."
“Women wander about without work; send some of them, and they will cook [the meat] and bring it back,” he said.
The king sent him, saying, “Go, give this to them, but do not let it fall into the hands of anyone else; have them kill it themselves and cook it.
The junior attendant replied, “Very well, Your Majesty,” and having gone there and spoken thus, he was refused by those women, who said, “We do not commit the taking of life.”
Having returned, she reported that matter to the king. Māgaṇḍiyā said, “Great King, you have seen it;
now you will know whether they commit the taking of life or not. Tell the lord, ‘Let them cook [the food] and send it to the ascetic Gotama.
The king having spoken thus, he sent it. The other, acting as if he were going while taking those [messengers], departed.
Having given those two cocks to the domestic priest, he brought the dead cock to them and said, "It is said that you have cooked these two cocks and sent them to the Teacher.
They replied, "Master, bring it; this is our duty," and they went out to meet him and took it.
He went into the presence of the king, and when asked, "What is it, dear sir? he said, "To the ascetic..."
"As soon as it was said, 'Cook this and send it to Gotama,' they came along the very path and took it," she explained.
Māgaṇḍiyā said, "See, Great King! They do not act toward those like you;
do you not believe me when I say that they have their aspirations set elsewhere? Although the king heard this, he remained silent, simply acquiescing. Māgaṇḍiyā...
“What indeed shall I do? he thought.
At that time, however, the king spent seven days at a time, in turn, upon the terraces of the palaces of Sāmāvatī, Vāsuladattā, and Māgaṇḍiyā.
Then [he thought], “Tomorrow or the day after tomorrow, [it will be] Sāmāvatī’s...”
Knowing that he would go to the palace roof, Māgaṇḍiyā sent a message to her younger father:
“Let him wash his fangs with an antidote and send a snake. He did so and sent it.
The king always went to his destination taking his lute, *hatthikaṇṭhavīṇā*, which had a single hole in its hollow body. Māgaṇḍiyā—
Having inserted a snake through that opening, he blocked the hole with a cluster of flowers. For two or three days, the snake remained inside the lute.
On the day the King was to depart, Māgaṇḍiyā asked, “To which woman’s palace will you go today, Your Majesty?
When it was said, “To Sāmāvatī’s,” she replied, “Today, Great King, I have seen an unpleasant dream. It is not possible—”
“Go there, Your Majesty. “We shall go,” he replied. Having been dissuaded as many as three times, she said, “If that is the case, I too will go with you, Your Majesty.
Although she was being turned back, she did not desist; saying, “I do not know what will happen, Your Majesty,” she went along with the king.
The king, having put on the garments, flowers, perfumes, and ornaments given by the Sāmāvatī-missikās, and having eaten a fine meal, laid down upon his bed with the lute placed at his head.
Māgaṇḍiyā, as if moving back and forth, removed a cluster of flowers from the hollow of the lute. A snake that had been without food for two or three days emerged through that hollow.
Breathing out, he coiled his hood and lay down upon the surface of the bed. Seeing this, Māgandiyā cried out in a loud voice, "Woe, woe!
O King, it is a snake! She reviled both the king and the women, saying, "This blind, foolish king is ill-fated;
he does not listen to my words. And these shameless, ill-behaved women—what indeed do they not receive from the presence of the king?"
"Do you think that you will live happily now that he is dead? While he was alive, you lived in misery!
Even when I tried to stop you, saying, 'Today I have seen a bad dream; it is not right for you to go to Sāmāvatī’s palace,' you did not listen to my words, O queens!
Having seen the snake, the king, terrified by the fear of death, said, "Even such as this..."
"They will do it! Oh, these wicked women! Even when she was telling me of their evil nature, I did not believe her words.
First they sat there having made holes in their own wombs; then, when I sent them a cock, they sent one back;
today they have released a snake upon my bed! Thus he became as if ablaze with anger.
Sāmāvatī also gave this exhortation to the five hundred women: "Ladies, we have no other refuge;
maintain a mind of loving-kindness equally toward the Lord of Men, the Queen, and yourselves, and do not harbor anger toward anyone.
The king, taking his horn-bow with a thousandfold strength, strung its bowstring and took up poisoned [arrows].
Having aimed his arrow and placed Sāmāvatī at the front, he had them all stand in a row and released the arrow at Sāmāvatī’s breast.

By the power of her loving-kindness (*mettā*), the arrow turned back and stood facing the path from which it had come, as if entering the king's very heart. The king thought: "The arrow I shot would have pierced even a rock..."
"It has passed right through; there is no place in the sky where it could have been obstructed. Yet, this arrow has turned back and come directly toward my heart!
Indeed, even this inanimate, lifeless arrow knows her virtue, while I, though a human being, do not.
Having thus spoken, he cast away his bow, joined his palms in reverence, and [addressed] Sāmāvatī.
Sitting on his haunches at the soles of [the Buddha’s] feet, he spoke this verse:
“I am bewildered, I am utterly confused; all the directions are dark to me.
O Sāmāvatī, protect me; may you be my refuge.”

Having heard his words, Sāmāvatī—the female disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One—did not say, "Very well, Your Majesty, go for refuge to me. Instead, she said this: "Great King, go for refuge to that very one to whom I have gone for refuge.
Then she spoke: "Do not go for refuge to me;
to him to whom I have gone for refuge, To him, Great King, is the Buddha; he is the unsurpassed Buddha."
"Go for refuge to that Buddha, and you too shall be my refuge," he said.
Having heard his words, the king said, "Now I am even more afraid," and spoke this verse:
"I am utterly bewildered; all the directions are confusing to me."
“Sāmāvatī, protect me; you must be my refuge.
Then, having again refused him in the same manner as before, when she said, “In that case, I go for refuge to you, and I go for refuge to the Teacher;
I grant you the boon,” he replied, “Let the boon be accepted, Great King.”
He said: "Having approached the Teacher, gone for refuge, and invited him, he gave a great almsgiving for seven days to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
Then, addressing Sāmāvatī, he said, 'Arise and choose a boon. She replied, 'Great King, I have no need for gold or other wealth;
however, grant me this boon and act accordingly, so that the Teacher..."
“He comes here regularly together with five hundred bhikkhus; we shall listen to the Dhamma.
The King paid homage to the Teacher and said, “Venerable Sir, please come here regularly together with five hundred bhikkhus;
Sāmāvatī and her retinue say, ‘We shall listen to the Dhamma. “Great King, for Buddhas, in one [place]...”
"It is not appropriate to go regularly; the great multitude awaits the Teacher’s arrival.
"In that case, Bhante, please command one bhikkhu. The Teacher commanded the Elder Ānanda.
From then on, taking five hundred bhikkhus with him, he went regularly to the royal palace. Those queens also [went] regularly...
They fed the Elder together with his retinue and listened to the Dhamma.
On one occasion, having heard the Elder’s discourse on the Dhamma and being filled with faith, they performed an offering of the Dhamma by presenting five hundred upper robes (*uttarāsaṅga*).
Each upper robe was worth five hundred pieces of gold.
Seeing them wearing only a single robe, the king asked, "Where is your upper robe? "It was given to us by our master," they replied.
"Was it taken by him? "Yes, it was taken. The king approached the Elder, paid homage, and asked whether the upper robes had been given away by those women.
Having heard that they had indeed been given and that the Elder had accepted them, he said, "Venerable sir, is it not true..."
“There are far too many robes; what will you do with so many? he asked.
“Great King, we shall take enough robes for ourselves and give the remainder to the monks whose robes are worn out. “What will they do with their own worn-out robes?
“They will give them to those whose robes are even more worn out. “And what will they do with their own more worn-out robes?”
“What will they do with them? “They will make bedspreads.
“What will they do with the old bedspreads? “They will make floor coverings. “What will they do with the old floor coverings?
“They will make foot-wipers, Great King. “What will they do with the old foot-wipers? “They will tear them into pieces.”
“Having pounded it and kneaded it with clay, they will plaster the wall. “Venerable sir, even after making so much, what has been given to the noble ones does not go to waste, does it?
“Yes, Great King,” he replied. The king, being inspired with faith, had another five hundred garments brought and placed at the feet of the Elder.
It is said that the Elder accepted only garments worth five hundred [pieces of gold].
Having placed five hundred coins at the feet [of the Blessed One], he received them back five hundred times;
having placed a thousand coins worth a thousand at the feet, he received them back a thousand times;
having placed a hundred thousand coins worth a hundred thousand at the feet, he received them back a hundred thousand times. One, two...
However, there is no counting the number of those obtained by way of three, four, five, ten,

and so forth. It is said that after the Tathāgata had attained final Nibbāna, the Elder traveled throughout the whole of Jambudīpa and gave to the monks in all the monasteries his own bowl and robes as their property.
Then Māgaṇḍiyā thought, “Whatever I do turns out otherwise than intended; what indeed shall I do now?
Thinking, “There is this means,” she sent a message to her younger brother while the king was going on a pleasure excursion to the park:
“Go to Sāmāvatī’s palace, open the stores of cloth and the stores of oil, and—”
“Let him soak cloths in oil-filled vessels, wrap them around the pillars, gather them all together, close the door,
place a mechanical device outside, and then go down and depart while setting fire to the house with torches.
He ascended the palace, opened the storehouses, and soaked cloths in oil-filled vessels, wrapping them around the pillars.
He began to wrap them. Then the women, headed by Sāmāvatī, approached him saying, "What is this, little father?
He replied, "Ladies, the king is having these pillars wrapped with oil-soaked rags for the sake of strengthening them;
in a royal palace, indeed, what is appropriate and what is inappropriate is difficult to discern. Do not stay near me, ladies. Having said this—
When they had arrived, she ushered them into the womb, closed the doors, secured a mechanical bolt outside, and descended while setting fire to it from the very beginning.

Sāmāvatī gave them this instruction: "As we have wandered through the cycle of existence since time immemorial, even with the wisdom of a Buddha it would not be easy to determine the limit of our bodies thus consumed by fire; therefore, be heedful."

“Let it be so. While burning in their homes, those women applied their minds to the meditation subject of the discernment of feelings (*vedanā-pariggaha-kammaṭṭhāna*), and some attained the second fruit, while others attained the third fruit. Therefore it is said:
“Then, after the meal, when they had returned from the alms round, a number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One...”
They sat down to one side, and while seated to one side, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, here the inner palace of King Udena was burned when he had gone to his park, and five hundred women, headed by Sāmāvatī, have died.
Venerable sir, what is the destination of those female lay followers? What is their future bourn? “There are, in this case, [two possibilities]...”
“Bhikkhus, there are female lay followers who are stream-enterers; there are those who are once-returners; there are those who are non-returners.

All those female lay followers, bhikkhus, have passed away without their attainment being fruitless. Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired exclamation (udāna):
“The world is bound by delusion, yet it appears as if it were real;
the fool, bound by acquisitions and enveloped in darkness,
seems to exist eternally, though for one who sees, nothing exists.”
Having spoken thus, he taught the Dhamma, saying: "Monks, beings wandering in saṃsāra do not at all times perform only meritorious deeds by being heedful;
rather, being heedless, they also perform evil deeds. Therefore, as they wander in saṃsāra, they experience both happiness and suffering."
When the king heard that Sāmāvatī’s house was reportedly burning, he came with great speed, yet he was unable to reach it before it had already been consumed by fire.
Upon arriving, while extinguishing the house, he sat down surrounded by his retinue of ministers, overcome with intense grief.
Recalling the virtues of Sāmāvatī and wondering, "Whose deed could this be? he thought of Māgaṇḍiyā.
Knowing that [the matter] would come to pass, and thinking, "If she is questioned while being threatened, she will not speak;
therefore, I shall question her slowly by means of a stratagem," he said to his ministers: "Friends, previously I was constantly rising from my seat, filled with suspicion and apprehension;
Sāmāvatī was always seeking an opportunity against me. But now my mind will be at peace."
"And we shall be able to live in comfort. They asked, "By whom, O King, was this done?
He replied, "It must have been done by someone out of affection for me. Māgandiyā, who was standing nearby, heard this and said, "No one else could have done it;
it was done by me, O King. I had my younger brother give the orders and had it executed. [He said,] "Her..."
"Except for this, there is no other being who has affection for me; I am well-pleased and grant you a boon.
Summon your circle of kinsmen. She sent a message to her relatives: "The king is pleased with me and grants a boon; let them come quickly.
The king provided great honor for each one as they arrived. Seeing that, even those who were strangers to her...
Having given a bribe, they came saying, "We are relatives of Māgaṇḍiyā.

The king had them all seized, and having have a pit dug in the royal courtyard deep enough to reach their navels, he had them sit therein; then, having filled it with earth and scattered straw over the top, he had fire set to it.
When their skin was burnt away, he had them ploughed with iron ploughshares until they were cut into pieces.
He had her ground like a diamond. From Māgaṇḍiyā’s own body as well, he tore out the flesh from the thick parts with a sharp blade;
then, having placed an oil pan on the hearth, he had it cooked like cakes and made her eat that very flesh.
In the Hall of Truth, the monks also raised this discussion: "Indeed, friends, it is unbecoming for such a person..."
“Such a death as this has befallen a female lay follower who was clear in her faith.
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?

When they replied, “About this very matter,” he said, “Monks, for women headed by Sāmāvatī, such an occurrence as this is unseemly in this present existence. It is the result of karma performed in the past.”
"But it is indeed fitting that they have obtained these [rewards]," he said. When they requested, "Venerable sir, tell us what was done by these women in the past," he related the past:
"In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, eight Paccekabuddhas resided constantly in the royal palace."
They ate. Five hundred women attended upon them. Among them, seven paccekabuddhas departed for the Himalayas;
one remained on the riverbank where there was a thicket of grass, and having entered a state of meditative absorption (jhāna), he sat there.
Then one day, when the paccekabuddhas had gone, the king took those women and went to play in the water in the river.
He went there. Having spent part of the day playing in the water, those women emerged;
oppressed by the cold and wishing to warm themselves by a fire, they wandered about saying, "Look for a place where we may make a fire.
Seeing that thicket of grass, and perceiving it as a "pile of straw," they surrounded it and set it on fire. As the grass burned and fell away, [he emerged].
Seeing the Paccekabuddha, they thought, "We are lost! A Paccekabuddha is meditating in our king's palace;
once the king finds out, he will have us executed. We must burn him to death. So all those women brought wood from here and there and piled a heap of timber over him.
It became a massive pile of wood. Then, having set it on fire, they said, "Now he shall burn!"
They departed. Having previously been unintentional, they were not bound by that karma; but now, subsequently, through intentional action, they were bound by karma.

However, even if one were to bring wood in carts by the thousands and set fire to a Paccekabuddha while he was in meditative absorption, they would not be able to produce even the slightest heat. Therefore, on the seventh day, having arisen...

She departed as she pleased. Because of having committed that deed, after being cooked in hell for many hundreds of thousands of years, through the remaining ripening of that very same karma, they were burned in this very manner in their homes throughout one hundred successive existences.
This was their prior karma.
When this was said, the bhikkhus questioned the Teacher: "Venerable sir, by what kamma was Khujjuttarā born hunchbacked;
by what kamma did she become possessed of great wisdom; by what kamma did she attain the fruit of stream-entry;
and by what kamma was she born as one who must carry out the errands of others? "Bhikkhus, it was during the reign of that very king in Bārāṇasī..."
At the time of his birth, the Paccekabuddha was somewhat hunchbacked.

Then a female attendant, having wrapped herself in a blanket and taken a golden vessel, thought, "Our Paccekabuddha moves about in such and such a manner," and she, becoming hunchbacked herself, imitated his way of walking.
As a result of that, he was born hunchbacked. Now, regarding those Paccekabuddhas...
On the first day, having seated them in the royal palace, she had bowls brought and filled with milk-rice (pāyāsa), and gave them to them.
When the bowls were full of the hot milk-rice, the Paccekabuddhas took them by turning them over and over.
Seeing them doing so, the woman gave her own eight ivory bracelets and said, "Take them after setting these here."
When they had done so and stood looking at them, he understood their intention and said, "Venerable sirs, we have no need for these.
They are given to you alone; take them and go. Taking them, they went to the Nandamūlaka Cavern.
Even today, those bracelets remain quite intact. This was due to the power of that deed.
As a result of that [merit], she has now become one who upholds the Tipiṭaka and possesses great wisdom.
Furthermore, as a result of having performed service for Paccekabuddhas, she attained the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). This was her prior karma during the interval between Buddhas.
However, in the time of the Sammasambuddha Kassapa, she was the daughter of a merchant in Bārāṇasī; when the shadow had grown long, she took a mirror...
Having taken it, she sat down while adorning herself. Then a certain trusted bhikkhunī whose taints were destroyed went to see her;
for even bhikkhunīs whose taints are destroyed like to visit the families of their supporters in the evening.
At that moment, however, there was no female messenger near the merchant’s daughter, so she said, “I pay homage.”
“Noble lady, please take this jewelry box and give it to me,” she said. The Elder Nun thought:
“If I do not give this to her after taking it, she will harbor resentment toward me and be reborn in hell.
But if I do give it to her, she will be reborn as a messenger for others. Yet, being a messenger for others is surely better than the torment of hell.”
“It is better,” she replied. Out of compassion, she took it and gave it to her. As the result of that deed, she was born as one who carries out the errands of others.
Then, on another day, the monks initiated a discussion in the Hall of Truth, beginning with Sāmāvatī: “...headed by Sāmāvatī...”
"Five hundred women were burned by fire in their house; Māgaṇḍiyā’s kinsmen, having set fire to straw above them, were split apart with iron ploughs;
Māgaṇḍiyā was cooked in boiling oil. Who indeed here are called 'living,' and who are called 'dead'?
The Teacher, having arrived, asked, "Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?"
Having asked, and being told, "It was indeed by her," [the Buddha said], "Monks, whoever is negligent, even if they live for a hundred years, they are as good as dead.
Those who are diligent, even if they have died, they truly live. Therefore, Māgaṇḍiyā, though she lives, is as good as dead;
the five hundred women headed by Sāmāvatī, though they have died, are truly alive. For, monks,..."
Having said, "The heedless indeed die," he spoke these verses:
"Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless; heedlessness is the path of death.
The heedful do not die; those who are heedless are as if already dead."
“Having understood this distinction, the wise take delight in heedfulness;
they rejoice in heedfulness, finding pleasure in the domain of the Noble Ones.
Those meditators, constant and always firm in their exertion,”
“The wise touch Nibbāna, the unsurpassed security from bondage.

In this context, the word *appamāda* (heedfulness) illuminates a great significance; it stands having grasped a great significance. For even if the entirety of the Buddha’s word in the Three Piṭakas were brought forward and explained, it would all converge upon the very term *appamāda*. Therefore it was said:
“Bhikkhus, just as whatever footprints of forest animals there may be, they are all encompassed within the footprint of the elephant...”
they all converge upon it; the elephant's footprint is declared to be their foremost by way of its size.
Even so, bhikkhus, whatever wholesome states there are, they are all rooted in heedfulness, they converge upon heedfulness, and heedfulness is declared to be the foremost among those states.”
In its essential meaning, this is called "non-separation from mindfulness. It is so named because mindfulness is constantly established.
"The deathless state" (*amatapada*): the "deathless" (*amata*) refers to Nibbāna. For it does not grow old nor does it die, because it is unborn;
therefore, it is called "deathless. "State" (*pada*) means that by which one goes; the meaning is that they reach the deathless. The "state of the deathless" is *amatapada*.
It means "the means for attaining the Deathless. "Heedlessness" (*pamāda*) is the state of being negligent;
it is a name for the relinquishing of mindfulness, which is characterized as forgetfulness (*muṭṭhassati*). "Of death" (*maccuno*) means of dying. "Footstep" (*pada*) means a means or a path.
For one who is heedless does not transcend birth; once born, he both decays and dies. Thus, heedlessness is called the "footstep of death," that is, of death itself.
"He approaches. "The heedful do not die" means that those endowed with mindfulness, being heedful, do not die. "They become ageless and immortal" is not to be taken literally;
for there is no sentient being whatsoever who is called ageless and immortal.

However, for the heedless, the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is indeed unlimited, whereas for the heedful, it is limited. Therefore, because the heedless are not liberated from birth and the rest, [they are said to die].

Even while living, they are as if dead; however, those who are diligent, having increased the characteristic of heedfulness, will quickly realize the paths and fruits and will not be reborn in a second or third existence.
Therefore, whether they are living or dead, they are indeed said not to die. But those beings who are negligent are, as it were, already dead by way of the death of negligence.
Because of death; for just as those who are dead due to the severance of the life-faculty are like a block of wood, devoid of consciousness, so too do they become.
For even among those householders who are like the dead, not even a single thought arises such as, "We shall give alms, we shall guard our virtue, we shall perform the Uposatha rites";
and even among those who have gone forth, [no thought arises regarding] duties toward teachers, preceptors, and so forth.

According to the view that [the thought], "We shall fulfill [the perfections], we shall undertake the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), we shall increase our meditation," does not arise [in those who are negligent], how then can they be distinguished from the dead?
Therefore it was said: "Those who are negligent are as if dead. Thus, having understood the distinction:
for one who is negligent there is no escape from the round of existence (vaṭṭa), whereas for one who is diligent there is.
Having thus understood this distinction specifically: who, then, understands this distinction?
"The wise are intent on heedfulness"—those who are wise, intelligent, and possessed of discernment, who, established in their own heedfulness, increase that heedfulness;
they alone understand the cause of this distinction. "They delight in heedfulness"—having understood this, they themselves delight in their own heedfulness, with faces beaming with joy.

They are joyful and exultant. "Delighting in the domain of the Noble Ones" means that, rejoicing thus in heedfulness, they increase that heedfulness and become delighted, devoted, and fully absorbed in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—such as the four foundations of mindfulness—which are reckoned as the domain of the Noble Ones (the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddha), as well as in the ninefold supramundane dhamma. This is the meaning.

"Those meditators": those who are diligent and wise are meditators by means of two kinds of meditation—namely, the "meditation on the object" (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna), which consists of the eight attainments, and the "meditation on characteristics" (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna), which consists of insight, the path, and the fruit.
"Constant": from the time of their initial renunciation until the attainment of the path of Arahantship, they possess constant physical and mental energy. "Always firm in exertion."

"Whatever can be attained by human strength, human energy, and human exertion—that which they have not reached, their energy will not cease"—thus, with such energy, they are endowed with unflagging persistence and firm exertion that proceeds continuously.
"They touch": here there are two kinds of touching—touching by knowledge and touching as fruition.
In this context, the four paths are called "contact through knowledge," and the four fruits are called "contact through fruition.

Of these, it is contact through fruition that is intended here. The wise and learned ones, realizing Nibbāna by means of the noble fruit, touch it and realize Nibbāna through that contact with fruition.
[The phrase] "the unsurpassed security from bondage" refers to those four...

The yogas cause the great multitude to sink into the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*); because they are the best among all mundane and supramundane phenomena due to being secure and fearless, they are called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*).
At the conclusion of the teaching, many became stream-enterers and so forth. Thus, the teaching became beneficial for the great multitude.
The First Story of Sāmāvatī.
2. The Story of the Merchant Kumbhaghosaka.
While staying at Veḷuvana, the Teacher gave this Dhamma teaching concerning Kumbhaghosaka, beginning with the words: "One who is diligent in exertion..."
He related the story. For in the city of Rājagaha, a snake-epidemic broke out in the house of the treasurer of Rājagaha.
When it arose, starting from the flies and continuing down to the cattle, the animals died first;
after them, the slaves and laborers; and last of all, the owners of the house. Therefore, that disease eventually seized both the treasurer and his wife. Because of the disease, they...
Stricken with grief, they looked at their son standing nearby and, with eyes filled with tears, said to him:
"Dear son, it is said that when this disease breaks out, only those who break through the wall and flee can save their lives. Yet you have fled without looking back at us;
now, having returned alive, you have buried forty crores of wealth for us in such-and-such a place."
“Having set them aside, you should remove them and provide for your livelihood.
Having heard their words, weeping and bowing to his parents, he fled in fear of death, broke through a wall, and went into a mountain thicket.
Having lived there for twelve years, he returned to the place where his parents resided.
Then, because he had gone away during his childhood and returned when his hair and beard were grown, no one recognized him.
Following the instructions given to him by his parents, he went to the place where the wealth was kept; having ascertained that the wealth was safe and sound, he thought:
"No one recognizes me. If I were to extract the treasure and put it to use, people would say, 'A poor man has extracted a hidden treasure.'"
“They might seize me and mistreat me; what if I were to live by working for wages?
Then, putting on a tattered rag as a lower garment, he reached the street of laborers, asking, “Is there anyone who needs a hired hand?
When the laborers saw him, they said, “If you will do one task for us, we shall give you food and wages. “What [task]?”
“What kind of task is this? “It is the task of awakening and exhorting. If you are able, rise early in the morning and, having wandered about, announce:
‘Sirs, arise! Prepare the carts! Yoke the oxen! It is time to go for the elephants and horses’ fodder!
Ladies, you too arise! Cook the rice-gruel! Cook the meal! He replied, “Very well.”
He accepted it. Then they gave him a house for his residence. He performed that work every day.
One day, King Bimbisāra heard a sound; he was one who understood all sounds.
Therefore, he said, "This is the sound of a man of great wealth. Then a female attendant standing near him [said]: "The King..."
Thinking, "He will not tell me this or that; it is necessary for me to know this," he sent a man, saying, "Go, dear son, find out about him.
That man went quickly, saw him, and returned, reporting, "This is a poor man who works as a hired laborer among the servants.
When the king heard his words, he remained silent, and on the second day as well—
On the third day as well, having heard that sound, she spoke in the same manner.

That female attendant, likewise reflecting in the same way and sending her again and again, thought: "When it was said, 'This is a poor man,' the king did not believe it even after hearing those words;
yet he says over and over again, 'This is the sound of a very wealthy man.'"
“There must be a reason for this; it is fitting to understand this according to its true nature.
She said to the king, “Your Majesty, if I receive a thousand [pieces of gold], I will take my daughter, go, and cause this wealth to enter the royal palace.
The king had a thousand given to her.
Taking her daughter and having her put on a single soiled cotton garment, she departed from the royal palace with her.
Acting as if she were traveling along a road, she went to the street of laborers, entered a certain house, and said, "Mother, we are travelers on the road;
we shall rest here for a day or two and then depart. "Mother, there are many..."
“There are people in the house; it is not possible to live here. This house of Kumbhaghosaka is empty;
go there. Having gone there, she said, “Husband, we are travelers on the road;
we will stay here for one or two days,” but even though she was repeatedly refused by him, she said, “Husband, having stayed for just this one day today, we will depart at dawn.”
She did not wish to go out. Staying right there, on the following day at the time of his departure for the forest, she said, "Husband, give me your fodder and go;
I will cook food for you. When he replied, "Enough, mother, I myself will cook and eat," she pressed him repeatedly until he gave her just enough to take with him, which she took from the market.

Having had vessels and pure rice and other ingredients brought, she prepared very pure boiled rice according to the cooking methods used in the royal palace, along with two or three delicious soups and condiments, and gave them to him when he returned from the forest.
Then, knowing that he had eaten and had become softened in heart, she said, "Master, we are weary; please stay right here for one or two days."
"Let us perform the fire sacrifice," he said. He accepted, saying, "Very well.
Then she cooked sweet food for him both that evening and on the following day and gave it to him.
Then, perceiving his gentle disposition, she said, "Master, we shall stay right here for a few days. While staying there, with a sharp knife... of him—
He cut the crossbars beneath the bed here and there. As soon as the bed approached and sat down upon it, it hung down below.
He asked, "Why has this bed come apart like this? [The mother replied], "Master, I am unable to stop the young children;
they keep crowding right here. [He said], "Mother, this suffering of mine is because of you."
“It has happened. For previously, whenever I was going anywhere, I used to go after closing the door.
“What can I do, dear? I am not able to stop you,” he replied. In this very manner, she cut [the ropes] two or three days in succession.
Although she was being reproached and censured by him for that, she spoke in the same way; then, having set aside one or two ropes, she cut the rest. Him—
On that very day, as soon as he sat down, all his wealth fell to the ground; his head and knees became joined together.
Rising up, he said, "What shall I do? Where shall I go now? You have made me like one who has no owner even for my bed.
[The other replied: "Dear son, what can I do? To prevent the children of our neighbors..."
“I cannot; let it be, do not worry—where would you go at such an hour?
Having thus addressed his daughter, he said, “My child, prepare a place for your brother to lie down.
She lay down on one side and said, “Come here, Master. The other also told her, “Go, dear, lie down with your sister. He, by her...
Having lain down together on the same bed, they became intimate that very day; the young woman wept.
Then her mother asked her, "Daughter, why do you weep? "Mother, this has happened," she replied. "Be still, daughter; what can be done?
You too must receive one husband, and he too must be your servant at your feet."
He made him his son-in-law. They lived together in harmony.
After a few days had passed, she sent a message to the king: "Let a festival be held in the street of the hired laborers.
