And let a proclamation be made: 'A fine of such-and-such an amount shall be imposed on whoever does not hold a festival in their house. The king—
He did exactly so. Then his mother-in-law said to him, "Dear son, by the king’s command, a festival must be held in the street of laborers;
what shall we do? "Mother, even though I work for wages, I cannot make a living; what can I do?
"Dear son, those living the household life indeed take on debt; it is not permitted to disobey the king's command. From debt..."
"There is no way to be released by any means whatsoever; go and bring one or two kahāpaṇas from somewhere," she said.
Feeling resentful and distressed, he went and brought back only a single kahāpaṇa from a place where there were forty million pieces of wealth.
She sent that kahāpaṇa to the king, and having celebrated the festival with her own kahāpaṇa, after a few days had passed—
In that same manner, she sent a message. Again, the king likewise commanded: "Let them hold a festival; for those who do not, let there be such-and-such a fine.
Once more, being pressured by her after speaking to him in the same way, he went and brought three kahāpaṇas.
She sent those kahāpaṇas to the king as well, and after a few days had passed, she again sent a message in the same manner: "Now..."
“Send men and have him summoned,” he said. The king sent them. The men went and, having asked, “Which one is Kumbhaghosaka?
they searched for him; finding him, they said, “Come, sir, the king summons you.
Terrified, he thought, “The king does not know me,” and so on, and did not wish to go. Then, by force—
They seized him by his hands and other limbs and dragged him away. When that woman saw them, she rebuked them, saying, "Hey, you ill-behaved ones!
It is utterly improper for you to seize my son-in-law by his hands and other limbs. Then, taking her daughter with her, she said, "Come, dear, do not be afraid;
once we have seen the king, I will have the hands of those who seized you cut off right then and there," and went before him toward the royal palace.
Having assumed a disguise and adorned herself with all her ornaments, she stood to one side. They then dragged the other woman along and brought her as well.
When she had paid homage and stood before him, the king asked, "Are you Kumbhaghosaka by name? "Yes, Your Majesty," she replied.
"For what reason do you live by deceiving people out of great wealth? "From where, Your Majesty, could I have such wealth? I live by working for wages."
"Do not do this; why do you deceive us? "I am not deceiving you, Your Majesty; I have no wealth," he replied.
Then the king, showing him those kahāpaṇas, asked, "To whom do these kahāpaṇas belong? Having recognized them, he thought, "Alas, I am a fool!
How indeed did these come into the king's hand? Looking here and there, he saw those two women, adorned with ornaments.
Standing at the entrance of the womb, she saw them and thought, "This is surely a grave matter; these must have been dispatched by the king.
Then the king said to her, "Tell me, sir, why do you act in this way? "I have no patron, Your Majesty," he replied.
"It is not fitting for one such as I to be your patron," [the king said]. "It would be well, Your Majesty, if Your Majesty were my refuge."
“I am here, sir. How much wealth do you have? “Forty crores, O King.
“What must be obtained? “Wagons, O King. The king had several hundred wagons yoked and sent them;
having had that wealth brought and piled up in the royal courtyard, he caused the inhabitants of Rājagaha to assemble and said: “Is there...”
When he asked someone in this city, "How much wealth does he have? they replied, "There is none, Your Majesty.
"But what is it appropriate for him to do? "He should be honored, Your Majesty," they said.

Having established him in the position of treasurer with great honor and given his daughter to him, [the King] went together with him into the presence of the Teacher. Having paid homage, he said, "Venerable Sir, look at this..."
"Among men, there is no one so steadfast as this; even though he possesses a fortune of four hundred million, he shows neither a trace of arrogance nor the slightest conceit of 'I am.
Like a pauper, he lives by wearing rags and working for wages on the street of laborers.
By such means I have come to know him. Having learned of him, I summoned him and [learned] his state of possessing wealth."
“Having had that wealth accepted and brought back, he was established in the position of treasurer, and my daughter was given to him by me.
Venerable sir, never before have I seen anyone so resolute,” he said.
Having heard this, the Teacher said, “In this way, O Great King, the livelihood of one who lives is called a righteous livelihood; it is not theft or suchlike deeds.”
But it oppresses and harms one both in this world and in the next; consequently, there is no such thing as happiness arising from that source.
For when a man’s wealth is lost, his livelihood—whether earned through farming or by labor—is indeed a righteous livelihood.
For one such as this, who is endowed with energy, endowed with mindfulness, whose bodily and verbal actions are purified, and who acts with circumspection through wisdom—
“Indeed, for one who is restrained in body and so forth, who lives a life of righteousness, and who abides without being separated from mindfulness, sovereignty increases.
Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“For one who is industrious and mindful...”
"For one who performs deeds of purity, who acts with reflection,
who is self-restrained, who lives according to the Dhamma,
and who is heedful, glory increases."
In this context, "possessing initiative" means one who possesses the energy of exertion. "Possessing mindfulness" means one who is endowed with mindfulness.
"Pure in action" means one who is possessed of faultless and blameless bodily actions and so forth. "Acting with circumspection" refers to having such a basis as:
"If it will be thus, I shall do thus," or "When this action is performed in this way, such a result will follow."
For one who, having observed and reflected upon all tasks as if treating a disease, performs them after careful consideration;

for one who is restrained—that is, restrained in body and so forth, being without flaw; for one who lives by the Dhamma—that is, for a householder who avoids cheating with scales and the like and subsists through agriculture, cattle-rearing, and so forth, and for a homeless one who avoids the practice of medicine, acting as a messenger, and the like, and lives according to the Dhamma.
"For one who maintains his livelihood by an even course of alms-gathering; for one who is heedful" means for one whose mindfulness does not depart.
"His fame increases" means that his fame—consisting both of the possession of power and wealth and of the recounting of his praise and reputation—increases.

At the conclusion of the verse, Kumbhaghosaka was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). Many others also attained the fruits of stream-entry and so forth. Thus, the teaching of the Dhamma became beneficial to the great multitude.
The second story, concerning the merchant Kumbhaghosaka.
3. The Story of the Elder Cūḷapanthaka.
While residing at Veḷuvana, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma instruction concerning the Elder Cūḷapanthaka, beginning with the words: “By exertion and by heedfulness.”

It is said that in Rājagaha, when the daughter of a wealthy merchant family reached marriageable age, she was being strictly guarded by her parents on the upper floor of a seven-storied palace. Intoxicated by the pride of youth, she became lustful for men;
having formed an intimacy with her own slave, she became afraid that others might discover this conduct of hers.
He spoke thus: “We cannot live in this place. If my parents discover this fault, they will cut me to pieces.
We shall go and live in a foreign land. Taking their portable wealth, they departed through the main gate, thinking, “Wherever it may be, we shall go to a place unknown to others and live there.”
Both of them went there. While they were living in one place, through their cohabitation, a fetus was conceived in her womb.
When the fetus reached maturity, she consulted with him: "The fetus has reached maturity;
for both of us to give birth in a place devoid of kinsmen and relatives will bring suffering."
"Let us go to our own family home. He thought, "If I go there, I shall not survive," and out of fear, he let the days pass, saying, "We will go today," or "We will go tomorrow. She reflected:
"This fool does not venture to go because of the greatness of his own fault; parents are indeed solely for one's welfare—let him go, or..."
"Or else, I shall go myself. When he had departed from the house, she put away the household utensils, informed her neighbors that she had gone to her own family home, and set out on the road.
He too, having returned home and not seeing her, questioned his neighbors; hearing that she had gone to her family home, [he followed].
Having pursued her with speed, he caught up with her on the way. There, she too gave birth right then and there.
He asked, "What is this, dear lady? "My lord, a son has been born to me. "Now what shall we do?
"The very purpose for which we were going to our family home has been accomplished right here on the road. Thereupon—
Thinking, "What shall we do by going? We shall turn back," they both turned back with one mind.
Because that child was born on the road (*pantha*), they gave him the name Panthaka. Not long after, she conceived another fetus.
Everything is to be detailed in the same manner as before. Because that child also was born on the road, [he was named] after the first-born...
Having given the name Mahāpanthaka to the elder, they gave the other the name Cūḷapanthaka.
Taking both boys with them, they returned to their own dwelling place.
While they were living there, the boy Mahāpanthaka heard other children calling their parents "little father" and "great father," or "uncle" and "aunt," and he questioned his mother.
“Mother, other children say, ‘uncle’ and ‘aunt,’ and also ‘great-uncle’ and ‘little-uncle.
Do we have no relatives at all? “Yes, dear, we have no relatives here.
But in the city of Rājagaha, you have a grandfather named Dhanaseṭṭhi; there we have many relatives. “Why do we not go there?”
“Go, my dear,” she said. Without telling her son the reason for her not going, as her children urged her again and again, she said to her husband:
“These children are distressing me greatly; will our parents eat us raw upon seeing us?
Come, let us show the children their grandfather’s family. “I must be present in person…”
“I shall not be able to [bring them back], but I will lead them there. “Very well; by whatever means possible, it is right for the children to see their grandfather’s family.
Both people took the children and, traveling by stages, eventually reached Rājagaha.
Entering a certain hall at the city gate, the mother of the children took hold of the two boys and informed her parents that she had arrived.
He had it announced. Having heard that message, they said, "In the course of wandering through saṃsāra, there is no one who has not previously been our son or daughter;
they have committed a great offense against us and cannot remain within the range of our sight.
Let these two people take this much wealth and go to a comfortable place to live; as for the children—"
"Send them here," they said, and having given the wealth, they dispatched a messenger.
Having received the wealth sent by them, [the parents] placed the children in the hands of the very messengers who had arrived and sent them off.
The children grew up in the family of their maternal grandfather. Among them, Cūḷapanthaka was very young, but Mahāpanthaka, together with his maternal grandfather—
He went to hear the Dhamma discourse of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers. As he went constantly into the presence of the Teacher, his mind inclined toward the going forth.
He said to his grandfather, “If you would grant me permission, I would go forth.
“What do you say, dear? Even for the whole world, your going forth would be more auspicious than my own; if—”
“Are you able? Go forth! Having brought him into the presence of the Teacher, when the Teacher asked, “Householder, have you obtained a son?
he replied, “Yes, venerable sir; this is my grandson, and he wishes to go forth in your presence.
The Teacher commanded a certain monk who was wandering for alms, “Ordain this boy. The Elder [then performed the ordination] for him.

Having explained the meditation subject of the five aggregates, he ordained him. Having mastered much of the Buddha’s word and received full ordination after completing his years of training, he practiced the meditation subject with wise attention and attained arahantship.
Passing his time in the bliss of jhāna and the bliss of fruition, he thought: "Would it be possible for Cūḷapanthaka to attain this same bliss?"
“Let him be given! Then, having gone into the presence of the Elder Merchant (Ayyakaseṭṭhi), he said, “Great Merchant, if you would grant permission, I shall ordain Cūḷapanthaka.
“Ordain him, venerable sir,” he replied. It is said that the merchant was well-pleased with the Teaching;
and when asked, “Whose daughters’ sons are these? he answered, “They are the sons of my runaway daughter.”

He felt ashamed; therefore, he granted them permission to go forth with ease. The Elder, having ordained Cūḷapanthaka, established him in the precepts. Yet, even after going forth, he was slow-witted.
"Just as the fragrant red lotus..."
“In the morning it may be in full bloom, its fragrance not yet faded;
behold the son of Aṅgīrasa shining brightly,
like the sun scorching in the sky.”
He was unable to learn this single verse even after four months.
It is said that during the time of the Sammasambuddha Kassapa, he had gone forth and, being wise, engaged in a joking mockery while another slow-witted bhikkhu was receiving his oral instruction.
That bhikkhu, feeling ashamed because of that mockery, neither received the instruction nor practiced recitation.
Due to that karma, even after going forth, he became dull-witted; whatever word he grasped would be lost as he attempted to grasp the next one in succession.
Four months passed while he was striving to master this very verse.
Then Mahāpanthaka said to him, "Cūḷapanthaka, you are incapable in this dispensation; in four months you have not mastered even one..."
"You cannot even learn a single verse; how then will you bring the duties of one who has gone forth to their completion?
Depart from here! Thus he was driven out of the monastery. Because of his affection for the Buddha’s teaching, Cūḷapanthaka did not desire the state of a householder.
At that time, Mahāpanthaka was the distributor of meals. Jīvaka Komārabhacca had brought many garlands, perfumes, and ointments.

Taking [the mangoes], he went to his own mango grove, honored the Teacher, and having heard the Dhamma, rose from his seat, paid homage to the One of Ten Powers, and approached Mahāpanthaka, asking, "Venerable sir, how many bhikkhus are there in the presence of the Teacher?
"About five hundred bhikkhus," he replied. "Tomorrow, venerable sir, [let us invite] the five hundred bhikkhus headed by the Buddha..."

“Take it and receive alms at our residence. The Elder replied, “Lay follower, there is a monk named Cūḷapanthaka who is slow and of a nature that does not grow; excluding him, I accept the invitation for the rest.
Upon hearing this, Cūḷapanthaka thought: “The Elder, while accepting the invitation for so many monks...”
"If he accepts me as an outsider, there is no doubt that my brother’s heart has turned away from me;
what use have I now for this religious life? I shall live as a householder, performing meritorious deeds such as giving.
On the following day at dawn, he set out to leave the order.
At the very time of dawn, the Teacher, surveying the world, saw this circumstance.
Going there first, he stood walking back and forth at the gatehouse on the path by which Cūḷapanthaka was traveling.
As Cūḷapanthaka was going along, he saw the Teacher, approached him, paid homage, and stood to one side. Then the Teacher said to him, "Where are you going, Cūḷapanthaka, by this [path]?"
“Are you going at the wrong time? he asked. “Venerable sir, my brother is driving me out; that is why I am going away to disrobe,” Cūḷapanthaka replied.
“Cūḷapanthaka, your going forth belongs to me. Why did you not come to me when driven out by your brother?
Come! What is the use of the life of a householder? You shall remain with me. And with his hand, whose palm was marked with a wheel, [the Buddha took him by the hand].
Having touched him on the head and taken him away, he seated him at the entrance of the Fragrant Chamber and said,
"Cūḷapanthaka, facing eastward and rubbing this piece of cloth while saying, 'Dust-remover, dust-remover,' remain right here.
Having given him a perfectly pure piece of cloth prepared through supernormal power, and when the time had been announced, he sat surrounded by the community of monks.
Having gone to Jīvaka’s house, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Cūḷapanthaka, meanwhile, looking at the sun and rubbing that rag, sat there saying, "Dust-remover! Dust-remover! As he was rubbing that piece of rag, it became soiled.
Then he thought: "This piece of rag was extremely pure, yet now..."
“Relying upon this personal existence, having abandoned its former nature, it has thus become defiled; impermanent indeed are conditioned phenomena!
Thus, establishing the contemplation of their destruction and fall, he increased his insight. The Teacher, knowing that Cūḷapanthaka’s mind had ascended to insight, said:
“Cūḷapanthaka, you have been regarding even a mere ragged piece of cloth as defiled, thinking, ‘It is dust, it is dust.’”
"Do not form a perception; however, within you there are the dusts of passion and so forth—remove them!
Having said this, he emitted a radiance and, appearing with a visible form as if sitting before him, spoke these verses:
"Passion is called 'dust,' but it is not called 'dust' in the sense of a particle."
"Passion" is a designation for "dust.
Having utterly abandoned this dust, O monks,
they dwell in the teaching of the One Free from Dust.
“Defilement is called ‘dust,’ not the pollen of the air;
this is a designation for defilement, namely ‘dust.
Having completely abandoned this dust, O monks,”
“They dwell in the teaching of the One Free from Dust.
“Delusion is dust, and it is not called ‘dust’ in the sense of soil;
this is a designation for delusion: ‘dust.’”
“Having utterly abandoned this dust, O monks, they dwell in the teaching of Him who is free from dust.
At the conclusion of this verse, Cūḷapanthaka attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Along with those very analytical knowledges, the three Piṭakas came to him.
It is said that formerly, when he was a king, while performing a circumambulation of the city, sweat broke out from his forehead;

he wiped his forehead with a pure cloth, and the cloth became soiled. Thinking, "Depending upon this body, even such a pure cloth has abandoned its natural state and become soiled—impermanent indeed are conditioned phenomena," he cultivated the perception of impermanence.
He obtained them. Because of that, the dust-remover itself became the requisite for him.
Jīvaka Komārabhacca also offered water for the Teacher’s ablution.
The Teacher covered the bowl with his hand, saying, "Jīvaka, are there not monks in the monastery? Mahāpanthaka said, "Venerable Sir, are there not [monks] in the monastery?"
“There are no monks,” he said. The Teacher replied, “There are, Jīvaka.
Jīvaka then sent a man, saying, “In that case, go and find out for yourself whether there are monks in the monastery or not.
At that moment, Cūḷapanthaka thought, “My brother says there are no monks in the monastery; [let us see] in the monastery...”
“...I shall demonstrate the presence of these monks,” he thought; thus, he filled the entire mango grove with nothing but monks.
Some monks were engaged in sewing robes, some were engaged in dyeing, and some were engaged in recitation.
In this way, he established a thousand monks who were each unlike one another. That man [saw] many monks in the monastery.
Having seen this, he turned back and informed Jīvaka, saying, "Venerable sir, the entire mango grove is filled with bhikkhus.
The Elder, right there, [recited:
"Having manifested himself a thousand times, Paṭṭhaka..."
“Sit in the delightful mango grove until the time for the announcement.
Then the Teacher said to that man, “Go to the monastery and say, ‘The Teacher summons the one named Cūḷapanthaka.
When he had gone and spoken thus, [Cūḷapanthaka replied] with a thousand voices, “I am Cūḷapanthaka! I am Cūḷapanthaka!”
“Get up! That man went back again and said, “Venerable sir, it seems that all of them are indeed named Cūḷapanthaka.
“In that case, go and take hold of the hand of whoever first says, ‘I am Cūḷapanthaka’; the rest will vanish.
He did so, and at that very moment, about a thousand bhikkhus vanished.
The Elder also went along with that man. At the conclusion of the meal, the Teacher addressed Jīvaka:
“Jīvaka, take the bowl of Cūḷapanthaka; he shall offer you the blessing. Jīvaka did so.
The Elder, letting out a lion’s roar like a young lion, stirred up the three Piṭakas and offered the blessing.
The Teacher rose from his seat and, surrounded by the community of monks, went to the monastery.

When the monks had performed the customary duties, he stood at the entrance of the Fragrant Chamber, gave the Sugata’s exhortation to the community of monks, and after teaching them a meditation subject, dismissed the assembly.
He then entered the Fragrant Chamber, which was perfumed with fragrant scents, and lay down on his right side in the lion’s posture.
Then, at the time of evening, the bhikkhus gathered from here and there and sat down as if surrounded by a red woolen rug;
they began a discussion on the virtues of the Teacher, saying, "Friends, Mahāpanthaka, not knowing Cūḷapanthaka’s disposition,
was unable to have him learn a single verse in four months, thinking, 'This man is slow-witted.'"

"He was cast out from the monastery; however, through his own state as the unsurpassed Dharma-King, the Perfectly Enlightened One bestowed upon him Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) during that very same single meal. The three Piṭakas also arrived along with the analytical knowledges themselves.
Oh, how great indeed is the power of the Buddhas!"
Then the Blessed One, having understood this conversation taking place in the Dhamma Hall, thought, "It is fitting for me to go today.

Rising from his Buddha-recluse posture, he donned his bright red inner robe, fastened his waistband like a flash of lightning, and put on his Great Robe of the Well-Gone One, which resembled a crimson woolen blanket.
Emerging from the fragrant Perfumed Chamber, he displayed the majestic gait of a noble elephant in rut or a lion’s stretch.
Having gone to the Dhamma assembly with infinite Buddha-play, he ascended the excellently prepared, noble Buddha-seat in the center of the decorated circular pavilion.
Emitting the six-colored rays of a Buddha and agitating the depths of the ocean like the morning sun upon the peak of Mount Yugandhara, he sat down in the middle of the seat.
As soon as the Perfectly Enlightened One had arrived, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus—
How did he become silent after cutting them off? The Teacher, looking upon the assembly with a mild and loving heart, thought:
"This assembly shines exceedingly; not a single person has any anxiety regarding their hands or feet, nor is there the sound of coughing or sneezing.
All these people are full of reverence out of respect for the Buddha, and are struck with awe by the Buddha’s majesty."
“While I am sitting here without having spoken even for the duration of a single lifetime, they will not initiate the first conversation.
The duty of initiating conversation must be known by me alone; I myself shall speak first.
Addressing the bhikkhus with a sweet, Brahma-like voice, he asked, “Bhikkhus, about what topic are you gathered here now?”
Having asked, "And what was your interrupted conversation? and being told, "It was this very one," [the Buddha said], "Monks, it is not only now that Cūḷapanthaka is slow;
he was slow even in the past. It is not only now that I have become his support;
I was indeed his support even before. Furthermore, in the past, I made him the master of this worldly household."
"Now, regarding the supramundane family," having said this, being requested by the monks who desired to hear that matter in detail, he related the past:
"In the past, monks, a young brahmin living in the city of Bārāṇasī went to Takkasilā for the purpose of learning a craft;
there, as a student of the Dhamma under a world-renowned teacher, he was among five hundred young brahmins."
He was extremely helpful to his teacher, performing all duties such as massaging his feet;
however, due to his dullness, he was unable to learn anything. Although the teacher thought, "This man is very helpful to me;
I shall instruct him," and strove to do so, he could not teach him anything. After living there for a long time, he was unable to learn even a single verse.
Unable to remain and becoming weary, he asked his teacher for permission, saying, "I shall go. The teacher thought: "This man has been helpful to me;
I expect him to become wise. I cannot let him go; I must certainly repay his kindness.
I will compose a charm for him and give it to him. He led him into the forest and said, "Strike..."
Having bound this mantra—“He strikes; for what reason does he strike?
I too know it, I know it!”—and having had him recite it many hundreds of times while teaching it to him, he asked, “Do you understand it?
When he replied, “Yes, I understand,” he said, “A craft that has been mastered through diligent effort will certainly not be lost.”
Having reflected thus, he gave him provisions for the journey and sent him forth, saying: "Go;
you shall live by means of this mantra, but you must constantly recite it so that you do not lose it.
Then, when he arrived in Bārāṇasī, his mother, thinking, "My son has returned after learning his craft," accorded him great honor and hospitality.
Then the King of Bārāṇasī, reflecting, "Is there perhaps some fault in my bodily actions and so forth?
and seeing no deed whatsoever that he himself disapproved of, thought: "One's own fault is not perceived by oneself;
it is perceived by others. I shall investigate the citizens. Having thought thus, he went out in the evening dressed in the guise of a stranger.
“After eating their evening meal, when people are sitting together, their conversation will take many forms:
‘If I were to rule the kingdom unrighteously, we would have been destroyed by that wicked and unrighteous king through punishments, taxes, and the like.
Or they will say, ‘If he rules the kingdom righteously, may our king live long,’ and so forth, thus speaking of my virtues.”
He wandered along the walls of those various houses.
At that moment, tunnel-thieves were breaking through a tunnel between two houses, using a single tunnel to enter both houses.
When the king saw them, he stood in the shadow of a house. As they were breaking through the tunnel—
When he entered the house and was looking at the belongings, the young man woke up and, reciting that mantra, said: "You have struck me! You have struck me!
For what reason have you struck me? I too know it, I know it! Hearing this, they thought, "It seems we have been discovered by him;
now he will destroy us. Terrified, they even cast off their lower garments and fled from right in front of him.
They fled. Seeing them fleeing and hearing the sound of the other man’s recitation of the mantras, the king determined that his own house was safe, took charge of the city, and entered his residence.
When the night had turned to dawn, early in the morning, he summoned a certain man and said: “Go, my good man, to such-and-such a street, to the house where—”
“One limb is missing; there is a young brahmin who has returned from Takkasilā after learning his craft there—bring him here.
He went and, saying, “The king summons you,” brought the young brahmin.
Then the king said to him, “Dear son, are you the young brahmin who has returned from Takkasilā after learning his craft? “Yes, Your Majesty,” he replied. “We too [require] that same...”
“Teach me a craft,” he said. “Very well, Your Majesty; sit on an equal seat and learn it,” he replied.
The king did so, and having received the mantra, he gave him a thousand pieces, saying, “This is your teacher’s fee.
At that time, the commander-in-chief asked the king’s barber, “When will you shave the king’s beard? “Tomorrow or the day after tomorrow,” he replied.
Or rather,” he said. Having given him the thousand pieces and saying, “I have a task to attend to,” when asked, “What is it, master?
he replied, “Acting as if you were performing the king’s shaving, sharpen your razor excessively and cut his windpipe.
You shall be the general, and I shall be the king. He accepted, saying, “Very well,” and on the day the king was to have his beard shaved—
Having moistened his beard with scented water and sharpened the razor, he took hold of it by the handle and thought, "The razor has a slightly blunt edge;
it must cut the throat in a single stroke. Then, standing to one side again, he sharpened the razor.
At that moment, the king recalled his own mantra and, while reciting it, said: "Strike! Strike! What..."
"Why did you strike me? I too know, I know your reason," he said. Sweat broke out on the barber's forehead.
Thinking, "The king knows my reason," he became terrified; throwing his razor to the ground, he prostrated himself at the king's feet with his chest.
Kings are indeed clever, so the king spoke thus to him: "Hey, you wicked barber! Do you think, 'The king does not know me'?"
“Are you making a sign? [He replied: “Grant me safety, Your Majesty. [The King said: “Let it be; do not fear. Speak. [The man said:
“Your Majesty, the general gave me a thousand [pieces of gold] and said, ‘Cut his windpipe as if you were shaving the king’s beard;
when I become king, I will make him the general. When the king heard this, he thought, “My life depends upon my teacher.”
Thinking, "I have received [my life]," he summoned the general and said, "Ho, general!
What indeed have you not received from me? I cannot bear to see you now; depart from my kingdom!
Having thus banished him from the kingdom, he summoned his teacher and said, "Teacher, it was by depending on you that I regained my life."
Having paid him great honor, he gave him the position of commander-in-chief. "At that time, Cūḷapanthaka was that person, and the Teacher was the world-renowned master.
Having brought up this past event, the Teacher said, "Thus, monks, even in the past, Cūḷapanthaka was indeed slow-witted."
"Even then, having become her support, I established her in a worldly household," he said. Then, on another day,
when the talk arose— "Oh, how the Teacher became a support for Cūḷapanthaka!"—
he related the past-life story from the Cūḷaseṭṭhi Jātaka and said:
“Even with a small load, the wise and discerning man raises himself up, like a tiny fire when it is fanned.
Having spoken this verse, he said: “Monks, it is not only now that I have become a support for him; in the past, too, I was his support.”
"Previously, I made this man the master of a worldly household; now, he is the master of a supramundane household.
For at that time, Cūḷantevāsika was Cūḷapanthaka, while I myself was the wise and capable Cūḷaseṭṭhi, skilled in the stars," he said, thus identifying the Jātaka.
On another day, in the Hall of Dharma, they raised this discussion:
"Friends, although Cūḷapanthaka was unable to grasp even a four-line stanza in four months, he established himself in Arahatship without ever relinquishing his energy;
now he has become the master of the household of the supramundane Dhamma. The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, what is it that you are discussing?"
Having asked, "For what discussion are you sitting together here now?
and being told, "For this one indeed," he said, "Monks, in my teaching, a monk who has aroused energy is surely the master of the supramundane Dhamma," and spoke this verse:
"By exertion, by heedfulness, by self-restraint, and by self-mastery;"
"A wise person should make an island, which the flood cannot overwhelm.
In this context, "should make an island" means by means of these causal factors: exertion known as vigor; heedfulness characterized by the state of non-negligence through mindfulness;
restraint characterized by the fourfold purification of virtue; and the taming of the sense faculties.

Endowed with these four qualities, a wise person possessed of the wisdom of the foundations of mindfulness (*dhamma-ñāṇa*) should make for themselves an island—the fruit of Arhatship—which serves as their own firm footing in this ocean of *saṃsāra* that is exceedingly deep and extremely difficult to find a footing in.

"Should make" means they would be able to make it. Of what kind? That which the flood does not overwhelm—that which, even though it is fourfold... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
The flood of defilements is unable to overwhelm or destroy it; indeed, it is impossible for the flood to overwhelm one who has attained Arahantship.
At the conclusion of the verse, many became stream-enterers and others. Thus, the teaching became fruitful for the assembled assembly.
This is the third story, concerning the Elder Cūḷapanthaka.
4. The Story of the Proclamation of the Bāla-Nakkhatta:
"Those who indulge in negligence"—the Teacher related this teaching on the Dhamma while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Bāla-nakkhatta.
For at one time in Sāvatthī, a festival called the Bāla-nakkhatta was proclaimed. During that festival, fools...
Foolish people smear their bodies with ashes and cow dung, and for seven days they wander about uttering indecent speech.
They have no sense of shame even when seeing a relative, a close friend, or one who has gone forth into homelessness.
Standing at every door, they speak indecently. Unable to bear hearing their indecency, people [rebuke them] according to their strength.
They sent half a [coin], a quarter, or a kahāpaṇa. Having received whatever they obtained at their door, those people departed.
At that time, however, about fifty million noble disciples were residing in Sāvatthī; they sent a message to the Teacher, saying:
"Bhante, may the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, not enter the city for seven days."
"Let it take place right here in the monastery. And so, for those seven days, they prepared rice gruel, alms-food, and other offerings within the monastery itself and sent them there;
they themselves did not even leave their homes.
When the festival had concluded, on the eighth day, they invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, escorted him into the city, and offered a great almsgiving.
Sitting to one side, they said, "Venerable sir, seven days have passed for us in extreme suffering.
Hearing the unseemly words of fools, our ears are nearly shattered; no one has any shame toward anyone else.
Because of this, we did not dare enter your city, nor did we even leave our own homes. The Teacher [spoke] to them...
Having heard this, he said, “Such indeed is the conduct of fools who lack wisdom,
whereas the wise, guarding heedfulness like the essence of wealth, attain the great bliss of the Deathless Nibbāna,” and then spoke these verses:
“Fools, those people of little wisdom, devote themselves to negligence;”
The wise person guards heedfulness as one would guard the most excellent wealth.
“Do not indulge in negligence, nor in intimacy with sensual pleasures;
for by being heedful and meditating, one attains vast happiness.”
In this context, "fools" (*bāla*) refers to those possessed of folly who do not understand the welfare of this world and the world beyond. "The dull-witted" (*dummedha*) means those lacking wisdom.
Not seeing the danger in negligence, they devote themselves to negligence, engage in it, and pass their time in negligence.
However, the "wise man" (*medhāvī*)—the learned one endowed with the wisdom born of the essence of the Dhamma—is the best and most excellent one descended from a noble lineage.
One guards heedfulness as if it were the wealth of the seven treasures. For just as people, seeing the benefits in wealth, guard that supreme treasure— thinking,
"By means of this we shall attain the excellence of the strands of sensual pleasure, we shall support our children and wife, and we shall clear the path for the journey to the next world"—
so too the wise person who is heedful [guards it], thinking, "I shall attain the first jhāna and the others."

"May I attain the paths and fruits; may I accomplish the three knowledges and the six direct knowledges"—seeing such benefits in heedfulness (*appamāda*), one guards heedfulness as if it were the most excellent wealth; this is the meaning. "Do not be heedless":

therefore, you should not devote yourselves to heedlessness, nor should you let your time pass away in negligence. "Do not [indulge] in intimacy with the delight of sensual pleasures": regarding both objective sensual pleasures (*vatthukāma*) and defilement-sensual pleasures (*kilesakāma*).
"Do not indulge even in intimacy with craving known as delight; do not think of it; do not acquire it.
For by being heedful—meaning by one who is heedful through the establishment of mindfulness—one who meditates attains the vast and sublime bliss of Nibbāna.
At the conclusion of the verse, many became stream-enterers and others. Thus, the teaching of the Dhamma became fruitful for the great multitude.
The fourth story: The Story of the Proclamation on an Inauspicious Constellation.
The fifth: The Story of the Elder Mahākassapa.
While residing at Jetavana, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma teaching—"By heedfulness, overcome heedlessness"—referring to the Elder Mahākassapa.
For one day, while residing at Pipphali Cave, the Elder, having walked for alms in Rājagaha and returned from his almsround after the meal,

sat down and, increasing his vision, surveyed with his divine eye— both attentive and inattentive— the beings passing away and being reborn among the waters, the earth, the mountains, and so forth. Meanwhile, the Teacher was at Jetavana.
While still seated, [the Buddha] wondered, "In what state of abiding is my son Kassapa dwelling today? Examining this with his divine eye, he understood:
"He is dwelling observing the passing away and rebirth of beings. He realized, "The passing away and rebirth of beings is not fully discerned even by the knowledge of a Buddha;
having taken rebirth-linking in a mother’s womb, they do so without informing their parents."
"It is impossible to set a limit to those beings who are passing away; it is not within your scope to know them, Kassapa. Your scope is but small;
however, to know and see all those who are passing away and being reborn is the domain of the Buddhas alone.
Having said this, he emitted a radiance and, as if sitting right before him, spoke this verse:
“When the wise man dispels negligence with diligence,
having ascended the palace of wisdom, he— being free from sorrow— looks down upon the sorrowing multitude.
Like one standing on a mountain looking at those on the ground, the steadfast one observes the fools.”

In this context, "he pushes away" means: just as when fresh water enters a lotus pond, it agitates the old water and, not giving it space, pushes it and drives it out by pressing against its very crest;
even so, when the wise man, cultivating the characteristic of heedfulness, does not allow any room for heedlessness, then—by the force of his heedfulness—he [pushes away that...].

He pushes away and removes it; then, having dispelled negligence, he—fulfilling the appropriate practice for that palace of wisdom known as the "divine eye" which is purified by its state of loftiness—ascends it like a palace by means of the ladder of that practice.

Being himself free from sorrow due to having abandoned the dart of grief, he beholds the multitude of beings, the assembly of creatures, who are possessed of sorrow because they have not abandoned the dart of grief.
With the divine eye, he surveys and sees both those passing away and those being reborn.

How so? Just as one standing on a mountain peak sees those standing on the ground, or as one standing on an upper terrace sees those standing in the courtyard of the palace without difficulty—so too does that wise, learned person, whose great taints are destroyed and whose seeds of the round of existence are not yet severed.
"He beholds with ease those who are passing away and those who are being reborn among the foolish.
At the conclusion of this verse, many realized the fruit of stream-entry and other higher attainments.
This is the fifth story, concerning the Elder Mahākassapa.
6. The Story of the Two Companions, One Negligent and One Diligent The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning two companion monks.
It is said that after receiving a meditation subject from the Teacher, they entered a forest hermitage. Of these two, one—
Having brought firewood at the very early hour and prepared a charcoal brazier, he sits through the first watch of the night warming himself while conversing with the young novices.
One of them, practicing the duty of a recluse with diligence, exhorts the other:
"Friend, do not act thus; for one who is negligent, the four states of misery are like his own home. The Buddhas, indeed, [do not speak] out of deceit..."
“...he cannot be won over,” he did not listen to his advice. The other, thinking, “This man is not patient with words,” said nothing to him and practiced the duty of a recluse with diligence.
The Elder Alasa, having warmed himself during the first watch of the night, entered the hut at the moment the other had finished walking up and down and entered;
he said, “Great indolent one, you have gone to the forest for the sake of lying down and sleeping...”
“You have entered [the Order]; having received a meditation subject from the presence of the Buddhas, is it not fitting for you to rise and practice the duty of a recluse?
Having said this, he entered his own dwelling, lay down, and fell asleep.
The other, having rested during the middle watch, rose in the last watch and practiced the duty of a recluse. Thus dwelling with such diligence, he—
Before long, he attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), while the other spent his time in negligence alone.
When they had completed the rains retreat, they went into the presence of the Teacher; having paid homage to the Teacher, they sat down to one side.
After the Teacher had exchanged greetings with them, he asked: "Bhikkhus, I hope you have practiced the duty of a recluse with diligence?"
“Has the duty of one who has gone forth reached its culmination for you? he asked. The first monk, who had been negligent, replied:
“Venerable sir, how could there be diligence for him? From the time he left, he spent his time lying down and sleeping.
“And you, monk? [The second monk replied: “I, venerable sir, having brought firewood early in the morning, prepared a bed of embers...”
“Having prepared himself, he spent the time sitting through the first watch of the night, warming himself and remaining awake.
Then the Teacher said to him, “You have spent the time negligently and yet you say, ‘I am diligent.
You are making the diligent negligent. In order to further reveal the fault in negligence and the benefit in diligence, [the Teacher said], “You, my...”
“Like a weak horse whose speed has been cut short in the presence of its colt,
but like a swift horse in your presence,” he said, and spoke this verse:
“Vigilant among the heedless, wide awake among those who sleep;”
“Just as a swift horse leaves behind the weakling, so does the wise one depart.
In this context, “heedful” refers to the one whose taints are destroyed, being endowed with heedfulness through the attainment of fullness of mindfulness.

“Among the heedless” refers to beings who stand at the point of losing their mindfulness. “Among those asleep” refers to those who, due to the absence of mindfulness and wakefulness, are as if slumbering in all postures.
"One who is wide awake" means established in great wakefulness characterized by vast mindfulness.

"Like one with weak strength" means like a noble Sindhu horse of swift speed that is weak in strength despite having a crippled foot and severed tendons. "One of good intelligence" means one of supreme wisdom. Having abandoned such a person—both in terms of scriptural tradition (*āgama*) and personal realization (*adhigama*)—he goes on.
For while those of dull intelligence exert themselves merely to grasp a single discourse (*sutta*), [the wise man] proceeds further.
The wise man takes up one section; thus, for the time being, he proceeds by abandoning [the practice] through the authority of the tradition (*āgama*).
However, when those of dull wit strive to establish night-quarters and day-quarters, they should first learn the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) and recite it.
Then, even at the preliminary stage, the wise man, having entered a night-quarter or day-quarter prepared by another, should contemplate the meditation subject and abandon all defilements.
Having discarded [the world], he does not even place supramundane states within his grasp; thus he departs having abandoned them through realization.
Furthermore, having abandoned and cast off the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa), he indeed departs as one emerging from saṃsāra.
At the conclusion of the verse, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and the other stages.
The sixth story: The Helper in Overcoming Hatred for the Negligent and the Non-Negligent.
7. The Story of Maghavā.
This teaching on the Dhamma, beginning with "By heedfulness one becomes Maghavā," was related by the Teacher while dwelling at Vesālī in the Gabled Hall, concerning Sakka, the king of the gods.
Now, in Vesālī there lived a Licchavi named Mahāli. Having heard the Tathāgata’s teaching on the Sakkapañha Sutta, he thought:
"The Fully Enlightened One spoke of the great prosperity of Sakka; did he speak having seen it, or without having seen it?
Does he know Sakka, or does he not? He thought, "I shall ask him. Then...
Then, Mahāli, the Licchavi approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, Mahāli, the Licchavi said this to the Blessed One:
"Has the Blessed One seen Sakka, the lord of the devas? "I have seen Sakka, Mahāli."
“‘The lord of the gods,’ [he said]. ‘Surely, Bhante, he must be an imitation of Sakka. For Sakka, the lord of the gods, is difficult to see, Bhante.
‘Mahāli, I indeed know Sakka, and I know the qualities that constitute being Sakka;
I know those qualities by the undertaking of which Sakka attained the status of Sakka.’”
Mahāli, when Sakka, lord of the devas, was formerly a human being, he was a young brahmin named Magha; therefore, he is called “Maghavā.
Mahāli, when Sakka, lord of the devas, was formerly a human being, he gave gifts in his youth; therefore, he is called “Purindada.
Mahāli, when Sakka, lord of the devas, was formerly a human being, he gave gifts with great care and respect; therefore, he is called “Sakka.”
Mahāli, in the past, when Sakka, lord of the devas, was a human being, he gave away a dwelling; therefore, he is called Vāsava.
Mahāli, Sakka, lord of the devas, can contemplate a thousand matters in a single moment; therefore, he is called Sahassakkha.
Mahāli, the daughter of the asuras named Sujā was the wife of Sakka, lord of the devas; therefore, he is called Sujampati.
Mahāli, Sakka, the lord of the gods, exercises sovereignty, overlordship, and kingship over the Tāvatiṃsa devas; therefore he is called "Lord of the Gods.

Mahāli, in a former life when Sakka, the lord of the gods, was a human being, there were seven rules of conduct that he fulfilled and undertook, and by virtue of having undertaken them, Sakka attained the status of Sakka. What are these seven rules of conduct?
"For as long as life lasts, may I support my mother and father; for as long as life lasts, may I honor those who are senior in the family;
for as long as life lasts, may I be gentle in speech; for as long as life lasts, may I be free from slanderous speech;

for as long as life lasts, may I dwell at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, being open-handed, pure-palmed, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to the practice of giving, and rejoicing in sharing gifts."
“For as long as life lasts, may I be truthful in speech; for as long as life lasts, may I be free from anger; and even if anger should arise in me, may I quickly subdue it.

Mahāli, these seven rules of conduct were fully undertaken and observed by Sakka, lord of the devas, when he was formerly a human being; and because they were undertaken, Sakka attained the state of Sakka.
“A person who supports their mother and father, who honors the elders of the family,
who speaks gently and kindly, who has abandoned slanderous speech,
who is devoted to the removal of stinginess, who is truthful, and who has overcome anger— ”
“The Thirty-three gods indeed call him a true man.

Having said, “Mahāli, this was the deed performed by Sakka when he was the young man Magha,” he was then asked by one who wished to hear his conduct in detail: “Venerable sir, how did the young man Magha conduct himself? To him, [the Buddha] replied: “In that case, listen...”
"Mahāli, listen," he said, and then related a story of the past:
"In the past, in the kingdom of Magadha, at a village called Macala, a young brahmin named Magha went to a place where village work was being done.
Having cleared away the dust with the edge of his foot from the spot where he stood and made it pleasant, he remained there. Another [man] [pushed him] with his arm..."
Having struck him, he moved him away and stood there himself. Without becoming angry at him, the other made another place beautiful and stood there.
Then yet another came, struck him with his arm, moved him away, and stood there himself.
Without becoming angry at him either, he too made another place beautiful and stood there. Thus, they departed from that house.
The men who had gone out struck him with their arms and removed him from every spot where he stood.
He thought, “All these people have become happy by depending on me; this must be due to some meritorious deed of mine that bestows happiness.
On the following day, taking a spade, he made a delightful place the size of a threshing floor. All—
Having gone there, they remained right where they were. Then, during the cold season, he provided them with fire; in the hot season, he provided them with water.
Thereupon, thinking, "A pleasant place is dear to everyone; there is nothing that is not dear to anyone.
From now on, it is fitting for me to travel about leveling the road," he set out at dawn and [prepared] the road.
Leveling the ground and cutting it down, he wandered about carrying away whatever tree branches were suitable to be removed.
Then another man saw him and asked, "Friend, what are you doing? "I am making for myself the path leading to heaven, friend," he replied.
"In that case, I too shall be your companion," said the other. "Be so, friend; for that which is called 'heaven' is pleasing even to many and abounds in happiness."
From that time on, there were two people. Seeing them and having questioned and heard from them in the same manner, another became their companion;
and so another, and yet another, until all thirty-three people had come together.
All of them, with spades and other tools in hand, went along making the road level for a distance of one or two yojanas.
Seeing them, the village headman thought: “These people are engaged in an improper task;
if they were to bring fish, meat, and such from the forest, or if they were to brew liquor and drink it, or perform some other similar work, I too would receive something.
Then, having summoned them, he asked: “What are you doing as you wander about? “The path to heaven,” they replied.

“Yes, sir. [The teacher replied: “It is not permissible for those living in the household life to do such things as go into the forest to bring back fish, meat, and so forth, to brew and drink liquor, or to engage in various kinds of manual labor; however, it is permissible [for you].
They rejected his words, and even though they were told this again and again, they continued to reject them. He became angry and said, “I shall expel you!”
Having gone into the presence of the king, he said, "Your Majesty, I see thieves wandering about in groups.
When the king replied, "Go, seize them and bring them here," he did so; having bound them all, he brought them and presented them to the king.
Without even investigating, the king commanded, "Have them crushed by an elephant! Then Magha gave the remaining men this advice:
—“Friends, there is no other refuge for us except loving-kindness (*mettā*).

Without giving way to anger toward anyone—toward the king, the village headman, the elephant that trampled us, or even toward ourselves—remain with hearts made equal through a mind of loving-kindness.
They did accordingly. Then, by the power of their loving-kindness, the elephant was not even able to approach them. The king—
“Having heard that matter and seeing many people, will he not be unable to trample them?
he said. “Go, cover him with a mat and have him trampled. Although the elephant was sent to be trampled after being covered with a mat, he retreated from afar.
When the king heard this report, he thought, "There must be a reason for this," and having summoned them, he asked:
"Sirs, what is it that you do not receive through me? "What is this you say, Your Majesty?
"It is said that you have become bandits by forming a gang and are wandering in the forest. "Who says so, Your Majesty? "The village headman, sirs. "No, Your Majesty..."
“Your Majesty, we are thieves; however, while clearing our own path to heaven, we perform this and that [good deed].
The village headman, wishing to destroy us for not following his word after inciting us to unwholesome actions, spoke thus in anger.
Then the king, hearing their words, was filled with joy and said, “Sirs, this animal—of you...”
“Recognizing his virtue, he said, ‘I was unable to recognize it while I was a human being; forgive me.
Having spoken thus, he gave the village headman together with his wife and children as their slave, the elephant fit for riding, and that village for their use as they pleased.
They thought, ‘Right here we have seen the fruit of merit performed,’ and so they practiced even more extensively.”
With hearts full of faith, they mounted that elephant in turn and, as they went along, deliberated:
"Now we must perform even greater merit; what shall we do? Let us build a permanent rest-house for the public at the crossroads of the four great paths.
Having summoned a carpenter, they began the construction of the hall. Among the women...
However, because his desire had vanished, they did not grant women ownership of that hall.
Now, in the house of Magha, there were four women: Nandā, Cittā, Sudhammā, and Sujātā.
Among them, Sudhammā, having conspired with the carpenter, said, "Brother, make me the chief woman of this hall."
He gave a bribe. Having accepted it with the words, “Very well,” the carpenter first dried a tree for the sake of the pinnacle, cut it, and bored it;
having completed the pinnacle, he carved the letters, “This hall is named Sudhammā,” wrapped them in cloth, and set them aside.
Then, after the carpenters had finished the hall, on the day of the pinnacle-erection—
“Alas, masters, we have forgotten one thing that ought to be done,” he said. “What is it, sir? “A door-bolt.
“Very well, we shall bring one. “It cannot be made now with a tree that has already been cut down;
it is necessary to obtain a bolt that was previously cut, planed, and bored out and set aside. “What should be done now? “If—”
“There is a lotus stalk for sale that was prepared and set aside in someone’s house; it should be sought out.
While they were searching, they saw it in Sudhammā’s house. Although they offered a thousand coins, they could not obtain it even for its price.
When she said, “If you dedicate the hall to me, I will give it to you,” they replied, “We do not dedicate [merit] to women.”
Then the carpenter said to them, "Sirs, what are you saying? There is no place other than the Brahma-world that is devoid of women;
take the pinnacle-block. This being so, our work will reach completion.
Saying, "Very well," they took the pinnacle-block, finished the hall, and divided it into three parts. In one portion [they assigned] the masters.
They established two dwelling places: one for the poor and one for the sick. Thirty-three people, having prepared thirty-three wooden planks, gave instructions to the elephant:

“When a traveler arrives and sits upon whichever plank has been spread out, take him and establish him in the very house of the owner of that plank; provide him with foot-massage, back-massage, water, hard food, soft food, and a bed.”
“All the burden shall belong to the owner of the plank alone. Thus, whenever an elephant arrived, he would take it and lead it to the house of the plank-owner.
That day, the owner performed for him whatever service was required.
Magha planted a *koviḷāra* tree not far from the hall and spread a stone slab at its base. Every person who entered the hall would look up at the capital of the pillar.
After teaching them the letters, they said, "This hall is named Sudhammā. The names of the thirty-three people were not known.
Nandā thought: "While these people were building the hall, they made us non-participants;
but Sudhammā, through her own cleverness, made herself a participant by acting as the central beam (kaṇṇikā). It is right for me too to do something; what indeed shall I do?"
Then it occurred to her: "It is fitting that those who come to the hall should have both drinking water and bathing water;
I shall have a lotus pond dug. She had the lotus pond constructed. Citta thought:
"Sudhammā has given the central pillar, and Nandā has had a lotus pond made; it is fitting that I too should do something. What indeed shall I do?"
Then it occurred to her: "It would be fitting for those who come and go to drink water, bathe, and put on garlands when they depart;
I shall have a flower garden constructed. She had a delightful flower garden built.
In that garden, there was almost no flowering or fruit-bearing tree of which one could say, "Such-and-such a tree does not exist here."
Sujā, however, thought: "I am both Māgha’s maternal cousin’s daughter and his personal attendant; the deed he has done is mine alone, and what I have done is his alone.
Thinking thus, she did nothing at all, but spent her time merely adorning her own person.
Māgha, moreover, attended upon his mother and father, performed the duty of honoring those senior in the family, and maintained truthful speech and gentle speech.
Having fulfilled these seven factors of conduct— listening to the Dhamma, subduing stinginess, and being free from anger—
one [should honor] the person who supports their mother and father, who shows respect to the elders of the family,
who is gentle and speaks with kindness, and who has abandoned slanderous speech.
“The man who is intent on the subduing of stinginess, who is truthful, and who has overcome anger—
him indeed the gods of the Thirty-three call a ‘true person.
Having thus attained a state worthy of praise, at the end of his life, he became Sakka, the king of the gods, in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
He was reborn there, and his three companions were also reborn in that very place; the carpenter was reborn as Vissakamma, the son of a deity.
At that time, the asuras were dwelling in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. When they heard, "New sons of the gods have been reborn," they prepared divine drinks.
Sakka gave a signal so that no one in his own retinue would drink. The asuras—

Having drunk divine liquor, they became intoxicated. Sakka, thinking, "What use have I for a kingdom shared with these?", signaled to his own retinue, had them seized by the feet, and cast them into the great ocean. They fell into the ocean head-first.
Then, through the power of their merit, a celestial mansion of the asuras called Sineru-heṭṭhimatala was manifested, and a tree called Cittapāṭali was manifested.
Furthermore, when the Asuras were defeated in the battle between the Devas and Asuras, the city of the Thirty-three known as Tāvatiṃsadevanagara arose, measuring ten thousand yojanas.

Between its eastern and western gates there was a distance of ten thousand yojanas, and likewise between its southern and northern gates. That city was provided with a thousand gates and adorned with groves and lotus ponds.

In the center of that hall, by way of its radiance, there arose the palace named Vejayanta, made of the seven precious gems and seven hundred yojanas in height, adorned with banners three hundred yojanas tall. On golden shafts were jewel-banners;
on jewel-shafts were golden-banners; on coral shafts were pearl-banners; and on pearl-shafts were coral-banners.
Upon pillars made of the seven precious gems were banners of the seven precious gems; the banner standing in the center was three hundred yojanas in height.
Thus, by the power of the *sālā* tree, the palace arose with a height of one thousand yojanas and was composed entirely of the seven precious gems;
and by the power of the *koviḷāra* tree, the *pāricchattaka* tree arose, measuring three hundred yojanas in circumference on all sides.
As a result of the stone slab, at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree, there appeared the Paṇḍukambala Rock, sixty yojanas in length, fifty yojanas in width, and fifteen yojanas in thickness;
it was the color of the *jayasumana* flower or red woolen cloth.
When one sits upon it, half the body sinks in, and when one rises, the depression is filled back up.
The elephant, however, was reborn as a son of the gods named Erāvaṇa. For there are no animals in the world of the gods;
therefore, at the time of departing for the pleasure garden, he cast off his divine form and became an elephant named Erāvaṇa, measuring one hundred and fifty yojanas.
For the sake of the thirty-three [gods], he fashioned thirty-three frontal globes (kumbhas) by means of his trunk.
In the center of all those [pools], which measured forty-five yojanas in extent, he had a thirty-yojana high cauldron named Sudassana constructed for the sake of Sakka.
Above it was a jeweled pavilion twelve yojanas in height.
There, at intervals, banners made of the seven precious gems rose up to a height of one yojana. Along its perimeter, a network of small bells hung down.
From it, stirred by a gentle breeze, there issued forth a sound like the music of celestial songs, blended with the resonance of the fivefold musical instruments.
In the center of the pavilion, a jeweled couch one *yojana* in length was prepared for the sake of Sakka; there Sakka sat down.
Thirty-three sons of the gods each sat upon jeweled couches within their own jars. Within each of those thirty-three jars—
In the Kumbha [palace], he had seven by seven tusks measured out. Each one was fifty yojanas in length.
On each tusk there were seven lotus ponds; in each pond, seven clusters of lotuses;
in each cluster, seven flowers; and on each flower, seven petals.
In each bowl, seven celestial maidens dance. Thus, throughout the fifty *yojanas* on all sides, there are theatrical performances upon the very tusks of the elephant.
Sakka, the king of the gods, wanders about enjoying such great glory.
Sudhammā, too, having passed away and gone, was reborn right there. Her palace, named Sudhammā, is nine hundred *yojanas* in extent.

The assembly hall of the gods (devasabhā) was established. It is said that there is no other place more delightful than that, and on eight days of every month, a hearing of the Dhamma takes place right there.
To this day, whenever people see a certain delightful place, they say, "It is like the Sudhamma assembly hall of the gods. Nandā also, having passed away, went and was reborn in that very same place.
For her, a lotus pond named Nandā, five hundred yojanas in extent, came into being. Cittā also, having passed away and gone there, was reborn in that very place;

for her too, a grove of cittā-creeper vines (cittalatāvana) five hundred yojanas in extent came into being, where they wander about, leading and deluding the sons of the gods who have previously been born there. Sujā, however, having passed away, [was reborn] in one...
In a mountain cave, she was reborn as a female crane. Sakka, surveying his own attendants, thought, "Sudhammā has been reborn right here, as have Nandā and Cittā; where then has Sujā been reborn?
Seeing that she had been reborn there, he reflected, "Foolish girl, having performed no merit at all, you have now been reborn in the animal realm."
"Now, it is fitting to perform that merit and bring him here," he thought.
Then, relinquishing his own form, he went to her in the guise of a stranger and asked, "What are you doing wandering about here? "Who are you, sir?
"I am your husband, Magha. "Where have you been reborn, sir? "I have been reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa deva-world."
“But do you know where your companions have been reborn? “I do not know, Master.
“They too have been reborn in my very presence; you shall see those companions. “How shall I go there?
Sakka said, “I will take you there,” and placing him upon the palm of his hand, he led him to the deva-world to the Nanda lotus pond.
Having released her on the bank, she informed the other three: "You will see your companion Suja.
"Where is she, lady? they asked. "She is standing on the bank of the Nandā lotus pond," she replied.
The three of them went there and said, "Oh, such is the fruit of our noble lady’s adornment of her own form! Now look at her beak; look at her feet!"
"Look at her calves! Indeed, her physical form is beautiful," they said, and having made sport of her, they departed.
Again, Sakka went to her presence and said, "Have you seen your companions? When she replied, "They have seen me and left after mocking me;
take me right there," he led her to that very spot, cast her into the water, and said, "Have you seen them?"
He asked, “What are their perfections? “They have been seen, O King,” she replied. “It is fitting for you as well to take the means to be reborn there.
“What must I do, O King? “Will you keep the counsel given by me? “I will keep it, O King.
Then, having given her the five precepts (*pañca-sīla*) and saying, “Guard them with heedfulness,” he departed. From that time on, she...
From that time on, she would search for and eat only dead fish that she had caught herself. After a few days had passed, Sakka went there to test her;
he lay down on the surface of the sand like a dead fish, turned over on his back. Seeing him, she took him up under the impression that it was a dead fish.
As she was swallowing him, the fish wagged its tail. She [realized] "It is a live fish! and [threw it] into the water.
He released him. After waiting a short while, he lay down again in front of her, face upwards.
Again, thinking it was a dead fish, she seized him; as she was swallowing him, he moved his fore-toe. Seeing this, she released him, thinking, "It is a live fish.
Having thus tested him three times and made himself known as one who "protects his virtue well," he—
“I have come here for the purpose of testing you; you guard your virtue well. Guarding it thus, you will before long be reborn in my presence;
be heedful,” he said, and then departed.
From that time on, however, she would sometimes obtain fish that had died of themselves and sometimes not. When she failed to obtain any, after the lapse of a few days—
Having withered away and passed away, she was reborn as the daughter of a potter in Bārāṇasī by the fruit of that merit.
Then, when she was fifteen or sixteen years old, Sakka, reflecting on where she had been reborn,
saw her and thought, "It is now time for me to go there," appearing in the form of an elephant with tusks like ivory.
Having filled a carriage with the seven kinds of jewels and driving it, he entered Bārāṇasī and set out upon the street, crying out, "Mother!
Father! Take some long peppers! Take some! But when people returned having taken mung beans, black gram, and other such things, he said, "I will not give them for a price.
When they asked, "How then will you give them? he replied, "I will give them to a woman who guards her virtue."
He said: "Master, what is this so-called virtue like? Is it black, or is it blue and other colors?
[The man replied: "You do not even know what virtue is like; how then will you protect it? However, I shall give it to one who protects virtue. [The woman said:
"Master, this daughter of a potter wanders about saying, 'I protect virtue. Give it to her! She too—
She said, "In that case, Master, give them to me. He asked, "Who are you? She replied, "I am one who has not abandoned the five precepts.
"These were brought by me specifically for you," he said. Pushing the cart, he went to her house;
having ensured it was not accessible to others, he gave her the money belonging to Devadatta, which was the color of *eḷāluka* fruit, and identifying himself, he said, "This is for your livelihood."
"O Dhana, having made the five precepts unbroken and so forth, guard them well," he said, and then departed.
She, too, passed away from there and was reborn in the realm of the Asuras as the daughter of the chief of the Asuras, appearing in the enemy's house of Sakka.
Because she had well-guarded the precepts during those two existences, she became beautiful, golden-hued, and possessed of extraordinary splendor.
Endowed with the splendor of beauty, the asura lord Vepacitti, thinking to himself, "None of you are worthy of my daughter," did not give her to anyone.
Instead, he assembled the asura host, saying, "My daughter herself will choose a husband who is worthy of her; choose a husband who is worthy of you."
He placed a garland of flowers in her hand. At that moment, Sakka, surveying her place of rebirth and learning of this occurrence, thought, "It is now fitting for me to go and bring her back.
He assumed the form of an old asura, went there, and stood at the edge of the assembly. She too, looking here and there, saw him the very moment she looked.
With her heart overwhelmed by a great flood of affection arising from their former association, she thought, "He is my husband," and threw a flower garland over him.
The asuras said, "Our king has not found a suitable match for his daughter for so long;
now he has found one. This man alone is more venerable than her grandfather and is a fitting match for her."
Ashamed, they departed. Sakka, seizing him by the hand, cried out, "I am Sakka! and leapt into the sky.
The asuras pursued him, thinking, "We have been deceived by old Sakka. Mātali, the charioteer, brought forth the Vejayanta chariot and halted on the way.
Sakka placed him upon it and set out toward the city of the gods.
Then, when he arrived at the Sippali forest, the young Garuḍas, terrified by the sound of the chariot, cried out.
Hearing their cries, Sakka asked Mātali, “Who is it that is crying out? “It is the young Garuḍas, O Lord. “For what reason?
“Because they have heard the sound of the chariot and are afraid of death. “Because of me alone, so many birds—”
"Lest he be crushed by the speed of the chariot and perish, turn back the chariot! He too, having given the signal with his staff to the thousand horses, turned the chariot back.
Seeing this, the asuras thought, "Jarasakka, who had been fleeing from the city of the asuras, has now turned his chariot back;
surely he must have found some support. Having thus reflected, they turned back and followed the very path by which he was coming.
Having entered the city of the Asuras, they did not lift up their heads again.
Sakka, too, having led Sujā, the Asura maiden, to the celestial city, established her in the position of senior among two and a half koṭis of apsarases.
She requested a boon from Sakka: "Great King, in this world of the gods, my parents, brothers, or sisters..."
"Or else, wherever you go, you must take me with you.

He agreed to her request, saying, "Very well. From that time on, whenever the *cittapāṭali* tree blossomed, the asuras would ascend to heaven for the sake of battle, thinking, "It is now the time for the divine *pāricchattaka* tree to bloom in our place of birth."
Sakka assigned protection over the Nagas in the lower ocean, then over the Supannas, then over the Kumbhandas, then over the Yakkhas, and finally over the Four Great Kings.
Furthermore, for the purpose of averting calamities, he stationed statues of Indra with thunderbolts in hand at the gates of the celestial city.
Even when the Asuras, Nagas, and others arrived after having been defeated, they would see the statues of Indra from afar.
Seeing him, they fled, thinking, "Sakka has come out! Thus, Mahāli, the young brahmin Magha practiced the way of heedfulness.
Having attained such sovereignty through this heedfulness, he ruled over two divine worlds.
Indeed, this heedfulness is praised by the Buddhas and others; for it is by relying on heedfulness that all mundane and supramundane [attainments] are achieved.
Having stated that "there is the attainment of distinctions," he spoke this verse:
"By heedfulness Maghavā attained preeminence among the gods;
They praise heedfulness, and heedlessness is always censured."
In this context, "by heedfulness" means by the heedfulness beginning with the clearing of the site of land at Macalagāma.
"Maghavā": now, the young brahmin Magha, known as "Maghavā," has attained the preeminence among the gods through his status as king over the two divine worlds.
"They praise": the wise ones, such as the Buddhas and others, extol and laud only heedfulness.
For what reason? Because it is the cause for the attainment of all mundane and supramundane distinctions.
"Negligence is always censured" means that negligence is constantly censured and condemned by those noble ones. For what reason?
Because it is the root of all failures. Indeed, whether it be human misfortune or rebirth in the woeful states, everything is rooted in negligence alone.
At the conclusion of the verses, Mahāli the Licchavi was established in the fruit of stream-entry, and many others in the assembled crowd were likewise established as stream-enterers and so forth.
This is the seventh story, concerning Maghavā.
8. The Story of a Certain Bhikkhu.
"The bhikkhu who delights in heedfulness"—the Teacher spoke this teaching on the Dhamma while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain bhikkhu.

It is said that after having the Teacher explain a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) to him up to the level of Arahantship, he entered the forest and, though striving and exerting himself, was unable to attain Arahantship. Thinking, "I shall have the meditation subject explained with greater distinction," he then...
Having departed and while coming into the presence of the Teacher, he saw a great forest fire breaking out along the way.
Hastening to the top of a certain bare mountain, he sat down; seeing the forest being consumed by the fire, he took it as his object of meditation:
"Just as this fire proceeds, burning both large and small fuels..."
“In this way, one must proceed by burning away both the great and the small fetters with the fire of the knowledge of the Noble Path.
The Teacher, while seated within the Gandhakuṭī, knowing the movement of his mind, said: “It is even so, bhikkhu;
just as with the great and the small, so too do the clingings arise within these beings.”
"It is fitting to burn away the fetters, both subtle and gross, with the fire of knowledge and render them incapable of arising again.
Having said this, he emitted a radiance and, appearing as if seated directly in front of that bhikkhu, spoke this verse of illumination:
"A bhikkhu who delights in heedfulness, seeing danger in negligence..."
“Burning away the fetter, whether subtle or gross, he goes like a fire.
In this context, “delighting in heedfulness” means one who delights in and is devoted to heedfulness; the meaning is that one passes one’s time through heedfulness.
“Seeing danger in negligence” means seeing negligence as a source of fear—such as the arising in hell—and so forth; or it means seeing the arising of those [unwholesome states].

Seeing negligence as a source of fear because it is the root [of all evil], he understands "fetter" (*saṃyojana*) as the bond that joins one to the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa-dukkha*), the tenfold fetter capable of causing one to sink into the round of rebirth.
"Minute and gross" means both great and small. "He goes like a fire consuming" means just as this fire goes toward both the great and the small.

"He goes as if burning up clinging. The meaning is this: in this way, that bhikkhu, delighting in heedfulness, goes along burning away this fetter with the fire of knowledge attained through heedfulness, making it incapable of arising again.
At the conclusion of the verse, while remaining seated exactly where he was, that bhikkhu incinerated all his fetters together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Having attained arahantship, he came through the air, praised and extolled the golden-hued body of the Tathāgata,
and departed while paying homage.
This is the eighth story, concerning a certain bhikkhu.
9. The Story of the Elder Tissa the Town-Dweller "Delighting in heedfulness"—the Teacher gave this Dhamma teaching while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the elder named Tissa the Town-Dweller.
For there was a certain son of noble family who had been born and raised in a market town not far from Sāvatthī, and who [entered] the Teacher’s dispensation...
Having gone forth and received full ordination, he became known as the Elder Tissa of the Market Town—a man of few desires, contented, secluded, and energetic.
He wandered regularly for alms only in his own native village.
Even while Anāthapiṇḍika and others were making great offerings, and even while Pasenadi of Kosala was making incomparable gifts, he did not come to Sāvatthī.
The bhikkhus, having raised the matter, reported it to the Teacher, saying, “This Elder Tissa, a resident of this town, lives constantly associating with his kinsmen;
even when Anāthapiṇḍika and others are making great offerings, and even when Pasenadi of Kosala is making an incomparable gift, he does not come at all.
The Teacher summoned him and asked, “Is it true, bhikkhu, that you...”
Having asked, "Do you act in this way? [the monk replied]: "No, venerable sir, I have no association with kinsmen.
Relying on these people, I receive food for consumption, whether coarse or refined.
Since I have obtained enough to sustain myself, why seek further food? Thus I do not go; indeed, venerable sir, I have no association with kinsmen."
