When this was said, the Teacher, who already knew his disposition by nature, gave him his approval, saying, “Excellent, excellent, monk!
Then, having said, “It is not surprising, monk, that you have become one of few desires after obtaining a teacher such as myself;
for this quality of fewness of desires is my lineage, my tradition,” he spoke to the monks.
Being requested, he recalled the past:
"In the past, on the banks of the Ganges in the Himalayas, there lived many thousands of crows in a certain fig forest (*udumbara-vana*).
There, a king of the crows, when the fruits of his own dwelling-tree were exhausted, [ate] whatever sprout remained."
Whether it was a leaf or bark, having eaten this or that and drunk water from the Ganges, being supremely desirous of little and contented, he did not go elsewhere.
By virtue of his state of fewness of wishes and contentment, Sakka’s palace shook.
Sakka, reflecting upon it, saw him; and for the purpose of testing him, by means of his own supernatural power, he [transformed] that tree—

He caused it to dry. The tree, broken down and reduced to a mere stump, stood there with holes here and there, emitting a sound like that of something being struck when the wind blew against it. From its holes, fine dust emerged.
King Suva, having eaten that dust and drunk water from the Ganges, did not go elsewhere; disregarding the wind and heat, he remained upon the top of the Udumbara stump.
He sat down. Sakka, knowing his supreme state of fewness of desires, thought:
"I shall make him speak of the virtue of friendship, grant him a boon, and then return after turning the Udumbara tree into the fruit of immortality.
Thus, becoming a king of swans and placing the Asura maiden Sujā before him, he went to the Udumbara grove and sat upon the branch of a tree not far away. Then, by him—
Speaking together, he recited this verse:
“There are trees with shimmering leaves, many trees with manifold fruits;
why indeed does your mind delight in a withered, leafless *koḷāpa* tree?”
The entire *Suvajātaka* should be expanded in accordance with the method already given in the *Navakanipāta*.
For the only difference there and here is the occasion for the discourse (*aṭṭhuppatti*); the rest is exactly the same.

Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher said, “At that time Ānanda was Sakka, and I myself was King Suvā,” and added, “Thus, monks, this thing called fewness of desires (*appicchatā*)—”
This is my lineage, this is my tradition. It is no wonder that my son, Tissa the townsman, has attained such fewness of wishes after finding a teacher like me.
Indeed, a bhikkhu must be as few in his wishes as Tissa the townsman;
for a bhikkhu such as this is incapable of falling away from the states of tranquility and insight, or from the paths and fruits.
"Indeed, he is close to Nibbāna itself," he said, and then recited this verse:
"The bhikkhu who delights in heedfulness, seeing danger in heedlessness, is incapable of decline; he is indeed close to Nibbāna."
In that regard, "incapable of falling away" means that such a bhikkhu is incapable of falling away from the states of serenity and insight, or from the paths and fruits;
he does not fall away from those already attained, nor does he fail to reach those not yet attained.

"In the very presence of Nibbāna" means precisely in the presence of both the Nibbāna of the extinction of defilements (*kilesa-parinibbāna*) and the Nibbāna through non-clinging (*anupādā-parinibbāna*).

At the conclusion of the verse, the Elder Tissa, resident of the market town, attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). Many others also became Stream-enterers and so forth. Thus, the teaching of the Dhamma became fruitful for the great multitude.
This is the ninth story, the Story of the Elder Tissa, Resident of the Market Town.
The commentary on the Chapter on Heedfulness is finished. This is the second chapter.
3. Cittavagga 1.
The Story of the Elder Meghiya "Unsteady and fickle is the mind"—the Teacher gave this teaching on the Dhamma while dwelling on Mount Cālikā, concerning the Venerable Meghiya.
To explain the background of this matter, the entire Meghiya Sutta should be cited in detail.
However, because he was distracted by three types of thoughts, the Teacher was unable to apply himself to striving in that mango grove;
therefore, he addressed the Elder Meghiya who had arrived and said, "Meghiya, you have done what is too much. Wait, Meghiya, for a while..."

“Thinking, ‘I am alone until some other bhikkhu arrives,’ it is not fitting for a bhikkhu who abandons one who is begging him to depart while being thus under the sway of his mind. This mind is indeed fickle;
it is fitting to bring it under one’s own control. Having said this, he spoke these two verses:
“The flickering and restless mind is difficult to guard and hard to restrain;
the wise man makes it straight, just as a fletcher straightens his arrow-shaft.
Like a fish cast onto dry land and pulled from its watery home,”
“This mind quivers; it must abandon Māra’s realm.
In this context, “quivering” means vibrating among objective bases such as forms and so forth.
“Fickle” means that, like a village child who does not settle into a single posture, it is fickle because it does not settle upon a single object. “Mind” means consciousness (*viññāṇa*).
However, it is called "citta" (mind) because of its diversity due to variations in its basis, object, function, and so forth.
It is "difficult to guard" (*dūrakkha*) because, like a bull eating grain in a cramped place, it is difficult to settle upon each and every suitable object alone.
It is "difficult to restrain" (*dunnivāraya*) because it is hard to prevent from going toward an unsuitable object.

"Like a fletcher straightens an arrow": just as a fletcher, having brought a crooked shaft from the forest, strips its bark, smears it with lime and oil, heats it over a bed of coals, and presses it against a wooden frame, thereby making it straight, free of bends, and fit for piercing targets;
and having done so, he demonstrates his craft to kings, royal ministers, and great officials.

Just as one receives great honor and respect, so too does a wise, learned, and discerning person—having made this mind, which by nature is like a fickle tree, barkless and stripped of its coarse defilements through dwelling in the forest of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga);

having moistened it with the moisture of faith; having heated it with bodily and mental energy; and having pressed it upon the anvils of serenity and insight—make it straight and free from crookedness.
He renders himself free from worldly attachment; and having done so, by comprehending conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) and shattering the great mass of ignorance (*avijjā*),
he places within his own grasp this distinction— namely, the three knowledges (*tisso vijjā*), the six direct knowledges (*cha abhiññā*), and the nine supramundane states—
and thereby attains the status of being most worthy of offerings.
"Like a fish gasping for water" means like a fish cast onto dry land, either by hand, by foot, or by being thrown onto the shore by some means such as a net.
"Released from his watery home" (*okamokataubbhato*): in the phrase "with robes full of water," *oka* refers to water;
in the phrase "having abandoned his home, wandering homeless," it refers to a dwelling place (*ālaya*). Here, both meanings are applicable. Thus, "released from his watery home."
For here, "from home to home" means from the abodes known as water; "drawn out" means pulled up.

"This mind quivers"—just as a fish drawn out from its watery abode and cast upon dry land quivers because it finds no water, even so this mind, which delighted in the abode of the five strands of sensual pleasure, having been extracted from that, [quivers] within the cycle of existence known as Māra’s realm.
When cast into the meditation subject of insight, it quivers, being tormented by physical and mental energy;
though it cannot remain stable, nevertheless, the wise person, without laying down the burden, makes it straight and workable in the manner already described—this is the meaning.
According to another method: without having abandoned this realm of Māra, the cycle of defilements...

A settled mind wavers like a lotus in water; therefore, the realm of Māra must be abandoned. Since it is by means of that which is called the cycle of defilements—the very realm of Māra—that the mind wavers, that must be abandoned.
At the conclusion of the verse, the Elder Meghiya was established in the fruit of stream-entry, and many others as well became stream-enterers and attained further stages.
The First Story of the Elder Meghiya.
The Second: The Story of a Certain Bhikkhu.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana in Sāvatthī, delivered this teaching on the Dhamma concerning a certain bhikkhu: "Light is he who is difficult to restrain."
It is said that in the kingdom of the King of Kosala, at the foot of a mountain, there was a densely populated village named Mātikagāma.
Then one day, about sixty bhikkhus, having received a meditation subject from the Teacher up to the level of Arahantship, went to that village and entered it for alms.
Now, the owner of that village was a man named Mātiko; his mother—
Having seen him, she had him sit in her house, served him with various kinds of excellent rice-gruel and food, and asked, "Venerable sir, where do you wish to go?

"To whatever place is convenient, Great Laywoman," he replied. She, perceiving that he was likely seeking a place for the rains retreat, prostrated herself at his feet and said, "If, Venerable sir, you will stay here for these three months, I..."
"I shall take the three refuges and the five precepts and perform the Uposatha ceremony," she said.
The monks consented, thinking, "Supported by her, we shall be able to escape from existence without being exhausted by seeking alms.
She then maintained the monastery where they lived and gave it to them.
While dwelling right there, they gathered together one day and exhorted one another: "Friends, it is not fitting for us to live in negligence.
For us, the eight great hells stand with their doors wide open as if they were our own homes.

Moreover, we have come here having received our meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) in the presence of a living Buddha; and Buddhas, indeed, [must be honored] even by one who merely follows their footsteps."
It is not possible to please him through deceit; he can only be pleased according to his own inclinations.

Be diligent! We two must not stand or sit together in one place. However, we shall be together in the evening at the time of attending upon the Elder, and in the morning at the time of going for alms; at all other times, the two of us shall not be together. Moreover, furthermore:
“Let us come when the bell has been struck in the middle of the monastery by the monk who is unwell, and having arrived at the signal of the bell,
let us prepare medicine for him.
While they were dwelling there after making this agreement, one day that female lay devotee had ghee, oil, molasses, and other such items brought.
Surrounded by male and female slaves, laborers, and others, she went to that monastery in the evening.
Not seeing any bhikkhus in the midst of the monastery, she asked the men, "Where have the masters gone?
When they replied, "They will likely be sitting in their respective night-quarters and day-quarters, mistress," she said, "What must I do so that I may see them?"
Then, people who knew the formal agreement (*katikavatta*) of the Saṅgha of monks said to her, “Noble lady, they will assemble once the gong has been struck.

She had the gong struck. Hearing the sound of the gong, the monks thought, “Someone must be unwell,” and leaving their respective places, they assembled in the middle of the monastery. Both [of them]...
There were no people who had come by the same path.

Seeing each person arriving from a different place, the laywoman thought, "A quarrel must have broken out among my sons," and after bowing to the Saṅgha of monks, she asked, "Venerable sirs, did you perhaps quarrel? "We did not, Great Laywoman. "If..."
“Venerable sir, there is no quarrel among you; then why is it that, instead of all coming together as you did when you came to our house, you have each come from a different place?
“Great laywoman, we have been practicing the duty of a recluse while sitting in each of our respective places. “But what, venerable sir, is this so-called ‘duty of a recluse’?”
“Let us recite the thirty-two aspects and establish the dissolution and passing away of the individual existence, Great Female Lay Follower.
“But, venerable sir, is it only for you that it is appropriate to recite the thirty-two aspects and establish the dissolution and passing away of the individual existence, or is it for us as well?
“This Dhamma is not forbidden to anyone, Great Female Lay Follower.”
“In that case, venerable sirs, give me the thirty-two aspects as well, and explain the establishment of the decay and fall of this personal existence.
“In that case, learn them, Great Laywoman,” they said, and they had her learn it all.
From then on, having recited the thirty-two aspects and established the decay and fall within herself, she—
The monks had already attained the three paths and the three fruits prior to her.
Through the path itself, the four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) and the mundane superknowledges (*abhiññā*) came to her.

Emerging from the bliss of the path and fruit, she looked with her divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*) and, investigating, wondered, "When indeed was this Dhamma attained by my sons? As she considered, she saw that all of them—
They possess lust, hatred, and delusion; they do not have even a mere fraction of *jhāna* or *vipassanā*.

Having reflected, "Do my sons have the necessary support (*upanissaya*) for *arahantship*, or do they not?", he saw that they did. Then, having reflected, "Is there a favorable environment regarding their lodgings (*senāsana*), or is there not?", he saw that there was.
Finally, he reflected, "Do they obtain a favorable environment regarding the persons [with whom they associate]?"
She reflected, "Do they receive what is suitable for them as individuals? Do they receive what is suitable as food, or do they not?

Observing that they did not have what was suitable as food, she began from then on to prepare various kinds of rice gruel, many sorts of snacks, and meals of diverse choice flavors; then, having seated the bhikkhus in her house, she...
Having offered water for the guest-offering, he dedicated it, saying, "Venerable sirs, please take whatever pleases you and enjoy it.
They took the rice-gruel and other foods according to their preference and partook of them. As they received nourishment suitable to their needs, their minds became one-pointed.
Having developed insight with one-pointed minds, they attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) before long, and reflected:
"Oh, how the Great Laywoman has become our support! Had we not received suitable food, there would have been no penetration to the Paths and Fruits for us.
Now, having completed the rains retreat and performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony, [we shall go] to the Teacher..."
“We shall go into his presence. They asked the Great Female Lay Disciple (mahā-upāsikā), “We wish to see the Teacher.
She replied, “Very well, noble sirs. Having followed them for a short distance, they spoke many affectionate words, saying, “Venerable sirs, please look after us,” and then turned back.
Those monks, having gone to Sāvatthī and paid homage to the Teacher, stood to one side.
When he had sat down and asked, “Bhikkhus, I hope you are keeping well; I hope you are getting along;
I hope you are not distressed for lack of almsfood,” they replied, “We are keeping well, Bhante; we are getting along, Bhante, and we are by no means distressed for lack of almsfood.
For there is a certain female lay follower who is our maternal grandmother, and having understood our mental disposition, she thinks, ‘Oh, may she prepare such food for us!’”
“Having prepared food exactly as she had thought of it, she gave it to him,” they said, speaking in praise of her virtues.
Having heard this account of her virtues, a certain bhikkhu desired to go there;
he took a meditation subject from the Teacher, requested leave from the Teacher, saying, “Venerable Sir, I shall go to that village,” and departed from Jetavana.
Having reached that village by stages, on the very day he entered the monastery, he thought: "It is said that this female lay devotee knows whatever one thinks;
I am weary from the road and will not be able to tend to the monastery. Oh, would that she would send someone to look after the monastery for me!
While sitting at home, the lay devotee, reflecting [on his thoughts], perceived it.
Having understood the matter, she sent a person with the message: "Go, look after the monastery, and then return. The other [monk], wishing to drink water, thought:
"Oh, if only she would send me some sugar-water! The laywoman sent that as well. On the following day, he thought:
"Let her send me thick rice gruel with a side-dish (uttaribhaṅga) early in the morning! The laywoman—
He did exactly so. Having drunk the rice-gruel, he thought, "Oh, would that she were to send me such solid food as this!
The female lay devotee sent it to him as well. He thought, "This female lay devotee sends me everything I have ever thought of;
I am longing to see her. Oh, would that she were to have various kinds of choice food prepared and come here herself!"
The female lay follower, thinking, "My son wishes to see me;
he is waiting for my arrival," had food prepared, went to the monastery, and gave it to him. When he had finished his meal, he asked, "Are you my mother's mother, Great Lay Follower?
"Yes, dear," she replied. "Do you know the minds of others? "Why do you ask me that, dear? "By me..."
“He has done everything exactly as he thought it; therefore, I ask you about that. “There are many bhikkhus who know the minds of others, dear father.
“I am not asking about others; I am asking you, lay follower.
Even though this was so, the lay follower did not say, “I know the minds of others,” but said, “Sons who know the minds of others act in such a way. He [thought], “This is a grave matter.”
“Alas, what a task this is! Ordinary people think both beautiful and ugly thoughts.
If I were to think anything improper, it would bring me to ruin, like seizing a thief by the crest while he is still clutching his loot.
It is best for me to flee from here,” she thought, and said, “Laywoman, I am going. “Where? [he asked.]
“Noble lady? “To the presence of the Teacher, lay follower. “Then stay here for a while, venerable sir.
“I will not stay, lay follower; I shall indeed go,” he said, and having departed, he went into the presence of the Teacher.
Then the Teacher asked him, “Monk, why do you not stay there? “Yes, venerable sir, it is not possible to stay there.”
“For what reason, monk? “Venerable sir, that female lay devotee knows everything we think, even as we think it.

And ordinary people, indeed, think both the beautiful and the ugly. ‘If I were to think anything improper, she would bring me to ruin, like one who seizes a thief by the topknot along with his stolen goods,’ thinking thus, I have come. “Monk, …”
“It is fitting for you to dwell right there,” [he said]. “I cannot, Bhante; I will not dwell there.
“In that case, monk, will you be able to guard just one thing? “What is it, Bhante? “Guard your own mind alone.
This mind is indeed difficult to guard; restrain your own mind, and not anything else.”
"Whatever one thinks, this mind is indeed difficult to restrain," he said, and then spoke this verse:
"The taming of the mind is good—the mind that is difficult to restrain, light, and falling wherever it pleases; a tamed mind brings happiness."
In this context, "mind" (citta) is called "difficult to restrain" (dunniggaṇha) because it is seized by suffering. It is "swift" (lahu) because it arises and ceases rapidly.
Of that which is difficult to restrain and swift: "falling wherever it wishes" means having the nature of falling upon just anything whatsoever.
For this [mind] falls upon whatever place may be obtained—whether a place that should not be obtained, a suitable place, or an unsuitable place.
He does not know; he does not look at birth, nor clan, nor age. Wherever he wishes, there he falls;

thus he is called "one who falls wherever he desires. For such a mind, its taming is good—its state of being tamed by the four noble paths—and its being made compliant so that it becomes free from wildness is likewise good.
For what reason? Because this mind, when tamed, brings happiness; when rendered free from vice, it brings the bliss of the paths and fruits as well as the bliss of ultimate Nibbāna.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many in the assembled multitude became stream-enterers and so forth, and the Dhamma instruction became fruitful for the great mass of people.
Having given this exhortation to that bhikkhu, the Teacher said: "Go, bhikkhu, without thinking of anything else..."
“Dwell right there,” she sent him off. Having received the Teacher’s exhortation, that bhikkhu went there.

He did not think of anything external whatsoever. The Great Laywoman, observing with her divine eye, saw the Elder and thought, “Now my son has returned, having obtained a teacher who gives exhortations. Then she—
Having discerned this through his own knowledge, he prepared suitable food and gave it to him.
By partaking of that wholesome diet, the monk attained *arahantship* within just a few days.

Spending his time in the bliss of the path and its fruition, he thought, "Oh, the Great Laywoman has become my support; by relying on her, I have attained escape from existence. Then, regarding her...
"This is the foundation established for my selfhood; but as I have wandered through saṃsāra, has this same foundation ever existed in other selfhoods before?
While reflecting thus, he recollected ninety-nine previous existences.
During those ninety-nine existences, her heart had been bound to another, and she had taken his life. The Elder [considered] her...
Seeing such a lack of virtue, he thought, "Alas! Our great female lay disciple has committed a grave deed.
The Great Female Lay Disciple, while sitting at home, was reflecting, "Has my son’s task of going forth been accomplished, or not?
When she realized that he had attained Arahatship, she reflected further and [thought], "My..."
Having attained arahantship, the son thought, "Oh, how this female lay devotee has become a great support for me!
Then, reflecting, "Has she indeed been my support in the past as well, or not? he recollected ninety-nine previous existences.
He saw that during those ninety-nine existences, he had been together with others and had deprived her of life.
She committed a transgression, and seeing this fault of mine, she thought: "Oh, what a heavy deed has been done by this laywoman!
Then, reflecting, "Has there ever been any benefit done for my son as I wandered through this cycle of existence?
she recollected seven previous existences beyond that; in her seventh existence, she had been his female attendant.
“Having offered a gift of life in this very place where my life was nearly taken, oh!
I have previously performed a great service for my son,” she said, while still sitting in her house. Having distinguished the matter further, she said, “Consider this!
Hearing the sound with his divine ear-element, he distinguished it and recollected his seventh previous existence; there, by her, of his own life—
Seeing that he had been given [alms], he thought, "Oh, what great service this noble laywoman has previously rendered me!
Being thus glad at heart, he explained the question regarding the four paths and fruits right there to her, and then attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue.
This is the second story, concerning a certain bhikkhu.
3. The Story of a Certain Discontented Bhikkhu.
This teaching on the Dhamma, "Extremely Difficult to See," was related by the Teacher while residing at Sāvatthī concerning a certain discontented bhikkhu.
It is said that while the Teacher was residing at Sāvatthī, a son of a wealthy merchant approached a senior elder who was a family friend of his own clan.
“Venerable sir, I wish to be freed from suffering; please tell me one means by which I may be released from suffering,” he said.

“Very well, friend, if you wish to be freed from suffering, give *salākabhatta* (tickets for meals), give *pakkhikabhatta* (fortnightly meals), give *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robes), give requisites such as robes, and divide your own property into three portions.”
“Employ one [son] in business, support your wife and children with one, and give one to the Buddha’s teaching,” he said.
“Very well, Bhante,” he replied, and having done everything according to the instructions, he asked the Elder again:
“What else should I do beyond that, Bhante? “Friend, take the three refuges and take the five precepts.”
Having accepted those as well, he asked for more than that. [The teacher said: “In that case, take the ten precepts.
“Very well, venerable sir,” he replied, and he took them. Because he had thus performed meritorious deeds in successive stages, he became known as Anupubbaseṭṭhiputta.
Then, having asked again, “Venerable sir, there is still more to be done,” [the teacher said: “In that case, go forth into homelessness.”
Having been thus addressed, he went forth and became a monk. He had one teacher who was an Abhidhamma bhikkhu and one preceptor who was a master of the Vinaya.
Once he had received full ordination, when the teacher came into his presence, he posed an Abhidhamma question to him:
"In the Buddha’s Dispensation, this is permitted to do and that is not permitted. His preceptor, too—
When he came into his presence, he asked a question regarding the Vinaya: "In the Buddha's teaching, it is said that this may be done and that may not be done;
this is permissible and that is not permissible. He thought: "Alas, this is a heavy task!
I went forth desiring to be freed from suffering, yet here there is not even room for me to stretch out my hand."
"It is evident that it is possible to be freed from suffering even while remaining at home; it is fitting for me to remain as a householder.
From that time on, being dissatisfied and finding no delight, he did not recite the thirty-two-fold meditation subject, nor did he take up the formal lessons;
he became emaciated, haggard, with veins protruding over his body, overcome by indolence, and covered in scabs.
Then the young novices asked him, "Friend, why have you been standing where you stood and sitting where you sat?
You are overcome by jaundice, emaciated, haggard, with veins protruding over your body, overcome by lethargy, and covered in scabs; what has happened to you?
"I am weary, friends," he replied. "For what reason? He told them the whole occurrence.
He reported it. They informed his preceptors and teachers. Taking him with them, the preceptors and teachers went into the presence of the Teacher.
The Teacher asked, "Monks, why have you come? "Venerable sir, this monk has become dissatisfied with your teaching.
"Is that so, monks? "Yes, venerable sir. "For what reason?"
“Venerable sir, I went forth desiring only to be freed from suffering.
However, my teacher spoke to me about the Abhidhamma, and my preceptor spoke to me about the Vinaya; consequently, I reached the conclusion:
‘There is not even room here for me to stretch out my hand. It is possible to be freed from suffering while remaining a householder; I shall become a householder.’”
“Venerable sir,” [the monk replied]. “Bhikkhu, if you are able to guard even one thing, there is no need to guard the rest.
“What is it, venerable sir? “If you are able to guard your own mind alone.
“I shall be able to do so, venerable sir. “In that case, guard your own mind; it is possible to be liberated from suffering. Having given this exhortation, [the Buddha departed].
Having given this, he spoke this verse:
"The wise one should guard the mind, which is very difficult to see, extremely subtle, and which falls wherever it desires; a guarded mind brings happiness."
In this context, "very difficult to see" means extremely hard to perceive. "Exceedingly subtle" means very refined and most delicate.

"Falling wherever it pleases" refers to that which has the nature of falling anywhere at all—in appropriate or inappropriate places, whether one should receive something or not—without regard for birth and so forth.
"The wise person should guard the mind": an ignorant fool of dull wit is truly incapable of guarding his own mind.
There is no [other cause]; by falling under the power of the mind, one meets with ruin and disaster. However, it is only the wise and intelligent person who is able to guard the mind;
therefore, you too must guard the mind alone. For this mind, when guarded, brings about happiness, bringing forth the bliss of the paths, fruits, and Nibbāna.

At the conclusion of the teaching, that bhikkhu attained the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti), and many others also became stream-enterers and so forth; thus the teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.
The third story: The Case of a Certain Lonesome Bhikkhu.
The fourth story: The Story of the Elder Saṅgharakkhita’s Nephew.
Regarding this teaching on the Dhamma beginning with the words "Dūraṅgamaṃ," the Teacher spoke while residing at Sāvatthī concerning a bhikkhu named Saṅgharakkhita.

It is said that in Sāvatthī, a certain son of good family, having heard the Teacher’s teaching on the Dhamma, went forth into homelessness and, upon receiving full ordination, became known as the Elder Saṅgharakkhita;
in just a few days, he attained arahantship. His younger sister, having given birth to a son, gave him the Elder’s name. Thus, having become known as Bhāgineyya-Saṅgharakkhita, he reached maturity.
Having gone forth in the presence of that very elder and received full ordination, he entered the rains retreat at a certain village monastery.
There, having obtained two sets of robes for the rainy season— one seven cubits long and one eight cubits long— he observed the eight-cubit one, thinking,
"This shall be for my preceptor," and considered the seven-cubit one, thinking, "This shall be for me."
Having completed his rains retreat, he was traveling along the road, thinking, "I shall see my preceptor," while wandering for alms.

Upon arriving, even before the elders had reached the monastery, he entered the monastery, swept the elder’s daytime resting place, prepared water for washing the feet, arranged a seat, and sat down waiting, looking toward the path by which [the elder] would come. Then, perceiving that he was on his way—
Having seen him, he went out to meet him, received his bowl and robe, and said, "Please sit down,
venerable sir. Having seated the elder, he took a palm-leaf fan and fanned him, gave him water to drink, washed his feet, brought that garment and placed it at his feet,
saying, "Venerable sir, please use this," and stood there fanning him.
Then the Elder said to him: “Saṅgharakkhita, my robe is complete; you alone should use it.
“Venerable sir, from the moment I received it, this has been regarded by me as yours alone;
please use it. “Let it be so, Saṅgharakkhita; my robe is complete; you alone should use it. “Venerable sir, do not—
“Do this; when you have used it, it will be of great fruit for me.
Although he spoke thus to him again and again, the Elder still did not consent.
While standing there fanning him, he thought: “In my time as a householder, I was the Elder’s nephew; now that he has gone forth...”
“My co-resident said, ‘Even so, my preceptor does not wish to share possessions with me.
Since he will not share possessions with me, what is the use of my ascetic life? I shall become a householder. Then this thought occurred to him:
“Household life is difficult to maintain; having become a householder, how indeed shall I live? Thereupon, he reflected:
“I will sell my eight-cubit cloak and buy a she-goat; for a she-goat gives birth quickly, and I shall sell each offspring as it is born to recover my initial cost.
Once I have accumulated a large capital from these sales, I will bring home a wife who will bear me a son.
Then, having given that child the name of my maternal uncle, I shall place him in a small carriage...”
Having had them seated, I will take my son and wife and come to pay homage to my maternal uncle.
On the way while coming, I will say to my wife: "Bring my son first; I shall carry him.
She, saying, "What use have you for your son? Come, drive this carriage," will take the son and say, "I shall carry him."
“Having led him away, she will be unable to sustain him and will cast him onto the path of the wheels.
Then the wheel will pass over his body. Then, saying, ‘You gave my son neither to me nor were you able to sustain him;
I am ruined by you!’, she will strike him on the back with a goad-stick.”
While standing there thinking in this way and fanning him, he struck the elder on the head with his palm-leaf fan.
The elder, wondering, "Why have I been struck on the head by Saṅgharakkhita?", investigated and came to know everything that had been thought by him.
He said, "Saṅgharakkhita, you were unable to strike a woman; who here [is more foolish] than an aged elder?"
“...is a fault,” he said. [The man] thought, “Alas, I am ruined! It seems my every thought has been known by my preceptor;
what use have I for the life of a recluse? Casting aside his palm-leaf fan, he began to flee.
Then the young monks and novices pursued him, took hold of him, and brought him into the presence of the Teacher. The Teacher—
Upon seeing those monks, he asked, "Monks, why have you come? Have you captured one of my young monks?
"Yes, venerable sir; we have come before you having caught this youth who had fled out of dissatisfaction.
"Is it true, monks? "Yes, venerable sir. "For what purpose, monks, did you commit such a grave deed?"
“Is it not true,” he said, “that you are the son of a Buddha who has exerted heroic effort?
Having gone forth in the dispensation of a Buddha such as I, you were unable to train yourself so as to be called a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arahant;
for what purpose did you commit such a grave deed? “I am weary, Bhante,” he replied.

“Why are you distressed? he asked. Having related the entire account—from the day he received the rains-cloths for the residence until the elder’s blow with the palm-leaf fan—he said, “It is for this reason, venerable sir, that I have fled.
Then the Teacher said to him, “Come, bhikkhu; do not worry, for the mind is something that remains even when far away.”
"An object of perception is by nature receptive; therefore, one ought to strive for the sake of being liberated from the bonds of lust, hatred, and delusion.
Having said this, he spoke this verse:
"It travels far, wanders alone, is bodiless, and dwells in a cave."
“Those who restrain the mind will be released from the bonds of Māra.
In this context, “far-reaching” means that for the mind there is no coming and going even as much as the length of a spider’s thread toward directions such as the east;
rather, it is called “far-reaching” because it perceives an object even when that object is at a distance.
However, there are no seven or eight types of consciousness that are joined together like spokes in a hub and capable of arising simultaneously.
At the time of their arising, only one consciousness arises at a time; when that has ceased, another single consciousness arises again.
Thus, it is called "moving alone" (*ekacara*). Furthermore, consciousness has neither a physical shape nor any variety of color such as blue and so forth.

It is called "bodiless" because it has no physical form. It is called "dwelling in a cave" because the cave refers to the cave of the four great elements, and this [consciousness] arises depending upon the heart-organ (hadayarūpa).

"Those who [do not let arise]" means any persons—whether men or women, whether householders or those gone forth—who do not allow unarisen defilements to arise, and who abandon arisen defilements through the loss of mindfulness.
“They will restrain the mind; they will make it restrained and undistracted.

They will be freed from Māra’s bonds”—this means that by the absence of the bonds of the defilements, they will all be released from the round of existence in the three realms, which is designated as "Māra’s bonds.

At the conclusion of the teaching, the Elder Saṅgharakkhita, the nephew, attained the fruit of stream-entry; many others also became stream-enterers and so forth, and the Dhamma teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.
The fourth story: The Elder Saṅgharakkhitabhāgineyya. The fifth:
The Story of the Elder Cittahattha.
Regarding the words "Of one whose mind is unsteady," the Teacher delivered this teaching on the Dhamma while dwelling at Sāvatthī concerning the Elder Cittahattha.
It is said that a certain clansman living in Sāvatthī, while searching for a lost ox, entered the forest; at midday,
having found the ox and released it back into the herd, he thought, "I will certainly receive some food from the masters," and being oppressed by hunger and thirst,
he entered the monastery, approached the bhikkhus, paid homage, and stood to one side.
He sat down. At that time, there was food remaining in the alms-bowls of the monks after they had eaten;
seeing him oppressed by hunger, they said to him, "Take some food from here and eat.
And during the time of a Buddha, food arises with many soups and condiments; taking from it just enough for his sustenance, he ate.
Having drunk water, washed his hands, and paid homage to the bhikkhus, he asked, "Venerable sirs, did the masters go to a place of invitation today?
"No, lay follower; the bhikkhus receive [alms] regularly according to this very routine.
He thought, "Even though we rise again and again and perform our work continuously day and night, such sweetly seasoned food as this—"
Thinking, "We do not receive alms; these people, it seems, eat at fixed times. What is the use of my being a householder?
I shall become a monk," he approached the monks and requested the going-forth. Then the monks, saying, "Very well, lay follower," ordained him.
Having received full admission, he performed every kind of duty and service. He [was affected] by the gains and honors that arise for Buddhas...
After a few days, his body became stout. Then he thought, "What is the use of my life wandering for alms?
I shall become a householder. Having left the order, he entered his home. While performing work in his house, his body withered away within just a few days.
Then, thinking, "What is the use of this suffering? I shall become a recluse," he went back once more.
He went forth. After spending a few days there, he became weary once more and left the order; however, during his time as a monk, he had been helpful to the bhikkhus.
After only a few days, becoming weary again, he thought, "What use is the life of a householder to me?
I shall go forth. He went to the bhikkhus, paid homage to them, and requested ordination. Then, because of his previous helpfulness, the bhikkhus ordained him once again.
In this manner, having gone forth six times according to this very pattern, he disrobed.
Because the monks saw that he wandered about under the sway of his mind, they gave him the name Thera Cittahattha (Hand-Mind Elder).
While he was wandering back and forth in this way, his wife became pregnant. On his seventh turn, from the forest...
Taking his tools and going home, he set down his belongings and entered the inner room, thinking, "I will take my own saffron robe.
At that moment, his wife was lying down and sleeping.
Her lower garment had slipped off, saliva was trickling from her mouth, she was snoring, her mouth was open, and she was grinding her teeth.

It appeared to him like a bloated corpse. Having gained the perception that "this is impermanent and suffering," he thought, "Having gone forth for so long, I have been unable to remain steadfast in the state of a monk because of this.
Grasping the corner of his saffron robe, he tied it around his belly and departed from his home.
Then his mother-in-law, who was staying in the house next door, saw him departing in that manner and thought, "This man must be filled with longing;
having just returned from the forest, he has left the house with his saffron robe tied around his waist and is walking toward the monastery.
What could this mean? Entering the house, she saw her daughter sleeping and, upon seeing her, [thought: "Having seen this..."
Knowing that he had departed feeling remorseful, she struck her daughter and said, "Get up, you ill-omened girl!
Your husband saw you sleeping and, filled with remorse, has gone away; from now on, he is no longer yours.
[The daughter replied,] "Go away, go away, mother! How could he have gone? He will return again in just a few days."
He said: "Even he, having declared, 'It is impermanent, it is suffering,' attained the fruit of stream-entry as he went along and went along.
Having gone there and paid homage to the monks, he requested the going forth. [The monks replied: 'We shall not be able to ordain you;
how can you have the status of a recluse? Your head is like a whetstone for a razor. "Venerable sirs, now—"
“Out of compassion for me, please ordain me once. They ordained him out of a sense of gratitude.
In just a few days, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
They said to him: “Friend Cittahattha, you yourself should know the time for your departure; in this matter—”
“Venerable sir, you have delayed for too long. “Bhante, we went while our association still existed;
that association of ours has now been severed, and we have become those who are no longer subject to coming together.
The monks went into the presence of the Teacher and said, “Bhante, when we spoke to this monk in such a manner, he replied thus; he explains it otherwise and speaks what is untrue.”
They said: "The Teacher replied, 'Yes, monks, when my son was of unsteady mind and did not understand the True Dhamma, he went back and forth;
but now his merit and evil have been abandoned. Having said this, he spoke these two verses:
"For one of unsteady mind, who does not understand the True Dhamma..."
For one whose faith wavers, wisdom does not reach fulfillment.
“For one whose mind is untainted, whose heart is unassailed,
who has abandoned both merit and evil— there is no fear for such a vigilant person.”
In that context, "of one whose mind is unsteady" means that this mind has nothing fixed or stable for anyone.
However, a person who— like a pumpkin placed on the back of a donkey, like a charred stump pounded upon a heap of husks,
or like a kadamba flower placed on the head of a bald man— does not settle anywhere, might at times become a disciple of the Buddha.
Sometimes he is an Ājīvaka, sometimes a Nigaṇṭha, and sometimes an ascetic (tāpasa). Such a person is called one whose mind is unsettled.

Of him, whose mind is unsettled, and who does not understand the True Dhamma—that is, who does not understand this True Dhamma consisting of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—because his confidence is either wavering or unstable.
It shows that wisdom (paññā) does not reach fulfillment through its divisions such as those pertaining to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) and the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara).

If even wisdom pertaining to the sense-sphere is not fulfilled, how could wisdom pertaining to the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara), or the supramundane (lokuttara) ever be fulfilled?

"Of one whose mind is untainted" means of one whose mind is not moistened by lust (rāga). "Of one whose heart is unassailed" refers to the state described in the passage, "one whose heart is assailed and become callous," where it is [assailed] by hatred (dosa).
The state of the mind to be abandoned has been mentioned; here, however, the meaning is "of one whose mind is unimpeded by hatred.
"Of one who has abandoned merit and demerit" refers to the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), for whom both merit and demerit have been abandoned by means of the fourth path.

"There is no fear for the watchful" is stated as if to describe the state of fearlessness belonging specifically to the one whose taints are destroyed while they are awake. Furthermore, [he is endowed] with faith and the other [faculties].
One is called "awake" because of being endowed with the five factors of wakefulness.
Therefore, whether he is awake or not awake, there is no fear of defilements for him, because the defilements do not recur.
Indeed, the defilements do not pursue him, because the defilements abandoned by each respective path do not return. For this very reason it was said: "By the path of stream-entry..."
“Those defilements that have been abandoned, he does not repeat, he does not return to, he does not go back to those defilements;
those defilements that have been abandoned by the path of the once-returner, the non-returner, and the arahant, he does not repeat, he does not return to, he does not go back to those defilements.
Thus the teaching was beneficial and fruitful for the great multitude.
Then one day, the monks raised a discussion in the Hall of Truth, saying, "Friends, these defilements are indeed burdensome!

Even a clansman endowed with such a strong predisposition for Arahantship was churned by defilements, becoming a householder seven times and going forth seven times. When the Teacher heard this conversation of theirs, he said:
Having gone to the Dhamma assembly by walking at a pace suited to that moment and sitting upon the Buddha’s seat, he asked, “Monks, about what topic are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very one,” he said, “Monks, it is exactly so;
the defilements are indeed heavy. If these were material things, such that they could be placed somewhere, [they would weigh down the earth].”
"The world-system would be too cramped and the Brahma-world too low; there would be no space for them.
These people even throw a person like me—a thoroughbred man endowed with wisdom—into confusion; what then can be said of the rest?
'For I myself, relying on a mere half-nāḷi of excellent *coraka* grass and a blunt hoe, went forth six times and previously disrobed. "When?"
“Venerable sir, when will the Sugata [speak]? “Listen, monks. “Yes, venerable sir. “Then listen,” he said, and related the past:
“In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, a wise man named Kudāla went forth into the ascetic life of an outsider.
After dwelling in the Himālaya for eight months, during the rainy season when the ground was saturated with water, he thought: ‘In my home...’”
"I have a single measure of *varakaca* seeds and a blunt hoe; let not the *varakaca* seed be lost.
Having thus left the monastic life, he plowed a spot with his hoe, sowed that seed, and built a fence.
When it was ripe, he harvested it, set aside a measure of seed, and ate the rest. He thought, "What use have I now for a house? Once again..."
Thinking, "I shall go forth in one month," he departed and went forth.
Following this very routine, relying upon a measure of sugar-cane, some *varakacoraka* grass, and a blunt hoe, he became a householder seven times and went forth seven times.
Then, on the seventh occasion, he thought: "Six times I have gone forth as a householder by means of this blunt hoe; at some point..."
"I shall discard it. Having gone to the bank of the Ganges, he thought, "If I descend, I might see the place where it fell;
therefore, I shall discard it in such a way that I do not see the place where it falls.
He tied a handful of seed in a piece of cloth, fastened the cloth to a hoe-blade, and grasped the handle of the hoe.
Standing on the bank of the Ganges, he closed his eyes, whirled [the head] three times over his own head, and threw it into the Ganges.
Turning back and looking, and not seeing the place where it had fallen, he cried out three times, "Victory is mine! Victory is mine!
At that moment, the King of Bārāṇasī, having suppressed the border regions, arrived and encamped his army on the riverbank.
Having descended into the river to bathe, he heard that sound. Now, for kings, the cry "I have conquered! is unpleasant to hear.
He went to him and asked, "I have just returned after crushing my enemies, crying 'I have conquered!
But you, on the other hand, are shouting 'I have conquered! I have conquered! What is this? Kudālapaṇḍita said, "You..."
"Victory over an external thief is indeed a victory, yet it is a victory that can be lost again. But I have conquered the internal thief of greed;
he shall not conquer me again. His defeat alone is truly a victory. Having said this, he spoke this verse:
"It is no true victory to win what is then lost again; it is a true victory when, once won, it is never lost."
“That which is conquered is well-conquered, that which is conquered is not to be conquered again.
At that very moment, looking at the Ganges, he developed the water-kasiṇa and, having attained this distinction, sat cross-legged in the air.
Having heard the Great Man’s discourse on the Dhamma, the king paid homage to him, requested the going-forth, and together with—
He went forth with a military force; his retinue was about a yojana in extent.
Another neighboring king, having heard of his renunciation, arrived thinking, "I shall seize his kingdom.
Seeing that prosperous city thus empty, he thought, "The king who abandoned such a city to go forth will not have gone forth in a lowly place; I too shall go forth."
Thinking, "It is fitting," he went there, approached the Great Man, and requested the going-forth; together with his retinue, he went forth.
In this same manner, seven kings also went forth. There was a hermitage extending for seven *yojanas*.
The seven kings, having renounced their wealth and taken such a multitude of people with them, went forth. The Great Man lived the life of celibacy.
Having mastered [the teachings], he went to the Brahma-world.
Having delivered this Dhamma instruction, the Teacher said: "Bhikkhus, at that time I was the wise Kudāla; such are these defilements, so heavy.
This is the fifth story, concerning the Elder Cittahattha.
6. The Story of the Five Hundred Bhikkhus.
The Teacher, while residing at Sāvatthī, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning those bhikkhus who had begun the practice of insight (āraddhavipassaka).
It is said that five hundred bhikkhus in Sāvatthī, having received a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) from the presence of the Teacher, [practiced] up to the stage of Arahantship.
Thinking, “We shall perform the duties of a recluse,” they traveled a road of one hundred leagues and arrived at a large village settlement.
Then those people, seeing them, had them sit on prepared seats and served them with excellent rice gruel, food, and other offerings.
Having asked, “Venerable sirs, where are you going? and being told, “To whatever place is comfortable,” they said, “Venerable sirs, this...”
“Dwell right here for three months; we too, having established ourselves in the refuges in your presence, will observe the five precepts,” they requested.
Having understood their consent, [the laypeople] said, “Venerable sirs, there is a great forest grove not far from here;
dwell there,” and thus they sent them off. The monks entered that forest grove.
The deities dwelling in that grove thought, "Noble sirs, you who are virtuous have arrived at this grove;
it is indeed improper for us to dwell in trees with our wives and children while the noble ones are living here.
Descending from the tree and sitting on the ground, they reflected: "Noble sirs, for one night today in this place..."
“Having stayed for a while, they will surely depart tomorrow. On the following day, the monks too, having wandered for alms within the village, returned once more to that very forest grove.
The deity thought, “The community of monks must have been invited by someone for tomorrow’s meal;
therefore they are returning. They will not go today; I suspect they will depart tomorrow. By this means...
They remained on the ground for only half a month.
Then they thought: "The venerable ones will likely stay right here for these three months;
and while they are staying right here, it is not fitting for us to climb our trees and sit upon them, nor [should we do so] during the three months while their wives and children [are there]."
“Having seized them, it would be right to cause these monks to flee by making even their places for sitting on the ground painful and by doing something to terrify them.
They began to display headless trunks at various night-stations, day-stations, and the ends of the walking-paths, and they started to produce non-human sounds.
The monks were afflicted with diseases such as vomiting and diarrhea.
Questioning one another, "Friend, what is troubling you?
and saying, "I have a cough," or "I have a fever," they would say, "Friend, today at the end of the walkway I saw a headless corpse;
at night in the watch-tower I saw a headless trunk; by day in the daytime station I heard the voice of non-human beings; this is something to be avoided."
“That place has become uncomfortable for us here; we shall go into the presence of the Teacher.
Having departed, they went by stages into the presence of the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down to one side.
Then the Teacher said to them: “Monks, were you unable to dwell in that place? “Yes, Venerable Sir.”
“Venerable sir, while we were living in that place, such terrifying objects appeared to us and such discomfort arose;
therefore, thinking, ‘This place is unfit to be inhabited,’ we abandoned it and came into your presence.
“Monks, you ought to go back to that very place,” [he said]. “No, Venerable sir...”
“It is possible, Bhante. “Monks, you went there without taking up weapons; now go, having taken up weapons.
“What kind of weapon, Bhante? The Teacher said, “I will give you a weapon;
go, having taken the weapon given by me,” and then—
“Whatever should be done by one skilled in the goal, having realized the state of peace:
one should be capable, upright, and very upright; easy to speak to, gentle, and free from pride.
Having recited the entire *Mettasutta*, [the Buddha said]: “Monks, starting from this grove outside the monastery...”
“Enter the interior of the monastery while reciting,” he dismissed them.

They paid homage to the Teacher, departed, and after traveling by stages, they reached that place. Having performed group recitation in the outer monastery, they entered the forest grove while continuing their recitation.
The deities throughout the entire forest grove, having conceived a mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*), came out to meet them.
They requested permission to receive their bowls and robes; they requested permission to massage their hands and feet;
they arranged for protection here and there for them, and sat down as if steeped in fragrant incense oil.
Nowhere was even the sound of a non-human being heard. The minds of those bhikkhus became one-pointed. In the places where they stood by night and by day...
Seated there, they directed their minds toward insight (vipassanā), established within themselves the contemplation of dissolution and passing away, and developed insight, thinking:
"This so-called individual existence (attabhāva) is like a clay vessel in its sense of being subject to breaking and its sense of impermanence.
While seated in the Fragrant Chamber (gandhakuṭī), the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), knowing that their insight had been commenced, [addressed] those bhikkhus...
Having addressed them, saying, “In just this way, monks, this so-called personal existence (attabhāva), by virtue of its perishable nature and its state of being subject to destruction,
is exactly like a potter’s vessel,” he emitted a radiance and, though standing a hundred yojanas away, appeared as if sitting right before them;
emitting six-colored rays and manifesting a visible form, he spoke this verse:
“Having understood this body to be like a jar, and having established this mind as being like a city, fight Māra with the weapon of wisdom;
guard what has been won, and be one who dwells nowhere.
In this context, “like a jar” means that, in terms of its lack of strength and weakness, it is non-enduring and temporary—referring to this collection of hair and so forth.
Having understood the body to be like a jar, similar to a potter's vessel, one should establish this mind as being like a city.

A so-called "city" is firm on the outside, surrounded by deep moats and walls, provided with gates and watchtowers, and possesses well-laid-out streets, crossroads, and junctions within its marketplaces; [one should think], "We shall plunder it," regarding that which is outside.
Just as thieves, unable to enter after arriving, depart as if struck by a mountain, even so the wise clansman,
having made his own mind of insight firm like a city and stationed himself within that city,

[overcomes the defilements] with the various kinds of weapons such as the single-edged blade— namely, those consisting of insight and those consisting of the Noble Path— just as one would [defeat] a host of thieves.
And with the weapon of wisdom, warding off the Māra of defilements that is to be slain by each respective path, you should fight—that is, strike down—each of those Māras of defilement;

this is the meaning. "Guard what has been won" means: having cultivated the conditions conducive to the dwelling, the season, food, persons, and hearing the Dhamma for the nascent insight that has arisen, and having entered meditative attainment (samāpatti) from time to time and emerged therefrom with a purified mind, [one should contemplate] formations (saṅkhāra).
Reflecting thus, one should guard oneself. "One should be without a dwelling" means one should be without attachment.
Just as a warrior at the head of the battle, having formed a defensive line, fights against his enemies, even when he is hungry or thirsty, or when his armor is loose or his weapons are failing...
Having fallen [into battle], he enters the fortified camp, rests, eats, drinks, arms himself, takes up his weapons, and emerging once more, he fights and crushes the enemy army;
he conquers what is unconquered and protects what is conquered.
For if, while stationed in the fortified camp, he were to remain there resting and enjoying those pleasures, the kingdom would fall into the hands of the enemy.

In the same way, bhikkhu, having attained the recently acquired insight again and again, and having emerged from those attainments, one who contemplates formations with a pure mind is able to guard it; through the subsequent attainment of the paths and fruits, one conquers the Māra of the defilements.
But if one relishes the attainment itself, [then] with a pure mind again and again—
One who does not comprehend mental formations (*saṅkhāra*) is unable to penetrate the Path and its Fruit.

Therefore, while guarding that which ought to be guarded, one should be "without a dwelling" (*anivesana*); having made meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) one's dwelling, one should not settle therein—that is, one should not create a basis for attachment (*ālaya*).
"Surely you too act in this way," thus the Teacher taught the Dhamma to those bhikkhus.

At the conclusion of the teaching, the five hundred bhikkhus, while still seated in their places, attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Praising, extolling, and worshipping the golden-hued body of the Tathāgata, they departed.
This is the sixth story, concerning the five hundred bhikkhus. 7.
The Story of the Elder Pūtigattatissa.
The Teacher, while residing at Sāvatthī, delivered this Dhamma teaching, "Soon indeed this body," concerning the Elder Tissa with the Putrid Limbs.
It is said that a certain son of good family from Sāvatthī, having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, placed his heart in the Dispensation and went forth;
having received full ordination, he became known as the Elder Tissa. As time passed, in his body...
A disease arose. Boils the size of mustard seeds appeared;

these gradually grew to the size of mung beans, then the size of kalāya peas, then the size of jujube stones, then the size of *āmalaka* fruits, and finally the size of young bamboo shoots and full-grown bamboo. They burst open, and his entire body became perforated with holes.
Thus, the name "Thera Pūtigatta-Tissa" (the Foul-Bodied Tissa) arose for him. Then, at a later time...
His bones broke; he became incapable of self-care. His lower and upper garments became smeared with pus and blood, resembling a net of cakes.
His co-residents and others, unable to tend to him, abandoned him.
Thus, having become destitute, he lay there.
For the Buddhas, indeed, the twice-daily surveying of the world is never abandoned.
Surveying the world at dawn, they direct their knowledge toward the fragrant chamber (*gandhakuṭī*) starting from the rim of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa-mukhavaṭṭi*) and look out;
surveying it in the evening, they direct their knowledge outward starting from the fragrant chamber and look out. At that time, for the Blessed One—

Within the net of his knowledge, the Elder Pūtigattatissa appeared. Seeing that this bhikkhu possessed the necessary support for attaining Arahatship, and thinking, "He has been abandoned by his fellow residents and others;
now, apart from me, he has no other refuge," the Teacher emerged from the Fragrant Chamber and, as if wandering on a tour of the monastery, went to the fire-hall.
Having gone there, he washed the cooking pot, added water, and placed it on the stove;
then, waiting for the water to reach the boiling point, he remained right in the fire-hall. Once he knew the water was hot, he went and seized the monk by the corner of his bed.
At that moment, the monks took up the bed, saying, "Go away, venerable sir! We will take him," and carried him to the fire-hall.
They brought it. The Teacher had Ambaṇa fetch it, poured hot water over it, and had those monks take his outer robe, knead it in the hot water, and hang it out in the mild sunlight.
Then, standing near him, he moistened his body with the hot water, rubbed it, and bathed him;
at the conclusion of his bath, the outer robe was dry. Then—
Having had him undress, they had him wring out his worn *kāṣāya* robe in water and then spread it out in the sun.
As soon as the water was drawn away from his body, that [robe] too dried up. He put on one *kāṣāya* as an undergarment and the other as an upper robe;
with a lightened body and a one-pointed mind, he lay down upon the couch. The Teacher stood at his head and said: "Bhikkhu, this body of yours..."
"Having departed from consciousness and become useless, he will lie upon the earth like a piece of wood," he said, and then recited this verse:
"Soon indeed this body will lie upon the earth,
Abandoned, devoid of consciousness, Like a useless log of wood."
In this context, "before long indeed" means that before long this body will lie upon the earth;
it will lie upon this earth which is already accustomed to being a natural resting place. "Cast away" means discarded;
it shows that, having become empty through the departure of consciousness, it will lie there. Like what? Like a useless log—meaning something devoid of purpose and of no further utility.

Like a piece of wood. For when people seeking building materials enter the forest, they cut straight wood with a straight shape and crooked wood with a crooked shape, and take away the building materials;
but having cut the rest—which is hollow, rotten, pithless, or knotted—they discard it right there. Other people seeking building materials...
There are no takers who come and take it; rather, having observed it, people take only what is beneficial to themselves, while the rest remains simply as earth.
Furthermore, by various means, that [earth] might even be fashioned into bedstead supports, footstools, or wooden seats.
However, regarding these thirty-two constituent parts of this physical body:
"There is not even a single part of this body—whether it be the bedstead’s supports or anything else—that can be grasped as being of benefit;
it is merely like a useless log. This body, devoid of consciousness, will lie upon the earth within a few days.
At the conclusion of the teaching, the Elder Pūtigattatissa attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), and many others did so as well.
They became stream-enterers and so forth. The Elder, too, having attained Arahatship, passed away into Parinibbāna.
The Teacher, having had his funeral rites performed and having taken his relics, caused a cetiya to be built. The bhikkhus asked the Teacher:
"Venerable Sir, where has the Elder Pūtigattatissa been reborn? "He has passed away into Parinibbāna, bhikkhus. "Venerable Sir, for one such as this..."
"But for what reason did the limbs of this bhikkhu, who was endowed with the necessary conditions for Arahantship, become putrid;
for what reason were his bones shattered; and what was the cause by which he attained the state of being a necessary condition for Arahantship?
"Monks, all of this arose solely through the kamma performed by him himself. "But what, [was that]?"
“Venerable sir, what has been done? [The Buddha said: “In that case, monks, listen. He related the past:
“In the time of the Sammasambuddha Kassapa, this man was a fowler; having killed many birds, he served them to people of high status.
He sold the remains of what had been given to them, thinking: ‘If the leftovers from what has been sold are not killed and set aside, they will become putrid.’”
He would break their leg bones and wing bones so that they were unable to fly, pile them up, and set them aside;
then, on the following day, he would sell them. When he had obtained a great quantity, however, he would have them cooked for his own consumption as well.
One day, while the meat broth was being cooked, a monk whose taints were exhausted (khīṇāsava) was wandering for alms.
He stood at the door of his house. Upon seeing the elder, he felt faith in his heart and thought, "I have killed and eaten many living beings, yet this noble one stands at my door;
there is flavorful food within my home, so I shall give him almsfood.
Taking the elder’s bowl and filling it, he gave him almsfood of excellent flavor, and having paid homage to the elder with the fivefold prostration, he—
“Venerable sir, may you reach the pinnacle of the Dhamma seen in this very life,” he said. The Elder gave his blessing, saying, “So be it. [The Buddha said:
“Monks, this was accomplished for Tissa through the power of the deed performed at that time;
as a result of breaking the bones of the birds, Tissa’s limbs became putrid and his bones were shattered, even though he was one whose taints were destroyed.”
“By the result of giving a gift of a lump of flavored food, he attained Arahatship.
This is the seventh story, the account of the Elder Pūtigattatissa. 8.
The Story of Nanda the Cowherd.
"Everywhere," the Teacher said this discourse on the Dhamma concerning Nanda the cowherd while staying in the Kosala country.
It is said that at Sāvatthī, Anāthapiṇḍika the householder had a cowherd named Nanda who guarded a herd of cattle;
he was wealthy, affluent, and of great means. It is said that just as Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic lived in the guise of a renunciant, so did Nanda live in the guise of a cowherd.

Avoiding the royal tax, he protected his own family. From time to time, taking the five products of the cow, he would come into the presence of Anāthapiṇḍika, see the Teacher, listen to the Dhamma, and request the Teacher to allow him to return to his own dwelling place.
The Teacher, awaiting the ripening of his wisdom, waited until its state was fully matured.
Having learned this, one day, while wandering on a journey surrounded by a great community of monks,
he descended from the road and sat down at the foot of a certain tree near Nanda’s dwelling place. Without going to the Teacher’s presence to pay homage and exchange greetings,
Nanda invited the Teacher, saying, "May the Teacher accept for me tomorrow a gift of the five products of the cow, excellent food, for the community of monks headed by the Buddha."
He gave it. On the seventh day, the Teacher, having offered words of thanksgiving, delivered a gradual discourse consisting of various topics such as the discourse on giving.
At the conclusion of the discourse, Nanda the cowherd was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
Taking the Teacher’s bowl and following him for some distance, he was told by the Teacher, “Stop, lay follower. Being thus turned back, he paid homage and returned.
Then a certain hunter pierced him and killed him. The monks who were coming from behind saw him, went to the Teacher, and said:
"Venerable sir, the cowherd Nanda, because you had come here, gave a great gift and followed after you;
as he was returning, he was killed. Had you not come, his death would not have occurred."
The Teacher said, “Monks, whether I have come or not, there is no means for one who wanders through the four cardinal directions and the four intermediate directions to escape from death.
For that which neither thieves nor enemies can do, it is the mind itself—internally corrupted and wrongly directed—that does this to these beings. Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“Whatever a hater might do to a hater, or an enemy to an enemy, a mind wrongly directed would do him even worse than that.
In this context, “diso disaṃ” means a thief [to] a thief. “Having seen” (*disvā*) is the ellipsis to be supplied. “Yaṃ taṃ kayirā” means whatever he might do to him.
He would bring about ruin and disaster. The same method applies to the second phrase as well. This is what is meant:
suppose one person, being a betrayer of friends and a thief, does not offend another’s children, wife, fields, lands, cattle, buffaloes, and so forth;
yet, seeing that very person—who has not offended him—acting as a thief, he [perceives him as such]. Or else, suppose there is an enemy with whom he has a settled enmity for some reason.
Having seen this, whatever ruin or calamity he might bring upon him through his own harshness and cruelty— whether by afflicting his wife and children,
destroying his fields and so forth, or even depriving him of life— his mind, being wrongly established and wrongly directed among the ten courses of unwholesome action,
makes that man even more evil than that [act]. Thus, it makes him far worse than before.
One might do so. In the manner described, an enemy or one who is hostile toward another might produce suffering for that person in this very life, or might bring about the end of their life.

However, a mind fixed upon these unwholesome courses of action brings ruin and disaster even in this present life, and [leads to suffering] throughout hundreds of thousands of future existences within the four lower realms.
"Having cast it down, he does not allow his head to be raised.

At the conclusion of this teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages. The teaching proved beneficial for the great multitude. However, as the deed performed by the lay devotee in a previous existence had not been asked about by the monks, it was therefore not mentioned by the Teacher.
This is the eighth story, the Case of the Cowherd Nanda.
9. The Story of the Elder Soreyya "Neither mother nor father could do this"—the Teacher gave this teaching on the Dhamma while residing at Jetavana in Sāvatthī concerning the Elder Soreyya.
The story originated in the city of Soreyya and was concluded in Sāvatthī. While the Fully Enlightened One was staying in Sāvatthī...

While residing in the city of Soreyya, the son of the Soreyya merchant, seated in a comfortable carriage together with a companion and accompanied by a large retinue, went out from the city for the purpose of bathing.
At that moment, the Elder Mahākaccāyana, desiring to enter the city of Soreyya for alms, was putting on his outer robe outside the city. To the Elder—
And his body was the color of gold. When the son of the merchant Soreyya saw him, he thought:
"Oh, would that this elder were my wife, or that the complexion of my wife's body might become like the complexion of this man's body!
At the very moment he thought this, his male characteristics disappeared and female characteristics appeared.
Feeling ashamed, she alighted from her carriage and fled. Her attendants, not recognizing her, asked, "What is this?
She too set out on the road to Takkasilā. Her companion, though searching here and there, did not see her.
After everyone had bathed, they went home. When asked, "Where is the merchant's son? they replied, "We thought he would have returned after bathing."
They spoke thus. Then his parents, having searched for him here and there and not finding him, wept and lamented;
thinking, "He must be dead," they offered a funeral meal. Seeing a caravan leader traveling toward Takkasilā, she followed closely behind his carriage.
Then, seeing her, the people said, "She follows right behind our carriage;
we do not know whose daughter she is. She replied, "You drive your own carriage;
I shall go on foot," and as she walked, she gave her finger-ring and made room for herself in one of the carriages. The people—
They thought, “In the city of Takkasilā, our merchant’s son has no wife;
we shall tell him of her, and there will be a great reward for us. Having gone to his house, they said, “Master, we have brought a jewel of a woman for you.
When he heard this, he summoned her and [found her] beautiful and pleasing, in accordance with his own age.
Seeing her, he conceived affection for her and took her home. For there are no men who have not previously been women, nor women who have not previously been men.

Indeed, men who commit adultery with another's wife, after dying and being boiled in hell for many hundreds of thousands of years, when returning to the human state, attain the female form in as many as a hundred successive existences.

The Elder Ānanda, a noble disciple who had fulfilled the perfections for a hundred thousand eons, while wandering through *saṃsāra*, was reborn in one particular existence within a family of blacksmiths.
Having committed the act of adultery with another's wife, he suffered in hell;
by the residue of that karma, he became a woman who served as a male’s foot-courtesan for fourteen existences, and for seven existences, she was one whose seed was extracted.
[She] attained [it]. However, women who have performed meritorious deeds such as giving, having dispelled their desire for the female state, resolve their minds thus:
"May this merit of ours lead to the acquisition of a male existence. Having passed away, they acquire a male existence.
Furthermore, by means of practicing correctly toward their husbands as deities, women also certainly acquire a male existence.
But this son of the merchant, having directed his mind improperly toward the elders, attained the female state in this very same existence.
Through her cohabitation with the merchant’s son in Takṣaśilā, a fetus was established in her womb.
After ten months had passed, she gave birth to a son; and at the time when that boy was beginning to walk, yet another...
She obtained a son. Thus, there were four sons in her womb: two who had lived there, and two who were born there in the city of Soreyya on account of him.

At that time, a friend of hers, the son of a merchant from the city of Soreyya, having gone from Soreyya to Takkasilā with five hundred carts, entered the city seated in a comfortable carriage. Then, him—

Standing on the upper terrace of the palace with the window open, looking down at the street, she saw her, recognized her, sent for a female servant to summon her, had her seated on the great floor, and bestowed upon her great honor and hospitality.
Then he said to her: "Lady, you have never been seen by us before; nevertheless, [you have come] to us..."
“You show them honor; do you know us? “Yes, sir, I know. Are you not the inhabitants of the city of Soreyya?
“Yes, lady. She then inquired after the health of her parents, her wife, and her children.
The other replied, “Yes, lady, they are well,” and said, “Do you know these people? “Yes, sir, I know them. One of them—”
“I have a son; where is he, Master? “Bhadde, do not speak of this.
One day we set out for a bath, sitting together with him in a comfortable carriage. We do not know his destination;
having wandered here and there and not seeing him, we informed his parents. They too, weeping and wailing, performed the funeral rites.”
“It was I, master,” she said. “Go away, lady! What are you saying? I am a man like a young god, your friend.
“Let it be, master; it was I. “Then what about this? “On that day, did you not see the venerable elder Mahākaccāyana?
“Yes, I saw him. “I too, having gazed upon the venerable elder Mahākaccāyana...”
“Alas, would that this elder were my husband, or that my husband’s complexion might be like the complexion of his body!”—thus I thought.
At the very moment of that thought, my male characteristics vanished and female characteristics appeared.
Then, feeling ashamed and unable to say anything to anyone, I fled from there and came here, my lord.
“Alas, what a grievous deed you have committed! Why did you not tell me? Nevertheless, has the Elder been asked for forgiveness?
“He has not been asked for forgiveness, Master. But do you know where the Elder is? “He is living right here, depending on this very city.
“If he should come here while wandering for alms, I shall provide my noble sir with food for his meal.”
“I would give it, sir. “In that case, quickly prepare the hospitality; we shall ask our noble master for forgiveness.
He went to the elder’s dwelling, paid homage, and sitting to one side, said, “Venerable sir, please accept my alms tomorrow.
“Are you not a visitor, son of a merchant? “Venerable sir, do not [be angry] with us.”
"Ask about the state of her being a visitor; take alms from me tomorrow," he said.
The Elder consented, and in the house, a great honor had been prepared for the Elder. On the following day, the Elder went to the door of that house.
Then, having seated him and served him with excellent food, the merchant's son took that woman, laid her at the feet of the Elder, and said:
“Venerable sir, please forgive my companion,” she said. “What is this? [The Elder asked. “Venerable sir, this person was formerly my dear companion;
having looked at you, he thought such a thing, whereupon his male characteristic disappeared and his female characteristic appeared.
Please forgive him, venerable sir. “In that case, stand up; I forgive you both.”
As soon as the Elder had said, "I forgive you," the female sex disappeared and the male sex appeared.
As soon as the male sex had appeared, the merchant’s son of Takkasilā said to him:
"Friend companion, since these two children lived in your womb and were born because of me, they are the sons of both of us."
