“Just so; we shall dwell right here, do not be distressed. “My dear friend, through one single existence, I first became a man and then attained the female state, and subsequently was born again as a man—thus I have undergone a transformation.
First, two sons were born depending on me; now, two sons have emerged from my womb. Thus, within a single existence...”
"Do not harbor the thought that he will live at home again after reaching such a state of distress; I shall go forth into homelessness in the presence of my noble master.
These two children are your burden, so do not neglect them," she said.

Having kissed her sons on the head, rubbed them all over, and laid them down upon her breast, she entrusted them to her father, departed, and went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Elder.

He made his request. The Elder, having ordained him and conferred full admission upon him, took him with him while wandering on tour and eventually arrived at Sāvatthī. He became known by the name Soreyya Thera.
When the inhabitants of the countryside learned of this occurrence, they were greatly stirred and filled with curiosity; they approached him and asked, "Is it true, venerable sir?"
“Yes, friends,” he replied. “Venerable sir, is there such a thing as a reason for this?
“It is said that two sons have been born in your womb; they were both produced depending on you. Between these two, which one do you feel the stronger affection for?
“The ones who dwelt in the womb, friend. They asked him the same thing repeatedly, each time someone arrived.
The Elder, repeatedly saying, “Affection for those born from one’s own womb is indeed powerful,” sat alone and stood alone, feeling ashamed.
Having thus attained solitude, he brought about the destruction and passing away of his individual existence and reached Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Then, as people came and went, they asked him: “Venerable sir, in this way...”
“Was it indeed so? “Yes, friends. “In what regard was your affection strong?
“I have no affection whatsoever for anyone. The bhikkhus thought, “This man speaks untruth;
previously he said, ‘My affection for the sons born from my own womb is strong,’ yet now he says, ‘I have no affection for anyone at all. He is giving a contradictory answer.”
"Venerable Sir," they said. The Teacher replied, "Monks, my son does not declare final knowledge (aññā) [in the conventional sense].
From the moment my son saw the Path through his rightly directed mind, no attachment has arisen toward anything whatsoever.
That attainment which neither mother nor father can provide for these beings is what has occurred within them."
"Only a mind rightly directed gives," he said, and then uttered this verse:
"Neither mother nor father could do it, nor any other relatives;
a mind rightly directed would make one better than that."
In this context, "that cause" (*taṃ kāraṇaṃ*) refers to that reason which neither mother, nor father, nor other relatives could provide.
"Well-directed" (*sammāpaṇihitaṃ*) means properly established within the ten courses of wholesome action (*dasasu kusalakammapathesu*).

"Better than that" (*seyyaso naṃ tato*) means that it would make one better, more excellent, and superior than from that cause; the sense is "it makes [one] so. For parents [provide] wealth for their children...
By giving, they are able to provide wealth for a comfortable livelihood without having to perform labor within a single lifetime.
Even the mother and father of Visākhā were so very wealthy and possessed of such great fortune that they gave her the means for a comfortable livelihood within a single lifetime.
Yet, they were not capable of bestowing the glory of a Wheel-Turning Monarch over the four continents.
Even one's mother and father cannot provide for their children, let alone divine prosperity or the attainment of the first jhāna and so forth;
there is no talk at all of bestowing supramundane success. However, a mind rightly directed is capable of granting all these forms of prosperity.
Therefore it was said: "It makes him better than that."
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages. The teaching thus became beneficial to the great multitude.
This is the ninth story, the account of the Elder Soreyya.
The commentary on the Cittavagga is finished.
The Third Chapter. 4.
The Chapter on Flowers. 1.
The Account of the Five Hundred Monks Absorbed in Discourse on the Earth.
The Teacher, while residing at Sāvatthī, delivered this discourse on the Dhamma concerning five hundred bhikkhus who were engrossed in talk about the earth.
It is said that these bhikkhus, having traveled through the countryside with the Blessed One and returned to Jetavana,
sat together in the assembly hall in the evening and discussed the various places they had visited, saying, "From such-and-such a village, traveling to such-and-such a place..."
They engaged in talk about the earth, saying, "It is even, it is uneven, it is full of mud, it is full of gravel, it is black clay, it is red clay.
The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, with what talk are you sitting gathered here now?
When they replied, "Venerable Sir, we were engaged in talk about the earth in the places where we have been wandering," he said, "Monks, this..."
"External earth, indeed, it is fitting for you to perform the preparatory exercise upon the internal earth," he said,
and then spoke these two verses:
"Who shall traverse this earth?"
Who, skilled like one gathering flowers, will pluck this well-taught verse of Dhamma from this world with its devas and the realm of Yama?
“The trainee shall traverse the earth,
as well as this world of Yama together with its devas;
the trainee [shall traverse] the well-taught Dhamma-footprint.”
“The skillful one will ripen [it] like a flower.
In this context, “who this” means who this earth, designated as the personal existence (*attabhāva*).
“Will discern” means he will investigate with his own knowledge, will understand, will penetrate, and will realize; such is the meaning. And “the world of Yama” refers to the fourfold...
"And the world of misery. "Who will discern, investigate, understand, penetrate, and realize this world together with its devas?"—this he asked. "Who [will realize] the well-taught Dhammapada?
Because it is spoken according to its true nature, it is "well-taught," consisting of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*).
"Skilled in the Dhamma-pada," means: like a skilled garland-maker selecting flowers, who will cook [them], that is to say, who will select, discern, examine, penetrate, and realize them.

"A trainee" (*sekha*) refers to one who trains in these three trainings—the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom—at the stage of the path of stream-entry.

Beginning from the stream-entry path up to the path of arahantship, the sevenfold trainee (sekha) will range over, investigate, discern, penetrate, and realize this earth—designated as this personal existence (attabhāva)—drawing away from it desire and lust by means of the path of arahantship.
And the world of Yama: both that world of Yama described in the manner mentioned above and this world of humans.
Together with the devas, he will investigate, examine, discern, penetrate, and realize the world with its devas.
"The trainee" (sekha) refers to the sevenfold trainee;
just as a skilled garland-maker, having entered a flower garden, avoids flowers that are still buds, those pierced by insects, those already withered, and those that have formed knots.
"Just as one selects beautiful flowers that are well-grown and of excellent quality, even so he will cook,
sift, examine, penetrate, and realize this well-spoken and well-explained path of the factors conducive to enlightenment through wisdom.
Thus the Teacher himself answered the question.

At the conclusion of the teaching, five hundred monks attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). The discourse on the Dhamma was also beneficial for the assembled multitude.
This is the first story: the account of the five hundred monks intent on talk about the earth.
2. The Story of the Elder Who Used the Mirage as a Meditation Subject (Marīcikammaṭṭhānika Thera).
The Teacher, while residing at Sāvatthī, delivered this teaching on the simile of the bubble concerning a certain monk who practiced the meditation subject of the mirage.
It is said that after receiving his meditation subject from the Teacher, that monk entered the forest with the intention, "I shall perform the duties of a recluse.
Although he strove and exerted himself, he was unable to attain Arahantship; thus, he [sought] a more distinguished meditation subject.
Thinking, "I shall relate this story," as he was approaching the presence of the Teacher, he saw a mirage on the road.

Reflecting on the meditation subject of the mirage, he thought: "Just as this mirage that arises in the summer season appears like a solid form to those standing at a distance, yet does not appear at all to those coming near, so too is this personal existence (attabhāva) of such a nature in terms of its arising and passing away. Thus he cultivated the meditation subject of the mirage.
Having arrived, weary from the road, he bathed in the Aciravatī River and sat in the shade of a tree on the bank of its fierce current.
Seeing large masses of foam rising up due to the force of the water and then breaking apart, he took hold of the object of meditation, thinking:
"This personal existence (*attabhāva*) is also just like this in the sense of arising and then breaking apart. Meanwhile, the Teacher was in the Fragrant Chamber (*gandhakuṭi*).
Standing right there, he saw the elder and said, “In this very way, monk, such a personal existence as this is like a mass of foam, like a mirage;
its very nature is to arise and perish,” and having said this, he spoke this verse:
“Having understood this body to be like a mass of foam, ...”
Fully awakening to the Dhamma of the mirage,
having cut off Māra’s flowering arrows,
one shall go beyond the sight of the King of Death.

In this context, "like a mass of foam" means that one has understood this body—consisting of the collection of head-hairs and so forth—to be similar to a lump of foam in its lack of strength, its weakness, its non-enduring nature, and its temporariness.

"Of the nature of a mirage" means that just as a mirage appears to those standing at a distance as if it were a form to be grasped and as if it were substantial, yet for those approaching it closely, it turns out to be empty, hollow, and ungraspable; [so too is this body].
In the same way, one who fully awakens to, realizes, and knows that "this body too is of the nature of a mirage" in the sense of appearing momentarily—

this is the meaning. Having severed with the Noble Path the threefold round of existence (vaṭṭa) known as Māra’s “blossoming flowers,” the bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed reaches a state beyond the sight and range of the King of Death.
"May I go to the deathless, the great Nibbāna!

At the conclusion of the verse, the elder attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Praising and extolling the Teacher’s gold-colored body, he approached while paying homage.
This is the second story, concerning the Elder who took the mirage as his meditation subject (marīcikammaṭṭhānika).
3. The Story of Viṭaṭūbha:
“Picking flowers indeed,” the Teacher gave this Dhamma teaching while dwelling at Sāvatthī concerning Viṭaṭūbha, who had been killed after being overwhelmed by a great flood along with his retinue.
Herein is the sequential account: for in Sāvatthī there was a son of the Great King of Kosala named Prince Pasenadi.
In Vesālī there was a Licchavi prince named Mahāli, son of the Licchavi king; and in Kusinārā there was a Malla prince named Bandhula, son of the Malla king.
These three went to Takkasilā to study the arts under a world-renowned teacher.
Having met in a hall outside the city, they asked one another the reason for their coming, their lineage, and their names.
Having become companions, they approached their teacher together and trained in the craft;
before long, having mastered the craft, they took leave of the teacher and departed together for their respective homes.
Among them, Prince Pasenadi, having demonstrated his father’s craft, was consecrated to the kingship by his father, who was well-pleased. Prince Mahāli [demonstrated] the craft of the Licchavis.
He showed it with great enthusiasm, and as a result, his eyes burst out and fell away.
The Licchavi kings thought, "Alas! Our teacher has met with the destruction of his eyes; we shall not abandon him, but shall attend upon him.
They gave him a gate that required a hundred thousand coins to open. Relying on that, he [taught] five hundred sons of the Licchavi kings.
While he was training in his craft, he became proficient. Prince Bandhula took sixty-six bamboo poles, inserted an iron rod through their centers, and stood them up in bundles of sixty.
When told by the Malla royal clans, "Cut these down," he leapt eighty cubits into the air and went along cutting them with a sword. At the final bundle, [he struck] against the iron rod...
Hearing the sound “kirī,” he asked, “What is this?
Upon learning that iron pins had been placed in all the bundles, he cast away his sword and, weeping, thought:
“Among all these kinsmen and friends, not even one has shown affection by telling me the reason for this. Had I known, I would have cut [the bundle] myself without making a sound with the iron pin.”
Having said this, he told his parents, "He will kill all of us and rule the kingdom.
They tried to dissuade him in various ways, saying, "My son, this is hereditary sovereignty; you must not do such a thing.
But he replied, "In that case, we shall go to my friend," and departed for Sāvatthī.
King Pasenadi of Kosala, having heard of his arrival, went out to meet him and, after ushering him into the city with great honor, appointed him to the position of commander-in-chief.
He summoned his parents and settled there to live.
Then one day, while standing on the upper terrace of the palace looking down at the street, the king saw Anāthapiṇḍika and Cūḷa-Anāthapiṇḍika...
Having seen many thousands of monks going daily to the houses of Visākhā and Suppavāsā for the purpose of their regular meal,
[the people] asked, "Venerable sirs, where are you going? and were told, "Your Majesty,
two thousand monks go every day to the house of Anāthapiṇḍika for the sake of the regular meals, the ticket-meals, the sick-meals, and so forth."

When it was said, "There are five hundred [meals] in the house of Cūḷa-Anāthapiṇḍika, and likewise for Visākhā and likewise for Suppavāsā," he himself, desiring to attend upon the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, went to the monastery and invited the Teacher together with a thousand bhikkhus.
Having personally given alms for seven days, on the seventh day, after paying homage to the Teacher, he said: "Bhante,..."
“Accept alms from me regularly, together with my five hundred bhikkhus,” he said.
“Great King, those called Buddhas do not accept alms regularly from a single place; many people look forward to the arrival of the Buddhas.
“In that case, then, send one bhikkhu regularly,” he said. The Teacher placed the responsibility upon the Venerable Ānanda.
When the Saṅgha of bhikkhus had arrived, the king took the bowl and, without even considering, "Let these [bhikkhus] partake," he himself partook for seven days.
On the eighth day, with a distracted mind, he became negligent.
Indeed, in a royal household, those who have not been commanded are not permitted to prepare seats, have the bhikkhus sit down, and serve them, thinking, "We are not allowed to remain here."
"We shall be able," they said, and many bhikkhus departed. On the second day as well, the king was negligent, and on that second day too, many bhikkhus departed.
On the third day he was negligent again; at that time, with the exception of the Elder Ānanda alone, all the others departed.
Those who possess merit are indeed subject to external conditions, yet they preserve the confidence of the families [who support them].
For the Tathāgata, there were two chief disciples, the Elder Sāriputta and the Elder Mahāmoggallāna;
two chief female disciples, Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā; among laymen, two chief laymen, the householder Citta and Hatthaka Āḷavaka;
and among laywomen, two chief laywomen, Veḷukaṇṭhakī Nandamātā and Khujjuttarā—beginning with these eight persons...
All the disciples who had attained their respective positions were of great merit and possessed of noble resolve (*abhinīhāra*), owing to their partial fulfillment of the ten perfections (*pāramī*).
The Elder Ānanda also, having fulfilled the perfections for a hundred thousand eons, was possessed of noble resolve and great merit;
yet, out of consideration for his family, he remained steadfast in maintaining their faith. They seated him alone and served him.
When the king returned after the monks had departed and saw the hard and soft foods left exactly as they were, he asked, “Venerable sirs, did you not come?
Hearing that “Only the Elder Ānanda came, Your Majesty,” he thought, “Surely they have caused me this much loss of food.
Becoming angry with the monks, he went into the presence of the Teacher and said, “Bhante, by me—”
“Alms have been prepared for five hundred bhikkhus,” he said, “but it is said that the Elder Ānanda has gone to the Ekakova;
the prepared alms remain exactly as they were, and the five hundred bhikkhus did not give notice in my house—what could be the reason for this?
The Teacher, without speaking of the fault of the bhikkhus, said, “Great King, regarding my disciples by you...”
"There is no mutual trust; therefore, they will not go [to such families]," he said.
Then, addressing the bhikkhus and explaining both the reasons for not visiting families and the reasons for visiting them, he spoke this sutta:
"Bhikkhus, a family endowed with nine factors is unfit to be visited, or even if visited, [is not fit for offerings]."
Or they are not fit to sit near him. By which nine [ways]? They do not rise up for him in a pleasing manner; they do not pay homage to him in a pleasing manner;
they do not offer him a seat in a pleasing manner; they conceal his presence; though there is much, they give little;
though it is excellent, they give coarse things; they give without respect, not with respect; they do not sit near him to listen to the Dhamma; they do not [respect] what has been spoken to him.

They do not wish to listen. Monks, a family endowed with these nine qualities is not fit to be approached if it has not been approached already, nor is it fit to be sat down near if it has been approached.
"Monks, a family endowed with nine qualities is fit to be approached if it has not been approached already, and once approached..."
Or it is sufficient for sitting down. By which nine? They rise up with agreeable courtesy; they pay homage with agreeable courtesy;
they offer a seat with agreeable courtesy; they do not conceal their presence from him; they give much even when they have little; they give choice things even when they have only choice things;
they give respectfully, not disrespectfully; they sit down to listen to the Dhamma; they [listen to] what he has spoken...
"They wish to listen. Possessed of these nine qualities, monks, it is fitting to approach a family that has not yet been approached, and once approached, it is fitting to sit near them.
Thus, Great King, my disciples did not fail to go to you because they could not obtain your confidence.
"For even the ancient wise men, though served with great care while they were in a state of non-trust, went only to a state of trust when they encountered death-pain.
When asked by the king, "When was that, venerable sir?", he related a past event:
"In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, a king named Kesava abandoned his kingdom and went forth as an ascetic."
He went forth into homelessness. Five hundred men followed him into the religious life. He became known as the ascetic Kesavatāpasa.
His barber, however, having also gone forth, became his pupil named Kappaka.
After the ascetic Kesavatāpasa had lived with his retinue for eight months in the Himalayas, he arrived at Bārāṇasī during the rainy season in order to partake of salt and sour gruel.
He entered for alms. Then the king, seeing him and being inspired with faith, obtained his promise to dwell in his presence for four months.
Having settled him in the royal park, the king himself went to attend upon him morning and evening.
The remaining ascetics, after staying for a few days, became distressed and agitated by the sounds of elephants and other noises; they said, "Teacher, we are weary."
“We are going,” they said. “Where to, dear ones? “To the Himalayas, Teacher.
“The king took a promise from us on the very day we arrived that we would stay here for four months.
How will you go, dear ones? “You gave us your promise without telling us; we cannot remain here. Not far from here—”
“We shall dwell in the place where you hear news of our progress. Having paid homage, they departed.
The teacher remained behind with Kappa’s pupil.
When the king came for his audience, he asked, “Where are the masters? “We have all grown weary,” they replied, and [they went] to the Himalayas.
"He has gone, Great King," he said. Not long after, the barber also became weary; though repeatedly forbidden by his teacher, he said, "I am unable," and departed.
However, instead of going to the others, he stayed in a place not far away, listening to news of his teacher's condition.
Later on, as the teacher was reflecting upon his disciples, a stomach ailment arose.
It arose. The king had it treated by physicians, but the disease did not subside. The ascetic said, “Great King, do you wish for my disease to be cured?
“Venerable sir, if I were able, I would make you well this very moment.
“Great King, if you wish for me to be well, send me to the presence of my pupils. The king said, “Very well.”
Saying, "Venerable sir," he had him laid upon a couch and dispatched four ministers, headed by the minister Nārada, with the instruction:
"Having learned of my noble master's condition, please send me word.
When the teacher Kappanta heard that his preceptor was approaching, he went out to meet him; when asked by the others, "Where is he?", he replied, "He is reportedly staying at such-and-such a place."
He said: "Having heard that their teacher was arriving, they too gathered together at that very spot;
having given the teacher warm water, they offered him various fruits. At that very moment, his illness subsided. Within just a few days, he became golden-colored.
Then Nārada asked him:"
“Having abandoned the lordship over men, who possess all the success of their desires,
how indeed does the Blessed One Kesī delight in the hermitage of Kappa?
There are sweet and delightful places, and there are charming groves.”
“O Nārada, these well-spoken words of yours delight me for an eon:
‘I eat fine rice, pure and served with meat;
how can you cover yourself with that saltless millet and wild grain?’”
“Whether it be delicious or not delicious, whether it be little or much;
wherever one may eat with confidence, confidence is the supreme flavor.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher, identifying the Jātaka, said: “At that time, King Moggallāna was [the king].”

Having said, "Nārada was Sāriputta, Ānanda was his attendant for many eons, Kesava was an ascetic, and I myself [was the king]," he added, "Thus, Great King, even in the past, the wise, upon encountering terminal sensations, went to those who were trustworthy.
I think that my disciples do not find trust with you. The king, together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus...
"I ought to place my trust in him; how indeed shall I do so? It would be right for the Perfectly Enlightened One to take his own kinswoman’s daughter into my household.

If this were to happen, thinking, 'The young novices and the Perfectly Enlightened One’s kinsman-king are here,' they will come to me constantly with confidence. Having thought thus, he said, "Give me one of your daughters."
He sent a message to the Sākiyas. Having asked, "Whose daughter is she among the Sākiyas?
and having said, "Having ascertained this, you should come," he commanded the messengers. The messengers went and requested the maiden from the Sākiyas.
They assembled and said, "The king belongs to another clan; if we do not give her to him, he will destroy us. Furthermore, there is no one equal to us in lineage."
"What indeed should be done? they deliberated. Mahānāma said, "I have a daughter named Vāsabhakhattiyā, born from the womb of my slave-woman, who has attained the pinnacle of physical beauty;
let us give her [to him]. Having said this, he spoke to the messengers: "Very well, we shall give our daughter to the King. [The messengers asked: "Whose daughter is she? [Mahānāma replied:
"She is the daughter of Mahānāma, the son of the paternal uncle of the Sammasambuddha."
“She is the daughter of Sakka, named Vāsabhakhattiyā.
They went and informed the king. The king said, “If that is so, very well; bring her quickly.
Kshatriyas are full of guile and might even send a daughter of a slave-girl; you must bring one who eats from the same vessel as her father.”
He sent [her]. Having gone there, they said, "Your Majesty, the king wishes for her to eat together with you.
Mahānāma replied, "Very well, dear ones," and after having her adorned, he had her summoned at his own mealtime;
showing her how to sit and eat together with him, he handed her over to the messengers. They took her and went to Sāvatthī, and...
They reported the event to the king. With a joyful heart, the king made her the senior among those five hundred women and consecrated her to the position of chief queen (*aggamahesī*).
Before long, she gave birth to a son of golden complexion.
Then, on the day of the child’s naming ceremony, the king sent him to his grandfather, saying: "The daughter of the Śākya king..."
“Vāsabhakhattiyā has given birth to a son; what name shall we give him?
Now, the minister who had gone to receive that message was somewhat deaf; having arrived, he reported it to the King’s grandfather.
Upon hearing this, he said, “Even before Vāsabhakhattiyā gave birth to her son, she surpassed all people; but now, moreover, for the King...”
She will become beloved,” he said. Having heard the word “beloved” indistinctly because he was deaf, the minister thought it was “Viṭaṭūbha.
Approaching the king, he said, “Your Majesty, you should give the prince the name ‘Viṭaṭūbha.
The king, thinking, “This will be an ancient name belonging to our lineage,” gave him that name.
While he was still in his childhood, the king, thinking, "I shall do what is pleasing to the Teacher," gave him the position of commander-in-chief.

As he grew up with the privileges of a prince, at the age of seven, seeing other princes having elephant figures, horse figures, and so forth brought from their maternal grandfathers' families, he asked his mother:
"Mother, presents are being brought from the maternal grandfathers' families for the others."
“Why has no one sent anything to me? Are you perhaps my mother or my father?
Then she deceived him, saying, “Dear son, your maternal uncles, the Śākya kings, live far away; that is why they send nothing to you.
When he was sixteen years old, he said, “Mother, I wish to see your maternal family,” to which she replied, “Enough, dear son; what is the use of going there?”
Even though he was being restrained with the words, "He will do it," he begged again and again. Then his mother consented, saying, "In that case, go.
Having informed his father, he set out with a great retinue.
Vāsabhakhattiyā had previously sent a letter, saying, "I am living happily here; let no one show any opposition to him on the part of his master. The Sākiyas—
Knowing that Viṭaṭūbha was approaching, they thought, "We are unable to go and pay him homage," and so they sent their youngest princes to the countryside.
When he arrived at Kapilavatthu, they assembled in the assembly hall. The prince went there and stood before them.
Then, saying, "This, dear son, is your maternal grandfather; this is your maternal uncle," they made him pay them homage. He paid homage to them all.
Having searched, and seeing not even a single person paying him homage, he asked, "Why is there no one to pay me homage?
The Śākyas replied, "Dear son, those younger princes have gone to the countryside," and they performed a great honor for him.
After staying for a few days, he departed with a large retinue. Then, in the assembly hall, a female slave—
Having reviled and reproached the seat with the words, "This is the seat of the son of Vāsabhakhattiya’s slave-girl," he washed it with milk and water.
A certain man, having returned after forgetting his own weapon, heard Prince Viṭaṭūbha’s sound of reviling;
upon asking the reason for it, [he learned that] Vāsabhakhattiya—
Having learned that Mahānāma Sakka had been born from the womb of a slave-girl, he informed his army.
A great clamor arose: "It seems Vāsabhakhattiyā is but the daughter of a slave! Hearing this, Viṭaṭūbha said, "Let them first wash the seat upon which I sit with milk-water;
but when I am established in the kingdom, I shall take the blood from their throats for my own..."
"I shall wash the seat where he sat," she resolved. When he had departed for Sāvatthī, the ministers reported this matter to the king.

The king, becoming angry with the Sākiyas for having given him his slave-girl, revoked the privileges granted to Vāsabhakhattiyā and her son, and ordered that they receive only what is due to slaves and slave-girls.
Then, after a few days had passed, the Teacher went to the royal palace and sat down on the prepared seat.
The king approached, paid homage, and said, "Venerable Sir, it seems your kinsmen have given me a daughter of a slave as a wife;
therefore, I have not withheld her maintenance for herself and her son, but have provided only what is due to a slave and a slave-girl. The Teacher said, "This was improper."
"Great King, this was established by the Sakyans: when giving, one should give to those of the same caste. Yet, Great King, I say this:
Vāsabhakhattiyā was the daughter of a Khattiya king and received her consecration in the house of a Khattiya king.
Vitatūba, too, was born from a lineage of Khattiya kings. What can a mother’s clan do? Only the father’s clan is authoritative."
"An ancient wise man gave the position of chief queen to a poor wood-gatherer woman;
the prince born from her womb, having obtained the sovereignty over Bārāṇasī, which was twelve yojanas in extent, became known as King Kaṭṭhavāhana," he said, and related the Kaṭṭhahāri Jātaka.
Having heard this discourse on Dhamma, the king thought, "Indeed, it is the father's lineage alone that is the standard."
Having smiled, he had the customary provisions provided for Vāsabhakhattiyā and her son.
Now, Bandhula the general’s wife, Mallikā—the daughter of the Malla kings from Kusinārā—had not borne a son for a long time.
Then Bandhula sent her away, saying, “Go back to your own family home. She...
Thinking, “I shall go only after seeing the Teacher,” she entered Jetavana, paid homage to the Tathāgata, and stood there.
When asked, “Where are you going? she replied, “Venerable Sir, my husband is sending me back to my family home. “For what reason? “It is said that I am barren and childless.
“If that is so, there is no need for you to go; please turn back. With a joyful heart, she did so.
Having paid homage to the Teacher and gone to her residence, she was asked, "Why have you turned back? Bandhula replied, "I was turned back by the One Possessed of the Ten Powers.
She accepted this, thinking, "The reason must have been seen by the One of Long Vision. Before long, she conceived a child;
when a pregnancy craving arose and she suffered from burning heat, she announced, "A craving has arisen in me. He asked, "What is the craving?"
“Master, I have descended into the consecration festival lotus-pool of the oligarchic clans in the city of Vesālī; having bathed, I wish to drink some water.

Bandhula said, “Very well,” and taking his thousand-fold-strength bow, he placed her upon the chariot, departed from Sāvatthī, and drove the chariot toward Vesālī by the gate granted to Mahāli the Licchavi.
He entered. Now, the residence of Mahāli the Licchavi was located right near the gate.
Hearing the sound of the chariot striking the threshold, he said, "This is the sound of Bandhula’s chariot; today fear will arise among the Licchavis.
Both inside and outside the lotus pond there was strong protection, and an iron net was spread over it, so that even for birds—
"There is no opportunity. But General Bandhula, alighting from his chariot, drove away the guard soldiers by striking them with a whip;
he cut through the iron net, bathed his wife in the middle of the lotus pond, and having bathed himself as well, he placed her back on the chariot.
Then, departing from the city, he set out by the very same path by which he had come. Those guard soldiers—
They informed the Licchavi kings. The Licchavi kings, becoming enraged, mounted five hundred chariots and set out, saying, "We shall seize Bandhula Malla.
They reported this occurrence to Mahāli. Mahāli said, "Do not go; for he will surely defeat you all.
But they replied, "We shall certainly go. [Mahāli said: "In that case..."
"Having seen the place where the rim of that chariot wheel has entered the earth up to its hub, you should turn back.
If you do not turn back from there, you will hear a sound like a thunderbolt ahead; you should turn back from that spot.
If you do not turn back from there, you will see a hole in the yokes of your chariots; you should turn back from that spot; do not go further forward."
Following his words, they did not turn back but continued to pursue him. Seeing them, Mallikā said, "My lord, the chariots are becoming visible.
"In that case," he replied, "inform me when only a single chariot becomes visible.
When all the chariots appeared as one, she then said, "My lord, only the front of a single chariot is now visible."
Bandhula said, "In that case, take these reins," and having given her the reins, he strung his bow while still standing on the chariot;
the wheel of the chariot sank into the earth up to its hub.
Even when the Licchavis saw that sight, they did not turn back. After traveling a short distance, the other [Bandhula] struck the bowstring, and it sounded like a clap of thunder.
It was as if they were being struck by lightning. Yet they did not turn back from there; they continued on, pursuing him. While still standing in his chariot, Bandhula discharged a single arrow;

it pierced through the front of the five hundred chariots, passed right through the neck-straps of the five hundred kings, and entered the earth. They, unaware that they had been pierced, [continued on].
“Stop, you! Stop, you! they cried, pursuing him. Bandhula stopped his chariot and said, “You are dead men;
there is no fighting for me with those who are dead. “We are not like those who are dead,” they replied.
“In that case, let the last one among you remove his armor. They removed it. As soon as it was removed—

Having spoken thus, he died and fell [into hell]. Then they all said, "In such a state as this, you should go to your own homes, make the necessary arrangements, instruct your wives and children, and then take off your armor.
Having done so, they all met their end. Bandhula also brought Mallikā to Sāvatthī; she gave birth to twins sixteen times.
She gave birth to twin sons. All of them were brave and endowed with great strength; they attained mastery in all arts and crafts.
Each had a retinue of one thousand men. As they went to the royal palace together with their father, the royal courtyard was completely filled by them alone.
Then one day, when some people who had lost their legal case through fraud saw Bandhula approaching, they raised a great outcry and informed the judges of the fraudulent judgment he had rendered.
He went to the court, investigated the matter, and restored the rightful owner to his property.
The great multitude broke into a loud clamor, offering shouts of "Well done! and applause.
The king asked, "What is this? and having heard the matter, he was pleased. He dismissed all those ministers and entrusted the administration of justice to Bandhula alone.
From that time forth, he administered justice correctly.
Consequently, those former ministers who had administered justice received no bribes and, being deprived of their income, spread the word in the royal court that "Bandhula aspires to the kingship."
They caused [the border] to be destroyed. The king, believing their words, was unable to restrain his mind.

Thinking again, "If he is slain right here, reproach will arise for me," he had the border attacked by his appointed men, summoned Bandhula, and said, "The border, it is said, has risen in revolt; go with your sons and—"

Having sent [messengers] with the command, "Seize his heart," he dispatched other capable great warriors along with them, saying, "Right here, cut off his head together with his thirty-two sons and bring it back.
Even as he was proceeding toward the frontier, the bandits who had been mobilized fled upon hearing, "The commander-in-chief is coming! He settled that region, established order there, and returned.
Then, not far from the city, those warriors cut off the heads of her sons along with [her husband].
On that very day, Mallikā had invited the two chief disciples together with five hundred bhikkhus.
Then, in the forenoon itself, they brought a letter to her and gave it, saying, "The head of your husband has been cut off along with your sons. She [read] it...
Knowing their conduct, she said nothing to anyone; instead, placing a leaf in her lap, she served the community of monks alone.
Then, as her attendants brought a vessel of ghee after giving the monks their meal, they broke the vessel of ghee in front of the elders.
The Dhammasenāpati said, "That which is subject to breaking has broken; there is no need for concern."
Taking the letter out from her lap, she said, “They brought this letter to me saying that my head would be cut off along with thirty-two sons;
even having heard this, I do not worry. What should I worry about, Venerable Sir, when a ghee-pot has been broken?
Then the Dhammasenāpati recited such verses as: “The life of mortals here is signless and unknown.”
Having spoken thus and taught the Dhamma, he rose from his seat and went to the monastery. She too, having summoned her thirty-two daughters-in-law, exhorted them:
"Your husbands were innocent; they received the fruit of their own past kamma.
Do not grieve, do not lament, and do not harbor malice toward the king."
Having heard those words, the king’s scouts went and reported their innocence to the king.
The king, overcome with a sense of urgency, went to her residence, asked Mallikā and her daughters-in-law for forgiveness, and granted Mallikā a boon.
She said, "Let the boon be considered as already accepted by me," and when he had departed, she gave a meal for the dead, bathed, and—
Having approached the king and paid homage to him, she said, "Your Majesty, you granted me a boon;
I have no other need than this: please grant permission for my thirty-two daughters-in-law and myself to go to our own homes.
The king consented. She sent her thirty-two daughters-in-law to their respective families, and she herself [proceeded] to the city of Kusinārā.
He went to his own family home.
The king, moreover, gave the position of commander-in-chief to Dīgha Kārāyaṇa, the nephew of the general Bandhula.
But he, thinking, "My maternal uncle was killed by this man," wandered about seeking an opportunity to harm the king. The king, for his part, [was aware that] he was innocent...
From the time Bandhula was killed, he became remorseful and could find no peace of mind; he did not enjoy the pleasures of sovereignty.
At that time, the Teacher was dwelling near the town of Medāḷupa belonging to the Sakyans.
The king went there, pitched his camp not far from the monastery, and with a small retinue approached the Teacher.
Thinking, “I shall pay homage,” he went to the monastery and, having given the five royal insignia to Dīghakārāyaṇa, entered the Perfumed Chamber all alone.
Everything should be explained according to the method in the *Dhammacetiya Sutta*.
When he had entered the Perfumed Chamber, Dīghakārāyaṇa took those five royal insignia and [went to] King Viṭaṭūbha.
Having left behind one horse for the king and one female attendant for the queen, he turned back and went to Sāvatthī.
After the king had exchanged friendly greetings with the Teacher and paid homage to him, he departed;
not seeing the army, he questioned that woman and, having heard what had happened, said, "I shall go and bring my nephew, Viṭaṭūbha..."
Thinking, "I shall take [it]," he set out for the city of Rājagaha; but when the gates were closed at the improper hour and he had reached the city, he lay down in a certain hall.
Exhausted by the wind and heat, he passed away right there during the night.
When the night had turned to dawn, the King heard the sound of that woman lamenting, "O Lord, the King of Kosala has become destitute! and [he went to her].
They informed him. He performed the funeral rites for his maternal uncle with great honor.
Viṭaṭūba, having obtained the kingdom, recalled that enmity and set out with a great army, thinking, "I will kill all the Sākiyas.
On that day, at dawn, the Teacher surveyed the world and perceived the destruction of his kinsmen.

Having seen this, he thought, "It is fitting to provide for my kinsmen. Then, having walked for alms during the morning and returned from his almsround, he lay down in the lion’s posture within the fragrant chamber.

In the evening, traveling through the air, he sat at the foot of a tree with dense shade on the outskirts of Kapilavatthu. Beyond that was a great, thickly shaded grove within the royal boundaries of Viṭaṭūbha.

There was a banyan tree. Having seen the Teacher, Viṭaṭūbha approached him, paid homage, and said, “Venerable sir, for what reason do you sit here at this time of intense heat at the foot of this tree with scanty shade?
Venerable sir, please sit at the foot of this banyan tree with abundant shade. [The Teacher replied], “Very well, Great King; the shade of one’s kinsmen is indeed cool.”
When this was said, he thought, "The Teacher must have come for the sake of protecting his kinsmen," and having paid homage to the Teacher, he turned back and returned to Sāvatthī itself.
The Teacher, too, having risen up, went straight to Jetavana.
The king, remembering the offense of the Sākiyas, set out once more; and having seen the Teacher there in the same manner, he again—
He turned back. On the third occasion as well, he went out, and seeing the Teacher in the same manner, he turned back again.

But on the fourth occasion, when he had gone out, the Teacher, having surveyed the past karma of the Sākiyas and knowing that the evil deed of their having thrown poison into a river on a single day was irremediable, did not come on the fourth occasion. Viṭaṭūbha...
Thinking, “I shall have the Sākiyas killed,” he set out with a great military force. Now, the kinsmen of the Sammasambuddha were known as the Asattaghātakas;
even though they themselves were facing death, they would not deprive others of life. They thought:
“We are well-trained, skilled, experienced, and great archers, yet it is not possible for us [to kill another].”
“Let us take his life; having shown him our own prowess, we shall drive him away. Having thus prepared themselves, they went forth and began the battle.
The arrows discharged by them passed through the gaps between the men of Viṭaṭūbha, emerging from the spaces between shields, the ears of armor, and other such openings.
Seeing this, Viṭaṭūbha said, “Is it not so, my men? “It is so, sir,” they replied. “The Sakyans...”
“They say, ‘We do not kill those who are not present,’ and yet they are banishing my men.
Then one man said to him, “Master, why have you turned back and looked? “The Sakyans are banishing my men.
“Not one of your men is dead. Come now, let them count them. As he was counting them, not even one—

He did not see their destruction. Turning back from there, he said: "O men, kill everyone who says 'We are Sākyans,' but grant life to those standing in the presence of Mahānāma the Sakyan, my maternal grandfather.
Not seeing anyone to seize, some of the Sākyans stood biting grass, while others stood holding reeds.
When asked, "Are you Sakyans, or not? since they would not speak a falsehood even while facing death, those who stood biting a blade of grass said, "We are not Sakyans;
it is grass. Those who stood holding a reed said, "We are not Sakyans; it is a reed.
And those who stood in the presence of Mahanama regained their lives. Among them, those who had been biting the grass...
Those who remained were called the Tiṇasākiyā; those who remained standing holding reeds were born as the Naḷasākiyā.
Viṭaṭūbha, refusing to release even the remaining infants who had been suckled at their mothers' breasts, had them executed and caused a river of blood to flow, with which he had a plank washed.
Thus was the Sākiya lineage cut off by Viṭaṭūbha.
Having thus caused Mahānāma the Sakyan to take hold [of him], he turned back, thinking, "I shall eat my morning meal at the time for the morning meal.
Having disembarked at a certain spot, when food was brought forward, he summoned his grandfather, saying, "We shall eat together.
However, even when giving up their lives, Kṣatriyas do not eat with the sons of slave-girls. Therefore, Mahānāma [went] to a certain lake...
Having observed him, he said, "I am covered in filth; I shall bathe, dear ones. "Very well, grandfather, bathe," they replied.
He thought, "This man will have me killed while I am eating alone; it is better that I die by my own hand.
So, loosening his hair and tying a knot at the top, he thrust his big toe into his hair and submerged himself in the water. By the power of his virtue—
The Nāga palace appeared hot. The Nāga king, wondering "What is this?
and having discerned the cause, approached him, seated him upon his own hood, and led him into the Nāga palace.
He dwelt right there for twelve years. Viṭaṭūba also thought, "My grandfather will come now; he will come now."
He sat down waiting. When he had waited for a very long time, he had the lake searched and even looked within the enclosures by the light of lamps;
not seeing anyone, he departed, thinking, "He must have gone. In the middle of the night, having reached the Aciravatī River, he encamped his army.
Some lay down on the sandy banks within the river, and some on the dry ground outside; among those who had lain down inside...
There were those who had not previously committed evil deeds, and there were also those who had previously committed evil deeds;
as they lay down, ants arose at their respective places. Those who had not committed evil deeds, thinking, "Ants are at my place! Ants are at my place!
climbed up and lay down on dry land, while those who had committed evil deeds descended and [lay down] in the sandy dunes.
They lay down. At that moment, a great cloud arose and rained down a heavy deluge.
A flood from the river came surging in and carried Viṭaṭūbha, along with his retinue, right into the ocean. There, they all became food for fish and turtles.
The great multitude raised a cry: "The death of the Sākiyas is unworthy; having thus crushed them again and again..."

"It is not fitting to say, 'The Sākiyans must be killed'. Having heard those words, the Teacher said, "Monks, although such a death for the Sākiyans in this present life is indeed improper, it is entirely appropriate that they have received it as a result of evil karma performed in the past.
[The monks asked: "But what, venerable sir, did they do in the past? [The Teacher replied: "All together—"
"Having offered it as a sacrifice, they threw the poison into the river. On another day, the monks raised a discussion in the Hall of Truth:

"After killing so many Śākyas, Viṭaṭūba was returning; before his own desires had even reached their fulfillment, he took such a great multitude with him and became food for fish and turtles in the great ocean. The Teacher, having arrived, asked: "What [discussion is this]?"
Having asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you sitting together now?

and being told, "For this very one," he said, "Before the heart's desires of these beings have even reached their peak, the King of Death severs the life-faculty—like a great flood sweeping over a sleeping village—and causes them to sink into the four oceans of the states of misery. Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“While a man is plucking flowers, his mind distracted, death seizes him and carries him away, as a great flood sweeps away a sleeping village.
In this context, “a man whose mind is distracted” means one whose mind is attached, whether to what has already arrived or what has not yet arrived. This is what is meant.

It is like this: just as a garland-maker, having entered a flower garden with the thought, "I shall gather flowers," might direct his mind toward the entire garden while gathering flowers from here and there, or he might not take flowers from that [specific spot] but direct his mind elsewhere; it is just like that.

While walking and gathering [fruit], one falls into negligence; in the same way, a certain person, having entered the midst of the five strands of sensual pleasure which are like a flower garden and having obtained a delightful form, yearns for one or another of the delightful sounds, smells, tastes, or tangibles.
Or, having obtained one of those, he yearns for another; or, having obtained a form itself—

Not desiring anything else, he relishes that very thing, or one among sounds and so forth. This same method applies to cows, buffaloes, female and male slaves, fields, lands, villages, market towns, provinces, and so on;
and for those who have gone forth, it applies to their cells, monasteries, bowls, robes, and so on.
Thus, while a man is plucking flowers known as the five strands of sensual pleasure—his mind distracted by sensual qualities whether they have been attained or not—he is like a sleeping village.

However, there is no such thing as "sleeping" in the case of a village or the walls of houses by way of actually falling asleep; rather, one is said to be "asleep" only with reference to the state of beings being drowsy and heedless.
In this way, death carries away the sleeping village—extending for two or three leagues—as if it were a great flood.
Just as that great flood leaves nothing remaining among women, men, cattle, buffaloes, chickens, and so forth, [so does death carry all away].

"Just as one who brings that entire village to the ocean makes it food for fish and turtles, even so, Death seizes the man whose mind is distracted, cuts off his life-faculty, and causes him to sink into the four oceans of the states of misery.
At the conclusion of this teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages. The teaching thus became beneficial to the great multitude.
The Story of Viṭaṭūbha, the Third.
4. The Story of the Maiden Patipūjikā.
The Teacher, while residing at Sāvatthī, gave this Dhamma teaching concerning a maiden named Patipūjikā. The story originated in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
It is said that there, a son of the gods named Mālabhārī entered a pleasure grove accompanied by a thousand celestial nymphs (accharā).
Five hundred celestial nymphs climbed a tree and plucked flowers; five hundred others took the fallen flowers and adorned the son of the gods.
Among them, one celestial nymph fell right from a branch of the tree, her body [falling like] the flame of a lamp.
...extinguished as if by fire. Having taken rebirth in a certain noble family in Sāvatthī, she was possessed of the recollection of her past lives (*jātissara*) at birth;

remembering, "I am the wife of the deva-son Mālabhārī," she performed worship with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings as she grew up, and prayed for rebirth in the presence of her husband. When she reached the age of sixteen, she went to another family's home...
Even when she had gone, she would give tickets for meals, fortnightly meals, and the rains-retreat meals, saying, "May this be a condition for my rebirth in the presence of my husband.
Then the bhikkhus gave her the name "Patipūjikā" (the Worshipper), saying, "This young woman, rising up again and again, prays only for him. She, too, constantly attended to the sitting-hall.
She prepared drinking water and arranged seats.
Other people, wishing to give offerings such as tickets for meals (*salākabhatta*), would bring them and say, "Mother, you should present these to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Following this routine, as she came and went, she attained fifty-six wholesome qualities (*kusaladhamma*) with every single step. For her—
A fetus was established in her womb. After the lapse of ten months, she gave birth to a son.
At the time when that son was able to walk, she obtained four more sons one after another.
One day, having given alms, performed worship, heard the Dhamma, and observed the precepts, at the close of the day—
At that very moment, having died from a certain illness that arose, she was reborn in the presence of her own husband.
The other woman, meanwhile, had been adorning the young god for all this time. Seeing her, the young god said, "You have not been seen since early morning;
where have you gone? "I have passed away, my lord," she replied. "What are you saying? "It is even so."
“Yes, Master. “Where were you reborn? “In a noble family in Sāvatthī. “How long did you remain there?
“After ten months had passed, I emerged from my mother’s womb;
at the age of sixteen, I went to another family, gave birth to four sons, performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms, and having made a wish for you, I came here into your very presence.”
“I have been reborn, Master. “How long is the lifespan of human beings? “About a hundred years, Master.

“Is it only that much? “Yes, Master. “Having received such a lifespan, do those reborn humans pass away while intoxicated by sleep and negligence, or do they perform meritorious deeds such as giving? “What can we say, Master? It is incalculable.”
"Human beings are constantly heedless, as if they had been born with a lifespan of a hundred years and were free from old age and death.
A great sense of spiritual urgency arose in the young deva Mālabhārī: "It is said that humans, having been born with a lifespan of only a hundred years, are heedless and lie down to sleep;
when indeed will they be freed from suffering? Now, a hundred years of human beings is [but a single day] for the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
One day and night of the devas consists of thirty such nights making a month;

twelve such months make a year. By that reckoning, the lifespan of the devas is one thousand celestial years, which by human calculation amounts to three hundred and sixty million years. Therefore, even a single day for that son of the devas—
The time was not yet past; it was as if it were but a single moment. Thus, for people of such short lifespans, negligence is indeed most improper.

On the following day, when the monks entered the village and saw that the rest-house had not been cleaned, the seats had not been prepared, and drinking water had not been set out, they asked, "Where is the attendant? [They replied: "Venerable sirs, where have you been?"
"You will see her; she died this afternoon, after the venerable ones had eaten yesterday and departed.

Upon hearing this, the ordinary monks (*puthujjana*), mindful of her kindness, were unable to restrain their tears. A sense of spiritual urgency (*dhammasaṃvega*) arose in those whose taints were destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).
Having finished their meal and gone to the monastery, they paid homage to the Teacher and asked: "Venerable sir,..."
“The laywoman named Patipūjikā, having risen again and again and performed various kinds of meritorious deeds, made a wish for her husband alone.
She has now died; where has she been reborn? “In the very presence of her own husband, monks.
“But, Bhante, there is no husband present here. “Monks, it was not that she wished for this husband,” he said.
“In the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, her husband was a deva named Mālabhārī;
having passed away from that place where she had been adorning herself with flowers, she went back and was reborn once again in his very presence. “Is it truly so, Bhante? “Yes, bhikkhus.
“Oh, Bhante, how fragile is the life of beings! Having served us in the morning, by evening she has been struck down by disease.”
“...so it is considered. The Teacher said, “Yes, monks, the life of beings is indeed short;

for that very reason, while these beings are still unsated with both sensual pleasures of the objects (*vatthukāma*) and sensual pleasures of the defilements (*kilesakāma*), the Ender (*antaka*), having brought them under his own power, takes them away as they weep and lament,” and having said this, he spoke this verse:
“While one is still plucking flowers, with a mind distracted,
and while one is still unsated with sensual pleasures, the End-maker brings one under his power. Therein,
“while plucking flowers” means just as a garland-maker in a flower garden [gathers] various flowers, so too [one gathers] those things bound to one’s own personal existence.
And while he was still plucking the flowers of the strands of sensual pleasure—which are bound up with requisites—he had a mind distracted by various modes of attachment:
by way of longing for what has not been attained, and by way of greed for what has been attained; thus, his mind was attached.

"Still unsatisfied with sensual pleasures" means: with respect to both objective sensual pleasures (*vatthukāma*) and defilement-sensual pleasures (*kilesakāma*), [he was unsatisfied] by way of seeking, by way of acquisition, and by way of enjoyment.

Even with his hoard, he remains truly unsatisfied. "The End makes him subject" means that Death, known as the reckoning of mortality, seizes him as he wails and laments while he is still living, and taking him away, brings him under its own power.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages; thus the teaching became beneficial for the great multitude.
The Fourth Story of the Maiden Who Honored [Her Parents].
5. The Story of the Stingy Merchant Kosika.
The Teacher, while residing at Sāvatthī, related this Dhamma teaching concerning the stingy merchant Kosika. The background of that story originated in Rājagaha.
It is said that not far from the city of Rājagaha there was a market town named Sakkara.
There lived a merchant named Macchariyakosiya, whose wealth amounted to eight hundred million [pieces].

He would not give even a drop of oil on the tip of a blade of grass to others, nor did he enjoy it himself. Thus, his entire accumulation of wealth went neither to his children and wife, nor to recluses and brahmins.
He experiences misfortune and remains unusable, like a lotus pond possessed by a rākṣasa. One day, at dawn,
the Teacher arose from the attainment of great compassion and, surveying those to be enlightened throughout the entire world-system,
[beheld] the merchant and his wife living forty-five yojanas away, who were destined for the fruit of stream-entry.

He perceived the decisive support (*upanissaya*). On the previous day, however, having gone to the royal palace to attend upon the king and returning after having performed his service, he saw a hungry countryman eating a bowl full of sour gruel and cakes.
Seeing this, a longing arose within him; he went to his own home and thought: "If I..."

"I shall say, 'I wish to eat a *kapallaka* cake'; many people will then desire to eat with me, and thus my large quantities of sesame, rice, ghee, molasses, and so forth will be exhausted. I will not tell anyone.
Thus, suppressing his craving, he goes about his way. As time passes, he becomes increasingly pale and thin, his body covered with a network of veins.
Having been born, he was unable to endure his craving; he entered the womb and lay down, hugging the bedstead.
Even though he had come to such a state, out of fear of losing his wealth, he said nothing to anyone.
Then his wife approached him, massaged his back, and asked, "What is it, my lord, that has caused you discomfort?"
He asked, "Is there anything that makes you unwell? "I have nothing that is unwell," he replied. "Then has the king become angry with you? "The king is not angry with me either.
"Then has your sons, daughters, or your slaves, laborers, and so forth, done anything unpleasant to you?
"There is nothing of that sort either. "But do you have any craving for anything? Even when this was said, out of fear of losing his wealth...
Without saying anything, he lay down in silence. Then his wife said to him, "Speak, master; do you have any desire for something?
As if swallowing back his words, he replied, "I have a desire.
"What is it you desire, master? "I wish to eat a *kapallaka* cake. "Then why did you not tell me? Are you poor?"
"Now I shall bake enough *kapallakapūva* cakes for all the inhabitants of the entire city. "What use have you for these?
They will eat them after doing their own work. "In that case, I shall bake enough for the inhabitants of one street.
"I know your great wealth. "I shall bake enough for everyone by making it near this house."
“I know that you have great intentions. “In that case, I will cook enough for just you and your wife and children.
“What need have you for them? “But what about enough for both you and me?
“What will you do with it? “In that case, I will cook enough for you alone. “In this regard...”

"When rice is being cooked, many people wait for their portions. Therefore, having set aside all the whole grains of rice, taking the broken grains and the potsherds from the hearth, and bringing a small amount of milk, ghee, honey, and molasses, I shall ascend to the uppermost floor of the seven-storied palace and cook it there;
I will sit there alone and eat it. She consented, saying, "Very well."
Having had what was to be taken collected and having ascended the palace, he dismissed the female slaves and summoned the merchant.
Starting from the bottom, the merchant closed the doors, fitted needle-hinges at all the doorways, ascended to the seventh floor, and having closed that door as well, sat down.
His wife also lit a fire on the hearth and placed a cauldron upon it.
He began to bake the cakes.
Then, early in the morning, the Teacher addressed the Elder Mahāmoggallāna:
"Moggallāna, in a village called Sakkāra, not far from Rājagaha, there is a miserly merchant who, thinking 'I shall eat cakes from a pan,' out of fear of others seeing him,"

"In the seven-storied palace, he is having cake-pies baked; go there, subdue the merchant, and making him harmless, have both husband and wife take the cakes, milk, ghee, honey, and molasses, and bring them to Jetavana by your own power.
Today I shall sit right here in the monastery with five hundred bhikkhus, [eating] only the cakes."
"I shall perform the meal-offering.
The Elder, having accepted the Teacher's word with "Very well, venerable sir," went at that very moment by the power of his psychic potency to that town;
and at the door of the lion-window of that palace, well-robed and well-clad, he stood in mid-air like a figure made of jewels.
stood there as if paralyzed. As soon as the Great Merchant saw the Elder, the flesh of his heart quivered.
He thought, "It was out of fear of seeing just such a person that I came to this place, yet here is this monk having come through the air and standing at the window.
Seeing no way to seize him, he began to sputter with rage like salt-crystals thrown into a fire.
He said this: “Ascetic, even if you stand in the air, what will you gain? Even if you walk back and forth, displaying footprints in the trackless sky, you will gain nothing at all.
At that very spot, the Elder walked to and fro. The merchant said, “Even if you walk, what will you gain?
Even if you sit cross-legged in the air, you will gain nothing at all. The Elder sat cross-legged...
He sat down with his legs crossed. Then [the king] said to him, "What will you gain by sitting in the air?
Even if you come and stand on the threshold of the window, you will gain nothing. The Elder stood on the threshold. [The king] said, "What will you gain even by standing on the threshold?
Even if you emit smoke, you will gain nothing indeed. The Elder also emitted smoke, and the entire palace became filled with smoke.
It was like the moment a merchant’s eyes are pierced by a needle;
yet, out of fear that his house might burn down, he did not say, "Even if you were to set yourself ablaze, you would not get him," but rather said to his wife, "This ascetic is very persistent;
he will not leave until he has obtained something. I will have him given a single cake. He said to her, "My dear, bake one small cake and give it to the ascetic."
“Give it to him and send him away. She put only a small amount of flour into a shallow bowl;
however, it turned into a large cake that filled the entire bowl and stood there puffed up.
Seeing this, the merchant thought, “You must have taken a great deal of flour,” and he himself, with the tip of his finger—
Taking a small amount of flour, he threw it in; the cake became larger than the previous one. In this way, whatever he baked, each one became increasingly large.
Becoming weary, he said to his wife, "My dear, give me one of these cakes.
As she was taking one from the stack, they all stuck together in a single mass. She—
He said to the merchant, "Master, all the cakes are stuck together; I am unable to separate them.
"I will do it," he replied, but he too was unable to do so. Both men, though they pulled at them from opposite ends, were simply unable to separate them.
Then, even as he continued to struggle with the cakes, sweat broke out from his body and his thirst was quenched.
Then he said to his wife, "My dear, I have no need for the cakes; give them to him along with the basket.

She took the basket, approached the Elder, and gave it to him. The Elder taught the Dhamma to both of them, spoke of the virtues of the Three Jewels, and [proclaimed] the fruit of giving gifts and so forth, saying, "There is what is given, there is what is sacrificed," as if [the fruit] were in the vault of the sky.
He appeared like the full moon.
Upon hearing this, the merchant, with a mind full of faith, said, "Venerable sir, please come, sit upon this couch, and partake.
The Elder replied, "Great merchant, the Sammasambuddha has sent me with five hundred bhikkhus, saying, 'We shall eat cakes.'"
“Sitting here together in this monastery, if it pleases you, I shall take you there;
have the merchant’s wife prepare cakes, milk, and other provisions, and we will go into the presence of the Teacher,” he said. “But where, venerable sir, is the Teacher at present?
“Mahāseṭṭhi, he is at the Jetavana Monastery, about forty-five yojanas from here.”
“Venerable sir, how shall we travel such a distance without exceeding the appointed time?
“Great merchant, if it pleases you, I will carry you by the power of my own psychic potency.
The top of the staircase in your palace shall remain in its original place, but the bottom of the staircase shall appear at the gateway of the Jeta Grove.”
“I shall lead you to Jetavana at the very moment you descend from the upper palace to the lower palace. He replied, “Very well, venerable sir.
The Elder fixed the top of the staircase right there and resolved, “Let the base of the staircase be at the gatehouse of Jetavana.
And so it was. Thus, from the moment the Elder had the merchant and the merchant’s wife descend from the upper palace to the lower palace—
He brought them to Jetavana very quickly. Both of them approached the Teacher and announced that it was time.
The Teacher entered the refectory and sat down upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared for him, together with the community of monks.
The great merchant offered the water of donation to the community of monks headed by the Buddha. His wife likewise [offered it] to the Tathāgata.

He placed the cake upon the bowl. The Teacher took only as much as was necessary for his own sustenance, and the five hundred bhikkhus likewise took only as much as was necessary for their sustenance.
Even as the merchant continued to give milk, ghee, honey, sugar, and other provisions, they did not come to an end.
The Teacher, together with the five hundred bhikkhus, completed the meal; the great merchant, along with his wife, [served] as much as they required.
They ate. Yet no end to the cakes could be seen; even after giving them to all the monks and the scavengers throughout the entire monastery, no limit could still be discerned.
They reported to the Blessed One, “Venerable Sir, the cakes do not reach exhaustion.
“Then throw them away at the gateway of the Jeta Grove,” he said. Then, not far from the gateway—
They discarded it on a mountain slope. Even to this day, that place is known as Kapallakapūvapabbhāra (the Slope of the Cake Pans).
The great merchant, together with his wife, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and stood to one side. The Blessed One gave a discourse of thanksgiving.
At the conclusion of the thanksgiving, both of them were established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), and having paid homage to the Teacher, they departed.
Having ascended the staircase at the city gate, they established themselves right there upon their own palace.
From that time forth, the merchant distributed eighty koṭis of wealth solely for the Buddha’s dispensation.
On the following day, in the evening, the monks seated in the Dhamma Hall said, “Behold, friends, the majestic power of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna!”
"Without harming his faith, and without harming his wealth, he subdued the merchant Macchariya in a mere moment, making him free from stinginess;
having had him take cakes and bring him to Jetavana, he established him in the fruit of stream-entry in the very presence of the Teacher—oh, how great is the power of this Elder!
Thus they sat, praising the virtues of the Elder. The Teacher, with his divine ear-element...
Having heard this and come [to the assembly], he asked, "Monks, about what topic have you been sitting together here now?
When they replied, "About this very one," he said, "Monks, it was as if a bee, without harming the faith,
without harming the wealth, and without wearying or vexing the family, were to take pollen from a flower."
Having approached as if [in a dream], he made known the Buddha’s qualities, saying, "My son Moggallāna was just like that," and after praising the Elder,
he spoke this verse: "Just as a bee,
without harming the color or fragrance of a flower,..."
“Taking its nectar, it departs; thus should a sage wander in the village.

In this context, “bee” refers to any species of honey-bee. “Flowers”: the meaning is that while wandering in a flower garden, it moves about without harming or destroying the flowers, their color, or their fragrance.
“It departs”: having wandered in this manner, it goes away as much as it requires.
Having drunk the sap, he takes more for the purpose of making honey and departs;
having thus entered deep into the forest thicket, he places that sap mixed with dust in a hollow of a tree and gradually turns it into sweet honey.
Because of his wandering through the flower gardens, neither the flower nor its color and fragrance are lost to him.

Then everything returns to its normal state. "Thus a sage should wander in the village" means that the sage who is neither a trainee nor one beyond training wanders through the village from house to house collecting almsfood.
For because of his wandering in the village, there is no decline in the faith or the wealth of the families; both their faith and their wealth remain as they were before. Thus...
Having walked for alms and departed, the monk-seeker then spreads his outer robe in a place with convenient water outside the village and sits down.
After consuming the almsfood while reflecting upon it by way of similes such as the axle-pin, the wound-covering,
and the child’s flesh, he enters a suitable forest thicket and applies himself to the internal meditation subject.
By comprehending the four paths, he brings the four fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala) directly into his own hands.

The Asekha-muni, moreover, devotes himself to dwelling in happiness in this very life (diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra). This is how his similarity to a honey-bee in the production of honey should be understood.
However, here it is specifically the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) who is intended.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
Having delivered this Dhamma instruction, the Teacher further elucidated the Elder’s virtues, saying:
"Monks, it was not only now that Moggallāna subdued the merchant Macchariya; in the past as well, having subdued him, he established his connection with the fruits of kamma."
Having said, "He made himself known thus," and in order to clarify this matter, he brought up the past, saying:
"Both were lame, both were crooked, both had squinting eyes;
pustules had grown on both of them, yet I did not recognize Illisa."
He related this Illisa-jātaka.
This is the fifth story, concerning the merchant Macchariya-Kosiya. 6.
The Story of the Ājīvaka from Pāveyya.
"Against the wishes of others"—the Teacher related this teaching on the Dhamma while residing at Sāvatthī concerning an Ājīvaka named Pāveyya.
It seems that in Sāvatthī, a certain housewife, having adopted an Ājīvaka named Pāveyya as a son, looked after him.
When people in the houses adjacent to hers heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, they came back and said, "Oh, how wonderful are the Buddhas!"

They praised the Buddha’s qualities in various ways, saying, “This is the teaching of the Dhamma. Having heard this discourse on the Buddha’s qualities, she went to the monastery desiring to hear the Dhamma.
She explained the matter to the Ājīvaka, saying, “Noble sir, I shall go into the presence of the Buddha. He tried to dissuade her, saying, “Do not go,” even though she entreated him again and again.
She stopped him. She thought, "He will not allow me to go to my monastery to hear the Dhamma; I shall invite the Teacher and listen to the Dhamma right here.
In the evening, she summoned her son and sent him, saying, "Go, dear, and invite the Teacher for tomorrow's meal.
As he was going, he first arrived at the dwelling place of an Ājīvaka.
Having gone there and paid homage to him, he sat down. Then the other asked him, "Where are you going? He replied, "I am going to invite the Teacher at my mother’s request.
[The other] said, "Do not go into his presence. "Enough, sir; I fear my mother, so I shall go," he said.
"We both shall eat the hospitality prepared for him; do not go," [the other] said.
“Enough, noble sir; my mother will scold me. “In that case, go;
but having invited her, do not tell her, ‘You must come to our house by such-and-such a place, or by such-and-such an alley, or by such-and-such a road.
Rather, standing nearby as if you were waiting, run away as if going by another path and then return. He [did as] the Ājīvaka had said.
Having heard this, he went into the presence of the Teacher, invited him, and performed everything according to the procedure prescribed by the Ājīvaka.
Then, having gone back to the Ājīvaka, when asked, "What have you done?", he replied, "Everything has been done, venerable sir.
[The Ājīvaka said], "Well done by you; we both shall eat that offering tomorrow. On the following day, at dawn, the Ājīvaka—
He went to the house. Having taken him, they had him seated in the inner chamber.

The neighbors, having smeared that house with fresh cow dung and scattered flowers with parched grain as the fifth ingredient, prepared a magnificent seat for the Teacher to sit upon. [There were] people who were not acquainted with the Buddhas.
For they do not know the arrangement of seats, and for the Buddhas, who are the teachers of the path, there is no further task to be done;
indeed, on the very day they attained full enlightenment after shaking the ten-thousandfold world-system at the foot of the Bodhi tree, [they knew]:
"This path leads to hell, this to the animal realm, this to the sphere of hungry ghosts, this to the human world, and this to the deva world."
"This is the great Nibbāna of the Deathless"—thus all the paths became manifest. However, there was no need to speak of the roads leading to villages, market towns, and so forth.
Therefore, early in the morning, the Teacher took his bowl and robe and went to the door of the Great Female Lay Disciple’s house.
She came out from the house, paid homage to the Teacher with the five-point prostration, led him into her residence, and having had him sit upon a seat, [she served him].
Having offered water for the guest-offering, she served him with excellent hard and soft food.

When the Teacher had finished his meal, the female lay follower, wishing to have him give a blessing of thanksgiving, took up his bowl. The Teacher began a discourse on the Dhamma as a blessing with a sweet voice.
The female lay follower listened to the Dhamma, applauding it and saying, "Excellent! Excellent! Even the Ājīvaka was in the rear of the hall.
While sitting there, he gave his approval to her as she listened to the Dhamma; however, upon hearing her voice, he was unable to restrain himself.

Thinking, "She is no longer mine," he went out and fled, reviling the laywoman and the Teacher in various ways, crying out, "You are ruined, you ill-omened woman! You show such honor to this man! The laywoman was ashamed by his words.
Her mind having become distracted, she was unable to direct her knowledge according to the teaching.
Then the Teacher asked her, "Upāsikā, why are you unable to bring your mind to follow the teaching? She replied, "Venerable Sir, my mind has become distracted by this talk.
The Teacher said, "How indeed can one speak to such a person who is of a different disposition?"
"It is not proper to pry into others' affairs; rather, without such preoccupation, it is proper to examine only what one has done and left undone oneself.
Having said this, he spoke this verse:
"One should not look at the faults of others, nor at what others have done or left undone."
“One should examine one’s own deeds, both those done and those left undone.
In this context, “not [the faults] of others” means that the contrary, harsh, and heart-piercing words of others should not be taken to heart.
Nor should one concern oneself with what others have done or left undone, such as thinking, “That certain lay follower is faithless and lacks confidence, nor does he…”
In his house, offerings such as ladlefuls of alms-food are given, but not ticket-meals and the like, nor is there any gift of requisites such as robes for him;
