likewise, such-and-such a female lay follower is faithless and lacks confidence, and in her house, offerings such as ladlefuls of alms-food are not given, nor ticket-meals and the like, nor is there any gift of requisites such as robes for her; likewise, such-and-such a monk is faithless.

"He has no faith; he does not perform the duties toward his preceptor, nor those toward his teacher, nor the duties for newcomers, nor for those departing, nor the duties regarding the shrine courtyard, nor the duties in the Uposatha hall, nor the duties in the dining hall, nor the duties in the sauna and so forth;
he possesses none of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), nor even the slightest effort toward delighting in meditation"—thus [he speaks] of others.
"One should not look at what has been done or left undone.

Regarding "one should examine oneself," this refers to the instruction that a son of good family who has gone forth out of faith should frequently reflect: "How are my days and nights passing? Recalling this advice, he should consider:
"Do I [apply] the three characteristics—'impermanent, suffering, non-self'—"
"Having applied myself to the practice, was I able to perform the work or not?"—in this way, one should examine what has been done and what remains to be done by oneself.
At the conclusion of the teaching, that female lay follower was established in the fruit of stream-entry, and the teaching became beneficial for the great multitude.
This is the sixth story, concerning the Ājīvaka of Pāveyyaka.
7. The Story of the Lay Disciple Chattapāṇi "Just as beautiful flowers bloom"—this teaching on the Dhamma was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Sāvatthī concerning the lay disciple Chattapāṇi.
For in Sāvatthī there was a lay disciple named Chattapāṇi, a master of the Tipiṭaka and a Non-returner (anāgāmī). He would observe the Uposatha from early morning onwards.

Having offered the sacrifice, he went to attend upon the Teacher. For noble disciples who are non-returners (anāgāmin), there is no such thing as a formal observance of the Uposatha by way of undertaking precepts;
rather, both their holy life (brahmacariya) and their practice of eating only one meal a day have come to them through the Path itself. Therefore it was said:
"Great King, Ghaṭīkāra the potter eats but one meal a day, lives the holy life, is virtuous, and possesses wholesome qualities. Thus it is for non-returners.
By their very nature, they were those who ate only one meal a day and lived the life of celibacy.

He too, having likewise observed the Uposatha, approached the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down to listen to the discourse on the Dhamma. At that time, King Pasenadi of Kosala came to attend upon the Teacher.
Seeing him approaching with the royal parasol in hand, the lay follower Chattapāṇi thought, "One must rise..."
Having reflected, "Should I or should I not? he thought: "I am sitting in the presence of the Supreme King;
it is not fitting for me to rise upon seeing these local kings. Yet the King will be angry with me if I do not rise. Even if he is angry, I shall not rise.
For when one rises upon seeing the King, the King is honored, but not the Teacher. Therefore..."
“I will not rise,” he said, and so he did not rise. Wise men indeed do not become angry when they see someone remaining seated in their presence without rising.
But the king, seeing that he did not rise, became displeased in mind;
having paid homage to the Teacher, he sat down to one side. The Teacher, perceiving his state of anger, said: “Great King, this Chattapāṇi...”
He spoke of the lay follower’s virtues, saying, “This lay follower is wise, has seen the Truth, is a bearer of the Three Piṭakas, and is skilled in discerning what is beneficial and what is harmful.
As the king listened to this account of his virtues, his heart became softened.
Then one day, while the king was standing on the upper terrace of the palace holding his parasol, he saw the lay follower Chattapāṇi returning with his parasol after having finished his meal.
Seeing him walking through the royal courtyard having mounted his sandals, he summoned him.
He removed his parasol and sandals, approached the king, paid homage, and stood to one side.
Then the king said to him, "O lay follower, why have you removed your parasol and sandals? "Hearing that 'the king summons me,' I removed them and came," he replied.
“Today our royal status must have become known to you,” [the king said]. “O Lord, we have always known your royal status,” [the minister replied].
“If that is so, why did you not rise when you saw me yesterday while sitting in the presence of the Teacher?
“Great King, I was sitting in the presence of the Supreme King; it is only upon seeing a local king that one rises.”
“I would display disrespect toward the Teacher; therefore, I did not rise. “Let it be, sir; let this matter rest.
“It is said that you are experts in what is beneficial and harmful for both the present life and the future, and as holders of the Three Piṭakas, you should recite the Dhamma in our inner palace.
“I cannot, Your Majesty. “For what reason? “The royal palace is a place of great reproach.”
“O gods, among these, those associated with the two [senses] and those associated with the two [objects] are the most serious. “Do not speak thus.
Do not feel remorse by thinking, ‘I did not rise when I saw you on the previous day. “Your Majesty, the place where householders roam is indeed very blameworthy.
Summon one renunciant and have him recite the Dhamma. The king said, “Very well, sirs; go now.”
Having sent him away, he went into the presence of the Teacher and made this request of the Teacher: "Venerable Sir, Queen Mallikā and Vāsabhakhattiyā say, 'We shall master the Dhamma.
Please go to my house regularly with five hundred bhikkhus and recite the Dhamma to them.
[The Teacher replied: "It is not the custom for Buddhas to go to one place regularly."
“There is not, Great King. “In that case, venerable sir, give another single bhikkhu,” he said. The Teacher placed the burden upon the Elder Ānanda.
The Elder went regularly and recited the lesson to them. Among them, Mallikā grasped it respectfully, rehearsed it, and mastered the lesson.
But Vāsabhakhattiyā did not grasp it respectfully at all.
She did not recite [the texts] herself, nor was she able to have them taught to her.
Then one day, the Teacher asked the Elder: “Ānanda, is the laywoman mastering the Dhamma?
“Yes, venerable sir. “Which one grasps it with diligence? “Mallikā, venerable sir, grasps it with diligence; she grasps it with diligence...”
“He recites them and is able to receive the formal instruction with due care.
But your own niece neither grasps them with care, nor recites them, nor is she able to receive the formal instruction.
Having heard the elder’s words, the Teacher said, “Ānanda, my Dhamma is indeed for one who listens with care and grasps it; it is not for one who does not listen with care and does not grasp it.”
"Without reciting it or teaching it, it is fruitless like a flower that possesses color but lacks fragrance;
however, for one who listens to it with due care and so forth, it becomes of great fruit and great benefit," he said, and then spoke these two verses:
"Just as a beautiful flower, though possessing color, is without fragrance..."
“Thus well-spoken words are fruitless for one who does not act upon them.
Just as a beautiful flower, though colorful and fragrant,
is so too are well-spoken words fruitful for one who acts upon them.”

In this context, *rucira* means beautiful. *Vaṇṇavanta* means endowed with color and shape; *agandha* means devoid of fragrance, such as the various kinds of *pālibhaddaka*, *girikaṇṇika*, *jayasumana*, and so forth.
Thus, "well-spoken speech" refers to the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Pitakas.
That is endowed with color and shape, yet it is like a flower that lacks fragrance. Just as...
Just as a scentless flower does not diffuse fragrance upon the body of one who wears it, so too this [Dhamma] does not bring forth the fragrance of what has been heard,

the fragrance of speech, or the fragrance of practice for one who does not respectfully attend to it through hearing and so forth— that is, for one who does not respectfully practice it and fails to perform what is to be done therein.
It becomes fruitless. Therefore it was said: “Well-spoken speech is fruitless for one who does not act.
“Possessing fragrance” means consisting of various kinds such as the *campaka* and blue lotus.

“In this way” means that just as the fragrance spreads from the body of one who wears that flower, so too does well-spoken speech—namely, the word of the Buddha comprised of the Three Piṭakas. “For one who acts” refers to one who listens with due care and so forth.

In that regard, he performs what ought to be done; for that person, it becomes fruitful, bringing the fragrance of learning, the fragrance of the scent, and the fragrance of practice—thus the meaning is that it is of great fruit and great benefit.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruits of stream-entry and the other stages. The teaching thus became meaningful for the great multitude.
The seventh story is that of the lay follower Chattapāṇi. 8.
The Story of Visākhā:

The Teacher, while residing at the Eastern Monastery near Sāvatthī, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning the lay follower Visākhā, beginning with the words: "Just as when one gathers a heap of flowers..."
It is said that she was reborn in the city of Bhaddiya in the Aṅga country as the daughter of the merchant Meṇḍaka and the chief queen,
Sumanādevī, of the merchant Dhanañjaya. When she was seven years old, the Teacher,

seeing the perfection of the supporting conditions (*upanissaya*) in her relatives who were to be awakened— such as the Brahmin Sela and others— set out on a journey accompanied by a great community of monks.
While traveling, he reached that city.
At that time, the householder Meṇḍaka was acting as the head merchant in that city, being the eldest among the five who possessed great merit.
These five of great merit were: the merchant Meṇḍaka, Candapadumā...
His eldest wife was [the mother of] him; his eldest son was named Dhanañjaya; his wife was named Sumanadevī;
and Meṇḍaka the merchant’s slave was named Puṇṇa. And it was not only Meṇḍaka the merchant who possessed such wealth;
rather, in the realm of King Bimbisāra, there were five others known as the Five of Immeasurable Wealth: Jotika, Jaṭila, Meṇḍaka, Puṇṇaka, and Kākavaḷi.

Among them, this merchant Meṇḍaka, having learned that the One Possessed of the Ten Powers had arrived at his own city, summoned his daughter Visākhā, the daughter of the merchant Dhanañjaya, and said: "My dear child, it is an auspicious occasion for you and an auspicious occasion for us as well;
therefore, together with five hundred young women of your retinue, prepare five hundred chariots."
“Mount [the chariot] and, surrounded by five hundred female slaves, go out to meet the One of Ten Powers. She consented, saying, “Very well,” and did so.
However, because she was skilled in discerning what was appropriate and what was inappropriate, she proceeded by carriage as far as the ground would allow for a vehicle;
then, alighting from the carriage, she approached the Teacher on foot, paid homage to him, and stood to one side.
Then, according to her temperament, the Teacher taught the Dhamma.

At the conclusion of that teaching, she, together with five hundred young women, was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The merchant Meṇḍaka also approached the Teacher, and having heard the discourse on the Dhamma, he too was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
Having invited [the Sangha] for the following day, on the next day, at his own residence, with excellent...
Having served the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, headed by the Buddha, with various kinds of solid and soft food, he gave a great almsgiving in this very manner for half a month.
The Teacher, having stayed in the city of Bhaddiya as long as he desired, departed.
Now at that time, Bimbisāra and Pasenadi of Kosala were brothers-in-law to one another.
Then one day the King of Kosala thought: "In the realm of Bimbisāra there dwell five men of immeasurable wealth and great merit, yet in my own realm there is not even one such as them.
What if I were to go into the presence of Bimbisāra and ask for one man of great merit?
Having gone there, he was received with a friendly welcome by the king, who asked: "For what reason..."
When asked, "Why have you come? he replied, "I have come thinking, 'In your kingdom there dwell five men of immeasurable wealth and great merit;
having taken one from among them, I shall depart. Give me one of them. [The king] said, "We are unable to move these great families.
He said, "I will not go unless I obtain one. The king consulted with his ministers.
“Shaking great families such as those of Jotika and others is like shaking the great earth.
There is a merchant named Dhanañjaya, the son of the great treasurer Meṇḍaka; after consulting with him, I shall give you my reply.
Having said this, he summoned him and said, “Dear one, the King of Kosala intends to go, saying, ‘I will take a single wealthy merchant along.’”
“He says: ‘Go with him. [The other replied: ‘I shall go, Your Majesty, when you have sent me. [The king said:
‘In that case, dear son, go after making a formal agreement. He did what was appropriate for himself to do.
The king also, having paid him great honor, dispatched him to King Pasenadi, saying: ‘Take this man and go. He took him—”
Taking [only his essentials] and traveling with the practice of staying only one night at every place, he reached a comfortable location and took up residence there.
Then the merchant Dhanañjaya asked him: "Whose domain is this? "Mine, merchant," he replied.
"How far is Sāvatthī from here? "It is at a distance of seven yojanas. "The city is crowded; our retinue..."
"Great sir, if it pleases you, let us dwell right here, O King.

The king, accepting with "Very well," had a city built in that place and gave it to him, and then departed. Because he himself had taken up residence in that region, the city came to be known by the name Sāketa.
In Sāvatthī, too, there was a son of the merchant Migāra named Puṇṇavaḍḍhana Kumāra who had reached maturity.
Then his parents said to him: "Dear son, find a maiden who pleases you.
"I have no need for such a wife," he replied. "Son, do not speak thus; a family that has no son..."
“He does not stay. Being told this again and again, he said, “In that case, if I can obtain a girl endowed with five auspicious qualities, I will do as you say.
“But what, dear father, are these so-called five auspicious qualities? “The excellence of hair, the excellence of flesh, the excellence of bone, the excellence of skin, and the excellence of age.”
For in a woman of great merit, when her hair is released and let loose, it becomes like a peacock’s tail-feather;
having struck the edge of her lower garment, it turns back and stands upright—this is called the excellence of hair (*kesakalyāṇa*).
Her lip-covering is like the *bimba* fruit, endowed with color, even, and well-polished—this is called the excellence of flesh (*maṃsakalyāṇa*). Her teeth are white, even, and without gaps.
They shine like rows of diamonds set upright or like rows of conch shells cut perfectly even; this is called "beauty of the bones.
Even when not smeared with black ointment and the like, the color of the skin remains glossy, resembling a wreath of blue lotuses;
and when white, it resembles a wreath of *kaṇikāra* flowers; this is called "beauty of the skin. Even one who has given birth ten times...
Furthermore, she was as if having given birth only once, remaining as though her youth had not yet departed; this is what is called "excellence in age.

Then her parents invited one hundred and eight brahmins, fed them, and asked, "Are there indeed women who possess the five excellences? "Yes, there are," they replied. "In that case, we must seek such a maiden."
"Let eight men go," he said, giving them much wealth and dispatching them, saying: "We shall know what must be done when you have returned;
go, seek out such a maiden as this, and when you have found her, give her this gold necklace worth a hundred thousand.
Having given him the gold necklace, they sent him forth.
Having traveled through those very great cities and searched for her, they returned without having seen a girl endowed with the five auspicious marks.
On the day of the *vivaṭa* constellation, as they were approaching Sāketa, they thought, "Today our task will be accomplished.
For in that city, the *vivaṭa* constellation occurs once every year.
It is called [the festival]. On that day, even families who do not usually go outside come out of their houses with their retinues and go to the riverbank on foot with their bodies uncovered.
On that day, even the sons of wealthy kṣatriyas and others think, "Having seen a pleasing girl from a family of our own kind, we shall encircle her with a garland," and so they [go].
They stood waiting by that path. Those brahmins, for their part, entered a certain *sāla* tree on the riverbank and stood there.

At that moment, Visākhā—having reached the age of fifteen or sixteen, adorned with all her ornaments and surrounded by five hundred young women—arrived at that spot, intending to go to the river to bathe; then a cloud...
Having risen, it began to rain. Five hundred maidens hurried away and entered the hall.
The brahmins, looking about, did not see even one among them who was endowed with the five auspicious marks. Then Visākhā entered the hall by her usual way;
her clothes and ornaments became wet. When the brahmins saw that she possessed four of the auspicious marks, they [examined] her teeth...
Desiring to see her, they said to one another, "Our daughter is of such a lazy nature; I imagine her husband will not even receive a mere ladle of sour gruel.
Then Visākhā asked them, "Whom are you talking about? "We are talking about her, mother," they replied.
For her voice issued forth as sweet as the sound of a bronze gong. Then she spoke to them again:
With a sweet voice, he asked, "For what reason do you say this?
They replied, "Your female attendants entered the sal grove quickly after their clothes and ornaments had become soaked;
yet you have not even the speed of coming to such a place, and you arrived with your clothes and ornaments already drenched. Therefore we speak thus, mother."
“Dear father, do not speak thus; I am stronger than they, but it was because I perceived a certain reason that I did not come by way of speed.
“What is it, mother? “Father, there are four types of people who do not shine when running, and there is yet another reason as well.
“Which are the four types of people who do not shine when running, mother? “Father, first of all, a consecrated king adorned with all his ornaments [does not shine].”
Having tied up one's loincloth and running about in the royal courtyard does not look well; people will only meet with reproach, thinking, "Why is this king running about like a householder?
He looks well only as he walks slowly. Even a king’s auspicious elephant, though adorned, does not look well when running;
it looks well only as it moves with the graceful gait of a tusker. Likewise, a renunciant does not look well when running.
“Why is this ascetic running like a householder?”—thus he receives nothing but reproach;
however, by walking with measured pace, he shines. A woman running does not shine; she is only to be reproached, [people saying], “Why is this woman running like a man?
or “Dear ones, these four people do not shine as they run. “But what is another reason?”
“Mother? “Dear ones, parents indeed raise their daughter by fashioning her limbs and members.
For we are like merchandise for sale; they raise us for the purpose of being sent to another family.
If, while racing, you should step on the hem of your lower garment or stumble and fall to the ground, and your hand or foot should break, it would be to the loss of the family itself.”
"It would be a burden; however, my ornaments will dry after being soaked. Having considered this reason, I did not run, dear ones.
At the time of her speaking, the brahmins, seeing the excellence of her teeth, said, "We have never before seen such perfection of teeth as this."
Having given her applause and said, "Mother, this is truly worthy of you," they fastened that golden garland upon her.
Then they asked her, "From which city have you come, dear? "From Sāvatthī, mother.
"What is the name of the merchant's family? "It is the merchant named Migāra, mother. "Who is the noble son?"
“What is his name? “His name is Prince Puṇṇavaḍḍhana, mother. Thinking, “This is a family of equal birth to ours,” she consented and sent a message to her father, saying, “Please send us a chariot.

For although she had come on foot at the time of her arrival, from the moment she was adorned with the golden garland, she was no longer permitted to go in that manner, as she was now a lady of noble rank.
Some travel by means of chariots and the like; others mount ordinary vehicles, or hold a parasol or a palm-leaf over their heads.
Even when these are unavailable, they simply go along lifting the hem of their lower garment and tossing it over their shoulders.
Her father, however, sent five hundred chariots. She, together with her retinue, mounted a chariot.
She had gone. The brahmins also arrived from one direction. Then the merchant asked them, "Where have you come from?

"From Sāvatthī, Great Merchant," they replied. "What is the merchant's name? "He is named Migāra, Great Merchant. "What is his son's name? "His son is named Puṇṇavaḍḍhana Kumāra, Great Merchant. "How much wealth does he have? "Forty crores, Great Merchant."
“As for wealth, we have not even a single kākāṇika’s worth; but since the time we obtained this girl merely for her protection, what need is there for any other reason?
Thus he consented. Having shown them hospitality and had them stay for one or two days, he dismissed them.
Having gone to Sāvatthī, they announced to Migāra the merchant, "We have obtained a girl for you. "Whose daughter is it? "The daughter of the merchant Dhanañjaya.
He thought, "I have obtained a girl from a great family; it is right that she be brought here quickly," and he informed the king of his intention to go there.
The king said, "This is a great family [obtained by me] from the presence of Bimbisāra..."
“Having brought him, he has been settled in Sāketa; it is fitting to pay him honor, and I too shall come,” he said.
He replied, “Very well, Your Majesty,” and sent a message to the merchant Dhanañjaya: “When I come, the King will also come.
You must be able to provide for such a great multitude of people and the vast royal army with what is appropriate.”
“You will not be able [to do so],” he said. The other also sent back a reply, saying, “Even if ten kings come, let them come.
Then the merchant Migāra, leaving only a house-guardian behind in that very large city, took the rest of his people and went forth;
stopping at a place half a *yojana* away, he sent word, saying, “We have arrived. The merchant Dhanañjaya—
Having sent many gifts, he consulted with his daughter: "My dear, it is said that your father-in-law has arrived together with the King of Kosala.
Which house should be assigned to him? Which to the king? And which to the viceroy and the others?
The wise merchant’s daughter, whose wisdom was as sharp as a diamond-point, who had made aspirations for a hundred thousand eons and was perfected in her resolve—

Having made arrangements, saying, “Look after such-and-such a house for my father-in-law, such-and-such a house for the king, and such-and-such houses for the viceroy and others,” he summoned his slaves and laborers and said, “So many of you shall perform the duties for the king; so many, for the viceroy and others.
You yourselves must also look after the elephants, horses, and so forth; and let the grooms and others come to the auspicious festival.”
"...will experience [this]. He made this arrangement for what reason?
"Lest some should say, 'Having gone to Visākhā’s auspicious ceremony, we received nothing; while guarding the horses and so forth, we did not enjoy ourselves.
On that very day, Visākhā’s father summoned five hundred goldsmiths and said, "For my daughter, a great *mahālatā* ornament..."
"Give her a name. He then had a thousand *nikkhas* of red gold given, along with corresponding amounts of silver, gems, pearls, coral, diamonds, and so forth.
After staying for a few days, the king sent a message to the merchant Dhanañjaya: "It is not possible for the merchant to support us for long;
now let him know it is time for the girl to depart. He too [sent a reply] to the king...
He sent a message: "The rainy season has now arrived; it is not possible to travel for four months.
Whatever your army requires shall be my responsibility; when I have sent word, you may depart.
From that time on, the city of Sāketa was like a permanent festival. Beginning with the king, all [the people]...
Garlands, perfumes, garments, and other such items were prepared beforehand. Then those people thought, "The merchant is showing honor to us alone.
In this way, three months passed, yet the decoration was still not finished.
The overseers of the work came and reported to the merchant: "There is nothing else lacking, but there is a need for firewood to cook food for the labor force."
“They are not enough. “Go, dear ones; take dilapidated elephant stables and other such ruins, as well as ruined houses, in this city and cook with them.
Even as they were cooking in this manner, half a month passed by. Then again, they reported, “There is no more wood.
[The King said: “At this time it is impossible to obtain wood; there are stores of cloth in the warehouses.”
“Open them, make wicks out of thick cloth, soak them in oil-lamps, and cook the rice. They did so for half a month.
In this way, four months passed; the ornament was also finished.
In that ornament, four *nāḷis* of diamonds were used, and eleven *nāḷis* of pearls.
There were twenty-two *nāḷis* of coral and thirty-three *nāḷis* of gems. Thus, it reached completion with these and other jewels.
They performed the function of thread for the ornament that was not made of thread using silver;
when fastened upon the head, it reached down to the surface of the feet. At various points, gold beads were joined together and fashioned [into it].

There were knots; the loops were made of silver. There was one bead at the top-center, two on each of the two shoulder-blades, one at the nape of the neck, two on each of the two upper arms, two on each of the two elbows, and two on each of the two sides of the waist.
In that ornament, they fashioned a peacock; on its right wing [were] those made of red gold.
There were five hundred feathers on the right side and five hundred feathers on the left;
the beak was made of coral, the eyes were made of gems, as were the neck and the plumage; the feather shafts were made of silver, as were the legs.
Standing upon the peak of a mountain in the middle of Visākhā’s head, he appeared like a dancing peacock. [He possessed] ten thousand feather shafts.
Her voice proceeded like celestial music and like the sound of the fivefold musical ensemble.
Only those who approached her close could perceive her state of intoxication. Her adornment was worth nine crores, and a fee of one hundred thousand was given for the labor of its crafting.
"By what karmic result did she obtain this adornment? It is said that during the time of the Sammasambuddha Kassapa, she...
Having given a set of robes to twenty thousand bhikkhus, she gave only her own thread, needles, and dye.
By the result of that gift of robes, she obtained this great jeweled ornament.
For women, the gift of robes reaches its highest point in the acquisition of great jeweled ornaments; for men, it is reached through miraculous bowls and robes.

Thus, after the great merchant had performed the betrothal ceremony for his daughter over the course of four months, while giving her wedding gifts, he gave five hundred carts filled with kahāpaṇa coins; five filled with golden vessels;
five filled with silver vessels; five filled with bronze vessels; five filled with pattuṇṇa cloth, cotton cloth, and silk cloth; and [five] filled with ghee.
He gave five carts filled with sesame oil, five filled with husked rice, and five hundred carts filled with farming implements such as ploughshares and the like.
It was his thought: "In the place where my daughter has gone, let her not have to send word to the doors of others' houses saying, 'I have need of such-and-such a thing.
Therefore, he had all the necessary equipment provided. On each chariot stood women adorned with every kind of ornament.
Setting aside three hundred female attendants for each of the three [queens], he gave him five hundred chariots.
He gave him fifteen hundred female attendants with the command: “Go about washing her, feeding her, and adorning her. Then it occurred to him:
“I shall give cattle to my daughter. He commanded his men: “Go, sirs, to the gate of Cūḷavaṅga.”
"Having opened [the gate], take three drums at the three *gāvutas* and stand there;
stand on both sides in a place one *usabha* wide. Do not allow the cows to go further than that. While standing thus, you must give the signal with the drums.
They did exactly as instructed. When the cows had emerged from the pass and reached the first *gāvuta*, they gave the signal with the drums.
They made a signal; when they had gone another half-yojana, they made a signal again.
Again, when they had gone three gavutas, they made a signal with the drum and forbade further movement across the breadth.
Thus, in a place three gavutas long and one usabha wide, the cows stood rubbing against one another.
The Great Merchant thought, "These many cows are enough for my daughter; close the gate," and had the iron gate closed.
When the gate was shut, by the power of Visākhā’s merit, the powerful bulls and milch-cows leaped up again and again and emerged.
Even as the people were trying to stop them, sixty thousand powerful bulls and sixty thousand [milch-cows]...
The cows departed, and as many vigorous calves followed them, leaping up and pursuing those cows.
"By what cause did the cattle go thus? [It was] because of the gift given while repeatedly trying to stop them.
It seems that in the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, she was Saṅghadāsī, the youngest of the seven daughters of King Kiki.
Having become known by that name, while giving the gift of the five products of the cow to twenty thousand bhikkhus, he would cover the bowls of the elders, the young monks, and the novices;
even as they tried to stop him, saying, "Enough, enough," he gave it on, saying, "This is sweet, this is pleasing.
Thus, as a result of that, the cows came forth even though they were being restrained. By the merchant, for so much...
At the time the wealth was being given away, the merchant’s wife said: “You have provided everything for my daughter, but you have not provided male and female slaves as attendants;
what is the reason for this? [The husband replied: “It is so that I may know who among those coming with my daughter has affection for her and who does not.
For I will not let anyone go by the neck when they come with her; rather, I shall send them in a vehicle.”
"I shall say: 'Let those who wish to go with her go at the very moment she mounts the vehicle; let not those who do not wish to go go,'" he said.
Then, thinking, "Tomorrow my daughter will depart," he sat in his inner chamber, had his daughter sit near him, and gave her this instruction:
"My child, for one living in her husband's family, it is necessary to observe such and such conduct. This too—
The merchant Migāra, sitting in the adjacent room, heard the advice of the merchant Dhanañjaya.
That merchant also advised his daughter thus:
"Mother, while living in your father-in-law's household, you must not let the internal fire go out to the outside, nor should you let the external fire enter within."
"Alms should be given only to one who gives; it should not be given to one who does not give. It may be given to both one who gives and one who does not give.
One should sit comfortably, eat comfortably, and lie down comfortably.
One should tend the sacrificial fire and pay homage to the deities within."
Having given this tenfold advice, on the following day he assembled all the troops and,
standing in the midst of the royal army, took eight householders as sureties, saying, "If any fault should arise concerning my daughter at the place where I have gone,
you must clear her. Then, having adorned his daughter with a great array of ornaments worth nine crores, he gave her a supply of bathing powder.

Having given fifty-four crores of wealth and having had [the people] mounted upon vehicles, he caused a drum to be beaten throughout the fourteen meal-villages belonging to him in the vicinity of Sāketa—villages as numerous as Anurādhapura itself—announcing: "Let those who wish to go with my daughters depart.
Upon hearing that sound, those fourteen villages thought: "What business do we have here when our noble lady is departing? and [they set out].

Did they depart without leaving anything behind? The merchant Dhanañjaya, having paid his respects to both the king and the merchant Migāra, followed them a short distance and then sent his daughter away with them.
The merchant Migāra, traveling at the very rear seated in his carriage, saw the army and asked, "Who are these people?"
He asked, "Are the male and female slaves your daughter-in-law's servants? "How many will she support? "Beat them and drive them away;
if they do not flee, inflict punishment upon them here. But Visākhā said, "Go on, do not stop him;
might indeed makes its own food. Even when this was said, the merchant replied, "Mother, we have no..."

“We have need of these; who will support them? Having thus beaten them with clods of earth, sticks, and other weapons, and having driven them away, she took the remainder, saying, “Enough for us with this much,” and set out. Then, when Visākhā reached the gate of the city of Sāvatthī, she reflected:
“Shall I enter sitting in a covered carriage, or shall I stand in the chariot? Then to her—
She thought, “If I enter in a covered carriage, the excellence of my great and costly ornaments will not be visible.
So, standing in her chariot and displaying herself to the entire city, she entered the town.
The residents of Sāvatthī, seeing Visākhā’s splendor, remarked, “This is indeed the one named Visākhā; such prosperity as this is truly worthy of her alone.”
They said: "Thus she entered the house of the merchant with great splendor.

On the day she arrived, all the inhabitants of the city, saying, "Our merchant Dhanañjaya has performed a great honor for those who have reached his own city," sent gifts according to their means and power.
Visākhā [received] each gift as it was sent in that very city.
She caused gifts to be sent to all the various families everywhere.

Thus, saying affectionate words appropriate to each person’s age—“Give this to my mother,” “Give this to my father,” “Give this to my brother,” “Give this to my sister”—and sending these presents, she treated all the inhabitants of the city as if they were her own kinsmen. Then, for her...
Immediately after the first watch of the night, the mare gave birth to her foal.
The maidservants took up torches, went there, bathed the mare with warm water, rubbed her with oil, and returned to their own quarters.
Meanwhile, the merchant Migāra, while preparing the auspicious marriage ceremony for his son, paid no heed to the Tathāgata even though he was staying at the Dhura Monastery.
Urged by a long-standing affection established among the shaven-headed ascetics, thinking,
"I shall also pay honor to my noble masters," he one day had several hundred pots of rice gruel cooked without water,
invited five hundred naked ascetics (acelakas) into his house, and said, "Let my daughter-in-law come and pay homage to the Arahants."
He sent a message to Visākhā. Having heard the words "Arahants," that noble female disciple, who was a stream-enterer, became joyful and delighted;
she went to the place where they were eating, and looking at them, thought, "Those who are devoid of shame and fear of wrongdoing cannot be called Arahants.
Why has my father-in-law summoned me? Thus reproaching the merchant with the words, "Fie! Fie! she—her own...
She went straight to the place where she was staying. When the naked ascetics saw her, they all reviled the merchant at once, saying:
"Householder, what have you not found elsewhere that you have brought here a female disciple of the ascetic Gotama, this great black-eared one?
Drive her out of this house immediately! He replied: "It is not possible for me to [comply] merely because of their words."
Thinking, "She is the daughter of a great family; they would have her expelled," he dismissed them, saying, "Noble sirs, young women may act whether knowingly or unknowingly;
you should remain silent. Then, sitting down himself upon a magnificent seat, he consumed honeyed milk-rice without water from a golden bowl.
At that time, a certain elder monk who lived on almsfood entered that house while wandering for alms.
Visākhā, standing there fanning her father-in-law, saw him and thought, "It is improper to inform my father-in-law.
She therefore stepped aside and stood where he could see the elder. But that foolish man, even though he saw the elder, acted as if he did not see him.

He was eating with his face turned downwards, as if he were already finished. Visākhā, realizing that even though her father-in-law had seen the Elder, he had not signaled for more food, said, "Please wait, venerable sir; my father-in-law is eating stale food.
Although the Elder had consented when the Nigaṇṭhas spoke, at the very moment Visākhā said, "He is eating stale food," he withdrew his hand and said, "This milk-rice..."
"Take him out from here! Drive him out of this house! He makes me appear like one who eats filth at such an auspicious time," she said.
Now, in that residence, all the slaves and laborers belonged to Visākhā;
who would dare to seize him by hand or foot? There was not even anyone capable of speaking to him with their mouth. Visākhā—
Having heard her father-in-law’s words, she said: "Father, we do not depart on this account alone.
I was not brought here by you like a slave-girl from a water-crossing; daughters whose parents are still living do not depart for such reasons alone.
For this very reason, when my father came here, he summoned eight householders..."
“‘If any fault arises regarding my daughter, you must clear her of it,’ she said, and placed me in their hands;
summon them and have them clear me of any charge or lack thereof.
The merchant, thinking, “She speaks well,” summoned eight householders and said, “At the time of this girl’s auspicious ceremony...”
“Having sat down, he says of me as I am eating plain rice porridge from a golden bowl, ‘He is an eater of filth.
‘Accuse her of this fault and drive her out of the house,’ [he said]. ‘Is that what you say, mother?
‘I do not say so; however, when a certain alms-collecting elder stood at my father-in-law’s door, my father-in-law gave him rice porridge with little water.’”
While he was eating the honeyed milk-rice, he did not pay attention to it;

thinking, "My father-in-law does not perform merit in this present life, he merely consumes the fruit of past merit," I said, "Please pass on, venerable sir, my father-in-law is consuming what is old.
[He replied,] "What fault is there in that for me? [I said,] "Noble sir, there is no fault here."
“‘Our daughter speaks appropriately; why are you angry? [He replied:
‘Lady, let that fault be for now, but one day during the middle watch of the night, she went out from the house surrounded by female slaves. [She asked: ‘Is it really so, mother? [He said:
‘Daughter, I did not go for any other reason; however, in this house, a noble mare had given birth.’”
"It is indeed improper to sit down without even forming a perception [of the situation]," she said;

and having had a torch brought and hot water and other necessities provided, she went with her female slaves and caused the care for the mare’s delivery to be performed. "What fault is there in this for me?
[the King asked]. "Noble Sir, there is no fault here; it is our daughter who performs such an act in your house as is not even to be done by female slaves."
"Do you see any fault in this?
"Noble lady, let there be no fault even in this matter for now; however, when her father was coming here, he gave her ten instructions while advising her in private and seclusion.
I do not know their meaning; please explain their meaning to me. To her—
But her father said, “The fire within must not be carried outside. She asked, “Is it possible for us to live without giving fire to our neighbors on both sides?
“It seems so, my dear,” he replied. “Father, he did not say this with that in mind.
Rather, he said this: ‘My dear daughter, having seen the faults of your mother-in-law, father-in-law, and husband...’”
“Do not speak while standing outside each respective house; for there is no fire like this kind of fire.
“Noble lady, let that be so for now. But her father said, ‘Fire must not be brought from the outside into the inside.
How can we avoid bringing fire from the outside when the fire within has already been extinguished? “Is that really so?”
“Mother,” [he said]. “Father, he did not say this with reference to me; rather, he said this with reference to this:

‘If women or men in neighboring houses speak ill of their mothers-in-law, fathers-in-law, or husbands, and you bring back what they have said, saying, “So-and-so speaks such and such ill of you,” then...’”
"Do not say: 'There is no fire equal to this fire. Thus, even in this matter, she remained entirely blameless.
And as it was here, so it was in the remaining cases as well.

Now, this is the intended meaning among them: for that which her father said—"What is given should be given only to those who give"—was said with reference to those who return borrowed utensils after having taken them."
The statement, “It should not be given to those who do not give,” was said with reference to those who, having borrowed something, do not return it.

The statement, “It should be given whether they give back or not,” was said with reference to poor relatives and friends who have arrived; whether or not they are able to repay it, it is proper to give to them.

The statement, “One should sit comfortably,” was also said with reference to the fact that it is not proper to sit in a place where one ought to rise upon seeing one’s mother-in-law, father-in-law, or master.

The phrase “one should eat comfortably” is said with reference to the fact that it is proper for her to eat only after her mother-in-law, father-in-law, and husband have eaten first; she should serve them, and having ascertained whether they have all received their portions, she may then eat herself.
The phrase “one should lie down comfortably” is also said with reference to the fact that she should not go to bed before her mother-in-law, father-in-law, and husband;
rather, after performing whatever duties and services are appropriate for them, it is proper for her to lie down herself afterwards.

“‘The fire is to be worshipped’—this was said with reference to the fact that one ought to regard one’s mother-in-law, father-in-law, and husband as if they were a mass of fire or like the kings of the nāgas.
‘The inner deities are to be revered’—this too was said with reference to the fact that one ought to look upon one’s mother-in-law, father-in-law, and husband as if they were deities.
Having thus heard the meaning of these ten instructions, the merchant gave his reply.
Not seeing [the ring], he sat down with his head bowed.
Then the householders asked him, "Is there some other fault in our daughter, merchant? "No, ladies," he replied.
"Then why did you have her, who was faultless, driven out of the house for no reason? When this was said, Visākhā—
She said, "Dear ones, although it was not proper for me to go first at my father-in-law's word, my father placed me in your hands for the purpose of clearing my name when he sent me here;
you have now ascertained that I am innocent, and it is therefore proper for me to go. She then told her male and female servants, "Prepare the carriages and other conveyances."
He gave the order. Then the merchant took his wife and said, "My dear, I spoke without knowing;
please forgive me. She replied, "Father, I shall indeed forgive you for what must be forgiven. However, I am the daughter of a family that possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha’s teaching;
we cannot live without the Saṅgha of monks. If it is according to my wish, [let them invite] the Saṅgha of monks..."
“I wish to attend upon him; I shall stay here. “Mother, you may attend upon your ascetics as you please,” he said.
Visākhā, having invited the One of Ten Powers, led him into her residence on the following day.
When the naked ascetics heard that the Teacher was going to the house of Migāra-seṭṭhi, they went there, surrounded the house, and sat down. Visākhā—
Having offered the water of hospitality, he sent a message saying, "All the honors have been prepared; let my father-in-law come and serve the One of Ten Powers.
Then, as he was wishing to go, the Ājīvakas restrained him, saying, "Householder, do not go into the presence of the ascetic Gotama.
He sent back another message, saying, "Let my daughter-in-law herself serve [the meal]."
Having served the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, and when the meal was finished, she sent a message again, saying:
“May my father-in-law come and hear a discourse on the Dhamma.
Then, as he was departing because he thought, “It is now highly improper not to go,” they spoke to him again out of a desire for him to hear the Dhamma: “In that case, [go] to the ascetic Gotama...”
“Listen to the Dhamma while sitting outside the curtain. Before he could even go, they went ahead and enclosed him with a curtain.

He went and sat down outside the curtain. The Teacher said, “Whether you sit outside the curtain, or on the other side of a wall, or on another mountain, or even across the entire world-system, I, who am called the Buddha, am able to make my voice heard by you.”
As if grasping the trunk of a great rose-apple tree and shaking it, and as if raining down the rain of the Deathless,
he began a gradual discourse to teach the Dhamma.
And while the Perfectly Enlightened One was teaching the Dhamma, even those standing in front and those standing behind [could hear], across a hundred world-systems.
Even those situated beyond a thousand world-systems, or even those dwelling in the Akaniṭṭha realm, say, "The Teacher looks only toward me;
he teaches the Dhamma only to me. For the Teacher was as if looking at each one individually and as if conversing with each one.
Indeed, Buddhas are like the moon; just as the moon [shines] in the midst of the sky...
Just as one standing [on a mountain] perceives to all beings, "The moon is above me, the moon is above me," even so,
to those standing anywhere, they appear as if standing directly in front of them. It is said that after having their heads adorned cut off,
their anointed eyes plucked out, and the flesh of their hearts torn away, sons like Jāli were given to others for the sake of slavery.
This is the fruit of the gift given by one who renounced daughters like Kaṇhājinā and wives like Maddi.

And the merchant Migāra, while sitting outside the railing as the Tathāgata was turning back from his teaching of the Dhamma, established himself in the fruit of stream-entry adorned with a thousand methods;
endowed with unshakable faith in the Three Jewels, he—

Free from doubt, he lifted the edge of his robe, approached, and taking his daughter-in-law’s breast with his mouth, said, “From this day forward, you are my mother,” and thus established her in the position of a mother. From that time on, she became known as Migāramātā.
Later, when she gave birth to a son, he too gave him the name Migāra.
The great merchant, having vacated his place for his daughter-in-law and departed, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s two feet;

massaging the feet with his hands and kissing them with his mouth, he announced his name three times, saying, “I am Migāra, Bhante! I am Migāra, Bhante! and added, “Bhante, for so long a time as I have been...”
"I did not know which two [gifts] yield great fruit, but now, through my daughter-in-law, I have come to know it.
I am liberated from all the suffering of the woeful states; this daughter-in-law of mine, coming to this house, has come for my welfare, benefit, and happiness. Having said this, he spoke this verse:
"Today I understand that place where what is given yields great fruit."
“Indeed, it is for my welfare that my auspicious daughter-in-law has come to our home.
On the following day, Visākhā again invited the Teacher. Then, on that next day as well, her mother-in-law attained the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala).
From that time forth, that household became an open gateway for the Dispensation. Thereupon, the merchant thought:
“My daughter-in-law has been very helpful to me; I shall show her my favor.
It is not possible for her to wear heavy ornaments at all times, so I will have light ornaments made that are suitable for her to wear during all postures, both by day and by night.
Having said this, he had ornaments called *ghanamaṭṭhaka*, worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], fashioned.

When that was finished, she invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, fed them with great care, bathed Visākhā with sixteen jars of scented water, placed her before the Teacher, and had her pay homage to him after she had been purified.
The Teacher, having given a blessing of thanksgiving, went back to the monastery. From then on, Visākhā also [performed] acts of giving and so forth.
Performing meritorious deeds and receiving eight boons from the presence of the Teacher, she became visible in the sky like a crescent moon and attained great prosperity through sons and daughters.
It is said that she had ten sons and ten daughters; for each of them, there were ten sons and ten daughters; and for each of those as well, there were ten sons and ten daughters.
Including her ten daughters, there were thus four hundred and twenty-eight thousand living beings belonging to her lineage through sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons. Therefore, the ancients said:
“Visākhā had twenty sons, and four hundred grandsons;”
“Eight thousand grandsons, well-known throughout Jambudīpa.
Her lifespan was one hundred and twenty years; not even a single grey hair appeared on her head, and she always appeared as if she were sixteen years old.
Seeing her going to the monastery surrounded by sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, [the people asked], “Who is this here?”
“Visākhā,” they ask, “are you inquiring? Those who see her walking think, “Let her walk a little more now;
while walking, our noble lady looks beautiful. Those who see her standing, sitting, or lying down think, “Let her lie down a little more now;
while lying down, our noble lady looks beautiful. Thus, regarding those four...
It cannot be said that she does not shine in one particular mode of deportment among the modes of deportment;

indeed, she possesses the strength of five elephants. When the king heard that Visākhā possessed the strength of five elephants, he went to her monastery, listened to the Dhamma, and at the time of his departure, wishing to test her physical power, [sent] an elephant...
He released it; the elephant raised its trunk and charged toward Visākhā.
Her five hundred female attendants fled, while some, not being terrified, asked, "What is this?
and were told, "Noble lady, it seems the king has released the elephant, desiring to test your strength. Having seen this, Visākhā—
Thinking, “What is the use of fleeing? How indeed shall I seize him?
and further considering, “If I seize him too firmly, he will perish,” she took him by the trunk with two fingers and sent him back.
The elephant was unable to steady himself and fell down on his knees in the royal courtyard. The great multitude gave a shout of applause. She, too—
Together with her retinue, she returned home in safety.
Now at that time, Visākhā Migāramātā had many sons and many grandsons in Sāvatthī;
her sons were healthy and her grandsons were healthy, and she was considered highly auspicious, for not even one among all those sons and grandsons had met with an untimely death.
There was no one [of her name]. When the residents of Sāvatthī, on festive and celebratory occasions, would invite Visākhā first and feed her,
it happened that on a certain holiday day, while the great multitude, adorned and bedecked, were going to the monastery to hear the Dhamma, Visākhā also—
having eaten at the place where she had been invited and having adorned herself with magnificent ornaments— went along with the great multitude.
Having gone to the monastery and removed her ornaments, she tied them into a bundle with her upper robe and gave it to her maidservant.
It was with reference to this that it was said:
“Now at that time there was a festival in Sāvatthī; people, adorned and prepared, [went] to the monastery.”
They were going [to the monastery], and Visākhā Migāramātā, having adorned herself and dressed in her finery, was also going to the monastery.
Then Visākhā Migāramātā removed her ornaments, tied them into a bundle with her upper robe, and gave them to her maidservant, saying, "Come now, girl, take this bundle."
As she was going to the monastery, she thought: "It is improper to enter the monastery with such costly ornaments fastened on my head and decorating me down to the soles of my feet.
So, taking them off and making them into a bundle, she placed them in the hands of a maidservant who, through her own merit, possessed the strength of five elephants.
She gave it to her. It was said that she alone was able to wear it. Therefore he said to her, "Mother, take this ornament;

I shall adorn myself with it on my way back from the presence of the Teacher. Having given it to her and adorned herself with that thick, solid ornament, she approached the Teacher and listened to the Dhamma.
At the conclusion of the discourse on the Dhamma, [she addressed] the Blessed One...
Having paid homage, she rose and departed. Her female slave had forgotten that ornament.
But when the assembly had departed after hearing the Dhamma, the Elder Ānanda would put away anything that had been forgotten;
thus, on that day, having seen the great *mahālatā* ornament, he informed the Teacher: "Venerable Sir, Visākhā has left her ornament behind."
“...having forgotten, they went away. “Set it aside for a moment, Ānanda,” [the Buddha said]. The Elder picked it up, hung it on the side of the stairs, and set it there.
Visākhā, together with Suppiyā, wandered about inside the monastery, thinking, “I shall learn what is appropriate to be done for those who have arrived, those departing, the sick, and others.
When those female lay disciples saw her inside the monastery, those who were in need of ghee, honey, oil, and so forth—
By their very nature, young novices used to approach with bowls and other such items; on that day as well, they did exactly the same.
Then, seeing a sick monk, Suppiyā asked, "What does the Venerable One require?
When he replied, "A covering cloth," she said, "Very well, Venerable Sir, I shall send it. However, on the following day, not obtaining any allowable meat, she—
Having performed the necessary task with the flesh of her own thigh, she returned to her natural form once again through her faith in the Teacher.
Visākhā, too, having looked upon the sick, the young novices, and the junior monks, departed by another door and stood on the outskirts of the monastery, saying, "Mother, bring me my ornaments;
I shall adorn myself. At that moment, the female slave forgot them.
Knowing that he had departed, she said, "Noble lady, I have forgotten it. She replied, "In that case, go, fetch it, and bring it back;
however, if my noble master, the Elder Ānanda, has picked it up and placed it elsewhere, do not bring it here, for I have already relinquished it to the noble one.
It seems she knew that people of good family would not take back an item they had forgotten.
“The Elder is putting it away”; thus he spoke. When the Elder saw that maidservant, he asked, “For what purpose have you come?
She replied, “My mistress has come having forgotten her ornaments. He said, “They were placed by me on this side of the staircase;
go and fetch them. She said, “Noble sir, these are articles touched by your hand.”
Having said, "My noble lady has made me foodless," she went away with empty hands. When Visākhā asked her, "What is it, mother? she related the matter. [Visākhā replied:
"Mother, I will not wear articles that have been touched by my noble sir; they have been relinquished by me.
But it is difficult to look after the noble ladies; therefore, having given up those [ornaments], [give them] allowable articles."
“I will bring it; go, fetch it. She went and brought it back. Visākhā, without even putting it on, had the goldsmiths summoned and had its value appraised.

When they replied, “It is worth nine crores, but for the cost of the workmanship, it is worth a hundred thousand,” she had the ornament placed in a carriage and said, “In that case, sell it. [She gave] the price for the food.
Once given away, no one will be able to take it back; for women who are worthy of adorning such an ornament are indeed rare.
Indeed, in this entire circle of the earth, only three women have obtained the Mahālatā ornament:
the great female lay disciple Visākhā, the wife of the general Bandhula Malla, and Mallikā, the daughter of the merchant of Benares.
Therefore, Visākhā herself gave him the price for it, loaded nine crores and one hundred thousand pieces of gold onto carts, and having brought them to the monastery, she paid homage to the Teacher.
Then she said, "Venerable Sir, my noble Elder Ānanda touched this ornament with his hand;
from the moment he touched it, I have been unable to wear it. Therefore—"
"But having sold it, I thought, 'I shall offer it as a permissible gift (kappiya),' yet finding no one else capable of taking it, I have come myself after paying its price.
In which of the four requisites (paccaya), venerable sir, shall I offer it?
"It is fitting for you, Visākhā, to build a dwelling place for the Saṅgha at the East Gate. "It is fitting, [Venerable Sir]."
"Venerable Sir," said Visākhā with a joyful heart, and she purchased the land for nine *koṭis*. With another nine *koṭis*, she began to build the monastery.

Then one day, as the Teacher was surveying the world at dawn, he perceived the excellence of the supporting conditions (*upanissaya*) of a son of a merchant named Bhaddiya, who had been reborn in the merchant family of the city of Bhaddiya after passing away from the deva-world.
Having finished his meal at the house of Anāthapiṇḍika, he turned toward the northern gate.
For it was the Teacher’s custom that after receiving alms at Visākhā’s house, he would depart by the southern gate and reside in Jeta’s Grove;
whereas after receiving alms at Anāthapiṇḍika’s house, he would depart by the eastern gate and reside in the Eastern Park. This refers to the northern gate.
Seeing the Blessed One even as he was departing, they knew that he would set out on his wandering tour.
On that day, Visākhā too, having heard that "the Teacher has gone toward the northern gate," went with haste, paid homage, and asked:
"Venerable sir, do you intend to go on tour? "Yes, Visākhā. "Venerable sir, having renounced so much wealth..."
“I shall have a monastery built for you; please turn back, venerable sir. “This is a journey from which there is no turning back, Visākhā.

Thinking, “The Blessed One will surely see someone who is endowed with the right causes,” she said, “In that case, venerable sir, please go after sending back one monk who can determine what has been done and what remains to be done for me. “Whomever you prefer...”
“Take the bowl, Visākhā,” he said. Although she was fond of the Elder Ānanda, she thought, “The Elder Mahāmoggallāna possesses supernormal powers;
by relying on him, my task will be quickly accomplished,” and so she took the Elder’s bowl.
The Elder looked toward the Teacher. The Teacher said, “Return, taking with you five hundred bhikkhus as your retinue.”

"Moggallāna," he said. He did accordingly. By his power, even people who had gone fifty or sixty yojanas for the sake of wood and stone returned on that very same day, bringing back massive trees and boulders.
They neither grew weary while loading the carts with the wood and stone, nor did the axles break. Before long—
They constructed a two-storied palace. With five hundred chambers on the lower floor and five hundred chambers on the upper floor, the palace was adorned with a thousand rooms.
He had the palace built upon a site of pure, fine-grained soil;
yet, thinking that a bare palace would not be beautiful, he surrounded it with five hundred huts for those engaged in ascetic practice.
He had five hundred small palaces and five hundred long halls constructed.
Then, after wandering on tour for nine months, the Teacher returned again to Sāvatthī.
Visākhā’s palace work was also completed in nine months. The pinnacle of the palace was made of solid, highly refined red gold, capable of holding sixty water-jars.

She had it built. Hearing that "the Teacher is going to the Jetavana Monastery," she went out to meet him, led the Teacher to her own residence, and requested his consent, saying, "Venerable Sir, please stay right here for these four months, taking the community of monks with you;
I shall perform a festival for the palace. The Teacher consented. From then on, [she served] the community headed by the Buddha...
She gave her gift specifically in the dwelling of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Then a certain female companion of hers, bringing a garment worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], arrived and said, "Friend, I wish to spread this garment as a floor-cover in your palace;
tell me where the place for spreading it is. She replied, "Very well, friend, if I am to..."
“I shall say, ‘There is no space,’ and you will think, ‘She does not wish to give me an opportunity.
Having yourself inspected two stories and a thousand chambers of the palace, find a place for the spreading out.
She took a cloth worth a hundred thousand [pieces] and, wandering here and there, seeing no cloth of less value than that, thought: “I am not...”
“I shall receive a share of merit in this palace,” she said, and overcome with grief, she stood weeping in one place.
Then the Elder Ānanda, seeing her, asked, “Why are you weeping? She related the matter to him.
The Elder said, “Do not worry; I will tell you where your portion is spread out,” and pointed to the foot-washing area at the base of the stairs.
"Make this a foot-wiping cloth and spread it out; the monks, having washed their feet and wiped their feet on it first, will then enter inside.
In this way, it will be of great fruit for you," he said. It is said that this was a point not previously considered by Visākhā.
For four months, Visākhā gave alms to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha while they were in residence within the monastery.
On the final day, she presented robe-cloths to the Saṅgha; those received by the newest members of the Saṅgha were worth a thousand pieces of gold.
Having filled the bowls of them all, she gave medicinal requisites. In her act of giving and relinquishment, nine koṭis were spent.

Thus, she renounced twenty-seven crores in total within the Buddha’s dispensation: nine crores for the acquisition of the monastery site, nine for the construction of the monastery, and nine for the festival of the monastery.

While remaining in the female state and living in the house of one holding wrong views, no other woman could possibly have made such a great renunciation. On the day the festival of the monastery was completed—
Surrounded by her sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, as the shadows grew long, she walked around the palace thinking,
"Everything that I previously aspired for has reached its fulfillment," and while doing so, she uttered this inspired exclamation in five verses with a sweet voice:
"When shall I [again] dwell upon this delightful palace, plastered with fine lime and clay?"
“I shall give a gift of a monastery; my intention has been fulfilled.
“When shall I give beds and stools, as well as cushions and pillows;
when shall I give furniture for the dwellings? My intention has been fulfilled.”
“When shall I give a ticket-meal, pure, with meat as a garnish?
My intention to give a gift of food has been fulfilled.
When shall I give cloth from Kāsī, and garments of linen and cotton?”
“I shall give a gift of robes; my intention is fulfilled.
“When shall I give ghee, fresh butter, honey, oil, and molasses?
I shall give a gift of medicine; my intention is fulfilled.”
The bhikkhus, having heard her voice, reported it to the Teacher: “Venerable sir, throughout all this time we have never before seen Visākhā singing;
today she is walking around the palace singing while surrounded by her sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons.
Is her bile perhaps disturbed, or has she become mad? The Teacher—
“Monks, it is not that my daughter sings; rather, her own aspiration has been fulfilled.
With a joyful mind, thinking, ‘The prayer I made has reached its fulfillment,’ she wanders about uttering this inspired utterance.
When they asked, “But when, venerable sir, was that aspiration made by her? he replied, “Listen, monks. “We shall listen, venerable sir,” they said.
When this was said, he brought up the past:
"In the past, monks, one hundred thousand aeons ago from now, a Buddha named Padumuttara appeared in the world.
His lifespan was one hundred thousand years, and he had a retinue of one hundred thousand whose taints were exhausted. His city was Haṃsavatī."
His father was a king named Sunanda, and his mother was Queen Sujātā.

A certain female lay devotee (upāsikā), who was his chief attendant, having requested eight boons and standing in the place of a mother, attended upon the Teacher with the four requisites and went to wait upon him morning and evening.
She had a female friend who used to go regularly to the monastery with her.

Having observed her confidential conversation and her state of intimacy with the Teacher, she thought, "What indeed has she done to become so dear to the Buddhas? and asked the Teacher, "Venerable Sir, what is this woman to you?
"She is the foremost among my female attendants," he replied. "Venerable Sir, by doing what does one become an attendant?"
“Will she become foremost? “She made a vow a hundred thousand eons ago.

“Is it possible, venerable sir, to obtain [the fruit] by making a vow now? “Yes, it is possible. “In that case, venerable sir, please accept alms from me for seven days together with a hundred thousand bhikkhus.
The Teacher consented. She gave the gift for seven days.
On the day of the robe-offering ceremony, having given a cloth garment to the Teacher, he prostrated before him and lay down at his feet, saying:
"Venerable Sir, it is not for the sake of any worldly sovereignty or such like that I seek the fruit of this gift;
rather, having obtained eight boons in the presence of a Buddha such as yourself, I wish to stand in the place of a mother and attend to you with the four requisites."
She made this aspiration: "May I become the foremost among those who possess the power of faith. The Teacher, wondering, "Will this aspiration of hers be fulfilled?
looked into the future for a hundred thousand eons and perceived: "At the conclusion of a hundred thousand eons, a Buddha named Gotama will arise;
at that time, you will become a female lay follower named Visākhā and, in his presence..."
"Having obtained eight boons, you shall become the foremost among those female attendants who stand in the place of a mother and care for me with the four requisites," he said.
That prosperity seemed as though it were to be attained by her that very day.
Having performed meritorious deeds for the duration of her life, she passed away from there and was reborn in the world of the gods; thus she wandered through the realms of gods and humans.
In the time of the Sammasambuddha Kassapa, there was a youngest daughter of King Kiki of Kasi named Saṅghadāsī.
Without going to another family, she performed meritorious deeds such as giving for a long time together with her elder sisters.
At the feet of the Sammasambuddha Kassapa, she made this aspiration: "In the future, may I occupy the position of the mother of a Buddha such as you."
"May I become foremost among those who provide the four requisites," she made this aspiration.
From then on, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, she was reborn in this present life as the daughter of the merchant Dhanañjaya, the son of the merchant Meṇḍaka.
She performed many meritorious deeds in my teaching. Thus indeed, monks, "not..."
"My daughter is singing, but seeing that her prayer has reached fulfillment, she utters this inspired utterance," said the Teacher,
and as he taught the Dhamma, he continued: "Monks, just as a skilled garland-maker, having made a great heap of various flowers,
weaves them into various kinds of garlands, even so were the various kinds of meritorious deeds performed by Visākhā."
Having said, "The mind inclines toward doing [good]," he spoke this verse:
"Just as one might fashion many garlands from a heap of flowers, so too,
by a mortal who has been born, much wholesome merit should be performed."
In that context, "from a heap of flowers" means from a heap of various kinds of flowers. "One should make" means one should perform.

"Many garland-strings" refers to many varieties of floral arrangements, such as single-stalked garlands and so forth. "By a mortal" means by a being who has received the name "mortal" due to the nature of having to die;
such a person should perform much wholesome action, consisting of the giving of robes and other such deeds. In this regard:
The taking up of the heap of flowers is for the purpose of showing many flowers. For if there are few flowers, even a skilled garland-maker cannot produce many garlands;
yet an unskilled one cannot do so even when there are many flowers.
However, when there are many flowers, a skilled, clever, and proficient garland-maker [can produce many garlands].

Just so, if someone’s faith is weak but their wealth is abundant, they are unable to perform many wholesome deeds; because their faith is weak and their wealth is meager, they are unable [to do much].
Furthermore, even with exalted faith, if their wealth is meager, they simply cannot [do much]. And as for [one who has] exalted...
When there is faith, one is able to acquire abundant wealth; and such was the lay follower Visākhā.
It was with reference to her that this was said: “Just as... [and so on] ...much wholesome merit ought to be done.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many became stream-enterers and others. Thus the Dhamma instruction became fruitful for the great multitude.
The Eighth Story: Visākhā;
The Ninth Story: The Question of the Elder Ānanda.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Sāvatthī, delivered this Dhamma teaching in response to a question posed by the Elder Ānanda, beginning with the verse: "The fragrance of flowers does not travel against the wind."
It is said that in the evening, while in seclusion, the Elder thought:
“The Blessed One has spoken of three supreme fragrances—the fragrance of roots, the fragrance of heartwood, and the fragrance of flowers—and their scent travels only with the wind, not against it.
Is there perhaps some kind of fragrance whose scent travels even against the wind? Then this occurred to him:
“What is the use of my deciding this for myself? I shall ask the Teacher himself. He approached the Teacher and asked him.
Thus it is said:
“Then, in the evening, the Venerable Ānanda emerged from seclusion and went to where the Blessed One was.”
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, there are these three kinds of fragrant substances whose fragrance travels only with the wind, and not against the wind."

“Which three? The scent of roots, the scent of heartwood, and the scent of flowers—these, venerable sir, are the three kinds of scents whose fragrance travels only with the wind, not against the wind.
Is there, venerable sir, any kind of scent whose fragrance travels with the wind, travels against the wind, and travels both with and against the wind?”
Then the Blessed One, answering his question, said:

"There is, Ānanda, a certain kind of fragrance whose scent travels with the wind, whose scent travels against the wind, and whose scent travels both with and against the wind. "But what, Bhante, is that kind of fragrance?"
“Whose fragrance travels with the wind, whose fragrance travels against the wind, and whose fragrance travels both with and against the wind?

“In this case, Ānanda, in whatever village or town a woman or a man has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and gone for refuge to the Saṅgha; who abstains from taking life...”

He abstains from taking what is not given, he abstains from sexual misconduct, he abstains from false speech, and he abstains from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence. He is virtuous and of good character;

with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, he dwells at home, open-handed, pure-handed, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to charity, accessible to requests, and rejoicing in the distribution of gifts.
“In the various directions, ascetics and brahmins speak his praise, saying: ‘In such-and-such a village or town,
a woman or a man has gone for refuge to the Buddha, has gone for refuge to the Dhamma,
and has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha… [and so on] … he delights in giving and sharing.’”

“Deities also proclaim his praise: ‘In such and such a village or town, a woman or a man has gone for refuge to the Buddha, has gone for refuge to the Dhamma, has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha… [and so on] …is devoted to generosity and sharing.
This, Ānanda, is that kind of fragrance whose scent wafts even with the wind.”
"The fragrance of flowers travels against the wind; the fragrance of sandalwood, tagara, or jasmine does not travel against the wind," he said, and then spoke these verses:

"The scent of flowers does not go against the wind, Nor does that of sandalwood, tagara, or jasmine; But the fragrance of the virtuous goes against the wind, Pervading every direction, both with and against the breeze."
The fragrance of the virtuous wafts even against the wind;
the person of integrity pervades all directions.
Whether it be sandalwood or tagara, blue lotus or jasmine—
"Of all these kinds of fragrances, the fragrance of virtue is unsurpassed.
In this context, "not the fragrance of flowers" refers to the Pāricchattaka tree in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, which is one hundred yojanas in height and breadth;
the radiance of its flowers extends for fifty yojanas, and its fragrance for one hundred yojanas.
That too travels only with the wind; however, it is not able to go even eight finger-breadths against the wind.
Such a floral fragrance does not come against the wind. "Sandalwood" means the fragrance of sandalwood.
"Tagara and jasmine"—the fragrance of these as well is intended here. For among the fragrances of heartwood, even red sandalwood, tagara, and jasmine [are included].

It blows only with the wind, not against the wind. But the fragrance of the virtuous—the fragrance of the moral conduct of true persons such as Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and their disciples—blows even against the wind.

Why is that? Because a true person pervades all directions; since a true person proceeds by completely overwhelming all directions with the fragrance of their virtue, it is said: "His fragrance does not blow against the wind."
It should not be said [that it does not go against the wind]. Therefore it was said: “it goes against the wind.

“Vassikī” means jasmine (*jātisumanā*). “Of these” means that among these types of fragrances such as sandalwood and so forth, the fragrance of virtue of virtuous and true persons is unsurpassed, peerless, and incomparable.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages. The teaching thus became beneficial to the great multitude.
This is the ninth story, concerning the questions of the Elder Ānanda.
10. The Story of the Almsfood Given by the Elder Mahākassapa.
"This fragrance is indeed small"—the Teacher gave this Dhamma teaching while dwelling at Veḷuvana concerning the alms-giving to the Elder Mahākassapa.
For one day, having emerged from cessation after seven days had passed, the Elder set out, thinking, "I shall go for alms by sequential rounds in Rājagaha.
At that time, there were female attendants of Sakka, the king of the gods, who had feet like those of a hen.
Five hundred celestial nymphs, inspired with the thought, "We shall give almsfood to the Elder," prepared five hundred portions of almsfood.
Taking them and standing on the path, they said, "Venerable Sir, please accept this almsfood; show us your favor.
He replied, "Go, you may go; I shall show favor to those who are destitute. "Venerable Sir..."
"Do not drive us away; show us favor. The Elder, having understood their intent, refused them once more.
When they continued to beg him, unwilling to depart, saying, "You do not know your own measure; go away," he snapped his fingers.
Hearing the sound of the Elder's finger-snap, they were paralyzed with fear; unable to stand before him, they fled.
Having gone to the world of the gods, they were asked by Sakka, "Where have you been?
They replied, "O gods, we went thinking, 'We shall give alms-food to the Elder when he has emerged from meditative absorption. But did you give it?
"He did not wish to accept it. "What did he say? "He said, 'I shall provide for those who are destitute,' O gods. "You..."
“In what manner did they go? “In this very manner, O King. Sakka, thinking, “What would those like you give as almsfood to the Elder?
and desiring to give it himself, transformed himself into an aged, decrepit man with broken teeth, grey hair, and a trembling body;
and having likewise made the celestial maiden Sujā an old woman of similar appearance, he [departed].
Having laid out the weavers’ street, he remained there spreading the warp.
The Elder, thinking, “I shall provide for those in distress,” was walking toward the city;
seeing that street just outside the city, he looked about and saw two men. At that moment, Sakka was spreading the warp, and Sujā [was weaving].
They were weaving cloth. The Elder thought: “Even at this advanced age they still work;
