I suspect there are none in this city more destitute than these. I shall show them favor by taking even as much as a ladleful or a handful of vegetables given by them.
He turned his face toward their house. As he was approaching, Sakka [saw him].
Seeing him, she said to Sujā, “My lady, my master is coming from here;
sit in silence as if you did not see him, and we shall deceive the elder for a moment and give him alms. When the elder arrived, he stood at the door of the house.
They, acting as if they did not see him and attending only to their own work, went on for a short distance.
Then Sakka said, "There stands one like an elder at the door of the house; go and investigate him. "Go and investigate him, Master," [the servant replied].

He went out from the house, paid homage to the elder with the fivefold prostration, and leaning on his knees with both hands, he stood up groaning and asked, "Which elder is the noble one? Stepping back a short distance, he looked into the eyes.
Having said, "It is smoking for me," he placed his hand on his forehead, looked upward, and said, "Alas, what suffering!
Venerable Mahākassapa Thera has come to the door of my hut after a long time;
is there anything in the house? Sujā, appearing somewhat distressed, replied, "There is, Master. Sakka said, "Bhante..."
“Without considering whether it is coarse or refined, do not fail to show them hospitality,” he said, and took the bowl.
The Elder thought, “Whether what they give be vegetables or a handful of broken rice, I shall accept their offering,” and gave back the bowl.
He entered the inner house, drew up a pot of rice called *ghaṭiodana* from a jar, filled the bowl, and [offered it] to the Elder.
placed it in his hand. That alms-food was provided with many soups and condiments, and its fragrance pervaded the entire city of Rājagaha.
Then the Elder thought: "This man is of little power, yet the alms-food is of great power, like the food of Sakka;
who indeed could this be? Then, recognizing him as Sakka, he said: "A heavy deed has been done by you toward those who are miserable."
“By plundering this wealth, someone who today gave me alms might have become a general or a merchant prince, even though they were poor.
“There is no one poorer than I, venerable sir.
“For what reason are you poor while experiencing the royal splendor in the world of the gods? “Venerable sir, it is indeed so; however, by me—”

When a Buddha has not yet appeared, meritorious deeds are performed; when the arising of a Buddha is occurring, by performing meritorious deeds, these three sons of gods—Cūḷaratha-devaputta, Mahāratha-devaputta, and Anekavaṇṇa-devaputta—have been reborn in a place near me as my equals, being more radiant than I.
For among those sons of gods, [I thought], "We shall play at the festival," and [sent] the female attendants...
“When they have taken [the goods] and descended into the middle of the street, I flee and enter my house.
For the heat from their bodies overwhelms my body, but the heat from my body does not overwhelm theirs. ‘Who, venerable sir, is more miserable than I? [I thought].
‘Even though this is so, from now on do not give alms to me by deceiving me in this way. “Having deceived [me],...
“When you have given this gift, is there merit for me or not? “There is, friend.
“If that is so, venerable sir, the performance of wholesome kamma is my burden.
Having said this, he paid homage to the Elder, took the ladle, circumambulated the Elder, rose up into the air, and exclaimed: “O, what a gift! What a supreme gift! To Kassapa...”
He uttered this inspired exclamation: "Well-established! Therefore it is said:
"At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, the Venerable Mahākassapa was dwelling in the Pippali Cave; he had been sitting for seven days in a single cross-legged posture, absorbed in a certain..."
Having entered into meditative absorption, the Venerable Mahākassapa emerged from that concentration at the end of those seven days.
Then, as the Venerable Mahākassapa had emerged from that concentration, this thought occurred to him:
"What if I were now to enter Rājagaha for alms?"
Now at that time, about five hundred deities were making an effort to obtain almsfood for the venerable Mahākassapa.
Then the venerable Mahākassapa, having declined those five hundred deities,
dressed in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms.
Now at that time, Sakka, lord of the devas, desired to give almsfood to the Venerable Mahākassapa.
Having manifested the form of a weaver, he was weaving thread, while the asura maiden Sujā filled the shuttle.
Then, as the Venerable Mahākassapa was walking for alms from house to house in Rājagaha, he came to where Sakka, lord of the devas...
He approached the dwelling. Sakka, lord of the devas, saw the Venerable Mahākassapa coming from afar;
seeing him, he went out from the house, went forward to meet him, took the bowl from his hand, entered the house, scooped rice from a jar, filled the bowl, and gave it to the Venerable Mahākassapa.
Thus the alms-food became possessed of many soups, many condiments, and many flavorful seasonings. Then it occurred to the Venerable Mahākassapa:
"Who might this being be, who possesses such power and majesty? Then it occurred to the Venerable Mahākassapa:
"This is Sakka, the lord of the devas. Having understood this, [he addressed] Sakka, the lord of the devas.
He said this: “What is this you have done, Kosiya? Do not do such a thing again.
“Venerable Kassapa, we too have need of merit; we too have work to be done with merit.
Then Sakka, lord of the devas, paid homage to the Venerable Mahākassapa and kept him on his right side.
Having ascended into the air, into the sky, he uttered this inspired exclamation three times: “O, what a gift!
A supreme gift, well-established upon Kassapa! O, what a gift! A supreme gift, well-established upon Kassapa! O, what a gift! A supreme gift, well-established upon Kassapa!”
Then the Blessed One, while still standing in his dwelling, heard that sound and addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, behold Sakka, lord of the devas, as he goes through the air after uttering this inspired utterance.
“But what did he do, Bhante? “Having deceived me, he gave alms-food to my son Kassapa.”
“Having given that, with a joyful mind, he departs uttering an inspired utterance (udāna). [The question was asked:
“Venerable sir, how was it known by him that ‘it is fitting to give almsfood to the Elder’? [The Buddha replied:
“Monks, having said, ‘Even the gods and humans long for an alms-collector such as my son,’ he himself uttered an inspired utterance. However, in the Sutta, only this much is recorded.

With his purified divine ear-element, surpassing that of humans, the Blessed One heard Sakka, lord of the devas, ascending into the air and uttering this inspired utterance three times in the sky: “O, what a gift! A supreme gift!
Well-established upon Kassapa! O, what a gift! A supreme gift! Well-established upon Kassapa! O, what a gift! A supreme gift!”
“...well-established upon Kassapa.
Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired exclamation:
“For a bhikkhu who lives on almsfood...”
The gods envy one who sustains himself alone and does not support others, who is such-like,
ever peaceful, and mindful.
Having uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*), he said, "Monks, Sakka, lord of the gods, came because of the fragrance of my son’s virtue and gave him almsfood," and then spoke this verse:
"Trifling is this fragrance, that which comes from tagara and sandalwood;
But the fragrance of those who possess virtue wafts supreme even among the gods."
In this context, "one who is heedful" means one of limited measure. As for the phrase "the fragrance of the virtuous":
the fragrance of those possessed of virtue is not limited like *tagara* or red sandalwood; rather, it is exceedingly sublime and far-reaching.
For that very reason, having become supreme, excellent, and best among the gods, he excels everywhere, both among gods and humans.
"It blows; it goes by blowing," he said.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages. The teaching became highly beneficial for the great multitude.
This is the tenth story concerning the alms-food given to the Elder Mahākassapa.

11. The Story of the Parinibbāna of the Elder Godhika "Of those who have perfected their virtue..."—the Teacher delivered this Dhamma teaching while dwelling at Veḷuvana near Rājagaha, concerning the parinibbāna of the elder Godhika.
For that venerable one, while dwelling on the Black Rock on the slope of Isigili, being diligent, ardent, and resolute, attained temporary [liberation].
Having attained liberation of mind, he fell away from it due to a certain incurable illness.
Having attained jhāna a second and a third time, he fell away again; but on the seventh occasion, having produced it, he thought:
"I have fallen away from jhāna six times. For one who has fallen away from jhāna, the destination is uncertain. Right now—"
Thinking, "I shall take up the knife," he took a hair-cutting razor and lay down on his side to cut his jugular vein.
Māra, knowing his mind, thought: "This bhikkhu desires to take up the knife;
those who take up the knife are indeed indifferent to life, and by establishing insight, they even attain Arahantship. If I..."
“I will try to dissuade him; he will not heed my words, so I shall have the Teacher dissuaded.
Having approached the Teacher in the guise of a stranger, he spoke thus:
“O Great Hero, O One of Great Wisdom, blazing with supernatural power and glory!
“O One who has transcended all enmity and fear, O Visionary, I bow at your feet.
‘I am your disciple, O Great Hero;
though death has overcome me, I still desire and intend [to live]. O Radiant One, restrain that [desire].’”
“How indeed, Blessed One, could a disciple of yours, delighting in your teaching, a trainee who has not yet attained his heart’s goal, pass away while people are listening?
At that moment, the Elder drew his knife. The Teacher, knowing “This is Māra,” spoke this verse:
“Thus indeed do the wise act; they do not long for life.
Having uprooted craving by its very root, Godhika has attained final Nibbāna.
Then the Blessed One, together with many bhikkhus, went to the place where the elder was lying after having taken his own knife.
He arrived. At that moment, Māra the Evil One, thinking, "Where indeed has his rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhiviññāṇa) settled?
became like a mass of smoke and like a thicket of darkness, searching for the Elder’s consciousness in all directions.
The Blessed One, having shown that state of smoke and darkness to the monks, said: "Monks, this is Māra the Evil One."
Māra searched for the consciousness of the clansman Godhika, thinking, "Where has the consciousness of the clansman Godhika been established?
He said, "Monks, with consciousness unestablished, the clansman Godhika has attained final Nibbāna.
Unable to find a place for his consciousness, Māra assumed the form of a young boy and [played] a yellow *veluva* lute.
Taking the Teacher, he approached him and asked:
“Above, below, across, in the quarters and intermediate directions—I have searched everywhere, yet I do not find him. Where has Godhika gone?”
Then the Teacher said to him:
“The wise man, endowed with fortitude, always delighting in meditation and devoted to jhāna,
devotes himself day and night, not craving for life.”
“Having conquered the army of Death, not returning to renewed existence,
having uprooted craving, Godhika has attained final Nibbāna.
When this was said, Māra the Evil One addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“Overcome with grief, his lute slipped from his armpit;
then that dejected yakkha vanished right there.

The Teacher also said, “What use is the place where the clansman Godhika has been reborn, O Evil One? For even a hundred or a thousand like you would not be able to see the place where he has been reborn,” and having said this, he spoke this verse:
“For those who are perfected in virtue, who dwell in heedfulness,
and who are liberated through right knowledge— Māra does not find their path. In this context,
“for those” refers to those such as the clansman Godhika, who attained final Nibbāna with consciousness that was non-anchored, and others.
Thus they attain final Nibbāna. "Of those with perfected virtue" means of those whose virtue is fulfilled.

"Dwelling in heedfulness" means dwelling in heedfulness characterized by non-forgetfulness of mindfulness (*sati*). "Liberated through right knowledge" means having known by way of cause, method, and reason:
[namely], liberation by way of its constituent part (*tadaṅgavimutti*), liberation by suppression (*vikkhambhanavimutti*), and liberation by eradication (*samucchedavimutti*).
"Of those liberated by liberation through subsiding and liberation by escape"— of those liberated by these five kinds of liberation,
Māra does not find their path. This means that even though Māra searches with all his might for the path of such great ones whose taints are exhausted,
he does not find it, does not obtain it, and does not see it.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages. The teaching became highly beneficial for the great multitude.
This is the eleventh story, concerning the final passing away of the Elder Godhika.
12. The Story of Garahadatta.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, gave this Dhamma teaching concerning a disciple of the Nigaṇṭhas named Garahadatta.
In Sāvatthī, there were two friends, Sirigutta and Garahadatta. Of these two, Sirigutta was a lay follower and a disciple of the Buddha, whereas Garahadatta was a disciple of the Nigaṇṭhas.
The Nigaṇṭhas would constantly say this to him:
“Why do you not advise your companion Sirigutta, saying, ‘Why do you approach the ascetic Gotama? What will you gain from being in his presence?
so that he might come to us and give us the things we should offer? Having heard their words, Garahadinna went frequently [to him].
While standing, sitting, or in other places, he would advise Sirigutta thus: "My good man, what have you to do with the ascetic Gotama?
What will you gain by approaching him? And why, noble lady, should it not be proper for you to approach me and give alms to them?
Although Sirigutta heard these words, he remained silent for many days and then became disillusioned.
One day he said, “Good sir, you come here constantly and, from the very place where I am standing, say to me:
‘What will you gain by approaching the ascetic Gotama? Lady, approach my [teacher] and give them alms.
Tell me then, lady, what do you know? “O Master, do not speak thus! Regarding my noble ladies...”
“There is nothing unknown to me; I know all—past, future, and present—and all bodily, verbal, and mental actions:
‘This will happen,’ ‘this will not happen’—I know all that is possible and impossible. “Do you say this? “Yes, I say it.
“If that is so, you have committed a very grave offense; for all this time, [you have withheld] this matter from me.”
“Without having spoken of it, today I have come to know the power of the noble ones’ knowledge. Go, friend, and invite the noble ones in my name.
He went to the presence of the Nigaṇṭhas, paid homage to them, and said, “My companion Sirigutta invites you for tomorrow.
“Was Sirigutta speaking to you personally? “Yes, noble ones,” he replied.
They became joyful and delighted, saying, "Our task is accomplished! Since the time Sirigutta gained faith in us, what prosperity indeed will not be ours?
Sirigutta also possessed a large residence; it was long on both sides between those two houses.
Having had a pit dug, he filled it with a mire of excrement.

Having had two stakes driven into the ground on both sides outside the pit and having had ropes tied to them, he had the front legs of the seats placed at the front edge of the pit and the hind legs placed upon the ropes.
Thinking, "When they sit thus, they will fall headlong in this way," he acted accordingly.
No pit was visible; thus he had rugs spread over the seats.

Having had large jars placed there, he had their openings bound with plantain leaves and white cloth, and keeping them empty, he had them placed outside at the rear of the house, smeared with rice gruel, boiled rice, husked rice, ghee, oil, honey, molasses, cakes, and flour.
Early in the morning, Garahadinna went quickly to his house and asked, "Is the hospitality for the noble ones prepared?
"Yes, friend, it is prepared," they replied. "But where is he? "In these many jars, this much rice gruel has been filled;
in these, the cooked rice; and in these, the ghee, molasses, cakes, and so forth. The seats have been arranged. He said, "Excellent!"
Having spoken thus, he departed. When he had gone, five hundred Nigaṇṭhas arrived.
Sirigutta went out from his house, paid homage to the Nigaṇṭhas with the fivefold prostration, and standing before them with palms joined in reverence, he thought:
"It is said that you know everything, including the distinctions of the past and so forth; such was told to me by your attendant."
"If you know everything, do not enter my house. For those who have entered my house, there is neither rice gruel nor food and such for you.
If you enter without knowing, I shall throw you into a cesspool and beat you.
Having thought thus, she gave the signal to the men. Thus, having recognized their intention to sit down...
“Standing at the back, you should remove the coverings from the seats, lest they be defiled by impurity.
Then he said to the Nigaṇṭhas, “Come this way, venerable sirs. Having entered, the Nigaṇṭhas began to sit down on the prepared seats.
Then the people said to them, “Wait, venerable sirs; do not sit down yet. “Why?”
“What is the reason? “It is proper to sit down after knowing the proper conduct (*vatta*) for noble ladies who have entered our house.
“What is it proper to do, friend? “It is proper for all of you to stand at the base of your respective seats and sit down simultaneously.
This, it is said, was his intention: “When one has fallen into a pit, [one should not say], ‘Friend, do not…’”
“Let him not be permitted to say, ‘Let the rest sit on their seats. They replied, “Very well,” and thought, “It is fitting for us to do whatever these men have said.
Then they all stood in a row at the foot of their respective seats.
Then, having said to them, “Venerable sirs, please sit down quickly all at once,” he [observed] their act of sitting.
Realizing this, they removed the coverings from atop the seats. The Nigaṇṭhas sat down all at once;
the legs of the seats, which had been placed upon ropes, gave way, and the Nigaṇṭhas fell headfirst into the pit.
When they had fallen, Sirigutta closed the door and said to those who were emerging one by one, "Why [do you not know] the past, the future, and the present?"
Having made them recite with sticks, saying, "Know this! This much shall suffice for them," he had the door opened. They went out and began to flee.
However, on their path of departure, he had the ground prepared with plaster made slippery.
Unable to stand there, as they fell again and again, he had them beaten once more, saying, "Enough! This much is enough for you."
He dismissed them. Crying out, "We have been cast out by you! We have been cast out by you! they went to the door of the supporter's house.
Seeing that misfortune, Garahadinna became enraged and thought:
"I have been cast out by Sirigutta—by me, who am a field of merit capable of giving as he wishes even to those in the world with its gods who approach him with hands outstretched in homage."
“Noble lady, you had him beaten and brought him to ruin! Having said this, he went to the royal palace and caused a fine of one thousand kahāpaṇas to be imposed upon him.
Then the king sent a message to him. He went and, having paid homage to the king, said:
“Your Majesty, impose the punishment after investigating the matter; do not do so without investigation. “I shall impose it after investigating,” [the king replied]. “Very well.”

“Sire,” [he said]. “In that case, take it,” [the king replied]. “Sire, my companion, a disciple of the Nigaṇṭhas, approached me and frequently spoke thus to me while I was standing, sitting, or in other positions: ‘Friend, what have you to do with the ascetic Gotama?
What will you gain by approaching him? Having begun with these words, Sirigutta reported the entire incident.
“Your Majesty, if it is appropriate to take punishment for this offense, then take it.
The king looked at Garahadinnaka and said, “Is it true that you spoke thus? “It is true, Your Majesty.
“While you were wandering about taking those who do not even know this much to be teachers, for what reason did you speak thus to a disciple of the Tathāgata, saying, ‘They know everything’?”
“Let the punishment you have imposed fall upon yourself! Thus he was made to bear the penalty himself, and his own family dependents were beaten and driven out.
He became angry at this and, from that time on, did not speak with Sirigutta for even half a month, thinking:
“It is improper for me to behave in this manner; I ought to bring ruin upon his family dependents as well.”
Having approached Sirigutta, he said, "Friend Sirigutta. "What is it, friend? "It happens that even among kinsmen and close friends there is quarreling and dispute;
why do you not say anything at all? Why do you act in this way? "Friend, because you do not speak with me, I do not speak.
"Friend, whatever has been done, let that be; we are not [to blame]."
“We shall break their friendship. From that time on, both of them stayed and sat together in one place.
Then one day, Sirigutta said to Garahadinna: “What do you have to do with the Nigaṇṭhas? What will you gain by approaching them?
Is it not fitting for you to approach my Teacher or give alms to the noble ladies? He too—
He expected nothing but this, and thus it was as if he had scratched the place where he had been itching with his fingernail.
He asked, "Sirigutta, what does your teacher know? "O friend, do not speak thus!
There is nothing that my Teacher does not know; he knows everything categorized as past and so forth, and he discerns the minds of beings in sixteen ways."
“I did not know this myself; why did you not tell me for so long?
In that case, go and invite your teacher for tomorrow’s meal. I shall feed him; ask him to accept my alms together with five hundred bhikkhus.”
Sirigutta approached the Teacher, paid homage, and said this: “Venerable sir, my companion Garahadinna is inviting you;
please accept his alms tomorrow together with five hundred bhikkhus.
On the previous day, however, I performed such-and-such for those who rely on his family, and I shall also provide a recompense for what I have done.”
“I do not know; I do not even know your desire to give alms with a pure heart. Having reflected, if it is appropriate, please accept;
if not, do not accept. The Teacher reflected, “Does he indeed wish to do something for us?
and seeing that between two houses he had caused a great pit to be dug, about eighty cartloads [of earth]—
“Having had logs of acacia wood brought and piled up, and having set fire to it, he intends to throw us into the charcoal pit and extinguish us.
He reflected again: “Is there any purpose for going there, or not?
Then he saw this: “I shall stretch out my foot into the charcoal pit; the palm-leaf mat placed there to conceal it will disappear.”
Having broken through the pit of embers, a great lotus the size of a wheel will emerge;
then, stepping upon the pericarp of that lotus, I shall sit upon my seat. Five hundred bhikkhus will likewise go and sit there, and the great multitude will assemble.
In that assembly, I will offer words of thanksgiving with two verses; at the conclusion of the thanksgiving—
"There will be a realization of the Dhamma for eighty-four thousand living beings;
Sirigutta and Garahadinna will become stream-enterers; and they will scatter their own heaps of wealth throughout the Teaching.
It is fitting that I go, depending upon this son of good family," he said, and thus he accepted the alms-food.
Sirigutta went and informed Garahadinna of the Teacher’s acceptance, saying, "Pay honor to the Chief of the World.
Garahadinna thought, "Now I shall know what is appropriate to do for him," and having had a large pit dug between two houses,
he had it filled with as much as eighty cartloads of acacia wood.
Having lit a fire and caused a heap of acacia charcoal to be prepared, he had it blown throughout the entire night and then had the heap of acacia charcoal piled up.
Atop the pit, he had tree-trunks placed, covered them with palm-leaf mats, and had them plastered with cow dung.
He laid out weak sticks along one side and made a path for walking, thinking, "In this way, as each step is taken..."

Thinking, "After wandering through Daṇḍaka and Bhagga, they will fall into a pit of glowing embers," he had the bowls placed at the back of his house according to the very arrangement established by Sirigutta, and he likewise prepared the seats in that same manner.
Early in the morning, Sirigutta went to his house and asked, "Friend, has your hospitality been prepared? "Yes, friend," he replied. "Where [are the bowls]?"
"But what about him? "Come, let us see," he said, and he showed everything exactly in the manner demonstrated by Sirigutta.
Sirigutta said, "Excellent, good man! The great multitude gathered. For when invited by one of wrong view, a vast assembly gathers;
even those of wrong view assembled, thinking, "We shall witness the failure of the ascetic Gotama."
Those possessed of right view also gathered together, thinking, "Today the Teacher will deliver a great discourse on the Dhamma;
we shall behold the domain of the Buddha and the play of the Buddha.
On the following day, the Teacher went to the door of Garahadinna’s house together with five hundred bhikkhus.
Thus, having gone out from his house, he paid homage with the fivefold prostration, stood before him with palms joined in reverence, and thought:

"Venerable sir, it was said to me by your attendant: 'It is reported that you know all things, categorized as past and so forth, and that you discern the minds of beings in sixteen ways. If you do indeed know this, [then please explain it] to me."
"Do not enter the house. For those who enter, there is neither rice gruel nor food and such; moreover, we shall throw you all into a pit of glowing embers and burn you.
Having thought thus, he took the Teacher’s bowl and said, "Come this way, Blessed One," adding, "Venerable Sir, please come after learning our household custom for those who have arrived."
“It is permissible,” he said. “What is it that is permissible, friend? “It is permissible for one person to enter first, go ahead, and sit down;
while he is sitting there, it is permissible for another to come in behind him. This was his thought:
“If I see one person falling into the pit of glowing coals as he goes ahead, the rest will not follow; thus, by making each one fall individually, I shall subdue them all. The Teacher—
Saying, “Very well,” he set out alone. Having reached the pit of glowing coals, Garahadinna stood back and said, “Go forward, venerable sir.
Then the Teacher extended his foot over the top of the pit of glowing coals;
the mat vanished, and having split the pit of glowing coals, lotuses as large as chariot wheels sprang up. The Teacher stepped upon the pericarps of the lotuses.
Having gone there, he sat down on the seat prepared for the Buddha; the monks also went and sat down in the same manner.
A burning fever arose from the body of Garahadinna.
He went in haste, approached Sirigutta, and said, "Master, be my refuge! "What is this? [Sirigutta asked].
“There is no rice-gruel or food, such as meals, in the houses of the five hundred monks; what indeed shall I do?

He asked, “But what have you done? [She replied: “I had a large pit filled with glowing coals dug between two houses, thinking, ‘I will throw them there and seize them. Then, having broken that [pit], great lotuses appeared.”
They rose up. Having stepped upon all the lotus calyxes and proceeded there, they sat down on the prepared seats and said, "Now what shall I do, Master?
[The man replied,] "Did you not just now show me, 'There are this many jars, this much rice-gruel, and this many grains of sesame and so forth'?
"That was a lie, Master; the jars were indeed empty. "Very well; go, and among them—"
"Look at the rice gruel and other foods in the bowls," he said.
At that very moment, those bowls in which "rice gruel" had been mentioned became filled with rice gruel; those in which "food and so forth" had been mentioned were already full of food and the like.
Upon seeing this success, the body of Garahadatta was suffused with rapture and gladness, and his mind became serene.

Thus, having served the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha with due respect, and desiring to have the Teacher offer words of thanksgiving after the meal was finished, he took up his bowl. As the Teacher was giving the blessing, he said:
"These beings, precisely because they lack the eye of wisdom, do not know the excellence of my disciples and the qualities of the Buddha’s teaching. For those who are bereft of the eye of wisdom..."
"Those who are called 'blind' are actually possessed of wisdom and have eyes," he said, and then spoke these verses:
"Just as a lotus might grow there in a heap of refuse cast away on the great highway— pure-scented and delightful."
“Thus, amidst those who have become like refuse, among worldlings who are like the blind, the disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One outshines them with wisdom.
In this context, *saṅkāradhāne* means in a place of refuse, that is, in a heap of rubbish. It is abandoned.

"On the great highway" means on the main road where [the body] has been discarded. "Pure-scented" means possessing a fragrant odor. "Delightful to the mind" means that the mind finds pleasure therein.

"Among those who have become like refuse" means among those who have become like rubbish. "Worldlings" (puthujjana) refers to the common people of the world so named because they give birth to manifold defilements (kilesa). This is what is meant: just as when [something] has been discarded on a great highway...
Just as a lotus of pure fragrance might grow within a heap of refuse that is impure,
loathsome, and repulsive— yet it would be delightful, dear, and pleasing to kings, royal ministers, and others, and would indeed be worthy of being placed upon their heads—

even so, though born among worldlings who are like a heap of refuse, and having arisen even amidst the common folk who lack wisdom and are without vision, [the noble one] by the power of his own wisdom...
Having seen the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefit in renunciation, one who has gone forth and become a monk outshines others by the mere fact of his going forth;
he outshines them even further by accomplishing virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
For a bhikkhu who is a disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One and whose taints are destroyed outshines, outshines, and shines brilliantly, surpassing the worldlings who are like blind men.
At the conclusion of the teaching, eighty-four thousand beings attained penetration of the Dhamma.
Both Garahadinna and Sirigutta reached the fruit of stream-entry. They distributed all their wealth throughout the Buddha’s dispensation.
The Teacher rose from his seat and went to the monastery. In the evening, the bhikkhus initiated a discussion in the Hall of Truth.
“Ah, how wonderful indeed are the qualities of the Buddha! For such a mass of acacia charcoal embers was pierced, and lotuses sprang up!
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, what discussion are you sitting here having now?
When they replied, “This very one,” he said, “Monks, it is no wonder that this occurred now while I have become a Buddha.”
"Lotuses have arisen from a heap of coals," he said, "and they arose even for me while I was still a Bodhisatta, though my knowledge was not yet mature.
When asked, "At what time, venerable sir? Tell us," he brought forth a past account:
"I would rather fall into hell, head downwards and feet upwards;..."
"I shall not act ignobly; come now, accept this alms-food.
Having thus related the *Khadiraaṅgāra Jātaka* in detail, he spoke.
This is the twelfth story, the Account of Garahadinna.
The commentary on the Pupphavagga is finished.
The Fourth Chapter. 5.
The Bālavagga (Chapter on the Fool).
1. The Story of a Certain Man "Long is the night for one who is awake"—the Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, gave this teaching on the Dhamma concerning King Pasenadi of Kosala and a certain man.
It is said that on a festival day, King Pasenadi of Kosala [beheld] a certain all-white elephant, fully adorned and prepared...
Mounting an elephant named Puṇḍarīka, he circumambulated the city with great royal majesty.

While the proclamation was being made, the great multitude of people, being struck by clods of earth, sticks, and other missiles, fled away; yet even as they ran, they would turn their necks and look back.
It is said that this is indeed the fruit of the gifts well-bestowed by kings. Even for a certain man of poor fortune—
The queen, standing on the upper terrace of the seven-storied palace, opened a window shutter, gazed at the king, and then withdrew.
To the king, he appeared like the full moon entering behind a bank of clouds.
His heart became so bound to her that he felt as if he were about to fall from the back of the elephant; thus, he quickly entered the city.
Having performed a circumambulation and entered the inner palace, he said to a trusted minister:
"In such-and-such a place, did you see the palace that was pointed out to me by me? "Yes, Your Majesty. "Did you see a woman there? "I saw her, Your Majesty.
"Go and find out whether she has a husband or not. He went and [ascertained] that she had a husband.
Having learned this, he went and reported to the king, "She has a husband.
Then, when the king said, "In that case, summon her husband," he went and said, "Come, sir, the king summons you.
He thought, "Surely some danger must have arisen because of my wife," and being unable to resist the king's command, he went to the king.
Having paid homage, he stood there. Then the king said to him, "Serve me from this day forward.
"Enough, Your Majesty; having performed my own work, I shall pay you tax. Let my livelihood be right here in my home.
"I have no need for your tax; from this day forth, serve me. [The king] gave him a wooden plank and a weapon.
He had [the man] executed. It was because he thought: "Having imputed some fault to him, I will have him killed and take his wife.
Then, terrified by the fear of death, he served [the king] with diligence.
Seeing no fault in him, as the king's lustful fever increased, [he thought]: "I will impute some fault to him and issue a royal command..."

Having summoned him with the words, "I shall do so," he spoke thus: "My good man, go to such-and-such a place by the river at a distance of one *yojana* from here, and at my evening bathing time, bring back white and blue lotuses as well as the mud from the Aruṇavatī.
If you do not return at that moment, I shall inflict punishment upon you. It is said that this servant was even more despised than the other four slaves.
For slaves such as Dhanakkītā and others, when they say, "My head aches" or "My back aches," they are indeed permitted to stay.
This is not the case for a servant; he must simply carry out whatever task he is commanded. Therefore, he thought: "I must certainly go.
In the Nāga abode called Aruṇavatī, there arise white and blue lotuses; where shall I find them?"
Thinking thus and terrified by the fear of death, he went home in haste and said, "My dear, my meal is ready.
"It is on top of the stove, master," she replied. Unable to wait until the rice had finished cooking, he had sour gruel brought in a ladle;
then, together with whatever condiments he could find, he crammed the raw rice itself into a basket and squeezed it down.
Having taken provisions for a journey of a league, he set out; as he was walking along, his meal became cooked.
Without making it stale, he removed a small portion of the food and was eating it when he saw a traveler.
Seeing him, he said, "There is a small amount of food here that I have set aside and kept from becoming stale; take it and eat it, sir. The other took it and ate. The first one also—
Having eaten a single handful of food, he threw it into the water, rinsed his mouth, and cried out with a loud voice:
"May the nāgas, supaṇṇas, and deities dwelling in this river region listen to my words!
The king, wishing to carry out my command, has ordered me: 'Bring mud from the Aruṇavatī together with white and blue lotuses' for a traveler."
“Whatever alms-food was given by me, that has a thousandfold benefit; whatever was given to the fish in the water, that has a hundredfold benefit.
Having assigned this much fruit of merit as a gift to you, bring me the clay from the Aruṇavatī River along with white and blue lotuses,” he proclaimed three times.
Thereupon, the Nāga king dwelling there, having heard those words, [appeared] in the guise of an old man.
Having gone into his presence, he asked, "What do you say?
When the other spoke in the same manner again and said, "Give me that portion," he replied, "I give it. When told again, "Give it," he said, "I give it, sir.
Thus, after having him bring the portion two or three times, he gave the clay from the Aruṇavatī river together with white and blue lotuses.
But the king thought: "Human beings are full of guile; if he should obtain [the seal] by some means or other, my purpose would not be accomplished.
Therefore, having had the gates closed at an early hour, he had the seal brought into his presence.
The other man, arriving at the very time of the king's bath, not finding the gate open, called out to the gatekeeper.
“Open the door! he said. “It cannot be opened; the king gave the seal early in the morning and had it brought to the royal palace.

Although he said, “I am a royal messenger, open the door,” finding no access to the door, he thought, “Now there is no life for me. What indeed shall I do? and [placed] a lump of clay upon the upper bolt of the door.
Having thrown [the stone] and hung flowers upon it, he raised a great cry, shouting three times:
"O inhabitants of the city, know that I have departed by the king's command; the king wishes to destroy me without cause!
Then, reflecting, "Where indeed shall I go? he thought, "Monks are indeed gentle-hearted; I will go to the monastery and lie down."
He made this resolution: "Indeed, these beings, while they are in a state of happiness, do not even know of the existence of monks, yet when overcome by suffering, they desire to go to a monastery.
Therefore, thinking 'I have no other refuge,' he went to the monastery and lay down in a comfortable place. Then, as the king also failed to obtain sleep that night—
As he was recollecting that woman, a fever of sensual desire arose within him. He thought:
"At the very moment of dawn, I shall have that man executed and bring that woman here.
At that very instant, four men appeared, born from a sixty-league iron cauldron that had been boiling.
Cooking by turning over like rice in a frying pan,
they reached the bottom after thirty thousand years and returned to the rim after another thirty thousand years. Raising their heads and looking at one another,
desiring to speak each a single verse but unable to do so, they uttered only a single syllable each.
Having turned over, they entered right into the iron cauldrons. The king, unable to find sleep, heard that sound immediately after the middle watch;
terrified and with a trembling mind, he thought, "Will there be some obstacle to my life, or perhaps to my chief queen, or will my kingdom perish? Thus he spent the entire night with eyes wide open.
He was unable to close his eyes. At the very time of sunrise, he summoned the royal chaplain and said, "Teacher, immediately after the middle watch, I heard great and terrifying sounds.
I do not know whether there will be an obstacle for the kingdom, for the chief queen, or for myself; that is why I have had you summoned. [The chaplain replied: "Great King,"
“What sounds did you hear? “Teacher, I heard these sounds: ‘du,’ ‘sa,’ ‘na,’ and ‘so. Consider their derivation.
To the brahmin, it was as if he had entered a great darkness; nothing was discernible.
When he said, “I do not know,” [the king] feared that his gain and honor would diminish, and said, “It is a grave matter, Great King!”
He asked, "What is it, teacher? "A threat to your life is perceived," he replied. Terrified twofold, he said, "Teacher, is there any means of warding it off?
"There is, Great King; do not fear. I know the three Vedas. "But what must be obtained?
"Having performed a sacrifice of all living beings, you will regain your life."

“O gods! [he asked. “What should be obtained? [They replied: “A hundred elephants, a hundred horses, a hundred bulls, a hundred cows, a hundred goats, a hundred sheep, a hundred chickens, a hundred pigs, a hundred boys, and a hundred girls.
Thus, having caused him to take a hundred of each species of living being, [the king thought: “If I cause only the species of deer to be taken, [people will say] ‘He is taking only his own food.’”
Thinking, "They will say, 'He has them captured,'" he had even the elephant-keepers and horse-keepers captured.
The king, thinking, "My very life is my gain," said, "Capture all living beings quickly! The men who were commanded captured even more than before.
And this was also said in the *Kosalasaṃyutta*:
Now at that time, a great sacrifice was being prepared for King Pasenadi of Kosala;

five hundred bulls, five hundred young oxen, five hundred heifers, five hundred goats, and five hundred rams had been led to the sacrificial posts for the sake of the sacrifice. Of those that belonged to him...
“Whether they be slaves, messengers, or laborers—even they perform their services with tearful faces, weeping, driven by the threat of punishment and the fear of danger.
The great multitude made a loud noise, lamenting for their own sons, daughters, and kinsmen; it was like the sound of the great earth quaking.

It was as if [the king’s senses were failing]. Then Queen Mallikā, hearing that sound, went to the presence of the king and asked, "Why is it, Great King, that your faculties are not clear; you appear as if exhausted?
"What do you mean, Mallikā? Do you not know that even a venomous snake is passing right by my ear? "And what is this?"
“O gods! [he asked]. “In the middle of the night, I heard such a voice as this:
‘I have consulted the royal priest, and it appears there is a threat to your life; by performing a sacrifice of all living beings, you will regain your life.
Having heard this, thinking, ‘My very life is my gain,’ he had these creatures seized. Queen Mallikā said, “You are a blind fool, Great King! Even though—”
“You are a great eater; you consume a meal of a *doṇa* measure of cooked rice with many varieties of soups and condiments.
You rule over two kingdoms, yet your wisdom is dull,” she said. “Why do you speak thus, Queen?
“Where have you ever seen it before that by the death of one person another gains life? How [could this be] for a blind fool of a brahmin?”
When it was said, "Having taken [him], why do you cast suffering upon the great multitude?
The Teacher, the Supreme Person for the world including the devas, whose knowledge regarding the past and so forth is unimpeded, dwells in the Dhuravihāra;
go and ask him, and act according to his advice," the king, together with Mallikā, went to the monastery in light vehicles and, being terrified by the fear of death, [approached him].
Unable to say anything, he paid homage to the Teacher and sat down to one side.
Then the Teacher was the first to address him, saying, "Well now, Great King, from where have you come so early in the day?
He remained silent. Thereupon Mallikā informed the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, it seems that the king..."
"Immediately after the middle watch of the night, a sound was heard. Then he informed the chaplain. The chaplain said, 'There will be a threat to your life;

to avert it, you must take five hundred living beings and perform a sacrifice with their throat-blood, and then you shall regain your life. The king had the creatures seized, and for that reason I have brought him here."
“Is it truly so, Great King? “It is so, Bhante. “What sound did you hear? He described it exactly according to what he had heard.
As soon as the Tathāgata heard this, he became composed. Then the beings said to him:
“Do not fear, Great King; there is no danger for you. Those who have committed evil deeds spoke thus while revealing their own suffering.”
“But what, venerable sir, did they do? Then the Blessed One, wishing to explain their karma, said, “In that case, Great King, listen,” and related the past:
“In the past, when the lifespan of humans was twenty thousand years, the Blessed One Kassapa appeared in the world. Among twenty [thousand]...”
Wandering on tour together with a thousand monks whose taints were exhausted, he arrived at Bārāṇasī.
The inhabitants of Bārāṇasī, whether two, three, or even more, gathered together and established an offering for guests.

At that time, there were four friends who were sons of wealthy merchants in Bārāṇasī, possessing a fortune of four hundred million. They deliberated: "In our homes there is much wealth; by means of it—"
"What shall we do? Not a single one among them said, "When such a Buddha is wandering on his alms-round, we will give gifts, we will guard our virtue, we will perform acts of worship.
Instead, one of them said, "We will wander about drinking strong liquor and eating sweet meat;
this is the fruit of our life. Another said, "Daily..."
“Let us go about eating rice mixed with perfumes three years old, along with various choice flavors,” said one. Another spoke thus:
“Let us go about eating various kinds of baked cakes and delicacies that we have had prepared. Yet another spoke thus:
“We shall do nothing else at all; when it is said, ‘We will give you wealth,’ we women who do not desire it—”
"There is no other way; therefore, let us entice him with wealth and commit the act of adultery. "Excellent, excellent!
they all agreed, accepting his words.
From then on, they sent wealth to beautiful women, and for twenty thousand years, they committed the act of adultery.

Having died, they were reborn in the Avīci hell. After being cooked in hell for the duration of one *buddhantara*, they died there and, due to the remaining karmic residue, were reborn in a copper cauldron sixty *yojanas* in height.
Reaching the bottom after thirty thousand years, and reaching the mouth of the cauldron again after another thirty thousand years, [they recited] each verse...
Desiring to speak but unable to do so, they uttered each syllable in turn and then turned back again, falling once more into the iron cauldrons.
"Speak, Great King; what was the first sound you heard? "The syllable 'du', venerable sir," he replied.
The Teacher, completing the verse that had been spoken by him in an incomplete form, spoke thus to show it in its fullness:
“We have lived a life ill-lived, we who, though being present, did not give;
while wealth was available, we did not make an island for ourselves.

Then, having explained the meaning of this verse to the king, he asked, “Great King, did you hear a second sound, a third sound, or a fourth sound? When the king replied, “I did,” he completed the remainder [of the teaching]:
“Sixty thousand years, in their entirety;
for those being cooked in hell, when will there be an end?
There is no end, whence could there be an end? No end is in sight.”
"For indeed, dear ones, evil has been committed by me and by you.
Surely, having gone from here and obtained a human birth,
being generous and endowed with virtue, I shall perform much wholesome merit."
Having spoken these verses in succession and explained their meaning, he said: "Thus indeed, Great King, those four persons, though desiring to speak each a single verse, were unable to do so;
having uttered only a single syllable each, they fell back again into the iron cauldron.
It is said that from the moment King Pasenadi of Kosala heard that sound, they began to sink downward.
"Even now, O Noble One, they do not exceed one thousand years. Upon hearing this teaching from the King, a great sense of spiritual urgency arose within him.

He thought, "Alas, how grave indeed is this act of adultery! It is said that after being boiled in hell for the duration of an entire interval between Buddhas, one who has passed away from there is reborn in a copper cauldron sixty *yojanas* in size, and remains there for sixty thousand years."
"Even after being cooked [in hell], no time for release from their suffering appears;
yet I too, having conceived a passion for another's wife, did not find sleep all night long. From now on, I shall not bind my mind to another's wife.
Having thought thus, he said to the Tathāgata: "Venerable Sir, today I have come to know the length of the night. That man also—

Sitting right there, having heard that conversation and thinking, "I have gained a powerful supporting condition," he said to the Teacher, "Venerable Sir, the king has indeed come to know the length of the night today, but yesterday I myself recognized the length of a *yojana*.
The Teacher, having reconciled the accounts of both, said, "For one person the night is long; for another..."
"A league is long, but for a fool, saṃsāra is long," he said, and while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
"Long is the night to one who is awake; Long is the league to one who is weary;
Long is saṃsāra to fools Who do not understand the True Dhamma."
In this context, "long" refers to the night; though it consists of only three watches, for one who is awake, it appears as if doubled or tripled and thus becomes long.
Even a great indolent person, having made himself food for a swarm of bedbugs by tossing and turning until sunrise, might still feel it is long;
whereas one who has eaten a fine meal and lies upon a splendid couch [perceives it otherwise].
Even one who indulges in sensual pleasures while sleeping does not know; nor does a practitioner of yoga who exerts effort throughout the entire night;
nor a preacher of the Dhamma while delivering a discourse; nor one standing near the seat listening to the Dhamma;
nor one overcome by pain, such as being afflicted by a disease of the head or having undergone the cutting off of hands and feet; nor a traveler journeying on a road at night.
And he knows [the distance]. A "yojana" is merely four *gāvutas*; however, for one who is weary and exhausted, it becomes long and appears as if doubled or tripled.

For instance, having traveled the road all day and becoming fatigued, upon seeing someone coming from the opposite direction, he asks, "How far is the village ahead? When told, "A yojana," he travels a short distance and...
Having asked again, and that person having replied, “A *yojana*,” he goes a little further and asks yet another.
He too says, “A *yojana*. As he asks again and again, they all say it is just a *yojana*. “How long indeed is this *yojana*!
I thought it was like one, two, or three *yojanas*. [The phrase] “of fools” refers to those who do not understand the welfare of this world and the world beyond.

However, for ignorant fools who are unable to bring an end to the cycle of saṃsāra, saṃsāra is said to be "long" because they do not understand that True Dhamma consisting of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, by knowing which they make an end of saṃsāra.
Indeed, it is long by its very own nature. And this has been said: "This [saṃsāra] is without discoverable beginning..."
“Monks, saṃsāra has no known beginning. But for the foolish, who are unable to find its limit, it is indeed too long.

At the conclusion of the teaching, that man attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), and many others attained the fruits of stream-entry and beyond. The Dhamma teaching became beneficial to the great multitude.
The King, having paid homage to the Teacher, released those beings from their bonds even as he was departing. Therein were women and men.

Released from their bonds and having washed their heads, as they were returning to their own homes, they spoke in praise of Mallikā’s virtues, saying: "May our noble Queen Mallikā live long! It is because of her that we have obtained our lives.
In the evening, the monks raised this discussion in the Hall of Truth: "Oh, how wise indeed is this Mallikā! Her own..."
“Relying on wisdom, he gave the gift of life to so many people.

Hearing the conversation of those bhikkhus while sitting in the Gandhakuṭī, the Teacher emerged from the Gandhakuṭī, entered the Dhamma Hall, sat down on the prepared seat, and asked: “Bhikkhus, about what talk are you gathered here now?”
When it was said, "Is her name indeed this?", [the Buddha] replied, "No, monks. It is not only now that Mallikā, relying on her own wisdom, gives the gift of life to the great multitude;
she gave it even in the past. Having said this, he related the past to illustrate that matter:
In the past, in Bārāṇasī, the king’s son approached a banyan tree (*nigrodha-rukkha*) and there [encountered] one who had been reborn...
He made a request to the deity: "Lord, King of Devas, in this Jambudīpa there are one hundred and one kings and one hundred and one chief queens;
if I should obtain the kingdom upon my father’s passing, I shall offer a sacrifice with their blood.
When his father had died and he had obtained the kingdom, [he thought]: "I have obtained the kingdom through the power of the deity; I must offer a sacrifice to him."

Thinking, “I shall do so,” he set out with a great army, brought one king under his control, and together with him, yet another and yet another—thus bringing all the kings under his control—he departed, taking them along with their chief queens.
Now, King Uggasena, the youngest of all, had a chief queen named Dhammadinnā who was heavily pregnant; [he took her as well].
Having departed and returned, [the king] cleared the foot of the tree, thinking, "I shall give this many people poison to drink and kill them.
A deity thought: "This king, while capturing so many kings, thinks, 'These were captured by means of me,' and thus desires to offer a sacrifice to me with their blood.
If he should cause these to be killed, then in Jambudīpa..."
"The royal lineage will be cut off; even at the foot of a tree, there will be impurity for me. Will I be able to prevent this?

Examining the matter, she realized, "I shall not be able," and having approached another deity, she reported this matter to her and asked, "Will you be able? She too refused; [she approached] yet another, and yet another.
Having thus approached the deities of the entire Cakkavāḷa and being refused by them as well, he went into the presence of the Four Great Kings. When they too refused him, saying, "We are not able;
however, our king is superior to us in merit and wisdom—ask him," he approached Sakka and reported the matter to him.
“Your Majesty, when you have fallen into a state of negligence, the lineage of the Khattiyas will be cut off;
therefore, be its refuge,” he said. Sakka replied, “I too shall not be able to ward it off, but I will tell you a stratagem.
Having spoken thus, he explained the stratagem: “Go, while the king is looking on, put on red garments yourself and [approach] him...”
Having emerged from the tree, show the manner of departing. Then the king, thinking, “A deity is departing;
I will make her turn back,” will entreat you in various ways. Then you should say to him:

“You must bring one hundred and one kings together with their chief queens and offer them as a sacrifice of blood from their throats; having thus entreated me, [you shall obtain] the queen of King Uggasena.”
"He has come here having abandoned [his duty]; I do not accept the tribute of such a liar.
"When this is said, the king will surely command him; she, having taught the Dhamma to the king, will grant the gift of life to all these people.
For this reason, Sakka explained this stratagem to the deity. The deity acted accordingly.
The king also gave the order. She came and paid homage only to her own king, even though she was sitting at the edge of the assembly of those other kings.
The king became angry with her, thinking, "While I stand as the eldest of all kings, she pays homage to her own husband, who is the youngest of all.
Then she said to him, "What concern have I for you? But this man is my husband."
“Since she is the giver of sovereignty, why should I worship her without first worshipping this one?
Even as the great multitude looked on, the tree deity said, “So be it, noble lady! So be it, noble lady! and honored her with a handful of flowers.
Again the king said: “If you will not worship me, then [worship] the deity of such great power who is the giver of my royal glory.”
"Why do you not pay homage? [He replied: "Great King, you took these kings by standing upon your own merit; they were not given to you by being taken from a deity.

Again, that deity said to him, "So it is, good sir! So it is, good sir! and honored him in that very same way. Then she said to the king: "You say, 'A deity took so many kings for me and gave them to me.'"
"Now, on the left side above you, a tree has been consumed by fire;
why was she unable to extinguish that fire, if she is so possessed of great power? Again, that deity said, "So it is, Blessed One! So it is, Blessed One!
and worshipped him in the same manner.
As she stood speaking, she both wept and laughed. Then the king said to her, "Are you mad?
She replied, "Why do you say this, Your Majesty? Women like me are not mad. Then he asked, "For what reason do you weep and laugh?
She said, "Listen, Great King. In the past, having been a daughter of noble family, while living in my husband's house, I [saw] my husband..."
Seeing that a guest had arrived, wishing to cook a meal for him, I gave a kahāpaṇa to a female slave, saying, “Bring some meat.

When she returned without having obtained any meat and said, “There is no meat,” I cut off the head of a she-goat lying in the back part of the house and prepared the meal. Thus, I [cut off] the head of a single she-goat.
"Having been cut up and boiled in hell, I have reached the point of having my head cut off for the remainder of the number of hairs on her body.
'When will you be released from this suffering after killing so many people?'— thinking thus,
I wept as I recollected your suffering," she said, and spoke this verse:
“Having cut the throat of one person, you will have to count the entrails by the number of hairs;
having cut the throats of many, what will you do, O Kshatriya?
Then [the king asked], “Why are you laughing? “Because I am satisfied that ‘I am freed from this suffering,’ O Great King. Again—
The deity, saying, "So be it, lady! So be it, lady! honored her with a handful of flowers. The king thought:

"Alas, what a grievous deed I have committed! It is said that this woman attained the cutting off of her head for every single hair on the body of one ewe she slaughtered as a remnant of her time in hell;
when, after having slaughtered so many people, shall I attain safety?"

Having released all the kings, he paid homage to those who were his seniors and, raising his joined palms to those who were younger, asked forgiveness from them all and sent them back to their respective places.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said: "Thus, monks, it was not only now that Queen Mallikā [acted in this way] toward herself..."
“Relying on wisdom, he gives the gift of life to the great multitude; indeed, he has given it even in the past,” he said, and then he synchronized the past:
“At that time, King Pasenadi of Kosala was the king of Bārāṇasī, Queen Mallikā was Dhammadinnā, and I myself was the tree deity.
Having thus synchronized the past, he further taught the Dhamma: “Monks, the taking of life...”
"One who takes life is not fit to be called by that name; for those who take life grieve for a long time. Having said this, he spoke these verses:
"He grieves here, he grieves after passing away;
the doer of evil grieves in both places."
Thus he grieves, he is tormented, having seen his own defilement by karma.
“If beings would know thus: ‘This birth is the source of suffering’;”
"One should not kill living beings; for the killer of living beings grieves.
The first account: the story of a certain man.
2. The account of the co-resident disciple of the Elder Mahākassapa.
“If one does not practice,” the Teacher spoke this teaching concerning a co-resident disciple of the Elder Mahākassapa while staying at Jetavana in Sāvatthī. This instruction originated in Rājagaha.
It is said that two co-resident disciples attended upon the Elder while he was dwelling in the Pippali Cave near Rājagaha.
Of these two, one performed his duties with due care, while the other, pretending as if he himself had done whatever the former had done, [neglected them].
Having learned that water for rinsing the mouth and tooth-sticks had been prepared, he said, "Venerable sir, water for rinsing the mouth and tooth-sticks have been prepared for me;
please wash your mouth. He spoke in the same manner at the time of washing the feet, bathing, and so forth.
The other thought: "This man always makes it appear as if whatever I have done were done by himself."
"Let it be; I shall do what is appropriate for him. Having eaten, while he was still sleeping, [the other] heated bathing water, placed it in a jar, and set it on the back of the wall.

However, he left about a reed's length of water remaining in the vessel used for heating the water, so that it continued to emit steam. When the former woke up in the evening, he [sensed] the steam...
Seeing him come out, [the young monk] thought, "He must have heated some water and placed it at the gatehouse.
He went quickly, paid homage to the Elder, and said, "Venerable sir, water has been placed at the gatehouse; please bathe. Having spoken thus, he entered the gatehouse together with the Elder.
Not seeing the water, the Elder asked, "Friend, where is the water? The young monk [went to] the fire-hall.
Having gone there and lowered his water-jar into the vessel, and realizing it was empty, he complained, "Look at the deed of that wicked man!
Having placed an empty vessel on the hearth, where has he gone? I announced, 'There is water at the gatehouse.
Carrying his jar, he went to the bathing place. The other, too, having fetched water from the flour-storehouse, set it down in the storehouse.
The Elder thought: "This young man, having said, 'I have heated water and placed it at the gate;
come, venerable sir, bathe,' now goes to the bathing place carrying a jar while complaining. What can this mean?
As he reflected, he realized: "For all this time, this young man has been presenting the service he performed as if it were done by himself."
Having learned this, she returned in the evening and, as he sat down, gave him this admonition:
"Friend, it is proper for a monk to say, 'I have done only what I myself did,' and not what was not done. Just now, you said, 'Water has been placed at the gate;
bathe, venerable sir,' yet when I had entered and was standing there, you went away carrying the water-jar and complaining. For one who has gone forth..."
"It is not proper to act in this way. Becoming angry, he thought, "See what the Elder has done;
on account of a mere bit of water, he speaks to me like this! On the following day, he did not enter for alms with the Elder.
When the Elder went to a certain place together with the other, [the latter] went to the family that supported the Elder after the Elder had departed.
When asked, “Venerable sir, where is the Elder? he replied, “The Elder has become unwell; he is sitting right here in the monastery.

[The other asked], “But what, venerable sir, should be obtained? When it was said, “It seems you should give him such food as this,” they prepared it according to those instructions and gave it to him.
He ate that meal while still on the way and reached the monastery.
He had gone. The Elder, too, having obtained a large, fine cloth at the place where he had gone, gave it to the young man who had traveled with him.
He dyed it and made it his lower and upper garment.
On the following day, the Elder went to that family of supporters and said, "Venerable sir, it is said that you have become unwell."
When he said, "We prepared and sent food exactly according to the instructions given by that young monk;
having eaten it, you have become comfortable," [the elder] remained silent. But having gone to the monastery, paid homage to that young monk while he was seated, and sat down, he said to him:
"Friend, it seems that yesterday this was done by you; this is not suitable for those who have gone forth. [Regarding] the formal request..."
“...it is not permissible to eat after making a formal request. Having become angry and harboring resentment toward the elders, he thought:
“On the previous day, because of a mere drop of water, they made me out to be a liar;
today, because I ate a handful of food at my own supporter’s family, they say to me, ‘It is not permissible to eat after making a formal request. Even for the sake of a cloth...”
Thinking, "It was given to his own attendant; alas, what a grievous deed this elder has committed!

I shall find out what ought to be done with him," on the following day, as the elder was entering the village, he himself remained behind in the monastery, took a staff, broke the vessels for use, set fire to the elder’s leaf-hut, and struck with a mallet whatever did not burn.
Having broken through [the wall], he escaped and fled. After he died, he was reborn in the Avīci Great Hell.
The great multitude raised a clamor: "It seems the Elder’s co-resident, unable to endure even a mere word of advice, became angry, set fire to the leaf-hut, and fled.
Then, at a later time, a certain bhikkhu departed from Rājagaha.
Desiring to see the Teacher, he went to Jetavana, paid homage to the Teacher, and after the Teacher had exchanged greetings with him, he was asked, "From where have you come?
He replied, "From Rājagaha, Bhante. "Is it well with my son Mahākassapa?
"It is well, Bhante; however, one of his co-residents, having become angry at a mere word of exhortation—"
“Having set fire to the leaf-hut, he has fled! The Teacher said, “It is not only now that he grows angry upon hearing advice; in the past, too, he was angry.
It is not only now that he destroys the hut; in the past, too, he destroyed it. Having said this, he related the past:
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, in a region of the Himalayas, a certain Siṅgila bird built a nest...
Having done so, he lived there. Then one day, while it was raining, a certain monkey, shivering from the cold, came to that place.
Seeing him, Siṅgila spoke this verse:
“Your head is like a human’s, yet your hands and feet are those of a monkey.”
“Now, for what reason is a house not found for you?
The monkey, thinking, “Although I have hands and feet, I lack that wisdom by which one might deliberate and build a house,” and wishing to make this matter known, spoke this verse:
“I have the head of a human, and my hands and feet are like those of a porpoise.”
“That wisdom which is the best among humans—that wisdom is not found in me.
Then, reproaching him, saying, “How will a life of householdership succeed for one such as you? Siṅgila spoke these two verses:
“For one whose mind is unsteady, whose mind is fickle, and who is treacherous;”
“For one whose virtue is not constant and secure, the state of happiness does not exist.
Therefore, O monkey, exert your power; transcend your mere virtue!
Build a hut to provide protection against the cold wind.”
The monkey thought, "This bird makes me appear unstable-minded, fickle, treacherous to friends, and lacking in steadfast virtue;
now I shall demonstrate his own treacherous nature. He then destroyed the nest and scattered it about.
Even as the bird was picking up the nest, he slipped out from one side and fled.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka:
"At that time, the monkey was the monk who defiled the hut, and the Siṅgila bird was Kassapa. Having thus identified the Jātaka, he said:
"Thus, monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, he became angry at the moment of admonition and defiled the hut. This was done by my son Kassapa..."
"Living together with such a fool, it is better to dwell all alone," he said, and then recited this verse:
"If, while wandering, one does not find a companion who is one's equal, one should resolutely pursue the solitary life; for there is no companionship with a fool."

In that context, "they move" should be understood as moving by way of the mind, without grasping at the movement of physical postures; the meaning is that they seek out a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitta*).
"If one does not find anyone superior or equal"—that is, if one should not find anyone superior or equal to oneself in the qualities of virtue, concentration, and wisdom.
"Solitary wandering": for among these, one who finds someone superior increases in virtue and the other qualities, while one who finds [someone] equal...

One who gains [virtue] does not fall away from it; however, by living together with one who is inferior and sharing in common enjoyment and use, one falls away from virtue and the other qualities. Therefore it was said:
"Such a person should not be served, should not be frequented, and should not be attended upon, except out of compassion and except out of pity. Thus, if [one acts] out of compassion...
If one can sustain that person—without expecting anything from them in return, thinking, "By depending on me, this person will grow in virtue and the other qualities"—then it is well.
If one cannot do so, one should make solitude firm;
having made the state of being alone stable, one should dwell entirely alone in all postures. Why? Because there is no companionship with fools. Thus ends the section on companionship.

These are: the Minor Precepts, the Intermediate Precepts, the Major Precepts, the ten bases of discourse, the thirteen qualities of the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), the qualities of insight (*vipassanā*), the four paths, the four fruits, the three types of higher knowledge (*vijjā*), and the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*). This quality of companionship does not exist for one who relies on a fool.

At the conclusion of the teaching, the visiting monk attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*); many others also attained the fruit of stream-entry and the other fruits; thus the teaching was fruitful for the great multitude.
The second story concerning the co-resident disciple of the Elder Mahākassapa.
3. The Story of the Merchant Ānanda.
The Teacher related this teaching on the Dhamma while dwelling at Sāvatthī with reference to the merchant Ānanda.
It is said that in Sāvatthī there was a merchant named Ānanda, possessing a fortune of forty crores, who was extremely stingy.
Every half-month he would assemble his kinsmen and advise his son, Mūlasiri, at three times of day:
"Do not perceive these forty crores of wealth as 'much'; one must not give away existing wealth, but must instead produce new wealth."
For even a single kahāpaṇa coin is exhausted for one who spends it. Therefore:
“Having seen the exhaustion of collyrium, the accumulation of termites, and the gathering of honey, the wise man should dwell at home.”

Then, at a later time, without having disclosed his five great treasures to his son, he died—defiled by the stain of stinginess regarding wealth—and was reborn in a certain village near the gate of that very city among a thousand families of caṇḍālas.
There, he took conception in the womb of one of the caṇḍāla women. When the king heard of his death, he...
Having summoned his son Mūlasiri, the merchant established him in the position of the head merchant.

Furthermore, that thousand-membered outcaste clan, which had previously lived by performing labor together for a single wage, no longer received wages from that time of his rebirth onward, nor even a mere morsel of food sufficient for their sustenance. They thought, "Even as we perform labor now..."
"We do not even receive a morsel of food; there must be some ill omen among us.
Dividing themselves into two groups, they shared [the household] until his parents separated;
then, concluding that "an ill omen has arisen in this family," they cast his mother out.
She too, having obtained barely enough sustenance with great difficulty for as long as he remained in her womb, gave birth to a son.
His hands, feet, eyes, ears, nose, and mouth were not in their proper places;
being thus endowed with such a deficiency of limbs, he was exceedingly deformed, like a demon of dust. Even so, however—
His mother did not abandon him; for the affection felt toward a son who has dwelt within one’s womb is powerful.

While she was supporting him with great difficulty, she would take him along when she went out, and having received nothing that day, she would provide for him at home herself by working for wages on the following day.
Then, when he was able to live by wandering for alms, she placed an alms-bowl in his hand.
“Father, it was because of him that we fell into great suffering; I am no longer able to support him now.
In this city there is food prepared for the poor, the destitute, and others; go there and live by wandering for alms,” he said, and thus dismissed him.
Wandering from house to house, he went to the place where he had lived during the time of the merchant Ānanda.
Having become a master of his own birth, he entered his own house; yet at the first three gate-towers, no one noticed him.
At the fourth gate-tower, however, the sons of the merchant Mūlasiri saw him and, their hearts filled with agitation, wept.
Then the merchant’s men, shouting, "Get out, you ill-omened one! beat him, cast him out, and threw him into a heap of refuse.
The Teacher, with the Elder Ānanda as his attendant monk, arrived at that place while wandering for alms.
Looking at the elder, he was questioned by him and explained the circumstances. The elder summoned Mūlasiri. Then a great crowd of people gathered.
The Teacher addressed Mūlasiri, asking, "Do you know this? When he replied, "I do not know," the Teacher said:

Having said, "Ānanda, your father was a merchant," he caused him to believe by having [the merchant] explain it, saying to the one who did not believe, "Merchant Ānanda, explain the five great treasures to your son.
He then went for refuge to the Teacher. While teaching him the Dhamma, the Teacher spoke this verse:
“I have sons, I have wealth”—thus the fool is distressed.
For he does not even possess a self; how then can he have sons? How can he have wealth?
The meaning of this is: “I have sons, I have wealth”—thus the fool, through craving for sons and craving for wealth...

He is struck and afflicted, he suffers; he is afflicted by the thought, "My children have perished," he is afflicted by the thought, "They are perishing," and he is afflicted by the thought, "They will perish.
The same applies to wealth. Thus, he is afflicted in six ways.
Even while striving in various ways by day and night on land and water routes and so forth with the thought, "I shall support my children," he is afflicted.
Even one who engages in farming, trade, and so forth with the thought, “I will produce wealth,” is still tormented.
For one who is thus tormented, there is no self of one's own; and for one who is unable to make that self, which is afflicted by such distress, happy, there is no self even in his continued activity.
This is also the case for one lying on the bed of death, overcome by the sensations of the moment of passing away.

Even for one who has bathed him twice daily, fed him thrice, adorned him with perfumes, garlands, and the like, and supported him throughout his life as a companion— while that person is being consumed as if by flames of fire,

while the joints of his body are being severed, and while the framework of his bones is being shattered— he closes his eyes to this world and opens them to the next; thus, even such support is no protection from suffering.
Because one lacks the power to act for oneself, one does not truly belong to oneself. How then could sons or wealth help?

At such a time, what indeed can sons or wealth do? Whether it was previously when the merchant Ānanda lay upon his deathbed, or now that he has encountered this suffering, he has established wealth for the sake of his son without giving anything to anyone else.
“Where are my sons? Where is my wealth? At that moment, what suffering did his sons or his wealth remove for him, or what happiness did they produce?
At the conclusion of the teaching, eighty-four thousand beings attained penetration of the Dhamma. The teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.
The Third Story: The Case of the Merchant Ānanda.
4. The Story of the Thug.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning a thug who broke open neck-ties. "He who is a fool... [he said].
It is said that those two companions went to Jetavana with a great crowd of people who were going for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma;
one of them heard the discourse on the Dhamma, while the other looked at his own waist-cloth.
Of these two, the one listening to the Dhamma attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), while the other obtained only five māsakas tied in the hem of a certain man’s garment. To him—
Cooked rice was prepared in his house, but in the other man’s house, no food was cooked.

Then the thief who was his companion, mocking him along with his own wife, said: "Because of your excessive cleverness, you have not even managed to provide the cost for the cooked rice in your own house.
But the other replied: "Indeed, it is only because of his foolishness that he imagines himself to be wise!"
Having gone to Jetavana with his kinsmen to report this matter to the Teacher, he informed him.
While teaching the Dhamma to him, the Teacher spoke this verse:
“He who considers himself a fool is thereby wise; but he who considers himself wise is truly a fool.”
“And the fool who fancies himself wise—he indeed is called a ‘fool.
In this context, “the fool” refers to one who, being blind and unwise, perceives and recognizes his own foolishness and state of folly, thinking, “I am a fool.
For that reason, such a person is either truly wise or resembles a wise man.
Or rather: for he, knowing "I am a fool," approaches and attends upon another who is wise;
being exhorted and instructed by that wise person for the sake of wisdom, and having accepted that instruction, he becomes either wise or even wiser.
He indeed is called a fool who, while being a fool himself, thinks, "Who else is my equal in being learned?"...
