Thinking, "There is a preacher of the Dhamma, or one who upholds the Vinaya, or one who upholds the ascetic practices," he thus fancies himself wise.
Without approaching or paying homage to another wise person, he neither learns the scriptures nor fulfills the practice;
he reaches only the state of absolute foolishness. He is like a thief who cuts through a knot [to steal]. Therefore it was said: "He..."
"He is called a fool.
At the conclusion of this teaching, at the end of the discourse, the great multitude together with the relatives of the other attained the fruit of stream-entry and the other fruits.
This is the fourth story, concerning the thief who broke the knot.
5. The Story of the Elder Udāyī "Even for as long as life lasts, the fool..."—the Teacher delivered this teaching on the Dhamma while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Elder Udāyī.
It is said that when the great elders had departed, he went to the Dhamma Hall and sat upon the Dhamma seat. Then, [the Teacher addressed] him...

One day, seeing some visiting monks, they thought, "This must be a learned great elder," and after asking him questions concerning the aggregates and so forth, finding that he knew nothing at all, they reviled him, saying, "Who is this?
Living in the same monastery as the Buddhas, he does not even know the mere aggregates, elements, and sense bases! They then reported this matter...
They informed the Tathāgata. As the Teacher was teaching the Dhamma to them, he spoke this verse:
“Even if a fool attends upon a wise man for as long as his life lasts, he does not understand the Dhamma, just as a spoon [does not know] the taste of the soup.”

The meaning of this is as follows: even if a fool were to approach and attend upon a wise person for the rest of his life, he would not come to know the Dhamma of the scriptures thus: "This is the word of the Buddha; this much is the word of the Buddha"; nor would he know: "This is the proper conduct, this is the dwelling, this is the behavior, this is the sphere of activity;
this is blameworthy, this is blameless; this is to be cultivated, this is not to be cultivated."
He does not know the Dhamma of practice and penetration in this way: "This is to be penetrated; this is to be realized. How is it like?
It is like a ladle and the taste of soup. For just as a ladle, even while being turned around in various kinds of prepared soups until they are completely exhausted, does not know:
"This is salty; this is unsalty; this is bitter..."
"Just as one who does not know the taste of a curry—thinking, 'This is pungent,' 'This is sour,' 'This is not sour,' or 'This is bitter'—does not understand it;
even so, a fool, though attending upon a wise man for as long as his life lasts, does not understand the Dhamma of the kind described.
At the conclusion of the teaching, the minds of the visiting bhikkhus were liberated from the taints.
The fifth story: The Elder Udāyī.
The sixth story: The Thirty Bhikkhus of Pāveyyaka.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, delivered this teaching on the Dhamma beginning with the words, "Even for a moment, if a wise man... concerning thirty bhikkhus from Pāveyya.
For while they were searching for a woman, the Blessed One first taught the Dhamma to them in a cotton-wood forest.

At that time, having all received the "Come, monk" (ehibhikkhu) ordination and wearing robes and bowls produced by supernormal power (iddhimaya), they undertook and observed the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅga).
Then, after a long period of time had passed, they again approached the Teacher and [heard] the teaching on the beginningless cycle of existence (anamatagga-dhammadesanā).
Having heard it, they attained Arahatship on that very seat. The monks, remarking, "Oh, how quickly the Dhamma was understood by these bhikkhus!
raised the matter in the Hall of Truth. The Teacher, hearing this, said: "Monks, it is not only now;
formerly also, when these thirty friends were rogues, while [listening to] Mahātuṇḍila in the Tuṇḍila Jātaka..."
"Even though they heard the teaching of the Dhamma, they quickly understood the Dhamma and undertook the five precepts.
By that very support, they have now attained Arahantship even on this very seat where we are sitting. Having said this, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
"If a wise person attends upon one who is learned, even for a moment;..."
“He quickly understands the Dhamma, just as the tongue perceives the flavor of soup.

This is its meaning: if a wise, learned person attends upon another wise person for even a moment, he quickly understands the Dhamma of the scriptures by learning from him and by questioning him. From that, [he understands] the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Having thus spoken, one who strives and exerts himself in practice understands even the supramundane Dhamma very quickly—
just as a person with an unimpaired sense of taste, having placed on the tip of the tongue various flavors such as salt and so forth for the purpose of discerning their taste,
perceives them exactly as they are. Thus does the wise person understand.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many bhikkhus attained arahantship.
This is the sixth story, concerning the thirty or so bhikkhus from Pāveyyaka. 7.
The Story of the Leper Suppabuddha.

"The foolish, the witless, wander about"—the Teacher delivered this Dhamma teaching while residing at Veḷuvana concerning the leper Suppabuddha. The story of the leper Suppabuddha has already appeared in the Udāna.
At that time, the leper Suppabuddha, sitting on the edge of the assembly, heard the Blessed One’s Dhamma teaching and attained the fruit of stream-entry.
Desiring to inform the Teacher of the quality he had acquired, yet being unable to venture into the midst of the assembly, [he remained there].

After the great multitude had paid homage to the Teacher and followed him for some distance, they turned back, and Suppabuddha went to the monastery. At that moment, Sakka, the king of the gods, knowing that the leper Suppabuddha desired to make manifest the qualities he had acquired through his Teacher’s dispensation, thought, “I shall test him,” and approaching while standing in the air, he said this: “Suppabuddha,The result of your actions is like a shadow that never leaves you. You have committed a grave offense against the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha. For that reason, you will suffer for an eon in hell. When he spoke thus, Suppabuddha replied, “Great King, I did not do it intentionally; I was driven by madness. Please forgive me. “Leper, even if you were driven by madness, you still committed a grave offense against the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha. For that reason, you will suffer for an eon in hell. A second time and a third time, Suppabuddha replied, “Great King, I did not do it intentionally; I was driven by madness. Please forgive me. A second and a third time, Sakka said, “Leper, even if you were driven by madness, you still committed a grave offense against the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha. For that reason, you will suffer for an eon in hell. Then Suppabuddha, with tears streaming down his face, cried out: “Venerable sir, I have committed a grave offense against the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha. May I be reborn in the Avīci hell! “Leper, even if you were driven by madness, you still committed a grave offense against the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha. For that reason, you will suffer for an eon in hell. Having spoken thus, Sakka departed. (1) Then Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, he said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, when the leper Suppabuddha was about to die, he made a solemn declaration. What is the destination, what is his future state? (2) “Ānanda, if Suppabuddha had died seven days ago, he would have been reborn in the Avīci hell. But because he has seen the Truth, he has attained the fruit of stream-entry. (3) Then the leper Suppabuddha, having made his solemn declaration, passed away and was reborn in the Avīci hell. (4) Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? (1) One who commits an offense intentionally and does not see it as an offense; (2) one who commits an offense unintentionally and sees it as an offense; (3) one who commits an offense intentionally and sees it as an offense; and (4) one who commits an offense unintentionally and does not see it as an offense. (5) “Bhikkhus, the person who commits an offense intentionally and does not see it as an offense is called the worst of persons. Why is that? Because he is unrepentant and does not seek purification. This person is reckoned the worst among persons. (6) “The person who commits an offense unintentionally but sees it as an offense is called a good person. Why is that? Because he is repentant and seeks purification. This person is reckoned a good person among persons. (7) “The person who commits an offense intentionally and sees it as an offense is called a middling person. Why is that? Because he is repentant and seeks purification. This person is reckoned a middling person among persons. (8) “The person who commits an offense unintentionally and does not see it as an offense is called a superior person. Why is that? Because he is unrepentant and does not seek purification. This person is reckoned a superior person among persons. (9) “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? (1) One who commits an offense intentionally and does not see it as an offense; (2) one who commits an offense unintentionally and sees it as an offense; (3) one who commits an offense intentionally and sees it as an offense; and (4) one who commits an offense unintentionally and does not see it as an offense. Because he is unrepentant and does not seek purification. This person is reckoned the worst among persons. Because he is repentant and seeks purification. This person is reckoned a middling person among persons. This person is reckoned a superior person among persons. (14) Then the leper Suppabuddha, having made his solemn declaration, passed away and was reborn in the Avīci hell. (22) “Bhikkhus, the person who commits an offense intentionally and does not see it as an offense is called the worst of persons. Why is that? Because he is unrepentant and does not seek purification. This person is reckoned the worst among persons. This person is reckoned a good person among persons. (24) “The person who commits an offense intentionally and sees it as an offense is called a middling person. Why is that? Because he is repentant and seeks purification. This person is reckoned a middling person among persons. This person is reckoned a superior person among persons. (26) Then the leper Suppabuddha, having made his solemn declaration, passed away and was reborn in the Avīci hell. (27) Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? (1) One who commits an offense intentionally and does not see it as an offense; (2) one who commits an offense unintentionally and sees it as an offense; (3) one who commits an offense intentionally and sees it as an offense; and (4) one who commits an offense
“You are a poor man, a wretched man among men; I shall give you boundless wealth. Say:
‘The Buddha is not the Buddha, the Dhamma is not the Dhamma, the Saṅgha is not the Saṅgha; enough for me of the Buddha, enough for me of the Dhamma, enough for me of the Saṅgha.
Then he said to him, “Who are you? “I am Sakka. “O blind fool!”
“O shameless one, you are not fit to speak with me!
You call me ‘miserable, poor, and wretched,’ yet I am neither miserable nor poor; I have attained happiness and possess great wealth:
‘The wealth of faith, the wealth of virtue, and the wealth of moral shame and dread of blame;’”
“Learning, wealth, and generosity, and wisdom indeed as the seventh treasure—
for whatever woman or man possesses these treasures,
they say of them, ‘He is not poor’; their life is not in vain.”
“I possess these seven kinds of noble wealth; for those who possess these seven riches are not called ‘poor’ by the Buddhas or the Paccekabuddhas.
When Sakka heard his words, he left him on the way and went into the presence of the Teacher, reporting all of that dialogue. Then the Blessed One—

He said: “No indeed, Sakka; even with a hundred or a thousand such as those, it would not be possible to make the leper Suppabuddha say, ‘He is not a Buddha,’ or ‘This is not the Dhamma,’ or ‘This is not the Saṅgha.
Then the leper Suppabuddha went into the presence of the Teacher, and having been greeted by the Teacher, he exchanged friendly greetings with him.
Having announced the qualities he had attained within himself, he rose from his seat and departed. Not long after he had left, a cow with a young calf took his life.
It is said that she was a certain *yakkhinī* who [had previously killed] the noble son Pukkusāti, Bāhiya Dārucīriya, and Tambadāṭhika the executioner.
Regarding Suppabuddha and Kuṭṭhi: in many hundreds of previous existences, he took the lives of these four people when they had been cows.
It is said that in the past, having been the sons of four wealthy merchants, they took a city’s most beautiful courtesan to a pleasure grove;
after enjoying the splendors of the day, at the time of evening, they deliberated thus: "In this place..."
“There is no other way; let us take this thousand kahāpaṇas and all her jewelry that we gave her, kill her, and go.
When she heard their words, she thought, “These men are shameless; having enjoyed themselves with me, they now wish to kill me.
I shall know what is appropriate to do for them. As she was being killed by them, she cried out, “I am a yakkhinī!”
Having made this offering, he formed a wish: "May they be able to kill me in exactly the same way that these men are killing me.
By the result of that [kamma], he killed these [men]. A number of bhikkhus, having reported his death to the Blessed One, asked:
"What was his destination, and for what reason did he fall into the state of a leper? The Teacher [declared] the fruit of stream-entry.
Having related how he had been reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and how, upon seeing the Paccekabuddha Tagarasikhī,
he had spat at him and passed him on his left side, and having explained that after suffering in hell for a long time he had now attained the state of a leper as a residual result of that karma,
[the Buddha said]: "Monks, these beings wander about performing for themselves deeds that result in bitter retribution."
Having spoken thus and established the connection, he taught the Dhamma further by reciting this verse:
“Fools of dull wit live as if they were their own enemies,
performing evil deeds that bear bitter fruit.”
“They wander there” means they roam about performing only unwholesome deeds through the four modes of conduct (*iriyāpatha*).

“Fools” (*bāla*) refers to those here who do not understand the welfare of this world or the welfare of the next world; such are called fools here. “Wiseless” (*dummedha*) means lacking discernment (*paññā*).
“As by an enemy oneself” (*attanā amitteneva*) means as if by one’s own self having become an enemy or a foe. “Bitter fruit” (*kaṭukapphala*) means sharp fruit, that is, fruit of suffering.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the seventh story, that of the leper Suppabuddha. 8.
The Story of the Farmer.
"This deed that has been done is not good"—this teaching on the Dhamma was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain farmer.
It is said that he was plowing a field not far from Sāvatthī.
Thieves entered the city through a drainage ditch, broke into the inner chamber of a wealthy family, and having taken much gold and bullion, [departed] by way of the same drainage ditch.

They departed. One thief, having deceived them, tucked a purse containing a thousand [pieces of gold] into his waistband, went to that field, divided the goods with them, and as he was departing taking his share, he failed to notice the purse of a thousand pieces falling from his waistband.
On that day, at dawn, the Teacher surveyed the world and beheld that farmer.
Seeing that he had entered the net of his knowledge, and reflecting, "What indeed will happen?", he perceived this:

"This farmer will go out to plow early in the morning; the owners of the goods, having followed the thieves' tracks, will see the purse containing a thousand pieces falling from his waistband and seize it; and there will be no witness for him other than me."
“...that name shall not exist; furthermore, he possesses the necessary support (upanissaya) for the path of stream-entry, so it is fitting for me to go there.
That farmer had already gone early in the morning to plow. The Teacher went there with the Elder Ānanda as his attendant monk.
Upon seeing the Teacher, the farmer went to pay homage to the Blessed One and then resumed his plowing. The Teacher [addressed] him...
Without saying anything further, he went to the place where the thousand-fold purse had fallen;
seeing it, he said to the Elder Ānanda, "Look, Ānanda, there is a venomous snake! "I see it, Bhante; it is a fierce-venomed one.
Hearing those words, the farmer thought, "This is a place where one wanders at any time, whether it be the right time or not; here is a venomous snake."
Thinking, "Is there perhaps something here? when the Teacher had spoken thus and departed, he took up his goad-stick with the intent, "I shall kill him," and went on.
Seeing a bundle of a thousand coins, he thought, "The Teacher must have been speaking with reference to this," so he took it and turned back;
out of incompetence, he set it aside in a secluded spot, covered it with dust, and went back to plow again.
He began. When the night had turned to dawn, people saw the work the thieves had done at their houses;
following the footprints step by step, they went to that field and, seeing there the place where the thieves had divided the goods, they saw the tracks of the farmer.
Following those tracks, they went on until they saw the place where [the goods] had been placed in a bag; there they cleared away the dust.
Taking his bag, they rebuked him, saying, "You wander about like one who, having plundered a house, is now plowing a field!
Having beaten and struck him, they led him away and presented him to the king. When the king heard of this incident, he ordered his execution.
The king’s men bound his hands behind his back and led him to the place of execution while lashing him with whips. As he was being whipped...
Without saying anything else, he went along saying, "See, Ānanda, it is a venomous snake; I see, Blessed One, it is a fierce-venomed one.
Then the king’s men asked him, "You speak as if you were the Teacher and the Elder Ānanda; what is this?
When he replied, "I shall speak when I am permitted to see the King," they led him into the presence of the King.
They related that occurrence to him. Then the king asked him, "Why did you speak thus?
He replied, "I am not a thief, Your Majesty," and recounted the entire sequence of events to the king from the time he had set out for the purpose of plowing.
Having heard his words, the king said, "Tell me, this man has taken as his witness the Teacher, the foremost person in the world."
“He makes excuses; it is not right to attribute fault to him. I shall know what must be done here.
Taking him with him, he went to the presence of the Teacher in the evening and asked the Teacher:
“Blessed One, did you go to that farmer’s field for plowing together with the Elder Ānanda? “Yes, Great King,” he replied.
“What did you see there? “A purse containing a thousand coins, Great King. “What did you say when you saw it? “We said, ‘This is it, Great King.
“Venerable sirs, had this man not identified someone like you, he would not have regained his life;
but because he spoke the words you spoke, he obtained his life. Thus it was.
Having heard this, the Teacher said, “Yes, Great King, I too went away after saying only this much. Indeed, a wise man should not perform such an action as that which causes remorse later.
Having spoken thus, he established the connection and, teaching the Dhamma, recited this verse:
“That deed is not well done which, having been done, one regrets;
for which, weeping with a tearful face, one experiences the result.
In this context, “that deed” refers to that action of a painful nature which is capable of causing rebirth in the hells and other such realms.
"Recalling," he regrets and grieves at the moment of what was recalled; that which was done was not good, not beautiful, and was fruitless.
"Whose face is wet with tears" means whose face is drenched with tears as he weeps while experiencing the result.
At the conclusion of the teaching, the lay follower who was a farmer attained the fruit of stream-entry, and the assembled monks also attained the fruits of stream-entry and the other stages.
The Eighth Story: The Farmer. The Ninth Story:
The Flower-Garland Maker Sumanas.
"That deed was well done"—the Teacher related this Dhamma teaching concerning the flower-garland maker named Sumanas while residing at Veḷuvana.
It is said that he received eight kahāpaṇas every day for attending upon King Bimbisāra at dawn with eight stalks of jasmine flowers.
Then one day, just as he had entered the city after taking those flowers,
the Blessed One— surrounded by a great community of monks and emitting six-colored rays of light— appeared with the magnificent majesty of a Buddha.
With the great grace of a Buddha, he entered the city for alms. For the Blessed One sometimes walks with his six-colored rays concealed by his robe,
like one of the ordinary alms-gatherers— as when he went out to meet Aṅgulimāla over a journey of thirty leagues—
and at other times he emits those six-colored rays, as when he entered Kapilavatthu and on similar occasions.
On that day as well, emitting rays of six colors from his body, he entered Rājagaha with great majesty of a Buddha and with the grand deportment of a Buddha.

Seeing the Blessed One’s physical form, which resembled a priceless jewel, and beholding the splendor of his body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor characteristics, the garland-maker’s heart was filled with serene faith.
Thinking, "What service indeed can I perform for the Teacher? and seeing no other way, he thought, "I shall honor the Blessed One with these flowers.
Then he reflected further: "These are the flowers regularly offered to the King;
if the King does not receive them, he might have me bound, or have me executed, or banish me from the kingdom. What then?"
"Shall I do it? Then this thought occurred to him: "The king might have me executed, or have me imprisoned, or banish me from the kingdom;
for even if he were to give to me, he could only give the wealth of mere life in this present existence.
But worship of the Teacher is sufficient for my welfare and happiness throughout many millions of eons. Thus, he surrendered his own life to the Tathāgata.
Thinking, "As long as my mind does not turn back from its faith, I shall perform worship for that long," he, joyful, delighted, and exultant, worshipped the Teacher.
How so? First, he threw two handfuls of flowers over the Tathāgata;
they remained suspended above his head like a canopy. He threw another two handfuls, and they—
Descending by way of the right side, which was covered with garlands and cloth, they stood there. Another threw two handfuls;
these also descended by way of the back and stood in the same manner. Another threw two handfuls;
these descended by way of the left side and stood in the same manner. Thus, having become eight *nāḷis* and eight handfuls, they were situated in four places.
They surrounded the Tathāgata. There was only enough space for him to pass through the front.
The flower stalks were on the inside, while the petals faced outward. The Blessed One proceeded as if encircled by silver plates.
Even though the flowers were insentient, by depending upon the Sentient One, they moved along with the Teacher as if they themselves possessed sentience, neither falling away nor being left behind.
They go; they stand wherever there is a place to stand. From the Teacher’s body, rays of light issued forth like hundreds of thousands of lightning flashes.

From the front, the back, the right, the left, and from the very top of his head, as the rays issued forth without interval, not even a single one fled from its position directly in front, but all remained.
Having circumambulated the Teacher three times, they grew to the size of young palm trunks and ran right before him.
The entire city was thrown into commotion. Within the city there were nine crores, and outside the city another nine crores;
among these eighteen crores of people, there was not a single man or woman who did not go out taking alms.
The great multitude went before the Teacher, letting out lion-roars and performing thousands of leaps.
The Teacher, too, in order to make the florist’s virtue manifest, traveled through the city—which measured three gavutas—by way of the path where the drum was beaten.
The entire body of the florist was filled with five-colored rapture.

Having thus traveled with the Tathāgata for only a short distance, as if submerged in liquid emerald and entered within the Buddha’s rays, he praised and paid homage to the Teacher. Taking an empty bowl, he returned home.
Then his wife asked him, "Where are the flowers? "The Teacher was honored by me," he replied. "What then of the King? she asked.
“Will you do it? [He replied: “Let the king have me executed or banish me from the kingdom;
I sacrificed my life to honor the Teacher, and all the flowers became only eight handfuls—such was the nature of the offering that arose.
The great multitude follows along with the Teacher, raising thousands of shouts of acclamation; as for this sound of the multitude’s acclamation...”

“At that place is he. Then his wife, out of blind folly, failing to conceive faith in such a miracle, reviled and abused him, saying, “Kings are indeed fierce; once provoked, they cause great harm by cutting off hands, feet, and so forth.
Because of the deed you have done, there may be harm for me as well. Taking her children, she went to the royal palace.
Having gone and been summoned by the king, when asked, "What is this?", she said:
"My husband, having worshipped the Teacher with flowers for your service, returned home empty-handed; when I asked him, 'Where are the flowers?', he spoke these words.
I rebuked him, saying, 'Kings are indeed fierce; once they are angry, they [punish] by the cutting off of hands, feet, and so forth.'"
"He has done much harm; because of the deed you committed, there might have been harm for me as well. Having abandoned him, we have come here.
Whether the deed he performed was well-done or ill-done, it belongs to him alone.
Know, O King, that he has been abandoned by me. At the very first sight of him, the King attained the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) and became full of faith.
The noble disciple, being full of faith, thought: "Alas, this woman is blind and foolish; she does not produce faith toward such qualities.
Acting as if angry, he said: "Mother, what are you saying? Was an offering made by her with those flowers intended for my service?
"Yes, sir," she replied. "It was a good deed done by her in discarding them, compared to one who performs an offering with my own flowers."
"I shall know what is appropriate to be done," he said; having dismissed him, he went swiftly to the presence of the Teacher, paid homage, and remained in the company of the Teacher.
The Teacher, perceiving the king's serene confidence, wandered through the city along the streets where the drums were beaten, and arrived at the door of the king’s palace.
He arrived. The king, taking the bowl, desired to lead the Teacher into his palace; however, the Teacher indicated by his posture that he wished to sit right there in the royal courtyard.
The king, perceiving this, commanded, "Erect a pavilion quickly! and had a pavilion constructed at that very moment.
The Teacher sat down together with the community of monks. But why did the Teacher not enter the king's palace?
Thus it occurred to him: "If I were to enter inside and sit down, the great multitude would not be able to see me, and the florist's merit would not become manifest.
But if I sit in the royal courtyard, the great multitude will be able to see me, and the florist's merit will become manifest. For the Buddhas [reveal] the merit of those who possess merit.
Only those who are capable can make this manifest; as for the rest of the people, they feel envy even while speaking of the virtues of the virtuous.
Four flower-canopies stood in the four directions. The great multitude surrounded the Teacher.
The King served the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, headed by the Buddha, with exquisite food. At the conclusion of the meal, the Teacher gave a blessing of thanksgiving.
Surrounded by four flower-cloths just as before, roaring his lion’s roar and encircled by a great multitude, he went to the monastery.
The King, having followed the Teacher and then turned back, summoned the florist and asked, "What did you do with the flowers I brought?
How did you honor the Teacher? The florist replied, "The King might have had me executed or banished from the kingdom..."
"May he ordain me," he said, and having renounced his life, he honored him, O gods. The king, saying,
"You are indeed a Great Man (Mahāpurisa)," brought forth from the royal palace eight elephants, horses, male slaves, female slaves, great ornaments,
eight thousand kahāpaṇas, eight women adorned with every kind of finery, and eight excellent villages.
He gave this gift known as the "Gift of All Eight.
The Elder Ānanda thought: "From early this morning, thousands of lion-roars and thousands of the waving of cloths have been occurring;
what indeed will be the karmic result for this garland-maker? He questioned the Teacher, who then [spoke] to him.
He said: "Ānanda, do not think that this garland-maker has performed only a trifling deed;
for he has performed this worship by sacrificing his own life. Having thus gained confidence in my heart, he will not go to a state of misery for a hundred thousand eons."
"Having attained the fruit of this deed among gods and humans,
he shall afterwards become a Paccekabuddha named Sumana," he said. Then,
having gone to the Teacher’s monastery at the time of entering the Gandhakuti, those flowers [were placed] at the door-porch.
They fell [at his feet]. In the evening, the monks initiated a discussion in the Dhamma hall:

“Oh, how wonderful is the work of this garland-maker! Having sacrificed his life for a living Buddha and performed an offering of flowers, he obtained at that very moment the name ‘All-Prosperous’ (Sabbatthaka).
The Teacher emerged from the Fragrant Chamber by one of the three ways of departing.
Having gone to the Dhamma Hall by means of his supernormal power and sat upon the Buddha’s seat,
he asked, “Monks, about what topic are you gathered here now? When they replied, “About this very one,” he said, “Indeed, monks,
regarding that deed for which there is no remorse after it has been done, and at every moment it is remembered, only joy arises.”
"Such a deed indeed ought to be done," he said, and joining the context together while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
"That deed is well done which, having been done, one does not regret;
That deed is well done whose ripening one enjoys with a joyful and happy mind."

In this context, "having done that" means: having performed wholesome action (*kamma*) characterized by happiness, which is capable of producing both the attainments of gods and humans as well as the attainment of *nibbāna*, one does not regret it;

rather, in this very life, at every moment of recollection, one becomes enraptured by the surge of rapture (*pīti*), cheerful through the surge of joy (*somanassa*), and thus gives rise to rapture and joy for the future.
He experiences the ripening [of that deed], thinking, "That deed done was good and auspicious.
At the conclusion of the teaching, there was a penetration of the Dhamma by eighty-four thousand living beings.
This is the ninth story, the Story of Sumanā the Garland-maker.

10. The Story of the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching beginning with the words, "As honey, so he thinks," concerning the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā.
It is said that she had made a resolution at the feet of Padumuttara Buddha and had performed meritorious deeds for a hundred thousand eons.
While wandering through births among gods and humans, she passed away from the world of the gods during this current dispensation of a Buddha and took rebirth in a merchant’s family in Sāvatthī.
Because her complexion was like the interior of a blue lotus, they gave her the name Uppalavaṇṇā.
Then, when she had reached maturity, kings and merchants throughout the whole of Jambudīpa [sought her hand] from that merchant...

They sent a message to him, saying, "Give us your daughter. There was no one who did not send such a request. Then the merchant thought, "I will not be able to satisfy everyone's wishes; however, I shall employ a certain stratagem. He summoned his daughter and said, "My dear child, will you be able to go forth into the religious life? Because she was in her final existence (*pacchimabhavikā*), she replied, "Father, I am able. The merchant thought, "If she goes forth, I shall be able to satisfy everyone's wishes. He then had a monastery built for her. When she had gone forth, he gave her a set of robes, a bowl, and other requisites, and provided her with a dwelling place. He then sent a message to all those who had requested her hand, saying, "My daughter has gone forth. Hearing this, they were filled with resentment and said, "We have been deceived by this merchant. They gathered together and went to the merchant’s house. The merchant, seeing them, rose from his seat and paid them homage. They said, "Merchant, why do you deceive us? You promised to give us your daughter, yet you have given her to another. The merchant replied, "Sirs, I did not deceive you. My daughter has gone forth. They said, "Merchant, we do not believe you. If you do not give her to us, we shall seize her by force. The merchant thought, "If I refuse them now, they will surely seize her by force; therefore, I shall employ a different stratagem. He then sent for his daughter and said, "Daughter, can you endure the hardships of the forest life? She replied, "Father, I can. The merchant then had a large, beautiful hut constructed in the forest and furnished it with every comfort. He placed a bed inside and provided her with food and drink. He then sent a message to those who had come seeking her, saying, "My daughter is staying in the forest; you may go and see her. They went there and saw her, and thinking, "She is indeed living in the forest," they departed. The merchant thought, "Now I have satisfied everyone's wishes. He then summoned his daughter and said, "Daughter, you have fulfilled your duty; you may return home. She replied, "Father, I have no desire to return to the household life. The merchant said, "Daughter, if you do not wish to return, at least come back once a month. She agreed to this. Thus, she would return once a month. The merchant then had a large, beautiful mansion built near the city gate and furnished it with every luxury. He provided her with a retinue of five hundred women and gave her all manner of fine garments and ornaments. He then sent a message to those who had come seeking her, saying, "My daughter is staying in the mansion; you may go and see her. They went there and saw her, and thinking, "She is indeed living in the world," they departed. The merchant thought, "Now I have completely satisfied everyone's wishes. He then summoned his daughter and said, "Daughter, you have fulfilled your duty; you may return home. She replied, "Father, I have no desire to return to the household life. The merchant said, "Daughter, if you do not wish to return, at least come back once a fortnight. She agreed to this. Thus, she would return once every fortnight. The merchant then had a large, beautiful mansion built near the city center and furnished it with every luxury. He provided her with a retinue of five hundred women and gave her all manner of fine garments and ornaments. He then sent a message to those who had come seeking her, saying, "My daughter is staying in the mansion; you may go and see her. They went there and saw her, and thinking, "She is indeed living in the world," they departed. The merchant thought, "Now I have completely satisfied everyone's wishes. He then summoned his daughter and said, "Daughter, you have fulfilled your duty; you may return home. She replied, "Father, I have no desire to return to the household life. The merchant said, "Daughter, if you do not wish to return, at least come back once a week. She agreed to this. Thus, she would return once a week. The merchant then had a large, beautiful mansion built near the palace and furnished it with every luxury. He provided her with a retinue of five hundred women and gave her all manner of fine garments and ornaments. He then sent a message to those who had come seeking her, saying, "My daughter is staying in the mansion; you may go and see her. They went there and saw her, and thinking, "She is indeed living in the world," they departed. The merchant thought, "Now I have completely satisfied everyone's wishes. He then summoned his daughter and said, "Daughter, you have fulfilled your duty; you may return home. She replied, "Father, I have no desire to return to the household life. The merchant said, "Daughter, if you do not wish to return, at least come back once every three days. She agreed to this. Thus, she would return once every three days. The merchant then had a large, beautiful mansion built near the city wall and furnished it with every luxury. He provided her with a retinue of five hundred women and gave her all manner of fine garments and ornaments. He then sent a message to those who had come seeking her, saying, "My daughter is staying in the mansion; you may go and see her. They went there and saw her, and thinking, "She is indeed living in the world," they departed. The merchant thought, "Now I have completely satisfied everyone's wishes. He then summoned his daughter and said, "Daughter, you have fulfilled your duty; you may return home. She replied, "Father, I have no desire to return to the household life. The merchant said, "Daughter, if you do not wish to return, at least come back once every day. She agreed to this. Thus, she would return once every day. The merchant then had a large, beautiful mansion built right next to his own house and furnished it with every luxury. He provided her with a retinue of five hundred women and gave her all manner of fine garments and ornaments. He then sent a message to those who had come seeking her, saying, "My daughter is staying in the mansion; you may go and see her. They went there and saw her, and thinking, "She is indeed living in the world," they departed. The merchant thought, "Now I have completely satisfied everyone's wishes. He then summoned his daughter and said, "Daughter, you have fulfilled your duty; you may return home. She replied, "Father, I have no desire to return to the household life. The merchant said, "Daughter, if you do not wish to return, at least come back every morning. She agreed to this. Thus, she would return every morning. The merchant then had a large, beautiful mansion built right next to his own bedroom and furnished it with every luxury. He provided her with a retinue of five hundred women and gave her all manner of fine garments and ornaments. He then sent a message to those who had come seeking her, saying, "My daughter is staying in the mansion; you may go and see her. They went there and saw her, and thinking, "She is indeed living in the world," they departed. The merchant thought, "Now I have completely satisfied everyone's wishes. He then summoned his daughter and said, "Daughter, you have fulfilled your duty; you may return home. She replied, "Father, I have no desire to return to the household life. The merchant said, "Daughter, if you do not wish to return, at least come back every evening. She agreed to this. Thus, she would return every evening. The merchant then had a large, beautiful mansion built right next to his own bedchamber and furnished it with every luxury. He provided her with a retinue of five hundred women and gave her all manner of fine garments and ornaments. He then sent a message to those who had come seeking her, saying, "My daughter is staying in the mansion; you may go and see her. They went there and saw her, and thinking, "She is indeed living in the world," they departed. The merchant thought, "Now I have completely satisfied everyone's wishes. He then summoned his daughter and said, "Daughter, you have fulfilled your duty; you may return home. She replied, "Father, I have no desire to return to the household life. The merchant said, "Daughter, if you do not wish to return, at least come back once every two days. She agreed to this. Thus, she would return once every two days. The merchant then had a large, beautiful mansion built right next to his own private quarters and furnished it with every luxury. He provided her with a retinue of five hundred women and gave her all manner of fine garments and ornaments. He then sent a message to those who had come seeking her, saying, "My daughter is staying in the mansion; you may go and see her. They went there and saw her, and thinking, "She is indeed living in the world," they departed. The merchant thought, "Now I have completely satisfied everyone's wishes. He then summoned his daughter and said, "Daughter, you have fulfilled your duty; you may return home. She replied, "Father, I have no desire to return to the household life. The merchant said, "Daughter, if you do not wish to return, at least come back once every four days."
Those words were like hundred-times-boiled oil poured upon her head. Therefore, she said to her father, "Father, I shall go forth.
He paid her great honor, led her to the nunnery, and ordained her. Not long after her ordination, it was her turn to serve in the Uposatha hall.
She lit a lamp, swept the Uposatha hall, and with the tip of the lamp-flame—
Having grasped the sign, she remained there looking again and again;

having generated the jhāna with the fire-kasiṇa as its object and making that very state the foundation, she attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) and the higher powers (abhiññā).
At a later time, after wandering through the countryside and returning, she entered the Blind Men’s Grove (Andhavana). At that time, for the bhikkhunīs...
Living in the forest was not prohibited. Thereupon, they built a small hut for her there, prepared a couch, and surrounded it with a screen of grass-cloth.
She entered Sāvatthī for alms and then departed. However, her maternal cousin, a young man named Nanda, had been in love with her since their time as laypeople.
Having heard that she had arrived, he waited for the elder nun to come out from her dwelling.
Having gone to the blind grove even earlier than usual, he entered that hut and hid beneath the bed.
When the elder nun arrived, entered the hut, closed the door, and had merely sat down on the bed—
still within the range of his vision before the darkness had fully vanished due to her having come from the sunlight outside— he emerged from beneath the bed and climbed onto it.
“Do not perish, fool! Do not perish, fool! Though he was being restrained by the elder nun, he overpowered her and went forth, having performed the deed he had desired.
Then, as if unable to bear his wickedness, the great earth split asunder.
Having entered the earth, he went and was reborn in the Great Avīci hell. The elder nun also [related] this matter to the bhikkhunīs.
She reported it. The bhikkhunīs reported this matter to the bhikkhus. The bhikkhus reported it to the Blessed One.
Having heard that, the Teacher addressed the bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, among bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, laymen, and laywomen, whoever is a fool committing an evil deed is like one eating something sweet-tasting, such as honey or sugar."
Connecting the context by saying, "Just as a man, joyful and elated, full of high spirits, acts [so does he]," the Teacher taught the Dhamma and spoke this verse:
"The fool imagines it is honey, so long as the evil has not ripened;
But when the evil ripens, the fool encounters suffering."

In this context, "it is sweet" means that for a fool performing evil, unwholesome karma, that action appears as something sweet-tasting like honey, desirable, lovely, and pleasing. Thus, he regards it as honey.
"As long as" means for as long a time. "The evil does not ripen" means that its result (vipāka) does not manifest either in the present life or in the future life.
As long as that [evil deed] has not yet ripened, he thinks thus. But when— that is, when,
either in this very life while various punishments for his deeds are being inflicted upon him, or in a future life while experiencing great suffering in the hells and other realms—
that evil ripens for him, then that fool undergoes, finds, and receives suffering.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
However, at another time, a great crowd of people raised a discussion in the Dhamma Hall:
"I suppose even those whose taints are destroyed still relish sensual pleasure and indulge in sense-desires; why would they not? For they are certainly not *koḷāpa* trees."
"And even the anthills are bodies of raw flesh; therefore, they too partake in sensual pleasure and indulge in sensual desires.
The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?
When they replied, "For this very discussion," he said, "Monks, those whose taints are destroyed do not partake in sensual pleasure, nor do they indulge in sensual desires."
"For just as a drop of water fallen upon a lotus leaf does not smear it, does not adhere to it, but rather rolls off and falls away;

and just as a mustard seed on the point of an awl does not smear it, does not adhere to it, but rather rolls off and falls away—in the same way, both kinds of sensual desire do not smear the mind of one whose taints are destroyed, nor do they adhere to it. Having thus established the connection, [he spoke].
While teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse in the Brahmāṇa-vagga:
“Like water on a lotus leaf, like a mustard seed on the point of an awl—
he who is not smeared by sensual pleasures, him I call a brahmin.”
The meaning of this will be made clear in the Brāhmaṇa Vagga itself. However, the Teacher summoned King Pasenadi of Kosala and said:

"Great King, in this dispensation, just as sons of noble family do, so too daughters of noble family renounce their vast circles of kinsmen and heaps of wealth, go forth, and dwell in the forest. While dwelling in such a manner..."
“Wicked persons, intoxicated by passion, harass them out of a sense of inferiority and superiority, and they even create obstacles to the holy life;
therefore, it is fitting for the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs to have a dwelling place within the city.
The king, accepting this with the words “Very well,” had a dwelling place for the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs constructed on one side of the city. Then—
"Ever since [the rule was established], the bhikkhunīs have been living only within the village.
This is the tenth story, the Story of the Elder Uppalavaṇṇā.
11. The Story of the Elder Jambuka.
"Month after month"—this teaching was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in the Veḷuvana forest concerning the Ājīvaka Jambuka.

It is said that in the past, during the time of the Sammasambuddha Kassapa, a certain householder living in a village built a monastery for an elder and served him there with the four requisites as he dwelt therein. The elder [stayed] constantly in his house...
He was eating. Then, while wandering for alms during the day, a certain bhikkhu whose taints were destroyed arrived at the door of that householder’s home.

Seeing him and being inspired by his deportment, the householder invited him inside, served him carefully with choice food, and gave him a large cloth, saying, "Venerable sir, please dye this cloth and wear it."
"Venerable sir, your hair is long; I shall bring a barber for you to have it cut, and I will return after having a couch brought for you to lie upon," he said.
A monk who was a regular visitor to that family and ate there constantly, seeing such hospitality, was unable to compose his mind, thinking: "This [man] has seen him for but a moment..."
Thinking, "He performs such honors [for others], yet he does not do so for me when I eat regularly at his house," he went to the monastery.
The other [monk] also went along with him, dyed the cloth given by the householder, and put it on.
The householder, taking the barber with him, went there, had the Elder's hair shaved, and had a couch spread out.
“Venerable sir, please lie down right here on this very bed,” he said, and having invited both elders for the following day’s meal, he departed.
The resident monk was unable to endure the honor being shown to him.

Then, in the evening, he went to the place where the elder was lying down and reviled him in four ways: “Friend, you are a visiting householder! You are a householder! You are a householder’s son! You are a householder’s grandson!”
"It is better to eat excrement than to eat food brought from a house;
it is better for one who has shaved his head to have his hair plucked out by a palm-stick than to have it shaved by a barber brought by a householder;
it is better to wander naked than to wear a garment given by a householder; it is better to lie on the ground than to lie on a bed brought by a householder."
The resident monk, thinking, "Lest this fool perish because of me," did not accept the invitation; instead, rising early in the morning, he departed at his own pleasure.
The resident monk, having performed the duties to be done in the monastery early in the morning, thought at the time for the alms-round, "Now the guest is still sleeping;
let him wake up by the sound of the gong," and so he struck the gong with the back of his fingernail.
Having struck [the gong], he entered the village for alms. The householder, having offered hospitality, was watching the path by which the elders would arrive;
seeing the resident monk, he asked, "Venerable sir, where is the Elder?
Then the resident monk said to him, "Friend, do not say anything; for yesterday, at the time you were departing, your own personal attendant entered the inner chamber."

“Having fallen asleep, even after rising early in the morning, he does not know when I am making the sound of sweeping my vihāra, nor the sound of pouring water into the drinking-water jar and the rinsing-water jar, nor even the sound of the gong,” he said. The householder thought:
“For my noble master, who is endowed with such perfection of deportment, it is only right that he should sleep until this time.”
“There is no one here by that name; however, seeing me paying such honor to him, he must surely have said something to this venerable sir.

Thinking thus, and out of his own sense of being wise, he respectfully fed him, thoroughly washed his bowl, filled it with food of various exquisite flavors, and said, “Venerable sir, if you should see my noble lady, please give her this message from me:”
"Please give this alms-food to him," he said.
The other, having taken it, thought: "If he eats such alms-food as this, he will become attached right here.
So, discarding that alms-food on the way, [he went] to the Elder's dwelling place.

Having gone there and looking about, he did not see him. Thus, because of having committed such an act, even though he had practiced the duties of a recluse for twenty thousand years, it was unable to protect him.

At the end of his lifespan, having passed away and been reborn in Avīci, he experienced great suffering for the duration of one Buddha-interval. Then, during this current appearance of a Buddha, in the city of Rājagaha...

He was reborn in a family with abundant food and drink. From the time he began walking on his own feet, he no longer wished to lie on a bed nor to eat food; he would consume only the filth from his own body.
Thinking, "Out of ignorance, he acts thus," they raised him. Even when he reached old age, he did not wish to wear clothes and wandered about naked.
He slept on the ground and ate nothing but his own bodily excrement. Then his parents thought, "This boy is not suitable for a household;
he is merely a shameless person, fit only for the Ājīvakas.
So they led him to them and gave him over, saying, "Ordain this child. They then ordained him. And as they were ordaining him, [they cut his hair] up to the level of his throat.
Having placed him in a pit and laid planks over his two shoulders, they sat upon them and tore out his hair with a palm-wood comb.
Then his parents invited him for the following day's meal and departed.
On the next day, the Ājīvakas said to him, "Come, let us enter the village. He replied, "You go; as for me—"
“I shall remain right here,” he did not wish to go. Then, having spoken to him again and again, they departed, leaving him behind as he refused to go.

He too, knowing that they had gone, opened the door-panel of the privy, descended, and with both hands, breaking it up morsel by morsel, ate excrement. The Ājīvakas sent food for him from within the village; that too—
He did not wish to go. Although he was told again and again, he said, "I have no need for this; I have obtained my food.
"Where was it obtained? "Right here. Thus, even when they spoke to him much on the second, third, and fourth days, he did not wish to go to the village, saying, "I shall remain right here.
The Ājīvakas [thought], "This man, day after day, neither..."
"He wishes to enter the village; he does not wish for us to bring food sent by him, but says, 'I have obtained it right here.
What indeed is he doing? We shall investigate him. As they entered the village, they left one or two men behind to keep watch over him and went on.
They remained hidden, as if they were following behind him. He too—
Knowing that they had departed, he descended into the latrine in the same manner as before and ate the excrement.
When the others saw his action, they reported it to the Ājīvakas. Upon hearing this, the Ājīvakas said, "Oh, what a grave deed!
If the disciples of the ascetic Gotama were to find out, [they would say], 'The Ājīvakas wander about eating excrement.'"
“They would proclaim our infamy; this man is not worthy of us,” they said, and they expelled him from their presence.

Once he had been expelled by them, there was a large flat rock spread out in a place where the common people voided excrement—a great pit situated against that flat rock, serving as the place where the common people voided excrement. He...

Having gone there and eaten excrement during the night, when the great multitude arrived for the purpose of bathing their bodies, he would grasp one end of a stone with one hand, lift one foot, and place it upon his knee;
facing the upward wind, he stood with his mouth wide open. When the great multitude saw him, they approached and paid homage to him.
“Venerable sir, why do you stand with your mouth open? he asked. “I subsist on air; I have no other food,” he replied.
Then [the other asked], “Why, venerable sir, do you stand with one foot placed upon your knee? “I am one of fierce asceticism and terrible penance.
When the earth is stepped upon by my two feet, it trembles; therefore, having lifted one foot—”
“I stand with my knees placed [on the ground]. For day and night I pass the time standing alone; I neither sit nor lie down.
Since people for the most part believe only what they hear, the inhabitants of Aṅga and Magadha for the most part thought:
“Oh, how wonderful! There are indeed ascetics such as these; we have never seen anyone like them before.”
Being greatly agitated, they approached him and brought him great honor month after month. He thought, "I shall subsist on air alone;
I will take no other food, for if I were to eat anything else, my asceticism would perish. Thus, he did not desire anything brought by them.
People said, "Venerable sir, do not destroy us! By the enjoyment [of these things] from one such as you, who possesses such terrible asceticism..."
"This will lead to our welfare and happiness for a long time," they entreated him again and again.

However, no other food pleased him. Pressed by the entreaties of the great multitude, he placed the ghee, molasses, and other items brought by them on the tip of his tongue with a blade of *kusa* grass and dismissed them, saying, "Go; this much is sufficient for your welfare and happiness."
Thus he spent fifty-five years naked, eating excrement, plucking out his hair, and sleeping on the ground.

Now, the Buddhas never fail to survey the world at dawn; therefore, one day as the Blessed One was surveying the world at the time of dawn, this Jambuka ascetic appeared within the net of his knowledge. The Teacher—
Reflecting, "What indeed will happen?", he perceived that this man possessed the necessary conditions for attaining Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). He thought:
"Beginning with him, I shall speak a single verse; at the conclusion of the verse, there will be a realization of the Dhamma by eighty-four thousand living beings.
By means of this noble son, the great multitude shall attain safety."
Having understood this, on the following day, after walking for alms in Rājagaha and returning from his almsround, the Teacher addressed the Elder Ānanda:
"Ānanda, we shall go to the presence of Jambuka the Ājīvaka. "Venerable Sir, will you go alone?
"Yes, I shall go alone. Having said this, the Teacher set out for his presence when the shadows were lengthening.

The deities thought: "The Teacher is going this evening to the presence of Jambuka Ājīvaka, and he dwells upon a back-slab of stone that is loathsome, defiled with excrement, urine, and tooth-sticks; it would be well to make it rain.
By their own supernatural power, they made it rain at that very moment. The back-slab of stone became clean and spotless.
Then they caused a rain of five-colored flowers to fall upon him.
In the evening, the Teacher went to the presence of Jambuka the Ājīvaka and called out, “Jambuka! Jambuka thought, “Who could this be?
Some wicked person is addressing me by the name ‘Jambuka,’” and he said, “Who is that? “I am a recluse. “What kind of great recluse? “Today, for me...”
“Give me a place to stay here for one night. “There is no place to stay in this spot, Great Ascetic.
“Jambuka, do not do this; give me a place to stay for one night.
Those who have gone forth indeed desire one who has gone forth—just as humans desire humans, and animals desire animals. “But have you gone forth? “Yes.”
“I have gone forth. “If you have gone forth, where is your gourd, where is your smoke-pipe, and where is your sacrificial cord?
“I have these things,” he replied, “but since wandering about carrying them separately is troublesome, I carry them within me.
He became angry, saying, “Will you wander about without taking up this [cord]? Then—
The Teacher said to him, “Be it so, jackal; do not be angry. Show me a place to dwell.
“There is no place to dwell here, Great Ascetic.
The Teacher pointed out a certain mountain cave not far from that jackal’s dwelling and said, “In this—”
“Who dwells in this mountain cave? he asked. “No one at all, Great Ascetic. “In that case, give this to me. “You yourself must know, Great Ascetic.
The Teacher spread out his sitting mat in the cave and sat down.
During the first watch of the night, the Four Great Kings came to attend upon the Teacher, illuminating the four directions with a single radiance. Jambuka—
Having seen the radiance, he thought, "What is this radiance? During the middle watch of the night, Sakka, the king of the gods, arrived.

Seeing him as well, Jambuka thought, "Who is this? During the last watch of the night, a Great Brahmā, capable of illuminating ten thousand world-systems with one finger, two fingers, or ten fingers respectively, made the entire forest a single expanse of light.
He arrived. Seeing him as well, the jackal thought, "Who could this be? and went to the Teacher early in the morning.
Having exchanged greetings and standing to one side, he asked the Teacher:
"Great Samana, who has come, illuminating the four quarters in your presence? "The Four Great Kings. "For what reason? "Me..."
“‘To attend upon me. ‘But are you superior to the four Great Kings? ‘Yes, jackal;
I am even more of a king than the Great Kings. ‘Then who came during the middle watch? ‘Sakka, the King of the Devas, jackal.
‘For what purpose? ‘Precisely to attend upon me. ‘But are you superior even to Sakka, the King of the Devas? ‘Yes, jackal.’”
“Even though I have been honored, I am superior; yet this one is like a novice attendant to me, like a *kappiyakāraka*.
“In the last watch of the night, who came along illuminating the entire forest?
“He whom the brahmins and others in the world, having spat and washed themselves, call out, saying ‘Homage to Mahābrahmā’—he himself is Mahābrahmā. “But what about you, compared even to Mahābrahmā?”

“Are you superior? “Yes, jackal; for I am even more exalted than Brahmā. “You are wonderful, Great Ascetic! Yet, while I have lived here for fifty-five years, not one of these has ever come to attend upon me. For all this time, I have spent it standing still, subsisting only on air. “Not so! [The Blessed One replied. “Why is that? “Because, jackal, I have been subsisting on air for twelve years. “If that is so, Great Ascetic, you are indeed superior to me. “I am not merely superior to you, jackal; I am superior to the whole world, including its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, to all beings, including ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans. “It is marvelous, Great Ascetic, it is truly wonderful how the Venerable Gotama speaks with such confidence and assurance. “Jackal, there are four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? [The Blessed One continued: “Here, jackal, some person dwells intent on the pursuit of sensual pleasures, which are low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial; he does not understand as they really are the suffering that arises from the pursuit of sensual pleasures, nor the escape from that suffering. This is called the first kind of person found existing in the world. Furthermore, jackal, some person dwells intent on the pursuit of sensual pleasures... [and so forth] ...he understands as they really are the escape from that suffering. This is called the second kind of person found existing in the world. Furthermore, jackal, some person dwells detached from sensual pleasures, detached from unwholesome states, possessing initial application and sustained application, born of seclusion, rapturous and joyful—this is the first jhāna.
