“Have they ever come to attend upon me before?
Then the Teacher said to him: “Jackal, you who were deceiving the ignorant masses in this world have now become intent on deceiving even me.
Did you not for fifty-five years eat nothing but dung and lie only upon the ground?”
He wandered about naked and tore out his hair with a piece of a palm stalk. Nevertheless, deceiving the world, you said, "I subsist on air;
I stand on one foot; I neither sit nor lie down. "You wish to deceive even me!
Previously, relying upon a wicked and base view, you were a consumer of excrement and a sleeper on the ground for so long a time."
“Wandering about naked, you reached the state of plucking out your hair with fragments of palm wood; even now, you still hold onto this evil, base view.
“But what have I done, Great Recluse? Then the Teacher explained to him the deed he had committed in the past.
Even as the Teacher was speaking, a sense of spiritual urgency arose within him, and shame and modesty were established. He—
He sat in the *ukkuṭika* posture. Then the Teacher threw him his water-cloak and gave it to him.
Having put it on, he paid homage to the Teacher and sat down to one side. The Teacher, having delivered a gradual discourse to him, taught the Dhamma.
At the conclusion of that teaching, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), and after paying homage to the Teacher, he rose from his seat.
He requested both the going-forth and the full ordination. At that point, his past karma was exhausted.
For after he had reviled the Great Elder Khīṇāsava with four insults, he was boiled in Avīci for as long as this great earth rose by more than three-quarters of a league;
then, due to the remainder of that [karma], he underwent this misfortune for fifty-five years.
Therefore, that karma of his was exhausted. However, it was not possible to destroy the fruit of the ascetic practice performed by him over twenty thousand years.
Consequently, the Teacher extended his right hand and said, "Come, monk;
lead the holy life for the complete ending of suffering. At that very moment, his layman’s marks vanished.
He appeared like a great elder of sixty years who carried the eight requisites.
It was said that this was the day he had returned after receiving honors from the inhabitants of Aṅga and Magadha;
therefore, when the residents of both kingdoms, having come to receive his honors, saw the Tathāgata, they wondered, "Is our noble master Jambuka large, or is it the Blessed One?"
Thinking, "The ascetic Gotama," they further reflected, "If the ascetic Gotama were great, he would have gone into the presence of the ascetic Gotama;
rather, because of Jambuka Ājīvaka’s greatness, the ascetic Gotama has come into his presence.
The Teacher, knowing the reflection of the great multitude, said, "Jambuka, regarding your supporters..."
"Please cut through my doubt," he said. The other replied, "Venerable sir, I too expect no more than this.
Having spoken thus, he entered the fourth jhāna, and rising from it, he ascended into the air to the height of a palm tree. Then, saying, "Venerable sir, the Blessed One is my Teacher;
I am his disciple," he descended, paid homage, and again rose to the height of two palm trees, then three palm trees, and so on, until he had risen to the height of seven palm trees.
Having ascended into the air and then descended, he made known his status as a disciple. Seeing this, the great multitude thought, "Oh, how wonderful!
These so-called Buddhas possess marvelous and incomparable qualities. As the Teacher conversed with the multitude, he spoke thus:
"For all this time, you have placed upon the tip of my tongue the honor you brought, as if it were but a blade of kusa grass."
“‘I shall fulfill my practice of austerity’—with this thought he has settled here;

yet even if he were to fulfill his practice of austerity for a hundred years by this means, the volition skilled in fasting that arises when he now refrains from eating out of scruples regarding the time or the meal does not equal even a sixteenth part of that practice of austerity.
Having thus established the connection, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
“Month after month, a fool might eat his food with the tip of a blade of kusa grass;
he is not worth a sixteenth part of those who have understood the Dhamma.
This is its meaning: if a fool, one who has not fully understood the Dhamma and is excluded from virtues such as moral discipline, has gone forth in a non-Buddhist sect...
“Thinking, ‘I shall fulfill the practice of austerity,’ one might eat food with the tip of a blade of *kusa* grass month after month for a hundred years.
That does not equal even a sixteenth part of those who have realized the Dhamma.

Those who have realized the Dhamma are called those who have known the Dhamma, those who have weighed the Dhamma. Among them, at the very least, a stream-enterer has realized the Dhamma; at the highest limit—
One whose taints are destroyed. Of these who have mastered the Dhamma, that fool is not worth a sixteenth part.
This teaching is expressed by way of individuals (*puggalādhiṭṭhānā*). However, the meaning here is this:

the volition of one who fulfills such ascetic practices for a hundred years, and the single skillful volition of those who have mastered the Dhamma who, having felt remorse over time or a meal, refrain from eating; [the latter outweighs the former].
Compared to that volition, the volition that has been active for a long time is not worth even a sixteenth part. This is what is meant:

if one were to divide the fruit of that volition of those who have mastered the Dhamma into sixteen parts, and then further divide each of those parts into sixteen parts again, the fruit of even a single one of those [final] parts is [the measure].
"Compared to that fool's practice of asceticism, this is far more fruitful.
At the conclusion of the teaching, eighty-four thousand living beings attained penetration of the Dhamma.
This is the eleventh story, the account of the Elder Jambuka.
12. The Story of the Snake-Preta "Indeed, an evil deed that has been done..."—the Teacher gave this Dhamma teaching while dwelling at Veḷuvana concerning a certain snake-preta.
For one day, among a thousand jaṭilas, were the Venerable Lakkhaṇa Thera and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera.
And as they were descending from Vulture Peak, thinking, "We shall go for alms in Rājagaha," the Venerable Elder Mahāmoggallāna saw a certain snake and manifested a smile.
Then the Elder Lakkhaṇa asked him the reason for his smile: "Friend, why do you manifest a smile?
"Friend Lakkhaṇa, this is not the time for this question; [it must be asked] of the Blessed One..."
“You should ask me about it when you are in the presence of the Blessed One,” said the Elder.

After those two had walked for alms in Rājagaha and gone to sit in the presence of the Blessed One, the Elder Lakkhaṇa asked, “Friend Moggallāna, as you were descending from Vulture Peak Mountain, you broke into a smile;
when I asked you the reason for your smile, you said, ‘You should ask me about this when you are in the presence of the Blessed One.’”
"Tell me now the reason for that. The Elder said: "Friend, having seen a certain peta, I manifested a smile.
Such was his form: his head was like a human head, but the rest of his body was like a snake.
This is indeed a snake-peta (ahipeta), twenty-five yojanas in length; from his head, a mass of flames rises as far as his tail."
“Flames of fire rise from their tails and reach their heads; flames rising from the middle of their heads go to both sides;

flames rising from both sides descend into the middle. It is said that the bodies of these two *petas* were twenty-five *yojanas* in length, while those of the remainder were three-quarters of a *gāvuta*. This was the case for this snake-*peta* and the crow-*peta*.
And it is twenty-five yojanas [in length]. Among them, this is first the Ahi-peta (Snake-peta).
Having seen the Kāka-peta (Crow-peta) being roasted on the summit of Vulture Peak, Mahāmoggallāna asked about his past karma and spoke this verse:
“Your tongue is five yojanas long, and your head is nine yojanas.”
“Your body has risen up twenty-five yojanas;
having performed what deed, have you attained such suffering?
Then the peta, explaining it to him—
“Venerable Moggallāna, I partook of the meal brought for the Saṅgha by the Great Seer Kassapa, according to my desire.
Having spoken this verse, he said: “Venerable sir, during the time of Buddha Kassapa, many bhikkhus entered a village for alms.”
Seeing the Elder, the people, filled with affection, had him sit in the assembly hall, washed his feet, anointed them with oil,
gave him rice gruel and hard food, and then sat down to listen to the Dhamma while waiting for the time of the alms-round.
At the conclusion of the discourse on the Dhamma, they took the Elders’ bowls, filled them from their own respective homes with various kinds of choice food, and...
They brought it. At that time, having become a crow, I was perched on the roof of the dining hall;
seeing him, I took three mouthfuls from a bowl held by one of them, filling my beak three times.
That food, however, did not belong to the Saṅgha, nor had it been specifically assigned to the Saṅgha, nor was it the remainder left over after the bhikkhus had eaten. Each person’s own...
It was food fit to be eaten by people, brought merely for the sake of the entire Saṅgha after being taken to their homes.
From that, I took three mouthfuls; such was my past karma.
Having died, as the ripening of that karma, I was cooked in Avīci, and with what remained of that [karmic] residue, I have now been reborn here on Vulture Peak as a crow-ghost.
“I am experiencing this suffering. This is the story of the crow-peta.
However, here the Elder said, “Upon seeing the snake-peta, he broke into a smile. Then the Teacher, acting as a witness, stood up and said:
“Bhikkhus, what Moggallāna has said is true. I too saw him on the very day he attained full enlightenment.”
Furthermore, he said: “I did not speak out of compassion for others, thinking, ‘If they were not to believe my words, it would lead to their harm.
For even in the *Lakkhaṇa-saṃyutta*, at the very moment Mahāmoggallāna saw [the marks], the Teacher, acting as his witness, spoke of the instances of his conversion;
this too was spoken by him in that same manner. Having heard that, the bhikkhus...
They asked about his past karma. The Teacher also explained it to them:
"In the past, it is said, near Bārāṇasī on the bank of a river, they built a leaf-hut for a Paccekabuddha.
While dwelling there, he went regularly into the city for alms. The citizens, too, with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings in their hands, [attended him morning and evening]."
People went to attend upon the Paccekabuddha. A certain man living in Bārāṇasī was plowing a field along that path.
As the great multitude went to attend upon the Paccekabuddha morning and evening, they passed through trampling that field.
Although the farmer tried to stop them, saying, "Do not trample my field," he was unable to prevent them. Then, to him—
It occurred to him: "If there were no leaf-hut for a paccekabuddha in this place, they would not destroy my field.
When the paccekabuddha had entered for alms, he broke the vessels used for eating and set the leaf-hut on fire.
Seeing that it was burnt, the paccekabuddha departed as he pleased. The great multitude...
Taking perfumes and garlands, he arrived and, seeing the leaf-hut burnt down, asked, "Where has our noble sir gone?
He too had gone with the great multitude, and standing right in the midst of the crowd, he said, "I have burnt that hut of his.
Then they said to him, "Seize this wicked man! Because of him, we were unable to see the Paccekabuddha."
“We did not get it,” they said, and having beaten him with sticks and other weapons, they brought about his death. He was reborn in Avīci;
having been cooked in hell for as long as this great earth has risen a mere *yojana* in height, he was reborn on Vulture Peak as a snake-spirit (*ahipeta*) by way of the remainder of his karma.
The Teacher, having related this past deed of his, said: “Monks, evil karma—”
"This is like milk; just as milk does not turn while it is being milked, so too karma does not ripen while it is being performed.
But when it ripens, one grieves with such suffering. Having thus established the connection, he taught the Dhamma by reciting this verse:
“Indeed, an evil deed that has been done does not curdle like fresh milk;
burning, it follows the fool, like a fire covered by ashes.
In this context, “like fresh milk” refers to the warm milk that has just issued from the udders of a cow at that very moment.
It does not discharge, it does not transform. This is what is meant: just as this fresh milk at that very moment does not discharge, does not transform, and does not abandon its natural state;

so too, having been poured into a vessel and taken up, as long as one has not added sour substances such as buttermilk there, and as long as one has not placed it in a curd-vessel or any other acidic vessel—
Just as a person does not abandon their natural state until they have reached it, and only afterwards does that state cease, even so, an evil deed does not ripen while it is still being performed.
If it were to ripen immediately, no one would be able to commit an evil deed. However, as long as the aggregates produced by wholesome karma persist, they protect that [evil deed].
Upon the dissolution of those [wholesome aggregates], it ripens within the aggregates produced in the states of misery (apāya).
"And as it ripens, it burns after the fool. "What is it like? "Like fire covered by ashes.

For just as a glowing ember hidden by ash does not burn immediately even when stepped upon because it is concealed by the ash, yet having heated the ash, it proceeds burning through the skin and so forth, all the way up to the brain; so too does this karma.
"In the same way, whatever evil deed has been committed by a fool follows him, burning as he is reborn in the hells and other realms in his second or third existence.
At the conclusion of this teaching, many became stream-enterers and others.
The Story of the Ahi-Peta, the twelfth.
13. The Story of the Saṭṭhikūṭa-Peta:
"Only for one's own harm"—the Teacher delivered this teaching on the Dhamma while dwelling at Veḷuvana, concerning the Saṭṭhikūṭa-peta.
For in the same manner as before, while the Elder Mahāmoggallāna was descending from Vulture Peak with the Elder Lakkhaṇa, he manifested a smile at a certain spot.
When asked by the elder for the reason for his smile, he said, "Ask me about this in the presence of the Blessed One.
Having gone for alms and approached the Teacher, he paid homage and sat down. At that time—
Being questioned again, he said: "Friends, I saw one peta with a body thirty gavyūtis in measure;
sixty thousand iron spikes, burning and blazing, fell repeatedly upon the top of his head and rose up again, splitting his skull;
as each was split, it would rise up once more—such was his body."
“Such a form as this has never been seen by me before; having seen it, I manifested a smile.
For in the *Petavatthu* it is said: “Sixty thousand peaks, complete in every way, fall upon your head, piercing right through your skull,” and so forth.
It was with reference to this very peta that it was said. Having heard the elder’s account, the Teacher said, "Monks, even while I was seated at the seat of enlightenment, I saw this being;
however, out of compassion for others, thinking, 'If they were not to believe my word, it would lead to their harm,' I did not speak of it. But now, with Moggallāna as my witness..."
“Having offered it, how did this happen? he asked. Having heard that, the monks asked about his past karma. The Teacher also told them:
“In the past, it is said, there was a cripple in Bārāṇasī who had attained perfection in the craft of arrow-making.
Sitting beneath a banyan tree at the city gate, he would shoot pebbles and cut through its leaves, saying, ‘An elephant figure…’”
When he was being addressed by village children saying, “Show us a horse! Show us a horse-form! he would show them whatever forms they desired and receive foodstuffs and other items from them.
Then one day, as the king was going to the park, he arrived at that place.
The children placed the cripple between the branches of a tree and fled. It was midday when the king stopped there.
As he had entered the foot of a tree, the dappled shadows covered his body. Thinking, "What indeed is this?
he looked upward; seeing figures of elephants and other forms upon the leaves of the tree, he asked, "Whose work is this?
Upon hearing that it was the work of cripples, he summoned one of them and said: "My chaplain is exceedingly talkative, even regarding trivial matters..."
“When he speaks much after what has been said, he will trouble me; will you be able to throw a reed’s worth of raw kidney-beans into his mouth?
“I shall be able, Your Majesty. Have the raw kidney-beans brought, and sit with the chaplain inside the curtain;
I shall know what must be done here. Then the king did so. The other [the snake] took a knife...
Having made a hole in the curtain, as soon as the mouth of the royal priest was open while he was conversing with the king, he threw a goat’s bladder into it one by one.
The priest swallowed each one as it entered his mouth. When the goat’s bladders were exhausted, the cripple shook the curtain.
By that sign, the king realized that the goat’s bladders had run out and said, "Teacher, I..."
"If I were to converse with you, how could I ever reach the end of the discussion?
Because of your excessive talkativeness, even while swallowing as many as a reed-bundle of *ajalaṇḍika* fish, you did not fall silent.
The brahmin became dejected, and from that time on, he was unable to converse with the king with his mouth open. The king [praised] the quality of the cripple...
Having remembered this, he summoned him and, being delighted, thinking,

"It was by depending on him that I obtained happiness," he gave him the wealth known as *sabbaṭṭhaka* and bestowed four excellent villages upon him in the four directions of the city. Understanding the significance of this matter,
a minister who advised the king in matters of welfare and righteousness spoke this verse:
“Truly, a craft is good, whatever its kind;
behold how, by the stroke of a cripple’s hand, villages were obtained from all four directions!
Now, at that time, that minister was none other than this Blessed One. Then, a certain man [observed] the prosperity attained by the cripple...
Seeing him, he thought: “Even though this man was once a cripple, by means of this craft he has attained great prosperity;
it is fitting that I too should learn this. He approached him, paid homage, and said: “Teacher, give me this craft.
“It is not possible, dear one, to give it,” he replied. Rejected by him, he thought: “Very well, I shall win [his favor].”
Saying, "No," he performed services for him such as massaging his hands and feet; after winning him over over a long period, he entreated him again and again.
The cripple, thinking, "This man has been exceedingly helpful to me," being unable to refuse him, taught him the craft.
When the skill was perfected, he asked, "My dear son, your craft is accomplished; what will you do now? [The other replied,] "I shall go outside and test my skill."
“What will you do? “I will strike and kill either a cow or a human being.

“Dear boy, for one who kills a cow there is a fine of a hundred [pieces], and for one who kills a human being there is a fine of a thousand; you, along with your wife and children, would not be able to pay that off.
Do not perish! Seek someone else who has no parents—such a person for whom there is no fine when struck.”
"Bring me one. Saying "Very well," he placed the pebbles in his lap and, wandering about while holding them in that manner, he saw a cow;
thinking, "This one has an owner," he did not dare to strike it. Seeing a human being, he thought, "This one has parents," and he did not dare to strike him.
At that time, a Paccekabuddha named Sunetta was dwelling in a leaf-hut near that city.
Seeing him entering the city for alms between the city gates, [the king] thought, "This man has neither mother nor father;
there is no punishment for striking him. Having struck him, I shall test his craft," and he struck the Paccekabuddha’s right ear-lobule.
Aiming [at him], he threw a pebble. It entered through his right ear and emerged from the left;
a painful sensation arose. The Paccekabuddha was unable to go on almsround;
he went through the air to the leaf-hut and attained final Nibbāna. When the Paccekabuddha did not return, the people thought, "Something must be wrong with him."
Having gone there and seen him attained to final nibbāna, they wept and lamented. He too, seeing the great multitude going there, went to that place;
recognizing him as a paccekabuddha, he said: "When this one was entering for alms, he came before me at the gateway, and I struck him while testing my own skill. The people [said]: "By this..."
"It seems a Paccekabuddha was struck by this evil man; seize him, seize him! they cried, and having beaten him, they brought about his death right there.

He was reborn in Avīci, and after being cooked there until the great earth rose up a full *yojana* high, he was reborn on the summit of Gijjhakūṭa as a spirit with sixty peaks (*saṭṭhikūṭapeta*) due to the remainder of the karmic result. The Teacher [spoke] this to him:
Having related his past karma, he joined the connection by teaching the Dhamma, saying: “Monks, the craft or power that arises for a fool arises only for his own harm;
for having obtained craft or power, a fool brings about only his own ruin,” and then he spoke this verse.
“As long as knowledge arises for a fool, it leads only to his harm;
it destroys the fool’s bright side and shatters his head.
In this context, *yāvadeva* is a particle used in the sense of defining a limit. *Ñattaṃ* means the nature of knowing—that craft which...
He knows that whatever sovereignty, fame, or prosperity he stands upon by which he is recognized by people, becomes manifest and well-known—this is his name.
For either a craft or the state of sovereignty and so forth arises only for the detriment of a fool;
relying on it, he brings about only his own ruin. "He destroys" means he annihilates. "The bright portion" refers to the section of wholesome states (*kusala*).
For when skill or sovereignty arises in a fool, it arises only by destroying his portion of the wholesome.
"The head" (*muddha*) is a name for wisdom (*paññā*). "They strike down" means they destroy it.
For that [skill or sovereignty], while striking at his bright portion, strikes and destroys the very head known as wisdom.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the thirteenth story, the Story of the Sixty-Peaked Petas.
14. The Story of the Householder Citta.

"One should desire the cultivation of what is non-existent"—this teaching on the Dhamma was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the Elder Sudhamma. The discourse originated in Macchikāsaṇḍa and was concluded at Sāvatthī.

For in the city of Macchikāsaṇḍa, a householder named Citta, seeing the Elder Mahānāma—who was among the group of five disciples—wandering for alms, gained confidence in his deportment; he took his bowl, led him into his home, and...
Having fed him, at the conclusion of the meal, while listening to a discourse on the Dhamma, he attained the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala).
Becoming one of unshakable faith and desiring to establish a monastic residence (saṅghārāma) in his own garden called Ambāṭakavana, he poured water into the Elder’s hand and dedicated it.
At that moment, thinking, "The Buddha's Dispensation is established," they made the water the boundary.
The great earth trembled. Having had a great monastery built in the park, the Great Merchant kept his doors open for monks arriving from all directions.
In Macchikāsaṇḍa, there was a resident elder named Sudhamma.
On another occasion, having heard a discourse on the virtues of Citta, the two Chief Disciples, desiring to show him favor, [went there].

They arrived at Macchikāsaṇḍa. When the householder Citta heard of their arrival, he went out to meet them for half a *yojana*, escorted them to his own monastery, and after performing the duties of hospitality for guests, he requested the General of the Dhamma, saying, "Venerable sir, I wish to hear a brief discourse on the Dhamma.
Then the Elder said to him, "Lay follower, we have come from a long journey."
“Exhausted in form as you are, listen for a moment,” he said, and preached the Dhamma to him. While listening to the Elder’s Dhamma, he attained the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).
Having paid homage to the two chief disciples, he invited them, saying, “Venerable sirs, please accept alms at my home tomorrow with a thousand bhikkhus.
Afterwards, he also invited the resident Elder Sudhamma, saying, “You too—”
“Venerable sir, please come with the elders tomorrow,” he invited him. Thinking, “This man is inviting me last,” the elder became angry and refused.
Although the lay follower entreated him again and again, the elder continued to refuse.
The lay follower said, “You will see, venerable sir,” and departed. On the following day, he prepared a great almsgiving at his own residence. The Elder Sudhamma also—
At the very time of dawn, thinking, "What kind of hospitality has the householder prepared for the two chief disciples?
I shall go tomorrow and see," he took his bowl and robe early in the morning and went to the householder's home.
Although he was addressed by the householder with the words, "Sit down, venerable sir," he replied, "I will not sit; I shall wander for alms."
Having spoken thus and observed the hospitality prepared for his two chief disciples, the householder, wishing to provoke him on account of his birth, said:
"Magnificent is your hospitality, householder, yet there is one thing missing here. "What is it, venerable sir? "Sesame balls, householder," he said.
Being rebuffed by the householder with the simile of the crow, he became angry and said: "This is your dwelling, householder—"
Having said, "I shall depart," although he was entreated three times [to stay], he departed anyway.

Going into the presence of the Teacher, he reported the words spoken by both Citta and himself. The Teacher, attributing the fault solely to him, saying, "A lay follower who is faithful and confident has been insulted by you with baseless words," had the formal act of reconciliation (*paṭisāraṇīyakamma*) performed against him and said, "Go to the householder Citta."
“Go and ask for his forgiveness,” he sent him. Having gone there, he said, “Householder, this fault is mine alone; please forgive me.
But being refused by the reply, “I will not forgive you,” he became dejected and was unable to obtain his forgiveness.
He returned once more to the presence of the Teacher. Although the Teacher knew that the lay follower would not forgive him, [he thought], “He is stiff with pride...”
“Let him go on this thirty-yojana road and then return,” he said, and sent him away without explaining the means for seeking forgiveness.
Then, when he returned with his pride humbled, [the King] gave him an attendant and said, “Go, go with him and ask the lay follower for forgiveness.
[The attendant replied], “How can a recluse say, ‘This is my monastery, this is my dwelling place’?”
“It is not fitting for one to harbor pride or envy, thinking, ‘He is my lay follower,’ or ‘She is my lay follower.
For in one who acts thus, the defilements such as desire and pride increase. Having established this connection, he taught the Dhamma by reciting these verses:
“One might wish for non-existent praise, And precedence among the bhikkhus;”

“Such is the intention of the fool; his desire and pride increase.
In this context, “non-existent” means that the foolish bhikkhu might desire non-existent esteem, thinking:
“Though I am actually faithless, may people know me as ‘faithful. According to the method explained in the *Niddesa* on evil desires (*pāpicchatā*), the fool is one who is “faithless...”
"Being immoral, of little learning, unsecluded, lazy, unmindful, unconcentrated, and of poor wisdom—yet while his taints are still unabandoned, may people know me thus:
'Oh, this person is faithful, virtuous, learned, secluded, energetic, mindful, concentrated, wise, and one whose taints are exhausted'! This is "honoring what is not worthy of honor."
He desires. "Preeminence" (*purekkhāra*) means being surrounded by a retinue.
Standing in such a course of desire, thinking, "Oh, that all the monks in this entire monastery would dwell surrounding me while asking me questions," he desires preeminence among the monks.

"In dwellings" (*āvāsesu*) refers to those communal dwellings; specifically, as for those superior lodgings in the middle of the monastery, he [desires them] for his own intimate friends and associates.
He desires lordship over the monasteries by assigning the monks, saying, "You stay here," while he himself occupies the best lodgings;
and he assigns inferior and even lodgings possessed by non-human spirits to other visiting monks, saying, "You stay here. Furthermore, he desires honor among other families.
He does not desire honor through the four requisites from others' families— neither from his parents nor from his relatives— with the thought, "Oh, may they give these to me alone, and not to others.
And as for that fool who thinks, "Let them consider it as done by me alone," [regarding] whatever is done in a monastery by way of constructing an Uposatha hall and so forth...
The thought arises: "May both householders and those gone forth alike think that all the new work (navakamma) has been completed by my elder alone;
thus, may they consider the preparatory work done entirely through my support. Furthermore, the thought arises:
"May both householders and those gone forth all remain under my sole authority," [referring to] carts, oxen, axes, hatchets, and so forth.

Or let them be obtained—even if it is only as much as a measure of rice-gruel, by heating it and drinking it, and so forth—in such matters, whether great or small, whether duties or non-duties, regarding any single task to be done, let them all proceed under my very authority; let them do everything only after having asked me for permission.
Such is the thought that arises. Thus, “of the fool” refers to that fool who possesses both that desire and this [thought].
A mere intention arises, but for him neither insight nor the paths and fruits increase.
Rather, just as the water of the ocean rises at the appearance of the moon, his craving and ninefold conceit alone increase as they arise through the six sense doors.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and the other stages.
The Elder Sudhamma, having heard this exhortation, paid homage to the Teacher, rose from his seat, and after circumambulating him to the right, went with that attendant monk.
Once within the sight of the lay follower, he confessed his offense and asked the lay follower for forgiveness.
The lay follower said, "I forgive you, venerable sir; if there was any fault on my part, please forgive me."
Having been sent back by the Teacher, he remained steadfast in the instruction given and attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) in just a few days.
The lay follower also thought: "I have attained the fruit of Stream-entry and established myself in the fruit of Non-returning without even seeing the Teacher;
it is fitting that I see the Teacher. He [prepared offerings] of sesame, rice, ghee, molasses, clothing, coverings, and so forth.
Having caused five hundred fully laden wagons to be prepared, he had it announced to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus: "Let those who wish to see the Teacher come;
they shall not be exhausted for lack of almsfood and other necessities. He likewise had it announced to the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs, and to the laymen and laywomen.
Together with him, there were five hundred bhikkhus and five hundred bhikkhunīs.

The laymen and laywomen also set out. He made arrangements so that for those three thousand people—both their own retinue and his own—there would be no lack of anything, such as rice gruel, solid food, and other provisions, along the thirty-league journey.
But having learned of his departure, at every league the deities established military encampments and provided divine rice gruel, snacks, meals, drinks, and so forth.
They attended upon that great multitude, so that no one lacked anything whatsoever.
Thus, being attended by the deities, traveling a league each day, he reached Sāvatthī in a month; the five hundred carts remained exactly as they had been filled.
He proceeded along, distributing the offerings brought by both deities and humans.
The Teacher said to the Elder Ānanda: “Ānanda, today, when the shadow has grown long, the householder Citta will come surrounded by five hundred lay followers and pay homage to me.
“But, venerable sir, will there be some miracle at the time of his paying homage to you? “There will be, Ānanda. “What is it, venerable sir?”
“Having arrived, at the time of my paying homage, he will cause a thick rain of five-colored divine flowers to fall over an area of eight karīsas—measuring as much as a knee-deep plowshare.
Having heard that report, the city-dwellers said, “It is said that the householder named Citta, who possesses such great merit, will arrive today to pay homage to the Teacher; such [a thing]...”
Thinking, "A miracle is about to take place; we too shall have the opportunity to see that great merit," they took gifts and stood on both sides of the road.
When they arrived near the monastery, five hundred monks came first.
Citta the householder said to the great female lay disciples, "Ladies, you are coming from behind."
Accompanied by five hundred lay followers, he went into the presence of the Teacher.
However, those standing or sitting in the presence of the Buddhas do not move here or there; they remain perfectly still on both sides of the Buddha’s path.
The householder Citta entered the great Buddha-path. By an Ariyan disciple who has attained the three fruits—
Every place he looked upon trembled. Thinking, "This must be the householder Citta," the great multitude gazed at him.
He approached the Teacher, entered within the six-colored rays of the Buddha, and grasping the Teacher’s feet with both his ankles, he paid homage.
At that very moment, a rain of flowers of the aforementioned kind fell, and thousands of shouts of "Well done! arose.
They caused [the festival] to proceed. He dwelt in the presence of the Teacher for one month;

while dwelling there, he had the entire Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha seated right within the monastery and gave a great almsgiving. Even those who had come with him, he kept within the monastery and looked after them.
Not even for a single day was there anything to be taken from his own carts, as [the place was filled] with gods and humans.
He gave the gift with the very same offerings he had brought and performed all his duties. Having paid homage to the Teacher, he said:
"Venerable Sir, while coming with the thought, 'I shall give a gift to you,' I spent a month on the road.
Here, that month has passed; I have not been able to take anything from the offerings I brought during all this time."
“I gave this gift only as an offering brought by gods and humans;
therefore, even if I were to dwell here for a year, I would not be able to find anything to give as a gift. I wish to go after unloading my carts;
please point out a place where I may store them. The Teacher said to the Elder Ānanda, “Ānanda, designate one spot and have it cleared for the lay devotee.”
The Elder did accordingly. It is said that the householder Citta was permitted to designate a *kappiya-bhūmi* (a place where things may be made allowable).
The lay devotee (*upāsaka*), together with the three thousand people who had come with him, set out again on the road with empty carts.
Devas and humans arose and said, "Noble sir, you have performed the act of traveling with empty carts," and [honored him] with the seven treasures.
They filled their wagons. He proceeded along, providing for the great multitude with the very provisions he himself had brought.
The Elder Ānanda, having paid homage to the Teacher, said: "Venerable Sir, even though I came into your presence a month ago, I have stayed here for another month;
during all this time, [the people] have provided for us solely with the provisions brought by gods and men."
He gave a great gift; now, having made five hundred carts empty, he will reportedly depart within a month.
But when gods and men rose up and said, "Noble sir, you have performed the act of departing with empty carts," they filled those five hundred carts with the seven kinds of jewels.
He, in turn, [satisfied] the great multitude with the very same offerings he had brought himself.
“...he will go along looking after it. “But, venerable sir, does this honor arise for him only when he comes into your presence, or does it also arise when he goes elsewhere?
“Ānanda, it arises for him both when he comes into my presence and when he goes elsewhere. For this lay follower is faithful...”
"Having confidence and perfected in virtue, whatever place such a person frequents, in that very place gain and honor arise for him.
Having said this, the Teacher spoke this verse from the Pakiṇṇaka-vagga:
"Confident, perfected in virtue, endowed with fame and wealth;"
"Whichever place he frequents, there he is honored.
Its meaning, however, will become clear right there.
When this was said, the Elder Ānanda asked about Citta’s past karma. Then the Teacher, explaining it to him, said:
Ānanda, this person had made a resolution at the feet of the Blessed One Padumuttara;
after wandering among gods and humans for a hundred thousand eons, he was reborn during the time of the Buddha Kassapa into a family of deer-hunters.
Having grown up, one day while it was raining, he took a spear and went into the forest to kill deer. While he was looking out for deer on an unworked mountain slope, [he saw...]
Having covered herself with a cloth including her head, she saw a certain bhikkhu sitting there and thought, "This noble one must be sitting performing his ascetic duties;
I shall bring him food. She hurried home, had meat brought from yesterday and rice cooked on one hearth, but then, seeing other bhikkhus wandering for alms, [she changed her mind].
Taking their alms bowls as well, he had them sit on prepared seats, prepared the meal, and having instructed another,
saying, “Noble ladies, serve the food,” he placed that food into bags, took them, and while walking along the road, gathered various flowers, put them into his bowl-bag,
and went to the place where the Elder was sitting, saying, “Venerable sir, please accept this favor for me.”
Having said, "Please do so," she took the bowl, filled it, and placed it in the Elder’s hand;

then, having made an offering with those flowers, she made this aspiration: "Just as this alms-food of delicious flavors has gladdened my heart along with this floral offering, so too, in each successive place of rebirth, may thousands of gifts come to me bringing joy to my heart, and may there be a rain of five-colored flowers."
"May it rain! he thus made his aspiration. Having performed wholesome deeds throughout his life, he was reborn in the world of the devas;
in the place where he was reborn, a rain of celestial flowers fell to the depth of his knees.

Now, on the very day of his birth, as well as upon his arrival here, there occurred the raining down of a shower of flowers, the presentation of gifts, and the filling of wagons with the seven precious gems.
"This is the natural outflow of that very same karma.
The fourteenth story, the Case of the Householder Cittaka. 15.
The Story of the Novice Tissa the Forest-Dweller.

"Indeed, there are other means for acquiring gain. The Teacher spoke this teaching on the Dhamma while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Elder Vanavāsika Tissa. This instruction originated in Rājagaha.
It is said that a friend of the Vangaṇṭa Brahmin, who was the father of the Elder Sāriputta, named the Brahmin Mahāsena, lived in Rājagaha.
One day, as the Elder Sāriputta was wandering for alms, he approached the door of that man's house out of compassion for him.
He arrived. However, his wealth was exhausted and he was poor. He thought, "My son must have come to the door of my house to wander for alms;
I am destitute, yet he likely does not know of my poverty, and I have nothing whatsoever to give.
Unable to stand before the Elder, he hid himself. The Elder—
Another day passed, and the brahmin remained hidden in the same manner. Although he thought, "If I obtain anything at all, I will give it," he obtained nothing.
Then one day, having received a bowl of milk-rice along with a coarse cloth from a certain brahmin reciter, he took it and went home;
as soon as he arrived, he remembered the Elder, thinking, "I must give this alms-food to the Elder."
"It is appropriate. At that moment, the Elder also entered a meditative absorption (*jhāna*), and upon emerging from that attainment, he saw the brahmin.
Thinking, "The brahmin has received the gift to be given and is waiting for my arrival;
it is appropriate for me to go there," he put on his outer robe, took his bowl, and revealed himself standing right at the door of the brahmin's house.
As soon as the brahmin saw the elder, his heart was filled with serene confidence. He then approached him, paid homage, and exchanged friendly greetings.
Having seated him within his house, he took a bowl of milk-rice and poured it into the elder’s bowl.
The elder accepted half of it and covered the bowl with his hand. Then the brahmin said to him, "Venerable sir, this is barely enough for one person."
“This is milk-rice; please accept it for the sake of my welfare in the next world, not for the sake of this world, for I wish to give it to you without reserve,” he said, pouring out everything.

The Elder ate right there. Then, at the conclusion of his meal, having given him even that single garment and paid homage, he said: “Venerable sir, may I too attain the very same state of direct realization as you have.”
The Elder, saying “So be it, Brahmin,” offered his blessing and, rising from his seat, departed.
Wandering on his journey by stages, he eventually arrived at Jetavana.

The Brahmin, thinking, “A gift given when one is in a state of poverty brings the greatest satisfaction,” felt deep faith and joy upon having made that offering, and developed an exceeding affection for the Elder.
Thus, having passed away out of affection, he took rebirth in Sāvatthī in a family that served the Elder.
At that very moment, his mother, realizing that a fetus had been conceived in her womb, informed her husband.
He provided her with the necessary care for her pregnancy.
Avoiding the consumption of things that were too hot, too cold, or too sour, and thus carrying the fetus comfortably,
a pregnancy-longing (dohala) arose in her: "O, if only I could invite five hundred bhikkhus headed by the Elder Sāriputta,
have them sit in my house, give them milk-rice with unadulterated milk, and having myself put on saffron-colored robes..."
“Taking a golden bowl and sitting at the edge of the seating area, she would consume this much of the leftover milk-rice from the monks.

It is said that her longing to wear the saffron robes was an omen of her son’s future going forth in the Buddha’s teaching while still in her womb. Then her relatives [said], “Our daughter’s desire is righteous...”
Thinking, "This is her pregnancy craving," they made the Elder Sāriputta the senior monk of the assembly and gave five hundred bhikkhus unadulterated milk-rice porridge.
She too, having dressed in one saffron robe and put on another as an upper garment, took a golden bowl and sat at the edge of the seating area;
she consumed the leftover porridge, and her craving was appeased. Thus it remained until her delivery.
On various other festive occasions as well— such as the celebrations following the birth of a son after ten months of pregnancy—

they gave only thin milk-rice mixed with honey and ghee to the five hundred bhikkhus headed by the Elder Sāriputta. It is said that this was the result of the milk-rice he had given previously when he was a brahmin boy.
On the day of his birth festival, they bathed the boy early in the morning, adorned him, and laid him upon a couch of glory over a blanket worth a hundred thousand pieces.
While still lying there, he looked at the Elder and thought, "This is my former teacher;
it was by depending on this Elder that I obtained this prosperity. It is fitting that I make a single gift to him."
When he was being brought to receive the precepts, he took that blanket by wrapping it around his little finger.
Then, thinking, "The blanket is caught on his finger," they began to pull it off him. He wept. His relatives said, "Go away;
do not make the child cry," and they brought him back along with the blanket. As he was paying homage to the Elder, [he pulled it from] the blanket...
Having pulled back his finger, he dropped the blanket at the feet of the Elder.
His kinsmen, instead of saying, "This was done by a young boy who did not know better," said, "Venerable sir, this was given by our son;

let it be considered as already relinquished. Then they said, "Venerable sir, please grant the training precepts to your servant, who has performed this act of worship with a blanket worth a hundred thousand pieces."
They asked, “What is the name of this boy? “Venerable sir, he has the same name as the noble one; his name shall be Tissa.
It is said that in his time as a householder, the elder had been a young brahmin named Upatissa. His mother also thought, “I must not thwart my son’s aspiration.
Thus, having performed the auspicious ceremony for naming the child, she then performed the auspicious ceremony for his first consumption of solid food.
Furthermore, on the auspicious occasions of his ear-piercing, his receiving of garments, and his tonsure ceremony,
they gave only honeyed milk-rice with little water to the five hundred bhikkhus headed by the Elder Sāriputta.
When the boy reached the age of seven years, he said to his mother, "Mother, I shall go forth in the presence of the Elder."
“Excellent, dear one! Previously, I made a resolve that I would not thwart my son’s aspiration;
go forth, my son! Having thus invited the elder and given him alms-food upon his arrival, he said, “Venerable sir, your slave says, ‘I shall go forth.
We will take him with us and return to the monastery this evening. Having dismissed the elder in this way, [he departed].
In the evening, having taken his son with great honor and respect to the monastery, he presented him to the Elder.
The Elder spoke with him: "Tissa, going forth is indeed difficult. When there is need for heat, one finds cold;
when there is need for cold, one finds heat. Those who have gone forth live with hardship, and you are accustomed to comfort."
“Venerable sir, I shall be able to do everything exactly according to the method you have taught.

The Elder said, “Very well,” and after explaining to him the meditation subject of the fivefold skin (the *tacapañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna*) by way of the contemplation of repulsiveness (*paṭikūla-manasikāra*), he gave him the going-forth.
For it is indeed appropriate to explain the entire set of thirty-two aspects (*dvattiṃsākāra*); however, for one who is unable to explain it all, [it is sufficient to explain the skin-fives].
This meditation subject of the five groups of charnel-ground corpses must indeed be explained. For this meditation subject has never been abandoned by any of the Buddhas.
There is no limit to the number of monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen who have attained Arahantship within each single category of these parts, such as the head hairs and so forth.
However, unskilled monks who ordain others [provide them with] the necessary support for Arahantship...
They destroyed [the obstacles]. Therefore, the Elder, having explained the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) and ordained him, established him in the ten precepts.

While his parents were performing the honors for their son’s renunciation, they gave nothing but rice-porridge with honey and little water to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha for seven days in the monastery itself.
The monks also [received] the constant supply of rice-porridge with honey and little water.
"We are unable to enjoy [it]," they complained. His parents also returned home on the evening of the seventh day.
On the eighth day, the novice entered the city for alms together with the monks.
The residents of Sāvatthī, thinking, "The novice is said to enter the city for alms today; we shall pay him honor," [prepared] five hundred robes.
Having fashioned them into bundles and prepared five hundred portions of alms-food, they stood on the path and gave them; on the following day, having come to the monastery’s grove, they gave them.

Thus, in just two days, the novice received a thousand robes along with a thousand portions of alms-food and had them given to the Saṅgha of monks. [This was] because of the coarse robe he had given during his time as a brahmin.
This was the result [of his merit]. Then the monks gave him the name Piṇḍapātadāyaka-Tissa (Tissa the Almsgiver).

On another day, while the novice was walking on alms-round through the monastery during the cold season, he saw the monks warming themselves here and there in fire-halls and other places, and he asked:
"Venerable sirs, why are you sitting here warming yourselves? "The cold oppresses us."
“Sāmaṇera,” he said. “Venerable sir, it is permissible to wear a woolen blanket during the cold season; for that is capable of warding off the cold.
The sāmaṇera replied, “You are one of great merit who can obtain a woolen blanket; where would we get a blanket?
“In that case, venerable sir, let those who need blankets come with me,” he announced throughout the entire monastery.
Then the monks, thinking, "We shall go with the novice and bring back the blanket," set out with about a thousand monks, relying upon a seven-year-old novice.
But he, without even giving rise to the thought, "How shall I obtain blankets for so many monks?
took them and set out toward the city. For it was the nature of Sudinna...
Such was the power of that gift. As he wandered from house to house outside the city, he obtained five hundred blankets and entered the city. People brought blankets to him from here and there.
However, one man coming through the market gate saw another man sitting with five hundred blankets spread out before him.
Seeing a shopkeeper, he said, "Hey, a novice monk is coming along gathering up blankets;
cover your blankets with yours! "But does he take what is given, or what is not given?
"He takes what is given. "That being the case, if I wish to give, I shall; if not, I will not. Go away," he dismissed him. [The shopkeeper was] stingy.
Indeed, foolish and blind people, having been stingy while others were giving such gifts, and seeing this peerless gift yet remaining stingy themselves, are reborn in hell like Kāḷa.
The shopkeeper thought: "This man came here according to his own nature and said to me, 'Cover yourself with my blanket.
Even if he says, 'Take what has been given,' I—" [He continued: "But as for me..."
“I said, ‘If I wish for what belongs to another, I shall give it; if not, I shall not give it.
However, shame arises in one who does not give back what has been seen [belonging to another], whereas there is no fault in one who conceals what belongs to oneself.
Of these five hundred woolen blankets, two blankets are worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold; it is fitting that he should conceal these very ones. Thus he spoke regarding the two blankets.
Having tied one cloth to another and tucked them between them, he concealed [the bundle].

The novice monk also arrived at that place together with a thousand bhikkhus. As soon as the shopkeeper saw the novice, a fatherly affection arose within him; his entire body became suffused with love.
He thought: "Let alone the woolen cloths; seeing this [novice], even my heart-flesh..."

"It is fitting to give them. So they both brought out two blankets, placed them at the feet of the novice, and after bowing down, said, "Venerable sir, may you be a partaker of the merit of this deed. He also offered a blessing for him, saying, "May it be so.
Within the city as well, the novice obtained five hundred blankets. Thus, on that very same day, he received a thousand blankets.
Having obtained it, he gave it to a thousand bhikkhus. Then they gave him the name Thera Kambaladāyaka Tissa.
Thus, on the day of his naming, the blanket given to him reached the state of being a thousand blankets by the time he was seven years old.
Indeed, apart from the Buddha’s dispensation, there is no other place where what is given in small measure becomes much, nor where what is given in abundance [becomes even more so].
What was given became even more abundant. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Such, monks, is this Saṅgha of bhikkhus, that in such a Saṅgha of bhikkhus, what is little given becomes much, and what is much given becomes even more abundant.
Thus, by the merit of a single blanket, the novice, though only seven years old, received a thousand blankets. Of him—
While dwelling in Jeta’s Grove, relatives and benefactors frequently came into his presence and engaged him in conversation.
He thought to himself: “As long as I remain here, it is impossible for me not to speak when these relatives and benefactors come and converse;
nor can I establish my own position through such extensive discourse with them. What if I were now to [go] to the Teacher?”
“Having learned the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) in the presence [of the Teacher], one should enter the forest.

Having approached the Teacher, paid homage, and requested the meditation subject up to the level of Arahantship, he paid homage to his preceptor, took his bowl and robes, and departed from the monastery, thinking, “If I dwell in a nearby place, my relatives will call for me. Thus, [he traveled] twenty...
He traveled a path of one hundred yojanas. Then, while passing through the gate of a certain village, he saw an elderly man and asked:
"Venerable lay follower, is there a forest dwelling for those living in this region?
"There is, Bhante," he replied. "In that case, show me the way. [To] the elderly lay follower...

But upon seeing him, affection for his son arose within him. Standing right there, he took the novice with him without saying a word, saying, "Come, venerable sir, I will show it to you," and they departed.

As the novice was walking along with him, he saw various places on the mountains and trees adorned with diverse flowers and fruits, and asked, "Upāsaka, what place is this? Upāsaka, what place is this?"
He asked, "What are their names? As he was telling him their names, they reached a forest dwelling.
He said, "Venerable sir, this is a comfortable place; please dwell right here. Then, having asked his name, saying, "Venerable sir, what is your name?
and being told, "I am the lay follower named Vanavāsītissa," he said, "Tomorrow it will be fitting for us to go for alms in our village."
Having spoken thus, he turned back and went right into the village. He announced to the people, "A monk named Vanavāsītissa has arrived at the monastery;
prepare for him rice porridge, alms-food, and so forth.
First, the novice himself was named Tissa, and then there were Piṇḍapātadāyakatissa and Kambaladāyakatissa.
Having received three names—Vanavāsī, Itthi, and Sāmaṇera—he received a fourth name within seven years.
On the following day at dawn, he entered that village for alms. After people gave him alms, they paid homage to him.
The novice said, "May you be happy; may you be freed from suffering. Even after one person had given him alms, he returned to his house again.
He was unable to go, and they all remained standing, looking on. He too took only what was necessary for his own sustenance.

All the inhabitants of the village prostrated themselves at his feet with their chests touching the ground and said, “Venerable sir, while you dwell here during these three months, we shall take the three refuges, establish ourselves in the five precepts, and observe the eight Uposatha observances each month.”
“Give us your promise to dwell here. Having observed their helpfulness, he gave them his promise and went on a regular alms-round in that very place.
At every moment he was saluted, he would depart after speaking only these two phrases: “May you be happy; may you be freed from suffering. There, for the first month and the second month as well...
When the third month had passed and was coming to an end, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Then, at the conclusion of the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā) at the end of the rains retreat, his preceptor approached the Teacher, paid homage, and said:
"Venerable sir, I shall go to the presence of the novice Tissa. "Go, Sāriputta," [the Teacher replied]. He—
Taking five hundred bhikkhus as his own retinue, he set out and said, "Friend Moggallāna, I am going to the presence of the novice Tissa.
The Elder Mahāmoggallāna replied, "I too will go, friend," and departed together with five hundred bhikkhus.
By this same means, the Elder Mahākassapa, the Elder Anuruddha, and the Elder Upāli [set out].
The Elder Puṇṇa and all the Great Disciples set out together with five hundred bhikkhus each.
The retinues of all the Great Disciples consisted of forty thousand bhikkhus.
Having traveled a road of two hundred yojanas, they arrived at their alms-resort village. A lay devotee who was the regular attendant of the novice stood right at the gate.
Having seen him, he went out to meet him and paid homage.
Then the Elder Sāriputta asked him: "Is there, lay follower, a forest dwelling in this region?
"There is, venerable sir. "Is it occupied by monks, or unoccupied? "It is occupied by monks, venerable sir. "What is its name?"
“Does he dwell there? “He dwells in the forest, venerable sir. “In that case, show us the way. “Who are you, venerable sirs?

“We have come to the presence of the novice. The lay follower looked around, recognized all the great disciples beginning with the Dhammasenāpati, and with his body suffused with uninterrupted rapture, said: “Wait!”
“Very well, venerable sir,” he replied. He hurriedly entered the village and shouted: “Venerable sirs!
These eighty great disciples, headed by the Elder Sāriputta, have come to the presence of the novice with their respective retinues.
Take your beds, chairs, rugs, lamps, oil, and so forth, and depart at once! The people immediately took the beds and other items for the elders.
Following step by step behind the elders, they entered the monastery together with them.
Recognizing the community of monks, the novice received the bowls and robes of several senior elders and performed his duties.
While he was still arranging the elders' lodgings and putting away their bowls and robes, darkness fell.
The Elder Sāriputta said to the lay followers, "Go, lay followers; darkness has fallen upon you.
"Venerable sir, today is the day for hearing the Dhamma; we will not go, we shall listen to the Dhamma, for there has been no hearing of the Dhamma since before this.
"In that case, novice, light a lamp and announce the time for the hearing of the Dhamma. He—
He did so. Then the Elder said to him, “Tissa, your attendants say, ‘We wish to hear the Dhamma.

Preach the Dhamma to them. At once the lay devotees rose up and said, “Venerable sir, our master knows no discourse on the Dhamma other than these two phrases he has established: ‘May you be happy’ and ‘May you be freed from suffering.’”
“Give us another preacher of the Dhamma,” they said. But even after the novice had attained Arahatship, he did not preach the Dhamma to them.
At that time, however, his preceptor asked him, “Novice, how indeed are they happy? How indeed are they suffering?”
“Please explain the meaning of these two phrases: ‘are being liberated’,” he said.

[The Elder] replied, “Very well, Venerable Sir,” took his fan, ascended the Dhamma-seat, and—drawing out the meaning and the reasoning according to the five Nikāyas—like a great cloud over the four continents pouring down a thick rain, [he explained] the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and the factors conducive to enlightenment.
Having delivered a discourse on the Dhamma analyzing it up to the pinnacle of Arahantship, he said: "Venerable sir, such is the happiness for one who has attained Arahantship;
having attained Arahantship, one is liberated from suffering. Other people, however, are not liberated from the suffering of birth and so forth, nor from the sufferings of hell and so forth.
"Excellent, novice! Your inspired speech is well-delivered. Now, [recite] the *sarabhañña*..."
"Speak! he said. He then recited the *Sara-bhañña*. As the dawn was breaking, the lay supporters of the novice were divided into two groups.
Some said, "Never before have we seen anyone so harsh.
How is it that one who knows such a Dhamma discourse could, for all this time, stand in the place of a parent while serving us?"
Some were angry, saying, "He did not speak even a single verse of Dhamma to human beings! Others were pleased, saying,
"It is indeed a gain for us that we served such a venerable one without knowing his virtues or faults,
and now we have been granted the opportunity to hear the Dhamma in his presence."

On that very day, at the time of dawn, the Perfectly Enlightened One, surveying the world, saw that the attendant of the novice Vanavāsī Tissa had entered within the net of his own knowledge. Reflecting, "What will happen? he considered this matter:
"Some of the attendants of the novice Vanavāsī Tissa are pleased, while others are angry; [they are] toward me..."
"But being angry with their son, the novice, they will be destined for hell; therefore, I must certainly go there.
Once I have gone, all those novices will develop a mind of loving-kindness toward him and be released from their suffering.
Those people, having invited the Saṅgha of monks, went to the village, had a pavilion constructed, and prepared rice porridge, alms-food, and other offerings.
Having prepared the seats, they sat waiting, looking along the path by which the Saṅgha would arrive.
The bhikkhus, too, having attended to their physical needs, as they were entering the village for alms at the time for the alms-round, asked the novice:
“Tissa, will you go with us, or will you come later? “I shall go only at the time of my own departure.”
“Go, venerable sirs,” they said. Taking their bowls and robes, the monks entered.
The Teacher, having put on his robe and taken his bowl right there in Jetavana, traveled in a single moment of thought and appeared standing before the monks.
Hearing that “the Perfectly Enlightened One has arrived,” the entire village was thrown into an uproar.
A great clamor arose. With joyful hearts, the people seated the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, headed by the Buddha, provided them with rice-gruel, and served solid food.
Even before the meal was finished, the novice entered the village. The villagers brought him out and respectfully gave him alms-food.
Having taken only what was necessary for his sustenance, he returned to the presence of the Teacher.
Having gone, he offered the bowl. The Teacher, saying, "Bring it here, Tissa," extended his hand, took the bowl, and said, "Behold, Sāriputta, the bowl of your novice," showing it to the Elder.
The Elder took the bowl from the Teacher's hand, gave it to the novice, and said, "Go, sit in your own place and attend to your meal."
The villagers, having served the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, paid homage to the Teacher and requested a blessing.

As the Teacher gave his blessing, he spoke thus: "It is indeed a gain for you, lay followers, that by relying on your own family attendant novice, you have [honored] Sāriputta, Moggallāna, Kassapa, Anuruddha, and the eighty great disciples."
“You have gained the opportunity for this vision; I too have come depending solely upon your family preceptor. It is by depending on him alone that you have obtained this vision of the Buddha.
It is a gain for you! It is well-gained for you! The people thought: “Oh, what a gain for us!
We have seen our noble lady, who is capable of propitiating both the Buddhas and the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus.”
“We have gained our goal; we shall even be able to give alms to him,” the people said, and they were satisfied with the novice.
Being satisfied, the people gained even greater confidence. At the conclusion of the expression of thanks, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
The Teacher rose from his seat and departed. The people followed the Teacher for a short distance, paid their respects, and then turned back.
The Teacher, traveling with the novice on an even pace, proceeded while asking him, "Novice, what is the name of this place?
What is the name of that place? regarding the locations previously pointed out to him by the lay follower.
The novice also proceeded, explaining to him, "Venerable Sir, this is such-and-such; this is such-and-such. The Teacher [continued] for him...
Having gone to the dwelling place, he climbed to the summit of the mountain. While standing there, the great ocean appeared to them.
The Teacher asked the novice: "Tissa, standing on the mountain top and looking here and there, what do you see?
"The great ocean, Bhante. "Upon seeing the great ocean, what did you think? "My..."
“‘Venerable sir, you must have thought: "When one weeps during times of suffering, the tears shed must exceed the waters of the four great oceans. ‘Excellent, excellent, Tissa! It is even so.
For the tears shed by each single being during times of suffering indeed exceed the waters of the four great oceans. Having said this, he spoke this verse:”
“The water in the four oceans is but little;
the flood of tears shed by a man afflicted by suffering is far more vast and immeasurable.”
“For what reason, friend, do you neglect [your duties]?
Then he asked him again: “Tissa, where do you live? “In this mountain cave, Bhante.
“But while living there, what do you think about? “That when I die, my body shall be deposited in this place.”
“I thought there was no limit to them, venerable sir. “Excellent, excellent, Tissa! It is even so.
For among these beings lying upon the earth, there is indeed no place called ‘the Deathless’,” he said, and added:
“Fourteen thousand named Upasāḷakas;”
“In this world everything is consumed by fire; there is nothing in the world that remains unburnt.
But where truth, Dhamma, non-violence, self-restraint, and self-control exist—this is what the Noble Ones cultivate;
this is what in the world remains unburnt. (Jātaka 1.2.31–32)

In this context, he related the Upasāḷaka Jātaka from the Dukanipāta. Thus, among beings who die by casting their bodies upon the earth, there is no one who dies in a place where the Deathless has never before been;
yet those like the Elder Ānanda attain final Nibbāna in a place where the Deathless has never before been.
It is said that when the Elder Ānanda was in his eightieth year, observing the constituent forces of his life-span, he realized they were exhausted.
“I shall attain final Nibbāna on the seventh day from now,” he announced.
Upon hearing this news, among the people living on both banks of the Rohiṇī River, those dwelling on this side said, “We have been of great service to the Elder;
he will attain final Nibbāna in our presence. Those dwelling on the opposite bank also said, “We have been of great service to the Elder...”
“He will attain final nibbāna in our presence,” they said. Having heard their words, the Elder thought:
“The inhabitants of both banks have been helpful to me; it cannot be said that these [latter] are not helpful.

If I were to attain final nibbāna on this side of the river, those living on the opposite bank would quarrel with them for the sake of obtaining my relics. If, however, I were to attain final nibbāna on the opposite bank...”

Thinking, "Those dwelling on this shore will act in the same way; even when a quarrel arises, it will arise because of me alone, and even when it is pacified, it will be pacified because of me alone," he reflected:
"Those dwelling on this shore are helpful to me, and those dwelling on the further shore are also helpful to me; there is truly no one who is not helpful. Those dwelling on this shore..."
"Let those dwelling on this side of the river gather on this side, and let those dwelling on the far side also gather on the far side," he said.
Then, on the seventh day, sitting cross-legged in the air at a height of seven palm trees in the middle of the river, he preached the Dhamma to the great multitude and declared:
"Let my body split in the middle; let one part fall on this side of the bank, and one part on the far side."
Having made a resolution while remaining seated as he was, he entered the fire-element (*tejodhātu*); flames burst forth. His body split down the middle;
one half fell on this side of the riverbank, and the other half on the opposite bank. Then the great multitude wailed;

the sound of their lamentation was like the roar of the earth’s quaking at the end of an eon. Even more piteous than the sound of lamentation at the Teacher’s final *parinibbāna* was [the sound of] the people—
"For four months they wandered about weeping and lamenting, crying out and wailing:
'While those who held the Teacher's bowl and robes remained, it was as if the Teacher himself were still present; now our Teacher has passed into Parinibbāna.
Then the Teacher asked the novice: "Tissa, do you fear the sounds of leopards and other wild beasts in this forest thicket?"
"Do you not fear? "I do not fear, Blessed One; moreover, upon hearing their sounds, a delight in the forest arises within me.
Having said this, she spoke a discourse called "The Description of the Forest" in about sixty verses.
Then the Teacher addressed her, saying, "Tissa. "What is it, Venerable Sir? "We are going; will you go with us, or will you turn back?"
“Venerable sir, if my preceptor goes taking me with him, I will go; if he turns back, I will turn back.
The Teacher set out together with the community of monks. However, the novice’s intention was only to turn back.
The Elder, knowing this, said to him, “Tissa, if you wish to turn back, then turn back. He [then left] the Teacher and the community of monks...
Having paid homage, he turned back. The Teacher went to Jetavana itself.
A discussion arose among the bhikkhus in the Dhamma Hall: "Oh, how difficult the novice Vanavāsī Tissa performs!
From the moment of his conception, his kinsmen have provided five hundred bhikkhus for the seven auspicious occasions."

They gave him only rice-milk with water and honey; for seven days after his going forth, they gave only rice-milk with water and honey to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha within the monastery.
On the eighth day after his ordination, while entering the village, he received a thousand portions of alms-food along with a thousand garments in just two days; and again on another day—
He received a thousand woolen blankets. While he was living here, great gain and honor arose for him;
now, having abandoned such gain and honor, he has entered the forest and subsists on mixed alms-food—what a performer of austerities is the novice Tissa!
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, what discussion are you currently seated around?”
Having asked this and being told, "It is indeed for the sake of gain," he said: "Yes, monks, the basis for gain is one thing, and the practice leading to Nibbāna is another.

For a bhikkhu who guards the basis for gain by undertaking the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), such as living in the forest, thinking 'I shall thus obtain gain,' the four states of misery stand with their doors wide open; but as for the practice leading to Nibbāna—"
Having abandoned the gain and honor arising from his practice, he entered the forest and, striving and exerting himself, attained arahantship.
Joining the context together and teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
“Indeed, the means to gain is one thing, while that which leads to Nibbāna is another.”
"Having thus understood this through direct knowledge, a bhikkhu who is a disciple of the Buddha should not delight in honor, but should cultivate seclusion.
In this context, "the means to gain is one thing, while that which leads to Nibbāna is another": the means to gain is indeed one thing, and [the path to Nibbāna] is another.
The path leading to Nibbāna. For a monk who seeks to acquire gains, it is permissible to perform a small amount of unwholesome action;
he must practice crookedness of body and so forth. For at whatever time he performs some such act as crookedness of body, at that time gain arises.
Indeed, for one who lifts up a bowl of milk-rice after inserting his hand straight down without making it crooked—
The hand becomes merely smeared [with food], but when one bends it down and lifts it up, the lump of milk-rice comes out as if being drawn up;
in this way, gain arises at the very moment of performing bodily crookedness and so forth.
This is called "unrighteous dependence on gain. Furthermore, there is the excellence of requisites: the wearing of robes, great learning, a retinue, and dwelling in the forest.
However, gain arising from such causes as these is called "righteous" (dhammika).
A monk who is fulfilling the path leading to Nibbāna must abandon crookedness of body and so forth.
He ought to be like one who is not blind acting as if blind, like one who is not mute acting as if mute, and like one who is not deaf acting as if deaf. He should be without guile and without deceit.

It is appropriate. Having understood that "it is thus" (evam etam) refers both to this method for acquiring gain and the path leading to Nibbāna, a monk who is a disciple—so called in the sense of being born from hearing the Buddha’s instruction or advice, or in the sense of hearing it—is one who awakens to all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena;
such a one should not delight in unrighteous honor consisting of the four requisites.

One should not reject what is in accordance with the Dhamma, but should cultivate seclusion such as physical seclusion and the rest. In this context, "physical seclusion" (*kāyaviveka*) is the solitude of the body.
"Mental seclusion" (*cittaviveka*) refers to the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*). "Seclusion from acquisitions" (*upadhiviveka*) is Nibbāna.
Among these, physical seclusion dispels association with crowds; mental seclusion dispels association with the defilements (*kilesa*); and seclusion from acquisitions...
He dispels attachment to mental formations. Physical seclusion is a condition for mental seclusion; mental seclusion is a condition for seclusion from acquisitions. For it has also been said:
"Physical seclusion belongs to those who dwell in seclusion and delight in renunciation;

mental seclusion belongs to those whose minds are purified and have attained supreme clarity; and seclusion from acquisitions belongs to persons who are without acquisitions and have reached the state beyond formations."
One should cultivate and increase this threefold seclusion; the meaning is that one should enter upon it and dwell therein.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the fifteenth story, the account of the novice monk Tissavanavāsi.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Foolish is finished.
The fifth chapter.
6. The Chapter on the Wise.
1. The Story of the Elder Rādha "Like one who brings forth treasures"—the Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this Dhamma teaching concerning the Venerable Elder Rādha.
It is said that in his time as a householder, he was a poor brahmin in Sāvatthī. He thought, "I shall live in the presence of the bhikkhus."

Having reflected thus, he went to the monastery; while clearing away the weeds, sweeping the courtyard, and providing water for rinsing the mouth and other necessities, he remained right within the monastery.
The monks took care of him, yet they did not wish to grant him the going-forth (pabbajjā).
Not obtaining the going-forth, he became emaciated. Then one day, at dawn, the Teacher surveyed the world.

Seeing that brahmin, he reflected, "What indeed is this? and knowing, "He will become an arahant," he went into the presence of the brahmin at the time of evening, as if walking on a tour of the monastery, and asked, "Brahmin, what are you doing as you wander about?
"I am performing the duties and services for the monks, venerable sir. "Do you receive any hospitality from them?"
“Yes, venerable sir, I receive a mere portion of food, but they do not ordain me.
On this occasion, the Teacher had the community of monks assembled, and having asked about the matter, he inquired:
“Monks, is there anyone who remembers a service rendered by this brahmin? The Elder Sāriputta replied: “I remember it, venerable sir; this [brahmin]—”
“While I was walking for alms in Rājagaha, she had me give her the portion of rice from my own bowl that she had brought;
I remember this service of hers. When the Teacher said to him, “Sāriputta, is it not right to release one who has done such a service from suffering?
he replied, “Very well, Bhante, I shall ordain him,” and he ordained that brahmin.
His turn to receive alms at the head of the meal row did not come until the very end of the seating order, and he suffered from hunger due to the lack of rice gruel, food, and other provisions.
The Elder took him along on his journey and constantly exhorted and instructed him, saying, "This is what you must do; this is what you must not do.
He was easy to speak to and accepted the instructions with deference. Therefore, practicing according to those instructions—
In just a few days, he attained Arahatship.
The Elder took him with him, went into the presence of the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down. Then the Teacher, having exchanged greetings with him, said:
"Sāriputta, is your pupil easy to speak to? "Yes, venerable sir, he is exceedingly easy to speak to."
“He has never been angry when any fault was spoken against him. “Sāriputta, if you were to obtain such companions in the holy life, how many would you take?
“Venerable sir, I would take even many,” he replied. Then one day, they raised a discussion in the Hall of Truth:
“It is said that the Elder Sāriputta is grateful and appreciative; [once] when he received only a spoonful of almsfood...”
"Recalling the favor [done to him], he ordained the poor brahmin. The Elder, being capable of receiving instruction, received instruction that was indeed suited to him.
Having heard their conversation, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, Sāriputta was grateful and mindful of benefits," and spoke this verse to clarify that matter:
