“Relying on Alīnacitta, the great army was uplifted;
they captured the joyful Kosalas alive.
Thus, a bhikkhu endowed with such support and possessing aroused energy...”
“Cultivating wholesome states for the attainment of security from bondage,
one shall gradually reach the destruction of all fetters.
Having related this *Alīnacittajātakam* in detail from the *Dukanipāta*, he then spoke of how, at that time, by means of the carpenters’ foot—

Having told this Jātaka concerning the Elder Sāriputta—explaining how the solitary elephant became the donor of a completely white elephant calf after recognizing his own benefit through the act of making [the calf] healthy—he then spoke concerning the Elder Rādha:
"Monks, a monk indeed must be easy to speak with, just like Rādha; having pointed out a fault..."
“Even when being exhorted, one should not become angry; rather, the one who gives exhortation should be regarded as a pointer-out of hidden treasure,” he said.
Then, joining the connection and teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
“One who sees faults in another, like a guardian of hidden treasures, should be seen as such.”
"One should associate with such a wise person who speaks with restraint;
for one who associates with such a person, it becomes better, not worse.
In this context, "treasures" refers to jars of treasure filled with gold, silver, and so forth, which have been deposited and placed here and there.

"An encourager" is like one who, out of compassion for a person living in hardship and misfortune, says, "Come, I will show you a means of living happily," leads them to the location of a treasure, extends his hand, and points it out, saying, "Take this and live happily.
"One who points out faults" refers to two types of fault-finders: [one who says], "By this unseemly conduct or lapse..."
Nor is one who seeks out faults with the thought, "I shall restrain him in the midst of the Saṅgha.

Rather, it is one whose nature is established in upholding [others] by looking for this or that fault for the purpose of making known what is unknown, for the purpose of supporting what is already known, and out of a desire for the growth of their virtue and so forth.
This is the one intended here. For just as a man in distress, even after threatening or beating someone with the words, "Take this!"...
When showing a treasure, one does not become angry; rather, one is joyful.
In the same way, when seeing such a person point out what is unbecoming or a lapse, one should not be angry, but should instead be glad, thinking:
"Venerable sir, you have performed a great service for me; standing in the place of my teacher and preceptor, you have exhorted me, and [you should] do so again."

"You should speak"—thus one must indeed invite correction. Regarding "one who speaks after having rebuked": for some, upon seeing an unseemly act or a lapse by their student (saddhivihārika) and so forth, might think, "This person attends to me with great care, providing water for my mouth and other services;
if I speak to him, he will no longer attend to me, and thus I shall suffer loss. Being unable to bring himself to address the matter, such a person is not "one who speaks after having rebuked."

He is called one who scatters chaff upon this teaching. But he who, having seen such a fault, restrains him in accordance with the fault, sends him away, inflicts punishment, and—expelling him from the monastery—trains him, is called one who speaks with censure, just like the Perfectly Enlightened One.
For it has been said: "Ananda, I shall speak after repeatedly censuring [the offender]."
"Having threshed it again and again, Ānanda, I shall speak; that which is the essence will remain.
"Wise" means endowed with the wisdom of the Dhamma-essence. One should associate with and attend upon such a person—such a wise one.
For a pupil who associates with such a teacher as this, it is better, not worse; there is only growth, not decline.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
Thus ends the first story, the Story of the Elder Rādha.
2. The Story of Assaji and Punabbasu.
"Should exhort and instruct"—this teaching on the Dhamma was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the monks Assaji and Punabbasu. However, the discourse originated at Kīṭāgiri.
It is said that although those two monks were pupils of the Chief Disciples, they were shameless and evil monks.
Dwelling at Kīṭāgiri together with five hundred monks who were their own evil followers, they...
“‘They plant flowering shrubs themselves and have them planted by others’”—performing such various kinds of improper conduct, they committed an act that defiles the families.
Sustaining their livelihood through the requisites arising from that, they made that residence an unfit dwelling for well-behaved monks.
When the Teacher heard of this occurrence, he went with a retinue of two [monks] in order to carry out the formal act of banishment against them.
Addressing his two chief disciples, he said: “Go, Sāriputtas;
toward those among them who do not follow your word, perform the formal act of banishment (pabbājanīyakamma). But as for those who do follow it, instruct and exhort them.
For one who instructs and exhorts is disliked and displeasing only to the unwise, but to the wise, he is dear and pleasing.”
Connecting the context and teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
“One should advise and instruct, and restrain one from what is unwholesome;
for such a person is dear to the virtuous, but is disliked by the wicked.”
In this context, "should advise" means that one is said to advise when speaking while a matter has already arisen;

one is said to instruct when pointing out what is yet to come by saying, "There may even be misfortune for you," and so forth, while the matter has not yet arisen. One is said to advise when speaking face-to-face;
one is said to instruct when sending a messenger or a message in the absence of the person. One is said to advise when speaking only once.
"Speaking again and again" means he instructs; or rather, "instructing" itself is what is meant by "instructing. Thus one should exhort and instruct.
"And from the ignoble" means one should restrain him from unwholesome states (*akusaladhammā*) and establish him in wholesome states (*kusaladhammā*);
this is the meaning. "For he is dear to the virtuous" means that such a person is dear to the True Persons (*sappurisa*), such as the Buddhas and others.

But for those who have not seen the Dhamma, who have not crossed over to the world beyond, who have eyes only for material things, and who have gone forth merely for the sake of a livelihood—for them, that instructor and adviser is unpleasant when they pierce him with the weapons of their mouths, saying:
"You are neither our preceptor nor our teacher;
why do you instruct us? Thus he becomes disliked.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
Sāriputta and Moggallāna also went there and exhorted and instructed those bhikkhus. Among them, some accepted the exhortation and conducted themselves properly;
some left the order; and some incurred the formal act of banishment (pabbājanīyakamma).
The Story of Assaji and Punabbasu, the second.
3. The Story of Elder Channa.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning Elder Channa, beginning with the words: "One should not associate with evil friends."

It is said that the Venerable One reviled the two chief disciples, saying: "At the time of the Great Renunciation, I went forth together with our noble son [the Buddha], and at that time I did not see even another person;
yet now these two wander about saying, 'I am Sāriputta,' 'I am Moggallāna,' and 'We are the chief disciples. The Teacher [addressed] the monks...
Having heard of this occurrence from those nearby, the Teacher summoned the Elder Channa and admonished him. At that very moment, Channa became silent;
yet, having gone back again, he continued to revile the Elders. When he had thus reviled them for a third time, the Teacher summoned him once more and, after giving him counsel, said:
"Channa, the two Chief Disciples are your spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitta), supreme persons. Toward such spiritual friends—"
Having said, "Serve them, associate with them," he spoke this verse while teaching the Dhamma:
"Do not associate with evil friends; do not associate with those who are base.
Associate with virtuous friends; associate with the most excellent of men."
The meaning of this is as follows: those who delight in unwholesome kamma such as bodily misconduct and so forth are called "evil friends" (*pāpamitta*).
Or, those base men who incite one toward improper acts, such as breaking the bond of kinship or the twenty-one kinds of wrong livelihood, are called "the lowest of men" (*purisādhamā*).
Both of these types are indeed evil friends and the lowest of men; one should not associate with them nor attend upon them. Conversely, there are virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitta*).
"Both these [false teachers] and true persons—those you should associate with and attend upon.
At the conclusion of this teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
However, even after hearing that advice, the Elder Channa continued to revile and abuse the monks in the same manner as before.
They reported this again to the Teacher. The Teacher said, "Bhikkhus, while I am living, you will not be able to train Channa;

but after I have attained final Nibbāna, you will be able. Then, at the time of his final Nibbāna, when the Venerable Ānanda asked, "Venerable Sir, how should we deal with the Elder Channa? the Teacher replied, "Ānanda,..."
“Brahmadanda must be imposed upon the monk Channa,” he commanded. When the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, Channa heard that the Elder Ānanda had announced the brahmadanda against him;
distressed and dejected, he fainted and fell to the ground three times. Having entreated him, saying, “Venerable sir, do not destroy me!
and fulfilling the proper conduct, he before long attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
The third story, the account of the Elder Channa.
4. The account of the Elder Mahākappina.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, delivered this teaching on the Dhamma concerning the Elder Mahākappina: "One who finds joy in the Dhamma sleeps in happiness."

In this regard, the gradual account is as follows: It is said that in the past, the Venerable Mahākappina, having made his aspiration at the feet of the Buddha Padumuttara, was wandering through *saṃsāra* and was reborn in a weavers’ village not far from Bārāṇasī, becoming a chief weaver there.
At that time, about a thousand *paccekabuddhas*, having dwelt in the Himālaya for eight months during the rainy season, [emerged].
They dwelt in the countryside for four months. Once, having disembarked not far from Bārāṇasī, they sent eight paccekabuddhas into the presence of the king with the message:
"Request manual labor for the purpose of preparing lodgings. At that time, however, it was the king’s festival of sowing.
Hearing that "the paccekabuddhas have indeed arrived," he departed at that very moment.
Having asked the reason for his arrival, he said, "Venerable sir, there is no opportunity today;

tomorrow is our auspicious plowing festival, so we shall do it on the third day," and having failed to invite the Paccekabuddhas, he went inside. The Paccekabuddhas departed, thinking, "We shall go elsewhere.
At that moment, the wife of the chief carpenter had gone to Bārāṇasī on some business.
As they were going along, they saw those Paccekabuddhas; having paid homage to them, they asked, “Venerable sirs, noble ones, why have you come at an unusual hour?

and then related the matter from the beginning. Upon hearing that account, the woman—endowed with faith and endowed with wisdom—invited them, saying, “Venerable sirs, please accept almsfood from us tomorrow. They replied, “Sister, we are many. She asked, “How many?”
“Venerable sir,” he asked. “About a thousand,” they replied. “Venerable sirs, there are about a thousand weavers living in this village.
Let each one give alms to one monk; please accept the alms, and I myself will build a dwelling place for you.
The Paccekabuddhas consented.
Having entered the village, she made a proclamation: “I have invited a thousand paccekabuddhas after seeing them;

prepare a place for the noble ones to sit, and provide rice porridge, food, and other offerings. Having had a pavilion constructed in the center of the village and seats arranged, on the following day, she had the paccekabuddhas seated and [served] with excellent solid food.
Having served them with solid food and at the conclusion of their meal, he took all the women of that village with him;
together with them, he paid homage to the Paccekabuddhas and requested their consent, saying, "Venerable sirs, please grant us your promise to dwell here for the three months of the Rains.
Having obtained their promise, he then made a proclamation throughout the village: "O mother and father, let one man from each family take an axe, a hatchet, and other such tools..."
“Having taken [materials] and entered the forest, bring back building supplies and construct a dwelling place for the noble ladies.
Hearing her very words, the village dwellers each took one [share] and, together with the sites for night-quarters and day-quarters, had ten thousand leaf-huts constructed;
and when the Paccekabuddhas had entered the rains retreat in their respective leaf-huts, [each thought], “I—”
"I shall attend upon them with reverence; I myself shall attend upon them with reverence," they said, and so they attended upon them.

At the conclusion of the rains retreat, having exhorted them, saying, "Prepare robes for the Paccekabuddhas who have completed their rains retreat in their respective leaf-huts," he caused a robe worth a thousand pieces to be given to each one. The Paccekabuddhas, having completed the rains retreat—
Having expressed their appreciation, they departed.
The village dwellers, too, having performed this meritorious deed, passed away from there and were reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, where they became known as the Gaṇadevaputtas.
Having enjoyed divine splendor there, during the time of the Sammasambuddha Kassapa, they were born in Bārāṇasī.
They were reborn in the houses of wealthy householders. The chief weaver became the son of the eldest householder, and his wife was the daughter of that same eldest householder.
When they all reached maturity and went to their respective husbands' families, they returned to those very same houses.
Then one day, a proclamation for a Dhamma discourse was made throughout the monastery: "The Teacher..."
Having heard that he would teach the Dhamma, all those householders went to the monastery with their wives, thinking, "We shall hear the Dhamma.
At the very moment they entered the middle of the monastery, it began to rain.
Those who had attendant monks or novice kinsmen entered their respective cells. But for those who were not such [as those],...
Finding no place anywhere to enter because they were unable to do so, they stood right in the middle of the monastery.
Then the head householder said to them, "Behold our misfortune! Is it not fitting for sons of noble family to feel such shame?
They replied, "Noble sir, what indeed shall we do? He said, "It is because we lacked a place of trust that we have come to this misfortune."
“Let us all pool our wealth and build a courtyard,” he said. “Very well, noble sir,” the eldest replied and gave a thousand;
the others each gave five hundred. The women each gave two hundred and fifty.
Having pooled that wealth, they began the construction of what was called the Great Courtyard, with a thousand gabled chambers as a surrounding for the Teacher’s residence.
Because the new construction was so vast and his wealth was insufficient, they gave him further amounts of money, each time half of what had been previously given.

When the courtyard was finished, while celebrating the festival of the monastery, they offered a great almsgiving for seven days to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, and prepared robes for twenty thousand monks.
But the wife of the eldest householder, not acting in the same way as everyone else but remaining firm in her own wisdom,
thought, "I shall honor the Teacher with something more exceptional. Taking a basket of *anōja* flowers along with a thousand-piece garment the color of *anōja* flowers,
she honored the Teacher with the *anōja* flowers at the time of the expression of thanks, and placed that garment at the feet of the Teacher.

Setting aside [other wishes], she made this aspiration: "Venerable Sir, in each place where I am reborn, may my body be the color of the *anoja* flower, and may my name be 'Anojā'. The Teacher gave his blessing, saying, "So be it.
They all lived out their full lifespans, and passing away from there, they were reborn in the world of the gods. Then, during the arising of this Buddha...
Having passed away from the world of the gods, the eldest householder was reborn in the royal family of the city of Kukkuṭavatī;
upon reaching maturity, he became known as King Mahākappina. The others were reborn into the families of the ministers.
The wife of the eldest householder was reborn in the royal family of the city of Sāgala in the kingdom of Madda; her body was the very color of the *anoja* flower.
They gave her the name Anojā. When she reached maturity, she went to the house of King Mahākappina and became known as Queen Anojā.
The other women, having been born into the families of the ministers, also reached maturity and went to the houses of those very same sons of the ministers.
They all enjoyed a prosperity equal to that of the king. When the king—
Adorned with every ornament, he would mount an elephant and roam about, and then they too would roam about in the same manner.
When he roamed about on horseback or in a chariot, they too would roam about in the same manner.
Thus, by the power of the merit they had performed together, they experienced prosperity together. As for the king’s [ministers], Balo and Balavāhano...
There were five horses: Puppha, Pupphavāhana, Supatta, and two others. The king himself mounted the horse Supatta, while he gave the other four horses to the cavalrymen to carry his commands.
Having fed them early in the morning, the king said to them, "Go, and after roaming for two or three leagues, [report on] the Buddha, or the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha..."
"Or, having learned that he has passed away, bring me the news of his welfare," he sent.
They departed through the four gates and wandered for three *yojanas*, but returning without having obtained the message, they came back.
Then one day, the king, mounting the horse Supatta and surrounded by a thousand ministers, was going to the pleasure garden.
Seeing five hundred merchants entering the city while exhausted from their journey, he thought, "These people are weary from the road;
surely I shall hear some excellent news from them. He had them summoned and asked, "Where have you come from?
They replied, "Your Majesty, there is a city named Sāvatthī at a distance of two thousand yojanas from here; we have come from there."
"But has any teaching appeared in your region? "Your Majesty, there is nothing else; however, a Perfectly Enlightened One has appeared.
At that very moment, the king’s body was suffused with five-colored rapture (*pīti*);
unable to perceive anything else, he waited for a short while and then asked, "Sirs, what are you saying? "A Buddha, Your Majesty, has appeared."
The king spent his time in the same manner for a second and a third time. On the fourth occasion, having asked, "What do you say, dear ones?
and being told, "A Buddha has appeared, Your Majesty," he said, "Dear ones, I give you a hundred thousand [pieces of gold].
Then he asked, "Is there any other message? "There is, Your Majesty; the Dhamma has appeared. The king [inquired about] that as well.
Having heard this, he let three rounds pass in the same manner as before;
when it was said on the fourth round, "The Dhamma has appeared," he said, "I shall give you another hundred thousand here as well," and asked, "Is there further news, dear ones?
"There is, Your Majesty; the Jewel of the Saṅgha has appeared. Having heard that too, the king let three rounds pass and on the fourth—

When the word "Sangha" was uttered in the verse, he said, "I shall give you another hundred thousand here as well," and looking at his thousand ministers, he asked, "Dear ones, what will you do? They replied, "Your Majesty, what will you do?
He said, "Dear ones, having heard that 'the Buddha has appeared, the Dhamma has appeared, the Sangha has appeared,' I shall not turn back again."
“I shall go to the Teacher and, having approached him, receive the going-forth in his presence. “We too, Your Majesty, will go forth together with you,” they replied.
The king had letters engraved upon a golden plate and said to the merchants:
“The queen named Anojā will give you three hundred thousand [pieces of gold], and you should speak to her thus: ‘It is said that the king—’”
“Relinquish your sovereignty; enjoy your prosperity as you please.
But if he asks, “Where is the king?”, you should report, “He has gone away, saying, ‘I shall go forth into homelessness for the sake of the Teacher.
The ministers likewise sent such a message to each of their own wives. Having dismissed the merchants, the king—
Mounting his horse and surrounded by a thousand ministers, he departed at that very moment.
On that same day, at the time of dawn, the Teacher, surveying the world, saw King Mahākappina together with his retinue and thought:
"Having heard from the merchants that the Three Jewels have appeared, this Mahākappina..."
"Having honored these words with three hundred thousand [offerings], he will renounce his kingdom and, surrounded by a thousand ministers, desire to go forth under me;
tomorrow he will depart. Together with his retinue, he will attain Arahantship along with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā);
I shall go out to meet him. On the following day, like a Wheel-turning Monarch (cakkavattī) going out to meet a minor village headman, [the Buddha set out].

Taking his own bowl and robes, he went out to meet him for a distance of one hundred and twenty leagues and sat down at the foot of a banyan tree on the bank of the river Candabhāgā, emitting rays of six colors.
As the King was approaching, upon reaching a certain river, he asked, "What is this? "It is called the Aparacchā, O Lord," they replied. "What is its extent, dear sir? he asked.
“‘In depth it is one *gāvuta*, O gods, and in width two *gāvutas*. ‘But is there a boat or a raft here?
‘There is none, O gods. ‘While we look for boats and such, birth leads us to old age, and old age to death.
Having become free from doubt, I have gone forth for the sake of the Three Jewels; by their power, this—”
“May we not become like water in water! Reflecting thus on the virtues of the Three Jewels and recollecting the Buddha with the formula, “Such indeed is the Blessed One:
the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One,” he and his retinue plunged onto the surface of the water with a thousand horses.
The thoroughbreds leaped forth as if onto a backstone; the tips of their hooves were not even wetted.
Having crossed that river, he went forward and, seeing another river, asked, "What is the name of this one?
"It is named Nīlavāhinī, O Lord," they replied. "What is its size? "In depth and in breadth, it is half a *yojana*, O Lord.
The rest is exactly as before. Upon seeing that river, he recollects the Dhamma, thinking, "Well-expounded is the Dhamma by the Blessed One."
He leaped up, recollecting [the Buddha]. Passing over that as well, he went on and saw another river and asked, "What is the name of this?
"It is called the Candabhāgā, O King. "What is its size? "In depth and in breadth, it is one yojana, O King.
The rest is exactly as before. But upon seeing this river, [he thought], "The Blessed One has entered the good path..."
He leaped forward while recollecting the recollection of the Saṅgha, thinking, "This is the Saṅgha of disciples.
Having crossed that river, as he went along, he saw the six-colored rays of light issuing from the Teacher’s body.
The branches, twigs, and foliage of the banyan tree appeared as if made of gold. The king thought: "But this radiance belongs neither to the moon nor to the sun."
"It is not one of the gods, Māras, Brahmās, Nāgas, Supaṇṇas, or others; surely, as I am coming for the sake of the Teacher, I must have been seen by the Great Buddha Gotama.

At that very moment, he dismounted from the back of his horse and, with body bowed low, approached the Teacher following the rays [of light], as if sinking into the essence of emerald-colored water amidst the Buddha’s rays.
Having entered within, he paid homage to the Teacher and sat down to one side together with his thousand ministers;
the Teacher delivered to him a gradual discourse. At the conclusion of the teaching, the king, along with his retinue, was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
Then they all rose and requested the going forth. The Teacher [considered]: "Will these sons of good family come?"
Reflecting on the phrase "alms-bowls and robes made by supernormal power," he understood: "These sons of noble family gave a thousand robes to a thousand Paccekabuddhas;
during the time of the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha Kassapa, they also gave twenty thousand robes to twenty thousand bhikkhus.
It is no wonder that these alms-bowls and robes have arrived through supernormal power. Having realized this, he raised his right hand.
Having extended his hand, he said, "Come, monks; lead the holy life for the complete ending of suffering.
At that very moment, wearing the eight requisites and appearing like elder monks of sixty years' standing, they rose into the air, descended, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down.
The merchants went to the royal palace and, having announced that they had been sent by the king, were told by the queen, “Let them enter.
They entered, paid their respects, and stood to one side. Then the queen asked them, “Sirs, for what reason have you come?
“We have been sent to you by the king; please give us three hundred thousand,” they replied.
“Dear ones, you are saying too much. What have you done for the king? For what reason is the king so pleased with you that he has had this much wealth given?
“Queen, we have done nothing else; however, we reported a certain message to the king.
“But can you report it to me as well, dear ones? “It is possible, Queen. “In that case, dear ones, please speak.”
“Queen, a Buddha has appeared in the world. Having heard this, her body thrilled with joy just as before, she failed to perceive anything for three times;
but on the fourth occasion, upon hearing the word “Buddha,” she asked, “Dear ones, what was given by the king for this word?
“A hundred thousand pieces of gold, Queen. “Dear ones, the king has acted unworthily.”
"Having heard such a message, you have sent word that you will give a hundred thousand [pieces of gold].
Indeed, I shall give you three hundred thousand as my gift for your distress; furthermore, what else did you report to the king?
They reported those two other messages as well, saying, "This and this. The queen, her body thrilled with joy as before, [spoke] three times...
Without paying close attention, he heard the same thing during the fourth round and caused three hundred thousand to be given each time;
thus, they all received twelve hundred thousand in total.
Then the queen asked them, "Where is the king, dear ones? They replied, "O Queen, [he has said], 'I shall go forth into homelessness for the sake of the Teacher.'"
“He has gone,” they replied. “What message did he give me?
“It seems he entrusted all his sovereignty to you, saying, ‘May you enjoy prosperity as you please,’ O Queen. “But where are the ministers, dear ones?
“They too have gone, O Queen, with the thought: ‘We shall go forth together with the king. She [then spoke] to their wives...
Having summoned them, she said, "Ladies, your husbands have gone forth with the king, saying, 'We shall go into homelessness.
What will you do? "But what message did they send us, O Queen?
"It is said that they entrusted their own prosperity to you; it is said that you may enjoy that prosperity as you please."

“But what will you do, Queen? “Mother, that king, upon hearing the message, even while standing on the road, worshipped the Three Jewels with three hundred thousand [pieces of gold] and, casting away his prosperity like a globule of spittle, set forth saying, ‘I shall go forth.
But as for me, having heard the message of the Three Jewels, I shall worship the Three Jewels with nine hundred thousand...”
“They have been honored, yet this prosperity is not painful for the king alone; it is painful for me as well.
Who would stand on their knees and take with their mouth a lump of spittle discarded by the king? I have no need for such prosperity;
I too shall go forth into homelessness, having gone to follow the Teacher. “Queen, we too [shall do so] because of you alone...”
“We shall go forth together. “If you are able, it would be well, my ladies,” he said. “We are able, O Queen,” they replied.
“Very well, my ladies; come then,” he said. Having had a thousand chariots harnessed, he mounted a chariot and set out with them.
On the way, seeing the first river, he asked about it exactly as the king had asked, and [they told him] the entire account.

Having heard this, she said, "Look for the path the king took. When they replied, "We do not see any hoofprints of the Sindhava horses, O Queen," she said, "The king has departed having made an act of truth (saccakiriya) directed toward the Three Jewels.
I too have set out directed toward the Three Jewels; by their very power, let this [water] not become like this!"
Having recollected the virtues of the Three Jewels, he dispatched a thousand chariots. The water became as solid as a stone slab;
not even the tips of the wheel-rims were wetted. By this very means, he crossed the other two rivers.
Then the Teacher, knowing of his arrival, acted so that the monks seated near him would no longer be visible.
She did exactly that. As she went along, seeing the six-colored rays of light emanating from the Teacher’s body, she thought the same thing and approached the Teacher.
Having paid homage, she stood to one side and asked:
"Venerable Sir, Mahākappina has gone forth for your sake; I suppose he has arrived here. Where is he? Please let us see him as well."
“Sit down for a moment; you shall see him right here. All of them, their hearts filled with joy, sat down, thinking, “Seated right here, we shall indeed see our husband.

The Teacher delivered a gradual discourse to them, and at the conclusion of the teaching, Queen Anoja and her retinue attained the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). Elder Mahākappina [delivered] a further discourse on the Dhamma to them...

Listening with his retinue, he attained *arahantship* together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). At that moment, the Teacher revealed to them those monks who had attained *arahantship*.

It is said that if they had seen their own husbands wearing the saffron robes and with shaven heads at the very moment they arrived, their minds would not have become one-pointed, and thus they would not have been able to attain the paths and fruits.
Therefore, at the moment they were established in unwavering faith, he showed them those monks who had already attained Arahatship.
Having seen them, they prostrated themselves with the fivefold salutation and said, "Venerable sir, your duty as renunciants has reached its culmination.
Having paid homage to the Teacher, they stood to one side and requested ordination. Thus...
When this was said, some say that the Teacher thought of Uppalavaṇṇā’s arrival.
But the Teacher said to those female lay disciples, “Go to Sāvatthī and receive the going-forth in the Bhikkhunī-upassaya.

As they proceeded by stages on their journey through the countryside, they received offerings of honor and hospitality from great crowds along the way, yet they traveled the two hundred leagues on foot.
Having gone to the nuns' quarters and gone forth, they attained arahantship.

The Teacher, too, taking a thousand bhikkhus, went by way of the air to Jeta’s Grove. There, indeed, the Venerable Mahākappina wandered about at his night-quarters, day-quarters, and other places, uttering this inspired exclamation:
"O what bliss! O what bliss! The bhikkhus reported this to the Blessed One.
“Venerable sir, Mahākappina wanders about uttering the exclamation, ‘Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!’;

I suppose he is speaking with reference to his own sensual pleasure and the pleasure of kingship. The Teacher summoned him and asked, “Is it true, Kappina, that you uttered such an exclamation with reference to sensual pleasure and the pleasure of kingship? “It is true, Blessed One.”
“Venerable sir, does he know whether that [utterance] was an inspired utterance (*udāna*) or not?
The Teacher replied, “Monks, my son does not utter an inspired utterance concerning sensual pleasure or the pleasure of kingship;

rather, in my son there arises what is called the joy of the Dhamma and what is called the delight in the Dhamma. It is concerning the great Nibbāna of the Deathless alone that he utters this inspired utterance.”
Connecting the context and teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
“The one who drinks the Dhamma sleeps happily with a serene mind;
the wise person always delights in the Dhamma proclaimed by the Noble Ones.”

In this context, "one who drinks the Dhamma" (*dhammapīti*) means one who drinks the Dhamma; that is, one who drinks the Dhamma. Now, this Dhamma cannot be drunk from a vessel like rice-gruel and other such things.

Rather, it is by touching the ninefold supramundane Dhamma with the mental body (*nāmakāya*), realizing it as an object, and penetrating the Noble Truths of suffering and so forth through the clear comprehension of full understanding (*pariññābhisamaya*) and the rest, that one is said to drink it.
"He drinks the Dhamma" means this. "He sleeps happily" is merely a figurative expression; the meaning is that he dwells happily in all four postures.
"With a serene mind" means with a mind that is untroubled and free from defilements.

"In the states proclaimed by the Noble Ones" refers to the factors conducive to enlightenment, such as the foundations of mindfulness and so forth, which have been proclaimed by the Noble Ones beginning with the Buddha. "He always delights" means he takes constant delight in such Dhamma-joy.
"Dwelling with a serene mind, endowed with wisdom, he always delights and rejoices.
At the conclusion of this teaching, many became stream-enterers and others.
This is the fourth story, concerning the Elder Mahākappina.

5. The Story of the Wise Novice (Paṇḍitasāmaṇeravatthu) The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning the wise novice, beginning with the words: "For they lead water.
It is said that in the past, the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, accompanied by a retinue of twenty thousand arahants whose taints were destroyed, went to Bārāṇasī.
Having observed their own strength, people joined together in groups of eight or ten and gave gifts such as food for travelers.
Then one day, at the conclusion of his meal, the Teacher offered this expression of appreciation:
"Lay followers, here some person thinks: 'It is proper to give only what belongs to oneself; why should one be exhorted by another?'"

One gives a gift oneself but does not encourage others to do so. Such a person obtains an abundance of wealth in every place where they are reborn, but not an abundance of followers. Another encourages others to give but does not give themselves.
Such a person obtains an abundance of followers in every place where they are reborn, but not an abundance of wealth. Still another neither gives themselves nor encourages others to give.
Thus, in whatever place he is reborn, he obtains neither abundance of wealth nor abundance of retinue;
he lives merely as one who subsists on the remnants of others. Another person gives himself and also encourages others to give.
He, in whatever place he is reborn, obtains both abundance of wealth and abundance of retinue.
Hearing this, a certain wise man standing nearby thought: "I shall now act in such a way that both types of success will be mine.
He paid homage to the Teacher and said: "Venerable Sir, please accept my almsfood tomorrow.
"How many monks do you require? "But how many do you have, sir?"
“Venerable sir, what is his retinue? “Twenty thousand bhikkhus. “Venerable sir, please accept alms from me tomorrow together with them all.

The Teacher consented. He entered the village and said, “Mother and father, I have invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, headed by the Buddha, for tomorrow; you should provide as many bhikkhus as you are able to feed.”
Having announced, "Give alms to that many," he wandered about; then, as each person observed their own strength and said,
"We will give to ten," "We will give to twenty," "We will give to a hundred," or "We will give to five hundred," he recorded everyone's words on a leaf starting from the beginning.
Now at that time, there was a certain man in that city who was known as "Mahāduggata" (the Great Poor) because of his extreme state of destitution.
Seeing him also present before him, he said: "Friend Mahāduggata, I have invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha for tomorrow's meal;
tomorrow the residents of the city will give alms. How many bhikkhus will you feed?"
“Master, what have I to do with monks? For those who possess wealth, indeed, there is need for monks;
but as for me, tomorrow I do not even have a single stalk of rice for porridge. I live by working for wages; what have I to do with monks?
One who exhorts others must be competent. Therefore, even when he was told “there is none,” that man did not remain silent, but spoke thus:
—“Good man Mahāduggata, in this city many people enjoy prosperity, eating fine food, wearing delicate garments, adorned with various ornaments, and reclining on beds of glory;
yet you, though working for hire all day long, do not even obtain enough to fill your belly. Even so, you think: ‘In the past...’”
“Do you not know that because no merit has been performed, one obtains nothing at all? “I know it, Master. “Then why do you not perform merit now?
You are young and endowed with strength; is it not fitting for you to give a gift according to your power, even by working for wages?
While he was speaking thus, the man became filled with a sense of spiritual urgency and said, “I too shall [give] one monk...”
"Put your name on the list; having done some small work for hire, I will give alms to one monk," he said.
The other replied, "What is the use of putting one's name on the list for a single monk? and so he did not put his name down.
The very poor man also went home and said to his wife, "My dear, the city dwellers will provide a meal for the Saṅgha tomorrow; I too was encouraged by the recruiter [to say], 'One..."
When he was told, "Give alms," she said, "We too shall give alms to one tomorrow.
Then his wife, without saying, "We are poor; why did you accept [the request]? replied, "Husband, you have done well.
Previously we gave nothing at all, yet now we have become destitute. Let us both work for wages and give alms to one."
“We will give it, sir,” they said, and both went out from their house and went to the place of labor.
When the great merchant saw him, he asked, “What is it, friend Mahāduggata, will you work for wages? “Yes, noble sir.
“What will you do? “I will do whatever you have me do. “In that case, tomorrow we shall—”
“We shall feed three hundred bhikkhus; come, split some wood. Having brought out an axe and a hatchet, he gave them to him.

Mahāduggata fastened his belt tightly and, exerting great effort, would take up the hatchet after putting down the axe, and take up the axe after putting down the hatchet, as he split the wood. Then the merchant said to him: “Good man, you—”
“Master, today you are working with extraordinary zeal; what could be the reason for this? “Sir, tomorrow I shall feed a single monk.
Hearing this, the merchant, with a mind full of faith, thought: “Oh, a difficult task has been undertaken by this man!
Without falling silent out of thinking ‘I am poor,’ he has resolved: ‘Having worked for wages, I shall feed a single monk.’”
“...so he says. When the merchant’s wife saw his wife, she asked, “My lady, what work will you do?
When she replied, “I shall do whatever you command,” the merchant’s wife had her enter the mortar-hall and provided her with mortars, pestles, and other tools.
She pounded and winnowed the rice as if she were dancing, joyful and exultant. Then [the merchant’s wife] said to her—
The merchant’s wife asked, “Mother, you are working with an expression of extreme joy;
what is the reason for this? “Noble lady, having earned this wage, we too shall feed a bhikkhu.
Upon hearing this, the merchant’s wife also gained confidence in her, thinking, “Oh, what a performer of difficult deeds she is! [Meanwhile,] the merchant [gave] to Mahāduggata...
When the timber was being split, she had four *nāḷis* of rice given to him, saying, "This is for your wages," and she had another four *nāḷis* given, saying, "This is for your gratuity.
Having gone home, he said to his wife, "I have obtained rice by working for wages; this shall be the seed-corn."
"Take curds, oil, pungent condiments, and spices with that wage you have received.
The merchant’s wife also had her give her another bowl of ghee, a vessel of curds, pungent condiments, and a measure of pure rice.
Thus, there were nine measures of rice for both of them. Thinking, "We have obtained the gift to be given," they were joyful and elated.
They rose early in the morning. The wife said to Mahāduggata, “Go, husband, seek out some leaves and bring them back.
Not finding any leaves in the market, he went to the riverbank; with a joyful heart, thinking, “Today I shall obtain food to give to the Noble Ones,” he gathered leaves while singing.
A fisherman standing there, having cast a great net, [saw] Mahāduggata’s...
Thinking, "He must have something to eat," he called him over and asked, "You are singing with an exceedingly joyful heart;
what is the reason for this? "I am gathering leaves, friend. "What will you do with them? "I shall feed a single bhikkhu.
"Oh, how happy that bhikkhu is! What will he eat of your leaves? "What can I do, friend? By myself—"
“Shall I feed you with the fish I have caught? “In that case, come along. “What shall I do, madam?
“Take these fish and make bundles worth one foot, half a foot, and one kahāpaṇa. He did so.
Then he gave the bound fish to the monks who had been invited by the city dwellers.
They took them for their own benefit. While he was still making offerings of fish, the time for the alms-round arrived.
Observing the time, he said, "Friend, I must go; this is the hour when the monks arrive.
"But is there any fish offering left? "No, friend, it is all gone. "In that case, [I shall take] what is for my own benefit..."
Having buried them in sand, he placed four rohita fish there and said, "If you wish to feed the bhikkhu,
take these and go," and he gave those fish to him.
On that day, however, at dawn, the Teacher surveyed the world with his net of knowledge and [beheld] a person of great poverty within his own sphere of wisdom.
Seeing that he had entered within, and reflecting, "What might this be?", he thought:
"Yesterday, a very poor man worked for hire with his wife, intending to feed a single monk; which monk will he obtain?
Then he considered: "People will take the monks, using the signal of the leaf-assignment, and seat them each in their own respective houses."
"He will not find another monk except me," he reflected. It is said that Buddhas feel compassion for those who are destitute.

Therefore, the Teacher, having attended to his bodily needs early in the morning, entered the Fragrant Chamber and sat down, thinking, "I shall look after Mahāduggata. Meanwhile, Mahāduggata had gone home after catching fish.
As he was entering, [the throne] manifested a hot appearance to Sakka’s Pandukambala stone seat. Looking about, [Sakka] wondered, "What could be the reason for this?
He thought, "Yesterday, a great pauper worked for hire with his wife, intending to give alms to a single bhikkhu; which bhikkhu will he obtain today? Then he considered, "He has nothing..."
"But another monk shall do so; however, I, the Teacher, will show favor to Mahāduggata," he said, while sitting in the Gandhakuṭī.
Mahāduggata would give even his own meager supply of rice-gruel, boiled rice, and leaf-vegetables to the Tathāgata. [The Teacher thought:
"What if I were to go to Mahāduggata’s house and perform the work of a cook? and thus, in the guise of a stranger—
Having approached the vicinity of his house, he asked, "Is there anything for anyone to do as wage labor?
Seeing him, the Great Poor Man said, "Friend, what work will you do? "Master, I am skilled in all crafts;
there is no craft that I do not know. I even know how to prepare rice gruel, cooked rice, and so forth. "Friend," [he replied].
“We have need of your work, yet we see no wages to be given to you. “But what is it that must be done?
“I wish to give alms to a certain bhikkhu; I desire the preparation of rice-gruel and food for him.
“If you will give alms to the bhikkhu, I have no need for wages; what merit [would there be] for me?”
"It is not proper. "If that is the case, it is well, friend; please enter," he said.
Having entered his house, he had oil, rice, and other provisions brought out, and then sent him away, saying, "Go and bring the monk who has received his alms-bowl.
The distributor of gifts also sent monks to the various houses according to the order already written down on the leaf.
The very poor man went to him and said, "Give me the alms-bowl belonging to me.
At that moment, the other regained his mindfulness and said, "I have forgotten your bowl.
The very poor man felt as if he had been struck in the belly with a sharp spear and cried out, "Master, why do you destroy me? It was by you that I was urged yesterday toward my wife..."
"Having worked for wages together for an entire day, today at dawn I have come back after wandering along the riverbank seeking leaves;
give me one alms-bowl," he lamented, raising his arms. People gathered and asked, "What is this, Great Destitute?
He related the matter to them. They asked a bystander, "Is it true, friend? he replied, "It is true."
“Did she, having made a promise, incite you by saying, ‘Give alms to one bhikkhu’? “Yes, noble lady.
“A grave deed has been done by you, you who, while providing for so many bhikkhus, did not give even one bhikkhu to him.
At their words, he became ashamed and said to her: “Friend Mahāduggata, do not ruin me!”
"Because of you, I have encountered great distress; people, according to the custom of placing their names on slips of paper, are taking away the alms intended for themselves.
There is no one who will take the bhikkhu sitting in his own house and give him [the food];
yet the Teacher, having washed his face, remains seated right there in the Gandhakuṭī. Then the king, the crown prince, the commander-in-chief, and others [came] from the Teacher’s Gandhakuṭī.
“While sitting and looking toward the departure, take the Teacher’s bowl and say, ‘We shall go. Buddhas indeed show compassion to those who are destitute;
go to the monastery, pay homage to the Teacher, saying, ‘Venerable Sir, I am destitute;
please take me under your care,’ and if you have merit, you will certainly receive it.”

Thus he went to the monastery. Then, because they had seen him in the monastery on other days as one who subsisted on the remains of food, the king, the crown prince, and others said to him, "Great pauper, it is not yet time for the meal;
why have you come? He replied, "I know, sirs, that 'it is not yet time for the meal.
However, I have come to pay homage to the Teacher. Having said this, he went to the Gandhakuti.
Placing his head upon the threshold and bowing with the fivefold prostration, he said, "Venerable Sir, there is no one more destitute than I in this city;
be my refuge and grant me your favor. The Teacher opened the door of the Perfumed Chamber, brought forth his bowl, and placed it in his hand.
He felt as though he had attained the glory of a wheel-turning monarch, and the king, the crown prince, and others—
They looked at one another’s faces. For there was no one capable of taking the bowl given by the Teacher through the power of authority.
Yet they spoke thus: "Friend Mahāduggata, give us the Teacher’s bowl;
we will give you so much wealth. You are poor, take the wealth; what use have you for the bowl?"
The very poor man said, "I will give it to no one; I have no need for wealth;
I shall feed the Teacher alone. The rest of them, having requested him and failed to obtain the bowl, returned.
But the king thought, "Even when tempted with wealth, the very poor man does not give the Teacher’s bowl, nor can anyone take the bowl given by the Teacher himself."
He was unable to do so, and thinking, "How much wealth will he have to give?
When he gives his gift, I shall take the Teacher with me to his house and offer him the food I have prepared," he went along with the Teacher.
Sakka, the king of the gods, likewise prepared rice gruel, hard foods, cooked rice, soups, leaf-vegetables, and other provisions.
Having prepared a seat worthy for the Teacher to sit upon, he sat down.
After leading the Teacher inside, Mahāduggata said, "Enter, Bhante. Now, his dwelling house was low;
it was not possible to enter without stooping. And indeed, when Buddhas enter a house, they do not enter by stooping.
For at the time of entering the house, either the great earth sinks down or the house rises up;
this is the fruit of their well-bestowed gift. When they have departed after leaving again, everything returns to its normal state.
Therefore, the Teacher, while still standing, entered the house and sat upon the seat prepared by Sakka. While the Teacher was seated—
The king said, "Friend Mahāduggata, even when we were begging from you, you did not give us the Teacher’s bowl;
let us see, then, what kind of honor you have paid to the Teacher. Then Sakka opened up the rice-gruel, the solid food, and so forth, and showed them to him.
The fragrance of those offerings pervaded the entire city. The king, having looked at the rice-gruel and the other items—
He said to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, I have come thinking, ‘How much of an offering will there be for the Great Poor Man?
Once this offering has been given, I will lead the Teacher home and give him the food I have prepared myself.
Such food as this has never been seen by me before; if I were to remain here, the Great Poor Man would become weary.”
"Let us go," he said, and having paid homage to the Teacher, he departed. Sakka also gave the Teacher rice porridge and other foods, serving him with great care.
When the Teacher had finished his meal and performed the expression of thanks, he rose from his seat and departed.
Sakka gave a signal to the great pauper; he took the bowl and followed after the Teacher. Sakka then turned back.
Standing at the door of the house of a man of great poverty, he looked up into the sky.
At that very moment, a rain of the seven precious gems fell from the sky, filling all the vessels in his house until the entire dwelling was full; there was no more room in his house.
His wife, taking her children by the hands, led them out and stood outside. He [approached] the Teacher.
Having returned from his pursuit, he saw the children outside and asked, "What is this?
They replied, "Master, our entire house is filled with the seven treasures; there is no room to enter.
Thinking, "Today the fruit of my giving has been bestowed upon me," he went into the presence of the king, paid homage, and when asked, "Why have you come? he said, "Your Majesty, [my] house..."
“[This vessel] is filled with my seven kinds of jewels; take that wealth.
The king thought, “Oh, the gift given to the Buddhas has reached its ultimate fulfillment this very day! and said to him, “What do you require to obtain?
“A thousand carts for the purpose of carrying the wealth, O King. The king sent a thousand carts and had the wealth brought to the royal courtyard.
He had it scattered. It became a heap as large as a palm tree. The king, having caused the people to assemble in the city, asked:
"Is there anyone in this city who possesses such great wealth? "There is none, Your Majesty," they replied. "What should be done for one of such vast wealth?
"It is fitting, Your Majesty, to grant him the position of chief treasurer. The king, having performed a great honor for him, [conferred the office].
He caused the site for a treasurer’s residence to be granted.

Then, having pointed out the site of a former treasurer’s house, he said, “When a tree grows there, have it cleared away, build a house, and live there. After he had cleared that site and leveled it, while the ground was being dug...
Treasure jars rose up, striking against one another. When this was reported to the king, he said, “These have arisen through your merit;
you alone shall take them. He had a house built and for seven days gave a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha.
Thereafter, remaining as long as his lifespan lasted, he performed meritorious deeds and at the end of his life was reborn in the world of the devas.

Having experienced divine prosperity for the duration of one *buddhantara*, when this Buddha appeared in the world, he passed away from that state and took rebirth in the womb of a merchant’s daughter in Sāvatthī, within the family of the Elder Sāriputta’s attendant.
Then, her parents, having learned that she was pregnant, provided her with the necessary care for the pregnancy. After some time, such as this occurred to her...
A pregnancy longing arose in her: “O, that I might give a gift of red fish-flesh to five hundred bhikkhus, beginning with the preacher of the Dhamma;
and having donned saffron robes, seated at the edge of their seats, I might eat the food left over by those bhikkhus. Having informed her parents, she did so.
She did so, and her craving subsided. Then, at seven subsequent auspicious occasions, they fed five hundred bhikkhus—headed by the Elder Dhammasenāpati—with the very same flesh of red fish.

All of this is to be understood according to the procedure already described in the account of Prince Tissa. This, however, was the result of that gift of red fish given during his time of extreme poverty.
[This was] the result. On the day of his naming, when his mother said, "Venerable sir, please give the precepts to your slave," the Elder asked, "What is this boy's name?

[She replied], "Venerable sir, from the moment of his conception in this child's womb, even those in this house who were dull-witted and mute have become wise; therefore, let my son be known simply as 'The Wise One' (Paṇḍita)."
“...will be his name. The Elder gave him the precepts. From the day of his birth, however, a thought arose in his mother’s mind: “I shall not thwart my son’s aspiration.
When he was seven years old, he said to his mother, “Mother, I will go forth into homelessness in the presence of the Elder. “Very well, dear one,” she replied, “I shall not thwart your aspiration.”

Having said, “I shall not break my word,” he invited the Elder, fed him, and then dismissed the Elder, saying, “Venerable sir, this slave wishes to go forth; I will bring him to the monastery this evening.
Then, having gathered his kinsmen together, he said, “Today itself we shall perform the honors due to my son for his time as a householder.”
Having accorded him great honor, he took him to the monastery and gave him to the Elder, saying, "Venerable sir, please ordain this man.
The Elder explained the difficulty of the life of renunciation; when the man replied, "Venerable sir, I shall follow your instruction," the Elder said, "In that case, come.
He then moistened his hair, taught him the meditation subject of the five aggregates (the *tacapañcaka*), and ordained him.
His parents also, staying in the monastery for seven days, gave alms to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha using only red fish-meat.
On the seventh day, they returned home in the evening. On the eighth day, as the Elder was going into the village, he went taking him with him;
he did not go together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. For what reason? Because his bowl and robes had not yet been taken.
or his deportment is pleasing; moreover, there is a duty to be performed by the Elder in the monastery.

For when the Saṅgha of bhikkhus has entered the village, the Elder wanders throughout the entire monastery, sweeps the places that have not been swept, sets out drinking water and water for washing in empty vessels, and [straightens] beds, chairs, and so forth that have been poorly arranged.

Having tidied up, he enters the village afterwards. Furthermore, thinking, "Lest the followers of other sects enter an empty monastery and say, 'See the places where the disciples of the ascetic Gotama sit!
he cleans the entire monastery and then enters the village. Therefore, on that day as well, having had the novice take his bowl and robes—
He entered for alms even earlier than usual.
As the novice was walking along with his preceptor, he saw a ditch on the way and asked, "Venerable sir, what is this?
"It is called a ditch, novice. "What do they do with it? "They direct water from here and there [into it]."
“Having brought it back, she performs her own agricultural work. “But, venerable sir, does water have consciousness?
“There is none, friend. “Then, venerable sir, they carry such a thing as this, which lacks consciousness, to wherever they wish?
“Yes, friend. He thought: “If even such a thing as this, lacking consciousness, can be carried to wherever one desires and perform its work...”
“If they cannot do so, why will those who possess minds not be able to bring their own minds under control and practice the Dhamma of a recluse?
Then, as he walked ahead, he saw fletchers heating bow-staves over a fire and straightening them by looking at them with the corners of their eyes.
He asked, “Venerable sir, who are these men? “They are called fletchers, friend. “What—”
“Do they do this? “They straighten a reed by heating it over a fire. “Venerable sir, does that [reed] have consciousness?

“It is without consciousness, friend. He thought: “If they take something without consciousness, heat it over a fire, and straighten it, why then should those with consciousness not bring their own minds under control and practice the Dhamma of a recluse?”

“They will be able to. Then, as he was walking ahead, seeing carpenters fashioning wood for the spokes, the nave, and so forth, he asked, “Venerable sir, who are these? “They are called carpenters, friend. “But what do they do?
“Friend, they take wood and make wheels and other parts for vehicles and such. “But are these things, venerable sir, endowed with consciousness?”
“Friend, they are mindless,” he said. Then it occurred to him:
“If they take mindless pieces of wood and fashion wheels and such things, why should sentient beings, having brought their own minds under control, not be able to practice the Dhamma of a recluse?
Having seen these reasons, he said: “Venerable sir, if you [were to give] your bowl and robe to me...”
"You take them, and I shall turn back. The Elder, without even giving rise to the thought, "This young novice who has only recently gone forth is following me and speaking thus," said, "Bring them,
novice," and took his own bowl and robes.
The novice, having paid homage to his preceptor as he was turning back, said: "Venerable sir, when you bring me food, you should bring it using only the meat of red fish.

"How shall we obtain it, friend? [he asked]. "Venerable sir, if you do not obtain it through your own merit, you will obtain it through my merit," he replied. The Elder thought, "Even while this young novice sits outside, there are obstacles..."
“May you do so,” he said, giving him a key and adding, “Open the door to my dressing room, enter within, and sit down.
He did accordingly; then, directing his knowledge toward his own physical body and contemplating his own selfhood, he sat there.
Thereupon, by the power of his virtue, Sakka’s throne manifested a sign of heat. Sakka wondered, “What now could be the cause of this?”
Reflecting, “The wise novice monk has given his bowl and robes to his preceptor and turned back, thinking, ‘I shall perform the duties of a recluse’;
it is fitting for me also to go there,” he addressed the four Great Kings,
saying, “Drive away the birds dwelling in the grove near the monastery and establish a guard all around,” and then [he spoke to] Candadevaputta.

“Draw in and seize the moon’s disk! he said; and having told the son of the gods Sūriya, “Draw in and seize the sun’s disk!”, he himself went and stood guard at the place where the pulling rope was fixed.
Not even the sound of a withered leaf falling in the monastery was heard, and the novice’s mind became one-pointed. While still during the midday meal, he—
Having reflected upon his own state of being, he attained the three fruits.
The Elder, thinking, "The novice is sitting in the monastery;

it will be possible to obtain suitable food for him at such-and-such a family," went to a lay supporter’s family with whom he shared a bond of affection and respect. And on that day, the people there—
Having caught a rohita fish, they sat waiting for the Elder’s arrival.

Seeing the Elder approaching, they said, "Venerable sir, it is a fortunate thing that you have come here," and having invited him into their home, they gave him rice gruel, hard food, and other provisions, and offered him alms-food consisting of the juice of the rohita fish. The Elder signaled his intention to take it. The people—
"Venerable sir, please eat; you will also receive the meal for the errand," he said.
At the conclusion of the elder’s meal, they filled his bowl with a dish of roasted fish and gave it to him. The elder, thinking, "The novice is hungry," went away quickly.
On that day, the Teacher, having eaten early and gone to the monastery, reflected thus:

“Will the novice Paṇḍita’s purpose for going forth be fulfilled? Reflecting thus, he observed that the novice had given his bowl and robes to his preceptor, turned back with the thought, “I shall perform the duties of a recluse,” and having understood that he had attained three of the fruits, he further examined whether or not there was the necessary condition (*upanissaya*) for Arahantship.
Seeing that it existed, [he resolved] before the meal:
While reflecting on whether he would be able to attain arahantship or not, he perceived that he would indeed be able.
Then it occurred to him: "Sāriputta is coming quickly, having taken the novice's meal;
he might even cause an obstacle for me. Therefore, I shall sit taking my post at the gatehouse and then question him."
"When this question is answered, the novice will attain Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Then, having gone there and standing at the gatehouse, he asked the Elder who had arrived four questions; as each question was asked, the Elder answered it.
Herein, this is the question and answer: the Teacher, it seems, said to him, "Sāriputta, what have you attained?"
“Food, venerable sir. “What does that which is called ‘food’ nourish, Sāriputta? “It nourishes feeling, venerable sir.
“What does feeling nourish, Sāriputta? “It nourishes form, venerable sir. “But what does form nourish, Sāriputta?
“It nourishes contact, venerable sir. The intended meaning here is this: for food consumed by one who is hungry nourishes that [body].

Having avoided what is unwholesome, one brings about pleasant feeling. Through the enjoyment of food, when pleasant feeling arises in one who is happy, there is excellence of physical beauty in the body. Thus, feeling brings about form.
Furthermore, one who is happy, experiencing happiness and joy born of the materiality produced by food, thinks, "Now a gratification has arisen for me," as he lies down or sits.
“...or does he obtain a pleasant touch?
When these four questions had been answered, the novice attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
The Teacher also said to the Elder: “Go, Sāriputta, give food to your novice. The Elder—

Having gone there, he knocked at the door. The novice emerged, took the bowl from the elder’s hand, set it aside, and fanned the elder with a palm-leaf fan. Then the elder said to him, “Novice, perform the meal duty.
“But what about you, venerable sir? “I have finished my meal duty; you do it. [The novice was] a seven-year-old boy.
Having gone forth, on the eighth day at that very moment, he attained *arahantship*, resembling a blossomed lotus or water-lily.
While sitting and reviewing the stage of his realization, he performed his meal duties.
When he had washed his bowl and put it away, the deity Candima released the lunar disk, and the deity Suriya released the solar disk. The four...
The great kings dispatched protection for the four quarters, and Sakka, the king of the gods, dispatched protection for the focal point.
The sun slipped from its central position and moved away.
The monks complained, “The shadow has become excessively long; the sun has slipped from its central position and moved away.”
"The novice has just now eaten; what indeed is this? The Teacher, having learned of that occurrence, came and asked, "Monks, what are you discussing?

"This very thing, Bhante," they replied. "Yes, monks, when one who possesses merit performs the duty of a recluse, the son of the Moon-god [Candadevaputta] appears as the moon's disk, and the son of the Sun-god [Sūriyadevaputta] appears as the sun's disk."
Having dragged him out, they seized him; the Four Great Kings took up their guard in the four directions around the monastery grove;

Sakka, the king of the gods, took up his guard at the drawbridge; and even I, thinking "I am the Buddha," could not remain sitting at ease, so I went and took up my guard at the gatehouse for my son, as well as over the water in the irrigation channels and ditches.
"Having observed these objects— those who draw a bow, fletchers straightening arrows, and carpenters fashioning wood—
the wise take them as their lesson, tame themselves, and attain Arahantship. Having said this, he connected the context and,
teaching the Dhamma, spoke this verse:
“Channel-makers lead the water; fletchers straighten the arrow-shaft;
carpenters bend the wood; the wise tame themselves.
In this context, “water” refers to having dug out a dry spot on the earth, filled it with a pit, or constructed a channel.
"Channel-makers" (*nettikā*) are those who, having set up a wooden trough for a tree, lead water to whatever place they desire.
"A shaft" (*tejana*) means an arrow. This is what is meant: channel-makers lead water according to their own preference;
fletchers also heat a shaft and bend it to make the arrow straight. Carpenters also, while carving wood for the sake of rims and other parts, [shape it].
They bend according to their own preference, making themselves straight or crooked.

Thus, by taking this much as an object, the wise, while giving rise to the path of stream-entry and so forth, discipline themselves; but those who have attained Arahantship are called "absolutely disciplined.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and the other fruits.
The fifth story: The Story of the Novice Paṇḍita. 6.
The Story of the Elder Lakuṇḍaka-Bhaddiya.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning the Elder Lakuṇḍaka-Bhaddiya, beginning with the verse: "Just as a mountain peak... (Selo yathā).
It is said that when ordinary people, such as novices and others, saw the Elder, they would seize him by his head, his ears, or even his nose, and say, "What, Little Father!
Are you not weary of the Dispensation? Do you take delight in it? The Elder felt neither anger nor ill will toward them.
In the Hall of Truth, they raised this discussion: "Behold, friends, the Elder Lakuṇḍaka-Bhaddiya!"
"Seeing that the novices and others were harassing him in such and such ways, he felt neither anger nor ill will toward them.
The Teacher approached and asked, "What are you discussing, monks?
When they replied, "This, venerable sir," he said, "Yes, monks, those whose taints are destroyed feel neither anger nor ill will. For they are like solid rock."
Having said, "Unshakable, immovable," and having established the connection, he taught the Dhamma by reciting this verse:
"Just as a solid mass of rock Is not stirred by the wind,
So too, amidst blame and praise, The wise do not waver."
Regarding the phrase "therein, blame and praise": although only two of the worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*) are mentioned here, the meaning should be understood in terms of all eight.

For just as a solid rock, without holes or crevices, is not stirred, moved, or shaken by the wind coming from the east and other directions, even so, when all eight worldly conditions overwhelm them, the wise do not flinch.
They did not waver or tremble, whether through aversion or attachment.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the sixth story, concerning the Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya.
7. The Story of Kāṇamātā "Even as a lake..."—the Teacher related this Dhamma teaching while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning Kāṇamātā. The background story is already recorded in the Vinaya.
At that time, however, Kāṇamātā, wishing to send her daughter—who had hands not empty—to her husband's family, [prepared] baked cakes four times...

When the Teacher had laid down the training rule regarding that matter at the time it was given to the four monks, Kāṇā—having been brought home by her husband as another wife—heard of this occurrence.
Thinking, "These [monks] have ruined my household life," she reviled and abused the monks whenever she saw them. Consequently, the monks were unable to enter that street.

The Teacher, having learned of this occurrence, went there. Kāṇamātā, having paid homage to the Teacher, had him sit on the prepared seat and gave him rice gruel and solid food. After he had finished his morning meal, the Teacher asked, "Where is Kāṇā?
"Venerable sir, she stands weeping, overcome with shame upon seeing you. "For what reason? "Venerable sir, these bhikkhus..."
“He reviled and abused me; therefore, upon seeing you, she stood there ashamed and weeping.
Then the Teacher summoned her and asked, “Kāṇā, why do you stand hiding and weeping upon seeing me? Then her mother related the deed she had committed.
Thereupon the Teacher said to her, “But Kāṇā’s mother, did my disciples [behave thus] toward you?”
“They took what was given; they did not take what was not given,” [the man replied]. “It was given, venerable sir,” [he said].
“If my disciples, while wandering for alms, reached the door of your house and took what was given by you, what fault is there in them?
“There is no fault, venerable sir, on the part of the noble ones. “The fault lies with her alone. The Teacher said to the blind woman: “Blind one, it is said that my—”
"The disciples, while wandering for alms, came to the door of the house; then, cakes were given to them by your mother. What fault indeed could there be here on the part of my disciples?
"There is no fault, Bhante, on the part of the noble ones; the fault is mine alone," she said, and having paid homage to the Teacher, she asked for his forgiveness.
Then the Teacher spoke to her in a gradual discourse, and she attained the fruit of stream-entry. The Teacher rose from his seat.
As he was going to the monastery, he proceeded through the royal courtyard. When the king saw him, he asked, "Is it said that this is the Teacher?
Upon being told, "Yes, Your Majesty," the king sent messengers, saying, "Go and announce my arrival to pay my respects.
Approaching the Teacher who was standing in the royal courtyard and bowing down, the king asked, "Venerable sir, where have you been? [The Teacher replied: "To Kāṇamātā..."
“...to my home, Great King. “For what reason, venerable sir? “It is said that she reviles and abuses the bhikkhus;
for that reason we have come. “But, venerable sir, has you made her stop abusing them? “Yes, Great King;
we have made her cease from abusing the bhikkhus, and she is now the mistress of the supramundane household. “Very well, venerable sir.”
“You have made her the mistress of the supramundane household; I, however, shall make her the mistress of the mundane household.

Having said this, the king paid homage to the Teacher and turned back. He sent a large covered carriage, summoned the blind man, adorned him with all kinds of ornaments, established him in the position of his eldest daughter, and said, “She is capable of supporting my daughter.”

"Let them take her," he said. Then a certain high minister, thinking, "I shall support the King's daughter," led her to his own home, entrusted her with all authority, and said, "Perform meritorious deeds as you please.
From that time on, Kāṇā stationed men at the four gates and [provided for] the monks who were to be served by her.

And although the bhikkhunīs searched for it, they did not find it. The hard and soft food prepared and set out at the door of the blind woman's house flowed forth like a great flood. In the Dhamma hall, the bhikkhus initiated this discussion:
"Friends, in the past four elder monks caused remorse in the blind woman; she was thus remorseful."
"Even though she had performed the sacrifice, it was by coming to the Teacher that she obtained the perfection of faith.
Furthermore, the Teacher made her house-door worthy for the monks to approach. Now, although she seeks monks or nuns to attend upon her, she finds none;
oh, how wonderful are the qualities of the Buddhas! The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, what is this?"
Having asked, "For what discussion are you sitting together now? and being told, "For this very one," he said:
"Monks, it is not only now that those elder monks have caused remorse for Kāṇā; they have done so even in the past.
Nor is it only now that I have made Kāṇā obedient to my word; I have done so even in the past. When the monks requested him to explain the meaning of this matter, he spoke as follows:
“Where one cat finds a kill, a second is born there;
a third and a fourth as well—this, O cats, is your den.
Having related this Babbu-jātaka in detail, [he said]: “At that time, the four elder bhikkhus were the four cats...”
Having identified the Jātaka by saying, "The blind mice were they, and I myself was the jeweler," and having said, "Thus, monks, even in the past,
those who were blind, dejected, turbid-minded, and distracted became serene in mind like a lake of clear water through my word," he joined the connection and, teaching the Dhamma, spoke this verse:
“Just as a lake that is deep, serene, and undisturbed, so too,
having heard the Dhammas, the wise become serene.
In this context, “lake” refers to a body of water such that it is not agitated even when a fourfold army enters it.
In every respect, however, the Great Blue Ocean, eighty-four thousand yojanas deep, is called a lake.
For in its lower portion, extending for forty thousand yojanas, the water is stirred by fish; in the upper portion, likewise extending for that same distance, the water is stirred by the wind;
and in the middle portion, extending for four thousand yojanas, the water remains perfectly still.
"This is called the deep lake. "Such are the teachings" refers to the teachings of the Dhamma. This is what is meant:

just as a lake is serene due to its lack of turbulence and undisturbed due to its stillness, so too, having heard my teaching of the Dhamma, the wise—by means of the path of stream-entry and so forth—attain a state of mind free from defilements and become serene; this is the case for those who have reached Arahantship.
But they became entirely serene.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other fruits.
This is the seventh story, that of Kāṇamātā.

8. The Story of the Five Hundred Bhikkhus "Everywhere indeed the virtuous renounce"—the Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, spoke this Dhamma teaching concerning five hundred bhikkhus. The teaching originated in Verañjā.
For during the first period after his enlightenment, the Blessed One went to Verañjā and was invited by the brahmin of Verañjā together with five hundred [brahmins].

He entered the rains retreat together with five hundred bhikkhus. The brahmin of Verañjā, ensnared by the enticements of Māra, did not give rise to mindfulness directed toward the Teacher for even a single day. Verañjā also suffered from a famine;
the bhikkhus, wandering for alms throughout the inner and outer parts of Verañjā, grew weary as they failed to obtain food. For them, horse-dealers brought bundles of parched grain.
They requested alms. Seeing that they were weary, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna desired to provide them with the essence of the earth and wished to send them for alms to Uttarakuru;
the Teacher forbade him. Regarding the alms-food, the monks did not have even a single day’s lack of confidence; they lived having abandoned all improper conduct. Therein, the Teacher—

Having stayed for three months in Verañjā, after taking leave of the brahmin Verañja and receiving the hospitality and honor he had extended, and having established him in the refuges, the Teacher departed from there.

Traveling by stages on his wandering tour, he eventually arrived at Sāvatthī and dwelt in Jeta’s Grove. At that time, the residents of Sāvatthī provided meals for the newly arrived Teacher. Then, however—
About five hundred scavenger-monks lived in dependence on that monastery, residing right within the vihāra.

Having eaten the choice foods remaining from the monks' meals, they would fall asleep; then, rising, they would go to the riverbank, where they roared, shouted, engaged in wrestling matches like those of boxers, and played about.
Thus, whether inside the vihāra or outside it, they wandered about committing only improper conduct. The monks...
In the Dhamma Hall, they raised this discussion: "Friends, see how these scavengers showed no sign of agitation in Verañjā during the time of famine;
yet now, having eaten such excellent food, they wander about displaying various kinds of agitation.
But as for the bhikkhus, even in Verañjā they lived with a tranquil appearance, and now too—"
“...dwelling in complete tranquility. The Teacher went to the Hall of Dharma and asked, “Monks, what are you discussing?
When they replied, “This very thing,” he said, “In the past, these five hundred were born in the womb of donkeys;
