having become five hundred donkeys, they drank the remains of the sour, salty beverage left over by five hundred noble thoroughbred horses—[the leftover] dregs and scum.”
Having said, "They drank the so-called 'hair-water'— which was thin and inferior because it had been squeezed through a cloth made of *makaci* fibers after being kneaded with water—
and wandered about roaring like those intoxicated by honey," he added:
"The hair-water was thin and inferior..."
Drinking [ordinary liquor], intoxication arises in donkeys;
but having drunk this exquisite essence,
no intoxication arises in Sindh horses.
“Having drunk only a little, that man of low birth becomes intoxicated by it when questioned, O Lord of Men;
whereas one born into a noble family, possessing steadfast virtue, remains sober.”
"One does not become intoxicated after drinking the finest liquor.

Having related this Vālodakajātaka in detail, he connected the narrative by saying: "In this way, monks, true persons, having avoided worldly conditions (lokadhamma), remain entirely unshaken both in times of happiness and in times of suffering."
While teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
“Everywhere indeed the virtuous abandon [unwholesome things];
the noble ones, seeking no sensual pleasures, do not prattle on.”
“Whether touched by pleasure or by pain, the wise do not display elation or dejection.
In this context, “in all things” means among all phenomena, such as the five aggregates and so forth. “Sappurisā” means good persons. “Cajanti” means they relinquish.

By drawing it out with the knowledge of the path to arahantship, they abandon desire and lust. "Those who crave sensual pleasures" means those who, for the sake of sensual pleasure and for the purpose of sensual pleasure, indulge in them.
"The peaceful do not prattle" means that the Buddhas and other noble ones, being peaceful, neither prattle themselves for the sake of sensual pleasure nor cause others to prattle.
For those who have entered for alms but remain in wanton conduct might ask, "What, lay follower, is happiness?"
When they say things such as, "For our children and wives, there is no misfortune among bipeds or quadrupeds due to kings, thieves, or the like," they are said to be "making them talk.
Having spoken thus, when they invite themselves by saying, "Yes, venerable sir, we are all well;
there is no misfortune at all. Our house now has abundant food and drink; please stay right here," they are inviting themselves.
They are said to "lament. But the virtuous do neither of these two. The phrase "whether touched by pleasure or by pain" is merely a pedagogical device;
rather, it means that when touched by the eight worldly conditions, the wise do not display high or low states of being—whether through elation or dejection, or through praise or blame.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the eighth story, concerning the five hundred bhikkhus. 9.
The Story of the Elder Dhammika.
"‘Not for one’s own sake’—the Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this Dhamma teaching concerning the Elder Dhammika.
It is said that in Sāvatthī there was a certain lay follower who lived his household life righteously and justly.
Desiring to go forth, he one day sat with his wife and, while conversing on pleasant topics, said: ‘My dear, I wish—’"
“Let me go forth,” he said. “In that case, master, wait for a while until I have given birth to the child in my womb.
He waited; and when the boy was able to walk on his own feet, he asked him again, saying, “Wait for a while, master, until this one has reached maturity.
To which [the boy] replied, “What do I care whether you have asked me or not? For myself—”
Thinking, “I shall bring about deliverance from suffering,” he went forth and became a monk.
Having taken up a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he strove and exerted himself, completing his duties as a renunciant.
Then, returning to Sāvatthī to see them, he delivered a discourse on the Dhamma to his son. He too went forth, and not long after having gone forth—
He attained arahantship. His former wife also thought, "Those for whose sake I lived the household life have both gone forth;
what now is the use of my household life? I shall go forth.
Having left home, she went forth, and not long after her ordination, she too attained arahantship. Then one day, in the Hall of Truth, this conversation arose:

They raised the topic: “Friends, the lay follower Dhammika, because he was firmly established in his own duty, went forth into homelessness, attained arahantship, and has become a support even for his wife and children.
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, what discussion are you having as you sit here now? When they replied, “This one,” he said, “Monks, by a wise man...”
Having established the connection by saying, "Success should not be sought for one's own sake nor for the sake of another;
rather, one must be righteous and take refuge in the Dhamma," he taught the Dhamma, reciting this verse:
"Neither for one's own sake nor for the sake of another..."
One should not desire sons, nor wealth, nor a kingdom;
one should not desire success for oneself through unrighteousness.
Such a person should be virtuous, wise, and righteous.
In this context, "not for his own sake" means that one called wise does not commit evil for the sake of himself or for the sake of another.

"He would not desire a son" means that he would not seek a son, wealth, or a kingdom through unwholesome action; the meaning is that even while desiring these things, he simply does not perform evil deeds.
"For the sake of his own prosperity" means that he would not seek even his own success through what is contrary to the Dhamma, nor for the sake of achieving such prosperity.
The meaning is that he does not commit evil. "He is virtuous" means that such a person as this alone may be both virtuous and wise, and righteous, and no other—this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and the other fruits.
The ninth story is that of the Elder Dhammika.
10. The Story of Listening to the Dhamma:
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, gave this discourse on the Dhamma concerning the listening to the Dhamma, beginning with the words, "Few indeed are those among men..."
It is said that in Sāvatthī, people living in the same street, having united as a group, gave a gift and held a Dhamma-listening session throughout the entire night;
however, they were unable to listen to the Dhamma for the whole night.
Some, being attached to sensual pleasures, returned home again; some, being attached to ill-will; some, being attached to pride; and others...
Being possessed by sloth and torpor, they sat right there and, nodding off, were unable to listen.
On the following day, the monks, having learned of this occurrence, initiated a discussion in the Hall of Truth.
When the Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, about what discussion are you gathered here now?", and they replied, "About this very matter," he spoke.
“Bhikkhus, these beings for the most part are dependent on existence; they dwell clinging to existences alone, while those who go to the further shore are few indeed.
Having thus established the connection, he taught the Dhamma by reciting these verses:
“Few among men are those people who go to the further shore;”
But then, other people merely run along the near shore.
However, those who follow the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma that has been rightly proclaimed—
those people will cross over to the far shore, the realm of Death so difficult to transcend.
In this context, "few" means small in number, not many. "Those who go to the further shore" means those who go to the further shore of Nibbāna.

"But this other generation" refers to that remaining generation which merely runs along the shore of the view of a self-existent body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*); the meaning is that this [other generation] is much more numerous.
"Well-expounded" means correctly expounded, well-spoken. "In the Dhamma" means in the Dhamma of the teaching. "Followers of the Dhamma" means...
Having heard that Dhamma and fulfilled the practice appropriate thereto, they are followers of the Dhamma by means of the realization of the paths and fruits.
"They will reach the further shore" means that such persons as these will go to the further shore of Nibbāna.

"The realm of Death" refers to the cycle of existence in the three realms, which is the dwelling place of Death, reckoned as the Māra of the defilements. "Hard to cross" refers to those people who are followers of the Dhamma.
The meaning is that, having crossed over and transcended this realm of Māra—which is so difficult to cross and so hard to overcome—they will go to the further shore of Nibbāna.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the tenth story, the Account of Listening to the Dhamma.
11. The Story of the Five Hundred Guest Monks:
"Having utterly abandoned dark states"—the Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, spoke this teaching of the Dhamma concerning five hundred guest monks.
It is said that five hundred monks, having spent the rains retreat in the kingdom of Kosala, and being now released from their vows, thought, "We shall see the Teacher."
Having gone to Jeta’s Grove and paid homage to the Teacher, they sat down to one side.
The Teacher, having observed their individual temperaments, spoke these verses while teaching the Dhamma:
“Having abandoned dark qualities, let the wise man cultivate the bright;”
“Having come from home to homelessness, to a solitude that is far away—
therein one should find delight, having abandoned sensual pleasures, possessing nothing.
The wise person should purify themselves of the defilements of the mind.”
“Those whose minds are well-developed in the factors of enlightenment,
who delight in the relinquishing of grasping through non-clinging,
those taint-destroyers, radiant ones— they have attained final nibbāna in this world.”
Therein, "having abandoned the dark state" means having relinquished and cast off unwholesome states classified as bodily misconduct and so forth.

"One should cultivate the bright" means that the wise bhikkhu, from the time of his initial renunciation up until the path of Arahatship, should cultivate the bright state classified as bodily good conduct and so forth. How?
"Coming from home to homelessness": "home" (oka) is said to be attachment; "homelessness" (anoka) is said to be—

"Without attachment (*anālayo*)," the meaning is: having emerged from attachment (*ālaya*), one should develop [the mind] depending upon and directed toward Nibbāna, which is designated as "without attachment," while aspiring for it.

"One should desire delight therein" means: one should desire delight in that seclusion designated as "without attachment"—in Nibbāna—which is difficult for these beings to find delightful. "Having abandoned sensual pleasures" refers to both objective sensual pleasures (*vatthukāma*) and defilement-sensual pleasures (*kilesakāma*).
The meaning is: having abandoned [worldly things] and become a possessor of nothing, one should desire delight in seclusion. "By means of mental defilements" refers to the five hindrances;
"one should purify oneself" means one should cleanse, wash, and thoroughly purify oneself. "In the factors of enlightenment" refers to the *sambodhyaṅgas*.
"The mind well-cultivated" means the mind has been properly developed and increased by way of cause and method. "In the relinquishing of grasping" [refers to the state of non-clinging].
"Grasping" (ādāna) is called "seizing"; the meaning is that those who delight in that non-grasping known as relinquishment, having not grasped anything by means of the four kinds of clinging.

"Radiant" (jutimanto) means possessed of majesty; the meaning is that they stand having illuminated the phenomena—such as the aggregates and so forth—by means of the radiance of the knowledge of the path to arahantship.
"In this world" (te loke) refers to those who have attained final nibbāna in this world of aggregates and so forth.

They are "parinibbūta" by means of two types of parinibbāna: by the parinibbāna with residue (saupādisesa), because the cycle of defilements (kilesavaṭṭa) has been exhausted from the attainment of Arahatship onwards;
and by the parinibbāna without residue (anupādisesa), because the cycle of aggregates (khandhavaṭṭa) has been exhausted through the cessation of the final consciousness.
The meaning is that they have reached the state of non-designation (apaṇṇattikabhāva), like a lamp that has gone out for lack of fuel.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the eleventh story, concerning the five hundred visiting bhikkhus.
The commentary on the Chapter of the Wise is finished.
The Sixth Chapter.
7. The Chapter on Arahants. 1.
The Account of the Question of Jīvaka.

The Teacher delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, "Gataddhino," while dwelling in Jīvakambavana, concerning a question asked by Jīvaka. The story of Jīvaka has already been related in detail in the Khandhaka.

On one occasion, however, Devadatta, having joined together with Ajātasattu and ascended Gijjhakūṭa mountain, threw down a rock with a malicious intent, thinking, "I shall kill the Teacher. Two mountain peaks caught it.
Then, having split apart, the splinter struck the Blessed One’s foot and drew blood, causing intense pains to arise.

The monks carried the Teacher to Maddakucchi. The Teacher, wishing to go from there to Jīvaka’s Mango Grove, said, “Take me there. Taking the Blessed One with them, the monks went to Jīvaka’s Mango Grove.
Having heard of this occurrence, Jīvaka went into the presence of the Teacher;
he administered a potent medicinal ointment for the treatment of the wound, bound it up, and said to the Teacher: "Venerable Sir, I have prepared medicine for a certain person within the city.
I shall go to him and return again; until my return, please keep this medicine."
"Let him remain bound by his own destiny. Having gone and performed the task for that man, he returned at the time of closing the gate but did not reach it in time.
Then this thought occurred to him: "Alas, a grievous deed has been done by me!
For I have applied sharp medicine to the foot of the Tathāgata, just as one would to the wound of some other man."
“The binding has been made; this is the time for its release. If it is not released, a fever will arise in the Blessed One’s body throughout the entire night.
At that moment, the Teacher addressed the Elder Ānanda: “Ānanda, Jīvaka, arriving this evening, did not reach the gate;
however, thinking, ‘This is the time for the release of the wound,’ he released it.”
"No," [the Elder replied]. The Elder released him, and the wound was removed like the bark from a tree.
Before the dawn had even broken, Jīvaka arrived in haste at the presence of the Teacher and asked, "Venerable sir, has a fever arisen in your body?
The Teacher gave this connection: "Jīvaka, for the Tathāgata, every fever was already stilled right at the seat of enlightenment."
Having synthesized the Dhamma, while teaching it, he spoke this verse:
“For one who has traversed the journey, who is free from sorrow, who is liberated in every respect,
and for whom all fetters have been abandoned— no fever exists.”

In this context, "one whose journey is completed" (*gataddhi*) refers to two kinds of journeys (*addhā*): the journey across a wilderness (*kantāraddhā*) and the journey through the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭaddhā*).

Among these, as long as one traveling through a wilderness has not yet reached the desired destination, one is merely a traveler (*addhika*); but when that destination is reached, one is called "one whose journey is completed.
Likewise, beings dependent on the cycle of existence are merely travelers as long as they dwell within the cycle. Why? Because of the [nature of] the cycle.

Because of having exhausted the journey. Stream-enterers and others are indeed those who have a journey remaining; however, one who stands having exhausted the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is called "one whose journey is gone" (*gataddhi*).
Of that one whose journey is gone. "Of the sorrowless one" (*visokassa*): because of the departure of sorrow rooted in the cycle of existence, he is sorrowless.
"Completely liberated in every respect" (*vippamuttassa sabbadhī*): completely liberated from all phenomena such as the aggregates (*khandha*), that is, one who has abandoned all fetters (*gantha*).
"Because of the abandoning of all four ties, for one who has abandoned every tie, no fever exists. Fever is of two kinds:

bodily and mental. Among these, although the bodily fever of one whose taints are destroyed is not extinguished—since it arises due to cold, heat, and so forth—it is with reference to this that Jīvaka asks.
But the Teacher, owing to his status as the King of Dhamma and his skill in the methods of teaching...
Turning back the teaching by means of the fever of mental states (*cetasika-pariḷāha*), he said: "Jīvaka, in the ultimate sense, no such fever exists for one whose taints are destroyed.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
The First Story of the Questions of Jīvaka.
2. The Story of the Elder Mahākassapa.
The Teacher delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, "Those who exert themselves," while dwelling at Veḷuvana, concerning the Elder Mahākassapa.
For at one time, having spent the rains retreat in Rājagaha, the Teacher announced to the bhikkhus: "In half a month, I shall set out on a walking tour.
It is said that this is the custom of Buddhas who wish to go on a walking tour with the bhikkhus:
[thinking], "In this way, the bhikkhus will prepare their own bowls, sew their robes, and dye them, so that they may travel comfortably," he says, "Now..."
“After the lapse of half a month, I shall set out on tour,” he announced to the bhikkhus.
While the bhikkhus were preparing their own bowls, robes, and other requisites, the Elder Mahākassapa also washed his robes.
The bhikkhus complained, “Why does the Elder wash his robes? In this city, both inside and outside, there are eighteen crores of people.”
“They dwell there. Among them, those who are not the elder’s kinsmen are his attendants, and those who are not his attendants are his kinsmen.
They show him proper honor with the four requisites. Abandoning such assistance, where will he go?
Even if he were to go, he would not go beyond the Māpamāda cave. Thus spoke the Teacher.
It is said that when monks who ought to turn back upon reaching a certain cave were told, "You should turn back from here;
do not be negligent," it was called the "Cave of Heedlessness" (*māpamādakandara*); it was with reference to this that it was said.
As the Teacher was setting out on his journey, he thought: "In this city, both inside and outside, there are eighteen koṭis of people."
“They are staying there. Since monks must go to the auspicious and inauspicious places of men, it is not possible to leave the monastery empty;
whom then shall we send back? Then it occurred to him: “These people are the kinsmen and supporters of Kassapa;
it is right to send Kassapa back. He said to the Elder: “Kassapa,…”
“It is not possible to leave the monastery empty; the monks have need of us for both auspicious and inauspicious occasions for people.
You should return with your own retinue. “Very well, venerable sir,” the Elder replied, and taking his retinue, he returned.
The monks were filled with envy and said, “Friends, did you not see how we just now spoke?”
"What we said—that 'Why is Mahākassapa washing his robes? He will not go with the Teacher'—has come true.
When the Teacher heard the monks' conversation, he turned back, stood still, and asked, "Monks, what is it that you are talking about?
"We were talking about the Elder Mahākassapa, Bhante," they replied, following the very same line of reasoning they had previously expressed.
They reported everything. Having heard this, the Teacher said, "Monks, you should not say of Kassapa that he is 'attached to families and requisites.
He turned back because he thought, 'I shall do as my teacher says. For even when he was formerly making his aspiration, he resolved:
'May I be unattached to the four requisites, like the moon, and capable of visiting families.'"
"May it be so," he made this aspiration. "There was no attachment in his family or to material requisites;
while I was teaching the practice of the moon-like way and the practice of the noble lineage, I taught beginning with my son Kassapa," he said.
The bhikkhus asked the Teacher, "Venerable sir, when was the aspiration established by the Elder? "Do you wish to hear? he replied.

"Is it so, monks? "Yes, venerable sir," they replied. The Teacher said to them, "Monks, one hundred thousand aeons ago from now, a Buddha named Padumuttara appeared in the world," and having said this, he recounted the entire previous life of the Elder, beginning with the aspiration made by him at the feet of Padumuttara.
This is already explained in detail in the Therapāḷi.

The Teacher, however, having related this Elder’s past conduct in detail, said: "Thus indeed, monks, beginning with my son Kassapa, I have taught both the practice of the moon-like simile and the practice of the noble lineages.
My son Kassapa has no attachment whatsoever to requisites, families, monasteries, or cells; he is like one who has descended into a pond."
“Having wandered there, my son goes on like a royal swan, unattached to anything whatsoever.
Having thus established the connection, he taught the Dhamma by reciting this verse:
“The mindful exert themselves; they do not delight in a fixed abode.”
"Like swans leaving a pond, they abandon home after home. In this context,

"the mindful exert themselves" means that those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsavā), having attained fullness of mindfulness, apply themselves and strive through the acts of adverting, entering, emerging, resolving,
and reviewing regarding the qualities they have personally realized, such as the meditative absorptions (jhāna) and insight (vipassanā).
"They do not delight in a dwelling" means that they have no attachment (*ālaya*) to their own abode. The phrase "like swans" is merely a heading for the teaching;
however, this is the meaning here: just as when birds leave a pond rich in food after taking their own provisions, they feel no attachment to that place, thinking, "This water is mine!
This lotus is mine! This blue lotus is mine! This seed-vessel is mine!"—so too [the noble ones].
Just as birds, without making anything their own and without looking back, leave that place, fly up, and go about sporting in the sky;
even so, though dwelling anywhere, those whose taints are destroyed dwell entirely unattached to families and the like,
and when it is time to depart, they leave that place and go away without clinging, thinking, "This is my dwelling, this is my courtyard, these are my attendants."
They proceed with equanimity. "From home to home" means from one abode to another; the meaning is that they abandon all abodes.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the second story, concerning the Elder Mahākassapa.
3. The Story of the Elder Belaṭṭhasīsa The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning the Venerable Belaṭṭhasīsa: "For those who have no accumulation...
It is said that after the Venerable had walked for alms through one street in the village and finished his meal, he would again [enter] another...
Having walked through the streets and taken some dry rice, he carried it back to the monastery, stored it away, and thought, "Seeking almsfood on a fixed route is indeed suffering.
Thus, for several days, he spent his time in the bliss of meditative absorption (jhāna), consuming that food only when there was a need for nourishment.
When the monks learned of this, they complained and reported the matter to the Blessed One. On this occasion, the Teacher [prohibited] for the future...
Although the Blessed One had laid down a training rule for the monks in order to avoid the practice of hoarding, the Elder—
demonstrating that there was no fault in his own action because it was performed out of fewness of desires before the rule was established— connected the context and,
teaching the Dhamma, spoke this verse:
“Those who have no hoarding, who have fully understood food,
for whom the void and the signless liberation is their domain—
their path is hard to trace, like that of birds in the sky.”
In this context, "accumulation" refers to two kinds of accumulation: the accumulation of kamma and the accumulation of requisites.
Among these, wholesome and unwholesome kamma is called the accumulation of kamma; the four requisites are called the accumulation of requisites.
In that regard, for a bhikkhu living in a monastery who sets aside a single lump of sugar, a quarter-measure of ghee, and one measure of husked rice—
There is no accumulation of requisites; beyond that, there is nothing more.

For those who have neither of these two kinds of accumulation, they are "those who have fully understood food" because they have fully understood food by means of the three kinds of full understanding (*pariññā*). For, the knowledge of rice-gruel and so forth as being rice-gruel and so forth is "full understanding through knowing" (*ñāta-pariññā*);
however, the full understanding of food by way of the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment is "full understanding through scrutinization" (*tīraṇa-pariññā*).

The knowledge that draws out desire and lust for edible food is the full understanding of abandoning (*pahānapariññā*). Through these three types of full understanding, those who have fully understood nutriment [attain the goal].
In the phrase "void and signless," the liberation of the wishless (*appaṇihita-vimokkha*) is also included.
These three are indeed names for Nibbāna itself; for Nibbāna is "void" because of the absence of greed, hatred, and delusion, and because of them...
"Emancipated" means emancipation by way of the void (suññatā-vimokkha). Likewise, because of the absence of the signs of lust and so forth, it is signless (animitta);

and because it is emancipated from them, it is called the signless emancipation (animitto vimokkho). Furthermore, because of the absence of the aspirations for lust and so forth, it is wishless (appaṇihita);

and because it is emancipated from them, it is called the wishless emancipation (appaṇihito vimokkho). For those who dwell making that [nibbāna] their object by means of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti):
This threefold liberation is the domain of those whose course is difficult to trace.
Just as the path of birds that have flown through the sky is difficult to trace and cannot be known because no footprints are seen, even so,
for those who possess neither these two kinds of accumulation nor have fully understood food by means of these three types of full understanding, their course is difficult to trace.

This liberation, as previously described, has as its range these five categories: the three states of existence (*bhava*), the four modes of birth (*yoni*), the five destinations (*gati*), the seven stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*), and the nine abodes of beings (*sattāvāsa*).
Because it is not known by what name this [liberation] goes among these five divisions, its destination is "untraceable" (*durannaya*); that is, it cannot be pointed out.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the third story, the account of the Elder Belaṭṭhasīsa.
4. The account of the Elder Anuruddha.
The Teacher delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, "Yassāsavā," while residing at Veḷuvana, concerning the Elder Anuruddha.
For one day, the Elder, his robes worn out, was searching for cloth among rubbish heaps and other such places.
In a previous existence three lifetimes back, his former wife had been reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven as a celestial maiden named Jālinī.
It happened that she saw the Elder searching for rags. Thinking to herself,
"If I offer these three divine cloths, thirteen cubits long and four cubits wide,
for the sake of the Elder, he will not accept them," she went before him as he was searching for rags and stood upon a heap of refuse.
He placed them so that only their bite-marks were visible. As the Elder was wandering along that path searching for rags, he saw their bite-marks;
seizing them right there and pulling them, he beheld divine cloths of the aforementioned measure.
Thinking, "Ah, this is truly the finest kind of refuse-rag," he took them and departed. Then, on the day he was making the robe—
The Teacher, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred bhikkhus, went to the monastery and sat down; the eighty great elders also sat down right there.
To sew the robe-cloth, the Elder Mahākassapa sat at the base, the Elder Sāriputta in the middle, and the Elder Ānanda at the tip.
The Saṅgha of bhikkhus wound the thread, the Teacher threaded the needle-eye, and the Elder Mahāmoggallāna...
He wandered about, bringing whatever was needed for each purpose. A daughter of the gods, having entered the village, said:

"Sirs, while our venerable Elder Anuruddha is making a robe, the Teacher, surrounded by eighty great disciples and together with five hundred bhikkhus, is seated in the monastery; [bring] rice-gruel and other offerings."
"Take this and go to the monastery," he urged, inciting the monks to beg for alms.
The Elder Mahāmoggallāna also brought back a large cluster of rose-apples (*jambu*) between meals, but five hundred monks were unable to finish eating it as it was exhausted.
Sakka prepared the ground around the place where the robes were being made; the earth appeared as if dyed with lacquer juice. Of the portions remaining after the monks had eaten...
There was a great heap of rice gruel, hard food, and cooked meals. The bhikkhus complained, "What is the use of so much rice gruel and other foods for so many bhikkhus?
Should we not rather observe moderation and bring only this much? They thought that their kinsmen and supporters would surely be told off.
The Elder Anuruddha, [aware of] the great number of his own kinsmen and supporters...
"I suspect he wishes to make this known. Then the Teacher asked them, "Monks, what are you discussing?
When they replied, "Venerable Sir, it is this," he said, "Monks, do you think that Anuruddha has caused this to be brought?
"Yes, Venerable Sir. "Monks, my son Anuruddha would not speak such words. For those whose taints are destroyed..."
Connecting the context by saying, "They speak a discourse connected with conditions, but this alms-food has been produced through the power of a deity," he taught the Dhamma and spoke this verse:
"Whose taints are utterly exhausted, and who is not dependent on nutriment;..."
"Empty and signless is the liberation that is his domain;
like the track of birds in the sky, his path is difficult to trace.
In this context, "whose taints" means whose four taints (*āsava*) have been completely exhausted. "And not dependent on nutriment" means with respect to nutriment...
Not dependent on craving or views, his track is difficult to trace. Just as it is impossible to know when birds are flying through the sky—
“they went by stepping here with their feet,” “they went by striking this spot with their breast,” “this with their head,” or “this with their wings”—
even so, for such a bhikkhu, [the track] by way of the path to hell...
He is unable to define the term by such methods as "gone to the realm of ghosts" or "born in the animal womb," and so forth.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the fourth story, concerning the Elder Anuruddha.

5. The Story of the Elder Mahākaccāyana The Teacher delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, beginning with the words "He whose faculties," while residing at the Eastern Monastery concerning the Elder Mahākaccāyana.
For on one occasion, during the Great Pavāraṇā ceremony, the Blessed One was seated below the palace of Migāra’s Mother, surrounded by the great disciples.
He sat down. At that time, the Elder Mahākaccāyana was dwelling among the people of Avantī.

That venerable one, having come even from afar, would always exert himself to listen to the Dhamma. Therefore, as the great elders were sitting down, they left a seat for the Elder Mahākaccāyana and then sat down.
Sakka, the king of the gods, arrived with a retinue of devas from two celestial worlds.
Having worshipped the Teacher with celestial perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, he stood there;
not seeing the Elder Mahākaccāyana, he thought, "Why is my noble lord not visible? It would indeed be well if he were to come.
At that very moment, the Elder arrived and showed himself seated upon his own seat. Seeing the Elder, Sakka gripped him firmly by the ankles.
Having taken him by the feet and said, "It is well indeed that you have come, noble sir;
I was waiting precisely for your arrival," he massaged his feet with both hands, honored him with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, and after bowing down, stood to one side.
The bhikkhus murmured in complaint: "Sakka pays honor only after looking at his face; what about the rest of the great disciples?"
“Without performing such honors, upon seeing Mahākaccāyana, he quickly took him by the ankles, saying, ‘It is well indeed that my noble lord has come; I was waiting precisely for your arrival.
Having massaged his feet with both hands, and having thus honored and paid homage to him, he stood to one side. When the Teacher heard this account from them, he said:
“Monks, those bhikkhus who, like my son Mahākaccāyana, have guarded the doors of their sense faculties, are dear indeed to both gods and humans.
Having said this, and having established the connection, he taught the Dhamma by reciting this verse:
“Whose faculties have attained tranquility...”
Like well-trained horses by a charioteer,
even the gods envy that steadfast one who has abandoned conceit and is free from taints.

The meaning of this is as follows: for that bhikkhu whose six sense-faculties have reached a state of being well-tamed, calmed, and rendered harmless—just like horses by a skilled charioteer—he has abandoned the ninefold conceit;
because he stands having abandoned conceit, he is "one who has abandoned conceit.
Because of the absence of the four taints (*āsava*), he is "taintless" (*anāsava*). "Tādi" refers to one who is established in suchness, one of such a nature.
"Even the gods envy them, and humans likewise long for the sight of them and their arrival.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the fifth story, concerning the Venerable Mahākaccāyana.
6. The Story of the Elder Sāriputta The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, gave this Dhamma teaching concerning the Elder Sāriputta.
For on one occasion, when the Venerable Sāriputta had completed the rains retreat and desired to set out on a journey, he took leave of the Blessed One.
Having paid homage, he departed together with his own retinue. Many other monks also followed the Elder.
As they went along, the Elder called out by name and clan those monks who were known by their names and clans, and thus made them turn back.
A certain monk, however, who was not well-known by name or clan, thought: "Oh, would that they would call me by my name and clan as well..."
“Having taken him by the hand and spoken to him, he should make him turn back. However, in the midst of the great community of monks, the elder did not notice him.
Thinking, “Unlike other monks, he does not take me by the hand,” the monk harbored resentment toward the elder.

Furthermore, the corner of the elder’s outer robe brushed against the monk’s body, and because of that, the monk likewise harbored resentment. He thought, “Now, when the elder reaches the vicinity of the monastery...”
Knowing that he would have passed away, [the monk] approached the Teacher and said, "Venerable sir,
the Venerable Sāriputta struck me as if breaking a pair of ear-rings, saying, 'I am your chief disciple,' and having departed on his journey without even asking for my forgiveness.
The Teacher summoned the Elder.
At that moment, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna and the Elder Ānanda thought:
“The Teacher does not fail to know that our eldest brother has not yet brought this bhikkhu; rather, he intends to make him roar the lion’s roar, so we shall assemble the company.
Taking keys in their hands, they opened the doors of the various courtyards and said, “Come forward, venerable sirs!”
“Come forward, venerable ones! Now the venerable Sāriputta will let out a lion’s roar in the presence of the Blessed One,” he said, and thus assembled the great community of monks.
The Elder also arrived, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down.
Then the Teacher questioned him regarding that matter. Without saying, “This monk was struck by me,” the Elder—
While speaking in praise of his virtues, he said, "Venerable sir, surely one in whose body mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*) is not established might here,
after having insulted a fellow celibate practitioner and failing to desist,
set out on a journey," and then continued in this manner: "Venerable sir, just as they place both the pure and the impure upon the earth," and so forth, regarding himself.
He explained his state of mind as being like earth, and his state of mind as being like water, fire, wind, a dust-sweeper, a young Caṇḍāla boy, a bull, and a bull with its horns broken off;
he also explained how he was repelled by his own body as if it were a snake’s carcass and so forth, and how he regarded his own body as one would regard a bowl of fat.
And as the Elder spoke of his own virtues through these nine similes, in all nine instances...
The great earth shook, making the ocean its boundary. However, at the time when the examples of the young outcaste boy who swept away dust and the omentum of a fat sheep were brought forth,
the bhikkhus who were ordinary worldlings were unable to restrain their tears, while a profound sense of spiritual urgency arose in those whose taints were exhausted.
As that monk, while speaking of his own virtues, was actually slandering [the Elder], a burning fever arose throughout his entire body.
He immediately fell at the feet of the Blessed One, confessed the fault of his slanderous speech, and admitted his transgression.
The Teacher addressed the Elder, saying, "Sāriputta, forgive this foolish man, for as long as..."

“Even if one’s head were split into seven pieces, it would not bear fruit,” he said. The Elder sat down in the *ukkuṭika* posture, raised his joined palms, and said, “Venerable sir, I ask forgiveness from that venerable one;
may that venerable one forgive me if there was any fault on my part.
The monks said, “See now, friends, the incomparable virtue of this Elder! To one such as this, [he spoke] with such false speech...”

“Without showing even the slightest anger or ill-will toward the monk who has made a false accusation, he himself sits down in the *ukkuṭika* posture, raises his joined palms, and asks for forgiveness. Having asked, “Monks, what did you think when you heard that story?
and being told, “This was our thought, venerable sir,” the Teacher said, “Monks, it is not possible for those like Sāriputta...”
"Monks, Sāriputta’s mind is like the great earth, like a city gatepost, and like a pond of clear water; it is impossible for him to give rise to anger or hatred.
Having said this, and having established the connection, he taught the Dhamma by reciting this verse:
"He is not disturbed, being even as the earth..."
Such a one of good vows is like an indakhīla pillar;
like a lake free from mud,
for such a one there are no further rounds of saṃsāra.
The meaning of this is: Monks, just as people place both pure things such as perfumes and garlands upon the earth, and impure things such as urine and excrement;
just as children and others splash and urinate upon the city-gate pillar that has been driven into the ground, while others honor it with perfumes, garlands, and the like—so it is there.
Just as there arises neither attraction nor repulsion toward a pillar planted in the earth,
even so this bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is "suchlike" (tādi) due to his unshakable state by the eight worldly conditions, and is "well-vowed" (subbata) because of the excellence of his vows.
He does not [think], "These people honor me with the four requisites, but these do not honor me," regarding both honor and dishonor.
He neither approves of nor disapproves of those who act [in such ways]; rather, he is like the earth and like a pillar.
And just as a lake free from mud has clear water, so too, by being free from defilements, he is unperturbed by the mud of passion and the like, remaining perfectly serene.
As for the term "tādi" (such-like), regarding one of such a nature, in both happy and miserable destinies...
"There are no so-called 'saṃsāras' by way of wandering through them.
At the conclusion of the teaching, nine thousand bhikkhus attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
This is the sixth story, concerning the Elder Sāriputta.

7. The Story of the Novice Tissa, Resident of Kosambī "His mind becomes peaceful"—the Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this Dhamma teaching concerning the novice Tissa, the Elder of Kosambī.
It is said that a certain son of good family from Kosambī went forth in the Dispensation of the Teacher; having received full ordination, he became known as "the Elder Tissa, Resident of Kosambī."
He became known. When he had completed the rains retreat at Kosambī, his attendant brought him a set of three robes as well as ghee and molasses and placed them at his feet.
Then the Elder said to him, "What is this, lay follower?
"Venerable sir, did I not have you spend the rains retreat? Those who have spent the rains retreat in our monastery receive such gains; please accept them."
“Venerable sir,” he said. “Enough, lay follower; I have no need for this. “For what reason, venerable sir?
“Friend, I do not even have a novice to act as my attendant for what is allowable.
“If there is no attendant, venerable sir, my son shall become a novice in your presence. The Elder consented. The lay follower [took] his seven-year-old...
Having brought his own son to the Elder, he gave him over with the words, "Ordain this one.

Then the Elder, having moistened the boy's hair and given him the meditation subject of the five aggregates (*khandha*), ordained him. At the very moment the razor touched his head, he attained Arhatship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
Having ordained him, the Elder stayed there for half a month and then, thinking, "I shall see the Teacher," [sent] the novice...
Taking his belongings, he set out on his way and entered a monastery along the road.
A novice monk took charge of the elder’s lodging and attended to it.
While the novice was still attending to it, evening fell, and he was unable to attend to his own lodging. Then, when the time for attendance had come, the elder approached and sat down.
He asked, “Novice, have you looked after your own dwelling? “Venerable sir, I did not find the opportunity to look after it.
“In that case, stay right here in my dwelling; it is difficult for you to live outside in a guest’s quarters.
Taking him with him, the elder entered the lodging. However, the elder was still an ordinary person (puthujjana), and as soon as he lay down, he fell asleep.
He lay down. The novice thought, “Today is the third day that I have been staying in the same lodging with my preceptor.
Thinking, ‘If I lie down and fall asleep, the elder might share the same bed,’ I shall spend the night sitting up.
Thus, having crossed his legs right there near his preceptor’s couch, he sat through the night.
He passed the time. At dawn, the Elder rose and, thinking, "It is time to have the novice leave," took up a fan placed at the side of the bed.
Striking the edge of the novice's straw mat with the tip of the fan blade and tossing the fan upward, he said, "Novice, go outside. The handle of the fan struck the novice in the eye.

At that very moment, his eye burst. He asked, "What is it, Bhante? and when told, "Get up and go outside," he did not say, "My eye has burst, Bhante," but instead covered it with one hand and went out.
Furthermore, at the time for performing his duties, instead of sitting in silence while saying, "My eye has burst," he took hold of the eye with one hand and with the other...
Taking a broom made of a fistful of grass in his hand, he swept the privy and the place for washing the face;
having set out water for washing the face, he swept the courtyard. While giving a tooth-stick to his preceptor, he gave it with only one hand.
Then the preceptor said to him: "This novice is indeed untrained; [he gives] to teachers and preceptors with only one hand."
“It is not proper to give a tooth-stick. “Venerable sir, I know that this is not proper;
however, one of my hands is not empty. “What is it, novice? He related the whole matter from the beginning.
Upon hearing it, the Elder was deeply moved and said, “Alas! What a grave deed I have committed! and added, “Forgive me.”
“Good man, I do not know this; please be my refuge,” he said, and raising his joined palms, he sat down in a squatting posture at the feet of the seven-year-old boy.
Then the novice said to him: “Venerable sir, I did not speak for that purpose;
I spoke thus only out of a desire to protect your mind. There is no fault in you here, nor—”
"It is my fault; it is the very nature of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). Do not worry; I did not tell you because I wished to protect you from remorse.
Although the Elder was thus consoled by the novice, he did not find comfort.
Feeling a surge of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), he took the novice’s belongings and set out toward the presence of the Teacher. The Teacher remained seated, waiting for his arrival.
Having gone there, he paid homage to the Teacher, exchanged greetings with him, and when asked, "Is it endurable for you, monk?
Is there anything that makes you unwell? he replied: "It is endurable, Bhante;
there is nothing that makes me unwell. However, there is another quality in me that is superior, like that of this young novice."
“I have never seen such a thing before. “But what has this monk done? He then related the entire incident to the Blessed One from the beginning, saying:
“Venerable sir, even when I was asking for his forgiveness in this way, he spoke to me thus:
‘In this matter there is no fault on your part, nor is there any on mine. This is simply the fault of the cycle of existence (saṃsāra); do not worry about it.’”
“Thus he merely comforted me; he felt neither anger nor ill-will toward me, Venerable Sir. Never before have I seen one so endowed with such virtues.
Then the Teacher, saying, “Monks, those whose taints are exhausted do not become angry with anyone, nor do they feel hatred;
their faculties are tranquil and their minds are peaceful,” and having established the connection, he taught the Dhamma by reciting this verse:
“His mind is peaceful, his speech and action are peaceful,
for him who is liberated through right knowledge, who is tranquil and such-like.
Therein, “his mind is peaceful” means that the mind of that novice whose taints are destroyed is indeed peaceful due to the absence of covetousness and the other [unwholesome states].

It becomes peaceful and extinguished. Likewise, through the absence of false speech and so forth, his speech is indeed peaceful; and through the absence of killing living beings and so forth, his bodily action is indeed peaceful.
"Of one liberated by right knowledge" means, by way of this cause—having known [the truth]—one who is liberated by the five kinds of liberation.
"Of one who is peaceful" means one who is peaceful through the internal pacification of lust and the other defilements. "Such a one" (tādi) means...
"Of one such as this, endowed with such qualities.

At the conclusion of the teaching, the Elder Tissa of Kosambī attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial for the rest of the great multitude.
Thus ends the seventh story, the account of the novice Tissa of Kosambī.
8. The Story of the Elder Sāriputta The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, gave this Dhamma teaching concerning the Elder Sāriputta.
For on one occasion, about thirty forest-dwelling bhikkhus came into the presence of the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down.

The Teacher, seeing that they possessed the necessary conditions for attaining Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), addressed the Elder Sāriputta and asked him a question concerning the five faculties:
"Sāriputta, do you believe that the faculty of faith, when developed and cultivated, has the Deathless as its goal and the Deathless as its consummation?
The Elder replied, "Venerable Sir, I do not [doubt this] regarding the Blessed One..."

"I go by faith; the faculty of faith... [and so on] ...has the deathless as its consummation. Venerable sir, those who have not known this, have not seen it, have not understood it, have not realized it, and have not touched it with wisdom, would go there by faith in others. The faculty of faith... [and so on] ...has the deathless as its consummation. Thus he answered that question. Having heard that, [He] said: "Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous how well this has been stated by the Blessed One: 'I go by faith; the faculty of faith... [and so on] ...has the deathless as its consummation. For, venerable sir, those who have not known this, have not seen it, have not understood it, have not realized it, and have not touched it with wisdom, would go there by faith in others. The faculty of faith... [and so on] ...has the deathless as its consummation. Having heard this, he said: "Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous how well this has been stated by the Blessed One. Then he paid homage to the Blessed One and departed keeping him on his right. Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus, this young brahmin Sela has great faith; he is one who has gone for refuge from today forward for as long as life shall last. Then the bhikkhus asked the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why the young brahmin Sela has such great faith, such great confidence in the Blessed One? The Blessed One replied: "Bhikkhus, the young brahmin Sela saw the five hundred white bulls, and having seen them, he spoke thus: 'Truly, these are auspicious signs; truly, these are signs of success. And when he saw the five hundred white bulls, he developed a mind of loving-kindness toward me. It was because of that, bhikkhus, that the young brahmin Sela developed such great faith, such great confidence in me. Then the bhikkhus asked the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why the young brahmin Sela developed a mind of loving-kindness toward the Blessed One? The monks raised this discussion: "The Elder Sāriputta has not relinquished his wrong grasp;
even today he still does not believe in the Perfectly Enlightened One. Hearing this, the Teacher said: "Monks, what is it that you are saying? For I have said:
'Without having developed the five faculties and without having increased serenity and insight, one cannot attain the paths and fruits.'"

I asked him, "Sāriputta, do you believe that there is one who is capable of realizing [these truths]? He replied, "Venerable sir, I do not believe that there is anyone who realizes them in such a way.
It was not that he did not believe in the fruit and result of what is given or done, nor did he disbelieve in the virtues of the Buddha and the others;
rather, it was regarding the states of jhāna, insight, the path, and the fruits which he had realized for himself.
“He does not follow out of faith in others; therefore, he is beyond reproach. Having said this, and having established the connection, he taught the Dhamma by reciting this verse:
“The man who is faithless, ungrateful, and a breaker of bonds—”
“Having had his opportunity destroyed and having vomited out [desire], he is indeed the supreme person.
The meaning of this is as follows: he does not believe in the qualities realized by himself when they are spoken of by others, thus he is “faithless” (assaddho).
He knows Nibbāna, which is unmade (akata), thus he is “grateful” (akataññū); the meaning is that he has realized Nibbāna. [He has severed] the junction of the round, the junction of saṃsāra.

"One who stands having cut [the bonds]" is one who has severed the connection (*sandhiccheda*). "One whose opportunity is destroyed" means that because the seeds of wholesome and unwholesome kamma have been exhausted, the opportunity for rebirth has been destroyed.
"One whose hopes are vomited out" means that all desires have been cast out by him because the task to be performed by the four paths has been accomplished.
Such a person is a "supreme man" (*purisuttama*), having attained the state of supremacy among men through the penetration of the supramundane Dhamma.

At the conclusion of the verses, those thirty forest-dwelling bhikkhus attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). For the rest of the people as well, there was a discourse on the Dhamma lasting for a month.
This is the eighth story, the Story of the Elder Sāriputta. 9.
The Story of the Elder Revata of the Acacia Forest.
"In the village..."—the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the Elder Revata of the Khadiravana.

For the Venerable Sāriputta, having gone forth after renouncing wealth worth seven hundred and eighty million, ordained three sisters—Cālā, Upacālā, and Sīsūpacālā—as well as two brothers, Cunda and Upasena; however, the youth Revata alone remained.

He remained behind at home. Then his mother thought: "My son Upatissa has gone forth, abandoning such great wealth, and he has caused three sisters and two brothers to go forth as well; Revata alone remains.
If he too goes forth, all this wealth of ours will perish and the family lineage will be cut off while he is still so young."
“I will not bind him with household life. The Elder Sāriputta also gave instructions to the monks beforehand:
“Friends, if Revata comes wishing to go forth, you should ordain him as soon as he arrives.
My parents hold wrong views; what is the use of asking them? I alone am his mother and father. His mother—
Desiring to bind the seven-year-old Revata Kumāra with the fetters of domestic life, his father sought a girl from a family of similar status,
fixed an auspicious day, adorned and prepared the boy,
and taking him along with a great retinue, went to the girl’s paternal home. Then, when the auspicious ceremonies for both had been performed, among their respective relatives—

When they had assembled, the relatives, wishing for the girl’s prosperity, placed her hand into a bowl of water, uttered auspicious words, and said, “See the destiny attained by your grandmother; live long, my child, just as your grandmother did.
Prince Revata thought, “What indeed was the destiny attained by this grandmother? and asked, “Which one is her grandmother?”

He asked. Then they said to him, "Dear son, do you not see this woman who is one hundred and twenty years old, with broken teeth, grey hair, wrinkled skin, limbs covered in moles, and bent like a rafter? This is her grandmother.
"But will she too become like this? "If she lives, dear son, she will. He reflected:
—"Even such a body as this will reach this state of disintegration through old age; my brother Upatissa must have seen this.
It is fitting that I flee and go forth into homelessness this very day.
Then his relatives, having placed him on a single carriage together with the young girl, took him and departed.
Having gone only a short distance, he made the pretext of needing to attend to bodily needs and said, "Stop the carriage for a moment; I will come down and return.
He descended from the carriage and went a little way into a thicket, making some delay.
Again, after going a short distance, he descended and re-ascended under that same pretext, and did the same once more. Then his kinsmen thought, "Surely these are his [last] exertions..."
Having observed that they were proceeding thus, they did not maintain an excessively tight guard.
He went a short distance further, then under that same pretext, he dismounted and said, "You go on ahead driving the carriage;
we shall follow slowly behind," and having dismounted, he headed toward a thicket. His kinsmen, perceiving that he would follow behind them, [prepared] the vehicle...
They went away brandishing their weapons. He too, having fled from there, went to a certain place where about thirty bhikkhus were dwelling;
having approached them and paid homage, he said, "Venerable sirs, please grant me the going-forth. "Friend, you are adorned with all kinds of ornaments;
we do not know whether you are the son of a king or the son of a minister, so how can we grant you the going-forth?"
“Venerable sir, do you not know me? “We do not know you, friend. “I am the younger brother of Upatissa.
“Who is this person named Upatissa? “Venerable sir, the venerable ones call my brother ‘Sāriputta’;
therefore, when I say ‘Upatissa,’ they do not recognize me. “But are you the younger brother of the Elder Sāriputta?”
“Yes, venerable sir,” he replied. “In that case, come; your brother has already given his permission.
Having said this, the monks had him remove his ornaments, set them aside to one side, and ordained him. They then sent word to the Elder.
Upon hearing this, the Elder reported it to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is said that Revata has been ordained by forest-dwelling monks.”
They sent word, saying, "Having gone there and seen him, we shall return. The Teacher said, "Wait a while, Sāriputta," and did not allow him to go.
After a few days had passed, the Elder again requested leave from the Teacher.
The Teacher said, "Wait a while, Sāriputta; we too shall come," and likewise did not allow him to go.

The novice thought, "If I remain here, my relatives will follow me and call for me," so he mastered his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) up to the stage of Arahantship in the presence of those monks. Taking his bowl and robes, he set out on a journey;
after traveling thirty yojanas, he went to a Khadira forest and dwelt there within three months.
Together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), he attained Arahatship. After the Elder had performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony, he asked the Teacher for permission to return there once more.
The Teacher said, "Sāriputta, we too shall go," and set out together with five hundred bhikkhus.
When they had traveled a short distance, the Elder Ānanda stood at a fork in the road and said to the Teacher, "Bhante, regarding Revata..."
“Regarding the paths for going to his presence: this is the circuitous route, sixty yojanas long, which is inhabited by humans;
this is the direct route, thirty yojanas long, which is under the protection of non-humans. By which shall we go?
“But Sīvalī, Ānanda, did he come along with us? “Yes, Bhante. “If Sīvalī has come, then take the direct route.”
The Teacher, it is said, did not say, "I shall provide you with rice gruel and food;
take the straight path," but rather, knowing that "this is a place for giving the fruit of merit to various people," he said, "Sīvali, if anyone has come, take the straight path.
When the Teacher had set out on that path, the deities [thought], "For our noble Elder Sīvali..."
Thinking, "We shall pay him honor," they had monasteries built every yojana;
not allowing anyone to travel further than one yojana, they rose at dawn, took celestial rice-gruel and other offerings, and wandered about asking, "Venerable Sir, where is our Elder Sīvali sitting?
The Elder caused what was brought for him to be given to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha. Thus...
The Teacher, together with his retinue, traversed the thirty-league wilderness as if experiencing the merit of the Elder Sīvali.

The Elder Revata, having learned of the Teacher’s arrival, constructed for the Blessed One a fragrant palace (*gandhakuṭi*), as well as five hundred gabled chambers, five hundred walking-places (*caṅkama*), and five hundred places for standing by night and day. The Teacher [stayed] in his presence.
He resided there for only a month. While residing there, he experienced only the merit of the Elder Sīvali.
However, at that time, two elderly monks thought as follows when the Teacher was entering the Khadiravana grove:
"This monk, while performing so much new construction work, how will he be able to practice the duty of a recluse? The Teacher..."
"He has come into the presence of such a novice monk merely to look at his face, thinking, 'He is the younger brother of Sāriputta.
On that day, the Teacher, having surveyed the world at dawn, saw those monks and understood the course of their thoughts.
Therefore, having stayed there for about a month, on the day of his departure, so that they...
The monks forgot their oil-flasks, water-pots, and sandals;
having resolved [to leave] while departing, he released his supernormal power (iddhi) at the moment they had gone outside the monastery precincts.
Then those monks, thinking, "I have forgotten this and that," and "I too have forgotten it," both turned back, yet they could not discern that place.
Having wandered about while being pierced by the thorns of *khadira* trees, they saw their own belongings hanging from a *khadira* tree;

taking them, they departed. The Teacher also, taking the community of monks, returned after only about a month while experiencing the merit of the Elder Sīvalī, and entered the Eastern Monastery (*Pubbārāma*).

Then those elder monks, having washed their faces early in the morning, went to the house of Visākhā, the provider of food for guests, thinking, "We shall drink rice-gruel," and after drinking the gruel and eating the solid food, they sat down.
Then Visākhā asked them: "Venerable sirs, have you also been with the Teacher at the dwelling place of the Elder Revata?"
“Have you come? “Yes, lay follower,” [he replied]. “Venerable sir, the Elder’s dwelling place is delightful.
“From what could it have delight, lay follower? It is a thicket of white-thorned acacia trees, like a haunt for hungry ghosts.
Then two other young bhikkhus arrived. The lay follower gave them rice gruel and solid food as well, and questioned them in the same manner.
They said, “It is impossible, laywoman, to describe the Elder’s dwelling place; it has been fashioned by supernormal power (iddhi) as if it were the Sudhamma assembly hall of the devas.
The laywoman thought, “The monks who arrived first spoke one way, but these speak another way. The monks who arrived first must have forgotten something regarding the supernormal power.”
Thinking, "Those [others] must have returned after being dismissed,

but these must have gone while they were being conjured up by means of psychic power," he understood this matter through his own wisdom and stood waiting, thinking, "I shall ask the Teacher when he has arrived.
Then, after only a short moment, the Teacher, surrounded by the community of monks, went to Visākhā’s house and sat upon the prepared seat.
She sat down. Having respectfully served the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, at the conclusion of the meal, she paid homage to the Teacher and asked:
"Venerable Sir, among the bhikkhus who went with you, some say that Revata Thera’s dwelling place is 'the Khadira forest,' while others say it is 'delightful. What indeed is it?"
"Is it so? Having heard that, the Teacher said, "Lay follower, whether it be a village or a forest, whatever place the Arahants dwell in is truly delightful.
Having established the connection and teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
"In a village or in a forest, in a valley or on a plateau;
"Wherever Arahants dwell, that ground is delightful.
In this regard, although Arahants may not obtain physical seclusion in the vicinity of a village, they certainly obtain mental seclusion;
for even objects resembling those of the divine realms cannot disturb their minds. Therefore, whether it be a village...
"Or any one of the forest dwellings, etc., where Arahants reside—that is a delightful spot on the earth";
the meaning is that such a location on the earth is beautiful.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
On another occasion, the bhikkhus raised a discussion: "Friends, for what reason did the venerable Elder Sīvali dwell in his mother’s womb for seven years, seven months, and seven days;
why did he suffer in hell; and by what consequence was he born having attained the pinnacle of gain and the pinnacle of fame? When the Teacher heard this discussion, he said:
“Monks, what are you discussing? Having asked this, when they replied, “Venerable Sir, this,” he spoke while recounting that venerable one’s past karma:
“Monks, ninety-one aeons ago, after the Blessed One Vipassī had appeared in the world, on one occasion, having wandered on a tour of the countryside, he returned to his father’s city.
The king [prepared] a guest-offering for the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha.”
Having made preparations, he sent a message to the citizens, saying, "Come and be my companions at my almsgiving.
They did so, thinking, "We shall give more than the alms given by the king," and having invited the Teacher, they prepared the offering on the following day and sent a message to the king.
When the king arrived and saw their almsgiving, [he thought], "More than this..."
Thinking, "I shall give," he invited the Teacher for the following day; yet neither was the king able to defeat the citizens, nor were the citizens able to defeat the king.

On the sixth occasion, the citizens thought, "Tomorrow we shall provide such a gift that it will not be possible to say, 'This or that specific thing is lacking in this offering,'" and on the following day, they prepared the gift.
Looking [for it], thinking, "What indeed is missing here?", they did not see any fresh honey;
however, there was much dried honey. They sent four thousand kahāpaṇas to the four city gates for the sake of obtaining fresh honey.
Then, a man from the countryside, while coming to see the village headman, [encountered them] on the way.
Having seen a honeycomb, he drove away the flies, cut off a branch, and taking the honeycomb along with the branch-staff, he entered the city thinking, "I shall give this to the village headman.
The headman, who had gone there for the sake of honey, saw him and asked, "Sir, is honey for sale? "It is not for sale, sir," he replied. "Well then, take this coin—"
“Give it to me! He thought, “This honeycomb is not worth even a single foot-measure [of gold], yet this man offers a kahāpaṇa.
I think it must be worth many kahāpaṇas; it would be right for me to increase the price. Then he said to him, “I will not give it.
“In that case, take two kahāpaṇas. “I will not give it even for two. In this way he continued to increase the price until—
“Then take this thousand,” he said, and offered him the bundle.
Then he said to him: “Are you perhaps mad, or do you not find a place to store your kahāpaṇas?
You say, ‘Take a thousand and give me honey,’ even though it is not worth a quarter! What on earth is this?”
“I know it, sir, but I have a certain business, and for that reason I speak thus. “What is that business, master?
“We prepared a great almsgiving for the Buddha Vipassī, who was accompanied by sixty-eight thousand monks; however, there was not even a single measure of fresh honey among it.
That is why I take it thus. “That being the case, I will not give you the price.”
"If I too shall receive merit from this gift, I will give," he thought. He went and informed the citizens of that matter.
The citizens, perceiving the strength of his faith, agreed, saying, "Very well, let him be the recipient.
They had the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, headed by the Buddha, seated, and having given them rice gruel and solid food, [they set out] a great golden bowl.
Having had it brought, they pressed the honeycomb. A jar of curd had also been brought by that same person as part of the gift;

he poured that curd into a bowl, mixed it with the honey, and gave it to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, starting from the very beginning. It reached everyone who took as much as they required.
There was still more remaining above. One should not wonder, "How did such a small amount of honey reach so many?
For it reached them through the power of the Buddha. The domain of the Buddhas is not to be wondered at;
for four things are said to be "inconceivable. One who wonders about them becomes a partaker of madness itself. That man [took] this much...
Having performed that deed, at the end of his life he was reborn in the world of the devas.

Wandering through the cycle of existence for such a long time, on one occasion, passing away from the deva-world, he was reborn into a royal family in Bārāṇasī. Upon the death of his father, he attained the kingship.
Thinking, "I shall seize a certain city," he went there and surrounded it, and sent a message to the citizens: "The kingdom..."

"Either give us the kingdom or give us battle! They replied, "We will neither give you the kingdom nor give you battle," and having said this, they went out through the small gates and brought firewood, water, and so forth, performing all their duties.
The other king, guarding the four great gates, besieged the city for seven years and seven months.
Then his mother asked, "What is my son doing? and having heard the report that "this is what he is doing, O Queen," she said, "My son is a fool.
Go and tell him, 'Shut even the small gates and besiege the city!
Having heard his mother's command, he did accordingly. And the citizens, unable to go outside, [remained within].
On the seventh day, they killed their own king and gave him the kingdom. Having performed this deed, at the end of his life he was reborn in Avīci;

having been cooked in hell for as long as it takes for the earth to rise by a yojana, because the four small gates were closed, when he passed away from there, he took rebirth in the womb of that very same mother.
Having dwelt within the womb for seven years and seven months, he lay across the birth canal for seven days.
Thus, monks, Sīvalī, having been seized through his past deed of besieging that city, was cooked in hell for such a length of time;
and because the four small gates were closed, when he passed away from there, he was reborn in the very womb of that same mother.
"Having taken rebirth in the womb, he dwelt there for so long a time;
because fresh honey was given [to his mother], he has become one who has attained the pinnacle of gain and the pinnacle of fame.
On another day, the bhikkhus initiated a discussion: "Oh, what a gain for the novice! Oh, what merit!"
“By whom alone were five hundred gabled houses and so forth made for five hundred bhikkhus?
The Teacher approached and asked, “Bhikkhus, about what conversation are you sitting here now?
When they replied, “About this very one,” he said, “Bhikkhus, my son has neither merit nor evil; both have been abandoned by him.”
In the Brahmana Chapter, he spoke this verse:
“He who here has transcended both merit and evil, both these attachments—
he who is sorrowless, stainless, and pure, him I call a brahmin.”
The ninth story: The Elder Revata of the Khadiravana Grove.
The tenth: The Story of a Certain Woman.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning a certain woman, beginning with the words, "Delightful are these..."
It is said that a certain alms-collecting monk, having received a meditation subject from the Teacher, entered a dilapidated park and practiced the duties of a recluse.
A city beauty, having made an appointment with a man, saying, "I will go to such-and-such a place; you should come there," departed. That man did not come.
Looking along the path of his approach and not seeing him, she became distressed and wandered here and there.
Upon entering that garden, she saw the Elder sitting with his legs crossed in the *pallaṅka* posture;
looking around here and there and seeing no one else, she thought, "This man alone is here; I shall delude his mind," and [she stood] before him.
Standing there, she repeatedly removed her lower garment and put it back on; she loosened her hair and tied it up again;
and she laughed, clapping her hands. A sense of spiritual urgency arose within the Elder and pervaded his entire body. He thought, "What indeed is this?
The Teacher also [thought], "Having received a meditation subject from my presence, he intends to practice the duties of a recluse."

Inquiring, "What indeed is the state of the monk who has gone away? he saw that woman, understood her improper conduct and the elder’s arising of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), and while sitting in the fragrant chamber (*gandhakuṭī*), spoke with him:
"Monk, that which is a place of no delight for those seeking sensual pleasures becomes a place of delight for those free from passion. And so it was said:
Having spoken thus, he pervaded [the area] with radiance and, while teaching him the Dhamma, uttered this verse:
“Delightful are the forest retreats, where people find no pleasure;
Those free from passion will delight there, not those who seek sensual desires.”
In this context, "forests" refers to delightful wildernesses adorned with groves of trees in full bloom and endowed with pure waters.
"Wherein" means in those forests, amidst blooming lotus groves, people seeking sensual pleasures do not find delight, just as village flies do not delight in them.
"Free from lust," however, refers to those whose taints are exhausted—the *khīṇāsava*—who are like bees and honey-makers.
They will delight in such forests as if they were groves of lotuses. Why? Because they do not enter into sense pleasures;
the meaning is that they are not seekers of sense pleasures.

At the conclusion of the teaching, that elder, while still sitting as he was, attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). Then, coming through the air and offering praise, he paid homage at the feet of the Tathāgata and departed.
The tenth story, concerning a certain woman.
The commentary on the Chapter on Arahants is finished.
The seventh chapter.
8. The Chapter on the Thousand (Sahassavagga) 1.

The Story of the Bandit-Executioner Tambadāṭhika The Teacher delivered this Dhamma teaching, beginning with the verse "Even if one were to speak a thousand words," while residing at Veḷuvana, concerning the bandit-executioner Tambadāṭhika.
It is said that there were four hundred and ninety-nine thieves who made their living by committing village raids and other such acts.
Then a certain man, with protruding yellowish-brown eyes and copper-colored teeth, went to them and said, "I too shall live with you.
Thereupon, they showed him to the chief of the bandits, saying, "This man also wishes to live with us."

They said this. Then the chief of the thieves, having looked at him, thought, "This man is too cruel; he is capable of cutting off his mother's breast or drawing blood from his father's throat and eating it.
Thinking thus, he rejected him, saying, "There is no need for him to live with us. Although thus rejected, he returned and, by attending upon one of that very man's disciples, won him over.
So, taking him with him, he approached the chief of the bandits and requested, "Master, this man is excellent and has been helpful to us;
please take him under your protection. Having thus secured the chief of the bandits, he concealed him.
Then one day, the citizens, joining together with the king’s men, seized those thieves and led them into the presence of the ministers of justice. The ministers—

They ordered that their heads be cut off with axes. Then, searching for someone who would kill them, thinking, "Who indeed will slay these?", and finding no one who wished to kill them, they said to the chief of the bandits:
"If you kill these men, you shall receive both life and honor; therefore, kill them! But he, because he had lived under their protection, did not wish to kill them.
He did not consent. By this means, they questioned four hundred and ninety-nine [men], and none of them consented.
Finally, they questioned that Nibbidhapiṅgala, who had copper-colored teeth; he agreed, saying, "Very well," and after killing them all, he obtained both life and honor.
By this same means, five hundred thieves were also [recruited] from the south of the city.
Having brought them and shown them to his ministers, when those ministers ordered that their heads also be cut off, he questioned them starting with the chief thief.
Seeing no one who wished to kill anyone else, he asked, "On the previous day, a man killed five hundred thieves;
where is he? When it was said, "He was seen at such-and-such a place," he had him summoned.
“Kill these men; you shall receive honor,” they commanded. He accepted, saying, “Very well,” and having killed them all, he received honor. Then, deliberating, “This man is excellent;
let us appoint him permanently to this very office of executioner,” they gave him that position and showed him honor. From the western direction as well...
Even those five hundred thieves brought from the northern direction were executed.
Having thus killed two thousand men brought from the four directions, he began from then on to kill each day one or two men as they were brought;
in this manner, he carried out the work of an executioner for fifty-five years.
Thus, in his old age, he was no longer able to cut off a head with a single stroke; striking two or three times, he caused the men to grow weary.
The citizens thought, "Another executioner will surely arise;
this man excessively exhausts the people—what is the use of him? and they removed him from that position. He [then resumed] his former work as an executioner.
While he was doing so, he did not obtain these four things: to wear unwashed robes, to drink milk-rice porridge prepared with fresh ghee, to wear jasmine flowers, and to anoint himself with perfumes.
On the day he was moved from his position, he said, "Cook milk-rice porridge for me," and having had them fetch unwashed garments, jasmine garlands, and ointments, he went to the river and bathed.
Having put on new garments, adorned himself with garlands, and anointed his body with perfumes, he returned home and sat down.
Then, having placed before him milk-rice gruel prepared with fresh ghee, they brought water for washing his hands.
At that moment, the Elder Sāriputta emerged from meditative absorption and thought, "Where indeed should I go today?"
Looking at his own alms-round, he saw milk-rice in that man’s house. Reflecting, "Will this man provide for me?
