and realizing, "Upon seeing me, he will offer me hospitality; and having done so, this son of good family will attain great prosperity," he put on his robe, took his bowl, and went to the door of that man's house.
He revealed himself while remaining right there.
Upon seeing the Elder, his heart was filled with faith, and he thought: "For a long time I have committed the work of an executioner;
many people have been killed by me. Now, milk-rice has been prepared in my house, and the Elder has arrived and is standing at the door of my home."
"Now it is fitting that I give a gift to the noble sir," he thought.

Removing the rice gruel that had been placed before him, he approached the Elder, paid homage, and having seated him inside the house, he poured milk-gruel into the bowl, added fresh ghee, and stood fanning the Elder.

Because he had not received milk-gruel for a long time, [the Elder]— Please note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "khīrayāguṃ" (milk-gruel). The translation reflects the available portion of the narrative.
He had a powerful desire to drink it. The Elder, knowing his intention, said, "Upāsaka, drink your own rice-gruel.
He gave the fan into the hand of another and drank the gruel. The Elder said to the man who was fanning him, "Go and fan the Upāsaka himself.
While being fanned, he drank his fill of gruel and returned.
While fanning the elder, he stood and took the bowl of the elder who had finished his meal. The elder began the expression of thanks (*anumodanā*).
He was unable to make his own mind follow the elder’s Dharma teaching.
The elder, having observed this, asked, "Lay follower, why are you unable to make your mind follow the teaching? [He replied,] "Venerable sir, for a long time by me..."
“A harsh deed was committed; many people were killed. Recalling that as my own karma, I was unable to bring my mind into accordance with the Noble One’s teaching.
The Elder, thinking, “I shall deceive him,” asked, “But did you do this of your own volition, or were you made to do it by others? “The king made me do it, Bhante. “What indeed—”

“In that case, lay follower, it would be unwholesome for you. When the elder had spoken thus, the lay follower, being of dull faculties, perceived, “There is no unwholesomeness in me,” and said, “In that case, venerable sir, please preach the Dhamma.
As the elder was offering the words of thanksgiving, he listened to the Dhamma with a one-pointed mind; yet, while still short of the path of stream-entry—
He produced a conformable patience (*anulomikā khanti*). The Elder, having offered words of thanksgiving, departed.
As the lay follower was following the Elder and turning back, a female spirit (*yakkhinī*) approached in the guise of a cow, struck him on the chest, and killed him.
Having passed away, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven. The monks initiated a discussion in the Hall of Dharma (*dhammasabhā*).
“The executioner, having performed cruel deeds for fifty-five years, was released from them this very day;
he gave alms to the Elder this very day and passed away this very day. Where, indeed, has he been reborn?
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now? When they replied, “About this very one,” the Teacher said:
“Monks, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven,” he said. “Venerable sir, what do you say?
Having caused so many people to be killed over such a long period of time, how could he be reborn in the Tusita mansion? “Yes, monks; he acquired a great spiritual friend.
Having heard Sāriputta’s teaching on the Dhamma, he developed conforming knowledge (anuloma-ñāṇa) and, passing away from here, was reborn in the Tusita mansion.”
Having said, "He has been reborn," he spoke this verse:
"Having heard well-spoken words in the city, the executioner of thieves,
having attained the patience of conformity, rejoices, gone to the triple heaven."
“Venerable sir, a discourse of thanksgiving is not powerful; the unwholesome karma committed by him is great.
How is it that he produced such a distinction by so little? The Teacher said, “Monks, do not take the measure of the Dhamma taught by me as being either small or great.
For even a single word, if it is grounded in the goal, is better. Having said this, he established the connection.
Teaching the Dhamma by way of synthesis, he spoke this verse:
“Even if one were to speak a thousand words consisting of meaningless phrases,
a single meaningful phrase is better, hearing which one attains peace.”
In this context, "even a thousand" is a term for limitation; that is, even if speech is limited by a thousand— such as one thousand or two thousand—
if those words are joined with meaningless phrases, such as descriptions of space, descriptions of mountains, descriptions of forests, and so forth,
which are expounded by those who do not point out the way to liberation and are devoid of purpose, then however many such [words] there may be, they are evil.

This is the meaning. As for "a single meaningful phrase": having heard such a single meaningful phrase as, "This is the body; this is mindfulness directed to the body; the three knowledges have been attained;
the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled," one becomes tranquil through the subsiding of lust and other defilements.
That [phrase] accomplishes the goal, is connected with Nibbāna, and elucidates the aggregates, elements, bases, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and foundations of mindfulness.
The meaning is: "even a single verse is better.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the first story concerning the executioner Tambadāṭhika.

2. The Story of the Elder Bāhiya Dārucīriya "Even if one were to recite a thousand verses..."—the Teacher related this teaching on the Dhamma while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the elder Bāhiya Dārucīriya.
For once, many people set out upon the great ocean by ship, and their vessel was wrecked within the great ocean.
They became food for fish and turtles. Only one among them, having seized a plank and exerted himself, reached the shore of the port of Suppāraka;

he had no undergarment or upper robe. Seeing nothing else, he wrapped some dry sticks with grass fibers to make an undergarment and an upper robe, and taking an alms-bowl from a shrine, [he entered] the port of Suppāraka.
He arrived; when people saw him, they gave him rice gruel, alms-food, and other offerings, and they honored him, thinking, "This one is an Arahant.

When garments were offered to him, he thought, "If I wear these as an inner robe or a cloak, my gains and honor will diminish," so he rejected those garments and continued to wear only bark-cloth. Then many people cried out, "An Arahant! An Arahant!"
As he was being addressed, this reflection arose in his mind: "Whoever in the world are Arhats, or have entered the path to Arhatship, I am one among them.
Then a deity who was formerly a blood-relative thought thus to him.
"Formerly a blood-relative" means those who previously practiced the duties of a recluse together. It is said that in the past, under the teaching of the Blessed One Kassapa...

Seeing the decline of the novices and others as they were withdrawing, seven monks were seized by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and thought, "As long as the Dispensation has not vanished, we shall establish our own foundation.

Having paid homage to the Golden Cetiya, they entered the forest; seeing a mountain, they said, "Let those who still have attachment to life turn back. Those without attachment [to life] shall enter this mountain."
Having said, "Please climb up," he fastened a ladder; they all climbed up, and once the ladder was removed, they practiced the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).
Among them, the senior of the Saṅgha attained *arahantship* after the lapse of only one night.
Having chewed a tooth-stick of *nāgalatā* at Lake Anotatta and brought back almsfood from Uttarakuru, he said to those bhikkhus: "Friends,..."
“Having chewed this tooth-stick and rinsed your mouth, eat this alms-food.
“But, venerable sir, did we make such an agreement as this: ‘Whoever first attains arahantship, the rest shall eat the alms-food brought by him’? “No, friends. “In that case, if we too—”
“We shall produce a distinction just like yours and, having brought [food] ourselves, we shall eat,” they did not wish [to accept].
On the second day, the second elder attained the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*). He too, having brought almsfood in the same manner, invited the others.
They said this: “But, venerable sir, was such an agreement made by us, ‘When the Great Elder [attains a distinction],’” and so forth?
“Shall we not eat the alms-food brought by us, but rather eat that which has been brought by our younger brother? “Certainly not, friend.
“If that is so, then like you, we too shall eat only after having achieved distinction through our own manly effort,” they said, and thus they did not wish to eat.
Among them, the monk who had attained Arahantship passed away into Parinibbāna; the Non-returner (Anāgāmī) [did likewise].
He was reborn in the Brahma-world. The other five elders, being unable to attain a higher distinction, withered away and passed away on the seventh day;
having been reborn in the deva-world, they passed away from there during this current dispensation of a Buddha and were reborn in various noble families.
Among them, one became King Pukkusāti, one Kumāra-Kassapa, and one Dārucīriya.

“Dabba Mallaputta alone, Sabhiya the wanderer alone. In this context, it is with reference to the bhikkhu who was reborn in the Brahma-world that it is said, “the deity who was formerly his blood-relative.
For this Brahmā thought: “This man, having bound a ladder together with me, climbed up the mountain...”
“He practiced the duties of a recluse; now, if he wanders about adhering to this view, he will perish. I shall cause him to be stirred.

Then, having approached him, he said this: “Bāhiya, you are not an arahant, nor have you entered the path to arahantship, nor do you possess that practice by which you might become an arahant or enter the path to arahantship.”
“...has entered [the attainment]. Standing in the air, Bāhiya looked at the Great Brahmā as he spoke and thought:

“Alas, a grave deed has been done! I thought, ‘I am an Arahant,’ yet this one says to me, ‘You are not an Arahant, nor have you entered the path to Arahantship. Is there perhaps another Arahant in the world? Then—
He asked her: "Is there currently, O deity, in the world an arahant, or one who has entered the path to arahantship?

Then the deity informed him: "There is, Bāhiya; in the northern regions there is a city named Sāvatthī, and there the Blessed One currently resides—the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. For that Blessed One, Bāhiya..."
“He is an Arahant and he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of Arahantship.

Having heard the deity’s words during the night, Bāhiya, with a heart stirred by spiritual urgency, departed from Suppāraka at that very moment and traveled twenty hundred yojanas to Sāvatthī in a single night’s stay. He traversed the entire road in just one night.
He departed. And as he went, he traveled through the supernatural power of a deity; some even say it was "through the supernatural power of the Buddha.

At that moment, the Teacher had entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having finished his morning meal, in order to dispel physical fatigue, he saw many bhikkhus walking back and forth in the open air and asked, "Where is the Teacher now? The bhikkhus replied, "The Blessed One..."
Having said, "I have entered Sāvatthī for alms," they asked him, "But from where have you come? "I have come from Suppāraka," he replied.
"When did you set out? "I set out yesterday evening. "You have come from afar;
sit down, wash your feet, anoint them with oil, and rest for a while. When you have arrived, [inform] the Teacher..."
“Will you see him? “Venerable sir, I do not know whether there is a threat to the life of the Teacher or to my own life;
having traveled this road of two hundred leagues without stopping or sitting down anywhere for even a single night, I shall rest only after seeing the Teacher.
Having said this, he entered Sāvatthī in great haste and [approached] the Blessed One with incomparable...
Seeing him walking for alms with the splendor of a Buddha, [the brahmin] thought, "At long last, I have seen Gotama, the Perfectly Enlightened One!

From the moment he saw him, he walked with his body bent low; having prostrated himself with the fivefold contact right there in the middle of the street, he grasped the Blessed One’s ankles firmly and said this:
"May the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma, may the Sugata teach me the Dhamma."
“...the Dhamma that would lead to my welfare and happiness for a long time. Then the Teacher rejected him, saying, “It is not yet the right time, Bāhiya;
we have entered among the houses for alms.
Having heard this, Bhante, as one wandering through the cycle of existence, no morsel of food has ever been obtained by me that was not [already] received from you.
"Or perhaps I do not know whether there will be an obstacle to my life; please teach me the Dhamma. For the second time, the Teacher declined. It occurred to him:
"From the moment he saw me, his entire body has been continuously overwhelmed by rapture (*pīti*).
With such a powerful surge of rapture, even if he hears the Dhamma, he will not be able to penetrate it; he must first attain equanimity (*majjhattupekkhā*)."
“Let that be for now; since he has come a path of two hundred leagues in a single night, his exhaustion is also great, so let that too be appeased.
Thus, having refused him twice, when requested a third time, while still standing in the middle of the street, [the Blessed One said]:
“Therefore, Bāhiya, you must train yourself thus: ‘In the seen, there shall be only the seen,’ and so forth.”
He taught the Dhamma by means of the method. While listening to the Teacher’s Dhamma, he exhausted all taints and attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
At that very moment, he requested the Blessed One for the going-forth (*pabbajjā*). When asked, "Is your bowl and robe complete?
he replied, "They are not complete. Then the Teacher said to him, "In that case, go and seek out a bowl and robe," and departed.
“It is said that for twenty thousand years he practiced the duty of a recluse,
yet thinking, ‘A bhikkhu who has obtained requisites himself may use them alone without looking to another,’ he did not provide for even a single bhikkhu with either a bowl or a robe;
therefore, the bowl and robe made of supernormal power will not appear to him.”
Having understood this, he did not grant him the going-forth by means of the "Come, monk" formula.
While he was still searching for that very bowl and robe, a certain female spirit (yakkhinī) approached in the form of a cow, struck him on the chest, and brought about his death.
The Teacher, having walked for alms and finished his meal, set out together with many monks and [saw] Bāhiya’s body.
Seeing that it had fallen in a place of refuse, he commanded the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus, standing at the door of a certain house, have a bier brought;
having carried this body out from the city, cremate it and erect a stupa.
The bhikkhus did accordingly. Having done so, they went to the monastery, approached the Teacher, and reported what they had done.
Having reported this, they asked about his future destiny. Then the Blessed One, having explained to them that he had attained final nibbāna, placed him in the foremost position, saying:
"Bhikkhus, among my bhikkhu disciples who possess swift direct knowledge, Bāhiya of the Bark Robe is the foremost.
Thereupon, the bhikkhus asked him: "Venerable sir, you..."
“You should say, ‘Bāhiya has attained arahantship. When did he attain arahantship? “At the time he heard my Dhamma, monks.
“But when, Bhante, was the Dhamma spoken by you to him? “While walking for alms, standing in the middle of the street.
“For it was only a trifle, Bhante, that you spoke while standing in the middle of the street.”
“How is it that he, having heard the Dhamma, produced such a distinction by merely that much?
Then the Teacher said to them, “Bhikkhus, do not take my Dhamma as a measure of ‘little’ or ‘much.
For even thousands of verses based on what is meaningless are not better than a single verse-foot based on what is meaningful. Having said this, he established the connection.
Teaching the Dharma by way of connection, he spoke this verse:
“Even if there are a thousand verses composed of meaningless words,
a single line of a verse is better, hearing which one attains peace.”

In this context, "even a single verse-line is better" means that even a single verse such as "Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless... [as taught] by me" is better. The rest should be understood in the same manner as before.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the second story, concerning the Elder Bāhiya Dārucīriya.
3. The Story of the Elder Nun Kuṇḍalakesī The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this teaching on the Dhamma concerning the nun Kuṇḍalakesī: "He who recites a hundred verses...
It is said that in Rājagaha there was the daughter of a wealthy merchant, sixteen years of age, who was beautiful, lovely to behold, and inspiring.
When she reached that age, the women became inclined toward men and lustful for men.
Then her parents had her reside in a bedchamber on the upper floor of a seven-storied palace. They gave her only a single female slave as an attendant.
Then, having seized a young man of good family who was committing theft and having bound his hands behind his back, they led him from crossroads to crossroads...
Having struck him with whips, they led him to the place of execution. Hearing the noise of the great crowd, the merchant’s daughter thought, "What is this?
Standing on the terrace of her palace, she looked out; seeing him, her heart became bound to him.
Longing for him, she refused food and lay down upon her couch. Then her mother asked her, "What is this, my dear?"
“If I obtain this man being led away after having been seized as a ‘thief,’ I shall live.
If I do not obtain him, there is no life for me; I shall die right here. “Mother, do not do this;
you will obtain another husband equal to us in birth, clan, and wealth. “I have no need for anyone else.”
“If I do not obtain him, I shall die. Unable to persuade her daughter, the mother informed her husband.

He too, unable to persuade her, thought, “What can be done? and sent a purse of a thousand coins to the king’s officer who was leading the thief away, saying, “Take this and give this man back to me.”
Saying, "Very well," he took the coins, released him, killed another man, and reported to the king, "The thief has been executed, Your Majesty.
The merchant also gave him his daughter.
From that time on, thinking, "I shall please my husband," she adorned herself with all her ornaments and personally prepared his rice-gruel and other food.
He was aware of this. After a few days had passed, the thief thought:
"When indeed shall I kill her, take her ornaments, sell them in a tavern, and obtain food to eat?
Thinking, "There is a way," he refused food and lay down upon his bed. Then she approached him and asked, "What is it with you?"
“Master, am I being harmed? she asked. “Nothing at all, my dear,” he replied. “But are your mother and father angry with you?
“They are not angry, my dear. Then she asked, “What is this then?
“My dear, on that day when I was bound and being led away, I promised an offering to the deity dwelling at the Robbers’ Cliff in exchange for my life.”
“I obtained it, my dear; you too have received it through her very power. I think, ‘This is an offering I have set aside for that deity,’ Bhadde.
“Husband, do not worry; I shall perform the offering. Tell me, what is required?
“With honeyed milk-rice mixed with little water, and flowers with parched grain as the fifth ingredient. “Very well, husband; I shall prepare it.”
Having prepared all the offerings for the ritual, she said, "Come, my lord, let us go.
He replied, "In that case, dear lady, dismiss your relatives, take costly garments and ornaments, and adorn yourself;
laughing and playing, we shall go happily. She did accordingly.
Then, when they had reached the foot of the mountain, he said to her, "Bhadde, from here on both of us shall go together;
have the other people return with the carriage, and you yourself take up and carry the vessel for the offering.
She did accordingly. The robber took her and ascended the mountain of the robbers' precipice. For on one side of it...
People would climb up [the mountain], but one side was a precipitous cliff. Standing on the summit of the mountain, they would hurl robbers down that side;
they would fall to the ground, broken into pieces. Therefore, it is called "Robbers' Precipice.
Standing on the summit of that mountain, she said to him, "Master, perform an offering for me. He remained silent.
So it happened. Again, when she asked him, "Why, master, are you silent? he said to her, "I have no need for the sacrificial offering;
rather, I have come here having deceived you and taken it. "For what reason, master? "In order to kill you, take your ornaments, and flee.
Terrified by the fear of death, she said, "Master, both I and my ornaments—"

“These are indeed yours; why do you speak thus? Though he was entreated again and again with the words, “Do not do this,” he replied, “I shall surely kill her. [She said: “If that is so, what use is my death to you?
Take these ornaments and give me my life. From now on, consider me as dead; or else, becoming your slave, I will perform service for you.”
Having spoken thus, he recited this verse:
“This golden armlet, these many pearls and beryl gems—
take all of it, O Blessed One, and declare me to be your slave.”
Hearing this, the robber said, "If you do this, you will go and tell your parents; I shall certainly kill you. Do not lament so bitterly," and he spoke this verse:
"Do not lament so bitterly; quickly bind up your bundle.
There is no life left for you; I am taking everything."
She thought: "Alas, this task is grave! Wisdom was not created for the purpose of cooking and eating;
rather, it was created for the purpose of investigation. I shall find out what must be done. Then she said to him:
"My lord, when you were seized as a 'thief' and led away, I informed my parents; they released a thousand pieces of gold."
Having had it brought, they placed it in their home. "From that time on, I have been your benefactress;
today, having looked upon me well, grant me leave to pay you homage. He replied, "Very well, lady; look upon me well and pay homage.
Having said this, he stood at the edge of the mountain. Then she circumambulated him three times and paid homage at four places.
“Master, this is the last time you shall see me; from now on, there will be no more seeing of you by me, nor of me by you.

Having embraced him from both front and back, and while he was thus distracted, she stood behind him who was standing at the edge of the mountain, took hold of his shoulder with one hand and his back with the other, and [threw him] over the mountain precipice.
He threw it. Striking against the interior of the mountain, it shattered into pieces and fell to the ground.
A deity dwelling at the top of the Corapapāta precipice, having witnessed the actions of both of them, gave her approval and spoke this verse:
“Indeed, it is not in all circumstances that a man is wise;”
“A woman too can be wise and discerning in every circumstance.
Having thrown the thief over the precipice, she thought: “If I go home, they will ask, ‘Where is your husband?
If, being asked thus, I say, ‘He was killed by me,’ they will say, ‘Having given a thousand [pieces of money] to this ill-behaved woman, you brought her back.’”
“Having had it brought back, they will now kill her,” she thought;
“Even if I say, ‘He intended to kill me for the sake of my ornaments,’ they will not believe me. Enough of this home!
Having cast away her ornaments right there and entered the forest, she wandered on by stages until she reached a hermitage of wandering mendicants.
Having paid homage, she said, "Venerable sir, please grant me the going-forth in your presence. Then they granted her the going-forth.
Having gone forth, she asked, "Venerable sir, what is the highest goal in your dispensation? [The Teacher replied:
"Bhadde, one must either produce jhāna by performing the preliminary work on the ten *kasiṇas*, or one must master a thousand discourses."
“This is the supreme goal of our renunciation. [He replied,] “Venerable sir, I shall not be able to produce jhāna for the time being, but I will learn a thousand arguments.
Then, having had him master those thousand arguments, they said, “You have mastered the craft;
now, as you wander over the surface of Jambudīpa, find someone capable of debating with you on a question.”
Having placed a branch of the Jambu tree in his hand, they dismissed him, saying: "Go, Bhaddā;
if anyone who has become a householder is able to discuss the Dhamma with you, become his wife;
if one who has gone forth is able, go forth under him."
Known by the name Jambūparibbājikā, she departed from there and wandered about asking questions of whomever she encountered.
There was no one capable of conversing with her; as soon as people heard that "Jambūparibbājikā is coming here," they would flee.
When she entered a village or town for alms, she would [pile up] a heap of sand at the village gate.

Having placed a branch of a rose-apple tree there and saying, "Let whoever is capable of conversing with me crush this rose-apple branch," he entered the village. No one was able to approach that place.
When that branch had withered, she took another rose-apple branch; wandering in this manner, she arrived at Sāvatthī.
Having made a heap of sand at the village gate and placed a branch of a rose-apple tree there, he spoke according to the aforementioned method and entered the village for alms.

Several village boys stood surrounding the rose-apple branch. At that time, the Elder Sāriputta, having walked for alms and finished his meal, was departing from the city and saw those boys standing around the rose-apple branch.
Having seen it, he asked, "What is this? The boys explained the situation to the Elder. He said, "In that case, boys, crush this branch.
"We are afraid, Venerable Sir," they replied. "I shall provide the answer; you simply crush it.
Encouraged by the Elder's words, they did as instructed, and while crushing it, they lifted up the jambu branch. The female wanderer—
Having arrived and rebuked them, he said, "I have no need for a question with you; why did you crush my branch?
They replied, "Venerable sir, we were made to crush it by our master. He asked, "Reverend sir, was my branch crushed by you?
"Yes, sister. "In that case, let us discuss a question together. "Very well, I shall discuss it."
When the shadows were lengthening, she went into the presence of the Elder to ask her question, and the entire city was thrown into agitation.
Thinking, "We shall hear the discourse of two wise men," the citizens went along with her, paid homage to the Elder, and sat down to one side.
The female wanderer said to the Elder: "Venerable sir, I ask you a question."
“Questions? “Ask, sister,” he said. She asked a thousand questions, and for each question asked, the Elder gave an answer.

Then the Elder said to her: “Are these all your questions, or are there others? “These are all of them, venerable sir. “You have asked many questions; we too shall ask one. Will you answer it? “If I know it, [I will answer].”
“I shall answer; ask, venerable sir,” she said. The Elder asked the question, “What is ‘one’?
Not knowing how this should be answered, she asked, “What is this, venerable sir? “It is called a question of the Buddha, sister.
“Give that to me too, venerable sir. “If you will become like me, I shall give it to you.”
“In that case, please ordain me. The Elder informed the bhikkhunīs and ordained her. Having been ordained and received full admission (*upasampadā*), she became known as the Elder Nun Kuṇḍalakesī;
after only a few days, she attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
The bhikkhus raised a discussion in the Hall of Truth: “The Elder Nun Kuṇḍalakesī [listened to] the Dhamma...”
"There is not much; she has reached the culmination of her duties as a renunciant, for it is said that she returned after engaging in a great battle with a certain bandit and defeating him.
The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, "About this very matter," he said, "Monks, regarding the Dhamma taught by me, whether it be little or much—"
"Do not take the measure [of a person] by their words; even a hundred meaningless phrases are not as good as a single word of Dhamma, which is indeed better.
There is no such thing as victory for one who conquers external thieves; but for one who conquers the thieves that are the internal defilements, there is true victory.
Having said this, he joined the connection and, teaching the Dhamma, spoke these verses:
“Better than a hundred verses spoken that are joined with meaningless words is a single word of Dhamma, hearing which one attains peace.
One who might conquer a thousand men in battle by the thousands— ”
"And one who should know but himself—he indeed is the supreme warrior.

In this context, "a hundred stanzas" means that person who might recite many stanzas, even numbering a hundred. "Connected with words of no meaning" means connected with words that are meaningless, such as descriptions of the color of the sky and so forth.
"A stanza of Dhamma" refers to that which accomplishes the goal and is associated with the aggregates (*khandha*) and other categories.
“Monks, there are these four Dhamma-footings. What are the four? Non-covetousness, monks, is a Dhamma-footing;
non-ill will, monks, is a Dhamma-footing; right mindfulness, monks, is a Dhamma-footing; and right concentration, monks, is a Dhamma-footing.
Among these four Dhamma-footings thus spoken of, even a single Dhamma-footing is better.

"Whoever conquers a thousand in battle"—this refers to one who, as a warrior in combat, might conquer a thousand multiplied by a thousand men in a single battle, bringing victory after defeating a hundred thousand human beings;

even such a conqueror of battle is not called the "supreme and most excellent. But "whoever should conquer but one—the self"—this refers to one who, in places for standing by night or day, [practices] the internal meditation subject (*ajjhattika-kammaṭṭhāna*).
By conquering his own defilements such as greed through right reflection, he should conquer himself.
"He is indeed the supreme victor in battle" means that he is the most excellent and preeminent among those who win battles, a warrior at the head of the fray.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
The third story: The Elder Nun Kuṇḍalakesī.
4. The Story of the Brahmin Who Asked About Harm.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, delivered this teaching on the Dhamma concerning the Brahmin who asked about harm.
It is said that the brahmin thought, "Does the Perfectly Enlightened One know only what is beneficial, or does he also know what is harmful? I shall ask him.
He approached the Teacher and asked: "Venerable sir, I imagine you know only what is beneficial, not what is harmful?
"Brahmin, I know both what is beneficial and what is harmful. "In that case, tell me what is harmful."
Then the Teacher spoke this verse to him:
“Sleeping late, laziness, irritability, and being a heavy drinker;
Going alone on a journey, and consorting with another’s wife.”
“O brahmin, practice this; it will lead to your harm.
Having heard this, the brahmin gave his approval, saying, “Excellent, excellent! Teacher of the group, elder of the group, you truly know both what is beneficial and what is harmful.
“In this way, brahmin, one who is called a knower of the beneficial and the harmful is described by me...”
“There is no one like him. Then the Teacher, having discerned his intention, asked: “Brāhmaṇa, by what work do you earn your living?
“By the game of dice, Master Gotama. “But do you win, or do you lose? “I both win and lose.
When this was said, [the Teacher replied]: “Brāhmaṇa, that is a mere trifle; as for one who conquers others, victory—”
“Indeed, victory over others is not as good as victory over oneself. But for one who conquers himself by overcoming the defilements, that victory is superior;
for no one is able to turn that victory into a defeat. Having said this, and having established the connection, he taught the Dhamma by reciting these verses:
“Victory over oneself is indeed better than victory over other people.”
For a person who has tamed themselves, who always conducts themselves with restraint—
neither a god, nor a gandhabba, nor Māra together with Brahmā could overturn what has been won by such a person.
In this context, *hava* is a particle. *Jitaṃ* is a change of grammatical gender;

the meaning is that by one’s own victory over defilements, the self is conquered, and thus it is superior. As for "this other generation"—meaning whatever remaining generation might be conquered by gambling, or by the seizure of wealth, or by battle, or by the overwhelming of force—the meaning is that what is conquered by such means is not superior.
But why is it that "only that is victory, this is not victory"? Because, as it is said: "For one who has tamed himself...

for such a person. This is what is meant: because for that person who has tamed himself through the absence of defilements—one who always conducts himself with restraint in body and so forth, and who is thus restrained by these things such as bodily restraint—for such a person...
Even if a deity, a gandhabba, Māra, or Brahmā were to rise up together and strive and exert themselves with the thought, "I shall cause his victory to become a defeat;
I shall cause the defilements abandoned through the cultivation of the path to arise again," they could not do so—
just as one who, having been defeated by wealth or other means, becomes an opponent and, by winning back what was lost, makes that victory a defeat.
“Thus, they would not even be able to bring about a defeat.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the fourth story, concerning the Brahmin who asked about what is harmful.

5. The Story of the Brahmin Maternal Uncle of the Elder Sāriputta The Teacher, while residing at Veḷuvana, gave this Dhamma instruction concerning the brahmin who was the maternal uncle of the Elder Sāriputta.
It is said that the Elder went to him and asked, "Brahmin, are you performing any wholesome deed whatsoever?"
“I do, venerable sir. “What are you doing? “I give gifts by relinquishing a thousand [pieces of gold] every month. “To whom do you give them?
“To the Nigaṇṭhas, venerable sir. “With what in mind? “The Brahma-world, venerable sir. “But is this the path to the Brahma-world?
“Yes, venerable sir. “Who says so? “My teachers.”
“I have told you, Bhante. “You do not know the path to the Brahma-world, nor do your teachers;
the Teacher alone knows it. Come, Brahmin, I shall explain the path to the Brahma-world to you.
Taking him with him, he led him into the presence of the Teacher and, having reported what had occurred, said, “Bhante, this Brahmin spoke thus; it would be well for him...”
“Tell me the path to the Brahma-world. The Teacher asked, “Is it true, brahmins?

When they replied, “Yes, Master Gotama,” he said, “Brahmin, for you who give in this manner, even a single moment’s look at my disciple with a clear mind, or the gift of a mere ladleful of alms-food, is more fruitful than the giving of gifts for a hundred years.”
Having spoken thus and established the connection, while teaching the Dhamma, he uttered this verse:
“Though one were to offer a thousand [pieces of gold] month after month for a hundred years,
Yet if one were to honor for even a moment a single person of developed self— ”
"That very worship is better than a hundred sacrifices offered for a hundred years.

In this context, "with a thousandfold" means by the relinquishing of a thousand. "Whoever should sacrifice for a hundred years" means that one who, giving away a thousand [pieces of gold] month after month for a hundred years, should give gifts to the common people of the world; and "one who has cultivated the self"—that is, one who has developed the mind through meditation.
But if one were to honor— with the offering of a spoonful of alms-food, or with food sufficient for maintenance, or even by the mere gift of a coarse garment—

a person who has developed their own self through the excellence of qualities such as virtue, being at the lower limit a stream-enterer and at the upper limit one whose taints are destroyed, upon arriving at their house—
this very act of honoring would be superior to the other’s performance of sacrifice for a hundred years.
"Better. "Best" means "supreme"—this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, that brahmin attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), and many others also attained the fruits of stream-entry and the rest.
This is the fifth story, the account of the brahmin who was the maternal uncle of the Elder Sāriputta.
6. The Story of the Nephew of the Elder Sāriputta The Teacher, while dwelling at Veḷuvana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning the nephew of the Elder Sāriputta.
The Elder had approached him and asked, "Brāhmaṇa, are you performing wholesome deeds? To which he replied, "Yes, venerable sir."
“What are you doing? “Every month I slaughter one animal and tend the sacrificial fire. “For what purpose do you do this?
“It is said, sir, that this is the path to the Brahma-world. “By whom was it told to you thus? “By my teachers, venerable sir.
“Neither you know the path to the Brahma-world, nor do your teachers. Come, let us go into the presence of the Teacher.”
“Let us go,” he said; and having led him into the presence of the Teacher and reported the matter, he said, “Venerable sir, please explain the path to this Brahmā-world for him.

The Teacher asked, “Is it indeed so? When the other replied, “It is so, Master Gotama,” the Teacher said, “Brāhmaṇa, even if one were to tend the fire in this manner for a hundred years, your fire-tending would not equal even a sixteenth part of my disciple’s [practice].”
"Even for a mere moment, one does not obtain even a fraction of that merit," he said, and having established the connection, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
"But if a person were to tend a fire in the forest for a hundred years,
And were to honor for even a moment one whose self is cultivated— [The latter would yield greater fruit]."
"That very worship is better than a hundred years of sacrifice.

In this context, "jantu" is a designation for sentient beings (*satta*). "One should tend the fire in the forest" means that even after entering the forest with the aspiration for the state of non-proliferation (*nippapañca*), one should tend the fire there. The rest is exactly as before.
At the conclusion of the teaching, that brahmin attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), and many others also attained the fruits of stream-entry and the other stages.
The sixth story concerning the nephew of the Elder Sāriputta.
The seventh story concerning the brahmin friend of the Elder Sāriputta.

The Teacher, while residing at Veḷuvana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning the brahmin who was a friend of the Elder Sāriputta, beginning with the words: "Whatever sacrifice has been offered..."
The Elder approached him as well and asked, "Brāhmaṇa, are you performing any wholesome deed?
"Yes, venerable sir," he replied. "What are you doing? "I am performing a sacrifice. "In that case, perform that sacrifice with great renunciation.
Thereafter, the Elder questioned him in the same manner as before, led him into the presence of the Teacher, and—
Having reported his journey, he said, "Venerable sir, please tell me the path to this Brahmā-world. The Teacher asked, "Brāhmaṇa, is it so?

When the brāhmaṇa replied, "It is so, Master Gotama," the Teacher said, "Brāhmaṇa, while you were performing the great sacrifice for a year, the gift given by you to the common folk of the world with a devout heart [was surpassed by] the gift given by me to my disciples..."
"Even a mere fourth part of the wholesome volition that arises in those who pay homage does not equal [the merit of giving]," he said;
then, joining the connection and teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
"Whatever sacrifice or offering there may be in the world..."
One seeking merit might sacrifice for a year,
yet all that does not equal even a fourth part of the excellence of paying homage to those who are upright.

In this context, "whatever" (*yaṃ kiñci*) is a term that includes everything without exception. "Sacrificed" (*yiṭṭha*) refers mostly to the giving bestowed on occasions such as auspicious ceremonies.
"Offered" (*huta*) refers both to the hospitality given after having prepared [the food], as well as to the giving performed with faith in both the action and its fruit.
"One should sacrifice for a year" means that one should give the aforementioned kinds of gifts continuously for the duration of one full year.
One might give [this] even to the worldly multitude throughout the entire Cakkavāḷa. "Seeking merit" means desiring merit.
"Among those who have gone straight" means, at the lower limit, among stream-enterers (sotāpanna), and at the upper limit, among those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava). This is what is meant:

"The fruit that arises from the wholesome volition of one who, with a mind of confidence, bows the body and pays homage to such persons—even a fourth part of that [fruit would not equal the merit of another]."
"All that gift does not equal it; therefore, among those who are upright, merely paying homage is better.
At the conclusion of this teaching, that brahmin attained the fruit of stream-entry, and many others also attained the fruits of stream-entry and the higher stages.
This is the seventh story, the account of the brahmin who was a friend of the Venerable Sāriputta.
8. The Story of the Boy Āyuvaḍḍhana The Teacher delivered this Dhamma teaching while dwelling in a forest hut near Dīghalaṅghika, concerning the boy Dīghāyu.
It is said that two brahmins living in the city of Dīghalaṅghika had gone forth into the renunciant life of outsiders, and after forty-eight years...
They practiced ascetic penance for many years. Among them, one thought, "My lineage will perish; I shall disrobe.
Having reflected thus, he sold the merit of the penance he had performed and, together with a hundred cows and a hundred kahāpaṇas, obtained a wife and established a household.
Then his wife gave birth to a son. But his other companion—
Having gone abroad, he returned once more to that city. Hearing that he had arrived, the father took his wife and children and went to see his friend.
Upon arriving, he placed his son in his mother’s hands and first paid homage himself;
the mother, in turn, placed her son in his father’s hands and paid homage. He said, "May you live long," but as for the son—
When he was being paid homage, [the Elder] remained silent.

Then [the brahmin] said to him, “Venerable sir, why is it that after we had paid homage to you, you said, ‘May you be long-lived,’ yet at this time of paying homage to him, you say nothing? “There is a certain obstacle for him, brahmin.
“How long will he live, venerable sir? “Seven days, brahmin. “Is there a means to ward it off?”
“Venerable sir,” he asked. “I do not know the reason for my being repelled. “But who, venerable sir, would know?
“The ascetic Gotama would know; go to him and ask him. “In going there, I fear a loss of my ascetic penance.
“If you have affection for your son, then go to him and ask, without considering the loss of your penance.”
Thus, having gone into the presence of the Teacher, he first paid homage himself. The Teacher said, "May you live long.
When Pajāpatī paid homage, he spoke to her in the same way; but when it was time for his son to pay homage, he remained silent.
The man questioned the Teacher in the same manner as before, and the Teacher likewise gave the same reply. It is said that this brahmin had not yet penetrated the knowledge of omniscience.
He compared his own counsel with the knowledge of omniscience, yet he did not know the means of warding it off.
The Brahmin asked the Teacher: “But, Bhante, is there a means of warding it off? “There might be, Brahmin.
“What might it be? “If you were to have a pavilion erected at the door of your house and a small throne placed in its center—”
“Having had that constructed and surrounded it, if you were able to prepare eight or sixteen seats, have my disciples sit upon them,
and perform a protective recitation (*paritta*) continuously for seven days,
then his obstacle would perish. “Master Gotama, while I am able to construct the pavilion and such, how shall I obtain your disciples?”
“When you have finished this much, I will send my disciples. “Very well, Master Gotama,” he replied.
Having completed all his business at the door of his own house, he went into the presence of the Teacher. The Teacher sent forth monks;
they went there and sat down, and they had the boy lie down upon a small couch. For seven days and nights, the monks—
They recited the *Paritta* continuously. On the seventh day, in the evening, the Teacher arrived. When he had arrived, all the deities of the world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*) assembled.
However, a certain *yakkha* named Avaruddhaka, having served Vessavaṇa for twelve years and receiving a boon from him, obtained this:
"On the seventh day from now, you should take this boy."
Therefore, he too came and stood there.

But when the Teacher had gone there and the highly influential deities had assembled, the deities of little influence, being crowded back repeatedly and finding no space, retreated for twelve yojanas. Avaruddhaka did likewise.
He withdrew, and the Teacher also performed a protective recitation (*paritta*) throughout the entire night. When seven days had passed, the captor did not obtain the boy.
But on the eighth day, as soon as the dawn had risen, they brought the boy and had him pay homage to the Teacher.
The Teacher said, "May you live long. "But for how long, Master Gotama, will the boy remain? "For one hundred and twenty years."
“O Brahmins! Then they gave him the name “Āyuvaḍḍhanakumāra” (Life-Increasing Prince).
As he grew up, he traveled about surrounded by five hundred lay followers. Then one day, in the Hall of Truth, the monks started a conversation: “See, friends!
It was said that Prince Āyuvaḍḍhana ought to have died on the seventh day; yet now—”
“Having lived for two hundred years, he wanders about surrounded by five hundred lay followers;
surely there must be some cause for the increase in the lifespan of these beings. The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what topic are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very matter,” he said, “Monks, it is not only the increase in lifespan alone...”
"But these beings, by honoring and revering those possessed of virtue, increase in four ways, are freed from perils, and remain for as long as their lifespan lasts.
Having said this, and having established the connection, he taught the Dhamma by reciting this verse:
"For one whose nature is to pay homage, who always honors the elders..."
"Four things increase: life-span, beauty, happiness, and strength.
In this context, "one whose nature is to pay homage" means one whose nature is to bow down; the meaning is one who is constantly intent on the duty of salutation.
"One who honors the elders" refers to a householder [honoring] even a young novice monk who has gone forth that very day, or a monastic [honoring] his seniors.
The meaning is: for one who shows respect to those senior in years or superior in virtue—whether by way of going forth or full ordination—or who constantly honors them with salutation.
"Four things increase" means that while life-span increases, for as long as it increases, the others likewise increase. For by that [life-span], which conduces to a lifespan of fifty years...
A wholesome deed has been performed; should a threat to life arise for him at the age of twenty-five, it is pacified by his habit of paying homage.
He remains for the full span of his natural lifespan, and his beauty and other qualities increase along with that very life-span.
This same principle applies even beyond this. There is no such thing as an "increase" of a life-span that proceeds without obstruction.

At the conclusion of the teaching, Prince Āyuvaḍḍhana, together with five hundred lay followers, was established in the fruit of stream-entry; many others also attained the fruits of stream-entry and the higher stages.
Thus ends the eighth story, the Story of Prince Āyuvaḍḍhana. 9.
The Story of the Novice Saṅkicca.
The Teacher, while residing at Jeta’s Grove, spoke this teaching on the Dhamma concerning the novice Saṅkicca: “He who lives for a hundred years...
It is said that in Sāvatthī, about thirty young men of good family, having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, placed their trust in the Dispensation and went forth.
When they had received full ordination and reached five years of seniority, they approached the Teacher and took up the burden of study.

Having heard that there are two types of practice—the burden of insight (vipassanādhura) and [the burden of study]—and thinking, "We have gone forth in old age," they made no effort in the burden of study.

Desiring to fulfill the burden of insight, they had the meditation subject explained to them up to the stage of Arahantship, and then asked the Teacher, "Venerable Sir, we shall go to a certain forest retreat. The Teacher said, "Which place?"
Having asked, "Will you go? and being told, "To such-and-such a place," he understood: "There, fear will arise for them because of one who eats the remains of offerings;
however, that fear will be pacified when the novice Saṅkicca has departed, and then their task of going forth will reach completion."
The novice Saṃkiccasāmaṇera was seven years of age at birth; he was the novice of the Elder Sāriputta.
It is said that his mother was the daughter of a wealthy family in Sāvatthī. When he was conceived in her womb, she died instantly from a certain illness.
As she was being cremated, everything except the flesh of the fetus was consumed by the flames. Then, as for that flesh of the fetus—
Having brought him down from the funeral pyre, they pierced him with stakes in two or three places. The tip of a stake struck the corner of the boy’s eye.
Having thus pierced the flesh of the womb, they threw him onto a heap of charcoal, covered him with the very coals, and departed.
The flesh of the womb was consumed by the fire, but on top of the embers, the boy—resembling a golden image—remained within the interior of a lotus.
He remained as if lying there. For it is impossible for a being in his final existence (*pacchimabhavika*) to meet with death before attaining *arahantship*, even if Mount Sineru were to crush him.
On the following day, those who had come thinking, "We shall extinguish the funeral pyre," saw the boy still lying in that same position;
struck with a sense of wonder and amazement, they thought, "How is it that while so much wood has been consumed..."
"When the entire body was being burned, the boy did not burn; what indeed will happen? Thinking this, they took the boy into the village and questioned the fortune-tellers.
The fortune-tellers said, "If this boy shall live as a householder, his kinsmen will remain in poverty for seven generations. But if he goes forth [into homelessness], by means of the five..."
"He will wander about surrounded by hundreds of ascetics," they said.
Because his eye was pierced by a thorn, they gave him the name Saṅkicca; thus, after some time, he became known as Saṅkicca.
Then his relatives thought, "Very well, when he has grown up, we shall have him ordained in the presence of our noble Sāriputta," and so they raised him.
Thus, at the age of seven, having heard the talk of the boys—"While you were dwelling in your mother’s womb, your mother passed away;
even while her body was being cremated, you yourself were not cremated"—he thought, "I am indeed released from such dangers as these;
what use have I for the household life? I shall go forth. He informed his kinsmen, who said, "Excellent, dear one!"

Having led him into the presence of the Elder Sāriputta, they handed him over, saying, "Venerable sir, please grant him the going-forth. The Elder gave him the meditation subject of the five aggregates (the *tacapañcaka kammaṭṭhāna*) and ordained him.
At the very moment the razor touched his hair, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
This was the novice Saṅkicca. The Teacher said, "When he has gone, that fear will be stilled; then their purpose for going forth will reach fulfillment."
Knowing that he would depart, [the Buddha] said, "Monks, go after looking back at the Elder Sāriputta, your eldest brother.
They replied, "Very well," and went into the presence of the Elder. When he asked, "What is it, friends?
they said, "Having received a meditation subject from the Teacher, we wished to enter the forest and took our leave."
Then our Teacher said to us, "Go after looking for your eldest brother. We replied, "It was because of that that we came here.
The Elder thought, "The Teacher must have sent these men here upon seeing a certain reason;
what could it be? Having reflected and understood the matter, he asked, "But do you have a novice, friends?"
“There is none, friend. “If there is none, then take this novice Saṅkicca and go. “Enough, friend.
With a novice as our support, we will have an impediment; what need have those living in the forest for a novice?
“It is not that you will have an impediment because of him, friend, but rather that he will have an impediment because of you.”
"It will come to pass. The Teacher sent you to me while also expecting to send a novice with you;

take this and go. Having consented by saying "Very well," those thirty-one people, together with the novice, took leave of the Elder, departed from the monastery, and as they were wandering on their journey, they reached a point two hundred yojanas away.
They reached a village of one thousand families.
When the people saw them, their hearts were filled with faith; they served them with great care and, having asked, "Venerable sirs, where will you go?
and being told, "To whatever place is convenient, friends," they prostrated at their feet and said, "Venerable sirs, we..."
“Venerable sirs, while you dwell in this place for the duration of the rains-retreat, we shall undertake the five precepts and perform the Uposatha ceremony,” they requested.

The Elders consented. Then, having prepared resting places at night, sitting places during the day, walking paths, and leaf-huts for them, the people attended upon them with great enthusiasm, saying, “Today we will serve; tomorrow we will serve. On the day of the entry into the rains-retreat, the Elders—
They made a formal agreement, saying: "Friend, we have received our meditation subject in the presence of the Buddha who is currently living.
It is not possible to please the Buddhas except through the perfection of practice. Furthermore, the doors to the states of misery stand wide open for us;
therefore, apart from the time for alms-round in the morning and the time for attending upon the elders in the evening, at all other times..."
“Let us not be in one place; whichever of us feels unwell shall go to the other when the bell is struck and prepare medicine,
while at all other times, whether by night or by day, we shall apply ourselves diligently to our meditation subject.”

While they were dwelling there having made such an agreement, a certain poor man who was living in dependence upon his daughter set out on the road when a famine arose in that place, desiring to live by depending upon another daughter.
The Elders, too, having wandered for alms in the village and returning to their dwelling place, bathed in a certain river along the way.
Having sat down on a sandy bank, they performed their meal duties. At that moment, the man arrived at that place and stood to one side.
Then the elders asked him, "Where are you going? He explained the matter to them.
The elders, having conceived compassion for him, said, "Lay follower, you are very hungry; go, bring some leaves."

Having said, "We will give you each a single morsel of food," they prepared it with soups and condiments according to their own respective eating habits and gave him one morsel each when he brought the leaf-plate. It is said that this was the established custom:
that when giving food to one who has arrived at the time of a meal, the monk should not give him the first portion, but rather [prepare it] according to his own manner of eating.
"Whether it be little or much, it should be given. Therefore, they gave accordingly. Having finished his meal and paid homage to the elders, he asked:
"Venerable sirs, have the masters been invited by anyone? "No, lay follower; there is no invitation.
People give such food as this every day. He thought: "We always rise early and exert ourselves..."
"Even while working, we are unable to obtain such food; what is the use of my going elsewhere?
I shall live right here in their presence. Then he said to them, "I wish to live in the presence of the noble ladies, performing the duties and services.
"Very well, lay follower," they replied. He then went with them to the place where they lived.
By performing his duties and counter-duties with great diligence, he won the monks over exceedingly;
then, after two months had passed, wishing to see his daughter, he thought, "If I ask permission, noble ladies, they will not let me go; I shall depart without asking.
Without informing them, he departed. Indeed, this was the only significant transgression he committed: that he left without announcing his departure to the monks.
Now, on his way there was a forest. There, it was the seventh day since five hundred thieves had been dwelling after making a vow to a deity, saying:
"Whoever enters this forest, we shall kill him and perform an offering for you with his flesh and blood.
Therefore, on the seventh day, the chief of the thieves—
Climbing a tree and looking out, he saw him approaching and gave the signal to the thieves.
Knowing that he had entered the middle of the forest, they surrounded him, seized him, and bound him tightly.
Producing fire by means of a fire-drill, they gathered wood and, having made a great mass of fire, carved stakes.
Seeing their action, he asked, "Master, neither pigs nor deer and the like are seen in this place;
for what reason are you doing this? They replied, "Having killed him, we shall perform an offering to the deity with your flesh and blood.
Terrified by the fear of death, he disregarded the kindness of the monks and thought only of himself.
Protecting his own life, he spoke thus: "Master, I am a *vighāsāda* (scavenger-eater), raised on leftover food;
a *vighāsāda* is indeed an ill-omened one. But these masters, though they have gone forth after leaving here and there, are still Kṣatriyas.
In such-and-such a place thirty-one bhikkhus reside; kill them and perform a sacrificial offering."
“The deities will be exceedingly pleased with you. Hearing this, the robbers thought, “He speaks auspiciously;
what is the use of this ill-omened man? We shall kill a khattiya and perform a sacrificial offering.

Thinking thus, they said, “Come, show us their dwelling place,” and making that very man their guide, they reached that spot. Not seeing any monks in the midst of the monastery, [they proceeded further].
“Where are the monks? they asked him. Since he had lived there for two months, he knew their established practice and said:
“They are sitting in their own daytime and nighttime resting places;
strike this bell, and by the sound of the bell they will assemble. The chief robber struck the bell.
When the monks heard the sound of the gong, thinking, "The gong has been struck at an improper time;
someone must be unwell," they came and sat down in a row on stone slabs prepared in the middle of the monastery.
The senior monk of the Sangha looked at the robbers and asked, "Lay followers, by whom was this gong struck? The chief robber replied, "By me."
“Venerable sir,” they said. “For what reason? “We have made a request to the forest deity;
we shall go taking one bhikkhu with us to perform an offering for her. Hearing this, the Great Elder said to the bhikkhus:
“Friends, a task that has arisen for younger brothers must be resolved by the eldest brother. I shall sacrifice my own life for you.”
“I shall go with these; may no obstacle befall any of you. Be diligent in performing the duties of a recluse.
The junior elder said, “Venerable sir, the duty of an elder brother is the responsibility of the younger;
I shall go, while you remain diligent. In this manner, each saying, “I alone, I alone,” they all spoke in turn until thirty had spoken.
The people rose up and said, "In this way, they were neither the sons of one mother nor the sons of one father, nor were they free from passion;
nevertheless, for the sake of the rest, they sacrificed their lives in succession.
Among them, not even a single person was able to say, 'You go.'"
Having heard their words, the novice Saṅkicca said, "Venerable sirs, you stay; I shall go, sacrificing my own life for yours.
They replied, "Friend, even if we were all to be executed together, we would not release you alone.
"For what reason, venerable sirs? "Friend, because you are the attendant of the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma."
“If we release the novice, the Elder will scold us, saying, ‘They took my novice away and handed him over to the bandits.
We will not be able to withstand that reproach; therefore, we shall not release him.
“Venerable sir, even when the Perfectly Enlightened One sent you to my preceptor... [the preceptor continued: “...my preceptor—”
"Even when sending me with you, he sent me for this very reason. You stay here; I myself will go.
Having paid homage to the thirty monks, he said, "Venerable sirs, if there is any fault in me, forgive it," and departed.
At that moment, a great sense of spiritual urgency arose among the monks; their eyes filled with tears and their hearts were moved.

He shook his head. The Great Elder said to the robbers, “Upāsakas, this young man will be frightened when he sees you making the fire, carving the stakes, and spreading the leaves; set him aside in a secluded spot and perform those tasks.
The robbers took the novice with them, went to a secluded place, set him down there, and performed all their duties.
At the conclusion of his task, the chief thief drew his sword and approached the novice.
As the novice was sitting down, he entered into a state of meditative absorption (jhāna) and remained seated. The chief thief turned his sword and brought it down upon the novice’s shoulder;
the blade bent and struck edge against edge. Thinking, "I have not struck correctly," he [prepared to strike again].
He straightened it and struck him. The sword, wrapping itself like a palm leaf, went to the base of the pillar.
At that time, there was no one capable of killing the novice even if Mount Sineru were to crush him, let alone with a sword.
Seeing that miracle, the chief of the thieves thought: "Formerly, my sword [could not even cut] a stone pillar or a khadira post..."
“Or it cuts like a bamboo shoot; now it has bent once and become like a palm-leaf sheath.
This sword, though being insentient, knows this man’s virtue, whereas I, though sentient, do not.
Throwing the sword upon the ground, he prostrated himself at the man’s feet with his chest and said, “Venerable sir, for the sake of wealth...”
"We have entered the forest; even when we see us from afar, thousands of people tremble and are unable to utter two or three words.
Yet you do not have even the slightest fear;
your face shines like gold in a furnace or like a full-blown *kaṇikāra* flower. What indeed is the reason for this?"—asking thus, he spoke this verse:
“You have no fear; rather, your complexion brightens.
Why do you not lament in such a great terror?
The novice, emerging from meditation and teaching him the Dhamma, said: “Friend village headman, for one whose taints are destroyed, the personal existence [is ended].”
"It is as if a burden has been placed upon one's head; when that [burden] breaks or is lost, he is simply satisfied and does not fear," having said this, he spoke these verses:
"There is no mental suffering, O village headman, for one who is free from longing."
All fears have been transcended by one whose fetters are exhausted.
For one whose craving for existence has been destroyed, seeing things as they truly are in this very life,
there is no fear of death, just as when a burden is laid down.
Having heard his words, he looked at the five hundred thieves and said, "What will you do? "As for us, Master," they replied.
"First, my good men, having seen such a miracle, I think there is no more work for me in the midst of the household;
I shall go forth into homelessness in the presence of this noble one. We too shall do exactly the same. "Excellent, dear friends! he said, and then—
The five hundred thieves also, having paid homage to the novice, requested the going-forth.
He, using the very edges of their swords, cut off both their hair and the hems of their garments;
he dyed them with red clay, had them don those saffron robes, established them in the ten precepts, and while departing taking them with him, he thought: "If I go without seeing the Elders..."
“They will not be able to perform their duties as recluses. For from the moment the thieves took me and departed, not one among them was able to restrain his tears;

as they wonder, ‘Has the novice been killed or not?’, their meditation subject will not remain present before them. Therefore, I shall depart upon seeing them. Thus, surrounded by five hundred monks, he set out.

Having gone there, when those men, who had gained consolation by seeing him, asked, "Good man Saṅkicca, have you obtained your life?", he replied, "Yes, venerable sirs. These men, wishing to kill me but being unable to do so, became confident in my virtues;
having heard the Dhamma, they went forth into homelessness. I came thinking, 'I shall depart as soon as I have seen you.'"
“Be diligent and practice the duty of a recluse; I shall go into the presence of the Teacher.
Having paid homage to those monks and taken the others with him, he went into the presence of his preceptor. When the preceptor asked, “Saṅkicca, have you found disciples?
he replied, “Yes, venerable sir,” and reported the matter to him. The Elder said, “Go, Saṅkicca, and see the Teacher.”
When this was said, they replied, “Very well,” and having paid homage to the Elder, they took him and went into the presence of the Teacher.
When the Teacher asked, “Saṅkicca, have you found disciples? he replied, “Yes, Bhante,” and related what had occurred.
The Teacher asked, “Is it true, monks, that such is the case? and when they replied, “Yes, Bhante,” he said, “Monks, this is indeed your work as thieves.”
"Rather than living for a hundred years established in immorality, it is better now to live even a single day established in virtue.
Having said this, he joined the connection and, teaching the Dhamma, spoke this verse:
"And he who lives for a hundred years, immoral and unconcentrated..."
"A single day’s life of one who is virtuous and meditative is better.

In this context, "immoral" means lacking virtue. "Of one who is virtuous" means that compared to an immoral person living for a hundred years, the life of one who is virtuous—even for a single day or a single moment—while meditating with the two *jhānas*, is better; the meaning is that it is superior.

At the conclusion of the teaching, those five hundred monks attained *arahantship* together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), and the Dhamma teaching was beneficial for the great multitude of people who had gathered.
At another time, after Saṅkicca had received full ordination and reached ten years of seniority, he took a novice.
This novice was his own nephew, named Adhimutta. Then, when the novice’s age was complete, the Elder addressed him, saying:
"I shall grant you full ordination; go and ask your relatives about the required age limit."
"Come," he sent him off. As he was going to his parents, on the way he was being led out to be sacrificed as an offering by five hundred bandits.
Having taught them the Dhamma, they became filled with faith and released him, saying, "You must not tell anyone that we are in this place. Then his parents arrived along the opposite path.
Even as they were setting out upon that very same path, he did not inform them, guarding the truth.
Hearing the lamentations of those being harassed by bandits— who cried out, "It seems you too have joined sides with the bandits,
for you do not inform us!"— and learning that they had not told even his parents, they conceived a clear faith and requested ordination.

Just like the novice Saṅkicca, he ordained them all, brought them into the presence of his preceptor, and having been sent by him to the Teacher’s presence, went and reported the matter. The Teacher asked, “Is it so, monks?
When they replied, “Yes, venerable sir,” he joined the narrative together in the same manner as before and, teaching the Dhamma, spoke this very verse:
“And though one might live for a hundred years, immoral and unconcentrated,
better is a single day’s life of one who is virtuous and meditative.
This story of the novice Adhimutta is exactly as previously described.
The ninth story: The Story of the Novice Saṅkicca.
The tenth story: The Story of the Elder Khāṇu-koṇḍañña.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, spoke this teaching on the Dhamma concerning the Elder Khāṇu-koṇḍañña: "And he who should live for a hundred years... [and so forth].
It is said that the Elder, having received a meditation subject from the presence of the Teacher and dwelling in the forest, attained Arahantship.
Thinking, "I shall inform the Teacher," he was returning from there when, exhausted on the way, he left the path and sat down upon a flat rock, where he entered into jhāna.
Then, five hundred thieves, having plundered a village, according to their own strength...
Having tied up their bundle and carrying it on their heads, they traveled a long distance until they were weary.
Thinking, "We have come far; we shall rest here on this flat rock," they left the road and approached the rock.
Upon seeing the Elder, they perceived him as "just a tree stump. Then one of the robbers [placed] the bundle on the Elder's head.
He placed his bundle down; another, relying on him, also placed his bundle down. In this way, five hundred thieves surrounded the Elder with five hundred bundles and sat down themselves.
They fell asleep, and at the time of dawn, having woken up and each taking their own bundle, they saw the Elder and, perceiving him to be a non-human being (*amanussa*), began to flee.
Then the Elder said to them, “Do not be afraid, lay followers; I am one who has gone forth.
They prostrated at the feet of the Elder and asked his forgiveness, saying, “Venerable sir, forgive us; we took you for a mere stump.
When the chief of the bandits said, “I shall go forth in the presence of the Noble One,” the others said, “We too shall go forth,” and so they all—
Having become single-minded, they requested ordination from the Elder. Just as Saṅkicca the novice, the Elder ordained them all.
From that time forth, he became known as Khāṇu-koṇḍañña. He went with those bhikkhus into the presence of the Teacher.
When the Teacher asked, "Koṇḍañña, have you obtained disciples? he related the circumstances.
He reported this. The Teacher asked, "Is it truly so, monks? When they replied, "Yes, venerable sir;

we have never before seen such power in anyone else, and for that reason we went forth," he said, "Monks, compared to living for a hundred years established in such deeds of lack of wisdom, the life of even a single day lived now by you who are possessed of perfected wisdom is superior."
Having said, “It is better,” and having established the connection, he taught the Dhamma by reciting this verse:
“Better than one who lives for a hundred years, lacking wisdom and unconcentrated,
is a single day’s life of one who possesses wisdom and practices meditation.”
In this context, "one lacking wisdom" means one who is witless. "Of one possessing wisdom" means of one who is wise. The rest is exactly as before.

At the conclusion of the teaching, those five hundred bhikkhus attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). The Dhamma teaching was also beneficial for the great multitude of people who had assembled.
This is the tenth story, the account of the Elder Khāṇu-koṇḍañña.
11. The Story of the Elder Sappadāsa The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this teaching on the Dhamma concerning the elder Sappadāsa: "He who might live for a hundred years...
It is said that in Sāvatthī, a certain son of good family, having heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, went forth and received full ordination.
At a later time, becoming weary [of the world], he thought, "For a clansman such as I, the state of a householder is indeed improper;
it would be better for me to die while remaining in the life of a renunciant. Thinking thus, he wandered about contemplating a means for his own death.
Then one day, early in the morning, after the monks had finished their meal and returned to the monastery, they saw a snake in the fire-hall and placed it in a certain...
Having placed [the snake] in a jar and sealed the jar, they took it and departed from the monastery.
The discontented monk, returning after having finished his meal, saw those monks and asked, "Friends, what is this? When told, "A snake, friend," he said, "What will you do with this?
They replied, "We shall throw it away. Having heard their words, [he thought], "By this, [one might harm] oneself..."
Thinking, "I will have him bite me and then die," he said, "Bring it; I will make him spit it out.
Taking the jar from their hands, he sat down in one place and had himself bitten by that snake, but the snake did not wish to bite.
He reached his hand into the jar and stirred it here and there; having opened the mouth of the fierce snake, he thrust his finger—
He threw it in, but the snake did not bite him at all. Thinking, "This is no venomous serpent;
this is just a house-snake," he left it and went to the monastery. Then the monks said to him, "Friend, you have discarded a snake.
"Friends, that was no fierce serpent; this was just a house-snake. "Friend, it was indeed a fierce serpent; it had spread its great hood and was hissing."
"He was seized by us with pain; for what reason do you speak thus? they asked.
"Friends, even though I had him bite me and even though I put my finger in his mouth, I could not make him bite," he replied.
Upon hearing this, the monks became silent.
Then one day, a barber took two or three razors, went to the monastery, placed one on the ground,
and shaved the hair of the monks with the other. Taking the razor he had placed on the ground, he thought,
"I shall cut my own throat with this and die," and placing his neck against a tree, he stood there with the edge of the razor pressed against his jugular vein.
Reflecting upon his own virtue from the time of his full ordination (*upasampadā*) onwards, he beheld that virtue as stainless as the orb of the spotless moon or a well-polished crystal gem.
As he gazed upon it, a rapture (*pīti*) arose that pervaded his entire body.
Suppressing that rapture and increasing his insight (*vipassanā*), he attained *arahantship* together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), and [took] the razor...
Taking it, he entered the midst of the monastery. Then the monks asked him, "Friend, where have you been?
"Friends, I went there thinking, 'With this razor, I shall cut my windpipe and die. Then they asked, "Why did you not die?
"Because I have now become incapable of taking up a weapon. For I had thought, 'With this razor, I shall cut my windpipe.'"
"They cut off all defilements with the hoof of knowledge. The monks reported to the Blessed One, "This man has declared final knowledge through what is untrue.
Having heard their words, the Blessed One said: "Monks, those whose taints are destroyed do not deprive themselves of life with their own hands.
"Venerable Sir, you call this man one whose taints are destroyed; thus he is endowed with the necessary conditions for attaining Arahatship."
"Why is this man distressed? What is the supporting cause for his attainment of Arahatship, such that 'why does that snake not bite him?
" [The Teacher replied: "Monks, in the third previous existence before this one, that snake was his slave;
therefore, he did not dare to bite the body of his own master. Thus, first of all, the Teacher gave them this one reason.
He explained it. From that time forth, that bhikkhu became known as Sappadāsa.
It is said that during the time of the Sammasambuddha Kassapa, a certain son of good family, having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
Having gone forth and received full ordination (*upasampadā*), at a later time, when dissatisfaction had arisen within him, he [spoke] to a companion...
He informed the monk. That monk frequently spoke to him of the dangers inherent in the life of a householder.
Having heard this, the other took delight in the Teaching; he sat on the bank of a river, cleansing his monastic requisites—which had previously been stained with dirt—until they were spotless.
His friend was sitting right beside him. Then he said to him:
“Friend, when I was about to disrobe, I intended to give these requisites to you. Having conceived greed, he thought:
“What is the use of this man’s being ordained or disrobed? I shall take the requisites now.
From that time on, he said: “Friend, what is the use of our living, we who [wander] with begging bowls in hand?”
"‘We wander for alms among other families; we do not engage in conversation or social chatter with wives and children’—speaking thus, he described the virtues of the householder’s life.
Having heard his words, the king became distressed once more and thought:
“When I previously said, ‘I am distressed,’ he first spoke of the disadvantages of the householder’s life, but now he speaks of it constantly...”
He spoke of the virtues [of the monastic life], and thinking, "What indeed could be the cause?
he realized, "It is because of greed for these requisites of a recluse," and thus he turned his own mind back by himself.
