Thus, because he had caused dissatisfaction in a certain bhikkhu during the time of the perfectly enlightened Buddha Kassapa, dissatisfaction has now arisen in him. Furthermore, he who at that time [had been] for twenty thousand years...
"The ascetic duty was performed; now, for him, the necessary condition for attaining Arahatship has arisen.
Having heard this matter from the Blessed One, those bhikkhus asked further:
"Venerable Sir, it is said that this bhikkhu, having placed a razor-edged tube around his neck while standing, will attain Arahatship. Will it arise?"

“In that very moment, the path to arahantship arises. “Yes, monks, for a monk who has aroused energy, the path to arahantship arises even before his foot has reached the ground when he lifts it and places it down.
For the life of a person who has aroused energy, even if it lasts but a single moment, is better than the life of a lazy person lasting for a hundred years.”
Having said, "It is better," and having established the connection, he spoke this verse:
"Better than one who lives for a hundred years, lazy and lacking in energy,
is a single day lived by one who exerts firm energy."
In this context, "lazy" refers to a person who passes his time with the three types of thoughts, beginning with sensual desire.
"Of weak energy" means lacking vigor. "Firmly initiating energy" refers to one who initiates a firm energy capable of producing the two kinds of jhāna.
The rest is exactly as before.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the eleventh story, the Story of the Elder Sappadāsa. 12.
The Story of the Elder Nun Paṭācārā.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this teaching on the Dhamma concerning the Elder Nun Paṭācārā, beginning with the words: "Though one should live for a hundred years...
It is said that she was the daughter of a merchant in Sāvatthī who possessed a fortune of four hundred million; she was exceedingly beautiful.
When she reached the age of sixteen, they had her reside on the top floor of a seven-storied palace, guarding her strictly. Nevertheless, by means of a single...

She acted improperly toward her own junior attendant. Then her parents, having agreed to give her to a youth from a family of equal status, fixed the date for the wedding. When that time drew near, she said to the junior attendant:
"They say they will give me to a certain family; once I have gone to my husband’s house, take my bridal gifts..."
“Even if you come there, you will not gain entrance; if you have any affection for me, take me right now and flee by whatever way you can.
“Very well, my dear,” he replied. “In that case, I shall stand at such-and-such a place at the city gate tomorrow morning at dawn; you should find a way out and come there.”
Having spoken thus, he stood at the appointed place on the following day.

She too, having dressed early in the morning in soiled garments, disheveled her hair, smeared her body with clay, and taking a water-jar as if she were going out with female servants, departed from her house and went to that spot.
He took her and, having traveled a long distance, arrived at a certain village.
Having established her dwelling in the forest, she plowed the field and brought back wood, leaves, and other provisions.
The other woman, having carried water in a jar, performed the work of pounding and cooking with her own hands, experiencing the fruit of her own evil deeds.
Then, a fetus was conceived in her womb. When her pregnancy was full term, she thought, "I have no one here to assist me; my parents..."
"Women are tender-hearted toward their children; take me to them, for there my delivery shall take place," she entreated her husband.
He refused, saying, "What are you saying, dear lady? Upon seeing me, your parents would subject you to various forms of punishment;
it is not possible for me to go there. Although she entreated him again and again, [he still refused].

Unable to go herself, when he had departed for the forest, she addressed her neighbors, saying, "If he returns and, not seeing me, asks 'Where have you gone?', you must tell him that I have gone to my own family home.
Having said this, she closed the door of her house and departed. He too returned, and not seeing her, questioned the neighbors.
Having heard of that event, [the husband] pursued her, thinking, "I will not let her go back. Upon seeing her, although he entreated her in many ways, he was unable to make her turn back.
Then, at one spot, the kamma-born winds (kammajavātā) within her began to stir.
She entered a narrow path and, saying, "Husband, the kamma-born winds have stirred within me," she lay down upon the ground and began to roll about.
Having given birth to the child with great difficulty, she thought, "The purpose for which I went to my father's house has been accomplished.
She returned home with him once more and took up residence there.
At a later time, she became pregnant again. When her pregnancy was full term, she [proceeded] in the same manner as before.
Having failed to obtain permission from her husband to go, she set out just as before, carrying her son on her hip.
When he pursued them and told her to stop, she did not wish to turn back. As they were traveling, a great unseasonable storm arose;
the sky was as if ablaze with lightning on all sides, and it was like a mass of clouds being torn apart, with a continuous downpour of torrents of water.
It became as clear as the sky. At that moment, the winds born of her karma stirred within her. She addressed her husband, saying, "Husband, the winds born of my karma have stirred;
I am unable to sustain myself. Find for me a place sheltered from the rain.
Taking an axe in his hand, he searched here and there, and upon the top of an anthill, he saw a thicket growing.
Having seen it, she began to cut it down. Then, a fierce and venomous cobra emerged from an anthill and bit her.
At that very moment, her body turned blue as if being consumed by flames rising from within, and she fell right there.
The other woman, experiencing great suffering, was watching for his arrival, but not seeing him, she [fainted] once more.
She gave birth to a son. The two infants, unable to endure the force of the wind and rain, cried out with a great clamor.
Taking both of them between her breasts, she pressed them against the ground with her two knees and hands, and remained standing in that very position throughout the night.
Her entire body became as pale as a withered leaf, appearing as if devoid of blood. When dawn had risen...
At dawn, carrying one son on her hip who was the color of a piece of raw meat and holding the other by his finger, she said, "Come, dear child,
your father has gone from here," and as she walked along the path her husband had taken,
she saw him lying dead at the top of an anthill— his body blue in color and stiffened. Seeing this, she thought, "Because of me, my husband has died on the road."
Weeping and lamenting, she went forth.
Having spent the entire night in rain, she saw that the Aciravatī River was filled with water reaching up to her knees, her waist, and even her breasts;
yet, due to her own dull-wittedness, she proceeded to enter the water together with her two children.
Unable to bear the weight, she left her eldest son on this side of the river, took the other one, and having gone to the opposite bank, spread out some broken branches and laid him down.
Thinking, "I shall go to the other one's side," she abandoned her young child;
unable to swim, she turned back again and again, looking back, and set out. Then, when she had reached the middle of the river—
A hawk, seeing the prince from the sky, mistook him for a piece of meat and swooped down.
Seeing it swoop down for the sake of her son, the mother raised both her hands and let out three loud cries of "Sūsū!
The hawk, however, failing to hear her because of the distance, seized the boy and flew off into the air. On this side of the shore...
Seeing her middle son standing in the middle of the river with both hands raised, letting out a great cry, she thought, "He is calling for me," and plunged into the water with speed.
Thus, her youngest son was carried off by a hawk, and her eldest son was swept away by the water.
Weeping, she cried: "One son of mine has been seized by a hawk, one has been swept away by the water, and my husband lies dead on the road."
As she was walking along lamenting, she saw a man coming from Sāvatthī and asked him, “Where do you live, dear sir?
“I live in Sāvatthī, mother. “In the city of Sāvatthī, in such-and-such a street, there is a family of such-and-such a name;
do you know it, dear sir? “I know it, mother, but please do not ask me about that. If [you wish to know] anything else…”
"Do you know? Is it a question? "I have no other business; I ask about that very thing, dear father.
"Mother, you do not allow yourself to be told [the truth]. Today, the rain was seen falling all night long upon you.
"It was seen by me, father; it rained all night for me alone, not for anyone else. But as for the reason why it rained for me, later—"
“I shall tell you; first, tell me what has happened at that merchant’s house.
“Mother, tonight the merchant, the merchant’s wife, and the merchant’s son—all three of them—fell into the house while they were rolling about, and they are burning on a single funeral pyre.
This smoke is visible, mother. At that moment, she [tore] her lower garment...
Not realizing she was falling, having fallen into a state of madness, she wept and lamented according to her nature:
"Both my sons have passed away; my husband died on the road;
my mother, father, and brother are burning in a single funeral pyre."
Lamenting, she wandered about. Seeing her, people cried out, "A madwoman! A madwoman!
and, seizing refuse and dust, they scattered it over her head and struck her with clods of earth.

The Teacher, seated in the midst of the eightfold assembly at the Great Monastery of Jetavana, while teaching the Dhamma, saw her approaching—she who had fulfilled the perfections for a hundred thousand eons.
Endowed with the supreme aspiration.

It is said that during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, having seen the Teacher Padumuttara take a certain Elder Nun who was a master of the Vinaya by the arm and place her in the Nandana Grove as if appointing her to the position of "foremost," she thought: "May I too [become like you]..."
Having made an offering, she established a prayer, saying, "May I obtain the foremost position among the elder nuns who are masters of the Vinaya in the presence of a Buddha.
The Buddha Padumuttara, extending his knowledge of the future, understood that her aspiration would be fulfilled;
he declared, "In the future, in the dispensation of the Buddha named Gotama, this woman shall be known by the name Paṭācārā as the foremost among the elder nuns who are masters of the Vinaya."
“...she will become the foremost,” he prophesied.

When the Teacher saw her approaching from afar—having thus made her aspiration and perfected her resolve—he thought, “There is no one else capable of being a refuge for her except me,” and he acted so that she would come directly toward the monastery. As soon as the assembly saw her, they [said]:
"Do not allow this madwoman to come from here," she said. The Teacher replied, "Go away;
do not stop her. When she had reached a spot not far off, he said, "Regain your mindfulness, sister!
At that very moment, through the power of the Buddha, she regained her mindfulness. At that time, she noticed that the garment she was wearing had fallen.
Having established a sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing, she sat down in the *ukkuṭika* posture. Then a certain man threw her an upper garment.
Having clothed herself in it, she approached the Teacher, prostrated with the fivefold contact at his gold-colored feet, and said:
"Venerable Sir, be my refuge; be my support. For a hawk has seized one of my sons."
"One was swept away by water; my husband died on the road; both my mother and father, as well as my brother, remain behind at home, burning together upon a single funeral pyre.
Having heard her words, the Teacher said, "Paṭācārā, do not grieve; I shall become your protection, your refuge, and your support."
You have come into the presence of one who is indeed capable. For just as now you have one son seized by an army,
one swept away by water, and one fallen dead on the road, while both parents and a brother remain stranded at home—
just so, in this cycle of existence (saṃsāra), when sons and others die, the tears that flow from you as you weep would equal the waters of the four great oceans.
Having said, "There is more water than that," he spoke this verse:
"The water in the four oceans is but a trifle;
The water of tears shed is far greater and not small."
“When a man is touched by suffering, why, mother, do you neglect him and grieve?
While the Teacher was thus delivering the discourse on the beginningless cycle of existence (*anamatagga-pariyāya*), the grief in his body subsided. Then—
Knowing that her grief had become attenuated, the Teacher addressed Paṭācārā again:
“Paṭācārā, sons and the like are unable to serve as a protection, a shelter, or a refuge for one going to the world beyond; therefore, even though they exist, they are as if non-existent.
A wise person, however, having purified their virtue, [should quickly] [clear the path leading to their own Nibbāna].”
Having said, "It is right to purify [the mind]," he spoke these verses while teaching the Dhamma:
"Children are no refuge, nor father, nor kinsmen;
for one seized by the End-Maker, there is no refuge among relatives."
“Having understood this meaning, the wise person, restrained by virtue,
should quickly purify the path leading to Nibbāna.
At the conclusion of this teaching, Paṭācārā, having incinerated defilements as numerous as the particles of dust on the great earth, attained the fruit of stream-entry.
She was established [in the fruit], and many others also attained the fruits beginning with stream-entry (*sotāpatti*).
Having become a stream-enterer, she requested ordination from the Teacher. The Teacher sent her into the presence of the bhikkhunīs and had her ordained.
Having received full admission (*upasampadā*), she became known as Paṭācārā because of her previous conduct. One day, while washing her feet after taking water in a small pot, she...
She poured water, which flowed a short distance and then ceased. On the second occasion, the water she poured went further than that. On the third occasion, it went even further still.
Taking that very object as her focus, she delimited the three stages of life and reflected:
"Just like the water I first poured, these beings die even in their first stage of life; further than that..."
She thought: "Those who die in middle age are like water poured out on the second occasion; those who die even later than that are like water poured out on the third occasion.
While seated within the Gandhakuṭī, the Teacher emitted a radiance and, as if standing before her and speaking, said: "It is even so, Paṭācārā."

"Rather than living for a hundred years without seeing the arising and passing away of the five aggregates, it is better to live for even a single day—or even a single moment—seeing their arising and passing away.
Having said this, he joined the connection and, teaching the Dhamma, spoke this verse:
"And one who might live for a hundred years, Without seeing the arising and passing away..."
"One day’s life is better for one who sees arising and passing away.
In this context, "not seeing arising and passing away" means not seeing the arising and passing away of the five aggregates by way of their twenty-five characteristics.
"Seeing arising and passing away" means seeing their arising and passing away. For the other [who does not see], it is the opposite.
"Even a single day of life is better than living without it.
At the conclusion of this teaching, Paṭācārā attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
This is the twelfth story, the account of the Elder Nun Paṭācārā.
13. The Story of Kisāgotamī The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, spoke this teaching on the Dhamma concerning Kisāgotamī: "He who lives for a hundred years...
It is said that in the house of a certain merchant in Sāvatthī, forty million pieces of wealth remained as nothing but glowing embers.
When the merchant saw him, grief arose within him; he refused food and lay down upon his couch.
A certain friend of his went to the house and asked, "Friend, why do you grieve? Having heard what had happened, he said, "Friend, do not grieve;
I know a stratagem, so do it. "What shall I do, friend? [The other replied: "In your own shop, [hang] a palm-leaf mat..."
Having spread them out there and made a heap of those embers, sit as if you were selling them.
To the people who come one after another and say, "Other people sell cloth, oil, honey, molasses, and so forth,
but you sit here selling embers," you should reply, "What can I do if I am not selling what belongs to me?"
But if someone were to say to you, "Other people sell cloth, oil, honey, molasses, and so forth, yet you sit here selling gold and bullion," you should ask him, "Where is the gold and bullion?
When he says, "Right here," you should say, "Bring it here first," and receive it in your hands. Thus, the gold and bullion given in this manner would be in your hand.
"She will exist. Moreover, if she is a girl, you should bring her to your house as a wife for your son, hand over forty million in wealth to her, and then enjoy whatever she gives you.
If it is a boy, you should give your daughter, who has reached marriageable age, to him in your house, hand over forty million in wealth to him, and then enjoy whatever he gives you. He...
Thinking, "This is an excellent stratagem," he sat down as if selling charcoal from his own shop.
To those who said to him, "Other people sell cloth, oil, honey, molasses, and so forth;
why are you sitting here selling charcoal?", he gave this reply: "What should I do if I am not selling what belongs to me?"
He gave it away. Then a young girl named Gotamī, known as Kisāgotamī because her body was so emaciated, the daughter of a decayed family, went to the shop door on some business of her own;
seeing the merchant, she said to him: "What is this, father?
While other people sell cloth, oil, honey, molasses, and such things, you sit here selling gold and bullion?"
“Where, mother, is the gold and bullion? “Did you not say, ‘You are sitting right there holding it’?
Bring it here, mother. She took a handful and placed it in his hands; it became gold and bullion once again.
Then the merchant asked her, “Which house is yours, mother? and when she replied, “The one named so-and-so,” he [gave it to her].
Having learned that she was without a husband, he secured her wealth, brought her to his own son, and entrusted him with forty million in riches.
All of it consisted solely of gold and bullion. At a later time, she became pregnant.
After ten months had passed, she gave birth to a son. He died at the time of taking his first steps. Because she had never before seen death, she—
When they were carrying him out to cremate him, she stopped them, saying, "I will ask for medicine for my son.
Taking the corpse on her lap, she wandered from house to house asking, "Do you know of any medicine for my son?
Then people said to her, "Mother, you have gone mad; you are asking for medicine for a dead son."
They said, "She wanders about. Thinking, "I will certainly find someone who knows the medicine for my son," she wandered about. Then a certain wise man, seeing her, thought:
"This daughter of mine has given birth to her first child and has never before seen death; it is fitting that I should become her support."
Having reflected, he said, "Mother, I do not know medicine, but I know one who knows medicine.
"Who knows it, dear? "The Teacher knows it, mother; go and ask him. She said, "I will go, dear;
I will ask him, dear," and having approached the Teacher, she paid homage to him and stood to one side.
He asked, “Venerable sir, you say that you know a medicine for my son? “Yes, I know it. “What must be obtained?
“It is necessary to obtain white mustard seeds, just enough to be grasped by two fingers.
“I shall obtain them, venerable sir. “In whose house must they be obtained? “In a house where there is no son or daughter at all.”

“Has he ever been dead before? She replied, “Very well, Bhante,” and having paid homage to the Teacher, she took the dead child on her hip, entered the village, and stood at the door of the first house, saying, “Is there any white mustard seed in this house?
It is said that this is medicine for my son. When they said, “There is,” she said, “In that case, give it to me. They brought some white mustard seeds. Regarding those white mustard seeds—
When they were being given away, she asked, "Mother, is there no son or daughter in this house who has ever died?

When she was told, "What are you saying, mother? There are only a few who are living; those who have died are many," she returned the seeds, saying, "In that case, take these mustard seeds yourselves; these are not medicine for my son."
In this manner, she wandered about from the very beginning, questioning him. Not having obtained even a single mustard seed in one house, she thought at the time of evening:
"Alas, what a heavy task! I had the perception that only my own son was dead;
yet in the entire village, those who are dead are more numerous than those who are living. As she was reflecting thus,
Her heart, once soft with affection for her son, became hardened.
She abandoned her son in the forest, went into the presence of the Teacher, paid homage, and stood to one side.
Then the Teacher said to her, "Have you obtained even a single grain of mustard seed? "I have not, Bhante; in this entire village, those who are dead are more numerous than those who are living."
Then the Teacher said to him, “You perceived, ‘Only my son has died,’ yet this is the inevitable law for all beings.
For King Death drags away all beings while their aspirations are still unfulfilled, casting them into the ocean of the states of woe as if with a great flood.
Having said this, he taught the Dhamma and spoke this verse:
“Death carries away that man who is intoxicated by children and cattle, whose mind is distracted,
just as a great flood sweeps away a sleeping village.
At the conclusion of this verse, Kisāgotamī was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), and many others also attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
She then requested ordination from the Teacher; the Teacher sent her into the presence of the bhikkhunīs and ordained her.
Having received full admission, she became known as the Elder Kisāgotamī. One day, having reached her turn in the Uposatha hall, she sat down after lighting the lamp.
Seeing the flames of the lamp arising and breaking, she thought: "In this very same way..."
“Beings arise and pass away; it is only those who have attained Nibbāna who do not appear,” she thought, and thus she took that as her object of meditation.
While still seated within the fragrant chamber, the Teacher emitted a radiance and sat as if directly in front of her, speaking to her:
“Just so, Gotamī, these beings arise and pass away like the flickering of a lamp’s flame.”

"Furthermore, those who have attained Nibbāna are no longer perceived at all; thus, for one who does not see Nibbāna, even a hundred years of life are inferior to the life of one who sees Nibbāna, even for a mere moment.
Having said this, and having established the connection, he taught the Dhamma by reciting this verse:
“And though one should live for a hundred years without seeing the deathless state, a single day’s life of one who sees the deathless state is better.
In this context, “the deathless state” (amataṃ padaṃ) means a portion free from death; the meaning is the great Nibbāna, which is deathless. The rest is exactly as before.
At the conclusion of the teaching, Kisāgotamī, while remaining seated as she was, established herself in Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
This is the thirteenth story, the Story of the Elder Nun Kisāgotamī.
14. The Story of the Elder Nun Bahuputtikā.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, spoke this teaching on the Dhamma concerning the Elder Nun Bahuputtikā.
It is said that in a certain family in Sāvatthī there were seven sons and seven daughters.
When they all reached maturity, they established themselves in their own households and lived happily according to their own nature. Later on, their father—
She passed away. Although her husband had died, the great female lay devotee did not yet divide the household estate.
Then her sons said to her, "Mother, now that our father has passed away, what use have you for the household? Are we not capable of looking after it?
Having heard their words, she remained silent; but when they spoke to her again and again, she said, "Sons..."
“They will look after me; what need have I for a separate household? she said, and having divided her entire estate into portions, she gave it away.

Then, after a few days had passed, the wife of the eldest son said, “Oh, our noble lady comes to this very house as if she were giving us two shares each, thinking, ‘He is my eldest son. The wives of the other sons also [said the same].
They spoke to her in this very way. Even when they went to their respective homes, beginning with the eldest daughter, they spoke to her in the same manner.
Having been thus humiliated, she thought, "What is the use of living in the presence of these people? I shall live as a bhikkhunī.
She went to the bhikkhunī residence and requested ordination. They ordained her. Having received full admission (upasampadā), she—
She became known as the Elder Nun Bahuputtikā. Thinking, "I have gone forth at an advanced age;
I must be diligent," she performed the duties and services for the bhikkhunīs.

Thinking, "I shall practice the ascetic's duty throughout the entire night," she would take hold of a pillar on the lower terrace with her hand and practice the ascetic's duty while pulling it back and forth. She did so even while walking in meditation.

Thinking, "In this place of darkness, my head might strike against a tree or something else," she takes hold of that tree with her hand and performs the duties of a recluse while merely pulling it toward herself.

Thinking, "I shall practice only the Dhamma taught by the Teacher," she attends to the Dhamma and performs the duties of a recluse while recollecting the Dhamma. Then the Teacher, in the Fragrant Chamber—
Remaining seated, he pervaded her with radiance as if sitting face-to-face with her.

Speaking with her, he said, "O Bahuputtikā, it is better to live for even a moment while seeing the Dhamma taught by me than to live for a hundred years without reflecting upon or seeing the Dhamma taught by me. Having thus spoken, he established the connection and [taught] the Dhamma.
Declaring this, he spoke this verse:
“Though one should live for a hundred years without seeing the supreme Dhamma,
Better is a single day’s life of one who sees the supreme Dhamma.”
Therein, "the supreme Dhamma" refers to the ninefold supramundane Dhamma (*lokuttara-dhamma*). For that indeed is called the supreme Dhamma.
Indeed, for one who does not see it, even a life of a hundred years is inferior to the life of even a single day or a single moment for one who sees and penetrates that Dhamma;
thus, the latter's life is better.
At the conclusion of the verse, the Elder Nun Bahuputtikā was established in Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
This is the fourteenth story, the Story of the Elder Nun Bahuputtikā.
The commentary on the Sahassa Chapter is finished.
The Eighth Chapter.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
In the Minor Collection (Khuddakanikāya).
Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā (Second Part) 9.
Pāpavagga (The Chapter on Evil)

1. The Story of the Brahmin Cūḷekasāṭaka The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching beginning with "One should hasten toward the good," concerning the Brahmin Cūḷekasāṭaka.
For in the time of the Buddha Vipassī, there was a Brahmin named Mahāekasāṭaka; but this [Brahmin] is now—
In Sāvatthī there was a man named Cūḷekasāṭaka. He had only one lower garment (*nivāsana-sāṭaka*), and his brahmin wife also had only one.
They shared a single upper robe (*pārupana*); whenever it was time to go outside, either the brahmin or the brahmin woman would put it on.
Then, one day, when the announcement for the Dhamma discourse in the monastery had been made, the brahmin said: "Madam, the announcement for the Dhamma discourse has been made."
“Will you go to hear the Dhamma by day, or by night? For because we lack an upper garment, it is not possible for us to go together.
The brahmin lady said, “Husband, I shall go by day,” and having put on her wrap, she departed.
The brahmin spent the day at home and went by night, sitting down right in front of the Teacher.
He heard the Dhamma. Then, as it pervaded his body, five-colored rapture arose within him.
Desiring to honor the Teacher, he thought, "If I give this garment, there will be nothing left for my wife to wear, nor for myself.
Thereupon, a thousand thoughts of stinginess arose in him, and then a single thought of faith arose once more.
Having overcome that [faith], a thousandfold stinginess arose once more. As if binding and seizing it, this powerful stinginess obstructed his mind of faith.

While he was still thinking, "I will give," or "I will not give," the first watch of the night passed and the middle watch arrived. Even during that watch, he was unable to give. Then, in the last watch...
When it was time for him to depart, he thought: "Two watches of the night have already passed while I have been struggling between my mind of faith and my mind of stinginess.
If this mind of stinginess continues to grow to such an extent, it will not allow me to lift my head from the four states of misery;
therefore, I shall give it. Having thus overcome his thousandfold stinginess, he directed his mind toward faith.
Having performed his duties as a courtier, he took his upper garment, placed it at the feet of the Teacher, and three times raised a great shout: "Victory for me! Victory for me!
King Pasenadi of Kosala, while listening to the Dhamma, heard that sound and said, "Ask him; what indeed has he conquered?
When questioned by the king’s men, he explained the matter. Hearing this, the king [said], "It is difficult..."
The brahmin said, "I shall provide him with a gift," and had a pair of garments given to him. He gave even those to the Tathāgata alone.
Again, the king had twice as many given—two, four, eight, and sixteen. He gave all of those to the Tathāgata alone.
Then the king had thirty-two pairs given to him. The brahmin, not taking anything for himself, [gave] whatever he received...

Saying, “I shall indeed give them away,” for the sake of releasing himself from his vow, he took two pairs—one for himself and one for the brahmin woman—and gave thirty pairs to the Tathāgata alone. Even as the king was giving for the seventh time, he still desired to give more.
Previously, when he had offered the great single robe, he had taken two out of the sixty-four pairs of robes.
But when he had obtained thirty-two [blankets], he took two. The king commanded his men:
"My good men, this brahmin has performed a difficult feat; have two blankets brought from my inner palace. They did so.
The king had two blankets worth a hundred thousand pieces given to him. The brahmin thought, "These shall not be of use for my body..."
"These are indeed worthy of the Buddha's dispensation," he said;

then, having made one blanket into a canopy over the Teacher’s bed inside the Perfumed Chamber, he tied it there, and having made another into a canopy over the place where a monk who regularly ate in his house finished his meal, he tied that there as well. In the evening, the king went into the presence of the Teacher.
Recognizing that blanket, he asked, "Venerable sir, by whom was this offering made?
When it was told to him, "By the Ekasāṭaka," he said, "The brahmin has placed his faith in my very place of inspiration.
Then [he gave him] four elephants, four horses, four thousand kahāpaṇas, four women, four female slaves, four male servants, and four excellent villages.
In this manner, he had four sets of four garments given to every single being until all fourfold sets were distributed.
Then the bhikkhus raised a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: "Oh, how wonderful is the deed of Cūḷekasāṭaka!
In that very moment he obtained all the fourfold sets; the fruit of the wholesome deed performed today has been granted this very day."
The Teacher came and asked, "Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?

When they replied, "About this very matter," he said, "Monks, if this man with a single robe had been able to give it to me in the first watch of the night, he would have obtained all sixteen [of my robes].
If he had been able in the middle watch, he would have obtained all eight. In the powerful final watch..."
"Because it was given, he obtained all four [rewards]. For one performing a wholesome deed, the thought that has arisen must be acted upon at that very moment without letting it pass.
For a wholesome deed performed sluggishly bestows prosperity only sluggishly;
therefore, a wholesome deed should be performed immediately after the arising of the thought. Having said this, he established the connection [between the stories].
While teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
“Hasten toward the good; restrain the mind from evil.
For one who performs merit slowly, the mind delights in evil.”
In this context, "one should hasten" means one should act with great urgency and speed.
For when a householder’s thought arises, "I shall perform some wholesome deed such as giving *salākabhatta* (tickets for meals)," he must act with such haste, thinking "I first!
I first!", so that others do not obtain the opportunity. Or, when a monastic [thinks] regarding the duties toward his preceptor (*upajjhāya-vatta*) and so forth...
While performing it, one should act with great haste, saying "I first! I first!", without giving another the opportunity.
One should restrain the mind by all possible means from evil—either from unwholesome mental states or from evil deeds such as bodily misconduct.
For he who acts sluggishly thinks: "Shall I give? Shall I not give? Will it succeed for me? and so forth.
Thus, like one walking along a muddy path, he performs merit sluggishly;
for him, as if he were a single-robed man, a thousandfold evil of stinginess finds an opening. Then his mind takes delight in evil;
for it is only at the time of performing wholesome deeds that the mind delights in the wholesome, but once released from that, it becomes inclined toward evil.
At the conclusion of the verses, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the first story, that of the Brahmin Cūḷekasāṭaka.
2. The Story of the Elder Seyyasaka.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning the Elder Seyyasaka.
For that elder was a co-resident disciple of the Elder Lāḷudāyi;

having informed him of his own lack of spiritual delight, he was incited by him to commit the first *saṅghādisesa* offense, and whenever such lack of delight arose, he committed that offense. When the Teacher heard of his conduct, he spoke.

Having summoned him and asked, "Is it true that you have done this?", and he having replied, "Yes, Venerable Sir," [the Buddha] rebuked him in various ways, saying, "Why did you commit such a grave deed? It is unbecoming, O foolish man!
Having thus laid down a training rule, he declared: "For such an action leads to suffering both in the present life and in future lives."
Having spoken thus and established the connection, while teaching the Dhamma, he uttered this verse:
“If a person should do evil, he should not do it again and again;
he should not take delight in it, for the accumulation of evil is suffering.”
The meaning of this is as follows: If a person should commit an evil deed even once, he should reflect upon it at that very moment and not do it again, thinking, "This is improper;
this is gross. Even if a desire or a liking for it should arise within him, he should dispel that as well and certainly not perform it.
Why? Because the accumulation of evil is suffering. For the accumulation of evil...
"Prosperity brings only suffering, both in this world and in the world beyond.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the second story, concerning the Elder Seyyasaka.
3. The Story of the Daughter of the Lāja Devas The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning the daughter of the Lāja devas. The story originated in Rājagaha.
For the Venerable Mahākassapa, while dwelling in the Pippali Cave, had entered into meditative absorption (*jhāna*) and on the seventh day—
Having risen and surveyed the area for alms with his divine eye, he saw a woman at the edge of a rice field taking ears of rice and making them into parched grain.

Wondering, "Is she faithful or faithless? and having ascertained that she was faithful, he reflected, "Will she be able to provide hospitality for me or not? and perceived that she was a confident and noble lady.

Knowing, "He will accept me as a follower, and having done so, he will attain great prosperity," she put on her robe, took up her bowl, and stood right near the rice field. Upon seeing the Elder, the noble daughter’s heart was filled with serene faith;
her body thrilled with five-colored rapture, she cried out, "Wait, Venerable Sir! and taking parched rice, she hurried toward him.

Having poured [the food] into the elder’s bowl and paid homage with the five-fold prostration, she made this aspiration: "Venerable sir, may I be a partaker of the Dhamma seen by you. The elder gave his blessing, saying, "May it be so.
She too, having paid homage to the elder and reflecting upon the gift she had given, turned back. And on that path leading along the boundary of a field—
In a certain hole lay a serpent of deadly venom. It was unable to bite the Elder’s calf, which was covered by his saffron robe.
As she was returning while reflecting upon her gift, she arrived at that spot. The serpent emerged from its hole, bit her, and dropped her right there.
With a mind full of serene faith, she passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven in a palace thirty yojanas in size.
She was reborn with a body thirty *gāvutas* in height, adorned with every ornament, like one who has just awakened from sleep within a golden celestial mansion.
Wearing one divine garment as an undergarment and another as an upper robe, she was surrounded by a thousand nymphs;
and for the purpose of manifesting her former deeds, she was adorned with a hanging golden vessel filled with golden parched rice.
Standing at the door of her celestial mansion, she surveyed her own prosperity and wondered, "What indeed have I done to obtain this fortune?
Examining the matter with her divine eye, she realized: "This was obtained as the result of the gift of a tooth-cleansing stick given by me to the noble Elder Mahākassapa."
Having obtained such prosperity through that very limited deed, she thought, "It is no longer fitting for me to be negligent;
by performing service and duties for my noble master, I shall make this prosperity stable.
Having reflected thus, at dawn she took a golden broom and a basket for throwing refuse, and went to the Elder.
Having swept the courtyard, she set out drinking water and water for washing. Seeing this, the Elder observed, "Some young bhikkhu or novice must have performed the duty.
On the second day as well, she did exactly the same, and the Elder likewise observed it. But on the third day, the Elder [heard] the sound of her sweeping.
Having heard [the sound] and seeing the radiance of her body entering through the gaps between the palm trees and other openings, he opened the door and asked, "Who is this sweeping?
She replied, "Venerable sir, I am your attendant, Lājadevadhītā. He said, "Do I not have no attendant by that name?
She replied, "Venerable sir, while guarding the rice field, I gave you parched grain with a mind full of faith..."
“Returning, I was bitten by a snake and passed away, only to be reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa deva-world. It is by relying on you, Noble One, that I have obtained this prosperity.
Now, having come here with the thought, ‘I shall make this prosperity stable by performing service for you,’ I have arrived, Venerable Sir.
“Yesterday and the day before yesterday as well, it was you who swept this place; it was indeed by you—”
“Water and food have been prepared,” [she said]. “Yes, venerable sir,” [she replied]. “Begone, daughter of a deva!
Let the duty you performed be considered as finished; from now on, do not come to this place. “Venerable sir, do not destroy me!
Allow me to perform your duty so that I may make my prosperity firm. “Begone, daughter of a deva! Do not come before me.”
The Dhamma-preachers, having taken their mental seeds and sat down, said:
"It is said that a certain daughter of the gods came to the Elder Mahākassapa, performed her duties of service, and offered him drinking water and water for washing. Then they said:
"From now on, do not come here; go back! She [the goddess] cried out again and again, "Venerable sir, do not destroy me!"
She continued to beg. The Elder, thinking, "She does not listen to my words," struck her with his finger, saying, "You do not know your own measure.

Unable to remain there, she leaped into the air; then, raising her hands in *añjali*, she stood weeping in mid-air, crying out, "Venerable Sir, do not destroy the prosperity I have gained; grant me the power to make it permanent!"
While sitting in the Perfumed Chamber in Jeta’s Grove, the Teacher heard the sound of her weeping.
Emitting a radiance, he sat as if face-to-face with the goddess and spoke to her: "Goddess, it is my son Kassapa’s burden alone to maintain restraint;
however, for those seeking merit, once they have recognized, 'This is our goal,' it is the performance of meritorious deeds alone."
“It is a burden. For the performance of merit brings happiness both in this world and in the life to come,” he said.
Then, having established the connection and teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
“If a person should do what is meritorious, let him do it again and again;”
“One should cultivate desire for that, for the accumulation of merit is blissful.
Its meaning is as follows: if a person should perform a meritorious deed, he should not rest content, thinking, “I have performed merit once;
that is enough,” but should indeed perform it again and again. Even at the moment when he is not performing it, he should maintain desire and inclination toward that merit.

"Exert yourselves indeed! For what reason? Because the accumulation of merit is blissful. Indeed, the accumulation and increase of merit is called "blissful" because it brings about happiness in both this world and the world beyond.
At the conclusion of the teaching, the goddess, while still standing fifty-four *yojanas* away, attained the fruit of stream-entry.
This is the third story, that of the Goddess Lājā.
4. The Story of the Merchant Anāthapiṇḍika "Even an evil person may see what is auspicious"—the Teacher gave this Dhamma teaching while dwelling at Jetavana concerning Anāthapiṇḍika.
For Anāthapiṇḍika, having dedicated his wealth of four hundred and fifty million to the Buddha’s Dispensation, built a monastery specifically for that purpose.
While the Teacher was dwelling at Jetavana, he went for the three great daily audiences;
and as he went, his empty-handed hands were never seen, for he thought, "Lest the novices or the young monks should look even at my hands and wonder, 'What has he brought with him?
When going early in the morning, he would go only after having rice-gruel brought; and when he had finished his breakfast, he would take clarified butter, fresh butter, and other such items.
Medicines. At the time of evening, she would go out having had garlands, perfumes, ointments, garments, and so forth brought for her.
Thus, at all times, day after day, she gave alms and observed the precepts. Later on, her wealth was completely exhausted.
Furthermore, those who lived by trade took eighteen crores of wealth from her hand as a loan, as did those belonging to her own family.
Eighteen crores of gold, which had been buried on the riverbank, entered the great ocean when the bank collapsed due to the water.
In this way, his wealth gradually came to total exhaustion. Even in such a state, he continued to give alms to the Saṅgha;
however, he was no longer able to provide them with high-quality offerings.
Thus, one day when the Teacher asked, "Householder, is alms given in your family?
he replied, "It is given, Bhante, but it is only broken rice with sour gruel as the second course. Then the Teacher said to him, "Householder, do not think, 'I am giving coarse alms.
For when the mind is noble, there is no such thing as coarse alms given to the Buddha and his disciples."

"Moreover, you give gifts to the eight types of noble persons (ariyapuggala), whereas I, even when giving a great almsgiving after having made the whole of Jambudīpa free of ploughs during the time of the Velāma festival, did not obtain anyone who had gone for refuge to the Triple Gem.
Thus, those worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇeyya) are indeed difficult to find. Therefore, do not think, 'My gift is coarse,'" he said, and then recited the Velāmasutta to him.
He preached the Dhamma. Then, when the Teacher and his disciples were entering the house, the deity dwelling at the gateway was unable to withstand their majesty.
Thinking, "I shall cause dissension among these householders so that they do not enter this house," she desired to speak;
yet, despite her desire to say something during the time of their sovereignty, she was unable to utter a word.
Then, thinking, "Now this poor man will take my word," she entered the treasurer’s bedchamber during the night and stood in the air.
When the treasurer saw her, he asked, "Who is this?
She replied, "I am the deity residing at the fourth gate-tower, O Great Treasurer; I have come to give you counsel. He said, "In that case..."
"Give him advice. "Great merchant, without even looking toward the end of your life, you have squandered much wealth in the teaching of the ascetic Gotama;
now that you have become destitute, you still will not let go of it. If you continue in this way, in just a few days you will not obtain even enough food and clothing.
What use have you for the ascetic Gotama? You have been far too generous."
“Restrain your work and manage the household,” he said. “This is the advice given to me by you. “Yes, householder. “Go!
I cannot be shaken even by a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand like you.
What you have said is improper; who is it that you think is living in my house? Leave my home immediately!”
Having heard the words of the noble disciple who had attained the stream, she was unable to remain where she was; taking her children, she departed.

Finding no other place to dwell after leaving, she thought, "I shall ask the merchant for forgiveness and live right there," and so she approached the city-protecting deva-son, explained the offense she had committed, and [spoke].
"Come, take me to the presence of the merchant, ask for his forgiveness, and have him give me a place to stay," she said.
He refused her, saying, "What you have said is improper; I do not venture to go into his presence.
She then went to the presence of the Four Great Kings, but was refused by them as well. Finally, she approached Sakka, the king of the gods.

Having related her circumstances, she entreated him even more earnestly, saying, “Your Majesty, unable to find a place to live, I wander about helpless with my children in my arms; please grant me a dwelling.
Then he said to her, “I too shall not be able to speak to the merchant on your behalf, but I have a certain expedient for you.”
“I shall tell you,” he said. “Very well, Your Majesty, please tell me.

“Go, take the guise of an official of the treasurer, hand over the letter from the treasurer’s hand, and by your own power clear the eighteen crores of wealth that were seized by those living off trade;
then, having filled the empty storehouses with the eighteen crores of wealth that had entered the great ocean...”
“There is also eighteen crores of wealth belonging to no one in such-and-such a place;
gather it all together, fill his empty chamber with it, and after inflicting punishment upon him, ask for his forgiveness.
She replied, “Very well, Your Majesty,” and having done everything exactly as instructed, she stood again in the sky, illuminating his bedchamber. When he asked, “Who is this? she said:
"I am the blind, foolish deity dwelling at the fourth gate-tower. Forgive me for the foolishness with which I spoke to you.
Indeed, at the word of Sakka, I gathered forty-five crores of wealth and performed the punitive task of filling empty wombs; now, finding no place to dwell, I am suffering."
Anāthapiṇḍika thought: “This deity says, ‘I have performed my penance,’ and she confesses her own fault;
I shall bring her before the Perfectly Enlightened One. He led her into the presence of the Teacher and related everything that the deity had done.
The deity prostrated herself at the feet of the Teacher with her head and said, “Venerable Sir, whatever—”
"Out of my blind folly, not knowing your virtues, I spoke wicked words;

please forgive me for that," he said, and having asked the Teacher for forgiveness, he asked the Great Merchant to forgive him as well. Then the Teacher, instructing both the merchant and the deity according to the ripening of their wholesome and unwholesome kamma, said:
"In this world, householder, even a wicked person [is not known as such] as long as his evil does not yet ripen."

“As long as one’s good karma ripens, one sees only what is auspicious; but when one’s evil karma ripens, then one sees only what is evil. Even a person of noble character, as long as his own good karma has not yet ripened, sees only evils; but when his good karma ripens, then he sees only what is auspicious.
Having said this, and having established the connection, he taught the Dhamma by reciting these verses:
“Even the wicked man sees what is good, as long as his evil does not ripen;
but when his evil ripens, then the wicked man sees his own evils.
Even the good man sees what is evil, as long as his goodness does not ripen.”
“And when his merit ripens, then the meritorious person sees auspicious things.
In this context, “the evil-doer” refers to a person endowed with unwholesome kamma such as bodily misconduct and so forth.
For even he, while experiencing the happiness produced by the power of previous good conduct, sees what is auspicious. “As long as the evil does not ripen” means as long as that [evil]...
That evil deed does not yield its result either in the present life or in the future life.

But when it does yield its result—whether in the present life or in the future life—then, experiencing various punishments in the present life and the suffering of the states of deprivation in the future life, that evil person sees only evil things. In the second verse as well, by means of bodily good conduct and so forth...
The "good person" is one who is engaged in wholesome action. For even he, while experiencing the suffering produced by the power of past misconduct, perceives that it is evil.
"Until the good ripens" means as long as that wholesome karma does not yield its result, either in the present life or in a future existence.
But when it yields its result, then there is happiness such as gain and honor in the present life.
"And in the future life, experiencing the bliss of celestial prosperity, that noble one sees only what is noble.
At the conclusion of the teaching, that deity was established in the fruit of stream-entry, and the Dhamma discourse was beneficial for the assembled company as well.
This is the fourth story, concerning the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika.

5. The Story of the Monk with Unrestrained Requisites "Do not underestimate evil"—this teaching on the Dhamma was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a monk who had unrestrained requisites.
It is said that whatever requisites he used outside, such as beds, chairs, and so forth, he would simply discard them right there.
Requisites are destroyed by rain, by heat, and even by termites and the like.
When other monks said to him, "Friend, should not requisites indeed be put away? he replied, "Friends, I have done very little;
these have no mind, nor do they have bile. And so he continued to act in that same way. The monks reported his conduct to the Teacher.
The Teacher summoned him and asked, "Is it true, monk, that you act in this way?
Although questioned by the Teacher, he replied with the same contempt as before, saying, "What is this, Blessed One? It is a trifle I have done; he has no heart, nor has he bile.
Then the Teacher said to him, "It is not permissible for monks to act in this way; it is an evil deed..."
"One should not underestimate even what is called 'small.

For just as a vessel placed in the open with its mouth uncovered may not be filled by a single drop when it rains, yet becomes full as the rain falls again and again, even so a person who commits evil gradually builds up a great heap of evil. Having said this, he established the connection [between the present and the past].
While teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
"Do not despise evil, thinking, 'It will not come to me.
By the falling of water drops, even a water jar is filled; [so too is a fool filled with evil,] even if it comes little by little."
“The fool is filled with evil, gathering it even little by little.

In this context, *māvamanyetha* means one should not despise [it]. *Pāpassa* means evil. *Na mandaṃ āgamissati* means one should not despise evil, thinking, “Only a small amount of evil has been done by me; when will this ripen? Thus is the meaning. *Udakumbhopi* means...
Just as any earthenware vessel placed with its mouth open while it rains will gradually become full by the falling of even a single drop of water,
so too the foolish person, accumulating, performing, and increasing evil even little by little, becomes full of evil; such is the meaning.

At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages. The Teacher also laid down a training rule, saying: "By spreading out a bed in the open air and failing to put it back in its proper place, one incurs such-and-such an offense.
This is the fifth story, concerning the monk who did not restrain his requisites. 6.
The Story of the Merchant Biḷālapādaka.
"Do not despise small merit"—this teaching on the Dhamma was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the merchant Biḷālapādaka.

For on one occasion, the residents of Sāvatthī were giving alms to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha in groups. Then one day, as the Teacher was offering the blessing of thanksgiving, he said:
"Lay followers, here someone gives a gift himself but does not encourage others to do so. In whatever place he is reborn..."
One person acquires an abundance of wealth, but not an abundance of followers. Another does not give gifts themselves, but encourages others to do so;
they acquire an abundance of followers in every place where they are reborn, but not an abundance of wealth.
Another neither gives gifts themselves nor encourages others to do so; they acquire neither an abundance of wealth nor an abundance of followers in every place where they are reborn.
“He does not possess an abundance of followers; rather, he wanders about as one who eats the scraps of others. But a certain person gives himself and also encourages others to give.
He obtains both an abundance of wealth and an abundance of followers in every place where he is reborn.
Then, having heard that teaching on the Dhamma, a certain wise man thought: “Oh, how wonderful is this principle! Now, I—”

Thinking, "I shall perform an act of merit that will lead to the perfection of both [this life and the next]," he rose as the Teacher was about to depart and said, "Venerable Sir, please accept our alms tomorrow. "By how many monks do you require them?
"By all the monks, Venerable Sir. The Teacher consented. He too, having entered the village, said, "Mother, Father, by me..."
He wandered about proclaiming: "The Saṅgha of bhikkhus, headed by the Buddha, has been invited for tomorrow.
Whoever is able [to provide] for as many bhikkhus as they can, let them give rice and other provisions for that many; we shall have it cooked in one place and offer the gift."

Then, a certain merchant, seeing him arrived at the door of his own shop, became angry, thinking, "This man does not invite enough monks for his own needs, but wanders about inciting the entire village [to give]," and said, "Bring the vessel you have taken.
Grasping him with three fingers, he gave him a small amount of rice, and likewise mung beans, and likewise beans. He—
From that time on, he became known as the merchant Biḷālapādaka (Cat’s Paw).
Even when giving ghee, molasses, and other offerings, he would place them in a basket, set it in a corner, and give only small amounts, letting them drip drop by drop.
The lay follower gathered what was given by the others together, but kept what was given by this man entirely separate. The merchant observed his conduct...
Seeing this, he thought, "Why does he take separately what has been given by me?
Having reflected thus, he sent a junior attendant after him, saying, "Go and find out what he is doing.

The attendant went and, thinking, "May it be of great fruit for the merchant," added one or two grains of rice for the sake of the rice-gruel, the meal, and the cakes, as well as some mung beans and peas.
He even dropped drops of oil, molasses, and other substances into all the vessels. The junior attendant went and reported this to the merchant.
Upon hearing this, the merchant thought: "If he speaks ill of me in the midst of the assembly, I shall strike and kill him the very moment my name is mentioned.
Having fastened a dagger within his lower garment, on the following day...
Having gone there, he stood at the head of the meal-hall. After that man had served the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, he said to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, I gave this gift after exhorting a great multitude of people.
Among those people whom I exhorted, some gave much and some gave little—rice and other provisions—each according to their own means; for all of them, it will be of great fruit."
“Let it be so. Having heard this, the merchant thought: “I came thinking, ‘When my name is mentioned—saying that rice and other provisions were given by a certain nymph—I will kill him.

But this man, acting as the general overseer, [says] that for all those who gave by measuring with measures such as the *nāḷi*, and for all those who gave having taken [the food] with their hands from a nymph...”
"May it be of great fruit," he said. "If I do not ask his forgiveness for such a thing, the divine punishment will fall upon my head.
He prostrated himself at the other's feet and said, "Forgive me, Master.
When the other asked, "What is this? he related the entire incident. Seeing that deed, the Teacher asked, "What is this?"
He questioned the steward of the offerings. The steward reported the entire sequence of events starting from the previous day.
Then the Teacher asked him, "Is it true, householder? When he replied, "Yes, venerable sir," the Teacher said, "Lay follower, one must not underestimate merit, thinking it is 'insignificant.
[Even] for a Saṅgha of monks headed by a Buddha such as myself..."

"Having given a gift, one should not despise it as 'small. For wise people, when performing meritorious deeds, are filled with merit step by step, just as a vessel that is open is gradually filled with water.
Having said this, and having established the connection, he spoke this verse while teaching the Dhamma:
“Do not despise even small merit, thinking, ‘It will not come to me.
By the falling of water drops, even a water jar is filled;
so too the wise person is filled with merit, gathering it little by little.”
The meaning of this is as follows: a wise person, having performed a meritorious deed, should not despise or underestimate that merit by thinking, "Only a small amount was done by me;
it will not come back with a dull result. Where will such a trifling action find me, or where shall I find it?
When will this ripen? For just as [a drop of water] continuously...
"Just as a clay vessel set out to be filled becomes full by the falling of drops of water, even so,
a wise and learned person who accumulates merit little by little becomes full of merit.
At the conclusion of the teaching, that merchant attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), and the Dhamma discourse was beneficial for the assembled multitude as well.
The sixth story: The Story of the Merchant Biḷālapādaka.
The seventh story: The Story of the Very Wealthy Merchant.
Regarding the merchant Mahādhanavāṇija, the Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching beginning with the words, "He is like a merchant."
It is said that five hundred thieves, seeking an opportunity to break into that merchant’s house, could find no opening.
On another occasion, the merchant filled five hundred carts with goods and announced to the monks:
"I am going to such-and-such a place for trade; those of you, venerable sirs, who wish to go to that place, please set out."
“They will not grow weary on the road seeking alms. Having heard this, five hundred bhikkhus set out on the path together with him.
Those bandits, thinking, “It is said that the merchant has set out,” went and waited in the forest.
The merchant also traveled on, stayed for two or three days in a village at the entrance of the forest, and made arrangements for his oxen, carts, and so forth.
They, however, continued to give alms-food to those monks regularly.
When the robbers waited too long, they sent a man, saying, "Go; find out the day on which he will depart and come back to us.
He went to that village and asked a friend, "When will the merchant depart? The friend replied, "In two or three days."
“But for what purpose do you ask? he said. Then the other explained to him, “We are five hundred thieves stationed in this forest for his sake.
The other replied, “In that case, go; he will depart soon. Having sent him away, he thought, “Shall I ward off the thieves, or the merchants?
Then he considered, “What have I to do with thieves? Relying on the merchants, [these] five hundred...”
"Let me give a signal to the merchant so that the monks can live [in safety]. Thinking thus, he went to the merchant's presence and asked, "When will you depart?

When told, "On the third day," he said, "Do as I say; it is said that five hundred thieves are stationed in the forest for your sake—do not go yet. [The merchant asked,] "How do you know this? [He replied,] "Among them, I..."
“I have a companion; I know him from our conversation. He said, “In that case, thinking ‘What is the use of going further? I shall turn back and go home itself.
While he was delaying, another man sent by those thieves returned, questioned that companion, heard the news, and [reported], “He says he will indeed turn back and go home itself.”
Having gone there, he informed the thieves. Upon hearing this, the thieves departed from that place and stood on another path.
While he was lingering there, the thieves again sent a man to him.
He, having learned of their presence there, informed the merchant once more. The merchant said, "In this matter too, I have no deficiency; such being the case, neither..."
“I will go from here, not from there; I shall remain right here,” he said, having approached the bhikkhus:
“Venerable sirs, it seems robbers are stationed on the road wishing to plunder me; hearing that I would turn back, they have stationed themselves on the other road.
Without going either from here or from there, I shall stay for a short while right here. Venerable sirs, do you wish to dwell right here?”

“Stay, or if you wish to go, do as you please. The monks said, “If that is the case, we shall turn back,” and having taken leave of the merchant, they returned once more to Sāvatthī. There they paid homage to the Teacher and sat down.
The Teacher asked, “Monks, why did you not go along with the great wealthy merchant? They replied, “Yes, venerable sir.”
When it was said, "Thieves lay in wait on both paths in order to plunder the wealthy merchant; therefore he remained right there,
but we have come after taking leave of him," [the Buddha replied], "Monks,
the wealthy merchant avoids the path because of the presence of thieves, just as a man who desires to live avoids the *halāhala* poison."
The monk, having understood that "the three states of existence are like a road infested by robbers," ought to avoid evil.
Having said this, and having established the connection, he taught the Dhamma by reciting this verse:
"Just as a merchant with great wealth, traveling alone on a dangerous road..."
“Just as one who desires to live would avoid poison, so should one avoid evil deeds.
In this context, “fearful” means that which is to be feared; the meaning is that it is dangerous because it is infested with thieves. This is what is intended:
just as a wealthy merchant with a small caravan [would avoid] a dangerous road, and just as one who desires to live...
"A wise bhikkhu should avoid even minor evils, just as one avoids the *halāhala* poison.

At the conclusion of this teaching, those bhikkhus attained *arahantship* together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), and the Dhamma discourse was beneficial for the great assembly that had gathered.
This is the seventh story, the Story of the Wealthy Merchant.
8. The Story of Kukkuṭamitta the Hunter The Teacher delivered this Dhamma teaching while dwelling at Veḷuvana concerning a hunter named Kukkuṭamitta.
It is said that in Rājagaha, there was a daughter of a wealthy merchant who, having reached marriageable age, was kept for protection in a bedchamber on the upper story of a seven-storied palace.
Having been provided with a single female attendant and being supported by her parents, one day in the evening, while looking out through a window toward the street,

she saw five hundred snares and five hundred stakes; and having seen a hunter named Kukkuṭamitta who, after killing five hundred deer, was carrying away a large cart filled with their meat along with a single live cock.
Seeing him filling his cart and sitting upon it as he entered the city for the purpose of selling meat,
the courtesan, her heart bound to him, gave a gift into the hand of a female attendant and sent her off, saying, "Go, give this gift to him,
and when you know it is time for him to leave, come back. She went, gave the gift to him, and asked, "When..."
“...will you go? He replied, “Having sold my meat today, I shall leave early in the morning by such-and-such a gate and depart.
When she heard what he had said, she came and reported it to her. The merchant’s daughter prepared the garments and ornaments suitable for herself to take;
then, having dressed in soiled clothes early in the morning and taking a water-jar, [she set out] with her female slaves.
As if going to a ford for water, she went out, reached that place, and stood watching for his arrival.
He too set out early in the morning, driving his cart. She followed right after him.
Seeing her, he said, "I do not know you as the daughter of such-and-such a person; do not follow me, mother!"
He said, "You are not calling me; I am coming here by my own nature. You, however, should remain silent and drive your own cart. He continued to try to dissuade her again and again.
Then she said to him, "Husband, it is not right to turn away Fortune (Siri) when she comes of her own accord into one's presence. He [then understood] her reason for coming without any doubt.
Having learned this, he placed her on a cart and departed. Her parents, having searched for her here and there and finding no trace of her, assumed she must be dead and prepared funeral offerings.
She, meanwhile, through living together with him, gave birth in succession to seven sons;
when they reached maturity, she bound them with the bonds of the household.

Then one day, as the Teacher was surveying the world at dawn, he saw that Kukkuṭamitta, together with his son and his daughter-in-law, had entered within the net of his knowledge. Reflecting, "What might this be?

he perceived that all fifteen of them possessed the necessary spiritual support (*upanissaya*) for the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*). Taking his bowl and robe early in the morning, he went to the place where his snare was set.
On that day, not even a single deer had been caught in the snare. The Teacher, having pointed out the tracks leading to the base of the snare, sat down in the shade beneath a certain thicket ahead.
At dawn, Kukkuṭamitta took his bow, went to the place of the snare, and while looking at it from the beginning, he saw not a single deer caught in the snare, but only the tracks of the Teacher.

He saw him. Then it occurred to him: "Who is this wandering about, releasing my bound deer? Carrying a grudge against the Teacher, as he went along, he saw the Teacher sitting at the foot of a bush and thought, "This man must have released my deer;
I shall kill him! He drew his bow. The Teacher allowed him to draw the bow.
He did not give it up. Unable to discharge the arrow nor even to lower it, he stood there looking exhausted, with his ribs seemingly breaking and saliva trickling from his mouth.
Then his sons went home and said, "Our father is delaying; what could this be? To which their mother replied, "Go, dear ones, to your father's side."
Having been sent forth with bows, they went and saw their father standing there;
thinking, "This man will be our father’s enemy," all seven drew their bows. By the power of the Buddha, however, they stood exactly as their father was standing.
Then their mother, saying, "Why indeed are my sons also delaying? together with her seven daughters-in-law—
Having gone there and seeing them standing thus, she wondered, "Whose bows are these that they stand holding drawn?
Looking about, she saw the Teacher; throwing up her arms, she raised a great cry: "Do not destroy my father! Do not destroy my father!
Hearing that cry, Kukkuṭamitta thought: "Alas, I am ruined! My father-in-law..."
"Alas, this is my father; oh, what a grave deed I have committed! his sons thought, "This is our grandfather;

oh, what a grave deed he has committed! Kukkuṭamitta established a mind of loving-kindness toward him, thinking, "This is my father-in-law," and his sons also established a mind of loving-kindness toward him, thinking, "He is our grandfather. Then their mother—
The merchant’s daughter said, “Quickly cast away your bows and ask my father for forgiveness.
The Teacher, knowing their hearts had become softened, gave them permission to lower their bows.
They all paid homage to the Teacher, asked for his forgiveness, saying, “Venerable Sir, forgive us,” and sat down to one side. Then the Teacher [instructed] them with a gradual discourse...
How did he preach? At the conclusion of the teaching, Kukkuṭamitta, together with his sons and daughters-in-law—himself being the fifteenth—was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
After the Teacher had wandered for alms, he returned to the monastery after the meal.
Then the Elder Ānanda asked him, "Venerable Sir, where have you been? [The Teacher replied: "To Kukkuṭamitta."
“Ānanda, it is so. Venerable sir, who is this person among you who has not committed the deed of taking life? “Yes, Ānanda.

He, being the fifteenth member of that group, having established himself in unwavering faith and being free from doubt regarding the Three Jewels, has become one who has not committed the deed of taking life.
The monks said, “Venerable sir, does he not have a wife? “Yes, monks, she does.”
“Having been a young girl in a noble family, she attained the fruit of stream-entry. The monks raised this discussion:
“It is said that Kukkuṭamitta’s wife, having attained the fruit of stream-entry while still a young girl, went to his house and bore him seven sons;
for all this time, she was told by her husband, ‘Bring the bow, bring the arrows, bring the spear, bring the javelin,’ and so forth.”
When she was told, "Bring the net," she gave them to him. He too, taking what she had given, went and committed the taking of life.
[The bhikkhus thought: "Could it be that even a stream-enterer commits the taking of life? The Teacher, having arrived, asked, "Bhikkhus, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, "About this very matter," he said, "Bhikkhus, a stream-enterer does not [commit such an act]."
They commit the taking of life; however, she did so thinking, "I am carrying out my husband's word.
She had no intention such as, "Having taken this, let him go and commit the taking of life.
For just as poison cannot burn one who takes it when there is no wound on the palm of the hand, even so, in the absence of unwholesome volition (*akusalacetanā*), evil does not arise.
"Even for one who does not [intend harm], there is no such thing as evil, even if they draw out a bow or other weapons and give them away," he said.
Then, establishing the connection and teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
"If there were no wound upon the hand, one might take poison with the hand."
“Poison does not follow one who is woundless; there is no evil for one who does no wrong.
In this context, *nāssa* means “it would not exist for him. *Hareyya* means “it would be able to carry away. For what reason?
Because poison does not follow one who is woundless (*nābbaṇaṃ*), for poison is unable to enter a hand that has no wound. In the same way, having drawn out the bow and so forth...
Because even that unwholesome volition is absent, there is no such thing as "evil" for one who does not commit evil;
like poison on a woundless hand, evil does not follow his mind.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.

At another time, the monks initiated a discussion: “What indeed was the supporting condition for Kukkuṭamitta and his son and daughter-in-law to attain the path of stream-entry, and for what reason were they reborn in a family of hunters?
The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, about what discussion are you sitting here now? and they replied, “About this very one.”
“Bhikkhus, when they were preparing the relic shrine for Kassapa the Great Seer in the past, they said:
‘What indeed will be the clay for this shrine? What will be the water? Then it occurred to them:
‘Yellow orpiment and red arsenic shall be the clay; sesame oil shall be the water. So they [prepared] the yellow orpiment and red arsenic...”
Having pounded [the gold], mixed it with sesame oil, and combined it with brick, they inlaid it with gold on the inside;
however, the exterior surface consisted entirely of solid gold bricks. Each one was worth a hundred thousand.
When the stupa was completed up to the point of the relic chamber, they thought: "At the time of depositing the relics, with much wealth..."
"What is the purpose? Whom shall we appoint as the presiding elder?
Then a merchant living in a village said, "I shall be the presiding elder," and he placed one hundred million pieces of gold into the relic casket.
Seeing this, the inhabitants of the kingdom thought, "This city merchant is merely amassing wealth; such a person..."
They complained, saying, "The one from the monastery cannot become the senior; however, the village dweller, having contributed a hundred million, has become the senior.
When he heard their talk, he thought, "I shall give two hundred million and become the senior," and so he gave two hundred million.
The other thought, "I alone shall be the senior," and gave three hundred million. Thus...
Increasing it again and again, the city-dweller gave eight *koṭis*.
However, the village-dweller had only nine *koṭis* of wealth in his house, whereas the city-dweller had forty *koṭis*. Therefore, the village-dweller thought:
"If I give nine *koṭis*, he will say, 'I will give ten *koṭis*,' and then my poverty will become known."
So he spoke thus: "I will give this much wealth, and together with my sons and wife, I shall become a slave to the Cetiya.
Taking his seven sons, his seven daughters-in-law, and his wife, he dedicated himself along with them to the Cetiya.
The inhabitants of the kingdom thought, "Wealth can indeed be acquired; but this man has dedicated himself, together with his sons and wife."
"Let this one alone be the eldest," they said, and they made him the eldest. Thus, all sixteen of those people became slaves to the Cetiya, while the inhabitants of the kingdom made them free men.
Even so, having looked after the Cetiya itself, they remained for as long as their lifespan lasted;
then, passing away from there, they were reborn in the world of the gods. Among them, for the duration of one interval between Buddhas, they remained in the world of the gods.
In this current dispensation of a Buddha during the spring season, his wife passed away from that state and was reborn in Rājagaha as the daughter of a wealthy merchant.
While still a young girl, she attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*).

However, because a rebirth for one who has not yet seen the Truths is a grave matter, her husband, after wandering through various existences, was reborn into a family of hunters. Together with him...
At the mere sight of the merchant’s daughter, his former affection overwhelmed him. As it is said:
“Whether through former association or through present benefit, Affection arises in this way, like a lotus in the water.”
Out of her former affection, she went to the family of hunters. Her sons, having passed away from the world of the gods, took rebirth in her very womb;
and her daughters-in-law, having been born here and there and reached maturity, likewise went to that same household.
Thus, they all then tended to the cetiya, and by the power of that karma—
"He has attained the fruit of stream-entry.
The eighth story: The Case of Kukkuṭamitta and Naṭasāda. 9.
The Story of the Dog-Catcher Kokā.
"Whoever [harms] one who is unoffended"—the Teacher spoke this teaching on the Dhamma while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a dog-catcher named Koka.

It is said that one day, in the morning, as he was going to the forest with his bow and surrounded by dogs, he saw a monk entering for alms along the way; becoming angry, he thought, "I have seen a bringer of misfortune."
Thinking, "Today I shall receive nothing," he departed. The Elder, too, having wandered for alms in the village and finished his meal, set out again toward the monastery.
