The other, having wandered in the forest and returned without obtaining anything, saw the Elder once more and thought, "Today, having seen this ill-omened one, I went into the forest and received nothing; now, because of him..."
Thinking, "He has appeared once more; I shall have him eaten by the dogs," he gave the signal and released the dogs.
The Elder also pleaded, "Do not do this, lay follower! He replied, "Today I received nothing because you were present before me;
now that you have come into my presence again, I shall certainly have you eaten," and he drove the dogs forward. The Elder—
With great speed, he climbed a tree and sat down at a height equal to a man's stature. The dogs surrounded the tree.
The hunter went up and, saying, "Even by climbing this tree you will not escape," pierced the elder’s sole with the point of his arrow.
The elder entreated him, saying, "Do not do this! But the other, disregarding his plea, did so again and again.
He pierced him. While one sole of the elder’s foot was being pierced, the elder lifted it up; while the second foot was being pierced, he lifted that one up as well.
Thus, disregarding his request, they pierced both soles of his feet.
The elder’s body became like something set ablaze by torches. He became subject to the sensations [of pain].
He was unable to establish mindfulness and did not even notice that his wrapped robe was slipping off.
As it fell, it fell wrapping itself around his head from the crown downwards.
Thinking, "The Elder has fallen," the dogs entered between the robes, tore away their own master, and ate him until nothing but his bones remained. From within the robes, the dogs...
Having gone out, they stood outside.
Then the elder broke off a dry stick and threw it; seeing the elder, the dogs realized, "Our master has been eaten by us," and fled into the forest.
The elder felt remorse, thinking, "Between my robes..."
"Having entered, this lay follower has perished; is my virtue indeed intact?
Descending from the tree, he went into the presence of the Teacher and, reporting the entire occurrence from the beginning, asked: "Venerable Sir, that lay follower has perished because of my robe;
is my virtue intact? Do I still possess the status of a recluse? The Teacher—
Having heard his words, [the king] said, "Monk, your virtue is healthy; you truly possess the state of a recluse.
He met with destruction because he wronged one who was innocent of malice; and not only now, but in the past as well, he likewise met with destruction by wronging those who were innocent.
Having said this, he related the past to illustrate that matter:
In the past, it is said, a certain physician, having wandered through a village for the sake of medical practice and failing to obtain any work, went out with a hungry heart.
Seeing many boys playing at the village gate, he thought, "I shall get food by having these bitten by a snake and then treating them.
He then showed them a snake that was lying with its head protruding from a tree hollow.
“Ho there, young men! This is a young myna bird; catch it! he said. Then one young man, seizing the snake firmly by the neck, pulled it out;
and realizing it was a snake, he cried out and hurled it at the head of the physician standing nearby.
The snake coiled itself around the physician’s spinal vertebrae, bit him firmly, and remained right there.
"He brought about his death; thus this fowler, having previously wronged one who was innocent, has met his destruction.
Having related this past event and established the connection, the Teacher, while teaching the Dhamma, spoke this verse:
“He who offends an unoffending man, a pure person free from blemish—the evil returns to that very fool, like fine dust thrown against the wind.
In this context, *appaduṭṭhassa* means one who is not hostile toward himself or toward all beings. *Narassa* means a sentient being.
*Dussati* means she offends. *Suddhassa* means of one who is indeed innocent. *Posassa*—this too is another way of designating a sentient being (*sattādhivacana*).
*Anaṅgaṇassa* means of one free from defilements (*nikkilesa*). *Pacceti* means she falls upon [him].
*Paṭivātaṃ* means just as when a fine particle of dust is thrown by a person wishing to strike someone standing upwind, it strikes that very person.

It falls back upon him alone; even so, when a person offends by striking with the hand or the like against one who is not hostile toward him, that evil ripens for that very fool—either in this very life or in the future—in states such as the hells, and he "receives" it through the suffering of its maturation. This is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, that bhikkhu was established in Arahatship, and the Dhamma instruction was fruitful for the assembled company as well.
Thus ends the ninth story, the Story of the Dog-Catcher Kokasunakha. 10.
The Story of the Elder Tissa, the Householder’s Patron of the Jewel-Makers.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this teaching on the womb (*gabbha*) concerning the Elder Tissa, who had been a family associate of a jeweler.
It is said that for twelve years this elder ate at the house of a certain jeweler.
In that household, the husband and wife stood in the place of parents and attended upon the elder. Then one day, that jeweler, in the presence of the elder—
He was sitting there cutting meat. At that moment, King Pasenadi of Kosala sent a precious gem, saying, "Wash this, pierce it, and send it back.
The jeweler received it with his hand still stained with blood, placed it on top of a chest, and went inside to wash his hands. Now, in that house, there was a domestic *koñca* crane.
It was there. Driven by the scent of blood and perceiving it as meat, he swallowed that gem right before the Elder’s very eyes.
When the jeweler returned and did not see the gem, he asked his wife and sons one after another, "Who has taken the gem?
When they replied, "We did not take it," he thought, "The Elder must have taken it. Then, together with his wife...
He thought, "The Elder must have taken the gem. "Master, do not speak thus;
for all this time I have never seen any fault in the Elder, nor would he take such a gem.
The gem-maker asked the Elder, "Venerable sir, was a precious gem taken by you in this place? "I did not take it, lay follower."
“Venerable sir, there is no one else here; it must have been taken by you yourself. Give me the jewel.
When he did not consent, she spoke again to her husband: “The Elder has taken the jewel; let us press him and ask. He said, “Wife, do not ruin us!
It would be better for us to enter into slavery than to [press] the Elder.”
"Let us act in such a way. Thinking, "If we all submit to slavery, we shall not even be worth the price of the jewel," he took a rope, wrapped it around the Elder’s head, and struck him with a staff.
Blood flowed from the Elder’s head, ears, and nose; his eyes bulged out as if about to fall from their sockets, and overcome by the pain, he fell to the ground.
The crane went away with the scent of blood and drank the blood.
Then, with the force of anger that had arisen toward the Elder, the jeweler struck him with his foot, saying, "What are you doing? and threw him down.
He died instantly and lay on his back. Seeing this, the Elder said, "Lay follower, first loosen the turban on my head and look at this crane."
“Is he dead, or not? Then he said to him, “Like this man, you too shall die. “Lay follower, by this [man] that jewel was swallowed;
had he not died, even though I were dying myself, I would not have told you of the jewel.
Having slit his belly and seen the jewel, he trembled, and with a heart filled with agitation, he stood at the feet of the Elder.
Having lain down, he said, "Venerable sir, please forgive me for what was done by me unknowingly. "Lay follower, there is no fault in you, nor is there any in me;
this is merely a fault of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). I forgive you.
"Venerable sir, if you will forgive me, please sit in my house according to your usual custom and receive alms. "Lay follower, from now on, I shall not [go there]."
"From now on, I shall not enter the inner roofed area of another's house; for this fault lies precisely in entering the interior of a house.
From this day forth, even when my feet are being led inside, I shall stand at the very door of the house and receive alms.
Having spoken thus, he undertook the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) and recited this verse:
“Food is being cooked for the sage, little by little, in family after family.
I shall wander for alms; I still have strength in my legs.
Having said this, the elder, due to that very illness, attained final nibbāna before long. (The story of) Koñca the jeweler.
He took rebirth in his wife’s womb. Having died, the jeweler was reborn in hell.
Because of her soft-heartedness toward the Elder, the jeweler’s wife, having died, was reborn in the world of the devas.
The monks asked the Teacher about their future destiny. The Teacher said, “Monks, here some are born in the womb, while others—”
"Evil-doers are reborn in hell; some who have performed wholesome deeds are reborn in the world of the devas; but those free from taints attain final Nibbāna.
Having said this, and having established the connection, he taught the Dhamma by reciting this verse:
"Some are born in a womb; evil-doers go to hell;
“Those of happy destiny go to heaven; those free from taints attain final Nibbāna.
In this context, “womb” (gabbha) refers specifically to the human womb. The rest here is of plain meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
The tenth story: The Story of the Elder Tissa, the Supporter of the Jewel-Makers.

11. The Story of the Three People. The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, related this teaching on the Dhamma concerning three individuals, beginning with the words: "Not in the sky... (Na antalikkhe).
It is said that while the Teacher was dwelling at Jetavana, a large number of bhikkhus, coming to see the Teacher, entered a certain village for alms.
When they arrived, the village dwellers took them and seated them in the assembly hall;
having given them rice gruel and solid food, they sat listening to the Dhamma while waiting for the time of the alms-round. In that [place]...
At that moment, while one woman was cooking rice and fumigating the curry and condiments, a flame of fire rose from her vessel and seized the roof-covering.
Then, a single grass torch rose up and, burning, leapt into the air.
At that very instant, a crow flying through the sky thrust its neck inside; wrapped in the grass and creepers, it was consumed by the flames.
He fell in the middle of the village. When the monks saw him, they thought, "Oh, what a grievous deed! Look, friends, at the calamity brought about by a crow;
who but the Teacher could know the karma performed by this man?
We shall ask the Teacher about his karma," and with these thoughts, they departed.
As other monks were also traveling by boat to see the Teacher, their vessel came to a standstill in the midst of the ocean.
The people thought, "There must be someone ill-omened on board here," and they drew lots.
The boatman’s wife—standing in the prime of her youth, beautiful and pleasing to behold—drew the lot. [The boatmen said: "Let us draw the lot again..."
Having said, "Consider it," they considered it up to three times, and it fell upon her alone on all three occasions.
The people looked toward the face of the boatman and asked, "What is it, master? The boatman said, "It is not possible to destroy a great multitude for the sake of one person;
throw her into the water. As she was being seized and thrown into the water, she was terrified by the fear of death.
She cried out. Hearing this, the boatman said, "What is the use of these lost ornaments?
Strip off all the jewelry, have her put on a single rag, and cast her out!
I cannot bear to see her floating upon the surface of the water; therefore, so that I do not see her, place a basket of sand around her neck."
"Bind her and throw her into the ocean. They did so. Yet, even at the very spot where she fell, fish and turtles devoured her.
When the bhikkhus learned of this occurrence, they thought, "Aside from the Teacher, who else could know the karma performed by this woman?
We shall ask the Teacher about her karma. Having reached their desired destination, they...
Having disembarked from the boat, they departed.
Furthermore, seven other bhikkhus, while traveling to see the Teacher, entered a certain monastery in the evening and asked for a place to stay.
There were seven beds in a single cave; having obtained that very place, they stayed there.
While they were lying there during the night, a boulder as large as a gabled hall rolled down and closed the entrance to the cave.
The resident monks thought, "We have made this cave available for visiting monks, yet this great boulder has stood blocking the entrance;
we must remove it. So they gathered people from the seven surrounding villages.
Even though they strove, they were unable to move the rock from its place. The monks who had entered inside also continued to strive;
yet, despite this, they were unable to move the stone for seven days. For seven days, the visiting monks suffered great hardship with empty stomachs.
On the seventh day, the rock rolled away of its own accord. The monks emerged.
Thinking, "Who other than the Teacher will know of this evil of ours? We shall ask the Teacher," they departed.

Meeting with those who had gone before on the way, they all approached the Teacher together, paid homage, and sat down to one side. When the Teacher had exchanged greetings with them, each related what he himself had seen and experienced.
They asked about the causes in successive order.
The Teacher also explained to them in that same sequence: "Monks, that crow experienced the very result of his own deed.
For in the past, in Bārāṇasī, there was a certain farmer who was unable to tame his ox while he was training it."
Thus his ox, having gone only a short distance, lay down; though beaten and made to rise, he went only a short distance further and again lay down in the same way.

Unable to subdue him despite his efforts, overcome by anger, [the man thought], "From this day forward you shall sleep in comfort," and wrapping the ox's neck with straw like a bundle of hay, he bound it.
“The fire-giver, the ox, perished right there, consumed by flames. At that time, monks, that evil deed was committed by that crow.
Having been boiled in hell for a long time as a result of it, and through the remainder of that karmic ripening, he was reborn seven times in the womb of a crow;
in each case, he died just like this, consumed by flames in the air.”
Monks, that woman too experienced only the result of her own actions. In the past, in Bārāṇasī, she was the wife of a householder.
She herself performed all the household duties, such as fetching water, pounding grain, and cooking.
A certain dog used to sit watching her as she performed all these tasks in the house. When it was time for the meal in the field—
When she goes into the forest for the sake of wood, leaves, and so forth, he goes along with her.
Seeing them, young men mock them, saying, "Look, here comes a dog-catcher! Today we shall have meat to eat.
She, becoming dejected by their talk, strikes the dog with clods, sticks, and the like, and drives it away.
The dog turned back and followed her again. It is said that in a third previous existence, he had been her husband;

therefore, he was unable to sever his affection for her. For although there is no one who has not previously been one's wife or husband throughout the beginningless cycle of saṃsāra, nevertheless, there is an excessive attachment toward kinsmen in lives that are not far removed. Thus, that dog—
He was unable to abandon it. Having become angry with him, she went to fetch rice-gruel for her husband, placing the rope in her lap as she departed;
the dog went along with her. After she had given the rice-gruel to her husband, she took an empty pot, went to a certain watering place, filled the pot with sand, and looked around nearby.
She made a noise at the dog as it stood there. Thinking, "At long last, I have received sweet words today," the dog wagged its tail and approached her.
She seized him firmly by the neck, tied one end of the rope to the water-jar, and tied the other end of the rope around the dog's neck, then turned the jar toward the water.
She overturned it. A dog, pursuing the basket, fell into the water and died right there.

As the ripening of that karma, she suffered in hell for a long time; then, as a remainder of that ripening, in a hundred successive existences, a basket of sand was tied around her neck and she died after being cast into the water.
Monks, you too have experienced the very result of the deeds you yourselves committed.
Long ago, seven young cowherd boys living in Bārāṇasī were wandering with their cattle through a certain forest region every seven days.
One day, after they had finished tending the cattle and were returning, they saw a large iguana and pursued it. The iguana fled and entered a...
He entered the anthill. That anthill had seven openings. Thinking, "We will not be able to catch it now;
we shall come back tomorrow and catch it," each of the seven boys took a handful of broken twigs and closed one of the seven openings, then they departed.
On the following day, they ignored that lizard and [went elsewhere].
Having searched for the cows in the area, on the seventh day they set out taking the cows with them;
seeing that anthill, they regained their mindfulness and, thinking, "What has become of that lizard?", each opened the hole they had covered up.
The lizard, having no hope for life and reduced to mere bone and skin, emerged, quivering. They—
Seeing her, they felt compassion and said, "Do not kill her; she has gone without food for seven days.
Having rubbed her back, they released her, saying, "Go in peace. Because they did not kill the lizard, they did not fall into hell for that long.
However, those seven people, having come together, [experienced suffering] for seven days each during fourteen successive existences.
“They were those who had their wives cut off. At that time, monks, you yourselves, having been those seven cowherds, performed that deed.
Thus the Teacher answered each question as it was asked by them.
Then a certain monk said to the Teacher: “But, Bhante, what evil deed did he commit such that even though he leapt into the air...”
“There is no escape even for one who has leapt into the ocean or entered between mountains.
The Teacher said, “It is even so, monks; there is not even a single spot in the sky or elsewhere where one might stand and be released from evil karma.
Having spoken thus, he joined the connection and, teaching the Dhamma, uttered this verse:
“Neither in the sky, nor in the midst of the ocean, nor by entering a cleft in the mountains—there is no place found in this world where one could stand and be released from evil karma.
The meaning of this is: for if someone, thinking “By this means I shall be released from evil karma,” were to sit in the sky...
One might enter the great ocean, eighty-four thousand yojanas deep, or sit amidst mountains;

yet one would not be released from evil karma. There is not even a space as small as a hair’s tip among the regions of the earth, such as the eastern quarters and so forth, where one could stand and be able to escape from evil karma.
At the conclusion of the teaching, those bhikkhus attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages; the Dhamma discourse was also beneficial for the great multitude that had gathered.
This is the eleventh story, concerning the three leagues.
12. The Story of Suppabuddha the Sakyan.
The Teacher delivered this Dhamma teaching, "Not in the sky," while residing at the Nigrodha Monastery, concerning Suppabuddha the Sakyan. It is said that Suppabuddha,
having conceived resentment toward the Teacher for two reasons— namely, "He went away after abandoning my daughter" and "Having ordained my son, he has taken his place as an enemy"— one day...
Thinking, "I will not give him the opportunity to go to my invitation and eat," he blocked the path and sat in the middle of the street drinking liquor.
Then, when the Teacher arrived at that place surrounded by the community of monks, they announced, "The Teacher has arrived.
He said, "Tell him to go on ahead; this man is not older than I am."
"Even though he was told again and again, 'I will not show you the way,' he sat there saying the same thing.
Since the Teacher could not obtain the way from his maternal uncle, he turned back from there. He [the uncle] also sent a spy, saying, 'Go, and having heard what he says, come back.
As the Teacher was returning, he smiled, and the Venerable Ānanda asked, 'Who is it, Bhante?"'
When asked, "What is the condition for the manifestation of his smile? he replied: "Ānanda, do you see Suppabuddha? "I see him, Bhante.
"That man has committed a grave deed by refusing the path to one such as me, a Buddha;
on the seventh day from now, he will sink into the earth at the foot of the stairs on the lower terrace. A spy overheard this conversation.
Having heard this, he went to Suppabuddha and, when asked, "What did my nephew say as he was returning?
he reported exactly what he had heard. Upon hearing his words, Suppabuddha thought, "Now there is no fault in my nephew's speech;
certainly, what he says is exactly so. Even though that is the case, I shall now [accuse him] with a lie."
"I shall subdue him. For he did not say to me vaguely, 'On the seventh day he will enter the earth,' but rather said, 'At the foot of the stairs on the lower terrace, he will enter the earth.
From this moment on, I will not go to that place; instead, by making him fail to enter the earth at that spot, I shall subdue him with a lie."
Having placed all his personal belongings atop the seven-storied palace,
having had the stairs removed and the doors closed, and having stationed two wrestlers at each door,
he said, "If I should wish to descend below through negligence, you must restrain me," and sat down in the bedchamber on the seventh floor of the palace.
When the Teacher heard this account, he said, “Monks, let Suppabuddha fly up into the air from the palace roof, or sit in mid-air, or leap into the ocean from a ship, or enter between mountains;
there is no such thing as a double outcome for the word of the Buddhas. He shall sink into the earth at the very spot where I have spoken.”
Having spoken thus and established the connection, while teaching the Dhamma,
he uttered this verse: “Neither in the sky, nor in the midst of the ocean, nor by entering a cleft in the mountains,
is there any place found in the world where one could stand and not be overcome by Death.”

In this context, "where death would not prevail" means that there is not even a spot the size of a hair-tip on the earth where death, once it has arrived, could not overcome or conquer one. The rest is exactly as before.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
On the seventh day, at the time when the Teacher’s alms-round had ceased, while Suppabuddha was in the lower palace—
The horse Maṅgala, having become unbridled, struck various walls. Sitting above him, Suppabuddha heard the noise and asked, "What is this?
"The horse Maṅgala has become unbridled," they replied. However, that horse would settle down as soon as it saw Suppabuddha.
Then, wishing to seize him, Suppabuddha rose from his seat and went toward the doors; [he found] the doors...
The doors opened by themselves, and the staircases remained in their respective places. The Mallas standing at the door seized him by the neck and hurled him headlong down.
By this same means, the doors on all seven terraces opened by themselves, and the staircases remained in their places. At each level, the Mallas seized him by the neck and hurled him headlong down.
They threw him down. Then, as soon as he reached the foot of the stairs on the lower terrace, the great earth split open and received him;
having gone there, he was reborn in Avīci.
This is the twelfth story, the account of Suppabuddha the Sakyan.
The commentary on the Chapter on Evil is finished.
The ninth chapter.
10. The Chapter on Punishment.
1. The Story of the Group-of-Six Monks:
"All tremble" — The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, spoke this Dhamma teaching concerning the Group-of-Six monks.
For on one occasion, when the dwelling had been prepared by the Group-of-Seventeen, the Group-of-Six monks said, "Depart! [We will take it]."
"We are older; this belongs to us," they said. When those [other monks] replied, "We will not give it up;
we looked after it first," they struck the monks of the group of seventeen. Terrified by the fear of death, the group of seventeen let out a great cry.
The Teacher, hearing their sound, asked, "What is this? and when told, "It is this," he spoke.
When this had been reported, [the Blessed One] laid down the training rule regarding the giving of blows, saying:
"Monks, from this time forward, a monk must not act in this way; whoever does so incurs such-and-such an offense. Then he said:
"Monks, a monk, knowing that 'just as I am, so too others tremble at punishment and fear death,' [should treat another...]"
Having said, "He must not be struck, he must not be killed," and having established the connection [to the previous discourse], he taught the Dhamma by reciting this verse:
"All tremble at punishment; all fear death.
Making oneself the analogy, one should neither strike nor cause others to strike."
In this context, "all tremble" means that all beings indeed tremble when punishment falls upon themselves.
"Of death" means they are likewise afraid even of death. In this teaching, the phrasing (*byañjana*) is exhaustive, but the meaning (*attha*) is not;
for just as when a king causes a drum to be beaten with the command, "Let everyone assemble," even though the royal ministers...

Excluding those [four], the rest assemble; likewise, here, although it is said "all tremble," one should understand that with the exception of these four—the thoroughbred elephant, the thoroughbred horse, the thoroughbred bull, and the one whose taints are destroyed—it is only the remainder who tremble.

For among these, the one whose taints are destroyed, because he has abandoned the view of a self-identity (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), does not see a being subject to death and thus does not fear; the others, however, do.
Because the three types of personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) are powerful, they do not fear, as they do not perceive a being who is their own adversary.
"Neither should one kill nor cause to kill" means that just as I am, so too are other beings; thus, one should neither strike another nor cause them to be struck.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*) and the other fruits.
The First Account of the Group of Six Monks.
2. The Account of the Group of Six Monks:
Regarding the teaching on the Dhamma beginning with "All tremble," the Teacher spoke while residing at Jetavana concerning the Group of Six Monks.
For at that very same time and for that very same reason, they struck the group of seventeen monks regarding the previous training rule;
for that very same reason, they raised their palm-strikes against them. Here too, the Teacher, having heard their noise, asked, "What is this?
and when it was reported, "It is this," he said: "Monks, from now on, indeed, no monk..."
“Thus it must be done; whoever does so incurs such-and-such an offense.
Having thus laid down the training rule regarding the hand-strike, he said: “Monks, a monk, knowing that ‘just as I do, others also tremble at punishment;
and just as my life is dear to me, so is theirs,’ must not strike another nor cause them to be killed.”
Having spoken thus and established the connection, while teaching the Dhamma, he uttered this verse:
“All tremble at the rod; to all, life is dear.
Making oneself the analogy, one should neither kill nor cause to kill.”

In this regard, with the exception of those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), the life of all other beings is dear and sweet; however, one whose taints are exhausted remains equanimous toward both life and death. The rest is just as before.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*) and the other fruits.
This is the second story, concerning the group of six bhikkhus (*chabbaggiya-bhikkhu*).
3. The Story of the Many Boys.
While residing at Jetavana, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning many boys, beginning with the words, "All beings desire happiness.
For on one occasion, while the Teacher was entering Sāvatthī for alms, he encountered many boys along the way.
Seeing a house-snake species being struck with a stick, he asked, "Boys, what are you doing?
When they replied, "We are striking a snake with a stick, Venerable Sir," he asked again, "For what reason?
When they replied, "Out of fear of its bite, Venerable Sir," he said, "While you strike this [snake] thinking, 'We shall bring ourselves happiness,' in every place where you are reborn..."
“You shall not obtain happiness. For one who desires his own happiness ought not to strike another,” he said.
Then, establishing the connection and teaching the Dhamma, he spoke these verses:
“He who harms with a stick beings who desire happiness—”
“Seeking his own happiness, he does not find happiness after death. But he who,
seeking his own happiness, does not harm with a rod beings who also desire happiness—
he finds happiness after death.”
In this regard, "he who with a stick" refers to that person who harms others with a stick, a clod of earth, or similar objects.
"And having passed away, he does not obtain happiness" means that such a person, in the next world, does not obtain human happiness, divine happiness, or the ultimate happiness of Nibbāna.
In the second verse, "and having passed away, he obtains" means that such a person, in the next world, [obtains] the aforementioned kind [of happiness].
The meaning is that he obtains all three kinds of happiness.
At the conclusion of the teaching, those five hundred youths were established in the fruit of stream-entry.
This is the third story concerning the many youths.
4. The Story of the Elder Koṇḍadhāna "Speak not harshly to anyone"—the Teacher gave this Dhamma teaching while residing at Jetavana concerning the elder Koṇḍadhāna.
It is said that from the very day he went forth, a certain female form would accompany the elder wherever he went.
The Elder did not see him, but the great multitude did. As he was walking for alms within the village, people would give him one portion of alms and say, "Venerable sir, let this be for you;
but this one is for your companion," and they would give a second portion as well.
What was his past karma? It is said that during the time of the Sammasambuddha Kassapa, there were two friends who were monks;
they were born from the same mother’s womb and were exceedingly harmonious.
During the era of a long-lived Buddha, monks would assemble for the Uposatha ceremony either every year or every half-month. Therefore, those two also thought, "We shall go to the Uposatha hall."
They departed from their dwelling place. A certain deity who had been reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, seeing them, thought:
"These bhikkhus are exceedingly harmonious; is it possible to cause a schism among them? Having thought this, due to his own foolishness, he arrived immediately after that thought.
When one of them said to him, "Friend, wait a moment; I have need of a bodily function," she—
A deity, having assumed the form of a human woman, entered between the elder and another monk;
as she was emerging, she adjusted her mass of hair with one hand and her lower garment with the other, and thus emerged behind him.
He did not see her, but while waiting for her arrival, the monk standing in front turned around and looked back.
Having done so, he saw him as he was departing. Knowing that he had been seen by him, she vanished.
When the other monk returned to his presence, he said to him, "Friend, your virtue is broken. "Friend, I have not done such a thing," he replied.
"Just now, as you were going out, I saw a young woman doing this very thing behind you."
“I have seen it with my own eyes; why do you say, ‘I do not have such a thing’? He replied, as if struck on the head by a thunderbolt, “Friend, do not destroy me!
I truly do not have such a thing. The other said, “I have seen it with my own eyes; how can I believe you?
And like a split bamboo stalk, he broke away and departed, even saying in the midst of the Uposatha assembly, “I am not [associated] with this man.”
“I shall observe the Uposatha together with him,” he thought, and sat down. The other said to the monks, “Venerable sir, I do not have even a speck of blackness in my virtue.
He too replied, “I have seen it myself. Seeing that he was unwilling to observe the Uposatha with him, the deity thought, “A grave deed has been committed by me,” and said: “Venerable sir, …”
"There is no breach of virtue on the part of my noble master; however, this was done by me for the sake of testing him.
Perform the Uposatha together with him," she said. Believing her as she stood speaking in the air, he performed the Uposatha;
yet he was not as gentle-minded toward the Elder as he had been before. Such was the previous deed of the deity.
At the end of their lives, those elders were reborn in the world of the devas according to their pleasure. As for the female deva, she was reborn in Avīci;
after being cooked there for the duration of one *buddhantara*, she was reborn in Sāvatthī during this current appearance of a Buddha.
Having reached maturity and gone forth in the Dispensation, she received full ordination (*upasampadā*). From the day of her going forth, that female form [vanished].
He appeared exactly like that. Therefore, they gave him the name Thera Koṇḍañña.
Seeing him wandering about in such a manner, the bhikkhus said to Anāthapiṇḍika: "Great merchant, expel this immoral man from your monastery.
For because of him, infamy will arise among the rest of the bhikkhus. "But, venerable sirs, did the Teacher [permit] in the monastery..."
“Is there no one? “There is, Venerable Sir, the lay follower Visākhā. “In that case, Bhante, the Teacher himself will know,” they said.
The monks went and spoke in the same manner to Visākhā; she too gave them the same reply.
Since the monks’ words were not accepted by her, they reported it to the King: “Great King, the Elder Koṇḍañña—”
“Wandering about with a certain woman, he has brought disgrace upon all of you; drive him out from your kingdom!
“But where is he, Bhante? “In the monastery, Great King. “In which dwelling does he reside? “In such-and-such a place.
“Then go; I shall take him myself. At evening time, he went to the monastery.
Having gone to that lodging and had it surrounded by men, he proceeded toward the elder’s dwelling place.
Hearing the great noise, the elder emerged from the monastery and stood at the entrance. The king also saw that womanly form standing behind him.
Knowing that the king was approaching, the elder ascended into the monastery and sat down. The king [approached] the elder...
He did not bow, nor did he see that woman. Although he looked between the door-posts and even beneath the couch, failing to see her, he said to the Elder:
"Venerable sir, I saw a certain woman in this place; where is she? "I do not see her, Great King," he replied.
Even when the king said, "Just now I saw her standing behind you," the Elder simply said, "I do not see her."
The king, wondering, "What could this be? said, "Venerable sir, please depart from here for now.
When they had gone out and were standing at the entrance, she stood again behind the elder. The king, seeing her, climbed back up to the upper floor;
knowing that he had arrived, the elder sat down. Again, the king looked about in all directions.
Having looked, he asked the Elder again, “Venerable sir, where is that woman? “I do not see her, Great King,” replied the Elder.
“What are you saying, venerable sir? Just now I saw her standing behind you!
“Indeed, Great King; even the great multitude says, ‘A woman is walking right behind me,’ yet I do not see her.”
“I see him. The king, observing that this must be a mere likeness, said again to the Elder, “Venerable sir, please descend from here first.
When the Elder had descended and was standing at the entrance, the king saw him standing behind his back and ascended to the upper floor once more.
He did not see him again. Having questioned the Elder once more, he received the same reply: “I do not see him.”
Having concluded that "this is indeed appropriate," he said to the Elder:
"Venerable sir, as long as such corruption follows behind you, no one else will give you alms;
please enter my house regularly, and I myself will attend to you with the four requisites. Having thus invited the Elder, he departed.
The bhikkhus complained, saying, “See, friends, the evil deed of the king!
When he said, ‘Take this man out from the monastery,’ the Elder came, invited him with the four requisites, and then departed. They also said to that Elder, “Ho, you of immoral conduct!
Now you have become a royal attendant! He too, being previously unable to say anything to the bhikkhus, replied, “You yourselves are of immoral conduct!”
“You Koṇḍas! You go about taking hold of women,” he said. They went and reported this to the Teacher:
“Venerable Sir, when we spoke to the Elder Koṇḍañña, he reviled us, saying things such as, ‘You are immoral,’ and so forth.
The Teacher summoned him and asked, “Is it true, monk, that you speak thus? “It is true, Venerable Sir,” he replied.
“For what reason? “Because we were conversing with him. “Why, monks, did you converse with him?
“Because, venerable sir, we saw a woman walking behind him.
“It is said that these people spoke upon seeing a woman walking with you; why did you speak? Having seen them first...”
They said, "Why do you converse with these people even without seeing them?
Was this not previously brought about solely by your own evil view? Why do you now again adopt that evil view?
The monks asked, "But, venerable sir, what did he do in the past? Then the Teacher explained his former karma to them.
“Bhikkhu, it is because of this evil deed that you have come to this miserable state.
Now, it is not fitting for you to again adopt such an evil view. Do not speak anything further with the bhikkhus;
remain silent, like a bronze bowl with its rim broken off. By acting in this way, you will be one who has attained Nibbāna.”
Having spoken thus and established the connection, he taught the Dhamma by reciting these verses:
"Do not speak harshly to anyone; when spoken to, they may answer you back.
For contentious speech is painful, and retaliatory blows may strike you."
“If you do not harm yourself, like a gong that has been struck, you have reached Nibbāna; no further conflict exists for you.
In this context, “Do not speak harshly to anyone” means: do not speak harshly even to a single person. “Spoken by you”—this refers to what was said by you.
If others are called "immoral," they might likewise retort against you. This is a contentious speech, a counter-argument that seizes upon an equal footing;
it is indeed painful. As for "counter-blows": if you strike another with the physical rod or other means, such counter-blows may fall upon your own head.
"If you remain peaceful" means if you are able to keep yourself motionless.
Kaṃsa is like a bronze bowl that has been struck, its rim broken off and reduced to the mere base;
for even when struck with hands, feet, or a staff, it makes no sound.
"If you can become such as this"—if you are able to fulfill this practice, then although you have not yet reached it now...

"One who has attained Nibbāna. "In you, no provocation is found": this being so, the meaning is that even "provocation," characterized by the speech of further retaliation such as "you are immoral" or "you all are immoral," is not found in you, nor will it ever exist.

At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages; the Elder Koṇḍañña, too, abiding by the instruction given by the Teacher, attained Arahantship and, before long, leaping into the air, took the first voting ticket.
The fourth story, concerning the Elder Koṇḍadhāna.
5. The Story of the Women Observing the Uposatha.

The Teacher, while residing at Pubbārāma, delivered this Dhamma teaching beginning with the words, "As if with a staff," concerning the observance of the Uposatha by Visākhā and other female lay devotees.
It is said that on a certain great Uposatha day in Sāvatthī, about five hundred women went to the monastery having observed the Uposatha.
Visākhā approached those elderly women and asked, "Aunties, for what purpose have you become observant of the Uposatha?
When they replied, "Having aspired to celestial excellence," she then questioned the middle-aged women.
When they said, "For the sake of being released from rebirth in the realms of existence," she asked young women;
when they said, "For the sake of obtaining a son in the first pregnancy," she asked unmarried girls;
and when they said, "For the sake of going to their husbands' families while still in youth," she heard all that they said, took them with her, and went into the presence of the Teacher in order.
She reported this. Having heard it, the Teacher said: "Visākhā, for these beings, birth and the rest are like cowherds with clubs in their hands.
Birth sends one into the presence of old age; old age into the presence of sickness; and sickness into the presence of death.
Then death, as if cutting with an axe, severs life. Even so, there are none who aspire toward the turning away from existence (nibbāna)."
"But they only aspire for the round of existence," he said. Having established the connection, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
"Just as a cowherd drives his cattle to pasture with a staff, So do old age and death drive living beings toward the end of their life-span."

In this context, "he drives them" means that a clever cowherd, having warded off with his staff the cows entering the middle of a field, leads them to a grazing ground where grass and water are easily obtained while striking them with that very same stick.
"They drive away life" means they cut off and cast away the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
For old age and death are like the cowherd; the life-faculty is like the herd of cows; and death is like the grazing ground.
In this regard, birth first sends beings toward old age; old age toward sickness;
and sickness toward death. That very death goes on, cutting them down as if with an axe;
this is the application of the simile here.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the fifth story, concerning the women who observed the Uposatha.
6. The Story of the Ajagara Preta.
Then, while residing at Veḷuvana, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning the Ajagara peta.
For on one occasion, as the Elder Mahāmoggallāna was descending from Vulture Peak with the Elder Lakkhaṇa,
he saw with his divine eye a peta named Ajagara, twenty-five yojanas in length, with flames of fire issuing from its head.
Rising from the base, they go to the limit; rising from the limit, they go to the head;
rising from both ends, they descend into the middle. Seeing this, the Elder smiled. When asked by the Elder Lakkaṇa for the reason for his smile, he replied:
"It is not the right time, friend, to answer this question; you should ask me in the presence of the Teacher."
Having spoken thus, after walking for alms in Rājagaha and returning to the presence of the Teacher, he was asked by the Elder Lakkhaṇa and said:
"There, friend, I saw a certain peta; such was its physical form. Upon seeing it, I broke into a smile, thinking:
'Indeed, never before have I seen such a physical form as this! The Teacher said: "You have become one who possesses vision..."
Having established the Elder’s statement by saying, "Monks, it is disciples who dwell thus," he continued:
"Monks, I too saw this peta right at the Seat of Enlightenment; however, I did not speak of it, thinking, 'If they were not to believe my word, it would be to their detriment.
Now, having obtained Moggallāna as a witness, I speak of it."
Having spoken thus, when questioned by the monks regarding his past karma, he explained:
"It is said that during the time of the Buddha Kassapa, there was a merchant named Sumaṅgala.

Having paved the ground with golden bricks over an area of twenty usabhas, he built a monastery for a sum of wealth equal to that amount, and with an equal amount of wealth, he held a festival for the monastery. One day..."
Early in the morning, while going into the presence of the Teacher, he saw at the city gate a certain thief lying in a hall with his head covered by a saffron robe and his feet smeared with mud.
He said, "This man, whose feet are smeared with mud, must have been wandering about at night and is now lying down during the day. The thief opened his mouth and, seeing the merchant, [spoke].
Saying, “Very well, I shall know what you must do,” he harbored a grudge and burned his field seven times;
he cut the legs of the cattle in the pen seven times; and he burned his house seven times.
Being unable to extinguish his anger even by that much, he established a friendship with Cūḷūpaṭṭhāka and said, “What...?”
When asked, "What is dear to those merchants? he heard that "there is nothing dearer to him than the Perfumed Chamber.

Thinking, "Very well, I shall extinguish his anger by burning the Perfumed Chamber," he broke the water-pots for drinking and washing while the Teacher had entered for alms, and set fire to the Perfumed Chamber.
Hearing that the Perfumed Chamber was being burned, the merchant came along.
When it was time to burn [the Gandhakuti], he came and, looking upon the burning Gandhakuti, felt not even as much dejection as the tip of a hair.
He rubbed his left arm and, with his right hand, gave a great clap.
Then those standing nearby asked him, "Why, Master, did you give such a clap at the time of burning the Gandhakuti for which you had spent so much wealth?"
Thus he said: "Sons, I have obtained this much wealth to store away in the Buddha’s teaching, which is not shared with fire and other such things.

Thinking, 'Once again, by spending this much wealth, I shall be able to build a fragrant chamber for the Teacher,' he clapped his hands in a joyful heart. Having again spent that same amount of wealth, he had the fragrant chamber constructed.
He gave alms to the Teacher, who was accompanied by a retinue of twenty thousand bhikkhus. Seeing this, the robber thought:
"I shall not be able to carry out my plan unless I kill him; very well, I will kill him.
He fastened a dagger within his lower garment and, though he wandered through the monastery for seven days, he found no opportunity. The great merchant also [spent] seven days...
Having given alms to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha and having paid homage to the Teacher, he said:
"Venerable Sir, one man of mine has burnt my field seven times, the hooves of my cattle have been cut off by a bull seven times, and my house has been burnt down seven times;
now even this Gandhakuṭi will surely be burnt by that same man."
"I give the first portion of this gift to him.
Hearing this, the robber thought: "Alas, what a grave deed I have committed! Even toward me, who has committed such an offense, he shows not even the slightest anger;
instead, he gives me the very first portion of this gift. I am betraying him—how can one act in such a manner?"
"If I do not ask this man for forgiveness, even the divine rod of punishment might fall upon my head.
Having said this, he went and prostrated at the feet of the merchant, saying, "Forgive me, Master! When the merchant asked, "What is this? he replied, "Master, an improper deed was committed by me;
forgive me for that. Then the merchant said to him, "This and that were done by you for me..."
Having questioned him about everything, when he replied, "Yes, it was done by me," [the treasurer] asked, "I have never seen you before;
why did you do this out of anger toward me? He recalled the words spoken by the man who had left the city one day and said, "It was for this reason that my anger arose.
The treasurer remembered what he himself had said and replied, "Yes, dear son, it was said."
Having asked the thief for forgiveness, saying, "Forgive me for that," he said, "Rise up, dear one; I forgive you; go, dear one. [The thief replied:
"If you, Master, forgive me, make me and my wife and children slaves in your house. [The man said:
"Dear one, after I had spoken to you so much, you committed such an act of violence; however, it is not possible for anyone living in the house to do anything [against me]."
"I have no need for you living in my house; I forgive you, go, dear one.
Having committed that deed, the robber was reborn in Avīci at the end of his lifespan; after being cooked there for a long time, he now suffers as a residual result on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Having thus related his past karma, the Teacher said, "Monks, fools do not realize when they are performing evil deeds;
but later, being consumed by the very actions they themselves have committed, they become like a forest fire to themselves.
Having established the connection, he taught the Dhamma and spoke this verse:
“Then, performing evil deeds, the fool does not realize it;
through his own actions, the witless one burns like one consumed by fire.
In this context, “then, evil deeds” means that the fool does not perform evil deeds solely out of anger; rather, even while performing them, he does not...
The meaning is "he awakens. There is no one who, while committing an evil deed, does not recognize, "I am committing an evil deed.
It is said that he "does not awaken" because of his lack of knowledge regarding the fact that "such is the ripening of this karma.
The meaning is that by means of those actions belonging to himself, that foolish person devoid of wisdom, having been reborn in hell, suffers like one scorched by fire.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the sixth story, the *Ajagara-petavatthu*. 7.
The Story of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Veḷuvana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning the Elder Mahāmoggallāna.
For on one occasion, the heretics gathered together and deliberated:
"Friends, do you know for what reason such great gain and honor have accrued to the ascetic Gotama? We do not know, but you perhaps do?"

"Yes, we know; it arose depending on one named Mahāmoggallāna. For he would go to the world of the devas, ask the devas about the karma they had performed, and upon returning, tell humans: 'By doing such-and-such, one obtains such-and-such prosperity.
He would also ask those reborn in hell about their karma, and upon returning, tell humans: 'This..."

“Having given him such a name, he experiences suffering like this. When the people heard his words, they brought him great wealth and honor, thinking, “If we can kill him, that wealth and honor will accrue to us.
They all became of one mind, saying, “There is a way; by doing whatever it takes, we shall have him killed,” and [they resolved] themselves...
Having incited his attendants, he obtained a thousand kahāpaṇas.
Then, having summoned some wandering thieves who were engaged in the business of murdering men, he gave them the money and said, "The Elder Mahāmoggallāna dwells on Kāḷasilā; go there and kill him.
Out of greed for the wealth, the thieves accepted the offer and went, thinking, "We shall kill the Elder."
They surrounded his dwelling place. When the Elder realized he was hemmed in by them, he went out through a keyhole and departed.
Those thieves, not seeing the Elder on that day, went again one day later and surrounded him once more.
The Elder, knowing this, broke through the circular window-frame and leaped into the air. Thus it was during the first month and also during the middle month.
They were unable to seize the Elder. But when the last month arrived, the Elder, knowing that the consequences of his own past actions were drawing near, did not depart.
The bandits went and seized him, and while reducing his bones to the size of mere rice-grains, they broke them apart.
Then, perceiving that he was dead, they threw him onto the back of a bush and departed.

The Elder, thinking, "I shall attain final Nibbāna only after seeing the Teacher," enveloped his physical body in the shroud of jhāna, made it firm, and went through the air into the presence of the Teacher. Having paid homage to the Teacher, he said, "Venerable Sir, I shall attain final Nibbāna.
"Will you attain final Nibbāna, Moggallāna? "Yes, Venerable Sir. "Where will you go? "To the region of Kāḷasilā."
“Venerable sir,” he replied. “In that case, Moggallāna, preach the Dhamma to me and then depart.

For at this time, there is no such disciple as you remaining to see me. “I shall do so, venerable sir,” he said, and having paid homage to the Teacher, he rose into the air and, like the Elder Sāriputta on the day of his Parinibbāna, performed various kinds of supernatural powers while preaching the Dhamma.
Having spoken thus and paid homage to the Teacher, he went to the Kāḷasīla forest and attained final Nibbāna.
The report that "the thieves had killed the Elder" spread throughout the entire land of Jambudīpa. King Ajātasattu dispatched secret agents to search for the thieves.
While those thieves were drinking liquor at a tavern, one struck another on the back and knocked him down.
Thus, having incited him, he said, "Ho, you ill-behaved one!
Why did you fall upon my back? But what of it, you wicked thief? Was not the Elder Mahāmoggallāna struck first by you?
"Do you not know that I was the one who struck him? Hearing these words of theirs as they each claimed, "I struck him! I struck him!"—
Those scouts, having captured all those thieves, reported it to the king. The king had the thieves summoned and asked, "Was the Elder killed by you?
"Yes, Your Majesty," they replied. "By whom were you incited? "By the naked ascetics, Your Majesty.
The king had the five hundred naked ascetics seized and, together with the five hundred thieves, brought them into the royal courtyard.
Having had them buried in pits as deep as their navels and covered with straw, he had fire set to them.
Then, knowing they were burnt to death, he had them ploughed up with iron ploughs and had them all reduced to pieces.
The bhikkhus raised a discussion in the Hall of Truth: "The Elder Mahāmoggallāna has done something truly unworthy of himself..."

“He has met his death. The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now? When they replied, “About this very matter,” he said, “Monks, Moggallāna has met a death that was not worthy of this very person; rather, he has met a death that is entirely consistent with the karma he performed in the past. Having said this, he related the story: In times long past, there was a certain king who ruled over a kingdom.

He had a son named Prince Mahāpanāda, who was exceedingly handsome and possessed of great majesty. As he grew up, he became proficient in all the arts and sciences. One day, as the prince was walking about, he saw a poor man carrying a load of wood on his head. Seeing him, the prince felt compassion and thought, “How miserable it is for this man to carry such a heavy burden! He then took the load from the man’s head and carried it himself. At that time, a certain deity living in the sky saw this and thought, “This prince is performing a deed of great merit; I must test him. She then transformed herself into a hideous old woman, bent over and leaning on a staff, and stood before the prince. The prince, seeing her, spoke kindly to her and said, “Old lady, why do you carry such a heavy load? Let me take it from you. The old woman replied, “Prince, I am indeed old and feeble; I cannot carry this load any further. But even if you were to take it, I would not let you go. The prince insisted, “I will certainly take it; please let me help you. The deity, wishing to test him further, said, “If you truly wish to help me, you must first give me half of your own body. The prince, without hesitation, agreed. The deity then manifested her true form and said, “Prince, I am a deity who dwells in the sky. I came to test you because I saw your compassionate heart. Since you have given half of your body out of compassion, I shall grant you a boon. The prince replied, “If you are pleased with me, may I always be able to give away my body to those in need. The deity granted his wish. Because of that deed, when the prince later became king, he was known as King Mahāpanāda. One day, while wandering through the city, he saw a poor man suffering from leprosy. Feeling pity, the king gave him half of his own body to heal the man’s wounds. Because of that act, he eventually passed away and was reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three. There, he enjoyed celestial pleasures for many eons. When his merit was exhausted, he passed away from that realm and was reborn in the human world as the son of a wealthy merchant. He was named Sīvali. From birth, Sīvali was endowed with great beauty and virtue. He grew up to be a wise and noble youth. One day, while he was walking in the forest, he encountered a band of robbers who were about to kill a traveler. Seeing their intent, Sīvali offered himself to the robbers in exchange for the traveler’s life. The robbers were amazed by his selflessness and released the traveler. Because of that deed, Sīvali eventually passed away and was reborn in the Brahma-world. From there, he descended to be born as the son of the Buddha’s mother, Queen Māyā.

Thus, Moggallāna had met a death that was not inconsistent with his previous deeds, but was entirely in accordance with the karma he had performed in the past. The Teacher, having finished the discourse, declared: “Monks, one who performs wholesome deeds will experience the fruit thereof, whether in this very life or in a future existence. He then pronounced the following verses: “Just as a seed, when planted in good soil, Grows and bears fruit in due season, So too, a deed well done, whether small or great, Will surely bear its fruit for the doer. Therefore, one should always perform good deeds, For the fruit of merit is sweet and enduring. By doing what is right, one finds happiness, Both in this world and in the next. Having spoken thus, the Teacher rose from his seat and returned to the monastery. The monks, having heard the Teacher’s words, were filled with joy and practiced accordingly. Thus ends the story of Moggallāna’s death.
“Venerable sir, what was his past karma? Being thus asked, he explained in detail:
“In the past, it seems, a certain son of good family living in Bārāṇasī looked after his mother and father while performing the work himself, such as pounding and cooking.
Then his parents said to him, ‘Dear son, you are all alone; both in the house and in the forest—’”
Having said, "While you perform your work, you will grow weary; we shall bring a young girl for you," they were refused by him, who replied, "Mother and father, I have no need for such a thing;
as long as you live, I shall serve you with my own hands.
Yet, after repeatedly entreating him, they brought a young girl. After she had served them for only a few days, later on—
Not wishing even to see them, she complained, saying, "It is not possible to live in one place with your mother and father.

When he would not accept her words, and while he was away, she took pieces of bark-cloth and the froth of rice-gruel, scattered them here and there, and when he returned and asked, "What is this? she spoke.
—"This is the behavior of these blind old people; they wander about making the entire house filthy.

It is not possible to live in one place with them. As she spoke to him thus again and again, even that being who had fulfilled the perfections was separated from his parents. He thought, "Very well, I shall find out about them."
Having fed them, saying, "It must be done," he said, "Mother and Father, your relatives at such-and-such a place are waiting for your arrival;
let us go there. Having placed them on a carriage and taken them along, when they reached the middle of a forest, he said, "Father, take the reins;
the oxen will follow by the sign of the goad. Robbers dwell in this place; I..."
Saying, "I am descending," he handed the reins to his father, descended, and as he went along, he changed his voice and made the sound of bandits rising up.
Hearing the noise, the parents, thinking that bandits had risen, said, "Dear son, we are old;
you must protect yourself. Even though his parents were crying out thus, he [continued] with the sound of bandits...
Having done so, he beat him, killed him, threw him into the wilderness, and returned.

The Teacher, having related this past deed of his, said: "Monks, after Moggallāna had performed such karma and was boiled in hell for many hundreds of thousands of years, by the remainder of the karmic result, he was beaten in this very same manner in a hundred successive existences."
“Crushed to pieces, he met his death. Thus Moggallāna received a death that was exactly in accordance with his own karma, along with the five hundred thieves.
For one who offends against those who have not offended him meets only with ruin and disaster for ten reasons.
Having said this, and having established the connection, he taught the Dhamma by reciting these verses:
“He who, with a stick, offends those who do not deserve a stick,
or who offends those who are innocent, will swiftly encounter one of ten states:
he will experience harsh pain, loss of wealth, or the breaking up of his body.”
One may encounter a severe illness, or even a derangement of the mind;
or a calamity from a king, or a terrible accusation;
or the ruin of kinsmen, or the fragility of wealth.
“Or else his houses the fire consumes;
at the breaking up of the body, that one of poor wisdom is reborn in hell.

In this context, “toward those who do not wield the rod” refers to those whose taints are destroyed and who are free from the rod of bodily action and so forth. “Toward those who are not malevolent” refers to others or to oneself.
"Or toward those who are innocent. "One of ten grounds" means one of the ten causes of suffering.
"Suffering" refers to harsh sensations such as diseases of the head and so forth. "Loss" refers to the loss of wealth acquired with great difficulty.

"Torture" refers to bodily mutilation such as the cutting off of hands and so forth. "Severe" refers to various conditions such as being paralyzed on one side, blindness in one eye, lameness, leprosy, skin diseases, and so forth.

"Serious illness" means a grave affliction. "Mental derangement" means insanity. "Calamity" means a misfortune from the king, such as the loss of one's reputation, being dismissed from the position of commander-in-chief, or the confiscation of property.
"False accusation" means a harsh accusation, such as when one has not seen, heard, or even thought of something, yet is told:
"You committed this act of breaking into houses and so forth, or this act of treason against the king. "Complete ruin" [refers to the total destruction of one's wealth].
"Or relatives" means the destruction of those relatives who are capable of being one's support. "Frail" means the state of being fragile or the state of rotting.
For whatever grain there is in his house, that reaches a state of rot; gold reaches the state of charcoal; pearls reach the state of cotton seeds;
a kahāpaṇa coin reaches the state of potsherds and the like; and bipeds and quadrupeds [reach their end].
The meaning is that they become one-eyed, crippled, and so forth. Regarding "fire burns":

even if there is no other fire to burn it twice or thrice within a single year, it may still burn when struck by a thunderbolt-fire, or it certainly burns when the fire arises through its own inherent nature. Regarding "hell":
even after reaching any one of these ten states in this very life (diṭṭheva dhamme), one will certainly [suffer] in the future life (samparāye).
To show what is to be attained, it was said: "He goes to hell.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the seventh story, concerning the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.
8. The Story of the Monk with Many Possessions (*Bahubhaṇḍika-bhikkhu-vatthu*) "Going about naked is not [the way]":
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, gave this Dhamma teaching concerning the monk Bahubhaṇḍika.
It is said that a certain householder living in Sāvatthī, after his wife had died, went forth into homelessness. When he was going forth, he [took] his own...
Having constructed a courtyard, a fire-hall, and a storehouse, he filled the entire storehouse with ghee, honey, oil, and other provisions, and then went forth.
Having gone forth, he summoned his own slaves and ate whatever food they prepared according to his liking.
He possessed many goods and many requisites; at night, he wore one set of lower and upper garments, and...
During the day he has one set of lower and upper robes; during the day he dwells at the edge of the monastery.
One day, while he was drying his robes and bedding, monks wandering through the lodgings saw him and asked, "Whose are these, friend?
When he replied, "Mine," they said, "Friend, the Blessed One has permitted only three robes, yet you..."
"But having gone forth in the teaching of the Buddha, who is himself so modest in his desires, how have you come to possess such a great abundance of requisites?
Having brought him before the Teacher, they reported, "Venerable Sir, this bhikkhu has far too many belongings.
The Teacher asked, "Is it true, bhikkhus, that this is so? When they replied, "It is true, Venerable Sir," he said, "But why, bhikkhu, have you..."
“While I was teaching the Dhamma out of fewness of desires, such a great quantity of requisites has arisen,” he said.
At that very moment, becoming angry, he thought, “I shall now live according to this manner,” and casting off his upper robe, he stood in the midst of the assembly wearing only a single garment.
Then the Teacher, supporting him, said: “Was it not you, monk, who formerly sought a sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing, even during the time of the water-demon?”
"Seeking shame and fear of wrongdoing, he lived for twelve years;

why then, having gone forth in this so weighty teaching of the Buddha, do you stand here in the midst of the fourfold assembly having cast off your upper robe and abandoned shame and fear of wrongdoing?
Having heard the Teacher’s words, he established shame and fear of wrongdoing, put on that robe, and [approached] the Teacher.
Having paid homage, he sat down to one side. The bhikkhus requested the Blessed One to clarify the meaning of that matter.
The Blessed One brought up the past and spoke:
"In the past, it is said, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in the womb of the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī. Of him..."
On the day of his naming ceremony, they gave him the name Mahimsaka Kumāra. His younger brother was named Candaka Kumāra.
When their mother passed away, the king appointed another woman to the position of chief queen.
She too gave birth to a son, and they gave him the name Suriya Kumāra. Seeing him, the king was delighted and said, "I grant a boon to your son."
"I give it," he said. She, for her part, replied, "Your Majesty, I shall take it at the time I desire.
When her son reached maturity, she said to the king, "Your Majesty, you granted me a boon at the time of my son's birth; now, grant the kingdom to my son.
The king said, "My two sons wander about like blazing masses of fire; it is not possible for him..."

Although he had refused to grant the kingdom, seeing that [the mother] was still entreating him again and again, he thought, "This woman might even bring harm to my sons," and so he summoned his sons, saying, "Sons, at the time of Prince Sūriya’s birth, I granted him a boon;
now his mother asks for the kingdom. I am not willing to give it to him, but his mother—[is she] yours..."
"He might even bring about our ruin; go now, and after dwelling in the forest, come back and take the kingdom upon my passing," he commanded.
When they had paid homage to their father and were descending from the palace, Suriyakumāra, who was playing in the royal courtyard, saw them;
having understood the reason for their departure, he went out with them. At the time when they had entered the Himālayas, the Bodhisatta—
Having left the road and sat down at the foot of a certain tree, he said to Sūriyakumāra:
“Dear son, go to that lake, bathe, drink, and bring water for us as well on lotus leaves.
Now, that lake had been obtained from Vessavaṇa by a certain water-demon (*dakarakkhasa*). And Vessavaṇa had said to him: “Excepting—”
“Whoever knows the divine qualities (*devadhamma*), and others who enter this lake, you may eat them.
From that time on, he would ask those who entered the lake about the divine qualities and eat those who did not know them.
Sūriyakumāra also entered the lake without even investigating it, and when asked, “Do you know the divine qualities? he replied, “The so-called divine qualities...”
He replied, "The moon and the sun. Then, [the rakkhasa] thinking, "You do not know the divine qualities (devadhamma)," made him enter the water and placed him in his own abode.
The Bodhisatta, seeing that he was taking so long, sent Prince Candaka.
He too, when asked by him, "Do you know the divine qualities? replied, "The divine qualities are the four quarters. The water-rakkhasa...
Having caused that water also to enter [the lake], he left it right there.
When the Bodhisatta waited for him for a long time and thought, "There must be some obstacle," he went there himself.
Seeing only the footprints of the two of them leading into the water, and realizing, "This lake is possessed by a rākṣasa," he fastened his sword and took up his bow.
He stood there. Seeing that he was not descending, the rakkhasa approached in the guise of a forest worker and said:
"O man, you are weary from the road; why do you not descend into this lake, bathe, drink, eat the lotus roots and stalks, adorn yourself with the flowers, and then depart?
As soon as the Bodhisatta saw him, he recognized, "This is that yakkha."
Having understood this, he said, "You have seized my brothers. "Yes, they were seized by me," she replied. "For what reason?
"Because I receive them whenever I enter this lake. "But do you receive all of them? "I receive all except those who know the divine qualities (devadhamma).
"Do you have need for these divine qualities? "Yes, I have need of them. "Then I shall explain them to you."
"In that case, tell me," [the Bodhisatta said]. "It is not possible to speak with a defiled body," [the yakkha replied].
The yakkha bathed the Bodhisatta, gave him water to drink, adorned him, and having placed him upon a couch in the center of the decorated pavilion, sat down at his feet.
Then the Bodhisatta, saying to him, "Listen attentively," spoke this verse:
“Those endowed with moral shame and fear of wrongdoing, concentrated in wholesome qualities—the virtuous and true persons in the world—are called ‘those who possess the divine nature.
Having heard this teaching on the Dhamma, the yakkha was inspired with faith and said to the Bodhisatta: “O wise one, I have confidence in you.”
“I give you one brother; which shall I bring? “Bring the youngest. “O Wise One, you know only the divine qualities (*devadhamma*), but you do not practice them.
“For what reason? “Because by setting aside the eldest and causing the youngest to be brought, you do not perform the duty of honoring the elder.
“Yakkha, I indeed know the divine qualities,” he said.
And I shall serve them; for it was by depending on him that we entered this forest.

Indeed, it was for his sake that our mother requested the kingdom from our father, yet our father, instead of granting her that boon, permitted him to dwell in the forest for the purpose of protecting us.
That prince has come along with us, not turning back. [He is alone in the forest.]
"Even if it were said, 'A *yakkha* has eaten him,' no one would believe it. Therefore, fearing the danger of reproach, I had him brought back here.
The *yakkha*, having gained confidence in the Bodhisatta, said, "Excellent, wise man!

You alone know the divine qualities (*devadhamma*), and you conduct yourself according to those divine qualities," and he brought the two brothers and gave them back. Then the Bodhisatta [explained] the disadvantage in the state of a *yakkha*.
Having spoken thus, he established him in the five precepts. With his protection well-arranged by that means, he lived in that forest;
then, when his father passed away, he took the yakkha with him, went to Bārāṇasī, and seized the kingdom.
He gave the position of viceroy to Prince Canda and the position of commander-in-chief to Prince Suriya, and having had a shrine built for the yakkha in a delightful place, he—
He acted in such a way that he attained the pinnacle of gain.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the Rakkhasa was the monk Bahubhaṇḍika;
Suriyakumāra was Ānanda; Candakumāra was Sāriputta; and Mahiṃsakumāra was none other than myself."

Having thus related the Jātaka, the Teacher said: "In this way, monk, having formerly wandered about endowed with moral shame and dread of blame while seeking the qualities of a deity, you have now acted improperly by standing in this manner in the midst of the fourfold assembly before me and saying, 'I am one of few desires.
For it is not merely by the rejection of a garment and such things that one becomes a recluse. Having said this, he spoke further.
Connecting the context and teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
“Neither nakedness, nor matted hair, nor mud, nor fasting, nor lying on the bare ground,
nor the dust and dirt, nor the exertion of squatting— these do not purify a mortal who has not crossed over doubt.”
In this context, *nānāsaka* means not abstaining from food; the meaning is "those who have rejected meals. *Thaṇḍilasāyika* means those who sleep on the bare ground.
*Rajojalla* refers to the dust settled upon the body in the form of a coating of mud. *Ukkuṭikappadhāna* is the exertion of energy undertaken in a squatting posture. This is what is meant:
for that mortal who thinks, "In this way, I shall [attain] that which is called the escape from the world..."
Thinking, “I shall attain purification,” if one were to adopt and practice any of these practices such as nakedness and the like,
one would only increase wrong view and partake in exhaustion. For even if these are well-undertaken,
they do not purify a mortal who has not crossed over doubt, because of the state of not having crossed over the doubt concerning the eight bases.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the eighth story, concerning the monk Bahubhaṇḍika. 9.
The Story of the Minister Santati.
"Even though he was adorned," the Teacher related this Dhamma teaching while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the minister Santati.

At one time, having returned after suppressing a rebellion on the frontier of King Pasenadi of Kosala, the king, being pleased with him, granted him sovereignty for seven days and gave him a woman skilled in dance and song. For seven...

Having been intoxicated by liquor for several days, on the seventh day, adorned with all his ornaments and mounted upon the back of a noble elephant, he was going to the bathing place when he saw the Teacher entering through the gateway for alms.
While still seated upon the back of the noble elephant, he nodded his head, paid homage, and departed. The Teacher smiled and said, “Venerable sir, who is it that has caused you to smile?”
When asked by the Elder Ānanda, "What is the cause? he explained the reason for his smile, saying: "See, Ānanda, the minister Santati!
Today, having come into my presence adorned with all his ornaments, he will attain Arahantship at the conclusion of a four-line stanza;
then, sitting in the air at the height of seven palm trees, he will pass into Parinibbāna. The great multitude [gathered] together with the Elder...
As he was speaking, he heard the words of the Teacher. Thereupon, those of wrong view thought:
“Behold the conduct of the ascetic Gotama! He speaks only what has already reached his ears.
Today, it is said, he will attain final Nibbāna after hearing the Dhamma from him while still intoxicated with liquor and adorned as he is; today we shall refute him with a lie.”

Those possessed of right view thought: "Oh, how great is the majesty of the Buddhas! Today we shall be able to behold both the playful grace of the Buddha and the playful grace of the minister Santati.
The minister Santati, too, having spent part of the day sporting in the water at the bathing place, went to the pleasure garden and to the drinking hall.
He sat down. That woman also descended into the center of the stage and began to perform dance and song.

As she was displaying her dance and song that day—having been without food for seven days in order to show off the grace of her body—winds like knives arose within her womb, tore through the flesh of her heart, and departed.
At that very moment, she [vomited] from her mouth...
He passed away with his eyes wide open. Minister Santati, saying, "Examine [the body]," was told, "It has ceased, sir.
At that very moment, being overwhelmed by intense grief, the seven days of liquor he had drunk vanished like a drop of water from a hot pan.
He thought, "No others can extinguish this sorrow of mine."
“Will they be able [to extinguish it] without the Tathāgata? Surrounded by his retinue, he went to the presence of the Teacher in the evening, paid homage, and spoke thus:
“Venerable Sir, I have come thinking, ‘Such grief has arisen within me;
will you be able to extinguish it for me? Be my refuge. Then the Teacher said to him, “To extinguish this grief…”
"You have come into the presence of one who is indeed capable.
For the tears that flowed from you while weeping at the time of this woman's death in this very manner would exceed the water of the four great oceans. Having said this, he spoke this verse:
"Dry up what was before; let there be nothing for you hereafter."
“If you do not grasp at the middle, you will wander in peace.
At the conclusion of this verse, the minister Santati attained arahantship.
Looking into his own life-force (*āyusaṅkhāra*), he realized that it would no longer continue and said to the Teacher, “Venerable Sir, please grant me permission for final Nibbāna. The Teacher—
Even though he knew the deed that had been done by him, he reflected: "The holders of wrong views who have assembled here for the sake of suppressing him with false speech will find no opportunity;
