however, the holders of right view who have assembled thinking, 'We shall behold both the grace of the Buddha and the grace of the Great Minister Santati,' will, upon hearing of this deed performed by him, apply themselves with diligence to meritorious deeds. Having thus observed, [he said]: "By him..."
“Tell me the deed she committed against me; and when you speak, do not stand on the ground, but speak while standing in the air at the height of seventy palm trees,” he said.

“Very well, Bhante,” he replied, and having paid homage to the Teacher, he rose to the height of one palm tree, descended, paid homage to the Teacher again, and as he rose once more, he ascended in succession to the height of seventy palm trees.
Sitting cross-legged in the air, he said, "Listen to me, venerable sirs, regarding my past karma," and spoke thus:
"In the ninety-first aeon from now, during the time of the Sammasambuddha Vipassi, I was reborn in a certain family in the city of Bandhumatī.
Reflecting on what kind of deed would not cause harm or oppression to others, I investigated and found the work of Dhammaghosa."
Having seen this, from that time forth, while performing that work, I have wandered about inciting the great multitude, proclaiming: "Perform meritorious deeds!
Observe the Uposatha on Uposatha days! Give gifts! Listen to the Dhamma!
There is nothing else equal to the Jewels of the Buddha and the rest; show honor to the Three Jewels! Thus it was for me.
Upon hearing the sound, the Great King Bandhumatī, the father of the Buddha, summoned me and asked, "Dear son, what are you doing as you wander about?

When I replied, "Your Majesty, I am wandering about proclaiming the virtues of the Three Jewels and exhorting the great multitude toward meritorious deeds," he asked me, "Where do you sit while wandering? and I said to him, "On foot, Your Majesty."
When this was said, [the king] replied, "Dear son, you ought not to wander about in such a manner;
put on this flower garland and wander about while seated upon the back of a horse. Having given me a flower garland resembling a string of pearls, he gave me a well-trained horse.
Then, as I wandered about being proclaimed with the same honors bestowed by the king, the king summoned me once again.
“Father, what are you doing as you wander about? he asked. When I replied, “The same thing, Your Majesty,” he said, “Father, even a horse is not suitable for you;
sit here in this chariot and wander. He then gave me a chariot yoked with four thoroughbred horses.
On the third occasion as well, the king heard my voice, had me summoned, and after asking, “Father, what are you doing as you wander about? I replied, “The same thing.”
When he said, "O gods," [the king replied], "Son, even this chariot is not worthy of you.
Having given me a great mass of wealth and magnificent ornaments, he gave me an elephant.

Thus, adorned with all my finery and seated upon the back of that elephant, I performed the work of proclaiming the Dhamma for eighty thousand years; during all that time, the fragrance of sandalwood issued from my body.
A fragrance like that of a blue lotus wafted from his mouth. "This is the deed I have done," he said.
Having thus recounted his own past karma, while still seated in the air, he entered the fire-element and attained final Nibbāna.
A mass of flames rose from his body and consumed the flesh and blood; only his relics remained, like jasmine flowers.
The Teacher spread out a clean cloth, and the relics fell upon it.
Having placed them in a bowl, he had a stupa built at the crossroads, thinking, "The great multitude, by worshipping it, shall partake in merit.
The monks raised a discussion in the Hall of Truth, saying, "Friends, the minister Santati, having attained Arahatship at the conclusion of the verses, was adorned and arrayed just as he was..."
“Having sat in the air, he attained final Nibbāna; is it appropriate to call him a ‘recluse’ (samaṇa), or rather a ‘brahmin’ (brāhmaṇa)?
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what discussion are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very matter,” he said, “Monks, it is appropriate to call my son a ‘recluse,’ and it is also appropriate to call him a ‘brahmin.’”
"It is indeed proper to speak," he said, and while teaching the Dhamma, he uttered this verse: "Even if one is adorned,
if one should live in harmony—
peaceful, self-controlled, resolute, and leading the holy life;"
“He who has laid aside the rod toward all beings—he is a brahmin, he is an ascetic, he is a monk.
In this context, “adorned” means embellished with clothes and ornaments; its meaning is: adorned with garments, jewelry, and so forth.
Even if a person should conduct himself with equanimity in body and so forth— being peaceful through the subsiding of lust and other defilements,
tamed by the restraint of the faculties, fixed by the certainty of the four paths, chaste through the practice of the highest conduct,

and having laid aside the rod toward all beings by virtue of having lowered the physical rod and the rest— such a one, because he has banished evil, is a *brāhmaṇa*, and because he has stilled evil, is a *samaṇa*.
Because their defilements have been shattered, they should indeed be called "bhikkhus.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the ninth story, the account of the minister Santati.
10. The Story of the Elder Pilotika-Tissa "Restraint through moral shame (*hirīnisedho*)"—the Teacher related this teaching on the Dhamma while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the elder Pilotika.
For on one occasion, the elder Ānanda, having taken a bowl and a tattered rag-robe for alms, [was walking along].
Seeing the boy wandering about, he said, "Is renunciation not better for you than living while wandering like this?

When the boy replied, "Venerable sir, who will ordain me? he said, "I shall ordain you," and taking him with him, he bathed him with his own hands, gave him a meditation subject, and ordained him. Furthermore, that piece of ragged cloth which had been worn as a lower garment—
Looking around after stretching out his hand, and seeing no spot at all suitable for receiving even the mere act of straining water,
he placed it together with the bowl upon a branch of a tree. Having gone forth and received full ordination, while enjoying the gains and honors that had arisen for the Buddhas,
and wandering about clothed in costly robes, he became stout of body and grew weary of the world.
Thinking, “What is the use of my wandering about wearing robes given in faith by people?
I shall wear only my own rags,” he went to that place, took up the rag, and said: “O shameless and immodest one!
Having abandoned the covering of such garments as these, you go forth with a bowl in hand to wander for alms while wearing this mere fragment of a rag!”
Making that rag his object of focus, he exhorted himself by means of himself; and as he was thus exhorting himself, his mind became settled.
He tucked that rag away right there, turned back, and went to the monastery. After a few days had passed, becoming weary once more, he spoke in the same way and returned;
again he did the same, and so on. As he was wandering back and forth in this manner—
Seeing him, the bhikkhus asked, "Friend, where are you going? He replied, "Friends, I am going to my teacher.
Following that very same routine, he took his own ragged cloth as his meditation object and restrained himself;
in just a few days, he attained Arahantship. The bhikkhus said, "Friend, why do you no longer go to your teacher's presence?"
“You are going; surely this is your path for wandering? “Friend, when there was association with my teacher, I went;
but now that association has been severed for me, therefore I do not go into his presence. The monks reported this to the Tathāgata:
“Bhante, the elder Pilotika is making a different declaration. “What did he say, monks? “This,” [he replied].
“Yes, venerable sir,” he replied. Having heard this, the Teacher said, “Yes, monks, when there was association, my son went into the presence of his teacher;
but now that association has been severed, having restrained himself by himself, he has attained Arahantship.
Having said this, he spoke these verses:
“There is found in this world a certain man restrained by a sense of shame,
who rouses himself from sleep like a noble horse struck by a whip.
Like a noble horse touched by the whip...”
Be ardent and filled with a sense of spiritual urgency;
through faith, virtue, and energy,
through concentration and discernment of the Dhamma.
"Having perfected knowledge and conduct, being mindful, you shall abandon this no small suffering.
In that context, one who restrains unwholesome thoughts arisen within by means of moral shame is "one restrained by shame" (*hirīnisedha*). "Someone in the world... [refers to]...
Such a person is rare; they exist only somewhere in the world.

One who, being diligent, practices the duty of a recluse while sleeping, and by warding off the sleep that has arisen within himself, awakens—that is, causes himself to wake up—is like a noble horse which, when the whip falls upon it, wards off the whip and does not allow it to fall upon itself. Such is one who [wardes off] sleep...
"He awakens [others]; he is difficult to find—this is the meaning.

This is the summary of the second verse: "Monks, just as a noble horse, having fallen into negligence, makes an effort later on, thinking, 'I too have been struck by the whip,' even so, you too should be ardent."
Be filled with a sense of spiritual urgency; having become thus endowed with the two kinds of faith— mundane and supramundane— with the fourfold purification of virtue,
with physical and mental energy, with the concentration of the eight attainments, and with the discernment of Dhamma characterized by the knowledge of what is possible and impossible,
[you shall attain] the three or eight clear knowledges and the fifteen [aspects of the path].

"By the perfection of conduct, you shall be endowed with both knowledge and conduct (*vijjācaraṇa*). By being mindful through the establishment of mindfulness (*upaṭṭhitasati*), having become possessed of awareness (*patissata*), you will abandon this no small suffering of saṃsāra.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*) and other stages.
The Tenth Story: The Elder Pilotika-Tissa.
11. The Story of the Novice Sukha.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning the novice Sukha, beginning with the words: "For they lead away the water..."
In the past, there was a son of the chief merchant of Bārāṇasī named Gandhakumāra.
When his father passed away, the king summoned him, comforted him, and with great honor bestowed upon him that very position of chief merchant.
From then on, he became known as Gandhaseṭṭhi. Then his treasurer opened the door of the treasury.
"Master," they said, "this much is your father’s wealth, and this much is that of your grandfather and the others," and having brought it out, they showed it to him.
He looked at that heap of wealth and said, "But why did they not go away after taking this wealth?
"Master, there are none who have gone away after taking wealth; for beings depart taking only with them their own wholesome and unwholesome deeds."
He thought: "They have departed after securing their wealth through their foolishness; I, however, shall go only after taking this all.
While thinking thus, he did not consider, "I shall give alms or perform an offering," but instead thought, "I shall eat all of this and then depart.
He spent a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] and [purchased] one made of crystal...
He had a bathing pavilion constructed; having paid one hundred thousand [pieces of gold], he had a bathing slab made of crystal;
having paid one hundred thousand, he had a sitting couch made; having paid one hundred thousand, he had a food bowl made;
and having paid another hundred thousand, he had a pavilion built for the dining area; and having paid yet another hundred thousand, he had a foot-stand made to be placed beneath the food bowl.
He had a lion-window constructed at his house and gave a thousand coins for his own breakfast and another thousand for his dinner.
On the full-moon day, however, he caused a hundred thousand to be given for the meal;
on the day that meal was eaten, he spent a hundred thousand, decorated the city, and had the drum beaten, proclaiming: "It is said that for the merchant Puṇṇama..."
“Let the great multitude look at the manner of his eating.
The great crowd gathered, having tied their beds one above the other.

He too, sitting upon a plank worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] in a bathing pavilion worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], bathed with sixteen jars of scented water and [entered] that lion-window.
Having opened it, he sat down upon that couch. Then, having placed that bowl upon that filled footstool, they increased the food to the value of a hundred thousand pieces of gold.
Surrounded by his theatrical troupe, he partook of that food amidst such splendor.
At another time, a certain village man, for the purpose of bringing provisions for himself—
Having placed wood and other materials in a carriage, he went to the city and took up residence in his friend’s house.
At that time, it was the full moon day. The king caused a drum to be beaten throughout the city, proclaiming: "Let everyone behold the dining splendor of the Perfume Merchant.
Then his friend said to him: "Friend, have you ever seen the dining splendor of the Perfume Merchant before?"
“Never before have I seen such a thing, Sir. “In that case, come, let us go;

the drum is sounding in the city, let us see this great prosperity,” he said, and taking the country-dweller with him, he departed. The great multitude also climbed onto one couch after another to watch.
A village-dweller, having merely smelled the fragrance of the food, said to the city-dweller: “To me...”
“From eating this portion of alms-food, thirst has arisen. “Good man, do not crave for this; it cannot be obtained.

“Good man, if I do not obtain it, I shall not live. Being unable to dissuade him, he stood at the edge of the assembly and, after letting out a great cry three times, saying, “I bow to you, Master,” he was asked, “Who is this? and replied, “It is I, Master.”
“What is this? [They asked. “This one village-dweller has raised thirst for a morsel of food in your bowl;
give him a morsel of food. “It is not possible to obtain it. “What, friend, have you heard?
“I have heard it, but even so, if I obtain it I shall live; if I do not obtain it, death will come to me. He cried out once more.
—“Master, it is said that this man will die if he does not receive anything; please grant him his life.
“Friend, a single morsel of food is worth a hundred, even worth two hundred. If I were to give to whoever asks, what would I have left to eat?
“Master, this man will die if he does not receive anything; please grant him his life. “It is simply not possible.”
"It would be in vain to obtain [it]; however, if he cannot live without it, let him work as a hired servant in my house for three years, and I will have a bowl of rice given to him.

When the villager heard this, he said to his companion, "So be it, good sir," and abandoning his wife and children, he declared, "I shall work as a hired servant for three years for the sake of a bowl of rice."
He entered the house of the merchant. While performing his labor, he carried out all his duties with great care.
Whether in the house or in the forest, by night or by day, every task that was to be done was found to have been completed by him.

When it was said, "The hired laborer," he became known throughout the entire city. Then, when the day had come to an end, the steward of the meal-offering [said] to the hired laborer: "Hired laborer..."
"Master," he said, "the day is full; for three years he has worked as a hired laborer, and not even a single task has ever been spoiled by him.
Then the merchant gave two thousand [pieces] for his own evening and morning meals, and one thousand for the other's morning meal.
Having caused three thousand [pieces of gold] to be given, he said: "Today, perform for him alone the service that is my duty.
Having spoken thus, and having set aside his beloved wife named Cintāmaṇi, he told the rest of the people as well: "Today, attend upon him alone," and he entrusted all his prosperity to him.
He [the merchant] [bathed] with the bathing water of the merchant... him alone.
Seated on that plank in the courtyard, having bathed and dressed himself in that very same lower garment and cloak, he sat upon that very same couch.
The merchant also caused a drum to be beaten throughout the city, proclaiming:
"The food-servant has obtained his bowl after serving three years in the house of the Perfume Merchant; let the great multitude behold the excellence of his meal. The great multitude—
Having climbed from one couch to another above it, he looked out; the spot where the villager was looking back at him began to tremble.
The actors stood surrounding him and placed a bowl of food before him.
Then, at the time when he was about to wash his hands, a Paccekabuddha on Mount Gandhamādana emerged from meditative attainment on the seventh day.
Having risen, he reflected, "Where indeed shall I go today for alms? While considering this, he saw a hired laborer receiving his meal.
Then he reflected, "This man has worked for hire for three years and received a bowl of rice;
does he have faith, or not? Perceiving that he did have faith, [he thought], "Faith too is a form of assistance."
Thinking, "They are not able to do it; will he indeed be able to provide for me?

and realizing, "He will indeed be able to do so, and by means of my providing for him, he will obtain great prosperity," he put on his robe, took his bowl, rose up into the air, went through the midst of the assembly, and showed himself standing right before him.

Thus, seeing the Paccekabuddha, he thought: "In the past, because of my stinginess, I worked as a laborer in another's house for three years for the sake of a single bowl of rice; yet this rice will sustain me for only one day and night.
But if I give it to this noble one, it will sustain me for many thousands of millions of aeons."

“I shall give it to the Noble One himself. Having worked for hire for three years, he refrained from putting even a single morsel of the food he had received into his mouth, thereby subduing his craving.

He then lifted the bowl himself, went into the presence of the Paccekabuddha, placed the bowl into another’s hand, prostrated with the fivefold salutation, and took hold of the bowl with his left hand.
With his right hand, he poured the food into the bowl of the Paccekabuddha. When half of the meal remained, the Paccekabuddha covered the bowl with his hand.
Then he said to him: "Venerable sir, there is but one portion;
it cannot be divided into two. Do not favor me with this world; favor me only with the world beyond. Do not leave any remainder."
“I shall give it entirely without remainder. For when one gives even a small portion of one’s own property without leaving anything behind, it is called a gift without remainder;
such a gift is of great fruit. Acting accordingly, he gave everything away. Then, having bowed once more, he said:
“Venerable sir, for three years I have experienced suffering working as a hired laborer in another’s house on account of this single bowl of rice.”
"Whatever has been experienced by me, may there now be only happiness for me in every place where I am reborn; may I be a partaker of the very same [happiness] you have seen in this present life.

The Paccekabuddha, offering words of appreciation, said: "May it be so! May your mental resolves grant all your desires like a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi), and may they fulfill them like the full moon."
“May everything you desire and aspire to be fulfilled for you;
may all your intentions be accomplished, like the moon on the fifteenth day.
May what you desire and long for be fulfilled for you very quickly.”
"May all my intentions be fulfilled, just like the wish-fulfilling gem (maṇi jotirasa).
Having said this, he resolved: "Let this great multitude remain watching me until we reach Mount Gandhamādana," and he went through the air to Gandhamādana.
The great multitude also remained standing, watching him. Having gone there, he offered that alms-food to five hundred paccekabuddhas.
Having divided it, he gave it away. Everyone took as much as they could carry. One should not think, "The alms-food is small; how can you manage?
For four things are said to be inconceivable, and among them, this is the domain of the Paccekabuddhas.
When the great multitude saw the alms-food being distributed and given to the Paccekabuddhas, they raised a thousand shouts of "Sādhu! (Excellent!).
It was like the sound of a thunderbolt striking the earth. Hearing it, the merchant Gandha thought:
"I suppose this hired laborer was unable to maintain the prosperity bestowed upon him by me; therefore, this great crowd has gathered and is shouting out in derision.
To find out what was happening, he sent men. They returned and said: "They are indeed 'upholders of prosperity'..."

"Master, let it be so," they said, and reported the matter to him. Upon hearing this, the merchant’s body was suffused with five-colored rapture, and he thought, "Oh, what a difficult task he has performed!
For all this time, though established in such prosperity, I have not been able to give anything. He had the man summoned and asked, "Is it true that you did this?"
Having asked, "What was it named? and being told, "Yes, sir," he said, "Well then, take a thousand [pieces of gold] and give me a share in your gift.
He did so. The merchant also gave him everything belonging to himself, dividing it in the middle.

For there are four kinds of excellence: excellence of the object (*vatthusampadā*), excellence of the requisites (*paccayasampadā*), excellence of the volition (*cetanāsampadā*), and excellence of superior qualities (*guṇātirekasampadā*).
In this context, the "perfection of the recipient" (*vatthusampadā*) refers to one who has attained the cessation-attainment (*nirodhasamāpatti*), namely an Arahant or a Non-returner (*anāgāmī*).

The "perfection of the requisites" (*paccayasampadā*) refers to the arising of the requisites through lawful and equitable means. The "perfection of volition" (*cetanāsampadā*) refers to the state of volition being accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge throughout the three periods of time: before the giving, at the time of giving, and after the giving. Regarding the recipient...

The state of having emerged from meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) is called the perfection of the excellence of qualities. Furthermore, for this [offering], the one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), namely the Paccekabuddha, is the field of merit;
the condition arising through the Dhamma by virtue of what is obtained after performing service is the object; the volition (*cetanā*) pure throughout the three times is the intention;
and the mere fact that the Paccekabuddha has just emerged from meditative attainment is the excellence of qualities—thus all four perfections (*sampadā*) are accomplished.
By the power of these [meritorious deeds], they attain great prosperity even in this very life. Therefore, that man received prosperity from the merchant.

Later on, when the king heard of the deed he had performed, he summoned him, gave him a thousand [pieces of gold], and having accepted the gift, being well-pleased, bestowed upon him a vast mass of wealth and granted him the position of chief merchant.
They gave him the name Bhaṭṭabhatika-seṭṭhi. Having become a friend to the merchant Gandha-seṭṭhi, eating and drinking together with him, he lived out his full lifespan;
then, passing away from there, he was reborn in the world of the gods.

After enjoying divine splendor for the duration of one interval between Buddhas, during this present arising of a Buddha, he was born in Sāvatthī into a family that served as attendants to the Elder Sāriputta.
He took rebirth. Then, after his mother had received the necessary care for her pregnancy, after a few days had passed, she thought:
"Oh, that I might give delicious food to five hundred bhikkhus along with the Elder Sāriputta;
and having dressed myself in saffron robes and taking a golden bowl, sitting at the edge of their seats, I might consume the remnants of what those bhikkhus have left over."
Having become pregnant with longing, she satisfied that longing by acting accordingly. She likewise gave gifts on other auspicious occasions as well;
then, after giving birth to a son, on the day of the naming ceremony, she said to the Elder, "Venerable Sir, please give the precepts to my son.
The Elder asked, "What is his name? [She replied: "Venerable Sir, from the time my son took rebirth..."
When it was said, "From the time he was born, no suffering has ever occurred in this house;
therefore, his name shall be 'Sukhakumāra' (Joy-Child)," they took that very name for him and gave him the precepts.
At that moment, a thought arose in his mother's mind: "I will not thwart my son's aspiration."
She gave him gifts in the same manner even for auspicious occasions such as the piercing of his ears.
When the boy was seven years old, he said, "Mother, I wish to go forth into homelessness in the presence of the Elder. She replied, "Very well, dear son;
I shall not thwart your intention," and having invited the Elder and fed him, she said, "Venerable sir, my son wishes to go forth..."

“I wish to bring him to the monastery this evening. Having dismissed the elder and gathered his kinsmen, he said, “Today we shall perform the duties that must be done for my son during his time as a householder.
He adorned his son and, leading him with great splendor and majesty to the monastery, entrusted him to the elder. The elder also addressed him, saying, “Dear son, the going-forth...”
Having said, "It is indeed difficult [to live as a monk]; will you be able to find delight [in it]?
and being told in reply, "Venerable sir, I shall follow your advice," he gave him a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) and ordained him.

His parents, honoring his ordination, provided food of a hundred flavors for the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha within the monastery itself for seven days, and in the evening they returned to their own home.

They arrived. On the eighth day, when the Saṅgha of bhikkhus had entered the village, the Elder Sāriputta performed whatever duties were to be done in the monastery, had the novice take his bowl and robes, and entered the village for alms.
Along the way, seeing the water-channels and other features, the novice questioned them just like a learned novice; the Elder likewise answered him accordingly. The novice—
Having heard those reasons, he said, "If you would take your own bowl and robes, I shall turn back.
Without breaking the Elder's resolve, the Elder said, "Novice, give me my bowl and robes.

When the bowl and robes had been taken, the novice paid homage to the Elder and, as he was turning back, said, "Venerable sir, while providing food for me, [you have provided] food of a hundred flavors..."
"Bring it," he said. "Where shall we obtain that? "If you cannot obtain it through your own merit, you shall obtain it through my merit, venerable sir.
Then the Elder gave him the key and entered the village for alms.
He too, having returned to the monastery, opened the Elder’s cell, entered, closed the door, and sat down, directing his knowledge into his own body.
By the power of his virtue, Sakka’s seat showed signs of becoming hot. Sakka, wondering, "What can this be?", looked around;
seeing the novice, he thought, "The novice Sukha has given his own bowl and robes to his preceptor and turned back, thinking, 'I shall practice the duties of a recluse.
It is fitting for me to go there. Having thus reflected, he summoned the four Great Kings.
“Go, dear ones, and drive away the noisy birds in the grove of the monastery,” he commanded.
Having done so, they took up their posts as guards around it. He ordered the moon and sun, “Remain holding your celestial mansions.
They did likewise. He himself took up a guard at the entrance. The monastery was completely settled.
He became silent. With a one-pointed mind, the novice increased his insight and attained the three paths and fruits.
The Elder, reflecting, "The novice said, 'Please bring food with the hundred flavors'; in whose house could this possibly be obtained?
saw a devoted attendant who possessed the right disposition. Having gone there, he said, "Venerable sir,..."
“It is well done by you today for coming here,” he said. With delighted minds, they took his bowl, seated him, and gave him rice gruel and solid food.
When they requested a Dhamma talk until mealtime, he delivered a discourse on the qualities that lead to harmony.
Having observed the time, he brought the teaching to a conclusion. Then, after they had given him food of a hundred flavors, he—
Seeing the Elder desiring to depart after taking his bowl, they said, "Eat, venerable sir;
we shall give you more," and having fed the Elder, they gave him another bowl full. The Elder took it and, thinking, "The novice is hungry," set out for the monastery with great haste.
On that day, the Teacher had gone out early in the morning and, while sitting in the Perfumed Chamber, reflected:
“Today, after giving his bowl and robes to his preceptor, the novice Sukha turned back, thinking, ‘I shall perform the duties of a recluse.
Has he accomplished his task? Seeing that he had attained the three paths and fruits, and further investigating, [the Elder] perceived:
“This novice will be able to reach Arahantship today; however, Sāriputta said—”
Thinking, “He thinks, ‘I am hungry,’ and will leave in haste taking his food; if he brings the food before attaining Arahantship, there will be an obstacle for him.
It is fitting that I go and take up guard at the gate-tower,” he emerged from the Gandhakuṭī, stood at the gate-tower, and took up guard.
The Elder also brought food. Then, in the same manner as described above, he asked him four questions.
At the conclusion of the answers to the questions, the novice attained Arahatship. The Teacher addressed the Elder, saying, "Go, Sāriputta, give this novice his meal.
The Elder went and knocked at the door. The novice also came out to his preceptor.
Having performed his duties, when he was told, "Perform your meal duty," the boy realized that the Elder had no need for food;
at that very moment, the seven-year-old boy attained Arahatship. Reflecting on his low seat, he performed his meal duty and washed his bowl.
At that time, the Four Great Kings assigned him protection, and even the moon and sun [did so].
They released their celestial chariots. Sakka, too, stationed his guards at the points of entry.
The sun appeared as soon as it had passed the middle of the sky. The bhikkhus said, "It is now evening, yet the novice has just finished his meal;
why is it that today the forenoon was so powerful and the afternoon so weak? The Teacher arrived and—
“Monks, for what discussion have you gathered here now? he asked. When they replied, “Venerable sir, today the morning was strong and the evening has become weak;
the novice has just finished his meal, yet the sun is already seen to have passed the meridian of the sky,” the Buddha said, “Monks, it is even so for those possessed of merit.”
At the time of performing the duties of a recluse. For today the Four Great Kings have taken up their positions as guards nearby;
the moon and sun have taken their celestial mansions and stood still; Sakka has taken up his guard at the drawbridge; and I too have taken up my guard at the gate-tower.
Today, while the novice Sukha is fetching water from the pond, and the fletcher is straightening his arrow—
"Having seen carpenters fashioning wheels and other objects, he tamed himself and attained arahantship," he said, and then recited this verse:
"The channel-makers lead the water; the fletchers straighten the arrow-shaft;
the carpenters bend the wood; but those of good vows tame themselves."
In this context, "well-trained" (*subbatā*) means well-disciplined; the sense is that they are easily to be exhorted and instructed. The remainder is exactly as explained in the method below.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and the other fruits.
This is the eleventh story, the Story of the Novice Sukha.
The commentary on the Daṇḍavagga is finished.
The tenth chapter. 11.
The Jarāvagga (Chapter on Old Age).
1. The Story of Visākhā’s Friends "What laughter?
What joy?"—the Teacher related this Dhamma teaching while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the friends of Visākhā.
It is said that in Sāvatthī there were five hundred sons of noble families who thought, "In this way, these women shall dwell in heedfulness."
Each of them entrusted their wives to Visākhā, the Great Laywoman. Whenever they went to a park or a monastery, they went together with her.

At one time, when the festival was announced with the cry, "For seven days there will be a liquor festival," each of them prepared liquor for their respective husbands. For those seven days, the liquor festival...
Having played, on the eighth day, when the work-bell rang out, they went to their respective workplaces.
Those women thought, "We were not permitted to drink liquor in the presence of our husbands; there is still liquor remaining, so we shall drink it in such a way that they do not know.
They went to Visākhā and said, "Noble lady, we wish to go to the park."
Having said, "I have seen them," and being told, "Very well, mother; having performed the duties that must be done, you may depart," she went with her.
They had wine brought out in a concealed manner, drank it in the park, and wandered about intoxicated.
Visākhā thought, "What these women have done is improper; now they will say, 'Visākhā, the disciple of the ascetic Gotama, [drank] wine...'"
Thinking, "The followers of other sects will also censure us, saying, 'Having drunk [liquor], she wanders about,'" he said to those women: "Ladies, you have done what is improper;
disgrace has been brought upon me as well, and your husbands will be angry. What will you do now? They replied, "Noble sir, we shall feign illness.
He said, "In that case, you will be known by your own deed. They went home.
Having gone there, they made a pretense of being ill. Then their husbands asked, "Where are so-and-so and so-and-so?
When they heard that they were ill, they reflected, "Surely these women must have drunk the remaining liquor," and having beaten them, they brought them to ruin and disaster.
On another festival day as well, they desired to drink liquor in the same manner.
Having approached Visākhā and said, "Noble lady, please take us to the park," they were refused by her, who replied, "Previously you caused me ill repute;

go away, I will not take you. Having deliberated among themselves, saying, "We will not act this way now," they approached her again and said, "Noble lady, we wish to perform an offering to the Buddha; [we wish to go to] the monastery..."
“No, indeed. “Then it is fitting now, mother; go and prepare the festival offerings.
They had fragrant garlands and other items placed in baskets, hung small vessels filled with liquor from their hands, and covered themselves in large cloths.
Approaching Visākhā and entering the monastery with her, they went to one side and, using those very small vessels...
Having drunk the liquor and discarded their garments, they sat down in the Dhamma hall in front of the Teacher.
Visākhā said, "Venerable Sir, please preach the Dhamma to these women.

At that moment, their bodies were trembling from the force of intoxication, and they gave rise to the thought, "Let us sing! Let us sing! Then, a certain deity belonging to the host of Māra, having taken possession of their bodies—
Thinking, "I shall display a performance before the ascetic Gotama," he took possession of their bodies.
Some among them began to clap their hands and laugh before the Teacher, while others began to dance.
The Teacher, reflecting on what this was, understood the reason and thought: "Now the hosts of Māra will find no opportunity."
“I shall give [my life]. For I have not fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) for so long a time for the sake of finding an opportunity against the hosts of Māra,” he said.
To stir them with a sense of urgency, he emitted rays from the hairs of his eyebrows; instantly, there was a blinding darkness.
They became terrified, struck by the fear of death. By that means, the wine in their wombs was digested. The Teacher—
Vanishing from his seated cross-legged posture, he stood upon the summit of Mount Sineru and emitted a ray of light from the hair between his eyebrows;
at that very moment, it was as if a thousand moons had risen simultaneously. Then the Teacher addressed those women:
"It is not fitting for you to come into my presence while being heedless. For it is through your own negligence that the deities belonging to Māra’s host—"
“Having found an opportunity, you caused laughter and the like to be performed even at a time when laughter and the like were inappropriate;
now it is fitting for you to exert yourselves in order to extinguish the fires of lust and the other defilements. Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“What laughter, what joy can there be, while [the world] is constantly ablaze?”
“Enveloped in darkness, you do not seek a lamp.

In this context, *ānanda* means joy. This is what is meant: while this dwelling in the world is constantly ablaze with the eleven fires such as lust and the rest, what laughter or joy can there be for you? Is this not indeed something that ought not to be done?
"Enveloped as you are by the darkness of ignorance consisting of eight bases,
for what reason do you not seek nor produce the lamp of knowledge in order to dispel that very darkness?
At the conclusion of the teaching, those five hundred women were established in the fruit of stream-entry.
The Teacher, knowing that their faith was firmly established and unshakable, descended from the summit of Sineru and sat upon the Buddha’s seat.
Then Visākhā said to him: “Venerable Sir, this liquor is indeed evil.
For such women as these, sitting before a Buddha like you, were unable to maintain even their basic posture.”
“Having risen and clapped their hands, they began laughing, singing, dancing, and so forth. The Teacher said, “Yes, Visākhā, this so-called ‘liquor’ is indeed evil.
For by depending on it, many beings have met with ruin and disaster.
When she asked, “But when, Bhante, did it first arise? he brought forward the past in order to relate its origin in detail.
He related the Kumbha-jātaka.
This is the first story concerning Visākhā’s companions.
2. The Story of Sirimā.
The Teacher delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, "Behold the mind-made," while dwelling at Veḷuvana, concerning Sirimā.

It is said that she was a beautiful courtesan in Rājagaha. However, during one rainy season, having offended the wife of the merchant Puṇṇaka—the daughter of the merchant Sumanaseṭṭhi, a lay follower named Uttarā—and desiring to appease her, he...
Having finished his meal with the community of monks at home and having asked the Teacher for forgiveness, he listened that day to the Teacher’s expression of gratitude for the meal and said:
“Conquer anger with non-anger; conquer the wicked with goodness.”
“One should conquer the miser with generosity, and the speaker of falsehood with truth.
At the conclusion of this verse, he attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). This is the summary here;
the detailed explanation, however, will appear in the commentary on the verses of rejoicing in the *Kodhavagga*. Having thus attained the fruit of stream-entry, Sirimā...
Having invited the One Possessed of the Ten Powers, on the following day he gave a great almsgiving and caused the Saṅgha to receive a regular meal of eight dishes.
From that time forward, eight bhikkhus went to his house regularly. Saying, "Take ghee!
Take milk! and so forth, he filled their bowls. What one had received, [he would share] with three or even four.
It was sufficient. Every day, almsfood was provided for him at a cost of sixteen kahāpaṇas.
Then one day, a certain bhikkhu ate a meal of eight-course food at her house and went to a monastery three leagues away.
When he was sitting in attendance upon the Elder that evening, they asked him: "Friend, from where did you come after receiving alms?"
“Sirimā said, ‘I have eaten a meal of eight kinds of curry. [The other replied,] ‘She gives it with affection, friend.
‘It is impossible to praise her meal; she gives it having prepared it with extreme refinement. What one person receives is enough for three or four.
Yet, even compared to her gift, the sight of her is superior. For such is that woman, and such is she.’”
Thus he praised her virtues.
Then, one bhikkhu, having heard this account of her virtues, developed an affection for her despite never having seen her;
thinking, "It is right for me to go and see her," he stated his seniority and asked that bhikkhu about the order of precedence.
Having heard, "Friend, tomorrow in that house you will receive the eight-course meal as the senior monk of the Saṅgha," he took his bowl and robes at that very moment and departed;

yet, having entered the hall for the distribution of voting tickets (salākagga) early in the morning when the dawn had risen, he stood there as the senior monk of the Saṅgha and received the eight-course meal in that house. But as for the bhikkhu who, having eaten yesterday...
She departed, and at the very moment of her departure, a disease arose in the horse’s body. Therefore, she removed her ornaments and lay down.
Then her female slaves, having received food for the eight [monks], saw the monks who had arrived and informed her.
Unable to take the bowls with her own hands to have them sit down or to serve them, she commanded her slaves: "Ladies..."

“Noble ladies, having taken the bowls, having had [the bhikkhus] sit down, having given them rice-gruel, and having given them fresh food, fill their bowls at the time for the meal and give them to me.

They replied, “Very well, noble lady,” and having ushered the bhikkhus in, given them rice-gruel, given them fresh food, and filled their bowls with the meal at the time for the meal, they informed her. She said, “Escort me, having surrounded me.”
Having said, "Noble ladies, I shall pay homage," she was escorted by them to the presence of the monks;
with her body trembling, she paid homage to the monks. That monk, looking at her, thought: "Such is the beauty of her form even while she is ill;
but when she is healthy, adorned with all her ornaments, what kind of perfection of form will she possess?"
Then, after many tens of millions of years, a defilement that had been accumulated within him became active. Having become ignorant, he was unable to eat his meal;
taking his bowl and going to the monastery, he covered the bowl, set it aside in a corner, spread out his robe, and lay down.
Then, even though one of his companions tried to entreat him, he was unable to feed him. Thus, he remained with his meal cut off.
On that very day, in the evening, Sirimā passed away. The king sent a message to the Teacher:
“Venerable Sir, Sirimā, the younger sister of Jīvaka, has died. When the Teacher heard this, he sent a message back to the king:
“There is no need for the cremation of Sirimā; let her be placed in the raw-corpse cemetery so that crows, dogs, and other such creatures do not devour her.”
“Having laid him down in that manner, guard him. The king did exactly so. After three days had passed in succession, on the fourth day the body swelled;
worms oozed out from the nine openings of the wounds, and his entire body became as shattered as a bowl of cooked rice.
The king caused a drum to be beaten throughout the city, proclaiming: “With the exception of the household guards...”
“A fine of eight kahāpaṇas shall be imposed on those who do not come to see the child Sirimā.
He also sent a message to the Teacher, saying: “Let the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, headed by the Buddha, come to see Sirimā.
The Teacher announced to the bhikkhus: “We shall go to see Sirimā. That young bhikkhu also—
For four days he lay down without taking any food, having rejected the words of anyone. The food in his bowl became putrid, and filth arose within the bowl.
Then that companion monk approached him and said, "Friend, the Teacher is going to see Sirimā.
Although his stomach was thus famished, at the very word "Sirimā," he [arose].
Rising up suddenly, he asked, "What are you saying? When it was said, "The Teacher goes to see Sirimā; will you go as well?
he replied, "Yes, I shall go. Discarding his meal, washing his bowl, and placing it in its bag, he went forth together with the community of monks.
The Teacher stood to one side surrounded by the community of monks, and the community of nuns also [stood there].
The assembly of kings, the assembly of laymen, and the assembly of laywomen also stood on each side.
The Teacher asked the king, "Who is this, Great King? "Venerable Sir, she is Jīvaka’s sister;
her name is Sirimā. "Sirimā, is it? "Yes, Venerable Sir. "In that case, have the drum beaten in the city, saying: 'Having given a thousand [pieces of gold]...'"
“Let them take it for a price. The king did so. Not even one person said, “I will,” or “I shall.
The king reported to the Teacher, “They do not take it, Bhante. “In that case, Great King, set a price,” he said.
The king had a drum beaten, proclaiming, “Let them take it for five hundred [pieces],” yet no one would take it.

Having seen this, he had a drum beaten, proclaiming: "Let those who wish to take the glory give two hundred and fifty, two hundred, one hundred, fifty, twenty-five, ten, five, one, half a kahāpaṇa, a quarter, a māsaka, or even a kākaṇika!
No one desired it. He then had the drum beaten again, saying: "Let them take it for free!"
He caused [it] to be proclaimed: "There was no one who would say 'Yes' or 'No'. The King said, "Venerable sir, there is no one at all who will take her even for nothing.
The Teacher said, "See, monks, how dear this woman is to the great multitude!
Previously, in this very city, they obtained her by paying a thousand [pieces of gold] on a single day; now, there is no one who will take her even for nothing. Such is she..."
"Behold, monks, this diseased personal existence—name-and-form that has reached its end and dissolution," he said, and then uttered this verse:
"Behold this painted image, a heap of sores piled together;
Diseased and full of many thoughts, it has no lasting stability."
In this context, *cittakaṃ* means "variegated," the sense being that it is made variegated by garments, ornaments, garlands, lac, and so forth.
*Bimbaṃ* refers to the physical form (*attabhāva*) configured with long and other such limbs and members in their respective places.

*Arukāyaṃ* refers to a body that has become a wound (*aru*) by way of the nine openings. *Samussitaṃ* means "constructed" or "assembled" by means of three hundred bones. *Āturaṃ*... [means "afflicted"].
"Always ill" means that one must constantly attend to him through the postures and other such means. "Conceived in many ways" means it is conceived in many ways by the multitude of people.
"Of which there is no permanent stability" means that for which there is neither a state of permanence nor a state of stability;
its nature is exclusively one of breaking up, scattering, and destruction—look at this! is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, eighty-four thousand beings attained penetration of the Dhamma, and that monk also was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
This is the second story, concerning Sirimā.
3. The Story of the Elder Nun Uttarā.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, "All this is utterly decayed," concerning a nun named Uttarā Thera.
It is said that when the nun, who was one hundred and twenty years of age, went for alms and received food, she saw a certain monk in the middle of the street;
she invited him to share her alms, and as he took it all without declining her offer, [she gave it to him].

Having given [the food], she remained without food. In this same way, on the second and third days as well, having given alms-food to that very bhikkhu at that very spot, she remained without food. But on the fourth day, while wandering for alms, she saw the Teacher in a crowded place;
as she was stepping back, she stepped on the corner of her own robe which was hanging down.
Unable to remain steady, she turned over and fell. The Teacher went to her side and, saying, "Sister, this body of yours is decayed;
it will soon break apart," he spoke this verse:
"This form is utterly decayed, a nest of disease, fragile;”
"The putrid body breaks apart, for life ends in death.
This is its meaning: Sister, this form of yours, known as the body, is worn out by old age;
moreover, it is a nest of disease in the sense that it is the dwelling place of all diseases. Just as even a young jackal...
It is called a "cracked jackal"; even a young *gaḷocī* creeper is called a "rotten creeper.
Likewise, although this body is golden-hued when first born, it is fragile due to its state of rot from the quality of constant oozing.
Being thus rotten, this body of yours breaks apart; it should be understood that it will break apart before long. For what reason? Because it ends in death.
"Because for all beings, life ends in death"—this is what is meant.
At the conclusion of the teaching, that elder nun attained the fruit of stream-entry, and the Dhamma instruction was beneficial for the great multitude as well.
This is the third story, the Story of the Elder Nun Uttarā.
4. The Story of the Many Arrogant Bhikkhus Regarding the teaching "Those who are arrogant," the Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke concerning many arrogant bhikkhus.
It is said that five hundred bhikkhus, having received a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) from the presence of the Teacher, entered the forest and applied themselves to it.
Exerting themselves, they attained meditative absorption (*jhāna*) and thought, "Our purpose in going forth has been fulfilled by the non-manifestation of the defilements;
we shall report the qualities we have acquired to the Teacher.
When they had reached the outer gateway, the Teacher said to the Elder Ānanda: "Ānanda, let these monks enter so that I may see them."
“There is no need for work; let them go to the raw charnel ground and, returning from there, see me. The Elder went and informed them of this matter.

They replied, “What use have we for the raw charnel ground? However, without saying more, thinking, “The Buddha, who sees far into the future, must have seen a reason,” they went to the raw charnel ground. While looking at the corpses there—some fallen for one or two days—[they saw...]
Having conceived hatred toward the corpses, they gave rise to lust for those fresh bodies that had fallen at that very moment;

at that instant, they recognized their own state of defilement. While seated in the Fragrant Chamber, the Teacher radiated light and, as if speaking directly in the presence of those bhikkhus, said: "Bhikkhus, is this not unbecoming?"
“Having seen such a heap of bones as yours, how could you give rise to the delight of passion? Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“These things which are unlovely, like dried gourds in the autumn— Seeing these bones, grey as pigeon-droppings, what delight can there be?”
In this context, "cast away" means discarded.
"In autumn" means during the autumn season, like gourds scattered here and there, battered by wind and sun. "Dove-colored" means having the color of doves.
"Having seen those"—having seen such bones as these—what pleasure do you find? The meaning is: surely it is not even fitting to take the slightest pleasure in sensual desires.
At the conclusion of the teaching, those bhikkhus, having attained Arahantship while remaining exactly where they stood, approached and paid homage to the Blessed One while offering him praise.
This is the fourth story, concerning the many conceited bhikkhus. 5.
The Story of the Elder Nun Rūpanandā, the Beauty of the Land.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, gave this Dhamma teaching concerning the nun Rūpanandā, the "Beauty of the Land," beginning with the words: "A city has been built of bones.

It is said that one day she thought to herself: "My elder brother, having renounced the glory of kingship, went forth and became a Buddha, the Supreme Person in the world; his son, Prince Rāhula, has also gone forth; and my husband too has gone forth."
“My mother has also gone forth; since so many of my kinsmen have gone forth, what shall I do staying at home? I too shall go forth.
She went to the nuns’ quarters and went forth out of affection for her relatives, not out of faith; however, because of her great beauty, she became known as Rūpanandā.
[The people said: “It is said that the Teacher teaches: ‘Form is impermanent, suffering, and non-self; feeling... perception... volitional formations...’”
Having heard it said, “Consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and non-self,” she thought, “He might speak of faults even in my own form,

which is so beautiful and lovely,” and thus she did not go into the presence of the Teacher. Meanwhile, the residents of Sāvatthī, having given alms early in the morning and observed the Uposatha vows,
with their upper robes purified and carrying perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in their hands, [assembled] at Jetavana in the evening.
Having assembled, they listen to the Dhamma. The community of bhikkhunīs, too, having developed a desire for the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, goes to the monastery and listens to the Dhamma.
Having heard the Dhamma, as they enter the city, they enter while speaking only of the Teacher’s virtues.
In this world inhabited by the four measures, those beings are indeed few who do not develop faith upon seeing the Tathāgata.
For some, having seen the Tathāgata’s golden-hued body adorned with the primary and secondary marks, develop faith;
while others, having heard the Teacher’s voice—which has proceeded for many hundreds of lifetimes—develop faith.
Having heard the sound of his virtues and the sound of his teaching of the Dhamma endowed with the eight factors, they gain confidence;
those who take the coarse as their standard gain confidence because of the coarseness of his robes and so forth, while those who take the Dhamma as their standard gain confidence, thinking:
"Such is the virtue of the One Possessed of Ten Powers, such is his concentration, such is his wisdom; the Blessed One is peerless and has no equal in qualities such as virtue."
As they spoke thus of the Tathāgata’s virtues, their mouths could not suffice.
Having heard this discourse on the virtues of the Tathāgata from the bhikkhunīs and laywomen headed by Rūpanandā, she thought:
“They speak only of my brother’s virtues; how much could he possibly say in a single day were he to speak of the faults in my form? What if now I—”
“Having gone with the bhikkhunīs, let her go without showing herself, see the Tathāgata, listen to the Dhamma from him, and then return.
She announced to the bhikkhunīs, “I too shall go today to hear the Dhamma.
The bhikkhunīs said, “It has been a long time indeed since Rūpanandā felt such a desire to go into the presence of the Teacher. Today—”
Thinking, "Relying on this, the Teacher will teach the Dhamma in various ways through diverse methods," they departed with joyful hearts, taking her with them.
From the moment she left, she thought to herself, "I shall not show myself.
The Teacher thought, "Today Rūpanandā will come to attend upon me; what kind of Dhamma teaching will she receive?"
Thinking, "What is suitable? he reached the conclusion: "She is one who prizes physical form and has a strong attachment to her own person;
therefore, just as a thorn is extracted with a thorn, the crushing of her intoxication with form by means of form itself is what is suitable.
Then, at the time of her entering the monastery, [he saw] a beautiful woman about sixteen years of age, dressed in red garments.
By means of his supernormal power, he manifested a woman adorned with every ornament, who stood near him fanning him.
Both the Teacher and Rūpanandā saw that woman.
Having entered the monastery together with the bhikkhunīs, she stood behind the bhikkhunīs and prostrated herself before the Teacher with her five limbs touching the ground.

Having paid homage, she sat among the bhikkhunīs; looking at the Teacher from the tips of his feet upward, she beheld the Teacher’s body, variegated with the primary marks, radiant with the secondary characteristics, and encircled by a fathom-wide halo.
Then, gazing upon his face, which possessed the splendor of the full moon, she saw a female form standing nearby. Having looked at that, she looked at her own body.
She despised herself as being like a female crow in the presence of that golden royal swan.
Indeed, from the very moment she saw that form created by psychic power, her eyes rolled about. Thinking, "Oh, how beautiful are her hair! Oh, how beautiful is her forehead!
her mind was completely captivated by the splendor of every part of that body, and she felt a powerful attachment toward that form.
The Teacher, knowing her attachment there, while teaching the Dhamma, caused that form to pass beyond the appearance of a sixteen-year-old and made it appear as a twenty-year-old.

Upon looking at it, Rūpanandā thought, "This form is indeed not like the former one," and her mind became slightly dispassionate. The Teacher, by gradual stages, [then showed] that woman... once again.
He showed her the forms of women of different ages: a middle-aged woman, and an old, decrepit, elderly woman.

She too, in due course, thought, "This one has vanished, that one has vanished," and as she grew weary of them, upon seeing one who was aged and decrepit—with broken teeth, grey hair, a bent back like a roof-rafter, leaning on a staff, and trembling—she became utterly disgusted.
Then the Teacher, having caused her to be overcome by that disease, showed her [the woman].
At that very moment, she cast away both her staff and her palm-leaf fan, let out a great cry, fell to the ground, and wallowed back and forth, submerged in her own urine and excrement.
Seeing this as well, Rūpanandā became utterly disgusted. The Teacher also [foretold] the death of that woman.
She displayed it. At that very moment, it became bloated; pus and maggots flowed from its nine openings, and crows and other scavengers gathered and tore at it. Seeing this, Rūpanandā thought:
"This woman has reached old age right here, she has reached sickness, she has reached death; even for her—"
"In this very way, old age, sickness, and death will come to my own selfhood (attabhāva). Thus she saw the selfhood as impermanent.
Because it was seen as impermanent, it was necessarily seen as suffering and non-self.
Then the three realms of existence (bhava) appeared to her like a house on fire and like a corpse tied to her neck; [her mind] turned toward the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).
Her mind leapt forward. The Teacher, knowing that she had perceived the state of impermanence, looked to see whether she would be able to establish her own footing by herself;
thinking, "She will not be able; it is necessary for her to obtain external conditions," he taught the Dhamma according to what was suitable for her and said:
“Behold, Nanda, this body: afflicted, impure, and putrid;
oozing and trickling, it is craved by fools.
As is this, so is that; as is that, so is this.”
“See [the world] as empty by way of its elements; do not return to the world again.
Having abandoned desire for existence, he will wander, being at peace.
Thus indeed, with reference to the bhikkhunī Nandā, the Blessed One spoke these verses. Nandā, following the sequence of the teaching...

Having directed her knowledge [toward this], she attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). Then, in order to explain the meditation subject of emptiness (*suññatā-kammaṭṭhāna*) for the sake of her cultivation of insight (*vipassanā-parivāsa*) for the three higher paths and fruits, [the Teacher] said:
"Nandā, do not form the perception that 'there is an essence in this body.
For there is not even the slightest essence here; this is merely a city of bones constructed by piling up three hundred bones."
Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“A city has been built of bones, plastered with flesh and blood;
therein are laid down old age and death, pride and hypocrisy.”

The meaning of this is as follows: Just as people build an external house called a "city" for the purpose of storing rice, grain, and so forth— by piling up timber, binding it with creepers, and plastering it with clay—
so too is this internal [body] constructed by piling up three hundred bones, bound together with sinews, plastered with flesh and blood, covered with skin, and characterized by decay.

This city was built for the purpose of depositing death, which has the characteristic of aging and dying, pride, which has the characteristic of conceiving based on the perfection of one's ascent and so forth, and hypocrisy, which has the characteristic of destroying well-done causes.
For it is precisely such physical and mental affliction that has been deposited here; beyond this, there is nothing further to be grasped.
At the conclusion of the teaching, that elder nun attained Arahatship, and the Dhamma instruction was fruitful for the great multitude as well.
Thus ends the fifth story, the Story of the Elder Nun Rūpanandā, the Beauty of the Land.
6. The Story of Queen Mallikā.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, "They decay," concerning Queen Mallikā.
It is said that one day, having entered the bathing pavilion and washed her face, she began to wash her legs with her body bent over.
A favorite dog of hers had entered along with her; seeing her thus bent over, [he...]
Having seen her, he began to engage in unrighteous intimacy with her. She stood there, relishing his touch.
The king, looking down from the upper palace through a window, saw her; when she returned, he said, "Begone, you outcaste! Why have you done such a thing?
"What have I done, Your Majesty? "Intimacy with a dog! "That is not so, Your Majesty. "By me..."

“I have seen it myself; I will not believe you. Begone, you outcaste! “Great King, anyone who has entered this courtyard appears as one person yet seems to be two when viewed through this window,” she said, speaking what was untrue.
“Your Majesty, if you believe me, enter this courtyard; I shall [show you] through this window.”
"I shall look," she said. The king, being of deluded nature, believed her words and entered the inner chamber.
The queen, standing at the window and looking out, said, "O blind fool, Great King, what is this?
Are you having an intimacy with a goat? Even when he replied, "I do not do such a thing, my lady," she [continued], "By me in person..."
“I have seen it; I will not believe you,” she said.
Hearing this, the king thought, “Surely this man has entered the inner chamber alone, yet he appears as two”;
thus he believed her. Mallikā thought: “This king has been deceived by me through my foolishness; a wicked deed has been done by me, and he—”
"Having been falsely accused, this deed of mine the Teacher will know, and the two Chief Disciples and the eighty Great Disciples will also know;

alas, what a heavy deed I have committed! It is said that she was a companion to the king during his peerless almsgiving, and on one occasion there, she made a renunciation of wealth worth fourteen koṭis.
The white parasol, the sitting couch, the footstool, and the foot-stand belonging to the Tathāgata—these four, however, were priceless.
At the time of her death, she did not recall such a great act of relinquishment, but instead recalled that very evil deed;
having passed away, she was reborn in Avīci. To the king, moreover, she was exceedingly dear.
He was overcome by intense grief. After performing the funeral rites for her body, he went into the presence of the Teacher, thinking, "I shall ask where she has been reborn.
The Teacher acted in such a way that he did not remember the reason for his coming.
When he heard the discourse on the qualities that lead to remembrance (*sāraṇīya-dhamma-kathā*) in the presence of the Teacher, he remembered it upon entering his home. He thought, "Alas! I..."

Thinking, "I will go to the presence of the Teacher and ask about the place where Mallikā was reborn," she went to the Teacher but forgot; thinking, "I will ask again tomorrow," she went there on the following day as well.
For seven days in succession, the Teacher acted in such a way that she did not remember.
Having been cooked in hell for exactly those seven days, she passed away from there on the eighth day.
He was reborn in the Tusita heaven. But why did the Teacher cause her to become homeless?

It is said that she was exceedingly dear and pleasing to him; therefore, upon hearing that she had been reborn in hell, he fell into a wrong view, thinking, "If one so endowed with faith can be reborn in hell, what is the use of giving alms? and thus adopted such a misconception.
If one were to cause the permanent meal provided for five hundred bhikkhus in a house to be taken away, one would be reborn in hell; yet,
because the Teacher had rendered that person refuge-less for seven days, on the eighth day, while wandering for alms,
he went of his own accord to the gate of the royal palace.
When the king heard that the Teacher had arrived, he went out, took his bowl, and began to ascend the palace.
However, the Teacher signaled that he wished to sit in the chariot-hall.

The king had the Teacher sit right there, honored him with rice gruel and solid food, and after bowing down, remained seated and said: "Venerable Sir, as for the place where Queen Mallikā was reborn..."
Thinking, "I shall ask," he went there, but he forgot; he asked, "Venerable sir, where has she been reborn?
"In the Tusita realm, Great King. "Venerable sir, since she was not reborn in the Tusita realm, who else will be reborn there?
Venerable sir, there is no woman equal to her. For wherever she sat or stood, [she would think], 'Tomorrow I shall give this to the Tathāgata.'"
"Having made this provision for giving, thinking 'I shall do this,' there is no other duty for her at all, venerable sir;
from the moment she passed away to the next world, my body has not been able to carry on.
Then the Teacher said to him, "Do not worry, Great King; this is the constant law for all," and he asked, "Great King, to whom does this chariot belong?"
Having heard this, the king placed his palms together in reverence upon his head and said, "Venerable Sir, that belongs to my grandfather.
"And whose is this? "Venerable Sir, it belongs to my father. "But whose is this chariot? "Venerable Sir, it is mine.
When this was said, the Teacher replied, "Great King, your grandfather’s chariot was not of the same appearance as your father’s chariot," and so forth.
"Your father’s chariot has reached [old age], but your chariot has not yet reached it;

even for such a thing as a wooden block, old age arrives—how much more so for a physical body? Great King, indeed, only the Dhamma of the True Men is free from old age, but there are no beings who are called 'ageless,'" and having said this, he spoke this verse:
“Indeed, even well-adorned royal chariots wear out,
and likewise the body also succumbs to decay;
but the Dhamma of the virtuous does not age.”
“Sages indeed proclaim this to the virtuous.
Herein, *ve* is a particle. Even the chariots of kings—well-adorned with the seven jewels and other chariot ornaments—wear out.
“The body too”: not only the chariots, but even this well-tended body [wears out].
One who reaches states such as being broken or maimed undergoes aging.
But for the "good"—that is, for the Buddhas and others—the ninefold supramundane Dhamma does not undergo any impairment; thus it is said that they do not undergo aging.
"They proclaim" means that the good ones, the Buddhas and so forth, speak together with the wise and learned.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the sixth story, that of Queen Mallikā. 7.
The Story of the Elder Lāḷudāyin.
"Those who have heard little," the Teacher spoke this teaching on the Dhamma while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the Elder Lāḷudāyi.
It is said that he would go to the houses of those performing auspicious rites and speak inauspicious things in such a manner as, "They stand beyond the walls," and so forth;
whereas when going to the houses of those performing inauspicious rites, he would say what ought to be said regarding the "beyond the walls" and other such matters: "And generosity... [and so on].
He would recite either the *Maṅgala-gāthā* according to the method beginning with "The practice of Dhamma," or the *Ratana-sutta* beginning with "Whatever wealth there is here or in the world beyond.
Thus, even when he was reciting one thing while intending to recite something else in those various places, he did not realize, "I am reciting something else.
When the monks heard his discourse, they reported it to the Teacher: "What is this, Bhante?"
“Because Lāḷudāyin goes from auspicious places to inauspicious ones, he says one thing when something else ought to be said.
The Teacher said, “Monks, it is not only now that he speaks thus; in the past as well, he said one thing when something else ought to be said.
Having said this, he related the past:
It is said that in the past, in Bārāṇasī, a son of a brahmin named Aggidatta, Prince Somadatta by name, attended upon the king.
He was dear and pleasing to the king. However, the brahmin lived by means of agricultural work;
he had only two oxen, and one of them died. The brahmin said to his son: "Dear Sonadatta, [go to] the king..."
“Go and ask for one ox from me. Somadatta thought, “If I ask the king myself, my insignificance will be made known,” and so he said, “Dear son, you yourself must ask the king.
When told, “In that case, dear son, take me with you and go,” he reflected:
“This brahmin is dull-witted; he does not even know how to speak such words as ‘approach’ (abhikkama) and so forth.”
"He does not know; he says one thing when something else ought to be said.

However, after I have had him trained, I shall take him away. Taking him with him, he went to a cemetery called Bīraṇatthambhaka, tied bundles of grass together, assigned names to them—saying, "This is the king, this is the viceroy, this is the commander-in-chief"—and showed them in succession to his father, saying, "By you, the royal family..."
"Having gone there, you must advance in this manner, retreat in this manner; the king must be addressed thus, and the viceroy thus.
But having approached the king, saying 'Victory to you, Great King!', and standing thus, you should recite this verse and ask for the ox. And he had them learn the verse:
“Great King, I have two oxen with which we plow the field;
one of them is dead, O Lord, so give me the second, O Khattiya.
For he, having mastered that verse in the space of a single year, informed his son of its mastery.
When he said, “In that case, dear son, take some kind of gift and come;
I will go on ahead and wait in the presence of the king,” they replied, “Very well, father.

Having taken the gift, while they were standing in the presence of King Somadatta, he went to the royal palace with great enthusiasm. Being greeted with a joyful mind by the king, [the king said], “Dear son,…”
When he was told, "It has been a long time indeed that you have come; sit on this seat and say what you need," he spoke this verse:
"O Great King, I have two oxen with which we plow the field;
one of them is dead, O Lord, so take the second, O Khattiya."
When the king said, "What are you saying, dear? Speak again," he recited that same verse.
The king, having become disenchanted with him and realizing the state of his speech, smiled and said, "Somadatta, I imagine there are many oxen in your house.
When [the brahmin] replied, "There will be many, Your Majesty, those given by you," the king was pleased with the Bodhisatta and [bestowed wealth] upon the brahmin.
Having given sixteen oxen, ornaments, and a village for his residence as a royal grant (*brahmadeyya*), he sent the brahmin away with great honor.
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said: "At that time, King Ānanda was [the king], the brahmin was Lāḷudāyī, and Somadatta..."
"But it was I myself," he said, identifying the Jātaka. "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, because of his own lack of learning, this man would say one thing when something else ought to be said. For a man of little learning is indeed like an ox.
Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“This man of little learning grows old like an ox;
his flesh increases, but his wisdom does not increase.
In this context, “of little learning” means having learned only one or two *paññāsakas*. Alternatively, it refers to the very least of the *vaggas*.
By way of limited comprehension, he is one who has heard little because he lacks even one or two discourses (*suttanta*).
However, having mastered a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) and applying himself to it, he is indeed one who has heard much. "He grows old like a bullock":

for just as a bullock, while growing old and increasing in size, does not grow for the benefit of its mother, nor its father, nor its other relatives, but rather increases in vain; so too is this person.

It decays; even so, this person too does not perform the duties toward his preceptor, nor the duties toward his teacher, nor the duties toward newcomers and so forth, nor does he apply himself to the delight of meditation.
He decays in vain, his flesh merely increasing—just like an ox in the forest that has been abandoned because it is "incapable of pulling the yoke, the plough, and so on."

Just as the flesh of one who wanders about, eats, and drinks increases, so too, for this person who has been left by his preceptor and others, who relies on the Saṅgha and obtains the four requisites, and who nourishes the body by performing purgatives and other treatments, the flesh increases;
he wanders about having become stout-bodied. "His wisdom" refers to both mundane and supramundane wisdom.

His wisdom does not increase by even a single finger’s breadth; rather, the meaning is that craving and the ninefold conceit increase in dependence upon the six sense-doors, like the *gaccha* and *lata* creepers in the forest.
At the conclusion of the teaching, the great multitude attained the fruit of stream-entry and the other stages.
The seventh story: The Elder Lāḷudāyi.
8. The Story of the Udāna:

"Through many a round of births..."—the Teacher, while seated at the foot of the Bodhi tree, uttered this teaching on the Dhamma as an inspired utterance (*udāna*). Later, when asked by the Elder Ānanda, he explained it.
For while sitting at the foot of the Bodhi tree, even before the sun had set, he shattered the host of Māra during the first watch;
in the middle watch, he dispelled the darkness that obscures the recollection of past lives and purified his divine eye;
and in the last watch, out of compassion for sentient beings, he applied his knowledge to the nature of conditions and, contemplating them in forward and reverse order, [attained full awakening].

At the time of sunrise, having fully awakened to supreme perfect enlightenment, he uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*) that has never been abandoned by hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, and spoke these verses:
“Through many births in saṃsāra, I have wandered without finding rest;”
Seeking the house-builder, one undergoes birth again and again, which is suffering.
"O house-builder, you are seen! You shall build no more houses.
All your rafters are broken; the ridge-pole is demolished."
“The mind has reached the unconditioned; it has attained the destruction of craving.

In this context, “seeking the house-builder” means: while seeking the builder of this house—which is designated as the self-existence—the mason that is craving—I [sought] for the sake of that Bodhi-knowledge by which it is possible to see him, at the feet of Dīpaṅkara.

"Having made the resolution, for so long a time throughout this cycle of existence—consisting of many births, numbering many hundreds of thousands of births—I have wandered and transmigrated, failing to find and failing to obtain that knowledge;
'aparāparaṃ anuvicariṃ' means I moved about from one state to another. 'Birth is suffering again and again' refers to the search for the builder of the house."

This is a statement of the reason. Because this thing called birth—mingled with aging, sickness, and death—is painful to undergo again and again, and because it does not cease as long as that [birth] is not seen;
therefore, the meaning is that they will run on in search of it. "You have been seen" means:
"Now you have been seen by me, who has penetrated the knowledge of omniscience. "Again to the house" means: again into this cycle of saṃsāra.
"You shall not build my house, which is known as the self-body (attabhāva). All your rafters are broken"—all your remaining rafters of defilement (*kilesa*) have been shattered by me.
"The peak of the house is destroyed"—the central pillar (*kaṇṇika-maṇḍala*) of this house of the self-body built by you, which is known as ignorance (*avijjā*), has also been demolished by me.
"The mind has reached the unconditioned (*visaṅkhāra*)"—now...
My mind has gone to, has entered into, Nibbāna which is beyond all formations, by way of making it its object.
"I have attained the destruction of craving"—that is, I have realized Arahantship, which is known as the destruction of cravings.
This is the eighth Udānavatthu.

9. The Story of the Son of the Wealthy Merchant Mahādhana "By not practicing," the Teacher related this teaching on the Dhamma while dwelling at Isipatana in the Deer Park, concerning the son of the wealthy merchant Mahādhana.
It is said that he was born in Bārāṇasī into a family possessing a fortune of eight hundred million. Then his parents thought:
“In our family there is a vast mass of wealth; having placed it in the hands of our son, we shall enjoy it as we please.
There is no need for him to perform any other work. Thus they had him trained solely in dancing, singing, and instrumental music.
In that same city, a daughter was also born into another family possessing eighty crores of wealth. Her parents likewise—
Having thought thus, they taught him nothing other than dancing, singing, and instrumental music. When they reached maturity, they were married.
Subsequently, their parents passed away. Two hundred and eighty million pieces of wealth were in a single household.
The merchant’s son went to attend upon the king three times a day. Then, while he was there—
In the city, the scoundrels thought: "If this son of a merchant is a drunkard, it will be convenient for us;
