let us teach him the habit of drunkenness. Taking liquor, they tied snacks, meat, salt, and sugar to the ends of their garments, and carrying radish roots, they [waited] for him as he was returning from the royal palace.
Sitting there and watching the road, they saw him approaching;
having drunk liquor, thrown salt crystals into their mouths, and bitten into radish roots, they said, "Live for a hundred years, Master, son of a merchant!
Because of you, we shall become capable of eating and drinking. Hearing their words, he [looked back] at those coming from behind.
He asked his junior attendant, "What are these people drinking? "A certain drink, sir. "Is it of a pleasant kind? "Yes, sir;
in this world of the living, there is nothing else fit to be drunk like this.
Thinking, "If that is so, it is right for me to drink it too," he had it brought to him in small amounts and drank it. Then, before long, those rogues...
Knowing his state of intoxication, they surrounded him. As time passed, his retinue became large.

Having had wine brought by means of a hundred or even two hundred [coins], he drank while, in this very sequence, placing heaps of kahāpaṇas at his various sitting and standing places as he drank the wine, saying:
"With this, bring garlands; with this, perfumes; this person is skilled in jewelry."
"This is for dancing, this for singing, this for instrumental music. Give a thousand for this one, two thousand for that one.
Wasting his own wealth in this manner, he soon exhausted eighty million pieces of gold.
When it was said to him, "Your wealth is exhausted, sir," he replied, "Does my wife have nothing belonging to her? "She has, sir. "In that case, bring it here."

Having squandered that as well in the same manner, he gradually consumed everything belonging to him—fields, monasteries, parks, and so forth, down even to vessels and utensils, rugs, coverlets, and mats—after selling them all.
Then, in his old age, those by whom his family’s house had been sold and taken over expelled him from that house. He [addressed] his wife...
Taking up residence by leaning against the wall of another person’s house,
he began to wander for alms with a broken potsherd and eat the leavings of people.
Then one day, while standing at the door of the dining hall, he saw the leavings of food being given to young novices.
Seeing him receiving [the alms], the Teacher manifested a smile. Then the Elder Ānanda asked the reason for the smile. As the Teacher explained the reason for the smile, he said:

"Behold, Ānanda, this son of a wealthy merchant who has squandered eighty-two crores of wealth in this city, yet having taken a wife, wanders about for alms. For if he had been in his first stage of life..."
If he had not squandered his wealth but had applied himself to business, he would have become the foremost merchant in this very city.
But if he had gone forth into homelessness, he would have attained Arahantship, and his wife would have been established in the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmiphala).
If, in middle age, he had not squandered his wealth but had applied himself to business, he would have become the second merchant; [and] having gone forth...
If he had gone forth [in his youth], he would have become a non-returner (*anāgāmī*). His wife, too, would have been established in the fruit of a once-returner (*sakadāgāmiphala*).
If, in his later years, instead of squandering his wealth, he had applied himself to his business, he would have become the third merchant;

even if he had gone forth after renouncing the world, he would have become a once-returner, and his wife would have been established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*). But now, even from his household wealth...
"He has fallen away even from the state of a recluse. Having fallen away, he has become like a heron in a dry pond," and having said this, he spoke these verses:
"Having failed to practice the holy life, and having failed to acquire wealth in youth..."
They meditate like old herons in a pond whose fish have been exhausted:
"Having lived without practicing the holy life and having gained no wealth in their youth,
they lie down sighing over the past, like arrows shot from a bow."
In this context, "not having lived it" means not having dwelt in the life of celibacy (*brahmacariya*).
"In youth" means at a time when one is capable of acquiring wealth that has not yet arisen, or protecting wealth that has already arisen; [such people] do so even without obtaining any wealth.
"Like fish in a dried-up pond": those fools, like aged cranes whose wings are worn out in a pond where the fish have perished due to a lack of water, brood in distress.
This is what is meant: just as there is an absence of water in a pond, so too there is an absence of a dwelling place for these;
just as there is an absence of fish when they have perished, so too there is an absence of wealth for these;
and just as there is an absence of flight for cranes whose wings are worn out, so too these are now incapable of securing wealth by means of sea, land, or other paths.
Therefore, like cranes whose wings have been clipped, they remain stuck right there and do not fly away.
"Exhausted from the bow" (*cāpātikhīṇā*) means exhausted beyond [the range] of the bow; the meaning is that they are released from the bow. This is what is intended:
just as arrows released from a bow travel according to their momentum and fall, and when no one picks them up to lift them, they become food for the termites right where they lie, so too...
These three, having passed beyond their prime, will now approach death because they are incapable of saving themselves.
Therefore it is said: "They lie like arrows shot from a bow.
They lie lamenting and grieving, reminiscing about things done in the past—such as eating, drinking, dancing, singing, and playing music—thinking, "Thus we ate; thus we drank."
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the ninth story, concerning the son of the wealthy merchant.
The commentary on the Chapter on Old Age is finished.
The Eleventh Chapter.
12. The Chapter on the Self. 1. The Story of Prince Bodhi.
The Teacher delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, "Attānañca," while dwelling in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, concerning Prince Bodhi.

It is said that after having a palace named Kokanada built— unlike any other on the surface of the earth, appearing as if it were soaring into the sky— he asked the architect, "Have you ever before built such a palace elsewhere?"
"Or is this your very first craft? When he replied, "It is my very first craft, Your Majesty," the King thought:
"If he builds such a palace for anyone else as well, this palace will cease to be extraordinary.
It is right that I should have him killed, or have his hands and feet cut off, or pluck out his eyes. Thus...
“He will not build another palace. He told this matter to his dear friend, the young brahmin named Sañjīvakaputta.
The latter thought: “Without a doubt, he will cause the carpenter to perish;
he is an artisan of priceless skill. Let him not perish while I am looking on; I shall exercise restraint over him. He approached him and said, “Regarding the palace—”
Having asked them, "Is your work finished? and being told, "It is finished," he said, "A prince wishes to destroy you;
you must protect yourself. The carpenter replied, "Master, you have done us a great service by informing me;
I shall know what needs to be done here. [The king] asked, "What is it, my friend? Is the work on our palace finished?"
Questioned by the prince, he replied, "Not yet, Your Majesty; much remains unfinished. "What work remains? [the prince asked].
"I shall explain later, Your Majesty; for now, have timber brought," he said. "What kind of timber?
"Timber that is sapless and dry, Your Majesty. Having had it brought, he gave it to him. Then he said to him: "Your Majesty..."
“From this day forward, you must not come into my presence. For what reason?
Because when I am performing delicate work while conversing with others, my work is distracted; however, at the time for food, my wife alone shall bring me my meal.
The prince agreed, saying, “Very well. He too sat down in a private chamber.
Having cut those logs, he fashioned a Garuḷa bird capable of sitting inside his own house for his wife and children;
then, at the time for food, he said to his wife, "Sell everything available in the house and take the gold and bullion.
The prince, meanwhile, surrounded the carpenter’s house with a guard to prevent him from leaving.

He placed [the bird] there. When the carpenter had finished his work with the bird, he said to his wife, "Come today taking all the children with you," and having eaten his morning meal, he caused his wife and children to sit inside the belly of the bird, exited through a window, and fled.
He went while they were still crying out, "Your Majesty, the carpenter is fleeing! and reached them.
Having descended into the Himalayas and established a city, he became known as King Kaṭṭhavāhana.

The prince, thinking, "I shall build a palace," invited the Teacher and, having decorated the palace with four kinds of fragrant scents, spread out a cloth from the very first flight of steps. It is said that he was childless.
Therefore, thinking, "If I obtain either a son or a daughter, the Teacher will step upon this," he spread it out.
When the Teacher arrived, he prostrated himself before the Teacher with the fivefold greeting, took his bowl, and said, "Enter, Bhante.
The Teacher did not enter; he requested him a second and a third time. Without entering, the Teacher—
He looked toward the Elder Ānanda. The Elder, by the mere sign of being looked at, understood that the cloths were not being stepped upon;
he had the cloths gathered up, saying, "Prince, let the cloths be gathered; the Blessed One will not step on a cloth-mat;
the Tathāgata is looking toward future generations. Having had the cloths gathered, he [led] the Teacher into the inner residence.
Having entered and honored him with rice gruel and solid food, he sat to one side, paid homage, and said:
"Venerable sir, I am your benefactor; I went for refuge three times. It is said that while still in the womb, I went for refuge once;
a second time when I was a young child; and a third time when I had attained the age of discretion. Why, then, [do you give me] only this rag-robe?"
“Did he not step on it? “But what were you thinking, young man, when you spread out the cloths?
“Thinking, ‘If I obtain a son or a daughter, the Teacher will step upon my cloth-covering,’ I did so, venerable sir.
For that reason, he did not step on it. “But am I not going to obtain a son or a daughter, venerable sir?”
“Yes, Prince. “For what reason? “Because in a previous existence I fell into negligence with my wife.
“At what time, Bhante? Then the Teacher brought up the past and showed it to him:
“In the past, it is said, many hundreds of people set out upon the ocean in a great ship. In the middle of the ocean, the ship—”
The ship broke apart. The husband and wife took hold of a single plank and entered an intermediate island;
all the others died right there. Now, on that island lived a great flock of birds.
Seeing no other food, and being tormented by hunger, they roasted the bird eggs in the embers and ate them. When those were insufficient, they [ate] the fledglings.
They took them and ate them. Thus they continued eating in the first stage of life, in the middle stage of life, and even in the final stage of life.
They did not attain heedfulness in even a single stage of life, nor did even one among them attain heedfulness.
Having shown this past karma of his, the Teacher said, "If you, young man, at that time—even in a single stage of life..."
If you had practiced heedfulness together with your wife, a son or daughter might have been born to you even at one stage of life.
But if even one of you had been heedful, then on that account a son or daughter would have been born to you.
Prince, by regarding oneself as dear, one must protect oneself through heedfulness during all three stages of life; thus—
"Even if one is unable [to protect oneself], one must at least guard against even a single lapse," he said, and then spoke this verse:
"If one should know oneself to be dear, one should guard it well-guarded;
during one of the three watches of the night, the wise person should remain awake."

In this context, the Teacher taught by designating one of the three stages of life as "yāma" (the watch) due to his own mastery of the Dhamma and skill in teaching; therefore, the meaning here should be understood in this way:
"If he would know himself to be dear, he would guard him well-guarded"—that is, he would guard him in such a manner that he becomes well-guarded.
In this regard, even if one is a householder and, thinking "I will protect myself," enters a well-guarded inner chamber on the upper floor of a palace and dwells there with full protection;
or even if one has gone forth and dwells in a cave where doors and windows are well-secured and closed—one still does not truly protect oneself.
However, being a householder, one [protects oneself] by means of giving, virtue, and so forth, according to one's ability.
One who performs meritorious deeds, or one who has gone forth and exerts himself in the duties, the secondary duties, and the study of the scriptures, is said to protect oneself.
Thus, even if a wise person is unable to do so during all three stages of life, he still looks after himself in at least one of them.
For if, while being a householder in the first stage of life, he fails to perform wholesome deeds due to being addicted to play and pleasure—
If one is unable [to practice in youth], one should perform wholesome deeds with diligence during middle age.
If, while supporting one's wife and children during middle age, one is unable to perform wholesome deeds, then they must certainly be performed in old age.
Even by acting in this way, one has truly looked after oneself. However, for one who does not act thus, even their own self is not beloved; such a person is destined solely for the states of misery.

He does not do it. However, if one who has gone forth falls into negligence while reciting, memorizing, or teaching in the first stage of life, or while performing his duties and obligations, then in the middle stage of life he must practice the duty of a recluse with diligence.

If, having mastered the scriptures in the first stage of life, he asks questions regarding the commentaries, the detailed expositions, and what is appropriate or inappropriate in the middle stage of life...
One falls into negligence; therefore, even in the final stage of life, the duty of a recluse must indeed be performed with heedfulness.
By acting in this way, one truly looks after oneself. But for one who does not act thus, there is no such thing as a "dear self"; rather, it torments him with subsequent remorse.
At the conclusion of the teaching, Prince Bodhi was established in the fruit of stream-entry, and the discourse on the Dhamma was fruitful for the assembled multitude as well.
The First Story of Prince Bodhi.
2. The Story of the Elder Upananda the Sakyan:
Regarding this Dhamma teaching, "First, one must master oneself," the Teacher spoke while residing at Jetavana concerning Upananda the Sakyan.
It is said that the Elder was skillful at preaching the Dhamma.
Having heard his discourse on the Dhamma connected with fewness of desires and other virtues, many bhikkhus honored him with their three robes and undertook the ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas).
He alone took possession of the requisites they had relinquished. When one rainy season was drawing to a close, he went to the countryside. Then, in a certain...
In another monastery, young novices, out of affection for the preacher of the Dhamma, said, "Venerable sir, please spend the rains retreat here.
Having asked, "How much is received here as the rains-retreat gift?
and being told by them, "One robe each," he left his sandals there and went to another monastery. Having gone to that second monastery, he asked, "What is received here?"
Having asked, when it was said, "Two garments," he placed his walking staff there. Going to the third monastery, he asked, "What is obtained here?
When it was said, "Three garments," he placed his water-pot there.
Going to the fourth monastery, he asked, "What is obtained here? When it was said, "Four garments," [he said], "Excellent, here..."
Thinking, "I shall dwell there," he entered the rains retreat at that place and gave Dhamma discourses to both householders and monks.

They honored him with many cloths and robes. Having completed the rains retreat, he sent word to the other monasteries as well, saying, "Because I have set aside requisites, I am entitled to receive the *vassāvāsika* (rains-retreat gift); let them send it to me."
Having had everything brought forth and filled a carriage, he set out.

Then, in a certain monastery, two young bhikkhus, having obtained two pieces of cloth and one woolen blanket, were unable to divide them—saying, "Let the cloths be yours, the blanket is mine"—and so they sat down near the road and quarreled. He [the king] saw them...
Seeing the elder approaching, they said, "Venerable sir, please divide [the robes] for us and give them to us. He replied, "You yourselves must divide them.
They said, "We cannot do it, venerable sir; you yourself must divide them for us. He said, "In that case, will you abide by my word? "Yes, we will abide by it.
"Then very well," he said, and giving them two pieces of cloth, he said, "This one shall preach the Dhamma..."
"This is worthy of being worn by us who are speaking," he said, and taking a costly woolen blanket, he departed.
The young bhikkhus, filled with remorse, went into the presence of the Teacher and reported the matter to him.
The Teacher said, "Bhikkhus, it is not only now that he has taken what belongs to you and caused you remorse; he did so in the past as well."
Having said this, he related a story from the past:

"In the past, two large fish named Anutīracārī (The Shore-Walker) and Gambhīracārī (The Deep-Walker), having caught a great rohita fish, fell into a dispute, saying, 'Let my head be mine, and let your tail be yours.
Unable to divide it, they [sought the help] of a jackal..."
Seeing him, they said, "Uncle, divide this and give it to us. I replied, "I have been appointed by the king to the seat of judgment;
having sat there for a long time, I have come here for the sake of walking meditation. Now I have no leisure. They said, "Uncle, do not do this;
divide it and give it to us. "Will you abide by my word? "We will abide by it, Uncle."
“Very well,” he said, and having cut off his head, he placed it to one side, and his tail to another side.
Having done so, he addressed them, seeking to convince them: “Sirs, let him who has been moving along the shallow bank take the tail;
let him who has been moving in the deep water have the head. But this middle section shall belong to me, as I abide by the law of justice. Thus he informed them.
“The tail shall move along the bank, the head shall move in the deep water, and the middle section shall remain motionless; thus shall it belong to one established in the Dhamma.
Having spoken this verse, he took the middle section and departed. They too, feeling remorseful, stood looking after him.
Having shown this past event, the Teacher made the monks understand by saying, "In this very way, even in the past,
he caused you to feel remorse," and while censuring Upananda, he said, "Monks, one who advises another must first establish himself in what is appropriate," and spoke this verse:
“First, one should establish oneself in what is suitable;
then one may instruct others, and thus the wise person will not be defiled.
In this context, “establish in what is suitable” means one should settle [oneself] in appropriate virtues. This is what is meant: whoever...

One who desires to instruct another in qualities such as fewness of wishes, or in the practice of the noble lineages (ariyavaṃsa), and so forth, should first establish himself in those very qualities. Having established himself thus, he may then instruct others in those qualities.
For one who, without settling himself therein, instructs only others, becomes defiled when he receives blame from others.
"Indeed, by establishing oneself there [in virtue] and instructing others, one receives praise from others; therefore, one is said not to be defiled.
Acting thus, the wise man would not be defiled.
At the conclusion of the teaching, those bhikkhus were established in the fruit of stream-entry, and the Dhamma discourse was beneficial for the great multitude as well.
The second story: The Elder Upananda the Sakyan.
The third story: The Elder Padhānika Tissa.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning the Elder Padhānika Tissa, beginning with the words, "And himself..."
It is said that after receiving a meditation subject from the Teacher, he took five hundred bhikkhus and entered the rains retreat in the forest.
Having exhorted them, saying, "Friends, you have received your meditation subjects in the presence of the living Buddha;
therefore, practice the duty of a recluse with diligence," he himself went to lie down and fell asleep. During the first watch of the night, those bhikkhus...
Having walked for meditation during the middle watch, they enter the monastery.
He, having fallen asleep, goes to them when he awakens and says, "Did you come here thinking, 'We shall lie down and sleep'? Quickly go out and perform the duties of a recluse!
Having said this, he himself goes back and sleeps just as before. The others, having walked for meditation outside during the middle watch, [return].
In the last watch of the night, they entered the monastery.
He woke up again, went to them, led them out of the dwellings, and having returned himself, lay down to sleep just as before.
While he was constantly acting in this way, those monks were unable to attend to their recitation or their meditation subject; their minds became distracted.
Thinking, "Our teacher is exceedingly energetic; we shall keep watch over him," they kept watch.
Seeing his activity, they said, "We are lost, friends! Our teacher is crying out an empty cry.
While they were excessively exhausted by sleepiness, not even a single bhikkhu was able to produce any distinction [in spiritual attainment]. Having completed the rains retreat...
Having gone into the presence of the Teacher, they were received by him with greetings;

when asked, "Monks, what have you been doing while practicing the duty of a recluse with diligence? they reported that matter to him. The Teacher said, "Monks, it was not only now that he created an obstacle for you;
even in the past he did so," and at their request—
“Reared neither by mother nor father, dwelling in a family that knows no discipline, this cock does not distinguish between the proper time and the improper.
Having related this *Akālarāvī-kukkuṭa-jātaka* in detail, he said: “For at that time, that cock was this very Elder Tissa the Striver (*padhānika*).”
“Those five hundred monks were those young brahmins, and I myself was the teacher renowned throughout the land,” the Teacher said, having related this Jātaka in detail.
Then, saying, “Monks, one who advises others must first make himself well-tamed;
for it is by being thus tamed that one truly disciplines others,” he spoke this verse:
“If one would act toward oneself as one instructs another, then, being well-tamed oneself, one should tame [others];
for indeed, it is said that the self is difficult to tame.
The meaning of this is: when a bhikkhu, having said to another, “One should walk back and forth during the first watch and so forth,” gives him such advice...

When one is undertaking the walking meditation and other practices, if one were to act toward oneself in the same way that one instructs others—thinking, "In this way, being well-tamed, one should tame"—then by whatever quality one instructs another, one should tame oneself having become well-tamed by that very quality.
For it is said, "The self is indeed difficult to tame"; for this which is called the "self" is indeed hard to tame. Therefore, just as that [other] is well-tamed...
"He exists; he must be tamed accordingly.
At the conclusion of the teaching, those five hundred bhikkhus attained arahantship.
This is the third story, concerning the Elder Tissa the Striver.

4. The Story of the Elder Nun Kumārakassapa’s Mother The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching beginning with “Self is indeed the lord of self,” concerning the mother of the elder Kumārakassapa.
It is said that she was the daughter of a wealthy merchant in the city of Rājagaha, and from the time she reached the age of discretion, she requested ordination.
Then, although she requested again and again, she did not obtain the going forth from her parents;
having reached marriageable age, she went to her husband's family and lived at home as one who treats her husband as a deity.
Not long after that, a fetus was established in her womb. Without realizing that a fetus had been conceived, she gratified her husband and [sought] the going forth.
She made her request. Then, having led her to the nuns' quarters with great honor, he—being unaware of the situation—ordained her in the presence of the nuns who were partisans of Devadatta.
At a later time, when the nuns learned of her pregnancy, they asked her, "What is this?
She replied, "I do not know, noble ladies, what this is; my virtue, indeed, has remained entirely intact."
The bhikkhunīs, having led her into the presence of Devadatta, asked, "This bhikkhunī has gone forth out of faith;
we know that she is pregnant, but we do not know the time [of conception]. What shall we do now?
Devadatta, thinking only, "Let no disgrace arise for the bhikkhunīs who give me instruction," said:
“Expel her! he said. Hearing this, the young woman said, “Noble lady, do not destroy me!
I did not go forth for the sake of Devadatta; come, lead me to the Teacher at Jetavana. They took her and went to Jetavana and informed the Teacher.
Although the Teacher knew that she had conceived a child while she was still a householder, [he acted] for the purpose of clearing away the slander of others.
Having summoned King Pasenadi of Kosala, Mahā Anāthapiṇḍika, Cūḷa Anāthapiṇḍika, the female lay follower Visākhā, and other prominent families, he commanded the Elder Upāli:
“Go, perform the formal act for this young bhikkhunī in the midst of the fourfold assembly. The Elder, having summoned Visākhā in the presence of the king, said:
He concealed that legal matter. Having had a curtain wall erected, she watched from within the curtain the hands, feet, navel, belly, and limbs of that woman;
then, calculating the months and days, she realized, "This woman conceived while still a householder," and informed the Elder of this matter.
Then, in the midst of the assembly, the Elder established her innocence. At a later time, she...
She gave birth to a son of great majesty who had made his aspiration at the feet of Buddha Padumuttara.
Then one day, as the king was passing near the nuns' quarters, he heard the sound of the child and asked, "What is this?
When it was told to him, "Your Majesty, a son has been born to a certain nun; this is his cry," he [took] that boy...
Having led him to his own home, he gave him to the nurses. On the day of his naming ceremony, they gave him the name Kassapa;
and because he was raised with the care due to a prince, they came to know him as Kumāra-Kassapa.

While playing in the playground, he struck some boys, and when they said, "We have been struck by one who has no mother or father," he approached the king and said, "Your Majesty, [they say] 'I am one who has no mother or father'..."
Having asked, "Tell me, point out my mother," and after the king had shown him the nurses, saying, "These are your mothers," he replied, "These are not my mothers;
there must be one who is my true mother. Point her out to me.
The king, thinking, "It is not possible to deceive him," said, "My dear, your mother is a bhikkhunī; you [should go] from me to the bhikkhunīs' quarters..."
"He has been brought here. At that very moment, having become deeply moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), he said, "Father, let me go forth into the homeless life.
The King replied, "Very well, my son," and with great honor, he caused him to go forth in the presence of the Teacher.
Having received full ordination, he became known as the Elder Kumāra Kassapa. Having taken a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) from the Teacher, he entered the forest.

Being unable to produce a distinction despite his efforts, he went back to the Teacher’s presence with the thought, “I shall take up the meditation subject again after refining it,” and dwelt in the Andha Forest. Then,
having practiced the duties of a recluse together during the time of the Buddha Kassapa and having attained the fruit of Non-Returner (anāgāmiphala), he was reborn in the Brahma-world.
A bhikkhu who had been reborn there came from the Brahma-world and asked fifteen questions.
[The Buddha] sent him away, saying: "Apart from the Teacher, there is no one else capable of answering these questions; go and learn their meaning in the presence of the Teacher.
He did so, and at the conclusion of the answers to the questions, he attained Arahatship. Of him—
However, from the day he departed until twelve years had passed, tears flowed from the eyes of his mother, the bhikkhunī.
Distressed by the suffering of separation from her son, she wandered for alms with a tear-stained face;
seeing the Elder in the middle of the street, she cried out, “My son! My son! and as she rushed toward him to seize him, she fell over backward.
Rising up with milk flowing from her breasts, she went, clad in wet garments, and seized the Elder. He thought:
"If she receives kind words from me, she will perish. I shall speak with her while remaining stern.
Then he said to her: "What are you doing as you wander about? Do you have even a trace of affection?"
“You cannot cut it. She thought, “Oh, how harsh is the Elder’s speech!
and said, “What are you saying, dear? When he spoke to her again in the same way, she thought:
“Because of him, I have not been able to restrain my tears for twelve years; yet he remains so hard-hearted—what use have I for him? Thus she felt the affection for her son.
Having severed those [fetters], he attained Arahatship on that very same day.
At a later time, in the Hall of Truth, they raised this discussion: "Friends, Devadatta has ruined both Kumāra Kassapa—who was so endowed with a favorable basis for attainment—and the Elder Nun;
yet the Teacher became their support. Oh, how wonderful are the Buddhas!"
“...compassionate toward the world. The Teacher, having arrived, asked, “Monks, about what topic are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “About this very one,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that I have become their support and refuge;
in the past as well, I was indeed their support. Having said this—
“One should resort to the banyan tree alone, and not dwell among the branches;
death under the banyan is better than life among the branches.
Having related this *Nigrodha-jātaka* in detail, [he said]: “At that time, the deer Sākha was Devadatta, and his retinue...”
Having thus correlated the Jātaka— wherein Devadatta’s retinue was present, the Migadhenu Therī was the one who had reached her turn [to give birth],
his son was Kumārakassapa, and the Nigrodha, the king of deer, who went forth after the pregnant doe sacrificed her own life—
it was I myself— and having severed his affection for his son, he declared that he himself had established the Therī as his refuge: "Bhikkhus, because..."
"One cannot become destined for heaven or destined for the path by relying on another; therefore, oneself alone is one's own refuge—what can another do?
Having said this, he spoke this verse: "Self indeed is the lord of self; for who else could be the lord? ... [The rest of the verse follows]"
"By means of one's own well-tamed self, one finds a protector that is difficult to find.

In this context, "protector" (nātha) means a support. This is what is meant: because it is possible for one who is established in themselves, endowed with self-mastery, to perform wholesome deeds and thereby reach heaven, or to develop the path, or to realize the fruit; therefore—
For indeed, the self alone is one's own support; who else indeed could be the support for anyone?
By means of the self alone, when well-tamed and free from deceit, one obtains the rare protector known as the fruit of arahantship.
It is with reference to arahantship that it is said here: "one obtains the rare protector."
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the fourth story, the Story of the Elder Nun Kumārakassapa’s Mother.
5. The Story of the Lay Follower Mahākāla.
"By oneself indeed is evil done"—the Teacher gave this teaching on the Dhamma while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a lay follower named Mahākāla who had attained the fruit of stream-entry.
It is said that for eight days of each month, he would observe the Uposatha and listen to discourses on the Dhamma throughout the night in the monastery.
Then one night, thieves broke into a certain house, took goods, and [made a noise] with the sound of iron vessels.
Pursued by their awakened owners, they abandoned the stolen goods and fled.
The owners pursued them as well, and they scattered in all directions. However, one of them took the path to the monastery;
having heard the Dhamma talk from Mahākāla during the night, he abandoned his bundle in front of a man who was washing his face at the edge of a lotus pond early in the morning and fled.

The people who had come following his core followed him, and upon seeing the bundle, they said, "You have broken into our house, stolen this bundle, and yet you wander about as if listening to the Dhamma!
Seizing him, they beat him, killed him, discarded him, and departed.
Then, early in the morning, the young novices who had gone to fetch water saw him and [cried out], "In the monastery..."
Having heard this, they reported it to the Teacher, saying, "The lay follower Sayita has met an untimely death.
The Teacher said, "Yes, monks, in this present existence he met an untimely death;
however, he received exactly what was appropriate for the karma he had performed in the past. When requested by them, the Teacher related his past deed:
It is said that in the past, within the realm of the King of Bārāṇasī, bandits would attack at the entrance of a certain frontier village.
The king stationed a royal officer at the entrance of the forest; taking wages, he would escort people from this side to the other, and bring them back from the other side to this one.
Then, a certain man, having placed his beautiful wife upon a small carriage, set out.
He went to that place. As soon as the king’s servant saw the woman, affection arose within him;
thus, even when she said, "Master, please take us across the forest," he replied, "It is now late; we shall cross it in the morning. She said, "Master, it is still the right time;
take us right now! He said, "Turn back, sir! Food and lodging will be provided for you right here in our own house."
Thus, he did not wish to turn back. The other man, having given orders to the men, had the carriage turned around;
and though the prince was unwilling, he provided him with lodging at the gatehouse and prepared food for him. Now, in his house there was a precious jewel;
he had that placed inside the carriage, and at dawn, he heard the sound of the thieves entering.
He had it made. Then his men reported to him, "Sir, the jewel-treasure has been stolen by thieves.
He stationed guards at the village gates and said, "Search those who are departing from within the village. The other [the thief] also yoked his carriage early in the morning and set out.
Then, while they were cleaning his carriage, they saw the jewel-treasure he himself had placed there; having intimidated him, they...
“Having taken the jewel, you are fleeing! they cried, and after beating him, they showed him to the village headman, saying, “Sir, we have caught the thief.
The headman thought, “Alas! After providing lodging and food for my servant in my house, he has taken the jewel and gone.
Catch this wicked man! Having ordered him to be beaten and killed, he had him cast away. This was his past deed.

Passing away from there, he was reborn in Avīci; having been cooked there for a long time, by the remainder of the karmic result, he met his death after being struck in that very same manner one hundred times in successive existences.

Having thus shown Mahākāla his past karma, the Teacher said, "Bhikkhus, in this way it is their own evil deeds committed by themselves that crush these beings in the four states of misery," and spoke this verse:
“Indeed, the evil done by oneself, born of oneself, originating from oneself, grinds the fool down, just as a diamond grinds a gem made of stone.
In this context, “a diamond grinds a gem made of stone” means: just as a diamond [grinds] a gem made of stone. This is what is meant.
Just as one might take a diamond— a stone-made gem originating from stone— and, having chewed that very stone-gem which is its own source and place of origin,
reduce it to hole after hole and fragment after fragment until it is rendered unusable; even so,
a foolish person lacking wisdom [destroys] the evil he has himself committed, born within himself, and originating from himself, in four ways.
"It crushes, carves up, and destroys [beings] in the states of misery.
At the conclusion of the teaching, the assembled bhikkhus attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the fifth account, the Story of the Upāsaka Mahākāla.
6. The Story of Devadatta The Teacher, while staying at Veḷuvana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning Devadatta, beginning with the words: "He who is utterly immoral...
For one day, the monks raised a discussion in the Hall of Truth, saying: "Friends, Devadatta..."
“Being immoral and of evil character, through the cause of his immorality, he strengthened his craving;

having won over Ajātasattu and produced great gain and honor for himself, he incited Ajātasattu to kill his father and, acting in concert with him, strove in various ways to bring about the death of the Tathāgata.
The Teacher approached and asked, “Bhikkhus, what is it that you are discussing?”
Having asked, "Are you sitting here gathered for this discussion? and being told, "Indeed we are," he said, "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, Devadatta strove in various ways for my death.
Having spoken thus, he related the Kuruṅgamiga Jātaka and others, saying, "Monks, for a person who is utterly immoral, craving arises on account of that immorality like a *māluvā* creeper."
"Having completely entwined a sal tree and breaking it apart, she casts it into the hells and other realms," he said, and then spoke this verse:
"He whose extreme immorality has overspread him like a creeper over a sal tree,
He makes himself exactly as his enemy would wish."
In this context, "absolute immorality" (*accantadussīlya*) means the state of being exclusively immoral.

One who, as a layperson from birth, commits the ten courses of unwholesome action, or one who, as a renunciant from the day of full ordination, incurs a grave offense (*garukāpatti*), is called absolutely immoral.
However, here it refers to the state of immorality that has followed one through the course of two or three successive existences.
This was said with this intention. And here, "the state of immorality" should be understood as the craving that arises in an immoral person by way of the six doors.

"As a creeper envelops a sal tree": just as a *māluvā* creeper envelops a *sāla* tree, when it rains, the creeper receives the water with its leaves and, by means of breaking [the branches], covers it; so too for that person, this immorality known as craving...
It completely envelops everything; thus it stands having covered and enveloped the personal existence (*attabhāva*).

Like a tree that, when broken by a *māluvā* creeper, falls to the ground, so too one who is broken by that craving known as immorality falls into the states of misery (*apāya*), just as one who desires his ruin wishes for him.
The meaning is: "he makes himself [his own].
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other fruits.
This is the sixth story, concerning Devadatta.

7. The Story of Devadatta’s Attempt to Cause a Schism in the Saṅgha "Easy it is," this teaching on the Dhamma was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Veḷuvana, concerning Devadatta’s attempt to cause a schism in the Saṅgha.
For one day, as the Venerable Ānanda was walking for alms, Devadatta, striving to cause a schism in the Saṅgha, [approached him]...
Having seen him, he declared his intention. Hearing this, the Elder went into the presence of the Teacher and said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, this morning, having dressed myself and taken my bowl and robe, I entered Rājagaha for alms.
Venerable sir, Devadatta saw me as I was walking for alms in Rājagaha. Having seen me..."
He approached me, and having approached, he said this to me:
“From this day forward, friend Ānanda, apart from the Blessed One and apart from the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, I shall perform the Uposatha and the formal acts of the Saṅgha.
Today, the Blessed One [foretells that] Devadatta will split the Saṅgha and will perform the Uposatha and the formal acts of the Saṅgha. When this was said, the Teacher—
“Good is easily done by the good; good is difficult for the evil to do.
Evil is easily done by the evil; evil is difficult for the noble ones to do.

Having uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*), he said, “Ānanda, it is easy to perform an action that is harmful to oneself, but it is indeed difficult to perform an action that is beneficial,” and then spoke this verse:
“Easy to do are things that are unwholesome and harmful to oneself;
but that which is truly beneficial and wholesome—that indeed is most difficult to do.
The meaning of this is: those actions which are unwholesome, blameworthy, and because they lead to the states of misery, are themselves harmful to oneself.
Those [actions] are easy to perform. However, that karma which leads to a happy destination because it is beneficial to oneself and is good in the sense of being blameless—
and which leads both to a happy destination and to Nibbāna— is exceedingly difficult to perform,
like diverting the Ganges river, which flows toward the east, and making it flow toward the west.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the seventh story, concerning the attempt to cause a schism in the Saṅgha. 8.
The Story of the Elder Kāla.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this teaching on the Dispensation concerning the Elder Kāla.
It is said that in Sāvatthī, a certain woman, acting as a mother to him, attended upon that elder.

When people in her neighbor’s house had heard the Dhamma from the presence of the Teacher and returned, they exclaimed, "Oh, how wonderful are the Buddhas! Oh, how marvelous is the teaching of the Dhamma!"
They praised her, saying, "She is sweet. When that woman heard their talk, she informed him, "Venerable sir, I too wish to hear the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma.

He forbade her, saying, "Do not go there. Although she was forbidden by him on the following day and again on the next, up to the third time, she remained desirous of hearing it. Why, then, did he forbid her? It was because—so [it is said].
The thought occurred to her: "Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he will break with me.

One day, having eaten her morning meal early and undertaken the Uposatha vows, she instructed her daughter, saying, "Daughter, you must serve the noble one very well," and then went to the monastery. When that bhikkhu arrived, her daughter served him.
When asked, "Where is the great female lay disciple? she replied, "She has gone to the monastery to hear the Dhamma.
Upon hearing this, burning with the fever that had arisen within his belly, he thought, "Now she has betrayed me," and went in haste.
Seeing her listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he said to the Teacher, "Venerable Sir, this woman is dull-witted and subtle..."

“He does not know the Dhamma discourse; instead of speaking on the subtle Dhamma connected with the aggregates and so forth, it would be appropriate for him to speak on the discourse of giving or the discourse of virtue. The Teacher, knowing his intention, said:
“You are of poor wisdom; relying on an evil view, you revile the teaching of the Buddhas. You are merely striving for your own destruction.”
Having spoken thus, he recited this verse:
“The foolish man who, relying on an evil view, reviles the teaching of the Arahants, the Noble Ones who live by the Dhamma;”
“Like the *kaṭṭhaka* tree, he bears fruit for his own destruction.

This is its meaning: that foolish person, out of fear of the loss of his own honor, relies on an evil view and, when others say, “We shall listen to the Dhamma or we shall give alms,” he reviles the Arahants, the Noble Ones who live according to the Dhamma.
He rejects the teaching of the Buddhas; that rejection of his and that evil view are like the fruits of the *kaṭṭhaka* tree known as the bamboo.

Therefore, just as the *kaṭṭhaka* tree, when bearing fruit, bears them for its own destruction—that is, it bears them solely for the purpose of its own ruin—so too he bears fruit for his own destruction. And this has also been said:
“Fruit indeed destroys the plantain tree; fruit destroys the bamboo and the reed;
honor destroys the base man, just as the fetus destroys the mule.
At the conclusion of this teaching, the female lay devotee was established in the fruit of stream-entry, and the Dhamma discourse was beneficial for the entire assembled company.
The Eighth Story: The Elder Kāla.
9. The Story of the Lay Disciple Cūḷakāla.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this teaching on the Dhamma concerning the lay disciple Cūḷakāla, beginning with the words: "For by oneself indeed [is it done]."
One day, in the manner described in the Mahākāla-vatthu, housebreakers who had been pursued by their owners heard a Dhamma talk in the monastery during the night.
Leaving the monastery at dawn, they fled and dropped a bundle in front of that lay follower as he was entering Sāvatthī. When people saw it, [they said], "This man committed a robbery at night..."
“Even while pretending to listen to the Dhamma, he behaves as if he were acting; seize him! they said, and they beat him.
When the water-carrier slave girls saw him going to the bathing place, they released him, saying, “Go away, master; he does not do such a thing.
Having gone to the monastery, he said, “Venerable sirs, I have been driven out by people; it is through the slave girls that I have obtained my livelihood.”
He informed the bhikkhus. The bhikkhus reported that matter to the Tathāgata.
Having heard their words, the Teacher said, "Bhikkhus, the lay follower Cūḷakāla obtained his livelihood by relying on the water-carriers and by his own abstention from wrongdoing.
For these beings, having committed evil deeds themselves, are defiled only by themselves in the hells and other realms of suffering."
"But by performing wholesome deeds, those going to a happy destination and to Nibbāna purify themselves by their own efforts," he said, and then spoke this verse:
"By oneself indeed is evil done; by oneself is one defiled.
By oneself is evil left undone; by oneself alone is one purified."
"Purity and impurity are personal; one cannot purify another.
This is its meaning: he by whom unwholesome karma has been committed becomes defiled by himself alone, experiencing suffering in the four states of misery.
But he by whom evil has not been committed goes toward both a happy rebirth and Nibbāna.

"One is purified by oneself alone. Purity, which consists of wholesome kamma, and impurity, which consists of unwholesome kamma, ripen individually within the very self of the sentient beings who are the agents.

It is said that one person does not purify another person, nor does one defile another; rather, it is the self that purifies itself, and it is the self that does not purify itself. It is not the case that one person purifies or defiles another.
At the conclusion of the teaching, Cūḷakāla was established in the fruit of stream-entry, and the Dhamma instruction was fruitful for the assembled multitude as well.
Thus ends the ninth story, the Story of the Lay Follower Cūḷakāla.
10. The Story of the Elder Attadattha.
"His own welfare": This teaching on the Dhamma was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning the Elder Attadattha.

For when the Teacher said at the time of his Parinibbāna, "Bhikkhus, four months from now I shall attain Parinibbāna," seven hundred ordinary monks, stirred by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), did not leave the presence of the Teacher, [asking] "What..."
“Shall we now do so, friends? they asked, as they wandered about deliberating. But the Elder Attadattha thought to himself:
“The Teacher, it is said, will attain final Nibbāna at the end of four months; yet I am not free from lust.
While the Teacher still lives, I shall strive for the sake of Arahantship. Therefore, he did not go into the presence of the monks. Then the monks [addressed him].
“Friend, why do you neither come to us nor say anything?
Having said this, they led him to the presence of the Teacher and reported, “Venerable Sir, this man is doing such-and-such. When the Teacher asked him, “Why are you doing this?
he replied, “Venerable Sir, it is said that you will attain final Nibbāna at the end of four months; I—”
"While you are still living, I shall strive for the attainment of Arahatship. The Teacher gave him his approval, saying:
"Monks, he who has affection for me ought to act for his own benefit as he did.
For it is not by worshipping me with perfumes and the like that they worship me; rather, they worship me through practice in accordance with the Dhamma. Therefore..."
"Others too should be like oneself in seeking their own welfare," he said, and then spoke this verse:
"One should not neglect one's own welfare for the sake of another's, however great it may be.
Having clearly understood one's own welfare, one should be devoted to one's own true goal."

The meaning of this is as follows: While still a householder, one should not, for the sake of even a *kākaṇika* (a small coin) of one's own interest, neglect an interest of another amounting to a thousand.
For he might produce food, whether hard or soft, for his own sake even for the value of a *kākaṇika*, but not for the sake of another.
However, this has been stated here under the heading of meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*) rather than being spoken in that manner [as a general ethical rule].

Therefore, thinking “I shall not neglect my own welfare,” a bhikkhu must not neglect any duty that has arisen for the Saṅgha, such as the restoration of a shrine, nor the service toward his preceptor and others.
For it is precisely by fulfilling the duties of proper conduct (*ābhisamācārika-vatta*) that one realizes the fruits of the Noble Ones and so forth;
therefore, this too is indeed one’s own welfare. However, one who is excessively energetic in insight (*accāraddha-vipassaka*) [thinking] “Today or tomorrow...”
Or, if one wanders about aspiring for penetration [of the truths], one should even neglect duties toward one’s preceptor and so forth, and perform only one’s own duty.
For, having clearly understood such a personal goal and observed, "This is my own welfare," one should be intent upon one's own welfare;
that is, one should be devotedly engaged in that which is one’s own purpose.
At the conclusion of the teaching, that elder was established in Arahatship, and the Dhamma instruction was fruitful for the assembled monks as well.
Thus ends the tenth story, the Story of the Elder Attadatta.
The commentary on the Attavagga is finished.
The Twelfth Chapter. 13. The Chapter on the World (Lokavagga). 1.
The Account of the Young Bhikkhu.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this teaching on the Dhamma concerning a certain young bhikkhu.
It is said that a certain elder went to the house of Visākhā early in the morning together with a young bhikkhu.
In Visākhā’s house, a constant supply of rice-gruel for five hundred bhikkhus was always prepared. Having drunk the gruel there, the elder—
Having seated the young bhikkhu, she herself went to another house.
At that time, Visākhā’s granddaughter—standing in her grandmother’s place—was performing services for the bhikkhus.
While straining water for the young man, she saw the reflection of her own face in a bowl and laughed; the young man also looked at her.
She laughed. Seeing him laughing, she said, "One whose head is severed is laughing. Then the youth reviled her, saying, "You are one whose head is severed;
even your parents have had their heads severed! Weeping, she went to her grandmother in the kitchen.
When asked, "What is this, mother? she related the matter to her. She then approached the youth and said, "Venerable sir..."

"Do not be angry; this is no great burden for a noble one who has had his hair and nails cut, who wears only a lower garment and a cloak, and who wanders for alms carrying a bowl broken in the middle," he said. "Yes, lay follower, it is true;
you know my state of having my hair and so forth cut. It would be appropriate for her to revile me by calling me 'one with a severed head.'"
Visākhā was unable to convince either the young man or the girl. At that moment, the Elder arrived and asked, "What is this, lay follower?
Having heard the matter, he spoke to the young man as he exhorted him: "Go away, friend!
This is not an insult to one who wanders for alms carrying a broken bowl in the midst of one whose hair and nails have been cut."
“Be silent! [she replied. “Yes, venerable sir; why do you scold me instead of scolding your own attendant?
Is it proper for you to revile me, calling me ‘one whose head is cut off’? At that moment, the Teacher arrived and asked, “What is this?
Visākhā related the entire incident from the beginning. The Teacher [perceived] the young man’s underlying predisposition for the fruit of stream-entry.
Seeing this, he thought, "It is fitting that I should comply with this youth," and said to Visākhā:
"But Visākhā, is it right for you to revile my disciples by merely cutting off your daughter's hair and so forth, as if they had their heads cut off?
At that very moment, the youth rose up, extended his hands in anjali, and said, "Venerable sir, you yourself [should answer] this question."
“You know well; our preceptor and our female lay disciple do not know well,” he said.
The Teacher, perceiving that the youth was well-disposed toward himself, said, “To laugh for the sake of sensual pleasures is a base quality;
it is not fitting to associate with negligence while practicing a base quality,” and he spoke this verse:
“One should not pursue a base thing; one should not dwell in negligence;
one should not pursue wrong view; one should not be a prosperer of the world.
In this context, “a base thing” refers to the things of the five strands of sensual pleasure. For that is indeed a base thing, [low] even among such animals as camels and oxen.
It should be practiced. That which causes one to be reborn in inferior places such as the hells is called "inferior"; one should not practice that.
"By negligence" means one should not dwell even with negligence characterized by the loss of mindfulness.
"One should not practice" means one should not adopt wrong view either. For he who acts in this way is indeed called a "prosperer of the world. Therefore, thus—
"By non-doing, one would not increase the world.
At the conclusion of this teaching, that young man was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), and the Dhamma teaching was fruitful for those who were present as well.
This is the first story, the Story of the Young Bhikkhu.
2. The Story of Suddhodana.
The Teacher, while dwelling at the Nigrodha Monastery, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning his father.
For on one occasion, having gone to Kapilavatthu on his first visit, the Teacher was met by his kinsmen.
Having arrived at the Nigrodha Park, in order to humble the pride of his kinsmen, he manifested a jeweled walkway in the sky;
walking upon it, he taught the Dhamma. With hearts full of faith, his kinsmen paid homage, beginning with King Suddhodana.
During that gathering of relatives, a rain of lotuses fell. When this was related by the great multitude, [the Buddha spoke].
“Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, even when my kinsmen were gathered together, a rain of lotuses fell,” he said, and then related the Vessantara Jātaka.
When his kinsmen had heard this teaching on the Dhamma and were departing, not a single one invited the Teacher.
The king also, thinking, “Where will my son go without coming to my house? did not invite him either.
He arrived. Having gone there, he had rice-gruel and other foods prepared for twenty thousand bhikkhus and arranged seats.
On the following day, as the Teacher was entering the city for alms, he reflected:
"Did the Buddhas of the past, upon reaching their father’s city, enter the family of their kinsmen directly, or did they wander for alms in regular succession?"
Having seen that they had been walking in succession, he set out on his alms-round starting from the first house.
Rāhula’s mother, sitting on the terrace of the palace, saw him and reported the matter to the king. The king, adjusting his garment, went out in haste, paid homage to the Teacher, and said:
“Son, why have you ruined me? You have gone about for alms far too much.”
“Shame has been aroused! Is it truly fitting for you to wander through this very city in golden palanquins and such, yet go about for alms?
Why do you put me to shame? “I am not putting you to shame, Great King; rather, I am following my own family tradition.
“But what, dear one, is this tradition of living by wandering for alms? Is that my lineage? “That is not so,” [he replied].
“Great King, that is your lineage, but this is my lineage. For many thousands of Buddhas have lived by wandering for alms alone.
Having said this, he taught the Dhamma and spoke these verses:
“One should rise up and not be negligent; one should practice the Dhamma of good conduct.”
One who lives according to the Dhamma sleeps happily, both in this world and in the next.
"One should practice the Dhamma well-conducted, and not practice what is ill-conducted;
one who lives according to the Dhamma sleeps happily, both in this world and in the next."
In this context, "rising up" means having risen and stood at the door of another's house regarding the alms that are to be received.
"One should not be negligent" means that one who, neglecting the proper conduct for wandering for alms, seeks out choice foods, is said to be negligent in rising;
however, one who wanders for alms in regular succession is said not to be negligent. Acting in this way, one should not be negligent in rising.
"Dhamma" means that, having abandoned improper modes of livelihood, one should practice that very same well-conducted way of life consisting of alms-gathering while wandering from house to house.

"He sleeps in comfort"—this is merely a figurative expression; the meaning is that by practicing this way of life of alms-gathering, one who lives according to the Dhamma dwells happily in this world through the four postures. "No misconduct [befalls him]" refers to [misconduct] such as that involving prostitutes and so forth.
"Walking in what is not one's proper sphere, one practices the way of the alms-round improperly; this is indeed called 'practicing misconduct.
Without practicing in such a manner, one should practice the Dhamma properly, and not practice misconduct. The rest has the same meaning as already stated.
At the conclusion of the teaching, the king was established in the fruit of stream-entry, and the Dhamma instruction was fruitful for those who were present.
The Story of Suddhodana, the second.
3. The Story of the Five Hundred Bhikkhus Practicing Insight.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning five hundred bhikkhus who were practicing insight. "Just as a bubble..."—it was with reference to these five hundred insight-practicing bhikkhus that he spoke.
It is said that those monks, having received a meditation subject from the Teacher and entered the forest, were practicing with diligence but had not attained any distinction.

Thinking, "We shall receive a distinguished meditation subject," they returned to the presence of the Teacher; while on the way, they continued to develop the mirage meditation subject as they came along.
At the very moment they entered the monastery, it began to rain.
Standing at various prominent spots there, they saw bubbles rising and bursting with the force of the current, and they took up the object of meditation, thinking:
"This body, too, having arisen, is just like a bubble in its nature of bursting.
While seated in the Gandhakuṭī, the Teacher looked upon those bhikkhus and, as if conversing with them, emitted a radiance.
Having pervaded [the world with compassion], he spoke this verse:
“As one would look upon a bubble, as one would look upon a mirage,
so for one who contemplates the world in this way, the King of Death does not see him.”
In this context, "mirage" refers to a ray of light. For although these appear from afar in the form of houses and so forth, they are ungraspable for those who approach them;

they are merely empty and void. Therefore, the meaning is that the King of Death does not see one who contemplates the world of the aggregates and so forth in the same way one would view a bubble—arising and then breaking away—as being empty and void by its very nature.
At the conclusion of the teaching, those bhikkhus attained arahantship at the very spot where they stood.
This is the third story, concerning the five hundred bhikkhus practicing insight meditation.
4. The Story of Prince Abhaya.
"Come, behold this world!"—this teaching on the Dhamma was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Veḷuvana concerning Prince Abhaya.

It is said that when Abhaya returned after having pacified the border regions, his father Bimbisāra, being pleased, gave him a dancing woman skilled in song and dance and granted him sovereignty for seven days.
During those seven days, he did not even step outside his palace, yet he [enjoyed] the splendor of royalty...
Having experienced this, on the eighth day he went to a river crossing, bathed, and entered a park;
there he sat watching the dancing and singing of that woman, just as the minister Santati had done before.
At that very moment, she passed away due to the force of the wind from the sword, like a female dancer of the minister Santati. The prince was overcome with grief at her death.
Thinking, "No one other than the Teacher will be able to extinguish this grief of mine," he approached the Teacher and said,
"Venerable Sir, please extinguish my grief. The Teacher comforted him and said, "For indeed, Prince,
throughout the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), there is no measure for the tears you have shed while weeping at the time of this woman's death in exactly this same way."
Having said, "There is none," and perceiving through that teaching that his grief had been diminished, he said, "Prince, do not grieve;
this is a place where foolish people sink," and spoke this verse:
"Come, behold this world, a mind like a king’s chariot."
"Where fools sink down, for the one who understands there is no attachment.
Therein, "you see him" refers specifically to the prince. "This world" refers to this personal existence (attabhāva), comprised of the aggregates (khandha) and so forth.
"Variegated" means adorned with garments, ornaments, and the like, just as a royal chariot is variegated with the seven precious gems and so on.
"Where fools [sink]" means that in this very personal existence (attabhāva), fools sink in such a manner.
"For those who understand" means that for the wise who understand, there is not even a single attachment among these, such as attachment through lust; this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, the prince was established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala), and the Dhamma teaching was fruitful for all those present.
The fourth story, the Story of Prince Abhaya.
The fifth, the Story of Elder Sammajjana:
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning Elder Sammajjana, beginning with the words, "He who, moreover, before..."
It is said that he would wander about constantly sweeping, without regard for the time—whether morning or evening.
One day, taking his broom, he went to the presence of the Elder Revata, who was sitting in the daytime quarters, and thought:
"This great indolent man sits here after coming and eating the offerings given in faith by the people; what indeed is his..."
“It is not proper to sweep one place after taking up the broom,” he said.
The Elder, thinking, “I shall give him some instruction,” said, “Come here, friend. “What is it, venerable sir? “Go, wash yourself, and then come back. He did so.
Then the Elder, having seated him to one side, spoke to him as he was giving instruction: “Friend, for a monk, indeed, at all times—”

It is appropriate to walk about while sweeping; however, having already swept in the morning, it is appropriate to go for alms, and upon returning from the almsround, to sit in either the night-quarters or the day-quarters, recite the thirty-two aspects (dvattiṃsākāra), contemplate the decay and fall of this physical body, and then rise in the evening to sweep again. One should not fail to sweep at all times.
“Indeed, one should even make room for oneself. Following the elder’s advice, he attained Arahatship before long.
That place became increasingly dirty. Then the monks said to him, “Friend Sammajjanatthera, why do you not sweep that place?
“Venerable sirs, it was done by me at a time of negligence.”

"Now I am diligent. When the monks reported to the Teacher, "This elder is speaking of something else," the Teacher said, "Yes, monks, in the past, when he was negligent, my son wandered about sweeping; but now, spending his time in the bliss of the paths and fruits, he does not sweep.
Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“But whoever, having been negligent in the past, later does not neglect, illuminates this world like the moon freed from clouds.

The meaning of this is: that person who, having previously been negligent—either by failing to perform duties and services, or by neglecting recitation and other such practices—[later becomes diligent].
Subsequently, as he passes his time in the bliss of the paths and fruits, he does not become negligent.
Like the moon freed from clouds and the like, he illuminates this world of aggregates and so forth with the knowledge of the path, making it a single expanse of light.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and the other stages.
The fifth story: The Elder Sammajjana.
The sixth story: The Elder Aṅgulimāla.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this teaching on the Dhamma beginning with the words, "Whose evil... regarding the Elder Aṅgulimāla. The background story for this should be understood according to the Aṅgulimāla Sutta.

But the Elder, having gone forth in the presence of the Teacher, attained arahantship. Then, while the Venerable Aṅgulimāla was dwelling alone in seclusion, experiencing the bliss of liberation, on that occasion he uttered this inspired utterance:
“He who, having been heedless in the past, is not heedless later, He illuminates this world like the moon freed from clouds.”
Having uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*) according to this method, he attained final *parinibbāna* in the element of *nibbāna* without residue.
The monks raised a discussion in the Hall of Dharma, saying, "Friends, where has the Elder been reborn?
The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now? They replied, "Venerable Sir, regarding the Elder Aṅgulimāla..."
When it was asked, "What is the account of his place of rebirth? [the Buddha replied], "Monks, my son has attained final Nibbāna.
[The monks asked], "Venerable sir, having killed so many people, has he attained final Nibbāna? "Yes, monks. Previously, not having found a good friend, he committed such evil;
but later, having found the condition of a good friend, he became diligent."
"It occurred. Therefore, that evil deed of his was covered over by a wholesome one," he said, and then spoke this verse:
"Whose evil deed is covered over by a wholesome one, He illuminates the world like the moon freed from clouds."
In this context, "by the wholesome" is said with reference to the path of Arahatship. The remainder is of plain meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other fruits.
This is the sixth story, the account of the Elder Aṅgulimāla.
7. The Story of the Weaver’s Daughter:
"Blinded" The Teacher delivered this teaching on the Dhamma while residing at the Aggāḷava Cetiya, concerning a weaver’s daughter.
One day, when the Teacher had arrived at Āḷavī, the inhabitants of Āḷavī invited him and gave an offering. The Teacher—
At the conclusion of the meal, while offering words of appreciation (*anumodanā*), one should thus cultivate mindfulness of death (*maraṇassati*): "My life is unstable; my death is certain.
I must certainly die; my life ends in death. Life itself is uncertain, but death is certain.
For those in whom mindfulness of death has not been cultivated, at the final stage [of life], they are like those who encounter a venomous snake...
"Having seen [the danger], they die in a state of terror, crying out with fearful cries like a man who has been struck by a blow and is terrified.

But those for whom mindfulness of death (*maraṇassati*) has been developed do not tremble at the time of their end; they are like a man who, having seen a venomous snake from afar, picks it up with a stick, discards it, and stands firm. Therefore, mindfulness of death should be developed," he said.
Having heard that teaching on the Dhamma, the remaining people became intent upon their own respective duties.
However, a weaver’s daughter about sixteen years of age thought, "Oh, how wonderful is the discourse of the Buddhas!
It is fitting for me to cultivate mindfulness of death," and she cultivated mindfulness of death throughout the day and night. The Teacher, having departed from there, went to Jetavana.
She arrived. That young girl, too, had been developing mindfulness of death for three years.
Then one day, as the Teacher was surveying the world at dawn, he saw that young girl entered within the net of his knowledge.
Reflecting, "What will happen? he perceived: "By this young girl, my..."
"From the day I heard the Dhamma teaching, I have cultivated mindfulness of death for three years.
Now, having gone there and asked this young woman four questions, and having given her applause at the four points as she answers them, I shall recite this verse.
At the conclusion of that verse, she will be established in the fruit of stream-entry. [He went] to her.

Knowing that "by relying on this, the teaching of the Dhamma will also be beneficial for the great multitude," he departed from Jetavana accompanied by a retinue of five hundred bhikkhus and, traveling by stages, arrived at the Aggāḷava Monastery.

When the inhabitants of Āḷavī heard that "the Teacher has arrived," they went to that monastery and invited him. At that time, the young girl also, having heard of the Teacher's arrival, [thought], "He has come..."
“My father, Master, was the teacher, the Great Gotama Buddha, whose face was like the full moon,” she said, her mind filled with joy.
She thought: “At the end of these three years, I have seen the Teacher of golden complexion;
now I shall be able to behold his golden body and hear his sweet and sublime Dhamma.”
As her father was going to the weaver’s workshop, he said: “My dear, I have taken up a garment belonging to another;
only a span’s width of it remains unfinished, and I shall finish it today. Quickly, spin my shuttle and bring it to me. She thought:
“I am desirous of hearing the Dhamma from the Teacher, yet my father says this to me. What indeed shall I do?”
“Shall I listen to the Dhamma, or shall I spin my father’s shuttle? Then it occurred to her:
“If my father does not have me spin his shuttle, he might even scold me or strike me; therefore, having spun the shuttle and given it to him, I will listen to the Dhamma afterwards.
Sitting down on a stool, she began spinning the shuttle.
The residents of Āḷavī also served the Teacher, and having taken his bowl, they stood waiting for the expression of thanks.
The Teacher thought, "Because of this daughter of good family, I have come a journey of thirty yojanas; yet even today she finds no opportunity.
Once she has found an opportunity, I shall give the expression of thanks. Thus he remained silent. Although the Teacher remained silent in this way, [the people continued to wait].
No one in the world, including the devas, was able to say anything against him. That maiden, having wound her shuttle and placed it in her basket, went toward her father;
yet, standing at the edge of the assembly and looking only at the Teacher, she remained there.
The Teacher also raised his neck and looked at her. By the very manner of that look, she recognized: "The Teacher..."
“Sitting right here in the midst of such an assembly, he gazes at me and awaits my arrival;
he is merely waiting for me to come into his presence. Having set down her shuttle-basket, she went into the presence of the Teacher.
But why did the Teacher look at her? It was because this thought occurred to him: “If she goes on from here, she will die as an ordinary worldling (puthujjana).”

"Having done so, she will be of uncertain destiny; but having come into my presence and departed, she will attain the fruit of stream-entry, become one of certain destiny, and be reborn in the Tusita heaven. It is said that on that day there was no escape from death for her.
She approached the Teacher by the very sign of his glance, amidst the six-colored rays of light.
Having entered within and paid homage, she stood to one side.
While seated in the midst of such an assembly, she paid homage to the Teacher who was silent and, at that very moment of standing, said to him: “Young girl, from where have you come?
“I do not know, Bhante. “Where will you go? “I do not know, Bhante. “Do you not know?”
“I know it, Bhante. “Do you know? “I do not know, Bhante. Thus the Teacher questioned him with four questions.
The great multitude murmured, “Ho! Look! This weaver’s daughter converses with the Perfectly Enlightened One about whatever she desires;
surely, when he asked her, ‘Where have you come from? she ought to have said, ‘From the weaver’s house.’”
“It should be said. When asked, ‘Where are you going? it may be said, ‘To the weaver’s workshop.
Having silenced the great crowd, the Teacher asked, “Young girl, when asked, ‘Where have you come from?
why do you say, ‘How could I not know? “Venerable Sir, you already know that I have come from my father’s weaver’s house.”
When they asked, "From where have you come?", they were asking, "Having come from where have you been reborn here?
But I do not know, "From where have I come to be reborn here? Then the Teacher, saying to her, "Excellent, excellent, young lady!
You have answered the very question I asked," gave his first applause and [continued with] the further [question].
He asked, “Where will you go? When she was asked again, he said, “Why do you say, ‘I do not know’?
“Venerable sir, you know that I am going to the weavers’ workshop taking this basket of woven cloth.
You ask me, ‘Having gone from here, where will you be reborn? But I, having passed away from here, do not know where I shall go to be reborn. Then the Teacher [spoke to her].
“Only the question asked by me has been answered by you,” he said, giving a second cry of approval, and then asked a further question:
“Then why, when asked ‘Do you not know? did you say ‘I know’? “I know the fact of death, venerable sir;
therefore I spoke thus. Then the Teacher said to her, “Only the question asked by me has been answered by you,” and gave a third [cry of approval].
Having given her approval, he asked further: “Then why, when asked ‘Do you know? did you say ‘I do not know’? She replied:
“Venerable sir, I know only the fact of my own death; however, I do not know that ‘I shall die at such a time,’ whether by night, by day, or in the morning, etc.;
therefore I spoke thus. Then the Teacher said to her: “The very question I asked...”
Having given a fourth "well done" after saying, "He was dismissed by her," he addressed the assembly:
"You do not know even this much that has been spoken by her; you do nothing but complain. For those who lack the eye of wisdom are indeed blind;
only those who possess the eye of wisdom are truly sighted. Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“This world has become blind; here, few see with insight.
Like a bird escaped from a net, few go to heaven.
In this context, “this world has become blind” means that the great mass of worldly people has become blind due to the absence of the eye of wisdom (*paññā-cakkhu*).
"Thin here" means that few people here practice insight (*vipassanā*) by way of impermanence and so forth.
"Like one freed from the net" means that when birds are being caught by a skilled fowler who has covered them with a net, only some are released from the net;
the rest enter back into the net itself. Likewise, among beings covered by the net of death, many go to the states of misery (*apāya*).
"Rare indeed are those beings who go to heaven, or reach a happy destination, or even Nibbāna"—this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, the young girl was established in the fruit of stream-entry, and the Dhamma instruction was beneficial for the great multitude as well.
She too, taking her shuttle-basket, went to her father's side; he, however, fell asleep while sitting. To her...
Without even noticing, she brought the shuttle-basket toward him; the basket struck against the end of the shuttle and fell with a sound.
He woke up and, following the very sign he had grasped, pulled the shuttle-end toward him.
The shuttle-end went and struck the young girl on the chest; she died right there and was reborn in the Tusita heaven.
Then her father, looking at her, saw that she had fallen dead with her entire body smeared with blood.

Great sorrow arose within him. Thinking, "No one else will be able to extinguish my grief," he went weeping into the presence of the Teacher, related the matter, and said, "Venerable Sir, please extinguish my grief. The Teacher [addressed] him—
