Having comforted him, he said, "Do not grieve, lay follower. In this beginningless cycle of existence (saṃsāra), the tears that have flowed from you alone at the time of your daughter's death are greater than the water in the four great oceans.

Having spoken thus, he delivered a discourse on the beginninglessness of existence. His grief having subsided, he requested the Teacher for the going-forth; having received full ordination, before long he attained Arahantship.
The Seventh Story: The Potter’s Daughter.
8. The Story of the Thirty Bhikkhus.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, related this Dhamma teaching concerning thirty bhikkhus, beginning with the words: "Like swans on the path of the sun."
On one occasion, about thirty resident monks approached the Teacher.

When it was time for the Elder Ānanda to perform his duties toward the Teacher, he arrived and, seeing those monks, thought, "Since the Teacher has already exchanged greetings with them, I shall perform my duties," and he stood at the gateway. The Teacher, meanwhile, was exchanging greetings with them.
Having done so, he taught them the *sāraṇīya-dhamma*. Upon hearing it, they all attained *arahantship* and, soaring up, departed through the air.

When those monks had been gone for some time, the Venerable Ānanda approached the Teacher and asked, "Venerable Sir, just now about thirty bhikkhus arrived; where have they gone? "They have gone, Ānanda. "By what [means]?"
“By what path, venerable sir? “By the sky, Ānanda. “But how is it, venerable sir, that those whose taints are destroyed [attain this]? “Yes, Ānanda;
having heard the Dhamma in my presence, they have attained arahantship. At that moment, swans arrived through the sky.
The Teacher said, “Ānanda, whoever has well developed the four bases of psychic power goes through the sky like a swan.”
Having spoken this, he recited this verse:
“Like swans they travel on the path of the sun; they travel through the sky by means of psychic power.
Having conquered Māra and his host, the wise are led out from the world.”

The meaning of this is as follows: these swans travel through the sky along the path of the sun. Those who have well-cultivated the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) also go through the sky by means of psychic power.
The wise and learned, having conquered Māra together with his host, are led out from this world of saṃsāra;
the meaning is that they reach Nibbāna.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the eighth story, concerning thirty bhikkhus. 9.
The Story of the Maiden Ciñcā.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this discourse on the "One Dhamma" concerning the young woman Ciñcā Māṇavikā.

For during the first period after his enlightenment, when the disciples of the One Possessed of Ten Powers had become numerous, when immeasurable gods and humans had entered the plane of the Noble Ones, and when the mass of virtues had spread abroad, great gain and honor arose.
At that time, the heretics were like the sun at its rising.
Deprived of gain and honor, they became like glow-worms. Standing in the middle of the streets, they sought to entice people by saying, "Is the ascetic Gotama alone the Buddha?
We too are Buddhas! Is it only to him that what is given bears great fruit? To us as well, what is given bears great fruit;
give to us too, and honor us! Yet even while thus soliciting people, they obtained no gain or honor.
Not being able to find him, they met together in secret and thought, "By what means might we create disrepute for the ascetic Gotama among the people and destroy his gain and honor?
At that time, there was a female wanderer in Sāvatthī named Ciñcā Māṇavikā, who possessed supreme beauty and had attained great fortune.
She was like a celestial nymph. Rays of light streamed forth from her body. Then one named Kharamantin said:
"By inciting a scandal against the young woman Ciñcā Māṇavikā, we shall cause the gain and honor of the ascetic Gotama to perish.
They agreed, saying, "There is indeed a way. Then she went to the monastery of the sectarians, paid her respects, and stood there. The sectarians—

They did not speak with her. She thought, "What fault could there be in me? and after saying, "I pay homage to you, noble ladies," up to three times, she said, "Noble ladies, what fault is there in me? Why do you not speak with me?
"Sister, do you not know that the ascetic Gotama is harassing us, making us lose our gains and honor as he wanders about? "I do not know."
“Noble ladies, what must I do in this matter? “If you, sister, desire our welfare, create disrepute for the ascetic Gotama by means of yourself and destroy his gain and honor.
She replied, “Very well, noble ladies; this burden is mine, do not worry,” and having said this, she departed and employed her feminine wiles.

From that time on, due to her proficiency, after hearing a discourse on the Dhamma from the residents of Sāvatthī, she would put on a cloak the color of an *indagopaka* insect at the moment of departing from Jetavana.
Carrying perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, she would walk toward Jetavana.
When asked, "Where are you going at this hour? she would reply, "What business of yours is it where I am going? and then [proceed] near Jetavana.

Having stayed in the monasteries of the non-Buddhist sects (titthiyārāma), when lay followers were departing from the city early in the morning with the thought, "We shall pay homage to the foremost [relics]," he would enter the city as if he had actually dwelt within Jetavana.
When asked, "Where did you stay? he would reply, "What business is it of yours where I stayed?
After the lapse of a month or half a month, when questioned further, he would say, "I stayed with a recluse (samaṇa) at Jetavana."

"I have stayed in the same fragrant chamber as Gotama. Having aroused doubt among ordinary people as to whether this was true or not, after three or four months had passed, she wrapped her belly in rags, assumed the appearance of being pregnant, and covered herself with a red cloth on top, saying to the blind fools:
"This pregnancy has arisen because of the ascetic Gotama."
Having caused them to have faith, and after the lapse of eight or nine months, she bound a wooden ring around her belly,
covered it with a cloth, had her hands, feet, and back massaged with a cow’s horn, and displayed her protruding breasts; then, with her senses exhausted,
she went to the Dhamma Hall at the time of evening when the Tathāgata was seated upon the decorated Dhamma-seat preaching the Dhamma, and [approached] the Tathāgata.
Standing before him, she said, “Great Ascetic, you have been teaching the Dhamma to the great multitude; your voice is sweet and your lips are tender.
Yet, having conceived a child because of you, I have become full-term, and you do not even know of my birth-chamber.
Without yourself providing the ghee, oil, and other necessities, nor even instructing any of your attendants, [you leave me to the] King of Kosala.”

“You do not say to Anāthapiṇḍika or the female lay follower Visākhā, ‘Do what is appropriate for this young girl Ciñcā,’ but you only know how to take pleasure; you do not know how to provide for the care of a pregnancy.
Having spoken thus, as if attempting to defile the lunar disk by seizing a lump of excrement, she reviled the Tathāgata in the midst of the assembly. The Tathāgata—
Setting aside the discourse on the Dhamma, he roared like a lion and said, "Sister,
as for whether what you have said is true or false, only I and you know. She replied, "Yes, Great Ascetic,
it has become so because it is known by both you and me."
At that moment, Sakka’s seat showed signs of heat. Reflecting on this, he realized, “The young woman Ciñcā is reviling the Tathāgata with untruth.
Thinking, “I shall clear up this matter,” he arrived accompanied by four deva-youths.
These deva-youths, having become young mice, [gnawed] the binding ropes of the wooden wheel in a single stroke.
They cut off her hands; the wind blew up the garment she was wearing; a wooden ring fell and struck the instep of her foot, severing both of her feet.
People cried out, "Shame on this ill-omened woman! She reviles the Perfectly Enlightened One!
Spitting on her head, they beat her with clods of earth, sticks, and other weapons, and drove her out of Jetavana. Then, while she was still within the range of the Tathāgata’s vision—
When the time had passed, the great earth split open and gave way; a mass of flames from the Avīci hell rose up.
As if she were putting on a woolen blanket given by a noble family, she went and was reborn in Avīci.

The gain and honor of the followers of other sects declined, while that of the One Possessing the Ten Powers increased even more. On the following day, they raised this discussion in the Hall of Dharma:

“Friends, Ciñcā Māṇavikā, having slandered the Perfectly Enlightened One—the possessor of such sublime qualities and the most worthy recipient of offerings—with what was untrue, has met with great ruin.
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?
When they replied, “For this one,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now; in the past as well, she slandered me with what was untrue.”
"Having reviled him, they have surely met their destruction," he said, and added: "The Lord,
who does not perceive even the slightest fault in others,
great or small, in every respect, would impose punishment himself without due reflection."
Having related this Mahāpaduma Jātaka in detail from the Dvādasanipāta, he said:
"At that time, it seems, this co-wife of the Bodhisatta Prince Mahāpaduma, having become the king’s chief queen, invited the Great Being with unrighteous intent;
but when she failed to win his heart, she brought about her own ruin."
Having feigned illness and shown her affliction, she reported to the king: "Your son has brought me to this state against my will.
Enraged, the king threw the Great Being over a precipice.
Then, a deity dwelling within the mountain’s interior caught him and placed him upon the hood of a nāga king. The nāga king [took] him...
Having led him to the abode of the Nāgas, he honored him with half the kingdom. Having lived there for a year, desiring to go forth, he reached a region of the Himālayas;
having gone forth, he developed the meditative absorptions and the higher knowledges.
Then, a forest-dweller seeing him, informed the king. The king went to him, exchanged greetings, and [learned] the entire account of his life.
Having recognized the Great Being, he invited him to the kingship; but when the Great Being advised him, saying, "I have no need for kingship,
but you, however, should rule the kingdom righteously, without violating the ten duties of a king and abandoning the path of ruin," he rose from his seat,
wept, and as he was proceeding toward the city, asked his ministers along the way, "Whom shall I rely upon to [obtain] such a person endowed with virtuous conduct?"
“Has he met with separation from his son? “It was because of the chief queen, O King,” they replied. The king had her seized by her feet and cast down into the thieves’ precipice;
then, having entered the city, he ruled the kingdom according to Dhamma.
At that time, the youth Mahāpaduma was the Teacher, and the mother’s co-wife was the young woman Ciñcā.

Having explained this matter, the Teacher said, “Monks, for one who has abandoned the single quality of truthful speech and is established in lying, having cast aside the world beyond, there is indeed no evil deed that he would not do,” and he spoke this verse:
“For a person who has transgressed the one quality,
The liar, who has cast aside the world beyond, There is no evil that he would not commit.”
In this context, "one thing" means truth. "Of a liar" refers to one for whom not even a single word among ten spoken words is true; such is the liar.
"One who has cast aside the next world" means one who has abandoned concern for the afterlife. For such a person does not perceive these three kinds of excellence:
human prosperity, divine prosperity, and ultimately, the excellence of Nibbāna. There is none... [end of fragment].
For one such as he, there is no evil that is not called "evil" and thus not to be done.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the ninth story, the account of the young woman Ciñcā.
10. The Story of the Peerless Gift "Truly, the miserly..."—the Teacher delivered this Dhamma teaching while residing at Jetavana, concerning the peerless gift.
For on one occasion, the Teacher, having wandered on tour, entered Jetavana accompanied by a retinue of five hundred bhikkhus.
The king went to the monastery, invited the Teacher, and on the following day, having prepared alms-giving for guests, he summoned the citizens, saying, "Let them see my gift.

When the citizens arrived and saw the king's gift, they invited the Teacher on the next day, prepared alms-giving, and sent word to the king, saying, "Your Majesty, let him see our gift as well. The king—
Seeing their gift, he thought, "They have done something superior to my own gift; I shall give a gift again," and on the following day he prepared a gift.
The citizens, seeing that too, prepared one the next day as well. Thus, neither the king was able to defeat the citizens, nor were the citizens able to defeat the king.
Then, on the sixth occasion, the citizens increased [their offering] a hundredfold and a thousandfold.
They prepared the gifts in such a way that it was impossible to say, "This or that is lacking in their gift.
When the king saw this, he lay down reflecting on a stratagem, thinking, "If I am unable to do something superior to this gift of theirs, what is the use of my life?
Then Queen Mallikā approached him and asked, "Why, Great King, are you thus..."
"You are lying down; why are your senses so weary? she asked. The king said, "Now you do not know, O Queen.
"I do not know, Your Majesty," she replied. He then explained the matter to her.
Then Mallikā said to him, "Your Majesty, do not worry. Where was the king, the lord of the earth, being defeated by the citizens?"
“Whether you have seen him before or heard of him, I shall provide for your gift.
Having spoken thus, O Great King, out of his desire to provide an incomparable gift, he said:

“Have a pavilion for sitting constructed within the enclosure with *sālakalyāṇī* footprints for five hundred bhikkhus; the rest shall sit outside the enclosure. [Prepare] five hundred white parasols...”
Have them made; having taken those, five hundred elephants shall stand holding them aloft above the heads of the five hundred bhikkhus.
Have eight or ten ships of refined gold made; they shall be in the middle of the pavilion.
Between each pair of bhikkhus, a single daughter of a khattiya shall sit and grind perfumes.
Each one of the Kṣatriya daughters will take seeds and stand fanning two monks each;
the remaining Kṣatriya daughters will carry perfumes from house to house and place them in golden boats.
Some of those Kṣatriya daughters will take bunches of blue lotuses and, having stirred the perfumes placed in the golden boats, will cause the fragrance to spread.
“The citizens have neither daughters of the kṣatriya caste, nor white parasols, nor elephants. For these reasons the citizens will be defeated;
act accordingly, Great King. The king said, “Excellent, Queen! You have spoken well,” and he had everything carried out according to her instructions.
However, there was one elephant that did not suffice for a single monk. Then—
King [Mallika] said to Mallikā: “My dear lady, one elephant is not enough for a single bhikkhu;
what shall we do? “Why, Your Majesty, do you have no five hundred elephants? “I have them, my queen, but they are rogue elephants;
upon seeing the bhikkhus, they become as fierce as the Verambha winds. “Your Majesty, I will provide one young rogue elephant for a single bhikkhu.”
“I know the place where he stands holding the parasol. “Where shall we set him down? “In the presence of the noble Aṅgulimāla.
The king did so. The young elephant thrust his tail between his thighs, dropped both ears, closed his eyes, and stood still. The great crowd [said], “Of such a fierce elephant as this...”
"This is the form," he said, looking only at the elephant.
After the king had served the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha and paid homage to the Teacher,
he said, "Venerable sir, whatever items in this gift— whether allowable or unallowable— all that I give to you alone."
He said: "In that gift, fourteen crores of wealth were relinquished in a single day.
Furthermore, the Teacher’s white parasol, sitting-couch, footstool, and foot-stand—these four were priceless.
After that, he was no longer able to give such a gift to the Buddhas; for that very reason, it became known as the 'Peerless Gift' (Asadisa-dāna)."
It is said that this occurs but once for all Buddhas, and for all of them, it is arranged by a woman alone.
Now, King [Kappina] had two ministers named Kāḷa and Juṇha. Among them, Kāḷa thought: "Alas, the decline of the royal family!
Fourteen crores of wealth are exhausted in a single day. After these men have consumed this gift and departed..."
Lying down, they will fall asleep; alas, the royal family is ruined! Juṇha thought: “Oh, how well given was the King’s gift!
Indeed, it is not possible for one who does not abide in the state of royalty to give such a gift;
there is no one who does not bestow a portion upon all beings. As for me, however, I shall rejoice in this gift.”
At the conclusion of the Teacher’s meal, the king took his bowl for the sake of an expression of thanks. The Teacher thought:
"A great gift has been given by the king, like one setting a mighty flood in motion; was the great multitude able to gladden their hearts, or not?
Having discerned the mental disposition of those ministers, he [considered]: "If I were to deliver a thanksgiving discourse appropriate to the king's gift..."
“I shall act; Kāḷa’s head will split into seven pieces, and Juṇha will be established in the fruit of stream-entry.
Knowing this, out of compassion for Kāḷa, he gave such a gift while the king stood there, and having spoken only a four-line verse, he rose from his seat and went to the monastery.
The bhikkhus asked Aṅgulimāla: “Friend, did you not say...”
“Did you not fear seeing the rogue elephant standing there holding the royal parasol? “I did not fear, friend.
They approached the Teacher and said, “Venerable sir, Aṅgulimāla has declared final knowledge. The Teacher replied, “Bhikkhus, Aṅgulimāla does not fear.
For among the bulls whose taints are destroyed, my sons who resemble me are the preeminent bulls.”
Having said, "They do not fear," he spoke this verse to the assembly of brahmins:
"The bull, the preeminent one, the hero, the great seer, the victor, the imperturbable,
the cleansed, the awakened— one such as that, I call a brahmin."

The king, overcome with grief, thought: "After I had given a gift to such an assembly, the Teacher rose from his seat and departed after speaking only a verse, without offering me the appropriate *anumodanā*.
I must have offered the Teacher an inappropriate gift instead of a suitable one; I must have given him what is not allowable (*akappiya*) instead of what is allowable (*kappiya*)."
“Either something must have been given by me, or the Teacher must be angry with me. For such a gift is indeed called an ‘unparalleled gift’;
it is fitting to offer a thanksgiving appropriate to that gift. Having gone to the monastery and paid homage to the Teacher, he said this:
“Venerable sir, was it that I did not give a gift worthy of being given, or rather, was there no suitable, allowable article appropriate for a gift?”
“Without giving anything else, only an improper object was given. “What is this, Great King?
“You did not offer me a thanksgiving appropriate for my gift. “Great King, your gift was indeed worthy of thanksgiving.
For this is called an incomparable gift; it can be given only once to a single Buddha, and such a gift as this is difficult to give again.”
“But why, venerable sir, did you not offer me a blessing appropriate to my gift?
“Because the assembly was impure, Great King. “What, venerable sir, was the fault of the assembly?
Then the Teacher explained the mental conduct of both ministers and declared that he had refrained from offering the blessing out of compassion for Kāḷa. The king—
Having asked, "Is it true, Kāḷa, that you thought such a thing?
and being told, "It is true," he said, "What harm have I done to you by not taking what belongs to you, while giving my own possessions to my wife and children?
Go, sir; let what was given to you by me remain given, but depart from my kingdom. Thus he sent him out of the kingdom.
Having sent forth the moonlight and summoned Juṇha, he asked, "Is it true that you thought such a thing?
When he replied, "It is true," [the king said], "Excellent, uncle! I am pleased with you.
Take my retinue and give alms for seven days according to the method prescribed by me. Having thus handed over the kingdom for seven days, he said to the Teacher: "Behold..."

“Venerable sir, it was the act of a fool; I struck him even though he had given me such a gift. The Teacher said, “Yes, Great King, those who are called fools do not rejoice in the gifts of others and thus become destined for an unhappy rebirth.
But the wise, having rejoiced in the gifts of others, become destined for heaven alone,” and having said this, he spoke this verse:
“Indeed, the stingy do not go to the world of the gods; fools truly do not praise giving.
But the wise person, rejoicing in the gift, by that very act becomes happy in the life hereafter.
In this context, “stingy” refers to those who are stubbornly miserly. “Fools” refers to those who do not understand this world and the world beyond. “The wise person” (dhīra) refers to...
"He is wise. "He is happy for the sake of others": by that very merit of rejoicing in the gift, he becomes happy in the next world while experiencing celestial prosperity.

At the conclusion of the teaching, Juṇha was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). The Dhamma teaching was beneficial for the assembled multitude as well. Having become a stream-enterer, Juṇha continued to give alms for seven days according to the same arrangement provided by the king.
This is the tenth story of incomparable giving.

11. The Story of Kāla, Son of Anāthapiṇḍika Regarding the teaching on the Dhamma beginning with “The sole sovereignty over the earth,” the Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke concerning a man named Kāla, the son of Anāthapiṇḍika.
It is said that although he was the son of such a wealthy merchant endowed with faith, he never went into the presence of the Teacher.
He did not wish to go, nor to see [his father] when he arrived at home, nor to hear the Dhamma, nor to perform services for the Saṅgha.
Even when his father said, "Do not do this, dear son," he would not listen to his words.
Then his father thought: "If he continues to wander about having adopted such a view, he will be destined for the Avīci hell."
"But it is not fitting that my son should go to hell while I am looking on.
Now, in this world, there is no being who cannot be won over by the gift of wealth; I shall break him with wealth.
Then he said to him: "Dear son, having observed the Uposatha, go to the monastery, listen to the Dhamma, and then come back; [I will give you] a hundred kahāpaṇas."
“I will give them to you. “Give them, dear,” [the father said]. “I will, son,” [the son replied].
Having obtained this promise three times, he went to the monastery while observing the Uposatha. However, he had no need for hearing the Dhamma;
having slept in a comfortable place, he returned home early in the morning. Then his father said, “My son observed the Uposatha; quickly [give him...]”
Having said, "Bring rice gruel and other foods," he had them served. The boy replied, "I will not eat without taking coins," and so he rejected whatever was brought to him.
Then his father, unable to endure the distress, had a hoard of coins provided. The boy took those in his hand and only then consumed the food.
On the following day, the merchant said to him, "Dear son, I will give you a thousand coins; stand before the Teacher..."
“Having learned even a single verse of the Dhamma, you may return,” he sent him. He too went to the monastery and, standing before the Teacher, learned only that one verse and intended to flee.
Then the Teacher made a sign of non-attention. Without having attended to that verse, he stood thinking, “I will learn the next verse,” and heard it immediately. [Thinking,] “I will learn it...”
It is said that one truly hears with respect only when listening attentively. And it is said that for those who listen in this way, the Dhamma bestows the path of stream-entry and the others.
He too listened, thinking, "I shall master this," yet the Teacher employed a method of non-observation toward him.
While he remained there listening, thinking, "I shall master the subsequent words," he was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
On the following day, he entered Sāvatthī together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
Seeing him, the great merchant thought, "Today my son's appearance is pleasing. It occurred to the boy as well:
"Oh, that my father would not give coins to the Teacher today! Because of those coins, my state of observing the Uposatha..."
“...should he conceal it? However, the Teacher had already recognized his state of observing the Uposatha on account of that single kahāpaṇa coin from the previous day.
Having caused rice-gruel to be given to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, the Great Merchant also caused it to be given to his son.
He sat down and drank the rice-gruel in silence, ate the hard food, and partook of the meal. The Great Merchant [then spoke] to the Teacher...
At the conclusion of his meal, he had a bundle of a thousand coins placed before his son and said, "Dear son, I told you that I would give you a thousand;
having thus made you undertake the Uposatha observance, I sent you to the monastery. Here is your thousand.
Seeing the kahāpaṇas being offered before the Teacher, he felt ashamed and said, "I have no need for these kahāpaṇas. [The father replied,] "Take them!"
Even when addressed as "Father," he did not accept it. Then his father, having paid homage to the Teacher, said, "Venerable Sir, today my son’s disposition is favorable.
When asked, "What is it, Great Merchant? he replied, "On the previous day, I sent him to the monastery saying, 'I will give you a hundred kahāpaṇas.
On the following day, however, he did not wish to eat without accepting the kahāpaṇas."
"But today, even when a kahāpaṇa coin is being offered, he does not wish for it," he said. The Teacher replied, "Yes, Great Merchant, today for your son,
the fruit of stream-entry alone is more excellent than even the attainment of a universal monarch, or the attainments of the world of the gods and the Brahma-world," and having said this,
he spoke this verse:
“Compared to sole sovereignty over the earth, or going to heaven, or lordship over the entire world, the fruit of stream-entry is superior.
In this context, “sole sovereignty over the earth” refers to the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*). “Or going to heaven” refers to the twenty-six types of heavenly realms.

"By the attainment of heaven. "By sovereignty over the entire world" means not merely by sovereignty over this much—a single world together with its *nāgas*, *supaṇṇas*, *vaimānikas*, and *petas*—but rather by sovereignty over the whole world.

They say that the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*) is superior because, even after exercising rule over such a place, one is still not released from hell and the other lower realms; whereas a stream-enterer, having closed the doors to the states of woe, remains so even though he may be very weak.
He is not reborn for an eighth existence; therefore, the meaning is that the fruit of stream-entry alone is excellent and supreme.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other fruits.
This is the eleventh story, concerning the son of Anāthapiṇḍika.
The commentary on the Lokavagga is finished.
The Thirteenth Chapter. 14.
The Buddhavagga.

1. The Story of the Daughters of Māra The Teacher, while dwelling at the Seat of Enlightenment (Bodhimaṇḍa), delivered this teaching on the Dhamma beginning with the words, "He by whom [the senses] are conquered," concerning the daughters of Māra. However, having originated the discourse at Sāvatthī, he later spoke it again to the brahmin Māgaṇḍiya in the kingdom of Kuru.
It is said that in the kingdom of Kuru, the daughter of the brahmin Māgaṇḍiya was also named Māgaṇḍiyā, and she possessed the most excellent beauty.
Desiring her, many wealthy brahmins and wealthy kshatriyas sent messengers to Māgaṇḍiya, saying, "Give us your daughter.
But he rejected them all, saying, "You are not suitable for my daughter.
Then one day, at dawn, the Teacher surveyed the world and saw that [the youth] had entered within the net of his own knowledge.
Seeing the brahmin Māgaṇḍiya, the Teacher reflected, "What might happen here?

and perceived that both the brahmin and his wife possessed the necessary spiritual predispositions (*upanissaya*) for the three stages of the path and its fruits. Meanwhile, the brahmin was constantly tending a sacrificial fire outside the village.
Early in the morning, the Teacher took his bowl and robe and went to that place. As the brahmin gazed upon the Teacher’s physical splendor, he thought:
Thinking, “In this world there is no man equal to him; he is a suitable match for my daughter, so I shall give my daughter to him,” he said to the Teacher: “Ascetic, I have a daughter.
Seeing no man suitable for her, I did not give her to anyone. But you are indeed a suitable match for her.”
“I wish to give you my daughter as your attendant; stay right here until I have brought her.
Having heard his words, the Teacher neither approved nor rejected them.
The brahmin, having gone home, said to his wife: “My lady, today I have found a man worthy of my daughter.”
“Since he has been seen, we shall give her to him. Having thus adorned his daughter and taken her with him, the brahmin went to that place together with his wife.

A great crowd of people, filled with curiosity, also came out. The Teacher, instead of standing at the spot where the brahmin had spoken, displayed a footprint-relic (*padacetiya*) there and stood in another place. For it is said that the footprint-relics of the Buddhas [are such that] this...
Having resolved, "Let such-and-such a person see [me]," one appears only at the very spot where one has stepped;

in any other place, there is no one who can see it. When the brahmin was asked by his wife, who was walking with him, "Where is he?", and she said, "Tell her to stand in this place," he looked down and saw the footprints, thinking, "These are his footprints."
She showed it to him. Because of her skill in the science of marks and mantras, she said, "Brahmin, this is not the footprint of one who enjoys sensual pleasures.
When the Brahmin replied, "Madam, you saw a crocodile in the water-vessel;
I saw that ascetic and told him, 'I will give you my daughter,' and he consented," she said, "Brahmin, although you speak thus..."
Having said, "But this is the station of one who is free from defilement," he spoke this verse:
"For the crouching stance belongs to the lustful;
for the hateful, there is the forceful pressing down."
“For the deluded man there is a downward-dragging state;
for one whose veil is lifted, such is this state.
Then the brahmin said to him, “Lady, do not cry out; come along in silence,” and as they were going, he saw the Teacher.
Having pointed him out to her, saying, “This is that man,” he approached the Teacher and said, “Ascetic, I shall give you my daughter.
The Teacher, without saying, “I have no need for your daughter,” replied, “Brāhmaṇa, I will tell you a certain reason;
will you listen? When the brāhmaṇa said, “Speak, noble ascetic, I will listen,” [the Teacher related] from the time of his Great Renunciation...
Having brought back the past, he showed it to him.
Herein, this is the summary of the account: the Great Being, having renounced the glory of sovereignty, mounted his horse Kaṇṭhaka and set out with Channa as his companion.
As he was departing, Māra, standing at the city gate, said: "Siddhattha, turn back; seven days from now..."
When it was said, "The Wheel-Treasure will appear," he replied, "I know this, Māra, but I have no need for it.
Then [Māra asked], "For what purpose then do you go forth? [He replied], "For the sake of omniscient knowledge.
[Māra said], "In that case, if from this day forward you should entertain even a single thought of sensual desire or any other such thought, I shall know what must be done to you."
He said: "From that time on, seeking an opportunity, he followed the Great Being for seven years.
The Teacher, too, having practiced austerities for six years and relying on his own personal effort, penetrated the knowledge of omniscience at the foot of the Bodhi tree;
then, experiencing the bliss of liberation, he spent the fifth week at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree."
He sat down. At that time, Māra thought, "Though I have followed him for so long, seeking an opening, I have seen not the slightest lapse in him;
he has now passed beyond my domain. Overcome with dejection, he sat down on the great highway.
Then his three daughters—Taṇhā, Arati, and Ragā—said, "Our father is not to be seen; where is he?"
"Is he still here now? Looking about, they saw him sitting in that manner; approaching him, they asked, "Why, dear son, are you so distressed and dejected?
He related the matter to them. Then they said to him, "Dear son, do not worry;
we shall bring him under our own control and fetch him back. "It is not possible, mothers; he cannot be brought under anyone's control."
“Father, we women shall now bind him with the snares of passion and bring him back;
do not worry,” they said. They approached the Teacher and said, “O ascetic, let us serve your feet.
But the Teacher paid no heed to their words, nor did he even open his eyes to look at them.
Again, the daughters of Māra thought, "The inclinations of men are indeed diverse;
some have love for girls, some for those established in the first stage of life, some for those established in the middle stage of life, and some for those established in the final stage of life.
We shall entice him in various ways. Thus, each one assumed a hundred forms, beginning with the appearance of a girl.

Having manifested young maidens—those who had not yet given birth, those who had given birth once, those who had given birth twice, middle-aged women, and elderly women—they approached the Blessed One six times and said, "O ascetic, let us serve your feet.
Yet the Blessed One paid no heed to them, for he was liberated through the unsurpassed destruction of the acquisitions (*upadhi*). Then the Teacher...
As they were following him even that far, he said to them, "Go away! Why do you strive thus? It is not fitting to act in such a manner before those who are free from passion.
The Tathāgata has abandoned lust and the other defilements; for what reason do you seek to bring him under your own power?
Having said this, he spoke these verses:

“He whose victory is never lost, whose victory no one in the world can overturn—that Buddha of infinite range, Please provide the text you would like me to translate. I am ready to assist you with your request. Please provide the text to be translated.
By what track can you lead the trackless one?
He for whom there is no ensnaring,
clinging craving to lead him anywhere.
“By what track can you lead that Buddha of infinite range,
who is trackless? In this context,

“for whom what was conquered is not to be reconquered” refers to that Perfectly Enlightened One for whom the host of defilements such as lust, which were conquered by various paths, [is no longer subject to recurrence].
Furthermore, because it is not practiced again, one does not fall away; there is no such thing as a "defeat. "He does not go forth" means he does not depart;
for him, no single defilement among the group of defilements such as lust and so on ever follows after him in the world—that is to say, it does not pursue him.
"Of infinite range" means having an unlimited range by virtue of omniscient knowledge, which has the infinite as its object.
"By what foot? means: for whoever has even a single "foot"—such as the foot of lust and so forth—you may lead them away by that foot.
But for the Buddha, there is not even a single foot; how then will you lead that trackless Buddha?
In the second verse, this thing called *taṇhā* (craving) is called the "weaver of the net" (*jālakārikā*) both because it is entangled and because it functions as a snare.

"Jālinī" means "net-like" because it is like a snare. It is called "visattikā" (clinging) because of its state of being attached, its state of being stuck, its state of creeping about, its flowering with poison, its fruiting with poison, and its poisonous enjoyment toward objects such as forms.
The meaning is: "By what path will you lead that Buddha who is trackless—that craving of such a nature which has no power to lead him anywhere in existence?"
At the conclusion of the teaching, many deities attained realization of the Dhamma. The daughters of Māra also vanished right there.

Having delivered this Dhamma instruction, the Teacher said, "Māgaṇḍiya, in the past I saw these three daughters of Māra endowed with bodies resembling lumps of gold, unobstructed by phlegm and other impurities."
"Even then, there was no desire for sexual intercourse. Your daughter’s body was filled with the thirty-two aspects of a corpse, like a beautiful vessel of impurity on the outside.
For even if my foot were smeared with filth and this [threshold] were standing in the place of a door-sill, I would still not let my foot touch her body," and having said this, he spoke this verse:
“Having seen craving, aversion, and lust,
there was no desire even for sexual union:
‘What is this thing filled with urine and excrement?’”
"I would not even wish to touch him with my foot.
At the conclusion of this teaching, both the husband and wife were established in the fruit of Non-Returner (Anāgāmi).
This is the first story concerning the daughters of Māra.

2. The Story of the Descent from Heaven (*Devorohaṇavatthu*) "Those wise ones who are devoted to meditation"—this teaching on the Dhamma was spoken by the Teacher at the gate of the city of Sāṅkāśya with reference to many gods and humans. However, the origin of the discourse was in Rājagaha.
For on one occasion, the merchant of Rājagaha, for the purpose of securing against danger and because his ornaments and other belongings had been lost through negligence, [set out to retrieve them].
Having had a net-basket constructed for the sake of protection, he played in the water-sports of the Ganges.
Then, a red sandalwood tree growing on the upper bank of the Ganges, its roots washed away by the river water, fell and was shattered against the rocks here and there, scattering about.
From that, a single piece the size of a water-jar, being ground by the rocks and struck by the waves of the water, [was formed].
Having become rotten, it was gradually carried along by the current until, covered with seaweed, it became caught in his net. The merchant asked, "What is this?
and upon hearing it was a "tree-stick," he had it brought to him. To determine what it was, he had it planed with the edge of a bamboo splinter.
At that very moment, red sandalwood the color of lac appeared. However, the merchant...
He was neither of right view nor of wrong view, but was neutral in nature. He thought: “In my house there is much red sandalwood;

what indeed shall I do with it? Then this occurred to him: “In this world there are many who say, ‘We are arahants, we are arahants,’ yet I do not see even a single arahant. Having prepared a fragrant paste in my house...”
“Having had a bowl inscribed and placed in a sling, I will have it suspended sixty cubits in the air by means of a succession of bamboo poles and say:
‘If there is an Arahant, let him come through the air and take this. Whosoever takes it, I shall go for refuge to him along with my sons and wife.
Thinking thus, he had the bowl inscribed according to his plan and [placed it] upon a succession of bamboo poles.
Having raised it up, he said, "Let whoever in this world is an Arahant come through the air and take this bowl.
Six teachers said, "This is worthy of us; give it to us alone. He replied, "Come through the air and take it.
Then, on the sixth day, Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta sent his disciples, saying, "Go..."
"Tell the merchant thus: 'This is truly worthy of our teacher;
do not go through the air for the sake of such a trifle, but please give him that bowl. They went and spoke to the merchant accordingly.
The merchant said, "Let only one who is capable of coming through the air take it. Nāṭaputta himself desired to go.
He gave an instruction to his pupils: "I shall act as if I am about to leap up after lifting one hand and one foot;
you must say to me, 'Teacher, what are you doing? Do not show the quality of Arahantship hidden for the sake of a wooden bowl to the great multitude,' and then seize me by my hands and feet."
“Dragging him along, you shall make him fall to the ground! He went there and said to the merchant, “Great merchant, this bowl is suitable for me;
it is not suitable for others. Let it not be that for the sake of such a trifle you should find my flying through the air disagreeable;
give me the bowl. “Venerable sir, take it by flying through the air! Then Nāṭaputta—
“Go away, then! Go away! Having sent his pupils away, he raised one hand and one foot, thinking, “I shall fly up into the air.
Then the pupils seized him by the hands and feet, saying, “Teacher, what is this that you are doing?
What is the purpose of showing off hidden virtues to the great multitude for the sake of a wretched, inferior wooden bowl? Thus they held him.
Having seized him and dragged him down, they threw him to the ground. He said to the merchant, "Great merchant, these men will not let me fly up;
give me back my bowl. "Go up and take it yourself, venerable sir! Thus, although the heretics exerted themselves for six days, they did not obtain that bowl at all.
On the seventh day, when the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and the Venerable Piṇḍolabhāradvāja had gone to Rājagaha with the thought,
“We shall go for alms,” and were standing on a flat rock while putting on their robes,
some ruffians started a conversation: “Friends, in the past six teachers wandered about in the world thinking, ‘We are Arahants.’”
“Today is the seventh day since the merchant of Rājagaha raised up his alms-bowl and said, ‘If there be any who are Arahants, let them come through the air and take it!
Yet not a single person has leaped into the sky saying, ‘I am an Arahant. Today, therefore, the absence of Arahants in the world has become known.
Having heard those words, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed the Venerable [Sāriputta]:
He said to Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja: “Friend Bhāradvāja, have you heard these words?
These men speak as if they were upholding the Buddha’s teaching. You possess great psychic power and great majesty; go, travel through the air, and take that bowl.
“Friend Mahāmoggallāna, you are the foremost of those possessed of psychic power; you [should take it].”

“Take it; if you do not take it, I shall take it. When he said, “Take it, friend,” the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja entered the fourth jhāna, the basis for direct knowledge, and arising from it, he lifted the three-league-long rock on his back into the air like a tuft of cotton wool, covering it with the sole of his foot, seven times over the city of Rājagaha.
He moved around it. He appeared like a covering for the city, which measured three hundred *gāvutas* in size.
The city dwellers, terrified that "the rock is seizing us by overwhelming us," placed their beds and other belongings upon their heads and hid here and there.
On the seventh round, the Elder broke through the back rock and revealed himself. When the great multitude saw the Elder, they—
“Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja, grasp the rock firmly; do not destroy us all!
The Elder kicked the rock with his toe and released it. It traveled and landed back in its very original place.
The Elder stood upon the roof of the merchant’s house. Seeing him, the merchant prostrated himself on his chest and said, “Come down!”
Saying, "Very well, sir," he had the Elder descend from the sky, had him sit down, and having caused an alms bowl to be brought down, filled it with the four sweet foods and gave it to the Elder.
The Elder took the bowl and set out toward the monastery.
Now, those who were in the forest or in empty huts did not witness that miracle. They gathered together and said, "Venerable sir, even for us..."
“Show us a miracle! they followed after the Elder. Having displayed various miracles for each of them, he went to the monastery.
The Teacher, following him and hearing the noise of the great crowd making a clamor, asked, “Ānanda, whose noise is this?
“Venerable Sir, Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja has leaped into the air and taken a sandalwood bowl; it is his—”
Having heard that "this sound is near," he summoned Bhāradvāja and asked, "Is it true that you did this?
When the elder replied, "It is true, venerable sir," the Buddha rebuked him, saying, "Bhāradvāja, why did you do such a thing?
He then had the bowl broken into pieces and gave them to the monks to be used as eye-salve, [and so forth] regarding the miracle.
He established a training rule for his disciples so that they would not perform such miracles.
When the members of other sects heard, "The ascetic Gotama, it is said, had that bowl broken and established a training rule for his disciples so that they would not perform miracles," they said,
"The disciples of the ascetic Gotama [disregard] the training rule he has established."
“Even for the sake of their lives they do not transgress [their vows]; the ascetic Gotama will surely protect that as well.

Now we have found our opportunity,” they proclaimed as they wandered through the city streets: “Protecting our own virtue, we previously did not reveal our virtue to the great multitude on account of a wooden bowl;
but the disciples of the ascetic Gotama, for the sake of a mere alms-bowl...”
For this reason, they showed their own virtues to the great multitude, saying, "The ascetic Gotama, out of his own cleverness, had his bowl broken and established a training rule;
now we shall perform a miracle in competition with him.
King Bimbisāra, having heard that report, went into the presence of the Teacher and said, "Venerable sir, it is said that you have performed a miracle..."
“Is it not true, Great King, that the training rule was laid down for the sake of preventing disciples from committing [such acts]? “Yes, Great King.
“Now the sectarians say, ‘We shall perform a miracle together with you’; what will you do now?
“If they perform one, I shall perform one too, Great King. “But did you not lay down the training rule? “No, Great King, I did not.”
“I have prescribed a training rule for myself, saying, ‘That is prescribed by me alone for my disciples.
But, Venerable Sir, apart from you, is there not a training rule prescribed elsewhere? “In that case, Great King, I shall question you on this very point:
‘Great King, do you have a pleasure grove in your realm? “I do, Venerable Sir. “If, Great King, [you were to give it away]...”
“If a great multitude of people were to eat mangoes and other fruits in your park, what should be done with them? “A punishment, Bhante.
“But do you yourself have permission to eat [from it]? “Yes, Bhante; I am not subject to punishment, for I am permitted to eat what belongs to me.
“Great King, just as your command prevails throughout your realm of three hundred leagues, so too does yours over your own property.”
“There is no punishment for one eating mangoes and such fruits in a park, whereas there is for others; even so, my command prevails over hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems.
There is no such thing as transgression of the training rules for myself, whereas there is for others;
I shall perform a miracle. When the sectarians heard this speech, they said, “Now we are lost; by this ascetic...”
It is said that Gotama had laid down training rules only for his disciples, not for himself.
Thinking, "He himself wishes to perform a miracle; what indeed shall we do? they deliberated.
The King asked the Teacher, "Venerable Sir, when will you perform the miracle? "In four months from now," he replied.
“On the full moon day of Āsāḷha, Great King. “Where will you perform it, venerable sir? “At Sāvatthī, Great King.
“But why does the Teacher point to such a distant place? “Because that is the place where all Buddhas perform the Great Miracle;
moreover, it is for the sake of assembling a great multitude of people that he chooses a distant location.”

...declared. When the sectarians heard this report, they said, “It is said that after four months have passed from now, the ascetic Gotama will perform a miracle at Sāvatthī. We shall follow him immediately without letting him escape;
when the great multitude sees us, they will ask, ‘What is this? Then we shall say to them, ‘We are [following] with the ascetic Gotama.’”
“We said, ‘We shall perform a miracle,’ and he fled; we followed him, not allowing him to escape.
The Teacher, having walked for alms in Rājagaha, departed. The sectarians also departed right after him and stayed at the place where the meal was being taken.
Having stayed there, they took their morning meal the following day. When they were asked by the people, “What is this? they replied: [as follows].
They announced [the arrival] according to the very plan they had previously considered. The great multitude also followed in pursuit, thinking, "We shall see the miracle.
The Teacher gradually reached Sāvatthī. The sectarians also went along with him;
having won over his attendants and received a hundred thousand [pieces of money], they had a pavilion constructed from acacia pillars and had it covered with blue lotuses.

Thinking, “We shall perform a miracle here,” they sat down. King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Teacher and said, “Venerable sir, the heretics have had a pavilion built; I too shall have a pavilion built for you.
“Enough, great king; I have one who builds my pavilion. “Venerable sir, who else but me would be able to build it?”
“Sakka, the king of the gods. “But where, venerable sir, will you perform the miracle? “At the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree, Great King.

When the sectarians heard that “he will indeed perform the miracle at the foot of the Amba tree,” they informed their own supporters and, within a distance of a league, uprooted even mango saplings that had grown that very day and threw them into the forest.
On the full-moon day of Āsāḷha, the Teacher entered the city.
At that time, the king’s park-keeper named Kaṇḍa saw a large ripe mango inside a leaf-cup fashioned by a reddish-brown cricket.
Driven by greed for its fragrance and flavor, he drove away the crows that were swooping down toward it and, taking it with him to give to the king to eat, he encountered the Teacher on the way.
Having seen it, he thought: "If the king were to eat this mango and give me eight or sixteen kahāpaṇas, that would not be enough for my livelihood even for a single lifetime.
But if I were to give this to the Teacher, it would certainly bring me benefit for a long time. He then offered that ripe mango to the Teacher. The Teacher—
He looked toward the Elder Ānanda. Then the Elder brought forth the bowl given by the Four Great Kings and placed it in his hand.
The Teacher extended the bowl, accepted the mango fruit, and demonstrated the manner of sitting right there.
The Elder spread out his robe and gave it to him. Then, once he was seated, the Elder strained some drinking water.

Having crushed ripe mangoes and made a drink from them, she gave it to him. After the Teacher had drunk the mango juice, he said to Kaṇḍa, “Plant this mango seed right here after clearing away the dust. He did so.
The Teacher washed his hand over it; as soon as his hand was washed, [the tree] became a trunk the size of a plowshare and fifty cubits in height.
A mango tree sprang up. It had five great branches—one in each of the four directions and one reaching upward—each fifty cubits long.
At that very moment, it became covered with flowers and fruit, bearing clusters of ripe mangoes at every spot.
The monks coming from behind arrived while eating mangoes as they went. The King [saw] such a...
Having heard that a mango tree had sprung up, he established a guard over it with the thought, "Let no one cut it down.
Because it was planted with a stalk (*kaṇḍa*), it became known as the Kaṇḍamba tree. Even the ruffians, having eaten the mango fruits, said: "Go, you wicked nuns!
'The ascetic Gotama, they say, will perform a miracle at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree,' so [you must go] by yourselves..."
Even mango saplings that had grown within a *yojana* were uprooted; saying, "This is what is called a *kaṇḍamba*," they struck them with mango seeds from their leftovers.
Sakka commanded the divine son Vātavalāhaka: "Uproot the pavilion of the sectarians with winds and cast it onto a dung heap."
"Throw it down! He did so. He also commanded the divine son Suriya, saying, "Scorch them, dragging down the solar disk.
He did so. Again, he commanded Vātavalāhaka, saying, "Go forth, raising up a whirlwind.
As he did so, he sprinkled the heretics—who were dripping with sweat—with a mass of dust until they resembled red clay.
They became so. He also commanded the rain-cloud, saying, "Let down large drops. It did so accordingly.
Then their bodies became like those of monkeys. Being ashamed, those Nigaṇṭhas fled in every direction they could face.
While they were thus fleeing, a certain farmer who was an attendant of Purāṇa Kassapa thought, "Now my masters..."
Thinking, “It is the time for the performance of the miracle; having gone there, I shall witness the miracle,” he released the oxen.
Taking the rice-gruel pot and the rope brought early in the morning, as he was coming along, he saw the old man fleeing as before.
He asked, “Venerable sir, today I am coming because I thought, ‘I shall witness the miracle of the noble ones. Where are you going? “What? [the other replied.]
"By means of this miracle, give me this water-pot and the rope. Taking the water-pot and the rope given by him, he went to the riverbank;
having tied the pot to his own neck with the rope, feeling ashamed, he said nothing and fell into the lake.
As he was rising amidst the water bubbles, he passed away and was reborn in the Avīci hell.
Sakka fashioned a jeweled walkway in the sky; one end rested upon the eastern rim of the world-system and the other upon the western rim.

As the shadow lengthened for the assembled assembly of thirty-six yojanas, the Teacher, perceiving that "the time for performing the miracle has now arrived," emerged from the Fragrant Chamber and stood at its entrance.

He stood there. Then a certain powerful laywoman named Gharaṇī, who was a non-returner (anāgāminī), approached him and said, "Venerable sir, while a daughter such as I exists, you have no need to trouble yourselves; I shall perform a miracle.
"How will you do it, Gharaṇī? "Venerable sir, [I shall take] the great earth within a single world-system..."
“Having made water, like a water-bird, I will dive and show myself at the eastern rim of the world-sphere;
likewise at the western, northern, and southern rims, and likewise in the center. When the great multitude sees me and asks, “Who is this?
they will say, “This is a housewife; such is the power of a single woman. What then of the power of a Buddha?”
"But what will it be like? "In this way, the heretics will flee even without seeing you.
Then the Teacher said to her, "I know that your wife is capable of performing such a miracle; however, this bouquet of flowers was not tied for your sake," and he refused.
She thought, "The Teacher does not grant me permission; surely there must be something superior [to what I can do]."
"Is there another capable of performing a miracle? he asked, and stood to one side.
The Teacher, thinking, "In this very way their virtue will become manifest; thus he shall roar the lion’s roar in the midst of this assembly extending thirty-six yojanas," questioned others as well:
"How will you perform the miracle? They replied, "In such and such a manner..."
“We shall do so, Bhante,” they said, and standing right before the Teacher, they let out a lion’s roar.

Among them, it is said, Cūḷa-Anāthapiṇḍika thought, “While there exist sons like me who are lay followers who have attained the stage of non-returning, there is no need for the Teacher to undergo exhaustion.
He then said, “Bhante, I shall perform a miracle. When asked, “How will you do it? he replied, “Bhante, I—”
“Having manifested a Brahmā-body twelve yojanas in height, I shall, in the midst of this assembly, clap my hands with a sound like the thundering of a great cloud;
this is called the ‘Brahmā-clap’. The great multitude, asking, “What kind of sound is this?
will say, “This is indeed the so-called ‘Brahmā-clap’ of Cūḷa-Anāthapiṇḍika. The sectarians [will say], “Of a householder...”
"Indeed, such is his power; but what will the power of a Buddha be like? Thinking thus, they fled even before seeing you.
The Teacher said, "I know your power," and having spoken to him in the same manner, he did not grant permission for him to perform a miracle.
Then, a seven-year-old novice nun named Cīra, who had attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), paid homage to the Teacher.
“I will perform a miracle, Bhante,” he said. “How will you do it with a cloth?

“Bhante, having brought Sineru, the Cakkavāḷa mountains, and the Himavat mountain, and having placed them here in a row, I shall go forth from each one like a female swan, moving without attachment; when the great multitude sees me—”

“Having asked, ‘Who is this?’, they will say, ‘A young novice nun. Then the heretics will think, ‘If such is the power of a novice nun who is only seven years old, what must the power of a Buddha be like?
and they will flee even before seeing you. From here on, such statements should be understood according to what has been said. Regarding her as well, the Blessed One said, “I know...”

Having said, "They possess such power," he did not grant permission for the performance of a miracle. Then a certain novice named Cunda, who was seven years of age, had attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), and was an arahant with taints destroyed;
he paid homage to the Teacher and said, "Blessed One, I shall perform a miracle.
When asked, "How will you do it? he replied, "Venerable Sir, from Jambudīpa..."
“Having seized the trunk of the great Jambu tree that serves as a banner, I shall shake it and bring back the great Jambu fruits to feed this assembly;
and having brought the flowers of the Pāricchattaka tree, I shall pay homage to you.
The Teacher, saying, “I know your power,” rejected his performance of such a miracle.
Then the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā, having paid homage to the Teacher, said, "Venerable Sir, I shall perform a miracle.

When asked, "How will you do it? she replied, "Venerable Sir, after I have shown the assembly extending twelve yojanas all around, I shall come as a Wheel-turning Monarch surrounded by an assembly thirty-six yojanas in circumference."
“I shall pay homage to you. The Teacher, saying, “I know your power,” likewise refused her request to perform a miracle.
Then the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, having paid homage to the Blessed One, said, “Venerable Sir, I shall perform a miracle.
When asked, “How will you do it? he replied, “Venerable Sir, I shall place Mount Sineru, the king of mountains, between my teeth.”
“Setting aside the bean and mustard seeds, I shall eat [the rest]. “What else will you do?
“I shall roll up this great earth like a mat and place it between my fingers. “What else will you do?
“I shall spin the great earth like a potter’s wheel and cause the multitude to eat the essence of the earth.”
“What else will you do? “Placing the earth in my left hand, I shall set these beings down on another island with my right hand.

“What else will you do? “Making Mount Sineru like the handle of a parasol, I shall lift up the great earth, place it upon that [handle], and like a monk holding a parasol, I shall walk through the air carrying it with one hand.”
The Teacher, saying, "I know your power," did not grant him permission to perform a miracle as well.
Thinking, "The Teacher surely knows that I am capable of performing a miracle even more excellent than his," he stood to one side.
Then the Teacher said to him, "Moggallāna, this basket of herbs was not tied for your sake. For I am one whose burden is peerless."
"There is no one else capable of bearing my burden. It is not surprising that there is now no one capable of bearing my burden;
even when I was reborn in the causeless animal realm, there was likewise no one else capable of bearing my burden.
Having said this, when asked by the Elder, "But when was that, venerable sir?", he brought up the past:
“Whenever there is a heavy burden, whenever there is a path that leads deep, it is then that they yoke the black bull; he indeed carries that burden.
Having thus related the Kaṇhasabha Jātaka in detail, he further showed that same story with specific distinctions:
“One should speak only what is pleasing, never what is displeasing;
for one who speaks what is pleasing, a heavy burden was lifted,
and he obtained wealth, whereby he became glad at heart.”
Having related this Nandivisāla Jātaka in detail, the Teacher ascended the Jewel Walk.
There was a retinue twelve yojanas long in front of him, and likewise behind, to the north, and to the south.
But in the midst of a retinue twenty-four yojanas long, stretching directly before him, the Blessed One performed the Twin Miracle.
That should first be understood from the text as follows: What is the Tathāgata’s knowledge regarding the Twin Miracle?
Here, the Tathāgata performs the Twin Miracle, which is not shared with his disciples:
from the upper part of his body a mass of fire issues forth, and from the lower part of his body a stream of water issues forth; from the lower part of his body a mass of fire issues forth.
A stream of water flows from the upper part of the body. From the front part of the body, from the back part of the body; from the back part of the body, from the front part of the body;
from the right eye, from the left eye; from the left eye, from the right eye;
from the right ear canal, from the left ear canal; from the left ear canal, from the right ear canal; from the right nostril, from the left nostril.
From the left nostril, from the right nostril; from the right shoulder, from the left shoulder; from the left shoulder, from the right shoulder;
from the right hand, from the left hand; from the left hand, from the right hand;
from the right side, from the left side; from the left side, from the right side; from the right foot, from the left foot.
From the left foot, from the right foot; from each finger, from the spaces between the fingers;
from the spaces between the fingers, from each finger— from each single pore of the body a mass of fire issues forth, and from each single hair a stream of water issues forth.
From each single hair a mass of fire issues forth, and from each single pore a stream of water issues forth, [in] six colors, blue...
[There were] yellow, red, white, madder-colored, and radiant [robes].
While the Blessed One walked up and down, the Buddha-emanation stood, sat, or lay down... [and so on] ...the emanation lay down while the Blessed One walked up and down, stood, or sat.
This is the knowledge regarding the Tathāgata’s twin miracle.
The Blessed One performed this miracle while walking back and forth on that very walkway.

By means of his attainment of the fire-kasiṇa, a mass of fire issued from the upper part of his body; by means of his attainment of the water-kasiṇa, a stream of water issued from the lower part of his body.
However, the mass of fire did not issue from the place where the stream of water issued, nor did the stream of water issue from the place where the mass of fire issued.
To show that the stream of water flows from its point of origin, it is said: "from the lower part of the body and from the upper part of the body.
This same method applies to all the locations. However, in this case, the mass of fire was unmixed with the stream of water, and likewise the stream of water was unmixed with the mass of fire.
It is said that both of these, having risen as far as the Brahma-world, [reached] the rim of the world-sphere.

It falls. As for what is called "the six colors," its six-colored rays—like molten gold being poured from jars, or like streams of liquid gold issuing from a mechanical pipe—rise up from within a single world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), strike the Brahma-world, turn back, and seize the very rim of that world-system. Within a single world-system...
The Bodhi-hall became as if its rafters were crooked, filled with a singular light.
On that day, the Teacher walked back and forth performing miracles, preaching the Dhamma to the great multitude from time to time.
And while preaching, he did not leave the people despondent, but provided them with an opportunity for encouragement. At that moment—
The great multitude broke into a cry of "Well done!
At the moment that applause arose, the Teacher, surveying the minds of such a vast assembly, discerned the mental disposition of each individual according to sixteen modes.
Such is the swiftness of the Buddhas' mental revolution. Whosoever was devoted to which teaching or which miracle, he discerned that person's inclination alone.
He preached the Dhamma and performed a miracle. While the Dhamma was thus being taught and the miracle being performed, there occurred a realization of the Dhamma among the great multitude.
But the Teacher, finding no one in that assembly who had grasped his mind and was capable of asking another question, manifested a created Buddha. To the question asked by that [created Buddha],...
The Teacher answered; he answered what was asked by the Teacher. When the Blessed One was walking, the created being performed one of the other postures, such as standing;
when the created being was walking, the Blessed One performed one of the other postures, such as standing.
To show this matter, it was said: "The created being walks," and so forth. While the Teacher was acting in this way...
Having witnessed the miracle and heard the discourse on the Dhamma, twenty koṭis of beings attained penetration of the Dhamma in that assembly.
While performing the miracle, the Teacher reflected: "Where indeed did the Buddhas of the past perform this miracle and enter the rains retreat?
Having reflected, he saw: "They entered the rains retreat in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and taught the Abhidhamma Piṭaka to their mothers."
Having seen this, he lifted his right foot and placed it upon the summit of Yugandhara; then, lifting his other foot, he placed it upon the summit of Sineru.
Thus, there were three strides covering a distance of sixty-eight hundred thousand *yojanas*, leaving two footprints.
It should not be thought that the Teacher stepped forward by extending his foot; for at the very moment he lifted his foot—
The mountains came to the foot of the Teacher’s path and received him;
when the Teacher stepped upon them, those mountains rose up and stood back in their own places. Seeing the Teacher, Sakka thought:
“I suspect the Teacher will spend this rains-retreat on the Paṇḍukambala Rock; it will be a great benefit to many deities. While the Teacher...”
"Furthermore, once the rainy-season residence has begun here, other deities will not even be able to place a hand upon it.
Moreover, this Paṇḍukambala Stone is sixty yojanas long, fifty yojanas wide, and fifteen yojanas thick;
even when the Teacher is seated upon it, it will remain empty. The Teacher [perceived] his intention.
Having understood that his own saṅghāṭi was being cast as a cover for the stone seat, he threw it. Sakka thought:
“He has thrown it merely to cover the robe, but he himself will sit on a very small space.
The Teacher, knowing his intention, sat upon the yellow-silk stone—just like a great wearer of rag-robes—on a low stool, within the fold of his inner robe.
Having done so, he sat down. The great multitude, looking for the Teacher at that very moment, did not see him;
it was as if the time had come for the moon to set, or as if the time had come for the sun to set. The great multitude thought:
"Has he gone to Cittakūṭa, or to Kelāsa, or to Yugandhara?"
“We shall not see the Perfectly Awakened One, the eldest in the world, the bull among men”—speaking this verse, he lamented. Others said, “The Teacher delights in solitude;
out of shame, thinking, ‘I have performed such a miracle before such an assembly,’ he must have gone to another kingdom or district.”
“We shall not see him now,” they lamented, and spoke this verse:
“The wise one, delighting in solitude, will not return to this world;
we shall not behold the Fully Awakened One, the eldest in the world, the bull among men.”

They asked Mahāmoggallāna, "Venerable sir, where is the Teacher? Although he knew for himself, out of a desire that the virtues of others might also become manifest, he said, "Ask Anuruddha. They asked the Elder in that manner, "Venerable sir, where is the Teacher? [He replied:
"Having entered the rains retreat upon the Yellow Marble Rock in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven..."
“He has gone to teach the Abhidhamma Piṭaka to his mother. “When will he return, Bhante? “After teaching the Abhidhamma Piṭaka for three months, on the day of the Great Pavāraṇā.
They thought, “We will not depart until we have seen the Teacher,” and they encamped their army right there.
It is said that the very sky served as their canopy. And because of that great assembly, there was a friction of bodies.
His name was not known; the earth opened up, and the surface of the ground became entirely pure.
The Teacher first said to the Elder Moggallāna: “Moggallāna, you should teach the Dhamma to this assembly;
Cūḷa-Anāthapiṇḍika will provide the food. Therefore, for those three months, it was Cūḷa-Anāthapiṇḍika alone who...
He provided for that assembly with rice gruel, boiled rice, hard foods, betel, oil, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments.
Mahāmoggallāna taught the Dhamma and answered the questions posed by those who had come to witness the miracles.
The Teacher also spent the rainy season on the Paṇḍukambala stone slab in order to teach the Abhidhamma to his mother.
The deities of the ten thousand world-systems gathered around him who had arrived. Therefore it is said:
“When the Buddha, the Supreme among Men, dwelt upon the yellow sandstone slab at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.”
“Deities from ten world-systems, having assembled together,
pay homage to the Perfectly Enlightened One as he dwells atop the Naga.
No deity whatsoever outshines the Perfectly Enlightened One in beauty.”
“Having surpassed all the gods, the Fully Enlightened One alone shines forth.
Thus, while he sat having outshone all the deities with the radiance of his own body, his mother came from the Tusita celestial mansion and sat on his right side;
and the deity Indaka also came and sat on the very same right side.
Aṅkura sat down on the left side. As the powerful deities were gathering together, he moved aside and found space at a distance of twelve yojanas;
Indaka remained sitting right where he was.
The Teacher, having observed both of them and desiring to make known how great the fruit is of a gift given to those worthy of offerings within his own dispensation, spoke thus: "Aṅkura..."
“During that long interval, for a period measuring ten thousand years, she prepared a row of hearths twelve yojanas in length and gave a great gift;
now, having come into my presence, she has found space in a place twelve yojanas wide—what indeed could be the reason for this? And so it was said:
“Having observed both Aṅkura and Indaka, the Perfectly Awakened One,
honoring them as worthy of offerings, spoke these words:
‘A great gift was given by you, Aṅkura, over a long interval of time.’”
“You are sitting too far away; come near me.
He, full of faith, reached the surface of the earth. The entire assembly heard him.
When this was said, Aṅkura, being exhorted by the One of Developed Mind, spoke as follows:
“What is the use of that gift to me, who am worthy of offerings?
This Indaka yakkha gives but a meager gift;
he does not outshine us, just as the moon does not outshine the host of stars.”
In that context, *dajjā* means "having given. When this was said, the Teacher asked Indaka, "Indaka, you are sitting on my right side;

why do you sit there without moving away? He replied, "Venerable Sir, like a farmer sowing a small seed in a fertile field, I have obtained the excellence of a worthy recipient (*dakkhiṇeyya*)," thus speaking in praise of the one worthy of offerings.
“Just as when much seed is sown in a field of barren soil,
it does not yield an abundant harvest, nor does it satisfy the farmer.
Even so, a great gift bestowed upon those who are immoral— ”
The fruit is not abundant, nor does it satisfy the donor.
"Just as when even a small seed is sown in a fertile field,
and the rain falls properly, the fruit satisfies the farmer."
“Even so, toward those who are virtuous and endowed with such qualities, even a small service rendered becomes a merit of great fruit. What was his past deed?
It is said that when the Elder Anuruddha had entered the village for alms, [he performed this act].
He had his own alms-food, which he had brought back in a ladle, given to him.

At that time, Aṅkura’s merit became far more fruitful than the gift given by [the other] who had constructed a row of cooking hearths twelve yojanas long for ten thousand years. Therefore, he spoke thus.
When this was said, the Teacher said: “Aṅkura, a gift ought to be given with discrimination; in this way, it brings comfort to those who are suffering.”
It becomes of great fruit, like a seed sown in fertile soil. But you did not do so; therefore, your gift has not become of great fruit.
Explaining this point, he said:
“Having discerned, one should give a gift where what is given bears great fruit…” and so forth.
“Having discerned those worthy of offerings in this world of the living— gifts praised by the Sugata—
what is given to them yields great fruit.”
"Seeds sown in a good field"—having said this, and teaching the Dhamma further, he spoke these verses:
"Fields have weeds as their defect; this generation has passion as its defect."
Therefore, what is given to those free from passion bears great fruit.
Fields have weeds as their blemish, and this generation has hatred as its blemish;
therefore, what is given to those free from hatred bears great fruit.
“Fields have weeds as their defect; this generation has delusion as its defect.
Therefore, what is given to those free from delusion yields great fruit.
Fields have weeds as their defect; this generation has craving as its defect.”
"Therefore, indeed, what is given to those free from craving bears great fruit.
At the conclusion of this teaching, both Aṅkura and Indaka were established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala), and the Dhamma instruction was beneficial for the great multitude as well.
Then the Teacher, seated in the midst of the assembly of devas, spoke concerning his mother: "Wholesome states, unwholesome states..."
“...the indeterminate phenomena,” he thus established the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. In this manner, for three months without interruption, he taught the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.

While teaching, at the time for the alms-round, he would create a manifested Buddha (nimmitabuddha), saying, “Teach this much of the Dhamma until my return,” and then go to the Himālaya mountains to eat a tooth-stick of *nāgalatā* and bathe in Lake Anotatta.
Having washed his face and brought almsfood from Uttarakuru, he sat in the Mahāsāla Māḷaka and performed his meal duties.
The Elder Sāriputta went there and performed his duty toward the Teacher.
At the conclusion of the meal, the Teacher said, "Sāriputta, today I have preached such and such a Dhamma; you [should teach it] to your own resident bhikkhus."

"Recite it," he said, and spoke thus to the Elder. It is said that five hundred sons of noble family, having gained confidence through the Twin Miracle (*yamakapāṭihīra*), went forth under the Elder. Referring to them, he spoke to the Elder in this way.

Having spoken, he departed for the world of the gods and himself preached the Dhamma, beginning from the place where the manifested Buddha had taught. The Elder also went and preached the Dhamma to those monks.
He taught them. While the Teacher was dwelling in the world of the gods, they became those who completed the sevenfold training.
It is said that during the time of Buddha Kassapa, they had been small bats;
hanging in a certain mountain cave, they heard the sound of two elders walking up and down and reciting the Abhidhamma, and they grasped the signs of the sounds.
Not knowing that "these are called the aggregates" and "these are called the elements," they merely grasped the sign in their memory;

having passed away from there, they were reborn in the deva world. After experiencing celestial prosperity for the duration of an interval between Buddhas, they passed away from there and were reborn in noble families in Sāvatthī.
Having developed serene confidence at the Twin Miracle, they went forth into homelessness under the Elder.
At the very beginning, they were those who had been engaged for seven days. The Teacher also taught the Abhidhamma for those three months in that same manner.
At the conclusion of the teaching, there was a penetration of the Dhamma by eighty-four thousand deities, and Mahāmāyā also became established in the fruit of stream-entry.
That assembly, thirty-six yojanas in circumference, having heard that "on the seventh day from now, the Great Pavāraṇā will take place," approached the Elder Mahāmoggallāna and said:
"Venerable sir, it is fitting to know the day of the Teacher’s descent;
for we shall not depart without seeing the Teacher. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna [considered] that matter...
Having heard this, he said, "Excellent, friend," and sank right there into the earth.

Having gone to the foot of Sineru, he resolved, "Let the assembly see me as I ascend," and like a yellow woolen cloth (paṇḍukambala) inlaid with a jewel, his form became visible as he ascended through the middle of Sineru.
The people also watched him, saying, "He has ascended one league; he has ascended two leagues."
They looked down. The Elder, as if lifting the Teacher’s feet with his head, climbed up, paid homage, and said:
