“Venerable Sir, the assembly wishes to depart as soon as they see you; when will you descend? “Moggallāna, where is your elder brother Sāriputta?
“Venerable Sir, he has entered the rains retreat at Saṅkassanagara. “Moggallāna,” [the Teacher replied].
"On the seventh day from now, I shall descend at the gate of the city of Sāṅkāśya for the Great Invitation (Mahāpavāraṇā). Those who wish to see me should come there;
from Sāvatthī to the gate of the city of Sāṅkāśya is thirty yojanas, and on such a journey there is no need for anyone to provide provisions.
Let those observing the Uposatha go to their own monasteries for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma."
“...you should inform them, saying, ‘Come as if you were [already here]. The Elder replied, “Very well, Bhante,” and having gone there, he informed them accordingly.
After the Teacher had completed the rains retreat and performed the *pavāraṇā* ceremony, he informed Sakka: “Great King, we shall go to the human realm.
Sakka constructed three stairways made of gold, gems, and silver. Their bases were at the gate of the city of Sāṅkāśya.
They established themselves, their heads upon the summit of Sineru. Among them, on the southern side, there was a golden staircase for the devas;
on the northern side, a silver staircase for the Mahābrahmās; and in the middle, a jeweled staircase for the Tathāgata.
The Teacher, standing upon the summit of Sineru at the time of his descent from the deva realm, performed the Twin Miracle.
Having done so, he looked upward; as far as the Brahma-world, it became a single open space. He looked downward; as far as the Avīci hell, it became a single open space.
He looked toward the cardinal and intermediate directions; hundreds of thousands of world-systems became a single open space.
Devas saw humans, and humans also saw devas; everyone saw one another face to face.

The Blessed One emitted rays of six colors. On that day, having beheld the splendor of the Buddha, there was not a single person among the assembly, which extended thirty-six *yojanas* in circumference, who did not aspire to Buddhahood.
The gods descended by a golden staircase, the Great Brahmas by a silver staircase, and the Perfectly Enlightened One by a jeweled staircase.

Otari. Pañcasikha, the son of the Gandhabba deities, taking his yellow-wooded lute (*veluvapaṇḍuvīṇā*), descended while standing on the right side, making an offering with the sound of the Teacher’s sweet, divine Gandhabba-lute.
Mātali, the charioteer, standing on the left side, took celestial perfumes, garlands, and flowers, and descended after paying homage and making an offering. Mahābrahmā...
Chatta held the parasol, and Suyāma held the yak-tail fan. The Teacher descended accompanied by this retinue and stood at the gate of the city of Saṅkassa.
When the Elder Sāriputta arrived and paid homage to the Teacher, he did so because the Elder Sāriputta had never before seen the Teacher descending with such splendor of Buddha-majesty. Therefore—
“Never before have I seen such a one, nor have I heard of anyone like him;
thus the Teacher, speaking so charmingly, has come from the Tusita realm leading his host.
Having thus expressed his own satisfaction with these words, he continued: “Venerable Sir, today all gods and humans alike long for you.”

“...they aspire,” he said. Then the Teacher, saying to him, “Sāriputta, Buddhas endowed with such qualities as these are indeed dear to gods and humans alike,” spoke this verse while teaching the Dhamma:
“The wise who are devoted to meditation, who delight in renunciation and tranquility;”
"Even the gods envy those mindful ones who are devoted to the Buddhas.

In this context, "those devoted to jhāna" refers to those who are engaged and intent upon these two types of jhāna—namely, the jhāna of contemplation on characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*) and the jhāna of contemplation on the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*)—through the processes of adverting, entering, resolving, emerging, and reviewing. In the tranquility of renunciation...
The "delight" (*rati*) mentioned here should not be understood as the delight in renunciation (*nekkhamma*);
rather, this is said with reference to the delight in Nibbāna, which is the subsiding of the defilements. "Even the gods" means that both gods and humans yearn for and long after them.
"Of the mindful ones" refers to those Fully Enlightened Ones who are endowed with such qualities as mindfulness. [They think: "O, may we become Buddhas!"
The meaning is that they desire the state of Buddhahood and conceal [their own inferiority].
At the conclusion of the teaching, there was a realization of the Dhamma for thirty million beings, and five hundred bhikkhus who were the Elder’s co-residents established themselves in Arahatship.
It is said that all Buddhas, having performed the Twin Miracle without exception, dwell for the Rains Retreat in the world of the gods, and then, at the gate of the city of Saṅkassa—
The entry. In that place, the spot where the right foot was set down is called the Acala-Cetiya site.
Standing there, the Teacher asked questions within the domain of worldlings and others;
the worldlings answered the questions within their own domain, but they were unable to answer the questions within the domain of stream-enterers. Likewise for once-returners and the rest.
Regarding the domain of the sense objects, those who have attained stream-entry and the like were present; regarding the domain of Mahāmoggallāna, the other great disciples were present;
regarding the domain of the Elder Sāriputta, Mahāmoggallāna was present; and even Sāriputta was unable to answer regarding the domain of the Buddha.
Starting from the eastern direction, he surveyed all directions, and everywhere it was but a single open space. In the eight directions, gods and humans...

From the Brahma-world above down to the earth-dwelling yakkhas, nāgas, and supaṇṇas below, they all raised their joined palms and said, “Venerable sir, there is no one here who can answer that question; please consider it right here.
The Teacher [thought], “Sāriputta is weary. For although he—
“Those who have mastered the Dhamma, and those various trainees here—being asked, O dear sir, tell me their mode of conduct, for you are wise.
Having heard this question concerning the domain of the Buddha, [the Venerable Sāriputta thought]: “The Teacher asks me about the path by which trainees and those beyond training arrive.”

He is free from doubt regarding the question, yet he doubts my intention, wondering by what approach I might be explaining this practice among the aggregates and so forth, thinking, "I will not be able to grasp the Teacher’s underlying intent.
Thinking, "If I do not provide him with the method (naya), he will not be able to explain it," and intending to show him the method, [the Blessed One] said: "This is real..."
"Do you perceive it thus, Sāriputta? he said. It occurred to him: "Sāriputta, grasping my intention as he speaks, will explain by way of the aggregates.

As soon as the method was given to the Elder, that question presented itself to him through a hundred methods, a thousand methods, and a hundred thousand methods. Standing upon the method given by the Teacher, he [explained] that question...
He spoke. Indeed, apart from the Fully Enlightened One, there was no one else capable of attaining the wisdom of the Elder Sāriputta.
For that very reason, the Elder stood before the Teacher and let out a lion’s roar:
"Venerable Sir, even if it were to rain throughout an entire eon, I could count how many drops have fallen into the great ocean and how many have fallen upon the earth."
“Is there anyone capable of counting ‘so many rocks on the mountain’ and recording it in writing? The Teacher replied to him, “I know, Sāriputta, that you are capable of counting.
There is no comparison for the wisdom of that venerable one. Therefore he said:
“The sands of the Ganges might run out, The water in the great ocean might run dry;”
“The clay of the earth may be exhausted, but my wisdom shall not be exhausted.

This is what was said: “For if, venerable Lord of the World endowed with wisdom, after I have answered a single question, I were to throw not even a single grain of sand, a single drop of water, or a single fragment of dust for every hundred questions...”
"Even if one were to cast each single [grain] from among the sands of the Ganges and so forth,
given away by the thousands or by the hundreds of thousands, the sands of the Ganges and so forth would sooner reach exhaustion than my answers to these questions.
For even a bhikkhu of such great wisdom, not seeing the end or the limit of a question within the domain of the Buddha, was thus addressed by the Teacher.
He answered the question while remaining strictly within the established method. Hearing this, the monks began a discussion:
"The entire assembly was unable to answer the question that was asked, yet the Dhamma-Senāpati Sāriputta alone answered it.
When the Teacher heard this discussion, he said, "It is not only now that Sāriputta has answered a question which the great multitude was unable to resolve..."
He was unable to release him, for he had been released by this very person even before. Having said this, he related the past:
“Even if more than a thousand ignorant people were gathered together, they might cry out for a hundred years;”
"A single wise man is better,
who understands the meaning of what is said"—
thus he related this Jātaka in detail.
The Second Story of Devorohaṇa.
3. The Story of the Nāga King Erakapatta.

The Teacher delivered this Dhamma teaching, beginning with the words "Difficult is the attainment of human birth," while dwelling near Bārāṇasī at the foot of a Sattasirīsaka tree, concerning the Nāga king named Erakapatta.
It is said that formerly, during the dispensation of Buddha Kassapa, he was a young bhikkhu traveling by boat on the Ganges.
While holding onto a blade of *eraka* grass, even as the boat moved with great speed, he did not let go;
the blade of *eraka* grass snapped and fell away. Thinking, "This is a mere trifle," he did not confess the offense, and for twenty thousand years—

Although he had practiced the duties of a recluse in the forest, at the time of death, as if his neck were caught by a blade of *eraka* grass, he felt remorse, thinking, "My virtue is not pure," even though he wished to confess his offense.
Not seeing another monk, he passed away from there and was reborn as a king of the *nāgas*, the size of a boat or a hollow in a single tree; his name was simply Erakapatta.
Thus, at the very moment of his rebirth, he looked upon his own physical form and became remorseful, thinking:
"Having practiced the duties of a recluse for so long a time, I have been reborn in a causeless womb in the place of those who eat frogs.
Later on, having obtained a daughter, he lifted up a large fruit from the surface of the water in the middle of the Ganges and [presented it] to his daughter.
Having placed him there, she had him dance and sing. This was his thought:
"Surely, by this means, when a Buddha has arisen here, I shall hear of his arising.
"To whoever brings back a response to my song, I will give my daughter along with a great Naga abode"—thus she proclaimed every half-month on the Uposatha day.
He placed his daughter upon the hood. Standing there and dancing, she asked:
"Who indeed is the sovereign king? Who is the king who rules over the realm?
How does one become free from passion? And how is one called a fool?"
She sang this song.
All the inhabitants of Jambudīpa, thinking, "We shall win the Nāga maiden," went there and, using their own power of wisdom, sang counter-songs.
She rejected them. Every half-month, standing upon her hood, she spoke thus:

They sang until one interval between Buddhas had passed. Then our Teacher, having arisen in the world, one day at dawn while surveying the world, saw that the youth named Uttara had entered the net of his own knowledge, starting from the time of Erakapatta.
Reflecting, "What indeed will happen?", he perceived: "Today, [the daughter] of Erakapatta..."
"This is the day for making the snake dance after placing it upon my hood;
this young brahmin Uttara, while receiving the counter-song given by me, will become a stream-enterer. Taking that [song] with him, he will go into the presence of the Naga King.
Upon hearing it, he will know, 'A Buddha has appeared,' and will come into my presence. When he has arrived, in that great assembly, I shall recite a verse."
He saw that "at the conclusion of the verses, there will be a realization of the Dhamma for eighty-four thousand living beings.
Having gone there, he sat down at the foot of one of seven *sirīṣa* trees that were not far from Bārāṇasī.
The inhabitants of Jambudīpa gathered together, bringing with them songs and counter-songs. The Teacher was walking in a place nearby.
Seeing Uttara Māṇava, he said, "Come, Uttara. "What is it, Bhante? "Come here first.
Then, when he had come and sat down after paying homage, [the Teacher] asked, "Where are you going? "To the singing place of Erakapatta’s daughter.
"Do you know how to sing a response to a song? "I know it, Bhante. "Then sing for me," he said. Then he—
To him who was speaking according to his own way of knowing, [the Teacher said]: “This is not a superior response;
I shall give you a response, and you may take it and go. “Very well, Bhante,” he replied. Then the Teacher said to him: “Uttara, at the time of Nāgamāṇavikā’s singing, you should say:
‘The King, the lord of the six gates, being impassioned, is the master of passion;’”
“Non-greed is free from passion; greed is called ‘foolishness’”—thus he said, “you should sing this counter-song.
The meaning of the young woman’s song is as follows: “What indeed is the sovereign king?”—what indeed is one called a sovereign king? What indeed...
"King, lord of the realm"—but how indeed does one become a king, a lord of the realm?
And "how is he stainless?"—how indeed does that king become stainless?
As for the meaning of the response: "The king is the lord of the six doors"—he who is the lord of the six doors, even in the case of a single door...
One who is not overcome by forms and the like is called a "king. But he who, being impassioned, is impassioned with respect to those objects is called one who is impassioned and a "lord of passion.
One who does not become impassioned, being free from passion, is called "stainless" (*viraja*).
He who becomes impassioned, being impassioned, is called a "fool."
Thus, having given this counter-song to him, [the Teacher said]: "Uttara, when you have sung this song, he will sing this counter-song to it:
'By what is the fool carried away? How does the wise man push back?
How does one become secure from the yoke? Tell me that when asked.'"
Then you should sing this reply to him:
"The fool is carried away by the flood, but the wise man pushes back the bonds;
one who is detached from all bonds is called 'one who has attained security from bondage'."

The meaning of this is as follows: “The fool is carried away by the fourfold flood, beginning with the flood of sensual desire; the wise man pushes back that flood by means of the practice known as right exertion. Being dissociated from all yokes, such as the yoke of sensual desire, he is called one who has attained security from bondage.
As Uttara was receiving this counter-song, he established himself in the fruit of stream-entry.
Having become a stream-enterer, he took that verse and went [to his companions], saying, “Friends, I have brought back a song in reply; give me an opportunity.”
As he walked, he stepped over the knees of the great crowd standing shoulder-to-shoulder.
Standing upon the hood of her father, the Naga maiden danced and sang the song: "Who indeed is the sovereign lord? Uttara sang the response:
"The king is the sovereign lord of the six gates. Again, the Naga maiden sang his song: "By what indeed is one carried away?"
Then, singing a counter-song, Uttara recited this verse: "He is being swept away by the flood.
Upon hearing it, the Naga King, realizing that a Buddha had appeared in the world, thought with a joyful heart, "In the interval between one Buddha and another, I have never before heard such a line;
indeed, a Buddha has arisen in the world! He then struck the water with his tail.
The great waves rose up, and both banks broke apart. People submerged in the water for a distance of about the length of a bull from here and there.
Having placed his hood beneath this great multitude and lifted them up, he established them on dry land.
He approached Uttara and asked, "Master, where is the Teacher? "He is sitting at the foot of a tree."
“Great King,” he said. “Come, Master, let us go,” he replied, and went together with Uttara. The great multitude also followed along with him.
Having arrived, the Naga king entered between the six-colored rays of light, paid homage to the Teacher, and stood there weeping.
Then the Teacher said to him, “What is this, Great King? “Venerable Sir, I am one such as you...”
Having become a disciple of the Buddha, I practiced the duties of a recluse for twenty thousand years; yet even that practice of the recluse was unable to deliver me.

On account of a mere trifle—the cutting of a blade of *eraka* grass—I took rebirth with no root-cause (*ahetuka-paṭisandhi*) and was born in the place where one wallows on one's chest. For an entire interval between Buddhas, I have not obtained human status.
“Hearing the true Dhamma is not easy, nor is seeing a Buddha such as yourself,” the Teacher said, having heard his words.
Then, saying, “Great King, human birth is indeed difficult to obtain; likewise is hearing the true Dhamma, and likewise is the arising of a Buddha;
this is gained only with hardship and great effort,” he spoke this verse while teaching the Dhamma:
“Hard to obtain is the acquisition of human status; hard for mortals is life;
hard is the hearing of the True Dhamma; hard is the arising of Buddhas.
Its meaning is as follows: because it is obtained through great effort and great skill, the acquisition of human status is hard.

Indeed, it is difficult and rare. Even for mortals who strive to maintain their livelihood by performing continuous agricultural labor and other such tasks, life is difficult because it is precarious and short-lived.
Furthermore, hearing the True Dhamma is difficult because a person who teaches the Dhamma is rare even over the course of many eons.
This is because the initial resolve (abhinīhāra) succeeds only through great effort, and once that resolve has succeeded...
Furthermore, because their appearance is difficult to encounter even in many thousands of millions of eons, the arising of Buddhas is indeed rare; it is exceedingly difficult to find.
At the conclusion of the teaching, eighty-four thousand beings attained the realization of the Dhamma.

On that very day, the Nāga king would have attained the fruit of stream-entry, but because he was an animal, he did not attain it. He [remained] among those states known as conception, the taking up of the physical body, the casting off of the body, waking from sleep, rising from sleep, sexual intercourse, and death.
In five instances they exhausted themselves by assuming only the body of a nāga; having attained a state of non-exhaustion in those [five], he was able to wander about in the form of a young brahmin.
This is the third story, the Account of the Nāga King Erakapatta.

4. The Story of the Questions of the Elder Ānanda The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, gave this teaching on the Dhamma, "To refrain from all evil," in response to a question posed by the Elder Ānanda.
It is said that while the Elder was sitting in his daytime resting place, he reflected: "The Teacher has [spoken of] the mothers and fathers of the seven Buddhas..."
"The lifespan, the awakening, the assembly of disciples, the assembly of chief disciples, and the attendant of the chief disciples—all this has been told;
but the Uposatha has not been told. Is it the same Uposatha for them as well, or is it another?
He approached the Teacher and asked about that matter. However, because there was only a difference in the time of those Buddhas...
There was no variation in their discourse. For the Perfectly Enlightened One Vipassī held the Uposatha every seventh year;
indeed, the instruction he gave on a single day was sufficient for seven years.
Both Sikhi and Vessabhū held the Uposatha every sixth year, as did Kakusandha and Koṇāgamana.
And every year, the Great Sage Kassapa observed the Uposatha every sixth month;
for the instruction he had given on a single day was sufficient for those six months.
Therefore, the Teacher, having announced this difference in their schedule, said, "But the verses of exhortation for them shall be these very ones," and established a single Uposatha for all of them.
Manifesting [this truth], he spoke these verses:
“To refrain from all evil, to cultivate the wholesome,
and to purify one’s own mind— this is the teaching of the Buddhas.”
“Patience is the supreme austerity, forbearance is the highest;
the Buddhas declare that Nibbāna is supreme.
For one who harms others has not truly gone forth.”
One who harasses others is not a recluse.
Non-censuring, non-harming, restraint according to the Pātimokkha,
moderation in food, and a secluded dwelling— these are the requisites for a recluse.
"And application to higher consciousness—this is the teaching of the Buddhas.

Therein, "of all evil" means of all unwholesome kamma. "The undertaking" refers to both the production of the wholesome from the time of going forth until the path of arahantship, and the cultivation of that which has been produced. "The complete purification of one's own mind" refers to...
The purification of one’s own mind from the five hindrances—this is the teaching of the Buddhas; this is the instruction of all Buddhas.
Patience—that which is called patience, characterized as endurance—is the supreme, highest asceticism in this dispensation.
"The Buddhas say that Nibbāna is supreme" refers to the Buddhas, the Paccekabuddhas, and the *anubuddhas* (those who have awakened after them).
These three Buddhas declare that Nibbāna is supreme. For one who harms others by seizing their hands or other limbs, or by inflicting injury, is not truly called a renunciant (*pabbajita*).
Likewise, one who harms another in the manner already described is certainly not a recluse (*samaṇa*) either.
"Non-reproach" means both not reproaching and not causing others to reproach. "Non-injury" means both not injuring and not causing others to injure.
"Pātimokkha" refers to the foremost virtue. "Restraint" (saṃvara) means closing off [the doors of the senses]. "Knowing the proper measure" (mattaññutā) is the state of one who knows the measure;

it is the knowledge of the right amount. "Secluded" (panta) means remote. "Higher mind" (adhicitta) refers to the higher mind consisting of the eight attainments (samāpatti). "Application" (āyoga) means the performance of practice.

Such is this teaching of all the Buddhas. For herein, verbal virtue is explained by "not censuring," bodily virtue by "not harming," and virtue is explained by the phrase "restraint according to the Pātimokkha. By "not harming" is meant bodily virtue;
and by the phrase "restraint according to the Pātimokkha" is meant both the virtue of the Pātimokkha and the restraint of the sense faculties.
Through moderation in food there is both purity of livelihood and the virtue of being content with the basic requisites; through secluded lodgings there is suitable lodging;
and through higher mental training there are the eight attainments. Thus, by this verse, all three trainings have indeed been explained.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
The Fourth Story: The Case of the Elder Ānanda.
5. The Story of the Dissatisfied Monk.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning a certain dissatisfied monk, beginning with the words: "Not even by a rain of kahāpaṇa coins..."
It is said that after he had gone forth in the Dispensation and received full ordination, he was sent by his preceptor with the instruction, "Go to such-and-such a place and learn the recitation.
He went there. Then a disease arose in his father.
Desiring to see his son, and finding no one capable of summoning him, the father, lamenting out of grief for his son, was on the verge of death.
Having made the offering, she placed a hundred kahāpaṇas in the hand of her youngest son, saying, “You should use this for the cost of the bowl and robes for my son,” and then passed away.
When the younger brother arrived, he fell at his feet, rolled about, and wept, saying, “Venerable sir, your father passed away while lamenting;
however, he placed a hundred kahāpaṇas in my hand.”
"What shall I do with it? he asked. The youth refused, saying, "I have no need for kahāpaṇas. Later, he thought:
"What is the use of my life wandering for alms among other families? It is possible to live supported by those hundred kahāpaṇas;
I shall disrobe. Oppressed by this lack of spiritual ardor, he abandoned his recitation and his meditation subject.
He became like one suffering from jaundice. Then the young novices asked him, "What is this?
and when he replied, "I am weary," they informed their preceptors and teachers. They then led him into the presence of the Teacher and presented him to him.
The Teacher asked, "Is it true that you are weary? and when he replied, "Yes, Bhante," the Teacher said, "Why did you act in this way?"
"But do you have anything for the support of life? he asked. "Yes, venerable sir," he replied. "What do you have? "A hundred kahāpaṇas, venerable sir.
"In that case, first bring some pebbles from somewhere; having counted them, we shall know whether it is possible to live on that much or not.
He brought the pebbles. Then the Teacher said to him: "First, for the sake of consumption..."
"Set aside fifty; twenty-four for the sake of two oxen; this much for seed; [this much] for the yoke and plough;
and [this much] for the hoe, axe, and adze. When calculated in this way, those one hundred kahāpaṇas were not enough.
Then the Teacher said to him, "Bhikkhu, your kahāpaṇas are few; how will you satisfy your craving by means of these? In the past..."
"Having ruled as a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti), he was capable of causing a rain of jewels, knee-deep, to fall over an area of twelve leagues by merely clapping his hands;
yet, even after ruling as a king of the gods for as long as thirty-six Sakka reigns last, he passed away at the time of death without having fulfilled his craving.
Having said this, at his request, [the Buddha] brought forth a story from the past.
Having related the Jātaka of Mandhātu in detail:
“As far as the moon and sun revolve, illuminating the quarters with their radiance—
all living beings established upon the earth are the servants of Mandhātu.”
Immediately after this verse, he spoke these two verses:
“No satisfaction is found in sensual pleasures even by a rain of coins;
sensual pleasures are of little gratification and full of suffering—thus has the wise man understood.”
“He finds no delight even in celestial pleasures;
the disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One delights in the destruction of craving.
In this context, “with a rain of kahāpaṇas” refers to that rain of the seven treasures which he caused to fall after clapping his hands.
It is said, "a rain of kahāpaṇas. For even by that, there is no satiety regarding either sense-objects as things (*vatthu-kāma*) or sense-objects as defilements (*kilesa-kāma*).
Thus, this craving is difficult to fill. It has "little gratification" because it yields only meager pleasure, being like a dream.

It is "suffering" because, according to the suffering described in the Aggregates of Suffering and so forth, it is indeed full of much suffering. "Having understood thus" means having known these sense-desires in this way. "Even those divine" means...
For even if he were invited by the gods with the objects of desire that provide enjoyment for them, the Venerable Samiddhi, like [the Buddha], would find no delight in those desires at all.
"Delighting in the destruction of craving" means he delights in both Arahantship and Nibbāna;
he dwells aspiring for that. "A disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One" refers to one of those taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One.
"By hearing the Dhamma, one becomes a monk who is a practitioner of yoga.
At the conclusion of the teaching, that bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry, and the teaching of the Dhamma was beneficial for the assembled company as well.
This is the fifth story, concerning the bhikkhu Anabhirata.

6. The Story of the Brahmin Aggidatta The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, gave this Dhamma teaching concerning the one named Aggidatta, the chaplain to King Pasenadi of Kosala, who was seated upon a heap of sand.
It is said that he had been the chaplain to Mahākosa; then, when his father passed away, King Pasenadi of Kosala...
Thinking, “He is my father’s chaplain,” out of respect he placed him in that very spot;
when the chaplain returned to attend upon him, he went out to meet him and provided him with a seat of equal status, saying, “Teacher, please sit here. The chaplain thought:
“This king shows me excessive respect, yet it is not always possible for kings [to do so].”
"I must seize my heart. For the happiness of kingship is indeed a pleasure only when shared with those of equal age;

I am now old, and it is fitting for me to go forth. Having thus obtained the king’s permission to renounce the world, he had a drum beaten throughout the city and, within seven days, distributed all his wealth through acts of giving, and then went forth as an outsider ascetic.
He went forth into homelessness. Ten thousand men followed him into the religious life.
Together with them, he took up residence between the kingdoms of Aṅga-Magadha and Kuru, and gave this exhortation:
"Sirs, whoever finds sensual thoughts and the like arising within them, let that person take a single handful of sand from the river and scatter it here. They replied, "Very well."
Having given their assent, they acted accordingly whenever thoughts of sensual desire and the like arose.
At a later time, there was a great heap of sand, which the Naga king named Ahicchatta received.
The inhabitants of Aṅga and Magadha, as well as those of the kingdom of Kuru, brought them great honor month after month and offered gifts. Then, among them, Aggidatta—
He gave this advice: “Go for refuge to the mountain; go for refuge to the forest; go for refuge to the grove;
go for refuge to the tree; thus you will be liberated from all suffering. He also advised his own pupils with this same counsel.
The Bodhisatta, having likewise gone forth and attained supreme enlightenment, was at that time dwelling in Jeta’s Grove near Sāvatthī;

looking over the world at dawn, he saw that the brahmin Aggidatta, together with his pupils, had entered within the net of his own knowledge, and [he perceived]: "All these are endowed with the necessary conditions for Arahantship."
Having understood this, at the time of evening, he said to the Elder Mahāmoggallāna:
“Moggallāna, do you see how the brahmin Aggidatta is causing a great multitude of people to leap over at a place that is not a ford? Go and give them instruction. “Venerable sir, these are many;
they are beyond the capacity of me alone. If you also come, they will become manageable. “Moggallāna,” [the Buddha replied].
“I too shall come; you go on ahead,” he said. As the Elder was walking along in front, he thought:
“These men are both powerful and numerous. If I say anything at the place where they all assemble, they will all rise up in a disorderly mob.
By his own supernatural power, he caused a heavy rain to fall. While it was raining heavily, they...
As they fell, they rose again and entered their respective leaf-huts. The Elder stood at the door of the brahmin Aggidatta’s leaf-hut and called out, “Aggidatta!
Hearing the Elder’s voice, he thought, “In this world, there is no one capable of addressing me by name;
who is it that calls me by name? Thus, due to his arrogance and stubbornness—
“Who is this? he asked. “I am, O brahmin,” he replied. “What do you say? “Tell me a place where I may stay here for one night.
“There is no place to stay here; there is but a single leaf-hut for one person.
“Aggidatta, people go to other people, cattle to cattle, and those who have gone forth to those who have gone forth.”
"Do not do that; give me a place to stay. "But have you gone forth? "Yes, I have gone forth.
"If you have gone forth, where is your pack-bag and goods? What are the requisites of one who has gone forth?
"I have my requisites, O Brahmin, but it is difficult to wander about carrying them separately; therefore, I wander about having taken them within myself."
Thus, [Aggidatta] became angry with the Elder, saying, "Having taken him, you will wander about. Then the Elder said to him, "Do not be angry with us, Aggidatta;
tell me where my dwelling place is. "There is no dwelling place here," he replied.
"But who lives on this heap of sand? "A certain Nāga king. "Give that one to me. "It cannot be given; it is a heavy burden."
“This is his work. “Let it be; give it to me. “In that case, you yourself must know how.
The Elder set out toward the heap of sand. Seeing him approaching, the Nāga king thought, “This ascetic comes from this direction;
he likely does not know of my presence. I shall kill him by emitting smoke. And so, he emitted smoke.
The Elder thought, "This Naga king imagines, 'I alone am able to emit smoke; others are not,' and he observes this," so he himself emitted smoke.
The smoke rising from the bodies of both reached as far as the Brahma-world.
Both streams of smoke did not afflict the Elder, but they afflicted the Naga king alone. Unable to endure the force of the smoke, the Naga king—
It blazed up. The Elder, having attained the fire-element, blazed up along with it. The flames of fire rose as far as the Brahma-world.
Both [the flames] did not afflict the Elder, but afflicted only the Naga king.
Then his entire body became as if set ablaze by meteors. The company of seers, looking on, thought: "The Naga king [is attacking] the ascetic..."
"He consumes us! Alas, what a wretched ascetic; having failed to heed our words, he is lost!

Having tamed the nāga king and rendered him harmless, the elder sat down upon a heap of sand. The nāga king coiled his body around the heap of sand and, fashioning a hood as large as the interior of a gabled chamber, held it over the elder.
Early in the morning, a group of people went to the Elder, thinking, "We shall find out whether the ascetic is dead or alive.

Seeing him sitting on top of that heap of sand, they raised their hands in reverence and, praising him, said, "Ascetic, we hope you were not harmed by the Naga king? "Do you not see me holding my hood over my head? he replied.
"Is he standing? they asked. "It is truly wonderful, sirs, that such a Naga king has been tamed by this ascetic!
Saying this, they stood surrounding the Elder. At that moment, the Teacher arrived. Seeing the Teacher, the Elder rose and paid homage to him.
Then the seers said to him, "He too is greater than you. "This is the Blessed One, the Teacher; I am his disciple."
“Sāvaka,” he said. The Teacher sat upon the top of the heap of sand. The company of seers, thinking, “This is indeed the power of a disciple;
but what will the power of this one be like? raised their joined palms and praised the Teacher.
The Teacher addressed Aggidatta, saying: “Aggidatta, you and your disciples and attendants—”
“Having said what did he teach them while giving his advice? [The Elder replied: “‘Go for refuge to this mountain; go for refuge to the forest, the grove, and the tree.
For one who has gone for refuge to these is liberated from all suffering’—in this way I gave them my advice.
The Teacher said: “Aggidatta, it is not by going for refuge to these that one is liberated from all suffering.”
"But by going for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, one is liberated from the entire suffering of the round of existence. Having said this, he spoke these verses:
"Many indeed are the refuges people go to: mountains and forests, groves, trees, and shrines—people driven by fear."
“This is not a secure refuge; this is not the supreme refuge.
By coming to this refuge, one is not liberated from all suffering.
But he who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha—”
One sees the four noble truths with right wisdom:
suffering, the origin of suffering, the overcoming of suffering,
and the noble eightfold path leading to the cessation of suffering.
“This indeed is the secure refuge, this is the supreme refuge;
by coming to this refuge, one is liberated from all suffering.
In this context, *bahu* means many. *Pabbatāni* refers to the various mountains such as Isigili, Veḷuva, and Vebhāra.
And there are forests such as Mahāvana, Gośīṅga, and Sālavana; and monasteries such as Veḷuvana and Jīvakambavana; and tree-shrines such as the Udena Shrine and the Gotama Shrine.
The meaning is that various people, driven by this or that fear and desiring to be freed from fear, or aspiring for the acquisition of sons and so forth, go to these for refuge.
"This is not a refuge" means that all of this [which has been mentioned] is certainly not a refuge.

It is not secure, nor is it supreme; and by relying upon it, not even a single being among those subject to phenomena such as birth is liberated from all suffering, beginning with birth—this is the meaning.
The phrase "And he who... is commenced for the purpose of showing the secure and supreme refuge after having shown that [other] refuge is insecure and not supreme.

Its meaning is as follows: whether a householder or one gone forth, [he who takes refuge] in the formula beginning, "Thus indeed is the Blessed One: the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One," and so forth...
Relying on the meditation subject of the recollection of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha, one goes for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha as the supreme.
Even for such a person, that going for refuge may be disturbed or shaken by acts such as paying homage to those of other sects.
However, in order to demonstrate its immovability, [the author], explaining that the refuge is attained precisely through the Path, sets forth the Four Noble Truths.

"He sees with right wisdom," it is said. For he who has gone for refuge by way of seeing these truths—this refuge is both secure and supreme—and that person, depending on this refuge, is liberated from the entire suffering of saṃsāra;
therefore, it was said: "This indeed is the secure refuge," and so forth.
At the conclusion of the teaching, all those seers attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Having paid homage to the Teacher, they requested ordination. The Teacher, extending his hand from within his robe, said: "Come, monks;
lead the holy life. At that very moment, they became endowed with the eight requisites, appearing like elders of sixty years' standing.
They were there. And that was the day on which he arrived, bringing with him the honors of all the inhabitants of the kingdoms of Aṅga, Magadha, and Kuru.

Having brought those honors and seeing that all those seers had gone forth into homelessness, they thought, "Is our brahmin Aggidatta great, or is it the ascetic Gotama?"—and because of the arrival of the ascetic Gotama...
“They think, ‘He is indeed like Aggidatta, the Great One. The Teacher, observing their disposition, said, “Aggidatta, dispel the doubt of this assembly.
He thought, “I too expect only this much,” and by the power of his psychic potency, he rose into the air seven times;
descending again and again, he paid homage to the Teacher and said, “Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is my Teacher.”
Having said, “I am a disciple,” he declared his status as a disciple.
This is the sixth story, the Account of the Brahmin Aggidatta. 7.
The Account of the Questions of the Elder Ānanda.
"This Dharma teaching is difficult to encounter," the Teacher said while dwelling at Jetavana, speaking in reference to a question posed by the Elder Ānanda.
For one day, as the Elder was sitting in his daytime resting place, he reflected: "A noble elephant is born in the Chaddanta lineage or the Uposatha lineage;
a noble horse is born in the Sindhava lineage or the Valāhaka-king lineage; a noble bull is born among cattle..."

While the Teacher was speaking of the Southern Land and so forth, he described the places of origin for noble elephants and other such beings, [but Ānanda thought,] "Where, then, does a noble person (purisājānīya) arise?
He approached the Teacher, paid homage, sat down to one side, and asked about this matter. The Teacher said, "Ānanda, a so-called 'noble person' arises everywhere."

It does not arise [everywhere]; rather, it arises in the Middle Country, which is three hundred yojanas in length from east to west, two hundred and fifty yojanas in width, and nine hundred yojanas in circumference.
Furthermore, when it arises, it does not arise in just any family, but arises only in one of the great clans of Kshatriyas or the great clans of Brahmins. Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“Hard to find is the thoroughbred man; he is not born everywhere.
Wherever that wise one is born, that family prospers in happiness.
In this context, “hard to find” means that the thoroughbred man is indeed hard to find; unlike the thoroughbred elephant and others, he is not easily found. He...

In all cases, he is not born in a border region or in a low-born family; even in the Middle Country, he is born into one of the noble families of kshatriyas or brahmins—a place where the great multitude performs honors such as salutation.
Being thus born, wherever that wise one of supreme wisdom, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is born, that family prospers in happiness; the meaning is that it indeed attains happiness.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the seventh story, the account of the Elder Ānanda’s question.
8. The Story of the Many Bhikkhus.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching, "Happy are those who have awakened," with reference to a conversation among a large number of bhikkhus.
One day, five hundred bhikkhus were seated in the assembly hall and initiated a discussion, saying, "Friends, what indeed is happiness in this world?
Thereupon, some said, "There is no happiness equal to the happiness of sovereignty."
They said: "Some say it is like the pleasure of sensual desires; others say, 'There is no such thing as pleasure that is like eating fine rice with meat and other delicacies.
The Teacher went to the place where they were seated and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?
When they replied, "For this very discussion," he said, "Monks, what are you talking about? For all of this..."

“Happiness is indeed comprised within the suffering of the cycle of existence; in this world, the arising of a Buddha, hearing the True Dhamma, harmony in the Saṅgha, and a state of mutual affection—this alone is happiness. Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“Happy is the arising of Buddhas, Happy is the teaching of the True Dhamma;”
“Happy is concord in the Saṅgha; for those in concord, austerity is happy.

In this context, “the arising of Buddhas”: because Buddhas, when they appear, deliver the great multitude from the wilderness of passion and so forth, therefore the arising of Buddhas is a supreme happiness. Because, by resorting to the teaching of the True Dhamma, the phenomena such as birth and so on—
Beings are liberated from birth and the other [stages of existence]; therefore, the teaching of the True Dhamma is blissful. "Harmony" means evenness of mind, and that too is indeed blissful.

Furthermore, because it is possible for those who are harmonious and of one mind to master the Buddha’s word, to observe the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), or to fulfill the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*), it is said that "the austerity of the harmonious is blissful."

Therefore he said: “As long as, monks, the monks assemble in harmony, rise from their meetings in harmony, and perform the duties of the Saṅgha in harmony, only growth, monks, is to be expected for the monks, not decline.
At the conclusion of the teaching, those monks were established in Arahatship, and the Dhamma instruction was beneficial to the great multitude as well.
The eighth story: The Story of the Many Bhikkhus.
9. The Story of the Golden Shrine of Kassapa the Great Seer.
The Teacher gave this Dhamma teaching concerning the golden shrine of Kassapa the Great Seer while he was wandering on his alms tour.
The Tathāgata, having departed from Sāvatthī and traveling by stages toward Bārāṇasī, reached a certain divine abode on the way near the village of Todeyya, accompanied by a great saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Seated there, the Sugata sent for Ānanda, the keeper of the Dharma-treasury, and had him summon a brahmin who was performing agricultural work not far away. He—
The brahmin arrived and, instead of paying homage to the Tathāgata, stood there having paid homage to that very spot where the deity resided.
The Sugata asked, "Brahmin, what do you think of this place?

"I pay homage to it, Master Gotama," he replied, "because it is the site of a cetiya that has come down through our lineage. "By paying homage to this place, you have done well, brahmin," said the Sugata.
He comforted him. Hearing this, the bhikkhus were struck with doubt, wondering, "For what reason did the Blessed One comfort him in such a way?

Then, in order to dispel their doubt, the Tathāgata recounted the Ghaṭikāra-sutta from the Majjhima Nikāya and, by means of his supernormal power, manifested a golden stupa one yojana high for Kassapa the Great Seer, as well as another golden stupa.
Having manifested [the Buddha] in the sky and shown him to the great multitude, he said, "Brāhmaṇa, it is even more fitting to pay honor to those such as these who are worthy of honor.

Having thus proclaimed the four types of persons worthy of a stupa— beginning with the Buddha— in the manner shown in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta, and having specifically elucidated the three types of shrines—
the bodily shrine (sarīracetiya), the shrine dedicated to relics (uddissacetiya), and the shrine of use (paribhogacetiya)— he spoke these verses:
“When one worships those worthy of worship— the Buddhas and their disciples—
who have transcended conceptual proliferation and crossed over sorrow and lamentation;
when one worships such as these, who have attained Nibbāna and are fearless from any quarter.”
“It is not possible for anyone to calculate even this much merit.

In this context, *pūjāraha* means one who is worthy of worship, one who is fit to be worshipped. “Worshipping those worthy of worship” refers to one who worships by means of salutations and so forth, as well as the four requisites.
He indicates those worthy of worship with the words beginning with “the Buddha. “The Buddha” means the Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*).
*Yadīti* means "whether" or "or"; that is the meaning. In this context, it refers to both the *paccekabuddhas* and the disciples (*sāvaka*).

"One who has transcended proliferation" (*papañcasamatikkanta*) means one who has transcended the proliferations of craving, views, and conceit. "One who has crossed over sorrow and lamentation" (*tiṇṇasokapariddava*) means one who has gone beyond sorrow and lamentation;
the meaning is that these two have been transcended. By these [epithets], his worthiness for worship is demonstrated.
“Those beginning with the Buddhas” refers to the Buddhas and others. “Such as these” is said by way of inclusion. “Nibbūta” means through the extinguishing of lust and the other defilements.
“Akutobhaya” means those for whom there is no fear from any source—whether from any state of existence (*bhava*) or any object (*ārammaṇa*);

they are the fearless ones. “Merit cannot be reckoned” means it is not possible to count the merit. If one asks how so? It is because of the phrase “even this much by anyone. This means “even this much.”
The word "api" (even/also) should be connected here with the phrase "by anyone [thinking] 'it is this much. In that context, "by a person" refers to that Brahmā or others.
"By means of conceit" (*māna*) refers to the threefold conceit: by way of measuring (*tīraṇa*), weighing (*dhāraṇa*), or filling (*pūraṇa*).
"Measuring" (*tīraṇa*) means measuring by way of method, thinking "it is this much. "Weighing" (*dhāraṇa*) means weighing with a scale.

"Fullness" (pūraṇa) means filling by means of half-pasata measures, pattha measures, nāḷika measures, and so forth. It is impossible for any person to calculate, by way of its result, the merit of one who worships the Buddha and others with these three kinds of pride, because it is boundless;

thus, regarding the two cases of one who worships, why is giving first [discussed]? Because it is impossible to calculate the merit of one who worships the Buddha and others while they are still living.

Furthermore, even when such persons have attained parinibbāna through the aggregates (khandha-parinibbāna) by means of the sign of the parinibbāna of defilements (kilesa-parinibbāna), it is impossible to calculate the merit of one who honors them;
thus, the distinction [between the two] is logical. For this reason, in the *Vimānavatthu*, it is said:
"Whether [the Buddha] is standing or has attained parinibbāna, the fruit is the same for those with equal minds."
"For by the cause of a mental aspiration, beings go to a happy destination.
At the conclusion of this teaching, that brahmin became a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*). The Golden Stupa, one *yojana* in height, remained suspended in the air for seven days;
there was a great gathering of people, and for seven days they honored the stupa with various kinds of offerings. Then...
A schism in their respective attainments arose among those who held different views;

however, through the power of the Buddha, that shrine returned to its original place, and at that very moment, it became a great stone shrine right there. At that assembly, eighty-four thousand beings attained penetration of the Dhamma.
The ninth [chapter], the Foundation for the Golden Shrine of the Fortunate One Kassapa, is concluded.
The commentary on the Buddha Chapter is finished.
This is the fourteenth chapter.
The first recitation section is finished.
15. The Chapter on Happiness. 1.
The Account of the Settlement of a Quarrel among Relatives.
"Truly, what happiness!"—the Teacher spoke this teaching on the Dhamma while dwelling among the Sakyans concerning his kinsmen, for the purpose of settling a dispute.

It is said that the Sakyans and the Koliyans had the river named Rohiṇī, situated between the city of Kapilavatthu and the city of the Koliyans, dammed with a single embankment and cultivated crops there. Then, in the month of Jeṭṭhamūla, when the crops...
As the waters were being diverted, the laborers from both cities also gathered together. Thereupon, the inhabitants of the city of the Koliyans said:
"If this water is carried off by both sides, it will be of no use to you nor to us;
however, our crops will ripen with this single supply of water, so give this water to us! The others replied likewise.

—“When you have filled up our granaries and stand there, we shall not be able to go about at your house doors with baskets, sacks, and other containers in our hands, carrying red gold, blue gems, and black coins;
our own crops too will ripen from this very same water. Give this water to us! — “We will not give it. — “Neither will we.”
Saying, "I will not give," they thus increased the dispute; one man stood up and struck another, and he too struck someone else, and so on.
Thus, by striking one another and provoking the lineages of the royal families, they escalated the quarrel.
The Koliyan laborers said: "You seize those who dwell in Kapilavatthu and shout at them! Those who are like dogs and jackals—"
“They lived together as if with their own sisters; what will these elephants, horses, and shields and weapons do for us?
The Sākiyan laborers also said, “Now you may roar, having taken up these leprous children—those who were helpless, destitute, and like animals living in *kolarukka* trees! Their [the Sākiyans']...
“What will our elephants, horses, shields, and weapons do for us?
Having gone there, they told this to the ministers appointed to that task; the ministers told it to the royal families.
Then the Sakyans, thinking, “We shall show our strength and power to those who have lived with our sisters,” went forth prepared for battle. The Koliyans did likewise.
Thinking, "We shall show our strength and power to those who dwell in the Kola tree," they set out prepared for battle.
At dawn, the Teacher, surveying the world, saw his kinsmen and thought, "If I do not go, these people will perish;
it is fitting that I go. He then traveled alone through the air and appeared in the sky over the middle of the Rohiṇī River.
He sat down cross-legged. When his kinsmen saw the Teacher, they cast away their weapons and paid him homage.
Then the Teacher said to them, "What is this quarrel, Great Kings? "We do not know, Bhante," they replied.
"Who then will know? "The viceroy will know; the commander-in-chief will know. By this means, they questioned everyone down to the slaves and laborers.
“Venerable sir, there is a quarrel over water,” they said. “What is water worth, Great King? “It is of little value, venerable sir.
“What are Kṣatriyas worth, Great King? “Kṣatriyas, venerable sir, are priceless.
“It is not fitting for you to destroy priceless Kṣatriyas on account of water that is of little value. They became silent. Then they...
The Teacher addressed him, saying: “Why, Great King, do you act in such a manner? If I were not here, a river of blood would flow today.
You have done what is improper; you dwell with the five kinds of enmity and with resentment, whereas I dwell without enmity.
You dwell afflicted by the defilements, whereas I am free from affliction. You dwell striving for the pursuit of the strands of sensual pleasure...”
Having said, "I dwell free from longing," he spoke these verses:
"Truly we live in great happiness, being without enmity among those who harbor enmity;
among men who are full of enmity, we dwell without enmity."
“Truly we live in great happiness, unafflicted among those who are afflicted;
among men who are afflicted, we dwell unafflicted.
Truly we live in great happiness, free from longing among those who long.”
“While people are full of longing, we dwell free from longing.
In this context, “very happy” (*susukhaṃ*) means truly happy. This is what is meant:
those householders who, by such means as breaking into houses, or renunciants who, by such means as practicing medicine, produce a livelihood and say, “We live happily,” [are not so].
"Because of them, we indeed live very happily: we who, amidst people with the five kinds of enmity, are free from enmity;

amidst people afflicted by defilements, are free from affliction through the absence of defilement; and amidst people eager for the pursuit of the five strands of sensual pleasure, are free from such eagerness through the absence of that pursuit. The rest is of plain meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the first account: the settling of a family quarrel.
2. The Account of Māra.
The Teacher delivered this Dhamma teaching, "Happy indeed is life," while residing in the brahmin village of Pañcasālā concerning Māra.
For one day, the Teacher, seeing that five hundred young women possessed the necessary conditions for attaining the path of stream-entry, stayed in dependence upon that village.
Those young women, too, having gone to the river on a festival day and bathed...
Adorned and fully prepared, they set out toward the village. The Teacher also entered that village and wandered for alms.
Then Māra, having taken possession of the bodies of all the villagers, acted in such a way that the Teacher could not obtain even as much food as would fit in a ladle.
Thus, as the Teacher was departing with his bowl as clean as when it had been washed, Māra stood at the village gate and said to him:
He said, “Did you receive almsfood, ascetic? “But why did you act in such a way, Evil One, that I might not receive alms?
“In that case, venerable sir, please enter again. It occurred to him:
“If he enters again, I will direct my power toward the bodies of everyone and strike him on the hand in front of them.”
“I shall engage in playful jesting. At that moment, those young girls reached the village gate;
seeing the Teacher, they paid homage and stood to one side. Māra also said to the Teacher: “Venerable sir, have you not received alms today, being oppressed by the suffering of hunger?
The Teacher replied: “Evil One, even though we have received nothing today, in the Ābhassara world—”
“Like the Great Brahmas, we shall pass our time in joy and happiness alone,” he said, and uttered this verse:
“Truly happy we live, for we possess nothing at all;
We shall subsist on rapture, like the Ābhassara deities.”
In this context, "for whom there is none" means for us there is not even a single "something" (*kiñcana*)—such as lust and so forth—among the "somethings" in the sense of being a hindrance.

"Feeding on joy" means: "O Evil One, just as the Ābhassara deities, being feeders on joy, pass their time through the very bliss of joy, so shall we also, having obtained nothing, become feeders on joy. This is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, five hundred maidens were established in the fruit of stream-entry.
This is the second story concerning Māra. 3.
The Story of the Defeat of the King of Kosala.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this teaching on the Dhamma entitled "Victory is Enmity" (Jayaṃ veraṃ), concerning the defeat of the King of Kosala.
It is said that while fighting against his nephew Ajātasattu near Kāsikagāma, he was defeated by him three times.
On the third occasion, he thought: "I have been unable to defeat even a child with milk on its lips."
"What is the use of my life? Having thus cut off his food, he lay down upon a couch. Then news of this event spread throughout the entire city.

The bhikkhus reported it to the Tathāgata: "Venerable Sir, it is said that King Kāsirāja, having been defeated three times in reliance on the village of Kāsika, has now returned after being defeated again, thinking: 'I was unable to defeat even a suckling infant.'"
"What is the use of my life? he said, and having cut off his food, lay down upon his bed. The Teacher, hearing their conversation, said:
"Monks, even the victor engenders enmity; but the defeated one surely lies in suffering. Having said this, he spoke this verse:
"The victor engenders enmity; the defeated one lies in suffering."
“One who is at peace sleeps happily, having abandoned victory and defeat.
In this context, one who conquers another incurs enmity.
One who is defeated, being vanquished by another, sleeps in suffering in all postures, thinking, “When indeed shall I be able to see the back of my enemy?”

The meaning is that he dwells in suffering alone. "Tranquil" means that with internal defilements such as lust calmed and the taints (āsava) destroyed, having abandoned both victory and defeat, he lies in peace;
the meaning is that in all postures he dwells in nothing but happiness.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
The third account of the defeat of the King of Kosala.
4. The Account of a Certain Daughter of a Family.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning a certain daughter of a family, beginning with the words: "There is nothing equal to passion."
It is said that on the day of her marriage, her parents invited the Teacher for the auspicious occasion.
The Teacher, surrounded by the community of monks, went there and sat down. The bride, meanwhile, moved back and forth performing tasks such as straining water for the community of monks.
Her husband stood watching her. As he watched her out of lust, [his mind became agitated].
An internal defilement arose within him. Overcome by ignorance, he paid no homage to the Buddha nor to the eighty great elders.
Instead, stretching out his hand, he set his mind on seizing that young woman.
The Teacher, observing his intention, acted so that the man could not see the woman. Not seeing her, he stood there gazing at the Teacher.
When the Teacher looked at him as he stood there, he said, "Young man, there is no fire equal to the fire of lust;
there is no misfortune equal to the misfortune of hatred; there is no suffering equal to the suffering of maintaining the aggregates;
and there is likewise no happiness equal to the happiness of Nibbāna," and having spoken thus, he recited this verse:
“There is no fire like lust, no misfortune like hatred,
no suffering like the aggregates, and no bliss higher than peace. In this context,
“there is no fire like lust” means that without showing smoke, flames, or embers, it burns from within.
There is no fire equal to passion that is capable of reducing everything to a handful of ashes. There is no offense equal to hatred, which is called "kalī.
"Equal to the aggregates" means equal to the aggregates; just as the aggregates, when maintained, are suffering, there is no other suffering like them.
"The supreme peace" means there is no happiness higher than Nibbāna.
"For other happiness is indeed merely happiness, whereas Nibbāna is the supreme happiness"—this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, both the girl and the boy were established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). At that moment, the Blessed One caused them to see one another.
This is the fourth story, concerning a certain daughter of a family.
5. The Story of a Certain Lay Follower (*Upāsaka*) Regarding the teaching on the Dhamma beginning with "Hunger," the Teacher spoke while residing at Āḷavī concerning a certain lay follower.
For one day, while seated in the Fragrant Chamber (*Gandhakuṭi*) in Jetavana during the early morning hours, the Teacher surveyed the world.
Having seen a certain poor man in Āḷavī and perceiving his spiritual potential (*upanissaya*), the Teacher went to Āḷavī accompanied by a retinue of five hundred bhikkhus.
The inhabitants of Āḷavī invited the Teacher for a meal.
That very same day, the poor man also heard that "the Teacher has arrived" and made up his mind, "I shall listen to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher. And on that very day...
One ox escaped. He thought, "Shall I search for the ox, or shall I listen to the Dhamma?
Deciding, "I will search for the ox first and listen to the Dhamma afterwards," he left his house early in the morning.
Meanwhile, the residents of Āḷavī had seated the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, served them, and took up their bowls for the giving of the blessing of thanksgiving.
The Teacher thought, "He who supported me as I came this thirty-league journey has entered the forest to search for his ox;
I shall teach the Dhamma only when he returns. Thus he remained silent.
That man, having seen his ox during the day, drove it back into the herd and thought, "Even if there is nothing else, at least I must pay homage to the Teacher."
Thinking, "I shall prepare it," although oppressed by hunger, he did not set his mind on going home;
instead, he hurried to the presence of the Teacher, paid homage to him, and stood to one side. While he was standing there, the Teacher asked the attendant for the alms-giving:
"Is there any food remaining over for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus? "Venerable Sir, there is all of it."
"In that case, serve him," [the Teacher said]. He had him sit down at the very place where the Teacher had spoken and served him respectfully with rice gruel, hard food, and soft food.

When he had finished eating, he rinsed his mouth. Indeed, apart from this instance, there is no mention of a meal being prepared for anyone else who has traveled to or from elsewhere within the three Piṭakas. As his fatigue subsided, [he...]
His mind became one-pointed. Then the Teacher, having delivered a gradual discourse, proclaimed the Truths to him.
At the conclusion of the teaching, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The Teacher, having offered words of thanksgiving, rose from his seat and departed.
The great multitude followed the Teacher for a distance and then turned back.
As the monks were walking along with the Teacher, they complained: "See, friends, the Teacher's conduct!
On other days it is not like this; but today, upon seeing a single person, he has had rice-gruel and other foods prepared and given them away.
The Teacher turned back and, while standing still, asked: "What are you talking about, monks? and [explained] that matter.
Having heard this, [the Buddha said]: "Yes, monks, as I was coming through a wilderness thirty *yojanas* in extent, I perceived the spiritual disposition (*upanissaya*) of that lay follower.
He was extremely hungry; having set out early in the morning, he had been wandering in the forest searching for an ox.
Thinking, 'If he is taught the Dhamma while suffering from the pain of hunger, he will not be able to penetrate it,' I [acted] thus."
Having said, "I have experienced it; there is indeed no disease like the disease of hunger," he spoke this verse:
"Hunger is the supreme disease; conditioned phenomena are the supreme suffering.
Knowing this as it truly is, Nibbāna is the supreme happiness."

In this context, "hunger is the supreme disease" means that while other diseases may be cured once and then disappear, or abandoned through the removal of their specific cause, hunger must be treated at all times; therefore, it is called the supreme among all other diseases.

"Formations" refers to the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandhā*). "Knowing this" means knowing that there is no disease equal to hunger, and no protection for the aggregates equal to [the protection against] hunger.
Having understood, as it truly is, the meaning that "there is no such thing as suffering," the wise man realizes *nibbāna*.
"Nirvana is the supreme happiness" means that it is the highest and most excellent of all forms of happiness.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
The Fifth Story of a Lay Disciple (Upāsaka).
6. The Story of Pasenadi of Kosala.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning King Pasenadi of Kosala, beginning with the words: "Health is the highest gain."
For at one time, the king was eating a doṇa-measure of rice with a corresponding amount of curry and condiments.
One day, having eaten his morning meal and not yet dispelled the drowsiness from the food, he went into the presence of the Teacher;
appearing exhausted, he rolled this way and that, and though overcome by sleep, being unable to lie down straight, he lay on one side.
He sat down. Then the Teacher said to him, "Why have you come so soon, Great King, without even resting?
"Yes, venerable sir, from the time I finished eating, great suffering has arisen for me. Then the Teacher, saying to him, "Great King, eating too much causes such suffering," spoke this verse:
“When one is drowsy and a great eater,
sleeping and rolling about in bed like a great boar fattened on fodder— ”
“Again and again the dull-witted enters the womb.
Having exhorted him with this verse, he further exhorted him, saying, “Great King, it is right to eat food in moderation; for one who eats in moderation finds happiness,” and spoke this verse:
“For a person who is always mindful...”
For one who knows the proper measure regarding food obtained,
sensations become slight;
he ages slowly, preserving his life.
The king was unable to learn the verse by heart, so he said to his nephew, a young brahmin named Sudassana, who was standing nearby, "Learn this verse, dear.
Having learned the verse, the youth asked the Teacher, "What shall I do, venerable sir?
Then the Teacher said to him: "When the king is eating, at the time of the final morsel..."

“You should recite this verse; then, having observed the matter, when the king discards a morsel of food, you should bring as many grains of rice as there are grains in that morsel for the time of cooking the king’s meal.

He replied, “Very well, venerable sir,” and both evening and morning, while the king was eating, he recited that verse at the time of the final morsel and [took the rice] from the morsel discarded by him.
By counting the grains of rice, he reduced his consumption of rice. When the king heard his verse, he also had a thousand coins given to him for each verse.
At a later time, having established himself on the practice of eating no more than a single *nāḷika* of cooked rice, he became one who had attained happiness and possessed a slender body.
Then, one day, having gone into the presence of the Teacher and paid homage to the Teacher, he said: "Venerable Sir, now I am happy."
I have become one capable of pursuing and capturing even deer and horses. Previously, there was only fighting between me and my nephew;

now, having given my daughter named Vajīrakumāri to my nephew, that village has been granted to her alone as the price for her bath-powder. Thus, the conflict with him has been pacified. By this means also—
For this reason, too, happiness has arisen for me. On the previous day, the royal jewel belonging to our family was lost from our house;
that, too, has now come directly into our hands—for this reason, too, happiness has arisen for me.
Desiring to establish a bond of trust with your disciples, we even took a kinsman’s daughter as a wife in our house—for this reason, too, happiness has arisen for me.
"It has been born," [the king said]. The Teacher replied, "Great King, health is indeed the supreme gain;
there is no wealth like contentment with what one has obtained, no kinsman like trust, and no happiness like Nibbāna. Having said this, he spoke this verse:
"Health is the supreme gain; Contentment is the supreme wealth;..."
“Trust is supreme among relatives; Nibbāna is supreme bliss.
In this context, “health is supreme among gains” means that the state of being healthy is the supreme gain. For one who is ill, even gains that exist are as good as non-existent;
therefore, for the healthy person, all gains are truly attained. That is why it is said: “Health is supreme among gains.”

"Contentment is the supreme wealth": for either a householder or one who has gone forth, contentment (*santuṭṭhi*) is the state of being satisfied with whatever one has obtained and belongs to oneself;
it is the supreme wealth compared to other forms of wealth. "Trust is the supreme kinsman":
whether it be a mother or a father, whoever lacks trust with another is as a stranger. With such a stranger...
However, there is trust (vissāsa), and that is the supreme, most excellent kinsman even if unrelated. Therefore it was said: "Trust is the highest of kinsmen.
Furthermore, there is no happiness like Nibbāna; for this very reason it was said: "Nibbāna is the supreme happiness.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
The Sixth: The Story of Pasenadi of Kosala. The Seventh:
The Story of the Elder Tissa.
Regarding the teaching on "the flavor of seclusion," the Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse while dwelling at Vesālī, concerning a certain bhikkhu.
For when the Teacher said, "Monks, four months from now I shall attain final Nibbāna," seven hundred monks in the presence of the Teacher were overcome with agitation;
a sense of spiritual urgency arose in those whose taints were exhausted, while ordinary worldlings were unable to restrain their tears. The monks, breaking into groups, asked: "What indeed..."
“We shall do so,” they said, and wandered about deliberating. Then a certain monk named the Elder Tissa thought, “The Teacher, it is said, will attain final Nibbāna at the end of four months;
yet I am not free from passion. It is fitting for me to attain Arahantship while the Teacher is still alive.
Thus he remained all alone, practicing the four postures by himself. He did not go into the presence of the monks, nor did anyone [approach him].
There was no conversation or discussion with him at all. Then the bhikkhus said to him, "Friend Tissa, why do you act in this way?
He did not listen to their words. They reported his conduct to the Teacher, saying, "Bhante, the Elder Tissa has no affection for you. The Teacher had him summoned and asked, "Tissa, why..."
Having asked, "Did you act thus?", and having been informed of his intention by him, [the Buddha] gave his approval, saying, "Excellent, Tissa!
Then he said, "Monks, let your affection for me be like that of Tissa. Even those who honor me with perfumes, garlands, and the like do not truly honor me;
it is only those who practice in accordance with the Dhamma who truly honor me," and he spoke this verse:
“Having drunk the flavor of seclusion, and the flavor of tranquility, one becomes free from distress and free from evil; drink the flavor of the joy of the Dhamma.
In this context, “the flavor of seclusion” means the flavor arising from seclusion; the meaning is the bliss of solitude. “Having drunk” means...
While performing the full understanding of suffering and so forth, he has "drunk" by way of realization through the object.
And "of tranquility" means having drunk the flavor of both the pacification of defilements and Nibbāna. He "becomes free from fever":

by that drinking of both flavors, the bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed becomes indeed free from fever and free from evil due to the absence of passion, agitation, and the like within him. The flavor...
Even while drinking the flavor of rapture that arises by way of the ninefold supramundane Dhamma, he becomes free from fear and free from evil.
At the conclusion of the teaching, the Elder Tissa attained Arahantship, and the Dhamma instruction was fruitful for the great multitude as well.
This is the seventh story, the Story of the Elder Tissa.
8. The Story of Sakka:
"It is good to see"—the Teacher delivered this Dhamma teaching while residing in the village of Veḷuva concerning Sakka.
For when the Tathāgata had relinquished the life-force, Sakka, having learned that the affliction of dysentery had arisen in him, [approached].
Sakka, the king of the gods, thought, "It is fitting that I go into the presence of the Teacher and attend to him while he is ill.
Having abandoned his physical form, which was three gavutas in height, he approached the Teacher and massaged his hands and feet.
Then the Teacher asked him, "Who is this? "I am Sakka, Bhante," he replied. "Why have you come? "Because of you..."

“Venerable sir, [I have come] to attend to the sick. “Sakka, the scent of humans is like a piece of rotting flesh tied around the neck of a god from a distance of a hundred leagues; go back, for I have bhikkhus to attend to the sick.
“Venerable sir, standing at a height of eighty-four thousand leagues, I have come having smelled the fragrance of your virtue; it is I myself [who have come].”
Thinking, “I shall attend upon him,” he did not allow anyone else’s hand even to touch the vessel for cleaning the Teacher’s body;
instead, holding it against his own chest as he carried it out, he did not even contract his face in the slightest, appearing as if he were carrying a vessel of perfumes.
Having thus attended to the Teacher, he departed at a time when the Teacher was feeling well.
The bhikkhus raised this discussion: “Oh, how great is Sakka’s affection for the Teacher!

Having abandoned such celestial splendor as this, he attended upon the Teacher, carrying the vessel for washing the Teacher’s body on his head, without even so much as a contraction of his face, as if he were merely carrying out a vessel of perfumes.
When the Teacher heard their talk, he asked: “What are you saying, bhikkhus?”
"It is not surprising that Sakka, the king of the gods, feels such affection for me.
For it was by relying on me that this Sakka, the king of the gods, abandoned his state as the aged Sakka, became a stream-enterer, and attained the status of the youthful Sakka.
Indeed, when he came before me, terrified by the fear of death and with the Gandhabba deity Pañcasikha leading the way—"
To him who was seated in the Indasāla Cave in the midst of an assembly of gods, [the Buddha said]:
“Ask me, Vāsava, whatever question you desire;
for each and every question, I shall bring you to its conclusion.”
Having spoken thus, I taught the Dhamma to dispel his doubt. At the conclusion of the teaching, there was a penetration of the Dhamma for fourteen koṭis of beings.
Sakka, even while remaining seated as he was, attained the fruit of stream-entry and became a "young Sakka.
In this way, I have been of great benefit to him. It is no wonder that he has affection for me, monks, for such is the nature of the Noble Ones.
"Seeing them is pleasant, and dwelling together with them in one place is also pleasant.
But all this [done] with fools is suffering. Having said this, he spoke these verses:
"It is good to see the Noble Ones; dwelling together with them is always pleasant."
One should always be happy by not seeing fools.
For one who walks in the company of fools grieves for a long time;
living with fools is always as painful as living with an enemy.
"A wise person is pleasant to dwell with, like a reunion with kinsmen.
Therefore— "One who is wise,
possessed of wisdom, learned, steadfast in virtue, observant of vows, and noble;"
“One should attend upon such a wise true person, just as the moon follows the path of the stars.
In this context, *sāhu* means beautiful and auspicious. Regarding “dwelling together”: it is not merely the sight of them;
rather, sitting in the same place with them, and even the state of being permitted to perform the duties and services for them, is likewise excellent.
"One who walks in the company of fools" means one who is a companion of a fool.

"For a long time" means that when he is addressed by his foolish companion, saying, "Come, let us commit the severing of embankments and so forth," he becomes of one mind with him and performs those acts;

having then undergone the cutting off of hands and other such punishments, he grieves for a long duration. "Always" means just as [one would suffer] with a sword-wielding enemy or with venomous snakes and the like.
"Living together with one [who is unwise] is always painful"—this is the meaning.
"The wise person is pleasant to dwell with": here, "pleasant to dwell with" means that dwelling in the same place with a wise person is pleasant.
How so? "Like the meeting of kinsmen": just as the meeting of kinsmen is pleasant, so too is this pleasant.
"Therefore" (*tasmā hi*): because dwelling with fools is suffering and dwelling with the wise is happiness;
