therefore, one should associate with those endowed with steadfastness (*dhiti*), who are wise (*dhīra*); with those endowed with wisdom (*paññā*), both mundane and supramundane; with those who are learned (*bahussuta*), endowed with scriptural knowledge and realization;
and with those of "bullock-like virtue" (*dhorayha-sīla*) due to their habit of bearing the burden defined as attaining *arahantship*, being virtuous and observant of precepts.
And one should associate with and attend upon such a true person— one who possesses the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), who is noble because he is far removed from the defilements,
and whose questions are beautiful— just as the moon associates with the sky known as the path of the stars;
this is the meaning of "one should associate with."
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the eighth story concerning Sakka.
The commentary on the Sukha Vagga is finished.
The Fifteenth Chapter. 16.
The Chapter on the Dear One. 1.
The Story of the Three Who Went Forth.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this teaching on non-yoga (*ayoga*) concerning three who had gone forth into homelessness.
It is said that in a certain family in Sāvatthī, there was an only son of his parents, beloved and dear to them.
One day, having heard the Dhamma talk from monks invited to his house as they were offering a blessing of thanksgiving, he desired to go forth.
Having made offerings to his mother and father, he requested their permission to go forth. They did not grant it.
He thought to himself, "I shall go forth after departing outside while my parents are still unaware.
Then, as his father was going out, he entrusted him to his mother, saying, "Please look after him," and as his mother was going out, she entrusted him to his father.
Then one day, when his father had gone out, his mother, thinking, "I will watch over my son," sat on the ground leaning against one doorpost with her feet pressed against the other, spinning thread.
He thought, "I will deceive her and go away," and said, "Mother, move aside for a moment; I wish to attend to my bodily needs. When she moved her feet, he—
Having departed, he went quickly to the monastery, approached the monks, and requested, "Venerable sirs, grant me the going-forth.
He was ordained in their presence.
Then his father arrived and asked his mother, "Where is my son? "Master, he was in this place," she replied.
Thinking, "Where indeed could my son be? he looked about; not seeing him, he thought, "He must have gone to the monastery.
Having gone to the monastery and seen his son ordained, he wept and wailed, saying, "Dear one, why have you destroyed me?
Then, thinking, "Now that my son has gone forth, what shall I do at home? he himself also requested the monks and went forth.
Then his mother also thought, "Why are my son and husband taking so long? Have they gone to the monastery and gone forth?
Looking for them, she went to the monastery and, seeing that both had gone forth, she thought, "What use have I for a home now that these two have gone forth?
She too went to the nuns' quarters and went forth. Having gone forth, they were unable to remain apart.
They were unable [to restrain themselves]; even in the monastery and in the nuns' quarters, they would sit together and spend the day conversing.
Because of this, both the monks and the nuns were troubled.
Then one day, the monks reported their conduct to the Teacher. The Teacher had them summoned and asked, "Is it true?"
Having asked, "Is it true that you do this? and being told, "It is true," he said, "Why do you do this?
This is certainly not the practice for those who have gone forth. They replied, "Venerable sir, we cannot exist without them.
He said, "To act in this way from the very moment of going forth is improper. For the sight of those one loves and the sight of those one dislikes is indeed suffering."
"Therefore, it is not fitting to treat anyone among beings or conditioned phenomena as either dear or undear," he said, and then spoke these verses:
"Yoking oneself to what is unfit and not yoking oneself to what is fit,
one who abandons the true goal for the sake of grasping at the dear, envies those devoted to their own task."
“Do not associate with those who are dear, nor ever with those who are unpleasant;
for not seeing those who are dear is suffering, and seeing those who are unpleasant is also suffering.
Therefore, do not hold anything dear, for the loss of what is dear is evil.”
“Those for whom there is neither the liked nor the disliked, for them no knots exist.
Herein, “non-application” (*ayogo*) refers to improper mental attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*), which is that which ought not to be applied.

For here, the cultivation of the sixfold non-range (*agocara*)—divided into such categories as frequenting the haunts of prostitutes—is what is called improper mental attention. In that improper mental attention, one [should place] oneself...
The meaning is "they apply themselves. Regarding "in yoga," the meaning is that they do not apply themselves to its opposite, which is wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*).
"Having abandoned the goal" means having abandoned that which is called the "goal"—namely, the three trainings beginning with higher virtue (*adhisīla*)—from the time of going forth.

"Grasping only what is dear" means grasping only that which is dear, namely, the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*). "One who delights in self-exertion" [refers to] through that practice...

Having fallen away from the Teaching and attained the state of a householder, he envies those who are devoted to self-exertion and, having accomplished virtue and the other perfections, receive honor from gods and humans;
the meaning is that he desires, "O, may I too become like this!
As for "may he not meet with those dear," it means that he should never, even for a single moment, come together with either dear beings or dear conditioned phenomena.

Likewise with those who are unpleasant. Why is that? For indeed, not seeing those who are dear due to separation from them, and seeing those who are unpleasant due to encountering them, is called suffering.
Therefore—because both of these are suffering—one should not make any being or any conditioned phenomenon dear.
"The loss of the dear" (*piyāpāyo*) means separation or parting from those who are dear. "Wretched" (*pāpako*) means miserable.
"Those for whom there are no ties" means that for those who have nothing dear, the bodily tie of covetousness (*abhijjhākāyagantha*) is abandoned;
for those who have nothing unpleasant, the bodily tie of ill will (*byāpādakāyagantha*) is abandoned. When these two are abandoned, the remaining ties are also abandoned.
Therefore, the meaning is that one should neither do what is dear nor what is unpleasant.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages. However, three people, thinking, "We cannot live without [the Sangha]," disrobed and returned home.
This is the first story concerning the three persons who went forth.
2. The Story of a Certain Householder.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning a certain householder.
For that man, having lost his sons and being overwhelmed by grief for them, went to the cremation ground and wept; he was unable to sustain himself against the sorrow for his sons.
At dawn, as the Teacher surveyed the world, he perceived that the householder possessed the necessary spiritual potential (*upanissaya*) for the path of stream-entry.
Having seen him, the Teacher returned from his almsround, took a junior monk as his attendant, and went to the door of that man's house.
Hearing that the Teacher had arrived, the man thought, "He must wish to exchange greetings with me," and so he ushered the Teacher inside,
prepared a seat in the middle of the house, and when the Teacher was seated, he came forward and sat down to one side.
Then the Teacher asked him, "Upāsaka, why are you suffering? When he had explained his grief over the loss of his son, the Teacher said, "Upāsaka, do not worry.
This thing called death does not occur in only one place, nor does it happen to only one person;
rather, as long as there is the arising of existence (bhavuppatti), it happens to all sentient beings. Not even a single conditioned phenomenon (saṅkhāra) is permanent."
"There is no such thing as a person who does not die. Therefore, one should reflect wisely: 'That which is subject to death has died;
that which is subject to dissolution has dissolved,' and one should not grieve. For even the ancient wise men, when their son died, did not grieve, thinking, 'That which is subject to death has died;
that which is subject to dissolution has dissolved,' but instead cultivated mindfulness of death. Having said this, [the king asked], "Venerable sir, who were those who did so?"
When did they do so? Tell me. Being thus requested, in order to explain that matter, he brought forward the past:
“As a snake casts off its worn-out skin, so does one go, leaving behind this body;
even so when the body is lifeless, discarded, and dead.”
“Burning, he does not know the lamentation of his kinsmen;
therefore I do not grieve for him, for he has gone to whatever destination belongs to him.
Having thus related in detail this *Uragajātakam* from the *Pañcakanipāta*, [the Buddha said]: “In this way, even the wise of old, when their beloved sons passed away...”
Just as you now wander about weeping, having abandoned your work and abstaining from food, they did not live in that manner;
rather, through the power of cultivating mindfulness of death, they consumed their food and attended to their work without succumbing to grief.
Therefore, do not worry, thinking, "My beloved son has died. For whatever sorrow or fear arises, it does so only because of what is dear.
Having said, "It arises dependent [on the beloved]," he spoke this verse:
"Sorrow is born from the beloved; fear is born from the beloved.
For one who is completely freed from the beloved, there is no sorrow—how then could there be fear?"

In this context, "dear one" (*piyata*) means that grief or fear arising from the root of the round of existence arises dependent upon either a dear being or a dear conditioned formation (*saṅkhāra*). However, for one who is completely liberated from these, neither of these two exists; this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, the householder was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), and the Dhamma teaching was fruitful for those who had gathered as well.
This is the second story, the Account of a Certain Householder.
3. The Story of Visākhā.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning the laywoman Visākhā, beginning with the words, "From love it is born.
It is said that she, having established her daughter Sudattā, a young maiden, in her own position within the household, [provided] for the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus in her home...
She performed services for her. At a later time, she passed away.
Having arranged for the disposal of her body, being unable to sustain her grief, she—suffering and dejected—went into the presence of the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down to one side.
Then the Teacher asked her, "Visākhā, why are you suffering and dejected, with a tearful face and weeping?"
“...seated,” he said. After she had reported that matter, she said, “Venerable sir, that young girl was dear to me and was perfect in her duties;
now I do not see anyone like her. “But how many people are there in Sāvatthī, Visākhā?
“Venerable sir, you yourself have told me there are seven million. “If this entire population were yours...”
“Would you wish to be like a daughter-in-law? “Yes, venerable sir. “But how many people die every day in Sāvatthī?
“Many, venerable sir. “In that case, venerable sir, would this not be a time for you not to grieve?
You would surely wander about weeping day and night. “Let it be so, venerable sir; I understand.”
Then the Teacher said to him, “In that case, do not grieve; for grief or fear arises only from affection,” and spoke this verse:
“From affection arises grief; from affection arises fear.
For one who is completely free from affection, there is no grief—how then could there be fear?”
In this context, "through affection" means that sorrow arises depending precisely upon the affection felt for one's sons, daughters, and so forth.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the third story, concerning Visākhā.
4. The Story of the Licchavis.
The Teacher delivered this Dhamma teaching, "Pleasure gives rise to [suffering]," while residing in the Gabled Hall near Vesālī concerning the Licchavis.
It is said that on a certain festival day, they adorned one another with various unique ornaments for the purpose of going to the pleasure grove.
They departed from the city. As the Teacher was entering for alms, he saw them and addressed the monks:
"Behold, monks, these Licchavis who have never before seen the gods of the Thirty-three; let them gaze upon them.
Having said this, he entered the city. They too, while going to the park, took a certain beautiful woman of the city with them and proceeded there.
Overcome by envy, they struck one another and caused blood to flow like a river.
Then, taking them up on a bed, they carried them away. The Teacher, having finished his meal, departed from the city.
Seeing the Licchavis being led away in that manner, the bhikkhus said to the Teacher: "Venerable Sir, the Licchavi kings, even at this early hour..."
“Adorned and prepared like gods, they have now departed from the city and, depending on a single woman,
have fallen into this calamity. Having said, “Monks, sorrow or fear, when they arise, arise indeed depending on pleasure,” the Teacher spoke this verse:
“From delight arises sorrow; from delight arises fear.
For one who is completely free from delight, there is no sorrow—how then could there be fear?
In this context, “from delight” means from delight in the five strands of sensual pleasure; the sense is: depending upon that.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the fourth story, concerning the Licchavis.
5. The Story of Prince Anitthigandha.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning the youth named Anitthigandha.
It is said that this being, having passed away from the Brahma-world, was reborn in Sāvatthī into a family of great wealth;
from the day of his birth, he did not wish to approach a woman, and when taken by a woman, he would weep. They [wrapped] him in a cloth swaddling-cloth...
Having taken [the child], they suckled him with breast milk. When he reached maturity, his parents said, "Dear son, we shall arrange a marriage for you.

He refused, saying, "I have no need for a woman. Although they entreated him again and again, he summoned five hundred goldsmiths, had them fashion a female figure out of a thousand pieces of red gold that was exceedingly beautiful and possessed of solid, well-proportioned limbs, and [gave it to them].
Having had him brought back by his parents, they said, "Dear son, if you do not take a wife, the family lineage will not be established;

we shall bring a maiden for you. When this was said, he replied, "In that case, if you bring me such a maiden as this, I will obey your word," and he showed them that golden image. Then his parents summoned renowned brahmins.
"Our son is of great merit; surely there must be a maiden who has performed merit together with him.
Go, take this golden image and bring back such a maiden," they sent forth.
Saying, "Very well," they set out on their journey and arrived at the city of Sāgala in the kingdom of Madda. And in that city, there was a maiden about sixteen years of age...
There was a beautiful young girl, whom her parents had stationed on the upper floor of a seven-storied palace.
Those brahmins, thinking, "If there is such a girl here, people will see her and say,
'She is as beautiful as the daughter of such-and-such a family,'" placed that golden image at a ford on the road.
They sat down to one side.
Then, the nurse of the girl, having bathed the girl and desiring to bathe herself as well, came to the bathing place;
seeing that effigy, she perceived it as her own daughter and said, "You are ill-behaved! I have just now come out after having you bathed."
“You have come here before me,” he said, striking her with his hand; perceiving both her stiff demeanor and her lack of emotion, he asked, “I took you for my daughter, ‘my child,’ but what is this?
Then those brahmins asked him, “Mother, is such as this your daughter? [He replied,] “What is she worth compared to my daughter? [The brahmins said,] “In that case, give us your daughter.”
"Show her to us. She went with them to the house and informed her husbands.
After exchanging greetings with the brahmins, they helped their daughter down and placed her beside a golden statue on the lower floor of the palace.
The golden statue lost its luster, while the young woman shone with radiance. The brahmins [perceived] her...
Having given away the maiden and sent her off, they went and informed the parents of the youth Anitthigandha.
With delighted minds, they said, "Go, bring her here quickly," and dispatched them with great honor.
When the youth heard of this occurrence, he thought, "It is said there is a girl more beautiful even than a golden image," and by the mere hearing of it...

Having conceived affection for her, he said, "Bring her back quickly. She too, having been placed upon a vehicle and being brought along, died on the very road due to a wind-disease produced by the jolting of the carriage because of her extreme delicacy.
The prince asked incessantly, "Has she arrived? Because he asked with such intense affection, they did not tell him immediately, but instead delayed for several days.

Having done so, they reported the matter to him. He, having become despondent at the thought, "I did not obtain union with such a woman as that," was overwhelmed by the suffering of grief as if by a mountain.
The Teacher, seeing his underlying potential (*upanissaya*), went to the door of that house while wandering for alms. Then his parents [invited] the Teacher into the house.
Having seated him, they served him with great care. At the conclusion of the meal, the Teacher asked, "Where is Prince Anitthigandha?
"Venerable Sir, he has cut off his food and is sitting in the inner chamber," they replied. "Call him here," he said.
When he had come and paid homage to the Teacher, he sat down to one side. The Teacher asked, "Prince, why is it that you are so deeply grieved?"

When he said, "It has arisen," [the Teacher asked], "Yes, venerable sir; having heard that such-and-such a woman died on the road, a powerful sorrow arose within me, and even food no longer appeals to me.
Then the Teacher said to him, "But do you know, prince, what it was that caused your sorrow to arise? "I do not know, venerable sir. "It was desire, prince."
"Powerful sorrow has arisen; for sorrow or fear arises depending upon sensual desire," he said, and then recited this verse:
"Sorrow is born from sensual desire; fear is born from sensual desire.
For one who is completely free from sensual desire, there is no sorrow—how then could there be fear?"

In this context, "from sensual pleasure" means from both the sensual objects (*vatthukāma*) and the defilements of sensual pleasure (*kilesakāma*); the meaning is that it is by depending on these two kinds of sensual pleasure.
At the conclusion of the teaching, the youth Anitthigandha was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).
This is the fifth story concerning the youth Anitthigandha.
6. The Story of a Certain Brahmin.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this teaching on the Dhamma concerning a certain brahmin.
It is said that one day, while holding wrong views, he went to the riverbank and cleared a field. The Teacher [observed] him...

Seeing his excellence as a supporting condition (*upanissaya-sampatti*), he went into his presence. Even upon seeing the Teacher, he remained silent without performing the proper etiquette of respect.
Then the Teacher addressed him first, saying, "Brāhmaṇa, what are you doing?
"I am clearing a field, Master Gotama. Having said only this, the Teacher departed. On the following day as well...
Having gone into the presence of him who had come to plow his field, he asked, "Brāhmaṇa, what are you doing?

Upon hearing, "I am plowing the field, Master Gotama," he departed. On the following day and subsequent days, having likewise gone and asked the same question, he heard, "Master Gotama, I am sowing the field, weeding it, and guarding it," and then he departed. Then, on one occasion...
The brahmin said: "O Gotama, you have come to me from the very day I began clearing my field.
If my crop succeeds, I shall share it with you; I will not eat anything myself without first giving to you.
From this day forward, you are my friend."
Then, on a later occasion, his crop flourished. Thinking, "My crop has flourished;

I shall have it reaped tomorrow," he was about to perform the necessary tasks for the reaping when, during the night, a great cloud rained down and carried away the entire crop, leaving the field looking as if it had been mown down.
However, on the very first day, the Teacher [had already known] that "that crop would not flourish."
He understood. Early in the morning, the brahmin went out thinking, "I will inspect the field. Seeing that the field was empty, he was overcome by intense grief and thought:
"From the time the ascetic Gotama arrived, which was when my field was being cleared, I have been waiting for him.
I thought: 'When this crop has been harvested, I shall share it with you; I will not eat it myself without first giving to you.'"
“From this day forward, you are my companion,” he said. Yet even that wish of his did not reach its fulfillment.
Having spoken thus, he cut off all food and lay down upon his bed. Then the Teacher came to the door of his house.
Hearing of the Teacher’s arrival, he said, “Bring my companion here and have him sit down with me. His attendants did accordingly.
The Teacher sat down and asked, "Where is the brahmin? When it was said, "He is lying in the inner chamber," he had him summoned.
Once the brahmin had come and was seated to one side, the Teacher asked him, "What is it, brahmin?
"Master Gotama, you have been coming here from the day I began clearing my field; I too have been thinking, 'When the crop has ripened, I will [give you]..."
"I said, 'I shall make a distribution [of wealth],' but that wish of mine has not been fulfilled; because of that, sorrow has arisen within me, and even food no longer pleases me.
Then the Teacher asked him, "But do you know, brahmin, on what account your sorrow has arisen? When he replied, "I do not know, Master Gotama, but you surely do," the Teacher said, "Yes."
“Brahmin, sorrow or fear that arises arises dependent upon craving,” having said this, he spoke this verse:
“From craving sorrow is born; from craving fear is born.
For one who is completely free from craving, there is no sorrow—how then could there be fear?”
In this context, "craving" refers to craving pertaining to the six sense doors; the meaning is that it arises depending upon this craving.
At the conclusion of the teaching, the brahmin was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
This is the sixth story, the Story of a Certain Brahmin.
7. The Story of the Five Hundred Boys The Teacher, while dwelling at Veḷuvana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning five hundred boys encountered on the road.
One day, the Teacher, accompanied by eighty great elders and a retinue of five hundred bhikkhus, entered Rājagaha for alms.
As he was entering, on a festival day, he saw five hundred children who, having been made to carry baskets of cakes, were departing from the city and going to the park.
They too, having paid homage to the Teacher, departed;
they did not even say to a single bhikkhu, "Take some cake. When they had gone, the Teacher said to the bhikkhus: "Will you eat?"
“Monks, there are cakes. “Where are the cakes, Bhante? “Do you not see those children who have passed by, having been made to carry away the baskets of cakes?
“Bhante, such children as these would not give cake to anyone.
“Monks, although these did not invite me or you with cakes, they were the owners of the cakes, monks.”
"He is coming from behind; it is better for you to go on after eating some cakes. For Buddhas have no envy or ill-will toward even a single individual;
therefore, having said this, he took the community of monks and sat down in the shade at the foot of a tree.
When the children saw the Elder Mahākassapa approaching from behind, their hearts were filled with affection and, through the force of their joy—

Having restored their bodies to full health, they took down their baskets, paid homage to the Elder with the fivefold prostration, and lifting the cakes together with the baskets, they said to the Elder, “Please accept them, Venerable Sir.
Then the Elder said to them, “The Teacher is sitting at the foot of a tree having taken the Saṅgha of bhikkhus; go, taking your offerings for him.”
“Distribute them among the community of bhikkhus. They replied, “Very well, venerable sir,” and turning back, they went with the Elder.
Having given the cakes, they stood to one side watching him; at the conclusion of his meal, they gave him water.
The bhikkhus complained, “Alms were given by these children while they looked at his face; [how can this be compared to giving to] the Perfectly Enlightened One?”
“Or, having failed to inform the great elders with cakes, they saw the Elder Mahākassapa and came along with the birds themselves.
When the Teacher heard their talk, he said, “Monks, a monk equal to my son Mahākassapa is beloved by gods and humans, and they indeed perform worship for him with the four requisites.”
Having spoken this, he recited this verse:
“People hold dear one who is endowed with virtue and insight, established in the Dhamma, a knower of truth, and who performs his own duty.”
In this context, "endowed with virtue and vision" means endowed with the fourfold purity of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*) and with right vision associated with the paths and fruits.
"Established in the Dhamma" means established in the ninefold supramundane Dhamma; the meaning is that he has realized the supramundane Dhamma.
"One who knows the truth" means one who, through the knowledge of truth, has realized the four truths in sixteen aspects.
"To one who knows the truth. "Performing his own duty" means fulfilling the three trainings, which are called one's own duty;

this is the meaning. "The people love him" means that the worldly masses hold that person dear; they truly desire to see him, desire to pay homage to him, and desire to honor him with requisites—this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, all those boys were established in the fruit of stream-entry.
This is the seventh story, concerning the five hundred boys. 8.
The Story of the Elder Eka-Nāgāmi.
"Born of Hatred": This teaching on the Dhamma was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain non-returner (anāgāmi) elder.
One day, his resident pupils asked him, "Venerable sir, have you attained any special distinction?
The elder replied, "Laypeople also attain what is called the fruit of non-returning; it is only when they reach Arahantship that I shall [share it] with them."
“I shall tell you,” he thought; yet, feeling ashamed, he passed away without saying anything at all and was reborn in the Suddhāvāsa heaven.

Then his pupils, having wept and lamented, went into the presence of the Teacher, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down to one side while still weeping. Then the Teacher said to them, “Bhikkhus, why are you weeping? They replied, “Our preceptor—”
“No, Bhante, he has passed away. “Let it be, monks; do not grieve. This is indeed the inevitable nature of things.
“Yes, Bhante, we know that. However, we asked our preceptor about his special attainments, and without saying anything at all, he passed away.
Because of that, we are suffering. The Teacher said, “Monks, do not grieve.”
"Your preceptor attained the fruit of non-returning;
thinking, 'These people will attain it as laymen,' and 'I shall tell them only after I have attained Arahatship,' he passed away while concealing it from you and was reborn in the Suddhāvāsa heaven.
Take heart, monks! Your preceptor has attained a state of mind unattached to sensual pleasures. Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“Having conceived desire for the unproclaimed, one should be touched by the mind;
with a mind unattached to sensual pleasures, one is called ‘one who flows upwards.
Herein, “having conceived desire” means having generated desire through the wish to act, having attained enthusiasm. “In the unproclaimed” refers to Nibbāna.
For that is called "undeclared" (anakkhāta) because it cannot be described as "done by such-and-such a person" or "of such-and-such a kind among blue and the other [colors].
And "it may be touched by the mind" means it would be touched—that is, filled—by the three lower path and fruition consciousnesses.
"With a mind unattached" means with a mind unattached to sense pleasures by way of the non-returning path. "One who flows upwards" refers to such a bhikkhu in the Aviha heaven.
Having been reborn there, from that point on proceeding toward the Akaniṭṭha heaven by way of rebirth-linking, he is called an "upward-streamer" (uddhaṃsota);
such was your preceptor—this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, those bhikkhus were established in the fruit of Arahatship, and the Dhamma discourse was beneficial for the great multitude as well.
The eighth story: The Elder Eka-anāgāmin. The ninth story: The Story of Nandiya.
The Teacher related this Dhamma teaching concerning Nandiya while staying at Isipatana, beginning with the words, "One who has been long away..."
It is said that in Benares there was a son named Nandika to a family endowed with faith;

he was worthy of his parents, possessed of faith, and a supporter of the Saṅgha. When he reached maturity, his parents desired to bring him a wife from their own household, a maternal cousin named Revatī.
However, she was lacking in faith and had a habit of not giving. Nandika—
He did not accept it. Then his mother said to Revatī:
"Daughter, you must plaster the seating area for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus in this house, prepare the seats, set out the footstools, and when the bhikkhus arrive, take their bowls and seat them;
after filtering water with a water-strainer, wash the bowls when they have finished eating."
"In this way, you will have won over my son. She did accordingly.
Then, having informed her son that she had become "capable of receiving instruction," and when he agreed by saying "Very well," they fixed a day and performed the marriage ceremony.
Then Nandiya said to her: "If you shall attend upon both the Saṅgha of monks and my parents, then..."
“You shall be allowed to live in this house; be heedful,” he said.
Having agreed, saying “Very well,” she served her husband for a few days with the appearance of faith, and gave birth to two sons.
When Nandiya’s parents also passed away, all the authority in the household belonged to her alone. And as for Nandiya, from the time his parents died...
Having become a great lord of almsgiving, he established a practice of giving to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
He also established a regular provision of cooked food at the doors of the houses of the poor, the destitute, and others.

Later on, having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma and perceiving the benefits of providing a dwelling place, he constructed a four-hall building adorned with four chambers at the Mahāvihāra in Isipatana.
Having had beds, chairs, and other furnishings prepared and having spread them out, he offered that dwelling to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha;
after giving the gift, he presented the water of dedication (*dakṣiṇodaka*) to the Tathāgata.
Simultaneously with the placing of the water of dedication in the Teacher’s hand, in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, extending twelve *yojanas* in every direction and rising one hundred *yojanas* in height—
A celestial palace made of the seven precious gems, filled with throngs of women, rose up.

Then one day, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, having gone on a tour of the deva realms, stood not far from that palace and asked the sons of the gods who had come into his presence: "To whom does this celestial palace belong, surrounded by a host of nymphs?"
“...has been reborn. Then the sons of the gods, pointing out the owner of the mansion, said:
“Venerable sir, this mansion has arisen for the sake of that householder’s son named Nandiya, by whom a monastery was built for the Teacher at Isipatana and offered to him.
And when the host of nymphs saw him, they descended from the palace and said: “Venerable sir, we [thought], ‘Nandiya’s...”
“We shall become her attendants. Having been reborn here, we are now deeply distressed because we do not see her;
it is like discarding a clay bowl to take up a golden one—having abandoned human excellence to seize divine excellence.
“Please speak to her so that she may come here. Thereupon, the Elder returned, approached the Teacher, and asked him about it.
“Venerable sir, does the attainment of divine success arise for those who have performed wholesome deeds while remaining in the human world?
“Moggallāna, did you not personally see the divine success that arose for Nandiya in the world of the devas?
Why then do you ask me? “Yes, venerable sir, it arises thus.”
Then the Teacher said to him, "Moggallāna, what is this you are saying?

It is just as if someone standing at the village gate, having seen a son or a brother who had been away for a long time returning from his journey, were to rush home in haste and announce, 'So-and-so has arrived!
and then his kinsmen, with faces beaming with joy, would come out in haste."
“‘You have come, dear one! You are well, dear one!’—thus they would greet him with joy.
In the very same way, when a woman or a man who has performed wholesome deeds leaves this world and goes to the next world, the deities go out to meet them, saying ‘I am ahead!
I am ahead! and greet them with joy, having brought ten kinds of divine gifts. Having said this, he spoke these verses:
“Relatives, friends, and well-wishers rejoice when a man who has lived abroad returns safely from afar.
In the very same way, those who have performed meritorious deeds rejoice when he passes from this world to the next.”
"Meritorious deeds receive him, like dear kinsmen who have returned.
In this context, "one who has been long away" means one who has been gone for a long time.

"Safely returned from afar" refers to one who has come back from a distant place without misfortune, having gained profit through trade or service to the king, and having achieved success. "Kinsmen and friends..."
"Kinsmen" (*suhajjā*) refers to relatives by way of family connection, friends by way of being seen together and so forth, and well-wishers by way of having a kind heart.
"They rejoice at his arrival" means that upon seeing him arrive, they rejoice either by the mere act of speaking words of welcome or by the mere act of joining their palms;
but when he has reached the house, they rejoice by presenting various kinds of gifts. "In the same way" [refers to the following].

In that very same manner, when a person who has performed merit passes from this world to the next world, the merits—which stand in the place of parents—rejoice and receive him, bringing with them these ten kinds of gifts:
celestial lifespan, beauty, happiness, fame, sovereignty, and the five celestial objects of sense pleasure:
forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles. "Dear kinsmen" refers to dear relatives in this world.
The meaning is that he came like a remaining relative.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
Thus ends the ninth story, the Story of Nandiya.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Dear is finished.
The sixteenth chapter.
17. The Chapter on Anger.
1. The Story of the Kṣatriya Maiden Rohiṇī The Teacher delivered this Dhamma teaching, "Abandon anger," while residing at the Nigrodha Monastery concerning a kṣatriya maiden named Rohiṇī.
It is said that on one occasion, the Venerable Anuruddha was at Kapilavatthu together with five hundred bhikkhus.
He arrived. Then his relatives, hearing that the Elder had come, went into his presence—with the exception of his sister named Rohinī.
The Elder asked his relatives, "Where is Rohinī? "She is at home, Venerable Sir. "Why has she not come here?
"Because a skin disease has broken out on her body, Venerable Sir; she did not come out of shame."
The Elder said, “Call her,” and having had her summoned, he put on a robe and cloak. When she arrived, he said to her, “Rohinī, why have you not come?
She replied, “Venerable sir, a skin disease has broken out on my body; therefore, out of shame, I did not come.
He asked, “But is it not fitting for you to perform meritorious deeds? She said, “What can I do, venerable sir? [He replied,] “The hall for the seats...”
“Have it built. “What shall I take with me? “Do you have no materials for decoration?
“I have them, Bhante. “What is their cost? “It will amount to ten thousand. “In that case, sell them and have the assembly hall built.
“Who, Bhante, will build it for me? The Elder looked at the relatives standing nearby and said, “You yourselves…”
"Let it be a burden," he said. "But what will you do, venerable sir? "I too shall remain right here.
"In that case, bring the timber and building materials for it. "Very well, venerable sir," they replied, and they brought them.
As the Elder was preparing the hall for the seats, he said to Rohinī: "Having had a two-storied hall for the seats built, on the upper floor..."
“From the time the floor-boards are laid down, sweep the lower hall continuously and arrange the seats;
set out the water-jars continuously. She replied, “Very well, Bhante,” and having set aside her ornaments, she had a two-storied assembly hall built.
From the time the upper floor-boards were laid down, she performed the sweeping and other duties of the lower hall.
She had it built. The monks sat down upon the seats that were arranged there. Then, even as she was sweeping the hall where the seats stood, her skin disease faded away.
When the hall for the seats was finished, she invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha;
and when the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha was seated, filling the hall for the seats, she served them with excellent food, both hard and soft.
She gave it. When the Teacher had finished his meal, he asked, "To whom was this gift given? "To my sister Rohinī, venerable sir," she replied.
"But where is she? "At home, venerable sir. "Summon her. She did not wish to come;
however, the Teacher summoned her even though she was unwilling. Having arrived and paid homage, as she sat down, he said:
“Rohinī, why did you not come? “Venerable sir, I have a skin disease on my body;
being ashamed because of it, I did not come. “But do you know by what this [disease] arose?
“I do not know, venerable sir. “This arose dependent upon your anger. “But what, venerable sir, did I do? “Well then, listen.”
Then the Teacher brought up the past for her.
In the past, the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī harbored a grudge against a certain female dancer of the king;
thinking, "I shall cause her suffering," she had large *kacchu* fruits brought and [sent] that female dancer to her presence.
Having summoned her, so that she would not know, he had itching powder placed upon her bed and among her curtains, coverlets, and so forth; then, as if playing, he scattered it over her body.
At that very moment, her body became inflamed and covered with pustules. Scratching herself, she went and lay down upon the bed.
There too, as she was being bitten by the powder of the *kacchu* tree, an even more intense pain arose. At that time, Rohinī was the chief queen.
Having brought up this past event, the Teacher said, "Rohinī, it was you who committed this deed then. Indeed, even the slightest anger or envy is not fit to be indulged in," and he spoke this verse:
"Abandon anger; let one cast away pride."
One should transcend all fetters;
for one who does not cling to name-and-form,
sufferings do not afflict that person who possesses nothing.
In this context, one should abandon anger in all its forms and the ninefold conceit (*māna*).
One should transcend all fetters (*saṃyojana*), including the ten types beginning with the fetter of sensual lust (*kāmarāga*). "Not clinging" (*asajjamāna*) means being unattached.
For he who grasps at name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) in such a manner as "form is mine, feeling is mine," and grieves when that [name-and-form] breaks up—
One who is afflicted is said to be "clinging" to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). One who does not grasp in this way and is not afflicted is said to be "not clinging.

For such a person who is not clinging, because of the absence of lust and the other defilements, they are "possessing nothing" (*akiñcana*); thus, sufferings do not "overcome" them—this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*) and the others. Rohinī also [attained] the fruit of stream-entry.
As soon as she was established [in that state], her body at that very moment became the color of gold.
Passing away from there, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven between four young gods (*devaputta*), becoming radiant and having attained the pinnacle of physical beauty.
When the four young gods saw her, they conceived affection for her and said, "Mine..."

Quarreling over whether [the child] was born inside the boundary or "born inside my boundary," they went into the presence of Sakka, the king of the gods, and said, "Your Majesty, a dispute has arisen between us concerning this; please settle it.
Sakka, too, looked at him and, having conceived affection for him, spoke thus: "From the moment you first saw her, how..."
“...our minds have arisen. Then one said: “As for my mind that has arisen, it was unable to settle down, like a war drum.
The second said: “My mind flows on swiftly indeed, like a mountain river. The third said:
“From the moment I saw her, my eyes have popped out like those of a crab. The fourth—
“My mind was unable to remain motionless, like a banner raised upon a shrine.
Then Sakka said to them, “Sirs, your minds are indeed agitated; but as for me, if I obtain this [fruit], I shall live, but if I do not obtain it, death will be my lot.
The sons of the gods replied, “Great King, there is no need for your death.”
Having dismissed her with the words, “There is none,” they departed. She became dear and pleasing to Sakka.
When it was said, “Let us go to such-and-such a festival,” Sakka was unable to refuse her request.
This is the first story, concerning the noble maiden Rohinī.

2. The Story of a Certain Bhikkhu The Teacher delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, beginning with the words "He who indeed [sees] what has arisen," while residing at the Aggāḷava Cetiya concerning a certain bhikkhu.
For when the Teacher had authorized lodgings for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and the merchants of Rājagaha and others were having lodgings constructed, [the following occurred].
A certain monk from Āḷavī, while preparing his own lodging, saw a beautiful tree and began to cut it down.
There, a young mother deity who had been reborn in that tree stood with her child on her hip and pleaded, "Sir, do not cut down my dwelling;
I shall not be able to wander about without a home, taking my child with me. He said, "I..."
“I will not find such a tree elsewhere,” he said, and did not heed her words.
Thinking, “Perhaps she will desist after looking at this boy,” she placed her son on a branch of the tree.
That monk, unable to withstand the raised axe, cut off the boy’s arm. The deity, overcome by powerful anger, [cried out] “Having struck—”
Thinking, “I shall kill him,” he raised both hands and reflected thus: “This monk is virtuous.

If I kill him, I will go to hell. Furthermore, when the other deities see monks cutting down their own trees, they will take me as their authority and [think], ‘The monk was killed by such-and-such a deity.’”
“They will kill him. And since this monk has a husband, I shall inform his husband himself.
Having said this, she drew back her raised hand, went weeping into the presence of the Teacher, paid homage, and stood to one side.
Then the Teacher asked her, “What is it, deity? She replied, “Venerable sir, your disciple has done such-and-such a thing to me; I too—”
“Desiring to kill him, she thought of this very thing, yet without having killed him, she has come here. She related that entire occurrence in detail.
Having heard it, the Teacher said, “Excellent, excellent, O deity! Well done by you who have thus restrained such a surging anger, like a racing chariot,” and he spoke this verse:
“He indeed who restrains arisen anger, as one would a racing chariot—”
“Him I call a charioteer; others are merely holders of the reins.

In this context, “uppatitaṃ” means arisen. “Rathaṃ bhantaṃ vā” means that just as a skilled charioteer, having restrained a chariot racing with excessive speed, stops it wherever he desires, even so is the person who [restrains] arisen anger.

"He is able to restrain and subdue [the horses]. "I call him a charioteer. But the other person—namely, the charioteers among kings, vassals, and others—is merely a holder of the reins; he is not a supreme charioteer.
At the conclusion of the teaching, a deity was established in the fruit of stream-entry, and the discourse on the Dhamma was fruitful for the assembled multitude as well.
But the deity, even though she had become a stream-enterer (sotāpanna), remained there weeping. Then the Teacher asked her, "What is it, O deity?
When she replied, "Venerable sir, my celestial mansion (vimāna) has vanished; what shall I do now?", he said, "Enough, deity; do not worry, I will give you a celestial mansion.
[He then brought] a certain deity who had passed away the previous day near the Gandhakuṭi in Jeta’s Grove.
Pointing to a tree, he said, "In such-and-such a place there is a secluded tree; go there.
She went there. From that time on, even powerful deities came thinking, "This celestial mansion belongs to one to whom the Buddha has given it," and they were unable to move it.
The Teacher, taking this as the occasion for a discourse, established the training rule regarding living plants for the bhikkhus.
The Story of a Certain Bhikkhu, the second.
3. The Story of the Laywoman Uttarā.

The Teacher, while residing at Veḷuvana, after having finished his meal at the house of Uttarā, spoke this teaching on the Dhamma concerning the laywoman Uttarā: "One should conquer anger with non-anger."
In this regard, this is the gradual account: It is said that in Rājagaha, a poor man named Puṇṇa lived by working for hire under the patronage of the merchant Sumanaseṭṭhi.
He had only two household dependents: his wife, named Uttarā, and their daughter.
Then one day, they made a proclamation throughout Rājagaha that a festival should be celebrated for seven days. Having heard this, the merchant Sumanaseṭṭhi...
Early in the morning, he called Puṇṇa and said, "Dear son, our household wishes to enjoy the festival;
will you take part in the festival, or will you work for wages? He replied, "Master, a festival is for those who have wealth.
But in my house there is not even a spoonful of rice for tomorrow's meal; what use have I for a festival? I would rather obtain oxen."
“I will go to plow. “In that case, take the oxen,” he said.
Taking the strong oxen and the plow, he said to his wife, “My dear, the city-dwellers are celebrating a festival. Because of my poverty, I must go to work for wages;
therefore, cook double the amount of fodder today and bring me my meal. Having said this to his wife, he went to the field.
The Elder Sāriputta, who had been absorbed in the attainment of cessation for seven days, emerged on that day and considered, "Whom should I favor today?
Looking about, he saw Puṇṇa had entered within the net of his own knowledge.
He then examined whether he was faithful and whether he would be able to receive his favor, and perceived his state of faith.

Knowing that he was capable of providing for them and that, as a result, they would obtain great prosperity, [the Elder] took his bowl and robe, went to the place where he was plowing, and stood watching a grove of trees on the bank of a ditch.
As soon as Puṇṇa saw the Elder, he set aside his plow, paid homage to the Elder with the fivefold prostration, and said: "With a tooth-stick..."
“There will be need for it,” he thought, and having made the tooth-stick allowable, he gave it to him. Then the elder took out his bowl and water-strainer and gave them to him.
He thought, “There will be need for drinking water,” and taking them, he strained the water and gave it to him.
The elder reflected: “This man lives in the last house of the village. If I go to the door of his house, [he will surely give me alms].”
“His wife shall not be able to see me. I will remain right here until she has taken her meal and sets out on the road.
Having lingered there for a short while and knowing that he had already set out on the path, he departed toward the interior of the city.
On the way, seeing the Elder, she thought: "Sometimes when there is something to give, I do not see the noble one;
sometimes when I am seeing the noble one, there is nothing to give. But today I have seen the noble one, and this gift is here;
will he perhaps show me favor? Having set down her food-bowl, she approached the Elder with the fivefold prostration.
Having paid homage, she said, "Venerable sir, without considering whether this is coarse or refined, please show favor to your servant.

The Elder held out his bowl; she supported the vessel with one hand and, as she was giving him the food with the other, he said, "Enough," and covered the bowl with his hand when half the food had been given. She—
“Venerable sir, there is only one portion; it cannot be divided into two.

Without providing for your servant in this world, please provide for him in the next world. We wish to give everything without remainder,” he said, and having placed it all into the elder’s bowl, he made the aspiration:
“May he be a partaker of the very things seen by you. The elder—
Saying, "So be it," he offered his thanks while still standing; then, sitting down at a pleasant spot by the water, he performed his meal.
She too turned back, sought rice, and cooked the food.
Meanwhile, Puṇṇa, having plowed a space measuring half a *karīsa*, being unable to endure the hunger, released his oxen and entered the shade of a single tree.
He sat down watching the road.
Then his wife, taking the food and walking along, saw him and thought: "This man, oppressed by hunger, sits here looking at me.
If he reproaches me, saying, 'My dear, you have been away far too long,' and strikes me with his goad-stick—"
Thinking, "The work I have done will be in vain; I shall report this to him at once," she said:
"Master, today for one day, please compose your mind; do not let the work I have done be in vain.
For this morning, while bringing your meal, I saw the Dhammasenāpati on the road and gave your meal to him."
Having gone again and cooked the meal, she returned and said, "Be gracious, Master, in your heart. He asked, "What are you saying, my dear?
and upon hearing that matter once more, he said with a mind full of faith, "My dear, you have done well indeed in giving me food for the Noble One;
I too gave him a tooth-stick and water for rinsing his mouth this very morning."
Having welcomed those words, his body weary from having obtained food so late at night, he placed his head on her lap and fell asleep.
Then, at dawn, the entire field that had been plowed stood there, covered with dust and appearing as radiant as a heap of *kaṇikāra* flowers made of pure gold.
Having woken up and looked, he said to his wife, "My dear, this is the field that was plowed..."
“Everything appears to me as gold; could it be that my eyes are spinning because I have received food so late?

“Master, it appears exactly the same way to me too. He rose up, went there, took a single clod of earth, struck it with the tip of his plow, and realizing its golden nature, exclaimed: “Oh, how wonderful! To the Master Dhammasenāpati...”
"The fruit of the gift I gave has been manifested this very day; however, it is not possible to consume such wealth while concealing it.
Having filled his wife's brought food-bowl with gold, he went to the royal palace.
Being granted leave by the king, he entered, paid homage to the king, and when the king asked, "What is it, dear one? he replied, "Your Majesty, today by me—"
“The entire plowed field remains as if filled with gold; it is right to have this gold brought back.
“Who are you? “I am named Puṇṇa. “But what did you do today?
“This morning, even at dawn, tooth-sticks and water for rinsing the mouth were given to me by the General of the Dhamma; my wife was also given his own meal to bring back for me.”
Having heard this, the king said, "It seems, sir, the fruit of the gift given to the General of the Dhamma has been shown this very day," and he asked, "Dear son, what shall we do?
[The son replied,] "Send many thousands of wagons and have gold brought back.
The king sent the wagons. As the royal men were taking it, thinking, "This belongs to the king," whatever they took turned out to be nothing but clay.
They went and informed the king, asking, "What did you say when you took it?
When they were questioned, they said, "It belongs to you. [The king replied: "Sons, it does not belong to me; go and take it, saying, 'It belongs to Puṇṇa.
They did so, and whatever they took was indeed gold. Having brought back all of it,
They piled it up in the royal courtyard, and the heap rose eighty cubits high.
The king, having assembled the citizens, asked, "Is there anyone in this city who possesses so much gold? "There is none, Your Majesty," they replied. "What, then, should be given to him?
"The parasol of a chief merchant, Your Majesty. The king said, "Let him be known as the merchant Bāhudhana," and [bestowed it] along with great wealth.
He gave him the merchant’s parasol. Then he said to him, “Your Majesty, for all this time we have lived in another’s house;
please give us a place to live. “In that case, look, this thicket appears;
have it cleared away and build a house there,” he said, pointing out the site of the former merchant’s house. Within a few days, he [cleared] that place.

Having had a house built, he performed the auspicious ceremony for entering the new home and the auspicious ceremony for the royal parasol together at once, and for seven days he gave alms to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
Then the Teacher, while offering a blessing of thanks, delivered a gradual discourse.
At the conclusion of the discourse on the Dhamma, the merchant Puṇṇa, his wife, and his daughter—
The three people from Uttarā became stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*).
Later on, the merchant of Rājagaha requested the daughter of the merchant Puṇṇa for his own son.
He replied, "I will not give her," but [Puṇṇa] said, "Do not do this; you have lived depending upon us for so long that your prosperity..."
When he said, "I have obtained [wealth]; give your daughter to my son," the other replied, "He holds wrong views; my daughter cannot live without the Three Jewels. I will not give him my daughter.
Then many sons of noble families, including groups of merchants and others, entreated him, saying, "Do not break off your friendship with him; give him your daughter. He, for their sake—
Having accepted the proposal, he gave his daughter on the full moon day of Āsāḷha.
From the time she went to her husband’s family, she was unable to approach a monk or a nun, give alms, or listen to the Dhamma.
Thus, when two and a half months had passed, she asked a female attendant standing nearby: “How much [time remains] now?”
“How much of the rainy season remains? “Half a month, noble lady. She sent a message to her father:
“Why have they cast me into such a prison? It would be better for them to brand me with the mark of a slave and announce that I am the servant of another.
It is not fitting to give me to a family of such wrong views. From the moment I arrived, regarding the visiting of monks and other such matters...”
“I do not even obtain the opportunity to perform a single act of merit.
Then her father, expressing his displeasure, thinking, “Alas, my daughter is suffering,” sent fifteen thousand kahāpaṇas, saying:
“In this city there is a courtesan named Sirimā who takes a thousand [kahāpaṇas] every day. With these—”
“Having brought him here with these kahāpaṇas, let her serve as her husband’s foot-attendant while she herself performs meritorious deeds.
She summoned Sirimā and said, “Friend, take these kahāpaṇas and attend upon your friend for this half-month.
She consented, saying, “Very well. Taking her with her, she went into the presence of her husband.
When he saw Sirimā and asked, "What is this?", she replied, "Master, for these half-months let my companion attend upon you;
as for me, during these half-months I wish to give gifts and to hear the Dhamma.
Seeing that beautiful woman, he felt a surge of affection and accepted her request, saying, "Very well."

Uttarā also, having invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, obtained the Teacher’s consent, saying, “Venerable Sir, for this half-month, please do not go elsewhere; alms should be received right here.
With a joyful mind, she thought, “From now until the Great Invitation ceremony (Mahāpavāraṇā), I shall have the opportunity to attend upon the Teacher and listen to the Dhamma.”
“Cook the rice-gruel in this way; bake the cakes in this way,” she moved about, supervising all the tasks in the kitchen.

Then her husband, thinking, “Tomorrow will be the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā),” stood at the window facing the kitchen and looked on, wondering, “What is that foolish woman doing as she moves about? He saw the merchant’s daughter, drenched in sweat.
Seeing him walking about after having arranged it thus—strewn with ashes and smeared with charcoal and soot—he laughed and departed, thinking: "Alas, what blind fools!
They do not enjoy such splendor and prosperity in a place like this; instead, they wander about with hearts delighted by the thought, 'We shall serve these shaven-headed recluses.'"
When he had departed, Sirimā, who was standing near him, thought, "What did he look at that he smiled?
Looking out through that very window, she saw Uttara and thought, "He smiled because he looked at her; surely there is an intimacy between him and her.
It is said that for half a month she had been a visiting woman in that house.
Although she was living there and enjoying that prosperity, she did not realize her own status as an outsider woman, but maintained the perception, "I am the mistress of the house.
Having harbored resentment toward Uttarā, thinking, "I shall cause her suffering," she descended from the palace, entered the kitchen,
took boiling ghee with a ladle from the place where cakes were being baked, and [stood] facing north.
Pāyāsi departed. Seeing her approaching, Uttarā thought: "My companion has done me a great service;
the world-system is too cramped and the Brahma-world is too lowly—the virtues of my companion alone are great.
For it was by depending on her that I was able to give alms and hear the Dhamma. If I have any anger toward her, let this ghee [be the expiation]."
"Let it burn me; if there is no [sin], let it not burn me. She suffused him with loving-kindness (*mettā*).
To her, that boiling ghee poured upon her head became like cool water.
Then, thinking, "This will be cool," Uttarā took a ladle full of it and was coming toward him.
Seeing her, the female slaves threatened her, saying, "Go away, you ill-behaved woman! You are not fit to pour boiling ghee on our mistress!
Rising up from here and there, they struck her with their hands and feet and threw her to the ground.
Although Uttarā tried to stop them, she was unable to do so. Then, pushing aside all the female slaves who were standing over her—
“Why have you committed such a grave offense? Having thus admonished Sirimā, he bathed her with warm water and anointed her with oil refined a hundred times.
At that moment, realizing she had been exposed as a courtesan, she thought:
“I have committed a grave deed for the sake of merely making my husband laugh—by pouring boiling ghee over her.”
She did not command her slave girls, saying, "Seize her! Even while tormenting me, she always warded off all the slave girls and did only what was appropriate for me.

"If I do not ask her for forgiveness, my head shall split into seven pieces," she said, as she prostrated at her feet and added, "Noble lady, forgive me. "I am a daughter with her father still living; toward her father..."
"Forgive me; I forgive you. "Very well, noble lady, I shall ask your father, the merchant Puṇṇa, to forgive you.

"Puṇṇa is my father who gives birth to the body (*vaṭṭa-janaka-pitā*); but when my father who gives birth to liberation (*vivaṭṭa-janaka-pitā*) forgives me, then I shall forgive him. "But who is that father of yours who gives birth to liberation?
"The Perfectly Enlightened One (*Sammāsambuddha*). "I have no acquaintance with him. "I shall arrange it. The Teacher will come tomorrow..."
"He will come here taking the community of monks with him; you should take whatever honor you have received, come right here, and ask his forgiveness.
She replied, "Very well, noble lady," and rising, she went to her own home.
Having commanded five hundred women in her retinue, she prepared various kinds of solid foods and soups. On the following day, she [prepared] that hospitality...
Having taken [the food], Uttarā returned to her home and stood there, unable to place it into the bowls of the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha.
Uttarā herself took all of that and made the necessary arrangements. At the conclusion of the meal, Sirimā also prostrated at the feet of the Teacher together with her retinue.
Then the Teacher asked her, "What was your offense? "Venerable Sir, yesterday I did such-and-such a thing;
then my companion, while she was harassing me, prevented the female slaves from doing so and instead rendered me a service.
Having recognized her virtue, I asked her for forgiveness. Then she said to me, 'I will forgive you when you have forgiven those [slaves].'"
He asked, "Is it truly so in Uttara? "Yes, venerable sir; my companion poured boiling ghee upon my head.
Then he asked, "What did you think [at that moment]? "The world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) was too narrow, and the Brahma-world was too low;
the virtue of my companion alone was great. For it was by relying on her that I was able to give alms and hear the Dhamma."
"Thinking, 'If there is anger in me toward this woman, let this [fire] burn me;
if not, let it not burn me,' I pervaded her with loving-kindness (*mettā*), venerable sir. The Teacher said, "Excellent, excellent, Uttara!

It is right to conquer anger in this way. For anger is indeed conquered by non-anger; one who reviles and insults is conquered by one who does not revile or insult; one who is stubborn and miserly..."
“By giving one’s own possessions, and by truthful speech, the liar is to be conquered,” he said, and then recited this verse:
“Conquer anger with non-anger; conquer the wicked with goodness;
conquer the miser with generosity; conquer the speaker of falsehood with truth.”
In this context, "by non-anger" means that an angry person must be conquered by one who is without anger. "The wicked" means one who is unwholesome must be conquered by one who is wholesome.
"The miserly" means one who is stubborn and stingy must be conquered by a mind of generosity toward what belongs to oneself.
"The speaker of falsehood" must be conquered by truthful speech. Therefore, he said: "Conquer anger with non-anger... [and so forth]."
"By truth, [I am] one who speaks no falsehood.
At the conclusion of the teaching, Sirimā, together with five hundred women, was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
This is the third story, the Story of the Laywoman Uttarā.

4. The Story of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna’s Question “‘One should speak the truth’—this teaching on the Dhamma was related by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a question asked by the Elder Mahāmoggallāna.
For on one occasion, the Elder, having gone on a journey among the devas, stood at the gate of a powerful deity’s celestial mansion.”
When she had come into his presence, paid homage, and stood there, he said to her: “Deity, you possess great prosperity;
what kamma did you perform to obtain this? “Do not ask me, venerable sir,” she replied.
It is said that the deity spoke thus because she was ashamed of her own minor deed. But when the Elder told her, “Speak indeed,” she said:
“Venerable sir, I have given no gift, performed no worship, and heard no Dhamma; I have merely guarded the truth alone.
The elder went to other doors of the celestial mansions and questioned the other goddesses who came there.
When they too, concealing the truth in the same manner, were unable to turn the elder away, one of them said: “Venerable sir, by me—”
There was nothing whatsoever done by me in the form of giving and so forth. However, during the time of Kassapa Buddha, I was another's slave.
My master was exceedingly fierce and cruel; with whatever stick or *kaliṅgara* he seized, he would split my head open.
When anger arose in me, I thought: "This husband of yours might even perform a *lakkhaṇāhata* [a ritual mark] on your nose and so forth..."
“I thought, ‘I am able to cut him down; let me not be angry,’ and having thus reproached myself, I did not give way to anger.
By that means, this prosperity was obtained by me. Another said, “Venerable sir, while guarding a sugar-cane field, I gave a stalk of sugar-cane to a certain bhikkhu.
Another gave a single *timbarusaka* fruit. Another gave a single *eḷāluka* root.
I gave one [seed]. Another gave one *phārusaka* fruit. Another gave a handful of roots.
Others, having each announced their own small gift of protection (*parittadāna*) by way of "a handful of neem," and so forth, said, "By this and that cause, we have obtained this prosperity."
Having heard what they had done, the Elder approached the Teacher and asked:
"Venerable Sir, is it possible to obtain divine prosperity merely by speaking the truth, merely by appeasing anger, or by such very small gifts as that of the *timbarusaka* fruit?
"Why do you ask me this, Moggallāna? Have you not heard from the deities about this?"
“Has the meaning been explained? “Yes, venerable sir; it seems that by this much one attains divine success.

Then the Teacher said to him, “Moggallāna, even by speaking only the truth, by abandoning only a measure of anger, and by giving only a small gift, one indeed goes to the world of the gods,” and he spoke this verse:
“One should speak the truth, one should not be angry, and one should give even a little when asked;
by these three qualities, one goes into the presence of the devas.
In this context, “one should speak the truth” means one should illuminate, express, or be established in truth. “One should not be angry” means...
One should not be angry with another. Regarding the term "one who asks": those called "askers" are indeed virtuous renunciants.
For although they stand at the door of a house even without saying "give," in actual fact, they are indeed asking.
Thus, when asked by such virtuous ones, if there is a small amount of property to be given, one should give even that little. "By these three" refers to these [three].
The meaning is that one might go to the world of the gods by even a single cause among these three.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the fourth story concerning the Elder Mahāmoggallāna’s question.
5. The Story of the Brahmin Buddhapita The Teacher delivered this Dhamma instruction, beginning with the question posed by the bhikkhus while residing in the Añjana Grove near Sāketa.
It is said that when the Blessed One, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, was entering Sāketa for alms, a certain resident of Sāketa...
As the elderly brahmin was departing from the city, he saw the One of Ten Powers at the gate of a house.
Prostrating at his feet and grasping them firmly by the ankles, he said, "Dear son, is it not true that in their old age parents ought to be cared for by their children?
Why did you not show yourself to us for all this time? I have seen you, but now I wish to see my mother as well."
Saying, "Come," he took the Teacher and went to his own home. The Teacher went there and sat down upon the prepared seat together with the community of monks.
The brahmin lady also came, prostrated at the Teacher’s feet, and said, "Dear son, where have you been for all this time?
Should parents not indeed be attended to when they have reached old age?"
He had his sons and daughters make obeisance, saying, "Come, pay homage to your brother. Both of them, with joyful hearts, served the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.

Then, having said, "Venerable sir, please accept almsfood from us here regularly," they were told, "The Buddhas do not accept almsfood regularly at only one place. To this they replied, "In that case, venerable sir,..."
"Those who come to invite you, you should send them to us," they said.
From then on, the Teacher sent those who came to invite him, saying, "Go and inform the brahmin.
They would go and say to the brahmin, "We are inviting the Teacher for tomorrow. On the following day, from his own house...
Taking the vessels for the rice and the vessels for the soup, he would go to the place where the Teacher was seated.
However, when there was no other invitation, the Teacher would take his meal in the brahmin’s own house.
Both of them, constantly giving their own offerings to the Tathāgata and listening to the discourse on the Dhamma, attained the fruit of the Non-Returner (anāgāmiphala).
The bhikkhus raised a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: “Friends, the brahmin knows that ‘Suddhodana is the father of the Tathāgata and Mahāmāyā is the mother.
Knowing this, he addresses the Tathāgata along with his wife as ‘our son,’ and the Teacher likewise accepts it.
What could be the reason for this? When the Teacher heard their conversation, [he went there].
“Monks, both of them call their own son ‘son,’” he said, and then related a story of the past:
“In the past, monks, for five hundred consecutive births this brahmin was my father, for five hundred births my paternal uncle, and for five hundred births my great-uncle.
And that brahmin woman likewise [was my mother] for five hundred consecutive births.”
"In five hundred births she was my mother; in five hundred births she was my junior mother; in five hundred births she was my senior mother.
Thus, for one thousand five hundred births I was reared in the hands of a brahmin, and for another one thousand five hundred births in the hands of a brahmin woman.
Having thus shown his state of being their son for three thousand births, he spoke these verses:
“In whomsoever the mind settles and the consciousness finds confidence—
even toward a person never seen before— one may indeed place trust in them.
Whether through former association or by present benefit,”
"Thus that love is born, like a lotus in the water.
For three months the Teacher dwelt depending upon that family. Both of them, having realized Arahatship, attained Parinibbāna.
Then, having performed great honors for them, they placed both of them together in a single coffin and carried them out. The Teacher also—
Accompanied by a retinue of five hundred bhikkhus, he went to the cremation ground together with them.
A great multitude of people came out, thinking, "It seems the parents of the Buddhas have passed away. The Teacher also entered a certain sal tree near the cremation ground and stood there.
After the people had paid homage to the Teacher and stood to one side, they said, "Venerable sir, do not grieve, thinking, 'Your mother and father have died. By the Teacher—

They exchanged greetings with him. Without rejecting them by saying, "Do not speak thus," the Teacher surveyed the inclinations of the assembly and, teaching the Dhamma appropriate for that moment, said:
"Truly brief is this life; ... [the rest of the verse follows]"
"One dies even before a hundred years have passed;
and even if one lives beyond that,
one still dies through old age."
He preached this Jarā Sutta. At the conclusion of the teaching, eighty-four thousand living beings attained penetration of the Dhamma.
The bhikkhus, not knowing that the brahmin and the brahmin lady had attained final Nibbāna, asked, "Venerable Sir, what is their future destiny?
The Teacher replied, "Bhikkhus, for such as these, who are Asekha Munis..."
“There is no such thing as a future life. For those like this attain only the deathless, the immortal, the Great Nibbāna,” he said, and then recited this verse:
“Those sages who are harmless and always restrained in body;”
“They go to the deathless state, having gone to which they do not grieve.
In this context, “sages” (munayo) refers to the asekha-sages who have attained the path and fruit through the practice of sagehood (moneyya). “By body” is merely a figurative expression;
the meaning is that they are well-restrained by all three doors. “Deathless” (accuta) means eternal. “State” (ṭhāna) means an unshakable state, a permanent state.
"Where" means: having gone to that Nibbāna where one does not grieve, does not sorrow, and is not afflicted, they go to that state—this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and the other fruits.
This is the fifth story, the account of the Brahmin who was the Buddha’s father.

6. The Story of the Maidservant Puṇṇā The Teacher delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, beginning with the words "Always remaining awake," while staying at Vulture Peak, concerning a maidservant named Puṇṇā belonging to a wealthy merchant of Rājagaha.
It is said that one day they gave her a large quantity of rice to be pounded. She lit a lamp and [began pounding] the rice even during the night.
Rubbing her limbs, which were dripping with sweat, she stood in the open air for the sake of rest.

At that time, Dabba Mallaputta was the assigner of lodgings for the bhikkhus. Having heard the preaching of the Dhamma, as the bhikkhus were going to their respective lodgings, he held up his finger for each of them to show the way ahead.

As he was walking, he emitted light for the bhikkhus. Seeing the bhikkhus wandering on the mountain by that light, Puṇṇā thought, "I am so afflicted by my own suffering that even at this hour I cannot find sleep;
for what reason, then, are the venerable ones not sleeping? She concluded, "Surely some bhikkhu must be unwell."
Thinking, "There will be trouble from the Dīghajātika [snake]," she took some rice-scum at dawn, moistened it with water, formed it into a cake on the palm of her hand, and cooked it over embers.

Placing it in the fold of her garment, she took a water-jar and set out toward the bathing place, intending to eat it on the path to the ford. The Teacher also entered that very village for alms and followed that same road.
Seeing the Teacher, she thought: "On other days, even when I saw the Teacher, I had no gift to offer;
and when I had a gift to offer, I did not see the Teacher. Now, however, I have a gift and the Teacher is present before me.
If he would accept it without considering whether it is coarse or refined, I would give it to him."
Setting down the cake and the pot in a secluded spot, she paid homage to the Teacher and said, "Venerable Sir, by accepting this meager gift, please show me your favor.
The Teacher looked toward the Elder Ānanda, who brought forward the bowl given by the Great King; the Teacher then accepted the cake. Puṇṇā, too, placed it into the Teacher’s bowl.
Having paid homage with the fivefold prostration, she said, “Venerable sir, may my success be realized even in this very life.
The Teacher, while remaining standing, offered words of appreciation, saying, “May it be so.
Puṇṇā thought, “Although my Teacher accepted the cake out of consideration for me, he will not eat it.”
“Surely she will give it to a crow or a dog, and then go to the house of a king or a prince to eat choice food.
The Teacher, wondering, “What indeed is she thinking? perceived her state of mind;
looking toward the Elder Ānanda, he signaled for him to sit down. The Elder spread out his robe and offered it to him.
The Teacher sat right outside the city and performed his meal.
The deities pressed together the essence suitable for gods and humans throughout the entire interior of the world-system, like a honeycomb, and infused it into that food.
Puṇṇā stood watching. At the conclusion of the meal, the Elder gave water. The Teacher, having finished his meal—
Having addressed Puṇṇa, he said, "Puṇṇa, why do you disparage my disciples? "I do not disparage them, Bhante," he replied.
Then [the Buddha asked], "What did you say when you looked at my disciples?
"As for me, Bhante, I cannot find sleep because of this distress; why do the venerable ones not find sleep? Surely someone must be unwell, or—"
“Venerable sir, this is all I thought: ‘There will be a danger from the Dīghajātika [serpent]’.
Having heard her words, the Teacher said, “Puṇṇā, you do not yet sleep because of the danger of suffering;
my disciples, however, do not sleep because they are constantly devoted to wakefulness,” and he spoke this verse:
“For those who are always wakeful, training day and night, and intent upon Nibbāna, the taints come to an end.
In this context, “training day and night” means for those training in the three trainings both by day and by night. Nibbāna...

"Those who are resolute" means those whose inclination is toward Nibbāna. "They go to their end" means that for such persons, all taints (āsava) go to their end—that is, to destruction and non-existence.
At the conclusion of the teaching, Puṇṇā, as she stood there, was established in the fruit of stream-entry; thus the Dhamma teaching was fruitful for the assembled company as well.
The Teacher, having performed his meal duties with the rice-cakes and charcoal-balls given by Puṇṇā, went to the monastery. The monks in the Dhamma hall started a discussion:
"It was difficult, friends, what was done by the Perfectly Enlightened One when he performed his meal duties with the rice-cakes and charcoal-balls given by Puṇṇā.
The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, what is the talk you are having just now?"
Having asked, "Are you sitting together? and being told, "We are indeed," he said, "Monks, it is not only now;
