in the past as well, I ate the broken rice given by this very woman. Having spoken thus, he related a story of the past:
"Having eaten grass for fodder, having eaten gruel and broken rice;"
“This was your food, sir; why do you not eat now?
“Where people do not know a person by birth or by discipline—there, Great Brahmā, even a great deal of mere rice-scum and broken grains is sufficient.”
“And you indeed know me, as this supreme horse is;
knowing this and being aware of it, I will not eat you, Kuṇḍaka.
Having related this Kuṇḍaka-Sindhava-Potaka Jātaka in detail, he spoke thus.
The Sixth Story: The Story of the Slave Girl Puṇṇā. The Seventh Story:

The Story of the Lay Follower Atula. The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, related this Dhamma teaching concerning a lay follower named Atula, beginning with the words: "This is an ancient saying."
For one day, a lay follower residing in Sāvatthī, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred lay followers, went to the monastery with those lay followers for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma.
Desiring to hear the Dhamma from the presence of the Elder Revata, he paid homage to the Elder Revata and sat down.
However, that venerable one delighted in seclusion and was like a lion walking alone; therefore, he did not engage in any conversation with him.
He preached. Thinking, "This elder said nothing at all," he rose up in anger, went to the presence of the Elder Sāriputta, and stood to one side.

When the Elder asked him, "For what purpose have you come?", he replied, "Venerable sir, I brought these lay devotees and approached the Elder Revata for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma; however, that elder said nothing to me."
He said, “He preached [the Dhamma], but having become angry with him, I have come here; please preach the Dhamma to me.
Then the Elder said, “In that case, lay follower, sit down,” and after making it extensive, he preached a discourse on the Abhidhamma.
The lay follower thought, “A discourse on the Abhidhamma is exceedingly subtle; the Elder has preached nothing but the Abhidhamma in great detail. For us, by this—”
"What is the point? he said, and in anger, taking his retinue with him, he went into the presence of the Elder Ānanda.
When the Elder asked, "What is it, lay follower?", he replied, "Venerable sir, we approached the Elder Revata for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma;
yet, having received not even a mere exchange of words from him, we became angry and [approached] the Elder Sāriputta."
“We went into his presence, but he spoke to us too much and too gently about the Abhidhamma alone. Thinking, ‘What use have we for this?
we became angry with him and came here. Please, Venerable Sir, give us a discourse on the Dhamma.
“In that case, sit down and listen,” said the Elder; and having made it easy for them to understand, he gave a brief discourse on the Dhamma.
Having become angry with that elder, they went into the presence of the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down to one side.
Then the Teacher said to them, “Lay followers, why have you come? “To hear the Dhamma, Bhante. “But has the Dhamma been heard by you?
“Bhante, we first approached the elder Revata; he [spoke] with us...”
“He said nothing at all; we became angry with him and approached the Elder Sāriputta, who taught us much of the Abhidhamma.
Failing to take note of that, we became angry and approached the Elder Ānanda, who taught us only a small amount of the Dhamma. Becoming angry with him as well, we have come here.”
The Teacher, having heard his words, said: “Atula, from ancient times this has been the established custom:
they indeed censure one who is silent, as well as those who speak much or speak little. For there is no one who is to be praised exclusively or censured exclusively.
Even kings—some condemn, while others praise. Even the great earth, and even the moon and sun...”
“Even when the Perfectly Enlightened One sits in the midst of the fourfold assembly and teaches the Dhamma, some disparage him while others praise him.
For the censure or praise of blind fools is of no account;
however, when he is censured by one who is wise and intelligent, he is truly censured, and when he is praised by such a person, he is truly praised. Having said this, he spoke these verses:
“This is ancient, O Atula; it is not as if it were only today:
they blame one who sits in silence, they blame one who speaks much, and they blame even one who speaks in moderation.
There is no one in the world who is not blamed.”
“There has never been, there will not be, nor is there found at present,
a person who is exclusively blameworthy or exclusively praiseworthy.
But that which the wise praise after investigating day by day— ”
“Who is fit to censure that wise one of flawless conduct, established in wisdom and virtue—like a coin of pure Jambūnada gold?
Even the gods praise him; he is praised even by Brahmā.”
In this context, "this is ancient" means it is something old. "Atula" addresses that lay follower by name.
"This is not as if it were today" means that this censure or praise is not something newly arisen at the present moment. "He sat in silence" is said as a reproach, implying:
"Why does he sit in silence like one who is mute, deaf, or as if knowing nothing at all?"
Regarding "one who speaks much," they criticize him, thinking: "Does he not rattle like a palm leaf struck by the wind?
There is no end to his talk. Regarding "one who speaks sparingly," they criticize him, thinking:
"Does he not remain silent after saying only one or two words, imagining his own speech to be like gold or bullion? Thus, in every way, he is unblamed in this world.
The meaning is that there is no such thing. "And it has not been" means that it did not exist in the past, nor will it exist in the future.
"And what a wise person... refers to the fact that the blame or praise of fools is of no account;
rather, it is that which the wise—having investigated day after day and having understood the grounds for blame or the grounds for praise—praise, or [that which pertains to] the flawless training.
Because he is endowed with a flawless mode of livelihood, they praise him as one of flawless conduct;

because he is endowed with the wisdom of the Dhamma-food, they praise him as wise; and because he is endowed with both mundane and supramundane wisdom as well as the fourfold purity of virtue, they praise him as one established in wisdom and virtue—just like a piece of Jambūnada gold, free from blemish and capable of enduring rubbing and polishing.
The meaning is: who is worthy of blame? "Even the gods" means that both deities and wise humans attend upon and praise that bhikkhu.
"Even by Brahmā" means that not only by gods and humans, but even by the Great Brahmā within the ten-thousandfold world-system is he indeed praised; this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, five hundred lay followers were established in the fruit of stream-entry.
This is the seventh story, the Story of the Lay Follower Atula.
8. The Story of the Group of Six.
"Agitation of the body": The Teacher delivered this teaching while residing at Veḷuvana concerning the group of six monks (*chabbaggiya*).

One day, while the Teacher was staying at Veḷuvana, he heard the loud clattering sound produced by those six monks as they walked back and forth on a stone slab, holding staffs in both hands and wearing wooden sandals.
“Ānanda, what is this sound? Having asked this and heard, “It is the clattering sound of the group-of-six monks walking while wearing sandals,” he laid down a training rule.
Then, saying, “A monk indeed ought to guard his body and so forth,” he taught the Dhamma and spoke these verses:
“One should guard against bodily anger and be restrained in body;
having abandoned bodily misconduct, one should practice good conduct with the body.
One should guard against verbal anger and be restrained in speech.”
Abandoning verbal misconduct, one should practice good conduct with speech.
One should guard against mental agitation and remain restrained in mind;
abandoning mental misconduct, one should practice good conduct with the mind.
“The wise are restrained in body, and likewise restrained in speech;
the wise are restrained in mind—they indeed are well-restrained.
In this context, “offense by body” refers to one who would guard against the threefold misconduct of the body. “Restrained in body” means [restrained] at the door of the body.
Having prevented the entry of misconduct, one should be restrained and keep the doors [of the senses] closed.

Since, however, by abandoning bodily misconduct and practicing bodily good conduct, one accomplishes both of these, it is therefore said: "Abandoning bodily misconduct, one should practice good conduct with the body.
The same method applies to the subsequent verses as well. "The wise who are restrained in body" refers to those...

The wise, by not committing killing and so forth with the body, by not committing false speech and so forth with speech, and by not giving rise to covetousness and so forth with the mind, are restrained;
the meaning is that they are well-restrained, well-guarded, well-protected, and have their doors well-shut in this world.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
The eighth case concerning the group of six.
The commentary on the Chapter on Anger is finished.
The seventeenth chapter.
18. The Chapter on Impurity (Malavagga). 1. The Story of the Son of a Cow-Slaughterer.
"Now he is like a withered leaf," the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain son of a cow-slaughterer.
It is said that in Sāvatthī there was a certain butcher who, having slaughtered oxen and taken the choice cuts of meat, would have them cooked;
then, sitting down with his wife and children, he would eat the meat and make his living by selling the rest for its price.
While he was thus performing the work of a butcher for fifty-five years, on one occasion, even as the Teacher was dwelling in the Dhura Monastery—
He did not give even a ladleful of rice gruel or boiled rice. He, however, would not eat a meal without meat.
One day, having sold some meat during the daytime, he gave a piece of meat to his wife to cook for himself and went to bathe.
Then a friend of his went to the house and said to the wife: "A little..."
“Give me some meat for sale; a guest has come to my house. “There is no meat for sale;
your friend sold his meat and has just now gone to bathe. “Do not say such a thing; if there is even a piece of meat, give it to me.
“There is nothing else except the meat left by your friend. He thought, “My friend’s...”
"There is no other meat besides that which was set aside for his sake; moreover, he does not eat without meat, so he will not give any.
Thinking this, she took the meat herself and departed.
When the cow-slaughterer had finished bathing and returned, she added her own cooked leaves to his meal as it was being served.
He asked, "Where is the meat? "There is none, sir," [the butcher] replied. "Did I not come and give you meat for cooking? [The butcher said:
"Your friend came and said, 'A guest has arrived; give me some meat to sell.
Even when I told him, 'I have no other meat than that set aside for your friend, and he does not eat without meat,' [he insisted]."
"By force he took that meat himself and went away. "I do not eat a meal without meat;
bring it," [the master said]. "What can be done? Eat, Master," [the servant replied].
He said, "I will not eat," and having had that meal removed, he took a knife and went to a bull standing in the back courtyard; approaching its mouth—
Having thrust in his hand and pulled out his tongue, he cut it at the root with a knife, took it away, and having roasted it over coals, placed it upon his meal;
sitting there, after eating one morsel of food, he put a piece of meat into his mouth.
At that very moment, his tongue was severed and fell into the bowl of rice. At that very moment—
He received a rebirth corresponding to his actions. That ox, too, having entered the house with blood streaming from its mouth, cried out as it moved about on its haunches.
At that time, the butcher’s son was standing nearby, watching his father. Then his mother—
He said: "Look, son, at this cow-slaughterer, who is wallowing on his knees in the middle of the house like an ox and crying out;
this suffering shall fall upon your head. Without even looking back at me, flee for your own safety!
Terrified by the fear of death, he paid homage to his mother and fled. Having fled, he went to Takkasilā.
The cow-slayer, too, like a bull, wandered about bellowing in the middle of the house and died, being reborn in the Avīci hell.
The bull also passed away. The cow-slayer’s son went to Takkasilā and mastered the craft of a goldsmith.
Then his teacher, while going to his village, said, "You should fashion such an ornament as this," and departed.

He too prepared such ornaments. Then his teacher, having returned and seen the ornaments, thought, "This boy is capable of making a living wherever he goes," and gave him his own daughter, who had reached marriageable age. He grew up with sons and daughters.
Later, when his sons reached maturity, they mastered their crafts and went to Sāvatthī, where they established a household life.
Having settled down and living there, they became faithful and confident. Their father also reached old age without having accomplished anything meritorious at Takkasilā.

Then his sons, thinking, "Our father is advanced in years," summoned him to their presence and, intending to give a gift for the sake of their father, invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha. On the following day, they...
Having seated the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, headed by the Buddha, within his home and having served them with great care, at the conclusion of the meal, they said to the Teacher:
“Venerable Sir, this ‘living-offering’ for our father has been given by us; please grant him your blessing.
The Teacher addressed him, saying: “Upāsaka, you are advanced in years, your body is fully ripened, like a withered leaf.”
"Since you have no provisions for the journey to the next world, establish your own firm footing; be wise, do not be foolish.
Speaking thus as an expression of appreciation, he recited these two verses:
"You are now like a withered leaf; ... [the rest of the verse]"
The messengers of Yama stand before you;
you stand at the gateway of departure,
and even provisions for the journey do not exist for you.
“Make an island for yourself;
strive quickly and be wise.
With defilements shaken off and free from blemish, [cross over the flood].”
"You shall ascend to the divine, noble plane.
In this context, "Now you are like a withered leaf" means, lay follower, you have now become like a withered leaf that has fallen to the ground after being severed.
"The messengers of Yama" refers to the envoys of Yama; however, this is said specifically with reference to death itself.
The meaning is that death has presented itself before you. "At the mouth of departure" means you stand at the point of decline and the point of non-increase.
"Provisions for the journey" means that, just as there are provisions such as rice for one going on a trip, you have no provisions of merit for going to the next world.
"Therefore, do it" means that you, like one whose ship has been wrecked in the ocean, [must now act] regarding what is called an island...
Establish for yourself a footing in wholesome states as if it were your own foundation. And while doing so, exert yourself quickly;
initiate energy with ever-increasing speed. By establishing a footing for your own wholesome kamma, become wise.
For he who performs wholesome deeds while still capable—before reaching the mouth of death—is called "wise"; be such as that, and do not be like a blind fool.
The meaning is as follows: By exerting energy in this way, you will reach the divine noble plane;

having removed the stains of lust and the other defilements, you will be one whose stains are cleansed (*niddhantamala*), who is without blemish (*anaṅgaṇa*) due to the absence of impurity, and thus free from defilement (*nikkilesa*). This is the sense of "you will attain the fivefold Pure Abode plane.
At the conclusion of the teaching, the lay follower was established in the fruit of stream-entry, and the Dhamma teaching was fruitful for those who were present.
On the following day as well, having invited the Teacher and given an offering, when the Teacher had finished his meal, they said at the time of the expression of thanksgiving:
"Venerable Sir, this too is the 'living-offering' for our father; please perform the thanksgiving for him alone.
As the Teacher was performing the thanksgiving for him, he spoke these two verses:
“Your youth has now been brought to an end,
and you have arrived in the presence of Yama;
there is no dwelling for you in between.”
And you have no provisions for the journey.
Therefore, make an island for yourself;
strive quickly and be wise.
"With impurities removed and free from blemish, you shall not again undergo birth and old age.
In this context, *upanītavayo*: *upa* is merely a particle; *nītavayo* means one whose youth has departed, one who has transcended youth—you are such.
The meaning is that you have now passed beyond the three stages of life and stand at the mouth of death.
"You have set out for the presence of Yama" means that you stand ready, prepared to go to the mouth of death.

"There is no lodging for you along the way" means that those who travel to the next world do not stay overnight on the road as people do when traveling a path, performing various tasks here and there.
For one going to the other world, it is not possible to say, "Please wait a few days; first I will give alms, first I will listen to the Dhamma," and so forth.
Rather, having passed away from here, one is simply reborn in the other world. It was with reference to this meaning that this was said.
As for the term "provisions for the journey" (*pātheyya*), although this has already been stated above, it is mentioned again for the sake of the lay follower (*upāsaka*).
It was spoken here by the Teacher as well for the purpose of strengthening [the understanding]. In this context, "birth and aging" includes illness and death as well.
While the path of the non-returner was explained by the preceding verses, the path of arahantship is explained here.
Even so, it is like when a king, having increased the size of a morsel of food to match the measure of his own mouth, offers it to his son.
Just as that youth took [the food] according to the size of his own mouth, even so, although the Teacher taught the Dhamma by way of the higher paths,
the lay follower— by virtue of his own underlying predisposition (*upanissaya*)— having already attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*),
reached the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmi-phala*) at the conclusion of this expression of thanks. The teaching of the Dhamma was also beneficial for the rest of the assembly.
The First Story of the Cow-Slaughterer’s Son.
2. The Story of a Certain Brahmin.
Regarding the teaching on the Dhamma beginning with "By gradual stages," the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain Brahmin.
It is said that one day, having set out early in the morning, he stood watching as the monks put on their robes at the place where the monks were dressing. Now, that spot was overgrown with grass.
As one monk was putting on his robe, the hem of the robe brushed against the grass and became dampened by drops of dew. The brahmin [thought]: "This..."
“It is proper to make this spot free of greenery. On the following day, taking a hoe, he went there, cleared the ground, and made it level like a threshing floor.

On the next day as well, having come to that place, he saw the corner of one bhikkhu’s robe fall to the ground and roll in the dust while the monks were putting on their robes; seeing this, [he thought], “I should scatter sand here.”
Thinking, "It is appropriate," he brought sand and scattered it.
Then one day, before the meal, when the heat was fierce, seeing the sweat pouring from the bodies of the monks as they put on their robes,
he thought, "It is appropriate for me to have a pavilion built here," and [he had] a pavilion [constructed].
He had it built. On the following day, at dawn, it rained; there was a heavy downpour. Even then, the brahmin remained standing, watching the monks;

seeing the monks with their robes soaked, he thought, "It is fitting for me to have a hall built here," and having had the hall built, he thought, "Now I shall perform a hall-consecration ceremony," and [invited] the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha.

Having invited them and having had the bhikkhus seated both inside and outside, at the conclusion of the meal, he took the Teacher’s bowl for the purpose of giving a blessing of thanksgiving, saying from the beginning:

"Venerable Sir, while I was standing here observing the bhikkhus at the time they were putting on their robes, seeing this and that, I caused this and that to be done. Thus he related everything in its entirety.

He reported the matter. Having heard his words, the Teacher said, "Brāhmaṇa, those called wise, performing even a little wholesome deed at every moment, gradually remove their own impurities of unwholesomeness," and spoke this verse:
"Gradually, the wise man, little by little, at every moment..."
"Just as a smith blows away the impurities from silver, so should one blow away one's own impurities.
In this context, "gradually" means in successive order. "Wise" means endowed with the wisdom born of the essence of the Dhamma (*dhammoja*).
"At every moment" means performing wholesome deeds at every opportunity. "Just as a smith [cleans] silver" means just as a goldsmith [cleans it] in a single instance.
Just as one cannot fashion a variety of ornaments from gold merely by heating it, crushing it, and removing its dross once;

but by heating and crushing it again and again, one removes the dross and can then create many kinds of ornaments—exactly so, a wise person performing wholesome deeds again and again should blow away the dross of their own lust and other defilements. Thus, with dross blown away...
The meaning is that he becomes free from defilement.
At the conclusion of the teaching, the brahmin was established in the fruit of stream-entry, and the Dhamma instruction was beneficial for the great multitude as well.
This is the second story concerning a certain brahmin.
3. The Story of the Elder Tissa While residing at the Jeta Grove, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma instruction concerning the monk named the Elder Tissa.
It is said that a certain son of a respectable family living in Sāvatthī went forth, and having received full ordination, he became known as the Elder Tissa.
Later on, having entered the rains retreat in a village monastery, he obtained a thick cloth eight cubits long.
When the rains were over and he had performed the *pavāraṇā* ceremony, he took it and went to place it in his sister’s hands.
She thought, "This cloth is not suitable for my brother," so she cut it with a sharp knife, tore it into pieces, pounded it in a mortar, and beat it into a paste.
Having wound fine thread and spun it, she had a robe woven.
The Elder, having prepared both the thread and the needles and gathered the young novice-monks who were robe-makers, went to his sister’s presence and said, "Give me that robe-cloth;
I shall have a robe made. She brought out a nine-cubit robe-cloth for her younger brother.
placed it in his hand. Having taken it, he spread it out and examined it, saying, "My cloth was thick and eight cubits long;
this is fine and nine cubits long. This is not my cloth; it is yours. I have no need for this; give me that very one instead.
"Venerable sir, this is indeed yours; please take it. But he did not wish to accept it. Then [the other said] to him:
Having reported everything he had done himself, he said, "Venerable sir, this is yours alone; please take it," and gave it to him.
He took it, went to the monastery, and began the work on the robe.
Then his sister prepared rice porridge, food, and other provisions for those making the robe. On the day the robe was finished—
However, he showed him excessive honor. Looking at his robe, the monk felt a surge of affection for it and thought, "I shall wear this tomorrow.

He folded it and placed it on the robe-rack; then, unable to digest the food he had eaten that night, he died and was reborn as a louse within that very robe. When his sister heard of his death, she...

As she rolled at the feet of the bhikkhus, she wept. After the bhikkhus had performed the funeral rites for her body, because there was no one to look after her while she was ill, the robe fell to the Saṅgha itself. Thinking, "We shall divide it," they had that robe brought out.
The louse, crying out, "They are plundering what belongs to me! ran hither and thither. The Teacher was in the Fragrant Chamber.
While sitting, having heard that sound with his divine ear-element, he said, "Ānanda, tell Tissa to set aside his robe for seven days without distributing it.
The Elder did accordingly. She too, having passed away on the seventh day, was reborn in the Tusita celestial mansion.
On the eighth day, the Teacher said, "Distribute and take Tissa's robe."

He gave the command. The bhikkhus did accordingly. In the Dhamma Hall, the bhikkhus raised this discussion: "Why has the Teacher allowed Tissa’s robe to be kept for seven days and then taken on the eighth day? The Teacher arrived and asked, "What is it that you are discussing? [They told him. The Teacher said, "Bhikkhus, if one were to take a robe immediately upon its being offered, there would be no opportunity to give it away to others. He then related the story of the past. At that time, there was a king named Mahāpanāda who ruled over a kingdom called Mahāpanāda. He had a son named Cūḷapanāda. One day, King Mahāpanāda went out hunting with his retinue. While wandering about, he saw a deer and pursued it. Having lost sight of the deer, he entered a dense forest. There, he saw a young man sitting at the foot of a tree. The king approached him and asked, "Young man, have you seen a deer pass by here? "Great King, I have not seen a deer; however, I see you, Great King. Why do you seek the deer? I shall show you the way. "Very well," the king replied, and they set out together. After traveling some distance, the young man pointed out a place where the deer had passed and said, "Great King, the deer went this way. The king followed that path and eventually caught the deer. As he was returning home with the deer, he saw a mango grove along the way. He thought, "I will eat the mangoes first and then go home. He ate the mangoes and then proceeded. When he reached the gate of the city, he thought, "If I enter the city now, the people will ask me, 'Where did you get this deer? and I shall have to tell them. It would be better to go directly to my palace. He went straight to the palace. His son, Cūḷapanāda, seeing his father arrive, asked, "Father, where have you been? "Son, I went hunting. "Father, why have you returned empty-handed? "Son, I caught a deer, but I ate some mangoes along the way and forgot to bring it back. "Father, please go and fetch the deer. The father went and brought the deer. The son, having received the deer, thought, "I will cook the meat myself and eat it. He prepared the meat himself and ate it. The father asked, "Son, did you cook the meat yourself? "Yes, Father. "Son, you are skilled in cooking; you should cook it for me as well. "Father, I am indeed skilled in cooking, but I have already eaten my fill. "Son, from today onwards, you must cook for me every day. "Father, I shall do so. From that day forth, the son cooked for his father daily. One day, while the son was cooking, he thought, "I will prepare a special dish for my father today. He prepared a dish of rice mixed with honey and ghee and presented it to his father. The father ate it and found it delicious. He asked, "Son, what is this? "Father, it is rice mixed with honey and ghee. "Son, prepare this for me every day. "Father, I shall do so. From then on, the son prepared that dish daily. One day, the son thought, "I will prepare a more excellent dish for my father today. He prepared a dish of rice mixed with sugar and ghee and presented it to his father. The father ate it and found it even more delicious than before. He asked, "Son, what is this? "Father, it is rice mixed with sugar and ghee. "Son, prepare this for me every day. "Father, I shall do so. From then on, the son prepared that dish daily. One day, the son thought, "I will prepare a most excellent dish for my father today. He prepared a dish of rice mixed with milk and ghee and presented it to his father. The father ate it and found it far more delicious than the previous ones. He asked, "Son, what is this? "Father, it is rice mixed with milk and ghee. "Son, prepare this for me every day. "Father, I shall do so. From then on, the son prepared that dish daily. One day, the son thought, "I will prepare a dish even more excellent than this for my father today. He prepared a dish of rice mixed with curd and ghee and presented it to his father. The father ate it and found it far more delicious than the previous ones. He asked, "Son, what is this? "Father, it is rice mixed with curd and ghee. "Son, prepare this for me every day. "Father, I shall do so. From then on, the son prepared that dish daily. One day, the son thought, "I will prepare a dish even more excellent than this for my father today. He prepared a dish of rice mixed with fresh butter and ghee and presented it to his father. The father ate it and found it far more delicious than the previous ones. He asked, "Son, what is this? "Father, it is rice mixed with fresh butter and ghee. "Son, prepare this for me every day. "Father, I shall do so. From then on, the son prepared that dish daily. One day, the son thought, "I will prepare a dish even more excellent than this for my father today. He prepared a dish of rice mixed with oil and ghee and presented it to his father. The father ate it and found it far more delicious than the previous ones. He asked, "Son, what is this? "Father, it is rice mixed with oil and ghee. "Son, prepare this for me every day. "Father, I shall do so. From then on, the son prepared that dish daily. One day, the son thought, "I will prepare a dish even more excellent than this for my father today. He prepared a dish of rice mixed with various spices and ghee and presented it to his father. The father ate it and found it far more delicious than the previous ones. He asked, "Son, what is this? "Father, it is rice mixed with various spices and ghee. "Son, prepare this for me every day. "Father, I shall do so. From then on, the son prepared that dish daily. One day, the son thought, "I will prepare a dish even more excellent than this for my father today. He prepared a dish of rice mixed with the juice of various fruits and ghee and presented it to his father. The father ate it and found it far more delicious than the previous ones. He asked, "Son, what is this? "Father, it is rice mixed with the juice of various fruits and ghee. "Son, prepare this for me every day. "Father, I shall do so. From then on, the son prepared that dish daily. One day, the son thought, "I will prepare a dish even more excellent than this for my father today. He prepared a dish of rice mixed with the essence of various medicinal herbs and ghee and presented it to his father. The father ate it and found it far more delicious than the previous ones. He asked, "Son, what is this? "Father, it is rice mixed with the essence of various medicinal herbs and ghee. "Son, prepare this for me every day. "Father, I shall do so. From then on, the son prepared that dish daily. One day, the son thought, "I will prepare a dish even more excellent than this for my father today. He prepared a dish of rice mixed with the essence of various precious substances and ghee and presented it to his father. The father ate it and found it far more delicious than the previous ones. He asked, "Son, what is this? "Father, it is rice mixed with the essence of various precious substances and ghee. "Son, prepare this for me every day. "Father, I shall do so. From then on, the son prepared that dish daily. One day, the son thought, "I will prepare a dish even more excellent than this for my father today. He prepared a dish of rice mixed with the essence of all flavors and ghee and presented it to his father. The father ate it and found it far more delicious than the previous ones. He asked, "Son, what is this? "Father, it is rice mixed with the essence of all flavors and ghee. "Son, prepare this for me every day. "Father, I shall do so. From then on, the son prepared that dish daily. One day, the son thought, "I will prepare a dish even more excellent than this for my father today. He prepared a dish of rice mixed with the essence of the nectar of immortality and ghee and presented it to his father. The father ate it and found it far more delicious than the previous ones. He asked, "Son, what is this? "Father, it is rice mixed with the essence of the nectar of immortality and ghee. "Son, prepare this for me every day. "Father, I shall do so. From then on, the son prepared that dish daily. One day, the son thought, "I will prepare a dish even more excellent than this for my father today. He prepared a dish of rice mixed with the essence of the supreme flavor and ghee and presented it to his father. The father ate it and found it far more delicious than the previous ones. He
“Monks, for what discussion are you sitting together now? he asked.
When they replied, “For this one,” he said, “Monks, three lice were born from your own robes.
While you were dividing [the cloth], they cried out, ‘They are plundering what belongs to me! and ran hither and thither. While you were taking the robe—”
"Having harbored malice toward you, she was reborn in hell; it was for that reason that I had her lay aside her robe.
But now she has been reborn in a Tusita mansion; therefore, I have permitted you to take the robe," he said.
When they replied again, "Venerable sir, this thing called craving is indeed heavy," he said, "Yes, monks, for these beings..."

“Craving is indeed heavy. Just as rust arises from iron and consumes that very iron, destroying it and rendering it useless, even so this craving, having arisen within these beings, causes those beings to be reborn in the hells and other realms, bringing them to ruin.
Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“Just as rust born from iron consumes that very iron for its own destruction,
so too does one who behaves with excessive license [consume himself].”
"Those deeds lead one to an evil destination.
In this context, "arisen from iron" means arisen from iron. "Having risen from that" means having emerged from that. "One who acts with excessive laxity":
here, "cleansing" (*dhonā*) refers to the wisdom that uses the four requisites after reflecting, "This is for this purpose."
One who wanders having transgressed that limit is called "one who wanders too far. This is what is meant:

just as rust arises from iron and, once arisen from it, consumes that very iron, even so, for one who uses the four requisites without reflecting, those actions—because they reside within him and are his own property—lead that person who wanders too far to a state of misery.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the third story, the account of the Elder Tissa.
4. The Story of the Elder Lāludāyi.
"Non-recitation is a defilement"—this teaching on the Dhamma was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the Elder Lāludāyi.
It is said that in Sāvatthī there lived about fifty million noble disciples (ariyasāvaka) and about two million worldlings (puthujjana).
Among them, after the noble disciples had given alms before the meal, they would afterwards give ghee, oil, honey, molasses, clothing, and so forth.
Having taken [the alms-food], they went to the monastery and listened to the Dhamma discourse.
After hearing the Dhamma, at the time of departure, they spoke in praise of the virtues of Sāriputta and Moggallāna.
Upon hearing their talk, the Elder Udāyī said, "If you speak thus after merely hearing the Dhamma from them, what indeed will you not say after hearing my own Dhamma discourse? The people—
Having heard his words, they thought, "This man will surely be a preacher of the Dhamma; it is fitting for us to hear the Dhamma from him as well.

On one day, having requested the Elder, they gave an offering to the Saṅgha, saying, "Venerable sir, today is our day for hearing the Dhamma," and added, "Venerable sir, may you preach the Dhamma to us during the day."
He also consented to them.

When they arrived at the time for hearing the Dhamma and said, "Venerable sir, please preach the Dhamma to us," the Elder Lāludāyi sat down on his seat, took up a fan, and while fanning himself, failed to utter even a single verse of the Dhamma; instead, he said, "I shall recite [the scriptures] aloud..."
“I shall speak; let another deliver a discourse on the Dhamma,” he said, and then descended from his seat.

They had another deliver a discourse on the Dhamma, and then they raised him back onto the seat for the purpose of reciting the *sara-bhañña*. Again, seeing nothing at all, he said, “I shall speak by night;
let another recite the *sara-bhañña*,” and he descended from his seat. They had another recite the *sara-bhañña*, and then—
They brought the Elder there at night. Seeing nothing at all during the night, he said, "I shall speak at dawn;
let someone else speak during the night," and then descended. They had another speak during the night, and again at dawn they brought him back.
He saw nothing at all once more. The great crowd, seizing clods of earth, sticks, and other weapons, cried out, "You blind fool! You [who oppose] Sāriputta and Moggallāna..."
Having threatened him, saying, "When your own praises were being told, you spoke thus and so; why do you not speak now?", he pursued him as he fled.
While fleeing, he fell into a certain latrine.
The great multitude raised a clamor: "Today Lāḷudāyin has fallen into a latrine because of his talk of the virtues of Sāriputta and Moggallāna!"
While the assembly was in progress, he grew impatient and, proclaiming his own status as a preacher of the Dhamma, received honor from the people.
When they said, "Let us hear the Dhamma," he sat upon the seat four times;

however, seeing nothing fit to be spoken, he [was struck] with clods of earth, sticks, and other things, [people saying], "You have entered into a rivalry with our masters, the elder Sāriputta and Moggallāna!"
“Having seized him and threatened him, as he was prattling on, he fell into the privy.
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, about what talk are you gathered here now? When they replied, “About this very thing,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, he was submerged in a pit of filth. Having said this, he related the past:
“I am four-footed, my friend, and you too, my friend, are four-footed.
Come, my friend, turn back; why do you flee in fear?
You are covered in filthy, putrid hair; you are foul-smelling, you pig!”
“If you wish to fight, friend, I shall grant you victory.
Having related this Jātaka in detail, he said: “At that time, Sāriputta was the lion and Lāḷudāyī was the boar.
Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher said: “Monks, only a very small amount of Dhamma was mastered by Lāḷudāyī.”
"But he did not even perform recitation; having mastered some portion of the scriptures, failing to recite them is indeed a defilement," and having said this, he spoke this verse:
"Recitation-less are the mantras defiled; neglectful are households defiled."
“Laziness is the stain of beauty; negligence is the stain of one who guards.

In this context, regarding the phrase “the stains of non-recitation,” it is said that “the mantras have non-recitation as their stain” because any sacred learning or craft perishes, or does not constantly remain present, for one who does not recite or apply oneself to it. Because...
However, for one living in the household life, if they do not rise early and attend to such matters as the repair of what is worn out, the house will fall into ruin;
therefore it is said, "Houses have non-exertion as their defilement.
Because the body of either a householder or a renunciant who, through laziness, fails to attend to the care of the physical frame or the maintenance of requisites—
He becomes ugly; therefore it is said, "Laziness is the stain of beauty.

Because when one is guarding cattle—whether through negligence while sleeping or while playing—those cattle may meet with destruction by leaping into improper fords and the like, or by the affliction of wild beasts, thieves, and so forth, or by descending into others' rice fields and eating [the crops]; and he himself [incurs] punishment...
Or he may encounter abuse; or else, when one who has gone forth fails to guard the six doors through negligence, the defilements descend upon him and cause him to fall away from the Dispensation.
Therefore it is said: "Negligence is the stain for one who guards.
The meaning is that it is called a "stain" because, by bringing about his ruin, it occupies the position of a stain.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the fourth story, the account of the Elder Lāludāyi.
5. The account of a certain son of good family.
The Teacher, while dwelling in Veḷuvana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning a certain son of good family.
It is said that they brought him a young woman from a family of similar status. From the day she was brought home, she became unchaste.
That son of good family, ashamed because of her misconduct and unable to appear before anyone, [remained in seclusion].
Having discontinued his attendance upon the Buddha and other duties, after a few days had passed, he approached the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down to one side.
When the Teacher asked him, "Lay follower, why are you not seen?", he related the matter to him.
Then the Teacher said to him, "Lay follower, in the past too I have said that women are like rivers and the like; therein, by a wise man, anger..."
"It was said that it should not be done, yet you did not perceive this because it was concealed by existence. Having said this, when requested by him, [the Buddha] spoke:
"Just as a river, a road, a tavern, an assembly hall, and a brothel—so too are women of the world; for them, no limit exists."
Having related the Jātaka in detail, he said: “Lay follower, for a woman, unchastity is a stain; for one giving a gift, stinginess is a stain;
in this world and the next, unwholesome action is a stain in the sense that it destroys beings; but ignorance is the supreme stain among all stains.
Having said this, he spoke these verses:
“Lack of generosity is the stain of a woman, and stinginess is the stain of one who gives.
Indeed, evil states are stains, both in this world and in the next.
But more stained than those stains is ignorance—the supreme stain.”
"Having abandoned this stain, O bhikkhus, be stainless.
In this context, "misconduct" (duccarita) refers to adultery. For even a husband will cast out from the house a woman who commits adultery;
even if she has gone to her parents' home, they will expel her, saying, "She has become disrespectful toward the family; she is not even to be looked upon with the eyes."
Wandering about without a protector, she encounters great suffering; therefore, her misconduct is called "dirt.

"Of the giver" means of the donor. For one who, at the time of weeding the field, thinks, "When this field is ready, I will give rice-gruel tickets and other gifts," yet when the crop has been harvested, stinginess arises and prevents the thought of generosity—such a person, through that stinginess...
When the mind of generosity does not grow, one does not obtain the three kinds of excellence—the excellence of human status, the excellence of divine status, and the excellence of Nibbāna.
Therefore it is said: “Miserliness is the stain for one who gives. The same principle applies to the remaining [vices] as well.
Furthermore, unwholesome states (pāpakā dhammā) are indeed a stain both in this world and in the world beyond.
"Than that" means than the impurity previously mentioned. "More impure" means: "I shall tell you of an even greater impurity.
Ignorance—that is, the eightfold lack of knowledge—is the supreme impurity. "Having abandoned it" means: "O monks, having cast off this impurity, you shall become stainless."
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the fifth story, concerning a certain son of good family. 6.
The Story of Cūḷasāri.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, delivered this teaching on the Dhamma concerning a certain co-resident disciple of the Elder Sāriputta named Cūḷasāri.
It is said that one day, having performed medical work and obtained excellent food, he was setting out with it when he saw the Elder on the road.
He said, "Venerable sir, this was obtained by me through performing medical work; you should not go elsewhere for such [food]."
“You will not obtain food; eat this. By performing medical work for you, I shall bring such food as this for you at all times,” he said.
Having heard his words, the Elder departed in silence.
The monks went to the monastery and reported the matter to the Teacher. The Teacher said, “Monks, one who is shameless is indeed impudent.”
“Having become like a crow and persisting in the twenty-one kinds of improper search, one lives happily; but one endowed with moral shame and dread of blame lives in suffering.
Having said this, he spoke these verses:
“Easy to live is life for one who is shameless, Who is as bold as a crow and a thief;”
Life is lived by one who is impudent, shameless, and defiled.
But it is hard to live for one who possesses a sense of shame, who constantly seeks purity,
who is not indolent or impudent, who lives a pure life, and who sees clearly.
In this context, "by one who is shameless" means by one whose sense of shame (*hiri*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*) have been severed.

For such a person, having declared even one who is not his mother to be "my mother," and likewise those who are not his father and so forth to be "my father" and so on, it is possible to live comfortably by resorting to the twenty-one kinds of improper search (*an-esanā*).
"By one as bold as a crow" means like a crow that is brazen; for just as a bold crow [enters] into noble families [for] rice-gruel and so forth...
Just as one wishing to steal might sit against a wall or similar place, and having perceived that he is being watched,
acts as if not looking, as if preoccupied with something else, and as if sleeping; and then, observing the negligence of the people, pounces upon them and,
even while they are crying out "Sūsū!", seizes a mouthful from the vessel and flees— in the same way, a person devoid of moral shame (*ahirikapuggala*) behaves toward the monks.
Having entered the village together with him, he designates the places for rice gruel, solid food, and so forth.
There, the monks, having wandered for alms and taken what is sufficient for their sustenance, go to the sitting hall;

they drink the gruel while reflecting on it, attend to their meditation subject, recite their lessons, and sweep the sitting hall. But he, instead of doing these things, heads straight toward the village.

For even while being looked upon by the monks with the words, "Look at this man," he acted as if not looking, as if distracted, as if sleeping, or as if fastening his belt or adjusting his robe; saying,
"I have such-and-such business to attend to," he rose from his seat, entered the village, and [went] early in the morning to whichever house had been designated.
Having approached the house, he would close the door slightly among the household members, sit at the entrance, and even while they were weeping, he would push open the door with one hand and enter.
Then, seeing him, they would—though unwillingly—seat him on a seat and give him whatever was available, such as rice-gruel and other foods.
Having eaten as much as he required, he would take the remainder in his bowl and depart.
This is what is called a "crow-hero. One lives well with such a lack of shame (*ahirika*).

He is a "destroyer" (*dhaṃsin*) because he destroys the virtues of others by saying things such as, "What, are we not of few desires? when others are saying, "The Elder named so-and-so is of few desires," and so forth.
Having heard such words from him, [others think], "He too possesses virtues such as fewness of desires..."
Thinking, "He is engaged [in this task]," people believe they should give him gifts.
However, from that point on, being unable to satisfy the minds of wise men, he falls away even from that gain. Thus, a person who is a spendthrift destroys the gain of both himself and others.
"Pakkhandinā" means by one who acts with zeal. Showing others' duties as if they were his own, he would rise early,
perform the duties such as those in the shrine courtyard (*cetiyāṅgaṇa*) among the monks, sit for a short while reflecting on his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*),

and then, when the monks rose and entered the village, he would wash his face and attend to himself by putting on the yellow saffron robes (*paṇḍukāsāva*), applying collyrium to his eyes, and anointing his head.
Having adorned himself, as if sweeping, he gave two or three strokes with the broom and stood facing the gateway.
Early in the morning, people arrived thinking, "We shall pay homage to the Cetiya; we shall perform flower offerings.
Seeing him, they said, "This monastery receives its maintenance because of this youth; do not neglect him."
They think it should be given to him. Even for one who is thus impudent (*pakkhandin*), life is easy to live.
"By one who is shameless" (*pagabbhena*) means by one endowed with bodily shamelessness and so forth. "A defiled life":
for a person living by maintaining such a livelihood, life becomes defiled; the meaning is that this is a miserable life, nothing but evil.
"By one possessed of moral shame" means by a person endowed with moral shame (*hirī*) and dread of wrongdoing (*ottappa*).

For such a person—refraining from calling those who are not his mother and so forth "my mother," and loathing unrighteous requisites as if they were excrement—seeks [requisites] in accordance with the Dhamma and justice, wandering for alms from house to house and maintaining his life;
thus, the meaning is that he leads a coarse life. "Seeking what is pure" means... pure things.
By one investigating bodily actions and so forth. "Unattached" means not clinging to the means of livelihood. "Seeing with a pure livelihood":

for such a person is indeed called one of pure livelihood. By such a person of pure livelihood, seeing that very pure livelihood as essential, it is difficult to live by way of a coarse life; this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the sixth story, the Story of Cūḷasāri. 7.
The Story of the Five Lay Disciples.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning five lay followers.
Among them, one observed only the training precept of abstaining from taking life, while the others observed the remaining ones.
One day, having fallen into a dispute, saying, "I am doing what is difficult; I am guarding what is difficult," they went into the presence of the Teacher, paid homage, and [said]:
They reported this matter to the Teacher. Having heard their words, the Teacher said, "Not even a single precept should be treated as minor;
all are difficult to guard," and he spoke these verses:
"He who takes the life of a living being, and speaks falsehood;..."
In this world, he takes what is not given and goes unto another’s wife.
That man who is devoted to the drinking of fermented liquor and spirits—
even in this very world, he digs up his own roots.
“Know this, O man: you are of evil character and unrestrained.
Let not greed and unrighteousness subject you for long to suffering.
In that context, “he who takes life” refers to one who, by even a single means among the six methods such as with one’s own hand, [deprives] another of life.
He cuts off the life-faculty. Regarding "false speech": he utters false speech that destroys the welfare of others.
Regarding "he takes what is not given in the world": in this world of beings, by even a single act of theft among such practices as robbery, he takes what is possessed by another.
Regarding "and he goes to another's wife": without offending against the goods protected and guarded by another, he engages in an illicit path.
He practices. "The drinking of fermented liquor and spirits" means the drinking of both *surā* and *meraya* by anyone whatsoever.
"Is devoted to" means he indulges in it and cultivates it habitually. "Digs up the root" means: let alone the next world;
even in this very world, whatever root—such as fields, land, and so forth—he might have used to establish himself, that too he either abandons or gives away for the sake of *sura*.
Drinking [the water] he digs up his own root; he wanders about helpless and miserable.
"O sir," she says, addressing a person who commits the five types of misconduct. "Of evil nature" means those of base character. "Unrestrained" means devoid of bodily restraint and so forth.
There is also the reading *acetasā*, which means "without mindfulness. "Greed and unrighteousness" refers to both greed and hatred; for both of these are indeed unwholesome.
"They torment for a long time" means that for a long duration these phenomena might not torment or crush him for the sake of the sufferings of hell and so forth.
At the conclusion of the teaching, those five lay followers were established in the fruit of stream-entry; thus the teaching of the Dhamma was fruitful for those who had gathered.
The Seventh Story of the Lay Disciple:
The Story of the Boy Tissa.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, "He gives and he enjoys," concerning the boy named Tissa.
It is said that he wandered about disparaging the gifts given by five crores of noble disciples, such as the householder Anāthapiṇḍika and the laywoman Visākhā;
indeed, even a peerless gift was subject to his censure. At various almsgivings, if he received something cool, he would disparage it, saying, "It is cold!
and if he received something hot, he would disparage it, saying, "It is hot! Even when people gave little, he would say, "Why do these people give so little?"
When someone gave little, he criticized them, saying: "I suppose there is no room to store things in these people's houses;
surely they should give at least enough for the monks' sustenance—why do they distribute so much rice-gruel and food to no purpose?
But when it concerned his own relatives, he would say: "Oh, how wonderful! My relatives' house is [a place] for those who come from the four directions..."
Having said, "It is a well for the monks," and so forth, he uttered words of praise. He, however, was the son of a gatekeeper;
while wandering through the countryside with carpenters, he arrived at Sāvatthī and went forth into homelessness.
Then, seeing him thus disparaging the gifts and other offerings of people, the bhikkhus thought, "We shall take him under our care."
Having reflected thus, they asked, "Friend, where do your relatives live?

Upon hearing that they lived in a certain village, they sent several young novices there. Having arrived, the villagers seated them in the assembly hall and, after offering them hospitality, they asked:
"There is a young novice named Tissa who has gone forth after leaving this village. Which..."
"Are they his kinsmen? The people thought, "There is no child here who has gone forth after leaving his family home; what indeed are these people saying?
They said, "Venerable sir, we have heard that a gatekeeper’s son, having wandered about with carpenters, went forth;
it is likely they are speaking of him. The young bhikkhus [spoke] to Tissa.

There, having learned of the absence of his lord and kinsmen, he went to Sāvatthī and reported the matter to the monks, saying, "Venerable sirs, Tissa wanders about lamenting for no reason at all. The monks, in turn, reported this to the Tathāgata.
The Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that he wanders about boasting; in the past, too, he was a boaster. Having spoken thus, at the request of the monks, he brought up a story of the past:
“Though he may boast much, having gone to another country, he might come back and cause ruin;
enjoy your wealth, O Kaṭāha!”—Having related this Kaṭāha Jātaka in detail, [the Buddha said]:
“Monks, whatever person, by others, whether for little or for much...”

"Whether it be coarse or refined, whether it is given after having first given to others or not given to oneself, one who is thus dejected will not give rise to jhāna, insight, or the paths and fruits.
Having said this, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke these verses:
"The people indeed give according to their faith, according to their confidence;..."
In this regard, he who is dejected regarding the food and drink of others does not attain concentration by day or by night.
But for one in whom this has been utterly cut off, uprooted, and destroyed at the root—
“Indeed, whether by day or by night, he attains concentration.
In this context, “he gives according to his faith” means that when a person gives anything—whether coarse or refined—they give precisely in accordance with their own faith.
“According to his confidence” refers to whichever [monk] among the elders, novices, or others...
Confidence arises; giving to such a person, one gives exactly according to their confidence, in accordance with one's own state of faith.
In that regard—meaning in the context of giving to another—one falls into a state of dejection, thinking, "I have received little," or "I have received coarse [food].
As for "concentration": that person, whether by day or by night, [attains it] either through access or absorption, or by way of the path and its fruition.

He does not attain concentration. "In whom this exists" means: in that person for whom this unwholesome state, known as agitation (*maṅkubhāva*) in certain situations, has been cut off and destroyed at the root by the knowledge of the path of Arahatship, he attains the aforementioned kind of concentration; such is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the eighth story, the Story of the Young Man Tissa. 9.
The Story of the Five Lay Disciples.
"There is no fire like lust"—this teaching on the Dhamma was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning five lay followers.
It is said that these men, desiring to hear the Dhamma, went to the monastery, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down to one side.

For Buddhas do not think, "This one is a khattiya, this one is a brahmin, this one is wealthy, this one is poor; having performed a grand service for this one, I shall teach him the Dhamma... [and so forth].

The thought does not arise in him, "I shall teach this, not that. When teaching the Dhamma concerning anything whatsoever, he teaches placing reverence for the Dhamma foremost, as if pouring down the celestial Ganges.
Now, among those sitting in the presence of the Tathāgata who was teaching in this manner, one sat and fell asleep;
another sat scratching the ground with his finger; another...
One sat fanning a tree; another sat looking up at the sky; but one listened to the Dhamma with great care.
As the Elder Ānanda was fanning the Teacher, he observed their demeanor and said to the Teacher:
"Venerable Sir, you preach the Dhamma to these people as if thundering like a great rain-cloud; yet they do not even pay attention to you."
"While they were preaching the Dhamma, these [beings] sat there doing this and that. "Ānanda, do you not know who these are?

"Yes, venerable sir, I do not know. "For among them, he who sits here sleeping has been reborn five hundred times in the womb of a snake, and having placed his head upon their coils, he has slept; even now, he is not yet satiated with sleep."
"No, it does not; my voice does not enter his ear. "But, venerable sir, do you speak in succession, or rather at intervals?
"Ānanda, for one who arises at intervals—sometimes as a human, sometimes as a deva, and sometimes as a nāga—it is impossible, even with omniscient knowledge, to describe all his successive births."
To determine this: in succession, he has been reborn five hundred times in the womb of a nāga, and even while sleeping, he remains completely overcome by sleep.
Even that man sitting there scratching the ground with his finger was reborn five hundred times in the womb of an ant, digging the earth;
even now, as he digs the earth, he does not hear my voice. This [man] [climbed] the tree...
Even the man who was sitting there shaking [the tree] was reborn in succession for five hundred births in the womb of a monkey;
even now, by virtue of his former habit, he continues to shake the tree, yet my voice does not reach his ear.
That man who was sitting looking up at the sky was also reborn for five hundred births as a reciter of the *nakkhatta* (astral) texts; even now—
Due to his former habit, even today he gazes only into the sky, and my voice does not enter his ear.

As for that man sitting there listening to the Dhamma with such care, he was born in succession through five hundred births as a Brahmin who had mastered the three Vedas and was a reciter of the mantras; even now, he listens attentively as if he were once again rehearsing those mantras.
“Venerable sir, your teaching of the Dhamma cuts through the outer skin and so forth, right down to the marrow of the bone;
why is it that these people do not listen attentively even when you are teaching them the Dhamma?
“Ānanda, I think you have the notion that my Dhamma is easy to hear. “But what, venerable sir, is difficult to hear? “Yes, Ānanda.”
“Why is that, Bhante? “Ānanda, the words ‘Buddha,’ ‘Dhamma,’ or ‘Saṅgha’ have never been heard by these beings even in many hundreds of thousands of millions of eons.
Because these beings, unable to hear this Dhamma, have come through the beginningless cycle of existence hearing only various kinds of worldly talk; therefore—”
“They wander about singing and dancing at places such as drinking parties and pleasure groves; they are unable to listen to the Dhamma.
“But on account of what, Bhante, are they unable to do so?
Then the Teacher said to him, “Ānanda, it is on account of lust, on account of hatred, on account of delusion, and on account of craving.”
They are unable [to do so]. There is no fire like the fire of lust; it burns beings, leaving not even ashes behind.
Although the fire that destroys an eon, arising by means of the appearance of the seven suns, also burns the world without leaving anything remaining, that fire burns only at certain times.
For the fire of lust, however, there is no time when it does not burn.
"Therefore, there is no fire equal to passion, no snare equal to hatred, no net equal to delusion, and no river equal to craving.
Having said this, he spoke this verse:
"There is no fire equal to passion, no snare equal to hatred;"
“There is no snare equal to delusion; there is no river equal to craving.
In this context, “no fire equal to lust” means that among smoke and the like, there is no fire equal to lust that burns by arising within [the heart] itself without showing anything outwardly.
“No seizure equal to hatred” means that among the seizures of *yakkhas*, *gahas*, pythons, crocodiles, and so forth, [there is none equal to hatred] in a single instance...
While they are able to seize only their own bodies, the seizing of hatred seizes everything without exception; thus, there is no seizure equal to hatred.
Furthermore, there is no net equal to delusion in the sense of its binding and entangling. Regarding "equal to craving":
among rivers such as the Ganges, one can perceive times when they are full, times when they are low, and times when they are dry.
But for craving, there is neither a time of fullness nor a time of emptiness; it is always perceived as deficient.
Thus, in the sense of being impossible to fill, there is no river equal to craving—this is the meaning.

At the conclusion of the teaching, the lay follower who had listened to the Dhamma with reverence was established in the fruit of stream-entry, and the teaching of the Dhamma was fruitful for all those who were present.
The ninth story of the lay follower (Upāsaka-vatthu).
10. The Story of the Merchant Meṇḍaka.
The Teacher related this Dhamma instruction, beginning with the words "Easy to see is a fault," while residing at Jātiyāvana near the city of Bhaddiya, concerning the merchant Meṇḍaka.
It is said that while the Teacher was wandering on tour among the Aṅguttarāpas, he perceived the supporting conditions for stream-entry in Meṇḍaka the merchant,
his wife Candapadumā, his son Dhanañjaya the merchant, his daughter-in-law Sumanadevī, his granddaughter Visākhā,
and his slave Puṇṇa; having seen this, he went to the city of Bhaddiya.
He dwelt in the Jātiyāvana monastery. The merchant Meṇḍaka heard of the Teacher’s arrival.

But why was this merchant named Meṇḍaka? It is said that in the rear part of his house, on a site measuring eight karīsas, golden rams as large as elephants, horses, and bulls sprang up, breaking through the earth and butting one another back and forth. In their mouths...

Balls made of five-colored threads were placed inside them. When there was a need for ghee, oil, honey, molasses, and so forth, or for clothing, coverings, gold, silver, and the like, they would remove these from the mouth of a single ball;

from the mouth of even a single ball, enough ghee, oil, honey, molasses, clothing, coverings, gold, silver, and wealth would come forth to satisfy all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa. From that time on...
He became known as Meṇḍaka the Wealthy.

But what was his past karma? It is said that during the time of Buddha Vipassī, he was the nephew of a householder named Avaroja, and he shared the same name as his uncle, being called Avaroja. Then his uncle [prepared] the Teacher’s fragrant chamber...
He began to build it. Having gone to his presence, he said, "Uncle, let us both do it together," but when the other refused,
saying, "I shall do it alone, making it something not shared with others," [the first] replied,
"In this place, once the Gandhakuṭī has been built, it is fitting that there be a structure called the Kuñjarasālā in such-and-such a spot."
Having reflected thus, he had building materials brought from the forest and caused one pillar to be fashioned inlaid with gold,
one inlaid with silver, one inlaid with gems, and one inlaid with the seven precious substances; likewise, having had the entire assembly of beams, doors, panels, windows, rafters, roof-boards,
and tiles made entirely inlaid with gold and the other precious materials, he [placed] the Tathāgata’s [image] made of the seven precious substances in the place directly facing the Gandhakuṭī.
He had an elephant-stable constructed. Upon it were canopies made of solid red gold, and the finial-pagodas were made of coral.
In the center of the elephant-stable, he had a jeweled pavilion built and established a Dharma throne.
Its legs were made of solid red gold, as were its four crossbars; furthermore, there were four golden deer.
Having had it made, he placed it beneath the four legs of the seat; having had two rams made, he placed them beneath the footstool;
and having had six golden rams made, he placed them surrounding the pavilion.
First, he had the Dhamma-seat woven with cords made of thread, and in the middle, with those made of golden thread, and above, with those made of pearls.
He had it woven with threads. He had a sandalwood support for it.

Having thus completed the Kuñjarasāla, while constructing the Sālāmahā, he invited the Teacher together with six million eight hundred thousand bhikkhus, gave alms for four months, and on the final day, he presented the three robes (*tricīvara*). Therein, the most junior member of the Saṅgha received one worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold.
Having performed meritorious deeds during the time of Vipassī Buddha and passing away from there, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans.
In this present Bhaddakappa, having been reborn into a family of great wealth in Bārāṇasī, he became known as the Bārāṇasī merchant.
One day, while going to attend upon the king, he saw the royal chaplain and asked, "Teacher, what is the auspicious moment of the lunar mansion?"
"Consider this," he said. "Yes, I shall consider it; what else is there for us to do? "In that case, what is the custom of the country?
"There will be one danger. "What kind of danger? "A fear of famine, householder. "When will it happen?
"After three years have passed from now. Having heard that, the merchant [prepared] much agricultural work...
Having had [the storehouses] built, he took only grain—even using the wealth available in his house—and had one hundred and twenty-five granaries constructed;

he filled all the granaries with rice. When the granaries were insufficient, he filled jars and other vessels, and buried the remainder in pits dug in the ground. Having mixed the remaining stock with clay, he had the walls plastered with it.
Then, at a later time, when a famine had arrived, he began consuming the grain as it had been stored;
and when the grain kept in the granaries, jars, and other vessels was exhausted, he summoned his dependents and said:
"Go, dear ones, enter the foothills of the mountains; when there is plenty and we are alive, come back to me."

"Do not wish to come back; live right there, wherever you may be. Weeping and with tearful faces, they paid homage to the merchant, asked for his forgiveness, and after staying for seven days, they did as he had said.
However, only one servant, a slave named Puṇṇa, remained in his presence; together with him, the merchant’s wife, the merchant’s son, and the merchant’s daughter-in-law—these five—[departed].

People existed. When even the grain stored in pits in the ground had been exhausted, they scraped off the clay from the walls, moistened it, and sustained themselves with the grain obtained therefrom.
Then, when a drought prevailed and the clay was being consumed, his wife scraped the remaining clay from the base of the wall, moistened it, and [obtained] about half an *āḷhaka* measure of rice.

Having obtained and husked a single measure of rice, she thought, "During times of famine, thieves are many," and out of fear of robbers, she placed it in a jar, sealed it, buried it in the ground, and left it there.
Then, when the merchant returned from his attendance upon the king, he said, "My dear, I am hungry; is there anything? Instead of saying that the rice was available, she replied, "There is nothing."
“There is one stalk of rice,” she said. “Where is it? “I buried it and left it there out of fear of thieves.
“In that case, dig it up and cook something,” he said. She replied, “If I cook rice-gruel, you will receive it twice;
if I cook a meal, you will receive it only once. What shall I cook, Master? [He said: “For us...”
"There is no other provision; we shall die after eating this meal, so please cook the food yourself.
Having cooked the meal, she divided it into five portions, increased the portion for the merchant, and placed them before him.
At that moment, a Paccekabuddha on Mount Gandhamādana was emerging from meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). Within that absorption—
It is said that through the power of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), hunger does not afflict them.
However, for those who have emerged from attainment, it arises with great intensity, as if burning the lining of the stomach. Therefore, they go about looking for a place where food may be obtained.
On the day they give alms, they obtain some form of prosperity, such as the position of a general or other high rank. Therefore—
He too, surveying with his divine eye, saw that a fear of drought had arisen throughout the whole of Jambudīpa,
and that five people were cooking a *nāḷika* of rice in the treasurer’s house. Seeing whether they were faithful and whether they were capable of performing an act of hospitality toward him,
and having observed both their faith and their capacity to provide such hospitality, he took his bowl and robe.
He showed himself standing right there at the gate in front of the great merchant. Upon seeing him, the merchant’s heart was filled with serene faith, and he thought:
"In the past, because I had not given alms, I have experienced such a famine as this; yet even this single meal would protect me for only one day.
But what is given to the Noble One will bring me benefit and happiness for many millions of aeons."
Having removed that bowl of food, she approached the Paccekabuddha, paid homage with the fivefold prostration, and led him into her house.
After washing his feet as he sat upon a seat and placing them on a golden footstool, she took the bowl of food and poured it into the Paccekabuddha’s alms-bowl.
When half of the food remained, the Paccekabuddha [covered] the bowl with his hand.
“Cover it. Then he said to him, “Venerable sir, this is one portion of cooked rice for five people from a single measure of rice;
it cannot be divided into two. Do not show me favor in this world;
I wish to give everything without reserve. Having said this, he gave him all the food. And having given it, he made an aspiration.
“Venerable sir, may I never again see such fear of famine in whatever place I am reborn.
From now on, may I be capable of providing seed-grain and food for all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa; may I not have to earn my livelihood by working with my own hands;
and having had one hundred and twenty-five granaries cleaned out, may I bathe my head and stand at their doors.”
“Having sat down, at the very moment I look upward, may streams of red rice fall and fill all my storehouses.
And in every place where I am reborn, may there be this very wife, this very son, this very daughter-in-law, and this very servant!
His wife also thought, “While my husband is tormented by hunger, it is not possible for me to eat.”
Having given her own portion to the Paccekabuddha, she made this aspiration: "Venerable Sir, in whatever place I am reborn henceforth, may I never behold such fear of famine;
and even as I stand before a bowl of rice providing food for all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa, may every spot from which I take the food remain filled until I rise."
"Let it be so! Let this very person be the master, let this very person be the son, let this very person be the daughter-in-law, and let this very person be the slave!
Then his son, having given his own portion to the Paccekabuddha, made this aspiration: "Venerable Sir, from this day forth may I never behold such fear of hunger;
and taking one thousand-fold purse for me, [may it serve] all those dwelling in Jambudīpa..."
"Even as I give away this single kahāpaṇa, may this bag of a thousand coins remain full; may these alone be my mother and father, this my wife, and this my slave.
His daughter-in-law also gave her own portion to the Paccekabuddha and made a resolution: "From this time forth..."
“May I never behold such fear of hunger; may no depletion be known even as I stand before a single granary, distributing seed and food to all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa;
in every place where I am reborn, may these same people be my father-in-law and mother-in-law, this same person be my husband, and this same person be my slave.
The slave also [made his aspiration] regarding his own portion for the Paccekabuddha.
Having given [the gift], he made this aspiration: "From now on, may I never behold such fear of famine;
may all these men become my husbands; and as I plow, may there be seven furrows each—three from this side, three from that side, and one in the middle—each as thick as a wooden pestle.
On that day, having aspired to the position of general, he obtained it.
Although he was capable, out of affection for his masters, he made this aspiration: "May these alone be my masters.
At the conclusion of everyone's speech, the Paccekabuddha said, "So be it," and added:
"May what you have desired and aspired to be quickly fulfilled!"
May all your intentions be fulfilled, like the moon on the fifteenth day.
May whatever you desire and aspire to be quickly accomplished;
may all your intentions be fulfilled, like the wish-fulfilling jewel, the Jotirasa.
Having offered an expression of thanksgiving with verses of the Paccekabuddhas, he thought, "It is fitting that I should inspire confidence in their hearts.
Having resolved, "May these men see me as far as Mount Gandhamādana," he departed.
They too remained standing, looking after him. He went and shared that meal among the five hundred Paccekabuddhas. That...
Through its power, it was sufficient for everyone. They remained standing, merely looking on.
But when midday had passed, the merchant’s wife washed the cooking pot, covered it, and set it aside.
The merchant, oppressed by hunger, lay down and fell asleep. Having woken up in the evening, he said to his wife:
“Bhadde, I am very hungry; is there perhaps some burnt rice on the bottom of the cooking pot?

Although she knew that the pot had been washed and set aside, she did not say, “There is none,” but thinking, “I shall open the pot and show it to him,” she rose, went to the base of the pot, and opened it.
At that very moment, [she saw] what was the color of a jasmine bud...
The cooking pot, full of rice, stood there with its lid removed. Seeing it, her body thrilled with joy, she said to the merchant:
"Rise up, master! I washed the pot and covered it; yet it is now filled with rice the color of jasmine buds.
Truly, meritorious deeds are things that ought to be done, and giving is what is fitting to be performed. Rise up!"
“Master, please eat. She gave food to the father and son. When they had finished eating and risen, she sat down with her daughter-in-law and ate;
then she gave food to Puṇṇa. Wherever she took from it, the supply was never exhausted;
only the place where the ladle had been dipped once remained visible. On that very day, the granaries and other stores were filled exactly as they had been before.
They filled it once more. He had a proclamation made throughout the city: "Food has been prepared in the house of the merchant; let those who need seed-food come and take it.
People took the seed-food from his house. All the inhabitants of Jambudīpa indeed obtained their livelihood by depending upon it.

Passing away from there, he was reborn in the world of the gods; wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha in the city of Bhaddiya into a family of merchants.
His wife, having been reborn into a family of great wealth, reached maturity and entered his very home.
