By virtue of that past karma of his, goats of the kind previously described arose in his house later on.
Their son was indeed their son, their daughter-in-law her daughter-in-law, and their slave his slave.
Then one day, desiring to test his own merit, the merchant had one hundred and twelve storehouses cleaned out; having bathed his head, he sat at the gate and looked upward.
All of them were filled with the aforementioned red rice. He [then considered] the merits of others as well.
Desiring to test his wife, his sons, and the others, he said, "I shall test your merit as well.
Then his wife, having adorned herself with all her ornaments, had rice measured out right before the eyes of the great multitude;
she had it cooked into a meal, sat down on a seat prepared at the gateway, and taking a golden spoon—
Having caused it to be proclaimed, "Let those who need food come," she filled the vessels brought by each person as they arrived and gave them away.
Even though she was giving throughout the entire day, only the place where her ladle had been held remained visible.
Furthermore, even under previous Buddhas, she would hold the cooking pot with her left hand and the ladle with her right hand for the Saṅgha of monks.

Having taken [the water], she filled her bowl in this very way; because she gave the food after filling it, the mark of the lotus (*paduma*) appeared on the palm of her left hand, and the mark of the moon (*canda*) appeared on the palm of her right hand.
Furthermore, because she took a water-strainer from her left hand, filtered water for the Saṅgha of monks, and moved about from one place to another while giving it, [these marks arose].
Because her right sole was filled with the mark of the moon and her left sole was filled with the mark of the lotus,
they gave her the name Candapadumā for that reason. Her son,
having washed his head and taken a bag containing a thousand coins, said, "Let those who have need of kahāpaṇas come!"
To each person who arrived, she filled their vessels and gave them away. In her purse, there was indeed a thousand kahāpaṇas.
Her daughter-in-law, having adorned herself with all her ornaments and taking a basket of rice, sat down in the courtyard and said, "Let those who need seed-rice come!
To each person who arrived, she filled their vessels and gave them away; yet the basket remained exactly as full as before.

[The king] was present. His slave, having adorned him with all ornaments, yoked two oxen with golden yokes and golden traces, took a golden goad-staff, applied fragrant ointments to the five-toed hooves of the two oxen, fastened golden bags to their horns, went to the field, and drove them.
"Three furrows here, three furrows there, and one in the middle"—thus were the seven furrows.
Having split [the wealth], they departed. The inhabitants of Jambudīpa took from the merchant’s house whatever they desired—food, seeds, gold, silver, and so forth.
These were the five of great merit.
When the merchant of such great power heard, "The Teacher has arrived," he thought, "I shall go out to meet the Teacher."
While departing, he saw some non-Buddhist teachers (tīrthikas) on the road.

Although they tried to stop him, saying, "Householder, why do you, being a proponent of action (kiriyavāda), go into the presence of the ascetic Gotama, who is a proponent of non-action (akiriyavāda)?", he disregarded their words, went on, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down to one side. Then the Teacher gave him a gradual discourse (anupubbikathā).

He preached the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the discourse, having attained the fruit of stream-entry, he informed the Teacher that although the Teacher had spoken dispraise of the sectarians, he himself had been restrained from doing so.
Then the Teacher said to him, "Householder, these beings indeed do not see even their own great faults;
yet they take non-existent faults in others to be existent and, in those various instances, [speak] excessively..."
Having said, "As if winnowing [the faults] of others," he spoke this verse:
"The fault of others is easy to see, but one's own is hard to see;
for one winnows the faults of others like chaff."
"But he conceals his own [faults], like a deceitful gambler concealing his losing throw.
In this context, "the fault of another is easy to see" means that even the slightest fault or lapse of another can be easily seen;
however, one's own [fault], even if very great, is difficult to see. "Of others" means for that very reason, that person...
In the midst of the Saṅgha and other such settings, he exposes the faults of others as if winnowing chaff, placing them in a high position.
Regarding the phrase "the cheat like a gambler’s ‘kali’": here, among birds, the state of being unable to escape is called *kali*;
the concealment by breaking branches and so forth is called *kitavā*; and the fowler is called *saṭho*. Just as a bird-trapper, having caught birds...
Like a gambler wishing to kill [his opponent], he conceals his own person; the meaning is that he thus hides his own fault.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the tenth story, the Story of the Merchant Meṇḍaka.
11. The Story of the Elder Ujjhānasaññin "Observing the faults of others"—the Teacher delivered this teaching on the Dhamma while residing at Jetavana concerning an elder named Ujjhānasaññin.
It is said that he used to wander about, seeking out even among the monks themselves, thinking, "He wears his lower robe like this; he wraps his upper robe like that."
The bhikkhus reported to the Teacher, "Venerable Sir, a certain elder named so-and-so acts in this way.
The Teacher said, "Bhikkhus, one who stands at the head of the duties and instructs in this manner is not guilty of fault-finding.
However, for one who constantly wanders about seeking out the faults of others with a mind intent on disparagement, not even a single distinction such as *jhāna* will arise."
“Only the taints increase,” he said, and then recited this verse:
“For one who observes the faults of others, who is constantly preoccupied with finding fault, the taints increase;
such a person is far from the destruction of the taints.”

In this context, "one who is full of complaints" refers to a person who, in seeking out the faults of others regarding how one should dress or how one should wear the robes—thinking, "It should be worn like this;
it should be covered like that"—does not increase even a single factor such as *jhāna*. On the contrary, his taints (*āsava*) alone increase.
For that very reason, he has gone far away, indeed at a great distance, from the destruction of the taints, which is synonymous with the path to *arahantship*.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the eleventh story, the Story of the Elder Ujjhānasaññin.
12. The Story of the Wanderer Subhadda.

"Ākāse" (In the air): This teaching on the Dhamma was spoken by the Teacher while lying upon his Parinibbāna bed in the Upavattana Sāla grove of the Mallas at Kusinārā, concerning the wanderer Subhadda.

It is said that in the past, when his younger brother gave the first-fruits of a harvest as a gift for nine successive years, he refused to give the gift himself, but finally yielded and gave it at the very end.
Therefore, during both the First and the Middle Enlightenments, [he failed to meet] the Teacher.
He did not succeed in seeing him. However, during his final enlightenment, at the time of the Teacher’s parinibbāna, he thought:
"I had asked three questions regarding my own doubts to the elder wanderers; because I perceived the ascetic Gotama as being 'young,' I did not ask him.
Now is the time for his parinibbāna, and later I shall have no opportunity to ask the ascetic Gotama about these matters."
"Would remorse arise? Though he approached the Teacher while being restrained by the Elder Ānanda, the Teacher granted him leave, saying, "Ānanda, do not restrain Subhadda; let him ask me questions.
Having entered the inner tent and sat upon a lower couch, [Subhadda asked], "O ascetic, is there such a thing as a footprint in the sky?"
He asked these questions: "Is there such a thing as an ascetic outside of this [teaching]? Are there such things as eternal conditioned phenomena?
Then the Teacher, explaining their non-existence, taught the Dhamma to him with these verses:
"Just as there is no track in the sky, so there is no ascetic outside."
“Beings delight in conceptual proliferation (papañca), but the Tathāgatas are free from proliferation.
Just as there is no footprint in the sky, there is no ascetic outside [the Dhamma];
there are no eternal conditioned phenomena, and there is no wavering in the Buddhas.”
In this context, "footprint" (*pada*) means that in this space there is no so-called footprint of anyone that can be designated as being of such-and-such a kind by way of color or shape.
"Outside" (*bahire*) means that outside my teaching there is no one who stands in the state of the path or its fruit and is called a "recluse" (*samaṇa*).

"The world" (*pajā*) refers to this world of beings known as *pajā*, which delights only in the conceptual proliferations (*papañca*) such as craving and the like. "Free from proliferation" (*nippapañca*) [refers to those] right at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
Because all conceptual proliferations (*papañca*) have been utterly cut off, the Tathāgatas are free from proliferation (*nippapañca*). "Formations" (*saṅkhāra*) refers to the five aggregates.
For among these, not even a single one is called eternal. Regarding "stirring" (*iñjita*):
the meaning is that among the stirrings of the Buddhas—such as craving, conceit, and so forth—there is not even a single stirring by which one might grasp formations as being eternal.
At the conclusion of the teaching, Subhadda was established in the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), and the Dhamma instruction was fruitful for the assembled multitude as well.
Thus ends the twelfth story, the Account of the Wanderer Subhadda.
The commentary on the Chapter on Impurities (Malavagga) is finished.
The Eighteenth Chapter. 19.
The Chapter on the Uprightness of Dhamma. 1.
The Case of the High Court Officials.
"It does not become one by that"—the Teacher spoke this teaching on the Dhamma while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the judges of the court.
One day, after walking for alms in the village of Uttaradvāra near Sāvatthī, the monks returned to the monastery through the center of the city after their meal.
At that moment, a cloud arose and it began to rain. As they were approaching...
Having entered the hall of justice, he saw the chief judges taking bribes and making those who were rightful owners ownerless.
Thinking, "Alas, these men are unrighteous, yet we believed they were administering justice according to the Dhamma," he waited until the rainy season had passed,
went to the monastery, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down to one side.

They reported that matter to the Teacher. The Teacher said, “Monks, those who, being under the sway of favoritism and the like, decide a case through rashness, are not called ‘upholders of the Dhamma.

Rather, it is only those who, having investigated the offense, pass judgment without rashness in accordance with the offense that are called ‘upholders of the Dhamma. Having said this, he spoke these verses:
“One does not stand firm in the Dhamma by leading a matter through force;
rather, the wise person is one who discerns both what is beneficial and what is harmful.
He leads others through non-forceful means, according to the Dhamma, and with impartiality.”
“The wise one who is guarded by the Dhamma is called ‘one established in the Dhamma.
In this context, “by that much alone” refers to this very reason. Regarding “established in the Dhamma”:

for a king, even if he remains within the legal principles (dhamma) of judicial decision-making that he ought to perform, he is not yet called “established in the Dhamma. “By which” means by which reason. “The matter” (attha) refers to the case that has been brought forward and must be adjudicated.
"An affair. "He decides by force" means that one established in desire (*chanda*) and so forth might decide through a lie committed by force.
For instance, one established in desire might say "He is a kinsman" or "He is a friend," and thus make what is ownerless have an owner;
one established in hatred (*dosa*) might speak falsely regarding those who are his enemies and make what has an owner ownerless; and one established in delusion (*moha*)...
Having accepted a bribe, at the time of judgment, as if distracted, looking here and there, he speaks falsely and dismisses the other, saying, "This one has won;
this one is defeated. Establishing himself in fear, even when someone of a powerful class is facing defeat, he attributes victory to them;
this is called conducting a case through violence. This is the one who stands on righteousness (dhammaṭṭha).
The meaning is that [the name] does not exist. "Both the beneficial and the non-beneficial" refers to both the real and the unreal cause.
"One who discerns both" refers to the wise person who speaks after having determined both the beneficial and the non-beneficial. "Without violence" means without false speech.

"According to the Dhamma" means according to the principle of legal judgment, and not by way of favoritism and so forth. "Impartially" means he leads others in accordance with their offense alone; [he grants] victory...
Or he brings about defeat. "Guarded by the Dhamma" means that he is protected by the Dhamma and shielded by the Dhamma;
being endowed with the wisdom born of the Dhamma, he is wise, and because he stands firm in the Dhamma as it has been determined, he is called "one who stands in the Dhamma.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other fruits.
The First Account of the Judicial Officers.
2. The Account of the Group of Six.
"One does not become wise by that"—the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Group of Six.
It seems they were wandering about, causing confusion in the dining halls both in the monasteries and in the villages.
One day, when the monks had finished their meal in the village and returned, they asked the young novices: "Friends, how was the dining hall?
"Venerable sirs, do not ask," [the novices replied]. "The group-of-six [monks] said, 'We alone are capable; we alone are wise. We shall strike these [others] down...'"
“Having scattered rubbish on their heads, we shall carry them out,” they said; then, seizing us by the backs and scattering rubbish [over us], they threw the dining hall into disorder.
The monks went into the presence of the Teacher and reported this matter to him.
The Teacher said, “Monks, I do not call one who causes harm to others by speaking much a ‘wise man’; rather, I call one who brings security...”
"But I say that one who is without enmity and possesses fearlessness is wise. Having said this, he spoke this verse:
"One does not become wise merely by speaking much;
One who is secure, without enmity, and fearless is called wise."
In this context, "to whatever extent" means that one does not become known as wise merely by speaking much in the midst of the Saṅgha and so forth for that reason.
Rather, the meaning is that he who is himself secure— being without enmity and fearless due to the absence of the five kinds of hostility—
or by whose presence the fear of the great multitude ceases, he is indeed called wise.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the second story concerning the group of six.
3. The Story of the Elder Ekudāna-Khīṇāsava.
"Not for long," the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the Elder named Ekudāna, whose taints were exhausted.
It is said that he lived all alone in a certain forest grove, and only a single *udāna* was familiar to him:
"For one of lofty mind who is heedful..."
For the sage who trains in the paths of silence,
for the one who is thus composed, peaceful, and ever mindful, no sorrows arise.
It is said that on the Uposatha days, he would himself announce the hearing of the Dhamma and recite this verse.
Like the sound of the earth quaking, there arose the sound of the deities' shouts of "Sādhu!
Then, on one Uposatha day, two monks who were bearers of the Tipiṭaka, each accompanied by a retinue of five hundred, went to his dwelling place. Upon seeing them, he was filled with joy.
“It was well done by you in coming here; today we shall hear the Dhamma from you,” he said.
“But, friend, is there anyone here who wishes to hear the Dhamma? “There is, Bhante; on the day of the Dhamma-recitation, this forest grove resounds with a single harmony of the ‘well done!
cries of the deities. Then one of them, a master of the Three Piṭakas, recited the Dhamma.
One person spoke. Even that single deity did not give a cry of approval.
They asked him, "Friend, you said that on the day of the Dhamma assembly, a deity in this grove gives a cry of approval with a great sound;
what does this mean? He replied, "Venerable sirs, on other days there was only one uniform sound of the cry of approval, but today I do not know."

“What is this? [they asked. “In that case, friends, you yourself speak the Dhamma first,” [he replied. Taking up a fan, he sat on his seat and recited that very same verse. The deities gave their applause with a great sound.
Then the monks who were their attendants complained, “In this forest grove, the deities give their applause merely by looking at our faces!”
"Even when so many bhikkhus who are masters of the Tipiṭaka were speaking, they did not offer even a single word of praise;
yet, when a single elder monk recited a single verse, they gave a great shout of 'Well done!
They too went to the monastery and reported this matter to the Teacher.
The Teacher said, "Monks, I do not call one a 'bearer of the Dhamma' merely because he learns or recites much.
But he who, having learned even a single verse, penetrates the Truths—he is called a bearer of the Dhamma.
Having said this, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
“One is not a bearer of the Dhamma merely by speaking much;
rather, one who, having heard even a little of the Dhamma, perceives it with the body,
is indeed a bearer of the Dhamma— he who does not neglect the Dhamma.”

In this context, "to whatever extent" means that one does not become a bearer of the Dhamma (*dhammadhara*) merely by speaking much through such means as learning, memorizing, and reciting; rather, such a person is called a protector of the lineage and a guardian of the tradition.
But he who, having heard even a little, practices in accordance with the Dhamma and in accordance with the meaning—this is one who truly upholds the Dhamma.
Having sacrificed, one who fully understands suffering and the other truths through the mental body sees the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths; he indeed is a bearer of the Dhamma.

As for the phrase "he who does not neglect the Dhamma": even he who, having aroused energy and desiring penetration day by day, does not neglect the Dhamma—he too is truly a bearer of the Dhamma; such is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the third story, concerning the Elder Ekudāna-Khīṇāsava.
4. The Story of the Elder Lakuṇḍaka-Bhaddiya.
"One does not become an elder by that alone"—the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching while residing at Jetavana concerning the Elder Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya.

One day, on the very day after that elder had gone to attend upon the Teacher and had just departed, about thirty forest-dwelling bhikkhus arrived, seeing him, and having paid homage to the Teacher, they sat down. The Teacher [perceived] their underlying potential for Arahantship...
Having seen him, he asked this question: "Do you see an elder who has gone from here? "We do not see him, venerable sir," they replied.
"Was anyone seen by you? "We saw a novice, venerable sir. "That was no novice, monks; that was an elder indeed.
"He is exceedingly small, venerable sir. "I do not [speak] of him, monks, on account of his physical stature..."

“I call one an elder merely by virtue of sitting in the seat of the elders. But he who, having penetrated the Truths, stands firm in non-violence toward the great multitude—he is truly named an elder. Having said this, he spoke these verses:
“One does not become an elder simply because his head is grey;”
“His age has ripened, yet he is called ‘one who is old in vain.
But he in whom truth, the Dhamma, non-violence, self-restraint, and self-control reside—
he indeed is the wise one whose impurities have been cast out, and he is truly called an ‘Elder’ (thera).”
In this context, "ripe" (*paripakka*) means matured; the meaning is that one has reached a state of old age.

"Futilely aged" (*mogha-jinna*) means one who is called "futilely aged" due to the absence of those qualities that constitute the state of an elder (*thera*). "But in whom truth and the Dhamma [exist]" (*yamhi saccañ ca dhammo ca*):
in that person, however, because the fourfold Truth has been penetrated in sixteen ways, and because the ninefold supramundane Dhamma has been realized through knowledge...

And there is [the following]: "Non-violence" (*ahiṃsā*) means the state of not harming. This is merely a way of teaching; the meaning is that in which all four kinds of development of the immeasurables (*appamaññā*) exist.
"Restraint" (*saṃyama*) and "taming" (*dama*) refer to both virtue (*sīla*) and the restraint of the sense faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*).

"One who has vomited out impurity" (*vantamala*) is one whose impurities have been extracted by the knowledge of the Path (*maggañāṇa*). "The wise one" (*dhīra*) is one endowed with steadfastness (*dhiti*). He is called "an elder" (*thera*) because he is possessed of these qualities that produce steadfastness.
The meaning is that he is called "Thera" (Elder).
At the conclusion of the teaching, those bhikkhus were established in Arahatship.
This is the fourth story, concerning the Elder Lakuṇḍaka-Bhaddiya.
5. The Story of the Many Bhikkhus: "Not by mere eloquence of speech.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, spoke this Dhamma teaching concerning a number of bhikkhus.
For on one occasion, some young bhikkhus and novices were performing tasks such as dyeing the robes for their own preceptors.
Seeing them performing services, some elders thought: "We too are skilled in the rules of phonetics;
we lack nothing ourselves. Suppose we were to approach the Teacher and say: 'Venerable sir, we are skilled in the rules of phonetics;
even though we have learned the Dhamma from others, [we wish to learn it] from these [elders]...'"
“Do not recite the scriptures until you have mastered them; rather, command the young novices to do so. For in this way, our gain and honor will increase.
They approached the Teacher and spoke thus.
Having heard their words, the Teacher said, “In this Dispensation, it is permitted to speak in such a manner only by way of tradition. These—”
"But knowing that you are dependent on gain and honor, I do not say of you that you are persons of good character merely because of your eloquence.
Only he in whom these states such as envy have been utterly eradicated by the path of Arahantship is truly a person of good character. Having said this, he spoke these verses:
"Not merely by eloquence, nor by beauty of complexion;..."
“A man may have the appearance of a good person, yet be envious, stingy, and deceitful.
But he for whom this [defilement] is utterly cut off, rooted out, and eradicated—
a wise man whose faults have ceased— is called one of good character.”
In this context, "not merely by way of speech" means not merely by way of verbal expression—that is, by mere words endowed with the characteristics of sound.
"Or by way of the beauty of complexion" means by way of the pleasing appearance of the body.
A "man"—by this much alone—is one who is envious of the gains and other benefits of others, possessed of the fivefold stinginess, and crafty due to a sycophantic disposition.

A person is not of good character. But for whichever individual this kind of envy and other faults has been cut off with its root by the knowledge of the path to arahantship, uprooted, and eradicated—having vomited out his faults and being endowed with the wisdom of the essence of the Dhamma—he is called "one of good character. This is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the fifth story, concerning a number of bhikkhus.
6. The Story of Hatthaka.
"One is not a recluse merely by being shaven-headed. The Teacher delivered this teaching on the Dhamma while residing at Sāvatthī concerning Hatthaka.

It is said that he, being eager for debate, would say, "You should come to such-and-such a place at such-and-such a time; we shall engage in debate," and having said this, he would go there beforehand.
Then [the other party] would say, "See, the sectarians have not come out of fear of me; rather, it is this very..."
Having said such things as, "They shall suffer defeat," he, being defeated in debate, wanders about prevaricating with one thing after another.
When the Teacher heard, "It seems Hatthaka acts in this way," he summoned him and asked, "Is it true, Hatthaka, that you act thus?
When he replied, "It is true," the Teacher said, "Why do you act in this way? For such false speech as this..."
"One does not become a *samaṇa* merely by the shaving of the head and so forth. But he who stands having stilled (*samitvā*) evil deeds, whether small or great—he alone is a *samaṇa*.
Having said this, he spoke these verses:
"One is not a *samaṇa* by being shaven, if one is unvirtuous and speaks falsehoods;..."
“What will become of a recluse who is possessed by desire and greed?
But he who pacifies evils, both subtle and gross, in every way—
he is called a ‘recluse’ (samaṇa) because of having pacified all evils.”
In this context, "by one who is shaven" means by one who has merely shaved his head. "Bare" means devoid of both the virtues of moral conduct (*sīla*) and the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*).
Speaking falsely—that is, speaking a lie—one is possessed of desire for objects not yet attained and greed for those already attained;
how then can such a person be called a "recluse" (*samaṇa*)? And he who "comes together," whether with things small or great...
The meaning is: "He quiets evil deeds; because of that quieting (*samitattā*), he is called a *samaṇa*.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the sixth story, the account of Hatthaka.
7. The Story of a Certain Brahmin “Not by that is one a bhikkhu. The Teacher gave this Dhamma teaching while residing at Jetavana concerning a certain brahmin.
It is said that after having gone forth in a non-Buddhist sect, he thought as he was wandering for alms: “The ascetic Gotama [is a bhikkhu] by his own...”
“One speaks of my disciples as ‘bhikkhus’ because they go about for alms; it is fitting to call me too a ‘bhikkhu.
He approached the Teacher and said, “Master Gotama, I too live by going about for alms;
please call me a ‘bhikkhu’ as well. Then the Teacher said to him, “Brahmin, I do not call one a ‘bhikkhu’ merely by the act of begging for alms.”
“Indeed, one who lives having undertaken a corrupt way of life is not called a bhikkhu.
But he who wanders about with discernment regarding all conditioned phenomena—he is called a bhikkhu. Having said this, he spoke these verses:
“One does not become a bhikkhu merely by begging from others;”
“By undertaking the way of the world, one is not a bhikkhu merely by that.
But he who, having cast aside both merit and evil here,
lives the holy life and wanders through the world with discernment— he indeed is called a bhikkhu.”
In this context, "as far as" means that one does not become a bhikkhu merely by begging for alms to the extent that others provide them.
One does not become a bhikkhu by practicing while adopting a "vissa" (putrid) state—either a corrupt doctrine or foul-smelling bodily actions and so forth.
"A warrior" refers to one here in this teaching who, through the holy life of the Path, [overcomes] both of these: merit and evil.

Having expelled and driven away [the defilements], he lives the holy life (*brahmacariya*). "Having reckoned" means by means of knowledge (*ñāṇa*). "In the world" refers to the world of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth;
having understood all phenomena thus—"these are internal aggregates, these are external"—he conducts himself.
Because his defilements have been shattered by that knowledge, he is called a "monk" (*bhikkhu*); this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the seventh story, concerning a certain brahmin. 8.
The Story of the Heretics.
"Not by mere recitation"—the Teacher related this teaching on the Dhamma while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove concerning the non-Buddhist ascetics (titthiyas).
It is said that when people were at their meal sites, those ascetics would say to them: "May it be safe; may it be well; may your life-span increase!
In such-and-such a place there is a quagmire; in such-and-such a place there is a thorn; it is not proper to go to such a place," and so forth.

Having uttered a blessing according to their custom, they departed. However, during the first period after the Enlightenment, when the practice of giving thanks (*anumodanā*) and so forth had not yet been authorized, the monks would depart from the dining hall without offering thanks to the people.
The people complained, saying, "We hear blessings from the followers of other sects, but these venerable ones depart in silence. The monks reported this matter to the Teacher.
They reported this to the Teacher. The Teacher gave permission, saying, "Monks, from now on, you may deliver blessings of thanksgiving (anumodana) as you please in the dining halls and other places;
you may engage in informal conversation and preach the Dhamma. They did accordingly.
Hearing these blessings and other discourses, the people became inspired; they went about inviting monks and providing them with hospitality.
But the sectarians complained, saying, "We practice the silence of a sage (muni), yet the disciples of the ascetic Gotama wander about engaging in great talk at the dining halls and other places.
When the Teacher heard this matter, he said, "Monks, I do not call one a 'sage' merely by his silence. Some..."
"Indeed, some do not speak because they do not know; others out of lack of confidence;

and still others out of stinginess, thinking, 'Let others not find out this superior matter of ours. Therefore, one is not a sage merely by silence; rather, one is called a sage by the subsiding of evil.
Having said this, he spoke these verses:
“One does not become a sage by silence, nor one who is dull-witted and ignorant;
rather, the wise man, having taken up the better course like a scale,
avoids all evils— and because he does so, he is a sage.”
“He who understands both worlds is therefore called a sage (muni).

In this context, although one is indeed called a sage by virtue of the knowledge of the path known as the practice of sagehood (*moneyya*), here the term “by means of silence” (*monena*) is stated with reference to the state of being silent. “Of deluded form” (*mūḷharūpa*) means of empty form. “Ignorant” (*avidvasū*)...
"Unwise. For one such as this is not called a sage (*muni*) even if he remains silent. Or rather, the meaning is that he is not called a sage by virtue of silence;

rather, he is empty-natured and unwise. And "who, like a scale, having taken up [the matter]"—just as one standing with a scale, if it is too heavy, takes away [weight], and if it is too light, adds [weight];
even so, he who [takes up] what is excessive...
He carries away and avoids evil as if removing it; he fulfills the wholesome as if adding to what is deficient.

And by acting in this way, taking hold of that which is excellent and supreme—namely, virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—he avoids evil unwholesome kamma.
"That sage" (sa munī) means that one is called a sage (muni). Therefore, he...
But why is he called a *muni*? If one asks, "Why is he a *muni*? the meaning is that he is a *muni* for the reason stated below.

He is a *muni* because he measures both worlds; that person who, as if weighing them on a scale, measures these two things in this world of aggregates and so forth according to the method beginning with, "These are internal aggregates, these are external," and so on—he is a *muni* by that [reason]. Thus he is called a *muni*.
For that reason, the meaning is that he is indeed called a "Muni.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the eighth story, concerning the heretics.
9. The Story of the Fisherman:
"One does not become noble by that. While residing at Jetavana, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse concerning a fisherman named Ariya.
One day, the Teacher, perceiving that the fisherman possessed the necessary spiritual potential for the path of stream-entry, [went] to a village on the northern gate of Sāvatthī.
Having wandered for alms, he was returning from there surrounded by the community of monks.
At that moment, the fisherman, who had been catching fish with a hook, saw the community of monks headed by the Buddha; he cast away his fishing rod and stood still.
The Teacher turned back and stood not far from him, and [asked] Sāriputta Thera and the others, "What is your name?"
He asked for their names. They each spoke their own names, saying, “I am Sāriputta,” and “I am Moggallāna.
The fisherman thought, “The Teacher asks for the names of all; I suppose he will ask for my name too.
The Teacher, knowing his intention, asked him, “Lay follower, what is your name? and he replied, “Venerable sir, I am Ariya.”
When he said, "Is that so?", [the Blessed One] replied, "No, lay follower, those who take life are not called 'Noble Ones' (ariya).
Noble Ones, however, abide in non-harming toward the great multitude," and spoke this verse:
"One does not become a Noble One by the fact that one harms living beings."
“Non-violence toward all living beings—one is called a noble one.
In this context, “non-violence” means by way of not harming. This is what is meant: for one does not become a noble one (ariya) by that cause through which one harms living beings;
rather, it is one who, because of non-harming toward all living beings by means of the hands and so forth, is established in the cultivation of loving-kindness and the like.
The meaning is: "He who stands aloof from harming is called a Noble One (ariya).
At the conclusion of the teaching, the fisherman was established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala), and the Dhamma teaching was fruitful for those who were present.
This is the ninth story, the Story of the Fisherman.
10. The Story of the Bhikkhus Endowed with Many Virtues, etc.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, gave this Dhamma teaching concerning a number of bhikkhus who were endowed with virtue and other qualities.
It is said that among them, some thought thus: "We are endowed with virtue; we are bearers of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga); we..."
"We are learned; we dwell in remote lodgings; we have attained the jhānas. For us, arahantship is not difficult to attain;

we shall reach arahantship on the very day we wish. Those among them who were non-returners (anāgāmin) also thought, "Arahantship will not now be difficult for us to attain. Then they all approached the Teacher on one day.
Having paid homage and sat down, they were asked by the Teacher, “Bhikkhus, have you reached the culmination of the purpose for which you went forth?
They replied, “Venerable sir, we are such and such; therefore, thinking, ‘We are capable of attaining arahantship at any moment we wish,’ we dwell [in this way].”

Having heard their words, the Teacher said, “Monks, it is not fitting for a monk to say, ‘Our suffering of existence is slight,’ merely on account of pure virtue and so forth, or merely by having attained the bliss of a non-returner.
Rather, until the destruction of the taints (*āsava*) has been reached, one should not give rise to the thought, ‘I am happy. Having said this, he spoke these verses:
“Not by mere rules and observances, nor even by great learning,
nor by the attainment of concentration, nor by a secluded dwelling,
do I touch the bliss of renunciation, which is not practiced by worldlings.”
"A bhikkhu may place his trust [in these], though he has not reached the destruction of the taints.
In this context, "by mere virtue and observance" means by mere virtue of the fourfold purification or by mere observance of the thirteen ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*).
"Or by great learning" means by the mere mastery of the three Piṭakas. "By the attainment of concentration" refers to the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
"By gain. "The bliss of renunciation" is the bliss of a non-returner (*anāgāmi*). It is by merely thinking, "I shall touch that bliss of a non-returner," or so.
"Not practiced by worldlings" means not practiced by ordinary persons (*puthujjana*), but practiced only by the Noble Ones (*ariya*).
"Bhikkhu"—he spoke thus addressing one of them. "He does not engender confidence" means he should not place his trust. This is what is meant: O Bhikkhu, by this...

A bhikkhu should not place his trust in the mere fact that he possesses perfected virtue and so forth, thinking, "My existence is slight and limited," until he has attained Arahantship, which is the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya).
For just as even a tiny amount of excrement is foul-smelling, so too even a slight amount of existence is suffering.
At the conclusion of the teaching, those bhikkhus were established in Arahatship; thus the Dhamma teaching was fruitful for those who had gathered there.
This is the tenth story, concerning the bhikkhus endowed with many virtues and other qualities.
The commentary on the Dhammaṭṭha-vagga is finished.
The Nineteenth Chapter. 20.
The Chapter on the Path. 1.
The Account of the Five Hundred Monks.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning five hundred bhikkhus.
It is said that when those bhikkhus returned to Sāvatthī after the Teacher had gone on a tour of the countryside, he sat in the assembly hall and spoke thus:
"The road from such-and-such a village to such-and-such a village is level; the road to such-and-such a village is uneven, stony, or free of stones," and so forth.
Following their own method, they engaged in a discussion concerning the path they had traveled.

The Teacher, perceiving that they possessed the necessary potential for the attainment of Arahatship, went to that place and sat upon the prepared seat. He asked, "Bhikkhus, about what topic have you been sitting together in conversation just now?
When they replied, "About this very one," he said, "Bhikkhus, this is an external path; by a bhikkhu..."
“It is fitting to perform the work on the Noble Eightfold Path; for by doing so, a bhikkhu is liberated from all suffering.
Having said this, he spoke these verses:
“The Eightfold Path is the best of paths; the Four Truths are the supreme words of truth.”
“Dispassion is the best of all things, and the Visionary is the best among bipeds.
This alone is the path, and no other, for the purification of vision.
Therefore, practice this, for it is the delusion of Māra.”
“Practicing thus, you will indeed bring an end to suffering;
the path for piercing the thorn of ignorance has been declared to you by me.
You yourselves must exert effort; the Tathāgatas are merely proclaimers.”
"Those who practice will be released from the bonds of Māra, for they are meditators. In this context,
"the eightfold path" refers to whether it be the paths of the legs and so forth, or the sixty-two paths of speculative views—
all these various paths are [defined] by the eight factors beginning with right view, as opposed to the eight [factors] beginning with wrong view.
For one who effects abandonment by taking cessation as the object and accomplishing the tasks such as the full understanding of suffering regarding all four truths,
the Eightfold Path is the best and supreme. Regarding the "four feet of the truths," this may refer to the truth of speech mentioned in the passage,
"One should speak the truth and not be angry," or to the various types such as "the Brahmin is truthful" and "the Khattiya is truthful."
Whether it be conventional truth (*sammutisacca*)— defined as "only this is true, all else is false"— or the truth of views (*diṭṭhisacca*),
or the ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*) categorized as "suffering is a noble truth" and so forth, for all these truths, suffering is [the primary object] in the sense of being fully understood,
in the sense of being realized, in the sense of being abandoned, in the sense of being developed, in the sense of a single penetration, and in the sense of a corresponding penetration.

The four terms beginning with "noble truth" (ariyasacca) are called supreme. Regarding the statement, "Dispassion is the supreme among phenomena," because of the words, "Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion is declared to be their foremost," dispassion—consisting of Nibbāna—is the supreme among all phenomena.
And regarding the phrase "the one-eyed among bipeds," this refers to all those distinguished as gods, humans, and so forth.
Among bipeds, the Tathāgata alone is supreme by virtue of his five eyes. The word *ca* has a conjunctive sense;
it includes non-material phenomena (*arūpadhamma*). Therefore, the Tathāgata is also supreme and foremost among non-material phenomena.
"For the purification of vision" means for the sake of the purification of the vision of the path and its fruition (*maggaphala*), regarding whom I have said he is "supreme."
"This alone is the path; there is no other. Therefore, you should practice this very way.
"This is the delusion of Māra" means it is called the deluding and the churning of Māra.

"The end of suffering" means you will bring about the limit and the final cessation of the entire suffering of saṃsāra. "For those pierced by the arrow of ignorance" refers to the arrows of passion and so forth.
Churning, rubbing, and pressing—this is the path. Having known this path through personal direct experience, and not merely by hearsay or other such means, I have declared it.

Now, for the sake of attaining that which is designated as "ardor" (*ātappa*) because of the heating (*ātāpana*) of the defilements, you must perform the task of right exertion (*sammappadhāna-vīriya*). For it is only the declarer who...

They are the Tathāgatas. Therefore, the meaning is that those who have practiced according to what was taught by them and are meditators possessing the two jhānas are liberated from the bonds of Māra, which are comprised of the round of existence in the three realms.
At the conclusion of the teaching, those bhikkhus were established in arahantship; thus the Dhamma teaching was fruitful for those who had assembled.
The First Story of the Five Hundred Bhikkhus.
2. The Story of the Characteristic of Impermanence:
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, delivered this teaching on the Dhamma concerning the five hundred bhikkhus, beginning with the words, "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent."
It is said that after receiving a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) from the Teacher and going to the forest to strive, they failed to attain *arahantship*.
Thinking, "We shall master the meditation subject more thoroughly," they returned to the presence of the Teacher. The Teacher, investigating what would be suitable for them, considered:
"During the time of the Buddha Kassapa, these [monks] spent twenty thousand years [contemplating] the characteristic of impermanence..."

Thinking, "They have been practicing accordingly; therefore, it is fitting to teach them a single verse by means of the characteristic of impermanence alone," he said, "Bhikkhus, all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhārā) within the realms of sensual desire, existence, and so forth, are indeed impermanent in the sense of having existed and then ceased," and spoke this verse:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent— When one sees this with wisdom..."
“Then one becomes disenchanted with suffering; this is the path to purification.
In this context, “all formations” refers to the aggregates that have arisen within the realms of sense-desire existence and so forth.

When one perceives through the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*) that they are impermanent because they cease right where they arise, then one becomes disenchanted with this suffering involved in maintaining the aggregates.
Becoming disenchanted, he penetrates the Truths by way of the full understanding of suffering and so forth.
"This is the path to purification" means that this is the path for the sake of purification and for the sake of cleansing.
At the conclusion of the teaching, those bhikkhus were established in Arahatship, and the Dhamma teaching was fruitful for the assembled multitude as well.
The second basis for the characteristic of impermanence.
3. The Basis for the Characteristic of Suffering.
The second verse also has exactly the same basis. For at that time, the Blessed One [taught] to those bhikkhus regarding the characteristic of suffering...
Knowing that he had made his resolve, [the Buddha] said, “Bhikkhus, all aggregates are indeed suffering in the sense of being oppressive,” and spoke this verse:
“When one sees with wisdom that ‘all conditioned phenomena are suffering,’”
“Then one becomes disenchanted with suffering; this is the path to purification.
In this context, “suffering” (dukkhā) is so called in the sense of being oppressed. The rest is exactly as before.
This is the third section on the characteristic of suffering.
4. The Section on the Characteristic of Non-Self (Anattalakkhaṇa-vatthu).
The same method applies to the third verse as well. For here, the Blessed One, having known that those bhikkhus had previously been devoted to the characteristic of non-self, said:
"Bhikkhus, all aggregates indeed are non-self in the sense of being devoid of mastery."
Having spoken this, he uttered this verse:
“When one perceives with wisdom that all phenomena are non-self, then one becomes disenchanted with suffering; this is the path to purification.”
In this context, "all phenomena" (sabbe dhammā) refers specifically to the five aggregates (pañcakkhandhā).

"Non-self" (anattā) means that they cannot be brought under one's control by thinking, "May they not age, may they not die"; thus, in the sense of being subject to lack of mastery, they are non-self, empty of self, ownerless, and without a lord.
The remainder is exactly as before.
The fourth story on the characteristic of non-self (Anattalakkhaṇavatthu).
5. The Story of the Elder Tissa the Striver (Padhānakammikatissattheravatthu):
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, delivered this teaching on the Dhamma concerning the Elder Tissa the Striver, beginning with the words, "At the time for exertion..."
It is said that five hundred sons of good family residing in Sāvatthī went forth in the presence of the Teacher; having received a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), they departed for the forest.
One among them remained right there. The rest, practicing the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*) in the forest, attained Arahantship.
Thinking, "We shall report the qualities we have acquired to the Teacher," they returned again to Sāvatthī. From Sāvatthī...
Seeing them wandering for alms in a village only a *yojana* away, a certain lay devotee honored them with rice gruel, food, and other offerings;
having heard their words of thanksgiving, he invited them for the following day as well.
On that very day, they went to Sāvatthī, put away their bowls and robes, and in the evening approached the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down to one side. The Teacher—
Expressing great joy in their company, he engaged them in friendly conversation.
Then, as they remained there, the monk who was his companion thought to himself: "The Teacher has no leisure to engage in conversation with these people;
however, because I lack the path and its fruits, he does not speak with me."
“Having attained Arahatship this very day, I shall approach the Teacher and converse with him.
Those monks, however, looked toward the Teacher, saying, “Venerable Sir, we have been invited for tomorrow’s meal by a lay follower along the road we came;
we shall go there early in the morning. Then their companion monk spent the entire night...
While walking back and forth, he fell upon a stone slab at the end of the walkway due to falling asleep; his thigh bone was broken.
He cried out with a loud voice. His fellow monks, recognizing the sound, ran hither and thither.
Even as they lit a lamp and performed the necessary duties for him, the dawn broke; they [then went] to that village.
They did not obtain the opportunity to go. Then the Teacher said to them, "Bhikkhus, why did you not go to the village for alms?
They replied, "Yes, venerable sir," and reported what had happened. The Teacher said, "Bhikkhus, it is not only now that this one creates an obstacle to your gains;
he did so in the past as well. Having been requested by them, he brought up a story from the past:
“He who desires to do later what ought to be done earlier, like one who breaks a branch of the *varuṇa* tree, he grieves afterwards.

Thus he related the *Jātaka* in detail. At that time, it is said, those five hundred monks were the young brahmins; this monk was the indolent young brahmin, while the teacher was none other than the Tathāgata himself.

Having delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, the Teacher said: "Bhikkhus, he who does not exert himself at the time for exertion, whose resolve is slack, and who is indolent, does not attain the distinction consisting of the jhānas and other such qualities. Having said this, he spoke this verse:
"One who does not exert himself at the time for exertion, though young and strong, yet given over to laziness..."
“One whose intention and mind are sunken, being lazy and indolent, does not find the path through wisdom.
In this context, “one who does not exert himself” means one who does not strive or make effort. “A youth, strong” means one who stands in the prime of youth and is endowed with strength.
Having eaten, he becomes possessed of sloth; having eaten, he lies down.

"With a mind whose right intention is utterly collapsed" means one whose mind has its right intention (*sammā-saṅkappa*) completely degraded by the three types of wrong thoughts (*micchā-vitakka*). "Languid" means lacking energy. "Slothful" means a great sloth;
not seeing the Noble Path which is to be seen through wisdom, he does not find it, that is the meaning—he does not obtain it.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the fifth story, concerning the Elder Tissa the Striver. 6.
The Story of the Boar-Peta.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Veḷuvana, delivered this teaching on the Dhamma concerning a hungry ghost (peta) in the form of a pig. For one day, as the Elder Mahāmoggallāna was descending from Gijjhakūṭa together with the Elder Lakkhaṇa, he broke into a smile at a certain spot. When the Elder Lakkhaṇa asked, "Friend, what is the cause for your breaking into a smile? [Moggallāna replied: "Friend, in the past, during the time of the Buddha Kassapa... [and so forth]. He related how, in that era, there were two brothers who were brothers-in-dharma; the elder brother was a forest-dweller, while the younger brother lived in a village monastery. The elder brother, having attained the four jhānas, passed away and was reborn in the Brahma-world. The younger brother, however, being negligent in his duties, fell from his status and was reborn as a hungry ghost in the form of a pig. One day, when the elder brother descended from the Brahma-world to visit his younger brother, he saw him suffering in the realm of hungry ghosts. Seeing him, he said, "Alas, friend, you have fallen from such a state! Hearing this, the younger brother wept and cried out, "I am indeed fallen! I am indeed fallen! Then the elder brother said, "Friend, if you wish to be released from this suffering, you must guard your speech. Having spoken thus, he departed. It was because of this event that the Elder Moggallāna smiled. The Teacher, knowing the full significance of this, preached the Dhamma to the bhikkhus, beginning with the words, "Vācānurakkhī" (Guarding one's speech). Thus he spoke. The Teacher then related the story of the pig-hungry ghost in detail. At the conclusion of the discourse, the bhikkhus, having heard it, attained the fruit of Stream-entry. The Teacher then addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus, if one does not guard one's speech, one will fall into such a miserable state as this. Having said this, he further explained: "Bhikkhus, in the past, during the time of the Buddha Kassapa, there was a brother-in-dharma who lived in a village monastery. He was negligent in his duties and fell from his status, being reborn as a hungry ghost in the form of a pig. One day, his elder brother, who had been reborn in the Brahma-world, came down to see him and said, 'Friend, you have fallen! Hearing this, the younger brother wept and cried out, 'I am indeed fallen! I am indeed fallen! Then the elder brother said, 'Friend, if you wish to be released from this suffering, you must guard your speech. Having spoken thus, he departed. It was because of this that the Elder Moggallāna smiled. The Teacher then taught the Dhamma, beginning with the verse: "Vācānurakkhī...". At the conclusion of the discourse, many hundreds of bhikkhus attained the fruit of Stream-entry. The Teacher then addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus, if one does not guard one's speech, one will fall into such a miserable state as this. Having said this, he further explained: "Bhikkhus, in the past, during the time of the Buddha Kassapa, there was a brother-in-dharma who lived in a village monastery. He was negligent in his duties and fell from his status, being reborn as a hungry ghost in the form of a pig. One day, his elder brother, who had been reborn in the Brahma-world, came down to see him and said, 'Friend, you have fallen! Hearing this, the younger brother wept and cried out, 'I am indeed fallen! I am indeed fallen! Then the elder brother said, 'Friend, if you wish to be released from this suffering, you must guard your speech. Having spoken thus, he departed. It was because of this that the Elder Moggallāna smiled. The Teacher then taught the Dhamma, beginning with the verse: "Vācānurakkhī...". At the conclusion of the discourse, many hundreds of bhikkhus attained the fruit of Stream-entry. The Teacher then addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus, if one does not guard one's speech, one will fall into such a miserable state as this. Having said this, he further explained: "Bhikkhus, in the past, during the time of the Buddha Kassapa, there was a brother-in-dharma who lived in a village monastery. He was negligent in his duties and fell from his status, being reborn as a hungry ghost in the form of a pig. One day, his elder brother, who had been reborn in the Brahma-world, came down to see him and said, 'Friend, you have fallen! Hearing this, the younger brother wept and cried out, 'I am indeed fallen! I am indeed fallen! Having said this, he further explained: "Bhikkhus, in the past, during the time of the Buddha Kassapa, there was a brother-in-dharma who lived in a village monastery. He was negligent in his duties and fell from his status, being reborn as a hungry ghost in the form of a pig. One day, his elder brother
When asked, he said, "Friend, this is not the time for this question; you should ask me in the presence of the Teacher.
Then, having walked for alms in Rājagaha together with the Elder Lakkhaṇa, and having returned from the alms-round, he went to the Veḷuvana, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down.
Thereupon, the Elder Lakkhaṇa asked him about that matter. He replied: "Friend, I..."
“I saw one peta; his body was three gavutas in height and resembled a human body.
However, his head was like that of a pig, and a tail had grown from his mouth, from which worms were oozing out.
Having seen him and thinking, ‘I have never before seen such a being,’ I broke into a smile. The Teacher said, “You are truly possessed of vision...”
"Indeed, monks, my disciples dwell thus," having said this, he continued: "I too saw this being right at the seat of enlightenment.
However, out of compassion for others—thinking, 'It would be to their detriment if they were not to believe me'—I did not speak of it.
Now, making Moggallāna my witness, I speak. Truly, monks, Moggallāna..."
He said, "Eat. Having heard this, the monks asked the Teacher, "Venerable Sir, what was his past karma?
The Teacher said, "In that case, monks, listen," and having brought up the past, he related his past karma.
It is said that during the time of Buddha Kassapa, two elders lived in harmonious residence together in a certain village monastery. Of those two, one—
One was sixty years old, and the other was fifty-nine. The fifty-nine-year-old, taking up the bowl and robes of the other, traveled about and performed every duty and service just like a novice.
As they lived in harmony like brothers born from the same mother’s womb, a Dhamma-preacher arrived at their dwelling place. It was then the day for listening to the Dhamma.
The elders took him under their care and said, "Good man, please give us a discourse on the Dhamma. He delivered a discourse on the Dhamma.
The elders were delighted, thinking, "We have found a preacher of the Dhamma," and on the following day they took him with them into the village ahead for alms.
Having finished their meal there, they said, "Friend, from just a little way beyond the place where you spoke yesterday..."
“Preach the Dhamma,” they said, and thus they caused him to preach the Dhamma to the people. Having heard the discourse on the Dhamma, the people invited him for the following day as well.
In this manner, for two days at a time, they went for alms together with him in the surrounding villages where the monks wandered for food.
The preacher of the Dhamma thought: “These two are too soft; having made them both flee, I shall [establish them] in this monastery.”
“It is proper for me to dwell there. In the evening, he went to attend upon the elder;
when the other monks had risen and departed, he turned back, approached the Great Elder, and said, “Venerable sir, there is something that must be said.
When the elder replied, “Speak, friend,” he reflected for a moment and then said, “Venerable sir, this kind of talk is highly blameworthy,” and having said this, he departed without speaking further.
He went to another person as well and did exactly the same.

On the second day he did likewise, and on the third day, when their curiosity had become exceedingly great, he approached the Great Elder and said, "Venerable sir, there is something that must be said, yet I do not dare to say it in your presence. The Elder replied, "Very well, friend; speak."
Being pressed, he said: "But, venerable sir, is the junior elder one who shares in communion with you? "Good man, what are you saying?
We are like sons born from the same mother's womb; whatever one of us has obtained, the other has also obtained.
Have I ever seen any fault in him for all this time?"
“Yes, venerable sir,” he replied. “Indeed, friend,” [the elder said]. “Venerable sir, this junior elder spoke thus to me: ‘Good man, you are a son of noble family;
this great elder is modest and virtuous. When engaging in social intercourse with him, you should do so after careful examination.
It is in this way that he has been speaking to me since the day I arrived.”
Upon hearing this, the Great Elder’s mind was filled with anger, and he shattered like a potter’s vessel struck by a staff.
The other also rose, went to his fellow monk, and spoke in the same manner; he too shattered in that very way.
Although not even one among them had ever gone out for alms separately during all this time, on the following day they did so separately.
Having entered for alms, the junior elder arrived first and stood in the assembly hall, while the senior elder arrived later.
Seeing him, the junior elder thought, "Should I receive his bowl and robe, or not?
Although he thought, "I will not receive them now," he added, "Never mind; this has never been done by me before."

Thinking, “It is not right for me to neglect my own duty,” he softened his heart, approached the elder, and said, “Venerable sir, please give me your bowl and robe. The other replied, “Go away, you ill-behaved one!
You are not fit to receive my bowl and robe,” and snapped his fingers at him. He [the novice] said, “Yes, venerable sir, I too am yours...”
When it was said, "He thought, 'I will not accept the bowl and robe,'" [the elder] replied, "Friend novice, what are you thinking?
Do I have any attachment to this monastery? The other also said, "But why, venerable sir, do you think thus:
'I have some attachment to this monastery'? This monastery is yours," and having said so, he [offered] the bowl and robe.
He took [the bowl] and departed; the other also departed. Although they were traveling by the same road, one took the path by the western gate and the other by the eastern gate.
The preacher of the Dhamma said, "Venerable sir, do not do this, do not do this!
When the other replied, "Stay here, friend," he turned back. On the following day, he entered the village ahead.
When people asked him, "Venerable sir, where have the venerable ones gone?", he replied, "Friends, do not ask;
your own preceptors left yesterday after having a quarrel and departed. Although I entreated them, I was unable to turn them back.
Among them, the foolish remained silent, but the wise thought, "For so long a time, we have never seen any lapse on the part of the venerable ones."
"Never before have we seen such a thing; surely this fear has arisen because of him," they thought, and fell into dejection.
Those elder monks, too, found no peace of mind in the place where they had gone. The Great Elder reflected: "Alas, a heavy task has been set for this young monk!
For a mere moment, he addressed a visiting monk whom he had just seen, saying: 'By the Great Elder...'"
"Do not engage in communal enjoyment with him. The other also thought: "Oh, what a grave deed the Great Elder has committed!
To see a visiting monk for a mere moment, he says to him: 'Do not engage in communal enjoyment with this one.
For them, there was neither recitation nor mental application. After the passing of a hundred years, in the western direction, they [reached] a certain...
They went to the monastery. Only one lodging was available for them. After the Elder entered and sat down on the couch, the other also entered.
As soon as the Elder saw him, he recognized him and was unable to restrain his tears.
The other, too, recognized the Elder and, with eyes filled with tears, thought, "Shall I speak? Shall I not speak?"
“‘He is not to be trusted,’ [thinking thus], he paid homage to the Elder and said, ‘Venerable sir, for all this time I have traveled about carrying your bowl and robes;
have you ever seen anything improper in my physical conduct or other doors?
‘Nothing has been seen, friend. Then why did you say to the Dhamma-preacher, ‘Do not [speak] with him’?”
“Did you have sexual intercourse? “Friend, I do not speak thus; it seems this was said by you in my presence.

“I too, venerable sir, do not say so. At that moment, realizing, “This must have been said by him because he wishes to cause a schism between us,” they both confessed their transgression to one another. For a hundred years, they had found no delight in the mind.
On that day, having assembled together, they set out, saying, “Come, let us drive him out from that monastery,” and in due course they arrived at that monastery.
When the preacher of the Dhamma saw the elders, he approached them to receive their bowls and robes. The elders said, “You are not [fit to stay] in this place.”
“He is worthy to dwell in this monastery,” they exclaimed, clapping their hands. Unable to remain, he departed and fled at once.
Then, the ascetic practice he had maintained for twenty thousand years could no longer sustain him;
falling from there, he was reborn in Avīci. After being cooked there for the duration of an entire *buddhantara*, he has now appeared on Vulture Peak in the manner described.
“He experiences suffering through his own person.
Having brought forward this past deed of his, the Teacher said, “Monks, a monk indeed must be one whose form is peaceful in body and so forth,” and spoke this verse:
“Guarded in speech, well-restrained in mind, ...”
And let one not perform unwholesome deeds with the body;
one should purify these three paths of action and attain the path proclaimed by the Seer.
The meaning of this is as follows: By avoiding the four types of verbal misconduct, one guards speech;
by not giving rise to covetousness and the like, one is well-restrained in mind; and by abandoning killing and so forth, one should not perform unwholesome deeds with the body.
In this way, one should purify these three paths of kamma. For one who purifies them in this manner, [one is protected] by the Buddhas and others, the seekers of the aggregate of virtue and the rest.
"May you attain the Eightfold Path proclaimed by the Seers.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the sixth story, the *Sūkarapeta-vatthu*.
7. The Story of the Elder Poṭṭhila The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, gave this Dhamma teaching concerning the elder named Poṭṭhila.
It is said that he was a master of the Tipiṭaka in the dispensation of seven Buddhas and taught the Dhamma to five hundred bhikkhus.
The Teacher thought: "This bhikkhu does not even have the thought, 'I shall bring about my own escape from suffering';
I will cause him to feel spiritual urgency. From that time on, whenever the elder came to attend upon him, [the Teacher would say]:
"Come, empty Poṭṭhila! Pay homage, empty Poṭṭhila! Sit down, empty Poṭṭhila! Go away, empty Poṭṭhila!"
He said, "Tucchapoṭṭhila has gone. Even after he had risen and departed, he would say, "Tucchapoṭṭhila has gone.
He thought: "I maintain the three Piṭakas together with their commentaries; I teach the Dhamma to five hundred bhikkhus in eighteen great assemblies.
Yet the Teacher constantly calls me 'Tucchapoṭṭhila. Surely the Teacher [knows] me regarding [the attainment of] jhāna and so forth..."
"Because of his absence, he speaks thus. Stirred by a sense of urgency, he thought, "Now I shall enter the forest and practice the duty of a recluse.
Having himself prepared his bowl and robes, he set out at dawn, after all others had finished their studies, together with a monk who was departing.
As they sat in the courtyard reciting, [the other monks] addressed him as "Teacher."
They did not recognize him. Having traveled a road of two hundred yojanas, he approached a forest dwelling where thirty bhikkhus were living;
having paid homage to the senior of the Saṅgha, he said, "Venerable sir, be my refuge.
[The elder replied: "Friend, you are a preacher of the Dhamma; we ought to learn something by depending on you. Why [do you say this]?"
"Do you speak thus? "Venerable sir, do not do so; be my refuge. Yet all of them were indeed those whose taints were exhausted (*khīṇāsava*).
Then the Great Elder, thinking, "On account of this man's grasping, pride still exists," sent him to another elder.
He too spoke to him in the same way. Following this procedure, as they all sent him forth, he sat down in the daytime resting place.
They sent him to a seven-year-old novice who was performing needlework and was entirely junior to him.
In this way, they stripped him of his pride.
With his pride humbled, he extended his joined palms toward the novice and said, "Be my refuge, O noble man!"
He said: "Aho! Teacher, what is this you say? You are elders and highly learned;
I should have some reason to learn from your presence. "Do not do so, good man; rather, be my support.
"Venerable sir, if you will be able to endure my instruction, I shall be your support. "I am so, good man."

"When you say, 'I shall enter the fire,' I will indeed enter the fire," he replied. Then, pointing out a lake not far away, he said, "Venerable sir, enter this lake just as you are, with your lower and upper robes on as they are.
Although he already knew that the monk was wearing expensive double-layered robes, he spoke thus while testing him to see whether or not he was capable of following instruction.

The elder also entered the water with a single word. Then, when his corner of the robe was becoming wet, [the other] said, "Come, venerable sir," and having come with a single word and stood there, he said: "Venerable sir, there are six holes in a certain anthill;
a monitor lizard has entered through one hole, and wishing to catch it, [I have closed] the other five holes."

“Just as one seizes [an object] through the very opening made by breaking the sixth [door], so too, you yourselves, having closed the remaining five doors, should apply yourselves to work at the mind-door regarding objects that enter through the six doors. For a learned bhikkhu, this was like lighting a lamp;
he thought, “Let it be just this much, O noble ones,” and [directed his attention] toward the physical body.
Having applied his knowledge, he began the practice of the ascetic life.

Even while seated at a distance of two hundred yojanas, the Teacher looked upon that bhikkhu and thought, "Just as this bhikkhu possesses vast wisdom, so too it is fitting for him to establish himself [in the Dhamma].
Having thus reflected, he [conversed] with him.
As if speaking, he pervaded the area with radiance and uttered this verse:
“From application indeed arises abundance; from non-application, the destruction of abundance.
Having known these two paths—leading to existence and leading to non-existence—”
“One should settle oneself in such a way that wisdom increases.
In this context, “exertion” (*yoga*) refers to wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*) directed toward the thirty-eight objects of meditation.

“Wisdom” (*bhūrī*) is a name for extensive understanding that is equal to the earth. “Destruction” (*saṅkhaya*) means ruin. “This twofold path” refers to this exertion and non-exertion. For existence...
"And for non-existence, for growth, and for non-growth. "In such a way" means: one should establish oneself in such a manner that this wisdom, called "abundant," increases.
At the conclusion of the teaching, the Elder Poṭṭhila was established in Arahatship.
The Seventh Story: The Elder Poṭṭhila.
The Eighth Story: The Story of the Five Elders.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Cut down the forest," concerning a large number of elderly monks.
It is said that in their time as householders, they were wealthy family men in Sāvatthī who were friends with one another.
Performing meritorious deeds together, they heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma and, thinking, “We are old; what is the use of the household life to us?
they requested the Teacher for the going forth and were ordained. However, because of their advanced age, they were unable to master the Dhamma.
Having had a leaf-hut built on the outskirts of the monastery, they lived there together.
Even when going out for alms, they mostly went to the house of their wives and children to eat. Among them, one man’s former wife was named Madhurapācikā;
she was helpful to all of them. Why? Because all of them would take the food they had received and give it to her.
"Are they sitting and eating right there in the house? She too served them whatever curries and side dishes were available.
Then, afflicted by a certain illness, she passed away. Thereupon those elder monks gathered in the leaf-hut of their friend the elder;
seizing one another by the neck, they lamented and wept, crying out, "The laywoman Madhurapācikā has died! The monks [asked]...
Running toward him from all sides, they were asked, "What is this, friends? and they replied, "Venerable sir, our friend’s former wife has passed away;
she was extremely helpful to us. Now, from where shall we obtain another such as her?
It is for this reason that we are weeping."
The bhikkhus initiated a discussion in the Dhamma hall. The Teacher, having arrived, asked, "Bhikkhus, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, "About this very matter," he said, "Bhikkhus, it is not only now;
in the past as well, having been reborn in the womb of crows and wandering on the shore of the ocean, they were swept into the sea by a wave of the ocean."
“Having killed the crow, they wept and lamented, saying, ‘We shall carry him out,’ and they grew weary while trying to drain the great ocean with their beaks.
Having thus brought up the past, he said:
“Are not the jaws weary? And does not the mouth dry up?”
“We cannot reach the near shore nor the far shore; the great ocean is merely filling up.
Having related this Kāka-jātaka in detail, he addressed those bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, it is by depending on the forest of lust, hatred, and delusion that you have encountered this suffering.
It is fitting for you to cut down that forest; in this way, you shall be free from suffering.”
Having said, "You shall become so," he spoke these verses:
"Cut down the forest, not the tree; from the forest fear is born.
Having cut down both the forest and the undergrowth, O bhikkhus, be free from the forest."
“As long as the thicket of passion for women, even the slightest, is not cut away from a man,
so long is his mind bound.”
“Like a calf still nursing at its mother.
In this context, when the Teacher said, “Cut down the forest,” a desire to cut down trees arose in those who had recently gone forth,
as they thought, “The Teacher is having us cut down the forest by taking up axes and other tools.”
Then, denying that [the previous statement] by saying, "Do not [think of] trees," he said, "I spoke this with reference to the forest of defilements such as lust, not to actual trees.
Regarding the phrase "from the forest" (*vanato*): just as fear of lions and other beasts arises from an ordinary forest, so too does fear of birth and the like arise from the forest of defilements;
this is the meaning. As for the expression "the forest and the thicket" (*vanañ ca vanathañ ca*): here, large trees are called "the forest" (*vana*).

Because they are situated within that forest, the minor [defilements] are called "undergrowth" (*vanatha*). Alternatively, trees that have arisen previously are called "forest" (*vana*), while those that arise subsequently are called "undergrowth.
In the same way, the most powerful defilements that drag one into existence are called "forest," while those that yield results during the course of existence are called "undergrowth.
Those that have already arisen are called "forest," while those that arise again and again are called "undergrowth."
Both of these must be severed by the knowledge of the fourth path. Therefore he said:
“Having cut down both the forest and the undergrowth, become free from the forest, O bhikkhus. To be “free from the forest” means to be free from defilements (*nikkilesā*).
For as long as even this slightest undergrowth of defilement is not severed in a man regarding women, for that long he is like a suckling calf.
The meaning is that he was one whose mind was bound and whose heart was attached to her, as if to a mother.
At the conclusion of the teaching, all five of those elder monks were established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*); thus the Dhamma teaching was beneficial for those who had gathered.
This is the eighth story, the Story of the Five Elder Monks.
9. The Story of the Elder Suvaṇṇakāra “Cut them off!”—this teaching on the Dhamma was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a pupil of the Elder Sāriputta.
It is said that a handsome son of a goldsmith went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Elder Sāriputta. The Elder [said], “For young people...”
Thinking, "His lust is excessive," he gave him the meditation subject of the foul (*asubha-kammaṭṭhāna*) in order to counteract that lust.

However, that was unsuitable for him. Therefore, having entered the forest and exerted himself for three months without obtaining even a moment of one-pointedness of mind, he returned again to the Elder.
The Elder asked, "Friend, has the meditation subject been established for you?"

When he had spoken, he reported that situation. Then the Elder said to him, "It is not right to fall into despondency because the meditation subject is not succeeding," and after explaining that same meditation subject thoroughly once more, he gave it back to him.
On the second occasion as well, being unable to produce any distinction, he returned and reported this to the Elder. Then the Elder [explained] to him with its underlying reason...
Having made a comparison, he explained that very same meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). The monk returned once more and reported that his progress with the meditation subject was unsuccessful.
The Elder thought: “A practitioner understands that sensual desire and the other hindrances exist when they are present within himself, and that they do not exist when they are absent.
This monk is a practitioner, not a non-practitioner; he is one who is practicing, not...”
"He has not practiced it, yet I do not know his underlying disposition; he will be one who is to be converted by a Buddha.
Taking him with him, in the evening, he approached the Teacher and reported the entire matter, saying: "Venerable sir, this is my co-resident;
for this reason, I gave him such-and-such a meditation subject. He related all that had occurred.

Then the Teacher said, "This knowledge of the underlying tendencies and latent dispositions is the domain only of Buddhas who, having fulfilled the perfections and caused the ten-thousandfold world system to resound, have attained omniscience. Having said this, he reflected, "From what family did this man go forth?
and perceiving that it was from a goldsmith's family, he looked back into his past existences and saw that [the man] had indeed been in a goldsmith's family.
Seeing five hundred successive lifetimes produced in succession, he thought: "For a long time this youth has been performing the work of a goldsmith;
thinking, 'I shall make *kaṇikāra* flowers, lotus flowers, and so forth,' he has refined only red gold.
Therefore, the meditation subject of the loathsome and repulsive is not suitable for him; a pleasant meditation subject alone is appropriate for him."
