Having reflected thus, he said, "Sāriputta, today you shall see that very monk whom you have caused to weary himself for four months with a meditation subject has attained Arahatship this very day, even after his meal; now go," and having dismissed the Elder,
he created by means of his psychic power a golden lotus the size of a wheel, from which drops of water were falling from both the petals and the stalks.

Having done so, he gave it [to him], saying, “Bhikkhu, take this lotus, place it on a heap of sand at the edge of the monastery, sit cross-legged in a spot facing it, and perform the preliminary exercise, thinking, ‘It is red, it is red.
As soon as he took the lotus from the Teacher’s hand, his mind became serene. He went to the edge of the monastery, piled up the sand, and...
There, having inserted a lotus stalk [into his nostril] and sitting cross-legged facing it, he began the preliminary work, thinking, "The blood, the blood.
At that very moment, his hindrances were suppressed and access concentration arose.
Immediately thereafter, having attained the first jhāna and mastered it through the five modes of mastery, he...
Remaining seated as he was, having attained the second jhāna and the others, he became masterful and sat playing with the play of jhānas through the fourth jhāna.

The Teacher, knowing that the jhānas had arisen in him, looked to see whether he would be able to produce a further distinction by his own natural capacity; perceiving that he would not be able, [the Teacher] said, "Let this lotus wither."
"Make a resolution. That lotus, which he had been pressing with his hands, became black in color as if it were wilting.
Emerging from meditation, he looked at it and thought: "Why does this lotus appear to be struck by old age?

If even that which is not subject to grasping (*anupādiṇṇaka*) is thus overcome by old age, there is no need to mention that which is subject to grasping (*upādiṇṇaka*). For even this will be overcome by old age."

He perceived the characteristic of impermanence (*aniccalakkhaṇa*). When that is seen, the characteristic of suffering (*dukkhalakkhaṇa*) and the characteristic of non-self (*anattalakkhaṇa*) are necessarily seen as well.
To him, the three realms of existence (*bhava*) appeared like a blazing fire or like corpses tied to a staff.
At that moment, some boys not far from him had descended into a lake, plucked water lilies (*kumuda*), and were making a heap of them on the bank.

Thus he gazed at the water-lilies both in the water and on the land. Then, to him, the water-lilies in the water appeared beautiful, as if dripping with water, while the others were withered at their tips.
He thought, "Old age strikes even that which is not clung to; what then will it not strike in that which is clung to?
Thus he saw the characteristic of impermanence and the other characteristics even more clearly. The Teacher—
Knowing, "Now this bhikkhu’s meditation subject has become manifest," the Teacher, while still seated in the fragrant chamber, emitted a radiance that struck him in the face.
As he looked up, wondering, "What is this?", the Teacher appeared as if standing right before him.
He rose and extended his hands in reverential salutation. Then the Teacher [spoke] what was suitable for him.
Having observed this, he spoke this verse:
“Cut off your own affection, as one plucks an autumnal lily with the hand;
cultivate only the path to peace, the Nibbāna taught by the Sugata.”
In this context, "cut off" means cut off by means of the path of arahantship. "Autumnal" means produced during the autumn season.
"The path of peace" refers to the eightfold path leading to Nibbāna. "Cultivate" means increase. For Nibbāna has been taught by the Sugata;
therefore, the meaning is: "Develop its path."
At the conclusion of the teaching, that bhikkhu was established in arahantship.
This is the ninth story, the Story of the Elder Suvaṇṇakāra. 10.
The Story of the Merchant Mahādhanavaṇija.
While staying at Jetavana, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning a merchant named Mahādhanavāṇija.
It is said that he had come from Bārāṇasī to Sāvatthī for trade, having filled five hundred carts with cloth dyed with safflower.
Upon reaching the riverbank, he unyoked his carts right there, thinking, "I shall cross the river tomorrow."
It rained. A great cloud arose during the night and it rained. The river remained full of water for seven days.
The citizens also celebrated a festival for seven days. The work with the saffron-dyed cloths was not finished.
The merchant thought: "I have come from afar. If I go back again, there will be much delay. I shall stay right here for the rains."
“Having lived here working for me during the winter and summer, I shall sell these [goods].
The Teacher, wandering for alms in the city, perceived his thought and broke into a smile. When the Elder Ānanda asked the reason for the smile, he said:
“Ānanda, have you seen that merchant of great wealth? “Yes, venerable sir,” he replied. [The Teacher continued: “He has perceived a threat to his own life.”
“Not knowing this, he thought while staying right here for this year that he would sell his goods.
“But, Bhante, will there be an obstacle for him? “Yes, Ānanda; having lived for only seven days, he will fall into the jaws of death,” the Teacher said, and spoke these verses:
“Today itself is the time for effort; who knows if death will come tomorrow?
For we have no appointment with Death and his mighty army.
Thus should one dwell, ardent and untiring by day and night.”
“The Sage who is at peace indeed proclaims this as ‘One Fortunate Night.
“I shall go, Bhante; I will inform him,” [Ānanda said]. “Go with confidence, Ānanda,” [the Elder replied].
The Elder went to the place where the carts were and wandered for alms. The merchant waited upon the Elder with food. Then the Elder said to him: “How much...?”
“Will you dwell here for a long time? “Venerable sir, I have come from afar. If I were to go back now, it would cause much delay;
I shall stay here for this year, sell my goods, and then depart. “Lay follower, the danger to life is difficult to foresee;
it is right to practice heedfulness. “But what, venerable sir, will be the danger?”

“Yes, lay follower, your life will continue for only seven days more. With a heart filled with agitation, he invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, gave a great almsgiving for seven days, and then took the bowl for the sake of the expression of thanks.
Then, as the Teacher was giving the expression of thanks, he said: “Lay follower, a wise man indeed should not think, ‘I shall dwell right here during the rains and so forth.’”
“It is not right to think, ‘I shall employ this or that deed,’ but it is right to think only of the danger to one’s own life.
Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“I shall dwell here during the rains, and here during the winter and summer;”
"Thus the fool reflects, not perceiving the danger.
In this context, "I shall dwell here for the four months of the rains" means that while staying in this place, performing such and such tasks, he will spend the rainy season.
"In winter and summer" means that even during winter and summer, [he thinks], "Performing such and such tasks, I shall dwell right here for four months."
Thus the fool ponders, not knowing the welfare pertaining to this present life and the life to come.
He does not perceive the obstacle to his own life, thinking, "I shall die at such a time, in such a place, or at such an age.
At the conclusion of the teaching, that merchant was established in the fruit of stream-entry; thus the Dhamma teaching was fruitful for those who had assembled.
The merchant also followed the Teacher, but turning back, he lay down upon his bed, saying, "A headache as it were has arisen for me.
While lying thus, he passed away and was reborn in the Tusita heaven.
This is the tenth story, the Story of the Merchant of Great Wealth.

11. The Story of Kisāgotamī "This world is intoxicated by children and cattle"—the Teacher related this teaching on the Dhamma while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning Kisāgotamī. The background story is found in the Sahassa-vagga:
"Though one should live for a hundred years, Without seeing the deathless state; Better it is to live for a single day, Having seen the deathless state."
“A single day’s life is better for one who sees the deathless state.
Having explained this at length in the commentary on the verse, the Teacher then said, “Kisāgotamī, have you obtained even a single mustard seed?
She replied, “I have not, venerable sir; it is said that in the entire village the dead are more numerous than those still living.”
Then the Teacher said to him, “You perceived, ‘Only my son has died,’ yet this is the inevitable law for all beings.
For King Death drags away all beings while their aspirations are still unfulfilled, casting them into the ocean of the states of misery as if with a great flood.
Having spoken thus, he taught the Dhamma by reciting this verse:
“Death carries away that man who is intoxicated by children and cattle, whose mind is distracted,
just as a great flood sweeps away a sleeping village.
In this context, “intoxicated by children and cattle” means having obtained children and cattle endowed with beauty, strength, and other such qualities.
"My sons are handsome, endowed with strength, wise, and capable of performing all tasks;
my oxen are handsome, healthy, and able to carry heavy burdens; my cow yields much milk"—thus a man who is attached to his children and livestock.
"With a distracted mind" means having acquired something, whether it be gold and silver or a bowl and robes, and then [becoming attached to them].
Or "with mind attached" means with a mind drawn toward a superior aspiration;
or "with mind distracted" means with a mind clinging to whatever has been obtained among the objects cognizable by the eye and so forth, or among the aforementioned requisites.
"The village asleep" refers to a group of beings who have fallen into sleep. "Like a great flood" means as [a flood sweeps through] such a village...
The meaning is that just as the vast, deep, and great flood of the mighty rivers goes on, carrying everything away without leaving behind even a dog,
so too does Death carry away a person of the kind described.
At the conclusion of the teaching, Kisāgotamī was established in the fruit of stream-entry, and the Dhamma teaching was beneficial for all those who were present.
The Story of Kisāgotamī, the eleventh.
12. The Story of Paṭācārā.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning Paṭācārā, beginning with the words, "There are no sons. The narrative is found in the Sahassa-vagga.
“Better to live for a single day seeing the rise and fall [of phenomena] than to live for a hundred years without seeing the rise and fall.
Having explained this at length in the commentary on the verse, the Teacher then recognized that Paṭācārā’s grief had become attenuated.
“Paṭācārā, children and the like cannot become a protection, a shelter, or a refuge for one going to the next world;
therefore, even though they exist, they do not truly exist. But it is fitting for a wise person, having purified their virtue, to purify the very path leading to their own Nibbāna.
Having said this, he spoke these verses while teaching the Dhamma:
“Sons are no protection, nor father, nor even kinsmen;
for one seized by the End-Maker, there is no refuge among relatives.
Knowing this fact, the wise person is restrained by virtue.”
“One should quickly purify the path leading to Nibbāna.
In this context, “for protection” means for the sake of a state of refuge, for the purpose of a firm foundation. “Relatives” refers to all kinsmen and friends, excluding one’s children and parents.
“Of one seized by the End-maker” means of one overcome by death. For in the course of worldly existence, children and the like—

Although they have been a refuge by means of giving food, drink, and so forth, and by rescuing one from arisen misfortunes, they are nonetheless said not to exist as a refuge or a shelter because they are incapable of warding off death by any means whatsoever at the time of death. For this very reason it was said:
"There is no refuge among kinsmen. This is the underlying meaning: thus, there is no mutual refuge among them.

Having understood the cause known as the state of being incapable [of attaining Nibbāna], the wise person, being restrained by the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla) and remaining guarded and protected, should quickly, very quickly, purify the Eightfold Path leading to Nibbāna; this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, Paṭācārā was established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala), and many others attained the fruits of stream-entry and the other stages.
The twelfth story, that of Paṭācārā.
The commentary on the Maggavagga is finished.
The twentieth chapter.
21. The Miscellaneous Chapter.
1. The Story of One’s Own Former Deeds.
Regarding the teaching on the Dhamma entitled "The Relinquishing of Limited Happiness," the Teacher delivered this discourse while dwelling at Veḷuvana, referring to his own former deeds.
For at one time Vesālī was prosperous, flourishing, populous, and crowded with people.
There, indeed, there were seven thousand seven hundred and seven kṣatriyas who ruled by turns.
For their residence, there were just as many palaces, just as many gabled houses, and pleasure gardens.
For the sake of monasteries, there were exactly that many parks and lotus ponds. At a later time, however, there was a famine and a failure of crops.
There, due to the fear of drought, first the destitute people passed away.
Because of the stench of their corpses discarded here and there, non-human beings (amanussa) entered the city. Due to this calamity caused by the non-humans...
Many more died. Because of the loathsome stench of their corpses, a plague broke out among the beings.
Thus, three fears arose: the fear of famine, the fear of non-human spirits, and the fear of disease.
The city-dwellers gathered together and said to the king: "Great King, there are three fears in this city."
“Such a danger as this has never arisen before, from now back through seven royal successions.
Indeed, such a danger arises only in the time of unrighteous kings. The king, having caused everyone to assemble in the assembly hall, said:
“If there is any unrighteousness in me, investigate it! Then all the inhabitants of Vesālī...
Investigating the lineage and finding no fault whatsoever in the king, they said, "Great King, there is no fault in you," and then deliberated,
"How indeed might this fear of ours be pacified? Thereupon, when some suggested, "By means of offerings, supplications,
and auspicious rites," they performed that entire ritual procedure, yet they were unable to ward it off.
Then others spoke thus: "There are six teachers of great power; when they have merely arrived here, this fear will be stilled.
Others said: "A Perfectly Enlightened One has appeared in the world. For that Blessed One teaches the Dhamma for the welfare of all beings;
he is of great psychic power and great majesty. When he has come here, these fears will be stilled. To them—
Having rejoiced in those words, they all asked, "Where does that Blessed One dwell at present?
At that time, as the commencement of the rainy season was approaching, the Teacher had given his promise to King Bimbisāra and was dwelling in the Bamboo Grove.
On that occasion, during the assembly with Bimbisāra, [he had attained] the fruit of stream-entry together with Bimbisāra.
The Licchavi named Mahāli was sitting in that assembly.

The inhabitants of Vesālī, having prepared a great gift and informed King Bimbisāra, sent the Licchavi Mahāli and the son of the family priest with the message: "Bring the Teacher here. They went and [delivered] the king's gift...
Having given that and reported the news, they requested, "Great King, please send the Teacher to our city.
The king did not accept, saying, "You yourselves must know best. They approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and requested:
"Venerable Sir, three dangers have arisen in Vesālī; these will be pacified when you have arrived."
"Come, venerable sir, let us go. Having heard their words, the Teacher reflected and understood:
"When the Ratana Sutta is recited in Vesālī, that protection will pervade hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems;
at the conclusion of the discourse, eighty-four thousand living beings will attain realization of the Dhamma, and those fears will be pacified. Knowing this, he said:
He accepted their words.
King Bimbisāra, having heard that the Teacher had indeed accepted the journey to Vesālī, caused a proclamation to be made throughout the city;
then, approaching the Teacher, he asked, "Venerable sir, has the journey to Vesālī been accepted?"
When he replied, “Yes, Great King,” the king said, “In that case, venerable sir, please wait; we shall prepare the road.

Having said this, he leveled the ground for five leagues between Rājagaha and the Ganges, established a monastery every league, and announced the time for the Teacher’s departure. The Teacher, together with five hundred bhikkhus, [set out].

He set out upon the road. At intervals of one *yojana*, the king had the ground strewn knee-deep with flowers of five colors, hoisted flags, banners, plantain trees, and other ornaments, and provided for the Blessed One a parasol over a parasol (*chattātichatta*).
He had two white parasols held above each individual monk, and together with his retinue, he honored them with flowers, perfumes, and other offerings.
While performing the worship, he had the Teacher stay in each monastery in turn, and after giving great alms and other offerings, he brought him to the banks of the Ganges in five days.
There, while decorating a boat, he sent a message to the people of Vesālī, saying:
"Prepare the road and go out to meet the Teacher. They [responded], "We shall perform double the worship," and from Vesālī...
Having leveled the ground for three *yojanas* between the [city] and the Ganges,
and having prepared parasols over parasols— providing four white parasols for the Blessed One and two white parasols for each individual monk—

they arrived while performing worship and stood upon the bank of the Ganges. King Bimbisāra, having joined two boats together and constructed a pavilion adorned with flower garlands and other ornaments...
Having had it adorned, he prepared a Buddha-seat made entirely of jewels. The Blessed One sat upon it.
The monks also, having boarded the boat, sat down surrounding the Blessed One.
Following after them, the king descended into water reaching up to his neck and said, "Venerable Sir, until the Blessed One returns, I shall remain right here on the bank of the Ganges."
Having spoken thus and dismissed the boat, he turned back. The Teacher traveled a distance of one *yojana* along the Ganges and reached the boundary of the Vesālī people.
The Licchavi kings went out to meet the Teacher, descended into the water up to their necks, brought the boat to the shore, and helped the Teacher disembark from the vessel.
As soon as the Teacher had stepped onto the bank, a great cloud arose.
A rain of lotuses fell. Everywhere, waters flowing knee-deep, thigh-deep, waist-deep, and so forth, carried all the corpses into the Ganges, and the ground became completely pure.
The Licchavi kings, having lodged the Teacher at intervals of one *yojana* each and given great alms, performed double the usual honor for three days as they proceeded toward Vesālī.
They led him away. Sakka, the king of the gods, arrived surrounded by a host of deities;
due to the gathering of these powerful devas, the non-human beings for the most part fled. In the evening, the Teacher stood at the city gate and addressed the Elder Ānanda:
"Ānanda, having learned this Ratana Sutta, wander through Vesālī together with the Licchavi youths."
“Perform a protective rite (*paritta*) within the space between the three walls.
Having learned the *Ratana Sutta* bestowed by the Teacher, the Elder took water in a stone bowl from the Teacher and stood at the city gate;
beginning from the [Elder’s] aspiration, he recited the Tathāgata’s ten perfections (*pāramī*) and ten near-perfections (*upapāramī*).
The ten ultimate perfections (*paramattha-pāramī*) comprise the thirty perfections (*pāramī*);

the three modes of conduct (*cariyā*), namely the conduct for the sake of the world, the conduct for the sake of one’s kinsmen, and the conduct for the sake of Buddhahood; the five great renunciations;

the descent into the womb in the final existence, the birth, the Great Departure, the practice of striving, the conquest of Māra at the seat of enlightenment, the penetration of omniscient knowledge, and the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma.

Having recollected all these qualities of the Buddha—namely, the nine supramundane states—he entered the city and wandered about throughout the three watches of the night, reciting the *paritta* within the three lines of the city wall.

Consequently, as soon as he uttered the words "Whatever there may be," the water thrown upwards fell upon the non-human spirits (*amanussa*). From the moment he began reciting the verse beginning with "Those beings here... [the protection was established].
Like silver ornaments, drops of water traveled through the air and fell upon the sick people.
At that very moment, their diseases were pacified, and the people rose up one after another and surrounded the Elder.
From the words "whatever [there may be]" onwards, all those touched by the spray of water—whether dwelling on heaps of refuse, against walls, or in other places—did not flee.
The non-human beings fled through this door and that door. The doors became blocked. Finding no other way out, they even broke through the rampart wall to escape.
The great multitude, having smeared the assembly hall in the center of the city with all kinds of perfumes, decorated its upper surface with golden stars and other ornaments.
Having strung up a canopy and prepared a seat for the Buddha, he brought the Teacher. The Teacher sat down on the prepared seat.
The community of monks and the Licchavi assembly also sat down, surrounding the Teacher. Sakka, the king of the gods, stood in a suitable place surrounded by a host of deities.
The Elder, too, having wandered through the entire city, [returned] with the great multitude whose diseases had been pacified.
Having arrived together and paid homage to the Teacher, he sat down. The Teacher, surveying the assembly, recited that very Ratana Sutta.
At the conclusion of the teaching, eighty-four thousand beings attained penetration of the Dhamma.
On the following day as well—and thus for seven days—he taught that same Ratana Sutta. Then, knowing that all fears had been stilled, [he addressed] the Licchavi host.
Having addressed them, he departed from Vesālī. The Licchavi kings, providing double the honor, led the Teacher back to the banks of the Ganges in three days.
The Nāga kings born in the Ganges thought: "The humans are paying honor to the Tathāgata; we..."

"What shall we not do? Having fashioned boats made of gold, silver, and jewels, and having prepared couches made of gold, silver, and jewels, they filled the water with lotuses of five colors and requested the Teacher, saying, "Venerable Sir, please show us favor as well," beseeching him to board their respective boats. "Both humans and nāgas..."
"Since they perform worship for the Tathāgata, why should we not do so?
Beginning with the earth-dwelling deities (*bhūmaṭṭhaka-deva*) and extending up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahmā-world, all the gods paid their respects.

Therein, the *nāgas* raised parasols and super-parasols a league in height. Thus, from below, the *nāgas* on the surface of the earth, those dwelling among trees, shrubs, and mountains, and the earth-dwellers—

The deities—the sky-dwelling gods of the atmosphere—beginning from the abode of the *nāgas* and extending as far as the Brahma-world at the edge of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), raised parasols upon parasols.

Between the parasols were banners; between the banners, flags; and in the intervals between them, there was honor paid with flower garlands, perfumes, powders, incense, and so forth. [They appeared] adorned with every kind of ornament.
The sons of the gods, assuming festive attire, wandered through the sky proclaiming their joy. It is said that there were only three great assemblies:
the assembly at the Twin Miracle, the assembly at the Descent from the Heavens, and this assembly at the Descent into the Ganges.
On the opposite bank, King Bimbisāra, having prepared twice the honor shown by the Licchavis, [prepared for] the Blessed One...

He stood waiting for the Teacher’s arrival. The Teacher, having observed the great generosity of the kings on both banks of the Ganges and having understood the inclinations of the Nāgas and others, manifested a created Buddha (nimmitabuddha) accompanied by a retinue of five hundred bhikkhus in each boat.
Each of these was attended by a white parasol, a wish-fulfilling tree (kapparukkha), and a canopy of flowers.

And below, he sat surrounded by hosts of *nāgas*. Among the earth-dwelling deities (*bhūmaṭṭhaka-devatā*) and others as well, in each respective place, he manifested a created Buddha (*nimmita-buddha*) together with his retinue.

Thus, when the entire interior of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) had become a single ornament, a single festival, and a single celebration, the Teacher, bestowing favor upon the *nāgas*, embarked upon a jeweled ship. [He did the same] for the monks as well.

Each one climbed up alone. The Nāga kings, having led the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha into the Nāga realm, listened to a discourse on the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher throughout the entire night.

On the following day, they served the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha with divine hard food and soft food. After the Teacher had given his expression of thanks, he departed from the Nāga realm.
Having departed, while being honored by the deities throughout the entire Cakkavāḷa, he crossed the river Gaṅgā in five hundred ships.

The King went out to meet him, helped the Teacher disembark from the ship, and having performed twice the honor that had been shown to the Licchavis upon his arrival, he escorted him to Rājagaha over the course of five days in the same manner as before. On the second day...
When the monks had returned from their almsround and were seated together in the Dhamma hall in the evening, they raised this discussion:
"Oh, how great is the majesty of the Buddhas! Oh, how great is the faith of gods and humans in the Teacher!
Along the eight-league road on both sides of the Ganges, the kings, out of faith directed toward the Buddha, have made the ground level."
"It was strewn with sand; various colored flowers were spread out to a depth reaching the knees;
by the power of the Nāgas, the waters of the Ganges were covered with five-colored lotuses;
and from the Akaniṭṭha realm upwards, parasols and super-parasols were raised, so that the entire interior of the Cakkavāḷa became as if a single ornament and a single festival. The Teacher arrived.
“Monks, for what discussion have you gathered here now? he asked.
When they replied, “For this very discussion,” he said, “Monks, this honor and hospitality was not produced by my own power as a Buddha, nor by the power of the nāgas, devas, or brahmās.
Rather, it was produced by the power of a small act of renunciation in the past. Having said this, being requested by the monks, he related the past.

In the past, in Takṣaśilā, there was a brahmin named Saṅkha. His son, a young brahmin student named Susīma, sixteen years of age, approached his father one day and said, "Father, I wish to go to Bārāṇasī to study the mantras.
Then his father said to him, "In that case, my son, such-and-such a brahmin is my friend;..."
“Go to him and study under him. Having assented with “Very well,” he traveled by stages to Bārāṇasī, approached that brahmin, and informed him that he had been sent by his father.
Then, accepting him as “the son of my friend,” the brahmin’s distress subsided, and on an auspicious day, he began to teach him the mantras.
Thus, grasping both quickly and extensively, and retaining what he had learned without loss—
like lion’s oil poured into a golden vessel— he soon mastered everything that was to be learned from his teacher.
While reciting it, however, he saw only the beginning and middle of the craft he had acquired, but not its conclusion.
So he approached his teacher and said, "I see only the beginning and the middle of this craft, but not its conclusion.
When the teacher replied, "I too do not see it, dear son," he asked, "Then who, teacher, knows the conclusion?
[The teacher said,] "These seers, dear son, dwell at Isipatana; they would know it. Go to them..."
When the teacher said, "Go and ask him," he approached the Paccekabuddha and asked:
"I have heard that you know the ultimate goal; is this true? "Yes, we know it. "Then please explain it to me.
"We do not explain it to those who have not gone forth. If you have need of the ultimate goal, go forth [into the religious life]. He accepted this, saying, "Very well."

He went forth in their presence. Then, saying to him, "First, train in this," they instructed him in the rules of proper conduct (*ābhisamācārika*) by way of such directions as, "It must be worn like this; it must be put on like this.

While training therein, because he was endowed with the necessary spiritual potential (*upanissaya*), he soon after awakened to the enlightenment of a Pacceka Buddha throughout the entire city of Bārāṇasī.
Manifest like the full moon in the vault of the sky, he attained the pinnacle of gain and the pinnacle of fame;

yet, because he had performed an action conducive to a short lifespan, he passed away into *parinibbāna* before long. Then both the *paccekabuddhas* and the great multitude, having performed the funeral rites for his body and taken his relics, erected a stupa at the city gate.
The brahmin Saṅkha, thinking, “My son has been gone for a long time;
I shall learn news of him,” and desiring to see him, departed from Takkasilā and eventually reached Bārāṇasī.
Seeing a great multitude of people gathered together, he thought, “Surely at least one among these will know news of my son. He approached them and asked, “Susīma—”
“A young brahmin named Māṇava has come here; do you know anything of his history? “Yes, brahmin, we know:
having mastered the three Vedas in the presence of such-and-such a brahmin, he went forth, realized pratyekabodhi, and attained final nibbāna;
this stupa has been erected for him. Having struck the ground with his hand, he wept.
Having wept, he went to that cetiya courtyard, cleared away the grass, brought sand in his upper robe and scattered it over the cetiya courtyard;
having sprinkled water from his water-pot and made an offering with wild forest flowers,
he fastened a banner with his robe, tied his own sunshade atop the stupa, and departed.
The Teacher, having brought up this past event, said: "Monks, at that time I was the brahmin Saṅkha.
I cleared away the grass from the terrace of the Paccekabuddha Susīma’s shrine;
as the result of that deed, they made a road eight yojanas long free of stumps and thorns, leveling it smooth. I scattered sand there."
By the result of that [merit], they scattered sand over a road eight yojanas long. I made an offering there with forest flowers;

by the result of that, various colored flowers were strewn over a road eight yojanas long, and in one place for a distance of one yojana, the water of the Ganges was covered with five-colored lotuses. There, I [sprinkled] the ground with water from my water-pot.
It was sprinkled [with water]; by the result of that act for me, a rain of lotuses fell upon Vesālī.

There, I raised banners and fixed up a parasol; by the result of that act for me, as far as the Akaniṭṭha realm, the entire interior of the world-system became like a single festival with flags, banners, parasols, and super-parasols. Thus indeed, monks, is this honor and hospitality.

"Neither by the power of a Buddha, nor by the power of a Nāga, a Deva, or a Brahmā was this produced for me; rather, it is through the power of small sacrifices made in the past," he said, and while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
"If, by sacrificing a small pleasure, one might see a vast happiness..."
“The wise man, seeing the vast happiness, should relinquish limited happiness.
In this context, “limited happiness” (*mattāsukha*) refers to a small amount of pleasure that is measured;
it is by the relinquishing of that. “Vast happiness” (*vipulaṃ sukhaṃ*) refers to sublime happiness, which is called the happiness of Nibbāna; “if he should see that” means...
The meaning is this: for one who prepares and eats a single bowl of food, a certain limited pleasure indeed arises;
yet, by relinquishing that [pleasure] and either observing the Uposatha or giving a gift, a vast and sublime pleasure called Nibbāna is produced. Therefore, if such [limited] pleasure of his...
"Through renunciation one sees vast happiness; thus, seeing that vast happiness correctly, the wise person should abandon that limited pleasure.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
The First Story on One’s Own Previous Deeds.
2. The Story of the Chicken-Egg Eater.
Regarding the teaching on the Dhamma beginning with "By causing suffering to others," the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain chicken-egg eater.
It is said that not far from Sāvatthī there was a village named Paṇḍura, where a certain fisherman lived.
While traveling to Sāvatthī, he saw tortoise eggs in the Aciravatī River; taking them with him, he went to Sāvatthī and had them cooked in a certain house.
As he was eating them, he gave one egg to a young girl in that house. After she ate it, from that...
From that time on, she desired no other kind of food. Then her mother took an egg from the place where the hen had laid them and gave it to her.
Having eaten it, she became bound by craving for its flavor; from then on, she herself would take the eggs from the hen and eat them.
Whenever the hen was about to lay, she would take her own eggs and eat them. The hen—[seeing her] taking her own eggs and eating them—[became distressed].
Having seen this, she was overcome by resentment; harboring ill will, she made a resolution:
"When I pass away from here, may I be reborn as a female *yakkha* capable of devouring your newborn child.
Having died, she was reborn in that very house as a cat. The other woman also died and was reborn in that same place as a hen.
A hen laid her eggs; a cat came and ate them, and did so a second and a third time as well.
The hen made this aspiration: “After eating my eggs three times, you now wish to eat me too.
Having passed away from here, may I be able to eat her along with her offspring. Having passed away from there, she was reborn as a leopardess. The other [hen] also...
Having died, she was reborn as a doe. At the time of her giving birth, a leopardess came and devoured her along with her fawns.
Thus, for five hundred successive existences, they caused suffering to one another while devouring each other;
finally, one was reborn as a female *yakkha* and the other was reborn as a daughter of a noble family in Sāvatthī. Hereafter—
This is to be understood according to the method stated in the verse: “For by hatred, hatreds are not stilled.
Here, however, the Teacher, having said, “For hatred is stilled by non-hatred, not by hatred,” spoke this verse while teaching the Dhamma to both of them:
“He who seeks his own happiness by inflicting suffering upon others...”
“Entangled in association with enmity, one is not released from that enmity.
In this context, “by inflicting suffering upon another” means by placing suffering upon another; the meaning is: by producing suffering for another.
“Entangled in association with enmity” refers to a person who [engages in] reviling, counter-reviling, striking back, counter-striking, and so forth.
"Entangled by association with enmity" means being involved with one another through the mutual practice of hostility.
"He is not released from enmity" means that, due to the persistence of enmity, he constantly encounters nothing but suffering.

At the conclusion of the teaching, the female spirit (yakkhinī) established herself in the refuges, undertook the five precepts, and was freed from her enmity; the other woman also attained the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). Thus, the teaching of the Dhamma was truly beneficial for those who were present.
The second story: The Story of the Chicken-Egg Eater.
3. The Story of the Bhikkhu Bhaddiya.
The Teacher delivered this Dhamma teaching, "For that which ought to be done," while dwelling in the Jātiyā Grove near Bhaddiya, concerning the bhikkhus of Bhaddiya.
They were, it seems, devoted to the practice of adorning their sandals. As it is said: “At that time, the Bhaddiya monks lived devoted to various kinds of practices for adorning sandals;
they made sandals of grass themselves or had them made, they made sandals of muñja-grass themselves or had them made, [as well as] sandals of pabbaja-grass, hintāla-grass, and kamala-grass.”
“They even make woolen sandals for themselves or have them made, and they neglect the recitation, the questioning, the higher virtue, the higher mind, and the higher wisdom.
When the monks learned that they were acting in such a manner, they complained and informed the Teacher.
The Teacher rebuked those monks, saying: “Monks, you have come with one purpose, yet you are occupied with something quite different.”
Having said, "Those who are engaged in what ought to be done," he spoke these verses while teaching the Dhamma:
"For when what ought to be done is neglected, and what ought not to be done is performed,
the taints increase for those who are arrogant and heedless."
“But for those whose mindfulness directed to the body is well-undertaken and constant,
who do not engage in what should not be done, but act with persistence in what should be done—
for those who are mindful and clearly comprehending, the taints come to an end.”

In this context, "duty" refers to such things as a bhikkhu’s guarding of the immeasurable aggregate of virtue from the time of his going forth, dwelling in the forest, maintaining the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), and delighting in meditation; these are what constitute duty.
However, by these [actions], whatever was his own duty has been cast aside and abandoned. "Non-duty" refers to a bhikkhu’s adorning himself with a sunshade or adorning himself with sandals.
Wearing sandals, using an alms-bowl stand, using a spittoon, wearing a waist-band, and wearing a shoulder-strap are called "improper acts.

For those who perform these, having cast aside the sense of shame (*hrī*), being arrogant in their conduct, and being negligent through the loss of mindfulness (*smṛti*), the four taints (*āsrava*) increase—this is the meaning.
"Well undertaken" means well-grasped. "Mindfulness directed toward the body" refers to the cultivation of the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupaśyanā*).
"Non-duty" (*akicca*) means they do not resort to or perform such things as the decoration of the parasol and so forth.

"Duty" (*kicca*) refers to the tasks to be performed from the time of going forth, such as the guarding of the immeasurable aggregates of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*). "Those who act with persistence" (*sātaccakārino*) means those who act constantly and without interruption.
For them, through the non-departure of mindfulness, there is "clear comprehension of what is beneficial for those who are mindful" (*satānaṃ sātthakasampajaññaṃ*).

The meaning is that for those who are clearly comprehending through the four kinds of clear comprehension—clear comprehension of what is suitable, clear comprehension of the range, and clear comprehension of non-delusion—the four taints go to their end; they reach exhaustion and non-existence.
At the conclusion of the teaching, those bhikkhus were established in arahantship, and the teaching of the Dhamma was fruitful for those present as well.
The Third Story of Bhaddiya.
4. The Story of the Elder Lakuṇḍaka-Bhaddiya.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning the Elder Lakuṇḍaka-Bhaddiya.

One day, a number of visiting bhikkhus approached the Teacher as he was sitting in the daytime resting place, and after paying homage, they sat down to one side. At that moment, the Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya was passing by not far from the Blessed One.
The Teacher, knowing the mental disposition of those bhikkhus, looked at them and said, "Behold, bhikkhus!"
"This monk, having killed his mother and father, goes on free from suffering. When the monks said to one another, "What indeed is the Teacher saying?
and looked at each other's faces with minds overcome by doubt, they asked, "Venerable sir, what is this you are saying?
Thereupon, teaching them the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
“Having slain mother and father, and two kshatriya kings, and having destroyed the kingdom along with its subjects, the brahmin goes free from affliction.
In this context, “along with its subjects” means together with the ministers and officials who carry out the king’s business. For it is said here: “Craving generates the person.”
Craving is called the mother because it gives birth to beings within the three realms of existence by way of speech.
The conceit "I am" (asmimāna) is called the father because the conceit arises dependent upon a father, such as thinking, "I am the son of such-and-such a king or a royal minister.
Just as the world follows a king, all speculative views fall under two categories: the views of eternalism and annihilationism.

Therefore, the two views of eternalism and annihilationism are called the two "Khattiya kings. The twelve sense-bases (āyatana), in their extensive sense, are called the "kingdom" because they resemble a realm.
Craving and lust, which depend upon them, are called the "retainers," like a subordinate official who seeks his own livelihood.
"Anigho" means free from suffering. A "Brāhmaṇa" is one whose taints (āsava) are exhausted. By means of the sword of the knowledge of the path to Arhatship, these [defilements] such as craving—
"The meaning here is this: having been freed from the taints and being one whose cankers are exhausted, he goes forth as one free from suffering.
At the conclusion of the teaching, those monks were established in Arahatship.
The story for the second verse is exactly like the first. For at that time, the Teacher spoke concerning the Elder Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya alone. While teaching them the Dhamma, he uttered this verse:
“Having slain mother and father, and two peaceful kings, and having slain the tiger as the fifth, the brahmin goes free from suffering.
In this verse, “two peaceful kings” refers to two brahmins. By means of his own mastery over the Dhamma, the Teacher [spoke] this verse.
And because of his skill in the methods of teaching, he spoke after having formulated [the discourse] regarding the two views of eternalism and annihilationism, as well as the two brahmin kings.
Regarding the term *Veyagghapañcama*: here, the path frequented by tigers (*byaggha*), which is perilous and difficult to traverse, is called "tiger-path" (*veyaggha*);

likewise, the hindrance of doubt (*vicikicchā-nīvaraṇa*) is called "tiger" (*veyaggha*) due to its similarity to that [path]. That [hindrance] is the fifth, thus it is the "pentad of hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa-pañcaka*).

This is called "The Leopard as the Fifth. Having completely destroyed this "Leopard as the Fifth" with the sword of the knowledge of the path to Arahatship, he goes free from distress—a brahmin; such is the meaning here. The rest is exactly as before.
This is the fourth story, concerning the Elder Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya.
5. The Story of the Wood-Cart Driver’s Son.
The Teacher, while residing at Veḷuvana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning the son of a wood-cart driver.
For in Rājagaha there were two boys, the son of a man with right view and the son of a man with wrong view, who constantly played with marbles.

They played together. Among them, the son of one with right view, while throwing the sugar balls, would recollect the recollection of the Buddha and, saying "Homage to the Buddha" again and again, he would throw the ball.
The other, enumerating the qualities of the heretics, would say "Homage to the Arhats" again and again and throw [his ball].
Of these two, the son of the one with right view won, while the other lost. He [the loser] said to him:
Seeing his deed, [the boy] thought, "By recollecting in this way and speaking thus while throwing the sugar, he defeats me; I too shall do the same.
Thus, he practiced the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*).
Then one day, his father, having yoked a cart and gone for the sake of firewood, took that boy along and went into the forest, where the cart was [loaded] with wood.
Returning after having filled [the cart], he released his oxen at a place convenient for water near a cemetery on the outskirts of the city and took his meal.
Then, as he was entering the city in the evening, those oxen entered the city along with a herd of cattle.
The cartwright, following after the oxen, entered the city; seeing the oxen there in the evening, he took them and departed.
He did not reach the gate; for even before he had arrived, the gate was closed.
Then his son, being alone, lay down beneath the cart during the night and fell asleep.
Now, Rājagaha was naturally abounding in non-human beings (amanussa), and he was lying near a cemetery. There, two non-human beings [approached him].
They saw him. One was an opponent of the Teaching with wrong view; the other had right view. Among them, the one with wrong view said, "This is our food;
we shall eat this. The other restrained him, saying, "Enough! Do not let it please you.
Although he was being restrained by him, he disregarded his words, seized the boy by the feet, and dragged him away. He...
Because his mind was cultivated through the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*), at that moment he said, "Homage to the Buddha!
The non-human being, terrified by great fear, retreated and stood back. Then the other said to him, "We have done what should not be done;
let us inflict punishment upon him," and remained there guarding him. Having entered the city, the one with wrong view [took] the king’s food-bowl.
Having filled it, they brought the food. Then, acting as his mother and father, they attended to him and fed him.

Saying, "Let only the king see these letters; let no one else," and announcing this matter, they carved the letters into the food bowl through the power of a *yakkha*, placed the bowl in a wooden cart, provided a guard throughout the entire night, and departed.
On the following day, making a clamor that "the thieves have carried off food and goods from the royal palace," they closed the gates and searched;
not seeing anything there, they departed from the city and looked here and there until they saw a golden bowl on a wooden cart.
Thinking, "This is the thief," they seized the boy and presented him to the king. The king [saw] the letters...
Having seen this, he asked, "What is this, father? [The son replied,] "I do not know, Your Majesty.
My parents came, fed me at night, and stood guarding me; thinking that my parents were protecting me, I fell asleep without fear.
This much I know. Then his parents also arrived at that place. The king [saw] him...
Having understood the situation, he took those three people with him, went into the presence of the Teacher, and after reporting everything, asked:
"Venerable Sir, is mindfulness of the Buddha alone a protection, or are mindfulness of the Dhamma and the others as well?
Then the Teacher said to him: "Great King, it is not only mindfulness of the Buddha that is a protection; rather, for those who [practice] in six ways—"
"Having well-cultivated their minds, they have no need for any other protection or shield, nor for mantras or medicinal herbs," he said,
and then, pointing out six conditions, he spoke these verses:
"The disciples of Gotama always awaken with a sound awakening;..."
“Those whose mindfulness is constantly directed toward the Buddha by day and by night,
those disciples of Gotama always awaken with a true awakening.
Those whose mindfulness is constantly directed toward the Dhamma by day and by night...”
“Always well-awakened they awaken, the disciples of Gotama,
for whom mindfulness directed toward the Saṅgha is constant by day and by night.
Always well-awakened they awaken, the disciples of Gotama.”
“Those whose mindfulness directed toward the body is constant, both by day and by night—
those disciples of Gotama always awaken with a true awakening,
their minds delighting in non-violence both by day and by night.”
“The disciples of Gotama always awaken with a true awakening,
they whose minds, by day and by night, delight in meditation. In this context,
“they awaken with a true awakening” means that while sleeping, they maintain mindfulness directed toward the Buddha, and having maintained it, [they awaken].
And those who awaken are said to awaken with a "good awakening.
"Always disciples of Gotama" means they are disciples of Gotama because they were born within the hearing of the Buddha of the Gotama clan and because of their listening to his very instruction.

"Mindfulness directed toward the Buddha" refers to that mindfulness which arises concerning the various qualities of the Buddha, beginning with the formula: "Thus indeed is the Blessed One... and so forth.
The meaning is that those who possess it at all times always awaken with a good awakening (*suppabuddha*).

However, those unable to do so even once, by attending to the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*) during three periods, two periods, or even one period of the day, are indeed said to awaken with a good awakening.
"Mindfulness directed toward the Dhamma" refers to the various classifications beginning with, "Well-expounded is the Dhamma by the Blessed One."

Mindfulness directed toward the qualities of the Dhamma (*dhammaguṇa*) is mindfulness arising with reference to the qualities of the Dhamma. Mindfulness directed toward the Saṅgha (*saṅghagata-sati*) is mindfulness arising with reference to the qualities of the Saṅgha, such as the various distinctions beginning with: "The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way.

Mindfulness directed toward the body (*kāyagata-sati*) is mindfulness arising by way of the thirty-two aspects, or by way of the nine cemetery meditations, or by way of the determination of the four elements, or by way of internal jhānas on the form-sphere kasinas such as the blue kasina.
"Being established. "Delighting in non-violence" means delighting in the cultivation of compassion as described thus: "He dwells pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with compassion.

"Cultivation" refers to the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā*). Although all remaining forms of cultivation are included here because the cultivation of compassion was discussed previously, in this context, specifically the cultivation of loving-kindness is intended. The rest...
This should be understood in the same manner as stated in the first verse.

At the conclusion of the teaching, the boy, together with his mother and father, was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). Later, having gone forth into homelessness, they all attained *arahantship*. Thus, even for those who had already attained [the fruits], the teaching of the Dhamma was truly fruitful.
This is the fifth story, the Story of the Wood-Cartman’s Son.
6. The Story of the Vajjiputtaka Bhikkhu.
This teaching on the difficulty of the religious life was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in the Great Forest near Vesālī, concerning a certain Vajjiputtaka bhikkhu.
With reference to him, it is said: "A certain Vajjiputtaka..."
A certain bhikkhu was dwelling at Vesālī in a certain grove. Now at that time, there was a festival at Vesālī lasting all night.
Then, having heard the sound of the noise of musical instruments, cymbals, and drums from Vesālī, that bhikkhu, lamenting, spoke this verse on that occasion:
“We dwell alone in the forest like a discarded log in the woods,
on a night such as this.”
"Who among us is more wicked than he?
It is said that this prince of Vajjiratta, having renounced the kingdom that had come to him by turn, went forth into homelessness;
and in Vesālī, together with the Four Great Kings, he made a continuous connection [of light] throughout the entire city, which was adorned with banners, flags, and other ornaments.
On the full moon of the month of Kattika, while the festival was taking place throughout the night,
having heard the sound of beaten drums and other instruments, and the noise of lutes and other musical instruments being played,
[he saw] those seven thousand kings, seven hundred kings, and seven kings in Vesālī, as well as their subordinate officers, generals, and so forth, all arrayed in their finery.

While walking on the sixty-cubit great promenade (*mahācaṅkama*) that had been set out in the street for the purpose of a festival of constellations, he saw the full moon situated in the midst of the sky.

Standing at the end of the promenade leaning against a wooden plank, and because he was devoid of head-dress and ornaments, he looked at his own body as if it were a piece of wood discarded in the forest, and thought: "Is there indeed anyone more wretched than we?"
Although by nature endowed with the qualities of a forest-dweller and so forth, at that moment, being oppressed by dissatisfaction, he spoke thus.
With the intention, "I shall cause this bhikkhu to feel spiritual urgency," a deity dwelling in that grove said:
"You dwell alone in the forest, like a piece of wood cast away in the woods."
"Many people envy you, just as those bound for hell envy those going to heaven.
Having heard this verse, on the following day he approached the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down.
The Teacher, understanding the situation and wishing to demonstrate the suffering inherent in the household life, combined five types of suffering and spoke this verse:
“Difficult is the going forth, difficult is the delighting therein; difficult are households, full of suffering.
Difficult is living together with others, and difficult is the traveler who is beset by suffering.
Therefore, one should not be a traveler, nor should one be beset by suffering.”
In this context, "difficult to go forth" means that it is indeed difficult to go forth by renouncing a mass of wealth, whether small or great, as well as one's circle of kinsmen,
and placing one’s chest [in resolve] within this teaching. "Difficult to find delight in" means that even for one who has thus gone forth,

while striving to maintain their livelihood through the practice of alms-gathering, there is the task of guarding the immeasurable aggregate of virtue and fulfilling the practice in accordance with the Dhamma.
It is difficult to find delight [in it]. As for "difficult to dwell in":

because one who dwells in a household must carry out the royal duties for kings, the masterly duties for masters, and must maintain both his dependents as well as righteous recluses and brahmins—even so, the household life is as difficult to fill as a leaking jar or the great ocean. Therefore, from the household life...
"These are difficult to dwell in; they are painful to live in—that is the meaning of 'painful' (*dukkha*).

'Painful is association with equals' means that even those householders who have gone forth together with others who are equal in birth, clan, family, and wealth, or those who have gone forth and are equal in virtue, conduct, and learning, may say things such as 'Who are you?
and 'Who am I? and become intent on legal disputes; these are called 'unequals' (*asamāna*)."
The meaning is that dwelling together with them is suffering. Regarding the phrase "one who goes on the path (addhagū) is beset by suffering":
those who are "goers on the path" because they have entered the path known as the round of existence (*saṃsāra*) are indeed beset by suffering. Therefore, "and not one who goes on the path":

since both the state of being beset by suffering and the state of being a goer on the path are themselves suffering, one should not be a "goer on the path" by virtue of traveling along the path known as the round of existence.
The meaning is: "May he not be afflicted by suffering of the kind already described.

At the conclusion of the teaching, that bhikkhu, becoming disenchanted with the suffering shown in these five instances, shattered the five lower fetters and the five higher fetters and was established in Arahatship.
This is the sixth story, concerning the bhikkhu Vajjiputtaka.
7. The Story of the Householder Citta.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this teaching on the Dhamma concerning the householder Citta.
The story has been related in detail in the commentary on the verse beginning with "One might wish for the cultivation of what is non-existent" in the Bāla-vagga. The verse is as follows:
It was stated right there. For this was said there:
"But, venerable sir, does this gain and honor arise only for one who comes into your presence, or does it also arise for one who goes elsewhere?
"Ānanda, it arises both for one who comes into my presence..."
“Even as he goes elsewhere, this arises for him. For this lay follower is faithful, confident, and possessed of virtuous conduct;
such a person, whatever place he frequents, in that very place gain and honor arise for him.
Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“Endowed with faith and perfected in virtue, possessed of fame and wealth, whatever region he frequents, there he is honored.

In this context, “faithful” means being endowed with both mundane and supramundane faith. “By virtue” refers to the virtue of a householder and the virtue of one who has gone forth from the household life.
Virtue is twofold. Of these two, it is the virtue of a householder that is intended here; thus the meaning is "one who is endowed with that.
"Endowed with fame and wealth" means: by a kind of household fame such as that of Anāthapiṇḍika and others, which consisted of a retinue of five hundred lay followers (upāsakas);
and by a twofold wealth—namely, the wealth consisting of money, grain, and so forth, and the sevenfold noble wealth—by such fame and such wealth he is endowed.

The meaning is "endowed with. Whichever region such a clansman frequents—among the directions beginning with the east—in each and every such place he is honored with such gain and honor; this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other fruits.
The Seventh Story: The Householder Cittaka.
8. The Story of Cūḷasubhaddā.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, gave this teaching on the Dhamma concerning the daughter of Anāthapiṇḍika named Cūḷasubhaddā, beginning with the words, "Though far away..."
It is said that from his youth, Anāthapiṇḍika had a friend named Ugga, the son of a merchant from the city of Uggā.
While they were learning their craft in the same teacher’s household, they made a pact with one another:
"When we have reached maturity and sons and daughters are born to us, whoever prevents their own son from marrying the other's daughter, by him [the penalty shall be paid]."
"should be given. When both had reached maturity, they were each established in the position of a guild-leader (*seṭṭhi*) in their respective cities.
Then, on one occasion, while Uggaseṭṭhi was engaged in trade, he went to Sāvatthī with five hundred carts.
Anāthapiṇḍika, having addressed his daughter Cūḷasubhaddā, said, "My dear, your father is Uggaseṭṭhi..."
“...has arrived; you must take full responsibility for everything that needs to be done for him,” she commanded.
She replied, “Very well,” and from the day he arrived, she personally prepared the soups, condiments, and so forth, and prepared the garlands, perfumes, ointments, and other requisites.
At mealtime, she had bathing water prepared for him, and from the time of his bath onwards, she diligently attended to all his needs.
Seeing her excellence of conduct, the merchant Ugga, with a mind full of faith, once sat down in pleasant conversation with Anāthapiṇḍika.
Reminding him, "In our youth, we made such an agreement," he requested Cūḷasubhaddā for his son.
However, he was by nature a holder of wrong views; therefore, [he did not wish to give her] to the One of Ten Powers.

Having reported that matter to the Teacher, and having been granted permission by the Teacher after he perceived Uggasena’s spiritual maturity, he consulted with his wife, accepted her advice, and fixed a date.
Then, like the merchant Dhanañjaya who gave his daughter Visākhā away, he arranged a great ceremony and, addressing Subhaddā, said: “My dear daughter, [give me your hand].”

"Living in her father-in-law’s family, she must not take the fire from within and carry it outside"— having thus given the ten precepts according to the method bestowed upon Visākhā by the merchant Dhanañjaya,
and having taken eight householders as guarantors with the words, "If any fault arises against my daughter while she is away,
you must clear her," on the day of her departure, [he addressed] the community headed by the Buddha...

Having given a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, as if demonstrating to the world the manifestation of the fruit of the wholesome deeds performed by his daughter in a previous existence, he sent his daughter away with great honor.
When she had gradually reached the city of Ugganagara, a great multitude of people went out to meet her along with her father-in-law’s family.
She too, like Visākhā, wishing to make her own glory and wealth manifest, entered the city standing in a chariot and displaying herself to the entire city.

She accepted the gifts sent by the citizens and, distributing them to each person according to their merit, made the whole city one with her own virtues. On auspicious days and other such occasions, however, for her—
The father-in-law, while performing honors for the naked ascetics (Acelakas), sent word saying, "Let him come and pay homage to our recluses.
She, being ashamed and unable to bear the sight of the naked ones, did not wish to go. Although he sent her again and again, she refused;
becoming angry, he said, "Throw her out! She thought, "It is not possible for them to attribute fault to me without cause."
Having summoned the householders, he informed them of the matter. They, knowing her innocence, persuaded the merchant.
He told his wife, "This woman did not pay homage to my ascetics because she is shameless.
She thought, "What kind of ascetics must these be that he praises them so excessively? and having summoned her, she said:
“What kind of recluses are they whom you praise so highly?
What is their virtue and what is their conduct? Answer me when I ask you this.
Then Subhaddā, proclaiming the qualities of both the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas, said:
“With peaceful faculties and peaceful minds, their state is peaceful whether moving or standing;
with downcast eyes and measured speech—such are the ascetics for me.
Their bodily action is pure, and their verbal action is untroubled.”
“Those ascetics of mine have their mental actions perfectly purified.
Stainless like conch shells and pearls, pure both within and without,
filled with wholesome qualities— such are the ascetics of mine.”
“The world is uplifted by gain and cast down by loss;
those who are the same in gain and loss, such as they are my true ascetics.
The world is uplifted by fame and cast down by infamy;”
“Those who are of one mind with fame and glory—such are my ascetics.
The world is uplifted by praise and likewise depressed by blame;
those who remain equanimous amidst both blame and praise—such are my ascetics.”
“The world is uplifted by pleasure, and it is depressed by suffering;
those who are unshakable amidst pleasure and pain—such are my ascetics.
With these and other such words, he satisfied his mother-in-law.
Then, saying to her, "Is it possible for you to show us the ascetics as well? and being told by her, "It is possible," they said, "In that case, act in such a way that we may see them.

She replied, "Very well," and having prepared a great almsgiving for the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, she stood on the upper terrace of the palace, facing toward Jetavana, and with due reverence performed the five-fold prostration.

Having paid homage, reflected upon the qualities of the Buddha, and performed an offering with perfumes, incense, flowers, and fragrant powders, he said, "Venerable Sir, I invite the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha for tomorrow;
may the Teacher know that I have invited him by this sign," and he threw eight handfuls of *sumana* flowers into the air. The flowers went and settled in the midst of the fourfold assembly.
As the Teacher was preaching the Dhamma, they stood above him like a canopy of garlands.

At that moment, Anāthapiṇḍika, having heard the discourse on the Dhamma, invited the Teacher for a meal on the following day. The Teacher said, "It has been accepted by me, householder, for tomorrow's meal.
[Anāthapiṇḍika asked: "Venerable sir, no one has arrived before me; for whom then have you accepted it?"
When he said, "It has been accepted," [the Venerable Ānanda] replied, "Householder, [the Buddha] has been invited by Cūḷasubhaddā.
When [the householder] asked, "But, venerable sir, does Cūḷasubhaddā not live far away, at a distance of two thousand yojanas from here? he replied, "Yes, householder;
for even those who dwell afar proclaim themselves as if they were standing right before one," and he spoke this verse:
“The virtuous shine from afar, like the Himālaya mountain;
the non-virtuous are not seen here, like arrows shot in the night.

In this context, “the virtuous” (santa) refers to the Buddhas and others who are called “virtuous” (santa) because of their tranquility (*santatā*) regarding passion and the other defilements. However, here [in the commentary], among the previous Buddhas...
"Beings who have performed their duties, whose roots of merit are abundant, and who have cultivated spiritual development" is what is intended by "those who exist.
"They manifest" means that even when standing at a distance, they come within the range of the Buddhas' knowledge and become visible. "Like the Himalayas" means:
for example, just as the Himalayas—extending three thousand *yojanas* in width, rising five hundred *yojanas* in height, and adorned with eighty-four thousand peaks—[are visible].
The Himavat mountain makes itself manifest even to those standing at a distance, as if it were standing right before them;

such is the meaning of "making manifest. "Those who are not good" refers to foolish persons who value the present life, have cast aside the world beyond, look only for material gain, and have gone forth into homelessness merely for the sake of a livelihood;
these are called "not good. They [are excluded] here from the circle of the knee of the Buddhas' sacrificial gift.
Even though they were sitting nearby, they were not seen and were not perceived.

"Thrown in the night" means that, like arrows shot in the darkness endowed with its four factors, they were not perceived due to the absence of a prior cause (*pubbahetu*) serving as a necessary condition (*upanissaya*); this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*) and the other fruits.
Sakka, the king of the gods, knowing that the Teacher had accepted Subhaddā’s invitation, commanded the divine son Vissakamma:
“Construct five hundred gabled mansions and lead the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, headed by the Buddha, to Ugganagara tomorrow.
On the following day, having constructed those five hundred gabled mansions, he stood at the gate of Jetavana. The Teacher—
Having selected five hundred who were pure and whose taints were destroyed, the Teacher, accompanied by his retinue,

sat within gabled chambers and proceeded toward the city of Ugga. The merchant Ugga, also with his retinue, following the same path as Subhaddā had indicated while watching the road for the Tathāgata’s arrival,
saw the Master approaching with great splendor and majesty, and with a mind full of faith—

Honoring him with great reverence through garlands and other offerings, he accepted [the Teacher] along with his retinue, paid homage, and after giving a great gift, invited him again and again for seven days and presented a grand almsgiving.
The Teacher, perceiving what was suitable for him, taught the Dhamma. Beginning with that, there was a realization of the Dhamma by eighty-four thousand beings.
The Teacher, saying, "Remain right here for the sake of favoring Cūḷasubhaddā," caused the Elder Anuruddha to turn back and returned to Sāvatthī itself.
From that time forth, that city became endowed with faith.
Thus ends the eighth story, the Story of Cūḷasubhaddā.

9. The Story of the Elder Ekavihārin Regarding the teaching on the Dhamma beginning with the words "A single seat," the Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, spoke concerning the elder named Ekavihārin.
It is said that this elder would lie down alone, sit alone, and walk for meditation alone. Alone...
"He stands" means he became visible within the fourfold assembly. Then the bhikkhus informed the Tathāgata, "Venerable Sir, such is this elder.
The Teacher, applauding him with the words "Excellent, excellent," spoke of the benefits of seclusion, saying, "A bhikkhu must indeed be secluded," and uttered this verse:
“Sitting alone, lying down alone, wandering alone and untiring, taming oneself alone,
one should find delight at the edge of the forest. Therein, “sitting alone,
lying down alone” means that even in the midst of a thousand bhikkhus, without abandoning one’s original subject of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna), by that very [means]...
For one sitting with attention (*manasikāra*), the seat is called "the single seat.

And even in a palace like the Lohapāsāda, or when there is a costly bed provided with various rugs and cushions in the midst of a thousand bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu who has established mindfulness and lies down on his right side with attention to his basic meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), that reclining is called "the single reclining. Such is...

The meaning is: one should resort to a single seat and a single bed. "Unwearied" means that by making a living through the strength of one's legs, one remains untiring and wanders alone in all postures;

the meaning is that one tames oneself alone by devoting oneself to the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) during night-stations and so forth, becoming solitary through the attainment of the paths and fruits.
"One should find delight at the edge of the forest": thus, by subduing oneself, one should take pleasure only in the forest edges that are secluded from the sounds of men and women and the like.
The meaning is that it is not possible for one who dwells in a crowded place to subdue oneself in this way.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages. From that time forth, the great multitude aspired only to dwell alone.
The Story of the Elder Ekavihāri, the ninth.
The commentary on the Miscellaneous Chapter is finished.
The Twenty-first Chapter.
22. The Chapter on Hell (Nirayavagga) 1. The Story of the Wanderer Sundarī.
Regarding the phrase "one who speaks what is untrue," the Teacher delivered this Dhamma teaching while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the wanderer Sundarī.
“At that time, indeed, the Blessed One was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped. This introductory narrative has already been related in detail in the *Udāna*.

Here, however, is the summary: it is said that when the Blessed One and the community of monks had received gains and honors comparable to the great floods of the five great rivers, the followers of other sects, having lost their own gains and honors, [approached] at the time of sunrise...
Becoming as lusterless as glow-worms, they gathered together and deliberated:
"From the time the ascetic Gotama appeared, we have been deprived of gain and honor; no one even knows that we exist.
With whom, then, can we join together to incite disparagement of the ascetic Gotama so that his gain and honor [shall diminish]?"
“Let us make her disappear. Then it occurred to them, “We shall be able to do so by being together with Sundarī.
One day, having entered the heretics’ monastery and paid their respects, they stood there without speaking to Sundarī.
Although she spoke to them again and again, receiving no reply, she asked, “But, Noble Ladies, have you perhaps been troubled by someone?”
“Sister, do you not see that the ascetic Gotama is wandering about having harassed us and deprived us of our gains and honor?
“What should I do in this matter? “Sister, you are beautiful and have attained great fortune;
by attributing infamy to the ascetic Gotama and causing the great multitude to adopt your words, deprive him of his gains and honor.”

“Do so. Having heard this and accepted it by saying “Very well,” she departed. From that time on, taking flowers, perfumes, ointments, camphor, cardamom, and other such items, she would go toward Jetavana every evening at the time when the great multitude, having heard the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, was entering the city.
And when asked, “Where are you going? she replied, “I am going into the presence of the ascetic Gotama; for I—”
Having said, "I lived with him in the same fragrant cell," she stayed for a while in a certain monastery of the non-Buddhist sects.
At dawn, having descended onto the path to Jetavana and coming toward the city, she was asked, "Sundarī, where have you been?
She replied, "I have come after living in the same fragrant cell with the ascetic Gotama and delighting him with the pleasures of the defilements."

Then, after a few days had passed, they gave money to some ruffians and said, "Go, kill Sundarī, place her body among the flower refuse near the Perfumed Chamber (gandhakuṭi) of the ascetic Gotama, and then return. They did exactly as instructed.
Thereupon, the sectarians raised a clamor, saying, "We do not see Sundarī," and having informed the king, [asked] "Where..."
When they were told, "There is a concern for you," they replied, "For these past days she has been staying at Jetavana, and we did not know her condition there.

Having been granted permission by the king with the words, "In that case, go and search for her," they took their own attendants, went to Jetavana, and while searching, they found her amidst the refuse of the flower garden. They placed her upon a litter and [returned] to the city.

Having laid her out, they informed the king: “The disciples of the ascetic Gotama, thinking, ‘We shall conceal the evil deed committed against our Teacher,’ have killed Sundarī and placed her among the floral refuse.
The king said, “In that case, go and search throughout the city. They went through the streets of the city, crying out: “Behold the disciples of the Sakyan-son ascetics!”

Having said, "It is the work of the monks," and so forth, they returned once more to the gate of the king’s residence. The king had Sundarī’s body placed upon a funeral pyre in the raw charnel ground and had it guarded.
With the exception of the noble disciples, the majority of the inhabitants of Sāvatthī—both within and outside the city—said, "Behold the work of the Sakyan-son ascetics," and so forth.
The monks were wandering about reviling [others]. The monks reported this matter to the Tathāgata.
The Teacher said, “In that case, you too should reprimand those men in this way,” and spoke this verse:
“The speaker of untruth goes to hell;”
Or he who, having done [an evil deed],
says, "I did not do it"— both of these, upon passing away,
become equal in the world beyond, being men of base actions.
In this context, "one who speaks what is untrue" refers to one who, having not seen the fault in another, utters false speech and slanders the other with what is empty.
"Having done" refers to one who, having committed an evil deed, says, "I did not do this.

"And after passing away they become equal" means that both those persons, having gone to the next world, become equal in their destination by way of entering hell. It is the destination alone [that is meant].
Their size is limited, but their lifespan is not limited. For having committed much evil karma, they burn in hell for a long time;
having committed little, only for a very short time. Since the karma of both these [types of beings] is indeed base, it is said:
"Base in their actions, men in the next world. Regarding the word *parattha*: [The commentary continues: ...of this...
However, the word *pecca* is connected with the following word.

The meaning is: having gone from here to the other world (*parattha*), those of inferior karma become equal [in suffering] in the next world. At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*) and the others.
The King dispatched men, saying, "Find out whether Sundarī was killed by others. Then those rogues... by them...
Drinking liquor with *kahāpaṇa* coins, they quarreled with one another. One said to another:
"You kill Sundarī all at once, throw her among the floral refuse, and then drink liquor with the *kahāpaṇas* you obtain from that—let it be, let it be!
The king’s men seized those rogues and presented them to the king. Then the king said to them: "By you—"
"She has been killed," he asked. "Yes, Your Majesty," they replied. "By whom was she caused to be killed? "By followers of other sects, Your Majesty.
The king had the followers of other sects summoned and questioned them. They spoke exactly as before.
Thereupon the king said, "In that case, go and wander through the city saying this: 'This Sundarī was killed by those who wished to cast blame upon the ascetic Gotama.'"
"We had him killed; there is no fault in the ascetic Gotama, nor in his disciples, but the fault lies with us alone.
They did accordingly. At that time, the foolish masses believed them, and even the heretics and rogues received the punishment for the murder of a man.
From then on, the honor shown to the Buddhas became great.
The First Story of the Wanderer Sundarī.
2. The Story of Those Oppressed by the Fruit of Evil Conduct.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Veḷuvana, delivered this teaching on the Dhamma concerning beings who were oppressed by the power of the fruit of their own evil conduct, beginning with the words, "Those with saffron robes around their necks..."
For the Venerable Moggallāna, while descending from Gijjhakūṭa together with the Elder Lakkhaṇa, saw the personal forms of hungry ghosts such as skeletons and smiled.
When asked by the Elder Lakkhaṇa the reason for his smile, he said, "It is not the right time for this question, friend;
you should ask me in the presence of the Tathāgata," and so he went into the presence of the Tathāgata.
