Questioned by the Elder, he explained that he had seen such beings as the skeleton-ghosts (aṭṭhisaṅkhalika-peta), saying:
"Friend, while descending from Vulture Peak Mountain, I saw a bhikkhu traveling through the air;
his outer robe was burning, blazing, and glowing... [and so on] ...even his body was burning," and he described this together with his bowl, robes, waist-belt, and other requisites.
While they were burning, he informed the five companions of his own religious order. The Teacher,
having explained the wicked nature of those who had gone forth in the dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa but were unable to act in accordance with their ordination,
spoke this verse at that moment to show the ripening of the evil deeds of the many wicked bhikkhus seated there:
“Many with saffron robes around their necks, evil-natured and unrestrained, those evildoers through their evil deeds are reborn in hell.
In this context, “with saffron robes around their necks” means having their necks wrapped in saffron-colored cloth. “Evil-natured” means possessing base qualities. “Unrestrained” means—
Devoid of restraint over the body and so forth, such evil persons are reborn in hell due to the unwholesome kamma they themselves have committed;
having been cooked there, when they pass away from that state, they are likewise cooked among the hungry ghosts (petas) by the remainder of the karmic result—this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
The second account concerning those oppressed by the fruit of misconduct.
3. The Account of the Bhikkhus from the Banks of the Vaggumudā River.

The Teacher, while residing in the Great Forest near Vesālī, delivered this teaching on the Dhamma—beginning with the words, "Better an iron ball [heated]..."—concerning the bhikkhus from the banks of the Vaggumudā River. The background story (vatthu) is already recorded in the *Pārājika* section regarding superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*).
Then the Teacher said to those monks, "Monks, why did you speak in praise of one another's superhuman states for the sake of your own bellies? When they replied, "Yes,
venerable sir," he rebuked those monks in many ways and spoke this verse:
“Better it would be to eat a glowing iron ball, hot as a flame of fire,
than that one who is immoral, unrestrained, should eat the alms-food of the land. In this context,
“than that one who is immoral” means than a person devoid of virtue who is unrestrained in body and so forth, [eating] what is provided by the inhabitants of the kingdom.
If one who professes, "I am an ascetic," were to accept and eat the alms-food of a kingdom given out of faith, it would be better and more excellent to eat a red-hot, glowing iron ball like fire.
Why is that? Because on account of that [iron ball], only a single lifetime might be consumed;
however, an immoral person, having eaten what was given in faith, will be cooked in hell for many hundreds of births—this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the third story, concerning the monks from the banks of the Vaggumudā River.
4. The Story of the Merchant’s Son Khemaka.
"Four states"—this teaching on the Dhamma was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a merchant’s son named Khemaka, the nephew of Anāthapiṇḍika.
It is said that he was handsome; for the most part, when women saw him, they were overcome by lust and were unable to maintain their composure.
He, too, was devoted to committing adultery with the wives of others. Then, one night, the king’s men seized him.
They presented him to the king. The king, thinking "I am ashamed before this great merchant," said nothing to him and had him released. Yet he did not desist.
Then the king’s men seized him a second and a third time and presented him to the king. The king released him each time as well.
Having heard of this occurrence, the great merchant took him with him and went into the presence of the Teacher.
Having reported that occurrence, he said, "Venerable sir, please teach him the Dhamma.
The Teacher, after delivering a discourse on spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), spoke these verses, pointing out the fault of adultery:
"A negligent man [misses] four states..."
One who commits adultery incurs these four things:
the acquisition of demerit, lack of restful sleep,
thirdly, censure, and fourthly, hell.
“Acquisition of demerit, a miserable rebirth,
and for one who is afraid, the pleasure with one who is afraid is trifling;
furthermore, the king inflicts a heavy punishment.”
"Therefore, a person should not consort with another's wife.
In this context, "grounds" (*ṭhānāni*) means causes of suffering. "Heedless" (*pamatto*) means one who is possessed of a lapse in mindfulness.

"Incurs" (*āpajjati*) means he reaches [the result]. "One who consorts with another's wife" (*paradārūpasevī*) means one who approaches another's wife, a traveler on a wrong path. "Gain of demerit" (*apuññalābham*) means the acquisition of unwholesome states.
"Not at will as to lying down" means that not obtaining a bed as he desires, he obtains a bed for only a short, unintended time.
"And the acquisition of demerit" means that this is his acquisition of demerit, and through that demerit there comes to be an evil destination known as hell.
"And little pleasure" refers to the pleasure he experiences when, being afraid, he is with a woman who is afraid.
Pleasure together with it is also slight and limited. "Severe" means that the king imposes a severe punishment, such as the cutting off of hands and so forth.
Therefore, because one who indulges with another's wife incurs these demerits and other consequences, the meaning is: "one should not indulge with another's wife.
At the conclusion of the teaching, Khemaka was established in the fruit of stream-entry. From then on, the great multitude spent their time in happiness.
What, then, was his previous karma? It is said that during the time of the Buddha Kassapa, he was a supreme wrestler.
Having hoisted two golden banners upon the Golden Stupa for the One Endowed with Ten Powers, he made this aspiration:
"May all women, with the exception of my own kinswomen and blood relatives, fall in love with me upon seeing me. This was his previous karma. Because of it, in every place where he was reborn...
Having seen this, they were unable to maintain their composure before the women of others.
This is the fourth story, concerning the merchant’s son Khemaka.
5. The Story of the Ill-Mannered Bhikkhu.
"Kuso yathā..."—the Teacher related this Dhamma teaching while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain monk who was difficult to speak with.
It is said that a certain monk, having unintentionally cut a blade of grass, felt remorse and approached another monk.
Having informed him of what he had done, he asked, "Friend, what happens to one who cuts grass?"
Then the other said to him, "You imagine that something happens because of the cutting of grass; nothing at all happens here.
One is released, however, by confessing. Having said this, he himself also tore out some grass with both hands and took hold of it.
The monks reported this incident to the Teacher. The Teacher, having rebuked that monk in many ways, said:
While teaching the Dhamma, he spoke these verses: "Just as kusa grass,
if grasped incorrectly, cuts the very hand, so the ascetic life,
if wrongly undertaken, drags one toward hell."
“Whatever action is slack, whatever vow is defiled, and a holy life that is dubious—none of these bears great fruit. If one should do it, one should do it thoroughly;
one should exert oneself with firm resolve.”
"For laxity indeed scatters dust even more.
In this context, "kusa" refers to any sharp-edged grass, even as much as a palm leaf.
Just as that *kusa* grass, when wrongly grasped, cuts and tears one's hand, even so is the state of a recluse (*sāmañña*), which is defined by the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).
Being of broken virtue and so forth, it is difficult to handle and drags one toward hell; the meaning is that it causes rebirth in hell.
"Lax" means any action performed by acting with hesitation, having made one's grasp loose.

"Defiled" means defiled by wandering among improper resorts such as those of prostitutes and the like. "Suspicious" means that which must be remembered with suspicion regarding duties such as the Uposatha.
Even upon seeing the Saṅgha assembled for some other business, he thinks, "Surely they have assembled because they know my conduct and wish to expel me.
Thus, his mind is haunted by such suspicions—suspected, alarmed, and apprehensive.
"It does not exist for him" means that for such a person, this holy life (brahmacariya), which is termed the duty of a recluse (samaṇadhamma), does not bear great fruit.
The meaning is that because it lacks great fruit for him, it likewise does not result in great fruit for those who give alms to him. "One should do" means:
therefore, whatever action one might perform, one should indeed perform it; "with firmness" means one should do it having made it firmly established and being resolute in its undertaking.
"A wandering ascetic" refers to one who, having acted with laxity, has fallen into a state of brokenness and so forth.

"Ascetic practice (*samaṇadhamma*). The meaning is that such ascetic practice is unable to remove the dust of passion and the like existing within; rather, it scatters even more dust of passion and the like upon it.

At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages. That monk also, having established himself in restraint and subsequently developed insight (*vipassanā*), attained Arahatship.
The fifth story: The Case of the Abusive Bhikkhu.
6. The Story of the Envious Woman.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning a certain woman who was overcome by envy.
It is said that her husband had an intimate relationship with one of his household slaves.
Possessed by jealousy, she bound the slave’s hands and feet, cut off her ears and nose, and threw her into a secret chamber.
Having closed the door to conceal the fact that she herself had committed this deed, she said, "Come, noble sir, let us go to the monastery."
Thinking, “Let us go and hear the Dhamma,” she took her husband and went to the monastery, where she sat down to listen to the Dhamma.
Then her visiting relatives came to the house, opened the door, and seeing that state of affairs, they released the female slave.
She went to the monastery and, standing in the midst of the fourfold assembly, reported the matter to the One of Ten Powers.
Having heard her words, the Teacher said, "One should not commit even the slightest misconduct thinking, 'May others not know of this.
Even if no one else knows, one should perform only good conduct.
For misconduct, even if committed in secret, later produces remorse; whereas good conduct generates only joy. Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“It is better not to do a misdeed, for a misdeed torments later;
it is better to do a well-done deed, having done which one does not regret.
In this context, “misdeed” (dukkata) refers to blameworthy action that leads to the states of misery; it is better, more excellent, and supreme simply not to have done it at all.
"He regrets later" means that indeed, at the time when one recollects it again and again, one suffers.
"Well done" means that it is better to have performed an action that is blameless, which bestows happiness, and which leads specifically to a happy rebirth.

"Having done what" means that having performed such an action, one does not suffer or regret at the time of recollection later on; rather, one becomes filled with joy—that is the meaning of "that action is excellent."

At the conclusion of the teaching, both the lay follower and that woman were established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). Furthermore, they set that female slave free right there and made her a practitioner of the Dhamma.
This is the sixth story, concerning a woman overcome by jealousy.
7. The Story of the Many Bhikkhus.
"Just like the city"—this teaching on the Dhamma was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a large number of visiting monks.
It is said that they had entered the rains retreat in a certain border region and lived happily during the first month.
In the middle month, however, bandits arrived, raided their alms-village, seized the tax-collectors, and departed. From that time on...
As people were fortifying that frontier city for the purpose of repelling bandits, those monks did not find the opportunity to attend upon them with proper care.
Having spent an uncomfortable rainy season retreat, they went to Sāvatthī after the rains to see the Teacher;
having paid homage to the Teacher, they sat down to one side. The Teacher exchanged greetings with them.
Having asked, "Monks, did you dwell happily? and being answered, "Venerable sir, we dwelt happily during the first month;

however, in the middle month, bandits attacked the village. From then on, as people were busy fortifying the city, they had no opportunity to attend to us properly. Therefore, we spent an uncomfortable rainy season."
“Enough, monks; do not worry. A comfortable dwelling is indeed always difficult to find.
A monk ought to guard his own person just as those people guarded the city,” and having said this, he spoke this verse:
“Just as a frontier city is guarded both within and without, so should you guard yourselves.
Let not the opportune moment pass you by;
for those who have let the moment pass grieve when they are consigned to hell.”
In this context, "with its interior and exterior guarded," monks, means:

just as that frontier city was made well-guarded with both interior and exterior by those people who made the gates, walls, and so forth firm on the inside, and made the watchtowers, moats, and so forth firm on the outside;
even so, you too, having established mindfulness and closed the six internal doors...

The meaning is: "Do not let go of the door-guarding mindfulness; by not grasping the six external sense bases in such a way that they lead to the injury of the internal ones, and by making them firm through non-grasping, wander about without abandoning the door-guarding mindfulness so as to prevent their entry, thereby protecting yourselves.
Do not let the opportune moment pass you by"—for one who acts thus...

One does not protect oneself; for such a person, this moment of the Buddha’s appearance, the moment of birth in the Middle Country, the moment of acquiring right view, and the moment of the completeness of the six sense bases—all these moments pass by.
May that moment not pass you by! As for those who have passed that moment, for those persons...
And the moment has passed; the meaning is that having been consigned to hell, they were reborn there and are now grieving.
At the conclusion of the teaching, those bhikkhus, having developed a sense of spiritual urgency, established themselves in Arahatship.
This is the seventh story, concerning a number of bhikkhus.
8. The Story of the Nigaṇṭhas:
Regarding "Out of Shamelessness. While residing at Jetavana, the Teacher related this Dhamma teaching concerning the Nigaṇṭhas.
For one day, having seen the Nigaṇṭhas, the bhikkhus initiated a discussion: "Friends, [they are] entirely uncovered..."
"Compared to these naked ascetics, these Nigaṇṭhas are superior, for they at least cover even one side of their front;
I suppose they are modest. Hearing this, the Nigaṇṭhas said, "We do not cover ourselves for that reason;
rather, it is because there are individuals such as Paṃsu and Rajā who are bound by the life-faculty (jīvitindriya), so that they may not fall into our alms-bowls."
Having said, "For this reason, let us conceal it," they engaged in much discussion with them through the exchange of arguments and counter-arguments.
When the monks approached the Teacher and were seated, they reported that occurrence to him.
The Teacher said, "Monks, those who feel shame where there is no need for shame, and feel no shame where there is need for shame, are indeed destined for an evil rebirth."
Having said, "They exist," he spoke these verses while teaching the Dhamma:
"Those who feel shame for what is not shameful, and feel no shame for what is shameful;
through the adoption of wrong view, beings go to a state of misery."
“Those who see danger in what is not dangerous, and see no danger in what is dangerous, go to an evil destination because of their adoption of wrong view.
In this context, *alajjitāya* means that which is not to be shunned. For indeed, the alms-bowl is called that which is not to be shunned; yet they [shun it].
Those who wander about having covered [their private parts] are said to be "ashamed. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of what is shameful":
one ought to be ashamed because of the private organ (*hirikopīnaṅga*) which is not to be uncovered. However, those who wander about without covering it are not truly ashamed of what is shameful.

Thus, they feel shame regarding that which is not shameful, and lack shame regarding that which is shameful; this is due to their state of grasping what is false and their state of grasping things otherwise than they are.

And there is wrong view. The meaning is that those who wander about having adopted that [wrong view]—beings who have undertaken wrong view—go to an unhappy destination, distinguished by such states as hell.

Regarding "fearless" (*abhaya*): because fear of lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, views, defilements, and misconduct does not arise in dependence upon the alms-bowl, the alms-bowl is called "fearless.
However, those who conceal it with fear when it is actually fearless...

"Those who see no danger" (bhayadassino) refers as follows: because lust and other defilements arise in dependence upon the limb of shamelessness (ahirika-kopīnaṅga), that [shamelessness] is called "danger.

By not concealing it, they are those who see no danger where there is danger. Because they have adopted such a false apprehension of reality, the meaning is that through the adoption of wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi-samādānā), beings go to an evil destination (duggati).

At the conclusion of the teaching, many Nigaṇṭhas, their minds filled with spiritual urgency, went forth into homelessness; thus the Dhamma teaching was beneficial even to those who had merely gathered there.
This is the eighth story, the Story of the Nigaṇṭhas. 9.
The Story of the Disciples of the Heretics.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, delivered this teaching on the Dhamma concerning the disciples of the sectarians.
On one occasion, some disciples of other sects saw their own sons playing with the sons of lay followers who held right view, accompanied by their respective retinues.
When they returned home, [the parents said]: "The recluses, sons of the Sakyans, are not to be saluted by you."
"Nor should you enter their monastery," they made this oath. One day, while playing near the gate-tower outside the Jetavana Monastery, they became thirsty.
Then they sent a layman’s son, saying, "Go there, drink water, and bring some for us too. He entered the monastery and [approached] the Teacher.

Having paid homage and drunk the water, he reported the matter to the Teacher. Then the Teacher said to him, "You yourself, having drunk the water, go and send the others here as well for the purpose of drinking water. He did accordingly. They arrived and drank the water.
The Teacher summoned them and, having delivered a discourse on the Dhamma suitable for them, established them in unwavering faith.
Having done so, he established them in the refuges and the precepts. They went to their own homes and reported the matter to their parents.
Then their parents, overcome with grief, lamented, saying, "Our children have become possessed of perverted views.
Thereupon, many clever neighbors came to them for the purpose of allaying their sorrow.

They preached the Dhamma. Having heard their discourse, [the parents] thought, "We shall entrust these children to the ascetic Gotama himself," and they led them to the monastery together with a large circle of kinsmen. The Teacher, observing their underlying disposition, spoke these verses while teaching the Dhamma:
“Those who perceive the blameless as blameworthy, and the blameworthy as blameless,
go to a state of misery through their adherence to wrong view.
But those who know the blameworthy as blameworthy, and the blameless as blameless...”
"By undertaking right view, beings go to a happy destination.

In this context, "he censures" refers to the ten-based right view and the phenomena that serve as its supporting conditions (*upanissaya*). "Those with a mind of censure" means those whose minds have arisen [thinking], "This is blameworthy.
Furthermore, regarding the ten-based wrong view and the phenomena that serve as its supporting conditions...

And for those who see fault in what is faultless: having recognized the fault in this as fault and the faultless as faultless, because they have adopted the wrong view characterized by grasping, the meaning is that beings go to a state of misery due to the adoption of wrong view.
The meaning of the second verse should be understood by way of the opposite of what was stated [in the first].
At the conclusion of the teaching, they all established themselves in the three refuges; as they listened to the Dhamma again and again, they were established in the fruit of stream-entry.
This is the ninth story, the Account of the Disciples of the Heretics.
The commentary on the Hell Chapter is finished.
The Twenty-Second Chapter. 23.
The Chapter on the Elephant. 1.
The Story of Self-Taming.

“I am a Nāga”—this teaching on the Dhamma was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Kosambī concerning himself. The story has already been related in detail in the commentary on the opening verse of the Appamādavagga (The Chapter on Heedfulness). For it is said there:
“Māgaṇḍiyā, being unable to do anything to them, thought, ‘I shall do what must be done to the ascetic Gotama himself.
She gave a bribe to the citizens and [instructed] the slaves, laborers, and servants: ‘When the ascetic Gotama enters the city and wanders about, [seize him].’”
“Accompany him, revile him, and drive him away! he commanded. Those of wrong view, lacking faith in the Three Jewels, followed the Teacher who had entered the city and said:
“You are a thief! You are a fool! You are deluded! You are a rogue! You are a camel! You are an ox!
You are a donkey! You are bound for hell! You are a creature of the animal realm! There is no happy rebirth for you; only an evil destiny awaits you!”
“...this is to be expected from you,” they reviled and abused him with ten grounds for abuse.
Hearing this, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Teacher: “Venerable Sir, these people of the city are reviling and abusing us;
let us go elsewhere. “Where, Ānanda? “To another city, Venerable Sir. “Among the people there...”
“Ānanda, when they are reviling and abusing us, where shall we go? “To another city than that, Bhante.
“When the people there are reviling and abusing us, where shall we go, Ānanda?
“To another city than that, Bhante. “Ānanda, it is not proper to act in this way. Wherever there is a legal dispute...”
“When it has arisen, it is appropriate to go elsewhere once it has been pacified right there. But who, Ānanda, are those who are abusing you?
“Venerable sir, everyone from the slaves and laborers upwards are abusing me. “Ānanda, I am like an elephant that has entered the fray.
For it is the burden of an elephant that has entered the fray to endure arrows coming from the four directions.”
"Even so, enduring the words spoken by many who are immoral is indeed my burden," he said,
and while teaching the Dhamma concerning himself, he spoke these verses:
"Just as an elephant in battle [endures] an arrow shot from a bow, I endure the words of the wicked."
I shall endure harsh words, for the majority of people are ill-behaved.
"They lead the tamed one to the assembly; the king mounts the tamed one.
Among humans, the tamed one is best—he who endures harsh words."
“Better than mules, better than thoroughbred Sindh horses, and better than great tusker elephants is one who has tamed himself.
In this context, “like an elephant” means like a *nāga*. “Fallen from a bow” means discharged from a bow. “Exceeding speech” refers to the eight kinds of ignoble modes of expression.

"Transgression" refers to the act of overstepping. "They shall endure" means that just as a well-tamed great elephant in battle endures being struck by spears and other weapons released from bows, remaining unperturbed when arrows fall upon it, even so shall I endure such harsh speech;
the meaning is that I shall bear it. "For one who is immoral"—for this refers to the common people of the world.
One who is very immoral wanders about, provoking others by uttering whatever words he pleases; in such a case, my burden is simply to endure it and maintain equanimity.

"Tamed" means that when people go into the midst of a great crowd at places such as pleasure gardens or festive circles, they lead tame breeds of oxen or horses harnessed to their vehicles. "Kings" [do so] with such very same draft animals.
Even when traveling, the king mounts only a tamed elephant. Regarding "among men": even among men, one who is tamed by the four noble paths and free from wickedness is the best.

"He who endures harsh words": he who, even when such transgressive speech is repeatedly spoken to him, remains patient, does not resist, and is not distressed—such a tamed person is the best; this is the meaning.
*Assatara* means born from a mare and a donkey. *Ājānīya* refers to those capable of quickly understanding whatever task a skilled horse-tamer causes them to perform.
*Sindhava* means horses born in the kingdom of Sindhu. *Mahānāga* refers to great elephants, so called because they are like tuskers.
"Self-tamed" means that these mules, Sindhu horses, and elephants are better when tamed than otherwise.
"Untamed. But he who, through the four noble paths, has tamed himself by his own self-taming and is free from worldly attachments—he is superior even to that;
the meaning is that he is higher than all of these.

At the conclusion of the teaching, that entire multitude of people—who had previously stood in market streets, crossroads, and other places, taking bribes, reviling, and abusing [the monks]—attained the fruits of stream-entry and the rest.
The First Story on Self-Restraint.
2. The Story of the Monk Formerly a Trainer of Elephants.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, delivered this teaching on the Dhamma concerning a certain monk who had previously been a trainer of elephants. "For not by these... [he said].
It is said that one day, on the bank of the Aciravatī River, he saw an elephant trainer who was unable to teach the elephant the specific task he desired, thinking, "I will tame this elephant.
Seeing him thus, he addressed the monks standing nearby and said:
"Friends, if this elephant trainer were to prick this elephant at such-and-such a spot, it would immediately..."
“...you should train him in this manner. Having heard his words, he did so and tamed that elephant until it was well-trained.
Those monks reported this matter to the Teacher. The Teacher summoned that monk and, having asked, “Is it true that you spoke thus?
and being told, “It is true, Bhante,” he rebuked him, saying, “What—”
"Those fools, you have elephant-vehicles or other vehicles that are well-tamed. Indeed, there is no place that cannot be reached by means of such vehicles;
however, it is possible to reach a place never before reached only by one who has himself been well-tamed.
Therefore, tame yourself alone; what is the use of taming these? Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“One cannot go to the realm not yet reached by means of these vehicles, as one who is tamed goes by means of a well-tamed and tamed self.
The meaning of this is: as for those vehicles such as elephant-vehicles and so forth, no person whatsoever can go by means of these vehicles even in a dream.
Because it has not been gone to before, one should go toward the direction of Nibbāna, which is designated as "the untraversed," in such a way that—

just as a person who is tamed, free from worldly trappings, and wise goes toward that previously untraversed direction and reaches the ground of taming by means of the subduing of the faculties in the prior stage and the cultivation of the Noble Path in the subsequent stage— one likewise proceeds. Therefore, the meaning is that the taming of oneself alone is superior to that.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the second story, concerning the monk who was formerly a master elephant trainer.
3. The Story of the Son of the Aged Brahmin.
The Teacher, while residing at Sāvatthī, delivered this Dhamma instruction concerning the sons of a certain aged brahmin.
It is said that in Sāvatthī there was a brahmin with a fortune of eight hundred thousand [pieces of gold].
After he had provided his four grown sons with wives, he gave them four hundred thousand [pieces of gold] each. Then, when his brahmin wife passed away, his sons divided the inheritance.
“If he brings another brahmin woman, the family inheritance will be divided among the children born of her womb;
come now, let us support him. Thus, attending to him with excellent food, clothing, and other necessities, and massaging his hands and feet, they waited upon him.
One day, when he had risen from his midday sleep, they attended to him.

Massaging his hands and feet, they spoke of the specific dangers of the household life and entreated him, saying, "We shall attend upon you for as long as we live in this manner; please give us the remainder of your wealth as well.
The Brahmin gave another hundred thousand to each of them, setting aside only what was necessary for his own clothing and robes, and [gave] all his other articles of enjoyment and use.
Having divided [the inheritance] into four portions, he assigned them. His eldest son attended upon him for several days.
Then one day, as the son was returning after bathing, his daughter-in-law stood at the gatehouse and said to him:
"Did you give your eldest son a hundred or a thousand more than the rest? Was it not the case that two hundred thousand were given to each of all?"
"Do you not know the way to the house of my other sons? He too, becoming angry and saying, "Begone, you outcaste woman!
went to another's house. After a few days had passed there as well, having been driven away by that same means, he went to yet another;
thus, failing to gain entrance even into a single house, he went forth into the white-robed renunciation and, wandering for alms, after the lapse of time—
Worn out by old age, his body withered by the suffering of poor food and a miserable bed, he returned from wandering for alms and lay down on a bench.
Having fallen asleep and then waking up, he sat up and looked at himself; seeing no support among his sons, he thought:
"The ascetic Gotama, they say, is one who does not hide his face, whose countenance is open, who is pleasant to speak with, and skilled in welcoming."
“It would be possible to approach the ascetic Gotama and receive a friendly greeting.
Having adjusted his lower garment and outer robe, and taking his alms bowl and staff, he went into the presence of the Blessed One. And this has also been said:
Then a certain wealthy brahmin, coarse and wearing coarse clothing, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he sat down to one side. The Teacher, having exchanged greetings with him as he sat to one side, said this:
"Why is it, brahmin, that you are so shabby and clad in such coarse robes? "Sir Gotama, here I have four sons;
they have driven me out of my house along with my wives after consulting among themselves. "In that case, brahmin..."
Having mastered these verses, when the great multitude has assembled in the assembly hall and your sons are seated together, speak thus:
“Those by whose birth I would rejoice, and for whom I would desire existence—ask them about their wives; they alone will restrain the boar.”
“‘Truly, these wretched people call me “Father, Father,” O dear one;
they are demons in the form of sons who abandon one when one has reached old age.
Like a worn-out horse, no longer fit for use, he is removed from his fodder.’”
The elder is the father of these children, yet he begs for alms at the houses of others:
“A staff, they say, is better for me than disobedient sons;
for it restrains even a fierce bull and even a fierce dog.”
“In former times there was darkness; one who stood on firm ground sank into the deep.
By the power of a staff, having stumbled, he stands up again.
Having learned these verses in the presence of the Blessed One, on a day when brahmins had assembled, while they were adorned with all their ornaments—

Having entered that assembly hall while the sons of the Brahmins were seated upon magnificent seats in their midst, [the Buddha], thinking "this is my time," entered the center of the hall, raised his hand, and said, "Sirs, I wish to speak verses to you;
will you listen? When they replied, "Speak, Brahmin, we shall listen," he spoke while still standing.
At that time, it was the custom among men that "anyone who eats what belongs to his parents but does not support them should be put to death.
Therefore, those sons of the brahmin fell at their father's feet and pleaded, "Father, give us our lives!
Out of the softness of his heart, the father said, "Do not destroy my two little sons!"
“They possess it,” he said. Then the people said to his sons, “If you do not properly attend to your father from this day forward, we shall have you executed.
Terrified, they seated their father on a chair, lifted him up themselves, and brought him home;
they anointed his body with oil, massaged it, and bathed him with fragrant powders and the like.
Having summoned the brahmin women, they said, "From today onwards, attend properly to our father;
if you fall into negligence, we shall restrain you," and then fed him with choice food.
By means of this excellent food and comfortable rest, after a few days had passed, the brahmin regained his strength and his faculties became refreshed.

Having looked upon his own person and thinking, "This prosperity of mine has been obtained by relying on the ascetic Gotama," he took a pair of garments as a gift and went into the presence of the Blessed One. After exchanging greetings, he sat to one side;
having placed that pair of garments at the feet of the Blessed One, he said, "We Brahmins, Master Gotama, [regard] the teacher..."
“Let us seek the teacher’s fee; may the venerable Gotama, as my teacher, accept this teacher’s fee,” he said.
Out of compassion for him, the Blessed One accepted it and taught the Dhamma.
At the conclusion of the teaching, the brahmin established himself in the refuges and spoke thus: “Master Gotama, four regular meals have been provided by my sons.”
“Therefore, I give two [meals] to you both. Then the Teacher said to him, “Excellent, brahmin;

however, we shall go only to where it pleases us,” and he dismissed him. The brahmin went home and said to his sons, “Sons, the ascetic Gotama is my friend; I have given him two regular meals. You [should also give] to him...”
"Do not be negligent when the opportunity has arrived. They accepted this, saying, "Very well.
On the following day, as the Teacher was wandering for alms, he came to the door of the eldest son's house.
Seeing the Teacher, he took his bowl, led him into the house, seated him upon a magnificent couch, and offered him exquisite food.
On the following day, the Teacher went in turn to the houses of all of them, one after another.
They all likewise paid him the same honor. One day, when an auspicious occasion had arisen, the eldest son said to his father, "Father, to whom shall we give the blessing?
"I know no others," he replied, "except for the ascetic Gotama, who is my friend."
“In that case, invite him for tomorrow along with five hundred bhikkhus. The brahmin did so.
On the following day, the Teacher went to his house accompanied by his retinue.

Having had the Buddha and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus seated in his house, which was smeared with fresh cow dung and adorned with every ornament, he [served] them with milk-rice mixed with honey and water, as well as with choice food.

And he served him with solid food. While the meal was still in progress, the Brahmin’s four sons sat down near the Teacher and said, “Master Gotama, we have looked after our father and never neglected him; look at his physical form!
The Teacher said, “You have done well; indeed, the support of mother and father was the very custom of the ancient sages.”
Having said this, and having related in detail the Mātuposaka Nāgarāja Jātaka from the Eleventh Book (Ekādasanipāta), beginning with the words:
“Because of that nāga’s absence, the sallakī and kuṭaja trees have grown,” he spoke this verse:
“The elephant named Dhanapāla...”
“Crushing with a pungent bite and difficult to restrain, the elephant,
though bound, does not eat his morsel,
but remembers the elephant forest.”

In that context, "named Dhanapāla" refers to the name of the elephant that had been captured in the delightful Nāgavana forest by the King of Kāsi, who had sent a master of elephants for the purpose. "With a pungent rut-fluid" means possessing a sharp *mada*.
For at the time of their rut, the temples (*kaṇṇacūḷikā*) of elephants burst open; even by nature, at that time, elephants [become agitated] toward the goad or the spear-point.
They do not count [the consequences] and they become fierce; he, moreover, was exceedingly fierce. Therefore it is said:
"He is one who breaks with bitterness and is difficult to restrain. "Bound, he does not eat a morsel":

having been bound and led to the elephant stable, he was placed upon the ground surrounded by various screens, adorned with fragrant pastes, and covered above by a variegated canopy provided for the king by the monarch.
Even when served with food of various exquisite flavors, he did not wish to eat anything;

it was with reference to this fact that it was said, "Bound, he does not eat a morsel. He remembers the Nāga Grove means that he recalls the Nāga Grove, thinking, "That is my delightful dwelling place. [He reflects:
"But my mother fell into suffering in the forest due to separation from her son; the duty of attending upon one's mother and father..."
"It does not fill me; what use have I for this food? he thought, and thus he recalled his righteous duty of service toward his parents.
Since that duty could be fulfilled while standing right there in the Nāgavana grove, it was said: "The elephant remembers the Nāgavana.
Even as the Teacher was recounting this account of his own former conduct, all [the deities]...
Having shed streams of tears, they became soft-hearted and gave ear. Then the Blessed One, perceiving what was suitable for them, proclaimed the Truths and taught the Dhamma.
At the conclusion of the teaching, the brahmin, together with his sons and daughters-in-law, was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
The third story: The Story of the Worn-out Brahmin’s Son.
4. The Story of Pasenadi of Kosala.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning King Pasenadi of Kosala, beginning with the words: "When one is drowsy..."
For at one time, the king was eating a doṇa-measure of rice with sauce and condiments prepared accordingly.
One day, having finished his breakfast, he went into the presence of the Teacher without having dispelled the drowsiness caused by the meal;
appearing exhausted, he rolled this way and that, and though overcome by sleep, he was unable to lie down straight.
He sat down to one side. Then the Teacher said to him, "Why have you come so soon, Great King, without even resting?
"Yes, venerable sir, from the time I finished eating, I have experienced great suffering.
Then the Teacher, saying, "Great King, excessive eating causes such suffering," spoke this verse:
“When one is drowsy and a great eater,
sleeping and rolling about in bed like a great boar fattened on fodder— ”
"The dull-witted one enters the womb again and again.

In this context, *middhī* means one who is overcome by sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*). *Mahagghaso* means one who eats excessively, like any one of those who eat with their hands, or those who wear a cloth over the shoulder, or those who eat from a bowl, or those who eat like crows, or those who eat until they are full.
*Nivāpapuṭṭho* means nourished on the fodder of pigs, such as broken rice and the like; for a domestic pig, from the time it is young...

Having been raised from birth, when his body had become stout and he was unable to go outside the house, he would lie rolling about on the lower couches and such, merely breathing in and out. This is what is meant:
when a man is both slothful and gluttonous, like a great boar filled with fodder, he is unable to maintain himself by any other posture.
Being unable [to remain awake], having a habit of sleeping, and rolling about while lying down, he was then unable to attend to the three characteristics—“impermanence, suffering, and non-self.
Due to his failure to attend to them, being of dull wisdom, he enters the womb again and again and is not released from dwelling in the womb.
At the conclusion of the teaching, the Teacher, by way of his assistance to the king—
“For a person who is always mindful, who knows the proper measure regarding the food he has received, his pains become slight; he ages slowly, preserving his life.
Having spoken this verse and caused the young man Uttara to learn it, [the Buddha said], “At the time of the king’s meal, you should announce this verse to him.”
“By this means you should cause yourself to lose weight,” he said, and explained the method; he did accordingly.

At a later time, having restricted himself to no more than a single *nāḷika* of rice, his body became very light and healthy, and having attained happiness, he placed his trust in the Teacher and offered an incomparable gift for seven days.
Through the expression of appreciation for that gift, the great multitude attained a vast distinction.
The fourth story, concerning Pasenadi of Kosala.
5. The Story of the Novice Sānu.
This teaching on the Dhamma was related by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a novice named Sānu.
It is said that a certain laywoman had an only son. She ordained him while he was still a mere child.
From the time of his ordination, he became virtuous and perfect in his conduct;
he performed his duties toward his teachers, preceptors, and visiting monks. Rising early on the eighth day of the month, he would prepare water in the water-shed.
Having swept the assembly hall for the hearing of the Dhamma, prepared the seats, and lit the lamps, he announced the recitation of the Dhamma with a sweet voice.
The bhikkhus, perceiving his strength, requested him, saying, "Recite the *sarabhañña*, novice!
Without offering any reply such as, "My heart is aching" or "My body is afflicted," he ascended the Dhamma-seat.

Having ascended [the sky], as if causing the celestial Ganges to descend while delivering a *sara-bhañña* recitation, he descends and says, "I give the merit of this *sara-bhañña* to my mother and father.
However, the people do not know that he has given the merit to his parents.
In his immediately preceding existence, however, his mother had been reborn as a *yakkhinī*; she, together with the deities—
Having come and heard the Dhamma, he says, "I rejoice in the alms-bowl given by the novice, dear ones.
Because "a bhikkhu endowed with virtue is indeed beloved by the world including the devas," the deities feel shame and reverence toward that novice;
they regard him as Mahābrahmā would, or like a mass of blazing fire. Out of reverence for the novice, [they treat] that yakkhinī...
They regard her with respect. At assemblies for listening to the Dhamma, gatherings of *yakkhas*, and other such occasions, they say, "The mother of Sānu!

The mother of Sānu! and offer the foremost seat, the foremost water, and the foremost alms-food to that *yakkhinī*. Even powerful *yakkhas*, upon seeing her, step off the path and rise from their seats.

Then the novice, having reached maturity, his faculties fully developed, being oppressed by discontent and unable to dispel it, with hair and nails grown long and his robes and undergarments soiled, went alone to his mother’s house without telling anyone, taking his bowl and outer robe.
When the laywoman saw her son, she paid homage to him and said: "What is it, dear son?"
“Previously you used to come here with your teachers, preceptors, or young novices;
why have you come alone today? He explained his state of dissatisfaction.
That laywoman, having shown him the various dangers of the household life and admonishing her son, was unable to convince him; she thought, “Perhaps even by my own nature...”
Having urged him, saying, "Please take note," she said, "Wait, dear son, until I have prepared your rice gruel and meal;
after you have drunk the gruel and finished your meal, I will bring out some pleasing garments and give them to you. Having spoken thus, she prepared a seat and offered it to him.
The novice sat down. In a mere moment, the laywoman prepared the gruel and solid food and gave it to him. Then...
Thinking, "I shall prepare the meal," she sat down nearby and began washing rice.
At that moment, the yakkhinī, reflecting, "Where is the novice? Does he receive alms-food, or not? perceived through her insight that he was sitting there with a desire to disrobe.
She thought, "The novice might cause shame to arise among the powerful deities."
Thinking, "I shall go and create an obstacle to his departure," he returned, became obsessed with his son's body, twisted his neck, and fell to the ground with saliva trickling from his mouth.
Seeing this calamity befall her son, the female lay devotee went in haste, embraced her son, and laid him down upon her lap. All the inhabitants of the village arrived.
They performed the rites for averting evil and other ceremonies. But the female lay devotee, lamenting, spoke these verses:
"On the fourteenth and the fifteenth, and on the eighth day of the fortnight, and during the fortnight of miracles, she was perfectly endowed with the eight factors [of the Uposatha]."
“Those who observe the Uposatha and lead the holy life— with them the *yakkhas* do not sport;
so I have heard from the Arahants.
But today I see that very thing: the *yakkhas* are sporting with Sānu.”
Having heard the words of the female lay follower:
“On the fourteenth and the fifteenth, and on the eighth day of the fortnight,
and during the fortnight of miracles, one should be well-endowed with the eight factors.”
“Those who observe the Uposatha and lead the holy life—the Yakkhas do not play with them.
Well done, you have heard from the Arahats.
Having said this, he spoke further:
“You should address Sānu when he has awakened with these words of the *yakkhas*:
‘Do not commit an evil deed, whether in public or in private.
And if you have committed or are committing an evil deed,’” [he said].
"There is no escape from suffering for you, even if you fly up and flee.
Having said that there is no liberation for him even if he flies up and flees like a bird after committing such evil karma, the yakkhinī released the novice.
He opened his eyes and, with his hair disheveled, looked at his weeping mother.

Seeing her breathing and weeping while all the villagers had gathered around, and not knowing that he had been seized by a *yakkha*, he thought, "Previously I was sitting on a seat and my mother was sitting nearby washing rice;
but now I am lying on the ground—what could this be? And while still lying there, he said to his mother:
“They weep for one who is dead, or for one who is alive but not seen;
seeing me alive, mother, why do you weep for me?

Then his mother, pointing out the danger in returning for the sake of renouncing again after having already gone forth by abandoning both the objects of sense-desire and the defilements of sense-desire, said:
“They weep for a dead son, or for one who is alive but not seen;
but they weep even more for that son who, having abandoned sensual pleasures,
returns here again— for he, though living, is as good as dead.”
Having spoken thus, and having made household life appear like glowing embers and like hell, she showed the dangers of domestic life and spoke again:
"My dear, you have emerged from glowing embers, yet you wish to fall back into the embers;
my dear, you have emerged from hell, yet you wish to fall back into hell."
Then, in order to illustrate this meaning—“Son, may it be well with you;

however, thinking ‘this son of ours is being burned,’ we brought him out from the house like household goods and ordained him in the Buddha’s teaching. Now you wish to burn again in the life of a householder?
To whom shall we complain about this, and to whom shall we appeal for help?”—he spoke this verse:
“Run away, O venerable one! Whom shall we blame?
You have already carried out goods from a burning house; do you now wish to set it on fire again?
As his mother spoke thus again and again, he reflected and realized, “I have no need for the state of a householder.”
He said: Then his mother, delighted, saying "Very well, dear," fed him with choice food. Having asked, "How many years old are you, dear?
and knowing that he had reached the full age, she prepared the three robes for him.
With his bowl and robes complete, he received full ordination. Not long after his ordination, the Teacher, inspiring him with zeal for the restraint of the mind, said:
“Indeed, for one who does not restrain this mind as it wanders among various objects for a long time, there can be no safety; therefore,
one must apply oneself to the restraint of the mind, just as one restrains a rutting elephant with a goad,” and having said this,
he spoke this verse:
“In the past this mind wandered on its journey wherever it wished,
wherever it desired, and as it pleased;
today I shall restrain it thoroughly and wisely.”
“Like one holding a goad for an elephant in rut.

Its meaning is as follows: this so-called mind, prior to this [moment], has been wandering according to its own desire and according to its pleasure—following wherever its lust arose and by whatever means it desired toward objects such as forms and so forth.
"It was pleasant; thus, wandering as I pleased, I have traveled on tour for a long time.

Today, like a skilled elephant trainer known as a *hatthācariya*, I shall—with the use of a goad—subdue with wise attention this rutting elephant that has broken loose, just as one would with a hook, and I will not allow it to transgress."
At the conclusion of the teaching, many deities who had approached together with Sānu to listen to the Dhamma attained realization of the Truth (dhammābhisamaya).
Having mastered the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas, that venerable one became a great preacher of the Dhamma;
after living for one hundred and twenty years, having caused a great stir throughout the entire land of Jambudīpa, he passed away into Parinibbāna.
The fifth story: The novice Sānu.
6. The Story of the Elephant of Pāveyyaka.
While residing at Jetavana, the Teacher gave this Dhamma teaching concerning the elephant named Pāveyyaka belonging to the King of Kosala, beginning with the words: "Delighting in heedfulness..."
It is said that once, when the elephant was in his youth and possessed great strength, at another time he was struck by the force of old age and wind;
having entered a large lake, he became stuck in the mud and was unable to emerge.
When the great multitude saw him, they raised a discussion, saying, "Even such an elephant as this has come to such a state of weakness. The king [heard] this...
Having heard of the occurrence, he commanded the elephant trainer: "Go, master, and pull that elephant out from the mud.
He went to that place, displayed the front of a battle, and had the war-drum beaten.
Being of a proud nature, the elephant rose up with speed and established itself on dry land. When the bhikkhus saw this event, they reported it to the Teacher.
The Teacher said, “Monks, that elephant rescued himself from the natural mire of the swamp, but you have plunged into the swamp of the defilements.
Therefore, by applying yourself with wise effort, you too must rescue yourselves from it. Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“Be devoted to heedfulness; guard your own minds well.”
"Rescue yourselves from the difficult path, like an elephant stuck in the mud.
In this context, "delighting in heedfulness" means you should take delight in not being separated from mindfulness.

"Guard your own mind" means protect your own mind regarding objects such as forms, etc., so that it does not commit transgression. "From the difficult path" means, just as that [elephant] in the mud...
Just as an elephant, having exerted effort with its trunk and feet, pulls itself out from a difficult mire and establishes itself on firm ground,
so too you should pull yourselves out from the difficult mire of the defilements and establish yourselves on the firm ground of Nibbāna—
this is the meaning. At the conclusion of the teaching, those bhikkhus were established in Arahatship.
The sixth story: The Elephant of Pāveyyaka.
7. The Story of the Many Bhikkhus.
"If one should obtain..."—the Teacher gave this Dhamma teaching while staying at the Protected Grove near Pālileyyaka.

While dwelling there, he spoke concerning a large number of bhikkhus. The background story has already appeared in the commentary on the verse “And others do not perceive” in the Yamaka-vagga. For it was said:
the fact that the Tathāgata was residing there while being attended upon by the elephant Hatthināga was well known throughout the whole of Jambudīpa.
From the city of Sāvatthī, great clans such as those of Anāthapiṇḍika and the Great Laywoman Visākhā sent a message to the Elder Ānanda, saying: "Venerable sir, please let us see the Teacher.
Five hundred resident monks who had completed the rains retreat also approached the Elder Ānanda and said: "Friend Ānanda, it has been a long time since we have heard from you."
“In the presence of the Blessed One, a discourse on the Dhamma—O friend Ānanda, it would be well for us to receive a discourse on the Dhamma from the presence of the Blessed One,” they requested.

The Elder, taking those bhikkhus with him, went there and said, “For three months we have been living together in seclusion; it is not fitting for the Tathāgata to approach the presence of so many bhikkhus.”
Thinking, "This is improper," he placed those monks outside and approached the Teacher alone.
When Pālileyyaka saw him, he took up his staff and rushed forward. The Teacher looked at him and said, "Go away, go away, Pālileyyaka! Do not stop him;
he is an attendant of the Buddha. Thereupon, he dropped his staff right there and received the Teacher's bowl and robes.

He asked for permission. The Elder did not grant it. The Nāga thought, "If he has mastered the proper conduct (*vatta*), he will not place his own requisites upon the stone seat where the Teacher sits. The Elder placed his bowl and robes on the ground;
for those perfected in proper conduct do not place their own requisites upon the seats or beds of their superiors.
The Elder paid homage to the Teacher and sat down to one side. The Teacher asked, "Have you come alone?
When he heard that he had come with five hundred bhikkhus, he asked, "But where are they?
When the Elder replied, "I left them outside because I did not know your mind," the Teacher said, "Call them here. The Elder did so. Then the Teacher [addressed] them...
Having exchanged greetings with the monks, when those monks said, "Venerable sir, the Blessed One is delicate both as a Buddha and as a kshatriya;
it must have been difficult for you to remain standing or sitting alone for three months,
and I imagine there was no one to perform the duties of service nor anyone to provide water for rinsing the mouth and other necessities," [the Blessed One replied], "Monks,..."
“The Pālileyyaka elephant has performed all my duties. For one who obtains such a companion as this, it is fitting to dwell alone;
for one who does not obtain such a one, the state of wandering alone is better. Having said this, he spoke these verses regarding the herd of elephants:
“If one could find a prudent companion...”
One should wander, joyful and mindful, with that steadfast companion who lives rightly, having overcome all dangers.
“If one does not find a wise companion,
a steadfast friend who walks with one and dwells in virtue,
then like a king abandoning a conquered kingdom, one should wander alone.”
One should wander alone like an elephant in the Matanga forest:
"The life of one who wanders alone is better;
there is no companionship with fools."
“One should wander alone and commit no evil deeds, free from anxiety like an elephant in the Mātaṅga forest.
In this context, “wise” means endowed with analytical wisdom (*nepakkapaññā*). “Virtuous in their dwelling, steadfast” means one who dwells in an auspicious manner.

"A wise person. "Regarding dangers": finding such a companion who dwells in loving-kindness, one should overcome all dangers—both manifest dangers such as lions, tigers, and the like, and hidden dangers such as the fear of lust, the fear of hatred, and the fear of delusion—and should travel with him contented and established in mindfulness; this is the meaning.
"Like a king who has left his kingdom"—this means he departed like King Mahājanaka. This is what is intended:
just as a king who has conquered a territory thinks, "This sovereignty is a great occasion for negligence; what use have I for ruling?
and, abandoning the conquered realm, enters the great forest all alone and goes forth into the ascetic life, [he dwells] in the four...
"He wanders alone among the postures; thus, one should wander alone. "Just like a noble elephant in the forest" means:
"I indeed dwell crowded with male elephants, female elephants, elephant calves, and elephant cubs;
I eat grass with its tips broken off, and they eat my broken-off branches; [the waters] are turbid..."
"I drink water, and when I have emerged from the bathing place, female elephants pass by, rubbing their bodies against mine.

What if I were to dwell alone, withdrawn from the herd? Having reflected thus, this great elephant, known as Mātanga because of his gait, abandoned the herd and remained in all postures in this forest.
"He wanders alone in happiness; thus, one should also wander alone"—this is the meaning.
"Of the one" means that for one who has gone forth, from the very moment of going forth, it is better for the one who delights in solitude to wander alone.

"There is no companion in a fool"—this refers to the Shorter Code of Ethics (Cūḷasīla), the Intermediate Code of Ethics (Majjhimasīla), the Greater Code of Ethics (Mahāsīla), and the Ten Subjects of Discourse (Dasa Kathāvatthūni).

The thirteen ascetic virtues (*dhutaṅga*), insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*), the four paths, the four fruits, the three types of higher knowledge (*tisso vijjā*), the six direct knowledges (*cha abhiññā*), and the deathless Great Nibbāna—this indeed is called "companionship. Since it is not possible to attain these by relying on fools, there is no companionship with fools.
For this reason, expressed by the word "alone," one should wander all alone in every posture, even regarding minor matters.

"And one should not commit evil deeds. The meaning is: just as that noble elephant Mātanga, free from anxiety and without attachment, wanders happily wherever he desires in this forest, so too should one wander alone and not commit even the slightest evil deeds.
Therefore, for those who do not find a suitable companion, it is fitting to be a lone wanderer; such is the point.
The Teacher, bestowing this Dhamma instruction upon those bhikkhus, taught it to them.
At the conclusion of the teaching, all five hundred bhikkhus were established in Arahatship.
This is the seventh story, concerning many bhikkhus.
8. The Discourse on Māra.
The Teacher delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning Māra while dwelling in a forest hut in the Himalayan region.
It is said that at that time, kings were ruling by oppressing their subjects. Then the Blessed One [spoke] regarding those unrighteous kings...
Seeing people oppressed by the administration of punishments in the kingdom, he reflected out of compassion:
"Is it possible to exercise sovereignty righteously—without killing or causing to kill, without conquering or causing to conquer, without grieving or causing to grieve?
Māra the Evil One, knowing this reflection of the Blessed One’s, thought: "The ascetic Gotama has reflected, 'Is it possible to exercise sovereignty?'"
Thinking, "Now he will wish to exercise sovereignty; and sovereignty is indeed a ground for negligence, and while he exercises it, it is possible to find an opportunity;
I shall go and incite him," the Teacher approached the Master and said:
"May the Blessed One exercise sovereignty, may the Sugata exercise sovereignty—without killing, without causing slaughter, without conquering, without subjugating."
“I have caused no one to be born, I have caused no one to grieve, nor have I caused anyone to grieve, in accordance with the Dhamma.

Then the Teacher said to him, “But what do you see in me, Evil One, that you speak to me thus? [Māra replied: “Venerable sir, the four bases of psychic power have been well-developed by the Blessed One.
If the Blessed One so desired, he could resolve that the Himalayas, the king of mountains, be ‘gold.’”
When he had said, "Let that [treasure] be gold alone, and I too shall perform my duties with wealth,
while you shall rule the kingdom according to the Dhamma," [the king replied]:
"The entire mountain of gold, of refined metal..."
"Two are not enough for one"— knowing this, one should live in harmony.
"How could a person who has seen suffering and its source bow down to sensual pleasures?"
“Having understood the substrate, one should train for its removal in this world.

Having stirred him with these verses, he said: “Evil One, your instruction is one thing, mine is another; there is no common discussion of the Dhamma between you and me. For I instruct thus,” and he spoke these verses:
“Friends are a joy when misfortune arises;
contentment with whatever one has is a joy;
merit is a joy at the end of life’s span.”
The abandoning of all suffering is happiness.
“In this world, filial devotion toward one’s mother is happy,
and likewise, filial devotion toward one’s father is happy.”
Happy is the state of being a recluse in this world,
and happy too is the state of being a brahmin.
Happy is virtue maintained until old age, and happy is faith firmly established.
"Happy is the acquisition of wisdom; happy is the refraining from evil deeds.

In this context, "in matters" refers to whatever task arises—whether for one who has gone forth, such as making robes or settling a legal dispute, or for a householder, such as agricultural work or overcoming those who rely on a powerful faction.
The meaning is that those who are able to accomplish or pacify such tasks are "pleasant companions. Regarding "contentment is happiness":

because householders, being dissatisfied with their own lot, engage in such acts as breaking into houses, and because renunciants likewise engage in various kinds of improper search, they do not find happiness at all. Therefore, that which consists of being content with whatever is available...
Contentment with whatever belongs to oneself, whether it be small or great—this alone is happiness; such is the meaning.
Furthermore, "merit" refers to the very act of merit performed according to one's aspiration at the time of death; that indeed is happiness.
Moreover, "of all"—namely, the abandonment of the entire suffering of saṃsāra, which is known as Arahantship—is what is called happiness in this world.
*Matteyyatā* means proper conduct toward one’s mother. *Petteyyatā* means proper conduct toward one’s father.

By both terms, what is described is specifically the act of attending upon one’s parents. For indeed, when parents realize their children are not attending to them, they either bury their own possessions in the ground or hand them over to others, thinking, "They do not attend upon us."
Their censure increases as well, and with the breakup of the body, they are reborn even in the Feces Hell (*gūthaniraya*).
However, those who attend upon their mother and father with diligence obtain both the wealth belonging to them and receive praise;
with the breakup of the body, they are reborn in heaven. Therefore, it is said that "both of these are happiness. Regarding "the state of being common":
"Right practice toward those who have gone forth" means precisely right practice toward the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and their disciples, who have banished evil.
By both [terms], the state of providing for them with the four requisites is described;
this too is what is called "happiness in the world."
“Virtue” (sīla): For ornaments such as jewels, earrings, and fine garments shine only upon those established in their respective stages of life.
An ornament for the young does not shine at the time of old age, nor does an ornament for the elderly shine at the time of youth;
rather, it produces only fault by giving rise to censure, such as, “I suppose this person is mad. [This applies to] the various divisions of the five precepts, the ten precepts, and so forth.
Moreover, virtue shines indeed at all stages of life, whether one is young or old;
by inspiring praise such as, "Oh, how virtuous this person is," it brings about nothing but gladness. Therefore it is said: "Virtue is happiness until old age.
"Faith is firmly established" means that faith—both mundane and supramundane—is established, being unshakable. "Happiness through wisdom..."

"Acquisition" means the acquisition of mundane and supramundane wisdom is blissful. "The non-doing of evil" means that, by way of destroying the bridge [to rebirth], the non-doing of evil is bliss in this world; such is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, there was a penetration of the Dhamma for many deities.
The eighth discourse on Māra is finished.
The commentary on the Nāga Chapter is completed.
This is the twenty-third chapter.
24. The Chapter on Craving (Taṇhāvagga) 1. The Story of Kapilamaccha:
Regarding the phrase "Of a human being," the Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this Dhamma teaching concerning Kapilamaccha.
It is said that in the past, at the time of the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One Kassapa, two brothers from a noble family went forth and received the going-forth in the presence of the disciples.
Of them, the elder was named Sāgata and the younger was named Kapila.
Their mother was named Sādhinī and their younger sister was named Tāpanā; they too went forth among the bhikkhunīs. Thus...
When they had both gone forth, the two brothers lived performing their duties and services toward their teachers and preceptors.
One day, having asked, "Venerable sir, how many duties (dhura) are there in this Dispensation?

and having heard the reply, "There are two duties: the duty of study (ganthadhura) and the duty of insight (vipassanādhura)," the elder brother, thinking, "I shall fulfill the duty of insight," [served] his teachers and preceptors for five years.
Having lived in his presence and received a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he entered the forest and, through diligent effort, attained *arahantship*.

The younger brother, thinking, "I am still young; I shall fulfill the duty of insight (*vipassanā*) in my old age," established himself in the duty of study (*ganthadhura*) and mastered the Three Piṭakas.
Relying on his mastery of the scriptures, he gained a great following, and because of that following...

Relying on him, gain arose. Intoxicated by the pride of his great learning and overcome by craving for gain, out of excessive conceit in his own wisdom, he would call what was permissible "impermissible" and what was impermissible "permissible";
he called what was blameworthy "blameless" and what was blameless "blameworthy. Then those virtuous bhikkhus said to him, "Friend Kapila, do not..."

Having spoken thus, even while he was being instructed after he had shown both the Dhamma and the Vinaya, he continued to act with contempt and derision, saying such things as, "What do you know? You are like empty fists!
Then the monks reported this matter to his brother, the Elder Sāgata. He too approached him and said, "Friend Kapila, for those such as you..."
“Right practice is what is called the life-span of the Dispensation; therefore, do not speak thus, rejecting right practice while upholding only what is allowable and so forth,” he advised.

But he did not heed his words either. Even so, after advising him two or three times, the Elder realized, “This man will not follow my advice,” and knowing this, said: “By that, friend, you shall be known.”
Having said, "By one's own karma," he departed. From that time on, other well-behaved bhikkhus abandoned him.

Living as one of evil conduct surrounded by those of evil conduct, one day at the Uposatha hall, thinking, "I shall recite the Pātimokkha," he took a fan, sat upon the Dhamma-seat, and said, "Friends, it is appropriate for those assembled here..."

Having asked, "The Pātimokkha for the bhikkhus," and seeing that the bhikkhus remained silent when he said, "What is the use of giving an answer to this?", he remarked, "Friends, there is neither Dhamma nor Vinaya; what is the use of the Pātimokkha, whether heard or not heard?
Having said this, he rose from his seat. In this way, he [rejected] the teaching of the scriptures of the Blessed One Kassapa.
He caused [him] to be expelled. On that very same day, the Elder Sāgata also attained final Nibbāna. At the end of his lifespan, Kapila was reborn in the great Avīci hell.
His mother and sister, following his example, reviled and abused the virtuous monks and were reborn in that very same place.
At that time, five hundred men who had lived by robbery, having committed acts such as plundering villages, were pursued by the people of the countryside.
While fleeing, they entered a forest; finding no refuge there, they saw a certain forest-dwelling bhikkhu.
Having paid homage to him, they said, "Venerable sir, be our refuge. The Elder—
“There is no refuge equal to your virtue; therefore, all of you undertake the five precepts,” he said.
Having accepted with the words, “Very well,” they undertook the precepts. Then the Elder exhorted them:
“Now that you possess virtue, you must not transgress your virtue even for the sake of your lives, nor should you harbor malice in your minds.”

They accepted, saying, "Very well. Then, when the people of the countryside reached that place and searched here and there, they saw those thieves and took the lives of them all. Having passed away, they were reborn in the world of the devas;
the chief thief became the eldest son of the devas.

Having wandered through the world of the devas for one interval between Buddhas by way of both forward and reverse order, they were reborn at the time of this Buddha’s appearance in a fisherman village near the gate of the city of Sāvatthī, consisting of five hundred families.
The eldest son of the devas took conception in the house of the chief fisherman, while the others were conceived in their respective homes. Thus, on that very same day, they all underwent conception.

And there was his emergence from his mother’s womb. The elder Kevaṭṭa, having had it investigated whether there were any other children born in this village that day, and having learned of their birth, gave the means for their upbringing with the thought, "These shall be companions for my son.
They all became friends, playing together in the dust.
In due course, they reached maturity. Among them, the eldest son of the fisherman Keṭubha was the foremost man in terms of both reputation and splendor.

As for Kapila, having been boiled in hell for the duration of one Buddha-interval, he was reborn at that time as a golden-colored fish with a foul-smelling mouth in the Aciravatī River as a result of the remaining karmic fruition. Then one day, those companions [saw] the fish...
Thinking, "We shall catch it," they took their nets and other gear and cast them into the river. Then that fish entered inside their net.
Seeing this, all the inhabitants of the fishermen's village raised a great shout: "When our sons first caught fish, they caught a golden fish!
Now the king will give us much wealth! And those friends...
Having placed the fish in a boat and hoisted the boat up, they went into the presence of the king.
When the king saw it and asked, "What is this?", they replied, "It is a fish, Your Majesty.
Upon seeing the golden-colored fish, the king thought, "The Teacher will know the cause of its golden color," and having had the fish taken, he went into the presence of the Blessed One.
He arrived. As soon as the fish opened its mouth, the entire Jeta Grove became exceedingly foul-smelling.
The King asked the Teacher, "Venerable Sir, why has the fish become golden-colored, and why does a foul odor blow from its mouth?"
"Great King, in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, there was a bhikkhu named Kapila who was learned and had a large following.
Overcome by craving for gain, he reviled and abused those who did not accept his words;
he caused the teaching of that Blessed One to decline. Because of that karma, he was reborn in Avīci, and due to the remainder of its ripening..."
Now he has been born as a fish. However, because he recited the Buddha’s word for a long time and spoke of the Buddha’s virtues, by the result of that merit he obtained this golden complexion.
Because he was one who reviled and insulted the bhikkhus, a foul odor emanates from his mouth. “Shall I speak with him, Great King? “Speak with him.”
“Venerable sir,” he replied. Then the Teacher asked him, “Are you Kapila? “Yes, venerable sir, I am Kapila. “Where have you come from?
“From the Great Niraya of Avīci, venerable sir. “Where has your elder brother Sāgata gone?
“He has attained final Nibbāna, venerable sir. “But where is your mother Sādhinī? “She has been reborn in the Great Niraya, venerable sir.”
“And where is your younger sister Tāpanā? “She has been reborn in the Great Hell, Bhante.
“Where will you go now? “To the Great Niraya of Avīci itself, Bhante,” he said;
then, overcome by remorse, he struck his head against the boat, died instantly, and was reborn in hell. The great multitude was deeply moved, their hair standing on end with awe.
Then the Blessed One, having observed the mental disposition of the assembly gathered at that moment,

spoke these verses after reciting the Kapila Sutta from the Sutta Nipāta— beginning with “The practice of Dhamma, the holy life; this they call the supreme treasure”— in order to teach the Dhamma appropriate for that occasion:
“For a person who wanders heedlessly, craving grows like a creeping vine.
He leaps from one state to another, like a monkey in the forest seeking fruit.
That miserable craving which clings to the world—this is what he endures.”
His sorrows increase like bīraṇa grass after heavy rain.
But for him who endures this foul craving, so difficult to overcome in the world,
his sorrows fall away from him like drops of water from a lotus leaf.
“I say this to you, may it be well with you, all you who have gathered here:
dig up the root of craving, as one seeking fragrant grass digs up the *bīraṇa* weeds.
Let not Māra break you again and again, as the reed breaks the *naḷa* cane.”
In this context, "one who wanders negligently" refers to a person whose conduct is negligent due to negligence characterized by the loss of mindfulness;
for such a person, neither meditation (*jhāna*), nor insight (*vipassanā*), nor the paths and fruits (*maggaphala*) increase.
Just as the *māluvā* creeper grows by entwining and enveloping a tree to its destruction, so too, in dependence upon his six sense doors...
The meaning is that craving increases because it arises again and again.
"He floats from here to there" means that this person, being subject to craving, drifts and runs from existence to existence. How is this like what? It is like a monkey in the forest desiring fruit;
just as a monkey desiring the fruit of trees runs through the forest from branch to branch of this tree or that tree.
Just as a monkey, having let go of one thing, seizes another; and having let go of that, seizes yet another;

does not incur the description, "it sits down because it could not find a branch"—even so, a person subject to craving, running from here to there, does not incur the description, "he has reached a non-occurrence of craving because he could not find an object."
That person whom this craving— reckoned as "visattikā" (clinging) because it is base, vile, feeds on poison, has poisonous flowers, has poisonous fruits,
involves the use of poison, and because it clings to and adheres to forms and so forth— overcomes by means of its sixfold gateway,
just as the *vīraṇa* grass is overwhelmed when repeatedly rained upon by a god raining during the rainy season.
It increases; the meaning is that for such a person, the sorrows rooted in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) increase within.

"Hard to transcend" (*duraccaya*): but as for the person who endures—that is, overcomes—craving, which is "hard to transcend" because it is difficult to pass beyond or abandon in the manner described, from that person the sorrows rooted in the cycle of existence fall away. Just as...
"Just as a drop of water fallen upon a lotus leaf does not remain—meaning it does not settle—so too [it does not remain].
"I tell you this" means: for that reason, I say this to you. "May there be welfare for you" means: may there be well-being for you;
do not meet with destruction like Kapila. "The root" refers to this sixfold craving by means of the knowledge of the path to arahantship.
"Dig up the root! What is it like?"—it means: "Just as a man seeking *usīra* grass digs up the *bīraṇa* grass with a large hoe because he needs the *usīra*, so too dig up its root.
"Lest Māra break you again and again like the reed by the river"—this means: "Lest the river current, having arrived with great force, break the reed growing in the river's flow."
The meaning is: "May the defilement-māra, the death-māra, and the devaputta-māra break [him] again and again.
At the conclusion of the teaching, the five hundred sons of fishermen were moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega);

aspiring to bring an end to suffering, they went forth in the presence of the Teacher. Before long, having brought an end to suffering, they enjoyed the Dhamma through the attainment of the imperturbable abiding (āneñjavihārasamāpatti) together with the Teacher.
"They were shared by only one person.
This is the first story, the Story of the Tawny Fish.
2. The Story of the Sow's Farrow.
