The Teacher delivered this Dhamma teaching, "Just as the root," while dwelling at Veḷuvana, concerning a young sow.
It is said that on one occasion, while the Teacher was entering Rājagaha for alms, he saw a young sow and manifested a smile.
Seeing the circle of light from his teeth emerging from the opening of his mouth as he smiled, the Elder Ānanda—
“Venerable sir, what is the reason for your breaking into a smile? he asked, inquiring about the cause of the smile.
Then the Teacher said to him: “Do you see this little sow, Ānanda? “Yes, venerable sir.
“In the dispensation of the Blessed One Kakusandha, she was a hen living near a certain assembly hall. She [acted as] the object of insight meditation for a certain practitioner of yoga.”
Having heard the sound of the Dhamma while he was reciting it, she passed away from there and was reborn in a royal family as a princess named Ubbarī.
Later, having entered the place where the body was being washed and seeing a heap of maggots, she conceived the perception of maggots toward that heap and attained the first jhāna.
Having remained there for the duration of her lifespan, she passed away from there and was reborn in the Brahma-world.
"...was reborn. Having passed away from there, wandering again through the cycle of existence, it has now been reborn in the womb of a pig.
Seeing this cause, I manifested a smile. Upon hearing this, the monks headed by the Elder Ānanda were seized with great spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
Having aroused their sense of urgency, the Teacher, demonstrating the peril of craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*), said:
Standing right there in the middle of the street, he spoke these verses:
"Just as a tree, though cut down, grows forth once again if its root remains unharmed and firm;
Thus, as long as the underlying tendency of craving has not been uprooted,
this suffering arises again and again.
For one who has thirty-six streams that flow intensely with what is pleasing—
“Intentions based on passion carry away one’s wrong view.
Streams flow everywhere; a creeper arises and stands.
Seeing that creeper has grown, cut its root with wisdom.”
“Beings have desires and endearments,
and they experience joys; being addicted to pleasures and seeking happiness, [they suffer].”
Truly, those people go to birth and old age. Led by craving,
beings run about like a trapped hare.
“Bound by the fetters and attachments,
beings encounter suffering again and again for a long time.
Led on by craving, the worldling— ”
They run about like a trapped hare;
therefore, one who desires their own dispassion should dispel craving.
In this context, "root" refers to a tree that has five types of roots extending straight downward and out in the four directions;

when it is not afflicted by any calamity such as being cut, split, cooked, or pierced, and possesses firm leaves and a strong trunk, that tree will grow back again through its branches even if it is severed at the top. In the same way, regarding the craving of the six doors...

The meaning is that while the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) have been struck down by the knowledge of the path to *arahantship* but not yet completely eradicated, this suffering— consisting of the various divisions such as birth and so forth— continues to arise again and again in each respective existence.
"Of whom" means of whichever person [there are] these eighteen modes of craving-conduct (*taṇhāvicarita*) based on the internal [clinging], and [those based] on the external [clinging].
Regarding the eighteen modes of craving’s wandering (*taṇhāvicarita*): through these modes of craving’s wandering, one is possessed of thirty-six streams;
thus craving flows and proceeds toward agreeable forms and so forth, and is therefore called "agreeably flowing" (*manāpasavanā*). This craving becomes excessive and powerful.
Because it arises again and again with great magnitude due to the person’s corrupted knowledge and wrong view, [it is so described].
The meaning is that, having become great, they flow as intentions based on lust, without depending on either jhāna or insight.
"They flow everywhere like streams" means these streams of craving flow in every way by way of the doors of the eye and so forth, because they flow toward all objects such as visible forms;
or alternatively, they flow everywhere because they flow through all states of existence, including all craving for forms... [and so on] ... up to craving for mental phenomena.
“Latā”: It is called a creeper (*latā*) because it is like a creeper in the sense of entwining and in the sense of binding.
“Arising and standing”: having arisen through the six doors, it stands upon objective fields such as visible forms and so forth. “And seeing that”:
having seen that creeper of craving by way of its place of birth—thinking, “It is here that this craving arises when it arises”—by means of wisdom (*paññā*), which is like a sword.
The meaning is: "Cut them at the root with the wisdom of the path, like a creeper grown in the forest.
"Saritāni" means those that have flowed out or spread forth. "Sinehitāni" means those that are moistened by the moisture of attachment occurring toward robes and so forth;
the meaning is that they are smeared with the moisture of craving (*taṇhā*). "Somanassāni" refers to such things belonging to a person who is under the sway of craving.
There are states of joy. "Those who are dependent on gratification" means that those persons, being under the sway of craving (*taṇhā*), become dependent on gratification and dependent on pleasure;
thus they become seekers of pleasure and pursuers of pleasure. "And those" refers to such men as these:

they certainly undergo birth, aging, sickness, and death, and are therefore called "those who go to birth and aging. *Pajā* refers to these beings; because it causes fear, it is called "craving" (*tāsī*).
"Preceded by craving that has reached its full measure" means being preceded and surrounded by it.
"Bound" means they crawl about and tremble with fear like a hare caught in a net by a hunter in the forest.
"Attached by the snares of the fetters" means bound by the tenfold snares of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and by the sevenfold snares of passion (*rāga*) and so forth, they are attached to that.
Or having become attached. "For a long time" (*cirāya*) means that they repeatedly undergo suffering, such as birth, for a long duration and over a vast period.

"Therefore" (*tasmā*) means: because beings are preceded by craving—that is, enveloped by it—therefore a bhikkhu who desires and longs for his own fading away (*virāga*), the departure from lust and the rest, which is Nibbāna, should dispel this craving by means of the path to Arahantship.
"Having pushed it out and removed it, one should discard it"—this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
That sow, too, passed away from there and was reborn in a royal family in Suvaṇṇabhūmi; passing away from there, she was reborn in Bārāṇasī.
Passing away from there, she was reborn in the house of a horse-merchant in the city of Suppāraka; passing away from there, she was reborn in the house of a mariner in the city of Kāvīra;
passing away from there, she was reborn in the house of a noble family in Anurādhapura;
and passing away from there, she was reborn as the daughter of a householder named Sumanas in the village of Bhokkanta to the south of that same city, with the very name Sumanā.
Having made an offering, she was reborn. Then her father, when that village had been abandoned, went to the kingdom of Dīghavāpi and lived in a place called Mahāmunigāma.
There, a minister of King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi named Lakuṇḍaka Atimbara, having gone there on some business, saw her;
after performing a great auspicious ceremony, he took her and went to Mahāpuṇṇagāma. Then him—
The Elder Mahā-Anuruddha, who dwelt in the Mahāvihāra on Mount Koṭapabbata, while wandering for alms there, stood at the door of that house and spoke with the monks:
"Friends, the sow named Sūkarapotikā has attained the status of wife to the minister Lakuṇḍaka-Aṭimbara; oh, how wonderful! Having heard those words, she recalled her past birth.

She attained the knowledge of recollecting past births. At that very moment, overcome with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), she requested permission from her husband and, with great magnificence, went forth under the five *balaka* therīs.

Having heard the discourse on the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta at the Tissamahāvihāra, she was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti*). Later, when the suppression of the Damilas had been accomplished, [she went] to the dwelling place of her kinsmen.
Having gone specifically to the village of Bhokkanta and residing there, she heard the *Āsīvisopama-sutta* (The Simile of the Venomous Snake) at the Kallama Mahāvihāra and attained *arahatta*.
On the day of her *parinibbāna*, when questioned by the monks and nuns, she recounted this entire account in detail to the community of nuns;
then, in the midst of the assembled community of monks, [she spoke] with the Elder Mahātissa, a reciter of the *Dhammapada* who resided at Maṇḍalārāma.
Having compared [the accounts] together: "In the past, having been reborn in the human womb, I passed away from there and became a hen;
there, having received a decapitation at the hands of Sena, I was reborn in Rājagaha. Having gone forth among the female wanderers, I was reborn in the plane of the first jhāna;
passing away from there, I was reborn in a family of wealthy merchants, and before long, having passed away from there..."
"Having gone to the womb of a pig, passing away from there, she went to Suvaṇṇabhūmi; passing away from there, to Bārāṇasī; passing away from there, to the port of Suppāraka;
passing away from there, to the port of Kāvīra; passing away from there, to Anurādhapura; and passing away from there, to Bhokkantagāma.
Having thus undergone these thirteen successive existences, both favorable and unfavorable, she now became weary of the world, went forth into homelessness, and attained Arahantship.
"May you all also accomplish this through diligence," he said, and having inspired the four assemblies with a sense of urgency, he attained final Nibbāna.
This is the second story, that of the sow’s piglet.
3. The Story of the Deserted Bhikkhu.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Veḷuvana, gave this Dhamma teaching concerning a certain monk who had fallen away from the order.
It is said that a certain disciple of the Elder Mahākassapa, although he had attained the four jhānas, saw a disagreeable object in the house of his maternal uncle, a goldsmith;
his mind became bound to it there, and he fell away from the order.
Then, because of his laziness, people expelled him from his home for being unwilling to work. Under the influence of evil companions, he wandered about making his living through criminal acts.
One day, they seized him, bound his hands tightly behind his back, and led him to the place of execution, lashing him with whips at every crossroads. Meanwhile, the Elder was wandering for alms.
As he was entering, seeing him being led out through the southern gate, he had his bonds loosened and said, "Recall again the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) you previously cultivated.
Through that instruction, the man regained mindfulness and once more attained the fourth jhāna.
Then, thinking, "Let us take him to the execution ground and have him executed," they impaled him on a stake.

Thus he does not fear, nor is he terrified. Then, even though people standing in various directions brandish weapons such as swords, spears, and lances, they see him remaining entirely unperturbed and exclaim, "Look, sirs, at this man!
In the midst of hundreds of men with weapons in their hands, he neither trembles nor quakes; oh, how wonderful! And so they are filled with a sense of marvel and amazement.
Having let out a great roar, they reported the matter to the king. When the king heard the reason for this, he said, "Release him.
They also went into the presence of the Teacher and reported the matter to him. The Teacher, pervading the area with radiance, taught the Dhamma to him and spoke this verse:
“Behold this person here: though seeking the state beyond the forest and intent on escaping the forest,
being already freed from the forest, he runs right back into the forest.”
“The freed one runs back to the very bondage.

Its meaning is as follows: that person who, having abandoned the thicket (vanatha) known as attachment in the state of a householder, has become free from the thicket through the act of going forth, and is intent upon the forest of austerity known as the divine abodes—[yet remains bound] by the craving-thicket known as the bondage of household life...
"Having been released, he runs again toward that very forest of craving known as the bondage of the household life. Come, look at this person!
Having been freed from the bondage of the household life, he runs right back to the bondage of the household life.
Upon hearing this teaching, even while sitting on the tip of the stake among the royal guards, he established the contemplation of arising and passing away.
Having applied the three characteristics and contemplated conditioned phenomena, he attained the fruit of stream-entry.

Experiencing the bliss of meditative attainment, he leaped into the air and went through the sky to the presence of the Teacher. Having paid homage to the Teacher, he reached Arahantship right there in the midst of the assembly, including the king.
The third story: The Case of the Deserted Monk.
4. The Story of the Prison.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, related this Dhamma teaching concerning a prison. "That is not strong"—this was said with reference to the prison.
It is said that once, having brought many thieves—cut-purses, highwaymen, and murderers—the King of Kosala presented them to him.
The king had them bound with handcuffs, rope-bonds, and iron chains.
Meanwhile, about thirty monks from the countryside, desiring to see the Teacher, arrived; having seen him and paid homage, they stayed for the following day in Sāvatthī.
While wandering for alms, they went to a prison; having seen the thieves there, they returned from their almsround and approached the Tathāgata in the evening, saying:
"Venerable Sir, today, while we were wandering for alms, we saw many thieves in the prison bound with iron shackles and other fetters, experiencing great suffering. Having cut those bonds..."
“They were unable to escape; is there, venerable sir, another bond more firm than those bonds?

they asked. The Teacher replied, “Monks, what kind of bonds are these? But as for that bond of defilement known as craving—which consists of wealth, grain, children, wives, and so forth—that is a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousandfold [stronger] than these.”
"Even this very firm and great bond, which is so difficult to sever, was severed by the wise of old;
having done so, they entered the Himavat mountains and went forth into the homeless life. Having said this, he related a story of the past:
In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a certain poor household.
He was born. When he reached maturity, his father passed away. He supported his mother by working for wages.
Then, against his own will, his mother brought a daughter of good family into the home, and later she too passed away.
Subsequently, a fetus took root in the womb of his wife. Without even knowing that a fetus had taken root, he said, "My dear, you..."
“Live by performing labor; I shall go forth into the religious life,” he said. She replied, “Master, has not a pregnancy been established in me?
Once I have given birth and seen the child, you may go forth. He consented, saying, “Very well.
When she had given birth, he asked her, “Bhadde, you have given birth safely; now I shall go forth. Then she said to him regarding the son—
"Wait until the time comes for you to depart from this place of nursing," he said, and then she conceived again.
He thought to himself, "It is not possible to leave after having deceived her; rather, I shall flee without telling her and go forth into the religious life.
Without telling her, he rose during the night and fled. Then the city guards seized him.
Thus, saying, "Master, I am known as a supporter of my mother; please release me," he had himself released.

Having lived in one place for a time, he went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*, attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and dwelt sporting in the play of *jhāna*.
While dwelling there, he thought: "Even such a bond of wife and children, so difficult for me to sever—"
He uttered this inspired utterance: "The bond of defilements has been severed.
Having brought up this past event, the Teacher, proclaiming the inspired utterance thus uttered, spoke these verses:
"The wise do not call that a strong bond; it is the bond of craving that they say is strong. It is difficult to sever, like a diamond-tipped arrow; but when one has severed it, one goes to heaven."
That which is for iron, wood, or bamboo;
that passion and attachment for jewels and earrings,
and that longing for children and wives.
“The wise call this a strong bond—
carrying one away, slack yet difficult to release;
having cut even this asunder, they wander forth.”
“Having abandoned sensual pleasure, they are free from longing.
In this context, “the wise” refers to the Buddhas and other learned men. That which is called a shackle (*saṅkhalika*) is made of iron;
that which is called a fetter (*andu*) is made of wood; and there is also that where one makes a rope from grasses used for asceticism or from other materials such as *vāka* grass.
The meaning is that they do not say a rope-bond is "firm" because it can be cut with swords and other such weapons.
"Sārattarattā" means being attached and impassioned; the meaning is "colored by a very thick passion.
"Maṇikuṇḍalesu" means both in jewels and in earrings, or in earrings variegated with jewels. "This is firm" refers to those [bonds] regarding jewels and earrings.
"Intensely impassioned": the passion they have, as well as the craving that is concern for their children and wives—this is the bond consisting of defilements which wise men call "firm.
"Carrying away": it is called "carrying away" because it drags one down and casts one into the four states of misery;
it carries away and takes one downward. "Loose": it does not cut through the skin, hide, and flesh at the place of bondage.
It is "slack" because one does not extract the blood, nor does one allow the binding to be made known before permitting the performance of works by land, water, and so forth.

It is "difficult to release" because a bond of defilement that has arisen even once through the power of greed is difficult to free from its place of attachment, like a tortoise; thus it is "difficult to release. "Having cut this too" means this...
Having severed even the firm fetters of the defilements with the sword of knowledge, they go forth as wanderers, abandoning sensual pleasure without looking back;
"they set out" and "they go forth" is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and the other fruits.
The Fourth Story of the Prison.
5. The Story of the Elder Nun Khemā.
The Teacher delivered this discourse on the Dhamma beginning with the words, "Those who are dyed by passion," while residing at Veḷuvana, concerning the chief queen of King Bimbisāra named Khemā.
It is said that she, having made her aspiration at the feet of Padumuttara Buddha, became exceedingly beautiful and charming.
However, having heard that "the Teacher speaks of the defects of physical form," she did not wish to go into the presence of the Teacher.
The King, perceiving that she was intoxicated with pride in her own beauty, had songs composed concerning the description of the Veḷuvana Grove and [entrusted them] to actors and others.
He had it performed. Hearing the sound of them singing, the grove of Veḷuvana seemed to her as if never seen before and as if never heard before.
She asked, "Which park are you singing about?
When they replied, "O Queen, it is your very own Veḷuvana park," she desired to go to the park. The Teacher, knowing of her arrival, [stood] in the midst of the assembly.
Having sat down, while preaching the Dhamma, he created a beautiful woman who stood at his side holding a palm-leaf fan and fanning him.
As Queen Khemā was entering, she saw that woman and thought:
"They say the Perfectly Enlightened One speaks of the faults of physical form; yet here is a woman standing near him, fanning him. I am not..."
"I do not approach even a sixteenth part of her; never before have I seen such female beauty.
I suspect they are slandering the Teacher with untruth," she thought. Without even listening to the sound of the Tathāgata’s speech, she stood there gazing only at that woman.
The Teacher, knowing the great admiration she had conceived for that form, [transformed] that form...
Having shown [the body] by way of its successive stages beginning with the first stage of life, he showed it ending at last in mere bones, according to the method already explained below.
Seeing this, Khemā thought: "Even such a form as this has reached destruction and decay in a mere moment;
indeed, there is no core to this form. The Teacher, observing her state of mind, said: "Khemā..."
“You thought, ‘There is essence in this form’; now see its lack of essence! Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“Behold, Khema, this heap of misery—afflicted, impure, and putrid;
oozing and trickling, it is craved by fools.”
At the conclusion of that verse, she was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).
Then the Teacher said to her, "Khema, these beings, stained by lust, corrupted by hatred, and bewildered by delusion, are unable to cross over the stream of their own craving;
they remain stuck right there," and while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
“Those who are stained by passion follow the stream,
like a spider following the web it has woven itself.
Having cut even this asunder, the wise go forth.”
“Having abandoned all suffering, they are free from longing.

In this context, “like a spider with its web”: just as a spider, having spun a thread-web, lies in the middle at its navel-center, and then quickly goes out and pierces a cricket or a fly that has fallen upon the edge [of the web].

Just as one who has drunk the juice returns and lies down in that very same place, even so those beings who are intoxicated by lust, corrupted by hatred, and deluded by ignorance follow the stream of craving they have created themselves; they are unable to transcend it.
Thus it is difficult to transcend. "Having cut even this, the wise go on"—the wise ones sever this bond.
"Having severed [the fetters], being free from longing and without attachment, they go by means of the path of Arahatship, having abandoned all suffering"—this is the meaning of "they go.
At the conclusion of the teaching, Khemā was established in Arahatship, and the Dhamma instruction was beneficial for the great multitude as well.
The Teacher said to the king: "Great King, it is fitting for Khemā either to go forth or to attain Parinibbāna."
“Venerable sir, let him go forth; enough with final Nibbāna. Having gone forth, she became an eminent female disciple (agga-sāvika).
This is the fifth story, the account of the Elder Nun Khemā.
6. The Story of Uggasena.
The Teacher, while residing at Veḷuvana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning Uggasena.
It is said that five hundred actors would go to Rājagaha every year or every six months;
having performed a festival for the king for seven days, they received much gold and silver. From time to time, there came an end to their period of receiving gifts.
There was none. The great multitude stood upon one couch after another and watched the festival.
Then a daughter of a rope-dancer climbed a bamboo pole, whirled about on its top, and danced and sang while walking through the air along its edge.
At that time, a merchant’s son named Uggasena, together with a companion, [stood] upon a couch after another...
Standing there, he gazed at her; feeling affection arise for her through the movements of her hands and feet, he went home and said, "If I obtain her, I shall live;
if I do not obtain her, my death shall be right here. Having cut off his food, he lay down upon a couch.
Although his parents asked him, "Dear son, what is ailing you? he replied, "If I am to obtain that daughter of the dancer..."
"I have life, but if I do not obtain her, my death shall be right here," he said. Even when his father replied, "Dear son, do not act thus;
we shall bring you another maiden suitable for our family and its wealth," he spoke in the same manner and lay down.
Then his father, having entreated many others but being unable to persuade him, summoned his friend.
Having given a thousand kahāpaṇas, he sent [the man], saying, "Taking these kahāpaṇas, give your daughter to my son.

He replied, "I will not give her for the sake of taking kahāpaṇas; however, if he cannot live without obtaining her, then let him travel with us, and I shall give him my daughter. Thus spoke his parents to their son.
They reported this matter to him. He said, "I shall travel with them," and disregarding their pleas even as they entreated him, he departed and went into the presence of the actor.
The actor gave him his daughter in marriage, and together with him, he traveled through villages, market towns, and royal capitals, displaying his craft.
She too, after living with him for a short while, gave birth to a son;
and while playing with him, she would say, "Son of a cart-watcher! Son of a pack-carrier! Son of one who knows nothing!
He, for his part, would bring grass for the oxen at the place where they stood while turning the carts, and at the place where he displayed his craft, he would pick up the goods he had obtained.
He takes [her away]. It is said that with reference to this very matter, the woman, while playing with her son, spoke thus.
He, having understood her intention regarding himself from her singing, asked her: "Are you speaking with reference to me? "Yes, I am speaking with reference to you.
"If that is so, I shall run away. She said: "But what does it matter to me if you run away?"
"Or has she come?"—thus he sang that same song again and again. It seems she, relying on her own physical beauty and her acquisition of wealth, did not respect anyone at all.
He, wondering, "What indeed is she relying upon for this pride of hers?", realized it was "relying on her craft.
Thinking, "Very well, I shall learn the craft," he approached his father-in-law.
Having mastered that craft, while demonstrating his skill in villages, market towns, and other places, he eventually arrived at Rājagaha.
He had it proclaimed: "On the seventh day from now, Uggasena, the merchant’s son, will display his craft to the city-dwellers.
On the seventh day, the city-dwellers had platforms and tiered seats erected and assembled there. He [then] [prepared] a sixty-cubit...

Having climbed the bamboo pole, he stood upon its top. That morning, as the Teacher surveyed the world, he saw that the youth had entered within the net of his own knowledge. Reflecting, "What might happen? he perceived:
"Tomorrow, thinking 'I shall display my craft,' the merchant's son will stand atop the bamboo pole; for the sake of seeing him, a great multitude..."

"He will assemble there; I shall teach a four-line verse, and upon hearing it, eighty-four thousand living beings will attain the realization of the Dhamma, and Uggasena too will be established in Arahatship.
Having understood this, on the following day, the Teacher, having observed the proper time, entered Rājagaha for alms, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

He entered. Even as the Teacher had not yet fully entered the city, Uggasena, for the purpose of making a great proclamation to the people, gave a signal with his finger and, standing upon the top of a bamboo pole, spun around seven times in the air;
then descending, he stood once more upon the top of the bamboo pole. At that moment, as the Teacher was entering the city, so that the assembly would not...
He looked [at them]; having done so, he caused himself to be looked at as well. Uggasena, looking at the assembly and becoming dejected because "the assembly does not look at me," thought:

"This is the craft I am to display for a year; yet as the Teacher enters the city, the assembly does not look at me but looks only at the Teacher. Alas, my demonstration of the craft has become in vain!"
The Teacher, knowing his mind, addressed Mahāmoggallāna, saying, "Go, Moggallāna, and tell the merchant’s son:
'It is said you will display your craft. The Elder went and, standing at the base of the bamboo, called out to the merchant’s son and spoke this verse:
“Come now, see, son of a dancer, Uggasena of great strength!
Perform on the stage before the assembly and make the great multitude laugh!
Hearing the Elder’s words, he became joyful in mind and thought, “The Teacher, I suppose, wishes to see my craft. While still standing at the top of the bamboo pole, he spoke this verse:
“Come, see, O one of great wisdom, Moggallāna of great psychic power!
I shall provide a spectacle for the assembly and bring laughter to the great multitude.
Having spoken thus, he rose up into the air from the top of the bamboo pole and, while still in the sky, performed fourteen somersaults.

Having climbed up, he stood upon the top of the bamboo pole. Then the Teacher said to him, "Uggasena, it is fitting for one called wise to abandon attachment to the aggregates of the past, future, and present, and thus be liberated from birth and the rest," and he spoke this verse:
"Let go of what is before; let go of what is behind."
“Relinquish the middle of existence and go to the further shore;
with a mind liberated in every respect,
you shall not again undergo birth and old age.”
In this context, "release first" means: release attachment, affection, cleaving, longing, obsession, grasping, misapprehension, and craving toward the past aggregates.
"Behind" means: release those same [states] toward the future aggregates as well. "In the middle" means: release them toward the present aggregates as well.
"One who has gone beyond existence": when this is so, by way of direct knowledge, full understanding, abandoning, development, and realization, one has gone beyond the threefold existence.

"Having become one who has reached the further shore (*pāragū pāraṅgato*), dwelling with a mind liberated from all conditioned things—such as the distinctions of the aggregates (*khandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*)—one does not again undergo birth, aging, and death; this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, eighty-four thousand living beings attained penetration of the Dhamma (*dhammābhisamaya*). The merchant’s son also [attained it] at the top of the bamboo pole.
Remaining standing, he attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Descending from his lineage and approaching the presence of the Teacher, he paid homage to the Teacher by prostrating himself on his five limbs and requested the going-forth (pabbajjā).
Then the Teacher, extending his right hand, said to him, "Come, monk. At that very moment, he was endowed with the eight requisites like a sixty-year-old elder.

It was as if he were falling. Then the monks asked him, "Friend Uggasena, did you feel no fear at all as you descended from the top of that sixty-cubit bamboo pole? When he replied, "Friends, I had no fear," they reported it to the Teacher:
"Venerable Sir, Uggasena says, 'I am not afraid. Having spoken what is untrue, he gives a false explanation."
The Teacher said, "Monks, monks who have severed the fetters like my son Ugga Sena do not fear,
nor are they terrified," and having said this, he spoke this verse in the Brahmā Section:
"Having severed all fetters, he who indeed does not tremble..."
“One who has transcended attachment and is disjoined from it—him I call a brahmin.
At the conclusion of this teaching, many attained realization of the Dhamma. On another day, the bhikkhus raised a discussion in the Hall of Truth:
“Friends, for a bhikkhu who is thus endowed with the necessary conditions for attaining Arahatship...”
"Is the reason for wandering about with actors because of his attachment to the daughter of an actor the same as the cause for the support of arahantship?
The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, about what conversation are you gathered here now?
When they replied, "About this very matter," he said, "Monks, both of these were done by him alone," and in order to clarify that point, he related a story from the past.

It is said that in the past, while a golden cetiya was being constructed for Kassapa the Great Seer, a number of noble sons from Bārāṇasī loaded much solid and soft food onto carts and set out for the site of the cetiya, thinking, "We shall do manual labor.
On the way, they saw an elder entering for alms. Then, a certain noble daughter, having looked at the elder—
She said to her husband: "Husband, noble sir, he is entering for alms. We have much food, both hard and soft, in the carriage;
bring him his bowl, and we shall give him alms. He brought the bowl, filled it with hard and soft food, and placing it in the Elder’s hand, they both made a wish: "Venerable sir, by you..."
“May we become partakers of the very same state as he who has seen the Truth. That elder was also one whose taints were destroyed;
therefore, looking at them and knowing that their aspiration would be fulfilled, he smiled. Seeing this, the woman said to her husband, “Master, he is smiling at us;
he will surely become a dancer. Her husband replied to her, “It shall be so, my dear.”
Having said this, he departed. This was their prior karma. Having remained there for the duration of their lifespan and been reborn in the world of the gods, they passed away from there;
she was reborn in the house of a dancer, and the man in the house of a merchant.
Because he had given her the reply, "So be it, my lady," he associated with the dancers. [As for the alms-food given to the Elder whose taints were destroyed...]

Relying upon him, she attained arahantship. That dancer’s daughter also, thinking, "Whatever be the destination of my husband, that shall be my own destination," went forth and established herself in arahantship.
This is the sixth story, concerning Uggasena.

7. The Story of the Wise Young Archer, Cūḷadhanuggaha "Of one whose thoughts are agitated..."—the Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, spoke this Dhamma teaching concerning the wise young archer, Cūḷadhanuggaha.
It is said that a certain young bhikkhu, having taken his own bowl-ticket at the distribution of tickets and having received the ticket-gruel, went to the refectory.
Having gone there, he drank. Not finding water there, he went to a house for the sake of water.
Seeing him there, a young girl felt affection arise and said, "Venerable sir, if you have need of drinking water again, please come right here.
From then on, whenever he could not find water, he would go to that very place. She [would fill] his bowl...
Having taken it, he gave him water. As time passed in this manner, after having given him an offering of rice porridge, on another day he seated him right there and gave him a meal.
Sitting near him, he initiated a conversation, saying, "Venerable sir, there is nothing at all lacking in this house;
we simply cannot find anyone to serve as an attendant. After only a few days had passed, he...
Having heard her words, he became despondent. Then one day, some visiting monks saw him and asked, "Friend, why are you so emaciated and pale?
When he replied, "I am despondent, friends," they led him to his teachers and preceptors.
They, in turn, led him to the presence of the Teacher and reported the matter to him. The Teacher said, "Is it true..."
Having asked, "Is it true, monk, that you are dissatisfied?

and being told, "It is true," he said, "Why have you, having gone forth in the teaching of a Buddha like me who has aroused such energy, failed to declare yourself a 'stream-enterer' or a 'once-returner,' but instead made yourself out to be 'dissatisfied'?
You have committed a grave act. To which [the monk] replied, "For what reason?"
“Are you distressed? he asked. When [the monk] replied, “Venerable sir, a certain woman said this to me,” [the Buddha] said, “Monk, that woman’s action is not surprising.
For in the past, she abandoned the most skilled archer in all of Jambudīpa and, having conceived an affection for one seen only for a moment, brought him to his death.
Having said this, at the request of the monks to clarify the meaning of that matter—

In the past, during the time of the wise Cūḷadhanuggaha, after he had mastered his craft in the presence of a world-renowned teacher at Takkasilā, he took his daughter—whom the teacher had given him out of satisfaction—and was traveling toward Bārāṇasī.
At the entrance of a forest, he killed forty-nine bandits with forty-nine arrows; when his arrows were exhausted, he captured the leader of the bandits.
Having thrown him to the ground, when he said, "My dear, bring me my sword," she felt affection for the thief at that moment;
placing the sword in the thief's hand, she revealed that the archer had been killed by the thief,
and as the thief was taking her away, she thought, "If this woman sees another man, she will treat him like her own husband."
"He will have me killed; what use is she to me? Thinking thus, he saw a river, set her down on the near bank, and taking her belongings, said, "Stay right here while I bring the bundle across.
Having thus abandoned her right there and revealed his intention to depart, he spoke:
"Having taken all the goods, you have crossed to the far shore, O Brahmin."
“Return quickly and swiftly, and rescue me from this as well.
“You have exchanged me, who am unfamiliar to you, for one long-acquainted;
you have traded the unstable for the stable, O lady!”
“I too, lady, will assign another [task];
I shall go from here to a place much further away.
“In a thicket of *eḷagalā* creepers, he makes himself a *ahuhāsiya* [nest].”
“Here there is no dancing or singing, nor is there well-timed drumming;
it is not the time for amusements, O fair-hipped one. Why do you laugh, O beautiful lady?
“O jackal, fool, witless one, you are lacking in wisdom, O jackal!”
“Having lost both your fish and your meat, you meditate like a beggar.
“The faults of others are easy to see, but one’s own are hard to see;
having lost both your husband and your lover, I think it is you alone who are meditating.”
“‘So it is, O King of Beasts, just as you say, jackal!
Surely, having gone from here, I shall become subject to the will of my husband.
He who would take away my clay bowl, he too would take away my bronze vessel.’”
“You have indeed committed evil; you will surely do so again.
Having related this Cūḷadhanuggaha Jātaka in detail from the Pañcaka Nipāta, he said:
“At that time, you were the wise Cūḷadhanuggaha, and that woman was this very girl; he who came in the form of a jackal and rebuked her was [the Bodhisatta].”

Having said, "I am Sakka, the king of the gods," he advised him, saying, "In this way, that woman, out of affection for one seen only for a moment, took the life of the foremost wise man in all of Jambudīpa;
having severed the craving you have conceived toward that woman, live on, O bhikkhu. Then, teaching the Dhamma further, he spoke these two verses:
“For a person whose thoughts are agitated,
who is possessed of intense passion and contemplates on the beautiful,
craving increases all the more.”
He indeed makes his bondage firm.
But he who delights in the stilling of thoughts,
who constantly cultivates the perception of foulness while being mindful—
"He indeed will make it clear;
he will cut through the bonds of Māra.
In this context, "of one who is crushed by thoughts" means of one who is crushed by thoughts such as sensual desire-thoughts (*kāmavitakka*). "Of one with intense passion" means...

"Of one with intense passion. "One who contemplates the beautiful" means one who contemplates as "beautiful" because of the unrestrained state of mind resulting from grasping at the sign of beauty in a desirable object.
"Craving": for such a person, not even a single factor such as jhāna increases;
rather, craving alone, pertaining to the six doors, increases further. "This one indeed" refers to this individual whose bond of craving is firm.

He makes it firm. He quiets discursive thought (*vitakkūpasameti*) in the first jhāna among the ten kinds of foulness (*asubha*), which is characterized by the subsiding of wrong thoughts and the like.
"Always mindful" (*sadā sato*): he who, being delighted in this [practice], develops that foulness-jhāna while remaining mindful through constant established mindfulness.
"He will make it clear" (*byanti kāhitīti*): this bhikkhu [will make clear] the craving that arises within the three realms of existence.
"He will bring it to an end. "The bond of Māra" means that he will also sever the bond of Māra, which is comprised of the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) of the three planes of existence.
At the conclusion of the teaching, that bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala), and the teaching of the Dhamma was fruitful for those who were present as well.
The seventh story: The Story of the Wise Man Cūḷadhanuggaha.
8. The Story of Māra.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, related this Dhamma teaching concerning Māra, beginning with the words: "He has reached the goal."
One day, at an improper time, several elder monks entered the Jetavana monastery, went to the dwelling place of the Elder Rāhula, and woke him up.
Not seeing another place to stay, he lay down in front of the Tathāgata’s fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭī).
At that time, the Venerable One had already attained Arahatship and was still quite young. [Meanwhile], Māra was in the Vasavatti heaven...
Standing there, he saw that venerable one lying at the entrance of the fragrant chamber and thought:
"The finger that causes pain to the ascetic Gotama lies outside, while he himself lies inside the fragrant chamber;
as his finger is being pressed, he too will be pained. Having conjured up the form of a great king elephant, he approached.
Circling around the head of the Elder Soṇḍa, he let out a loud, piercing cry.
While seated within the Gandhakūṭī, the Teacher, recognizing his nature as Māra, said:
"Māra, even with a hundred thousand like you, it is impossible to arouse fear in my son. For my son is fearless, free from craving, and possessed of great heroism."
Having said, "He is one of great wisdom," he spoke these verses:
"He has reached the goal, free from fear; he is without craving, without blemish.
He has severed the thorns of existence; this is his final body."
“Free from craving, without grasping, skilled in the analysis of words;
one who knows the combination of syllables as well as their preceding and following relations—
he indeed is one whose body is his last.”
"One of great wisdom is called a Great Man.
In this context, "one who has reached the goal" (*niṭṭhaṅgato*) means that for those who have gone forth in this teaching, *arahantship* is what is called the "goal";
the meaning is that he has reached and attained it. "Fearless" (*asantāsī*) means one who does not tremble with fear because of the absence of internal fears such as passion (*rāga*). He cut off...
"The arrows of existence" (bhava-salla): he cut through all the arrows leading to renewed existence. "The heap" (samussaya): this is his final body. "Without grasping" (anādāna):
free from clinging toward the aggregates and so forth. "Skilled in the analysis of language" (niruttipada-kovida):

the meaning is that he is proficient in all four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), namely, in etymological analysis and the remaining three categories. "He would know the combination of syllables, as well as what precedes and what follows."
He knows the cluster of syllables known as their combination, and he knows the subsequent syllable by means of the preceding syllable, and the preceding syllable by means of the subsequent syllable.

"He knows the subsequent syllable by means of the preceding syllable" means that when the beginning is discerned, even if the middle and the end are not discerned, [he knows]: "Of these syllables, this is the middle."

He knows: "This is the conclusion. He is said to know the preceding syllable by means of the succeeding syllable—when the end is discerned, even though the beginning and middle are not discerned, he knows:
"Of these syllables, this is the middle; this is the beginning. Even when the middle is discerned, he knows:
"Of these syllables, this is the beginning; this is the end. Thus he is one of great wisdom. Sa...
"His final body" means his body standing at the ultimate limit.
He is "of great wisdom" because he is endowed with the great wisdom that encompasses the great meanings, teachings, terminology, and eloquence, as well as the aggregate of virtue and so forth.
And he is called a "Great Man" (mahāpurisa) by virtue of his liberated mind, according to the statement: "Sāriputta, because my mind is liberated, I call myself a Great Man. This is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages. The Wicked Māra, thinking, "The ascetic Gotama knows me," vanished right there.
This is the eighth story, concerning Māra. 9.
The Story of Upaka the Ājīvaka.
The Teacher delivered this teaching on the Dhamma concerning the Ājīvaka Upaka while on the road.
For at one time, having attained omniscient knowledge at the Seat of Enlightenment and spent seven weeks there,
the Teacher took his bowl and robe and set out for Benares, a journey of eighteen yojanas, in order to turn the Wheel of the Dhamma.
While traveling along the road, he saw the Ājīvaka Upaka. Seeing the Teacher, Upaka asked: "Friend, your faculties are serene;
your complexion is pure and bright. Under whom, friend, have you gone forth?
Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you profess? Then the Teacher [replied to him].
Having said, "I have neither preceptor nor teacher," he spoke this verse:
"I am the conqueror of all, the knower of all;
I am unsullied by all phenomena."
"Having abandoned all, liberated through the destruction of craving, having realized it for himself through direct knowledge, whom would he point to?
In this context, "all-conqueror" (sabbābhibhū) means one who has conquered all phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence. "All-knower" (sabbavidū) means...
He has known all phenomena of the four planes. Regarding "in all phenomena": he is unstained by craving and views even amidst all those phenomena of the three planes.
"The abandoner of all": he stands having abandoned all phenomena of the three planes. "Liberated in the destruction of craving":

he is liberated by the liberation of one beyond training (asekhā vimutti) in the state of Arahantship, which is termed the "destruction of craving," having been produced at the end of the destruction of craving.
"Having known by oneself" means having personally realized the various phenomena to be directly known and so forth. "Whom should one point to?
means whom indeed should one designate, thinking, "This is my preceptor" or "This is my teacher"?

At the conclusion of the teaching, Upaka the Ājīvaka neither rejoiced in the Tathāgata’s words nor did he reject them. Instead, shaking his head and licking his lips, he took a path that led away from the road and went to a certain haunt of hunters.
The Ninth Story: The Case of Upaka-jīvaka.
10. The Story of Sakka’s Questions.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, gave this Dhamma teaching concerning Sakka, the king of the devas, regarding the gift of all things.
For on one occasion, the deities in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven assembled and raised four questions:
"Of all gifts, which gift is the foremost? Of all flavors, which flavor is the foremost? Of all delights, which delight is the foremost?
And why is the destruction of craving alone called the foremost? Not a single deity was able to resolve these questions. However, one...
One god asked another, and he in turn asked yet another; thus questioning one another, they wandered through ten thousand world-systems for twelve years.

Even after such a length of time, having seen no resolution to the questions, the deities of the ten thousand world-systems assembled together, went into the presence of the Four Great Kings, and asked: "Why, dear sirs, is there this great assembly of deities?"
When he had spoken thus, they said, "We have come to you because we were unable to resolve four questions after having formulated them.

"What are these questions, dear sirs? "We have come because we were unable to resolve these questions: 'Among the delights of the flavor of giving, which indeed is the best delight of the flavor of giving? And why is the destruction of craving itself the best? Dear sirs, we too—"
“We do not understand the meaning of these things; however, our king, having considered a matter contemplated by a thousand people, understands it at that very moment.
He is superior to us in wisdom and merit. Come, let us go into his presence.
Taking that very host of gods with them, they went into the presence of Sakka, the king of the gods, and he too asked, “What is it, dear ones? It is a great matter.”
When it was said, "It is a gathering of the devas," they reported that matter [to the King]. [The King] asked, "Dear ones, no one else is able to understand the meaning of these questions;
they belong to the domain of the Buddha. Where does the Teacher dwell at present?

Having been told, "In Jeta’s Grove," and hearing that he was there, he said, "Come, let us go into his presence," and together with the host of devas, during the night, [he went through] the entirety of Jeta’s Grove.
Having illuminated [the world] and approached the Teacher, he paid homage and stood to one side.
When the Teacher asked, "Great King, why have you come with such a great host of deities? he replied, "Venerable Sir, this assembly of deities has raised these very questions;
there is indeed no one else capable of understanding their meaning. Please explain their meaning to us."

The Teacher said, “Excellent, Great King! Indeed, it was for the sake of severing the doubts of those like you that I, having fulfilled the perfections and made great renunciations, realized omniscient knowledge.

For among all gifts, the gift of the Dhamma is supreme; among all flavors, the flavor of the Dhamma is supreme; among all delights, the delight of the Dhamma is supreme. Regarding the questions asked by you: [he continued].
"But the destruction of craving is indeed supreme, because it brings about the state of Arahantship," he said, and then recited this verse:
"The gift of the Dhamma surpasses all gifts;
the taste of the Dhamma surpasses all tastes."
“Delight in the Dhamma conquers all delight in worldly things;
the destruction of craving conquers all suffering.
In this regard, “the gift of Dhamma is the best of all gifts”: for even if one were to fill the entire interior of the world-system, up to the Brahma-world, without interval...

If one were to give robes resembling the interior of a plantain tree to the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and those whose taints are exhausted as they sit together in assembly, the mere expression of appreciation made by means of a four-line verse at that gathering would be superior.
For that gift does not equal even a sixteenth part of the value of that verse. In this way, the teaching of the Dhamma, its recitation, and its hearing [are likewise supreme].
It is great. And for whichever person that hearing of the Dhamma was caused to be held by many, the benefit belongs to him alone as something great.

Even more than the gift of excellent alms-food given by filling the bowls of such an assembly, or the gift of medicine consisting of ghee, oil, and so forth given by filling their bowls, [there is the merit of] monasteries similar to the Mahāvihāra and palaces similar to the Lohapāsāda.

Even compared to the gift of dwellings made by having many hundreds of thousands of palaces constructed, or the relinquishment made by Anāthapiṇḍika and others regarding monasteries, the gift of Dhamma alone—whether it be as much as the expression of appreciation for even a four-line verse—is superior and most excellent. Why is that?
Because those performing such meritorious deeds [attain their results] only after hearing the Dhamma.
They act thus, not without having heard [the Dhamma]. For if these beings were not to hear the Dhamma, they would not give even a ladleful of ghee or a spoonful of cooked rice.
For this reason, among all gifts, the gift of the Dhamma alone is supreme.
Furthermore, setting aside the Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas, there is no one capable of counting the drops of water while the rain falls upon the gods for an entire aeon.
Even those such as Sāriputta, though endowed with wisdom, were unable to attain the fruit of stream-entry and the other fruits by their own natural disposition;

rather, having heard the Dhamma spoken by the Elder Assaji and others, they realized the fruit of stream-entry, and through the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, they realized the disciple’s perfection-knowledge (sāvakapāramīñāṇa). For this reason also, O Great King:
The gift of the Dhamma alone is supreme. Thus it is said: “The gift of the Dhamma surpasses all other gifts.

Furthermore, even all other flavors—such as perfumes and tastes—even the flavor of the ambrosial food of the deities at their highest excellence, serve only as conditions for being cast into the cycle of existence and for the experience of suffering. However, that which is known as the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment...
And the flavor of the Dhamma, which is comprised of the nine supramundane states, is indeed the best of all flavors. Therefore it was said:

"The flavor of the Dhamma conquers every other flavor. As for those various kinds of pleasure—distinguished as the pleasure of sons, the pleasure of daughters, the pleasure of wealth, the pleasure of women, and the pleasures of dance, song, music, and so forth—even that, by causing one to fall into the cycle of existence, is merely a condition for the experiencing of suffering. Whatever...
When he preaches, listens to, or recites this Dhamma, the rapture that arises within him produces a state of elation, brings forth tears, and causes the hair on his body to stand on end.
This culminates in the end of the cycle of existence and results in the attainment of Arahantship.
Therefore, among all forms of delight, this delight in the Dhamma alone is the most excellent. Thus it was said: "Of all delights..."

“Delight in the Dhamma conquers”: moreover, the destruction of craving—that is, Arahantship, which arises at the moment of the destruction of craving—is the most excellent of all because it overcomes the entire suffering of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*). Therefore it is said: “The destruction of craving conquers all suffering.
While the Teacher was thus explaining the meaning of this verse, there was a penetration of the Dhamma by eighty-four thousand living beings.
It happened thus. Sakka, too, having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma and having paid homage to the Teacher, spoke as follows:
“Venerable Sir, why do you not allow us to receive the merit from such a supreme gift of the Dhamma?
From now on, Venerable Sir, please inform the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus and allow us to receive the merit. Having heard his words, the Teacher convened the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus.
“Monks, from this day forward, whether it be at a great Dhamma-listening, an ordinary Dhamma-listening, or even during a seated discussion, you should,
after delivering a discourse of thanksgiving, dedicate the merit to all sentient beings,” he said.
This is the tenth section, the Story of Sakka’s Questions.

11. The Story of the Childless Merchant “Riches destroy,” with these words the Teacher gave this Dhamma instruction while residing at Jetavana, concerning a merchant named Aputtaka (The Childless One).
It is said that after King Pasenadi of Kosala heard of his death, he asked, “To whom does the property of one who dies without a son belong?”
Having asked him and heard that it was for the king, he had the wealth brought from that man’s house to the royal palace within seven days.

Then, approaching the presence of the Teacher, when the Teacher said, "Well now, Great King, from where have you come so very early in the day?", he replied, "Venerable Sir, here in Sāvatthī a householder, a merchant, has died; I am bringing his estate, as he left no sons."
“I will bring [it] to the royal palace and return,” he said. Everything is to be understood according to the method already set forth in the Sutta.
It is said that when various kinds of choice food were brought in a golden bowl and presented to him, he said, “Do people eat such things?
Why do you play with me in this house? and, as the food was being served, [he struck them] with clods, sticks, and so forth.
Having struck them and driven them away, he ate broken rice with sour gruel as his second course, thinking, "This is the food of men.
Even when beautiful garments, vehicles, and parasols were presented to him, he drove those men away by striking them with clods of earth, sticks, and the like;
he wore hempen rags, traveled in a dilapidated little cart, and was shaded by a leaf-parasol—thus it was by the king.
When this was reported, the Teacher related his past karma:
"In the past, O Great King, that householder who was a merchant provided alms-food to a Paccekabuddha named Tagarasikhī.
Having said, 'Give alms to the ascetic,' he rose from his seat and departed. It is said that regarding him..."
When the foolish faithless man had spoken thus and departed, his wife, who was faithful and devout, thought:
"At long last I have heard the word 'give' from his mouth; today, fulfilling my own heart's desire, I shall give almsfood.
Taking the bowl of the Paccekabuddha and filling it with exquisite food, she gave it to him. He, too, as he was returning—
Seeing him, [the householder] asked, "What is it, ascetic? Have you received anything?
Taking the bowl and seeing the excellent alms-food, he became remorseful and thought: "It would have been better if these slaves or laborers had eaten this alms-food.
For they, having eaten it, will perform work for me; but this man, having gone and eaten it, will go to sleep."
“‘That alms-food of mine is lost! he cried. Furthermore, for the sake of his brother’s only son and his inheritance, he deprived him of life.
It is said that as the boy was wandering about holding his finger, the merchant would say things such as, ‘This carriage is my father’s property;
this is his ox. Then the merchant said to him, ‘Now he speaks thus to you; to him—’”
"But when he has reached maturity, who will protect the wealth in this house?
Having said this, he led him into the forest, seized him by the neck at the foot of a certain bush, slit his throat like a radish-root, killed him, and discarded him right there.
This was his prior karma. Therefore it is said:
“Great King, because that householder, the merchant, provided almsfood to the Paccekabuddha Tagarasikhī,
through the ripening of that kamma he was reborn seven times in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
And as a remainder of the ripening of that very same kamma, he has served as a merchant seven times in this very Sāvatthī.”
Great King, because that householder merchant, after giving, later felt regret, thinking,
"It would have been better if these alms-foods had been eaten by slaves or laborers," as the ripening of that karma,
his mind does not incline toward enjoying excellent food, nor toward enjoying excellent clothing, nor toward enjoying excellent vehicles.
His mind did not incline toward the enjoyment of the five kinds of sensual pleasures. However, Mahārāja,
because that householder merchant deprived his brother’s only son of life for the sake of the inheritance, as the ripening of that kamma,
he [suffered] in hell for many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, and many hundreds of thousands of years.
He was roasted; as a residual result of that very karma, this seventh time his wealth passes into the royal treasury because he is childless.
Moreover, Great King, that householder merchant’s former merit has been exhausted, and no new merit has been accumulated.
Today, Great King, that householder merchant is being roasted in the Mahāroruva hell.”
Having heard the Teacher’s words, the king said, “Alas, Bhante, what a grave deed!
While such vast wealth existed, he neither enjoyed it himself nor performed meritorious deeds for Buddhas like you who dwell in the foremost monasteries.
The Teacher replied, “It is even so, Great King; those who are dull-witted, having obtained wealth, do not [seek] Nibbāna.”
"Craving that arises in dependence on wealth destroys these very people for a long time," he said, and then recited this verse:
"Wealth destroys the foolish one, but not those who seek the further shore;
through craving for wealth, the fool destroys others as well as himself."
In this context, "but those who seek the further shore" refers to those individuals who seek the further shore of Nibbāna; it is they whom wealth does not destroy.
"One slays oneself, as it were another" means that a person of poor wisdom, by means of the craving arising dependent on wealth, slays himself just as if he were slaying another.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
The eleventh story, the Story of the Childless Merchant.
12. The Story of Aṅkura.
While residing on the Paṇḍukambala Rock, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning Aṅkura, beginning with the words: "Grass is a fault..."
He related the story. The narrative has already been explained in detail under the verse beginning, "Those wise ones devoted to jhāna.

For it was said there concerning Indaka: It is said that when the Elder Anuruddha entered his village for alms, Indaka had him provided with a portion of food measuring only a single ladle-full from what he himself had brought. By that merit, for ten thousand years...
By constructing a row of hearths twelve yojanas long, the gift he gave became even more fruitful.
Therefore, he spoke thus. When this was said, the Teacher replied: "Aṅkura, a gift ought to be given with discernment; in that way, it becomes as highly fruitful as seed sown in a fertile field.
But you did not do so; therefore, your gift did not become highly fruitful."
Elucidating this meaning:
“Having discriminated, one should give a gift where what is given yields great fruit;
having discriminated, one should give a gift praised by the Sugata.”
"Those who are worthy of offerings in this world of the living—
to them, gifts given bear great fruit,
like seeds sown in a fertile field."
Having spoken thus, while teaching the Dhamma further, he uttered these verses:
“Fields have weeds as their blemish; this generation has lust as its blemish.
Therefore, what is given to those free from lust bears great fruit.”
“Fields have weeds as their blemish; this generation has hatred as its blemish.
Therefore, what is given to those free from hatred bears great fruit.
Fields have weeds as their blemish; this generation has delusion as its blemish.”
Therefore, what is given to those free from delusion yields great fruit.
"Fields have weeds as their blemish, but this generation has desire as its blemish;
therefore, what is given to those free from desire yields great fruit."
In this context, "the defects of weeds" refers to grasses such as *sāmāka* that, when they sprout, spoil the fields of early and late crops;
because of this, those fields do not yield much fruit. In the same way, passion arising within beings spoils them;
therefore, what is given to them does not bear great fruit. However, what is given to those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) bears great fruit. Thus it was said:
“Fields have weeds as their blemish; this generation has lust as its blemish.
Therefore, what is given to those free from lust becomes of great fruit.
This same method applies to the remaining verses as well.
At the conclusion of the teaching, both Aṅkura and Indaka were established in the fruit of stream-entry; thus the Dhamma teaching was fruitful for those who had assembled.
This is the twelfth story, the Story of Aṅkura.
The commentary on the Tanhāvagga is finished.
The Twenty-fourth Chapter. 25.
The Chapter on Monks. 1.
The Account of Five Monks.
"Restraint by means of the eye"—the Teacher spoke this teaching on the Dhamma while dwelling at Jetavana concerning five bhikkhus.
It is said that among them, each one guarded only a single one of the five doors, such as the eye-door. Then one day, having assembled and quarreled, saying, "I guard what is difficult to guard;
I guard what is difficult to guard," they decided to ask the Teacher.

Thinking, "We shall come to know this matter," they approached the Teacher and asked, "Venerable Sir, while we are guarding the doors of the eye and so forth, each of us considers his own guarded door to be difficult to guard; among us, who then is it that guards what is difficult to guard?
The Teacher, without singling out even a single bhikkhu, said, "Bhikkhus, all of these are indeed difficult to guard."
"Moreover, it is not only now that you were unrestrained in these five matters;

previously as well you were unrestrained, and because of that very lack of restraint, failing to abide by the advice of the wise, you met your end. Having said this, when they asked, "When was that, venerable sir?
he related in detail the story of the Takkasilā Jātaka from the past, concerning how [the king] came under the power of the ogresses in the royal palace.
When the Great Being had reached the end of his life and was seated upon the royal throne beneath the white parasol following his consecration,
he surveyed his own glorious majesty and, as an inspired utterance, exclaimed: "In the instruction of what is wholesome,
through steadfastness and firm resolve..."
And because of my fearlessness toward the fear of not turning back,
we did not fall under the power of the rākṣasīs;
that state of safety was for me amidst great danger.

Having shown this verse, [the Buddha said]: "At that time as well, you five men, having set out from Takkaśilā with weapons in hand to surround the Mahāsatta for the purpose of seizing the kingdom, were traveling along the road.

On the way, because you were unrestrained regarding the objects of form and so forth presented to the eye-door and the other senses by the rākṣasīs, and because you did not abide by the advice of the Wise One but faltered, you were [seized] by the rākṣasīs."

"Those who ate [the food] met their end. But among them, I alone am the one who, having remained well-restrained toward those objects of sense and disregarding the celestial-looking *yakkhinī* who followed close behind me, reached Takkasilā in safety and attained the kingship.
Having thus identified the Jātaka, he said: "Monks, for a monk indeed, all doors—"
"These things must be restrained. For by restraining these very things, one is liberated from all suffering. Having said this, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke these verses:
"Restraint of the eye is good; restraint of the ear is good;
restraint of the nose is good; restraint of the tongue is good.
“Restraint in body is good, restraint in speech is good;
restraint in mind is good, restraint in all things is good.
A bhikkhu restrained in all things is liberated from all suffering.”

In this context, "by the eye" means: when a visible object comes into the range of a bhikkhu’s eye-door, if he does not become lustful toward a desirable object, does not become angry toward an undesirable object, and does not produce delusion through lack of equanimity, then restraint—meaning the fixing, closing, guarding, and protection—is said to have been established at that door. Such is his [practice] by means of the eye.
Restraint is good. This same method applies to the ear-door and the others as well.
However, restraint or non-restraint does not arise in the eye-door and the others; rather, it is obtained later in the impulsion-series (*javana-vīthi*).
For at that time, when non-restraint arises—consisting of lack of faith, impatience, laziness, forgetfulness, and ignorance—it is fivefold in the unwholesome series.
It is obtained. When restraint arises, these five factors—faith, patience, energy, mindfulness, and knowledge—are obtained within the wholesome cognitive process (*kusala-vīthi*).
As for the phrase "restraint by body," both the body of serene confidence (*pasādakāya*) and the physical body of movement (*copanakāya*) are included here. And yet, both of these are...
It is simply the door of the body. Regarding that, restraint and non-restraint have already been explained in the case of the sensitive door (pasādadvāra).
In the case of the impulsion door (copanadvāra) as well, there are killing, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct based on that same physical basis.

When these arise together with unwholesome cognitive processes (akusalavīthi), that door is unrestrained; when they arise together with wholesome cognitive processes (kusalavīthi), such as the abstinence from killing and so forth, it is restrained.

Regarding the phrase "good speech": here too, "speech" includes both the preliminary speech (*copana-vācā*) and the actual speech itself. Through that [preliminary speech], along with the false speech (*musāvāda*) and so forth that arise together with it, that door remains unrestrained;
through the abstention from false speech and so forth, it is restrained. Regarding the phrase "restraint by mind":

here too, there are no covetousness (*abhijjhā*) and other such states associated with a mind other than the impulsion-mind (*javana-manas*). However, at the moment of impulsion within the mind-door (*manodvāra*), [these states do exist].
When covetousness and the like arise, that door is unrestrained; when non-covetousness and the like are present, it is restrained.
"Restraint is good in all cases" means that restraint is good in all those doors, beginning with the eye-door.
To this extent, eight doors of restraint and eight doors of non-restraint have been explained. One who stands within those eight doors of non-restraint...

A bhikkhu who is not established in the doors of restraint is not liberated from the suffering rooted in the entire cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*); however, one who stands firm in the doors of restraint is liberated from all suffering rooted in the cycle of existence.
Therefore it was said: “A bhikkhu restrained in every way is released from all suffering.
At the conclusion of the teaching, those five bhikkhus were established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), and the Dhamma teaching was fruitful for those who had gathered as well.
The First Story of the Five Monks.
2. The Story of the Swan-Killer Monk.
"One who restrains his hands"—the Teacher gave this Dhamma teaching while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain monk who had been a swan-killer.
It is said that two friends living in Sāvatthī, having gone forth among the bhikkhus and received full ordination, mostly wandered about together.
One day, having gone to the Aciravatī River and bathed, they stood basking in the sun, engaged in friendly conversation.
At that moment, two swans were traveling through the air. Then, one young bhikkhu—
Taking a pebble, he said, "I shall strike the eye of one of the young swans. The other replied, "I will not be able to do that.
[The first man said: "Let it be; I shall strike the eye on this side; I shall strike the eye on the opposite side. [The other replied:
"Even for this, you simply will not be able to succeed. [The first man said: "In that case, hold it steady. Taking a second pebble, he threw it at the rear of the swan, and the swan—
Hearing the sound of the pebble, he turned back and looked.
Then, taking another round pebble, he struck the other swan’s eye from the side and forced it out through the other eye. Crying out, the swan turned around and fell right at their feet.
Seeing him there, the monks standing in various places said, "Friends, having gone forth in the Buddha’s teaching, this is most unbecoming!"
"By you, who committed this act of taking life," he said, and taking them along, he went and showed them to the Tathāgata.
The Teacher asked, "Is it true, monk, that you committed the taking of life?
When he replied, "It is true, Bhante," the Teacher said, "Monk, why did you do such a thing after having gone forth in this liberating teaching? In ancient times, the wise..."
"Before the Buddha had appeared, while living in the midst of household life, they felt remorse even over very minor matters;
yet you, having gone forth in such a teaching as that of the Buddha, did not feel even the slightest bit of remorse.
Having said this, when requested by them, he related a story of the past.
In the past, while Dhanañjaya was ruling the kingdom in the city of Indapatta in the Kururaṭṭha country, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in the womb of his chief queen.
Having gradually reached the age of discretion and mastered the arts at Takkasilā, he was established by his father as viceroy;
subsequently, upon the passing of his father, he attained the kingship and [observed] the ten royal duties.
Without causing provocation, he lived according to the *kurudhamma*. The *kurudhamma* consists of the five precepts; the Bodhisatta, having made them perfectly pure, guarded them.

And just as the Bodhisatta did, so too did his mother, the chief queen, his younger brother, the viceroy, the court chaplain who was a brahmin, the rope-holder, the minister, the charioteer, the guild-leader, the grain-measurer, the high official, and the gatekeeper.

While these eleven people—including the courtesan Nagarasobhinī—were thus observing the Kurudhamma, no rain fell upon the kingdom while Kaliṅga was ruling in the city of Dantapura in the kingdom of Kaliṅga.
However, the Great Being possessed an auspicious elephant named Añjanasannibha, who was endowed with great merit. When the inhabitants of the kingdom brought him [before the king],...
“The god will send rain,” they announced to the king with this perception. The king dispatched brahmins to bring that elephant.
Having gone, they entreated the Great Being, the elephant. To show them the reason for their request, the Teacher said:
“Having recognized your faith and virtue, O lord of men;”
“We shall bestow our beauty upon Kaliṅga in exchange for the color of collyrium.
Thus he related this Jātaka from the Tika-nipāta. Even when the elephant had been brought back, the rain did not fall;
yet, with the conviction that “that king protects the Kurudhamma, and therefore the rain falls in his kingdom,” they said: “That which he protects as the Kurudhamma...”
“Write it on a golden plate and bring it here,” Kāliṅga sent forth again the brahmins and his ministers.
When they had gone and made their request, the king and all the others, having each committed some slight lapse in their respective moral precepts, refused, saying, “Our virtue is not pure.
Yet, [the king] said, “A breach of virtue does not occur merely by this much. By them—
Being asked again and again, they each recounted their own precepts.
Upon seeing the Kurudhamma that had been brought back after being inscribed on a golden plate, Kāliṅga took it up and fulfilled it with great care.
Rain fell in his kingdom, and the land became secure and well-supplied with food. Having brought forth this past account, the Teacher said:
“Uppalavaṇṇā was the courtesan, and Puṇṇa was the gatekeeper at that time;
Kaccāna was the rope-handler, and Kolita was the measurer of grain.
Sāriputta was the guild-leader then, and Anuruddha was the charioteer.”
The Elder Kassapa the Brahmin, the wise Uparājānanda,
the Great Queen Rāhulamātā, Queen Māyā the mother,
and the Bodhisatta as King of Kuru— thus should you remember this Jātaka.
Having correlated the Jātaka, [the Buddha said]: "Monk, even in the past, the wise, when even a slight remorse arose, were apprehensive of a breach in their virtue;
yet you, having gone forth in the dispensation of a Buddha such as I, have committed an exceedingly grave deed by taking life.
Indeed, for one who is a monk, [it is forbidden] by hand, by foot, or by speech..."
And having said, "One must be self-restrained," he spoke this verse:
"Restrained in hand, restrained in foot,
restrained in speech— one who is thus restrained is supreme."
“Delighting in the internal,
composed, alone, and contented— him they call a bhikkhu. In this context,
“restrained in hand” means by virtue of the absence of hand-games, playing with the hands, or striking others with the hands.
"Restrained in hand": the same method applies to the second word as well. "Restrained in speech," however, means restrained in speech by not committing false speech and so forth.
"Supremely restrained" (*saṃyatuttama*) means one whose physical being is restrained; the meaning is that he does not perform such things as bodily movements, raising the head, or facial contortions.
"Delighting in the internal" (*ajjhattarata*) means delighting in the cultivation of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), which is designated as the "internal range."
“Samāhita” means well-established. “Eko santuṣita” means being alone, he is well-contented;
from the time he begins the practice of insight (vipassanā), his mind is satisfied by his own attainment.

Starting with the virtuous worldling (puthujjanakalyāṇaka), all those in training (sekkha) are called “santuṣita” because they are contented by their own attainments; however, the Arahant is absolutely and exclusively contented. It is with reference to him that this was said.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the second story, concerning the monk who killed the swans.
3. The Story of Kokālika.
"He who is restrained in speech"—the Teacher delivered this teaching on the Dhamma while dwelling at Jetavana concerning Kokālika.
The narrative background is already recorded in the Sutta, beginning with: "Then the bhikkhu Kokālika approached the Blessed One.
Its meaning should also be understood according to the method explained in the Aṭṭhakathā.
When Kokālika had been reborn in the Paduma Hell, the monks in the Dhamma Hall raised this discussion: "Alas!
The monk Kokālika has met his destruction because of his own mouth;
for while he was reviling the two Chief Disciples, the earth opened up to swallow him. The Teacher approached and asked, "Monks, what discussion are you having just now?"
Having asked, "Are you seated together? and being told, "We are indeed," he said, "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, the monk Kokālika was ruined by relying on his own mouth. When the monks, desiring to hear that matter, requested it, he related the past for the purpose of explaining it.
