In the past, in a region of the Himalayas, a tortoise lived in a certain lake.
Two young swans, while wandering about for food, became acquainted with him and formed a firm bond of friendship. One day, they asked the tortoise:
"Friend, our dwelling place in the Himalayas, at the foot of Mount Cittakūṭa in the Golden Cave, is delightful."
“Friend, you shall go with us. “My good man, how shall I go?
“We will carry you, provided you can keep your mouth shut. “I will keep it shut; take me and go, my good man.
Saying, “Very well,” they had the turtle bite onto one end of a stick, and they themselves bit onto both ends of it.
They leapt into the sky. As they were being carried away by the swans in that manner, village boys saw them and said, "Two swans are carrying off a tortoise with a stick!

The tortoise, wishing to say, "If my friends are taking me away, what is it to you here, you wicked servants?", [was carried] by the great speed of the swans to the royal palace in the city of Bārāṇasī.
When the upper part reached [the ground], it released the stalk from the place where it was gripped and fell into the open space, splitting into two.
Having brought this past event to mind, the Teacher said:
“Alas, he has slain himself, the tortoise who uttered a sound.”
When the wood was firmly gripped, he struck with his voice but once.
"Seeing this too, O best among men of valor,
one should release speech that is wholesome and not excessive."
“You pass by the tortoise who has fallen into calamity because of his excessive talkativeness.

Having related this *Bahubhāṇijātaka* in detail from the *Dukanipāta*, the Blessed One said, “Monks, a monk indeed must be restrained in speech, of even conduct, undisturbed, and with a mind extinguished,” and spoke this verse:
“The monk who is restrained in speech, Measured in his words, and undisturbed;”
“He illuminates the goal and the Dhamma; his speech is sweet.

In this context, “restrained in speech” means that even slaves, outcasts, and the like do not say to him, “You are ill-born,” or “You are immoral,” and so forth, because he is restrained by his mouth.
“Measured in speech” (*mantabhāṇī*): *manta* refers to wisdom (*paññā*); he is one whose habit is to speak with that [wisdom]. “Not arrogant” (*anuddhata*):...
"With a mind extinguished" (*nibbutacitto*). "He illuminates the meaning and the Dhamma" means he speaks both the meaning of what was said and the Dhamma of the teaching.
"Sweet": the speech of such a bhikkhu is called sweet.
However, the speech of one who accomplishes only the meaning and not the text, or who accomplishes only the text and not the meaning, or who accomplishes neither, [is not so].
"There is no such thing as 'sweet,'" he said.
At the conclusion of this teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the third story concerning Kokālika.
4. The Story of the Elder Dhammārāma The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, gave this teaching on the Dhamma concerning the elder Dhammārāma.
It is said that when the Teacher announced, "Four months from now my final passing away (parinibbāna) will take place," many thousands [of monks gathered].

The monks wandered about surrounding the Teacher. Therein, the ordinary monks (*puthujjana*) were unable to restrain their tears, while in those whose taints were destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), a sense of spiritual urgency regarding the Dhamma arose.
All of them, wondering, "What indeed shall we do?", wandered about in groups. However, a certain monk named Dhammārāma did not [join] the company of the monks.
He approached. When addressed by the bhikkhus, "What is it, friend?", he gave no reply;
thinking, "The Teacher will indeed attain final nibbāna at the end of four months, and I am not yet free from passion;
while the Teacher is still living, I shall strive and reach arahantship," he dwelt alone and reflected upon and contemplated the Dhamma taught by the Teacher.
He recalled this. The bhikkhus informed the Tathāgata: “Venerable sir, Dhammārāma has not even a trace of affection for you.
He does not even consult with us, saying, ‘The Teacher is about to attain final nibbāna; what indeed shall we do?
The Teacher had him summoned and asked, “Is it true that you act in this way? “It is true,” he replied.
“Venerable Sir,” he said. “For what reason? [The Elder replied: “It is said that you will attain final Nibbāna at the end of four months.
Since I am not yet free from passion, I reflect upon, contemplate, and recollect the Dhamma taught by you, thinking: ‘While you are still living, I shall strive and reach Arahantship.’”
The Teacher, giving him his approval by saying, "Excellent, excellent!", said:
"Monks, even a monk who possesses affection for me must be like one who delights in the Dhamma. For those who honor me with garlands, perfumes, and the like do not truly honor me;
rather, it is only those who practice in accordance with the Dhamma who honor me."
Having said, "It is called 'name'," he spoke this verse:
"The bhikkhu who delights in the Dhamma, rejoices in the Dhamma, reflects upon the Dhamma,
and recollects the Dhamma, does not fall away from the true Dhamma."

In this context, one who has a "pleasure grove" (*ārāma*)—meaning a state of delight—in the phenomena of serenity and insight in the sense of dwelling within them is a "delighter in the Dhamma" (*dhammārāma*).
One who takes pleasure in that very same Dhamma is "one who delights in the Dhamma" (*dhammarata*). By means of repeatedly reflecting upon that very Dhamma, he is "contemplating the Dhamma";
the meaning is that he adverts to and attends to that Dhamma. He "recalls" means he is recollecting that very same Dhamma.
"Saddhamma" means that such a bhikkhu does not fall away from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*) and the ninefold supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*).
At the conclusion of the teaching, that bhikkhu was established in Arahatship, and the Dhamma instruction was fruitful for those who were present as well.
The fourth story: The Elder Dhammārāma. The fifth:
The Story of the Bhikkhu Who Associates with Opponents.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Veḷuvana, delivered this teaching on the Dhamma concerning a certain bhikkhu who associated with opponents, beginning with the words: "Salābhaṃ... (Seeking gain...).
It is said that he had a certain monk as a companion who belonged to Devadatta’s faction.
Seeing him returning after having finished his meal, after walking for alms together with the monks, [the companion] asked, "Where have you been?
"I went to such-and-such a place for alms," he replied. "Did you obtain alms-food? "Yes, I obtained it. "In this matter, for us..."
“There will be great gain and honor; stay right here for a few days. Following his words, he stayed there for a few days and then returned to his own place.
Then the monks reported this to the Tathāgata: “Venerable Sir, this man is enjoying the gain and honor that has arisen for Devadatta; he is Devadatta’s partisan. The Teacher summoned him.
“Is it true, indeed, that you did such a thing? he asked. “Yes, venerable sir, I stayed there for a few days relying on a certain young man, but I do not approve of Devadatta’s doctrine.

Then the Blessed One said to him, “Even though you do not approve of his doctrine, you conduct yourself as if you were someone who approves of the doctrine of those you have seen and those you have encountered.”
"You are not acting like this only now; even in the past you were exactly like this," he said.
When the bhikkhus requested, "Venerable sir, we have seen him with our own eyes just now, but previously he wandered about as if approving of the views of others;
please explain it to us," he brought up the past and related the following:
Having listened to the words of old thieves,
Mahilāmukha wandered about beating [them];
for having listened to the words of those who are well-restrained—
“The best of elephants stood firm in all virtues.
Having related this Mahiḷāmukha Jātaka in detail, [the Buddha said]: “Monks, a monk must indeed be content with whatever gain he receives;
it is not proper to long for the gains of others. For one who longs for the gains of others, regarding the jhānas, vipassanā, the path, and the fruits—”
"Even a single quality does not arise [in one who is discontented]; however, for one who is content with whatever gain they receive, the meditative absorptions (jhāna) and other such states do arise.
Having said this, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke these verses:
"One should not despise one's own gain, nor should one live envying the gains of others."
“A bhikkhu who envies others does not attain concentration.
But if a bhikkhu, though receiving little, does not despise his own gains,
the gods indeed praise him as one of pure livelihood and untiring.”
In this context, "one's own gain" (*salābha*) refers to the gain that arises for oneself.
For one who avoids wandering from door to door (*sapadānacāra*) and maintains a livelihood through improper search (*anesanā*) is said to "despise," "contemn," and "loath" one's own gain.
Therefore, by not acting in such a way, one should not despise one's own gain. The meaning is: "One should not live envying others," that is, longing for the gains of others.
"He does not attain concentration" means that a bhikkhu who, envying the gains of others, becomes preoccupied with providing them with robes and other requisites,
does not attain either absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*) or access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*).

"He does not despise his own gain" means that even when he has little gain, a bhikkhu who wanders for alms from house to house in regular order among high and low families does not despise his own gain.

"By name. "The gods praise and extol such a bhikkhu"—that is, one who lives purely through his mode of livelihood, who is untiring due to his non-indolence in maintaining his life by means of the strength of his own legs; this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
The fifth story is that of the monk who served his adversaries.
6. The Story of the Brahmin Who Gave Five Gifts of the Best:
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, related this Dhamma teaching concerning a brahmin named Pañcaggadāyaka (Giver of Five Gifts of the Best).
It is said that when the crop stands in the field, he gives what is called the "field-peak";

at the time of threshing, he gives what is called the "threshing-floor-peak"; at the time of the threshing-basket, he gives what is called the "basket-peak"; at the time of the mortar, he gives what is called the "pot-peak";
and when it has increased in the bowl, he gives what is called the "bowl-peak. Thus he gives these five "peak-gifts" to whoever has arrived.
"He does not eat without having given," so he became known by the name "The Giver of the Five Offerings.
The Teacher, perceiving the underlying potential for the three fruits in both that brahmin and his wife, went to him at the time of his meal and stood at the door.
He too was sitting at the entrance facing inward toward the house, eating, when the Teacher stood at the door.
He did not see him standing there. But the brahmin lady, while serving him, saw the Teacher and thought:
"This brahmin eats after giving the first portions in five places; now the ascetic Gotama has arrived and is standing at the door.
If the brahmin sees him and takes his own food to give it to him, I will have to cook again."
“I shall not be able to. Thinking, “In this way he will not see the ascetic Gotama,” she turned her back toward the Teacher and stood behind him, shielding him from view;
she bent down and stood as if covering the full moon with her hand.
While standing thus, she looked at the Teacher with a sidelong glance, wondering, “Has he gone away yet? or “Has he not?”
He looked back. The Teacher remained right where he was.
Out of fear that the brahmin might hear him, he did not say, "Pass on," but stepping back slightly, he said very slowly, "Pass on. The Teacher shook his head, signaling, "I will not go.
When the Buddha, who honors the world, shook his head saying, "I will not go," she was unable to restrain herself.
He laughed a great laugh. At that moment, the Teacher emitted a radiance toward the house.
Even though the brahmin was sitting with his back turned, he heard the sound of the brahmin woman’s laughter; looking up at the radiance of the six-colored rays, he saw the Teacher.
For indeed, whether in a village or in the forest, the Buddhas do not fail to reveal themselves to those who possess the necessary causes.
They did not depart. The brahmin, too, having seen the Teacher, said, "Sir, I have been ruined by you;
it was a grave offense on your part that you did not inform me when the prince arrived and stood at my door.
Having taken his half-eaten bowl of food, he went into the presence of the Teacher and said, "Master Gotama, I am the foremost in five respects..."
“I eat only after giving; from this meal, having divided it in the middle, I have eaten only one portion, while one portion remains.

Will you accept this food from me? The Teacher, instead of saying, “I have no need for your leftover food,” replied, “Brāhmaṇa, even the top portion is suitable for me, as is the half-eaten portion remaining after dividing it in the middle.”
“Even a final morsel of food is suitable for me alone, for we, O brahmin, are like departed spirits who subsist on what is given by others.
Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“Whether from the beginning, the middle, or the end, [of a meal]...”
One who lives on what is given by others may receive almsfood;
such a person is neither capable of praise nor of disparagement,
and the wise call even him a sage.
Upon hearing this, the brahmin became filled with faith and thought, "Oh, how wonderful!
The prince named Dīpasāmika will not say, 'I have no need for your leftover food,' but will speak thus. Standing right at the gate, he asked the Teacher a question:
"Master Gotama, you call your own disciples 'bhikkhus. In what sense is one a bhikkhu?"
“What kind of Dhamma teaching would be suitable for him? the Teacher reflected. He considered:
“These two men both heard the word ‘name-and-form’ (nāmarūpa) during the time of Kassapa Buddha;
it is fitting that I teach them the Dhamma without letting go of the term ‘name-and-form. Thus he said: “Brahmin, without being attached to name and form...”
"Being unattached and not grieving, one is called a bhikkhu," having said this, he spoke this verse:
"One for whom there is no sense of 'mine' in name-and-form in every respect,
who does not grieve over what is non-existent— he indeed is called a bhikkhu."

In this context, "all" refers to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as it occurs by way of the five aggregates—the four beginning with feeling (*vedanā*) and the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*). "Not cherished" means that there is no grasping for it as "I" or "mine.

And "he does not grieve over what is non-existent" means that when that name-and-form has reached destruction and passing away, he does not grieve, thinking, "My form is destroyed... [and so on]... my..."
“Consciousness has been exhausted,” he does not grieve, nor is he distressed; he sees: “That which is subject to destruction and passing away has been exhausted for me.

“He indeed”—meaning one such as this, who, even while name-and-form still exist, is free from the sense of “mine,” and who does not grieve because of that which is no longer present—is called a bhikkhu.
At the conclusion of the teaching, both husband and wife were established in the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), and the teaching of the Dhamma was fruitful for those who had gathered there.
The Sixth Story: The Brahmin Who Gave the Five Products of the Cow.
The Seventh Story: The Story of Many Bhikkhus.
While residing at Jetavana, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma instruction concerning many bhikkhus, beginning with the words: "One who dwells in loving-kindness..."

For on one occasion, while the Venerable Mahākaccāna was dwelling on Mount Pavatta near Kuraraghara in the country of Avanti, a lay follower named Soṇa Koṭikaṇṇa, having gained confidence through the Elder’s discourse on the Dhamma, desired to go forth in the presence of the Elder. The Elder said to him:
“Soṇa, it is difficult to live on a single meal a day, to sleep alone, and to lead the holy life for as long as life lasts.”
Although he was refused twice after speaking thus, he was exceedingly eager for the going forth; having requested the Elder a third time, he went forth.
Because there were few monks in the Southern Land, three years passed before he received full ordination.
Desiring to see the Teacher face to face, he took leave of his preceptor and, receiving the message given by him, departed.
Having gone to Jeta’s Grove by stages, he paid homage to the Teacher. After exchanging greetings, he was assigned a lodging in the very same Fragrant Cottage as the Teacher.

Having spent much of the night pacing back and forth in the open air, he entered the Fragrant Cottage during the latter part of the night and passed that portion of the night in his own assigned lodging.
Then, at the time of dawn, he was requested by the Teacher.
He recited all sixteen chapters of the Aṭṭhakavagga by heart.
At the conclusion of his recitation, the Blessed One, expressing his appreciation, gave him his approval, saying, "Excellent, excellent, monk!
Hearing the Teacher's words of praise, the earth-dwelling devas, nāgas, and supaṇṇas—indeed, as far as the Brahma-world—raised a single shout of "Excellent! in unison.

At that moment, even the deity dwelling in the house of the Elder’s mother, the Great Laywoman (Mahā-upāsikā), in the city of Kuraraghara, which was two hundred yojanas from Jetavana, gave a great cry of "Sādhu! with a loud voice. Then the laywoman asked her:
"Who is this giving a cry of 'Sādhu!'? She replied: "It is I, sister. "Who are you? "I am the deity dwelling in your house."
"O deity! Previously you never gave me a word of praise; why do you give it today?
"I am not giving you a word of praise. "Then to whom have you given it? "To your son, the Elder Soṇa Koṭikaṇṇa. "What has my son done?
"Today your son dwelt in the same fragrant chamber as the Teacher and [heard] the Dhamma..."
He taught; having heard the Dhamma from your son, the Teacher was pleased and gave his approval (*sādhukāra*).

Therefore, I too have given him my approval. For when the Perfectly Enlightened One receives his approval, it spreads as a single act of approval from the earth-dwelling deities upward as far as the Brahma-world. But what, Master, did my son [do] for the Teacher?
“Has the Dhamma been taught? Has the Teacher taught it to my son? “It has been taught by your son to the Teacher.
As the deity was speaking thus, five-colored rapture arose in the laywoman and pervaded her entire body.
Then this thought occurred to her: “If my son has lived together with the Teacher in the same fragrant chamber and [taught] the Teacher...”

“He is capable of preaching the Dhamma; he will certainly be able to preach it for me as well. When my son returns, I shall have him listen to the Dhamma and I myself will hear the discourse on the Dhamma.
Then the Elder Soṇa, thinking, “Now is the time to announce the message given to me by my preceptor,” [went] to the Blessed One in the border regions.
Having requested five boons, beginning with full ordination by a community consisting of a quorum of five including a master of the Vinaya,
and having stayed for a few days in the very presence of the Teacher, he took leave of the Teacher, saying, "I shall see my preceptor. Departing from Jetavana,
he proceeded by stages until he arrived in the presence of his preceptor.
On the following day, the Elder, taking him with him while wandering for alms, went to the door of the female lay devotee’s house.
Seeing her son, she was delighted at heart; having paid homage and served him with great care, she asked:
"Is it true, my dear, that you stayed in the same fragrant chamber as the Teacher and delivered a discourse on the Dhamma to the Teacher? "It is so, lay devotee."
"By whom was this said to you? "Father, a deity dwelling in this house gave a great shout of 'Well done!
When I asked, 'Who is this?', she replied, 'It is I,' and spoke thus and so.
Upon hearing that, it occurred to me: 'If my son can speak the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he should speak it to me as well.'"
‘He will be able. Then she said to him, ‘Dear son, since you were able to explain the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, you will certainly be able to explain it to me as well.
On such-and-such a day, having arranged for a hearing of the Dhamma, I shall listen to your teaching of the Dhamma, dear son.
He consented. The laywoman, having given alms and performed worship for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, [said] regarding her son—
Thinking, “I shall hear my son’s discourse on the Dhamma,” she left only a single female slave to guard the house,
took all her attendants with her, and went to the pavilion built within the city for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma;
there, having ascended the decorated Dhamma-seat while her son was teaching the Dhamma, she sat down to listen to his discourse on the Dhamma.
At that time, nine hundred thieves were wandering about, looking for an opportunity to break into that laywoman’s house.
Her house was surrounded by seven walls and provided with seven gate-towers; in various places therein, they had tethered fierce dogs.
Furthermore, in the interior of the house, at the place where water dripped from the roof...
Having dug a moat, they filled it with tin. During the day, it remained as if melted and boiling due to the heat;
at night, it remained hard and solid. Immediately after that, they laid large iron plates continuously upon the ground.
Thus, [they guarded] both this protection and the fact that the laywoman remained within her own house.
Finding no opportunity because they were dependent [on her], those thieves learned of her departure that day;
they broke through the wall and entered the house by way of the lower part of the triple moat and the iron grating.
Then they sent the chief thief to her, saying: "If, upon hearing that we have entered here, she turns back and heads toward the house..."
“He is coming; strike him with a sword and kill him. He went and stood near her.
The thieves, having lit a lamp inside the house, opened the door to the treasury room where the coins were kept.
Seeing the thieves, the slave girl went to the laywoman and said, “Noble lady, many thieves have entered the house and opened the door to the treasury room.”
“[The thieves] have opened [the silver chest],” she reported. “Let the thieves take the coins they themselves have seen;
I am listening to the Dhamma talk for my son, do not create an obstacle to my Dhamma—go home,” she said, and sent her away.
The thieves, having emptied the chest of coins, opened the chest of silver. She went back again and reported that matter. The laywoman...
Thinking, "Let the thieves take what they desire; let them not cause me any obstacle," she sent her back again.
The thieves made the silver chamber empty and opened the gold chamber. She went back once more and reported the matter to the laywoman (*upāsikā*).
Then the laywoman addressed her, saying, "Lady, you have come to my presence many times, [saying], 'The thieves..."
"Let them take it as they please; I am listening to the Dhamma talk for my son, so do not create an obstacle for me.
Even though she was told this by me, she does not heed my words and continues to come back again and again.
"If you come now, I shall know what must be done with you; go home at once," she sent her away.
Having heard her words, Corajeṭṭhaka thought, "If those who seize the property of such a woman were to do so, a thunderbolt might fall and shatter their heads.
He went to the thieves and said, "Quickly restore the laywoman's property to its original state!
They [replaced] the chest of coins with coins, and the chests of silver and gold with silver and gold.
They filled it once more. Indeed, this is the natural law: that the Dhamma protects those who live according to the Dhamma. Therefore it was said:
“The Dhamma truly protects the one who lives by the Dhamma;
the Dhamma well-practiced brings happiness.”
“This is the benefit when the Dhamma is well-practiced:
one who lives according to the Dhamma does not go to a state of misery.
Then the thieves also went and stood at the place where the Dhamma was being heard. The Elder, having finished preaching the Dhamma, [waited] until the night had turned to dawn.
She descended from her seat. At that moment, the chief of the bandits fell at the feet of the female lay follower and said, "Forgive me, noble lady.
"What is this, dear? she asked. "For I stood here having conceived hatred toward you, wishing to kill you," he replied.
"In that case, my dear, I forgive you," she said. The other bandits also spoke in the same manner, and when she said, "I forgive you, dear ones," they were appeased.
They said, “Noble lady, if you will forgive us, please grant our son’s ordination in your presence.
She paid homage to her son and said, “Dear son, these thieves have gained confidence in my virtues and in your discourse on the Dhamma;
they are requesting ordination. Please ordain them. The Elder said, “Very well,” and [took] the robes they were wearing...
Having had their hair and beards shaved and having had them dyed with red clay, he ordained them and established them in the precepts.
At the time of their full ordination, he gave each of them a separate meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Those nine hundred bhikkhus, having each taken one of the nine hundred meditation subjects, ascended a mountain and [sat] in the shade of various trees.
Having sat down, they practiced the duties of a recluse.
Even while seated at the great monastery of Jetavana, two hundred yojanas away, the Teacher gazed upon those bhikkhus;
having determined the teaching on the Dhamma according to their respective temperaments, he emitted a radiance and sat as if right before them, speaking.
He spoke these verses as if [remembering them]:
“The bhikkhu who dwells in loving-kindness, with confidence in the Buddha’s teaching,
shall attain the peaceful state, the bliss that is the subsiding of all conditioned formations.”
“Empty this boat, O monk; once emptied, it will go swiftly for you.
Having severed both lust and hatred, you shall thereafter reach Nibbāna.
Cut off five, abandon five, and cultivate five further.”
The bhikkhu who has overcome the five attachments is called one who has crossed the flood.
"Meditate, bhikkhu, do not be negligent;
let not your mind delight in the strands of sensual pleasure."
Do not, being heedless, swallow a lump of iron, lest you cry out while being burned, "This is suffering!
"There is no meditation for one without wisdom; there is no wisdom for one who does not meditate."
He in whom there is both meditative absorption and wisdom is indeed close to Nibbāna.
For the bhikkhu who has entered an empty dwelling, whose mind is tranquil,
there is a superhuman delight as he clearly penetrates the Dhamma through insight.
“From whatever point one contemplates the arising and passing away of the aggregates,
one gains rapture and gladness— that which is the deathless for those who understand it.
In this regard, this is the beginning for a wise bhikkhu here:”
Guarding the sense faculties, contentment, and restraint according to the Pātimokkha;
associate with virtuous friends who are pure in livelihood and untiring;
be hospitable in conduct and skilled in proper behavior.
"Then, abounding in gladness, he will make an end of suffering.

In this context, "one who dwells in loving-kindness" (mettāvihārī) refers to one who either practices the meditation subject of loving-kindness or, by way of loving-kindness, has attained and remains established in the third and fourth jhānas;
such a person is indeed called one who dwells in loving-kindness. Furthermore, "one who is confident" (pasanno) refers to one who has confidence in the Buddha’s teaching.
The meaning is: he indeed delights in confidence. "Peaceful state" (*padaṃ santaṃ*) is a name for Nibbāna.

For such a bhikkhu attains and finds Nibbāna—which is called "peaceful" because it is the subsiding of all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārūpasama*), and which has received the name "bliss" because it is the supreme bliss—namely, that peaceful constituent part of all conditioned things. This is the meaning.
"Empty this boat, O bhikkhu"—empty this boat known as the selfhood (*attabhāva*), casting out the water of wrong thoughts.

"Once emptied, it will go lightly": for just as a boat filled with water in the great ocean, once its leaks are stopped and the water has been baled out, becomes light and does not sink in the great ocean;
so too, when this selfhood is emptied of the water of wrong thoughts, it becomes light and does not sink in the great ocean of saṃsāra.
Just as [a boat] goes quickly to a good port, so too for you:

this boat of the self, filled with the water of wrong thoughts, having closed the openings of the eye-door and so forth with restraint, will—because it has been drenched by the sprinkling of the water of arisen wrong thoughts—become light and, without sinking into the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), will go quickly to Nibbāna. "Having cut" means having severed the bonds of lust and hatred.
"Cut them off. For by cutting these off, you will attain *arahantship*, and thereafter you will go to, reach, even *nirvana* without remainder (*anupādisesa-nibbāna*); this is the meaning.
"Cut the five" refers to the five lower fetters (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) that lead to the lower realms, like a rope tied to one's feet.

A man might cut [the bonds] with a sword by means of the three lower paths. "He abandons five" means that one should abandon, should relinquish, and should cut—as a man would a rope tied around his neck—with the path of Arhatship the five higher fetters (*pañcoddhambhāgiyasaṃyojana*) which lead to rebirth in the upper deva-worlds;
this is the meaning. "He develops five further" is for the purpose of abandoning the higher fetters.
One should further develop the five faculties beginning with faith. Regarding the phrase “one who has transcended the five attachments”:

when this is so, because he has transcended the five attachments—namely, attachment consisting of lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, and views—the bhikkhu who has transcended the five attachments is called “one who has crossed the flood”; the meaning is that he is indeed called “one who has crossed the four floods.
“Meditate, O bhikkhu”: you, bhikkhu, should meditate by means of the two jhānas, and [you should also meditate] regarding bodily action and the rest.
"By dwelling in heedfulness, do not be negligent. "Let not your mind delight"—let your mind not take pleasure in the fivefold strands of sensual desire (*kāmaguṇa*).
"Do not swallow a ball of iron"—for those who are negligent through heedlessness, characterized by the loss of mindfulness, swallow glowing balls of iron in hell;
therefore I say this to you: "Do not, being negligent, swallow a ball of iron; do not, burning in hell, cry out, 'This is suffering! This is the meaning.
“There is no jhāna”: for one lacking the wisdom of effort that produces jhāna, there is indeed no such thing as jhāna. “There is no wisdom”:
for one who does not practice jhāna, there is no wisdom characterized by the statement, “A bhikkhu concentrated knows and sees things as they truly are.
“In whom there is both jhāna and wisdom”: the person in whom both of these exist [is fit] for Nibbāna.
The meaning is: "standing right nearby.
"Of one who has entered an empty place" means: of one who, in some secluded spot, has not abandoned the meditation subject and is seated with attention directed toward that meditation subject.
"Of one whose mind is peaceful" means: of one whose mind is extinguished (*nibbuta*). "Properly" means: of one who is practicing insight (*vipassanā*) into phenomena by way of cause and reason.
The meaning is that both the superhuman delight known as insight (*vipassanā*) and the divine delight known as the eight attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*) arise.
"In whatever way he comprehends" means that while performing the work upon the thirty-eight objects of meditation,
in whichever manner, at whatever times such as before the meal, or at whatever time he himself prefers, or in whichever meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) he prefers, he performs the work.

He practices full comprehension. "Arising and passing away" refers to the arising of the five aggregates by way of twenty-five characteristics, and their passing away by way of those same twenty-five characteristics.

"Rapture and gladness": thus, while comprehending the arising and passing away of the aggregates, he attains rapture in the Dhamma and gladness in the Dhamma. "The Deathless": that [Deathless] is found in name-and-form together with its conditions.

The rapture and gladness that arise when [the Dhamma] appears manifest and stands before one is "the Deathless itself" for wise people who understand it, because it leads to the attainment of Nibbāna, the Deathless;

this is the meaning. "In this regard, this is the beginning" means that in this context, this is the starting point; this is the preliminary stage. "Herein, for one possessed of wisdom" means in this [Dhamma].

In the Dispensation of a learned bhikkhu. Now, showing the preliminary stage (pubbaṭṭhāna) mentioned as "that foundation" (taṃ ādi), he says "guarding of the sense faculties" (indriyagutti) and so forth.

For the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla) is indeed called the preliminary stage. Therein, "guarding of the sense faculties" means restraint of the sense faculties (indriyasaṃvara). "Contentment" (santuṭṭhi) means contentment with the four requisites.
By this, both the purity of livelihood (ājīvapārisuddhi) and the virtue dependent on the requisites (paccayasannissita-sīla) are explained.
"Pātimokkha" refers to the fulfillment of the preeminent virtue known as the Pātimokkha.

"Associate with virtuous friends" means: avoiding those who neglect their duties and those who are unsuitable companions, one should associate with virtuous friends—those of pure livelihood for the sake of a noble life, who are not indolent but diligent in making a living by the strength of their own legs.

"Serve" is the meaning. "One who lives with hospitality" means one whose way of life is perfected through both material hospitality and hospitality in the Dhamma; the meaning is that he should be a performer of hospitality.
"Skilled in conduct": conduct includes both moral virtue (*sīla*) and the performance of duties (*vatta-paṭivatta*); one should be skilled in these, that is, one should be proficient in them.

The meaning is as follows: "Then, full of gladness" means that by becoming full of gladness through the joy in the Dhamma (*dhammapāmojja*) arising from such hospitable conduct and skill in proper behavior, he will bring an end to the entire suffering of saṃsāra.
Thus, at the conclusion of each of these verses taught by the Teacher, one hundred monks [attained realization].
Having attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) right where they were seated, they rose up into the air;
and all those bhikkhus, having crossed the two-hundred-and-forty-league wilderness by way of the sky,
paid homage at the feet of the Tathāgata while extolling and praising his gold-colored body.
The seventh story: The Group of Many Bhikkhus. The eighth story: The Story of the Five Hundred Bhikkhus.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, related this Dhamma teaching concerning five hundred bhikkhus, beginning with the words: "Like jasmine flowers."

It is said that those monks, having received a meditation subject from the Teacher and practicing the duties of a recluse in the forest, saw vassika flowers blooming at dawn and dropping from their stalks by evening. Seeing this, they exerted themselves with the thought:
"Just as these flowers are released from their stalks, may we be released first from lust and the other defilements. The Teacher, observing those monks, said: "Monks,..."
"A monk must indeed strive to be liberated from suffering, just as one releases jasmine flowers from their stalks," he said,
and while seated in the Perfumed Chamber, radiating light, he spoke this verse:
"Just as one releases the delicate jasmine flowers, so too should one release the mind from the body."
“Even so, O bhikkhus, you should utterly cast off lust and hatred.
In this context, *vassikā* refers to the jasmine (*sumanā*). *Maddavāni* means withered. This is what is meant:
just as the jasmine flower sheds its blossoms that bloomed yesterday, releasing them from their stalks on the following day when they have become old, even so you too—
"Cast off the faults such as lust and the rest.
At the conclusion of this teaching, all those bhikkhus were established in arahantship.
This is the eighth story, concerning the five hundred bhikkhus.
9. The Story of the Elder Santakāya While residing at Jetavana, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma instruction concerning the elder named Santakāya.
It is said that he had no fidgeting with his hands or feet; being free from bodily restlessness, his very person was tranquil.
He was indeed an elder who had come from a lion’s womb. It is said that once, after lions had taken their prey, they would enter one of the caves made of silver, gold, gems, or coral;
there, on a slab of emerald, they would lie for seven days amidst powdered yellow orpiment.
On the seventh day, rising and looking at the place where they had lain, if [they saw] any trace of their tail, ears, hands, or feet—

Seeing that the emerald, green vitriol, and lime powders had been disturbed and scattered about, they thought, "This is not worthy of your birth or your lineage," and lay down again for seven days without food. But when the powders were no longer scattered, [the Bodhisatta] thought, "This is befitting of your birth and lineage";
thus, emerging from his lair, stretching his limbs, and surveying the directions, he departed.
Having roared the lion’s roar three times, they set out for their range of food. This monk has come from such a lion-womb.
Having observed his bodily conduct, the monks reported it to the Teacher: "Venerable Sir, we have never before seen a monk like the Elder Santakāya.
For when he is seated, there is no movement of his hands, no movement of his feet, nor any stretching of his body."
"Or is there not? Having heard this, the Teacher said, "Monks, a monk indeed must be one who is tranquil in body and so forth, just like the elder Santakāya," and he spoke this verse:
"Tranquil in body, tranquil in speech, tranquil and well-composed;"
“The bhikkhu who has vomited out the bait of the world is called ‘peaceful.

In this context, “one whose body is peaceful” means one whose body is peaceful due to the absence of killing living beings and so forth; “one whose speech is peaceful” means one whose speech is peaceful due to the absence of false speech and so forth;
“one whose mind is peaceful” means one whose mind is peaceful due to the absence of covetousness and so forth; and “well-composed” means that all three—body and so forth—are perfectly concentrated.

The meaning is that because he has vomited up the worldly bait through the four paths, the bhikkhu is "one who has vomited up the worldly bait"; and because passion and the other defilements have been stilled within him, he is called "stilled.
At the conclusion of the teaching, that elder was established in Arahatship, and the Dhamma teaching was fruitful for those who had assembled as well.
The ninth story: The Elder Santakāya.
The tenth: The Story of the Elder Naṅgalakula.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this teaching on the Dhamma—“Exhort yourself by yourself”—with reference to the Elder Naṅgalakula.
It seems there was once a poor man who lived by working for hire. A certain bhikkhu, seeing him going along with a plough, his body clad in a mere patch of ragged cloth, said this to him:
"Is it not better for you to go forth from the household life than to live in this way?
"Who, venerable sir, would ordain me while I am living like this? "If you will go forth, I [will ordain you]."
"I will ordain him. "Very well, venerable sir; if you will ordain me, I shall go forth.
Then that elder, having led him to Jetavana, bathed him with his own hands, placed him in the courtyard, and ordained him.
Along with the fragment of rag-robes he was wearing, he had him place the plough at the very boundary of the courtyard upon a tree branch. Even at the time of his full admission, he...
He became known simply as the Elder Naṅgalakula. Living off the gains and honors that accrue to Buddhas, he became dissatisfied;

unable to dispel his dissatisfaction, he thought, "I shall no longer go about wearing these saffron robes given in faith," and having gone to the foot of that tree, he exhorted himself: "O shameless one! O devoid of modesty!"
"Having put on these robes and gone forth, he has become desirous of making a living by working for wages.

As he was thus admonishing himself, his mind became subdued. He turned back, but after a few days had passed, becoming weary once more, he admonished himself in the same way, and again his mind turned back. In this very manner, whenever he became weary...
Having gone there, he exhorted himself. Then, seeing him going there frequently, the bhikkhus asked him, “Friend Naṅgala Thera, why do you go there?
He replied, “I am going to the presence of my teacher, venerable sirs.
Within just a few days, he attained arahantship.
The monks, playing with him, said: "Friend Naṅgalatthera, your path for wandering has become like a forbidden track;

I suppose you no longer go into the presence of your teacher. "Yes, venerable sirs, we went there when there was association, but now that association has been severed, therefore we do not go," he replied. Having heard this, [the monks reported it].
The monks reported this matter to the Teacher, saying, "He has spoken falsely and then given a declaration of final knowledge. The Teacher said, "Yes, monks, my son,
having exhorted himself, has reached the pinnacle of the task of one who has gone forth," and while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke these verses:
“Exhort yourself by yourself, examine yourself by yourself;
for one who is self-guarded and mindful, a bhikkhu shall dwell in happiness.
For oneself is indeed one’s own refuge—what other refuge could there be?”
"For oneself is one's own refuge;
therefore, restrain yourself as a merchant restrains a noble horse.
In this context, "exhort yourself" means exhort and remind yourself by means of yourself. "Examine yourself" means [examine] yourself by means of yourself.

Examine this thoroughly. The meaning is: "O monk, since this is so, being yourself guarded through your own self-guarding, and being mindful through the establishment of mindfulness, you will dwell happily in all postures.
A "protector" (*nātha*) is a refuge and a support. For who else could be a protector? Because [the mind] is established within the individual existence (*attabhāva*) of another.

The meaning is: "Who indeed could be another protector? for it is impossible to become one who has realized the fruit by performing wholesome deeds or by developing the path with heaven as the ultimate goal;
therefore, since the self alone is one's own destination, foundation, and refuge, just as one seeking gain relies upon a noble thoroughbred horse...
Just as a merchant, having cut off the horse's wandering on uneven ground, bathes it, feeds it, restrains it, and looks after it three times a day,

so too you should restrain and protect yourself by preventing the arising of unarisen unwholesome states and abandoning unwholesome states that have arisen through negligence of mindfulness; when this is done, the first jhāna begins.
The meaning is: "Having done so, you will attain the distinction between the mundane and the supramundane.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the tenth story, the account of the Elder Naṅgalakula.
11. The Story of the Elder Vakkali The Teacher delivered this Dhamma teaching, "Abounding in gladness," while residing at Veḷuvana, concerning the Elder Vakkali.
It is said that this venerable one was born into a brahmin family in Sāvatthī; when he reached maturity, he saw the Tathāgata entering for alms.

Having seen and gazed upon the excellence of the Teacher’s physical form, and being insatiable from beholding that perfection of body, he thought, "May I always have the opportunity to see the Tathāgata.
Having gone forth in the presence of the Teacher with the thought, "In this way I shall see the Tathāgata at all times," he stood wherever he could see the One of Ten Powers,
abandoning his recitation, meditation subjects, mental attention, and other duties, gazing only at the Teacher.
He was reflecting. The Teacher, waiting for his knowledge to reach maturity, said nothing at first; then, knowing that "his knowledge has now reached maturity," he spoke and instructed him, saying:
"Vakkali, what is the use of seeing this foul body? He who sees the Dhamma, Vakkali, sees me;
he who sees me sees the Dhamma. Thus he [Vakkali] was instructed. So...
Even after being exhorted by the Teacher, he was unable to leave the sight of him and go elsewhere.
Then the Teacher, thinking, "This bhikkhu will not attain awakening without experiencing a sense of spiritual urgency," went to Rājagaha at the approach of the rains retreat.
On the day of entering the rains retreat, he dismissed him, saying, "Go away, Vakkali! Go away, Vakkali! He [thought], "The Teacher does not [wish to see] me..."
Thinking, "I am unable to stand before the Teacher for these three months," he said, "What is the use of my life?
I shall throw myself from the mountain," and ascended Vulture Peak.
The Teacher, perceiving his state of distress, [thought], "This bhikkhu, not obtaining consolation from my presence, regarding the paths and fruits..."
He emitted a radiance to reveal himself, thinking, “I shall destroy his underlying support.

From the moment he saw the Teacher, even that great sorrow of his was abandoned. Like filling a dried-up pond with a flood of water, the Teacher uttered this verse in order to arouse powerful rapture and joy in the Elder:
“A bhikkhu who abounds in gladness, having confidence in the Buddha’s teaching, shall attain the peaceful state, the bliss that is the stilling of all conditioned formations.
This is its meaning: a bhikkhu who naturally abounds in gladness finds delight in confidence toward the Buddha’s teaching; he, thus...
“Having full confidence in the Buddha’s teaching, may you attain Nibbāna—the peaceful state known by the name ‘the stilling of all conditioned formations, the bliss.
Having spoken this verse, the Teacher extended his hand to the Elder Vakkali and said:
“Come, Vakkali, do not fear; look upon the Tathāgata.”
“I shall lift you up, like an elephant sunk in the mud.
‘Come, Vakkali, do not fear; look upon the Tathāgata.
I shall release you, as the sun releases itself from the grasp of Rāhu.’”
“Come, Vakkali, do not fear; look upon the Tathāgata.
I shall release you, as the moon is released from the grasp of Rāhu.”—He spoke these verses.
Thinking, “I have seen the One of Ten Powers, and I have even received his summons, ‘Come!’,” he was filled with powerful joy.
Having thus attained it, and seeing no path for departure as he wondered, "Whither indeed should I go?", he leapt into the air before the One of Ten Powers.
While the Teacher’s verse was still being recited, his first foot remained upon the mountain;
then, while still in mid-air, he suppressed his rapture, attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), and descended while paying homage to the Tathāgata.
He stood in the presence of the Teacher. Later on, the Teacher placed him in the foremost position among those who were devoted through faith.
Thus ends the eleventh story, the Story of the Elder Vakkali.
12. The Story of the Novice Sumanas.
The Teacher delivered this Dhamma teaching while residing at the Pubbārāma monastery concerning the novice Sumanas. This is the sequential narrative:

During the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, a certain son of noble family saw the Teacher, in the midst of the fourfold assembly, appointing a certain bhikkhu to the position of foremost among those possessing the divine eye. Desiring that same attainment for himself, he [approached] the Teacher...
Having invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha and given a great almsgiving for seven days, he made this aspiration:
"Venerable Sir, may I too, in the future, become the foremost among those possessing the divine eye within the dispensation of a certain Buddha.
The Teacher, looking back over a hundred thousand aeons, perceived that the fulfillment of his aspiration was certain.
“One hundred thousand eons from now, in the dispensation of the Buddha Gotama, you will become the foremost among those possessing the divine eye,
named Anuruddha,” he prophesied. Having heard that prophecy, considering that attainment as if it were to be reached the very next day,
after the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, he asked the monks about the practice for developing the divine eye, and [traveled] seven yojanas...
Having surrounded the Kañcana-thūpa and caused many thousands of lamp-trees to be made, he performed a lamp-offering; passing away from there,
he was reborn in the world of the gods, and after wandering through existences among gods and humans for a hundred thousand aeons,
he was reborn in this aeon in a poor family in Bārāṇasī, where he earned his living as a grass-gatherer for the merchant Sumanaseṭṭhi.
He adopted [the child], and his name became Annabhāra. In that city, the merchant Sumanas was also constantly giving a great alms-offering.
Then one day, the Paccekabuddha named Upaṭṭha, having emerged from the attainment of cessation on Mount Gandhamādana, thought, "Whom shall I favor today? and then, "Today, I shall favor Annabhāra."
"It is appropriate to do so, for now he will return home from the forest having taken grass.
Knowing this, [the Elder] took his bowl and robe, traveled by means of psychic power, and stood waiting before Annabhāra.
Seeing him with an empty bowl in his hand, Annabhāra asked, "Venerable sir, did you receive alms? To which [the Elder] replied, "We shall receive them, O one of great merit!"
“In that case, venerable sir, please wait a moment. Having discarded the grass basket, he went quickly home and asked his wife, “Wife, is there the portion of food set aside for me, or not?
When she replied, “There is, husband,” he returned in haste, took the bowl from the Paccekabuddha, and said, “Since I have the desire to give, the gift... [is ready].”
"Previously, even when there was something to be given, I could not find a recipient. But today I have seen a recipient and there is something to be given;
what a gain for me! Having returned home, she had rice placed in a bowl, brought it back, and set it into the hand of the Paccekabuddha, saying:
“By this gift, may I not suffer poverty;
may the word ‘there is nothing’ never exist for me in any state of becoming.

He made this aspiration, saying: “Venerable Sir, may I be freed from such a miserable life, and may I never even hear the phrase ‘there is nothing. The Paccekabuddha replied, “So be it, O one of great merit,” and after giving his blessing, he departed.
The deity dwelling in the parasol of the merchant Sumanaseṭṭhin also said, "Oh, what a gift! A supreme gift!
It is well-established upon Upariṭṭha," and she gave her applause three times. Then the merchant said to her, "Did you not see me giving this much alms for all this time?
She replied, "I did not give my applause on account of your gift; rather, it was because of the weight of the food [upon] Upariṭṭha."
"Having become inspired upon receiving this alms-food, he uttered this word of praise for me. He thought, "It is truly marvelous!
For so long a time, while giving gifts, I was unable to cause even a deity to give a word of praise;
yet this Annabhāra, who lives depending on me, has caused a word of praise to be given by me with a single portion of alms-food. Having acted in a manner worthy of his gift..."
Thinking, "I shall make that alms-food my own," he summoned him and asked, "Did you give anything to anyone today?
"Yes, master; today I gave a portion of my meal to the Paccekabuddha Upāriṭṭha.
"Well then, sir, take this coin and give me this alms-food. "I will not give it."
“Yes, sir. He increased the amount until it reached a thousand, yet the other would not accept even a thousand.
Then he said to him, “Very well, sir; if you will not give alms-food, take a thousand and give me a ticket.
He replied, “I shall know after consulting with the noble one,” and quickly reaching the Paccekabuddha, he said, “Venerable sir, the merchant Sumanas has offered a thousand...”
"Having given it, he asks for your consent regarding the alms-food; what shall I do? he asked.

Then he [the other] brought him a simile: "Just as, O wise one, in a village of a hundred families, if a lamp were lit in one house, the others might take their own wicks, soak them in oil, and light them; the radiance of the original lamp—"
"It should be said that it exists, not that it does not exist. "Venerable sir, the radiance is even greater.
"In the same way, O wise one, whether it be a ladleful of gruel or a spoonful of alms-food, for one who gives a share of their own alms-food to others, it increases by as much as they give.
For you gave only a single portion of alms-food, yet through the merchant's gift..."
“Since it has been given, there are two portions of alms-food: one for you and one for him.
He replied, “Excellent, venerable sir,” and after paying homage to him, he went to the merchant and said, “Take this bowl, master.
[The merchant said,] “In that case, take these kahāpaṇa coins. [He replied,] “I do not sell alms-food; I give you the bowl out of faith.”
“I give,” he said. “You give out of faith; I too honor your virtues. Take this, dear son, and from now on do not perform manual labor yourself.
Build a house in the street and live there. Whatever you need, take it all from me.
However, the almsfood given by him who had emerged from the attainment of cessation was [consumed] on that very day.
It yields its fruit. Therefore, when the king heard of that occurrence, he summoned Annabhāra, took him into favor, bestowed great wealth upon him, and appointed him to the position of treasurer.
Having become a friend to Sumanaseṭṭhi, he performed meritorious deeds throughout his life; then, passing away from there, he was reborn in the world of the devas.
Wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he took rebirth in this present era of a Buddha’s appearance in the city of Kapilavatthu, in the house of the Sakyan Amitodana;
they gave him the name Anuruddha. He was the younger brother of Mahānāma the Sakyan and the son of the Teacher’s junior father;
he was exceedingly delicate and possessed great merit. One day, it is said, among the six khattiyas...
While they were playing with sugar, having made a wager on cakes, Anuruddha was defeated and sent word to his mother for more cakes.
She filled a large golden bowl and sent the cakes. After eating the cakes, he played again and, being defeated once more, sent word in the same way.
When the cakes had been brought three times in this manner, on the fourth occasion his mother said, "Now—"

“There is no cake,” she sent back. Having heard her words, because the word “there is not” was something he had never heard before, he formed the notion, “Now there will be such things as ‘no-cakes’ (natthipūva),” and sent her back, saying, “Go and bring some no-cakes.
Then his mother, when told, “Noble lady, please give me some no-cakes,” said, “My son has never heard the word ‘there is not’ before.”
Thinking, "How indeed might I make him know the state of non-existence? she washed a golden bowl, covered it with another golden bowl, and sent it off, saying, "Come, dear son, give this to my son.
At that moment, the deity who presided over the city thought, "In the past, when our master was Annabhāra, he gave a portion of alms-food to the Paccekabuddha Upaṭṭha..."
Thinking, “We have made a vow that we shall not even hear the word ‘there is not’;
if we were to know this matter and remain indifferent, our heads would split into seven pieces,” they filled a bowl with divine cakes.
That man brought the bowl, placed it before him, and opened it. Their fragrance pervaded the entire city.
As for the cake, however, as soon as it was placed in his mouth, it remained pervading seventeen thousand world-systems.
Anuruddha also thought: "I suppose my mother did not love me before this; for never before has she ever baked 'no-cake' for me.
He went and said to his mother: "Mother, I am not dear to you."
“Dear father, what are you saying? You are dearer to me than my own eyes or even the flesh of my heart.
“If I am dear to you, mother, why did you not give me such *natthipūva* cakes before?
She asked that man: “Dear father, was there anything in the bowl? “Yes, lady, the bowl was full of cakes; it was not such as mine.”
"Seen before. She thought: "My son has performed meritorious deeds; surely it must be deities who have sent him these divine cakes.
He too said to his mother: "Mother, I have never eaten such cakes before;
from now on, you must bake only plain cakes for me. From then on, whenever he said, "I wish to eat cakes," she [would take] a golden bowl...
Having washed it and covered it with another bowl, he sent it; the deities filled the bowl.
Thus, while living in the midst of the household, not knowing the meaning of the phrase "there is nothing," he consumed only divine cakes.
However, for the sake of being the Teacher’s retinue, as the Sakyan princes were going forth one after another according to family order, Mahānāma the Sakyan—
“Father, no one from our family has ever gone forth; either you must go forth, or I.
When this was said, he replied, “I am too delicate to be able to go forth. [The father said: “In that case, learn the craft of agriculture;
I shall go forth. [The son asked: “What is this so-called ‘craft of agriculture’? For he did not even know the place where food is produced.
He knows [only this]; what indeed could he know of the nature of action? Therefore he spoke thus.
For one day, Anuruddha, Bhaddiya, and Kimila—these three men—discussed among themselves: "From where does food arise? Among them, Kimila said, "It arises from storehouses.
It is said that one day he saw rice being put into a storehouse; therefore, "from the storehouse..."
He spoke thus because of the perception that "food arises [from within the body]. Then Bhaddiya said to him, "You do not know," and added, "Food, it is said, arises in the cooking pot.

It seems that one day, seeing food being increased from the cooking pot, he formed the perception that "it arises right here," and therefore he spoke in that manner. Anuruddha said to both of them, "You two..."
Having said, "You do not know," he replied, "Food indeed arises in a great golden bowl a ratana deep, within a basket.
It is said that they had never before seen rice being husked nor food being cooked;
they saw only the food placed before them after it had increased in the golden bowl. Therefore, they formed the perception: "This arises right within the bowl itself."
Therefore he spoke thus: "In this way, even one who does not know the proper place for rising from his seat—a clansman of great merit—what will he know of the management of a farm?

Having heard from his brother, who spoke in such a manner as 'Come now, Anuruddha, I shall instruct you in the business of household life; first, the field must be ploughed,' that the affairs of the farm were endless, [Anuruddha thought]: 'I have no need for the household life.'"
Having taken leave of his mother, he went forth together with five Sākiya princes headed by Bhaddiya.
Approaching the Teacher at Anupiya Mango Grove, he received the going-forth. Having gone forth, practicing the path of right conduct, he gradually realized the three knowledges;
while sitting on a single seat, with his divine eye, he saw [the world] as clearly as if looking at myrobalan fruits placed in the palm of his hand.
Having become capable of surveying thousands of world-systems as if they were right before his eyes, he declared:
“I know my former births; the divine eye is purified;
I am possessed of the threefold knowledge and have attained supernormal powers; the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”
Having uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*), he reflected, "What indeed did I do to obtain this prosperity? Seeing that it was because he had made a resolution at the feet of Padumuttara Buddha,
and further realizing that while wandering through *saṃsāra*, at a certain time in Benares, living in dependence on the merchant Sumanaseṭṭhi, he had been named Annabhāra— he understood all this.
“In former times I was Annabhāra, a poor grass-gatherer;
alms-food was given by me to the Neutral One, Upariṭṭha,” he said.
Then this thought occurred to him: “From that alms-food given by me to Upariṭṭha at that time, [I have obtained] kahāpaṇas...”
Having given the answer, he took hold of him and asked, "Where has my friend, the merchant Sumanas, been reborn now?
Then [the other] replied to him, "In the Viñjhā forest, at the foot of a mountain, there is a village called Muṇḍanigama;
there, the lay follower named Mahāmuṇḍa had two sons, Mahāsumana and Cūḷasumana. He has been reborn as that Cūḷasumana."
He saw him. Having seen him, he thought: "Will there be any benefit if I go there, or will there not?
While reflecting, he saw this: "If I go there, he will leave the world at the age of seven and go forth;
and at the very stroke of the razor, he will attain Arahantship. Having seen this, as the rainy season drew near, he went through the air...
Having gone there, he descended at the village gate. Now, the lay follower Mahāmuṇḍa had been a trusted friend of the Elder even before;
seeing the Elder putting on his robe at the time for alms, he said to his son Mahāsumana:
"Dear boy, the Venerable Anuruddha has arrived; go and take his bowl before anyone else does."

“Take it; I shall prepare a seat. He did so. The lay devotee, having served the Elder with due honor within his own residence, obtained his promise to stay for the three-month rains retreat, and the Elder consented.
Then, after attending to him for the three months as if looking after him every day, on the occasion of the Great Pavāraṇā, he offered him the three robes and—
Having brought sugar, oil, rice, and other provisions, he placed them at the feet of the Elder and said, "Please accept these, venerable sir.
"Enough, lay follower; I have no need for this. "In that case, venerable sir, this is known as the 'rainy-season residence gift';
please accept it. "I do not accept it, lay follower. "For what reason do you not accept it, venerable sir? "For my..."
“Nor is there even a novice to act as a preparer of allowable things nearby. “In that case, venerable sir, let my son Mahāsumana become a novice.
“I have no need for Mahāsumana, lay follower. “In that case, venerable sir, please let Cūḷasumana go forth.
The Elder, having consented with “Very well,” caused Cūḷasumana to go forth. At the very moment the razor touched his hair—

He attained arahantship. The Elder stayed right there with him for about half a month, and then, thinking, "I shall see the Teacher," he took leave of his kinsmen and traveled through the air, descending in a forest hut in the Himalayan region.
The Elder was already naturally possessed of aroused energy; as he walked back and forth there during the first and last watches of the night, [he attained even higher states].
Wind arose in his belly. Then, seeing him looking exhausted, the novice asked, "Venerable sir, what ails you?
"Wind has arisen in my belly," he replied. "Has it ever arisen before, venerable sir? "Yes, friend.
"By what means does it become comfortable, venerable sir? "When water is obtained from Anotatta, it becomes comfortable."
“Friend,” [the Elder said]. “In that case, Venerable Sir, I shall bring it. “Will you be able to do so, novice? “Yes, Venerable Sir.
“In that case, there is a Naga king named Pannaga at Lake Anotatta who knows me; inform him and bring back one water-pot for the sake of medicine.
“Very well,” he replied, and having paid homage to his preceptor, he rose into the air and traveled five hundred yojanas.
He went to that place. On that day, however, the Naga king, surrounded by his retinue of Naga dancers, was desirous of sporting in the water.
Seeing the novice approaching, he became angry, thinking:
"This shaven-headed monk wanders about scattering the dust from his own feet upon my head; he must have come to the Anotatta lake for the sake of drinking water. Now, I shall not [let him...]"
Thinking, "I shall give water," he lay down, covering the Anotatta Lake, which was fifty leagues in extent,
with his hood as if closing a great cauldron with a large pot. The novice, observing the serpent king's demeanor and realizing,
"He is angry," spoke this verse:
“Listen to me, O King of Nagas, you of fierce splendor and great power!
Give me a water-jar; I have come for the sake of medicine.
Having heard this, the Naga king spoke this verse:
“In the eastern quarter there is a great river named Gaṅgā;
it flows into the great ocean. From there, you must bring water.
Having heard this, the novice thought, “This Nāga king will not give it of his own accord; I shall take it by force.”

Thinking, "I shall take this water only after making him acknowledge my power and having overcome him," he said, "Great King, my preceptor has me fetch water from Anotatta itself; therefore, I shall carry it from here.
Go away, do not stop me," and spoke this verse:
“Water indeed will be my ruin; I have need of this very water-vessel.
If you possess strength and power, O King of Nāgas, then restrain it.
Then the King of Nāgas said to him:
“O novice, if you possess such valor and manliness, I welcome your words; bring me some water.
Then the novice, saying to him, “So be it, Great King, I shall bring it,” was told, “If you are able, then bring it.”

—"In that case, you must know it well," he said, and after obtaining their promise three times, he thought, "It is fitting for me to carry water after demonstrating the power of the Buddha's teaching.
Having thus reflected, he first went into the presence of the deities dwelling in the sky.
They came, paid homage, and stood before him, asking, "What is it, venerable sir? [He replied: "On this surface of Lake Anotatta..."
"A battle will take place between me and the Naga King Pannaga; go there and observe who wins and who loses," he said.
Following this very same procedure, he approached the four World-Protectors, as well as Sakka, Suyāma, Santusita, and Paranimmita-vasavatti, and reported the matter to them.
Thereafter, he proceeded in succession until he had gone as far as the Brahma-world.
There, Brahmās arrived from here and there, stood by him after paying homage, and asked, "What is it, venerable sir? He reported that matter to them.
Thus, excluding the non-percipient beings and the formless Brahmās, he traveled everywhere in a mere moment and reported it.
Having heard his words, all the deities [gathered] on the surface of Lake Anotatta like grains of rice placed in a winnowing basket.
Like flour-dust, they gathered together, filling the sky without any gaps.
When the assembly of devas had thus gathered, the novice stood in the air and said to the Naga king:
"Listen to me, O Naga king, you of fierce power and great strength!"
“Give me a water-pot, for I have come for the sake of medicine.
Then the Nāga said to him:
“Novice, if you possess valor and manliness;”
“I rejoice in your words; give me some water.
Having obtained the promise of the Naga king three times, he remained in the air and manifested a Brahma-body twelve yojanas in height.
Descending from the sky, he stepped upon the hood of the Naga king and pressed him down with his face turned downward. At that very moment—
As soon as he stepped upon the hood of the Naga king, it became like the skin of a snake crushed by a strong man;

the folds of the hood collapsed until they were only the size of a broom-handle. From the places where the Naga king’s hoods had been released, columns of water the thickness of palm trunks gushed forth.
The novice filled his water-vessel in mid-air, and the assembly of devas gave a shout of approval.
Then the Naga king, feeling ashamed, became angry with the novice; his eyes turned the color of *jayakusuma* flowers.
He thought, "This man has gathered the assembly of gods, taken water, and put me to shame.
Seizing him, I shall thrust my hand into his mouth and crush his heart-flesh, or else, seizing him by the feet, I shall cast him beyond the Ganges."
"I shall hurl it! he pursued with great speed; yet even as he pursued, he was unable to catch him.
The novice, having gone on, placed the drinking water in his preceptor’s hand and said, "Drink, venerable sir.
The Nāga king also came up from behind and said, "Venerable Anuruddha, this novice has come taking water that was not given by me; do not drink."
He said, "It is indeed so, venerable sir, that he is a novice. [The Nāga] said, "Venerable sir, drink this water brought by me as a gift.
Knowing that "there is no speaking of falsehood for a novice whose taints are exhausted," the Elder drank the water.
At that very moment, his affliction was pacified. Again the Nāga said to the Elder: "Venerable sir, I am the entire host of devas to this novice..."
“Having brought them together, I shall put him to shame; I will either split his heart asunder or, seizing him by the feet, hurl him across the Ganges.
“Great King, that novice is of great power; you will not be able to fight with the novice.
Go and ask his forgiveness. He himself already knew the novice’s supernatural power.

However, having followed him out of shame, he returned. Then, having asked his forgiveness according to the elder’s words and established a friendly intimacy with him, he said, "From now on, when there is need for water from Anotatta, there is no necessity for you to come;
you should simply send word to me, and I myself will bring it and give it to you. Having said this, he departed.
The Elder also set out, taking the novice with him. The Teacher, knowing that the Elder was approaching, sat in the Migāramātupāsāda waiting for the Elder’s arrival.
When the monks saw the Elder coming, they went out to meet him and received his bowl and robe.
Then some of them seized the novice by the head, some by the ears, and some by the arms.
Having shaken him, they said, "What is it, novice Cūḷakaniṭṭha? Are you not weary? The Teacher, seeing their conduct, thought:
"Heavy indeed is the task of these monks; like those seizing a venomous snake by the neck, they seize the novice without knowing his power.
Today, I shall make the virtue of the novice Sumanas manifest."
“It is fitting to do so. The Elder also came, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down.
After exchanging greetings with him, the Teacher addressed the Elder Ānanda: “Ānanda, I wish to wash my feet with water from Lake Anotatta;
give a water-pot to the novices and have them bring some water. The Elder [sent for] about five hundred novices at the monastery...
He assembled them. Among them, the novice Sumanas was the youngest. The Elder addressed the oldest novice:
"Novice, the Teacher wishes to wash his feet with water that has not yet been drawn; go, take a jar, and bring some water.
He replied, "I cannot, venerable sir," and did not consent. The Elder questioned the others in order.
They too, having spoken in the same manner, refused. “But are there no novice monks (sāmaṇera) whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava) here?
“There are,” they replied, “but they did not wish for it, thinking, ‘This garland-bunch is not bound for us; it is bound for the novice Sumanas alone.
As for the worldlings (puthujjana), however, they refused simply because of their own incapacity. Finally, at the turn of Sumanas—
When he had arrived, [the Teacher] said, "Sāmaṇera, the Teacher wishes to wash his feet with water from the Anotatta Lake; bring some water, having taken a water-jar.
He thought, "If the Teacher has me bring it, I shall bring it," and after paying homage to the Teacher, he said, "Venerable Sir, please have me brought water from the Anotatta Lake.
"Yes, Sumanā," he replied. Then, at the ponds built by Visākhā—
In his dwelling-cells made of solid gold, he took a great water-jar capable of holding sixty jars of water,
and thinking, "I have no need for this to be lifted up and placed upon my shoulder," he hung it by a sling,
rose into the air, and sped toward the Himalayas.

When the Nāga king saw the novice approaching from afar, he went out to meet him, took the water-jar upon his shoulder, and said, "Venerable sir, since you have slaves such as myself, why have you come yourself? When there was need of water, why did you not send even a mere message?
Having taken up the water in the jar himself, he lifted it up and said, "Go ahead, Venerable sir; I shall carry it."
“I shall bring it,” he said. “Stay here, Great King; I alone have been commanded by the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Having thus turned back the Naga king, he took the water-pot by its rim with his hand and went through the air.
Then the Teacher, seeing him approaching, addressed the monks: “Behold, monks, this novice!”
“Moving with grace, he shines like a king of swans in the sky,” he said. He too, having set down his water-jar and paid homage to the Teacher, stood there.
Then the Teacher said to him, “How many years have you been ordained, Sumanā? “Seven years, Bhante,” he replied.
“In that case, Sumanā, from this day forth be a bhikkhu. Having said this, he conferred upon him the inheritance-ordination (*dāyajja-upasampadā*).
He gave [them]. It is said that only two novices, both seven years of age—namely, this Sumana and Sopāka—received full ordination.
When he had thus been ordained, they raised a discussion in the Hall of Truth: "It is wonderful, friends!
Such power indeed belongs to a young novice; we have never before seen such power as this."
The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, with what discussion are you sitting together here now?
When they replied, "With this one," he said, "Monks, even one who is young in my teaching, if he practices rightly, surely attains such success as this.
Having spoken thus, while teaching the Dhamma, he uttered this verse:
“Whosoever is a young bhikkhu who applies himself to the Buddha’s teaching, he illuminates this world like the moon freed from clouds.

Herein, “applies himself” means he strives or exerts effort. “Illuminates” means that bhikkhu, by means of the knowledge of the path to arahantship, shines upon the world—the world consisting of the aggregates and so forth—just as the moon freed from clouds and other obscurations; the meaning is that he makes it a single expanse of light.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
Thus ends the twelfth story, the Story of the Novice Sumanas.
The commentary on the Bhikkhu-vagga is finished.
The Twenty-fifth Chapter. 26.
The Chapter on Brahmins. 1.
The Account of the Brahmin Abounding in Faith.
"Cut off the stream"—the Teacher gave this teaching while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a brahmin who was full of faith.
It is said that after hearing the Blessed One’s teaching, that brahmin, with a mind full of confidence, established a permanent meal offering for sixteen monks in his own home.
At the time when the monks arrived, he would take their bowls and say, "Please come..."
Whatever he said—whether "Venerable Arahants, please sit down" or "Venerable Arahants, please be seated"—he spoke only in connection with the talk of Arahants.
Among them, the worldlings thought, "He perceives us as Arahants," while those whose taints were destroyed thought, "He knows our state of having destroyed the taints.
Thus, all of them, being filled with remorse, did not go to his house.
Thus, being distressed and dejected, he thought, "Why indeed are the noble ladies not coming? He went to the monastery, paid homage to the Teacher, and reported the matter to him.
The Teacher addressed the monks, asking, "What is this, monks?
When they had reported the matter to him, he said, "But do you, monks, consent to the claim of being Arahants? They replied, "No."
“We accept it, Bhante. “If that is so, monks, this is merely a breach of the people’s confidence; there is no offense in breaching the confidence of those who have faith.
However, that brahmin has excessive affection for the Arahants;
therefore, you too ought to sever the stream of craving and attain Arahantship yourselves. Having said this, he taught the Dhamma and spoke this verse:
“Exerting yourself, cut off the stream; cast away sensual desires, O brahmin!
Having known the destruction of conditioned phenomena, you are one who has done what was to be done, O brahmin.
In this context, “exerting yourself” means that the stream of craving cannot be cut by mere slight effort; therefore—
Exerting great effort associated with wisdom, cut that stream. Cast out and remove both types of sensual desires.
"O Brahmin" is a term of address for those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*). "Having known the destruction of formations" means having known the exhaustion of the five aggregates.
"One who knows the unmade": this being so, [know] Nibbāna, which has not been made by anyone out of gold or other materials.
"By knowing [this], you have become one who is ungrateful.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the first story, concerning the brahmin abounding in faith.
2. The Story of the Many Bhikkhus.
When [the Teacher spoke] these words, "When there are two," the Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, related this Dhamma teaching concerning many bhikkhus.
For one day, about thirty bhikkhus dwelling in various directions arrived, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down.
The Elder Sāriputta, seeing the necessary conditions for their attainment of Arahatship, approached the Teacher and, while still standing, asked this question:
"Venerable Sir, it is said 'two things'; what indeed are those two things?
Then the Teacher, having said to him, "Sāriputta, by 'two things' are meant serenity and insight," spoke this verse:
“When a brahmin has reached the further shore regarding two things,
then all his fetters come to an end for him as he knows. In this context, “when” means at the time when,
by way of direct knowledge, mastery, and so forth, [he has reached the further shore] regarding the two kinds of states established as serenity and insight.
This one whose taints are destroyed is a "one who has gone to the further shore";
