the meaning is that for him who thus knows, all fetters—such as the yokes of sensual desire—which are capable of binding one within the cycle of existence, go to their destruction and end.
At the conclusion of the teaching, all those bhikkhus were established in arahantship.
The second account concerning a number of bhikkhus.
3. The Account of Māra:
"For whom there is no further shore..."—the Teacher related this teaching on the Dhamma while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning Māra.
Thus, on a certain day, having appeared as a certain man, he approached the Teacher and asked:
"Venerable sir, it is said 'the further shore, the further shore'; what indeed is this that is called 'the further shore'? The Teacher, knowing "This is Māra," said:
"Evil One, what have you to do with the further shore? For that is to be attained by those free from passion. Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“He for whom neither the further shore nor the near shore, nor both the further and the near shore, exist;
who is free from longing and detached—that one I call a brahmin.
In this context, the “further shore” refers to the six internal sense bases; the “near shore” refers to the six external sense bases; and the “both the further and the near shore” refers to...

"Neither of those two exists": the meaning is that for one in whom all this—whether grasped as "I" or "mine"—is absent due to the lack of such clinging, and who is thus free from distress through the disappearance of the afflictions (kilesa) and detached from all defilements, him I call a brahmin.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
The Third Discourse on Māra.
4. The Discourse on a Certain Brahmin.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, delivered this teaching on the Dhamma concerning a certain brahmin who was meditating.
He thought to himself: “The Teacher calls his own disciples ‘brahmins,’ and since I too am a brahmin by birth and lineage, would it not be appropriate for him to call me so as well?

He approached the Teacher and asked about this matter. The Teacher replied: “I do not call one a brahmin merely on account of birth and lineage; rather, I call one a brahmin who has attained the supreme goal, which is Arhatship.”
Having said, "I speak thus," he spoke this verse:
"One who sits in meditation, free from passion, having done what was to be done,
being without taints, and having attained the supreme goal— him I call a brahmin."

In this context, "meditating" means meditating with the two kinds of jhāna; sitting alone in the forest, stainless through the dust of sensual desire, having performed the sixteen tasks by means of the four paths, thus having done what was to be done, and being without taints due to the absence of *āsava*s—him who has attained the supreme goal of *arahantship*, I call a brahmin. This is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, that brahmin was established in the fruit of stream-entry; thus, the Dhamma teaching was fruitful for those who were present.
This is the fourth story, the Story of a Certain Brahmin.
5. The Story of the Elder Ānanda.
The Teacher, while residing at the Migāramātupāsāda, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning the Elder Ānanda.
It is said that on the occasion of the Great Pavāraṇā festival, Pasenadi of Kosala, adorned with all his ornaments and taking perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, went to the monastery.
At that moment, the Elder Kāḷudāyī had entered a meditative absorption (jhāna) at the edge of the assembly.
He was seated; however, this was merely his name, for his body was golden in color. At that moment, the moon was rising and the sun was setting.
As the Elder Ānanda gazed upon the radiance of the setting sun and the rising moon, he beheld the radiance of the king’s body, the radiance of the Elder’s body, and [the radiance] of the Tathāgata.
And he gazed upon the radiance of the Teacher’s body. Therein, surpassing all other radiance, the Teacher alone shone forth. The Elder, having paid homage to the Teacher, said:
“Venerable Sir, today as I was observing these radiances, it is yours alone that pleases me;
for your body shines, surpassing all other radiances. Then the Teacher said to him: “Ānanda, the sun...”
“The sun shines by day, the moon at night, and a king shines only when adorned with ornaments;
one whose taints are destroyed shines only within meditative absorption after abandoning the company of crowds. But Buddhas shine with fivefold splendor both by night and by day.
Having said this, he recited this verse:
“By day the sun shines, by night the moon glows;
the armored warrior shines, the meditating brahmin shines;
but the Buddha, throughout all day and night, shines with splendor.”
In this context, "shines by day" means it blazes during the daytime; however, at night, even its path cannot be discerned. As for the moon:
the moon also shines only at night when freed from clouds and the like, not by day.
"Armored" means that the king, adorned with all ornaments variegated with gold and gems, shines while surrounded by a fourfold army, and not in an unrecognizable guise.
"Steadfast. As for "the meditator," one whose taints are destroyed shines forth while meditating after having dispelled the crowd.

As for "by splendor": the Perfectly Enlightened One, having overwhelmed the splendor of immorality with the splendor of virtue, the splendor of the unvirtuous with the splendor of his qualities, the splendor of the unwise with the splendor of his wisdom, the splendor of demerit with the splendor of his merit, and the splendor of the unrighteous with the splendor of the Dhamma—by means of these five kinds of [splendor]...
The meaning is that he shines constantly with splendor.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the fifth story, concerning the Elder Ānanda.
6. The Story of a Certain Brahmin Who Went Forth The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, gave this Dhamma teaching concerning a certain brahmin who had gone forth.
It is said that a certain brahmin, having gone forth in the asceticism of an outsider, thought: "The recluse Gotama says of his own disciples, 'They have gone forth.'"

Thinking, "He says this, and since I too have gone forth, it is fitting for me to speak thus," he approached the Teacher and asked about this matter. The Teacher said, "I do not call one 'gone forth' merely by that;
rather, one is called 'gone forth' because of having gone forth from the impurities of the defilements," and spoke this verse:
“One who has banished evil is a brahmin; one of even conduct is called a recluse (samaṇa);
because he has cast out his own impurity, he is therefore called one who has gone forth (pabbajita).
In this context, “even conduct” means conducting oneself by having stilled all unwholesome states. “Therefore” means because of the state of having banished evil.
A brahmin is called a "recluse" (samaṇa) because he has gone forth by means of conduct after having gathered together unwholesome states;

therefore, the meaning is that whoever goes about driving out and dispelling the stains of passion and so forth within himself is also called "one who has gone forth" (pabbajita) by virtue of that very going-forth.
At the conclusion of the teaching, that brahmin-recluse was established in the fruit of stream-entry, and the Dhamma teaching was fruitful for those who had assembled as well.
The Sixth Story: The Account of a Certain Brahmin Who Went Forth.
7. The Story of the Elder Sāriputta.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning the Elder Sāriputta, beginning with the words: "Not for a brahmin..."
It is said that once, in a certain place, many people were speaking of the Elder’s virtues, saying, "Oh, our noble one is endowed with the power of patience;
even when others revile him or strike him, he does not have even the slightest anger.
Then, a certain Brahmin of wrong view asked, "Who is this who does not get angry? They replied, "Our Elder."
“Will it not be possible to make him angry? “This is impossible, brahmin. “In that case, I shall make him angry.

“If you are able, then make him angry. He thought, “Very well, I shall see what must be done,” and seeing the Elder entering for alms, he went behind him and struck a great blow with his hand on the middle of the Elder’s back. The Elder—
Without even looking to see what it was, he went on his way. A burning heat arose throughout the brahmin’s entire body.
Thinking, "Oh, this noble one is endowed with such virtue," he prostrated at the elder's feet and said, "Forgive me, venerable sir.
When asked, "What is this? he replied, "I struck you for the sake of testing you. [The elder said,] "Let it be; I forgive you."
“Venerable sir, if you will forgive me, please sit right here in my house and accept alms-food,” he said, and took the Elder’s bowl.
The Elder gave him his bowl. The brahmin led the Elder to his house and served him.
People became angry and said, “This man has struck our noble lord, though he was innocent; there shall be no release for him even by means of a staff.”
“Right here we shall kill him! they said, and with clods of earth, sticks, and other weapons in their hands, they stood at the door of the brahmin’s house.
As the Elder was rising and departing, he placed his bowl in the brahmin’s hand.
Seeing him going along with the Elder, the people said, “Venerable sir, take the bowl from him and turn the brahmin back. “What is this? [he asked.]
“Are you lay followers? “We were struck by the brahmin; we shall know what must be done for him.
“But were you struck by him, or was it me? “It was you, venerable sir. “This man struck me and asked for my forgiveness; you may go now,” he said.
Having dismissed the people and sent the brahmin back, the Elder went straight to the monastery. The monks—

They complained, “What is this? Elder Sāriputta has come back after sitting down in the very house of the brahmin who struck him and taking alms from him. From the moment he was struck by that man, whom will he be ashamed of now?
He will wander about beating the rest [of us]. The Teacher came and asked, “Monks, what is it that you are discussing now?”

Having asked, "Sitting together for what discussion? and being told, "For this one indeed," [the Buddha] said, "Monks, there is no such thing as a brahmin striking another brahmin; rather, a householder-brahmin must have struck a renunciant-brahmin.
This anger is something that is eradicated by the path of the Non-returner. Having said this, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke these verses:
“One should not strike a brahmin, nor should a brahmin release [anger] against him.
Woe to the one who strikes a brahmin, and even more woe to the one from whom he releases it.
For a brahmin, there is nothing better than this: that there is restraint of the mind regarding things that are dear.”
"From whatever [source] one who intends harm turns back, from that very source suffering is appeased.
In this context, "one should not strike": knowing "I am a brahmin whose taints are destroyed," one should not strike either another whose taints are destroyed or a brahmin by birth.
"Nor should he release [his blow]" means that even if he has been struck, that brahmin whose taints are destroyed...
The meaning is: "One who stands after having struck [another] should not release enmity; one should not harbor anger toward him. "Shame on the brahmin" means:

I censure the slayer of a brahmin whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*). Furthermore, "shame" on him who, when being struck by another, strikes back and releases enmity upon that person—I censure him even more than the former.

"Nothing is better for him": for one whose taints are destroyed, not reviling in return when reviled, or striking back when struck—this is "nothing better" for that brahmin whose taints are destroyed; it means there is no slight benefit, but rather an exceedingly great benefit.
"When the mind is restrained from what is dear": for to one who is prone to anger, the very arising of anger is dear to the mind.
It is called "anger" (*kodha*). For this anger offends even one's mother and father, and even the Buddha and others.

Therefore, the restraint of the mind against it—the suppression of the consciousness arising through the influence of anger—is not "anything superior" (*na kiñci seyyo*); such is the meaning. "One who harms" (*hiṃsamano*) refers to the angry mind.
As that [anger] is being eradicated from whatever object it arises by means of the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*), [it is said:]...
It turns back. The meaning is that from this and that—namely, from each respective basis—the entire suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*) indeed turns back.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*) and other stages.
This is the seventh story, the account of the Elder Sāriputta.

8. The Story of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, beginning with the words: "He who [guards] by body and by speech...
For when the eight *garudhammas* had been laid down by the Blessed One before the incident had arisen, a man of a decorative nature— [...the text continues...]
Having received it upon her head like a fragrant flower garland, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, together with her retinue, obtained full ordination;
she had no other preceptor or teacher. At a later time, concerning the Elder Nun who had thus obtained ordination, they raised this discussion: "Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī has no teachers or preceptors."

“They are appearing; she has herself taken the saffron robes. Having spoken thus, the bhikkhunīs, being apprehensive, neither performed the Uposatha nor the Pavāraṇā ceremony together with her. They went and reported the matter to the Tathāgata as well.
Having heard their words, the Teacher said: “I have [laid down] the eight Garudhammas for Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī...”

“I have given her away; I alone am her teacher, I alone am her preceptor. One should not harbor remorse regarding those whose taints are destroyed and who are free from bodily misconduct and the like.
Having said this, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
“He whose body, speech, and mind commit no wrong;”
“One who is restrained in three ways, him I call a brahmin.
In this context, “misdeed” (*dukkaṭa*) refers to blameworthy action that has suffering as its outcome and leads to the states of deprivation.
“In three ways” means that the doors [of the senses] are closed by these three factors—the body and so forth—in order to prevent the entry of bodily misconduct and the rest.
"I call him a brahmin"—this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the eighth story, that of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī.

The Blessed One replied: "Sāriputta, it is from me that you have heard the Dhamma. When the Elder had
Whenever he heard, “In such-and-such a direction the Elder resides,” he would raise his hands in reverential salutation and lie down right there with his head in that direction.
The monks reported this matter to the Tathāgata, saying, “Sāriputta holds wrong view; even today he wanders about worshipping the directions.
The Teacher summoned the Elder and asked, “Is it true, Sāriputta?”

Having asked, "Do you wander about worshipping the directions? and being told, "Venerable sir, you alone know whether I have the nature of worshipping the directions or not," [the Buddha said]: "Bhikkhus, Sāriputta does not worship the directions;
rather, having heard the Dhamma from the Elder Assaji and attained the fruit of stream-entry, he is worshipping his own teacher. For..."

“Relying upon a teacher, a bhikkhu understands the Dhamma; therefore, he should indeed be honored with the same care as the sacrificial fire by that brahmin,” having said this, he spoke this verse while teaching the Dhamma:
“From whom one may understand the Dhamma taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One...”
"One should honor him respectfully, as a brahmin honors the sacrificial fire.

In this context, "as a brahmin honors the sacrificial fire" means that just as a brahmin respectfully honors the sacrificial fire through proper attendance and by such acts as joining his palms in reverence,
so too should one honor the teacher from whom one learns the Dhamma proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
The meaning is: "One should revere him with diligence.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the ninth story, concerning the Elder Sāriputta.
10. The Story of the Brahmāṇa with Matted Hair "By matted hair, no," the Teacher spoke this teaching on the Dhamma while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain brahmāṇa with matted hair.
It is said that he thought: "I am well-born on both my mother’s and father’s side, having been reborn into a brahmāṇa family. If the ascetic Gotama..."
Thinking, "The Teacher calls his own disciples 'brāhmaṇas'; would it not be appropriate for me to call myself that as well?

he went into the presence of the Teacher and asked about this matter. Then the Teacher said to him, "Brāhmaṇa, I do not call one a brāhmaṇa merely because of matted hair, nor merely because of birth or lineage;
rather, I call one a brāhmaṇa who has penetrated the Truths," and having said this, he taught the Dhamma.
Declaring this, he spoke this verse:
“One does not become a brahmin by matted locks, nor by lineage, nor by birth;
he in whom there is truth and the Dhamma—he is pure and he is a brahmin.”

In this context, "Truth" (sacca) means that person in whom there exists both the knowledge of truth and the ninefold supramundane state, having penetrated the four truths in sixteen ways; he is pure, he is a brahmin—this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the tenth story, the Story of the Brahmāṇa with Matted Hair.

11. The Story of the Hypocritical Brahmin "What have you [done]?"—this teaching on the Dhamma was spoken by the Teacher while residing in the Gabled Hall concerning a hypocritical brahmin who practiced the "bat-vow.
It is said that he would climb a *kakudha* tree at the gate of the city of Vesālī, grasp a branch of the tree with both feet, and remain there.
Hanging with his head downward, he cried out: "Give me a hundred Kapila cows! Give me gold coins! Give me a female attendant!
If you do not give them, I shall fall from here and die, turning this city into a non-city! Thus he spoke.
At the time when the Tathāgata, surrounded by the community of monks, was entering the city, the monks saw that brahmin; and at the time of [the Buddha's] departure as well...
They saw him hanging there exactly as before. The citizens also thought, "If he continues hanging like this from dawn until he falls and dies, he will turn our city into a non-city.
Fearing the destruction of the city, they agreed, saying, "We shall give him whatever he asks for," and they gave it to him.
Having descended and taken everything, he departed. The monks were in the vicinity of the monastery...
Seeing him go away bellowing like a cow, they recognized him and asked, "Have you obtained what you sought, Brahmin?
Hearing him reply, "Yes, I have obtained it," they went inside the monastery and reported the matter to the Tathāgata.
The Teacher said, "Monks, this deceitful thief is not only a cheat now; in the past, too, he was a deceitful thief. Now..."
"However, while he may deceive foolish people, he was unable to deceive the wise," he said, and at their request, he related a story from the past.
In the past, a certain fraudulent ascetic made his dwelling near a village in Kāsī. A certain family looked after him;
they gave him a portion of whatever hard and soft food was prepared during the day, just as they would for their own children.

Setting aside the portion received in the evening, he gave it to him on the following day. Then one day, having obtained the meat of a monitor lizard in the evening and cooking it thoroughly, they set aside a portion from that and gave it to him on the second day.
Having eaten the meat, the ascetic, bound by craving for its flavor, asked, "What kind of meat is this? and was told, "It is the meat of a monitor lizard."
Having heard this, he went out for alms; having obtained ghee, curd, pungent condiments, and other provisions, he returned to the leaf-hut and set them aside at one side.
Now, not far from the leaf-hut, a bull-elephant lived in a termite mound.
From time to time he would come to pay homage to the ascetic. On that day, however, thinking, "I shall kill him," he hid his trunk.
He sat down not far from that anthill as if he were dozing.
As the king of the gods emerged from the anthill and approached him, he observed his demeanor and thought, "My teacher's disposition does not please me today," and so he turned back right there.
The ascetic, realizing that he had turned away, hurled his staff at him in order to kill him.
The staff slipped away and fell off. King Godhā, having entered the Dhamma-pit (the cave), then emerged with his head and, looking back along the path he had come, said to the ascetic:
"Thinking him to be a recluse, I approached one who was unrestrained."
Thus he struck me with a staff, just like one who is not an ascetic.
"What use have you for matted hair, O witless man? What use have you for your deerskin garment?
Your interior is a thicket, yet you polish only the exterior."
Then the ascetic, wishing to entice him with his own possessions, said this:
"Come, lizard, turn back! Eat rice and boiled grain;
I have oil and salt, and plenty of long pepper for me."
Having heard that, the bull-king said, "The more you speak, the more I feel a desire to flee," and he spoke this verse:
"I shall plunge even deeper into this anthill a hundred fathoms high;
you praise oil and salt, but pepper is harmful to me."

Having spoken thus, he said: "For all this time I have regarded you as a recluse, but now that you have hurled this staff with the intent to strike me, at the very moment it was thrown you ceased to be a recluse.
What is the use of matted locks for such a person of poor wisdom? What is the use of a deerskin complete with its hooves? For your interior is indeed dense with defilement."
“You are merely rubbing the outside,” he said. The Teacher, having brought up this past event, declared, “At that time this one was the fraudulent ascetic, and I myself was the king of the iguanas.
Having thus identified the Jātaka, he spoke this verse, showing how the wise iguana had then rebuked him:
“What use have you for matted hair, O witless one? What use have you for your deerskin garment?
Your interior is a thicket, yet you polish the exterior.

In this context, “What use have you for matted hair? means: “O you of dull wisdom, what is the purpose of these matted locks bound upon you, or even of this deerskin garment worn over your shoulders?”
"What is the purpose of this cloak of antelope skin? [The Buddha replied: "The 'interior'—for your interior is a thicket of defilements such as lust;
you are merely rubbing smooth on the outside, like elephant dung or horse dung.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
The Story of the Deceitful Brahmin is the eleventh.
12. The Story of Kisāgotamī:
The Teacher, while residing on Vulture Peak Mountain, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning Kisāgotamī, beginning with the words, "Wearing rag-robes..."
At that time, it seems, at the conclusion of the first watch of the night, Sakka approached the Teacher together with the assembly of devas;
having paid homage, he sat to one side to listen to a discourse on the Dhamma that inspires recollection.
At that moment, Kisāgotamī, thinking, "I shall see the Teacher," came through the air, but upon seeing Sakka, she turned back. Seeing her turn back after paying homage to him, Sakka...
She asked the Teacher, “Venerable Sir, who is this woman who, upon seeing you as she was coming along, turns back?
The Teacher said, “Maharaja, this is Kisāgotamī by name; she is my daughter and the foremost among the elder nuns who wear rag-robes. Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“A person wearing rag-robes, emaciated, with veins standing out all over;”
"One who meditates alone in the forest—him I call a brahmin.

In this context, "emaciated" refers to those who wear rag-robes (*paṃsukūlika*); for while fulfilling their practice appropriate to themselves, they become thin in flesh and blood, with their limbs covered by veins.
Therefore, he spoke thus. "Alone in the forest" means in a secluded place, by oneself.
"The meaning is: 'I call him a brahmin who meditates in the forest.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the twelfth story, the Story of Kisāgotamī.
13. The Story of a Certain Brahmin The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this teaching on the Dhamma concerning a certain brahmin. It is said that the brahmin thought:
"The ascetic Gotama calls his own disciples 'brahmins,' yet I too am born of a brahmin lineage."
“Is it appropriate for me as well to speak in this way? Having approached the Teacher, he asked about that matter.
Then the Teacher said to him, “Brahmin, I do not call one a brahmin merely by being born from a brahmin womb;
rather, I call him a brahmin who is without possessions and without grasping. Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“I do not call one a brahmin, O brahmin, by birth or by descent from a mother;
he is merely called ‘one who says ‘bho’’. But whoever is without possessions and without grasping—him I call a brahmin.”
In this context, "born from a womb" means born from a womb. "Produced from a mother" means produced in the belly belonging to a mother who is a brahmin woman.
"One who says 'bho'" means one who wanders about addressing others with "bho, bho" during greetings and the like; he is called a "speaker of 'bho'.

Furthermore, if he possesses any "belongings" such as lust and so forth, he is "one who has belongings. But I am one who has no belongings through lust and so forth, and [am free] from the four kinds of clinging.
"I call one who is without grasping a brahmin"—this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, that brahmin was established in the fruit of stream-entry, and the Dhamma teaching was fruitful for those who were present.
This is the thirteenth story, concerning the single brahmin.

14. The Story of the Merchant’s Son Ugga-sena The Teacher, while dwelling at Veḷuvana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning the merchant’s son named Ugga-sena. The background story has already been explained in detail in the commentary on the verse beginning, “Let go of what is before, let go of what is behind.
At that time, [the monks] said, “Venerable Sir, Ugga-sena says, ‘I am not afraid. I think he is answering falsely with something untrue.”
When the monks had spoken thus, [the Blessed One] said, "Monks, those like my sons, who have severed the fetters,
do not tremble at all," and he uttered this verse:
"Having severed all fetters, he who indeed does not tremble..."
"One who has transcended attachment and is disjoined from it—him I call a brahmin.
In this context, "all fetters" refers to the tenfold fetter. "Does not tremble" means he does not fear through craving.
"Him I call"—because he has gone beyond the attachments of lust and so forth, he is "one who has transcended attachment"; and because of the absence of all four bonds (*yoga*), [he is disjoined].
The meaning is: "I call one who is dissociated a brahmin.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the fourteenth story, concerning the merchant's son Ugga Sena.
15. The Story of the Two Brāhmaṇas "Having cut the bond"—this teaching on the Dhamma was related by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning two brāhmaṇas.
It is said that one of them had a bull named Cūḷarohita, and the other had one named Mahārohita. One day, they...
Having quarreled, saying, "My ox is strong; my ox is strong," they thought, "What is the use of our dispute? Let us find out by racing them.
On the bank of the Aciravatī River, they filled a cart with sand and yoked their oxen to it.
At that moment, some monks had also gone there to bathe. The brahmins set the oxen racing. The cart stood motionless; its leather thongs and straps—
However, they were cut. When the monks saw this, they went to the monastery and reported the matter to the Teacher.
The Teacher said, “Monks, these leather straps and thongs are external; anyone at all may cut them.
But it is fitting for a monk to cut the internal leather strap of anger and the leather thong of craving. Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“Having cut through the thong and the strap, the tether together with the rein;
the Buddha who has lifted the crossbar—that one I call a brahmin.
In this context, “thong” refers to anger, which functions as a means of striking; “strap” refers to that which functions as a bond.
Craving. The "fetter" refers to the sixty-two fetters of views together with the sequence of underlying tendencies;
having cut through all of this, he stands with the crossbar of ignorance lifted because that crossbar has been removed.
Because he has awakened to the four truths, he is the Buddha. The meaning is: "I call him a brahmin."
At the conclusion of the teaching, five hundred bhikkhus were established in Arahatship; thus the Dhamma teaching was fruitful for those who had gathered there.
This is the fifteenth story, the Story of the Two Brahmins.
16. The Story of Bhāradvāja the Abusive.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Veḷuvana, delivered this teaching on the Dhamma concerning Bhāradvāja the Abusive.
For the brahmin lady named Dhanañjānī, the sister of that Bhāradvāja, was a stream-enterer (sotāpannā).
Even when she spat, coughed, or sneezed, she would utter this inspired exclamation: "Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One."
She uttered an exclamation. One day, while the brahmin’s meal was being served, she stumbled and, in that very same way, uttered an exclamation with a loud voice.

The brahmin became angry and said, “In this very manner, this outcaste woman stumbles here and there and speaks in praise of that shaveling ascetic! Having said this, he added, “Now, you outcaste woman, go to him—”
“I shall refute the Teacher’s doctrine,” he said. Then she replied to him, “Go, brahmin;
I do not see anyone who could refute the doctrine of that Blessed One. Nevertheless, go and ask that Blessed One a question.
He went into the presence of the Teacher, and without even bowing down, he stood to one side and, asking a question, spoke this verse:
“What must one cut off to sleep in happiness? What must one cut off so as not to grieve?
Of what single thing, O Gotama, do you approve the destruction?
Then, answering his question, the Teacher spoke this verse:
“Having cut off anger, one sleeps happily; having cut off anger, one does not grieve.
O Brahmin, the Noble Ones praise the destruction of anger, which has poison for its root and sweetness for its tip; for having cut it off, one does not grieve.”
Having thus gained confidence in the Teacher, he went forth and attained arahantship.
Then his younger brother, Akkosaka-Bhāradvāja, hearing that "my brother has indeed gone forth," came in anger and reviled the Teacher with improper and harsh words.
He too was restrained by the Teacher through the simile of giving food and other provisions to guests, and he became confident in the Teacher.

Having gone forth, he attained *arahantship*. Furthermore, his two younger brothers, Sundarika-Bhāradvāja and Biliṅgaka-Bhāradvāja, who had been reviling the Teacher, were likewise tamed by the Teacher; they went forth and attained *arahantship*.
Then one day, in the Hall of Truth, they raised this discussion: "Friends, how wonderful indeed are the qualities of the Buddha!"
"When his four brothers were reviling him, the Teacher said nothing and became their very support.
The Teacher came and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you sitting together here now?
When they replied, "For this one," he said, "Monks, because I am endowed with the power of patience, I do not feel ill will toward those who are wicked."
Having said, "I shall indeed be a support for the great multitude," he spoke this verse:
"He who, free from malice, endures abuse, execution, and imprisonment— him,
possessing the army of the power of patience, I call a brahmin."

In this context, "one who is not angry" refers to one who, having become free from a mind of anger, endures verbal abuse through the ten bases of abuse, physical blows with hands and so forth, and binding with fetters and so on; because he is endowed with the power of patience, it is the "power of patience.
Because he is endowed with that very power of patience which acts as an army against repeated arising, it is the "army of power. This is what is meant.
The meaning is: "I call such a person a brahmin.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the sixteenth story, the Account of Bhāradvāja the Abusive.
17. The Story of the Elder Sāriputta The Teacher, while dwelling at Veḷuvana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning the Elder Sāriputta.
It is said that at that time, the Elder was walking for alms with five hundred bhikkhus when he arrived at the door of his mother’s house in the village of Nāḷaka.
He arrived. Then, having had him sit down and serving him food, she reviled him: "Hey, you eater of leftovers!
Having renounced eighty crores of wealth because you could not get leftover rice-gruel, you have come to eat rice-gruel from a ladle that has been rubbed against it in other people's houses.
You have ruined us; now eat! While she was giving food to the monks as well, she continued her abuse.
“Your son has made you his own junior attendant; now, eat,” she said.
The Elder took the alms-food and went back to the monastery. Then the Venerable Rāhula informed the Teacher of his alms-food.
Thereupon the Teacher asked him, “Rāhula, where have you been? “To my grandmother’s village, Bhante. “But what—”
“Was your preceptor addressed by your grandmother? “Venerable sir, my preceptor was reviled by my grandmother.
“What did she say? “This, venerable sir. “And what did your preceptor say to you? “Nothing, venerable sir.
Having heard this, the monks started a discussion in the Hall of Truth: “Friends, how wonderful indeed is the Elder Sāriputta!”
“Guṇa, when his mother was reviling him, not even a trace of anger arose in him.
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, what discussion are you sitting here having now?
When they replied, “This very one,” he said, “Monks, those whose taints are destroyed are indeed free from anger,” and spoke this verse:
“One who is free from anger, possessed of vows, virtuous, and without arrogance;
tamed, with this his final body—that one I call a brahmin.

In this context, “possessed of vows” means endowed with the ascetic practices (dhutanga); “virtuous” means possessing the fourfold purity of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla) through the absence of the swelling of craving (taṇhāussada).
"One who is free from pride, tamed by the subduing of the six sense-faculties, and who stands at the pinnacle with his final body—that person, O Brahmin, I call a brahmin. This is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
The seventeenth story: The Elder Sāriputta. 18.
The Story of the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā.
While residing at Jetavana, the Teacher gave this Dhamma instruction: "As water does not cling to a lotus leaf... concerning the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā.
He spoke with reference to this. The story has already been explained in detail in the commentary on the verse beginning, “The fool fancies himself as honey. For it is said there:
“On another occasion, a great crowd of people raised a discussion in the Hall of Truth:
‘I think even those whose taints are destroyed still relish sensual pleasure and indulge in sense-desires; why should they not? For these are not *koḷāpa* trees, nor are they anthills.’”
“All their bodies are made of flesh; therefore, they too relish sensual pleasure.
The Teacher approached and asked, “Monks, what discussion are you gathered here for now?

When they replied, “For this very reason,” he said, “Monks, those whose taints are destroyed do not relish sensual pleasure, nor do they indulge in sensual desire. For just as a drop of water fallen upon a lotus leaf...”
“It does not adhere, nor does it remain; rather, having turned away, it surely falls off.

And just as a mustard seed does not adhere to the point of an awl, nor does it remain, but surely falls off after turning away, even so, both kinds of sensual desire do not adhere to or remain in the mind of one whose taints are destroyed.
Having thus established the connection, he taught the Dhamma by reciting this verse:
“Like water on a lotus leaf, like a mustard seed on the point of an awl—he who is not smeared by sensual pleasures, him I call a brahmin.

In this context, “he who is not smeared” means: in this very way, he who is not internally defiled by either of the two kinds of sensual pleasure, and who does not settle upon that pleasure—him I call a brahmin; such is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the eighteenth story, the Story of the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā.
19. The Story of a Certain Brahmin.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, spoke this teaching on the Dhamma concerning a certain brahmin.
It seems that one of his slaves, when the training rules had not yet been laid down, fled, went forth into homelessness, and attained arahantship.
When the brahmin looked for him and did not see him, he one day saw him between the gates as he was entering with the Teacher for alms.
He firmly grasped his robe. The Teacher turned back and asked, "What is this, brahmin?
"It is my slave, Master Gotama. "This one has laid down his burden, brahmin. When he was told "he has laid down his burden," the brahmin perceived that he must be an arahant.
Therefore, when the brahmin replied again, "So it is, Master Gotama," the Teacher said, "Yes, brahmin."
Having said, "One who has laid down the burden," he spoke this verse:
"He who understands here and now the destruction of his own suffering,
who has laid down the burden and is detached— that one I call a brahmin."
In this context, "of suffering" means of the suffering of the aggregates (*khandha*).

"One who has laid down the burden" means one who has set aside the burden of the aggregates and is dissociated from the four bonds or from all defilements; that person, I call a brahmin—this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, that brahmin was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), and the Dhamma teaching was fruitful for those who were present as well.
The Nineteenth Story: The Brahmin.
The Twentieth Story: The Bhikkhunī Khemā.
While residing at Vulture Peak Mountain, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma instruction concerning the bhikkhunī named Khemā, beginning with the words, "Deep in wisdom."

One day, immediately after the first watch of the night, Sakka, the king of the gods, arrived together with his retinue and sat down to listen to a discourse on the qualities that inspire affection from the Teacher. At that moment, the bhikkhunī Khemā, thinking, "I shall see the Teacher," arrived;
but seeing Sakka, she paid homage to the Teacher while still standing in the air and then turned back. Sakka—
Seeing her, he asked, "Venerable sir, who is this woman who, as she approaches, remains suspended in mid-air, pays homage to the Teacher, and then turns back?
The Teacher replied, "Great king, this is my daughter named Khemā, possessed of great wisdom and skilled in discerning what is the path and what is not the path," and he spoke this verse:
“One who possesses profound wisdom, who is intelligent, skilled in what is the path and what is not the path,
and who has attained the supreme goal— him I call a brahmin. In this context,
“profound wisdom” means being endowed with the wisdom that functions regarding the profound aggregates and so forth, [specifically] the wisdom of the nourishment of the Dhamma (*dhammāhāra-paññā*).

The meaning is: I call him a brahmin who is wise, endowed with such expertise regarding the path and what is not the path—knowing, "This is the path to an evil destination; this is the path to a happy destination; this is the path to Nibbāna;
this is not the path"—and who has attained the supreme goal known as Arahatship.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the twentieth story, the account of the Bhikkhunī Khemā.
21. The Story of the Elder Tissa, the Cave-Dweller.
"Unassociated"—this teaching on the Dhamma was spoken by the Teacher while residing at Jetavana concerning the Elder Tissa the Cave-Dweller.
It is said that after receiving a meditation subject from the Teacher, he entered the forest and, while looking for a suitable dwelling place, came upon a rock cave.
At that very moment, his mind attained one-pointedness.
Thus he thought, "While dwelling here, I shall be able to accomplish the duties of one who has gone forth.
The deity residing in the cave also thought, "A virtuous bhikkhu has arrived; it is difficult to dwell in the same place as him.
However, he will stay here for only a single night before departing," and so she took her children and went away.
On the following day at dawn, the Elder entered the village for alms. Then, a certain female lay devotee, upon seeing him, felt maternal affection for him;
she had him sit down in her house, fed him, and requested that he dwell there under her protection for the three-month rains retreat.
He, thinking, "I can achieve the escape from existence by relying on her," consented and took up residence in that very cave.
He arrived. Seeing him approaching, the deity thought, "Surely he must have been invited by someone; he will go either tomorrow or the day after.
When half a month had thus passed, [the deity thought], "I suspect he will stay right here for the duration of the rains; however, because of his virtue and observance of precepts..."
"It is difficult to live in one place together with children, yet it is not possible to tell him 'Go forth.
Could there perhaps be some lapse in his virtue? Thus reflecting, she surveyed him with her divine eye;
seeing no lapse in his virtue from the time of his full ordination in the ordination hall onwards, she thought, "His virtue is pure. Whatever he has done, it must be for the sake of infamy."
Thinking, “I shall cause him to arise,” she fixed her mind upon the body of the eldest son of a female lay follower (upāsikā) in that supporter’s family and twisted his neck.
His eyes popped out and saliva dripped from his mouth. When the lay follower saw this, she cried out, “What is this?
Then a deity, in an invisible form, said to her: “He has been seized by me; even with an offering of food...”
“I have no need for it myself; however, you should ask the elder who visits your family for some *laṭṭhimadhuka*, and having prepared oil with it, give it to him as a nasal treatment (*natthukamma*).
In this way, I shall release him. “Let him perish or let him die;
I will not be able to ask the noble one for the *laṭṭhimadhuka*. [She thought: “If I am to ask for the *laṭṭhimadhuka*...”
“You cannot; tell him to put powdered asafoetida into his nose. “I cannot even say that.
“Then, taking the water for washing his feet, pour it over his head.

The laywoman thought, “This can be done,” and having seated the elder who had arrived at that time, she gave him rice gruel and solid food. While he was sitting during the midday meal, she [poured the water] on his feet.
Having washed his hands and taken water, he asked, "Venerable sir, shall we pour this water on the boy's head?
When [the Elder] said, "In that case, pour it," they did so. At that very moment, the deity released him and went to stand at the entrance of the cave.
The Elder also, having risen from his seat at the conclusion of his meal, was reciting the thirty-two aspects of the body (dvattiṃsākāra) without interrupting his meditation subject.
He set out. Then, when he reached the entrance of the cave, that deity said, "Great physician, do not enter here.
Standing right there, he asked, "Who are you? "I am the deity dwelling here," she replied.
The Elder, wondering, "Is there perhaps a place where I have performed medical work? began looking from the ordination hall onwards, [and saw] himself...
Without seeing any mark or blemish on his skin, he said, "I do not see any place where I have performed medical treatment;
why do you speak thus? [The other replied,] "Do you not see it? "Yes, I do not see it. "Then I shall point it out to you. "Yes, please point it out.
"Let aside for now what was done long ago; even today, look at the water used for washing the feet of the attendant’s son who was seized by a non-human spirit."
“Was it poured on your head, or was it not? “Yes, it was poured. “Do you not see this? “Is it with reference to this that you speak?
“Yes, it is with reference to this that I speak. The Elder thought: “Ah, how well-directed indeed is my mind!
My conduct is truly worthy of the Dispensation. Even the deities have placed a mark upon my fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*).”
Or having seen nothing black, he saw only the amount of water used for washing feet that had been poured onto the child’s head;
then, with respect to his virtue, a powerful rapture arose within him. Suppressing that [rapture], and without even removing his sandals, he attained Arahantship right there.
[The deity said: "Do not dwell here in this forest grove defiling a pure ascetic like me; you yourself must depart!"
Admonishing the deity, he uttered this inspired utterance:
“Pure indeed is my dwelling; I am a stainless ascetic.
Do not defile one who is pure; depart from this forest.”
Having stayed right there for those three months, he went into the presence of the Teacher after completing the rains retreat.
When the bhikkhus asked him, "Friend, have you brought your duties as a renunciant to their fulfillment?
he related to the bhikkhus the entire account of what had occurred from the time he entered the rains retreat in that cave. He said, "Friends, though you were being addressed thus by the deity..."
When it was said, "He became angry," he replied, "He did not become angry. The monks reported this to the Tathāgata:
"Venerable Sir, this monk explains things otherwise; even when being addressed thus by a deity, he says, 'He did not become angry.
Having heard their words, the Teacher said, "Monks, my son does not become angry at all. Whether by householders or by those who have gone forth..."
"Indeed, there is no such thing as 'association'; this one is unassociated, having few desires and being content. Having said this, while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
"One who is unassociated with both householders and those without homes, who wanders without a fixed abode and has few desires—him I call a brahmin."
In this context, "unassociated" (*asaṃsaṭṭha*) means unassociated by way of the absence of association through seeing, hearing, conversing, using [things], or physical contact.
"With both" (*ubhaya*) means unassociated with both householders and those who have gone forth. "Not wandering from home" (*anokasārī*) means one who wanders without a fixed abode;
such a person, O Brahmin, I call a brahmin—this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the twenty-first story, the account of the Elder Tissa who dwelt in a mountain cave.
22. The Story of a Certain Bhikkhu.
"Having laid aside the rod"—this teaching on the Dhamma was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain bhikkhu.
It is said that after receiving a meditation subject from the Teacher and striving in the forest, he attained Arahatship.
Thinking, "I shall report my attained qualities to the Teacher," he departed from there. Then, in a certain village, a woman [was with] her husband...
After they had quarreled, when he had gone outside, she set out on the road thinking, "I will go to my family home.
Seeing him on the way, she thought, "I will go along following this elder," and followed closely behind him. However, the elder did not see her.
Then her husband returned home; not seeing her, he thought, "She must have gone to her family village," and pursued her.
Seeing her, she thought, "It is not possible for her to enter this forest alone; whom does she rely upon as she goes?
Looking about, she saw the Elder and thought, "He must have set out taking her with him. Thinking thus, she threatened the Elder.
Then that woman said to him, "This venerable one neither sees me nor speaks to me; do not [let him...]"
He said, "I have not said anything. The man, his anger aroused, replied, "How could you possibly tell me that you saw yourself going along?
I shall do with him exactly what is fitting for you! With this, he struck the Elder with resentment toward the woman, took him away, and returned.
The Elder’s entire body became covered in swellings. Then, when he had gone to the monastery—
While the monks were massaging his body, they saw the swellings and asked, "What is this? He explained the matter to them.
Then the monks said to him, "Friend, when that man was striking you in such a way, what did you say?
Did anger arise in you? When he replied, "Friends, no anger arose in me," they went into the presence of the Teacher.

Having reported that matter, they said, "Venerable sir, when this bhikkhu was told, 'Anger arises in you,' he spoke falsely, saying, 'Friend, anger does not arise in me,' and thus gave an evasive answer.
When the Teacher heard their words, he said, "Bhikkhus, those whose taints are destroyed have laid down the rod; even when others strike them, they do not give way to anger."
Having said, "They indeed do so," he spoke this verse:
"Having laid aside the rod toward all beings, both the timid and the steadfast,
he who neither kills nor causes others to kill— him I call a brahmin."
In this context, "having laid aside" means having set down or cast away.

"Among the trembling and the firm" refers to those who are trembling due to the trembling of craving (*taṇhā*), and those who are firm due to the absence of craving. "He who does not kill" means he who, by being free from aversion toward all beings, has laid aside the rod;
he neither kills anyone himself nor causes others to kill—him I call a brahmin; such is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the twenty-second story, concerning a certain bhikkhu. 23.
The Story of the Novices.
“Not Contradictory”: This teaching on the Dhamma was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning four novices.

It is said that a certain brahmin woman, having prepared a meal for four monks, said to her husband, “Go to the monastery, have four elderly brahmins assigned to us, and bring them back. He went to the monastery and [said], “Four...”

“Designate them for me as Brahmins and give [them] to us,” he said. To him there came four novice monks (sāmaṇera) who were seven years old, wise, skilled in cooking, and free from the taints (khīṇāsava).
When the Brahmin’s wife, having prepared costly seats, stood waiting and saw the novices, she became enraged;
like salt thrown onto a fire, she began to sizzle and seethe, saying, “You [have brought these] to the monastery...”
Having said, "You went away and returned having taken four young boys with you, even though your own grandsons were not enough," he did not allow them to sit on those seats;
instead, having spread out low stools, he said, "Sit on these.
Then he said, "Go, brahmin, look for the elders and bring them here. The brahmin went to the monastery and [found] the Elder Sāriputta.
Seeing him, she said, "Come, let us go to our home," and brought him there.
When the Elder arrived and saw the novices, he asked, "Have these brahmins received alms? When they replied, "They have not," he realized that food had been prepared for only four people.
He said, "Bring me my bowl," and taking his bowl, he departed. The brahmin’s wife also asked, "What..."
Having asked, "Was it said by this [person]?", he took his own bowl and went away, saying, "It is appropriate to obtain food from these seated brahmins;
bring me my bowl. [The other thought: "He will not wish to eat here; having gone quickly, look elsewhere and bring [food].
The brahmin went, saw the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, spoke to him in the same manner, and brought [the food].
He too, seeing the novice, spoke in the same manner and, taking the bowl, departed.
Then the brahmin woman said to him, "These do not wish to eat; go to the Brahmanavādaka and bring back an elderly brahmin.
From early morning onwards, the novices sat there, oppressed by hunger as they received nothing at all. Then, for them—
By the power of his virtue, Sakka’s seat began to glow hot.
Reflecting on this, and perceiving that those [brahmins] had been sitting since early morning and were exhausted, he thought, “It is fitting for me to go there.
Assuming the form of an aged, decrepit, elderly brahmin, he sat upon the foremost seat of the brahmins among that assembly of brahmin disputants. When the brahmin saw him, he said, “Now...”
“Then my brahmin wife will be delighted,” he thought, and taking him with him, saying, “Come, let us go home,” he went to his house.
As soon as the brahmin woman saw him, her heart was filled with joy; she spread out the rugs for two seats but laid them down on only one, and said, “Noble sir, please sit here.
Having entered the house, Sakka [greeted] the four novices with the fivefold prostration.
Having paid homage, he sat down cross-legged on the ground at the edge of their seats. Then, seeing him, the brahmin’s wife said to the brahmin:
“Oh, you have brought back a brahmin! You have even come taking this madman with you;
he wanders about paying homage to his own grandsons. What is the use of him? Drive him out! He [looked] upon his shoulders, his hands, and his armpits...
Though being dragged away, he did not even wish to stand up.

Then the brahmin woman said, "Come, brahmin, you take him by one hand and I will take him by the other," and seizing both his hands, they pushed him out from the door of the house while striking him on the back. Sakka, however, remained seated right where he was.
He turned his hand around. Having turned back and seeing him still seated there, they let out cries of fear and released him.
At that moment, Sakka made known his identity as Sakka. Then they gave them food.
All five men took the food; one pierced through the circle of rafters, and another [pierced] the front part of the roof.
One went out by the western side, one sank into the earth, and Sakka also emerged through another spot;
thus they departed in five ways. From that time on, it is said, that house became known as the "House with Five Openings.
When the novices returned to the monastery, the monks asked them, "Friends, what was it like? [The novices replied,] "Do not ask us!"
From the moment we were seen, the brahmin woman, overcome by anger,
refused to let us sit on the prepared seats and said, "Quickly, quickly, bring the old brahmin! Our preceptor,
having arrived and seen us, thought, "It is right that these seated brahmins receive [alms]," and after having a bowl brought for them, he departed.
When it was said, “Bring another elderly brahmin,” the brahmin brought the Elder Mahāmoggallāna.
He too, upon seeing us, spoke in the same manner and departed. Then the brahmin’s wife sent the brahmin, saying, “These do not wish to eat;
go and bring one elderly brahmin from the school of the brahmin teachers. He went there.
“They brought Sakka, who had arrived in the guise of a brahmin; when he arrived, they gave him our food.
When they spoke thus, did you not get angry with them? “We were not angry. When the bhikkhus heard this, they reported it to the Teacher:
“Venerable Sir, these people are speaking falsely, saying ‘we were not angry,’ while explaining something else. The Teacher—
“Monks, those whose taints are destroyed do not indeed harbor enmity even toward those who are hostile,” he said, and then recited this verse: “One who is unhostile among the hostile,
who is extinguished among those who wield the rod,
who is without grasping among those who grasp— him I call a brahmin.”
In this context, "unopposed" means that even toward worldly people who are opposed by way of resentment, one is unopposed due to the absence of resentment.
It is "one who has laid down the rod" (nikkhittadaṇḍa) because, even though sticks or swords are not in hand, one refrains from striking others;
thus it refers to those among people who have laid down the rod. It is "free from grasping" (sādānesu) because of the absence of the grasping of the five aggregates as "I" or "mine."
The meaning is: "Because of the absence of grasping at that [clinging], one who is thus without appropriation—him, O Brahmin, I call a brahmin.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the twenty-third story, concerning the novices.
24. The Story of the Elder Mahāpanthaka The Teacher, while residing at Veḷuvana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning the Elder Mahāpanthaka.
That venerable one was unable to master a single stanza in four months, even though Cūḷapanthaka had been instructing him. [The Teacher said: "You..."
“You are incapable in the Teaching; you have fallen away even from the enjoyments of a householder. What is the use of your staying here? Depart from here!
Having thus driven him out of the monastery, he bolted the door. The monks raised a discussion, saying, “Friends, such was the deed done by the Elder Mahāpanthaka!
It seems that even those whose taints are destroyed can still give rise to anger. The Teacher came and asked, “What is this you are discussing?”
Having asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you sitting together here now?

and being told, "For this very one," he said, "Monks, there are no defilements such as lust in those whose taints are destroyed; this was done by my son out of regard for the welfare and regard for the Dhamma.
Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“He from whom lust and hatred, pride and hypocrisy have fallen away like mustard seeds from the point of an awl— him I call a brahmin. In this context,

“from the point of an awl” (āraggā) means that these defilements, such as lust and so forth, as well as hypocrisy— which is characterized by the smearing over of the virtues of others— have fallen away from him.
"Like a mustard seed cast down: just as a mustard seed does not remain steady on the point of an awl, so too [the mind] does not remain steady in the heart;
him I call a brahmin"—this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
The Story of the Elder Mahāpanthaka, the twenty-fourth.
25. The Story of the Elder Pilindavaccha.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Veḷuvana, delivered this Dhamma instruction concerning the Elder Pilindavaccha, beginning with the words: "Not harsh."
Thus, it is said that the Venerable One, speaking such words as, “Come, outcaste! Go away, outcaste! addressed both householders and those gone forth using only the term “outcaste.
Then one day, a number of bhikkhus reported this to the Teacher:
“Venerable sir, the Venerable Pilindavaccha addresses the bhikkhus with the term ‘outcaste. The Teacher had him summoned and asked, “Is it true?”
Having asked, "Is it true, Pilindavaccha, that you address the bhikkhus with the term 'outcaste'?
and being answered, "It is so, venerable sir," the Blessed One reflected upon that venerable one’s previous lives and said:
"Do not, O bhikkhus, find fault with the bhikkhu Vaccha; indeed, bhikkhus, Vaccha does not address the bhikkhus with the term 'outcaste' out of malice."
“Bhikkhus, for five hundred consecutive births, the bhikkhu Vaccha was reborn in every case in a brahmin family.
For a long time, he was accustomed to being addressed as ‘outcaste. Yet, for one whose taints are destroyed, there is no harsh or rough speech that strikes at the vital points of others.
It is merely by way of habituation that my son speaks thus.”
Having said, "He speaks thus," he uttered this verse:
"Let one utter speech that is not harsh, which is intelligible and true;
by which one does not revile anyone—that, I say, is a brahmin."
In this context, "not harsh" means not rough. "Informative" means informative of the meaning. "Truthful" means having a real meaning.
"One who does not provoke anger" means that by whatever speech one would not cause another to become angry;
one whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava) speaks only such speech as this. Therefore, the meaning is: "I call him a brahmin."
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the twenty-fifth story, the Story of the Elder Pilindavaccha.
26. The Story of a Certain Elder.
While residing at Jetavana, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma instruction concerning a certain elder, beginning with the words, "He who [sees] 'long'...
It is said that in Sāvatthī there was a certain Brahmin of wrong views who, fearing the odor of his own body, removed his upper robe, placed it aside, and sat facing the door of his house.
Then, a certain one whose taints were destroyed (an arahant), having finished his meal—

While returning from his monastery, he saw that garment; looking here and there and seeing no one else, he determined it was ownerless (*anissāmika*), resolved upon it as refuse-rag cloth (*paṃsukūla*), and took it.
Then the brahmin, seeing him, approached while reviling him and said, "Shaveling ascetic! You are taking my garment! "It is yours, brahmin. "Yes, ascetic."
“Without seeing anyone, I took this with the perception that it was a rag-robe;
take it,” he said, and having given it to him, he went to the monastery and reported the matter to the monks.
Then, hearing his words, the monks joked with him, saying, “Friend, is the robe long, short, thick, or thin? “Friend, let it be long...”
“Whether it be short or long, coarse or fine, I have no attachment to it; I shall take it with the perception of a rag-robe.
When the monks heard this, they reported it to the Tathāgata: “Venerable Sir, this monk speaks what is untrue and explains it as something else.
The Teacher said: “Monks, he speaks the truth. Those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) [regard] the property of others...”
Having said, "He does not take," he spoke this verse:
"He who here in the world does not take what is not given— whether long or short, fine or coarse,
pleasant or unpleasant— it is him that I call a brahmin."

The meaning of this is as follows: whether it be long or short among garments and ornaments, or minute or large among gems, pearls, and the like, or beautiful or ugly according to their high or low value—whosoever in this world does not take what is possessed by another, him, O Brahmin, I call a brahmin. This is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the twenty-sixth story, the Story of a Certain Elder.
27. The Story of the Elder Sāriputta.
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning the Elder Sāriputta.
It is said that the Elder, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred bhikkhus, went to a certain monastery in the countryside and entered the rains retreat.
When people saw the Elder, they promised him a great deal of requisites for the rainy season. After the Elder had performed the *pavāraṇā* ceremony, regarding all those rainy-season requisites...
While still on his way to the presence of the Teacher, he said to the bhikkhus:
“When people bring the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season) offerings for the young bhikkhus and novices, you should take them and send them [to me], or else set them aside and send word of them.
Having spoken thus, he went into the presence of the Teacher. The bhikkhus then raised the question: “Even today...”
"I suspect that the Elder Sāriputta still possesses craving;

for he has come after telling the monks, when people gave him the *vassāvāsika* (rain-retreat offerings), 'You should send the *vassāvāsika* to your own *saddhivihārika*s, or else send word to them by means of a message.
The Teacher, having arrived, asked, "Monks, about what conversation are you sitting here gathered now?"
Having asked, "Is it indeed she? and being told so, he said, "Monks, my son has no craving;
rather, he spoke thus so that there might be no loss for people through their merit, nor for young novices through their righteous gains.
Having said this, he uttered this verse:
“He in whom no desires exist, in this world or in the world beyond;
who is free from longing and detached—he, I call a brahmin.

In this context, “desires” (āsā) means craving (taṇhā). “Free from longing” (nirāsāsaṃ) means devoid of craving. “Detached” (visaṃyuttaṃ) means detached from all defilements; “him I call a brahmin”—this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the twenty-seventh story, the account of the Elder Sāriputta.
28. The account of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna.
"Of whomsoever [the mind is] detached..."—this teaching on the Dhamma was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the Elder Mahāmoggallāna.
The background story is the same as before. On this occasion, however, the Teacher, having described the Elder Moggallāna’s state of being free from craving, spoke this verse:
“He for whom attachments do not exist, who through final knowledge is free from doubt, and who has reached the immersion in the Deathless—him I call a brahmin.

In this context, “attachments” (*ālayā*) refers to craving (*taṇhā*). “Through final knowledge is free from doubt” means having understood the eight bases as they truly are, one is free from the doubt consisting of those eight bases.
"Free from doubt regarding doubt. "Having reached the depth of the Deathless" means having plunged into and attained the Deathless, which is Nibbāna;
that person, O Brahmin, I call a brahmin—this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
The twenty-eighth story: The Elder Mahāmoggallāna.
The twenty-ninth story: The Elder Revata.

The Teacher, while residing at Pubbārāma, delivered this Dhamma teaching, "He who here [accumulates] merit... with reference to the Elder Revata. The background story has already been explained in detail in the commentary on the verse beginning, "Whether in the village or in the forest. For it was said there:
Again, one day, the monks initiated a conversation: “Oh, what a gain for the novice! Oh, what merit!
For by him alone were five hundred gabled halls constructed for five hundred bhikkhus.
The Teacher came and asked, “Monks, with what conversation are you seated here now? When they replied, “With this very one,” he said:
“Monks, my son has neither merit nor evil; both have been abandoned by him. Having said this, he spoke this verse:
“He who here has transcended both merit and evil, both attachments— Sorrowless, stainless, and pure: him I call a brahmin.”
In this context, "both" means having abandoned both merits and evils. "Attachment" refers to the attachment consisting of passion and so forth. "Transcended" means he has gone beyond it.
Because of the absence of sorrow rooted in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), he is "sorrowless"; because of the absence of the dust of passion and the like within, he is "dustless";
and because of being free from defilements, he is "pure. This is the meaning of "I call him a brahmin."
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the twenty-ninth story, the Story of the Elder Revata.
30. The Story of the Elder Candābha.
The Teacher, while dwelling in Jeta’s Grove, delivered this teaching on the Dhamma concerning the Elder Candābha.

This is the sequential account: In the past, a merchant living in Bārāṇasī, thinking, "I will go to the borderlands and bring back sandalwood," took many goods such as clothing and ornaments and traveled to the borderlands with five hundred carts.
Having taken up residence at the village gate, he asked the cowherd boys in the forest, "Is there anyone in this village who works on the mountain slopes?
"Yes, there is," they replied. "What is his name? "He is called so-and-so.
"And what are the names of his wife and children? "They are such-and-such and such-and-such. "Where, then, is his house located?"

“[He said,] ‘At such-and-such a place. Having sat down in a comfortable carriage provided by them, he went to the door of her house, alighted from the carriage, entered the house, and called out to that woman by name, ‘Such-and-such!
She, thinking, ‘This must be some kinsman of ours,’ came quickly and prepared a seat for him. He sat there, gave his name, and said, ‘My…”
The companion asked, "Where are they? "They have gone into the forest, Master," he replied. "Where is my son named so-and-so? Where is my daughter named so-and-so?
he asked, calling out the names of them all. Then, giving [the boy] the names of each, he said, "You should give these clothes and ornaments to them;
and when my companion returns from the forest, you should give him these clothes and ornaments," and with that, he gave them to him.

Having paid him great honor, when her husband returned, she said to him, "Husband, from the time he arrived, he has called out the names of everyone and given this and that. He did for him what was appropriate to be done.
Then, as he sat on his bed in the evening, she asked him: "Friend, while wandering at the foot of the mountain, what did you obtain in abundance?"
“Have you ever seen it before? “I have not seen anything else, but I have seen many trees with red branches. “Many trees? “Yes, many.

“In that case, show them to us. Having gone with him, they cut down red sandalwood trees, filled five hundred carts, and while returning, he said to him: “Friend, at such-and-such a place in Bārāṇasī...”
"My house is called Nāma; you should come to my presence from time to time. I have no need for any other gift;
you should bring only red sandalwood trees. He replied, "Very well," and coming to him from time to time, he brought only red sandalwood, and he gave him much wealth in return.
Then, at a later time, after the Great Sage Kassapa had attained final Nibbāna and his golden stupa was established,
that man took a great quantity of sandalwood and went to Bārāṇasī. Thereupon, his merchant friend ground much sandalwood,
filled a bowl with it, and said, "Come, friend, let us go to the site where the cetiya is being built while the meal is cooking."
Thinking, "Let us go and return," he took him there and performed an offering of sandalwood.
His frontier-dwelling friend also drew a moon-circle with sandalwood upon the belly of the cetiya. This was his entire prior karma.
Having passed away from there and been reborn in the world of the gods, and having spent an entire interval between Buddhas there, in this current arising of a Buddha—
He was reborn in the city of Rājagaha into a family of great brahmin householders. From the circle of his navel, a radiance arose resembling the orb of the moon;
therefore, they gave him the name Candābha (Moon-Light). It is said that this was the result of his having fashioned the moon’s orb at the Cetiya.
The brahmins thought, “We can take this man and devour the world. [They placed] him in a vehicle...
Having seated him, they wandered about saying, "Whoever touches this body with their hand shall obtain such a perfection of sovereignty.
Only those who gave a hundred or a thousand [coins] were permitted to touch his body with their hands.
As they wandered thus, they arrived at Sāvatthī, at the city and the monastery.

And they took up residence along the way. In Sāvatthī as well, about five koṭis of noble disciples, having given alms before the meal, would go after the meal with perfumes, garlands, clothing, medicines, and other offerings in their hands to hear the Dhamma.
When the brahmins saw them, they asked, "Where are you going? They replied, "To the presence of the Teacher to hear the Dhamma."
"Come, what will you achieve by going there? There is no power equal to the power of our brahmin Candābha.
For those who touch his body receive such-and-such [benefits]; come and see!
"What power does your brahmin Candābha have? Our Teacher alone is of great power."
Being unable to convince one another, they took him and went to the monastery, thinking, "We shall know the power of either the moonlight or our Teacher.
As soon as he approached the Teacher's presence, the Teacher caused the moonlight to vanish. He—
In the presence of the Teacher, he was like a crow in a basket of glowing coals. Then they led him away to one side, and his radiance returned to normal.
When they brought him back again into the presence of the Teacher, the radiance vanished just as before.
Having gone there three times and seeing his radiance vanish each time, Candābha thought: "This man knows a spell for making radiance disappear."
"I think he knows," he thought. He asked the Teacher, "Do you know the incantation for making light disappear?
"Yes, I know it. "Then give it to me. "It cannot be given to one who has not gone forth.
He said to the brahmins, "Once this incantation is mastered, I shall become the foremost in all Jambudīpa; you stay right here."
“Having gone forth, I shall master the mantra in just a few days. He requested the Teacher for the going-forth and received full ordination.
Then [the Teacher] explained the thirty-two aspects (dvattiṃsākāra) to him. He asked, “What is this? [The Teacher replied,] “This is the preparatory exercise for the mantra;
it is fitting that you recite it. The brahmins also came from time to time and said, “Have you mastered the mantra?”
They asked him. He replied, "I will not accept [the invitation] yet. Within a few days, having attained Arahatship, when the brahmins returned and questioned him, he said, "Go now;
I have now become one whose nature is such that I shall not return. The monks reported this to the Tathāgata:
"Venerable Sir, this man speaks falsely and gives an evasive answer. The Teacher said, "This one, whose taints are exhausted, is now..."
“Monks, my son Candābha speaks only what is true,” he said, and then recited this verse:
“One who is like the moon—stainless, pure, serene, and undisturbed;
one for whom delight and becoming are utterly exhausted—that person I call a brahmin.”
In this context, "stainless" (vimala) means free from stains such as clouds; "pure" (suddha) means free from defilements; "serene" (vippasanna) means having a clear mind;

"untroubled" (anāvila) means free from the turbidity of defilements. "One whose craving for existence and delight has been exhausted" (nandībhavaparikkhīṇa) means one whose thirst for the three realms of existence has been completely destroyed;
that person, I call a brahmin—this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the thirtieth story, the Story of the Elder Candābha.
31. The Story of the Elder Sīvali.
This Dhamma teaching was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in the Kuṇḍadhāna Forest near Kuṇḍakoliya, concerning the Elder Sīvali.

For on one occasion, a daughter of the Koliyans named Suppavāsā, having carried a fetus for seven years and being afflicted with a difficult labor for seven days, was tormented by sharp, piercing, and bitter pains. She thought: "Truly, that Blessed One is a Perfectly Enlightened One!"

“Whoever teaches the Dhamma for the abandoning of such suffering as this; truly well-practiced is that Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples, who has practiced for the abandoning of such suffering as this;
truly most blissful is that Nibbāna, wherein such suffering as this is not found”—with these three thoughts, he [contemplates] that suffering.
Having consented, she sent her husband to the presence of the Teacher;
when he had reported her words and offered salutations to the Teacher, the Teacher said, "May Suppavāsā the Koliyan daughter be happy; may she be healthy and give birth to a healthy son.
At that very moment, being happy and healthy, she gave birth to a healthy son, and [she invited] the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
Having invited them, she gave a great almsgiving for seven days.
Her son, from the day of his birth, took a water-strainer and filtered water for the Saṅgha. Later, he went forth into homelessness, ordained, and attained Arahatship.
Then one day, the bhikkhus raised a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: "Behold, friends, such a person..."
“Indeed, even a monk endowed with the strong support (upanissaya) for Arahantship experienced such suffering in the mother’s womb for so long;
how much more so for others? Oh, how much suffering has he truly crossed over!
When the Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, about what discussion are you gathered here now? and they replied, “About this very matter,” [he spoke as follows].
“Yes, monks, my son has been freed from so much suffering and now dwells having realized Nibbāna,” he said,
and then spoke this verse:
“He who has crossed over this mire, this difficult path, this cycle of existence, and this delusion;”
“Crossed over, gone to the further shore, meditative, unshaken, free from doubt, without clinging, extinguished—he, I call a brahmin.
The meaning of this is: that bhikkhu who has crossed over this path of passion, this difficult ford of defilements, and this cycle of saṃsāra—of these four...
The meaning is: one who has transcended the delusion that fails to penetrate the Noble Truths; having crossed over the four floods, he has reached the further shore;
he is a meditator through the two kinds of jhāna; he is unshaken due to the absence of craving; he is free from doubt due to the absence of indecision;
and having not grasped due to the absence of clinging, he is extinguished by the extinction of defilements—him, O Brahmin, I call a brahmin.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the thirty-first story, the Story of the Elder Sīvali.
32. The Story of the Elder Sundarasamudda.
The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, delivered this Dhamma teaching concerning the Elder Sundarasamudda.
It is said that in Sāvatthī, a certain noble youth named Sundarasamudda was born into a great family possessing a wealth of forty crores.
One day, after his meal, he saw a great multitude of people with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in their hands, going for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma.
Seeing him going to the Jeta Grove, he asked, "Where are you going?
