When told, "To the presence of the Teacher in order to hear the Dhamma," he said, "I too will go," and having gone with him, sat down at the edge of the assembly.
The Teacher, knowing his disposition, delivered a graduated discourse. He [thought], "It is not possible for one living in a household..."
Thinking, "I shall lead the holy life (brahmacariya) as one who has polished away all stains," he gained the courage for the going-forth (pabbajjā) by means of the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma.

When the assembly had departed, he requested the going-forth from the Teacher; hearing that "the Tathāgatas do not grant the going-forth to one who has not been permitted by his mother and father," he went home and, like the noble youth Raṭṭhapāla and others, with great effort—

Having obtained permission from his parents, he went forth in the presence of the Teacher. Upon receiving full ordination, thinking, "What use have I for staying here?", he departed from there and went to Rājagaha, where he spent his time wandering for alms.
Then one day, on a festival day in Sāvatthī, his parents, with great splendor and majesty—
Seeing his young companions playing, they lamented, "This has become difficult for our son to obtain.
At that moment, a courtesan went to that family and saw his mother sitting there weeping;
she asked, "Mother, for what reason do you weep? "I weep because I am remembering my son," she replied. "But where is he, mother? she asked.
“He has gone forth among the bhikkhus. “Is it not permissible to make him leave the order? “It is permissible, but he does not wish to;
having departed from here, he has gone to Rājagaha. “If I were to make him leave the order, what would you do for me?
“We would make him the mistress of the household for this family of yours. “In that case, give me my travel expenses. [He gave] the travel expenses.
Having taken him with a large retinue and gone to Rājagaha, he observed the street where the Elder would walk for alms;
having secured a dwelling there, he prepared a sumptuous meal early in the morning. When the Elder entered for alms, he gave him the food.
After a few days had passed, [the householder said], "Venerable sir, please sit right here and perform your meal duties."
“Please do so,” he said, and took the bowl. He gave him the bowl.
Then, having served him with excellent food, he said, “Venerable sir, it is convenient to wander for alms right here.
Having had him sit in the courtyard for several days and fed him, he won over the children with cakes and said, “Come, you all...”
She said, "When the Elder arrives, even though I am keeping you away, you will come here and raise a cloud of dust.
On the following day, at the time of the Elder's meal, although she tried to keep them away, they raised a cloud of dust.
On the next day, she said, "Venerable sir, even though the children are being kept away, they do not listen to my words and raise a cloud of dust here; please sit inside the house."
Having seated them inside, she fed them for several days.
Then, gathering the children together, she said, "Even though you are being forbidden by me, you must make a great noise when it is time for the Elder to eat. They did exactly as she had said.
On the following day, she said, "Venerable sir, there is an exceedingly great noise in this place; even though the children are being forbidden by me, they do not listen to my words."
"Take them; sit right here in the upper palace," she said.
When the Elder consented, she ascended the palace with him in front, closing the doors as they went.
Although the Elder was one who practiced the alms-round by visiting only the highest houses, he ascended the seven-storied palace at her word, bound by his craving for flavors.
Having seated the elder, she said: "My dear Puṇṇamukha, there are indeed forty ways in which a woman surpasses a man:

she yawns, she bends, she swallows, she blushes, she scratches nail against nail, she treads foot against foot, she scratches the ground with a stick, she makes a child leap up and down, and she plays."
She plays, she kisses and causes [him] to kiss, she eats and causes [him] to eat, she gives and asks for [gifts], she imitates his actions,
she speaks loudly, she speaks softly, she speaks indistinctly, she speaks clearly, she laughs, looks on,
and moves her hips at dancing, singing, instrumental music, weeping, dalliance, and adornment; she displays her private parts.
“Fidgeting, exposing the thigh, covering the thigh, showing the breast, showing the waistband, showing the navel, rolling the eyes,
raising the eyebrows, tracing the lips with the tongue, licking the tongue, loosening the garment,
fastening the garment, loosening the hair on the head, and binding the hair on the head”— this is what is called "womanly affectation" as it has been handed down.
Displaying feminine charms, she stood before him and spoke this verse:
“Your feet are stained with red lac, O courtesan wearing sandals;
you too are young, and I am young for you.”
“Both of us shall go forth, we who are old and dependent on staffs.
At that moment, a great sense of spiritual urgency arose in the Elder as he thought, “Alas! What a grave deed I have done without due reflection!
At that very instant, the Teacher, while seated in Jeta’s Grove at a distance of forty-five yojanas, perceived this occurrence and smiled.
He manifested a smile. Then the Venerable Ānanda asked him: "Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason for manifesting a smile?

"Ānanda, in the city of Rājagaha, on the terrace of a seven-storied palace, a battle is taking place between the monk Sundarasamudda and a courtesan. "Venerable sir, who will be victorious, and who will be defeated?"

"Who will be the victor? The Teacher, declaring the Elder’s victory by saying, "Ānanda, Sundarasamudda shall be the victor and the courtesan shall be defeated," while remaining seated right there, radiated light and spoke this verse: "The monk has abandoned both sensual pleasures, being free from longing for them."
“Whosoever, having abandoned sensual pleasures here, goes forth as a homeless wanderer—him, whose craving for sense-pleasures and existence is utterly exhausted, I call a brahmin.

The meaning of this is: that person who, having left behind both types of sensual pleasures in this world, goes forth as a homeless wanderer—I call him a brahmin, he being one whose craving for sense-pleasures is exhausted and whose craving for existence is exhausted. This is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, that elder attained Arahatship.

By means of his psychic power, he rose up into the air, passed through the circular dome of the assembly hall, and having approached while still extolling the Teacher’s body, he paid homage to the Teacher.
In the Hall of Truth, they too raised this discussion: "Friends, Elder Sundarasamudda has lost his mind on account of a flavor cognizable by the tongue."
"But the Teacher has become his refuge. When the Teacher heard that conversation, he said, "Monks, it is not only now;
in the past as well, I became the refuge for this one whose mind was bound by craving for flavors.
Being requested by them, in order to clarify that matter, he brought up the past:
“There is nothing more harmful than flavors,
nor than dwellings or social attachments;
[it is like] a wind-animal dwelling in the deep forest.”
“While dwelling among sensual pleasures, Sañjaya was restrained.

Having related this Vātamiga Jātaka in detail within the Ekakanipāta, [the Buddha] identified the birth story, saying: “At that time, Sundarasamudda was the deer Vātamiga; however, I myself was the king’s chief minister who, after speaking this verse, caused him to be released.
This is the thirty-second story, the account of the Elder Sundarasamudda.
33. The Story of the Elder Jaṭila While residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, the Teacher delivered this Dhamma instruction concerning the Elder Jaṭila. The sequential account of this is as follows:
It is said that in the past, in Bārāṇasī, there were two brothers who were householders and possessed a large sugar-cane field.

...had them made. Then one day, the younger brother went to the sugarcane field and, thinking, "I will give one to my elder brother and one will be for me," he took two stalks of sugarcane, binding them at the place where they had been cut so that the juice would not flow out.
At that time, it seems, there was no need to crush the sugarcane with a machine; [it was simply taken] from the top or the bottom.
When it was cut and lifted, the sap flowed out of its own accord, just like water from a water-vessel.

Now, while he was on his way back from the field carrying sugarcanes, the Paccekabuddha emerged from meditative attainment at Gandhamādana and, reflecting, "Whom shall I favor today? perceived him within the net of his own knowledge.

Seeing that he had entered [the path] and knowing his capacity to provide support, [the Paccekabuddha] took his bowl and robes, arrived by means of psychic power (*iddhi*), and stood before him. Upon seeing him, the man’s heart was filled with faith;
he spread his upper garment on a higher spot of ground, said, "Venerable sir, please sit here," and having seated the Paccekabuddha, [offered] the bowl...
"Please offer it. Having loosened the binding at the stalk of the sugarcane, he placed it over the bowl; the juice flowed down and filled the bowl.
When the Pratyekabuddha had drunk that juice, [the man thought]: "The noble one has indeed drunk my juice well.
If my elder brother causes the price to be brought, I will pay the price. If he causes the bowl to be brought..."
Thinking, "I shall give him an alms-bowl," he said, "Venerable sir, please hold out your bowl to me," and for a second time, having crushed a stalk of sugarcane, he gave the juice.
It is said that he did not have even so much as a thought of deception, thinking, "My brother will go to another sugarcane field, bring back more sugarcane, and eat it.
However, the Paccekabuddha [accepted] the first sugarcane juice...
Because he was so delighted, wishing to share that sugarcane juice with others, he took it and sat down.
Perceiving his intention, [the Elder] prostrated himself on his five limbs and said:
"Venerable sir, by the result of this most excellent gift given by me, may I experience prosperity among gods and humans, and in the end, may I attain the very same Dhamma you have attained."

He made this aspiration: "May I attain [this]. The Paccekabuddha said to him, "So be it," and after offering a blessing with two verses beginning, "What you have desired and aspired for," he resolved that the man should see [himself] there.
Then, traveling through the air to Mount Gandhamādana, he gave that food to the five hundred Paccekabuddhas.
Having seen that miracle, he went to his brother and, when asked, "Where have you been?", replied, "I went to look at the sugarcane field.
When his brother said, "What was the point of going to such a sugarcane field?
Should one not rather have returned having taken one or two stalks of sugarcane?", he answered, "Yes, brother, I took two..."

“I took sugarcanes,” he said, “and upon seeing a certain Paccekabuddha, I gave him the juice from my sugarcane, saying, ‘I will give you either the root or the leaf. I have given the juice from my sugarcane to you as well;
shall you take its root, or rather its leaf? “But what was done by the Paccekabuddha? he asked.
“Having drunk the juice from my sugarcane stalk, I took the juice from your sugarcane stalks and went through the air to Gandhamādana,
where I gave it to five hundred paccekabuddhas. As he was saying this,
his body was suffused with uninterrupted rapture, and he thought, “May I attain the realization of the Dhamma even as that paccekabuddha did.”
Thus the younger brother made a wish for three attainments, while the elder brother made a wish for arahantship in a single phrase; this was their past karma.
Having lived out their full lifespan and passed away from there, they were reborn in the world of the gods and spent an entire interval between Buddhas there.
While they were still dwelling in the world of the devas, Vipassī, the Perfectly Enlightened One, appeared in the world.
Passing away from that heavenly realm, they took rebirth in a certain noble family in Bandhumatī; the elder was born as the eldest, and the younger as the youngest.
They gave the name Sena to the elder and Aparājita to the younger.

While they were living there after establishing their households once they had reached maturity, the sound of the Dhamma was proclaimed in the city of Bandhumatī by a Dhamma-preacher, saying: "The Jewel of the Buddha has appeared in the world;

the Jewel of the Dhamma and the Jewel of the Saṅgha have appeared. Give gifts, perform meritorious deeds! Today is the eighth day, today is the fourteenth day, today is the fifteenth day; observe the Uposatha and listen to the Dhamma!"
Having heard the proclamation, the householder Sena saw the great multitude giving alms before the meal and then proceeding after the meal to hear the Dhamma;

he asked them, "Where are you going? When they replied, "To the presence of the Teacher to hear the Dhamma," he said, "I shall go as well," and having gone along with them, sat down at the edge of the assembly.
The Teacher, having understood his intention, gave him a gradual discourse.
Having heard the Teacher’s Dhamma, he became eager for the going-forth and requested the Teacher for ordination. Then the Teacher asked him, "But do you have relatives who must be informed?
"I do, Bhante," he replied. "In that case, go and inform them and then return. He went to his younger brother.
Having gone there, he said, "Whatever property there is in this family, let all of it be yours.
"But what about you, Master? "I shall go forth in the presence of the Teacher. "Master, why do you say this? When my mother died, I obtained you as if I had obtained a mother;
when my father died, I obtained you as if I had obtained a father. This family possesses great wealth; even while remaining at home—"
"Virtuous deeds can indeed be performed; do not act in this way. "I have heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher.
It is impossible for one remaining in the midst of a household life to fulfill it. I shall certainly go forth; you, however, may return.
Having thus made his younger brother turn back, he went forth in the presence of the Teacher. Not long after receiving full ordination, he attained Arahantship.
The younger brother also, thinking, “I shall perform an act of honor for my brother who has gone forth,” gave alms for seven days to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha.
Then, having paid homage to his brother, he said: “Venerable sir, you have accomplished your own deliverance from existence;
however, I am bound by the five strands of sensual pleasure and, though I have gone forth, I am unable to renounce the world. In my house—”
“While you remain here, describe a great meritorious deed worthy of this place.
Then the Elder said to him, “Excellent, excellent, wise man! Build a fragrant chamber for the Teacher.

Having accepted with the words, “Very well,” he had various kinds of timber brought and had it carved for the sake of the pillars and other parts; one [chamber] was inlaid with gold, and one with silver.
Having had one pavilion inlaid with jewels and all the others inlaid with the seven precious gems, he had the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭī) constructed;
he then had it roofed with tiles likewise inlaid with the seven precious gems.
At the very time the fragrant chamber was being built, his nephew named Aparājita, who shared the same name as himself, approached him and said, "I too shall build one."
“Uncles, give me my share as well,” he said. “We will not give it to you, dear one; we shall make it something exclusive to others,” they replied.

Although he begged much, failing to obtain his share, he thought, “It is fitting to have an elephant stable in front of the Perfumed Chamber,” and thus he had an elephant stable made of the seven precious gems constructed.
In this current dispensation of the Buddha, he was reborn as Meṇḍaka the merchant.
Furthermore, in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī), there were three great windows made of the seven precious gems.
Facing them, below, the householder Aparājita had three lotus ponds constructed and paved with plaster;
having filled them with water scented with the four kinds of perfumes, he planted five-colored flowers for the time when the Tathāgata was seated within.
It was for the purpose of scattering the body with whirlwinds of dust raised by the force of the wind.
The bowl-shaped pinnacle of the Gandhakuṭī’s stupa was made of red gold, its spires were made of coral, and the tiles of the roof below were made of jewels.
Thus, it stood shining like a dancing peacock. Then, having ground whatever among the seven precious gems was suitable to be ground—
Taking all the rest, he filled the surrounding walkway by encircling the Fragrant Chamber with a wall reaching as high as his knees.
Having thus completed the Fragrant Chamber, the householder Aparājita approached the Elder Bhātika and said:
"Venerable sir, the Fragrant Chamber is finished; I hope for its use, for it is said that through its use, great [merit]..."
“...there is merit. He approached the Teacher and said, “Venerable Sir, it is said that this householder has had a fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭi) built for you, yet now he expects its use.
The Teacher rose from his seat, went toward the fragrant chamber, and after circumambulating it, stood at the gateway while gazing upon the heap of jewels that surrounded the fragrant chamber.
Then the householder said to him, "Enter, venerable sir. The Teacher remained right there and, on the third occasion, looked toward his brother, the elder.
Understanding this by the mere look, he said to his younger brother, "Come, dear one;
say to the Teacher, 'Protection shall be mine alone; you may dwell here as you please. He [the younger brother]—his...

Having heard these words, he paid homage to the Teacher with the fivefold prostration and said, "Venerable Sir, may you dwell here without concern, just as people enter beneath a tree and depart without looking back, or as those who have crossed a river abandon their raft without regard for it.
But for what purpose did the Teacher remain? It is said that his intention was this:
He thought: “Many people come to the presence of the Buddhas both before and after the meal;
when they depart taking jewels with them, we are unable to stop them.
If this householder sees so many jewels strewn about the courtyard and yet does not stop his own attendants from taking them, he will harbor resentment toward me and fall into the states of misery.”
For this reason, he remained standing there. But when the man said, "Venerable sir, let there be protection for me alone; you may stay," he entered.
The householder, having stationed guards all around, said to his men:
"Sirs, you must stop those who go away taking [the goods] in their laps, in baskets, or in bags; but do not stop those who go taking them in their hands."
In the city as well, he had it proclaimed: "I have strewn seven kinds of jewels in the courtyard of the Perfumed Chamber;
let the poor people, having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, take them as they go, filling both hands;
let even those who are well-off take some. For this was his thought: "Those with faith, desiring to hear the Dhamma, will certainly go; but even those without faith..."
"But having gone out of greed for wealth, they will hear the Dhamma and be liberated from suffering.
Therefore, he had it announced in this way solely for the sake of gathering the people. The great multitude took the jewels according to the very method prescribed by him.
Once the scattered jewels were exhausted, he had them scattered three times more, up to a depth of knee-high. At the foot of the Teacher, however, there was a quantity the size of a heap of tin.
He set down a priceless jewel-treasure. It was because he thought:
"Those who gaze upon the radiance of the jewel together with the golden-hued radiance from the Teacher’s body will never reach satiety. Therefore, he acted in this way.
And the great multitude gazed upon it insatiably.
Then one day, a certain brahmin of wrong views, thinking, "It is said that a precious jewel has been placed at the feet of the Teacher;
I shall take it," went to the monastery and entered through the midst of the great crowd who had come to pay homage to the Teacher.
As soon as the householder observed his manner of entering, he perceived that he intended to seize the jewel.

“Oh, what if I were not to take it? he thought. That man, as if bowing to the Teacher, extended his hand at the Teacher’s feet, took the jewel, tucked it into his waistband, and departed. The householder was unable to win his confidence.
At the conclusion of the Dhamma talk, he approached the Teacher and said: “Venerable Sir, three times I [offered] the Perfumed Chamber...”
“Having surrounded it, the seven treasures were strewn over an area as wide as the distance between my knees.
As they were taking them, I felt no resentment at all; rather, my mind became increasingly serene.
But today, thinking, ‘Oh, may this brahmin not take the jewel,’ when he had taken the jewel and departed, I was unable to compose my mind. Thus spoke the Teacher.
Having heard his words, [the Teacher] gave him this method: "Lay follower, are you not able to make your own property unseizable by others?
Standing upon the method given by the Teacher, he paid homage to the Teacher and said:
"From today onward, even if hundreds of kings or thieves should overcome me and seize even a mere thread from my clothing—"

He made this aspiration: "May they not be capable [of harming]; may my property not be consumed even by fire; may it not be swept away even by water. The Teacher granted him his blessing, saying, "So be it.

While he was constructing the Perfumed Chamber, he gave a great almsgiving for nine months right within the monastery to six million eight hundred thousand monks; at the conclusion of that gift-giving—
He gave a set of three robes to everyone. For the most junior member of the Saṅgha, the robes and garments were worth a thousand pieces of gold.
Having performed meritorious deeds in this way for as long as he lived, when he passed away from there, he was reborn in the world of the gods.
After wandering through the realms of gods and humans for so long a time, during the arising of this Buddha, he took conception in a certain merchant family in Rājagaha.
Having taken [the embryo], he dwelt in his mother’s womb for nine months and more than half a month. On the day of his birth, however, all weapons in the entire city burst into flames;
even all the ornaments worn upon the bodies of everyone emitted a radiance as if they were ablaze, and the city became a single mass of light.
The merchant also went to attend upon the king early in the morning. Then—
The king asked him: “Today all the weapons have burst into flame and the city has become a single mass of light;
do you know the cause of this? “I know it, Your Majesty. “What is it, merchant? “A slave of yours was born in my house;
it has come to pass through the power of his merit alone. “Could it be that he is a thief? “There is no such thing.”
“Your Majesty, this is a meritorious being who has made a formal resolve. “In that case, it is right to nourish him properly;
let this be his milk-money,” he said, and established a daily allowance of one thousand [pieces].
Then, on the day of his naming, because he became like a single lamp for the entire city, they gave him the name Jotika.
Then, when he had reached maturity and the ground was being cleared for the purpose of building a house, the palace of Sakka manifested a state of heat.
Sakka, reflecting on what this could be, realized, "They are taking the site for Jotika’s house.
Knowing that "he will not live in a house built by these men; it is fitting that I go there myself," he [assumed] the guise of a carpenter.
Having gone there, he asked, "What are you doing? "We are taking possession of Jotika’s house site," they replied. "Go away;
he will not live in a house built by you," he said, and he looked upon a patch of ground measuring sixteen karīsas.
At that very moment, it became as level as a *kasiṇa* disk. Again, [he thought], "In this place, having split open the earth..."
Thinking, "Let a seven-storied palace arise," he looked, and at that very moment such a palace arose.
Again, thinking, "Let seven walls made of the seven precious gems arise surrounding this," he looked, and such walls arose.
Then, thinking, "Let wish-fulfilling trees (kapparukkha) arise at their boundaries," he looked...
He looked, and such wish-fulfilling trees (*kapparukkha*) arose. Thinking, "Let four treasure-pots arise at the four corners of the palace," he looked, and it was exactly so.

Among the treasure-pots, one was a *yojana* in size, one was three-quarters of a *yojana*, one was half a *yojana*, and one was the measure of a *gāvuta*. [Such were] the treasure-pots produced at the birth of the Bodhisatta.
However, they were only the size of a single opening; below, they reached as far as the limits of the earth.
The measurement of the openings of the treasure-jars produced for Jotika has not been stated; all of them arose perfectly full, like palm fruits with their tops cut off.
At the four corners of the palace, there were four golden sugarcanes, each the size of the trunk of a young palm tree.
They were born. Their bowls were made of jewels and their stalks were made of gold;
these, it is said, were produced for the purpose of displaying their past karma.
At the seven gate-towers, seven *yakkhas* took up their guard. At the first gate-tower was Yamakoḷī.
The yakkha named Nāma took up the guard together with his own retinue of one thousand yakkhas;
in the second [group], the one named Uppala together with two thousand of his own retinue yakkhas; in the third, the one named Vajira together with three thousand;
in the fourth, the one named Vajirabāhu together with four thousand; and in the fifth, the one named Kasakanda.
Together with five thousand [guards], Kaṭattha by name took up the guard together with six thousand;
together with seven thousand, Disāmukha by name took up the guard in the seventh watch. Thus, there was a strict guard both inside and outside the palace.
"It is said that for Jotika, a seven-storied palace made of the seven precious gems arose."
Having heard that "seven walls, seven gate-towers, and four treasure-pots have arisen," King Bimbisāra sent for the merchant’s parasol. He was the merchant named Jotika.
A woman who had performed meritorious deeds together with him was reborn in Uttarakuru. Then, from there, a deity...
Having brought her, they had her sit in the inner chamber. As she was coming, she took a measure of rice and three fire-stones.
For as long as she lived, her food consisted of that very same measure of rice.
It is said that even if they wished to fill a hundred wagons with rice, that measure of rice would remain exactly as a measure. At the time of cooking the meal—
Having placed rice in a cooking pot, they set it upon those stones; the stones ignite at that very moment and extinguish as soon as the food is cooked.
By that very sign, they know the state of the food being cooked. The same method applies when cooking soups and other dishes.
In this way, their food is cooked by means of the fire-stones (*jotipāsāṇa*). And they dwell by the light of jewels, not by fire.
Nor did they even know the light of a lamp. It became renowned throughout the whole of Jambudīpa that such was the prosperity of Jotika.
Great crowds of people, having harnessed their carriages and other vehicles, came to see him.
The merchant Jotika had rice cooked from the grains of Uttarakuru and gave it as alms to all who arrived. [He said: "Let them take garments from the wish-fulfilling trees."
He commanded, "Let them take the ornaments. He further commanded, "Having caused the mouth of the treasure-pot one *gāvuta* deep to be opened, let them take enough wealth for their sustenance.
As those dwelling throughout the whole of Jambudīpa took the wealth and departed, not even a finger's breadth was lacking from the treasure-pot.
This, it is said, was the outflow of the jewels strewn upon the sand in the courtyard surrounding the Gandhakuṭī.

While the great multitude was thus departing, taking with them as much clothing, ornaments, and wealth as they desired, King Bimbisāra, though wishing to see his palace, could find no opportunity as the crowd continued to arrive.
Later on, when the people had thinned out because they were taking whatever they wished and had departed, the king said to Jotika’s father: “Regarding your son...”
“We wish to see the palace. He replied, “Very well, Your Majesty,” and having gone, he told his son:
“Dear son, the king wishes to see your palace. “Very well, father; let him come,” he said. The king went there with a great retinue.
At the first gate-tower, a slave girl who was sweeping and throwing away the refuse [caught] the king’s hand.
The king, feeling ashamed because he perceived her as the merchant’s wife, did not place his hand on her arm.
In the same way, at the other gate-towers, thinking they were the merchant’s wives, he did not place his hand on their arms either.
Jotika came forward, received the king, paid homage, and followed behind him, saying, “Please go ahead.”
"O King," he said. To the king, it appeared as if the jeweled earth were a precipice five hundred fathoms deep.
Thinking, "A pit has been dug here for me to fall into," he did not dare to set foot down.
Jotika appeared before him and said, "This is no pit, O King; follow behind me. At the moment the king stepped upon it, the ground—
Having entered, he wandered about, looking down at the palace from the lower floor.
At that time, Prince Ajātasattu, while wandering about holding his father’s finger, thought: "Oh, how blind and foolish my father is!
While householders dwell in palaces made of the seven precious gems, this king, having become a monarch, dwells in a house made of wood. Now I am the king..."
“Having sacrificed [this], I will not allow him to dwell in this palace.
Even as the king was ascending the upper stories, the time for the morning meal arrived. He addressed the merchant, saying, “Great merchant, let us eat our morning meal right here.
“I know, Your Majesty; the food for Your Majesty has been prepared,” he replied. Then, with sixteen...
Having bathed with jars of scented water, he sat upon the very seat-couch prepared for the merchant in the jeweled pavilion where the seat had been arranged.
Then, after they had given him water for washing his hands, they increased the quantity of the spoiled porridge in a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand [pieces] and placed it before him.
The king, perceiving it as "food," began to eat. The merchant said, "This is not..."
“Your Majesty, this food is spoiled gruel,” they said, and having added more food from another golden bowl, they placed it back into the first bowl.
It was said that it is pleasant to eat when one has risen from one’s meal. As the king ate the sweet food, he did not know moderation.
Then the merchant, having paid homage to him and raising his hands in *añjali*, said: “Enough, Your Majesty!”
"Let this much suffice; it is not possible to digest more than this," he said.
Then the king said to him, "Householder, why do you speak thus, making your own food seem so heavy? "Your Majesty, there is no such thing.
For this very food and these very condiments would suffice for your entire army. However, I am afraid of infamy."
"What is the reason? "If Your Majesty were to feel even a slight physical fatigue, I would fear the words, 'Yesterday the King ate at the merchant's house;
surely something must have been done by the merchant,' O Lord. "In that case, take the food and bring the water.
At the conclusion of the King’s meal, the entire royal retinue partook of that very same food.
While the king was seated engaged in pleasant conversation, he addressed the merchant, saying, "Is the merchant’s wife not in this house?
"Yes, sire," he replied. "Where is she? "She is sitting in the bedchamber, sire;
she does not know that you have arrived. For although the king had come with his retinue early in the morning, she did not know of his arrival.
He knew it as if he were seeing it. Then the merchant, thinking, "The king wishes to see my wife," went to her side and said, "The king has arrived;
why is it not right for you to see the king? While she was still lying down, she asked, "Who is this, master?
Who is this so-called 'king'? When he replied, "The king is our lord," she expressed her displeasure and said, "Misdeeds..."

"Alas for our meritorious deeds, we who even have a master! Having performed meritorious deeds with lack of faith, we have attained prosperity and been reborn in another's position of authority. Surely it must be that we gave gifts without having faith;
this is the fruit thereof. Having said this, she asked, "What shall I do now, Master?"
Taking a palm-leaf fan, she came and fanned the king.
As she was fanning the king with the palm-leaf fan, the fragrant breeze from the king’s turban struck her eyes, and streams of tears flowed from them.
Seeing this, the king said to the merchant: "Great merchant, women are indeed of little wisdom; [thinking], 'The king is my husband's...'"
"She seems to weep out of fear that she might lose her wealth; comfort her by saying, 'I have no need for your wealth.
"She is not weeping, Your Majesty. "Then what is it? "Tears have flowed from her because of the fragrance of your turban.
For she has lived and sat here using only the light of jewels, without ever seeing the light of lamps or the light of fires."
"And does he lie down? But the King will remain sitting by the light of the jewel, will he not? "Yes, O King.
"In that case, O King, sit from this day forward by the light of the jewel," she said, and gave him a priceless great mani-gem the size of a *tipusa* fruit.
The King, looking about his house, remarked, "Great indeed is the prosperity of the lamp-bearer! and departed. This is the story.
Such was the origin of Jotika.
Now, the origin of Jaṭila should be understood: for in Bārāṇasī there was a merchant’s daughter who was beautiful;
when she reached the age of fifteen or sixteen, [her father] gave her a maidservant for protection and [placed her] in a seven-storied [palace].
They had her reside in the bedchamber on the upper floor of the palace.
One day, as she was looking out through an open window, a certain *vidyādhara* traveling through the air saw her;
moved by affection, he entered through the window and engaged in intimacy with her. Through living with him, she soon became pregnant.
She obtained [the child]. Then, seeing her, the slave girl said, "Sister, what is this? When she was told by the other, "Let it be;
do not tell anyone," she remained silent out of fear. After ten months had passed, she gave birth to a son.
Having had a new vessel brought, she laid the infant down inside it, covered the vessel, and placed garlands of flowers upon it.
Setting this aside, he commanded a female slave, saying, "Lift this up with your head and cast it into the Ganges; and when asked, 'What is this?
you should say, 'It is an offering for my mistress. She did exactly as she was told.
Meanwhile, down by the river, two women who were bathing saw that vessel being carried along by the water, and one of them—
"This vessel is mine," she said. Another said, "Whatever is inside this belongs to me.
When the vessel was brought, she took it, placed it on dry land, opened it, and seeing the boy, one said, "Because it was said 'the vessel is mine,' the boy must belong to me alone.
The other said, "Because it was said 'whatever is inside the vessel belongs to me,' the boy is mine."
He said: "While they were disputing, they went to the place of legal adjudication and reported the matter;
when the ministers were unable to decide it, they went into the presence of the king. Having heard their words, the king said, 'You take the child;
you take the vessel. Now, she by whom the child was obtained was the female attendant of the Elder Mahākaccāna."
Therefore, she raised the boy with the thought, "I will have him go forth into homelessness in the presence of the Elder.
On the day he was born, because the impurities of the womb had not been washed away, his hair remained matted;
thus they gave him the name Jaṭila (the Matted-hair One). When he was old enough to walk about on foot, the Elder entered that house for alms. The female lay devotee...
Having seated the elder, she gave him food. When the elder saw the boy, he asked, "What is this, laywoman?
Have you obtained a son? "Yes, venerable sir," she replied. "I have supported this boy with the thought, 'I shall cause him to go forth into homelessness under you. Please let him go forth.
The elder said, "Very well," and taking him, as he was going along, [considered]: "Does he possess the prosperity of a householder..."
Looking about with the thought, "To experience the fruit of his meritorious deeds," he considered: "This being possesses great merit and will enjoy great prosperity;
however, he is still young, and his wisdom has not yet reached maturity. Having reflected thus, he took him and went to the house of a lay devotee in Takkasilā.
Having paid homage to the elder, he stood there and, seeing that boy, asked, "Venerable sir, have you found a boy?
"Yes, lay follower; he will go forth. Since he is still young, let him remain in your care for the time being.
"Very well, venerable sir," he replied, and placing the boy in the position of a son, he looked after him. Now, in his house, household goods had accumulated for twelve years.
As he was traveling from village to village, he took all that merchandise to the market, seated the boy in the shop,
and having explained the price of each item, he said, "When you have received this and that amount of wealth,
you should give it," and then he departed. On that very day, the deity who protects the city [appeared] even with as little as a pinch of black pepper and cumin.
They set it up right in front of his shop for those who were in need. Within twelve years, he sold off his abundant stock in a single day.
When the householder returned and saw nothing left in the shop, he said, "My dear son, you have ruined all your merchandise.
"I have not ruined it; I sold everything exactly according to the method you instructed. This was the cost of that item, and this..."

"Of such-and-such a person. The householder, having gained confidence, thought, "This man is priceless; he is capable of living anywhere," and so he gave him his own daughter who had reached marriageable age.
Having ordered men, saying, "Build a house for him," and once the house was finished, he said, "Go now, you may dwell in your own home."

Then, at the moment he was entering his house, as soon as he stepped upon the threshold with one foot, the ground in the rear part of the house split open and a golden mountain eighty cubits high rose up.

Hearing that a golden mountain had indeed risen by splitting the ground in Jaṭila Kumāra’s house, the king immediately sent him the parasol of a guild-president. Thus, he became the Guild-President Jaṭila.
...was his name. He had three sons. When they had reached maturity, he conceived the desire for the going-forth (pabbajjā) and thought:
"If there were a merchant family with wealth equal to ours, they would allow me to go forth; if not, they would not.
Is there perhaps in Jambudīpa a family with wealth equal to ours? For the sake of this inquiry, [he took] a golden...
Having had a brick made of gold, a golden goad-staff, and a pair of sandals fashioned, he placed them in the hands of men and dispatched them, saying:
"Go; taking these with you, wander about the surface of Jambudīpa as if merely looking around here and there.
Once you have ascertained whether or not there exists a merchant family with wealth equal to our own, return."
While wandering on their journey, they arrived at the city of Bhaddiya. Then the merchant Meṇḍaka saw them and asked, "Sirs, what are you doing as you wander about?

When they replied, "We are wandering about looking for someone," he said, "They have no need to wander about looking for anything by taking these [goods] with them; they are wandering about surveying the kingdom."
Having understood this, he said, “Sirs, enter our innermost house and look about.

There, in a space measuring eight karīsas, they saw the aforementioned golden rams—each as large as an elephant, a horse, or a bull—standing with their backs touching back to back, having burst through the earth. Having wandered among them, they emerged.
Then the merchant asked them, "Sirs, have you seen the one you were searching for?
When they replied, "We have seen him, Master," he sent them off, saying, "In that case, go.
They went from there, and when their own merchant asked, "Sirs, have you seen our merchant family of equal wealth?", they said, "Master, what do you have [to compare with it]?"
They related the entire account, saying, "In the city of Bhaddiya, the merchant Meṇḍaka possesses such great wealth.
Upon hearing this, the merchant was delighted and thought, "I have found one merchant family; is there perhaps another?
He gave them a blanket worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold and sent them off, saying, "Go, dear ones, and search for other merchant families as well."
Having gone to Rājagaha, they piled up a heap of wood not far from the house of the merchant Jotika, set fire to it, and stood there.
When asked, "What is this?", they replied, "We have a very valuable blanket for sale, but there is no buyer.
Even as we wander about carrying it, we fear thieves; therefore, we shall burn it and depart. Then—
When the merchant Jotika saw them, he asked, "What are these people doing? Upon hearing the matter, he summoned them and asked, "What is the price of this blanket?

When it was said, "It is worth one hundred thousand," he had the hundred thousand paid and sent them away with the very same hands, saying, "Clean the gateway and give it to the slave girl who throws out the refuse."
Taking the blanket, she went weeping to her husband and said, "Master, if I have committed some offense, is it not right for you to strike me?
Why have you sent such a thick blanket? How shall I wear this as an undergarment or as an upper robe?
"I did not send it to you for that purpose," he replied; "rather, wrap yourself in it..."
"I sent those [towels] for you to wipe your feet, which have been washed with scented water at the time you lie down after placing them at the foot of your bed;
are you not even capable of doing this? She replied, "I shall indeed be able to do this," and taking them, she departed.
Those men, having observed that situation, went to their merchant master and said, "What is it, dear sir?"
When he was told, "Have you seen the merchant’s family?", they replied, "Master, what do you have?
Such is the prosperity of the merchant Jotika in the city of Rājagaha," and having related all the splendor of his home, they explained the situation to him.
Upon hearing their words, the merchant was delighted in heart and, thinking, "Now I shall be able to go forth," went into the presence of the king.
“I wish to go forth, O King,” he said. “Very well, great merchant, go forth!

He went home, summoned his sons, and placing a golden staff and a diamond-tipped spade into the hand of his eldest son, said, “Dear son, go to the last house and extract a lump of gold from the golden mountain. Taking the spade, he went there.
He struck the golden mountain; it was as if he had struck a solid rock on his back.
Taking the spade from his hand, he gave it to his middle son and sent him off;
as that son struck the golden mountain, it was likewise as if he had struck a solid rock on his back. Then, giving it to his youngest son, he sent him off.
As he took that [gold] and struck and pounded it, it was as if he were striking a heap of clay.
Then the merchant said to him, "Come, dear son, enough of this much," and having summoned his other two elder brothers, he said, "This Golden Mountain was not produced for you;
it was produced for me and for my younger brother. By this..."
"Come together and eat with me," he said. But why was it produced for them alone, and why was the Jaṭila thrown into the water at the time of his birth? It was solely due to his own past action.
For while a shrine (cetiya) for the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa was being constructed, a certain one whose taints were destroyed (khīṇāsava) went to the site of the shrine.
Having looked at it, he asked, "Sirs, why does the face of the cetiya not rise up toward the north?
They replied, "There is not enough gold. He said, "I will enter the village and persuade [the people]; you must perform the work with diligence.
Having spoken thus, he entered the city and said, "Ladies, sirs, for one [part] of your cetiya..."
“Gold is not sufficient for the mouth; you must know this gold,” he said, as he went to the family of goldsmiths, exhorting the great multitude.
At that very moment, the goldsmith was sitting there quarreling with his wife.
Then the Elder said to him, “The gold taken by you for the cetiya is not sufficient for the mouth; it is necessary to know that.”
He said: "Out of anger toward his wife, he said, 'Go, throw your teacher into the water!
Then she said to him, 'You have committed an act of extreme recklessness; when I was angry with you, I should have been the one you scolded or struck.
Why did you harbor enmity toward the Buddhas of the past, future, and present? At that very moment, the goldsmith—"
Overcome with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), he said, "Forgive me, venerable sir," and prostrated himself at the elder's feet. "Dear boy, I have not said anything to you;
go and ask the Teacher for forgiveness. "How shall I ask for forgiveness, venerable sir? [The elder replied:
"Having fashioned three jars of golden flowers, place them inside the relic-chamber, and then, with wet clothes and wet hair..."
“Having offered them, ask for forgiveness, dear son.
He replied, “Very well, Bhante,” and while making golden flowers, he summoned his eldest of three sons, saying, “Come, dear son;
I spoke words of enmity to the Teacher, therefore, having made these flowers, at the relic-shrine...”
“Having placed [the matter] before him, I shall ask for his forgiveness; you too must become my companion,” he said. He replied, “I did not have you speak those hostile words to me;
you yourself should do it,” and thus he did not wish to do it. Having summoned the middle son, he spoke to him in the same way, but he too, having spoken likewise, did not wish to do it.
Having summoned the youngest son, he spoke to him in the same way; he, however, [thinking], “This is a duty that has arisen for our father...”
"Indeed, the burden belongs to the son," he said, and acting as the father's companion, he prepared the flowers.
Having completed three jars of cubit-sized flowers, the goldsmith placed them in the relic chamber; then, with wet clothes and wet hair, he asked the Teacher for forgiveness.
Thus, seven times during his births, he received the punishment of being cast into water. But this was the final instance.
His personal existence remained stable. Here too, by the very result of that same [merit], he was cast into the water.
However, because his two elder brothers—who were his sons—did not wish to be his companions at the time of making the golden flowers, for that reason a mountain of gold did not arise for them;
whereas for the matted-hair ascetic and his younger son, because they had acted together as one, [the mountain arose].
Thus he was reborn. Having thus instructed his sons, he went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher and attained *arahantship* in just a few days.
On another occasion, while wandering for alms with five hundred bhikkhus, the Teacher came to the door of his sons' house;
they gave alms-food for half a month to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
In the Dhamma hall, the bhikkhus started a conversation: "Friend Jaṭila, even today you still have craving for the golden mountain eighty cubits high and for your sons.
"Friends, I have no craving or pride regarding these things," he replied.
They said, "This Elder Jaṭila speaks falsely and gives an evasive answer. The Teacher [heard this].
Having heard their words, he said, "Bhikkhus, my son has neither craving nor pride toward them," and while teaching the Dhamma,
he spoke this verse: "He who,
having abandoned craving here, goes forth as a homeless wanderer;..."
"One whose craving and becoming are utterly destroyed—him I call a brahmin.
This is its meaning: he who, having abandoned here in this world craving or conceit pertaining to the six doors, being disinterested in household life, goes forth as a homeless wanderer;
because of the utter destruction of both craving and becoming, he is "one whose craving and becoming are utterly destroyed."
“Him I call a brahmin.
At the conclusion of this teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the thirty-third story, the account of the Elder Jaṭila.
34. The Story of the Elder Jotika.
The Teacher delivered this teaching on the Dhamma, beginning with the words "He who [has] craving here," while residing at Veḷuvana, concerning the Elder Jotika.
For Prince Ajātasattu, having allied himself with Devadatta, had his father killed and established himself in the kingdom.
Thinking, “I shall seize the great palace of the merchant Jotika,” he went forth prepared for battle.
Seeing his own shadow along with its retinue reflected in the jeweled wall, he observed, “The householder has gone out having taken up arms and gathered a force,” and did not dare to approach.
That day, the merchant had observed the Uposatha fast and, having eaten his morning meal early, remained there.
Having gone to the monastery, he sat down to listen to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher.
Meanwhile, a yakkha named Yamakoli, who was stationed at the first gate-post guarding the entrance, saw him and cried out, "Where are you going?
He then scattered the king's retinue and pursued them in every direction. The king, however, went straight to the monastery.
Then the merchant, seeing him, said, "What is it, Your Majesty? and rising from his seat, stood up.
"Householder, why have you sent your men, saying 'Fight with me,' and then come here and sit as if listening to the Dhamma?
But did Your Majesty go to my house to seize it? "Yes, we went. "Without my consent, to my house..."
“Even a thousand kings cannot take it, Your Majesty. He became angry and said, “But will you yourself become a king?
“I am not a king; however, even a single thread of my garment cannot be taken by kings or thieves against my will.
Shall I then take it according to your wish? “In that case, Your Majesty, here it is for you.”
"There are twenty rings on my ten fingers; I do not give these to you. If you are able, take them!
But that king, sitting on his haunches on the ground, would leap up and ascend to a height of eighteen cubits;
standing there, leaping again, he would ascend to a height of eighty cubits. Although he possessed such great strength, [he could not reach them] from here or there.
But even as he turned it over, he was unable to draw out even a single ring.
Then the merchant said to him, "Spread out your garment, Your Majesty," and straightened his fingers; twenty rings came forth.
Then the merchant said to him, "In this way, Your Majesty, what belongs to me cannot be taken without my consent," and [he described] the king's action.
Filled with a sense of spiritual urgency, he said, “Grant me permission to go forth, O King.
The king, thinking, “If he goes forth, I shall enjoy this palace in peace,” replied with a single word, “Go forth then.
Having gone forth in the presence of the Teacher, he attained Arahantship before long and became known as the Elder Jotika. His attainment of Arahantship—
At that very moment, all that prosperity vanished, and the deities even carried away his wife, named Satulakāyī,
back to Uttarakuru. Then one day, the monks addressed him, saying, "Friend Jotika, as for that palace of yours or that woman..."
Having asked, "Is there craving in him? and being told, "There is none, friend," they reported to the Teacher:
"Venerable Sir, this man speaks falsely and gives an evasive answer. The Teacher said, "Monks, there is indeed no craving for that in my son," and spoke this verse:
“He who, having abandoned craving, wanders as a homeless wanderer—
him, with craving and existence utterly exhausted, I call a brahmin.
The meaning of this verse is to be understood in the same manner as explained previously in the account of the Elder Jaṭila.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the thirty-fourth story, the Story of the Elder Jotika.
35. The Story of the Elder Naṭaputtaka.
"Having abandoned," the Teacher spoke this teaching on the Dhamma while dwelling at Veḷuvana concerning a certain son of actors.
It is said that while wandering about performing a theatrical performance, he heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, went forth into homelessness, and attained arahantship.
When he entered the city for alms together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha...
Having seen a certain actor’s son playing, the monks asked him, “Friend, this man plays every game you have ever played;
do you have any affection for him? When he replied, “No,” they said, “Venerable sir, this man speaks untruth and gives an evasive answer.
The Teacher, hearing their conversation, said, “Monks, my son has [mastered] all arts... ”
Having said, "He has transcended," he spoke this verse:
"Having abandoned human bondage and transcended divine bondage,
one who is detached from all bonds— him I call a brahmin."
In this context, "human bond" (*mānusaka-yoga*) refers to human life-span as well as the five strands of sensual pleasure.

The same principle applies to the "divine bond" (*dibba-yoga*). "He has transcended" means that one who, having abandoned the human bond, has gone beyond the divine bond—that person, being dissociated from all four bonds, I call a brahmin; such is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the thirty-fifth story, the Story of the Elder Naṭaputtaka.
36. The Story of the Elder Naṭaputtaka.
Having abandoned both delight and aversion—this teaching on the Dhamma was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling in Veḷuvana concerning a certain actor’s son.
The background story is the same as before. On this occasion, however, the Teacher said, “Monks, my son stands having abandoned both delight and aversion,” and spoke this verse:
“Having abandoned both delight and aversion, become cooled and free from acquisitions;
the hero who has overcome the entire world—him I call a brahmin.
In this context, “delight” refers to delight in the five strands of sensual pleasure. “Aversion” refers to dissatisfaction with dwelling in the forest. “Become cooled” means...

"Nibbūtaṃ" means one who has attained Nibbāna. "Nirūpadhiṃ" means free from defilements. "Vīraṃ" means one who stands having overcome this entire world of the aggregates (khandhaloka) and possesses heroic energy;
such a person, O Brahmin, I call a brahmin—this is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
The Thirty-sixth Story: The Elder Naṭaputtaka. The thirty-seventh story, concerning the Elder Vaṅgīsa:
"He who knows passing away"—the Teacher related this teaching on the Dhamma while dwelling at Jetavana, referring to the Elder Vaṅgīsa.
It is said that in Rājagaha there was a certain brahmin named Vaṅgīsa who, by striking the heads of deceased persons, would know:
"This is the head of one reborn in hell; this, of one in the animal realm; this, in the sphere of hungry ghosts; this, in the human world;
and this, the head of one reborn in the world of the gods. The brahmins thought, "By means of him, we can devour the world."

Having reflected thus, he had him clothe himself in two robes of red cloth; then, taking him along as they wandered through the countryside, they said to the people, "This brahmin named Vaṅgīsa knows the place where the heads of deceased persons are reborn;
ask him about the rebirth-place of your own kinsmen. People, according to their means, gave even ten kahāpaṇas.
Having given twenty or even a hundred [pieces of money], they asked about the place where their relatives had been reborn.

Traveling by stages, they eventually reached Sāvatthī and took up residence not far from Jetavana. After they had eaten their morning meal, they saw a great multitude of people going with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings to listen to the Dhamma;
having asked them, "Where are you going? they were told, "To the monastery to listen to the Dhamma."
When this was said, they replied, "What will you achieve by going there? There is no one equal to our brahmin Vaṅgīsa;
he knows the place where the heads of deceased persons have been reborn after being struck. Ask him about the rebirth-place of your kinsmen.
They, however, said, "What does Vaṅgīsa know? There is no one equal to our Teacher," and so it was with the others as well.

When it was said, "There is no one like Vaṅgīsa," he expanded upon that and said, "Come now, let us find out whether you or our Teacher possess the knowledge [of such things]. Taking them with him, he went to the monastery.
The Teacher, knowing of their arrival, [proceeded to describe] those reborn in the four places: in hell, in the animal realm, in the human world, and in the deva world.
Having had four heads and the head of one whose taints were destroyed—making five heads in total—brought and placed them in order, he questioned Vaṅgīsa as soon as they arrived:
"It is said that you can strike a head and know the place where those who have died have been reborn.
"Yes, I can," he replied. "Whose head is this? He struck it and said, "One who will be reborn in hell."
Then the Teacher, giving his approval by saying, "Excellent, excellent!", asked about the other three heads as well.
When the man answered each one correctly without missing a single point, the Teacher gave him his approval at every moment he spoke. Then, showing him the fifth head, He asked, "Whose head is this?
Having struck that one too, the man did not know the place where it had been reborn.
Then the Teacher said to him, "What is it, Vaṅgīsa, that you do not know? When he replied, "Yes, I do not know," the Teacher said, "I know it.
Then Vaṅgīsa entreated him, saying, "Give this spell to me. [The Teacher replied,] "It cannot be given to one who has not gone forth into homelessness.
He thought, "If I learn this spell, I shall become the foremost person in all of Jambudīpa."
Having dismissed those brahmins with the words, "You stay right there for a few days;
I shall go forth," he went into the presence of the Teacher and, having received full ordination, became known as the Elder Vaṅgīsa.

Then the Teacher gave him the meditation subject of the thirty-two aspects and said, "Recite the preliminary work of the mantra. While he was reciting it, from time to time [he was interrupted] by the brahmins...
When asked, "Have you mastered the spell? he replied, "Wait a moment, I am still learning it.
Within a few days, however, having attained *arahantship*, he was questioned again by the brahmins and said, "Friends, I am no longer able to go [to learn it].
Hearing this, the monks reported to the Teacher, "Venerable Sir, this man has given an answer based on what is untrue. The Teacher said, "Monks, do not..."
“You have spoken thus; now, monks, my son has become skilled in death and rebirth,” and having said this, he spoke these verses:
“He who fully understands the passing away of beings and their rebirth, who is unattached, well-gone, and awakened—him I call a brahmin.”
“Whose destination neither gods, nor gandhabbas, nor humans know— him,
the Arahant whose taints are exhausted, I call a brahmin. In this context,
“he who knows” means he who knows the passing away and rebirth of beings by making them manifest in every respect.

The meaning is: I call him a brahmin who is unattached due to his lack of clinging, a Sugata because he has gone well by means of his practice, and a Buddha because of his awakening to the Four Truths. "Of whom"—of whom these [beings] such as gods do not know the destination;
I call him a brahmin whose taints are exhausted because his defilements have been destroyed, and an Arahant because he is far removed from the defilements. This is the meaning.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the thirty-seventh story, the account of the Elder Vaṅgīsa. 38.
The Story of the Elder Nun Dhammadinnā.
“Of whomsoever,” the Teacher related this teaching on the Dhamma while dwelling in Veḷuvana, concerning the bhikkhunī named Dhammadinnā.
One day, her husband during their time as laypeople, the lay follower Visākha, having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher and attained the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), thought:
“It is fitting that I entrust my entire estate to Dhammadinnā. He...

Previously, when he was coming from that direction, he would smile upon seeing Dhammadinnā looking out through the window; however, on that day, he passed by without even looking at her as she stood at the window.
She thought, "What could this mean? and decided, "Very well, I shall find out at mealtime.
At the hour of eating, she brought the food to him. On other days, he would say, "Come..."
When he said, "Let us eat together," on that day he ate in silence. She thought, "He must be angry for some reason.

Then, at a time when Visākha was sitting comfortably, he summoned her and said, "Dhammadinnā, take charge of all the property in this house. She replied, "How can one who is angry take charge of property?"
They did not take it up, thinking, "What indeed is this? She said, "But you, Master," and added, "From now on, I shall not concern myself with anything.
"Who would take up the spittle discarded by you?
Since this is so, grant me permission to go forth. He agreed, saying, "Very well, lady," and with great honor...
Having led her to that nunnery, he ordained her. Once she had received full admission, she became known as the Elder Nun Dhammadinnā.
Out of a desire for seclusion, she went to the countryside with the other nuns and dwelt there;
before long, having attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), she thought, "Now, by depending on me, my kinsmen will perform meritorious deeds."
She returned once more to Rājagaha. When the lay follower heard that she had arrived, he thought, "For what reason has she come?
He went to the nuns' quarters, paid homage to the Elder Nun, and sat down to one side.
Thinking, "It would be improper to say, 'Are you weary, Noble Lady?'—I shall ask her a question," he [inquired] regarding the path of stream-entry.
He asked a question, and she answered it. By that same means, the lay follower asked questions regarding the remaining paths;
when he had passed beyond them, at the time his question was asked, she said, "The time has passed, friend Visākha.
When she added, "If you wish, you should approach the Teacher and ask this question," he paid homage to the Elder Nun, rose from his seat, and departed.
Having gone into the presence of the Teacher, she reported that entire conversation to the Blessed One.
The Teacher said, "Well spoken by my daughter Dhammadinnā; if I were to answer this question, I would answer it in exactly the same way," and while teaching the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
“He for whom there is nothing in the past, in the future, and in the present;
who is without possessions and without grasping—him I call a brahmin.
In this context, “in the past” refers to the aggregates of the past; “in the future” refers to the aggregates of the future; and “in the present” refers to the aggregates of the present.

Regarding the aggregates: "He has nothing" means that he in whom there is no "something"—that is, the "something" consisting of craving and grasping—at these points, him I call a brahmin who is "nothing" (akiñcana) due to the absence of the "something" of lust and so forth, and who is "without grasping" (anādāna) because of the absence of any seizing.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.

The Story of the Elderess Dhammadinnā, the thirty-eighth. 39. The Story of the Elder Aṅgulimāla The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, spoke this teaching on the Dhamma concerning the Elder Aṅgulimāla. The background story is already explained in the commentary on the verse beginning, “Indeed, the stingy do not go to the world of the gods. For it was said therein: [The story continues as follows: Once, when the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, the Venerable Aṅgulimāla approached him. Having paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: “O Aṅgulimāla, have you ever seen anyone who, having committed evil deeds, has gone to heaven? “No, Bhante,” he replied. “Have you ever seen anyone who, having done good deeds, has fallen into hell? “No, Bhante. “Then, Aṅgulimāla, have you ever seen anyone who, having committed both evil and good deeds, has experienced both suffering and happiness? “Yes, Bhante. “Then, Aṅgulimāla, have you ever seen anyone who, having abandoned both evil and good deeds, has attained final Nibbāna? “Yes, Bhante. When this was said, the Venerable Aṅgulimāla rose from his seat, adjusted his upper robe over one shoulder, prostrated himself with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, and said: “Excellent, Bhante! Excellent, Bhante! Just as one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—just so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May I receive the going-forth at the hands of the Blessed One; may I receive the higher ordination. “Come, bhikkhu,” the Blessed One said. “Well-taught is the Dhamma. Live the holy life for the complete ending of suffering. That very moment, the Venerable Aṅgulimāla became a bhikkhu. And within three days, through diligent application, he realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the supreme goal of the holy life, attaining it for his own sake, and he dwelt having realized it. He was one of the arahants. Then the Venerable Aṅgulimāla, being an arahant, free from lust, with a mind like a lake, went to the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: “Aṅgulimāla, how many kinds of persons are there in the world? “Bhante, there are four kinds of persons in the world: the person who goes to hell, the person who goes to heaven, the person who goes to both, and the person who attains final Nibbāna. “How is it, Aṅgulimāla, does the person who goes to hell do only evil deeds, or does he do both evil and good deeds? “Bhante, the person who goes to hell does only evil deeds; he does not do good deeds. “How is it, Aṅgulimāla, does the person who goes to heaven do only good deeds, or does he do both evil and good deeds? “Bhante, the person who goes to heaven does only good deeds; he does not do evil deeds. “How is it, Aṅgulimāla, does the person who goes to both do only evil and good deeds, or does he do neither? “Bhante, the person who goes to both does both evil and good deeds; he does not do neither. “How is it, Aṅgulimāla, does the person who attains final Nibbāna do only evil and good deeds, or does he do neither? “Bhante, the person who attains final Nibbāna does neither evil nor good deeds; he has abandoned both. “It is wonderful, Aṅgulimāla! It is marvelous, Aṅgulimāla! How well you have answered this question! Then the Venerable Aṅgulimāla, being an arahant, free from lust, with a mind like a lake, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. At that time, a certain brahmin woman, who was pregnant, was standing near the gate of the city of Sāvatthī. Seeing the Venerable Aṅgulimāla coming from afar, she cried out: “Stop, O Aṅgulimāla! Do not go further! Hearing her cry, the Venerable Aṅgulimāla thought: “This woman is calling me ‘Aṅgulimāla’; surely she must be referring to my past life as a bandit. Thinking thus, he turned back toward the city. But the Venerable Aṅgulimāla was an arahant, free from hatred, with a mind like a lake. Therefore, even though he turned back, he could not stop. He continued walking until he reached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: “Aṅgulimāla, why did you turn back? “Bhante, a certain brahmin woman, who was pregnant, stood near the gate of the city of Sāvatthī and cried out: ‘Stop, O Aṅgulimāla! Do not go further! Hearing her cry, I thought: ‘This woman is calling me ‘Aṅgulimāla’; surely she must be referring to my past life as a bandit. Thinking thus, I turned back toward the city. But, Bhante, I am an arahant, free from hatred, with a mind like a lake. Therefore, even though I turned back, I could not stop. “It is wonderful, Aṅgulimāla! It is marvelous, Aṅgulimāla!

That you were called ‘Aṅgulimāla’ by a brahmin woman who was pregnant, and yet you did not harbor ill will because of it. Then the Venerable Aṅgulimāla, being an arahant, free from lust, with a mind like a lake, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons in the world. What four? The person who goes to hell, the person who goes to heaven, the person who goes to both, and the person who attains final Nibbāna. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons in the world. Thus the Blessed One spoke. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had left, the Venerable Aṅgulimāla approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: “Aṅgulimāla, how many kinds of persons are there in the world? “Bhante, there are four kinds of persons in the world: the person who goes to hell, the person who goes to heaven, the person who goes to both, and the person who attains final Nibbāna. [The Blessed One repeated the question, and the Venerable Aṅgulimāla gave the same answer. “It is wonderful, Aṅgulimāla! It is marvelous, Aṅgulimāla! How well you have answered this question! Then the Venerable Aṅgulimāla, being an arahant, free from lust, with a mind like a lake, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons in the world. What four? The person who goes to hell, the person who goes to heaven, the person who goes to both, and the person who attains final Nibbāna. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons in the world. Thus the Blessed One spoke. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had left, the Venerable Aṅgulimāla approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he
The bhikkhus asked Aṅgulimāla, “Friend Aṅgulimāla, were you afraid when you saw that rogue elephant standing there holding a sunshade? “I was not afraid, friends,” he replied.
They approached the Teacher and said, “Venerable sir, Aṅgulimāla is declaring final knowledge. The Teacher said, “Bhikkhus, my son—”
“Aṅgulimāla is afraid. For among the bulls whose taints are destroyed, my sons—the monks who are like the preeminent bulls—do not fear,” he said, and then recited this verse:
“The bull, the excellent one, the hero, the great seer, the victor;”
“The one who is unshakable, washed clean, awakened—him I call a brahmin.
Its meaning is as follows: he is a “bull” (*usabha*) because of his bull-like steadfastness; “excellent” (*pavara*) in the sense of being supreme; a “hero” (*vīra*) due to his perfection of energy;
a “great seer” (*mahesi*) because he has sought out the great aggregates of virtue and so forth; and a “conqueror” (*vijitāvī*) because he has conquered the three Māras.
The meaning is: "I call him a *brāhmaṇa* who has washed away the defilements by bathing, and who is a Buddha by virtue of having awakened to the Four Noble Truths.
At the conclusion of the teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages.
This is the thirty-ninth story, the account of the Elder Aṅgulimāla.

40. The Story of the Brahmin Devahita Regarding the previous dwelling (*pubbenivāsa*), the Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, delivered this Dharma teaching concerning a question posed by the Brahmin Devahita.
For on one occasion, the Blessed One, having become afflicted by a wind-disease (*vātaroga*), sent the Elder Upavāna for hot water.
He sent [a messenger] to the presence of the Brahmin Devahita. Having gone there and informed the Teacher of his illness, he requested warm water.
Upon hearing this, the Brahmin became joyful in heart and thought, "It is indeed a gain for me that the Perfectly Enlightened One has sent a disciple to my presence for the sake of warm water.
He then had a man bring a carrying-pole for the warm water and a load of molasses.

He gave a honeycomb to the Elder Upavāṇa. Having taken it, the Elder went to the monastery, bathed the Teacher with warm water, and having stirred molasses with the warm water, he gave it to the Blessed One; at that very moment, his affliction subsided.
The brahmin thought: "To whom, indeed, does a gift given become of great fruit?"
“I shall ask the Teacher,” he thought. So he went into the presence of the Teacher and, asking about that matter, spoke this verse:
“Where should one give a gift? Where is what is given of great fruit?
How indeed does one who sacrifices succeed? How is an offering successful?”
Then the Teacher, saying, "What is given to such a brahmin as this bears great fruit," spoke this verse to explain who the brahmin was:
"The sage who knows his former abodes, sees heaven and states of woe,
has reached the destruction of birth, and is perfected in direct knowledge."
"One who has brought all undertakings to their conclusion—him I call a brahmin.
The meaning of this is: he who, having made his past lives manifest, knows them;

who sees with the divine eye the heavens divided into the twenty-six classes of deva-worlds and the fourfold states of misery; and who has moreover attained Arahantship, which is characterized by the destruction of birth.

Having directly known the state that is to be directly known, having fully understood the state that is to be fully understood, having abandoned what is to be abandoned, and having realized what is to be realized,
he has reached the goal, attained the consummation of his life, and is a sage because he has attained the state of silence through the wisdom of the destruction of the taints;
him I call the one who has reached the end of all defilements, the knowledge of the path of Arahantship, the dwelling in the holy life.
"One who has lived out his life in this way, I call a brahmin who has completed all that was to be completed.

At the conclusion of this teaching, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages. The brahmin, too, with a mind full of faith, established himself in the refuges and declared himself a lay follower.
This is the fortieth story, the Story of the Brahmin Devahita.
The commentary on the Brāhmaṇa Chapter is finished.

Having elucidated three hundred and five topics— twelve in the *Brāhmaṇa-vagga* and forty in each of the others—
the commentary on the meaning of the *Dhammapada*, composed in a measure of seventy-two recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*) and neither too concise nor too prolix,
is hereby completed. By that King of Dhamma, through whom the supreme *Dhammapada* was attained...
The verses in the Dhammapada spoken by that Great Seer number three hundred and twenty-four;
they were uttered by the one who discerns the Four Truths,
arising from three hundred and five subjects.
In this monastery, caused to be built by the grateful overlord,
while I was dwelling in the palace of King Sirikūṭa— [this work],
perfect in meaning and phrasing, is for the sake and welfare [of all].
Out of a desire for the true Dhamma to endure for the sake of the world and its Protector,
I have composed this very pure commentary on those [scriptures],
consisting of seventy-two recitation sections (bhāṇavāra) according to the measure of the Pāḷi.
By whatever merit has been attained, may all beings be made virtuous;
may all their aspirations be fulfilled, and may they obtain sweet fruit.
[This was composed] by one adorned with supreme purity of faith, wisdom, and energy, and endowed with a multitude of virtues such as morality, conduct, modesty, and gentleness.
To the great poet, the foremost of debaters, who spoke with words that were fitting, excellent, sweet, noble, and radiant—words flowing forth from the bliss produced by his perfect mastery of speech;

who was endowed with the analytical clarity of wisdom capable of penetrating and fathoming both his own tradition and the traditions of others; who possessed unimpeded power of knowledge regarding the Teacher’s Dispensation, including the Three Piṭakas and their commentaries;
who was adorned with the array of qualities such as the six supernormal powers and the analytical knowledges, which are accompanied by the four discriminations.
This is the Commentary on the Dhammapada composed by the Elder named Buddhaghosa— so called by his teachers—
whose intellect was vast and purified, who adorned the lineage of the Elders dwelling at the Mahāvihāra,
and who were lamps of the Elder tradition firmly established in superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma).
May he remain in the world for as long as there are seekers of deliverance from the world,
showing the way to sons of noble family through faith, wisdom, and the rest—
so long as even the name "Buddha" exists for that pure-minded Tathāgata.
"In this world, the Great Seer proceeds as the eldest in the world.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Dhammapada*, adorned with four hundred and twenty-three verses and one hundred and five illustrative stories, and comprising twenty-six chapters.
The Commentary on the Dhammapada is completed in its entirety.
